POURPIER. 273 Native plant of the family and genus whose name it bears. There are several varieties of purslane, all edible; but only the one called golden purslane is cultivated, which is an annual, low-growing, stalked, spreading plant, tender, fleshy, with wedge-shaped leaves; the flowers are soap-box-shaped and shed black seeds. The edible parts of purslane are the leaves and young shoots. GOLDEN PURSLANE CULTURE. - This cultivation is not very widespread and not very lucrative, because purslane is used only to garnish salads. Once it has been introduced into a plot, it perpetuates itself by sowing, and it is said that it is more beautiful when it sows itself than when it is sown by the gardener's hand; nevertheless, a little is sown in some marshes from the first days of May to the first days of August. After ploughing a piece of land, sow the seed more or less thickly, bury it with an 18 pitchfork, press it down with your feet, rake it over and cover it with a few millimetres of compost; if the season is dry, water immediately to encourage germination, and keep the young plant moist to hasten its growth. It's not that purslane fears heat and drought; but watering keeps it tender, and that's a quality. If sown thickly, all the purslane's branches are forced to rise straight up, and when they are 16 to 18 centimetres high, they are cut at a centimetre above the ground and sold by the bunch: In this way, the plant doesn't grow again, or grows so little that it's not worth keeping; but if you've sown lightly, the branches spread out and become stronger: then you pick them one after the other by hand, and you can make two or three successive pickings. PEAR. Plant of the Chenopoda family and the beet genus. It is a biennial, indigenous plant, with a taproot, broad, oval, petiolate leaves, and a thick, fluted, stalk, 1 meter or more high; numerous, clustered, very small, insignificant flowers, followed by small, kidney-shaped seeds. There are two cultivated varieties of pear, and their edible parts are the radial leaves, under the names pear and chard. CULTIVATION. - In the first days of May, at the latest, plough one or more plots of the usual width; trace, on each plot, with your feet, nine wide rays, the bottom of which is flat; sow the pear seed in the whole length of the ray, but clear enough so that the plant is not too tight; then pass your feet again, sliding, between each ray, to make the earth fall on the seed, pass the rake, finally spread on the plot 1 centimeter of compost or a very fine mulch. If the season is dry, wet as often as necessary. When the pear is 20 to 24 centimetres high, cut it off with a knife, this first time, at a or 3 centimetres from the soil, and sell it in small bunches. It grows again, but this time and the next, it is no longer cut, but the large leaves are picked one after the other by hand, and the central ones are kept for the next harvest, and so on. When you intend to grow pears during the winter, instead of sowing in beds 2 meters 35 centimeters wide, you sow in beds only 1 meter 66 centimeters wide, and in November, you place ooffers on them and cover them with frames; when the frosts arrive, we surround the boxes with a good O8 accot, cover the frames with straw mats, and, by this means, we have pear all winter and until May, when the plant goes to seed: even if you were more interested in growing pear in winter than in summer, it would be enough to sow the seeds in July. CARDE POIRÉE. This differs from the previous one in that the main rib of its leaves is wide and thick, and it is this part that is eaten cooked and seasoned like cardoons. GROWING. - We only sow it in June, because we expect the best product in April and May of the following year. So, in June, we sow cardoon pear in a piece of bed, and when the plant is 8 or 10 centimeters high, we water it, and an hour later, we carefully lift it and counter-plant it in one or more half-planted beds of romaine, or, better still, in a newly ploughed bed, where we put in eight rows, with the feet 56 centimeters apart in the rows, and water copiously during the dry weather. When the frosts come, we cover with large bedding, uncover during the mild weather, and, when there are no more frosts to fear, remove the bedding and clean the plants of damaged straw and leaves. At the end of April and in the first fortnight of May, the pear-shaped cardoon has regained its vegetation; its leaves have grown in size and appearance; it's then that we pull out the stalks, trim them, put three or four in a bundle and send them to the market. CARDON. Plant of the Compositae family, Carduaceae section and artichoke genus. A few varieties of cardoon are recognizable: they are biennial plants from the south of France, with a simple, taproot, very long, whitish, pinnatifid, often thorny root leaves; the stem grows to over 1 meter high, twining, and each shoot ends with a head of blue flowers to which fairly large, oblong seeds follow. The edible parts of the cardoon are the leaf stalks and ribs. CARDOONS DE TOURS. CULTIVATION. - In the past, only the Spanish cardoon was grown in our marshes, as it is not very thorny and has the disadvantage of hollow ribs. Today, and for a long time now, we only grow cardoon from Tours, which is thornier, but has the advantage of full ribs, making it far superior to the other. As cardoon is a very vigorous plant, it should be sown in the best and most substantial soil in the garden, and given frequent and abundant watering. If we sow it in April and neglect to wet it, many plants go to seed during the summer; this is why we wait until the first days of May to sow it, and sowing can be done in two ways, i.e. in the field or in a nursery. We sow it in place, because cardoon, with its simple, taproot and no hair, is difficult to pick up and may die several times during planting. Those who do not fear this difficulty sow it in a nursery and then plant it permanently. In a ploughed bed, 2 meters 33 centimeters wide, make two furrows 1 meter 33 centimeters apart; mark on a radius, every meter (3 feet), the place for a foot of cardoon; if the soil is sufficiently divided, soft and good, make a small basin in the places indicated, in which you place two or three cardoon seeds, which you bury 5 centimeters deep. If you want to do even better, remove a spade-head of soil from the marked places, and replace it with a layer of potting soil, in which you place two or three seeds, as before. When a row. O8 is sown, we sow the second, a third, etc., taking care that the whole sowing is in the same row.

chessboard. If the season is dry and hot, the seedling is held in water and sprouts in a few days: soon you can judge which will be the most beautiful plant in each sown spot, and you remove all the others. Those who, for whatever reason, have preferred to sow in a nursery, on a piece of bed or in the ground, wait until the seedling has 12 to 15 centimetres (4 to 5 inches) long leaves; lift it carefully, as its root is already very long, and plant it at the distance already indicated for sowing in place: when planting it, take care of its long root, insert it perpendicularly into the prepared trunk, lead it, water immediately and shade the plant until its recovery is assured. It's hardly until August that the cardoon begins to take on a rapid and vigorous growth, and, until then, the land wouldn't seem sufficiently occupied by cardoons 1 meter apart: so we spread a good mulch over the whole square and plant lettuce or romaine. We repeat, it's only through copious and abundant watering that we obtain beautiful cardoons in the Paris marshes; as they grow, we increase the dose, and, if the weather is dry and hot, we give a watering can of water to each plant every two days. In September, there are already cardoons strong enough to be blanched, and they are successively blanched until November. So, when we want to blanch cardoons from Tours, here's how we go about it: as we can hardly touch them because of their thorns, we bring their leaves together with a rope, and bind them at the bottom with a straw tie, then with another tie in the middle, then finally with a third tie towards the top; when the stalk is thus bound, we wrap it with large litter so as to deprive it of air and light, except for the tops of the longest leaves, and we tighten this litter with three ties like the cardoon itself. Market gardeners call this operation "swaddling" the cardoon; if the weather continues to be dry, we water the base of the cardoon, albeit swaddled, but only once. The cardoon needs three weeks of air and light deprivation for it to acquire the right whiteness and tenderness; then it is cut by the root between two plots of land, de-swaddled, its outer leaves and any defects removed, its collar trimmed, and delivered for consumption. If, in November, you want to preserve cardoons for the winter, bind them as described above. If, in November, you want to preserve cardoons for the winter, you bind them as described above, but do not swaddle them; you pull them out with part of their roots, and a root ball if possible, you take them to a cellar where you have deposited potting soil for this purpose, and you replant them in this potting soil almost without them touching each other; seven or eight days later, you visit them, to remove the outer leaves which usually rot first, and in fifteen or eighteen days they turn white : by continuing to visit them often to remove the spoiling leaves as you go along, you can keep them for two months. CELERI. A plant of the Umbelliferae family, in the Aminineae section, and of the parsley genus. There are several species or varieties of celery, all European, biennial: their roots are fibrous or tuberous, their leaves radical, large, twice winged, with broad, shiny leaflets; the stem is 3 to 6 decimeters high, twiggy, and bears umbels of small yellowish flowers followed by oval fruits. The edible parts of celery are the petioles, leaves and, in one species, the roots. LARGE-RIBBED CELERY. CULTIVATION.-In the first week of May, plow a piece of ground in the shade, and sow the seed of this celery, because, if sown in the sun, the plant could burn when it rises; when the seed is buried, spread a light layer of compost or very-short mulch over it, and water; We continue to give it a little wetting every day until it has risen, and we water it again very often to prevent it from hardening, until it is 10 to 14 centimetres high; then it's time to plant it. After ploughing one or more beds and covering them with mulch, use your feet to mark out ten or eleven radii on each bed, 2 metres 53 centimetres wide, and plant the young celery ao centimetres apart in the rows, immediately giving it a soft wetting; if the season is dry, we must water the celery abundantly at least every two days, firstly to prevent it from hardening off, secondly because it naturally likes water, and thirdly because we planted it close together to force it to grow quickly. When the celery is 40 to 46 centimetres tall, we need to think about blanching it, and we have two ways of doing this: 1° If we have old beds whose manure has been used up, we empty them by throwing the compost and manure over the edge to the right and left, and this creates a sort of trench in which we replant and govern the celery, corame O as we shall say in the following way, which is the most commonly used. 2° We dig a trench 1 meter 33 centimeters wide and 35 to 38 centimeters deep, at the sides of which there must be an empty space, 1 meter wide, for depositing the soil from the trench, and we loosen the bottom of this trench by plowing. When this is done, each celery plant with its root ball is lifted with a spade, and carefully planted in the bottom of the trench, making a dimple with the hand to receive the celery root ball, and covering it with earth which is slumped to sx it vertically: if some plants have side shoots or small eyelets, these are detached before replanting. In a trench 1 meter 35 centimeters wide, you can replant eight or nine celery plants per row, spacing the rows 18 to 22 centimeters apart; once the trench is planted, you immediately give it a copious moistening and, if the weather is dry, you water every day until the celery is well established. Twelve or fifteen days later, the celery should be sprouting from the heart; at this point, break up the earth deposited on either edge of the trench, and, if there are any leaves altered by the celery, remove them, and pour a 16-centimeter thickness of earth between the rows and stalks of celery, taking care that each stalk always retains its vertical direction. This first 08 operation is called "empiéter" (to encroach): twelve or fifteen days later, you can see that the celery has grown from the heart again; then you put loose earth back in between the rows and stalks of celery, to such a thickness that you can only see about 12 centimetres of the longest leaves: this second and final operation is called "rechausser" (to reshoot). After this second operation, the celery is blanched in twelve or fifteen days; then we pull it out, trim its roots, put it in bunches of six to seven feet per bunch, wash it, and finally send it to the market. TURKISH CELERY. This variety differs from the previous one in that it is much shorter and stockier; its ribs are a little larger and its heart fuller. Consumers now prefer it to large celery, and market gardeners are pleased with it because it is less costly to blanch than the other variety. CELERI-RAVE. This plant is sown at the same time and in the same way as the previous one, but it is only planted once and at a greater distance, so it doesn't grow so tall. In a bed 2 meters 33 centimeters wide, we plant seven rows of it, placing the plants 4o centimeters apart in the rows; we water it with as much care as the previous ones, until autumn, and when the frosts come, its root must be as big as a fist or the belly of a bottle; The tubers or roots are taken to the cellar, buried in sand if possible, and sold by the dozen throughout the winter. Celery root is excellent cooked. CELERY FOR CUTTING. This variety is distinguished by its smaller size and hollow ribs; its cultivation is also different and simpler. Sow in late March or April, broadcasting on a well-ploughed bed, and when the seed is buried and harrowed, cover with a centimetre of compost; When the plant has risen, it is moistened to encourage germination, and then tended with water to ensure that it remains tender at all times. When the plant has reached a height of 15 to 20 centimetres, it is cut, arranged in small bunches and sent to the market: It grows back immediately, and if care is taken to keep it moist, it can be picked every fifteen or eighteen days until the frosts. JUNE. RAIPONCE. Plant of the Campanulaceae family and the Campanula genus. It is a small native plant, biennial, with simple, taprooted roots, and radical, oval, lanceolate leaves; the stem is straight, slender, 5 centimeters or more high, sparsely twiggy, with bluish, campanulate flowers, followed by dried fruits that open at the sides to spread the seeds. The edible parts of this plant are the root and the radical leaves, which are eaten in salads. CULTIVATION. - Riponce is sown in June and July, to produce large roots in winter; those who prefer leaves to roots don't sow it until September. It is not necessary to plow the land where you want to sow raiponce; simply pass the push rake over it, to stir the soil to a depth of 2 centimeters. As this seed is very fine and very loose, it would be difficult to sow it alone without exposing yourself to putting too much in places, and it must be sown very lightly, as its leaves spread out in a circle on the ground: The seed is mixed with ash or fine, dry earth, and sown together on the prepared soil; then the soil is harrowed with a three-pronged fork to hide the seed, the earth is compacted a little so that it touches the seed on all sides, then a light, short mulch is spread over the whole, and finally the plant is watered as needed. Rapunzel is eaten from late December to February, or even later; it is pulled up with its root and rosette of leaves, peeled, washed and sold in small batches. The cultivation of raipouce is very restricted in our marshes, firstly because it is not lucrative, and secondly because country folk will pull it up where it grows naturally and supply the capital markets with it at very low prices. STRAWBERRY. A plant of the Rosaceae family, of the Dryadae order and of the genus whose name it bears. There are several species and many varieties of strawberry: all are small, herbaceous perennials, some native to Europe and others to America, 15 to 25 centimeters high, with trifoliate leaves and white flowers, followed by oval or rounded, sweet, red or white fruits, which bear seeds on their surface. The edible part of these plants is their fruit. OBSERVATIONS. - Strawberries are in everyone's taste, so strawberry cultivation has spread considerably around Paris, and gardeners within the city walls, where land is so expensive, can no longer compete in this crop, which has become a specialty. Of the eighteen hundred market gardeners in Paris, not even half a dozen grow strawberries naturally, and even fewer grow them under forced cultivation, which is the only way to expect any profit in Paris. Today, there are several varieties of strawberry whose fruit is larger and more attractive than that of the Alpine strawberry, but none of them bears fruit for as long, and their fruit is nowhere near as tasty as the Alpine strawberry. Its marketability is therefore more certain, and it is the only strawberry that market gardeners, who are still very few in number, can grow using forced cultivation only, with the hope of obtaining some profit. ALPINE OR FOUR-SEASON STRAWBERRY. FORCED CULTIVATION. - To cultivate the Alpine strawberry in this way, it must be renewed every year, either by sowing or dripping: renewal by sowing being the most advantageous, we will not deal with the other. At the end of June, we select a number of the most beautiful Alpine strawberries in a state of perfect maturity, crush them in water, and the seeds are easily extracted; when they have dried out, we plough a small corner of land, not in the shade, but which we can shade with a straw mat or two; and, when the top of the soil is well-divided and levelled with a rake, we sow the seed, on which we spread only a few millimetres of very fine soil or potting compost, and give it a light drenching; Repeat this drenching two or three times a day, if you don't shade with straw mats, as the top of the soil must not dry out until the seeds have risen, if you want them all to rise quickly; in less than 15 days, everything will have risen; six weeks later, i.e. two months after sowing, the plant will be ready to be transplanted into a nursery, where it will flower and produce runners, but we'll remove some as they appear. At the end of November, plough as many beds as you like, plant the strawberry plants 28 centimetres apart and, as soon as the frosts start, cover the beds with boxes and frames, so that the strawberry plants can continue to vegetate a little. We usually start forcing strawberry plants in February, when we remove all the soil from the paths to a depth of 54 centimetres, and fill them to the top of the collars with good new horse manure; Protect against frost by all known means, ventilate as needed, and rearrange and replace the stoves when you realize that they no longer provide enough heat for the strawberry plants, which must be kept clean and have 19 of their old leaves removed to allow light to penetrate everywhere, especially when the fruit begins to appear; finally, in the first days of April at the latest, the strawberry harvest can begin and last until the strawberry plants in the open ground give. There are other ways of forcing strawberry plants, in pots or greenhouses: some prefer runners to plants grown from seed, planting them in another season, etc.; but the cultivation method we have just described is the simplest and the only one practicable by market gardeners. TENDER TURNIP OF THE VIRTUES. We mention only this variety, which is oblong, white and very early, and could be sown at the end of June by market gardeners, if they still grew turnips; but they had to give up growing them a long time ago, because turnips are not a plant that can be forced, because they go to seed and stop growing if sown before June. All extramural growers sow turnips and can sell them much more cheaply than intramural market gardeners, where land is much more expensive. CHAMPIGNON. 291 A plant of the cryptogam family and the agaric genus; it grows naturally in France, on the lawns of dry meadows and woods, and at the foot of piles of horse manure: it's a white or grayish mushroom, fleshy, globose at first, composed of a stem and a cap whose blades, pinkish at first, become brown, even blackish, as the cap opens, spreading to a diameter of 10 centimeters; but then it's no longer saleable, though still good: it's when the mushroom is the size of a pigeon's egg to a hen's egg that it's most valuable, and most esteemed by consumers. In the past, market gardeners in Paris used to cultivate this mushroom at a profit; but since mushroom growers have been cultivating it at much lower cost in the quarries of Paris and the surrounding area, market gardeners have been making much less of it; they would even have been obliged to give it up altogether, if the mushrooms they bring in weren't whiter and more beautiful, and didn't have a better appearance and a higher price than those from the quarries. Although we are far from wishing to play the scholar, we will nevertheless note here, in favor of our colleagues, that scholars regard the white of this mushroom as the stems and branches of the plant, and the mushroom itself as its fruit. Although mushrooms can be made at any time of year, we prefer to make them in autumn. To do this, the manure must be prepared as early as July, in the manner described below. To judge the quantity of manure to be prepared, we first need to decide how many stacks to make; we usually make no less than two and no more than twelve stacks at a time, whose length we cannot determine here, although the most convenient are about 10 to 12 meters long. Manure preparation. - We take horse manure that we've been accumulating in piles for a month or six weeks, and bring it to the marshes on an empty, level, firm site; We then remove any large pieces of litter that have not been impregnated with urine, hay and any pieces of wood that may be present, as white does not set on these bodies. Striking the manure with the back of the fork, we lay it down in front of us in a floor at least 66 centimetres thick, pressing it down with the back of the fork. When the floor, which is almost always a long square, is made, it is stomped well, watered abundantly and stomped a second time, then left in this state for eight or ten days; then the manure ferments, scalds, sweats, and its surface is covered with a kind of white mold. After these eight or ten days, the floor must be remade from top to bottom on the same ground and rebuilt as before, with the necessary precaution of placing the manure from the edges of the floor into its interior, and the floor is left in this state for a further eight or ten days; at the end of this time, the manure should have acquired all the quality suitable for making millstones: on inspection, it should be found to be supple, soft, unctuous or greasy, without the smell of manure, and bluish-white inside, neither too wet nor too dry; if the tumier were not in all these conditions, there would be reason to fear that the millstones formed from it would not be very fertile. Mounting, larding and goptering. - The millstones must be 66 centimetres wide at the base, 66 centimetres high, and formed into a humpback shape, placed parallel to each other, 48 or 50 centimetres apart. The prepared manure is brought to the site; a man accustomed to this work, or better still, the market gardener himself, takes the manure in small bunches, lays them down in front of him, spreading them out and pressing them firmly against each other, and forms a humpback of the width and height indicated above; the man always works backwards, and when 08 he reaches the end, the humpback is finished: it is then combed, and beaten on the sides and top with the back of a shovel to make it smooth. In this state, the manure warms up, but can no longer take on very great heat; after a few days, we probe the wheel with the hand, and, if the heat is suitably gentle, we lard it. This operation consists of making small openings in the manure, the width of your hand, 5 centimetres from the ground and in a single line around the millstone, 33 centimetres apart (1). As you make these openings, you insert into each of them a small wafer of mushroom spawn (a mise, in market gardener's terms), three fingers wide and 8 or 10 centimetres long, and fold the manure over it so that it is well enclosed. Once this operation has been completed, the pack is covered with 10 to 1a centimetre-thick dry litter: this covering is called a chemise. Ten or twelve days later, we visit the millstones to see if the white has set; to do this, we lift the bottom of the liner, and look at the places where the white has been placed. When you see white filaments extending into the manure of the millstone, you know that the spawn has set and that it is good: if there are cakes or bets whose spawn does not (1) Some market gardeners place a second row of spawn 18 centimeters above the first. O8 not extend into the wheel, it's because it wasn't good; they are then removed and new ones put in their place; finally, when all the white is well set, and its filaments extend into the wheel, it's time to gopter it. This operation consists of coating the whole wheel with 5 centimetres of very fine, very soft earth: first, we remove the liner from over the wheel, plough the paths to a depth of about To centimetres, mix in potting soil and make everything as fine as possible; we lightly baste the entire surface of the wheel, and, while it's still wet, we take a shovel; This shovel is used to scoop up the earth prepared in the pathway, and to throw it against the grinding wheel, where it is held in place by applying the back of the shovel very sharply against the earth to prevent it from falling off, which requires dexterity and liveliness; as you gopt, you solidify the earth on the grinding wheel by striking it lightly with the back of the shovel, and then you put the shirt back on. When the millstones have been in this state for another fifteen or twenty days, they are inspected to see if the white is showing through the earth at the bottom of the millstones, and if the mushroom seed is forming, if all goes well, a few days later there will be mushrooms to pick: each time one is detached, a little compost is put in the hole left by the mushroom, and the part of the liner that was lifted is immediately put back on. When millstones are producing well, mushrooms can be picked every two days, and well-grown millstones usually produce mushrooms for two or three months; we've even seen millstones that, after producing a good crop and resting for two months, started again and produced a second crop. We have just described autumn mushroom cultivation as it is practiced in years that are neither dry nor rainy; but, in dry years, it is sometimes necessary to water the liner to maintain a slight humidity in the soil of the millstone; in rainy years, on the contrary, it is sometimes necessary to remove the excessively wet liner and replace it with a dry one. GROWING MUSHROOMS IN A CELLAR. CULTURE. - The manure is prepared in the open air in the marsh, as we have just said, and when it has reached the right point, it is lowered into the cellar: there it is arranged along the walls, so as to form a half-mill or a single-slope millstone; it can also be set up on shelves above the first. In the middle and on the floor of the cellar, millstones are built with two slopes, like those built in the open air: they are larded and gopted like the others, but they are not covered with a shirt; darkness takes its place: the skylights and doors are carefully closed, and the millstones, being sheltered from atmospheric influences, produce mushrooms for longer than those built in the open air. In the quarries in and around Paris, mushrooms are grown in the latter way, but in much greater quantities, and a prodigious amount of manure is consumed; but market gardeners' mushrooms are always preferred to the halle. Mushroom cultivation in the open air is rarely affected by the disease we call mole, but it frequently shows up in stacks built in cellars, sometimes taking over all the mushrooms and forcing the mushroom grower to establish his cultivation in another cellar. A mushroom affected by this disease has a warty cap, its leaves thicken, weld together, change color and become a shapeless mass that has lost the good odor of a healthy mushroom, has contracted another unpleasant one and is no longer saleable. How to make mushroom spawn. - Many market-gardeners take their spawn from old millstones that have ceased to produce, and store it in slabs in an attic or dry place; we have stored it in this way for a dozen years, and at the end of that time it was still good for larding millstones. Many of us thought that white from old millstones, which had already produced mushrooms who knows how many times, must have lost its fertility, and looked for a way to obtain some which had not yet produced mushrooms and which, therefore, could not be said to be exhausted. It's not that you can make spawn from scratch, but so little old spawn is used in the process that all the resulting spawn is considered new. Here's how it's done: first prepare a little manure, as you would for making millstones; then open a pelite trench at the foot of a wall, facing north, at least 66 centimetres wide and deep, and throw the earth over the edge of the trench. If you have a bit of old whitewash, divide it into small slabs and place them in two rows at the bottom of the trench, spacing the slabs 33 centimetres apart; then bring in the manure prepared in advance, arrange it neatly in the trench with a pitchfork and pack it down well. When the manure is 25 to 30 centimetres thick all over, you tamp it down well, then put the soil back on top, and tamp it down again. After twenty or twenty-five days, the spawn deposited in the bottom of the trench has vegetated and spread throughout the manure, which has itself become a mass of spawn; then the soil that covers it is removed, and with a spade the O8 manure is cut into square pieces 33 centimeters square and 20 to 24 centimeters thick: these pieces are split in two to facilitate their drying, and taken to an attic, where they are stored for four or five years, to be used for larding millstones. The best time to make this white is July. CHAPTER XI. Insect and disease damage to cheeses. To speak of insects and vegetable diseases in scientific terms is impossible for any market gardener, and the language of entomologists and nosologists will long be unfamiliar in our marshes. We have, however, felt it necessary to discuss insects and diseases in a work of the nature of this one, even though we can only designate them by trivial names, understood, it is true, by all market gardeners in Paris, but highly unintelligible to men accustomed to scientific language. In order to shorten this unattractive chapter, we name each vegetable in turn, as article headings, and below, in two columns opposite each other, we summarize the insects and diseases to which these vegetables are prone. As for the means of preserving them, we give very little information, as we are no more skilled in this area in market gardening than in field gardening. ASPARAGUS. Insects. When asparagus stalks go to seed, they are often attacked by the criocer, a red insect that eats the bark of the stalks and is sometimes so numerous that they are all covered with them. White grubs and moths also torment claws in the ground. Diseases. In greasy, damp soils, asparagus claws are prone to melting or rotting. AUBERGINE. Eggplant is prone to aphids and kermes; both can be destroyed by brushing the plant with water. This plant has no particular disease. CARDON. The cardoon's greatest enemy is a black fly that attaches itself to its leaves in huge numbers. We don't know whether this fly pumps juices or intercepts transpiration, but we do know that it slows and stops vegetation, and that the plant withers. As long as the cardoon is young and small, the moth also sometimes cuts the root and kills it. CARROT. A very formidable enemy of carrot seedlings in dry soils is a small spider that cuts young plants as they emerge: it can be destroyed by frequently watering the young plant. We know of no disease affecting carrots, apart from damping-off, which can affect them to some extent in unsuitable soils. CELERY. Celery leaves and ribs are quite prone to rust in its various stages of cultivation. Diseases. CELERY. Chervil has no known insects. Chervil is not prone to disease; only, Insects. Diseases. in summer, it can suffer from jaundice if the weather is very hot, and in unsuitable soils, it can be partially destroyed by damping-off. CURLY ENDIVE. In addition to the insects that harm romaine and lettuces, curly endive's other enemy is the cutworm, also known as the earthworm or large gray caterpillar. Curly endive is exposed to the same diseases as romaine and wild lettuce. We know of no other enemy to wild chicory, sown on a bed or under a frame, than the cattail, which, by making its galleries in all directions, reverses the germinating seeds and kills them. When grown on a bed and under a frame, little wild chicory is subject to only one disease: damping-off. Its name indicates its effect: the plant attacked by it melts in place, and the disease spreads by contagion. We attribute this disease to three causes: 1° a defect in the soil; 2° too much humidity; 3° lack of sunlight. You can't sow, nor can you plant. 303 plant in a place where melting has just wreaked havoc: everything will perish. CAULIFLOWER. Cauliflowers, like other cabbages, have many enemies; when sown in spring, they are liable to be devoured by flea beetles, which we call flea beetles and ground lice, as soon as the cotyledons emerge. The damage can be stopped by watering three or four times a day, or by shading the seedling. When the cauliflowers are free of this danger, caterpillars of several species arrive: yellow caterpillars, produced by white butterflies; large gray and green caterpillars, produced by butterflies of different colors. The caterpillar of the white butterfly eats only the leaves, but it devours quickly; it needs to be watched and destroyed often, as do the egg-layers that the butterflies deposit on the leaves. Having said what we know about the insects and diseases that damage or destroy vegetables, we feel it our duty to end this chapter with an account of the opinion, handed down by tradition among Paris market gardeners, concerning three atmospheric phenomena. Sensible people advised us not to talk about them in this book, because they thought there were errors or prejudices in the opinion in question: in spite of our deference to their advice, we were unable to comply; for, since we are writing the history of market gardening in Paris in 1844, and setting out its improvements, integrity dictates that we should also make known those beliefs likely to be regarded as errors or prejudices; subsequently, we can destroy them or explain the reason for them, if they have any foundation: here are the three phenomena. Rainbows. - Many market gardeners believe that when a rainbow appears, its influence can kill mushrooms that are in the seed stage in earthen millstones, albeit covered by their shirts. We don't all believe in this effect of the rainbow: many of us are inclined to attribute the loss of the mushroom seed, in this circumstance, to a sudden drop in temperature; but we haven't verified it, and leave the question as we found it. Thunder. - The loss of mushroom kernels by thunder, and even of mushrooms as large as hazelnuts, is far more proven than that caused by rainbows; there is not a single one of us who has not had the unfortunate experience of this in his millstones on earth. Those who make their millstones in cellars, in the quarries of Paris or the surrounding area, have never complained about it; its influence probably doesn't extend that far. Be that as it may, it's a fact that a violent thunderclap kills the fungus grain of shirt-clad millstones on the ground. Is it noise, is it electricity, is it a sudden cooling of the atmosphere, is it lightning that produces this unfortunate effect? No market gardener can answer these questions; but all can assure that the fact takes place. Trombe de vent. - This is the name given to the whirlwinds of wind and dust that rip up or break down trees and uncover the houses they pass through. There are hardly any market gardeners who haven't seen at least one of these pass through their marshes, and who don't know that such a whirlwind can take away manure, bells and sashes, and do appalling damage: In an old farm where a whirlpool was passing through, we saw the master, the girls and the boys running, shouting and waving anything they could get their hands on, such as spades, forks and rakes, in an attempt to break the whirling column of air; but all this noise and movement produced no effect, and the whirlpool continued on its way. Another method, whose effectiveness we ourselves have once tested, consists in throwing water against the whirlpool; one day we saved the last quarter of a line of frames that a whirlpool was taking away, by throwing water at it from the head of a watering can. One day, some physicist will be able to explain what we've just said about rainbows, thunder and waterspouts. CHAPTER XUI. Harvesting and preserving vegetable seeds. We felt it necessary, in a book on vegetable growing, to include a short chapter in which some information could be found on how we go about obtaining and harvesting the best seeds, and preserving them for as long as possible. We will have little to say that is not known to all gardeners, and especially to those who have been concerned with the organization of seeds, their tissues and the more or less alterable substances of which they are composed. What we will say here, once and for all, is that when the seeds are dry, they should be placed, species by species, in paper or canvas bags, and placed in a dry place, sheltered from the outside air, humidity and heat. ASPERGE. When, around June 15th, we stop picking asparagus, it rises and produces round, succulent, pea-sized, very red fruits, which ripen in autumn and contain, or should each contain, six black seeds; we crush these fruits in water to extract the seeds and dry them: they keep well for two or three years. AUBERGINE. When eggplants are harvested for sale, some are left to ripen completely; the seeds are then removed, and are lenticular or kidney-shaped, brick-colored and 2 millimeters in diameter: they are good for two years. CARROT. To obtain good carrot seeds, sow them at the end of July; during winter, cover them with litter to protect them from frost; when the thaw comes, uproot them and replant them 4o centimeters apart; water, if necessary, until mid-June, and in July the carrot seed ripens: This seed, as in parsley and other umbellifers, is a small fruit, divided into two parts, each containing a seed under a tough, oval-shaped envelope, 3 millimeters long, with four lines of long lamellar teeth on the outside, making them look bristly: These lamellae are usually broken by rubbing the seeds in the hands before sowing them, but this is not enough: when the seed is sown, it must be plumbed with the feet, to bring it into contact with the earth and speed up germination. Carrot seed is good for five or six years. CARDON. To obtain cardoon seed, in autumn, leave a few plants in place; as frost approaches, cut off the large leaves, mound them and cover them with litter, like artichokes; in spring, uncover them, grow their stalk, flower and ripen their seeds in October: these seeds are gray, almost straight and cylindrical, 8 to 9 millimeters long, with a few small longitudinal ridges: they are good for three or four years. CELERY. In November, select the most beautiful celery plants of each species, replant them in the ground at a distance of 53 centimeters, cover them over winter and uncover them in spring; they come up and ripen their seeds in August: these seeds are one or two times smaller than parsley seeds and of the same conformation; they are good for six years. CHERFEUIL. Seeds are obtained from chervil sown in September, which has overwintered and risen in the spring; they are linear, acute, 12 mm long and blackish: their germinative property is preserved for four or five years. 319 Cabbages, in general, are biennial plants that only produce seeds in their second year, and it is from cauliflowers sown in September that we collect seeds ten or eleven months later. So, in April, May and June, when the cauliflower harvest is at its peak, we mark a certain number of plants with the best apples, and we don't cut them off; we even leave a leaf or two on the apple, so that it doesn't harden, until we see several shoots coming out of the seed: then we remove these dry leaves and water to give the cabbage vigor. These shoots grow, branch out and flower; it's then that you must not spare the wetting; it's also the moment when, sometimes, the green aphid establishes itself, in immense quantities, on the young shoots of the shoots and would compromise the harvest of the seeds, if we didn't hasten to destroy it by all known means, among which we indicate this one, as the most expeditious and safest: wet the plant with a watering can and sprinkle powdered quicklime on the aphids; if the aphids return, start again. Soon the siliques grow and swell; when, in the course of August, you think they're ripe, you cut off I the little twigs that carry them, dry them on a sheet in the sun, where almost all the siliques open naturally and drop their seeds, which are round, blackish, as big as No. 9 shot; you winnow them, and, when they're quite dry, put them in bags: they're good for eight or nine years. CHOU-POMME. Under the name of apple cabbage, we include all cabbages that form an apple with their central leaves, from York sprouts to large cabbages. What we're about to say also applies to savoy cabbage. To collect seeds from all these cabbages, it is not essential to let the apple fall off, as is done in many places; when the apple is cut for sale or for cooking, enough of the core remains to produce shoots, flowers, siliques and seeds in large enough quantities for horticultural use, and these seeds are just as good as those that would have come from the apple. Most of these seeds are a little larger than those of cauliflower, equally round and of the same blackish color; they are harvested at various times of the summer and in the same way as we said for cauliflower: the seeds of apple and Milan cabbages are also good for eight or nine years. CURLY ENDIVE. To obtain seed for curly endive and its varieties, sow in a bed at the beginning of February and plant out in April. When the time comes to bind it for blanching, select a dozen of the best plants and do not bind them. The seeds are small, oblong, angular and 2 millimeters long, not including the small toothed crown at the end. The seeds of curly endive and wild chicory, and those of escarole, are very tightly packed in their calyxes, only coming out with great difficulty, and can remain on their stems for several years without falling off; they must therefore be beaten on a sheet with a flail to loosen them: they are good for five or six years. CUCUMBER. Cucumbers and gherkins are left to ripen completely, even to rot, before the seeds are collected; they are as long, but narrower, than those of melons: they are treated in the same way and keep just as long. 21 CRESS ALÉNOIS. The seed is chosen for sowing in April; it rises at the end of May and ripens in June; its seed is brick-colored, oval, 2 millimeters long: it is good for two years. SPINACH. When autumn-sown spinach has spent the winter, it rises quickly in spring and soon ripens its seeds, which are rounded or armed with a few sharp points: it is good for three or four years. LITTLE BLACK LETTUCE. In February, this lettuce is harvested, so we choose the best ones, lift them with a good root ball, replant them on a warm layer and place a bell on each one. In March, the cloches are removed, the lettuces grow taller, flower and set seed. By July, most of the seeds are ripe, so the plants are gently plucked, placed upright against a wall in the sun for a day or two, then shaken and beaten on a sheet in a van; left to dry in the sun for a few more days, they are beaten a second time, the seeds are winnowed out and, when well cleaned, put into bags (1). All lettuces have ellipsoid seeds, 3 millimeters long, black or whitish, with longitudinal striations; they can hardly be distinguished from each other except by their black or whitish color; the little black one (2) is black: it retains its germinative capacity for three or four years; the following ones retain it for the same length of time. GOTTE LETTUCE. This one is treated like the previous one, but (1) It's by ellipsis that we say petite noire; to complete the meaning, we should say petite laitue à graine noire. (2) This is the general way of harvesting lettuce seed; but those of us who insist on harvesting only perfect seeds leave the seed-bearing lettuces in place, and pick the seeds as they ripen, which can be recognized when their white aigrette rises out of the calyx and detaches the seeds; and, as these aigrettes only appear successively, we are obliged to return to the same seed-bearing lettuce eight or ten times to strip it of its good seeds. This way of harvesting the seed in detail, by pinching only the tips of the branches that carry it, is called pinching. It gives its seed a little later: this seed is whitish and can be collected like that of the little black one, as well as the three following ones. LETTUCEJROUGE. This lettuce heads in May. Its black seed is harvested in July. GEORGES LETTUCE. It heads and rises at the same time as red lettuce; its seed is black and it is harvested at the same time. GREY LETTUCE. This lettuce can be grown throughout the summer, but the best apples for seed are left to set in June; they are grayish-white and are harvested in September. ORDINARY LAMB'S LETTUCE. Having spent the winter, lamb's lettuce goes to seed in the first spring; but as its flowering lasts long enough, and its seed (or rather its berries) fall as it ripens, it is left to fall; The soil falls to the bottom, and the seed (or small fruit) floats to the surface through its two sterile, air-filled compartments. It is then washed, dried on a cloth, winnowed and bagged. The seed of ordinary lamb's lettuce is different in that it is not crowned: it is good for seven or eight years. REGENCE CITRUS. The seed of this variety can be recognized by its smaller size and the small toothed crown at the top. It is also harvested in spring and in the same way. MELON. Everyone knows that, when you eat a good melon, you can hope that its seed will reproduce other equally good ones; but you can never be sure. The way to avoid being deceived is not to prefer the seeds of the largest melons, but rather those that are the best of their kind; for melons of an extraordinary size for their species are subject to variation the following year: we therefore choose for grainc the melon that is the best of its kind; we let it ripen well, but not rot; we extract the seed, which we wash and dry well before putting it in a bag. All melon seeds are oblong, compressed, more or less large, leathery-skinned, yellowish-white and smooth; cantaloupe seeds are 11 millimeters long and 6 millimeters wide, while market melon seeds are only 1 centimeter long and 5 millimeters wide. We keep melon seeds for four or five years, but there are examples that show they can be good for twenty-five years or more. ONION. Having spent the winter in an attic, onions are planted in the open ground, in spring, 45 centimetres apart; soon they come up and their uprights are tied to stakes, to prevent the wind from breaking them. Around August and September, the numerous globular capsules, as large as peas, ripen and begin to open into three valves; the heads are then cut off, dried on a sheet in the sun, and rubbed in the hands to bring out the seeds, which are black, angular, irregular and less than 3 millimeters long: they are good for three years. ORDINARY sorrel: what we call the seed in sorrel is a triangular, brown, shiny, unilocular capsule, indehiscent and containing the true seed. Sorrel rises in spring, and its seed is easy to collect: it is good for three aus. PANAIS. The parsnip seed is treated like the carrot and grows at the same time; it belongs to the same family, but its seed is very different from that of the carrot; here it is very flat, oval, surrounded by a broad membrane no less than 5 millimeters high: this seed germinates for two or three years. PERSIL. After spending the winter, parsley rises in spring and ripens its fruit in June; these fruits are oval, longitudinally striated, 2 millimeters long, didymous or dividing into two bean-shaped parts, each containing a seed. Harvesting parsley berries or seeds is straightforward: they retain their germinative capacity for four or five years. PARSLEY. Burnet is not often sown in gardens, because it is a perennial plant that is usually propagated by bursting. When sown in spring, it sets seed the following year. The seed is brown, oval, wrinkled, ridged and has four wings; its length is 3 to 4 millimeters: it is good for three years. LEEK. The leek overwinters well in the open ground, so you can leave as much as you like, and it comes up in the spring; it bears fruit in exactly the same way as the onion, and its capsules are treated in the same way: its seed is black like the onion's, but a little smaller, more pointed at one end and less angular; it germinates equally well for three years. POIRÉE, CARDE-POIRÉE. These plants are stored over winter; the following spring, they come up and ripen their seeds in the summer. The seeds must be dried in the sun and beaten to detach them from the plant; these seeds are fruits as large as peas, very rough on the outside, black and hard as jet on the inside, and contain a single kernel: their germinative capacity is preserved for three or four years. PUMPKIN. The seeds of pumpkins and giraumonts vary according to species, not in shape, but in size; they are much smaller in the Jerusalem artichoke than in the large pumpkin; but they all resemble each other in the bead that surrounds them, whereas the seeds of melons and cucumbers lack this bead. In large pumpkins, the seeds are 2 centimetres q millimetres long, while in turbans, they are only 1 centimetre 8 millimetres. All these seeds are collected when the fruit is eaten, can be washed or not, and keep well for four or five years. RAIPONCE. The raiponce, sown in July, rises the following spring, and the seed ripens in July. This seed is as fine as dust, and is good for three years. BLACK RADISH. Black radishes, sown in June, are usually chosen as seed-bearing plants: at the end of December, the most beautiful ones are selected, planted 60 centimetres apart, covered during heavy frosts, and their seeds ripen in June; seeds that are harvested like those of pink radishes, which are the same color and size, and good for three years. RAVE, RADIS. When seeds are made for the trade, they are sown in spring in beds or fields of rabe or radish, and left to set seed; but market gardeners grow very little rabe, and among the radishes, pink is the most popular with consumers, so it's almost the only one they grow: When they need pink radish seed, they choose a certain number of the best from among the pink radishes they have sown in the spring, pull them out and replant them in the open ground, 40 or 45 centimetres apart; they are watered immediately, of course, and three or four more times as they come up, and the seed usually ripens in June. We then pull out the stalks and place them upright against a wall, facing south, to dry; but the siliqua of turnips and radishes does not open of its own accord like that of cabbages; it must be beaten and broken with a flail to bring out the seeds, which are once as large as those of cabbages, less round and of a C color tending towards brick: after having winnowed them, we lock them up and they are good for three years. ROMAN. These plants have seeds of the same shape and length as those of lettuces, also ridged, but a little narrower: all are grayish-white and retain their germinative capacity for three or four years. GREEN ROMAINE. At the end of April or beginning of May, when romaine planted in the ground is well capped, we let the most beautiful heads grow upwards, water them to give them vigor, and in the course of the summer, when they have deflowered and the calyxes are well swollen, we pull them up and place them upright against a wall, in the sun, as we said for lettuces, and collect the seed in the same way. Romaine seeds keep well for three or four years. BLOND ROMAINE. This is planted a little later in the ground, and the seed is harvested about a month later. GRAY ROMAIN. Grey romaine is sown in the open ground throughout the summer, so there are several times when the seed can be harvested. SCAROLE. As we don't grow escarole in spring, we get our seeds from the escarole we sow in August. In November, we mark the most beautiful plants and protect them from frost during the winter by covering and uncovering them as required. During the light frosts of spring, we cover them with cloches that we remove when the weather is fine; the escarole then rises, its seed ripens in September and we harvest it as we just said for curly endive: it is equally good for five or six years. 333 Calendar of market garden cultivation, or summary of work to be done and produce to be harvested in each month of the year. Having given, on page 92, the reasons which determined us to begin our presentation of market gardening with the month of August, these same reasons lead us to begin this calendar with the same month. AUGUST. In this month, the soil must continue to be covered with all the vegetables of the season, and to keep them moist and clean. Remember, too, that this month is the beginning of the horticultural year, and that it's time to start accumulating horse manure, which will need to be consumed prodigiously from November until April next year. As the melons, planted on the trench beds, are sold, the trenches are emptied of the sumier that formed the beds, filled with the soil that had been taken from them, ploughed and planted with hard and semi-hard cauliflower, escarole, coarse and semi-fine chicory and curly savoy cabbage, to be sold during the winter. After the 15th of the month, as the beds become emptier, we sow white onions, round-seeded and prickly spinach, to be sold from autumn to spring; radishes and lamb's lettuce, to be sold in October; half-long carrots, to be delivered for consumption the following spring. We also sow Dutch beans, which we cover with frames as the first frosts approach. Cardoon, celery, cauliflower, pear-cardoon, leek, sorrel and tarragon are all given heavy wetting, but escarole, chicory, cucumbers and gherkins are watered only moderately, unless the weather is very dry. Visit seedbeds often to purge them of insects, and collect seeds as they ripen. If you haven't started growing mushrooms in July, you can do so in this month and the next; however, you should use this latitude very sparingly, as it's always a good idea to get there first, and then eight days late can mean losing a season: finally, all vegetables should be weeded, hoeed and weeded in this month, as in all those of the year when vegetation is active. This month's crops are chicory, grey lettuce, blond romaine, summer cauliflower, leeks, carrots, a little spinach, purslane, escarole, chervil, parsley, melons, cucumbers, radishes, gherkins, sorrel, tomatoes, eggplants, pumpkins of all kinds. SEPTEMBER. The earth should be just as full of vegetables in this month as in the last. Autumn cauliflowers, escarole and chicory take pride of place, while romaine, melons and cucumbers gradually disappear. No more lettuces in our marshes, but then we sow early cabbages, such as York, pain-de-sucre and cœur-de-bœuf, to be transplanted later in nurseries; from the 8th to the 12th, we sow small and large salomon cauliflowers, half-hard and hard, to be transplanted either on ados or in trays, and then planted on beds or in the open ground when the season arrives. We sow little black or crepe lettuce to be planted under a bell or cold frame; we continue to sow lamb's lettuce and spinach, and, if the weather is dry, we need to water these plants to make them stand up. We continue to pile up manure to make layers in November, and to warm up white and green asparagus from the end of October; we also prepare some to make mushroom wheels. Towards the end of the month, we start tying and stuffing cardoons to blanch them; we replant celery in trenches or in old layers and pile it up; we sow pink radishes again, we sow chervil which will give in spring, we make a second sowing of small black lettuce which will be transplanted under cloche and planted on layers in November; At the same time, we also sow green romaine, to be transplanted under cloche, because it's romaine that we'll later plant between four lettuces per cloche on bed. Autumn cauliflowers are harvested as their heads reach perfection; a second sowing of raiponce is made to follow the one already made, escarole and chicory continue to be bound, and, if the weather is dry, cauliflowers, celery and anything else that seems to need it is wet. At the end of this month and in the following one, it's time to think about putting up the trunks and frames, and making straw mats; there's no time to take care of this during the day, and even the rain doesn't bring the market gardener or his people in; it's in the morning by candlelight and in the evening at night that all these things are prepared and put in order, so that when the time comes to use them, they're all ready to hand. In this month, we harvest chicory from Meaux and Rouen, escarole, cauliflower, carrots, parsnips, the last lettuces, the last melons, all sorts of supplies, sorrel, gherkins, pimentos, eggplant, tomatoes and pumpkins of all kinds. OCTOBER. In the first days of this month, you can also sow some of the seeds sown in the previous month: for example, you can still sow raiponium and lamb's lettuce; you can sow small black lettuce and early green romaine for bedding or coastal planting; and finally, you can sow chervil, which will be ready in spring: From one fortnight to the next, cardoons are stuffed and relined; celery is completely milled to bleach it and keep it available for sale; York, sugarloaf and oxheart cabbages, sown in the first days of September, are transplanted into the nursery. Cauliflowers sown at the same time are transplanted into boxes, so that they can be covered with frames at the first frost; if the asparagus stalks are dry, they are cut flush with the ground and the claws are lightly tilled. We continue to blanch cardoons and celery, and bind escarole and chicory; we begin to pick mâches sown in August, radishes and spinach. Towards the end of the month, we sow gotte, Georges, red and gray lettuces under cloche, to be transplanted onto teens and under cloche; we also sow blond and gray romaine in the same way, to be transplanted onto teens and under cloche or under chassis. Autumn cauliflowers are currently in full growth, and there are abundant heads to be cut every day and sent to the market; the white onion sown in August is being planted permanently. There are usually light frosts at the end of the month, so we put the frames on the cauliflowers we've transplanted into boxes and give them some air during the day. You can start heating green asparagus, even white asparagus; but it's in the following month that the big harvest of these early asparagus takes place. Chicory, escarole, cauliflower, premien cardoons, celery, carrots, parsnips, lamb's lettuce, raipons, eggplant, tomatoes, peppers, mushrooms, parsley, chervil, turnips, radishes, spinach and various pumpkins are harvested. NOVEMBER. This is the month when the early harvest begins in earnest, and a considerable supply of manure is needed to get the job done. From the very first days, white asparagus is heated, and sales continue to be heated; romaine, black, gotte, Georges, grey and red lettuces, sown in the previous month, continue to be transplanted, on ados and under cloche; some may even be sown again at the beginning of this month, if you are afraid of not having enough, as there is a huge consumption of forced lettuces and romaines in Paris. The first black lettuces are planted in beds, transplanted onto ados; York, pain-de-sucre and cœur-de-bœnf cabbages are planted in rows and even in furrows, and when frost threatens, a handful of litter is placed on each plant; We continue to plant white onions indefinitely; if it freezes at 3 degrees, we cut the remainder of the autumn cauliflowers, and cover the unbound escarole and chicory with litter. If the young romaine plant seems to be growing too fast, transplant it onto another bed; make supports around the beds and beds to prevent frost from penetrating; also replace cauliflower transplanted onto a frame for the same reason you transplanted romaine. As the frost increases, we spread straw mats over the beds and bells, pull out the unbound escarole and chicory and cover them with large quantities of dry manure, or take them to the cellar, where they are placed root up to blanch; we cover the celery trenches with litter, and put the cardoons in a greenhouse or cellar to protect them from the frost: In November, chicory, escarole, lamb's lettuce, raiponce, cardoons, celeriac and others, red cabbage and others, carrots, leeks, parsnips, mushrooms, chervil, spinach and various pumpkins are harvested. DECEMBER. Winter is usually more severe in this month than in the previous one, and the greengrocer must redouble his vigilance to preserve his plants: when the frost increases, we put short, dry manure between the bells of ados, we surround the layers already made with good accots, and we put new manure in the paths; we continue to heat the white and green asparagus; we continue to make layers to plant black lettuce under frame, to sow early carrots, turnips, radishes. We put manure on the soil where we have to make new layers, so that it doesn't freeze: whenever the sun is shining and the weather is mild, we give air to the frames, even to the bells: if severe frosts are forecast, short manure is put back between the bells on the bines, full-ground plants such as pear, carder-pear, sorrel, parsley and lamb's lettuce are covered with litter and uncovered as soon as it thaws; but, as sorrel and parsley are an everyday need, old plants are warmed up on beds and under frames: when snow has fallen on the straw mats that cover the frames and bells, and the frost continues without the sun coming out, you can leave this snow, which is a good shelter, for some time, but you mustn't let it melt on the layers or on the ados, which it would cool and make too damp. Those who did not sow snow peas or early peas under cold frames in the previous month can sow them in this one: we can prepare mushroom wheels that will yield in March; we can sow melons and cucumbers. We sell the last chicory and escarole, the last loose cauliflower; we continue to sell lamb's lettuce, celeriac, celery and celeriac, cardoon, mushrooms, parsley, chervil, leeks, red cabbage and others, spinach, sorrel, the first white and green asparagus, the first black lettuce. 08 JANUARY. This month's work is a continuation of the previous month's, and requires no less care to protect young plants from frost, and to give them as much sun and air as possible during the day, if only for an hour. So we continue to make new layers to plant black lettuce or crepe under frame, to heat sorrel, parsley, and sometimes other supplies, to sow turnips, radishes. We heat white and green asparagus; we make layers with bells, and we plant under each bell four lettuces and a romaine in the middle; we sow caroltes hátivest on layer and under frame, of the small wild chiconée also under frame. It goes without saying that we cover these new layers with good aggots, and that we line the paths with good meuf manure. Several types of cauliflower are planted under frames. At the end of the month, if it doesn't freeze, we plow the best coastal areas; and duty plants the first green romaine, which we preud on the teens. In November, we begin to pick black lettuce planted on beds and under chasers. Open ground yields little in this month, but if you have a few cofters and frame panels to shelter a bit of sorrel, parsley, chervil and periwinkle, these plants will still yield some produce: In this month, we harvest black lettuce, lamb's lettuce, celeriac, leek; celery and celeriac, red cabbage, Brussels sprouts and others, parsley, chervil, spinach, mushrooms, white and green asparagus, cauliflower kept in the cellar by the hub indicated on page 13a. = FEBRUARY. From the first days of February, a mother layer is made to sow cantaloupes of various varieties and cucumbers, which are transplanted eight or ten days later onto another layer known as the nursery layer, in potting soil or in small pots, according to the calculation made of the time to elapse until they can be planted permanently. By this time, greengrocers already have empty beds that have yielded black or crepe lettuce: these beds are turned over, mixed with new manure, rebuilt, and replanted with another season of small black lettuce, a first season of cauliflower, romaine; carrots, radishes, etc. are sown in them.: we make new layers to sow fine chicory, flax beans to transplant on other layers; we plant the first semi-hard cauliflowers in the open ground in a coastal where we have already planted green romaine, and which we will shelter if necessary with a handful of straw; carrots and radishes are sown in the open ground and only on the coast, at the same time as romaine and cauliflowers; leeks are sown in the sun to be planted in the open ground in spring; eggplants and tomatoes are sown in the sun and under a frame to be planted in the open ground after the frosts. If you haven't been able to plant all your white onions in autumn, as well as York, pain-de-sucre and cœur-de-bœuf cabbages, you finish planting them; you continue to heat white and green asparagus. During this time, you must make sure that frost does not penetrate under any cloche or frame, take advantage of the sun to give air to what needs it, get rid of excess humidity, clean and remove any damaged leaves from lettuces, romaine and other plants. After the 15th or 18th, the first melons and cucumbers are planted on beds that have been turned over and refurbished, and fitted with boxes and frames. Towards the end of the month, we plough the land where we'll be making trenches for cantaloupe melons in March; we sow carrots, spinach, parsley and chervil in the open ground; we plant the beans and beanslageolets we sowed and transplanted at the beginning of the month on beds; we cover them with trays, and sow others to succeed them. For sale this month: black lettuce, new radishes, green romaine, sorrel, lamb's lettuce, raipon, parsley, chervil, sorrel, celery and celeriac, leeks, parsnips, first green beans, mushrooms, white and green asparagus, preserved cauliflower, new lettuce for cutting. MARCH. In the first few days of this month, we start to open the trenches in which we will successively make layers on which we plant cantaloupe melons in large quantities and which we cover with frames as we plant them; we make layers to continue planting lettuces and romaines under cloche and under frame; we sow on layer and under frame other melons for a second or third season; green, blond and grey romaine, grey, red and Georges lettuces are planted in the open ground, and taken from the ados where they have spent the winter; and, as in this season there is usually no fear of heavy frosts, many more seeds are sown in the open ground in our marshes than elsewhere, and in strong, cold soils, they are only sown in April and May: so, in March, we sow short, half-long and long carrots, onions, leeks, fine and half-fine chicories, turnips and radishes, oscille, parsnips, Alençon cress; gotte, red and Georges lettuces; we do a second! of spinach to succeed the one sown in February. in February, and although we sowed fine and semi-fine chicory in the open ground, we also sow some on beds and under chassis, which will have come before that sown in the open ground; we make new beds in trenches, for beans; we sow eggplants and tomatoes on beds; we sow asparagus seed in the open ground, and we can start planting last year's seedling; finally we plant in the open ground many cauliflowers raised under chassis. In this month, there is usually a drying haze, which requires moderate and judicious watering of beds and soil. In this month, we have black lettuce, new radishes, green romaine, sorrel, parsley, chervil, the last lamb's lettuce and raipons, new carrots, green beans, leeks, spinach, small wild chicory, champiguon, tarragon, the last white and green asparagus, the last preserved cauliflower. 16 347 There are no longer any heavy frosts to fear; but we must always be on guard against late frosts, which are often fatal to over-confident early fruit growers. We continue to plant melons in trenches under panels, and we sow others to be planted on beds and under cloche; we prune and line melons under frames; we turn over old lettuce beds, as they are emptied, and we replant them with cloche melons. It's time to sow all the cucurbits that are to be planted in the open ground, such as the various pumpkins, giraumonts, cucumbers and gherkins. Tomatoes and eggplants are planted on beds; all market garden vegetables are sown and planted in the open ground in spring, summer and autumn, and it would be too long and tedious to list them here. The frames of the beds for carrots, turnips, radishes and chicory are removed and placed on top of the last ones, melons, which are planted in trenches. As the cold decreases, dryness usually increases: care must be taken to ensure that each vegetable does not lack the moisture it needs; finally, by the end of the month, no bare patch should be left in a swamp. In this month, we sell the last black lettuces, the first gotte and Georges lettuces, the first melons, petit prescott fond blanc and cucumbers; we continue to sell green romaine, carrots, turnips, radishes, sorrel, parsley, certeuil, tarragon, salad burnet, green beans, carde-poirée, mushrooms. MAY. A market garden must, in this month, represent a carpet of varied greenery, and one of the market gardener's main tasks is to sow in such a way that he always has plants ready to replace those that have reached maturity and are daily delivered for consumption, so that his marsh is always full until the end of autumn. We plant the last cantaloupe melons in trenches; we turn over the last empty lettuce and carrot beds, to plant other melons; we plant eggplants and tomatoes, if we weren't able to do so at the end of the previous month; if we're not too worried about competition, we sow a bed or two of green beans to replace those under chassis; we sow spinach and chervil, to replace those that have gone to seed; We sow all types of lettuce, except the little black one, which is no longer in season; we also sow the three types of romaine, but the green one will end with the month; we will only sow the blond and gray ones, which the escarole and chicory will make disappear in their turn in September; we sow the cardoons on a piece of bed to be replanted, or we sow them immediately in place. Celery is best sown on a piece of bedding, because it comes on faster and can be transplanted more quickly than that sown in the ground; however, small celery for cutting can be sown in the ground. Cauliflowers, whether bedded or planted in the ground, require a lot of watering and insect control. Pumpkins, giraumonts, cucumbers and gherkins sown on beds last month are planted permanently. Last year's pear, chard and parsley go to seed, and are replaced by new seedlings if this has not already been done. We sow pink radishes every ten days, black radishes for winter, carrots and parsnips to be delivered for consumption as they grow. Pruning melons takes up a good part of the market gardener's time, in this month and the next. This month sees the sale of red and grey lettuces, blond and grey romaine, cauliflower, melon, cucumber, chicory, York sprouts, sugar loaf, O8 beef hearts, green beans, radishes, turnips, parsley, chervil, spinach, sorrel, tarragon, burnet, watercress, carrot, chard, leek, white onion, spring onion. JUNE. In this month, as in the two preceding ones, the vegetable gardener must always remember how long it takes for this or that seed to sprout, how long it takes for the seedling to be ready for planting, and how long it takes for the vegetable to be ready for consumption, so that he always sows on time, and is not exposed to losing a season, or to seeing his land unoccupied. A few melons can still be planted in the first days of this month, if the plant is in good condition; hard and half-hard cauliflowers are sown to give their apples in autumn; those sown in May are planted; pear chard is also sown; romaine and the season's lettuces are sown. lettuces of the season, a few at a time, but every ten or twelve days; plant the cardoons sown on a piece of bed the previous month; you can even sow them in place if you haven't already done so; sow the Brussels sprouts, the Savoy cabbage fr. Brussels sprouts, curly Savoy cabbage and others are sown for the winter; we start transplanting celery, celery turcet and celery raye. Melons (I) are still taking up part of the market gardener's time this month. Supplies such as golden purslane, chervil and lady's mantle rise quickly in this season, and must be sown very often. Purslane and lady's mantle don't mind the sun, but chervil needs shade; the first escarole is sown this month. Much of the time is taken up with watering, without which no harvest can be expected. This is the month in which the frames and bells are omitted from the layers; the frames are stacked in a shed sheltered from the rain; the bells are stacked and set out in a corner of the marsh sheltered from shocks (see page 78). This month's produce includes cauliflower, York, painrde-sucre and cœur-de-bœuf cabbages, melons, cucumbers, green beans, ton ates, eggplants, cress alénois, cerfenil, parsley, salad burnet, sorrel, golden purslane, white onion, spring onion, chives, turnips and radishes, first celery for cutting, bonne-dame. JULY. No less foresight is needed in this month? than in the previous ones, since we have more or less the same sowing and planting to do, except for green romaine, which has given way to escarole. In the first few days of the month, celery continues to be transplanted; hard and semi-hard cauliflowers continue to be planted for the autumn; kale, Brussels sprouts, red cabbage and other types of cabbage are planted for consumption over the winter; chicory, escarole, turnips, radishes, chervil, maidenhair and anything else that can ripen before winter continue to be sown. As the melon trenches are emptied, the manure is removed from the trenches, and the trenches are filled with the soil from the trenches. The trenches are then ploughed and planted with autumn cauliflower, semi-fine chicory, Rouennaise chicory, Meaux chicory, escarole and other seasonal vegetables. Watering is usually even more frequent and more essential than in the previous month, and you can't expect to get beautiful cauliflowers or celery if they aren't abundantly watered. In this last month of the horticultural year, the marshes offer an abundance of melons, cucumbers, gherkins, fine and semi-fine chicories, blond and gray romaine, gray and red lettuces, sweetbread and beef cabbage, summer cauliflower, carrots, tomatoes, eggplant, parsnips, leeks, cut celery, pear, radish, parsley, sorrel, belle-dame, and all the season's supplies.
