remove dust from their leaves using a feather duster, a wet cloth or a watering can with very fine holes; for this watering, which should be done in the evening rather than the morning, you should use rainwater or river water in preference to any other water, and after cooling it down a little. Plants that are fat or have tough, glossy leaves can go a long time without water; plants with tender foliage suffer and die quickly from drought: 1° place them so that the base of the bulb rests on the rim of the decanter, and so that the tray and the roots emerging from it are completely immersed in the water; 2° give them air and light, without exposing them to too much heat; 3° change all or part of the water from time to time, but keep the decanter quite full; you can throw in a few grains of cooking salt to prevent the liquid from corrupting. When the roots are well developed and the buds are showing, the need for bright light diminishes and the onions can be placed back on the mantelpiece or on the furniture inside the apartment. This is how we care for Ornithogales, Amaryllis, Crocus, Hyacinths, Narcissus, Italian and Siberian Scillas, etc., etc., etc. Plants that require moderate heat and fear frost can be raised on double-framed windows; window greenhouses can be heated by hot-water basins with pipes, small thermosiphons, etc., etc. In good exposure, in the open air, often on balconies: Sweet peas, Nasturtiums, Ivy, Reseda, etc., etc. (1). (1) Flowers should never be kept in the bedroom at night. Means of plant propagation. - Sowing - Budding and Marcottage. - Cutting. - Grafting. - Crossbreeding. - Hybridization. The main aim of all horticulture is the multipli. cation of plants. Plants multiply by seed in their primitive, natural state; but we need to resort to artificial means in our cultivation. At the same time as sowing is the surest way of obtaining robust, fast-growing individuals, it also produces very curious varieties; roots, stems and branches perpetuate plants without alteration. Take well-ripened seeds, which you can tell by weight, color and inspection of the internal organs, which must be complete; not too old, with no wrinkles or alterations. The best way to preserve seeds is to enclose them in canvas bags of varying thickness, once they have been cleaned of all moisture. Large seeds with hard bark can be sown deeply; a thin layer of soil or pulverized compost is enough to cover the other fine seeds; the smallest seeds will even germinate without being buried; seeds with bumps, membranes or hairs should be rubbed between the hands for a few moments and mixed with ash or dust, to prevent them from attaching to each other. We hasten the germination of stone seeds (cherry, plum) and seeds with very hard skins by stratification, i.e. we hold these seeds for varying lengths of time in pots filled with soil or sand moist enough to ferment due to the action of the soil's heat, into which we push them at Om, 30 or Om, 40, at midday exposure, after which, the germ having developed, we sow in rows or broadcast. Seeds produce more hairs in soft, light soil than in heavy soil. Broadcast sowing. - This involves spreading the seeds as evenly as possible by throwing them with the hand from a distance. - Sowing in packets or pots. Holes are made at a greater or lesser distance depending on the species of plant, which is first surrounded with some of the soil removed, and then lightly tilled. - Sowing in terrines and pots. If the plants are very water-loving, there's no need to pierce the pots, which should be immersed up to a quarter of their height in the liquid, which gradually seeps through the walls, moistening the young roots sufficiently. Pierced pots or terrines should be lined with coarse sand to facilitate water drainage. - Ray sowing. Draw the rays with a chalk line, give them a depth of about Om, 03 to Om, 06; sow and cover the seed with the soil first raised. - Sowing in nurseries. Pips and seeds are broadcast and should be buried Om, 03 deep; pits are placed one by one, at a suitable distance, in Om, 06 holes. Mulch or leaves permanently against frost until spring. - Sowing on a bed. All seeds too delicate to be planted in the ground are planted in a bed or bell. Transplanting is any transplanting that is not permanent. Tubers are roots, underground stems or branches of underground stems of various shapes; separated and placed in the ground, they form new plants: Dahlia, Cyclamen, Potato, Jerusalem artichoke, etc. Each tuber eye produces true roots, stems, complete individuals in a word. If you cut large tubers into as many parts as there are eyes, each of these parts will produce a new plant. The stalks and bulblets should not be detached until they are ripe, which you can see by the complete desiccation of the leaves in whose axils these little bodies are born. Carnations are the rooted shoots that appear at the collar or on the roots of certain plants. Plants with perennial roots produce tufts of varying thickness, with seeds, buds or turions, which are broken off in autumn and towards the end of winter to produce new individuals. Strawberries and other plants have runners or stolons, which are spindly stems with buds at their joints; these buds, separated and placed in the ground, become new plants. Layering consists in burying a portion of a plant, one end of which protrudes outwards, while the other adheres to the mother plant, which is responsible for nourishing the cutting until it takes root and lives on of its own accord. A simple cutting is said to exist when a branch firmly fixed in this position by wooden hooks and covered with soil is placed in the ground at a depth of about Om, 08, 0, m10; marcotte 3 is said to be a serpentine marcotte when the top of the branch, instead of remaining freely erect out of the ground, is bent back in order to force it to give other marcottes; in marcotte by strangulation, the bark of the buried branch is tightened by means of an iron or linen wire, near and below an eye; in marcotte by circumcision, a circular strip of bark is removed below an eye, so as to maintain the descending sap at the base of the upper lip, and create a bead from which the roots grow; in marcotte by twisting, a branch with thin, fibrous bark is twisted at the point where it is to produce roots; in the simple incision method, the branch is split down the middle, and the separated parts are kept apart by placing a stone or other hard body between them; in the heel incision method, the branch is first split horizontally down the middle, then vertically upwards; in the complicated incision method, two perpendicular cuts are made on the horizontal slit made as above, and kept apart by placing small stones between them; in the amputation method, the cut piece is completely removed, as in the heel incision; finally, in the cepée method, after cutting a tree or shrub flush with the ground, the stumps are covered with soil; in this state, the stumps produce several shoots, which are removed once they have taken root. Annual shoots are often too high to be laid down or brought to ground level, or the wood is too brittle to lend itself to bending. In this case, after staking the branch, it is placed in a basket or pot with a deep indentation, in funnel-shaped glass vases, or in lead or zinc cups lined with soil; the soil is watered; the cutting is separated when it has taken root. Cuttings are young, fresh shoots that are placed in the ground at the cut end to take root. This operation is based on the inherent property of adventitious buds and all latent plant germs to convert into branches or roots, depending on the diversity of the environment in which they are found. In many cases, cuttings are an advantageous substitute for propagation by seed. Few plants are unwilling to undergo this operation. For cuttings to be successful, there must be an abundance of cellular tissue to prompt root development at the buried end of the shoot, and the soil must be as moist and warm as possible; it is important to prevent transpiration of the shoots and evaporation of moisture from the soil. Moist moss and heather soil encourage root development. Simple cuttings. - For very easy-to-grow trees: plane trees, poplars, willows and especially waterside plants, in December or March, cut off young branches two to six years old, prune them, leaving some of their shoots, and push them into deep holes, three to five decimeters square, filled with light soil and pressed in all directions. These branches will cover with leaves in the same season. For amenity trees that are difficult to regrow, in March, cut young shoots from the previous year below a node, divide them into sections of five or six buds, and bind them for a month up to a quarter of their length in fresh sand, sheltered from wind and frost; at the beginning of April, cut each section with a planting knife, in well-ploughed ground, facing north or east, leaving two or three eyes above the ground; water with gentle rain; mulch and keep cool at all times. Species which do not lend themselves to the two above-mentioned procedures can be cut with a bead or heel. As early as June of MULTIPLICATION OF PLANTS. the previous year, a circular ring is made on the young cutting, or a strong ligature is made with wire, so as to create a bead of abundant cellular tissue on this point; or, finally, a branch is broken off from the trunk, pulling up and down so as to remove with it the impasto naturally formed at its junction, and is planted. This procedure is detrimental to mother plants, and should only be used with caution. For Vines, Currants, many Roses, etc., cuttings are made from two-year-old wood or crossette: a fairly long piece of a two- or three-year-old branch is removed with the cutting; the old branch is pruned and placed in heather soil, to a depth of about Om, 12; finally, it is watered and covered with mulch. Orangery and greenhouse plants; herbaceous plants, Dahlias, etc. are generally cut under a bell. Here's how it's done: In terrines or deep pots of Om, 1 or Om, 2 lined with heather soil and potting compost, with a bed of sand, you will prick with an unsharp planter, the cuttings leafy in May and June, leaving them only the top and two leaves, after having well packed the soil, you will water; you will let it dry out in the shade; you will put the whole on a covered bed or in a warm place, in the shade. The air must be renewed with care and precaution; you must be sparing with watering, removing the vapors that settle on the inside walls of the bell and the moulds that often form around the young plants. We have always found the months of May and June to be particularly favorable for bell cuttings. Orange trees can even be propagated by taking cuttings from their leaves, while lilies, etc., can be propagated by taking cuttings from their scales. The aim of grafting is to make the branch or bud of one plant grow on another. For the operation to succeed, two main conditions must be met: 1° coincidence in the development of the branch removed, called the graft, and in the development of the plant on which it is placed, called the subject; 2° identity, if not of species and genus, at least of family and certain relationships between individuals. Let's take a look at the most frequently used grafts. Grafting by approach consists in strongly binding together two branches of neighbouring trees, after having first cut them to a quarter of their thickness. The wounds are protected from light, air and water, using Saint Fiacre's ointment or grafting wax. Most of the twigs above and below the graft are removed; little by little, the stem is incised, waiting to be cut until the welding is complete, which takes place in the course of the year. This grafting process gives new vigor to old espalier trees. To this end, two wildings of the same species are planted next to the exhausted tree; they are bent crosswise, or more or less, on the trunk of the first, a little above the other; suitable notches are made to graft them by approach; the following year, once the weld has been made, the two wildings are decapitated, their sole task being to provide the old tree with fresh, strong sap, to make it fertile, as in the days of its youth. Approach grafting can be used to form espaliers, hedges and fences. It is especially useful for delicate plants, at a time when the sap is moving. Herbaceous grafting is a type of approach grafting, with the difference that instead of operating on woody branches at least one year old, it is performed on herbaceous or barely woody plants, mainly on the terminal shoot of coniferous Fig. 9. Slot grafting. trees during the height of their vegetation. After cutting away the terminal shoot with a triangular section, the bevelled scion is placed in its place. Ligation must be done with care and skill; the lack of consistency of this type of graft makes it much more likely than the previous one to be strangled if it is too tight. Slot grafting, the most commonly used method for fruit trees, consists in cutting the tree or branches to be grafted horizontally at the base; on the flat part thus cut, or tray, a slot is made in the middle from Om, 03 to Om, 04 with a serpette and a hammer; the graft or scion (a well-aruged branch from the previous year) is taken. Fitted with 2, 3 or 4 eyes, this graft is beveled from the large end on both sides, and inserted into the slot so that the bark is at the same level and perfectly aligned. Two, three or four scions can be inserted if the tray is wide enough; then, without shaking the scions, the small wooden wedges holding the slits open are removed, tightened with woolen thread, and the wounds healed with grafting wax. For this operation to be successful, it is important that the subject is in good health, and that the scions have not yet grown. They can be cut in advance and kept fresh by burying them in the north; they can be grafted in the first spring, or in September (sleeping-eye grafting). In the latter case, the graft and subject will begin their winter sleep at the same time, and will be revived together in the spring. This does not destroy the general rule for scion grafting, which is as follows: the subject must be in sap and the graft must be about to enter it. Crown grafting is performed on subjects too large to be split. After horizontal amputation, a wedge of very hard wood is used to insert the scions, beveled on one side to a length of Om.04 to Om.05, between the sapwood and the bark, with the bark separated from the sapwood. A tie is placed around the scion, and grafting wax is applied. In this way, there are no cracks on the surface of the cut, which remains perfectly intact; such is the character of crown grafting. In this way, a large-diameter branch can receive ten or more scions. Flute or whistle grafting consists in amputating a branch at an eye, at a very smooth point, splitting the bark without damaging the wood, into two or three strips of Om, 06 in length; a ring of bark with its buds is removed from the graft, which should be as large as possible; it is threaded onto the sapwood of the subject, and the strips are raised without covering the eyes. If the subject's diameter is greater than that of the flute, the ring is trimmed to fit the designated place, and covered with one of the loose, falling strips; if the diameter is smaller, a strip is removed with a whistle, and the edges joined; grafting wax over the slits. This type of grafting is used mainly for walnut and chestnut trees. Grafting with a growing eye is done in May-June; grafting with a dormant eye is done in April and September; their distinctive feature is that they do not introduce any part of the grafted wood onto the subject. Here's how it's done: 1° After detaching a well-formed bud from the branch you wish to graft, you remove the leaf, but keep the part of the petiole adhering to the eye, which you remove with its bark, squarely above, pointed below, in the shape of an escutcheon, hence the name of this type of graft; 2° At the point reserved for the escutcheon, make an incision in the shape of a straight T or an upside-down ], penetrating all the way into the wood; using the spatula of your grafting tool, pull the two lips of the bark apart upwards; 3° Slide Fig. 10 - Escutcheon. Fig. 11. - Grafting the escutcheon. between the bark and the wood in the incision you've made on the subject, determining the most exact coincidence. Then bind the lips of the bark together to secure the bud, but without covering it. Don't cut the stem or branches just as you're grafting; you'll create an untimely shoot that's exposed to a lot of bad luck; so wait a few days, until it's perfectly fused; then pinch the end of your scions; cut halfway through; then retrench. If you have grafted with a dormant eye in autumn, postpone this part of the operation until the following spring. Loosen ligatures if they cause constrictions, and carefully remove any eyes that develop at the same time as the bud. English-style grafting or grafting by copulation can only be applied to subjects of exactly the same diameter as the scions; the top of the former and the bottom of the latter are cut at an angle so that all their parts overlap and the edges of the two barks coincide at all points. Ligature; grafting wax. Pontoise grafting, particularly used for ornamental trees and shrubs that retain their leaves in winter, is performed as follows: when the winter sleep is over and the sap begins to run again, you cut a triangular slit in the side of the subject, into which you insert the bottom of your wedge-cut graft, then bind it; but you must keep the shrubs thus grafted under a frame for two weeks or so; otherwise, the scion used, being loaded with leaves and often even flowers or flower buds, will perish through evaporation. As faun grafting is only a minor variety of flute grafting, we won't go into it here. Remember that, for all grafts, you need to choose a mild, rather humid than dry temperature; take trees rich in sap; don't let the sap abandon the grafts and, to this end, remove all the buds underneath them; loosen, a fortnight after the operation, the ligatures which often create harmful swellings; have sharp, clean, simple instruments that have been adopted 3. by experienced people: a clamp, a screwdriver, a scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors, a pair of scissors. by experienced people: ordinary serpette, serp, hand saw, slotted grafting tool; ties made of wicker, woollen thread, lime bark, iron, etc.; liquid grafting putty, Saint Fiacre's ointment; grafting wax to be used at a degree of heat such that it can be handled without burning. This phenomenon is often observed in plants that have been cultivated for a long time; these varieties sometimes remain so similar to themselves, through a long succession of generations, that one would almost believe oneself entitled to declare them true species: Onions, cabbages, melons and many vegetable plants; roses, carnations, daisy queens, azaleas, pelargoniums, dablias, etc. If you want to fix these new characters as much as you can, you will breed away from all other individuals of the same species, those in which these manifestations have occurred: this is what selection is all about. If you protect your chosen subjects from crossing with typical plants for a very long time, they will provide you with new types. Perennial varieties can be preserved by grafting, cuttings and layering. When a species has naturally produced a few clear-cut varieties, you can increase the number by artificial crossing or métissage, which is performed as follows: after allowing the races or varieties you wish to obtain mixed-breed forms to flower simultaneously, you place the pollen of one on the stigma of another. The operation is therefore quite simple; only it requires certain precautions to succeed, of which we'll say a few words. As soon as the foreign pollen has been deposited on the stigma, protect the flower from all contact with pollen from the plant itself or from other varieties. To this end, cut off all the other flowers, cover the artificially fertilized flower with a piece of canvas until the ovary swells; the smallest insects could bring it this pollen, the action of which would render all your care null and void. For hybridization, you will operate in the same way as for cross-breeding, with this crucial difference: the cross-breeding no longer takes place between races or varieties of the same species, but between different species, resulting in much greater uncertainty. There is a chance of success if the two species not only belong to the same natural family, but are also of the same genus, without differing too much from each other. Half-breeds and hybrids often take after both the father and the mother; half-breeds themselves are almost always as fertile as the typical species; hybrid flowers are affected by total sterility in the case of simultaneous abortion of their pollen, which has thus become unsuitable for fertilization, and poor conformation of the outer parts of the ovary or ovules; hybrid flowers are affected by partial sterility if the pollen alone is lacking, the ovary and ovules remaining in normal conditions. Some hybrid Petunias are very fertile; they fertilize themselves or cross between themselves, giving rise to many hybrid varieties. More or less fertile hybrids do not form a species; from their second generation, there is a tendency to revert to specific forms; then complete or incomplete return to these forms. In general, cross-breeding between races of the same species, or between different species, gives plants the ability to vary. Hybridization should never be practised for vegetable plants, to which it could only be harmful; we hardly know the results it would have on fruit trees - it is best to refrain from any imprudent attempt here. - ==="" ~πu======" =-==mo==-- -r==e=-==----=n =-"Sru FIRST SECTION. - PLANT DISEASES. There are diseases which, like plethora in men and animals, arise from an overabundance of life in plants. For example, certain branches, called gourmands for this reason, appropriate almost all the juices and leave the other parts of the plant without vigor; cut out the gourmands, reduce the manure; replace soil that is too fat, too substantial, with leaner, lighter soil. Trees that produce leaves instead of fruit are known as phyllomanes, or portfolios. Carpomante is the opposite of phyllomania: the tree has far too many fruits, but they are small, of poor quality and difficult to ripen; the problem is remedied by pruning and disbudding. Fasciation, so common in Compositae and Roses, consists in the accidental flattening of stems in branches that are naturally cylindrical; moreover, fasciation does not rob plants of their vigor and, because of this very monstrosity, makes them sought-after as ornaments. We can remedy the loss of vigor and languor of plants in poor soil or exposure, by moving them to another location and giving them manure, light, air and warmth. The ordinary causes of sterility are: cold, which freezes the fruiting bodies; heat, which dries out the stigma and makes it unsuitable for retaining pollen; and rain, which removes it from the stamens before it has fertilized the pistil. Hyacinth and gladiolus onions, etc., are subject to white glanders, caused by very bitter cold. Without destroying the outer forms of the tubers, white glanders changes them into a white, slimy, odorless, slightly acid and semi-liquid pulp. The progress of this serious disease is sometimes halted by removing the infected tunics and placing the onions in pots lined with sandy soil, in a warm location, but out of the direct action of the sun's rays. The garden potato species Marjolaine, Chaville, Schaw and Sept-Semaines are subject to a disease that manifests itself as frisole, or a peculiar folding of the leaves over themselves, changing from green to dark brown, and the appearance of brown spots on the surface of the stems; if you divide the tuber, you'll see that it has taken on a yellowish tint, then brown, spread irregularly in length and width. Immediately cut off all the outer parts of the plant at ground level; when you pull them out, you'll have small but mostly good potatoes. Just leave them exposed to the sun in the open air, then bring them in when the weather dries out. Don't be afraid to eat slightly damaged potatoes, as long as the damaged parts have been removed beforehand; starch factories will even buy the worst ones. 51 Dry sulfuring of vines is best carried out in full sunlight, from 10 a.m. to noon: once, when the vines begin to vegetate; again, when they flower; and again, when the bunches are in verjuice. Grapevine disease consists of the rapid multiplication of a microscopic fungus, Oidium Tuckeri, on leaves, shoots, bunches and grapes, which then appear to be covered with a whitish dust or powdery down. Examined under the microscope, this fuzz is made up of fine, ragged, compartmentalized filaments and oval or elliptical spores, joined end to end like grains in a necklace. Leaves twitch, fruits crack and dry out. The only remedy is sulphur flower, spread with a Gontier bellows on the diseased individual, which has been well bathed beforehand. The value of the crop saved in this way, in whole or in part, compensates for the pain and cost of the medication. Blanc de meunter is another disease similarly due to the development of a microscopic fungus, erysiphe, which attacks fruit trees in particular: Plum, Apple, etc.; ornamental shrubs: Rose, etc.; and some annual plants: Pansy, etc. We prevent erysiphe by keeping vegetation vigorous and energetic; curative means have yet to be discovered. Ulcers, from which gum or other juices from decomposed sap flow, gradually eat away at the heart of the wood and kill it, unless the damaged part is promptly and deeply cut away, taking care to line the scar with Saint-Fiacre ointment or grafting wax; later, the bark advances on both sides and covers the wound. The same precautions are taken against root ulcers. The rounded, more or less voluminous growths that appear on elm and other trees are called burls; if they are not so numerous as to interfere with the plant's growth, they are allowed to remain. Chlorosis or variegation alters the green color of leaves, making them mottled or variegated: Aucuba, Phalaris rubane, etc.; this morbid state is often seen, in reality, as an improvement, an amenity of the individual; variegation sometimes disappears when plants are given more substantial soil. Lightning shatters tree trunks and branches, stripping bark and wood, dividing the latter into longitudinal fibers: cleavage. The cold causes the champelure of the vine or death of young shoots and even branches, which are cut and disarticulated at the nodes, sometimes to such an extent that there is no wood left for pruning. Cracks in tree trunks are called frostbite, sometimes in the bark alone (simple frostbite), sometimes in the wood itself (interwoven frostbite). There is no remedy for champelure and gelivure; they can be prevented by sheltering trees with hedges and windbreaks; by shodding their feet with sand or dry earth; by rolling a rope of dry straw around their trunks, etc. Mercury, arsenic and baryte sprays, soda prussiates, copper acetate, quinine sulfate; soluble oxides of tin and copper; quicklime; sulfuric, prussic and muriatic acids; alcohols, ethers and extracts of hemlock, jimsonweed and black henbane poison plants. We therefore need to keep a close eye on the waste from soda factories and other chemical products that may be found in the vicinity of gardens. External causes, such as high winds, often lead to the decortication, tearing or fracture of certain parts of the tree; grafting wax should be used in preference to St. Fiacre's ointment to hasten the healing of these wounds; trees are often preserved by tying up branches that are too heavy, too laden with twigs or fruit. If the tear does not extend too deeply, we apply pieces of wood hollowed out like gutters to the two points opposite the split, and tighten them with hemp or iron ties, which should not be removed until five or six years later, when the wound has healed perfectly. Grafting wax, ointment of Saint Fiacre. If the broken part cannot be reattached, saw it low enough below the fracture to remove all traces of splitting or tearing on the amputated surface, then pare with grafting wax. Not only does hail cause purely mechanical damage to the parts of plants it hits, but the nitrous acid it suspends disorganizes them, as you will easily notice on the leaves and stems of melons, where hailstones leave spots that grow, turn from yellow to brown and kill the part hit. No remedy, but preservatives: glass frames and mats. Nails, bullets thrown by firearms, stones, animal horns, often remain in the wounds they have made; you will leave them there, unless you can extract them without enlarging the wound too much. Healing takes place very well on its own, and the bodies gradually buried in the wood do not interfere with the circulation of the sap. Necrosis or death of the wood is caused by bruising, burns, poor pruning, cold, etc., and can be seen in a portion of the wound. It is indicated by a dry, dead portion of wood, almost always longer than it is wide, enclosed in healthy tissue. Sometimes you leave necrosis to nature, sometimes you attack it with a gouge. You won't give rise to necrosis if, when pruning and trimming a tree, you cut obliquely from top to bottom, to make it easier for rain to run off, and if you cover the bare surface with tar or pitch. Entophytic helminths, small, thin, elongated, almost transparent worms, sometimes fill the pericarp of wheat (haggard or stunted wheat) and destroy it; humidity is favorable to their development and life; no means of destroying them is known. Entophytic fungi attack all parts of plants. Ergot is a disease of grass seeds, which elongate, become purplish-black, and emerge from between the bales in the form of small black horns or ergots. All these ravages, comparable to those of gangrene on living creatures, are probably due to the presence of a poisonous fungus. No cure. Oecidial fungi attack Compositae, Leguminosae and Umbelliferae; rœstélies fungi grow mainly on Pear trees; peridermium can be seen on Pine leaves; phragmidium on Roses, Raspberries, Strawberries, etc.; red rust destroys the leaves of Grasses; smut is found on Wheat, Oats, Barley, Millet, Corn, etc.; liming is often successful against smut. Fumaginia and honeydew, vegetal-animal products, cover the stomata on the upper surface of leaves, causing them to perish. Orange, lemon, myrtle, rockrose, maple and olive trees are particularly prone to the latter two diseases. The disease attaches itself preferentially to apple trees, willows, poplars, lime trees, etc.; more rarely to oak trees. Cuseute takes Serpolet, Flax and Vine as its victims; orobanche lives at the expense of Leguminosae, Serpolet, Mugwort, Hemp and Broad Bean. Melampyrus, rhinanthus and euphrasia feed on the juices of many plant species, exhausting them. These dangerous parasites must be destroyed by careful weeding. Byssus or root white develops on the roots and rootlets of Roses, Apples, Peaches, etc.; it looks like plaster. This fungus is very hardy; it often only shows its presence after killing the individual on which it has attached itself. Some plants affected by this kind of secret leprosy can be saved by uprooting them, cutting off the roots that are too diseased, washing all the roots that are still healthy or nearly so with plenty of water, even brushing them, and then replanting them in loose soil, away from the heat of the sun. SECTION TWO. - ANIMAL PESTS. Among the mammalian animals that are harmful to plants are the rat, the mole, the dormouse and the ferret. Rats like to take up residence in old, degraded walls, where they multiply and emerge, especially at night, to gather fruit from espaliers. The best trap for them is the "four de chiffre", so called because of the particular arrangement of the small sticks that hold a plank loaded with a heavy body in balance; it is primed with pieces of roasted bacon. The mole provides a real service by destroying insect larvae and certain bad plant onions, but on the other hand, it disturbs garden soil to such an extent that it has to be chased away. They are most active between ten and midday, when they are caught and killed with a spade. They live on fruit, and are caught in wicker cage traps, primed by a ripe fruit, but different from those available on the espalier tree; young dormice and ferrets can be tamed like squirrels. Among molluscs, slugs, especially in autumn and spring, cause great damage in gardens, multiplying rapidly and becoming a real nuisance; have the duck, which is very fond of them, chase them away; or throw cabbage or romaine leaves flat on the ground; The slugs will feed greedily on them, even sheltering in them at night so as to be ready for the next day's feast sooner; in the morning, before sunrise, remove them; instead of crushing them, feed them to your farmyard animals. Snails or escar gots are easy to catch after heavy showers in the summer, when they spread out everywhere in search of suitable and varied food: vegetables, ornamental plants, fruit, flower buds, etc. Destroy them mercilessly.You can protect your fruit trees and dahlias by defending the base of these plants with a circular pile of crushed oyster shells, whose sharp blades will be enough to keep your enemies at bay. Snails are widely traded in Burgundy and elsewhere. Insects. - The most harmful insect in our climate is the cockchafer. It usually appears in France in the second half of April as a larva, feeding on plant roots for three or four years; as a perfect insect, it devours the green parts; shake or warp the trees in the morning, and the beetles fall off; crush them and feed them mixed with other foodstuffs, to pigs, hens, etc., which are very fond of them. Female cockchafer beetles lay their eggs in the ground, in holes from Om, 08 to Om, 10 deep; the larvae that emerge from these eggs are called mans, worms or tures; moles destroy them, but by themselves upsetting the ground in such a way that the remedy is almost as damaging as the disease. Cantharids are more formidable as perfect insects than as larvae in May or June; in a single day, they destroy all the foliage of the Ash, Oak and Privet trees they attack: Cantharides fall numb on cloths previously laid on the ground; immediate immersion in vinegar kills them; well dried, enclosed in glazed pots inside, they can be kept for thirty or forty years; pharmacists buy them at a fairly high price. The kite larva (lucania) lives in the woody tissues of old oak and fruit trees; it can sometimes be partially destroyed by emptying the galleries it digs and injecting them with a burning liquid. The larva of the grain weevil appears in early spring and multiplies until autumn; we recommend covering piles of wheat devastated by this enemy with leaves of Walnut, Elder, Hemlock and Tansy; we doubt the effectiveness of this remedy; the best preservatives are silos, jars and dry, well-stoppered barrels. The green satin weevil pricks the leaves, making cones in which to deposit its eggs, from which white, hairless larvae emerge, already very voracious in this state. The following year, they're just as dangerous, in their perfect insect state; remove leaves, eggs and larvae and burn them. Cynips, diploptera and cecidomia create excrescences on the various parts of Oak, Pine, Willow, Elm, Maple, Rose, Ivy, etc., called galls if they are closed on all sides; false galls if they retain some communication with the outside. Vegetable garden pentatomas cause damage to flowers and vegetables; shake the plants affected by them over a wide-mouthed, well-glazed vase; the insects will fall in and you'll burn them. You'll easily recognize aphids by the two horns or nipples usually pointing upwards and attached to the tip of the abdomen; from these nipples emerge a sweet liquid which ants are very fond of sucking; hence the name "ant cows" given to aphids; these improvised mothers and their infants live together in harmony, frequenting each other day and night. Aphids sting and suck leaves, distorting them and soaking them in a viscous, highly-nuisible substance. The green aphid is a particular enemy of roses, destroying young shoots and buds; cabbages, cauliflowers, turnips and radishes. To get rid of them, smoke tobacco under a bell in the morning or evening, when the weather is calm. Remove the bell as soon as the aphids are asphyxiated, so that the smoke dissipates without harming the vegetation. The black aphid, which is rightly considered to be the same as the black aphid, and which undoubtedly owes its black color to the bean's juice, of which it is very avid, always attacks this plant from the top leaves; remove these leaves and burn them. The woolly aphid, quite different from the green and black aphids, has only one thing in common with them: its frighteningly rapid spread. It lives at the expense of the apple trees in our orchards, and of the ornamental apple tree with semi-double flowers, on whose bark it causes cankers of a bad nature, very often fatal. The sawfly is so called because it is armed with a kind of saw with which it cuts into the bark of the plant to which it entrusts its egg. Dragonfly or damselfly. - It is wrong to wage war on the dragonfly, so aptly named by Linnaeus as the sparrowhawk of insects, as it destroys hundreds of them in a single Fig. 28 - Depressed dragonfly (female). day, without harming any plant. Nightingales and warblers destroy caterpillars by the thousands; so attract these insectivorous birds by placing troughs full of water and boxwood cribs lined with mealworms at their disposal in the quietest part of your vegetable garden, in the shade of the cribs; You'll be amply rewarded for these inexpensive acts of kindness, but don't let this stop you from destroying all caterpillar nests at winter pruning, and looking for the eggs where the branches meet, in the cracks in the bark. If, in spite of your diligent care, the caterpillars multiply, catch them in the evening, just as they are about to go to sleep in bundles on the branches, and kill them by spraying them with soap water; then wash the area flooded with this corrosive liquid with fresh water. Cabbage worms pierce through the leaves of this plant, often leaving only the ribs and veins; hunt them at night, by candlelight, or in the morning, before sunrise; they hide in the ground to protect themselves from the heat of the day. Pigs' droppings, used to fertilize hops, sometimes protect them from their dangerous enemy: the hop hepiracle. The tent caterpillar, the most common of the caterpillars, owes its name to the longitudinal lines of various colors on its back; it is destroyed in spring in its easy-to-find nest. Spare the larvae of the sycophantine beetle, and even encourage their development: these larvae devour hundreds of processionary caterpillars in their nests. The golden-tailed caterpillar is very common, very fertile, hairy, brown and has sixteen legs. It lives on all kinds of trees, sticking large white silky bundles to their branches. The willow caterpillar chops small fragments of wood and, mixing them with silk, forms a very hard, very solid shell that must be destroyed. The peacock and half-night peacock are very common in gardens around Paris; they have thick, broad, gray wings, with brownish patches and zigzagging reddish lines; a wide, brown eye, edged with black, black in the center, occupies the middle of each wing. The moth is about Om, 020 long, with a brown head and first segment, green or yellowish in the other parts; it rolls the leaves where it shelters during the day, taking advantage of the night to commit its frightening ravages on the stems, flowers and bunches of the vine. Eggs are found covered in a greenish mucilage on the leaf surface. Warm up the vines, put the stakes on the fire; give chase to the perfect insect, the moth that comes dazedly to burn itself at the small fires lit at night, from distance to distance. There is no known preservative against the olive leaf beetle, which is so harmful to wheat, rye and barley. It is useful to wash the bark of fruit trees over winter with a strong milk of lime, to destroy, at least in part, the larvae of apple and pear moths, which are responsible for wormy fruit. The olive tree's enemy is the chiron or Dacus oleœ larva. Carefully defend your greenhouses and frames against armadillos (woodlice), and especially against the common sowbugs so numerous in cellars and damp places; they cut seedlings and eat them to the core. Use the same method as described above for earwigs. Perennial vegetables and vegetables proper: 1° Artichokes, Asparagus; - 2° Peas, Beans, Lentils. FIRST SECTION. - ARTICHOKES, ASPARAGUS. ARTICHAUT is a plant with long, strong roots, native to Barbary and southern Europe (Compositae). Its most remarkable varieties are: L'ARTICHAUT DE PROVENCE, or artichoke without hay, with an elongated head; it is less fleshy but earlier than those we will discuss below; it fears frost and can only be grown successfully in our southern departments. - The A, gros camus de Bretagne, with its broad, flattened, slightly dark-green head, is fairly early, but not very fleshy; it thrives particularly in Touraine and most of the departments of central France. - A. gros vert de Laon, with pointed, divergent scales, is the best, most esteemed and most widely grown artichoke in the climate of Paris and the surrounding area. - The early purple A is small, but very delicate, and is best eaten raw, with peppers, rather than cooked. Artichokes are propagated by separating the offshoots or eyelets, usually in mid-April, from the old stumps; each plant can produce 6 to 12 offshoots; the two or three most beautiful are kept on the stump, and the others are broken off as close as possible to the root, so that they can be removed with their heel; shorten the leaves to the length of Om, 16, and plant in a chessboard of Om, 80 at a distance of 1 meter, in previously well loosened and smoked soil; if possible, manure should be spread throughout the artichoke patch. The soil should be well moistened and watered every two days until vegetation is vigorous; the first harvest will take place in autumn. Artichokes fear the rigors of winter. As frosts approach, cut the stems close to the roots, and deadhead each plant in dry weather, so that the soil does not retain moisture that could lead to rot. In addition, cover each clump with leaves or litter, which are easy to lift when the air is warm, and easy to pull down when the cold returns. Towards the end of March, litter and leaves should be removed, and the mounds on each plant destroyed; the levelled soil should be ploughed well, and only two or three of the strongest eyelets should remain on each clump. It's always a good idea, as a precaution, to uproot a few plants before the frosts, which, if planted in a healthy cellar or storeroom, will escape the ravages of the bad season and form a valuable reserve. However, if winter has destroyed all the plants, there's still sowing. This can be done in February or March, on a warm bed and under a frame, in pots or in potting soil. Sowing can also be done at the end of April, or at the beginning of May, in beds, separating two or three seeds by each earthen dimple. An Artichoke plant will only give a good yield for four years, so renew it in the third year. At the end of summer, you can stuff and blanch your old shoots like cardoons. Artichoke seed retains its germinative properties for five or six years; it 3 curdles milk without imparting a bad taste to the cheese. ASPERAGE (Liliaceae) is a perennial root vegetable native to many parts of France, especially the Var region, with a claw-like perennial root that produces new stems every year, which die off at the end of summer. There are two main varieties: A, green or common; grosse-violette or A, from Holland. Asparagus seed is usually sown in nurseries in October, or from mid-February to the end of March, either broadcast or, better still, in rays. Choose light but fertile soil, strong but well-amended with plenty of ash or silica sand; cover the seed with Om, 02 to Om, 03 of soil and compost; water, weed and hoe gently, lest you remove, along with the weeds, the nascent asparagus, at first as small as threads and barely visible. This plant can be used from the first year, although it is customary to leave it to grow for two years; if this practice is followed, the care given in the first year will be continued in the second. The important and difficult thing is to establish the plant permanently. Some gardeners dig pits about 1 metre deep, from which they remove all the soil and replace it with more fertile soil spread on a bed of plaster, coarse sand, broom and heather detritus, etc., with fertilizer: peat, muds and ditch and pond curings, etc. Other gardeners content themselves with planting the plant in a pit of their own. Other gardeners simply make well-sealed trenches Om, 30 to Om, 40 deep; others simply plough and smoke the bottom, then plant and sow flat. They also vary the layout and spacing of the plants; sometimes they combine up to three or four rows of Asparagus in a pit or bed Om, 90 to Om, 60 wide with ados; sometimes they plant in isolated rows equally spaced Om, 50 to 1m,60 apart, using these large intervals for other crops. Without in any way wishing to criticize these methods, which have good results (despite the teens declared here to be harmful by experience), we recommend proceeding in this way; after smoking your soil, draw your lines with a chalk line in the beds running from east to west, mark the width of each bed with a small mound of earth, then on this very bed, and without delay, establish your claw, which fears the dryness of prolonged exposure to the air and wants its hair to be spared with the greatest care; top-dress each bed; water, hoe and weed. Towards the end of October or in November, cut off the dry stems. For subsequent cultivation, take the soil you need for your annual autumn replenishments from the gaps that are becoming increasingly gullied as the soil rises around the asparagus; in spring, do a light ploughing or forking; every two or three years, fertilize with short manure at the beginning or end of winter. If the subsoil is ungrateful and always damp, it's best to plant flat, maintaining intervals of Om, 60 between beds. If, instead of planting claws, you sow on the spot, here's what you need to do: With your soil well prepared, well smoked, as we said above, your lines drawn with a chalk line, and your distances fixed, dig a ditch, where in the first case you would have raised a mound, and sow at Om, 03 one from the other 3 or 4 seeds that you will cover with compost. When the plant has sprouted, pull out the weakest plants and keep only the most vigorous; all the rest of the seedling cultivation is similar to the claw cultivation, but you won't get the products of your seedling until a year later. In Paris and the surrounding area, asparagus is harvested as soon as it emerges from the ground as a slightly green and purple shoot, about a decimeter long. Use a short knife to avoid damaging the central plateau of the claws. Never try to grow Asparagus after Asparagus itself; it would tire the soil too much; it can only grow in the same place after an interval of at least ten years. The best Asparagus to force are those that have been planted for at least five or six years. When you want to heat them, dig up and remove the soil from the paths separating the beds, replacing it with warm, trodden manure; refill the beds with the soil from the paths mixed with fresh manure, and cover them with the glass frames. This operation is carried out in December or March. From time to time, we remove the manure from inside the frames and cut off the shoots, known as white asparagus, because they have little color. New manure replaces exhausted manure; at night, straw mats or bedding protect the asparagus from cold and damp, and are removed during the day if it doesn't freeze. The plant is left to rest for a year, then heated the following year. A similar process is used to produce forced green asparagus. SECOND SECTION. - PEAS, BEANS, LENTILLES, Peas (Papilionaceae) are native to southern Europe. It requires light, healthy soil, and should not be grown for several years in a row if it is to be rich and beautiful. It can be sown in clumps or rays, in warm locations. Make rays about Om 20 apart, and in each hole, dug Om 35 apart, plant 5 or 6 peas. Until harvest, hoe, weed and rake large species, and pinch out early species at 3rd or 4th flower. Peas from warm climates can only be grown in the open air when the frost has stopped; however, St Catherine's Peas can be grown along walls exposed to midday sun, even when the cold is still to be feared. For early plants, build layers covered with Om, 25 to Om 30 of soil; sow in November, December, January; tarpaulins, layers or frames. Pinch off 3 or 4 flowers; replant the nursery plant when it has reached Om, 08 or Om, 10. As soon as your Peas have reached Om, 22 to Om 25, before flowering, lay them down at the bottom of the frame, gently placing laths on their stems to keep them flat for three or four days; once the laths have been removed, the heads straighten up and continue to grow, with only their lower part remaining flattened; this artificial curvature greatly enhances the fruiting of this vegetable. Here are some of the most important pea varieties. Dwarf shelled peas. The early dwarf is usually sown before winter, at the foot of south-facing walls; its distinctive feature is that it flowers from the 2nd or 3rd node. - P. nain de Hollande, smaller than the preceding variety and of average season, has small pods and grains, and can be planted in borders in ordinary soils; it can also be raised under chassis. P. très-nain à châssis barely reaches Om, 16 in height, it is very early; its pod contains five seeds. - P. gros nain tardif produces large, good-quality seeds; strong and stocky, it requires more space than the preceding varieties. - P. dain vert petit and P. dain vert de Prusse are two productive species. - P. Michaux de Hollande is sown at the end of February or the beginning of March; pinched, it does not need oars; it has difficulty with winter and does not grow in damp soils. - P. Michaux or Petit Pois de Paris, as early as it is good, is sown before winter at the foot of south-facing walls; pinched at 3 or 4 flowers, it is rowed in good soils; its sub-variety, P. de Ruelle, requires the same care. - P. de Clamart or carré fin gives a tight, sweet grain; it is sown in open fields without oars, for the late season; in gardens it must be rowed. - P. gros vert normand à grandes rames is a late bloomer, but produces excellent quality dry grain. - P. géant is extraordinarily large, but soft and not very tasty. - P. carré blanc is good and sweet, but too often loses its stalks and leaves. - P. fève, a large, late variety, has large, tender berries that are not very sweet. - P. vert de Noyon is content with very ordinary soil; it is semi-hardy and productive. - P. wrinkled, originally from England, is unrivalled for its large, wrinkled, sweet kernels, enclosed in a long, large, full pod. - The dwarf P. wrinkled white heath combines the precocity of P. Michaux with the qualities of P. wrinkled. P. turc has two varieties, one with a red flower, the other with a white flower; it is very heavy and yields a grain that is not highly esteemed. - P. with a volette pod produces a grayish, very large, floury, slightly hard grain, enclosed in a purple-purple pod. When cooked, it takes on the hue of roasted coffee; it tastes like a small marsh bean. Peas without parchment or mange-tout. P, the dwarf, early parchmentless pea from Holland, does very well in the open ground; it is also grown under frames. The white P, without parchment, with large pods or ram's horn, is late and produces a lot in good soils. - P. sans parchemin with half-stems, less late than the previous variety, has a less wide, but fuller pod. - The ordinary dwarf P. sans parchemin has small pods, but very numerous and very tender. - The giant P. sans parchemin, grown mainly around Paris, outshines all other species in terms of the width and size of its pods. "11 The P. sans parchemin with yellow pods is grown like the ordinary P. sans parchemin, whose qualities it shares and which supplied it. - P. sans parchemin with white pods, so called because of the whitish color of its pods, is of fairly good quality; it wants to be rowed. Peas, especially the earliest ones, are enemies of the bruchid beetle, whose female lays eggs in each barely-formed seed, so that its larvae can find abundant food there from birth. The ravages of this insect could perhaps be avoided, at least in part, by sowing at the beginning of May or in April; besides, peas pierced by the bruchid beetle are still good for sowing when the germ remains intact, which often happens. Ripe Peas, kept as seed grains, should not be shelled until they are ready to be planted; they retain their germinative properties for several years. CHICKEN PEAS. - A close relative of the pea, but of a different genus, this plant is sown in spring and harvested in autumn in the Paris climate, where it does not ripen completely. Its naturally slightly tough grain, which is difficult to digest, is used to make crouton purées. In warmer climates, it is sown in autumn and harvested in summer. The low, stocky chickpea doesn't need oars. For northern Europe, we rightly prefer the brown-grained red chickpea, which is earlier than the common chickpea. HARICOT (Papilionaceae) is native to India; it does not require as much care as Pea. It needs a soft, light, slightly fresh, well-smoked soil with a well-consumed fertilizer; sow the early species in clumps around April 20: five or six seeds per hole; hoe twice, re-sowing lightly in the second. For the other species, wait until the first half of May; June and July for the Swiss species and, in particular, for the early Dutch dwarf and flageolet, preferred by market gardeners around Paris. If your soil is clayey and compact, increase the quantity of fertilizer, delay sowing, and cover the seed very little. In strong soils, rather than sowing in clumps, sow in rows, grain by grain at about Om, 08 apart, with row spacing of Om, 30 to Om, 40. Mix a small quantity of wood, peat or coal ash with the soil. Green bean sowing continues through July and even into mid-August; if you sow them in well-sheltered beds when the year is not too dry, these late products will not ripen before the frosts arrive, but as green beans or as fresh shelled beans, they will amply compensate you for your trouble. With the help of frames, manure and stoves, you can have new green beans for most of the winter and throughout the spring, by sowing on a warm bed; you transplant the very young plant onto less warm beds, in clumps of three or four plants, at intervals of Om, 30; you need to aerate from time to time and especially at flowering time; wipe off the steam that attaches itself to the glass; finally, water abundantly. The preferred variety in this case is the Dutch dwarf bean, which yields after two and a half to three months of cultivation; it should be neither bedded nor topped. New varieties include : Bicolore d'Italie without parchment. - The early yellow H. of six weeks, the early dwarf H. Valentin. dwarf early without parchment. The runner bean is an ornamental plant known for its beautiful bunches of scarlet-red flowers; its turnip-sized root is pulled out and stored in fresh sand in the cellar for replanting in March; it flowers and produces seeds indefinitely. 4- Fava (Papilionaceae). - Beans are happy in any soil, but prefer cool, well-smoked soil, not exposed to full sun. It is sown in February, March and April, in rows or clumps, with 3 or 4 seeds in each hole, spaced about Om, 30-35 apart; at the second hoeing, they are resown to strengthen them; as soon as the flower has passed, the ends of the stems and branches must be pinched to hasten the formation of the lower pods. If the bean is removed to a quarter or half of its normal volume, the stems are cut to ground level, defended against drought and, in this way, a second harvest is obtained in autumn. Among the main varieties are: the Fêve des marais, native to Persia; the grosse F, ordinary; the F. the red dwarf, the earliest and most dwarf of all; the late green F., a very productive breed, originally from China; the F. à lonque cosse, early and well-filled. Beans kept in their pods retain their germinative powers for more than five years. Lentil (Papilionaceae). - Lentils are sown in March and April, preferably in dry, sandy soils, in rows or clumps. A variety known as Lentille à la Reine, L. rouge, has a small, reddish, rounded seed; it has a finer taste than the common L.. Some people, in keeping with ancient practices, sprout Lentils before cooking them, to increase their sweetness; Lentils should not be threshed until they are ready to be sown or eaten, in which case they keep well for two years. GESSE is sown like Peas and eaten mashed. 5. Raves, Raiforts, Salsify, Scorzonera, Beetroot, Potatoes, Jerusalem artichokes (1). CARROTS. - The carrot is a biennial, indigenous plant (Umbelliferae). It has a large number of varieties; we will mention only the main ones. Among the reds, the most esteemed are: the short red of Holland, the English red of Altringham; the common red lonque; the red demi-lonque or Meaux carrot. - Red carrots are generally tastier than yellow and white ones. The short red Dutch carrot is early and of good quality, preferable for autumn and early spring sowing. Gardeners near Paris have obtained a highly sought-after sub-variety for stews; Altringham red and Meaux red have a beautiful color and a very pleasant flavor. R. lonque commune and R. pâle (1) These last two plants are wrongly classified as root vegetables, since the edible parts of the Potato and Topinambur are tubers and not true roots. de Flandre keep better from one year to the next than all the other carrots. Among the yellows, only the short yellow and the lonque from Achicourt, near Arras, are grown in gardens, and both are of excellent quality. Among the white varieties, the most esteemed for their sweetness and ability to keep for a long time are: common white, Breteuil white, transparent white, green-collared white; violet, yellow inside and very sweet, but prone to bolting if sown early, and very difficult to keep in winter. - The Spanish violet carrot, almost black in color, or the Indian black carrot, is more an object of curiosity than a real vegetable. Carrots need deep, rich soil or open, soft soil, smoked in the year or, at the latest, in the autumn before sowing. Sowing begins in February, when there is no need to worry about spiders or snails; sowing in March, April, May and June is more exposed to the attacks of these two dreaded enemies. The early Carrot is sown in September, and spends the winter in place, producing new roots in spring and early summer. Sow by broadcasting, or in rows spaced 15-20 cm apart, about 40 to 50 grams of seeds per acre; cover with a rake; sometimes add a little potting soil; if the soil is light and sandy, pack it down with a roller. Carrot seeds take a long time to germinate and require diligent care. Weed them and thin them out to leave at least an Om.15 space between each plant. When a plant is missing, transplant it, paying particular attention to the root tips. The seed used should be two years old, well scrubbed and free of hairs. Short carrots can be harvested early; long carrots can withstand frosts if protected by a layer of sawdust or litter; it is always wise not to wait for the harsh winter to bring them in and select the seed-bearing roots. For forced cultivation, we prefer to sow the Bell Carrot under a frame and on a bed filled with 20 to 25 cent. of potting soil; we thin out the plant if it is too tight, and give it air when the sun spreads a little heat. For spider mites (Theridium), water with a quantity of soot; or with an infusion of corporal tobacco: 60 grams in 12 liters of boiling water, which must be allowed to cool completely before use. NAVET. - Turnip is biennial and indigenous (Cruciferae). It requires light, slightly moist soil; drought makes it hard, stringy and pungent; it is broadcast from late June to October; spring sowing is sometimes dared with two- or three-year-old seed. The quantity of seed varies with the season, averaging 15 to 20 grams per acre. We cover with a rake; we thin and weed; we wage war on flea beetles. In fact, the surest way to protect turnips from this enemy is to choose ploughed, well-smoked soil for sowing, so that the vegetation is quickly strong enough to resist this insect, which attacks budding leaves in particular. Among dry turnips, let's mention: N. Freneuse, the most esteemed for stews, is russet, small and half-long; N. Petit Berlin, the smallest of all; N. jaune long, which does well only in sandy, soft soil; N. de Meaux, blond, shaped like a tapering carrot: Among the tender turnips, we grow the following in particular: N. blanc-plat hâtif, rouge-plat hâtif, précoce; N. des Sablons, white, half-round, very flavorful; N. des Vertus, N. de Claire fontaine, gros long d'Alsace, rave du Limousin, N. rose du Palatinat, etc. Among the semi-tenders, N. Boule-d'Or, N. jaune de Hollande, N. jaune d'Ecosse, N. gris de Morigny, N. jaune de Finlande, are very good and strong enough to withstand the first frosts. Turnips should be harvested before the first frosts, which, without destroying them, alter their tissues, give them a bad taste and even make them indigestible. They can be stored in a cellar or in a healthy yard, covered with fresh sand. Turnip seeds retain their germinative properties for three or four years. PANAIS. - Parsnip is a native, biennial plant (Umbelliferae). Sow outdoors, preferably in February or March. It is grown in the same way as carrots. The plant should be thinned out when the young individuals are the size of your little finger. The seed retains its germinative properties for only one year. There is a variety of parsnip known as the round or Metz parsnip, shaped like a top; it is preferable for soils with little depth, where the common species would be difficult to grow. RADISH (Cruciferae). - Annual plant from China. The main varieties are: early white radish, ordinary white radish, half-long radish, half-pink radish, summer gray radish, ordinary pink radish, early pink radish, summer yellow radish, early yellow radish, large winter purple radish, Chinese winter pink radish, etc. New: White Russian radish; Large winter radish, to be sown in June; keeps very well all winter. Most radishes, especially small round radishes, can be sown all year round. In spring, Radish seed is sown alone or mixed with lettuce and onion seed for transplanting; in other seasons, full soil is sufficient, at noon in winter, with a little shade in summer. The BLACK RADISH is sown in spring and harvested in autumn; well grown, well watered, in light, cool soil, it becomes very large, but remains tough. RAVE commune and its varieties, R. violette hâtive, R. rose, R. tortillée du Mans, R. rouge lonque, have the same cultivation and uses as Radishes; soft soil. Wild RAIFORT, with its pungent flavor, multiplies from seeds sown in summer in cool, shady soil, or from root sections planted in spring. Its grated root is eaten as German mustard or capuchin mustard. Winter Radish can be grown in a frame, with the same care as for early plants: warming, hoeing, weeding, etc. SALSIFIS. SCORSONERA. SPANISH BARK BEETLE. - These plants belong to the Compositae family and are all obtained by the same method of cultivation. They are sown broadcast, or even in rays, in March, April or July and August; they require substantial, well-disturbed soil, ploughed thoroughly, smoked from the previous year, and frequent watering in dry spells; they are thinned out, hoeed and weeded. The roots are harvested in autumn and into spring; summer seedlings only produce edible roots the following year. Salsify and Scorzonera seeds retain their germinative properties for two years; they never fully germinate. Scolyme d'Espagne should be sown in rows spaced about Om, 45 apart; plants should be placed at a distance of Om, 25 from each other; like Salsify and Scorsonera, Scolyme d'Espagne tolerates frost fairly well; however, if winter is too severe, Salsify should be covered with dry litter. BETTERAVE (Chenopodea). - Biennial plant native to southern Europe; its vegetable varieties include: ordinary red beet, the most widely cultivated of all and the least difficult to grow in the right soil; bark beetroot with chagrined bark; round red beetroot, a little rough, the most difficult to grow in the right soil. red, round, a little rough, very dark red; petite rouge de Castelnaudary with spindle-shaped root, rightly praised for its fine, delicate flesh; B. de Bassano, with delicate white flesh, much sought-after for the table; jaune ordinaire, very sweet; jaune globe, almost spherical with white, tight, sweet flesh, with orange stripes. Beet seed is broadcast in spring, in soil well loosened by one or two deep, smoky ploughings from the previous year; if sown in a nursery, the plant is transplanted when finger-sized; water often, until well established; weed and hoe. Plants should be about Om, 40 or Om, 50 apart. The roots are pulled out around Saint Martin's Day (first half of November). Once the leaves have been cut off, the beets are placed in a healthy cellar; the seed carriers are placed in gauges and covered with litter. These seeds retain their germinative properties for 4 or 5 years. POTATOES (Solanaceae). - Native to America. Gardeners cultivate only the earliest species. They should be planted in March, with good exposure, in sandy, light, unsmoked soil, simply covering each hole with a handful of litter to prevent frost. The tubers are planted either whole, or cut into pieces, each of which should have one or two good eyes. If planted in winter, the holes should be made deeper, leaving 50-60 cm between plants. Weed or ridge. For forced cultivation, tubers are taken from the germinator (1), where they have been placed since the end of November; (1) The germinator is a glazed frame with a box which is placed on a warm bed, under a frame, straw mats and bedding at night, but light is allowed to penetrate throughout the day; without this precaution, shrivelling is to be feared; a mild, uniform temperature is sufficient. The layout for each frame is 4 rows and 6 plants per row; at the start of vegetation, the spaces between rows will be advantageously occupied by Radish, Sorrel, Small Lettuce and Tomato seeds; but as soon as the Potato stems have gained strength, they need all the land; moderate watering at first, then more abundant: air as soon as the season allows. We only force the Marjolin variety. Potato seedlings are not to be scorned. These include: Pomme de terre de Jeaucé, half-ta rdive, round, yellow-fleshed, very good; P. comice d'Amiens, early, round, yellow; P. Shaw, yellow, round; P. Segonzae, early P.
