TOPINAMBOUR or POIRE DE TERRE (Composites). - Native to Brazil. It is 2 to 2 m high, 60 cm with flowers resembling small suns, and tastes like an artichoke. It thrives without fertilizer in the poorest soils, where it can be planted in the first spring in medium-sized whole tubers, to be harvested in autumn. It thrives and perpetuates itself, so to speak, indefinitely at the foot of a warm wall; the potatoes placed close together are removed as soon as they have sprouted shoots and roots. With Topinambours planted very close together, you can form good hedges that will protect delicate cold or temperate greenhouse plants planted in the open during the summer from gales. Two varieties of Topinambours are grown in the same months as Potatoes: one purplish-red, the other white or yellowish; they are harvested only as and when needed for consumption. 4 Vegetables with edible bulbs: Onions (species and varieties), Leeks (species and varieties), Garlic, Chives, Shallots. ONION (Liliaceae). - This perennial plant, but treated as a biennial in cultivation, offers many varieties that are easily modified by the influence of soil and climate: the large white onion and the early white onion, both good and sweet; the bulbous onion with rocambole or Egyptian onion, whose stem bears bulbs joined at the head, or rocamboles, hence its name; the white onion from Nocera, eaten candied in vinegar as an hors-d'oeuvre with gherkins; the sulfur-colored Spanish onion. d'Espagne, sulfur-colored, with tender, pleasant flesh; O. cornede-bœuf with bulbs Om, 30 long; O. globe, beautiful, but rather difficult to preserve in its spherical form; O. potato, giving neither seeds nor rocamboles and multiplying by cloves; the O, pear, flesh a little coarse and of a very strong taste; the O. jaune ou blond des Vertus and the O. de Cambrat, both large, very good and long-lasting; the O. de Madère, pale red, very large and of a sweet flavor; etc.., etc. The white onions are delivered for consumption in summer; the others, which keep better, are eaten in autumn and winter. In the North, onion seedlings are left in place; in the South, they are sown in nurseries before winter and planted in squares in spring. Both methods have undeniable advantages; we prefer the first, but will briefly explain both. Sowing in place. - Choose substantial, light, smoky soil from the previous year; roll to pack well; broadcast at a rate of 100 to 120 grams per are, in February or March; lightly bury with the rake, put in a little potting soil and pack again with the roller; very moderate watering at first; weeding and thinning. In August and September, lay down the tops to slow down the drying process and speed up ripening. Leave the crop to dry for a few days on bare soil, then bring it in during dry weather. Transplanting. - You should sow very thickly in August or September, and transplant before winter for white onions; for other species, postpone transplanting until spring. Once you've made your rays with a hoe, place your onions about 10 cm apart, covering only the roots, but keeping your bedding ready to protect them from the cold; water and weed as described above for seedlings. Harvest in August and September. Many gardeners rightly praise and practice the Nouvellon method. Here's how it works. You sow very thickly in a nursery, in August, watering only as much as is necessary for the seed to rise; you then leave the plant to form and dry on the ground; each seed thus produces an Onion from the size of a pea to that of a hazelnut. These are reserves to be transplanted in rows in spring. Watering, weeding, etc. All onions have a tendency to bolt in winter, and to exhaust themselves through premature sprouting. So keep them in a place where it doesn't freeze, but where it's cold rather than hot. As soon as they have elongated, seed-bearing onions should be given sturdy supports to protect them from gales. Ripe seeds retain their germinative properties for more than two years; leave them in the head capsules, bundle them and hang them in a dry place until you're ready to use them. POIREAU OR PORREAU (Liliaceae). - Native to Switzerland. Biennial. Leeks come in several varieties, the main ones being: the ordinary long leek, very good for sowing in the open ground; the large short leek, suitable only for spring sowing or for layering in the Paris climate; the large short leek from Rouen, which in Normandy sometimes reaches arm's length; the yellow leek from Poitou; the monstrous leek from Carentan, very large and very rustic. Leeks are sown thickly in February, March and July, in substantial soil, preferably amended the previous autumn with horse or sheep manure, grape marc or charrée, and not with the fresh manure of horned animals; replant, as soon as the individual has reached the size of a feather pipe, in rays about Om, 12 deep and Om, 15 to Om, 16 apart, after cutting off the tips of the leaves and roots; frequent watering during droughts; weeding. Some gardeners cut the leaves of Leeks up to 5 or 6 times in summer, to give them strength. To strengthen Leeks, they are sown on beds and under frames in mid-December, with stoves and blankets; they are replanted in February and delivered for consumption in July. Any plants that grow too quickly in spring should be pulled out and replanted in deep trenches. The seed comes from new plantings, also made in March, and retains its germinative properties for two years running. Well-formed leeks do not freeze, but even mild cold destroys the young plant. GARLIC (Liliaceae). - Native to Sicily. Garlic, cultivated mainly in southern France, comes in four main varieties: common garlic, Spanish garlic, early pink garlic and Oriental garlic. This plant needs dry rather than damp soil, amended with horse manure for a year or two, and warm exposure. Garlic is propagated by planting cloves Om, 15 or Om, 20 apart, in beds or, better still, in borders; plant in February or March to harvest in spring; also plant in spring to harvest in August and September. As soon as the leaves and flower stalks appear, twist and tie them together to stop the sap flowing to the garlic bulbs or pods; don't pull up the plants until the tops are completely dry; leave them to dry out in the sun, tie in bundles, and hang in a dry place. If you let a few plants grow, you'll be able to produce seeds, albeit with difficulty in the Paris climate; but in the first year, they'll only produce bulblets for planting, and the harvest will be a year late. Propagation by separating the cloves is therefore quite rightly the only method used. CIBOULE (Liliaceae). - The Ciboule is grown as a biennial or as a perennial; its seed is sown in spring like that of the Leek. Transplant when very young, keeping a distance of Om, 16 between clumps; harvest throughout the summer; sow towards the end of July for autumn. It needs light, substantial soil. Some gardeners prefer to plant perennial Ciboule in borders like Garlic, letting it form large clumps that they split twice a year. In addition to Ciboule commune and C. vivace, we'd like to mention: Civette-Saint-Jacques and its varieties, propagated by cloves in spring or autumn, in borders. Ciboulette or Cirette indigène et vivace, smaller than Ciboule, propagated by separate cloves in March, planted in beds or more usually in borders; good soil, warm exposure, watered in summer. Keep Ciboule and Ciboulette seeds enclosed in their capsules; they are good for 2 or 3 years. ECHALOTE (Liliaceae). - Native to Palestine. Cultivated like garlic, at the same time, in soft, healthy soil, smoked the previous year. The bulbs are planted in rays 0b.15 apart, up to the surface of the earth, in February-March, for harvesting in July and August; or in October-November, for harvesting in June of the following year; the leaves are pulled off when dry; the Shallots are left to dry out in the sun for a few days; then they are stored in an attic, dry and protected from the cold. The two main varieties of shallot are Jersey shallot and Alençon shallot, which are larger than the common species, but less delicate and less easy to preserve. Edible leafy and flowering vegetables: Cabbage (its varieties), Kohlrabi, Turnip cabbage (varieties), Spinach, Tetragon, Sorrel, Celery, Celeriac, Cardoons, Watercress, Alen cress, Rhubarb, Parsley, Chervil, Tarragon, Purslane, Fennel, Nasturtium, Borage. Cabbage (Cruciferous). - Indigenous. Biennial, triennial and almost perennial (in some varieties). This vegetable requires a great deal of care, but it suffices to summarize here the general principles of its cultivation, which is simple and easy. First and foremost, it needs fresh, loose, slightly strong soil, with plenty of smoke and a little shade. Carefully weed your young plant, thin it out if it's too tight, and protect it from ticks, slugs and worms (see Insect pests). Place them permanently, in staggered rows, at distances of Om 50 for small species, and Om 70-80 for larger ones. If you're transplanting in dry weather, water gently. Seedlings are planted in the spring; their enemies are aphids, just as shaped cabbages have caterpillars. Cabbages, in general, resist cold well, and you will often be content to pull them up and leave them on the ground, root up; they would perish if rain and snow melted between their leaves and turned them into icicles; you can also, after removing their largest leaves, store them in a cellar; they are measured at the foot of a wall, at a good exposure, with litter and straw mats. To make the best use of time and land, some gardeners counter-plant, i.e. place cabbage plants between rows of potatoes or other early plants; once these have been removed, a square of cabbage is planted. Let's look at some of the main species or varieties, and the special care they require. First, let's establish five main series: cabbages, Milanese cabbages, green or headless cabbages, rooted or fleshy-stemmed cabbages, cauliflowers and broccoli. The main sub-varieties of cabbage are: C. d'York, with its small, elongated head, highly prized and very early. - C. cœur-de-bœuf, very good. - Large white cabus with the following varieties: C. de Saint-Denis or C. blanc de Bonneuil with large head; C. cabus d'Alsace, very quick to form head; C. conique de Poméranie with regularly conical head; large C. d'Allemagne which gives a huge head in good soil; C. de Hollande, medium size, fairly early; C. Joannet and C. Joannet tardïf; C. de Vaugirard or pommé d'hiver, which ripens at the end of winter; vert glacé, which withstands cold well, etc. - C. hâtif or pain-de-sucre with elongated apples, tender and sought-after. - Red cabbage, highly prized and highly prized in the north, where it is even eaten in salads. All large cabbages are used to make sauerkraut. York sprouts are sown in August-September for planting in October-November; sometimes they are transplanted in nurseries and only replanted in February-March. C. cabus are generally sown: 1° in February in beds, if antomne plants are to be replaced; 2° at the beginning of March, in beds; 3° during the same month, until April, in potting soil; 4° especially at the end of July and during August, until September 8th. August seedlings are replanted in nurseries from October to November, and planted out in November-December in dry soil, or in February-March in cold soil. Savoy or curly cabbage. Varieties include: Very early Savoy cabbage from Ulm, not very large, but very tasty and quick to pick. Pancalier from Touraine. - Joulin, gros Milan, etc. - C. de Milan des Vertus, remarkable for its size and beauty; it grows like cabbages, and goes well with them, especially in well-smoked soil. - Norwegian Savoy is winter-hardy. - Brussels sprouts produce small, tender, delicate apples in the leaf axils, which are picked as they grow. They can withstand severe frosts, and are enjoyed from autumn through to the end of winter by successive sowing. Savoy cabbages are generally sown in August-September, at a distance varying from Om, 50 to 1 meter, depending on the size of the variety. Kale is more of a fodder plant than a vegetable in the strict sense of the term; however, the vegetable garden admits the dwarf kale and its two sub-varieties, the variegated kale, and the prolific kale, whose curious foliage on the veins of their leaves even earns them a place among ornamental plants. Kale is generally sown from March to May and July to August, from Om,80 to 1 meter for the larger species; to Om 60 for the smaller ones. ~--En- Kohlrabi. - Although the leaves of this plant are not eaten, we thought it appropriate to group it with the other cabbages, since it is a true cabbage with a stem that swells above the ground and forms a sort of ball at the top; the leaves are planted on the sides of this ball. Kohlrabi tastes like cabbage and turnip, and can withstand fairly hard frosts. It and its varieties are sown in nurseries from the end of March to the end of May; the plant is placed in cool, well-smoked soil; it must be watered abundantly, otherwise the ball develops poorly and remains stringy. The root is kept in crates or gauges, like turnips, unless you prefer to leave it on the spot, since in the Paris climate, this cabbage winters very well outdoors. Other varieties include: C. rave with dissected leaves; its elegant leaves are reminiscent of those of the Artichoke; small but delicate apples. - C. navet or C. turneps, with its varieties (C. navet ordinaire, C. navet blane and C. navet blane à collet rouge), capable of withstanding the coldest weather; they are sown lightly, from late May to late June, without the trouble of transplanting. - C. rutabaga or C. navet jaune, with rounded, yellowish roots, can be sown in the field from late May to mid-July. Seedbeds should be sheltered with bedding and straw mats; the seed keeps for 5 to 6 years. Cauliflower. - Cauliflower needs soft, well-smoked soil, plenty of watering, and a temperature that's more humid than dry or too hot; that's why it does better in spring and autumn than in summer. Sow in September in potting soil, at midday; prick out in a nursery and protect from frost; plant out in March at a distance of about Om.60; it produces in June and July. Hard and semi-hard cauliflower are rightly preferred for sowing. You can also sow, but very lightly, on a warm bed, under a bell or in a frame, in February, for transplanting in March and at the beginning of April, with straw mats, and plant in the open ground at the end of April; you'll have produce in June-July. Choose hard or soft varieties for sowing. During the second half of June, sow the demidur in an earthen bed, in the shade and without transplanting; set out in July; water abundantly in the evening and morning; produce in October-November. Cauliflowers can be stored in a dry place, on shelves or hung in a cellar or a healthy cellar, throughout the winter. When transplanting cauliflowers, space them at intervals of about Om, 50 to Om, 60 in all directions. As soon as the heads start to form, cover them with a few pieces of their fresh leaves laid flat to protect them from direct contact with air and light. There are three main breeds of cauliflower: the tender or salomon, with a leaf that is plainer, straighter and less wide than that of the others, and a head that is quick to form, but not very compact; the durum, with its thick, short stem and tight, heavy, compact head, which often doesn't form at all; and the demi-dur, which is a combination of the salomon and durum varieties, and outperforms them all. The following are also grown as sub-varieties of the above: Lenormand cauliflower with very large apples, Roscoff (Brittany) cauliflower, Malta cauliflower, Cyprus cauliflower, Dutch cauliflower, etc. As seedbeds, we reserve cauliflower plants sown in autumn, wintered under a frame, with strong stems and firm, tight, clean, white apples. Broccoli. - This is a species of cauliflower with wavy leaves and larger dimensions; it is grown like cauliflower, but is more sensitive to the rigors of winter. Its main varieties are white, purple and early dwarf purple or Sicilian black cauliflower. Broccoli is sown in May-June: when cold weather arrives, the stalk is covered with bedding and harvested in early spring. England has supplied us with the B. mammouth, a late breed, but whose head is equal in volume to that of the largest cauliflowers. Broccoli can only be grown successfully in the South, from the Loire onwards. We'll just say a few words about: 1° Chinese cabbage or Pe-Tsaï, an intermediate between cabbage and turnip; it grows quickly and can be sown most of the year, but is more successful in summer and autumn than in spring; 2° Marinated cabbage, whose perennial root produces stems and shoots every year; it needs healthy, deep soil and, preferably, saline fertilizers. Multiplication by seed and cuttings. SPINACH (Chenopodea). - From northern Asia, annual. Spinach can be sown very lightly every month, from March to the end of October, in well-smoked, slightly cool soil; water quite frequently; summer seedlings should be sown in semi-shade, as heat causes this plant to bolt very quickly; round-seeded varieties are preferable for this purpose. Sometimes, in winter, spinach leaves appear frozen; soak them in cold water, then let them dry out in the air, on very dry boards. The rays should be spaced Om, 16 apart. The beaten seed, as soon as it matures, can be kept for several years; we use the two-year seed for spring and autumn sowings. Male plants should be removed as soon as they have finished flowering. The main varieties are: thorny-seeded E., common E., English E., Dutch E., Flanders E., Esquermes E., the last three with smooth seeds. E. monstrueux de Viroflay, highly recommendable. TETRAGON, from New Zealand, quite common now in our gardens, replaces, at least during the Summer, Spinach, of which it has the color and taste. Sow it in beds or in holes filled with potting soil and spaced om, 50 apart; a single plant can cover an area of one square meter, watering frequently during the summer. Tetragonia's branch tips and leaves are eaten. CLOVER (Polygonaceae). - Perennial, common in meadows. Sorrel can be propagated by sowing in rows, in spring and autumn, in any soil and at any exposure; frosts slow its growth, but without destroying it or even attacking its leaves; however, it is wise to cover it with straw or dry litter. Sorrel can also be propagated by dividing clumps in spring and autumn, although sowing is still necessary from time to time to maintain the properties of each species. - Varieties: - Belleville sorrel, less acidic than common sorrel, with broader leaves, widely cultivated in the Paris area; - Virgin sorrel, very delicate, with blonder leaves, broader than those of common sorrel; it can be prevented from seeding, its male and female flowers are on separate stems; it is propagated by shattering; - Slap-leaved sorrel, still not very widespread; - Snow sorrel grows even under the snow. Sorrel seeds retain their germinative properties for 3 years. CELERY (Umbelliferae). - Native, biennial. Requires naturally cool soil, or frequent watering. It is sown from January to April, on a bed or under a cloche and under a frame; in the open ground, from April onwards in a sheltered position, in rows separated by sufficient intervals to allow the soil necessary for buttages to be taken up. This operation is carried out three or four times before heavy frosts; as the plants lengthen, they are tied up; the soil is first covered up to the first tie, then eight days later up to the second, and eight days later up to the third; only the tips of the leaves remain uncovered. In gique and northern France, gardeners transplant Celery stalks to the bottom of a ditch, bring 6. the soil up on either side and mound. With plenty of potting soil and a good bedding, some Celery can be left in the vegetable garden; the rest is brought into the vegetable greenhouse, mounded with sand or light earth, and blanched according to consumption needs; some is kept in reserve in gauges; the cold is fatal to Celery. In our northern departments, we are obliged to overwinter seedlings under frames, whereas in the south of France, we simply transplant them to a warm location with a cover. The seed retains its germinative properties for two or three years; the newest are the best. Main varieties: Céleri court hâtif, C. plein blanc, C. nain frisé, C. violet de Tours, C. creux, C. à couper, the last two are non-stopping. CELERI-RAVE (1), still little known and not widely grown, has an aromatic taste, which is not to everyone's taste; it is nevertheless an excellent vegetable; it needs deep, naturally cool or almost continuously watered soil. Seedlings are treated in the same way as other species. Plant at a distance of Om, 50; surround the beds, if possible, with gutters that retain water and thus provide Celery with the perpetual moisture it craves. This is the German method. Look for fibrous roots and cheyelu. Celery root plants are tucked in and surrounded in winter by sand or light earth; a few plants left outside in healthy soil brave the cold without the help of mats or bedding. CARDON (Compositae). - Barbary, Biennial. The various varieties of Cardoon are sown in May, in the very place where they are to grow to their full potential, as they do not tolerate transplanting. (1) The root is the only part of the celeriac plant that is eaten; nevertheless, we have not thought it necessary to separate this plant from the others listed in this chapter under the heading of edible-leaf plants. You'll make holes spaced Om, 80 to 1 meter apart in all directions, well-soiled and in each of which you'll place two or three seeds, reserving yourself to leave only the most beautiful plant afterwards; you'll treat these plants like those of Artichokes, but you'll need to water them more often when the leaves have reached 1m,50 to 2 meters; around mid-June, gather them together with wicker or straw ties, cover them with a straw shirt, and protect the base from the wind by a small ridge Om 06 high, to prevent them from shrivelling; don't forget that the ribs must be eaten as soon as they are white, otherwise they will rot. So, at the end of autumn, lift your cardoons intended for winter canning, plant them in fresh sand in a dry, frost-free place, and only stuff them as and when they are needed for consumption. Don't bind your seedbeds, simply stub them out like those for Artichokes; they'll flower the following summer and give you seed that keeps for five or six years. Varieties : C. de Tours, with full, thick ribs, wrongly preferred to the following; - C. inerme, almost as full as the C. de Tours; - C. d'Espagne, with hollow or half-hollow ribs; - C. à côtes rouges, very wide and very full; - C. Puvis, remarkable for its volume. Puvis, remarkable for its volume, wide and half-full ribs; many gardeners rightly proclaim it the best of the Cardons; it is certainly worth the Tours variety, with its dangerous spines; it has few prickles, sometimes none at all. CRESSON de fontaine (Crucifers). - Perennial, native. Watercress requires a trickle of running water or tubs half-filled with soil, and almost continuously covered with a sheet of water. Multiply with seeds or roots. Large artificial watercress beds can also be created when the soil lends itself to this type of cultivation. Varieties: C. des prés is sown in spring in moist soil; same properties, same care as for Cresson de fontaine. C. de terre is sown in damp, light soil, in spring, in rows; it also replaces Cresson de fontaine. CESSON ALÉNOIS Ou PASSERAGE CULTIVÉ (Crucifers). - Annual, from Persia. This plant owes its name to the pungent, acrid flavor of its leaves, which is quite similar to that of watercress. Passerage is short-lived and quick to bolt; it needs warm, dry soil with southern exposure; in summer, seedlings are renewed every two weeks. Three varieties: C. alénois frisé, C. à larges feuilles and C. doré. An excellent addition to early spring salads, which are always a little bland; very healthy. Cresson alénois is worthless once grown. - Water frequently in summer. RHUBARBE (Polygonaceae). - From Asia. Rhubarb can be propagated from seed, sown as soon as it matures in March, in a bed of light soil, to be planted after the first year in deep, healthy soil, with a distance of about 1.30 m between plants. They can also be propagated by separating clumps; water frequently. The best species are: Rhubarb ondulée, Rhubarb australe or Népaul, Rhubarb groseille, preferable to the two previous ones. We know that the English eat a lot of Rhubarb for their pies. Tartreum is just one variety of wavy Rhubarb. PARSLEY (Umbelliferae). - Parsley is one of the most widely used seasonings. The seeds of common parsley take a long time to germinate; they should be sown early in the spring, or, in large quantities, as early as February, in well loosened soil; the gutters should be Om, 35 apart, so that the soil can be easily hoeed in these intervals and weeded. In winter, Parsley is sold by weight and at a high price, so Paris market gardeners transplant a certain quantity of Parsley to the foot of a wall, to the south, with glass frames, as a guarantee against frost. Parsley does not flower or set seed until the third year, but then it dies. Some people, afraid of confusing it with hemlock, prefer to grow parsley with crisp leaves. Cultivated parsley varieties are: P. commun, P. frisé, P. nain très-frisé; S E ~ S O 7 M 8 Fig. 57. - Parsley. The last two are not constant and often revert to common parsley; the only truly distinct species is parsley with a large fleshy root, much sought-after in Belgium and Holland as a seasoning for fish; we use it little in France. CERFEUIL (Umbelliferae). - Native and annual. Chervil is sown in March, at the foot of a wall, in a warm spot; in June, in the north and in the shade, and in any spot between the end of March and September. The seed ripens within the year and keeps for three years. Varieties: C. frisé, C. musqué or d'Espagne, aniseed-flavored. Multiply by sowing in spring and separating plants. - Tuberous or bulbous C., sow from September to December, in soft, carefully weeded soil. - M M 2 7a E 4 2 E les~ Fig. 38 - Chervil. Q 2 AM E - C. de Prescott (from Russia), with edible root, widely used for stuffing turkeys, geese, etc., sown at the end of April; harvested at the end of August; stored in a dry place until March. Chervil should always be carefully peeled to avoid leaving behind the small hemlock (Ethusa cinapium), which you can recognize by the darker green and sharper divisions of its leaves. Large Hemlock is easy to recognize by its stems dotted with livid spots reminiscent of snake skin, its repulsive odor, its very bitter taste and the pungency of all its parts; Its leaves resemble those of Wild Chervil; they are twice and thrice winged, large and a little soft; the leaflets are pinnatifid, acute and blackish-green; the flowers are white, arranged in very open umbels, with 3 9 4° 4 2l 2 Fig. 29 - Small hemlock. several leaflets. POURPIER (Portulaceae). - Native to southern France, (1) Hemlock poisoning is treated with plant acids, vinegar, lemon juice, and promptly administered purgatives. annual. Once eaten as a salad, this plant is now eaten stewed. It is sweet and refreshing. It is sown in the open ground from May throughout the summer. In both cases, it's important to remember that the plant spreads quickly over the whole ground, so you need to be careful with the seed. Frequent potting. FENNEL (Umbelliferae). - Native to the southern regions of Europe, and much sought-after by the Italians, who consume huge quantities, it is not widely grown around Paris. It is sown from February-March in light, sandy, well-amended soil; broadcast or in nurseries; in the latter case, replanted: keeping a distance of about Om, 20 between each plant. Hoeing, weeding and watering. Fennel is very hot, so don't eat too much of it. It can be used to garnish stews, macaroni, etc., etc. CAPUCIN (Tropéolées). - Native to South America. We will only discuss the edible varieties here. The large one and its brown-flowered variety, the small one whose barely-formed flowers and still-green seeds are candied and used in place of capers; the fresh flowers are used to season salads. Sown in March along trellises and arbors, Nasturtiums bloom all summer long. BOURRACHE (Borraginae). - Native, annual. Sow in the open, in spring and autumn; its pretty blue flowers adorn salads like Nasturtium flowers; its leaves are a good sudorific. No cultivation care is required, just prevent Borage from invading the garden with its seeds. Salads: Spring, summer and winter lettuces, Roman lettuces, Chicory, Scarole, Wild chicory, Chicory with Nasturtium beard, Lamb's lettuce, Rapunzel LAITUES (Composites). - From Asia. All the many varieties of lettuce produced by cultivation can be grouped into two general divisions: 1° Head lettuces; 2° Roman lettuces or chicory. Among the lettuces in the first division, the earliest of all are called spring lettuces; the most voluminous and least prone to bolting are called summer lettuces; and those treated as biennials from autumn onwards, to be eaten in the spring of the following year, are called winter lettuces. This division also includes non-heading lettuces for cutting. In general, lettuces grow quickly and set with difficulty in soil that is too light, too hot and too dry; they grow extremely slowly in strong, cold soil. The main spring lettuces are: L. crêpe and L. gottes or gau, which are of little value, hold poorly, i.e. are far too quick to bolt before they have formed their heads or almost immediately afterwards, but are very early; this is their only merit. One variety, the -~~~] 7es 1* gotte à cordon rouge (red-stringed), can be grown on a coucne or in the open on a hillside, in the south, from the first days of spring. The dauphine variety, highly esteemed in England, is the best of the spring lettuces. The main summer lettuces are: L. blonde de Versailles, which is very delicate; L. blonde laesseuse, L. chou or L. de Batavia, L. de Gênes, L. rousse de Hollande, etc. L. chou is a very good apple, with a high yield. In many countries, this plant is grown only for pigs, which are very fond of it. In mediocre soils, you can plant the blonde pa vesseuse and the rousse de Hollande, which are very hardy and succeed on their own when left to their natural vegetation. The following are grown as winter lettuces: Passion lettuce, morine, petite crêpe and black lettuce, all of which are not very delicate in taste, but are very hardy and can overwinter in the garden if planted in a good spot. They are especially suited to the forced cultivation we'll be talking about later. Market gardeners call lettuces "cuttings", not particular species, but plants of Pancake or Gotti lettuces, sown very thickly: they cut them off at the root collar as soon as the fourth leaf appears and deliver them for consumption; Chicory and Spinach lettuces have this particular destination. Among the true novelties, we admit only the large white winter lettuce, which is easy to grow. Romaine lettuces include even more varieties and sub-varieties than round lettuces. We'll just mention the main ones: the early spring and summer green, the summer market garden green, the market garden grey, the largest known; the winter red, fairly insensitive to cold; the thick-leaf alphange, the blonde marai chère, the blonde de Brunoy, very large and quite similar to the alphange, needing, like it, to be tied. All are good and advantageous, but you'll rightly prefer the green summer romaine and the grey summer and late-season romaine, to which you can even add the tender, delicate, very large artichoke-leaf romaine, capable of withstanding the first white frosts. All Romaines are easily capped, i.e. they have a tendency to fold the tops of their leaves over each other; you can encourage this natural tendency by tying the leaves together at mid-height with a wet straw tie. Lettuce seed (whatever the species) should be sown in light rather than heavy soil, broadcast, very light, barely covering each other. Round-headed lettuces do not require transplanting, as they pump very well in place. Plant in staggered rows at distances varying from Om.40 to Om.20 between each plant, depending on the size of the individual plants; don't pack the soil too tightly so that the roots of your Lettuces sink easily into the soil, and mulch the beds so that the water from your watering doesn't make the soil too compact. Sow spring lettuces in March for transplanting in April, and summer lettuces from April 15 to the end of July, so that they follow one another uninterruptedly throughout the summer and provide you with good plants for transplanting; Winter lettuces in three or four different sowings, from August 15 to September 15, so that you can transplant them before All Saints' Day and leave them in place over winter with mulch and litter; lettuces for cutting, which cannot be transplanted, can be sown on a bed and under a frame in January; on a dull bed in the economic tarpaulin from mid-December, when winter is not harsh. When spring comes, you'll be able to start sowing outdoors again on a terra-cotta bed, and continue fortnight after fortnight throughout the summer. Watering and weeding. Lettuce's enemies are grubs. Romaine lettuces are grown in much the same way as round lettuces; the Romaine maraîchère plant is raised under a bell or under a frame, for forcing or transplanting in the open air, so that it can be delivered for consumption as early as the first spring. The plant is transplanted in rows, in a checkerboard pattern about Om, 04 apart; it can be partially planted in the open air from February to April, and sometimes as early as the end of December. Beware of frost and sunburn. For the forced cultivation practiced on such a large scale around Paris, you sow the seed of early lettuces under cloches, on an earthen bed, at noon, giving your plant as little air as possible (étouffée cultivation); you transplant under other cloches (at a rate of five individuals per cloche), then on beds, leaving only the necessary space between the surface of your bed and the glass, as your lettuces must not become large; You'll need to maintain a moderate but constant heat by using manure stoves, or even better, thermosiphon heaters. Be sure to wipe the steam condensed on the inside walls of your frames; the mist that falls on the leaves when they're cold causes stains. Set aside the best Lettuces of each variety for seedbeds, without tying them up; keep birds out in general, and goldfinches in particular, by means of small mirrors attached by strings to slightly inclined sticks, or by other scarecrows made of rags, etc. Lettuce seed retains its reproductive properties for three or four years; for your seedlings, you should preferably take the two- or three-year-old seed; the plant it provides grows more slowly than that which would come from the previous year's seed. CHICORÉE (Composites). - Indigenous and perennial. Chicory's bitterness must be forgiven, in view of the other qualities of this salad, the healthiest of all. It is very sensitive to cold, and can only be grown outdoors from April onwards. Bury little, if any, of the seed, which you should sow on a well-soiled bed. When planting, keep a distance of about Om 30-32 between each plant in all directions; give Chicory the same care as Lettuce until its leaves, spread out in a circle, meet on top of each other; bind them to blanch them. From April onwards, seedlings are renewed month by month and planted until September; if autumn is fine, you'll have easy-to-keep reserves in the cellar for winter supplies. Beware of the slightest frost. Gardeners who use forced cultivation sow curly chicory seed on a warm bed, under a frame, in February-March, and even sometimes in January, for the primeur, on a very warm bed; they always transplant on a very warm bed, leaving intervals of Om 20 in all directions. The main varieties of chicory are: Chicorée d'été or Chicorée d'Italie, highly sought-after for the early seasons, and even for autumn, as it fills up quickly and well; C. de Meaux, which is prone to bolting if sown before June and fills out slowly; Rouennaise or corne-de-cerf, with a full, yellow, tender heart; toujours blanche, a semi-full-grown variety especially suited to the Midi climate; Scarole or Escarole, or Endive, which is grown like ordinary curly chicory, but without forcing it; At the end of autumn, it is blanched on the spot by laying the leaves down at their ends and holding them in this position with a weight of soil proportionate to their strength; it is harvested as soon as the weather softens. Wild Chicory or Coffee Chicory grows in uncultivated areas, along roadsides; you can sow the seeds very abundantly, and pick the smallest leaves as soon as they appear, to eat in salads, alone or mixed with Lamb's lettuce or Lettuce. Market gardeners use wild chicory to make the salad known in Paris as Barbe-de-capucin. In spring, they sow the Scarole seed, tightly packed in poor sandy soils; in November, they uproot the plant, and after removing all the leaves except the emerging central leaf, they entrust it, in bunches about Om, 20 in diameter, to layers of hot manure prepared in advance in cellars, in vast abandoned quarries where neither outside air nor light reaches. New: Wild Chicory with a large root, very happily cultivated in the Brussels area; it makes a good Capuchin Beard. Chicory seed retains its germinative properties for five or six years; the old variety is preferred, as it produces plants that are less prone to climbing. MACHE, BOURSETTE, DOUCETTE, etc. (Valerianaceae). - Annual, native. Three varieties are available: Mâche commune, M. ronde, M. d'Italie or M. régence. Lamb's lettuce is sown from August to the end of October, broadcast, in loose soil, smoked from the previous year; for example, on beds that are still available after having produced several vegetable garden products; it is lightly covered and watered in dry weather; the most advanced Lamb's lettuce plants are picked as and when needed for consumption. Since the seed falls out of its own accord as soon as it is ripe, the seedstocks should be removed before they are fully ripe, and hung up in a healthy but not too dry place. The seed retains its germinative properties for at least five or six years. Lamb's lettuce is considered best when it has withstood frost once or twice. Lamb's lettuce that grows wild on its own in the harvest is called wheat or hare's ear lamb's lettuce. New: lettuce-leafed M., a beautiful white-green; a recommendable and easy-to-cultivate plant. RAIPONCE (Campanulaceae). - Campanula raiponce grows naturally in woods, along hedges; its leaves and roots are edible. Sow in midsummer, in light, well-soiled soil, barely covering it with the tines of a rake; if you forget to water, the root becomes so hard that it ceases to be edible. Wild Rapunzel has a finer, more delicate taste than cultivated Rapunzel. ε παιι πωσ Edible fruit plants: Strawberry (species and varieties), remontant strawberry plants, non-remontant strawberry plants, biferous highbush strawberry; Pineapples; Melons, Cantaloupes, Embroidered melons, Smooth-skinned melons, Watermelons, Cucumbers, Gherkins, Squash; Tomatoes, Aubergines, Peppers. STRAWBERRY (Rosaceae). - Perennial. The Strawberry, which is not very fussy about the choice of soil, is the first in our climate to give us its delicious fruit, and it gives us this fruit for longer than any other plant. It braves the most rigorous cold, even those of Siberia and Greenland, which last nine or ten months; nevertheless, it prefers substantial, slightly cool soil. All strawberry plants, except F. buisson and F. Gaillon, send around them, in all directions, nets or runners furnished with knots from distance to distance; these knots take root in their turn and give other nets; let them take free flight in August-September, if you want the plant by this means; otherwise cut them off or rather prevent them from developing, as they weaken the mother plants. F. buisson and F. Gaillon can be propagated by dividing clumps in spring and autumn, taking care that each clump retains a few roots. 7. Strawberry seeds should only be sown when the aim is to regenerate or maintain good species unaltered, or to create new varieties; this is how we have obtained all these large-fruited strawberry varieties of American origin. To sow, take the best ripe strawberries, crush them in water to separate the seeds, then place them in light, soft, well-divided, terra-cotta soil. Cover with Om, 001 sifted potting soil or heather; Warm exposure, but sheltered from the sun and strong winds, by means of straw mats; frequent watering; the seedling takes about fifteen days to emerge; at two months, it can be transplanted in situ or in a nursery. If you don't want to sow until the following spring, leave the seed to dry out and store it in a dry place. Strawberry plants are planted in borders or beds, with a distance of Om, 30 to Om, 40 between each plant, in soil that is neither clayey nor too compact, well tilled, well smoked and free of bindweed roots and other perennials; weeding, hoeing and watering are carried out; a thick mulch will protect the fruit from contact with bare soil, on which it would become dirty, and will prevent many weeds from reappearing. Renew the plant every two or three years if you want to keep your harvests good and plentiful. In the first half of September, we pull up wild strawberry plants in the woods. Strawberries are usually planted around mid-September. Strawberry plants with very large fruit require a spacing of Om, 35 to Om, 40 in all directions; small and medium-sized varieties are happy with spacing of Om, 25 to Om, 30. Watering should be frequent during the hot season; you should stop when the first white frosts are approaching. Strawberry plants have an enemy in white grubs, which you can prevent if, before planting, you line the bottom of the soil with a thick, well-trampled bed of carpenter's shavings or chestnut leaves; then, with the soil back in place, proceed as usual. Warm cattle urine, spread over the strawberry field, kills the cricket mole, one of the strawberry's most formidable enemies. For forced cultivation, use the nets produced in July by the young Strawberry plants of the Four Seasons, the Princess Royal and the Count of Paris, planted in March of the same year, and raise them in a nursery in part-shade until the beginning of September; Then you plant three plants in each of the pots prepared in advance, with good, light, substantial soil. You then arrange these pots (about forty) in a frame that's not too deep, so that your Strawberry plants are at most a few centimetres from the glass. In December, you will successively force your pots by transporting them either to the pineapple greenhouse, or under a frame, in tannin or warm bedding manure, always as close as possible to the glass, as they need light. Strawberry plants left in the open ground, in a suitable position, can also be harvested much more quickly if they are sheltered (straw mats, frames). Strawberries that produce several harvests in the same year are known as remontant strawberries. The two main varieties are The F. des Alpes, or four-season or all-month variety, is the best of the remontant strawberry plants, indeed of all the strawberry plants; its fruit is almost as delicate as that of the F. des bois, and can be harvested from April until the frosts, in the open ground, and during the winter in frames and hot greenhouses. It is sometimes necessary to renew it by sowing, as it degenerates quite easily; it offers the following sub-varieties: F. with white fruits, Gilbert's black with strongly colored fruits, les quatre saisons meudonnaises. F. buisson de Gaillon produces fruit similar to that of F. des quatre saisons and requires the same care in cultivation. It flowers a little later in the spring. It is usually used to garnish flowerbeds along driveways; in fact, as it has no netting, it is very suitable for this purpose. It needs to be renewed often, however, as overcrowded clumps choke, wither away in the middle and stop producing. A light mulch or moss protects F. Gaillon from sunburn and direct contact of the fruit with the ground. Distance between plants, Om, 30. White-fruited sub-variety, very good, like Gaillon proper, it produces more in the second season and autumn than in spring. Non-remontant F. are those that provide only one crop each year; all attempts to make large-fruited Strawberries remontant have failed. F. des boïs: round or elongated fruit, small but excellent. - F. de Montreuil, the largest and most productive of the F. des bois varieties, requires a dry, sandy site for planting, and fresh, rich soil for permanent transplanting. - Caprons, with their lightly-colored, slightly musky fruit, have their male and female flowers on separate plants: the male plants, which are naturally sterile, therefore occupy a precious place in the vegetable garden, but to no avail. - Pineapple F. have a bland, musky flavor that is not to many people's taste; their stalks swell and thicken as the fruit grows. - American F. have provided, and continue to provide, many varieties through hybrid crosses and seedlings; their rounded fruits are sweet rather than acidic, while their conical fruits are acidic rather than sweet. Among the American species most worthy of a place in the vegetable garden, we'd like to mention: Virginte scarlet, with high, bluish-green foliage, small, round fruit, pierced with deep cavities, very early; it bears from the end of May to the end of June. American scarlet, very productive; oblong, dark-red fruit, pink flesh. F. du Chili, very large fruit; requires substantial soil and southern exposure. - F. svperbe de Wilmot, very beautiful fruit, up to Om, 22 in circumference. Goliath, fruit almost as large as Wilmot. The F. queen Victoria, very beautiful, large fruit, dark red, glossy, with a fine, fragrant taste. British queen, very productive, the best of the American varieties, with rounded fruit. F. haut-bois is the name given to a strawberry plant remarkable for the height and elegance of its flowering stems, and for its fruit, which has a vinous flavor. It is biferous, meaning that, without being very remontant, it flowers again in autumn and gives a second harvest almost as abundant as the first. As large strawberries only produce once a year, the deyra gardener must grow several varieties, ripening at successive times over a two-month period, in the following order: First fortnight. Princesse Royale, Black Prince de Cuthill, Keen's seedling. Second fortnight. Comte de Paris, Caroline, Pineapple. Third fortnight. F. Elton, Duchesse de Treviso, Superb Wilmot, Queen Victoria. Fourth fortnight. British queen, Barne's large White, F. du Chili. ANANAS (Bromeliads). - From South America. Pineapples are grown exclusively in France, etc., under forced cultivation. The first two methods are almost always used; the third is used to obtain new varieties. Carnations and crowns are treated in the same way as cuttings from succulents; you don't plant them at the very moment you detach them, but let them dry out in the air, leaving the heel cut. Complete cultivation takes eighteen months to two years. You can start at any time. If you have planted your carnations at the beginning of November, in pots filled with heather soil and immersed in a layer that is always kept very warm, 20° centigrade at night and 25° centigrade during the day, you will wait until spring to put up a new, very warm layer, where the pineapples will quickly develop their roots; Ten or twelve hours later, they should be cut into pots larger than the first, filled with a mixture of equal parts of potting soil, heather soil and good garden soil. These pots should be placed in the tannage of a greenhouse, as close as possible to the glass. Watering and sprinkling from time to time; cleaning foliage with a damp cloth or sponge; high heat up to 35 and 40 degrees; strong fumigation with tobacco against parasitic insects, lice, cochineal insects and so on. Towards the end of summer, the plants are made or reeds; many gardeners, as soon as the flowering is over and the fruit has formed, subject the pineapple roots to an amputation almost as severe as that mentioned above. Replace each individual plant in a pot about Om.20 wide, immersed in new tannin, and make do with a temperature of -30°-32°. Distance between each plant, 0m,60. In recent years, many people have adopted the English method, which has always worked for us and which we believe is at least as good as the previous one. It consists in planting rooted Pineapples, after their first winter, in a tarpaulin soil Om, 60-80 deep, well heated by thermosiphon pipes; they are not transplanted or amputated later, distance between each foot, Om, 60. Frequent watering. Pineapple seeds, sown in spring in heather soil, sprout fairly quickly, but the plant only bears fruit after five years. Main varieties: A, providence and Enville, very early; Cayenne and its varieties: - A. Otaïti and A. de la Jamaique, very late; A. Comte de Paris, easy to grow; A. de la Martinique; A. Charlotte Rothschild; Princesse de Russie; Enville Pellevilain; Enville Mme Gonthier, etc. MELON (Cucurbitaceae). - Native to Asia. The first sowings are done in January, in pots of Om, 11 diameter outside, which you will bury in layers covered with frame and straw mats; at the rate of one seed for each pot; you can also sow in full compost, in small gullies of Om, 04 deep, leaving between each seed a dista nce of Om 08; or, finally, in terrines which you will entrust similarly to a warm layer. You'll need to provide air at the most favorable times of the day; you'll need to clear the glass of the fog that hangs on the inside walls. One month later, you'll set out, still on a bed, at a rate of two or three plants per panel, taking care to press each plant down to the cotyledons. When the plant has four leaves, you top it to encourage the growth of buds in the leaf axils; you prune the branches at the sixth or seventh leaf, and when there is a fruit, you pinch an eye above it. Bell Melons are sown in March-April, on a bed, under a frame, and are transplanted in clods and rows, at an average distance of Om, 80 to Om, 85, with a shaded bell, for a few days, on each plant until it has recovered well. Give air and light from time to time. Prune as above. In the South of France, sow four or five seeds in piles of manure, covered with soil. Choose the most beautiful plants as soon as they have emerged, and sacrifice all the others; the fruit obtained in this way is not very tasty. Don't grow Melons, Cucumbers, Potzrons, etc. too close together. The fertilizing dust, spreading in all directions, profoundly alters the species, giving you pumpkin melons with an unpleasant taste. Melon is sown in the open air, from May 10 to 20, on a bed of half-decomposed manure, inclined to the south, with potting soil mixed with good ordinary soil; there's no need to transplant; from time to time, spread a few handfuls of pigeon-hole around the melon plants, and water. The seed should only be harvested from fully ripened fruit, dried thoroughly and kept away from humidity; prefer old seeds to young ones. The best of all melons are Cantaloupes, and the best of all Cantaloupes are: the orange Cantaloupe, small, round, ribbed, with slightly firm red flesh; the earliest of all melons; consequently the most widely used early. Noir des Carmes, with round, green-black fruit, with ribs that are not very pronounced, but without scabs; red, vinous, very good flesh; very early under glass. - Prescott, the most esteemed in Paris; with more or less scabby ribs; shades varying from green to silver; small Prescott, with black or brown background, crown with protruding point in the center of the crown; - C. d'Alger, with red flesh; - C. de Hollande, etc. - M. maraîcher brodé. New: cantaloup d'Epinal; comes in at around 2 kilograms; fine, flavorful, beautifully colored flesh. For seedlings in the field, use preferably this last melon, the M. de Honfleur, the M. sucrin de Tours, the M. sucré vert d'Angers. In the south of France, we mainly grow: Melon de Malte, with white, melting, sweet flesh; early; medium size. - M. de Cavaillon or M. d'hiver, greenish-white flesh, juicy and fine. - M. d'Odessa, green with yellow stripes; melting green flesh; like the two preceding varieties. PASTEQUE or WATER MELON (Cucurbitaceae). - With red or white flesh, rather bland, can only be grown in France, in the departments of the Midi, where the orange tree lives; it comes in open fields, in holes previously filled with substantial earth and manure; we leave it to itself. Watering in the event of severe drought. CUCUMBER (Cucurbitaceae). - Native to India. Grows like melons, either on beds or in the open air. Sow in the first fortnight of May, keeping a distance of about 1.50 m between each plant from the center of the holes, each of which is about Om.50 in diameter and has been previously filled with fresh manure and good loam mixed with substantial earth. Mulch; water frequently. Concentrate all the sap on the fruit, by pruning and pinching. For early cucumbers, blane hâtif and hâtif de Hollande, remember what we said above about early melons. Bonneuil cucumbers are grown in the open air and turn into cucumber pomade. CORNICHONS (Cucurbitaceae). - These are cucumbers picked during the first period of fruit formation. The following are grown as Gherkins: 1° the small green Cucumber; in the open air, without pruning; frequent arr osage; 2° the C. serpent, so named because of the elongated, flexuous shape of its fruit; a less productive species than the previous one because it branches much less. Same care in cultivation. CUCUMBER (Cucurbitaceae). - They are sown in April-May, on piles of manure covered with potting soil, in damp, warm soil; holes are made similar to those for cucumber seeds, but larger, deeper and more widely spaced, depending on the size of the variety; when the seeds have sprouted, the best plants are selected, leaving one in each hole; They are usually left to develop naturally, with the exception of the Pumpkin, whose first stem is cut off above the second or third eye, and when the fruit is set, the branch bearing it is stopped two or three eyes above. Among the cultivated species and varieties, let's mention the main ones. The Pumpkin proper, often with huge, very heavy fruit, with the following varieties: P. d'Espagne, better than the previous one; P. de Chypre, with greenish flesh, not very thick; Giraumon-Turban, with yellow and greenish fruit, quite sweet. - The most esteemed varieties of squash are: Melonée or Muscade de Marseille, which ripens with difficulty around Paris, but does well in the south of France; - C. de Messine, with almost no inner cavity; C. de l'Ohio (America), with fruit weighing up to 3 or 4 kilograms; soft, sweet flesh; C. à la moelle or vegetal pith, with long fruit from Om, 14 to Om, 22; pale yellow; soft, melting flesh; highly prized by the English; the non-running Artichoke de Jérusalem; with fine, delicate flesh. - The Gourde de Pèlerin, the Courge Massue, etc., are not edible. Squash seeds retain their germinative properties for six to eight years. These plants are also propagated by cuttings and herbaceous grafting. New: Flat striped squash; waffle squash with spherical fruit weighing 6 to 7 kilograms; sweet, fine, golden-red flesh. TOMATO OR POMME D'AMOUR (Solanaceae). - From Mexico, annual. Like melons and squash, tomatoes fear the cold, and can only be sown in the open air from mid-May: the cold of autumn destroys many of these plants if they have not ripened by this time. It is therefore more prudent to sow in February and March, in the empty parts of melon plants; transplant to bed; then plant out as soon as the atmosphere is sufficiently warm. A little water and manure are all it needs to grow almost anywhere, with a good exposure to the south; pinch it to stop its wild shoots; press it to support its soft stems. Tomatoes are strengthened by sowing on a warm layer from the first days of January, then transplanting to another warm layer and planting out on a third warm layer; pruning is severe, leaving few fruits; harvesting takes place in June. For field tomatoes, if the autumn cold stops them ripening, simply place them in a warm greenhouse on shelves, or even on the kitchen mantelpiece, to turn red. New: Early dwarf red tomato; very productive variety; fine, tasty flesh. Seeds retain their germinative properties for three years. EDIBLE FRUIT PLANTS. AUBERGINE OU MÉLONGÈNE, Merangene (Solanées). - This plant, so widespread and easy to grow in the south of France, only produces good fruit in the Paris climate when it is forced, as the tomato is, with the difference that, to increase the volume of the eggplant, it is transplanted up to three times, eight or ten days apart each time, on very warm beds; it is planted in May and harvested in July. Sow on a bed in March, transplant on a bed in April, then plant in the open air, at the foot of a wall, in a warm spot. The following varieties can be distinguished: violette lonque, the most widely cultivated; V. ronde and panachée from Guadeloupe, with white, purple fruit; in the Midi, even the rather unhealthy fruit of A, poule-pondeuse or Plante-aux-Œufs is eaten. PIMENT (Solanaceae). - This plant is grown like eggplant. Sow on a bed in February-March or on compost in April; replant at the end of April or first fortnight of May, in a bed facing south, or in pots buried in a bed. Fruits are harvested within the year. Varieties: Long Pepper, Sweet Spanish Grey, Violet, Pepper-Tomato, with yellow, rounded, fairly sweet fruit, but which ripens with difficulty. - P. enragé des Antilles is a greenhouse shrub. Several chili peppers are grown as ornamental plants in the northern provinces of New France; Piment rouge d'Espagne, a very pretty breed of chili pepper with fruit 15 to 16 centimeters long, more or less cylindrical in its entire length. Fruit is a beautiful coral red, very fleshy and extremely sweet. When the spawn has penetrated all the way to the top of the millstone and has firmly attached itself, it is necessary to gopter, i.e. cover the entire surface with about Om, Ol of very finely sifted, slightly salty earth, which is applied with the back of the shovel; After harvesting, a little soil is added to the empty places left by the removed mushrooms; in this way, products can be obtained for another four or five months. Gardeners on the other side of the Channel don't lay these kinds of beds on the ground, but on shelves with ledges, in a warm yet dark shed leaning against the wall of a single-sided greenhouse; we have seen, in some Scottish homes, beds of Mushrooms in wide, deep drawers under large kitchen tables. Mushrooms, even the best and best-known ones, those that are grown in layers, become dangerous when they have aged, and should be eaten as soon as they hatch; if the edges have unfolded and the blades under the cap have turned from purplish pink to brown or black, throw them away; at the very least, they could give you terrible indigestion. Economic plants (1): ARACHIDE, PISTACHE DE TERRE, Arachys hypogœa (Papilionacées.) - From Mexico, its cultivation is very similar to that of beans. Sow in soft, light soil, warmed enough for rapid germination. Hoe between rays and clumps. Peanuts succeed in areas where melons are grown in open fields. SUGAR BEETS. - See. Beets, vegetables. CHAMELINE or CAMOMILE, Myagrum sativum (Cruciferae). - Oil-bearing plant. Sown in spring, at a rate of about 5 kilograms of seed per hectare, in soil at (1) See also Fodder plants. 8 *3 T" 1" wheat or sandy soil; harvest as soon as capsules turn yellow. CARDÈRE, CHARDON A FOULON, C. A BONNETIER, Dipsacus fullonum (Dipsaceae). - Biennial plant armed with strong, numerous hooks suitable for combing sheets. Good soil, sow in the spring in northern countries, in autumn in southern Europe; weed; distance between each plant, Om, 32. As soon as their heads turn yellow, you cut the stems, leaving a length of about Om, 30 to be able to bind them. CARTHAMUS, SAFRAN BATARD, Carthamus tinctorius (Compositae). - Dry, deep soils, sow as a broadcast crop, or better in rays, from March or early May, depending on the climate, when frosts are no longer to be feared. Space plants Om, 33 apart. Harvest florets in dry weather; store in a healthy, well-ventilated place. The seed yields an oil much used in the Orient; parrots usually feed on it. HEMP, Cannabis sativa (Cannabinis). - Hemp needs light, free, substantial soil, well loosened by ploughing in autumn and again in spring. Sow immediately after a fertilizing rain, burying the seed very lightly. Weed, thin out. Harvest the male plants, the first to mature, as soon as they turn yellow, and the female plants when the seed is almost ripe. Stir the seed often to prevent fermentation; keep it away from wind and birds. It makes good burning oil. 4 hectolitres are enough to sow one hectare. Piedmont hemp, which is taller and stronger than the previous variety, is especially suited to making ropes for ships; it thrives in very ordinary soil with little or no smoke; however, set aside a square of your hemp field, richer in humus and more fertile, for the hemp plants that are to supply you with seeds for sowing. Chinese Hemp, with wider, more extensive branches than common Hemp, sometimes reaches heights of up to 4 meters, but rarely flowers or seeds in the Paris climate, COLZA. See also CHOU. CORCHORUS TEXTILIS or LO-MA. - It differs little from Corchorus olitorius or Corette potagère, and produces a coarse filament. GARANCE, Rubia tinctorum (Rubiaceae). - Perennial and indigenous. It needs light, fresh, substantial, well-tilled, well-smoked soil; sow in March-April, broadcast or even in rays, in which you spread the seed as evenly as possible, at a distance of Om, 03 to Om, 04. Weeding, reloading in the first year. New weeding, new reloading the following year in November; you'll cut the plant as soon as it's in flower if you want to use it as fodder. The third year, in August-September, you harvest the roots, which sometimes sink into the ground to Om, 40 to Om, 50; you carry them to a very clean area, stir them with a fork to remove laterre; you put them to dry in a dry, ventilated place or in an oven. GAUDE, Reseda luteola (Resedaceae). - Biennial, usually sown in July in dry, sandy soils, among beans, etc. Weed in autumn and winter. Weed the following autumn and spring; in summer, we pull up the stems as soon as they turn yellow; we dry them in small bunches placed at a distance from each other; if they are too crowded, they risk fermenting. GUIZOTIA OLEIFERE (Composites). - Several unsuccessful attempts have been made to cultivate this plant, whose stems burst very frequently and which, in France, yields far fewer seeds than in Abyssinia, where it originated. HOPS, Humulus lupulus (Cannabinae). - Native to northern Europe and North America. Flowers dioecious, the males in paniculate clusters; the females in a scaly cone at the end of an ovular stalk, composed of large, membranous, russet-white, oval scales or bracts, concave at their base. Stems hard, angular, reaching heights of 6 and 7 meters, with the help of supports. Leaves large, rough, petiolate, opposite, saw-toothed. Hops thrive in damp, sheltered places, hedges and woodland edges; they fear heat and flower in July. Cattle like to feed on hop leaves and stems. The cones have a strong, narcotic, slightly worm-eaten odor and a bitter taste; they are used by brewers to make beer. In northern Germany and other parts of the world, young hop shoots are eaten in salads or prepared like asparagus. Its shoots, softened in water, make strong, flexible bindings; they can even be used to make a kind of coarse yarn. Hops are also used to decorate arbors, cradles, trellises, etc. As the limits of this work do not allow us to go into any detail on the cultivation of this important plant, we refer the reader to the special treatises. Suffice it to say that Hops require very rich soil and costly care. LINSEED, Linum usitatissimum (Linaea). - Cultivated for the oil yielded by its seeds and for the spun yarn obtained from its bark. Linen is sown in spring and sometimes in autumn; winter flax is preferred for autumn sowing. Flax needs light soil, ploughed in all directions and well smoked. Flax is broadcast; 1° thickly to obtain very fine flax; 2° lightly, if seed is desired. Riga seed is the most esteemed of all; its white-flowered sub-variety, also known as royal flax or white-flowered American flax, produces stalks with remarkably supple fibers. Other main varieties include: L. froid, L. chaud, L. de mars, L. de maz. White-flowered flax is distinguished from other flax breeds by its medium-sized, sparsely-branched stems, with seeds that ripen as soon as the plant is pulled up; it succeeds easily, produces regular products and does not degenerate. Its yarn is highly sought-after for mechanical spinning. Flax is harvested when the bolls have turned yellow; after removing the seed immediately, either by beating the stems or by passing them between the teeth of a rake, it is rolled on the meadow or in water. It has been calculated that between 100 and 175 kilograms of flax seed are needed per hectare. VIVACE LINSEED, Linum perenne. - This flax should be sown fairly thickly to force the stems to stand upright and lengthen; substantial, well-smoked soil. MADIA DU CHILI, Madia sativa (Compositae). - Very-rustic, fast-growing plant; yields good oil for eating, but with a flavor not to everyone's taste; also used for making soap, fulling sheets, etc.; ordinary but deep soil. Sow from mid-March to the end of June, in rows spaced Om, 40 apart, with plants from Om, 12 to Om, 15 in the row. 12 to 15 kilograms of seed are needed per hectare. Harvest when seeds take on a grayish hue. Madia's strong, unpleasant odor protects it from all insect attacks. COTTONED NETTLE, Chinese A-Poo, Urtica nivea (Urticeae). - Sow in a terrine or on a bed of soft earth, barely covering; plant out in the second year; cotton nettle is more successful in the south of France than in the north. Cultivation experiments are not yet very conclusive. PAVOT, OLIETTE OR ŒEILLETTE, Papaver somniferum (Papaveraceae). - This plant is grown particularly in our northern departments; it produces an oil that is less delicate than olive oil, but has none of the disadvantages often attributed to it. The poppy needs soft, substantial soil that is well loosened. Broadcast sow from the end of March through May and June: even in September in the Midi, on cleared clover and alfalfa, but not after oats; spread the seeds as evenly as possible, barely covering them; hoe several times, and thin so that the stems have a space between them of Om, 15 to Om, 23. In September, you'll pull up the poppies, whose maturity is announced by the gray color of their heads; you'll gather them in small heaps, beat them on the spot and drop the seeds onto cloths spread out on the ground. Two or three kilograms are enough to sow a hectare. Blind poppies (Willette aveugle) are poppies with large heads devoid of holes and opercules. The white poppy (Papaver somniferum album) is cultivated less for its seed than for its large capsules, which are used for medicinal purposes; they provide opium through incisions made on the stem. PERSICAIRE, INDIGO, RENOUÉE TINCTORIALE, LOUREIRO; Polygonum tinctorium (Polygonées, from two Greek words meaning: plants with many knots). - Perennial in China, treated as an annual in France and best propagated from seed rather than cuttings. Sow in mid-March for the Paris climate, in nurseries for transplanting, or in light, healthy, fertile soil. Cloches and frames. Plant in rows separated by a spacing of Om,50 to Om 65 to facilitate hoeing and harvesting. One square metre of nursery will give you a hundred or so good plants to plant when they have 4 or 5 leaves, in May or late April. Hoeing, weeding and watering. You'll need around two kilograms of seed per hectare for sowing in rows, and six kilograms per hectare for broadcast sowing. Water Pepper Knotweed, not to be confused with the preceding species, or Peach-leaved Persicaria, thrives in damp places, along streams; it has a pungent, burning, peppery flavor, hence its name; its whitish flowers, washed with red, bloom in the course of summer. It is sometimes combined with sorrel and raisins; its seeds are used instead of pepper in the preparation of some foods. It produces a greenish-yellow color that is rightly preferred to gaude, and is used as a fertilizer. Bistort owes its name (twice torsoed) to its large, fibrous root, folded twice on itself; all livestock, with the exception of the horse, are very fond of it; its tender leaves, like those of spinach, are prepared and eaten, and its seeds can be used to feed barnyard birds. Its root, which contains a lot of tannin and gallic acid, loses its stypticity through successive lotions, and yields a starch which, when mixed with wheat flour, even in fairly large quantities, does little to alter the quality of bread. Viviparous Knotweed, which is closely related to Bistort, likes the cold pastures of the Hautes-Alpes and the Pyrenees. The Samoyeds and Tartars grind its roots into flour. Amphibian Knotweed, with its bushy spikes of pleasant red flowers blooming in August-September, is eagerly eaten by sheep, horses and pigs, but disdained by cows; it is mown and added to the mass of manure. Renouée d'Orient, Cordon de Saint-Jean, Monte-auciel, Cordon de cardinal, Persicaire du Levant, with a six-foot stem, provides very good seeds for poultry. OLEIFER RADIUS, CHINESE RAIFORT: Raphanus sativus oleifer (Cruciferae). - This plant, brought from China to Italy and from Italy to France, yields an edible oil. It needs soft, slightly deep soil. Sow in autumn in our southern provinces; in spring in the north. Weed, hoe and thin out to leave an interval of about Om, 25 between each plant. Glycyrrhiza glabra (Papilionaceae). - The best-known species is Licorice, with hairless fruits, a long, tracing, woody root, yellowish on the inside, and a mild, sweet flavor. It has several stems three to four feet high, topped with leaves composed of six or seven pairs of leaflets, with one odd, hairless, oval, a little slimy. Requires soft, deep soil. Multiply by suckers or rooted plants, planted in spring at intervals of Om, 30. Manure. Roots take three years to develop their full potential. RHUBARB, Rheum (Polygonaceae). - We do not recommend large-scale cultivation of this plant, which requires a great deal of care and only produces its main product, the roots, after four or five years. Rhubarb needs light, deep soil that's slightly dry rather than damp, with a sunny exposure. Multiply by seed or suckers. Distance between each plant: 1 m to 1.30 m. Weeding and hoeing the first year; simple plowing in spring the following years. Harvest in late autumn. The roots are cut in fragments, about Om, 06 long; after removing the epidermis, they are gently dried, grated, the angles softened and rolled in a barrel. Commercial Rhubarb belongs to the Rheum dalmatum or Palm Rhubarb species, native to China. Wavy Rhubarb or Muscovy Rhubarb is highly prized by Russians, who eat its leaves raw or cooked like those of vegetables. The pulpy Rhubarb, native to Lebanon and Carmel, is praised as a remedy for inflammatory diseases; its stalks, eaten raw, are very pleasant to the taste, slightly acidic and refreshing; they are preserved in honey, sugar or grape must, and in this way are easily preserved all year round. Rhubarb compaete, native to Tartary and China, has large, heart-shaped, hairless leaves; its root is tonic in small doses and purgative in large. Rhubarb raponthic, native to Asia, the banks of the Volga, etc., is cultivated in our gardens under the name of Monk's Rhubarb. It has a large root, yellow inside, a little reddish outside; a strong, fleshy stem; very broad, heart-shaped leaves; small, yellowish-white flowers in paniculate clusters. In some regions, its leaves and young shoots are eaten prepared in various ways; the whole plant gives a yellow color and is used above all for dyeing leather. It has the same tonic and purgative properties as rale (1) : Eyes, Buds, Buds, Twigs, False Twigs, Branches, Stings, Bourses, Slats, Twigs, Stems, Pruning, Pruning, Pruning, Pruning, Pruning, Pruning, Pruning, Pruning, Pruning is an operation by which part of the branches or shoots of a tree are cut off, to give the tree a certain disposition, or to make it bear the most beautiful fruit, and, each year, almost the same number. Each variety of tree requires its own specific pruning; we will only discuss fruit tree pruning in this and subsequent chapters. Pruning varies according to considerations of age and terrain, as well as the state of health or disease of the plants, differences in climate and so on. However, practical experience has formulated general laws that should be known and followed. 1° Always direct the branches of fruit trees as close as possible to the (1) In the remainder of this book, we will indicate the specific pruning for each species of fruit tree. For grafting, the reader is referred to chapter III, Multiplication of plants. 2° Take care to maintain the balance between the various parts of the tree, inclining towards the ground any twig that gets carried away, and straightening, on the contrary, any twig that is not very vigorous, as the sap tends to rise. To apply pruning properly, you need to know some of the terms used in this operation. The eye is the part of the plant that gives rise to the leaves; the bud is the part of the plant that produces the flower; the bud is born from the eye; the lateral eye is the one on the side; the terminal eye is the one at the end of a shoot; the sub-eye is the rudimentary eye that is not visible, or the bud that replaces the one that has been destroyed; the gourmand bud is the one that grows larger; the single eye is the one that is solitary; the double, triple or multiple eyes are those joined by 2, 3 or more. Virtually every leaf has an eye at its base; this eye is the starting point for all pruning theories. The bud is the modified, developed eye, the proof of plant virility; it produces a herbaceous part, more or less covered with leaves, which is called a bud. Once the bud has completed its annual growth, it is called a shoot; when it is more than a year old, it is called a branch. The carpenter or mother branch is the one that determines the shape of the tree; - the wood branches, born from the carpenter branch, are much smaller than it; the fruit branches, born from the wood branches, give flowers or fruits; the replacement branches are those that are left to develop to replace the first ones struck by disease, and so on. Branches arising directly from the carpenter branch are also known as sub-mother branches or simply sub-mother branches; they are called lower sub-mother branches if they are below the mother branch; - upper sub-mother branches if they are above the mother branch; - lower sub-mother branches if they are below the mother branch. - Fig. 42. - Bursa and sting. above; - finally, the branches placed on the carpenters and intended to produce fruiting branches are called spurs. E Fig. 43 - Bourses with stalks and eyes. Fig. 44 - Twig on bursa. The short, not very large, mostly right-angled twigs, ending in a pointed eye, are stings; - the bursa is a nodosity developed by the influx of sap on a point where there are flowers or fruit. The lambourde is a short, thick twig, with closely-spaced leaves that seem to emerge from a fold or a kind of ring. Twigs are spindly, very branched branches, almost always indicating, for vigorous subjects, forthcoming fruiting; if the twig, instead of ending in a wood bud, shows a fruit bud at its tip, it is called a crowned twig. The "cochonnet" or "bouquet de mai" is a slender twig, simple if short, branched if large; it covers itself with buds and produces very good fruit; it is found on stone fruit trees, particularly peach. Notching is an operation which consists in making more or less tongued transverse cuts in the bark of trunks or branches in spring, before the sap rises, to temporarily stop the sap. If you want to speed up the development of one part of the tree, you make the cut above; if you want to slow it down, you make the cut below. De-budding consists in removing useless or misplaced eyes; this operation is performed during pruning or a little later on plants still devoid of their leaves. Disbudding is the removal of useless or misplaced buds, from the moment they have reached just a few centimetres to their full development; this operation is performed dry, i.e. on plants not yet covered with leaves; it requires great care. Pinching is an operation designed to stop or moderate the development of certain parts, by removing the bud tips. You pinch at one, two or three leaves, when you remove the tip of the bud above the first, second or third leaf from the base of the bud. Continuous pinching, which requires a great deal of reserve and care, is performed successively on the same buds, as they develop new production. Trellising consists in tying the buds of espaliered or counter-trellised trees along walls, trellises, etc., using rags or rushes. Trellising should be carried out as the tree develops, from June to August; only well-developed parts are tied. Breaking consists in breaking, towards the end of summer, the buds destined for the production of fruiting parts, stings, lambourdes, etc. Ring incision is designed to enlarge the fruit and hasten ripening. It consists in removing a piece of bark a few millimeters wide from the entire circumference of a stem or branch; a special instrument, known as shears or ring-nippers, is used for this operation. Bleeding is a longitudinal incision made in the very hard bark of certain trees: 1° to debride the tissues and facilitate the flow of sap; 2° to cure strangles in stone fruit trees. Arcure consists in bending rebellious branches to force them to bear fruit, or at least to assume a position favorable to the circulation of sap. Nursery. - General observations on tree and shrub seeds. - Stone fruit trees: Peach, Apricot, Almond, Plum, Cherry, Bigarreautier, Cherry, Olive. CONIFERS. - Many conifers are not cultivated in nurseries; their seedlings are taken from the woods, where they sow themselves. Before using the seeds, they are exposed to an oven, so that, under the action of moderate heat, the cone scales open and leave the seeds free. Cedar of Lebanon cones do not need to undergo this preliminary operation; they are carefully opened with a sharp instrument; the seedling will not remain in the nursery for more than two years; it is better to raise it in deep pots and then transplant it as a root ball; Cypresses should be treated in the same way.
