The PEACH tree (Rosaceae). - Native to Persia, has produced, through cultivation, a large number of varieties, either espaliered or in the open air. The different species are: - P. with downy fruit and flesh that does not adhere to the stone; - P. with downy fruit and adherent flesh; - P. with smooth, non-adherent fruit; - P. with smooth fruit and flesh that adheres to the stone. In the first class, the main varieties are: - the Pêche admirable, large, yellow, fine, sweet, which grows well in the open air; - the P. abricotée, a little mealy, reminiscent of apricot, from seed. - Avant-Pêche blanche, with white fruit, small, sweet, but not very fragrant; early. The tree that bears it is delicate. - Belle Beauce, very good quality, but a little late. - La Cardinale, marbled on the inside, like a beet; not much appreciated. - Chevreuse hâtive and Chevreuse tardive, of good quality. - Grosse mignonne ordinary, delicate and sweet, yellow on the shady side, red on the sunny side; divided into two lobes by a wide furrow. - Déesse hâtive and Galande, excellent quality. - Ma gdeleine blanche, with fine, musky white flesh. - Alberge jaune, yellow flesh around the circumference, red around the stone. - Belle de Paris, large fruit, marbled with red and very delicate. - P. de Vénus, with large fruit, topped by a nipple; delicate flesh, the best of all. The second class includes Pavie jaune, Pavie tardive, Pavie de Pomponne and Persée. The third class includes the small, apricot-like Jaune lisse and the red-mottled P. violette de Courson. In the fourth, we find Brug non, light red, very bright on the side exposed to the sun. In terms of ripening, peaches can be classified as follows: the white Avant-Pêche and the red Avant-Péche ripen in the second half of July. - Petite mignonne, Grande mignonne, Belle de Paris and Pourprée ripen in August. - P. de Vénus, Bourdine, Chevreuses, in September. - Pavie de Pomponne and P. abricotée, in October. - Brugnons ripen from early August to late October. - Pavie tardive, in November. Exposure. - South-facing: Chevreuse, Galande, Grosse mignonne, Avant-Pêche rouge, Belle Beauce, Nivette, Pourprée, P. de Vénus, Pavie, Violette de Courson and Jaune lisse. - The other species thrive in all exposures, except north. Cultivation. - Peach trees need soil that is light rather than strong, but deep and substantial. Some varieties can be propagated from seed: Pêche abricotée, Bourdine, Admirable, Grosse mignonne; for the others, grafting is used; sometimes hard-shelled almond trees are used for this purpose, as they are not very difficult to select and are not very prone to Peach tree diseases; sometimes plum trees and especially black P. de Damas, which does well in moist, shallow soil. Scion grafting is carried out from July to mid-September, at Om, 15 of soil for espaliers and at around 2 meters for open-air trees. Planting should only take place when the sap has been completely stopped by a hard frost. - Choose young plants with smooth bark, straight, moss-free stems and well-formed roots. The soil is loosened and even replaced with new soil, if it has already been used in previous years to grow peach, plum or apricot trees. The graft is raised to Om, 50 above the ground, keeping a distance of about 6 meters between each plant; a layer of manure Om, 10-12 thick covers the whole plantation. Watering, weeding, ploughing and fertilizing in autumn: in winter, use a fine broom to remove any frost or snow covering the branches. In summer, new watering should be stopped eight or ten days before the fruit ripens. Small mats to protect against the sun's heat. Harvesting takes place in August-September. Pruning. - As a general rule, the current year's branches alone produce flowers and fruit. When a young branch, born of a woody eye from the previous year, has borne fruit, we prune it on its lower eye, so that it opens onto a bud that will later become a fruiting branch. When a bud is born on one of the branches below the good wooden eye, it must be pruned to prevent the branch from growing longer and becoming exhausted. From the first year of transplanting, we begin to prune the peach tree and give it a particular shape; the rule, which must not be departed from, is this: provide a number of spur branches, regularly distributed, so that all parts of the espalier provide their quota of good peaches, and encourage, at the bottom of the branches that have borne fruit, the birth of replacement branches. The arrangements usually adopted are as follows: 1° SQUARE SPALER. - In February-March, the one-year-old grafted peach tree is cut back to a height of about Om, 25. Four of the best buds are selected Fig. 45. - Square peach tree (1st year). Fig. 46. - Square peach tree (2nd year). They are attached in a slightly oblique direction, but without obstructing the flow of sap. In the second year, from February onwards, the inner branches are arranged in an open V, forming a 45-degree angle, to form the mother branches; the other two branches, still in the same direction, but more oblique, will be the sub-branches; the mother branches are also pruned at the same height as the sub-branches, which will be born from the lateral eyes, while the terminal eyes, as they lengthen, will contain the mother9. branches. The first sub-mothers are pruned at about Om, 30, on a good eye that will extend them. If the first year has produced only two branches, instead of four, always prune in a V-shape, with two eyes, one of which, the upper, will continue the mother branch; and the other, the lower, lateral, will provide the first sub-mother. Fruiting branches should be pruned to a length of 10 to 15 centimetres, depending on their strength and position. Care should be taken to retain at least one eye (closest to the base), which will become the fruit-bearing replacement branch the following year. In the third year, if the tree is vigorous and well-balanced in all its parts, prune to encourage elongation, drawing in another sub-tree; if the tree is weak, simply prune the mother branches much shorter, without drawing in a sub-tree. The general care to be taken in the fourth and fifth years is the same as in the third; one or more sub-heads are pulled again, and any branches that get carried away are stopped. If everything is well balanced, attach the branches to the places intended for them; if the balance is badly established, lower the strong parts, straighten or free the weak par ties. Your tree should now have six lower limbs, three on each of its two branch-mothers. You'll dehair the youngest parts; you'll garnish the inside of your espalier, taking a branch from a spur of each of the mother branches, near the fork, which, raised almost vertically, becomes the first sub-mother. Keep an eye on its development. If it gets carried away, cut it back onto a weaker bud. Prune the other parts, taking into account their strength and the place they occupy; tie gently, without hindering the circulation of sap. When the tree is vigorous, you can prune several more branches that same year, at equal distances from each other, alternating as much as possible with the sub-mothers. A well-managed, complete square peach tree should have twelve limbs, six on each mother-branch; the well-filled carpenter-branches orffent numerous spurs which are themselves rich in buds. The square espalier very quickly covers the surface of a wall, thanks to the vertical position given to the inner limbs; but this upright position makes it Fig. 47 - Square peach tree (8th year) very difficult to maintain the balance of the sap. 2° The same can be said of the open V-shaped espalier or Montreuil espalier, which is similar in size but simpler than the previous one, and is rarely used today. 3° Espalier en Palmette. - This is the simplest, most widespread and most profitable type of pruning. For the simple Palmette, in February-March, the Peach tree (grafted one year old) is cut back to about Om.30 from the ground, giving a single shoot which will become the spire or central stem of the Palmette. The first pruning produces two lateral arms which are planted obliquely at the same height, one on the right, the other on the left; only force them to take up a horizontal position at the end of summer, when the annual shoot has come to an end; the following year, the arrow produces two other lateral arms which are extended parallel to the first two, and so on from year to year, until the peach tree reaches the height of the wall. Always leave the upper eye to extend the stem. Fig. 48. - Simple palmette (third year). Fig. 49 - Single palmette (2nd year). Double pallet. - Instead of one stem, you'll have two, due to the bifurcation of the main stem at birth; each of these stems has limbs on one side only. Here's how you get these two vertical mother branches. Assuming the tree has been grafted and planted in the usual way, cut back to about Om, 35 from the ground; as soon as the buds develop, choose two of the finest, as close together as possible and coming from either side of the stem; tie them obliquely or vertically, and only bring them back to the horizontal direction at the end of summer; make sure they strengthen equally. The following spring, prune these two branches over two eyes, one of which, the terminal, will extend the stem; the other, lower and outer, will form the first horizontal limb or first arm of the Palmette. Repeat the same operation every year, paying particular attention to pinching, disbudding and the overall balance of the tree. You can also form your secondary limbs with the end of the vertical branch, inclining it when it reaches the height where the lateral branch should be placed; you then continue your 5 OO Fig. 50. - Double palmette. vertical branch using the bud born at the point of curvature. In some fast-growing peach trees, it is not uncommon to obtain two levels of lateral branches in the same year: 1° by pinching the bud that extends the vertical part as soon as this bud is at the height where lateral branches are required; 2° by encouraging the birth of early buds, which are quick to appear after the pinching operation. The double pallet is less common and less advantageous than the single pallet. 4° To get an exact idea of the size of the U-shaped Peach tree, imagine the double Palmette described above, but without the side limbs. Once the two vertical branches have been established, all you have to do is keep them in balance, well furnished with fruit-bearing branches; if, despite all your care, the upper parts get carried away, bring them together on a lower bud. In other respects, same behaviour. Horizontal palms. - Plant several peach trees along an espalier, about 4 meters apart. Make the first pruning of all their stems on a front eye, keeping all the eyes below (except those in front or behind); they will give you the fruiting branches. At the next pruning, you cut all the shoots on a front eye to obtain the extension and, on a side eye on the right, to form the first row of cords. When the extension shoots have grown, prune them in the same way on a front eye; the side eye, on the left, will form the second row of cords at Om, 45 of the first. Follow the same procedure for the other three cords. As for the sixth, bend and palisade the end of the branch intended to form it as soon as this branch has passed the Om, 45 that should separate it from the previous one. Don't cut the ends of the cords until they touch the stems of the neighbor they're heading for, after which they should be bent over a branch or a false branch, suitably palmed and cut over a front eye. Sometimes, in order to obtain cords of the same height, you will bud in August at the appropriate place, and cut the following spring. 5° For the simple oblique cordon, you will plant one-year-old grafted peach trees with a single stem, at Om 75 from each other, inclining them all at an angle of 60 degrees, which you will reduce to 45 degrees the following year. Make sure that growth is regular, and that the eyes work together to form evenly-spaced spurs on the stem. This type of espalier should not exceed 3 meters in height. Fig. 51 - Oblique cordon. PEACH TREE DISEASES. - Blanc or Meunier is caused by a fungus and manifests itself as a whitish, farinaceous dust on the leaves and sometimes even on the fruit. - Grise is caused by the presence of myriads of small insects on the underside of the leaves, which they suck off and exhaust. Remedies: freshly slaked lime, 2 kilograms; 500 grams of sulfur flower, all mixed together; soak the diseased parts in the morning, before sunrise. Against peach aphid: tobacco water; soak 1/2 kilog. in hot water for 24 hours, add about 10 to 12 liters of cold water to this dissolution; sulphur flower sprayed on leaves with a bellows or a sulphur tassel. Water with a little iron sulfate dissolved in it. ABRICOTIER (Rosaceae). - From Armenia. Blooms in February-March; reproduces by sowing or grafting. The main varieties are: early apricot or Abricotin, second quality; blane with large fruit, peachy taste, very-good quality; A. de Provence, sweet and vinous; Alberge, abundant fruit; A, black, dark wine-red color, fiery-red flesh, third quality. A. d'Alexandrie; gros hâtif de Saint-Jean; gros rouge précoce, with large, orange fruit, first quality, ripens around mid-July and does very well in full wind; A. Angoumois hâtif, small and elongated, almost reddish-yellow, with strong odor, second quality, ripens in July; A, common, with large, round fruit, a little mushy when overripe, second quality; needs northern exposure and full wind; very productive; A. de Jacques, medium-sized, rounded, reddish-yellow, first quality, ripens around mid-August; A. de Hollande or Amande aveline, small, yellow, glassy, second quality; ripens around the end of July; A. Musch de Turquie, medium-sized fruit, rounded, dark yellow, pulp transparent enough to show through to the stone, fine and very pleasant taste; ripens around mid-July; requires espalier, first quality; A. Moorpark, quite similar to the peach apricot, ripens in mid-August; A. de Nancy, large, slightly flattened and rough, orange-yellow, melting, first quality; it is even rightly declared the best of all apricots; its stone is the only one where you'll notice a pinhole, reproduction by seed, many varieties; A. Pourret, with large, vinous fruit, second quality, ripens in mid-August; A. Beaugé, with large, rounded, yellow fruit, first quality, ripens at the beginning of September; A. précoce d'Esperen, with medium-sized, flattened, yellow fruit, first quality, ripens at the beginning of July; A. Royal, with round, orange, transparent, melting fruit, first quality; ripens at the end of July; all exposures, except north. Apricot fruit is only at its best when it comes from high-stemmed trees grown in the open air, rarely pruned in the first few years, then left to grow naturally. Pruning and cultivation. - Apricot trees thrive in light, deep soil with a southern or eastern exposure. Seedlings are selected from the best fruit, stratified and planted in autumn at a depth of about Om, 055. The Apricot tree is grafted in the form of an escutcheon, with a dormant eye; it is raVb M 2 Fig. 52. - Peacock's tail fan. beaten, at Om, 25 from the ground and, after the first year, two or four of the most vigorous buds are chosen and fixed in a slightly oblique direction. In the second year, prune longer or shorter, depending on the strength of the branches; pinch off any unnecessary buds. In the third year, we lengthen the carpenter branches, keeping some buds, so that if one of these branches is missing, it can be replaced by a well-placed bud that can be reattached to the same spot. Suppression of overabundant fruit production. The result is the Peacock's tail fan, the best shape for this tree. Protect the flowers from frost and the fruit from sunburn, using canvas and straw mats. AMANDIER (Rosaceae). - From Asia. Sow in autumn, in deep, chalky soil with warm exposure, using the kernels of naturally fallen fruit as seeds. It can be grafted and pruned for open-air or espalier planting, and requires the same cultivation care as the Peach and Apricot; the same precautions against frost and sunburn. Its varieties are classified into three divisions: 1° Ordinary hard-shelled almonds, ordinatre soft-shelled almonds, Princesse, Sultane, etc.; 2° Bitter almonds, 3° Almond-Peach, a hybrid of Peach and Almond. PLUM (Rosaceae). - From Asia. Blooms in March. Its varieties can be classified according to fruit color as yellow, violet, red or black. Yellow plums. - Apricot plum; elongated shape; yellowish on one side, red on the other; firm yellow flesh, more delicate than that of the apricot plum, with which it is often confused. Ripens in early September. - Reine-Claude, diaphanous, reddish-yellow, round; ripens in September. - Prune de Catalogne or de Saint-Barnabé, small, long and yellow. - Brignole, pale yellow on the shaded side, red on the sunny side; mediocre flesh. Very good quality; ripens in September. White plums. - The white P. Perdrigon, very healthy, very smoky, ripens in espaliers at the beginning of September. Green plums. - P. bifère, used in compotes; ripens in mid-July and mid-September. - ReineClaude, green apricot or Verte-bonne, large, spherical, speckled with gray and red; the best of all plums; ripens in August. Plum tree cultivation. - This tree thrives in the most ordinary soil, provided it is not marshy, loamy or too sandy; in southern countries, it thrives in all types of exposure; in northern countries, it thrives in the east or south. It can be propagated by sowing stratified cores or offshoots; the former is preferable for trees growing in the open air. Sow in spring and care for the young plant, either in a bed or in a nursery; let it gain strength before grafting, especially before slit grafting. Scion grafting is done in summer. Plum trees are planted the year after the first graft, and are cut back by 4, 6 or more eyes, depending on their vigor. Care is taken to destroy the useless offshoots, of which this tree is very prolific, by cutting them off at the root. Palmette pruning follows the general principles indicated for this operation. Plums are rarely espaliered; they like iron even less than apricots. Plum trees grown in the open air only need to be cleared of dead wood, useless branches and moss. Like Peach, this tree is subject to Gum and sometimes Powdery Mildew. Remedy: renew the soil around the base; sprinkle sulphur flower on diseased leaves; remove gum and heal wounds. Oven-dried plums keep very well. Plum wood is highly prized in joinery. CHERRY (Rosaceae). - From Asia Minor, we classify its 70 varieties into three categories: firstly, the Cherry trees proper; secondly, the Prickly Pear trees; thirdly, the Cherry trees. All these trees produce their flowers only on the previous year's wood; their fruit is round or heart-shaped, red, white, yellow or black, depending on the species. Cherry trees proper. - The German or Chaux cherry, with large, dark-red fruit, ripens towards the end of July. - L'Anglaise tardive, firm, pleasant-tasting flesh, top quality; ripens in early August. - Belle de Châtenay, large red fruit, firm, sweet flesh, first quality; ripens in early August. - Belle de Choisy or Dauphine, large, round, transparent, lightly colored, sweet flesh, first quality; ripens in late June. - Courte-queue or gros Gobet or Montmorency, very bright red; many varieties; ripens in mid-July. - Common cherry, with its varieties: Grosse, Madeleine, Cerise de pied. Small, acid fruit. Cannot be grafted; propagates by suckers. - Griotte commune, round, large, almost black, dark red flesh, second quality; ripens in early July. - C. du Nord, Belle Griotte; heart-shaped, bright red, second quality; ripens in September. Like all Griottes, it is preferred for preserving in brandy. - Cerise du Portugal, small Griotte, sweet-fleshed; ripens in early July. - C. Royale, early ripening, one of the best varieties; large, rounded fruit, turning from bright red to reddish-brown. - C. de la reine Hortense or Seize à la livre, large round fruit, bright red, fragrant; first quality; ripens in early July. - C. de la Toussaint, produced by a small tree with hanging branches like those of weeping willows, acid; third quality; ripens in July. The tree blooms for four months. - C. à Trochet, bright red, acidic, inferior quality; sometimes as many as six or eight of these cherries are found attached to the end of a single tail. Bigarreautiers - These trees are larger and stockier than the Merisiers, their twigs are more pendulous, and their fruit has a crunchy flesh that differs from that of the Guigne. Varieties: the Bigarreau, with its large red fruit, is of the highest quality and ripens at the end of July. - The B. à feuilles de tabac or four to the pound, curious for its leaves, but hardly worth cultivating, since it produces only small, few and poor-quality fruit. - B. de Metzel, with large, dark-red fruit, very pleasant taste, first quality, ripens in July. - B. hâtif, small, heart-shaped, light red, firm flesh with white fibers, first quality, ripens in June. - B. cœur de pigeon, heart-shaped, crisp flesh, the best of all Bigarreaux, ripens in July. - B. blanc, second quality, a little red on the sunny side, ripens in June. - B. belle de Richemont, with large, heart-shaped fruit of a beautiful shiny red, flesh-colored variety, first quality, ripens in mid-July. Wild cherry and guignier. - Wild cherry, the type found in our forests, is cultivated more for its wood than for its fruit. It thrives in granitic and sandy soils; its preferred variety is the Guignier, which itself gives us the most widespread varieties: the shiny black Guigne, the largest, shiniest and best of the Guignes; it ripens at the end of June. - Early black, the earliest and most common, but of third quality; ripens in the first half of June. - Early pink G., tender red, very watery. - G. grosse ambrée or grosse merise blanche, heart-shaped fruit, sweet, long from Om, 020, third quality, ripens from June to mid-July. Cherry trees with red or white fruit are used as subjects for grafting good cherry species. Cherry tree cultivation. - It's an essentially hardy, robust tree, adaptable to any kind of soil, provided it's neither too wet nor too clayey. We sow its pits in the woods. They can be grafted in buds or in slits, although the latter is less certain of success. Some good species can be espaliered; others can be planted in the open. The bark of the cherry tree is very hard and tight, compressing the sap juices; hence the custom of making longitudinal incisions in the bark from time to time, to facilitate the development of the trunk. Same diseases as stone fruit trees; same remedies. Cherries can be stored dry or in brandy. They are used to make a type of wine, kirsch, maraschino, jams and raisins. OLIVE (Jasmine). - From Asia. 8 to 10 meters high. The most commonly cultivated varieties are: O. Aglandeau or Caianne, with round fruit, very bitter, but yielding a superfine oil. - The O. d'Espagne, which produces a very large olive with very good candied, bitter oil. - Amellon or Amelline or plant of Aix, almond-shaped fruit; very good candied olive; sweet oil. - Picholine or Saurine, the best of the candied olives; sweet, fine oil. - L'O. Pointue or Rougette, esteemed oil. - L'O. Verdole or Verdau, with ovoid fruit that rots quickly when ripe. - Galininque or Laurine, with reddish fruit, resistant to cold, etc. Cultivation. - In France, olive trees require a very special region, known as the Oliviers region, and are propagated by seed, cuttings and suckers. Cuttings are the simplest way to produce good fruit; seedlings only bear fruit after 10 or 12 years and, like suckers, must be grafted. Crown grafting is preferred, although cleft and escutcheon grafting also work well. Olive trees are planted in staggered rows, at the edges, with a distance between plants of 10 to 13 meters, depending on the vigor of the species and the goodness of the soil. From time to time, they are smoked with manure made from scraps of wool rags, animal hair, horns and nails. The earliest fruits appear in November, and are harvested from then until March. In many countries, they are left on trees or fallen to the ground, but the best oil is obtained by removing them on a fine, warm day, laying them out for a week or so on a dry floor or on racks, and then pressing them without crushing the stones, as the oil from the kernels is inferior to that from the pulp. To preserve olives, they are picked before they are ripe, and their natural bitterness is corrected with a preparation based on sea salt. They are eaten ripe with a seasoning of oil, salt and pepper. Martin-Sire, P. Gros-Gilot, P. Frangipane, P. Picru, Gros-Certeau, P. FrancRéal d'hiver, P. Double fleur, P. de Sain, P. de Loup, etc. Growing and pruning Pear trees. - This tree needs deep, cool soil that is neither damp, cold nor clayey. Pear trees reproduce from seed and sowing. In autumn and spring, sow pear seedlings that have produced a type of cider known as perry. Choose loose soil for this purpose, make rays Om, 33 deep, at a distance of Om, 16; a little litter covers the seedling and keeps it cool enough to germinate. Weeding, hoeing and thinning are carried out, and seedlings that have become strong enough are placed in a nursery. The pivot is removed to encourage preduction of lateral roots, and the nursery is visited from time to time. Frequent hoeing. Two or three years later, grafting is carried out in the form of a slit or a dormant-eye escutcheon, on franc, in deep soils with a dry surface; on coignassier, in damp, cold soils. In general, trees grafted in the latter way produce fruit quickly, but do not live as long as those grafted on Francs. A Pear tree planted in good soil and left to its own devices lives for several centuries; the same variety pruned into cattails or pyramids rarely exceeds sixty years, as it usually dies out in twenty-five to thirty years. The Pear tree is fairly indifferent to the exposure given to it, as long as it receives sun all day long; a warm exposure seems preferable for winter Pear trees, whose fruit is picked last. The Pear tree can take any shape, but is best pruned into Pyramidal, Cattail, Palmette and Peacock-tailed Fan shapes. Pyramid pruning (first year). - In February, the tree, grafted one or two years old, is cut back to a height of Om, 30 to Om, 50 from the ground, on a good eye which, as it develops, should continue the axis or stem; in summer, the Fig. 53. pyramid-shaped pear tree (1st, 2nd and 3rd years). buds are pinched off, especially the buds close to the terminal, in order to activate the development of the lower buds; above all, the base must be well furnished. In the second year, lengthen the spire by about Om 20 to Om 40; prune the supporting branches, leaving the lower ones longer than the upper ones, so as to give the whole plant the shape of a 10. cone. Keep all the stalks, twigs and shoots, and prune near their base (cut to the thickness of a shield), the twigs developed on the stem, near the spire, and which are later to be carpenter branches. Prune all your lateral branches, according to their position and strength, on one eye outwards, so as to make them take a horizontal direction. Are you forced to change this direction? Prune on a side eye, but don't forget the result you want to achieve. Lateral branches should be inserted in spirals around the stem, without any of them being perpendicular above another, without any of them having a common point of insertion with the neighbor. Sometimes voids form on the axis; in this case, you can resort to longitudinal incisions or bleeding, which you make from bottom to top, towards the weak parts and a little above them; you also have the following remedies: grafting close to a neighbouring branch, and annular or partial incision. If the shoot is languishing, cut it back below, on a vigorous shoot that will replace it. If the branch is exhausted or has only fruit on it, return it to its crown. Avoid bifurcations, or allow them only with reservation, to fill a gap, take them only on the lateral parts of the carpenter branches and not above. Pruning should be more elongated on vigorous species that are slow to set fruit. Don't neglect the use of stakes and ties, but never let them stop the flow of sap; your tree would become counterfeit instead of symmetrical. In the third year, remember the general indications given for the second year. The tree which now forms a pyramid of about 1m, 35-45, if it has been well cared for, requires above all: 1° that you maintain a suitable spacing between the carpenter branches, using small wooden forks to serve Fig. 54. - Pyramid pruning, perfect condition. of buttresses; and that those which are too far apart be brought closer together, using wicker lliens; 2° that the ends of the carpenter branches be pruned more or less long, according to their vigor; 3° that the spurs be pruned short. The spindle-shaped pyramid hardly exceeds Om, 40 to Om 50 in diameter, but can reach 7 or 8 meters in height. To obtain the Cattail shape, the tree is cut back to around Om, 50 and all the eyes are left to develop; those that are too vigorous are pinched out; in August, they are broken at Om, 20 or Om, 25 in height. The following year, branches are pruned to three, four or five eyes; excessively long twigs are shortened, respecting stings and stalks. Cattail pruning, which is often confused with pyramid pruning, is rarely used today, although it has undeniable advantages. The most sought-after shape for espalier and counter-espalier pear trees is the simple palmette. To obtain this shape, the tree is lowered to about Om.30 above the ground, and the spire or central stem is pruned successively over two eyes, one on the right, the other on the left; the upper bud continues to form the stem; the buds are lowered and palisaded into an almost horizontal position, thus beginning a tier of the framework. The following year, during which the tree has been allowed only limited growth, will produce a second tier by the same procedure. The progress of vegetation in the cords of the palmette should be monitored, so that they grow equally and are of the same strength. By pinching and breaking the buds, the balance is maintained, and fruit production develops (stings, stalks, twigs). Pinching and breaking should only be carried out partially. Visit the trees every two or three days. Each year, we continue to add a new tier of branches to the tree. If one of the branches is destroyed, it is replaced by a branch taken from a neighbouring branch. Generally speaking, you should act in the same way as for Peach trees grown as palms. Double palmette. - Start by pruning two eyes, leaving the buds to grow vertically; each of these buds becomes the base of the tree's framework; they are allowed to grow lateral buds at equal distance from each other. For the rest, we proceed as in the simple palmette. Peacock-tail or fan shape. - After bringing the tree down to about Om, 20 above the ground, choose two of the most beautiful buds, pinch off and remove the others; the two buds thus preserved will be branches the following year; cut them at Om, 30, Om, 50 and even Om, 60, depending on their strength; fix them obliquely to the wall and you'll have the first rays of the fan. Then, to fill in the gaps left between the carpenter branches by their continual tendency to spread apart, choose vigorous buds and palisade them. Keep the spurs as short as possible, and keep them clear to avoid confusion. Spindle or candle shape. - We were wrong to abandon this shape, which, while not very pleasing to the eye, has many advantages: it is very easy to obtain, requires little care, takes up little space and favors fruit production. Cut back to around Om, 50, and even Om, 70, above ground level, leaving all buds to develop. In June-July, any buds that are too vigorous are pinched off; in August, they are all broken off at around Om, 20 in length. The following year, branches are pruned to five, four or even three eyes; excessively long twigs are shortened, leaving stings and shafts intact. Pinching and breaking in the usual way; removal of useless branches; columnar, vase, basket and girandole shapes; trigonal, tetragonal, pentagonal and hexagonal shapes, which are rarely used and are less advantageous than the palmette shape; single or double cords, sinuous cords, etc., etc., etc., etc... The fruit-bearing branches of the Pear tree only bear fruit after two or three years' waiting, but they remain fruitful for several years running. They are first announced in spring by the lambourdes, which bear fruit in year L 2 Fig. 55. - Pear trees in sinuous cords, with a double tier of branches. the following year and are then called bursas. These bursae produce stings. Twigs are born on the bursas and twigs, and should be pruned to a good eye at about half their length. Every year, in autumn, plough the base of espaliered Pear trees; weed and hoe them several times during the summer; every four or five years, give the bed where they stand a layer of rotted manure, Om, 04 or Om, 05 thick; A good mulch, left in place from mid-May, prevents the soil from hardening and splitting, stops the growth of most weeds, keeps the roots fresh, and makes watering less necessary. All varieties of Pear blossom around mid-April in the Paris climate; bunches naturally lose most of their blossoms as a result of the season's bad weather, or through lack of fertility (1). APPLE (Rosaceae). - Native, medium-sized. Blooms in May and therefore fears frost less than the pear tree; its formidable enemies are caterpillars, woolly aphids and weevils (2). Cultivation makes apple trees delicate. When grown in open fields, with as much air and space as it desires, it thrives and bears fruit abundantly. Cultivation and pruning - Even easier than the pear tree when it comes to choosing soil, the apple is content with soft, slightly moist soil, where its roots, which are more tracing than taprooted, settle easily; it even accepts sandy, chalky soil. It is propagated by pepins, which come from cider pomace and provide franks (known as Egrins), which can then be grafted onto high stems to form large open-air trees or beautiful cattails. Apple trees are grafted in slits and, even more often, in escutcheons. Besides, it doesn't like iron, and the only pruning that suits it in espalier is palmette pruning. How to obtain this shape: Graft from Doucin and Paradis, never from Franc; take care to elongate the supporting branches and severely pinch the vigorous buds that develop on them. The same care is used as for pear trees (see Pear trees). Cordon pruning is also very popular. (1) See also: Insectes nuisibles. (2) See: Harmful insects. One-year-old grafted Paradise trees are cut back to about Om, 45 above the graft, leaving only one vigorous bud attached to a stake and free to grow Fig. 56 - Palmette apple tree. vertically. At the end of summer, it is fixed horizontally on a wire or on small spikes. Then, year after year, the mother branches are lengthened and Fig. 57. - Apple tree in cords. to fill out with fruit crops along their entire length. Remove unnecessary or exhausted branches; allow only small fruit-bearing branches to grow in the spurs. For the record, let's mention bush pruning and goblet pruning. Normandie is a plantation of alternating lines of half-dwarf apple trees in small pyramids 1.50 m apart, and dwarf apple trees only 1 m apart. There is a spacing of 1.50 m between these lines. If the apple trees making up a Normandie are on Doucin and Paradis, the grafts must not be buried. Fg. 58. - Apple tree in vase. Fig. 58 bis. - Pear tree in vase. Every year, the apple tree is given a shallow ploughing: every three or four years, in autumn, a layer of soil about Om, 15 deep is removed from around the base to a distance of 2 meters; after amending it, it is put back in place; a little fat manure for dry soil; marl or lime for fresh soil. NÉFLIER (Rosaceae) native. - It differs from the Alisiers only in its bony cores, which vary from one to five, and its styles. The common medlar grows naturally in the woods of Europe. Cultivation causes it to lose its hardiness, giving us the large-fruited, monstrous-fruited, stone-less Beech. This tree is propagated by grafting onto Hawthorn or Coignassier. Seeds take two years to set. It thrives in all types of non-marshy soil and in all types of exposure. Pruning would reduce the number of fruits, so it is left to grow freely in the corner of a hedge or by the side of a path. The medlars are bitter and unpalatable; they only become good to eat after lying on dry straw for a while. ORANGE (Aurantiaceae). - From India and China. This tree, less fashionable in gardens than in the last century, because many shrubs with more varied flowers and leaves are rightly preferred to it, is still one of the most beautiful ornamental plants, and the object of considerable trade along almost the entire Mediterranean coast. The twelve dwarf species, forming one hundred varieties, are still cultivated with the care they deserve. The first orange tree was introduced into France in 1333; in 1500, there was still only one orange tree in the north of France; it was transported from Pamplona, then capital of Navarre, to Chantilly, then to Fontainebleau; in 1684, it was given to the Versailles orangery, where it has remained ever since: This is the Grand Bourbon, or Grand Connétable, or François I. The orange, lemon and all trees in the same family are propagated by seedlings and cuttings. A leaf or a piece of leaf can be rooted. Bigarade orange seedlings are preferred for sowing, as they grow more quickly. - Poire du Commandeur, Perrettes, etc., can be reproduced from seed without much alteration. Lemon seeds can be obtained cheaply from confectioners; they are planted Om, 035 apart in deep terrines of O 16 to Om, 25, lined with good heather; or one by one in small pots. Place terrines and pots in a warm layer. Ordinary care: heat, watering, etc. The seedlings sprout and, eight or ten months later, and sometimes only after two years, produce plants suitable for grafting. They are left to grow in varying degrees of strength, depending on the variety to be grafted. They spend their third year under frame in pots larger than those used the previous year; in the fourth year, they are placed in the open air for the whole of the summer. Orange trees can be grafted from three months to ten years of age; for small trees, mainly Chinese dwarfs, we use Pontoise grafting at Om, 20-30 from the ground; for larger trees, we use scion grafting. Cuttings are only successful for M 9 87e Fig. 59. - Orange tree. Poncires and Cedars. The marcotte technique is all but abandoned. Young orange trees must be changed into new pots every year; later, they are placed in crates which are renewed every two years, then every six or eight years; crates with movable panels, which can be removed separately, make it easier to examine the roots. The best time to repot and re-crate orange trees of all ages and species is the beginning of March. Pruning. - For field-grown orange trees, pruning is limited to a moderate amount every two or three years; the most important thing is to remove greedy branches and try to obtain as much fruit as possible; the flower gardener, on the other hand, wants flowers above all else; if he encourages the formation of fruit-bearing branches, it is with the intention of pinching them off as soon as they bear fruit. In the case of ornamental orange trees, as soon as the fruit has formed, the dead or diseased branches and those that cause confusion are simply cut back in September, in the open air. Every four or five years, the tree is pruned back thoroughly, removing any branches around the heads that would cause shocking irregularities in the overall shape. Orange trees can be rejuvenated very easily; the wood can be brought up to four, five, six and even ten years old; but, to be on the safe side, you should leave a year's interval between this operation and the re-growth. Sick orange trees are placed in very pure compost, even on the tarpaulin of a temperate greenhouse, after having cut off all the damaged parts of the roots and reduced the head by severe pruning on the main branches. Cultivation. - Like other orange-growing plants, orange trees don't like water; one or two wettings are enough for the strongest orange trees over winter. When they arrive in Paris in mid-October, they don't leave the greenhouse until around May 15th; but from mid-April onwards, you need to give them plenty of air, when the atmosphere outside is warm. As soon as they're out, they ask for the soil around their boxes to be ploughed, and for a layer of about Om, 055-80 of fat, well-wetted manure to be added; horse dung on the surface of the boxes prevents settling. Watering, showers on the foliage. The roots are left bare, as they like to be exposed to the direct influence of the air. Not only in Paris, but also in England and Holland, orange trees espaliered along the back wall of a forcing greenhouse produce almost ripe fruit. Bigarades and Limons are used to season meat and fish; small green oranges are candied in brandy. Orange blossom used to sell for 4 francs a pound, but today it's hardly worth more than a franc. It should be picked every other day, and even every day in hot weather, spread out on a dry white cloth and used two or three days later; the dwarf Chinese orange trees are the most highly prized flowers for making orange blossom water. Lemon, citron and lime trees and their varieties are cultivated and cared for in the same way as orange trees. There's no need to describe the orange tree and its fruit. Bigaradiers are lower in stem; their fruit is full of bitter, acidic juice. - Lemon or Citron trees have tapering, flexible, often thorny branches; their oval fruit is filled with an acid, tasty juice. - Citroniers differ from Limoniers in their shorter branches, larger, more warty fruit, firmer, thicker flesh, very good for candying. - Lime trees produce pale-yellow, oval, brownish fruit with a hint of nougat, bland or slightly bitter. - Grapefruits are recognized by their very large, rounded or pear-shaped, greenish fruit, with a more or less sweet taste (1). GRENADER (Myrtaceae). - From Africa; naturalized in southern France, etc. It is an evergreen shrub, with beautiful bright red flowers from July to September, and red, fleshy, watery and refreshing fruit3 23 Fig. 60. - Grenadier. sant. It is propagated from seed, cuttings and strangulated marcots in pots, whose soil must always be kept moist. These marcottes can be weaned at the end of summer. The Grenadier does not like iron; however, it is pruned like the Orange tree; naturally, it would only produce flowers on the tips of the current year's shoots; by pruning, we aim to produce annual sprays strong enough to flower. In winter, the tops of new shoots are pinched off as soon as they reach a certain length. In Paris and the northern départements, Grenadier is grown in crates and brought into the orangery at the start of winter, giving almost ripe fruit. It must be watered often and the soil changed every three years. When espaliered on the back wall of a single-sided greenhouse, it produces fully ripe fruit. Among the main varieties, let's mention the G. with acid fruit, which is very suitable for grafting with other varieties; the G. with white flowers and the G. dwarf with small fruit. VINEYARDS. - We need only refer here to species or varieties whose fruit is intended for table use, and not to those grown in large quantities to make wine. Vines require light, deep, moisture-free soil; a warm, south-facing or east-facing exposure in the Paris climate; pruning and training. - The vegetation of the Vine and that of the Peach are exactly the same; the pruning of these two fruit trees is based on the same principles; its aim is to obtain branches to replace those which, once they have borne fruit, will no longer do so; in the absence of branches capable of providing fertile shoots, there is no hope of a harvest the following year. After breaking up the soil to Om, 50 of its thickness, and loosening and even smoking it, the marcottes are placed at the foot of the wall, in a trench Om, 20-25 deep, with their heads turned towards the wall, Om, 50 apart; they are then 11. covered with earth. These young plants are planted in winter, at a good exposure, so that they can then spread out in horizontal cordons, etc., with the help of wire, trellis, etc. It's also in winter, when there's no frost, when vegetation is suspended, that each shoot is cut back on the two eyes closest to its base; in spring, these eyes will become productive shoots; this is how successive shoots are born on a first spur; if more than two buds grow on each spur, the others are removed, in order to have beautiful, well-stocked bunches. After a few years, the spur, which has in the meantime provided many good shoots, ages and becomes too long; it should be cut back on its lower eye during winter pruning. A well-pruned vine produces flowers in June, at which time the growth of shoots must be severely stopped, as they lengthen, attracting most of the sap and causing "coulure": the flowers don't set seed, and the aborted bunches turn into tendrils. Annular incision, recommended as a remedy against coulure caused by untimely rainfall, and condemned by practice in almost all cases, would be of no use here; destroy useless shoots, and also, by disbudding often renewed, at the right time, destroy all open eyes in false buds above the cutting; Without these precautions, there will be little or no harvest; disbud again after the grapes have formed; cut off the ends of the shoots; your bunches will ripen better and the lower eyes of the shoot, on which the winter pruning must be based, will become stronger. This repeated disbudding during the summer months constitutes summer pruning. Thomery method or horizontal cordon pruning. - The best method of vine training is the Thomery method. The vines are planted at Om 55 from each other, and the cordons are spaced Om, 50 apart. To line a 3-metre-high wall, plant five vines to form five cordons; the first cordon will be at Om, 50 from the ground, and the fifth at Om, 50 from the coping. Prune at two eyes above ground level; the upper eye should extend the stem; the lower eye forms the shoot. Fig. 61. - Thomery vine. The first stock forms the first cordon; the second, the second cordon, etc., each cordon will be 2.70 m long, divided into two arms of 1.35 m each. This length is sometimes exceeded, but this is almost always an inconvenience. All vines are pruned in this way: after pruning on two shoots, as mentioned above, the shoots are palisaded; at the next pruning, the bud of the extension is cut, according to its length and strength; the lateral shoot, resulting from the first pruning, is cut on its lower eye, in order to start a spur or fruit-bearing branch. Once you have reached the height of the cordon, wait until the prolona Fig. 62. - Vertical cordon vine. bud has passed the cordon line, and bend it to the right; pinch it at the top; a false bud will then emerge, which you will leave to grow freely, so that it will provide you with the left arm; you will thus have a more or less regular "T". While you're forming your cords, severely remove any unnecessary production from the stem. At the pruning that follows the formation of the T, you will cut both arms of the cordon on a terminal eye below, to extend them, and you will leave to grow only the top buds, which are necessary to you; choose two of the most vigorous at about Om, 16 one from the other; let them develop in freedom; you palisade the terminal buds in the horizontal direction, and those of the top in the vertical direction, but by pinching them by the top as soon as they arrive at the cordon immediately superior. Do the same for the other arm extensions, stopping them at the last spur as soon as they reach the desired length. Each year, you'll still have to prune the cordon spurs; you'll pinch off the shoot resulting from the first bud, and bring it back to the next pruning on the two eyes located furthest below; you'll pinch off the buds as soon as their growth requires it and, if they bear fruit, one leaf above the second bunch. L 6 - - 3 * 2 4 Q ~ 3 E ~ Fig. 63. - Serpentine vine. The following year, completely remove the farthest shoot at its heel, and prune the other on the two lower shoots. If the spur gets madly carried away, take advantage of the bud closest to the arm and cut back on it. - All pruning is done in the same way, so there's no need to go into too much detail here. Pruning shears are to be preferred to any other instrument. When the grapes are close to maturity, water them with a hand pump, expose them a little more to the direct action of the sun by removing a few leaves, and enclose them in paper or horsehair bags eight or ten days before they reach maturity, if they are to be kept on trellises until the frosts. After picking, place in a dry, well-ventilated place and sprinkle with crushed charcoal or sawdust. Always follow the principles briefly outlined above, and grow vines in vertical rows when the layout of the walls to be covered makes it impossible to use the Thomery method, which is undoubtedly the best. Vines planted in ordinary counter-spaliers or arbors are treated in the same way. We should also mention the serpentine shape, etc. (1). FRAMBOISIER (Rosaceae). - Native, trailing, biennial stems. This shrub grows in stony places, on mountains, and likes shade and cold. The fruit of the cultivated raspberry is highly sought-after for its flavor and refreshing qualities; it is used to prepare syrups, jams, ice creams, etc.; it gives wine a very pleasant taste; when fermented, it produces an alcoholic liquor; the Poles make an excellent mead from it, and the Russians a kind of wine. Raspberry should be given a special place in the garden, as it is always a bad neighbor, crumbling the soil and harming other plants too close to it. It is content with ordinary soil and half-shade exposure, and needs to be moved every four or five years, unless it is given a little fertilizer every autumn. It multiplies by suckers planted from November to March; in February, dead stems that have borne fruit are removed; pruning again from Om, 60 to one meter. Light ploughing.
