EPINE-VINETTE, VINETIER (Berberidae). - Native, forming a bush 2 to 2.5 meters high, and for this reason very often used as an impenetrable hedge; the red, acidic fruit is prized for jams. Preference is given to varieties with seedless fruit, white fruit, large fruit, purple fruit, purple leaves and sweet fruit. Propagate by marcottes, cuttings, offshoots, seeds. Separate, burst and replant in autumn. Wood and leaves, macerated in an alkaline lye, give a yellow dye suitable for coloring woodwork. The fermented berries produce an acidic liquor that deposits a salt similar to tartar. Vinetier flowers in spring, at the same time as Hawthorn. The very irritable stamens snap to the stigma as soon as they are touched with the tip of a needle. FIGUIER (Morées). - Grows naturally in the southern regions of Europe, in Greece, the Levant, etc., and has been cultivated for centuries. Cultivated for centuries, it has produced and still produces varieties whose number we won't even attempt to determine. It lives indefinitely, if not by its trunk, at least by its roots, from which new stems sprout when the old ones are cut. All it needs is a bit of good soil around its base, watering during hot spells, and the removal of dead branches or those too weak to bear fruit; we pinch off the strongest ones to force them to branch out; some gardeners rightly remove the woody bud from a newborn Fig: Other growers stick the tip of a large pin dipped in olive oil into Figs that have reached two-thirds of their normal size: the air introduced in this way, at the very heart of the fruit, activates the conversion of starch into juice. Fig trees are propagated by offshoots, cuttings, grafts and seeds: seeds are only used to obtain new varieties. Flute grafting is preferred to other types of grafting, but is rarely used, because the tree takes cuttings and suckers very well, and there are always many suckers growing from the base. Fig trees planted in staggered rows in the open ground need to be spaced at intervals of about 4 meters. Fig trees easily provide two harvests each year, one in July, the other in September-October; you shouldn't count too much on the second in Paris's climate. New Figs are pleasant and refreshing, but not very nutritious; dried, they are a great resource for the populations of Mediterranean regions. The ancients made a kind of wine from them, called sicyte (from the name of the Fig, in Greek). The juice of the fig, refined for twelve hours after picking, becomes a delicate syrup. Eaten before it has fully ripened, i.e. before it has begun to wilt, the Fig burns the lips and tongue, and causes indigestion. In addition to the huge consumption of fresh Figs at harvest time, many are dried out by placing them on racks in the sun; they are flattened as they lose their moisture. They are emollient, and are used as poultices to resolve tumors, gargles to soothe sore throats, and herbal teas to combat inflammatory diseases. Fig wood is light and spongy, easily soaked in oil and emery, and used by gunsmiths and locksmiths to polish their work. The milky, corrosive juice of the bark destroys warts, curdles milk and forms a sympathetic ink: characters traced on paper with this juice become visible only when exposed to fire. The Fig tree is remarkable for the singularity of its fruiting: the sexual organs are hidden in this fleshy, pear-shaped receptacle (commonly called fruit), pierced at the top by an umbilicus or small hole in the vicinity of which are the male flowers, while the female flowers can be seen lower down; the ancients didn't believe in the existence of these flowers; Later, they recognized the presence of female flowers in the cultivated Fig tree; but, still convinced that well-developed male flowers were lacking in the wild Fig tree, they resorted to caprification, still advantageously practiced today in many parts of the Levant. Olivier observed caprification in particular on the island of Naxos. Here's what he has to say on the subject: "The growers' methods consist in placing on Fig trees that produce only the second Fig, the species known as Fig flowers or first Figs, which appear and ripen a month and a half before the others. The second Figs ripen in August, and continue without interruption well into autumn. The Greeks thread together ten or twelve of these first Figs and hang them in various places on the Fig tree whose fruit they wish to fertilize. "The cynips psenes, a small black insect, also carries out caprification; it penetrates to the heart of the Figs, emerging covered with the dust of the stamens, which it then carries to the other Figs where it deposits its eggs. If you want a certain number of these Fig trees to bear only autumn fruit, take care to detach the summer Figs when they are as big as the tip of your finger, and cauterize the scars with a little lime or very fine plaster to prevent the milk from leaking out: the branch lengthens, the autumn Figs appear earlier and ripen before the frosts. In the Paris climate, only four or five varieties of Fig are grown, giving: the round white Fig, two seasons old, the best around the capital; the angelic yellow F., yellow with small green dots, pink flesh, not very delicate; the large red F. from Bordeaux, round, red, very good; the Madeleine, white lonque, fairly fine; the long red F. from Provence, reddish flesh, mediocre quality; the violet F., good when ripe. MURIERS (Morées). - From Asia Minor, Persia, China, etc. We can't go into the cultivation of the white mulberry for the sericulture industry, as that would take us too far. Everyone knows that its leaves are the food of silkworms; poultry love to eat its fruits, which humans rightly disdain. The main varieties of this tree are: the white Murier with shiny leaves; the M, hybrid; the M. Moretti; the M. de Tartarie; the M. Lou de Chine; M. Gasparin; M. multicaule; M. intermédia. The Red Mulberry, from North America, 12 to 15 meters high, produces a delicious dark-red fruit. The black mulberry produces an oval, almost black-purple fruit with a pleasant, refreshing taste. It is grown in espaliers or in the open air. As with other Mulberries, it needs shelter from strong winds, and soil that is somewhat mixed with rubble. Mulberries reproduce by seed, marcottes and cuttings. They are grafted onto trunks in the form of escutcheons or flutes. They don't need pruning, just the removal of dead branches. Black Mulberry fruit is used to make: 1° a delicious syrup to soothe inflammation of the mouth and back of the mouth; 2° a very fine vinegar. Its juice is used to color wines, syrups, liqueurs and certain jams. Turners value its wood; its bark is used to make rope and paper; its leaves replace those of the White Mulberry as food for silkworms. CHESTNUT (Amentaceae). - The common chestnut is a large, beautiful tree with polygamous flowers; native to southern Europe, it likes light, sandy, deep soil, and does not do well in water. There are several varieties of chestnut: the C. pourtaionne, with large, numerous fruits; the early C. printanière; the C. verte du Limousin, easy to store; the C. exalade, the best of all; the Marron de Lyon, d'Agen, de Luc, the M. d'Aubray; the latter, the largest of all, is very good, containing a single seed in each shell, instead of two or three; it lacks the tough membrane which, in ordinary chestnuts, marks the inner divisions of the fruit. In Corrèze, the main chestnuts grown are: C. hâtive noire, hâtive de mai, hâtive rousse, Huminaux, Huminaux roux, Carrive and Mastronne. The best Chestnuts are stratified before sowing and protected from frost; in February-March, they are planted in loose, unsmoked soil, Om 08 deep, Om 50 apart, in rays separated from each other by an interval of Om 80, traced in a north-south direction. Light ploughing; hoeing, the following summer, and so on until each individual has reached the right size for the nursery; it is then lifted, put in place, and the lateral branches are cut back. Ridging, trimming with thorns, a little straw or manure around the plant. - The second year, FRUITS ARE Grafted into flutes or buds with dormant eyes: pinching, delimbing. Chestnut trees should be placed 15 to 20 meters apart. The fruit is harvested when it falls off naturally. They should be exposed to the sun for a few days, and stored in a dry place. In some countries, chestnuts are dried in special ovens. Chestnut wood lasts a very long time in water, and is used to make hoops, trellises, etc. WALNUT (Juglandées). - Native to Asia. A large, beautiful tree cultivated for its wood, fruit and oil. Requires sandy or even stony soil. Walnuts are stratified before being sown in place at Om, 06 deep; at Om, 08 apart. Ordinary care of nursery plants. Young trees are grafted in slit, flute or escutcheon with growing eye or ring when they are Om, 10 or Om, 15 in circumference and one or 2 meters high. Ordinary precautions recommended for grafting. The following year, planting in Om, 80 to one-meter deep soil. At twenty years of age, the Walnut tree produces a fairly modest product; at sixty, it reaches its maximum fruitfulness; it supplies about half of all the oil consumed in France. Twenty vigorous walnut trees, in full production, on one hectare of land, can be estimated, without exaggeration, at 2,800 to 3,200 francs. When a Walnut tree comes of age, the tips of its branches dry out and must be immediately pruned back from Om, 70 to one meter from the trunk, if it is to continue to bear fruit; new scions soon form a new head. No pruning as such: just remove dead, broken, misplaced or over-vigorous branches that are detrimental to the overall balance. It is also when the Walnut has shown the signs of old age indicated above, that it should be felled to sell it as wood for joinery, etc.; left standing, it deteriorates very quickly. WALNUT (Amentaceae). - The Hazelnut is a shrub with stout, flexible stems; male catkins in groups of three or four at the same point of insertion, appearing towards the end of winter, well before the leaves. We grow: N. franc, with elongated, very delicate fruit; this species has produced two varieties: one with an almond covered by a red skin, the other with a white skin; - N. avelinier, with larger, less elongated fruit, with the following varieties: Rouge ronde, with a semi-hard shell; Rouge de Provence, with a soft shell; - N. à grappes, with very large, very delicate fruit. Hazelnuts ripen and detach from the tree in August-September. They are preserved like walnuts; they are used to make sugared almonds, and produce a more highly prized oil. They become acrid with age. The wood is used to make stiles, trellises, stakes, forks, etc. Multiplication by seed, sprouting and suckering: place Hazel in a northerly position, at some distance from vigorous trees that would smother it under their dense foliage. It requires no cultivation care, PISTACHIUM (Terebinthaceae). - From Syria. This tree is 7 to 8 meters tall, with strong spreading branches; its flowers are of different sexes, placed on separate individuals, which naturally makes it necessary to cultivate male and female individuals to obtain fruit; these fruits are oval, the size of an Olive, russet in color, wrinkled on the outside, containing a sweet, oily kernel called Pistachio. Through cultivation, the Pistachio tree has produced several varieties, all of which yield almonds of varying degrees of fineness, much sought-after by confectioners, etc.; softening, emollient, etc. They can be eaten raw or used to make sweets, ice creams, creams, etc. The most prized pistachios are the Tunis Pistachio, with its delicate green flesh; pork butchers use the Sicilian Pistachio. The Pistachio terebinth is a beautiful Barbary tree on which the Pistachio franco is often grafted, to enable it to withstand cold temperatures of 8 to 10 degrees C. Multiplication of marcottes, seedlings on a warm bed or under a frame; transplanting into pots. For three or four years, ordinary care given to orangery plants. Pistachio trees need light, open soil, south-facing exposure, espaliered, in the Paris climate; they should be placed 4 meters apart, with one male between three or four females, or better still, a male branch grafted in the middle of the branches of each female. The Pistachier-franc often freezes at 6 degrees below zero. SECTION I. - GRAMINES. AGROSTIS. - Agrostis grows, for the most part, among low turf, in arid and sandy soils; sheep are very avid for it. The largest and most remarkable species of Agrostis is Agrostis jouet des vents, common in our wheat fields. The stem reaches up to a meter in height; rough leaves, long and light panicle, with capillary peduncles, finely branched and loaded with numerous small flowers that end with long deciduous edges. It can be used to dye wool green. Agrostis traçante, or Stolonifère, or Trainasse, or Eternue, must be destroyed in well-cultivated land; but, as fodder, it has real advantages thanks to its active vegetation and its ability to keep fresh for a long time in winter. It thrives in cold, damp, peaty soils. Sow at a rate of around 10 kilograms of seed per hectare in March and September. Agrostis d'Amérique (Herd-Grass) is no more difficult than its predecessor when it comes to choosing a site; it is less successful when planted than when sown, and is an advantage12 in the formation of permanent meadows. Rough but nutritious forage. - Sow in March or September; 5 kg of seeds per hectare. Fig. 64. - Oats. - TALL OAT, FROMENTAL. - This oat needs high, not too damp ground, and the proximity of Sainfoin or some other leguminous plant, otherwise it dries out easily. It rebounds very well in regrowth. - 100 kilog. of seeds per hectare. MEADOW BROME. - If you have a chalky soil unfit even for Sainfoin, etc., etc., give it Meadow Brome, it will do well there; it can last up to fifteen or twenty years without any manuring. Bromegrass succeeds as an ornamental grass in soils where other grasses would quickly wither. Meadow FLOWER. - This plant thrives in clay or sandy soils, where it produces up to 1,000 to 1,200 bales per hectare of coarse but nutritious hay. Sow in September, at a rate of 8 kilograms of seed per hectare. PERENNIAL RYEGRASS. - Used as a mowing plant in temporary meadows on slightly cool ground. It grows back under the very teeth of cattle and becomes more vigorous the more it is grazed and trampled. It is sown in spring or autumn, at a rate of 50 kilograms per hectare for pasture; 100 kilograms per hectare for lawns. Rolling, topdressing. Lasts five or six years on average. Italian ryegrass. - Sods less than the previous variety, but recovers better after cutting and offers great continuity of vegetation. It likes humidity. It can give up to 7 or 8,000 kilograms of good dry fodder per hectare, for several years. Sow in autumn or spring, at a rate of 40 or 50 kilog. per hectare, half with red clover. Bailly ryegrass. - Succeeds in stony, half-burned soils, dry in summer, half-submerged in winter; fertilizer oxen feed on it readily. Sow at 20 to 25 kilograms per hectare. SECTION II. - LEGUMES. FÉVEROLLE. - Sow late February to April, broadcast or in rows. Hoeing. Several varieties: F. de Picardie coarse-grained; F. de Lorraine small-grained. 2 hectoliters per hectare. - Very suitable for preparing wheat harvests in clay soils. Ploughed in green, they are a first-rate fertilizer. CULTIVATED CHASTE OR SPANISH LENTIL. - Strong, light soil, but not too damp. Sow in March and April: one and a half hectoliters per hectare. Chickling is cut green as soon as the first pods ripen; it is fed to livestock, mainly sheep. In the south of France, its seeds are used to make a highly prized purée. LUPIN BLANC. - Good pasture for sheep; seed macerated in water for oxen. Sow in our northern provinces around mid-April, at a rate of 10 to 12 decaliters per hectare. Clay and gravel soils. ALFALFA. - Alfalfa needs well-tilled, very clean, deep soil, fertilized in the year preceding sowing, or at the time of sowing, with consumed fertilizers. Alfalfa is sown on barley or oats in spring, or, in summer, on flax, buckwheat or beans; or, in autumn, with spurge or rye. Hoe, lime and harrow at the end of winter. Fight dodder in May or June by cutting alfalfa plants affected by this parasitic plant to the ground; cover with dry straw and burn Fig. 65. - Field vetch. Cattle should never be allowed to graze on alfalfa still laden with dew or rain. 20 kilograms of seed per hectare. GREY PEA, LAMB PEA, EWE PEA, STRAWBERRY. - This annual plant is particularly successful on fallow land; the early varieties are sown in March; the P. gris d'hiver variety is sown in autumn at a rate of 25 to 26 decaliters of seed per hectare. Good fodder, especially for sheep. Land sown with grey pea should be smoked if it is to be used for wheat. SAINFOIN, ESPARCETTE, BURGUNDY. - Sandy, chalky soils suit it and it improves them. Sow in spring or autumn at a rate of 35 to 45 decalitres per hectare. Sainfoin à deux coupes produces a very abundant second cut, whereas ordinary Sainfoin gives only a rather weak regain; but it requires a less poor soil and a more abundant sowing: about 46 decaliters per hectare. COMMON VETCH. - It can be sown until June on strong, cool soils; its winter variety can be sown in autumn at a rate of 24 to 26 decaliters per hectare, in association with Rye or Oats. This fodder is cut as soon as it flowers and fed to livestock, but only after it has dried out and wilted. SECTION III. - ROOT FORAGES. CAVALIER CAULI (Cruciferae). - Very popular in our western provinces; rich in leaves. - Caulet de Flandre differs from the previous variety in its red hue. - C. Branchu or C. Mille-Têtes, less tall than Chou cavalier, but well furnished with vigorous shoots, is very useful for fertilizing oxen. Once the leaves have been harvested, C. moellier can be fed to livestock, cut into strips. - Perennial C. or C. de bouture is resistant to severe cold; its stems elongate, bend and root. - C. de Lannilis, with its large, blond leaves, provides good fodder for horned animals when cut into strips after the leaves have been harvested. It can withstand the winters of our northern departments. - Northern green kale differs from the preceding species in the way its leaves are cut. It withstands the harshest winters in our climates. In general, cabbages need strong, well-smoked soil. The larger species are sown from March to August in nurseries; set out in April, May, September, and in 12. rows spaced at one meter to Om, 65 apart. Hoeing, weeding. 200 to 250 gr. of seeds for a one-hectare plant. Turnip cabbage, Turneps cabbage, Lapland cabbage. - Sow in April at a rate of one and a half to 2 kilograms of seed per hectare, if sowing in the field. Resists the rigors of cold. Rutabaga cabbage, Swedish turnip. - Similar to Turnip Cabbage. Sow in rows spaced Om, 70 to Om, 80 apart. Can withstand frosts, but does not like humidity. Cabbage-Colza. - Broadcast on wheat stubble, turned over as soon as harvested; 4 to 5 kilograms of seed per hectare. Good green forage in early spring. Cultivation for seed requires more care. Sow on a bed from mid-July to the end of August, weed, transplant about two months later, in well-smoked soil, in rows spaced Om, 32. Replanting. Hoeing. Sometimes broadcast sowing in place. C. de mars is sown in March and April and produces ripe seed that summer. BETTERAVE CHAMPÊTRE, DISETTE (Chénopodées). - Biennial plant; needs soil loosened by one or two deep ploughings; sown broadcast or in rays, from mid-March to May; thin out so that plants are Om, 30 to Om, 50 apart, depending on soil quality. Weeding; hoeing. Seedlings are also sown in nurseries, to be planted when the root is the size of a finger, taking care not to let the tip fold up at the bottom of the hole. The roots are harvested in November and stored in a frost-free cellar. For sowing in rows, about 3 kilograms of seed are needed per hectare; for broadcast sowing, 4 to 5 kilograms; for transplanting, 2 to 2.5 kilograms are sufficient to provide the planting material needed for one hectare. As main sub-varieties, let's mention the Camel Disette; its length is about twice its diameter, with veined flesh. - D. corne de vache (cow's horn) with a very long root, curved and partly out of the ground, CARROT (Umbelliferae). - One of the best forage roots: it needs soil amended with well-consumed fertilizers. Sow from March to May and even June, at a rate of 4 to 5 kilograms per hectare, broadcast and preferably in rays. Light harrowing, rolling, weeding and hoeing. Harvesting takes place towards the end of November or in December. Store in cellars, trenches or frost-free pits. Among the many varieties grown for livestock, we recommend: jaune d'Achicourt, grosse blanche de Breteuil, blanche à collet vert, very productive, blanche des Vosges, whose large, clean roots are easy to store, NAVETS and RAVES (Crucifers). - Great winter resource. Sow late June to early August, broadcast or in rows. Weeding and hoeing, light, dry soil; 2 or 3 kilograms of seed per hectare. Among the best Raves are: Rave d'Auvergne à collet rouge. - Rabioule or Rave du Limousin, improperly called Turneps. - Rave du Norfolk, very good, quite late. - Turneps hâtif de Hollande, quick-growing and very strong-rooted. ALPISTE, Long millet, Birdseed, Canary seed (Grasses). - Good fodder for horses and horned animals. Sow in April in well-smoked soil. OAT-POTATO or Potato Oats. - Good quality, but a little prone to smut. Georgia oats. - Very early and very good for livestock; can be cut green first and left to seed on second growth. Siberian early oats. - Quite similar to the previous variety, but more vigorous. Joannette oats. - Gives good quality black grain, but must be harvested before full maturity. Brie black oats. - Short grain, swollen, early, good quality. Winter oats. - Straw and grain production, early, more successful in western France than in the north and east. Sow in September or January, preferably on dry land. ORDINARY FRUIT, barbless. - Its main varieties are: Blé blanc de Flandre, very beautiful and very productive, with white ears, white grain, oblong and slender. - Blé de Hongrie, white ear, narrow, white grain, very short. - Blé Touzelle or Tuzelle blanche de Provence, white grain, oblong. - B. Richelle white from Naples, very fine white grain. - Blé d'Odessa (Odessa wheat), barbless, red ear, fine straw and bent at the bottom. Sow in autumn or spring. - Blue wheat, hardy, productive, early. Sought-after for meslin and as a March wheat. - Talavera wheat, from Bellevue, with loose white ears. Sow in February or March. - Blé du Cap sans barbes, frankly from March, large grain, tight ear. - Blé de Saumur, a good sub-variety of Blé d'hiver ordinaire, with nourished ears, reddish grain, very white straw and higher than that of ordinary wheat, - Hardy red wheat, good for sowing on cleared clover, - Red March wheat, no beards, long ears. - Sicilian March wheat, grain Fig. 66. - Red, hard wheat of ordinary quality. - Hairy wheat from Crete, red, hairy head, light yellow grain. Sown in spring in Paris climate. Ordinary wheat, bearded. - Main varieties: Saissette de Provence, the best of the Bearded Wheats and perhaps of all the Wheats. - Bearded wheat from Naples, with beautiful elongated grain. - Caucasian wheat, bearded, elongated grain, reddish, hard, heavy. Sow in February. - Cape wheat, March wheat with very long ears, yellowish grain, heavy, good quality. - Ordinary bearded March wheat, early, good quality, frankly March. - Bearded March wheat from Tuscany, which provides the beautiful, fine straw used to make hats. - Victoria wheat, short straw, yellow ear, reddish grain, good quality. - Hedgehog wheat, short grain, small, reddish, heavy, good quality; spring and fall. - March wheat, bearded red, very early, therefore good for late sowing. Blé renflé, Poulard, gros Blé. - Main varieties: Nonette, semi-fine straw, coarse grain; autumn wheat. - Common Rivet wheat, blue ear, very tight, golden yellow grain, medium size, good quality, very rustic and very productive. - Black Petanielle wheat, large, almost round grain, long, hard, strong straw, very productive. - Miracle or Smyrna wheat, with stalked ears, large, rounded, yellowish-white grain; full, hard straw; needs good soil, fears severe cold and degenerates easily. Polish wheat or Russian rye, with large, long ears, very strong bales, elongated, hard, almost transparent grain, good quality, but not very abundant. Sow in spring, or better in autumn. Hard or African wheat. - Main varieties: Trimenia barbu from Sicily, abundant grain, fine straw, but a little hard; needs rich soil. - Aubaine rouge, very similar to the above. Sow in February or autumn. Barbless spelt, very good for fodder; very rustic, successful in cold, mountainous countries. - White bearded spelt, very early, very vigorous, good for spring and autumn sowing. White starch or March spelt. Sow in spring. Engrain commun or Petite Epeautre hardy, successful on siliceous soils. Sow in spring and autumn. Double grain, with rough ears and soft, unglazed grain. Sow in spring and autumn in chalky soils. Blés de mars, Blés de mai. - Blés de mars are early wheat varieties that fear the rigors of winter. Strictly speaking, there are no wheat varieties that, when sown in May, give an assured and complete harvest in the same year. CORN or TURKEY WHEAT, INDIA WHEAT, ZEA. - After rice and wheat, corn is the most useful of all grasses, and also one of the most universally cultivated. It can be sown on fallow land every two or three weeks, from May to mid-July, and will provide excellent green fodder for three or four months. Lines at Om, 55 or Om, 65 apart. Hoeing and weeding. Cut when the male flowers are showing their tips. Dry corn is a useful winter forage. It is estimated, without exaggeration, that the benefits of growing Corn are 50 per 100. SPRING BARLEY OR SPRING BARLEY. - After two-row bare barley, this is the earliest barley. Sows in May and sometimes June. Naked square barley, Celeste barley, Six-row barley. - Highly productive; grain less likely to blacken with rain; straw coarse, but soft and very good as fodder. Good soil. Sow in first spring. Guimalaye or Namto barley. - Short, rounded, greenish grain; short, firm, coarse straw. SARRASIN, BLACK WHEAT, BUCAIL, CARABIN (Polygonaceae). - Gives an abundant grain which man does not disdain and which chickens, pigeons, pigs, horses, etc., feed on very willingly. Sow for CEREALS. seed, from mid-June to early July, at a rate of half a hectoliter of seed per hectare; sow to bury as excellent fertilizer; one hectoliter per hectare. Poor, cold soils. Harvest early to avoid shattering. MARCH RYE. - Sown in March; fairly short but fine straw; very good grain. St. John's rye. - Northern rye with longer straw and ears, with smaller grains than Autumn rye, of which it is a variety. Cut as green fodder in autumn, or left to graze until late winter, to be harvested as grain the following summer. SORGHUM, MILLET. - Grain for chickens and pigeons; stalks provide good green fodder. A late-planting variety that is difficult to select. Sweet sorghum. - Stems 2 to 3 meters high, leaves smooth, flexuous and drooping, panicles of flowers first green, then purple, then crimson, seeds black and shiny. Same cultivation care as for Corn END OF PART ONE. GARDENER'S CALENDAR (1) January. - Fine days are rare at this time of year, under the foggy, cold skies of northern countries; however, you can have : 1° in the open ground, sweet coltsfoot, black hellebore or Christmas rose, Japanese calycanthus, tin laurel, common laurel, red and white laurel or Bois-Gentil, Alpine Iberid; 2° in greenhouses, a few Geraniums, Narcisse de Constantinople, Tulipe Duc de Thol, Clérodendrons, Ruellie à fleurs bleues, Begonias, a few hardy Orchids, some Cape Heather, Richardia, Canna, a few varieties of Rose du Bengale, a few early Camellias. In your hot greenhouses, place: Narcissus, Hyacinths, Daffodils, Cinereas, Chinese Primroses, Parma Violets, Frutescent Chrysanthemums, Lilacs, etc.., (1) This calendar was drawn up for the climate of Paris; it must therefore be modified if applied to the south of France; you must also take into account the changes in temperature that occur every year, and bring forward or postpone sowing, depending on whether the season is early or late. 19 transplant them, lining them with gravel, rubble, coarse gravel, fine gravel or river sand; destroy worn-out lawns with deep ploughing, and prepare the places where you will plant your Rosages, Bengals and Heather in March, in clumps or beds. From time to time, remove the litter from your herbaceous plants, but don't expose them to the still frequent frosts. February. - In the open ground, you'll have : Daisies, a few sweet-smelling violets, snowdrops, herbaceous heather, hill daphne, spring saffron and its many varieties, helleborine, small periwinkle, rosemary, gardeners' corchorus, hepatica and so on. In greenhouses, Jasmine, Peonies, Purple Cinerea, Camellia, variegated Oxalis, several Corréas, Ethiopian Richardia. Remove dead wood and harmful branches; plough your groves and flowerbeds, using a forked hoe rather than a spade, for fear of cutting the roots; sow your lawns; line the pits intended for your March rosages with heather soil; your flowerbeds will receive Julienne, Giroflée, Soleil vivace, Astère, Poetic Carnation and a few other perennials and biennials that you won't have to worry about in autumn. If you're no longer afraid of heavy frosts, plant your borders with Sage, Lavender, Hyssop, Daisy, Mignardise, Boxwood, etc., and place them in borders or posts. If the sun shines and heats up a little, carefully open some of your frames and renew the air in your greenhouses; hoe the soil in your pots, water, remove dead leaves; wage war on insects. March. - In the open ground you'll have: Sorbs, a few Spireas, some Thorns and Alisiers, several heathers, the dwarf Almond tree, the satin Almond tree, the A. Georgia, Andromeda, Tulips, Narcissus, 1ris, Hornbeam, Primrose, Spring Cynoglossa, Bear's Ear, Spring Orobium, Saffron, Arbouria, Leucoïum, Iberides, Double-flowered Populus, Sylvie and Apennine Anemones, and so on. Thanks to the forced heat, greenhouses and frames will easily give you several Acacias, Roses, Diosmas, Carmantines, Indigotier austral, Heather, Alisier de la Chine, Sparmannia d'Afrique, Camellias, etc., etc... Complete all your ploughing and planting of trees, shrubs and perennials, reserving only green and resinous trees for April. Rake and sand your driveways, keep an eye on your lawns, and follow up your autonine seedlings with borders, clumps or beds of annual flowers such as: Larkspur, Reseda, Poppy, Poppy, Mahon's Wallflower, etc. Sow on beds: Quarantaines, Zinnies élégantes, Balsamines; lay Dahlia tubers bare on a bed, cover them with a frame; when the heat brings out the buds, divide the clumps and put them in pots, but continue to keep them on a bed or at least under a frame; remove your diseased orange trees and other plants and revive their roots by laying them bare in the soil of the bed. Start taking cuttings under cloche and marcottes; protect your greenhouses with a light canvas, where young shoots have to fear the sometimes scorching rays of the March sun. April. - In the open ground : Bear's Ears, Primroses, Anemones, Narcissus, some Tulips, Corydalis, Bulbous Fumitory, European and Asian Trollius, Pansies, Chinese Glycine, Paulownia, False Ebony, Lilacs, Double-blooming Cherry and Cherry Trees, Cytises, Garden Coronilla; in greenhouses and under frames, Rhododendrons in trees, Indian Azaleas and the rest of the Camellias, many of which were in flower the previous month, wage war on caterpillars and other insect pests; clean your trees and shrubs; mow your lawns; plough your flowerbeds and beds. Your field-sown annuals are in full bloom; save your châsssis for sowing tropical seeds, or for weak or diseased plants. Cut under cloche, graft on approach, etc., give air to the greenhouses; multiply your watering as the heat increases and vegetation develops. May. - It would be superfluous to name all the many and varied flowers that have given this month its name: Bengal Roses, May Hazelnuts or Cinnamon, display their beauty and herald the thousands of Roses that will soon be in full bloom. From May 10 to 15, put your Dahlias in place, if you no longer fear frost; hoe your flowerbeds and beds; remove weeds from your lawns and mow them. Carry out your repottings instead of postponing them until autumn; take cuttings under cloches and make herbaceous, English and approach grafts. Towards the middle of the month, take out orange trees, and, at the end of the month, all orangery plants. Clear your greenhouses of their frames; place your heathers facing east, but keep them out of direct sunlight; provide soft light for Protées and Diosmas. June. - Roses are opening and spreading their fragrance; Dahlias are blooming. Flowers everywhere that it would be pointless to enumerate. Water, hoe; dry out your paths; mow your lawns; stake Asters, Primrose Roses, Dahlias, etc., stiles for Cobeas, Convolvulus, Clematis and other climbers. Leave weak or diseased plants in your unoccupied beds, bare or in pots, for varying lengths of time. Protect plants kept in greenhouses from excessive sunlight. Take cuttings under cloche and approach grafting, as in the previous month. July. - If June brings with it the most beautiful and fragrant Roses, July still has Bengale-Bourbon and Noisette, the King's Rose, Perpetual Roses, Hopper Roses, Dahlias, etc., not to mention many foreign shrubs to which the heat of this month is favorable. Raking, pruning, watering, autumn flower nurseries, marcotting carnations, separating onion cloves - there's plenty to keep you busy. Shelter your chests, frames, etc., keep a layer for sowing seeds in warm countries, and for your sick or delicate greenhouse plants. Re-tan your layers if you weren't able to do so in June. August. - We continue to enjoy Perpetual Roses, King Roses, Bengal Roses, etc., Asters, Dahlias, etc., to which we add Petunias, Verbena, Clematis, Phlox, Perennial Sun, Matricaria, Calf's Mufles, Julibrizin, Japanese Privet, Constantinople Acacia, Chinese and Virginia Bignones. In temperate greenhouses, Gesneria, ŒEchmea, Tillandsia, Stéphanotis, Passiflora, Fuchsia, Polygala Cordata, Metrosideros, Melaleuca, Lagerstrœmia, etc., etc., shine. At the beginning of this month, if you haven't been able to do so in July, lift all your autumn annuals into rootballs and put them in place: marigolds, daisy queens, balsamines, etc. Sow in place: Poppies, Poppy, Bluets, Adonis, Larkspur, Thlaspis, etc.; re-pot plants whose pots have remained buried during the summer, re-cutting roots and branches that have become too long; if you leave these plants in the shade, their vegetation will be re-established when you return them to the greenhouse or orangery. September. - This month's most beautiful and abundant flowers include: Cinereas, Amaryllis-Belladonna, Autumn Colchicum, Sarretes, Goldenrod, Silphium, Coreopsis and other radiata; always Asters, Dahlias, Oenotheras, Petunjas, Balsamines, Queen Daisies, Indian Carnations, Clarkias and so on. Same care and cleanliness as in previous months; in addition, watch the seeds and harvest them as they ripen; sow Quarantaines for transplanting on soil or in crates; sow Renoncules, Anémones, etc. If you need to make considerable changes to your gardens, choose this time of year: the soil transported will settle sufficiently before the next planting. Towards the middle of the month, you'll bring in your warm greenhouse plants, and finish repotting your temperate greenhouse and orangery plants; moderate arrangements in the morning rather than in the evening. Replace panels on tarpaulins, frames and temperate greenhouses at the end of the month. October. - You don't have to say goodbye to flowers just yet, because you've still got them: Roses de Berigale, Noisette; Muscades; Scarlet sage; Dahlias; Late gladioli; Asters; Phlox; Datura; Erica; Zinnia; Menziesia polyfolia; Hélianthus; XimenesiaEnceloïdes; Cosmos bipenné; Capucine; Hibiscus speciosus, militaris, roseus, palustris; Œnothera tetraptera, odorata; Tamarix gallica; Symphoricarpus; Chélone campanulata, rosea, glabra; Véronica præalta; Plumbago; Fuschia; Begonia discolor: - if you remembered to put these plants in the ground in May. Carry out your planting and planting out, finish your paths, collect dead leaves, remove the stems of perennials that no longer flower: Balsamines, Indian Carnations, Dyer's Coréopsis, Queen Daisies; in your cleaned, ploughed and smoked flowerbeds, plant, without delay, Scabieuses, Campanulas, Greek Valerian, Poetic Carnations, Calf's Mufles, etc., which will give you their flowers in spring, which will give you their flowers in spring; bring in large Giroflées before the frosts. Around October 15th, orange trees and orangery plants will be brought in and arranged so that those plants that do not need light (rose laurels, orange trees) form the back of your greenhouses, leaving room in front of them for evergreen, woody, herbaceous plants that like air and daylight; plough pots and crates, water moderately; graft in slits and cut Camellias under cloches, unless you reserve this operation for spring. Remake your layers of tannin in the hot greenhouses, giving them a thick bed of new manure or leaves as a base, and letting them build up their great fire and settle properly. Push the pots right up to the edge into this tannin, the larger ones at the back, the smaller ones at the front. November - If flowers are now becoming increasingly scarce, look after the ones you have left all the better: Bengal roses, Indian Chrysanthemums capable of withstanding four or five degrees of cold, the latter, potted, will last a long time in the temperate greenhouse. Collect dead leaves to cover delicate plants and make compost. Replace wilted annuals with perennials; plant 1° most of your ornamental trees, reserving resinous trees and heather shrubs for spring; 2° from November 1st to 15th, Narcissus, Hyacinth and Tulip Onions, etc. Monitor the temperature of your greenhouses and renew the air carefully. Water and keep clean. December. - Despite the cold, you will still be able to have, at the foot of the walls, Violette odorante; in sheltered places, Hellébore noir or Rose de Noël, Chimonanthus flagrans and its variety, Jasmin à fleur jaune; under frames come: Violette de Parme, Tulipe duc de Thel, Jacinthes blanches; in greenhouses: Cyclamens, Narcisses, Jacinthes, if you have taken care to plant them in October. Ripping for new lawns, repairing paths, pruning. Maintain the temperature of hot greenhouses at 10 to 20 degrees above zero, renew the air, and water around midday: if you squirt the water on your plants in the form of rain, you'll get a steam that's favorable to the development of vegetation. The same temperature applies to the pineapple greenhouse, where you can also place pots of Strawberries of the Four Seasons, Comte de Paris and Princesse Royale on the shelves. All you have to do is not let the thermometer fall below O degrees, but let the sun shine in at 5 to 10 degrees, and take advantage of the moment when it shines to renew the air and expel humidity by carefully opening the frames and windows, which you will close again before nightfall. There's no need to water large boxes of orange, pomegranate and rose-laurel in winter. Cover and mat the glass roof and the front of the windows, day and especially night, to prevent frost. Parterre. - Borders. - Lawns. - Assortment of flowers of various colors; laws to be observed in this respect. - Bedding plants, Fancy plants, Collection plants. - Parterre accessories. The Parterre or florist's garden is particularly intended for outdoor, hardy or semi-hardy plants, worthy of cultivation for their fragrance, their beauty, the brilliant shine of their corollas. The Parterre should never be too large; otherwise, the eye would not be able to take in the whole and the main details at the same time. Place it close to your home, so that it can be seen from the windows of your apartments. In northern countries, where the sky is often dark and rainy, you'll prefer the parterre to face south, south-east or south-west; never north. The proximity of tall trees, high walls and monumental greenhouses is detrimental to the parterre; at most, leave a few clumps of trees near the parterre to shelter it from the cold winds. In southern climates, follow instructions that are in many ways contrary to the above; remember, as a general rule, that it's enough for flowers to receive the sun's rays for a few hours each morning and evening. Rainwater should not be allowed to remain in the flower garden; the best soil is an average soil composed of roughly equal parts of ar ́ N C AHStI alllolan E 18 * M VIEI Fig. 1. - Parterre. gileous substance, calcareous substance and siliceous substance; this soil should be very loose and not subject to hardening or cracking in the sun. Use guano and odorless fertilizers. For very special crops, you'll need to set aside squares where the soil will offer the most suitable elements for the flowers you want to plant; primroses need 13. clay soil; Kalmias and Rosages need heather soil; bulbous plants need silica, etc. Sometimes the Parterre is flat throughout, sometimes it offers artistic reliefs rising from Om, 10 to Om, 15 and even to Om, 25 above the alleys; these reliefs must form gentle, rounded slopes from their perimeter to the center. Sometimes the parterre is shaped like a square, rectangle, trapezium, etc., sometimes it presents an irregular figure bounded by curved lines, with islands of flowers amid green lawns; unless you need to preserve the very style of an antique garden or constructions of some kind, avoid stiff, purely geometric shapes. Straight or curved paths determine the design of the parterre; in the largest gardens, they are rarely more than 4 meters wide; in the smallest, one meter is enough; they are sanded or covered with a layer of gravel one centimeter thick. For edging paths and walkways, we recommend: 1° Boxwood, planted in rooted splinters in a single row, 7 to 8 centimetres apart; allow it to reach an average height of around Om, 12 to Om, 18 by 6 to 8 centimetres thick, or even more, depending on the size of the parterre, the relief of the compartments to be bordered, etc.; 2° Thyme, planted in a single row, 7 to 8 centimetres apart.2° Thyme, large and small Periwinkle, double-flowered Daisy, Strawberry, Olympus Grass, Ivy, etc. Dry borders are those made of wood, iron or brick. Wooden edgings are usually made from thumb-sized strips of Oak, Beech or Hornbeam. Bricks should be well-fired, very hard, Om.25 by Om.60 c. long by Om.07 thick. Iron borders have the disadvantage of oxidizing rather quickly, despite the layers of minium. Lawns are made of a common grass that is allowed to grow quite high, and to which less care is given than to Turf; the latter is better suited to gardens of little extent. Never cut your lawns or turfs abruptly, by your flowerbeds whose true place is at the sides or towards the middle of the carpet of greenery, but on condition that you do not destroy the symmetry and overall view. You can establish your lawns by sowing or transplanting. Sowing is done by broadcasting on soil that has been well loosened, levelled and smoked; then you tread and water. Among our common grasses, preference is given to perennial species, which grow tall and fill out the ground well. Meadow grass (Poa pratensis), Timothy (Phleum pratense), Cynosure (Cynosurus cristatus), Sweet vernal grass (Anthoxanthum odoratum), Sheep's fescue (Festuca ovina), Perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne), Bentgrass (Agrostis canina and A. vulgaris); but we rightly recommend rejecting Cocksfoot (Dactylis glomerata), Bromes (Bromus erectus), etc.., Hoes (Holcus mollis and H. lanatus), large oats (Avena elatior). For transplanting, we take lawn tiles from the meadow and lay them, with all the soil adhering to their roots, on previously loosened and smoked soil; we carefully adjust them, roll them and water them. There are two main ways of distributing plants in a parterre: 1° Mixing species; 2° Growing or bedding flowers of the same species. In the mixing mode, remember that a parterre does not admit tall trees, and that simple shrubs two to three meters high are generally better on the sides than inside the compartments; a plant that is too large must not mask a smaller plant. The matching of flower colors requires special attention and a taste that nature inspires, but which the rules can leave a little guesswork. Especially in France, the harmonic arrangement of flowers is far too neglected in terms of color. The simple or primitive colors from which all the others are formed are red, yellow and blue. If you combine them two by two, they will give you orange from red and yellow, green from yellow and blue, violet from blue and red; mixing primitive colors two by two gives an unlimited number of intermediate shades between the darkest and the lightest. The complementary color is that which, added either to a combination of colors or to a single color, reconstitutes the triad of elementary colors; thus orange, derived from red and yellow, is complementary to blue; violet, composed of red and blue, is complementary to yellow; green, composed of blue and yellow, is complementary to red. Certain colors enhance, accentuate and nuance each other through their proximity. As a general rule, remember that: 1° All simple colors contrast happily with each other; 2° The binary combination of compound colors, presenting in each group the combination of three simple colors, is pleasing to the eye; for example, violet (red and blue) blends very well with orange (red and yellow) and green (yellow and blue); 3° Colors that are complementary to each other offer very attractive contrasts: blue and orange, violet and yellow; 4° White lends great relief to all colors, simple or compound, and softens the clash between colors that are naturally opposed to each other: red and orange, violet and red, blue and violet; 5° Black weakens the effect of all colors placed in too direct contact with it, with the exception of white; 6° Never bring simple colors closer to the composite colors in whose formation they enter; yellow contrasts unfavorably with orange (yellow and red) and with green (yellow and blue); blue with violet (red and blue) and with green (yellow and blue); red with orange (yellow and red) and with green (yellow and blue), and so on., etc. We've often seen binary and ternary combinations try out in flower gardens, rarely quaternary ones. The best binary combinations are obtained: 1° by contrasting white with all single or compound colors: bright yellow and white, orange and white, violet and white, green and white, pink or red and white, light blue or dark blue and white; - 2° by using single colors together or with their complementaries: yellow and blue, yellow and violet, orange and blue, red and yellow, red and blue, etc. Ternary combinations, where white almost always enters, are more varied than binary combinations: - white, yellow, blue and white; - white, yellow, green and white; - white, orange, white and violet; - white, orange, green and white; - white, red, blue and white; or white, red, white and blue; - yellow, red, white and yellow; - blue, orange, blue and white; or white, orange, white and blue, etc., etc., etc. The main bedding plants are: Balisiers or Canna. Parterre accessories are the various things that, without being necessary or really part of the garden, add to its pleasure or facilitate its upkeep, such as water fountains and basins, nurseries, benches, boxed trees, vases, fences, and so on. Don't make your fountain spin a tin dervish, or your pond carry badly-painted vessels: a water lily and goldfish will adorn it much better; no gilding on the seats; let them offer the means to stretch out comfortably and rest. As far as possible, and with a few exceptions established in practice, allow the trees in your boxes to grow naturally; it's enough for them to be cramped at the base, let the head spread out freely. Antique-shaped white vases are preferable to ugly pots laden with fantastic flowers which, even if well-painted, have too formidable rivals in your parterre itself. The nursery should be kept out of sight of visitors; it should contain all the utensils and equipment necessary for sowing, bedding, cuttings, grafting, etc., etc., etc., etc. It must be kept extremely clean. Landscaped gardens; their composition. - Rivers, streams, lakes, water features. - Paths and driveways. - Cuttings, embankments, artificial valleys and hills. - Tree and shrub distribution, etc. Fashion has caused the composition, arrangement and organization of landscape gardens to vary from century to century. If, in this area as in all others, beauty did not have its fixed rules, the simplest notions of taste and harmony would have been lost; On the one hand, French gardens sinned by an excess of symmetry; on the other, English gardens displayed a disorder that was not always an effect of art, nor an imitation of nature; moreover, this very imitation must have as its object only the beautiful and not the monstrous, the strange or the grotesque. Don't place, over an area of a few meters at the entrance to a middle-class house, confused masses of stones piled one on top of the other, under the pretext of representing rocks; don't dig under the feet of the over-confident walker holes of varying widths and depths which, in your opinion, will represent precipices, etc. Our fathers didn't admit the use of the word "precipice" in the French language. Our forefathers were accustomed to straight lines and flat surfaces; large areas of rough terrain were converted into terraces with rigorously geometric contours. Any tree, no matter how precious or ancient, disappeared if it had the misfortune to find itself out of Fig. 2. - Landscaped garden. alignment; in a word, our fathers proceeded in the construction of their vast landscaped gardens in a manner analogous to that of an all-too-famous modern aedile, whose love for the inflexible straight line will be attested to in future ages by the new Paris; but the Lenôtre, etc., thanks to their good taste, their skill and their ability to adapt to the new situation, were able to create their own landscaped gardens, thanks to their good taste and grandiose conceptions, created true marvels by means of processes that were in themselves ungrateful: the Gardens of Versailles, for example. Today, we prefer the picturesque effect to everything else; we're trying to get closer to nature; that's all well and good, but we mustn't conceal from ourselves the difficulties to be overcome. First of all, it's important to know all the details, all the accidents of the terrain on which you're operating; the general effect of the site, its natural resources, the objects to be preserved, their relationships with each other, deserve a great deal of attention. You draw your plan on paper, then on the ground. Milestones and stakes indicate the artificial hills and valleys, large and small elevations, the place of woods, copses and massifs; no steep, abrupt lines, but curves joined by gentle transitions; the capital S and half-circumferences are overused; good taste and the accuracy of the eye often replace the compass, an instrument that is always a little pretentious. If you have wide watercourses, trace or boldly modify their edges; don't let the detours be too close together; for narrow watercourses, you can multiply their sinuosities. Water is essential to a landscape garden; it gives it life. If your artificial river is 2 or 3 meters wide, you'll do well to divide it into two more or less equal arms, so as to form a small oblong island well planted with flowers, with a few rocks crowned with green trees or shrubs, with branches hanging down into the water: weeping willow, etc., etc... Artificial water features should be laid out in such a way that at least one of their edges is uncovered, allowing the view to extend over the entire body of water. On the shores, plant tall, isolated trees and low shrubs here and there. If the shores are too steep, boaters will be deprived of any perspective. There should always be a sufficient difference in level between the pond and the water outlet, so that the pond can be easily emptied when it's time to clear the water or fish in large quantities. In parts of the garden where you can easily bring in water, in basins or in tubs full of water, grow: Arundo donax; Typha; Lythrum; Butomus umbellatus; Spirea venusta and ulmaria; Epilobium spicatum rose and blane; PIris pseudo-acorus; Myosotis palustris; Caltha palustris flore pleno, etc.; Salix schubertea; Caltha palustris flore pleno.Salix schubertea; Cordamine pratensis flore pleno; Alisma flotant; Fléchière aquatique; Trèfle d'eau; Macre flottante; Nénuphar blanc, etc. If, with the help of a few millstones or other stones that retain moisture easily, you create an artificial rock, plant in the interstices : Cynoglossumomphalodes; Pulmonaria Virginica; Phalaris rubané, Marsh marigold; Trollius, Alyssum-saxatile; Crucianella odorata et stylosa; Alchemilla alpina; Doronicum caucasium; Ononis natrix; Rubus speciosus; Primula veris; Hepatics, Dianthus deltoides; Gypsophylla striata; Sedum sempervivum, Saxifraga géranoïdes; Lotus corniculatus flore pleno; Thymus serpillum; Thymus tomentosum; Narcissus poeticus; N. pseudonarcissus; Veronica-prostrata, etc. Populate your lakes and ponds with carp, tench, barbel, etc., and put goldfish in small basins. Bridges are built of wood, iron or stone; sometimes they are flat, sometimes domed; they must always retain a rustic appearance; ashlar abutments are preferable. Suspension bridges are becoming increasingly fashionable, but their elegance often detracts from their solidity. Alleys should not be so tortuous as to tire the walker; their edges should always be parallel to each other, whatever the shape and multiplicity of the circuits. Make the paths intended for cars 5 to 8 meters wide, and don't make them too winding; pedestrians need to be able to see crews and riders coming from afar. It's not in a landscaped garden that a coachman should have to show his skill at turning obstacles. Make pedestrian walkways 2.50 to 4 meters wide, so that several people can walk abreast, chatting, instead of being obliged to follow one another, as in a procession. A width of Om, 90 to 1m, 30 is sufficient for paths. If you can establish or preserve a few sunken paths, never incline their side slopes by more than 45 degrees; cover these slopes with Honeysuckle, Clematis and other shrubs or saplings with sarment stems; here and there, plant Hawthorn, Blackthorn, Dogwood. In general, remember: 1° don't over-multiply your paths, otherwise your tree beds and copses will look too thin and fragmented, and the picturesque effect will be destroyed; 2° don't let your paths end at the garden fences; 3° that the paths leading to the property's exit gates should only reach them via skilfully designed detours, so that the exits can only be seen from a short distance away; otherwise you'll destroy the illusion you've sought to create about the real extent of your garden. Once the layout has been completed, the earth and stones removed for the digging of lakes, basins, streams, etc., are immediately used for the artificial elevations, valleys, hills, etc. Assign a place in advance for the earth and stones to be removed. Assign a place for these materials in advance; organize the dumper service well, for the digging of bodies of water and valleys; always start by clearing a sufficient space for the dumper to circulate. When digging an artificial valley, proceed with transverse trenches in the direction of the width of the planned valley, rather than with random trenches; this way, you can easily follow the irregularities of the open line before your eyes, and the cross-section of the still-intact terrain will guide you as to the depth of the excavation. If you want to create a hill on level ground, place it not in the center, but at one of the ends, and let other well-planned undulations bring this hill into harmony with the garden as a whole. Leave the added soil to rest for a while, and then give the artificial hill its outward appearance, with plantings, pathways, etc.: the settling that occurs after these steps will have a positive effect on the garden. The settling that occurs after this work has been carried out will upset the hill from top to bottom. Tree distribution. - Here again, it's important to imitate nature as much as possible, which is never ridiculously symmetrical. There should be no overly fixed lines in your flowerbeds; no clashes in the contrast offered by trees of different greens; no trees whose strength of vegetation would so far outweigh the strength of vegetation of neighbouring trees, that the latter would soon wither away for lack of air, light and space. Each tree has its own particular kind of beauty: the Oak spreads its broad, rounded crown majestically; the Fir soars proud and bold; the Elm is both graceful and regular; the Poplar, noble and elegant. In general, Conifers have a serious, sad appearance, but their greenery withstands winter, and the snow that then covers their branches is very picturesque. Plant fir trees in groups of five, six or even ten; not far from them, plant trees of a lighter green. Here are a few tree associations that always succeed in favorable soil: Samaria Elm and Cytise, both with trifoliate leaves; Beech, Elm, Birch and Hornbeam. - False Acacia (Robinia), Japanese Varnish (Alianthus glandulosa). - Gleditschia and Sumae, etc., etc. Softwood trees recover with difficulty, or not at all, when planted after their fourth year; if they are over Om.03 or Om.04 in diameter, even if they are only three years old, nine times out of ten they die within a few weeks or months. A transplanted pine never acquires the vigor of one that grows in the place where it formed its pivot. Larch can be planted after two years in the nursery. Elm, Ash and Sycamore need only be nursed for one year. Oak, Beech and Chestnut need only spend two years in the nursery, provided they have been transplanted at one year old into deep, rich soil. Ornamental trees are planted in spring or autumn; the latter is generally preferable when the soil is of mediocre or poor quality and the plants have little strength; otherwise, it's better to choose spring. If a large tract of land is involved, planting should not be carried out simultaneously: light, dry soil should be planted in December-January; strong, moist soil in February-March; resinous trees, at the foot of which as much of their native soil as possible should be preserved, should be planted in the second half of April, if spring is far enough advanced. Care should be taken to compress the soil around the root collar. We recommend soaking the roots in a mixture of cow dung mixed with water. Alisier (tree 8 to 10 meters tall). Sea Buckthorn, with silvery foliage and thorny branches, making it ideal for hedges. Alder, very easy to grow in swampy areas, where it can reach heights of 20 meters, braving both heat and cold; it forms coppices that are exploited after seven or eight years of growth. Birch, 14 to 16 meters high, grows without deformities or knots, growing only flexible, hanging, tapering branches at the top. It thrives in arid, stony soils. The Catalpa, 10 meters high, native to America. The Common Hornbeam, so well-suited to forming graceful, thick hedges. Oak, king of our forests. Cypress, 10 to 12 meters high. Cytise des Alpes, with its beautiful clusters of hanging flowers. Maple and Sycamore, trees of great picturesque effect. Ash, tall, with a straight trunk, well-proportioned in its size, ending in an elegant but somewhat loose crown; it fears neither shade nor the proximity of other trees, which it quickly overtakes. Flowering Ash, etc., etc. Juniper (Juniperus), a hardy shrub, bristling with hard, sharp, very prickly leaves, with misshapen, twisted twigs, gathered into bushes, with a wild appearance; it is suited to arid, stony sites. The Beech, with a very straight, very large trunk; 30 meters high; vast crown; thick, glossy, light-green foliage; slightly pendulous branches; rivals the Oak itself; suitable for isolation. Holly, not very tall, with supple, bending branches, white flowers and bright, cheerful red fruit; it keeps its beautiful foliage and bright fruit even in the harshest winter weather. Magnolia trees, evergreen, with very large, beautiful flowers; the large-flowered M., which grows to 8 and 10 meters. - Deciduous Magnolias, all of which can grow in the open ground; the Yulan Magnolia, the Cordata Magnolia, with very large and beautiful flowers.

greenish-yellow, etc. Horse chestnut, remarkable for its magnificent foliage and graceful flowers. The Larch, with its thin, narrow, cheerful green leaves, arranged in rosettes along the branches. Micocoulier or Celtis, 15 to 16 meters high, with a noble habit and numerous, well-spread branches. Walnut, which should be placed at a suitable distance from other trees, which it would rather kill than support. Poplar, which has such a beautiful effect along streams and ponds. Pine, content with dry, arid, sandy soil, where no other tree could succeed. The Platane d'Orient, with its superb foliage and rounded green head, spreads shade and coolness all around it. It's one of the most beautiful and suitable trees for forming avenues and bordering large clearings in parks. Robinia or False Acacia, with clusters of elegant, fragrant white or pink flowers. Sumac, with winged leaves and bright red berries; dry, stony places. Elder, very fast-growing. Lime, ideal for shady alleys. It is less common in the modern landscape garden than in the old French garden. Japanese varnish (Ailanthus), 20 meters high and fast-growing. Picturesque accessories. - A landscape garden should be enough to please the eye, without borrowing anything from architecture; however, it does not reject artistic decorations, provided they are appropriate, well-understood and in the right proportions. If you find some ancient ruins on your property, preserve them with care, framing them in the landscape. If you're building a few pretty temples to rural divinities, to Pan, Flora, Pomona or the Seasons, prefer Greek architecture to Roman architecture, as it is purer and more graceful. It's better to copy a familiar model than to expose yourself to the ignorance and bad taste of many modern architects who, under the pretext of inventing new orders or adorning old ones, make a ridiculous mix of different styles. Never allow pagodas or Chinese pavilions; the elegance of some of their details does not prevent the bad effect of their whole. Since the last Paris exhibition, some large landscaped gardens have featured remarkable reductions of Moorish buildings, more suited to the climate of southern France than to our northern provinces. The Romanesque, Gothic and Renaissance styles are the only ones suitable for private chapels; reserve the Greek and Roman styles for temples dedicated to the pagan divinities mentioned above. Obelisks are still allowed in landscaped gardens, provided they are well-cut and well-proportioned; pyramids are ridiculous. Isolated columns may be whole or truncated; in the former case, they are topped with busts or statues; in the latter, they are topped with urns in antique form, with a few inscriptions, preferably borrowed from poets who have sung of the joys and brevity of life: Horace, Anacreon, etc. The statues must be few in number, but of truly remarkable craftsmanship. To the Faun, the grove and the thick thicket full of coolness and shade; to the Nymph, the limpid, murmuring water, the pond, the Weeping Willows, the Water Lilies, etc., etc., etc., etc. A simple but clean thatched cottage, well isolated in clumps of trees where birds sing and nest, and whose path the unwelcome visitor could not easily find, forms a pleasant contrast to the magnificent châteaux, and has always seemed preferable to those pretentious pavilions, with facades adorned with moldings, with windows trimmed with yellow, red, white glass, etc. A few antique marble vases, garnished with flowers rather than left empty, are a fitting ornament for the landscape garden as well as the parterre (1). ABIES, SAPIN (Conifers). - Name given particularly to a species of the Pinus genus. Pinus Abies is a resinous tree that grows very tall, although its roots are proportionately very small. Leaves are smooth green above and glaucous green below; male and female flowers are placed separately on the same individual; the fruit is called Cone, hence the name Conifer given to these trees. Fir wood is highly prized as firewood, for masting, etc.; it is fairly resistant to decay and rot; its maximum growth, in favorable soil, is 115 years; 76 years in poor soil. Fir does not do well in chalky soils, where it is better to plant Scots Pine and Maritime Pine. - Propagation by grafting for rare species; by seed for others. o Main species. Stems twiggy; branches inclined and then rising; very small cones. ACACIA (Mimosées), from a Greek word meaning spike (Leguminosae). - Not to be confused with the tree commonly known as Acacia, which belongs to the Robinia genus (false Acacia). Corolla funnel- or top-shaped, longer than the calyx, with qninquifid or, less often, quadrifid limb; indefinite number of stamens (8 to 200) inserted either in the style of the ovary, on the receptacle or at the bottom of the corolla; indefinite number of seeds contained in a bivalve envelope. - Trees or shrubs with or without prickles; leaves simple or compound or decomposed, stipulate; petiole and rachis often glandular; inflorescence axillary or terminal veryvaried; flowers sessile or rarely pedicellate, bracteolate, yellow, white or greenish. The Acacia genus comprises some 300 species, most of them native to the tropical regions of the Old and New Worlds: remarkable for the hardness of their wood and the materials they provide for medicine and industry; for example, Acacia Catechu yields a very astringent juice known as Cachou; Acacia Nigra is a tonic much-appreciated by Americans; tanners use the green fruits (neb-neb) of A. Nilotica; Senegal gum comes from A. Verck. Acacias with spines or prickles. A. Acacias are propagated from seed, which should be placed in a warm bed in early spring; very early plants can be planted about three weeks after their birth, in a new bed at Om, 10 or Om, 12 from each other, lightly watered, well sheltered by glass at night and aerated during the day; carefully removed after a month, leaving as much soil as possible on the roots, and placed separately in small pots filled with vegetable garden soil; immersed in a warm layer of tan; kept in the shade until they have formed new roots and, finally, treated like other tropical plants. Some species can be propagated by separating old plants when they have put down roots; perennial species survive the winter in warm greenhouses and produce ripe flowers and seeds the following summer. In June, remove creeping species from pots and expose them to the south; under cloches they live through the summer, but without gaining much strength; they are then condemned to perish at the first cold of autumn. ACANTHUS MOLLIS, Acanthus without thorns. Branc-ursine. From a Greek word meaning thorn (Acanthaceae.) - It was the beauty of its leaves surrounding a basket placed on a tomb that gave Callimachus the idea of the Corinthian capital. Perennial; single stem from Om, 70 to 1 meter; elegant, large, smooth leaves; graceful flowers; singular corolla: lower lip with three lobes, calyx with four divisions, one very large posterior, two very small intermediate and one anterior. Multiplication by seed or root division. Sow in dry, light soil towards the end of March, and if the season is mild, the plants appear in May; in damp soil, the roots rot over winter. Preferably grow A. du Portugal with long spikes of pinkish flowers; A. épineuse with tight, hairy, white flowers, spotted with lilac; in July and August. ACER, ERABLE (Acerineae). - Flower: calyx usually divided into five, more rarely into four, nine parts; pre-flowering imbricate; petals in equal number inserted on the circumference of a fleshy, hypogynous disk, sometimes missing; stamens inserted on this same disk, always in definite number, sometimes equal to the other parts of the flower, usually larger, rarely proportional to the number eight; ovary with two lobes; style. with two stigmas. Fruit separates into two mono- or di-sperm samaras. Seeds attached to inner corner of lodge. Fine, tight, white or gray wood, sought after by cabinetmakers for making musical instruments and for heating; it contains a certain amount of sugar. Maples grow to considerable size in our climates; they multiply easily by their seed, which should be sown in spring immediately after maturity and covered with about Om, 14 of light soil; it will then sprout within the year, fresh and substantial Sol. Propagate rare species and varieties by grafting them onto Sycamore or other common species. The native A. Pseudo Platanus or Sycamore, or False Platanus, reaches heights of 20 and 25 meters; yellowish-green flowers; - A. Platanoïdes or Plane is less tall, but more ornamental than the former; it has yellow flowers in graceful corymbs; - Montpellier Maple, very large, but not very tall. Yellowish flowers in corymbs; short-winged fruits that turn red when ripe. Finally, let's mention: the Country Maple, 6 to 10 meters high; the Cottony Maple, 10 to 12 meters high; the Sugar Maple, native to America, from which a sugar similar to cane sugar is extracted, etc., etc. ACER, NEGUNDO. V. Negundo. ACHILLEA (Compositae). - From the name of Achilles, pupil of the centaur Chiron; allusion to the real or supposed virtues of this plant. The main species are A, mille feuilles. Indigenous, perennial, cultivated for its variegated, blond, corymb-like flowers, which have an aromatic fragrance; purple-flowered variety much sought-after by sheep. Blooms all summer long. Multiplied by splinters. - A, tomentose, perennial, almost similar to A. with pectinate leaves; good for borders. Dry soil. Multipl. by splinters in spring. - Filependula, native to the East. Stems 1.50 m long; many yellow flowers in tight corymbs. Sow the seeds in a bed in March, and they'll give you flowers in September. Thanks to their long, fibrous roots, Achillea plants solidify embankments and slopes. LONG LEAF ACHIMENÈS (Gesneriaceae). - Native to Mexico. Stems from Om, 20 to Om, 30; flowers of a beautiful blue mixed with white. - Several species and numerous varieties: Achimenès with large leaves; A, with open leaves, etc. They are cared for in greenhouses like Orchids (see this word). Multipl, by rhizomes and cuttings. ACHYRANTHES. - From two Greek words meaning straw and flower (Amaranthaceae). Twelve species, most of which grow in the equatorial zone. A. de Vershaffelt is a tall plant of Om, 30-40, reddish-purple and crimson. Sought-after for borders and baskets. Multipl, from cuttings; warm, humid greenhouse; part-sun. ACONIT (Ranunculaceae). - From a Greek word: pointe, because savages used it to rub the tips of their arrows. A perennial plant growing in the open ground; from Om,70 to 1m,30 tall. Large, beautiful blue or yellow flowers, somewhat helmet-shaped and arranged in clusters or terminal panicles. Propagates easily by seed sown in light, soft soil in mid-shade, or by splitting and dividing clumps. Blooms in summer. The main species are: A, pyramidal, the first to produce long flower spikes of Om 70 in May and June. A, tueloup blooms from mid-June to August. A. des Pyrénées, 4.50 tall; yellow flowers in July. A. napel, 1.20 m high, with three varieties: one with white flowers, one with pink flowers and one with variegated flowers. Multipl, by splinters in spring or autumn. Water in dry weather; place in flowerbeds in the shade, leaving a distance of about Om 12 between plants. ACORUS CALAMUS, Sweet rush (Aroidea). - From two Greek words: without sloe, because, according to the ancients, this plant cured eye ailments. Native and herbaceous; attractive green leaves; fragrant flowers in cylindrical catkins. Japanese A. gramineus, with its green, white and pink ribboned leaves, is grown in orangeries or cold frames, in damp, shady heather soil. Multip, by splinters. ACROLINIUM ROSEUM, Pink-leaved Acrolinium (Compositae). - From Texas. Annual plant; stem about Om, 30 tall, leaves glaucous, linear: flowers with involucre of scarce leaflets, with golden-yellow disk in center. Sow outdoors in April. Sow outdoors in March-April; flowers keep as long as those of immortelle. ADHATODA VASICA, Indian or Ceylon walnut (Acanthaceae). - Height 3 to 4 meters. ÆSCULUS HIPPOCASTANUM, Horse chestnut (Hippocastaneae). - Native to the temperate climates of Asia; cultivated in Europe as early as 1591. Beautiful tree, 20 to 25 meters high; beautiful flowers dotted with pink spots on a white background, arranged in numerous vertical pyramids at the top of each branch; ample green foliage; strong, majestic trunk; astringent, bitter bark used for dyes; fruits of a repulsive harshness and quite similar in shape to those of the chestnut tree; sown in the ground or in troughs to transplant the seedling in the nursery. - M. d'Inde lives in all types of soil, but prefers substantial, cool soil; it tolerates pruning and shearing. We also grow the red-flowered Æsculus, with more embossed, greener foliage than the previous species; it flowers in the third or fourth year. AGAVE OF AMERIA, from a Greek word: Admirable (Amaryllidae). - General characteristics: tubular corolla, six deep divisions, six protruding stamens attached to the tube; ovary integral with the base of the corolla; three-located capsule; leaves large, numerous, very thick, armed with prickles; bare, candelabra-shaped spike 3 to 8 meters long, each branch terminating in a corymb of yellow flowers. Originally from America, this plant is now widespread in Italy, southern France, etc. It flowers quite often. Flowers quite often. Seed and carnation propagation; orangery. Aloe cultivation. For example: American aloe. Its leaf fibers are used to make ropes, fishermen's nets, carpets, wrapping cloths, etc., etc.; a honey-like juice, wine and vinegar are extracted from its stalk. Strong thorns make this plant sought-after for forming sturdy fences. - Yucca leaves. - Artichoke. - Variety mediapicta, yellow in the center. - Other: stricta, with striated and variegated leaves. ALOE, Aloe (Liliaceae). - Native to the Cape of Good Hope. Corolla tubular, almost cylindrical, divided into six lobes at its opening, enclosing six stamens attached to the receptacle; free ovary which converts into a capsule with three chambers, occupied by seeds arranged in two rows; - leaves are stiff, very fleshy, overlapping one another and forming pyramids or rosettes, sometimes glaucous green, sometimes with yellow or blood-red stripes; most are thorny or have strong, prickly teeth along their edges; - stems are very strong, sometimes woody; beautiful, short-lasting flowers; leaves yield a juice widely used in medicine (Succotrin). Aloes are treated like cacti, in light, nourishing soil; in winter, temperate greenhouse, no watering. - A. from Bourbon Island. Tall stem; flat, broad, hanging leaves with red margins; spikes of greenish-yellow flowers. - A. à corne de bélier (Africa). AZALEA, Azalea (Ericaceae). - Azaleas are divided into two distinct groups: 1° the Azaleas of America and the Caucasus, all of which are grown in light soil, or better still, in heather; 2° the Azaleas of India, which require a temperate greenhouse. The former are grown in the open air, in slightly shaded positions; flowerbeds. Temperate-greenhouse Azaleas bloom from April to June. As soon as they have finished flowering, they should be repotted with fine, rich heather soil, put back in the greenhouse, or left in the open air, but in the shade, then bury the pots up to Om, 06 from the edge, in a place well exposed to the sun. Drain pots; water moderately, preferably with rainwater; basin leaves in hot weather; slightly damp Dutch greenhouse in winter; plenty of light. Pinch after flowering, as it sprouts. Multiply by approach grafting, split grafting, veneering; reproduce by marcottes, by rooted splinters, under cloches, in a hot greenhouse. Seedlings produce the most beautiful varieties. CALCEOLARIA, Calceolaria (Scrophularinae). - Named for its yellow, purple, etc., clog-like flowers (calceolus). Woody species multiply by smothering cuttings and rooting splinters; herbaceous species multiply by dividing clumps. Prefer sowing in spring or autumn, in damp heather soil at moderate heat. Drain the bottom well and top with 17 CAL of heather soil. Sow and cover evenly with fine sand. Beat the top a little so that the seed receives the moisture more easily. Do not let the surface dry out; sowing should be done in half-shade. Transplant seedlings at their fourth leaf in potting soil or under a frame. When the young plants are strong enough, place them in pots of Om, 10. The best soil for them is a mixture of one-third heather soil, one-third potting compost and one-third free earth. Re-pot in November and December in om, 20 pots, leaving plenty of air and light. Smoke your plants every day to protect them from aphids.
