Also sow early peas with the recommended care, and replace any beans that have perished with those from Nice. FEBRUARY. If the ground is not frozen or covered with snow, continue to sow small lettuces and their supplies, radishes, mixed with carrots if desired; cabbage, kale, early Aleth cabbage, to bring them forward, and replant in place in March; michael peas, and others that may have been missed in previous months; asparagus, and artichokes for those that may be late; chicory-scarole for summer, curly-leaf lettuces, mousseronnes crêpes; parsley. You can also grow black-seeded romaine and Lombardy plants, eggplants; sow porreau, Lescure onion; early carrots, short Liège, very sweet white, very large with green collar; chili, ditto sweet; spinach, various species. Plant shallots, garlic and rocambola in light soil. Sow asparagus seed in the ground at the end of this month. Sow asparagus legs. Sow purple eggplants, tomatoes; sow autumn flowers. MARCH. This is the month when the earth opens up and calls for all the gardener's activity. Replant all the strawberry, sorrel and tarragon borders. We sow abundantly, and without fear, various kinds of snow peas, broad beans, several species of lettuce, romaine, escarole, Maux curly endive, wild chicory in borders or beds, chervil, parsley, onion, porreau, spring onion, carrots, beet, spinach, turnips and radishes, and all garden vegetables except beans, cardoons and eggplants. Asparagus can be planted, seedlings can be sown, and legs can be placed in the ground, if this was not possible the previous month. Aleth cabbage, if you missed it, early cabbage, York sprouts, salsify, scorzonera, ordinary tomatoes, large tomatoes, yellow tomatoes and plain tomatoes without Naples ribs. Repeat any missing seedlings. APRIL. We continue the previous month's work, sowing and planting all kinds of vegetables in abundance, weeding seedlings that have already been sown, thinning out those that are too thick, grommeting artichoke plants, and planting the most beautiful grommets to form a new plant if needed. Asparagus can still be planted at the beginning of the month. Watering should be done in the morning, during the day, and not in the evening, for fear of white frost. Sow various types of Savoy cabbage this month: milan des vertus, gros pointu, milan blanc doré de Russie, Bruxelles cabbage, rosette, or mille-têtes, known by all three names; haricot hâtif rond de Soissons, mange-tout; haricot-sabre à grandes rames. As vegetation becomes very active during this month, gardeners must not lose sight of plants that go quickly, such as turnips and radishes, spinach, chervil, romaine lettuce, peas, etc., so as to sow them often enough to avoid running out. Sow cucumbers and gherkins. If you haven't sown celery and cardoons by the end of March, hurry up and sow them at the beginning of the month. MAY. You can still sow spring onions, and any other vegetables (1) that have been forgotten. In May, you can still sow beets, carrots every fortnight, cucumbers, green gherkins, cauliflowers (1) I use the word légume in the general sense given to it in the French language, and which is used almost throughout the kingdom, but also of all kinds of vegetable plants. Holland hard and half-hard, recommending that they be sown, along with broccoli, eight days apart; cauliflower, from the end of May to the end of June; cardoons from Spain and Tours, lettuces for cooking, and romaine; a few small turnips and radishes, early turnips, beans, mange-tout of all kinds, early peas. April is infinitely more suitable for sowing. JUNE. Summer is harvest time: no more sowing or planting. However, spinach and supplies are still sown in mid-shade areas in June, but these weekly seeds have only one cutting. We sow large turnips, long radishes, small black radishes and large ones; we sow raiponce seed, as in August, watering it often; we sow lettuces for peeling, such as hollandaise, lazy, Batavia, Versailles cabbage lettuce, and chicory, beans, michael peas and carrots. From June through to winter, in addition to the seeds mentioned above that need to be sown in advance for the following year, other seeds are sown and paid for immediately. These are the weekly seeds, i.e. lettuce supplies, spinach, radishes, turnips, black radishes; lettuce and chicory plants are also raised, and even various leguminous seeds, such as prud'homme beans, early beans, especially michaux peas and Clamar peas. Although nothing sown after the summer solstice brings the seeds to maturity, since we're content here with these green seeds, we can harvest them. Finally, those who fear no expense in procuring rarities, sow cucumbers at the beginning of July, and harvest their fruits, by dint of manure, in December and January. JULY. Sowing of all vegetables whose produce can be obtained in less than three or four months continues as in the previous month, such as all kinds of salads and supplies, beans for eating green, peas, gherkins, eggplants, autumn cauliflowers, broccoli, kohlrabi, autumn carrots. Celery is ridged every two weeks, so that we always have some ready to eat. At the end of the month we sow cabbages, which we transplant in nurseries; we can also sow York cabbages, to enjoy them at the end of March: we sow chives and porreau to succeed those sown in spring; but it's good to remember that if the seeds we sow then to give their product the following spring were too new, the plants would be prone to go up : the safest time to sow these kinds of seeds is from August 10 to 15; this is the time to sow white onions for replanting in October, and scorzonera for overwintering. As can be seen from the list of cabbage, lettuce, etc. species not cultivated in our départements, with the exception of amateur gardens, and which are fixed at five or six varieties of each species, it necessarily follows that, for part of the year, we are deprived of vegetables. If we wanted early vegetables, it would be possible to obtain them, as well as late species, and enjoy the whole year the resources that nature provides. I'll mention peas and beans, which, because of their different species, can be eaten green, in the form of grain, or with their tender pods and without fillets: by experimenting, these various vegetables can be obtained almost all year round. Mashed potato peas are generally very neglected, yet this vegetable is a great resource at certain times, especially in years of unusual cold, such as the one we experienced at the end of 1829 and the beginning of 1830. The inhabitants of the north and of cold countries, more careful than we are, have their provisions ready, and are never without. There are well-educated gardeners who have wanted to sow foreign lettuces: when they take their produce to the market, they can't get rid of it, because the buyers don't know it. When, then, will the time come to cultivate with care the riches we owe to nature's inexhaustible resources? AUGUST. You won't see a single empty garden corner in this month, any more than in June and July. Cucumbers and gherkins need plenty of watering when it's not raining, and cauliflowers, cardoons and celery require copious watering even when it's raining a little. In addition to sowing and planting everything that will be eaten within the year, we must also take care of what can survive the winter and produce the following year; for example, we sow white onions, porreau, salsify, scorzonera, red passion lettuce, which we replant in the ground; spinach, chervil, turnips; carrots for spring. The gardener must carefully study his terrain and locality, in order to know the advantages and disadvantages: there are, in fact, terrains and sites where autumn sowing must be done a fortnight earlier or later than in others. In support of my argument, I'll cite our mountains, which lie within a radius of sixteen to twenty leagues from here: gardeners there sow early York sprouts a month earlier than in Toulouse, their plants remain covered in snow for three or four months, and the terrain is so favorable to them that York sprouts, which are very small among us, become much stronger in our mountains than our summer cabbages. Following our scorching summers, peas and green beans have often provided abundant supplies until the end of November. Bind chicory and escarole, and butter celery, often and sparingly at the same time. From the beginning of the month, sow early head cabbage, female beef cabbage, cabalan, Strasbourg cabbage, to have early crops; prud'homme beans: an excellent all-rounder, can supply until the frosts. SEPTEMBER. We continue to sow and plant everything that can be eaten or harvested. All sowings made during the previous month can be continued, as well as various lettuces, supplies, very early white turnips; chervil, spinach, yellow-pink radishes, yellow turnips, York sprouts, sugarloaf, cabbage (1), cabal, Strasbourg (all foreign cabbages sement in this month); parsley, broad-ribbed chard; spinach, to enjoy for a long time: small, pink, half-long radishes that last well through the winter; short, early Liège carrots; early white carrots; winter romaine lettuce. (1) Our gardeners sement flat summer cabbage every month of the year, to ohtenir primeurs; late sowings provide them with this species until the frosts. OCTOBER. Spinach and chervil can be sown during this month, and will bear fruit in March if the autumn is favorable; but crepe lettuce, gotte lettuce and romaine lettuce can be sown with advantage. At the end of the month, we sow a few snow peas at the foot of walls, in good exposure; we transplant young York cabbage, head cabbage sown in August, either in nursery, to be put in place only in February and March, or even immediately for a temperate climate. We sow the large Narbonne and Perpignan beans, and the early Nice ones. At the end of the month, asparagus stalks are cut, smoked and the soil ploughed; this is also the time to cut artichoke stalks, clean the stalks, shorten the outer leaves and plough to facilitate the ridging that will take place next month. Celery, cardoons, escarole and chicory continue to be blanched in the usual way. NOVEMBER. Radishes, lettuces, nasitort are sown: asparagus is sown in autumn with more success than in spring; large quarantine peas, Norman purée peas, long-shelled peas; large dwarf peas; Narbonne and Nice broad beans, if they could not be sown earlier. Cabbage seedlings sown in August or July are put in place; when placing them, care is taken to press them against the back of furrows made with a spade, so that they are sheltered from the north winds. DECEMBER. There is little to be done in the open ground during this month, unless there is some ripping to be done; however, if the vegetable garden is in strong soil, the earth in the empty squares can be ploughed roughly, so that the frosts penetrate it, and make it more crumbly; for it will heat up in the spring, and seedlings and plantations will thrive all the better for having been more divided. We sow lettuces, watercress, white mustard, lettuce supplies, garlic, radishes, Norman green peas, long-shelled and michaux peas, early peas, dwarf bouquet peas, dwarf green peas without parchment. These five species should be sown by anticipation, and little, in case of heavy frosts, observe that peas in the ground only fear frosts when the leaf has reached a certain elevation on the ground. VEGETABLE GARDEN. CHAPTER ONE. CATALOG OF VEGETABLE SEEDS. AlL. Alium sativum. Cloves are planted at the end of January, February and March, in beds four or five inches apart. Spanish garlic, or ROCAMBOLE. Scorodoprasum. Same cultivation: the bulblets of the stem and the cloves are used to multiply the plant, and are put to the same uses as garlic. Garlic is not cultivated. ARROCHE des Jardins, BONNE-DAME, BELLE-DAME. Atriplex hortensis. This annual plant is used to soften the acidity and overly green color of sorrel. It is sown in February, every two weeks, so as not to run out: any soil will do. ARTICHAUT. Cynara. There are several species: their cultivation is fairly well known. With large, long roots, they require deep, fresh, fertile, crumbly soil; they are usually propagated by eyelets around January, February and March. Here's the procedure to follow. When the old artichokes have leaves about 8 to 12 inches high, dig them up to the origin of their young stems with a spade, to expose them. There are usually from five to ten on each plant: we choose the two or four best to keep them, and we break off all the others as close as possible to the root, so as to remove them with the heel. These young stems are called "œilletons". We select the strongest ones and those with a good heel, from which new roots should emerge; we clean and smooth this heel with the serpette, if there are shreds, and we shorten the leaves to the height of 6 inches. This operation must be carried out immediately, and the leaves must not be allowed to wither. The Laon artichoke generally produces much higher yields than the southern varieties: its seed is sown in February and March. ASPERGE. Asparagus officinalis from southern France. Asparagus can be propagated in two ways, either by sowing in the field, or by raising plants in a nursery: the latter is the more common method. This operation is carried out in October or November. After preparing the soil to receive the legs, the squares are made as desired; from the length of the pits, three lines are drawn at equal distance, on which the places for the roots are marked, about fifteen to eighteen inches apart, by very small mounds of potting soil; the roots are laid out by hand on the mound, with their ends inclined, and the whole is immediately covered with two inches of soil. With these distances, it will be easy to hoe and water other plants that can be grown on the slope: low plants will suffice. Green Dutch asparagus seed and large Ulm violets are the best: sow the seed in March for sowing. BETTERAVE, Beta vulgaris. The red-black and yellow Castelnaudary beets are the most esteemed in our country; the yellow, white-fleshed beet, one of the best for extracting sugar, is grown like the other beets: it offers the grower a resource for speculation and income. It is widely cultivated in the north of France, and its sugar product is sold for consumption. It is to be hoped that this cultivation will spread to our southern departments, where the soil is highly suitable for the success of this plant. Once the soil has been well loosened by good ploughing, sowing is carried out in rays at the end of March and April: the plants must be thinned out so that they are at least a foot to eighteen inches apart: depending on the quality of the soil, fertilizer must be used; only consumed manure should be used. BASILIC. Ocymum Basilicum. Fine or broad-leaf, sow in March on a bed; outdoors in April. CARROT. Daucus Carota. There are a large number of cultivated carrots; I will mention the best species: the long red carrot from Toulouse, cultivated in large quantities, is a very good species; the long red from Holland, the short early (this species is very valuable for terre-fort, where the long carrot cannot rotate, as the soil is not soft); the short carrot can replace it with advantage: the short one can replace it with advantage; the red one, the white one, delicate to the taste, early (white carrot with green cockle out of the ground, very big: sow it clear, each seed at 5, 7 and 8 inches of distance, new species): the last two can be sown in September, October and February, to have them early, and replace those which, sown in June, begin to get woody. Carrots can be sown from February to the end of June, and can be taken up again in September; the first sowings, done a fortnight apart, provide for spring and summer; the last ones in June are used for winter until vegetation: this root requires deep, soft, sandy soil, well amended before autumn: they must be sown light, or thinned out so that those kept for winter are 5 to 6 inches apart (1). This thinning is done successively, and (1) Carrots are most often devoured at birth by the spider, not the one that crawls on trees, but the one that crawls on the ground, which is always on the move, and attacks several young seedlings, particularly carrots, whose tigelle it pricks to pump out the juices: the plant then withers and perishes. This spider is sometimes so numerous that it destroys seedlings of any size: there is only one way to keep it at bay; as it fears humidity, the plants are lightly watered every day, when the weather is limey and dry, with a decoction of lime water and soot. the torn carrots are used for cooking. Although I have just indicated, as far as I can, the qualities of the various carrots, it is nevertheless true to say that the nature of the soil influences this point, as much as and more than the quality of the seed, if the soil is not favorable to this plant: strong soil prevents the root from pivoting; the soil being too compact, it also loses its natural color, and becomes pale yellow. Cultivated celery. Apium graveolens. There are various species: dwarf, small to cut, whose leaves are used as salad supplies; Turkish or Persian celery; the large violet of Tours, remarkable for the thickness of its ribs, the size of its stalk and the entire volume of the plant, which is more considerable than in most others; and, finally, celeriac, whose large, turnip-shaped root is eaten cooked. To grow celery at different times of the year, sow from January to June in a light, well-amended bed of soil, staggered in rays about nine to ten inches apart; each plant is watered immediately to promote growth, and moistened every two or three days if it doesn't rain; when the plant is strong enough, it is blanched by tying it with three ties in dry weather, and covering it with dry straw, so that only the tips of the leaves are visible; or, after tying, the soil is heaped around the plant up to the first tie; after eight days, it is raised to the second tie, and finally to the third; eight days after this operation has been carried out, lettuces, chicory, etc. are planted to make use of the soil. In May and June, seedlings should be sown in the open air, and should be thinned out so that they can be left in place without being transplanted, in order not to retard growth. CAPUCIN, Tropœolum, The large and small varieties are grown to dress salads: the flower buds are barely formed and the seeds taken while still green are preserved in vinegar, replacing capers; the large, creeping variety is used to dress cabinets: it is sown in April and May. CARDON. Cynara cardunculus. From Barbary, we prefer Tours cardoon, which is very thorny, to Spanish cardoon, which is thornless, because the latter combines the disadvantage of being more prone to climbing with that of having thinner, less tender ribs: Both can be sown as early as February, in pots and under cover, if you want to have early cardoons, good for eating in June; but some always come up: to have them in winter, sow them only in May and June, in holes lined with consumed manure, spaced about three feet apart in all directions, where you place two or three seeds together, to leave only one plant. These plants should be grown in the same way as artichokes, but more watered and kept warmer, as they are more delicate; they should be blanched when they are strong enough: they should be mounded with earth, which should be piled up at the base; the leaves, which are often five feet long, should be brought together; they should be held together with wicker, or better still with straw; tightened in this way for three weeks, the cardoon will then have blanched, and its ribs will have softened: left any longer it would rot. CERFEUIL. Scandix cerefolium. Native and annual. It is sown at all times, from March to September, with the difference that it is sown in rays at the foot of a wall in March, in the north and in the shade during the summer, and at any exposure at other times. Curly chervil, very nice variety: same cultivation. CHENILLETTE. Scorpiurus. A small, indigenous annual plant whose bristly, scaly, furrowed fruits imitate either caterpillars, worms or snails; as a sort of mischief, they are sometimes added to salad supplies, to surprise people who are unfamiliar with them. They are sown in spring in ordinary soil. CHERVIS, CHERUI, CHIROUIS and GIROLLES. Sium sisarum. Fleshy, very sweet roots that can be eaten like scorsonera. Sow in spring or September, in soft, cool, deep soil, and water often. WILD CHICORY. Cichorium intybus. Native and perennial. Sow all year round, every two weeks; young leaves are used in salads. white or curly chrysanthemum. Cichorium endivia, summer or Italian chicory: the curly Meaux variety is sown in March; it is excellent for the early seasons, and even frequently used in autumn. There are several species. SCAROLE, the large, round one, which is quicker to produce, and has a very rounded, almost heady heart. Chicory seedlings are sown in the open ground in April, July, August and September: it is easy to grow and widely known. CHOU. Brassica oleracea. Biennial and indigenous. Several main breeds can be distinguished: cabbages with smooth, usually glaucous leaves; savoy cabbages with blistered, more or less dark green leaves; green or headless cabbages, which can last up to three years; those with fleshy roots or stems; and cauliflowers and broccoli. 1. cabbage or cabus. Its main sub-varieties, in order of earliness, are : YORK CABBAGE. Small, elongated, very early and highly prized. There are a few sub-varieties, such as cabbage-cabbage, or early super-fine, even smaller and a few days earlier; early dwarf cabbage, lower on the stem and with a slightly shorter head, as early as the previous one; large York cabbage, whose head acquires more volume and forms a little more quickly. SUGARLOAF CABBAGE. Slightly blond-green leaves, hooded, elongated head, sometimes in the shape of an inverted cone, tender and very good. BEEFHEART CABBAGE. Three sub-varieties: small, medium and large. The small forms its head almost as soon as the York cabbage; the large cabbage is quite similar to the large white cabbage. Both are good and widely grown. GROS CHOU CABUS BLANC, or summer cabbage. Highly cultivated in our regions, it is sown in September to produce early vegetables. Our gardeners sow it all year round. Sowing should begin at the end of January and continue until June, repeating often: this precaution is necessary for a good gardener; this one offers the greatest number of varieties; here are the best and most widely known: chou de Saint-Denis, or chou blanc de Bonneuil, very short stem, very glaucous leaves, large head, usually flattened, sometimes round; chou cabus d'Alsace, second season, slightly high stem, detached, rounded leaves, sometimes flat: one of the quickest to form a head among the large cabbages; large German, Alsatian or quintal cabbage, short stem, very large, broad, slightly scalloped leaves, lighter green than the preceding species, huge head in rich, cool soil; short-stalked, medium-sized, early Dutch cabbage, which is placed among the cabbages: it can occupy the same place given to lettuces; large Dutch cabbage, or cabbage, stubby Brunswick cabbage, with extremely short stem, medium-sized head, tight, flattened, with round, short, few leaves. ALETH CABBAGE, POINTED, VERY ATTRACTIVE. Sown in September and October, it is earlier than summer cabbage, and can also be sown at the end of January and February: at this time, it can replace summer cabbage plants that would have perished in a harsh winter. RED CABBAGE. There are two main breeds, large and small, known as Utrecht black cabbage: both are highly prized; many people eat them in salads; their apples, cut into small strips and pickled in vinegar, are excellent as pickles. Red cabbage is considered to be very heart-healthy, and is frequently used as such in medicine. All large cabbages are used to make saüer kraut, when their heads are full and tightly packed. Cabbages can be sown at several times: 1° from mid-August through September (York sprouts and other small hatives, June and July); the latter are planted out in October; the larger species can be planted out at the same time, or transplanted in nurseries, in proportion to their strength, to be planted permanently in February and March, at a distance of 15 inches for the small ones, 18 inches to 2 feet for the medium ones, 2.5 to 3 feet for the large ones. Sow York sprouts and cabbages in early soil as above; they come in apples from the beginning of April until May, and the others successively until August; 2° in February, at the foot of a wall facing south; 3° at the end of the same month and beginning of March, in well-soiled beds; 4° during March, in well-prepared soil: The plants from these seedlings are planted at the end of March and during April; their production follows that of the autumn seedlings, and continues until November and December. The larger species could be sown in April, and the smaller ones almost all year round; but it is still advantageous to grow kohlrabi, because they are preferable for late spring sowing. Cabbages in general, and large head cabbages in particular, require good, slightly consistent, well-smoked soil; when it is naturally fresh, they grow larger and more beautiful: for sowing, the soil should be light rather than strong, well loosened, with a little shade, which is especially essential for spring and summer sowing (1). If the weather is dry, you need to baste them regularly, and visit them to destroy any insects that might attack them, particularly the tiquet, or ground flea, which is sometimes very harmful to them. The best way to eliminate these insects is to sow ash on the young plant in the morning, when the dew falls. When replanting, visit the plant at the point where the roots start, and if you see a tumor, cut off half of it, and destroy the worm that causes it, which would stop the plant's development; water each plant at the time of planting, and then continue watering as long as the season requires. CABBAGE CABALAN GROS POMMÉ POINTU. A new species cultivated with great success. As it was not known two years ago, in September, I gave some seed to a few gardeners, and in June I received from one of them cabbages weighing eight pounds; I also received some from another gardener in Merville, which were very beautiful, since they weighed twenty-five pounds each: they have also been successful with various gardeners. Since that time, the seed has been much sought-after, and at the moment when I propose to deliver my opuscule for reprinting, I hear from all sides of its success. The quality is good, the head is sugarloaf-shaped and very firm; the leaves, pressed together, prevent caterpillars and slugs from lodging in them; the lateral leaves are of enormous extent, which means that it is advisable to plant this cabbage at twice the distance of cabbages. Only two cabbages should be planted on an ordinary-sized bed, given their large shape and the volume of their leaves. According to experience, kohlrabi should be sown in August and September, even in October; if the first sowings have failed, they can also be sown in January: it needs good soil, well amended and carefully smoked. Cabbage is all the more valuable for the countryside, as it grows almost without care. Only seedlings sown on benches require watering in July, August and September, to help the plant grow; once planted, at the end of October and November, it requires no further care; it can withstand the harshest winter: just weed and hoe in good time. Cabbages grown near Toulouse only received watering on transplanting, which is essential if the weather is dry. Today, cabbage is widely known and cultivated. It is easily distinguished from other cabbages by its yellow leaves, which are set aside and thrown into the manure. Their quality is so poor that they should not be grown, and I hasten to warn all those who will be growing them. This disadvantage is general to all plants; the only advantage this one has is that the bad plant is yellow, easy to recognize; whereas, for other cabbages, it is impossible for the most experienced gardener to choose the good from the bad plant. 2. MILAN CABBAGE, or curly cabbage. Its heads are less tightly packed, usually more tender, and less prone to muskiness: this often depends on the soil. The main varieties are the Ulm milan, with a slightly high stem, very quick to peel, not very large, excellent; the short milan, or dwarf, extremely stocky, very dark green, fairly quick to peel, tender and very good; the Touraine pancalier, low on the stalk, and very dark green, like the previous one, but with stronger ribs; the ordinary milan, or large milan cabbage, with a stronger head than all the preceding varieties; the long-headed milan, with a pointed head, not very large, but tender and excellent; the golden milan, whose color, a slightly blond green, becomes quite yellow in winter: Its apples are not very tight and very tender. MILAN-DES-VERTUS, or BIG GERMAN KOMPED CABBAGE. Its head is as large as that of large cabbages, which it resembles a little in the way it peels, and because it is less blistered and sometimes glaucous: it needs good soil. It is a valuable variety for large-scale cultivation; it is hardier, and keeps longer in winter, like the pancalier and the ordinary kite. CHOU DE BRUXELLES A JETS, CHOU ROSETTE, with a stem two to three feet high, producing small, tender, curly apples in the leaf axils, which are highly prized and picked as they grow, ending with the head. Kale could be sown, like cabbage, in August and September; but the most common practice is to sow it in spring, from the end of April to July, with the exception of green kale, which should not be sown later than May. The distance for small and medium-sized kites is eighteen inches to two feet, and two and a half to three feet for large ones. The first to be sown of the early varieties come in April and May, and the last to be sown at the beginning of winter, and keep until April: frost tenderizes them without destroying them, unless it is extraordinary. RUSSIAN CABBAGE. Russian cabbage has leaves cut right down to the rib in narrow, irregular strips, but which retain the stiffness peculiar to Savoy cabbage leaves, which contrasts with the elegance of the cuts. At the top of the stem, which is about a foot high, the leaves come together to form a rounded head of medium size, very tender, and of excellent quality. Sown in April, May and June, this cabbage is treated in the same way as the kites. CHOU-FLORI is sown in June and July; CHOU FEMELLE, in August and September: these species are very popular. Same cultivation as kites. 3. green cabbage, or non-apple. This name covers several varieties that do not form a head, some of which are green, others reddish, violet, variegated, etc. These cabbages are more resistant to cold than others. These cabbages are more resistant to cold than those of the other divisions, and most are only good to eat when frost has softened their leaves. Their new shoots are also eaten in spring, before the flowers have developed: they are not cut like the others when you want to use them, but the leaves are chopped as you need them. The main varieties are collards, large cow cabbages and tree cabbages, which grow up to six feet or more on a single stalk; their leaves are large and plain, very good to eat, and very useful for feeding cattle. CHOU MOELLIER, a sub-variety of the preceding one, whose stem increases in size from the middle to the top. CHOU CAULET DE FLANDRE, which differs from the cabbage cavalier only in its red color. CHOU VERT BRANCHU DU POITOU, less tall than the cavalier, but forming a considerable and very productive clump. CHOU VIVACE DE DAUBENTON, distinguished from the preceding variety by its lower branches, which lengthen and slope down to the ground, where they sometimes root naturally. GRAND FRISÉ VERT DUNORD, CHOU FRANGE. ou FRISÉ D'ECOSSE, and GRAND FRISÉ ROUGE. They are more resistant to cold than the others, and are also ornamental plants because of their habit and the elegant cut of their leaves; the same is true of the variegated variety. They can be sown throughout spring, summer and autumn, but are more commonly sown in April, May and June for winter and early spring produce, and in July and August for summer produce. Distance from two-and-a-half to three feet for the first five varieties, and two feet for the others. 4. ROOT cabbage, or CHARNUE ROOT. SIAMESE KOHLRABI. Distinguished by its swollen, ball-shaped stem, on the top and sides of which the leaves are planted. Half-sized kohlrabi is a good vegetable, when it has been watered a lot; it shares the taste of cabbage and turnip. It comes in three varieties: white, purple and early dwarf, the latter with its small, sparse leaves; its ball forms very quickly: it is dried in May and June, and the early dwarf until July. Kohlrabi can withstand fairly hard frosts. Kohlrabi, kohlrabi-turneps, Lapland kohlrabi, ordinary kohlrabi, early kohlrabi, quicker to form and more tender than the former, red-necked kohlrabi. They can withstand the coldest weather: same cultivation as kohlrabi. RUTABAGA. Yellowish Swedish turnip, preferred as a vegetable: sow from May to July. 5. FLOWER KALE. Brassica botrytis. There are three main varieties: tender, semi-hard and hard. These varieties have no clearly defined external characteristics that distinguish them from one another, but they do differ in quality. Cauliflower seed should be sown on benches to protect it from insects; it is sown from May 15 to the end of June. For the past two years, we have been deprived of cauliflower; the two summers that have just passed have been so rainy, and at the same time so cold, that cauliflower has not been able to peel; it has only risen: it needs the ordinary warmth of our summers, so that it can form its head. When the plant is a foot high, it is planted, taking care to plant it far enough into the ground, as they are often missed if this precaution is not taken, as they are likely to put a lot of leg into the soil: this is why only the leaves should be left to come out. Holes should be one foot square, with a bed of well-consumed horse manure at the bottom, and a layer of good soil on top: plant a cabbage in each hole, and top with a little short manure. In countries where cauliflowers come in very large quantities, take the precaution of leaving some soil around them, so that they can be resown; several sowings are necessary: if the first is not successful, as often happens, those that followed replace them. White broccoli should be treated in the same way. CABBAGE-WHITE BROCCOLI. Brassica botrytis cymosa. Resembles cauliflower, from which it differs only in its wavy leaves, its overall larger size and its color. The most widely grown varieties are white and purple, and are sown later than cauliflower, in late June and early July. CIBOULE. Allium fissile. It is sown in two seasons, in light, substantial soil: in February, to replant two plants together in April, and from the 15th to the end of September, to have them all year round. CHIVES, CIVETS; APPETITE. Allium schœnoprasum. Indigenous, multiplies by its cloves, which are separated in February to be planted in beds, and more usually in borders; it likes good soil and warm exposure: being delicate, it needs new soil. Russian gherkin, very small, almost round, comes in bunches; the earliest of all gherkins, since it is good at least three weeks before ordinary gherkins: its fruit must be picked as soon as it is born, otherwise it turns yellow. The English gherkin, stronger, elongated and of excellent quality, is abundant. All gherkins are sown in April and May. CUCUMBER. Cucumis sativus. A plant of warm climates: the long white cucumber, the small green candied cucumber, called green gherkin. All cucumbers like heat and water. SNAKE CUCUMBER. Cucumis fluxuosus. A very curious fruit: it owes its nickname to its elongated, flexuous shape. Used to make gherkins. Cucumbers are sown in manure-filled holes in April; green gherkins in April and May. CURRANGE. Cucurbita. Dark-fleshed melonne squash; long green melonne squash. LARGE TOMATOES. Several species of this genus are grown, and a large number of varieties: their cultivation is well known. GOURD. Powder pear, trumpet, etc. Several varieties: it produces fruits that are kept for their unusual shapes, and which are inappropriately called coloquintes. From April or May, they are sown like gherkins. ALENOIS CRESSON, and others. Can be sown at any time. Fountain cress can be sown at the edge of running water: plant a few roots. Para cress. ECHALOTE. Allium Ascalonicum. Bulbs are replanted in February and March, in beds or borders. SPINACH. Spinacia oleracea. There are two main species, with round or long leaves. For winter enjoyment, sow seeds from July to October in beds or borders. Spinach from England with long leaves, round from Flanders, with very wide leaves; from Holland, from New Zealand. The seed remains ungerminated for a long time. Transplant 25 inches apart, let the plant run on the ground, take the large leaves, cut them off by pulling towards the ground, so as not to shake the root, give it frequent watering. ESTRAGON. Artemisia dracunculus. Perennial, aromatic plant, propagated by bursting the stems in March and April. FÈVE DE NARBONNE, large, flat, called fève de Marais: sown at the end of October. FÈVE DE NICE, small, with long pods, early, good in green and for stewing; there is also a very large Windsor bean: the small dwarf bean is very good, very sweet and produces abundantly. In 1834, the harvest of this vegetable was nil: I have observed that the small dwarf bean alone has resisted drought and fog; its yield is fifty to one, and it is fed to horses with advantage: it deserves to be cultivated. I must point out, with regard to all types of broad bean, that they retain their fruiting germ for many years. What's more, two-, three- and four-year-old beans are more resistant to cold, more robust, load more, and don't provide branches or twigs that are useless for fruiting. I insist on this point, in order to fight as much as I can against a prejudice so strongly ingrained in me, that many people only want to sow this year's beans; and I am obliged to keep only new ones in my store, on pain of not selling them. I would also point out that broad beans and many other vegetables should be sown with a planter; then the ground is less raised, less loose, and ground rats and field mice have less opportunity in winter to devour the seeds and devastate the seedlings. FRAISIER. Fragaria. Multiplies by seed, by runners and by rooted splinters. There are six varieties: their cultivation is well known. HARICOTS A RAMES. From Soissons. White, flat, large seed. This dry bean is highly prized. Little cultivated in our departments, it is sought after elsewhere; it acquires a finesse of taste that makes it superior to other species. HARICOT-SABRE. White, flattened, medium-sized seed. This species is perhaps the best of all: it produces considerably; its pods are extraordinarily long and wide: when young, they make excellent green beans; when almost fully grown, they are still tender and fleshy, and can be eaten in this state, either fresh and broken into pieces, or in winter after having been cut into strips and candied in salt. It climbs very high, and requires large, strong oars. PREDOME, PRUDHOMME, PRODOMMET. White, round, small seed; it is an all-purpose eater par excellence; its pod is absolutely parchment-free, and still good when almost dry; the grain is dry and of esteemed quality: it is sown to be eaten green, in April, May, June, July, for the late season. The Lima bean, with its very high stalk, could become precious. Swiss bean. There are a large number of species. The cultivation of beans is generally too well known to enter into lengthy details: a soft, light and slightly cool soil is best suited to them. Beans without parchment are widely cultivated in this country; we have a species that is not of good quality; I urge amateurs to introduce the true prudhomme, which will be an excellent acquisition for the country. DOLIQUE. Dolichos. Following on from beans, I must mention a neighboring genus, the dolichos, which provides, especially in warm countries, several species and varieties cultivated for human consumption. Dolichos unguiculatus, known in Provence as Mongette and Bannette, is highly esteemed and produces a good yield, but has difficulty reaching maturity. The Egyptian or Lablab, which is grown in Egypt, is no less difficult: it is mainly used as an ornamental plant in our gardens. Finally, there is a third species known as the long-podded cowpea, asparagus bean, sesquipedalis, which, thanks to the extraordinary length of its narrow, fleshy pods, which are good in green, is accepted in amateur gardens. LETTUCE. Lactuca. Two species have given rise to two divisions: head and romaine lettuces, the former distinguished by its rounded shape, the latter by its more elongated form: the heart of the latter develops more easily, and it also has a much sweeter flavor. I'll list the most esteemed varieties, limiting myself to a much smaller number than exists, as few plants have varied as much as lettuce. SPRING HEAD LETTUCES. GOAT LETTUCE. Small, very blond, two sub-varieties with black seed, slow to bolt and, even in summer, bolts only very-difficulty. - Red-edged, or red cordon. - Dauphine. SUMMER HEAD LETTUCES. Versailles lettuce. Large, slightly high head, excellent for summer, fairly quick to bolt; difficult to bolt: white seed. - Blonde with black seed. - Berlin blonde. - Royal with black seed. - Batavia blonde, or Silesia, extremely large. - Turkish. - Genoa. - Big lazy brown. - Palatine. - Bloody or flagellated. All these summer lettuces should be sown from mid-June to the beginning of July: sowing several times, four to five days apart, will produce good results. WINTER LETTUCES. LAITUE PASSION, or DE LA PASSION, so named because it apples around Holy Week: white seed. - Morine: as large as an apple; lasts longer. - Small pancake. - Black head. CUTTING LETTUCE. Small species are usually preferred for this purpose, such as crêpes, gotte, lettuce-chicory, whose curled leaves imitate a small yellow chicory; lettuce-spinach, cut almost like an oak leaf. The latter grows back and can be cut several times. Spring lettuces can be sown in February, under cover, and replanted in April, or they can be sown in the field in February and March, among onions and carrots, etc. - Black-seeded Lombardy. Summer lettuces are sown at the same time as early lettuces, from March to July. Winter lettuces are sown from August to the end of September, and even in October: they can be transplanted along walls and shelters. Roman lettuces, or CHICONS. Early green. - Market green, gray. - Winter green. - Large gray. - Red apple. - Lombardy with white seeds. Head lettuces are ideally suited to Romans. We know that they need to be tied, so that their heads fill out better. MACHE, BOURSETTE, DOUCETTE, BLANCHETTE. Valeriana locusta. Annual plant. Sown every eight days, from late August to October. As lamb's lettuce is used whole, and only when young, picking the most advanced for consumption, the plant is sufficiently thinned out. Cultivated in our gardens, this species is more beautiful than the field variety. MELON. Cucumis melo. There are a great many varieties. They can be reduced to three main breeds: common or embroidered, cantaloupe and plain-skinned melons. Melon MaRAîcHeR. - Sucrin de Tours. - Small-seeded Sucrin. - Des Carmes: two varieties, one medium, the other small, very sweet. - White-fleshed Sucrin. - Green-fleshed pineapple. - De Honfleur: very large, elongated, ORANGE CANTALOUP. Small, round, ribbed. - Fine early. - Noir des Carmes. - Large black cantaloupe from Holland. - Large Portugal. All very good, but which the limits of this little book do not allow me to describe, since few of these species are grown, but the Saint-Nicolas-de-la-Grave melon, which is carried in very large quantities to our squares: they are rarely good. Roman melon. - From Cavaillon. These are two good varieties that do very well. I'm going to list a few more varieties, in the hope that the best will be selected and grown in the future. MELON DE MALTE, white-fleshed. - Maltese, red-fleshed. - From Peru. - From Morée. - From Candia. - From winter Malta. - From Persia, or Odessa. Green with yellow stripes, very long; green, melting flesh: winter like the previous one. Cultivation. For early crops, sow in March. The custom in our climate is to sow in April in holes in place: sometimes the plants don't succeed, either because of rain, or because they are eaten by insects: we sow again at the beginning of May on a bed in place; that is to say, and to explain myself more clearly, we make a hole of one foot, in which we put six inches of manure, which we cover with six inches of compost; then, we sow the melon seeds in it. When the fruit is set, prune the main branches, leaving them as long as possible according to their vigor, lengthening the strong ones more than the weak ones; four or five days after pruning, remove the harmful secondary branches: If there is more than one fruit on a branch, we cut them off, keeping the best fruit; if there is only one fruit, and it is rounded on one side but not on the other, we lightly pass the cutting edge of the pruning knife over the side that is not rounded. Some time later, we pinch off the ends of the fruit-bearing branches, and remove any unnecessary ones. If there are any good melons in Toulouse, we bring them from Bas-Languedoc. WATERMELON, PUMPKIN WATERMELON. Cucurbita citrullus. Red or white flesh, very melting: used for jams. MELONGENE, MERANGENE, EGGPLANT. Solanum Melongena. Sown in February on a bed and under a frame; failing that, sown in vases: a layer of manure is laid along a wall facing south, in a sheltered spot; after allowing the first fire to pass through the manure, the vases are immersed in it, covering them at night, and during the day when the weather is too cold. Violet and large brown. White eggplant, or egg-laying eggplant, is sown in the same way: water the vases (1). (1) Eggplant is particularly prone to destruction by the moth known as Courtilière, Courterole or Mole-Grillon. It wreaks havoc on seedlings, destroying tender plant roots, and we were mistaken when we thought it didn't eat them: it is very formidable, and we must make every effort to eliminate it from crops. The only way to destroy it is with water, on which a little oil is thrown. NAVET should be used. Brassica napus. The usual season for sowing turnips is from mid-June to September. There are several breeds of fine turnips: the soil has a great influence on their flavor. I'll just mention a few of them, and the best ones. The Freneuse turnip, small and half-long. - The Meaux turnip, very long and shaped like a tapering carrot. JAUNE de Hollande turnip, round shape, yellowish rind and flesh. - Scottish yellow is frost-resistant. - Maltese yellow. - Alsace black, long, usually very sweet and good, with enormous volume. These varieties, and all those belonging to the same section, succeed only in privileged, sandy, mild soils: they are turnips par excellence, especially for stewing; but in strong soils they become fibrous and worm-eaten, and are worth less than the common species. Foreign turnips are little cultivated, depending on the abundance of gardening in our regions; however, there are several turnip species that deserve to be known, having a delicious flavor, hunting it down, destroying it, and seeking it out to its furthest reaches. a thin, delicate rind: I recommend them to turnip lovers. Tender turnips include the white, half-round Sablons turnip, which is very good. - The pink turnip from the Palatinate, with a pink collar and very tender, sweet flesh. - Flat-white turnip, early. - The early red turnip, whose main merit is its earliness. - Maltot turnip - Limousin turnip, or rabioule, or turneps, which, although grown for livestock, is nevertheless very good in most non-sandy soils. OGNON. Allium cepa. This plant, one of the most important and useful of the root vegetables, is perennial by nature; its varieties are numerous, and change very easily with the influence of soil and climate. I'll mention the most esteemed. Pale red, the most widely grown. - Dark-red onion, broad and flat. - Yellow or blond. - Vertus. - Cambrai onion, excellent, large and good for keeping. - James onion, blond in color, slightly elongated, highly valued for its long shelf life. The Lescure onion is a good species, highly cultivated by our gardeners: consumption is very considerable for its quality. It is firm, slow to bolt, and keeps until Easter in ordinary years; but I must point out that 1834 was not a good year for it; we won't keep one, because of the heavy rains that fell during its development; we sow it at the end of January and throughout February: for early crops, if the plant is lacking at these two times, we must continue sowing in March. We grow the Saint-Michel red onion here, because it is sown at this time of year: it is used for tender early onions, which are needed for cooking at this time, as the others are past their prime. Straw onions are also advantageously sown in January and February, to be used for storage: the latter is more prone to cold than the former. Experience has shown that onions harvested from dry soil keep longer than those grown on oily soil. The latter rises more easily. The soil must be well prepared and fertilized, and the manure well consumed: it would be a good idea to have fertilized the soil for some time before sowing. When the onion is ripe, it is left for a few days in an alley, then brought in when the weather is dry. Another method is used in cold countries, where these seedlings are difficult to raise. In good, healthy soil, sow onion seeds in April and May, very thickly; water once or twice immediately after sowing: if the operation is successful, you'll obtain a multitude of pea-sized bubbles for harvest, which you can store in a dry place over winter, like other onions. After winter, lay out the ground in rays, six to eight inches apart, and plant the bubbles one by one, three or four inches apart: each one becomes a large, beautiful onion. Rumex acetosa. It is sown broadcast, in beds or borders, in spring, and better in autumn; it does well in all soils, although it prefers light, deep soil. Belleville sorrel, which has broader leaves than the common variety, is generally grown elsewhere. Virgin sorrel: less acidic. PANAIS. Pastinaca oleracea. Large biennial plant, long-rooted, simple, sweet and aromatic; adds flavor to soup. Same cultivation as for carrots: under the name of round parsnip, there is a spinach-shaped variety, earlier than the ordinary one, and better suited to soils with little bottom. PASTEQUE. See Watermelon. SWEET, EARLY POTATO. Convolvulus batatas. The long-rooted, yellow variety is preferred for its earlier maturity. The gardeners of Paris grow it successfully; my father raised it under simple frames, and then placed it in the ground at a good exposure. The gardener at the Jardin-des-Plantes grows it extensively, with great success. The southern départements could give themselves over to this crop, which would be perfectly successful in the open ground. PARSLEY. Apium petroselinum. Biennial plant: its seeds, which take three weeks to set, should be sown in the first days of March, then at the end of August and September, at the foot of a wall and at midday, to get them early. This plant goes to seed in the second year: there are several varieties, such as curly parsley, the very curly dwarf, a new variety remarkable for the beauty of its leaves and its slowness to rise; broad-leaved parsley, tuberosum, whose fleshy root is used in cooking; Naples parsley, with large ribs, or celery parsley, which produces a much larger plant than the others, and whose blanched ribs are eaten cooked like those of celery: the latter should be sown very lightly, or better still, replanted one foot in all directions. PICRIDIE CULTIVÉE, TERRE-CRÉPIE. Terra-Crepola. Cultivated in southern France and Italy, it is sown in March and successively cut young and green, and eaten as a salad. PEPPER. Capsicum. Several species of this genus are used as seasoning, the most common being the annual pepper, known as long pepper. - Coral. This plant is sown in February or March in potting soil and replanted in late April or early May in a bed facing south. - The ordinary chili pepper, the round one, the large one, the large Spanish round one, the sweet one, which we call tomato chili pepper, because of its shape, which is the same, but smaller in volume. TOMATO PEPPER. Yellow, rounded, tortuous fruit like the tomato, from which it takes its name: it is sweet and ripens more slowly than the ordinary pepper. PIMPRENELLE, garden, for salad. PORREAU, LEEK. Allium porrum. Requires light, substantial soil that has not been smoked for a long time. It is sown in February and March, and also in July: when it has reached the size of a feather pipe, take advantage of rainy, overcast weather to carefully remove it; and immediately replant it in a bed of the same well-disturbed soil, about six inches apart and three or five deep, after cutting off the tips of the leaves and roots. Water often during the summer. The German porreau is stronger and bigger than the one acclimatized in the country: same culture as for the previous one. POIRÉE or BETTe. Beta. The chard variety is generally adopted, because the ribs of its leaves, which are more tender and broader, can be cooked and eaten with white sauce; the most widely cultivated breed is the white chard; it is grown in two seasons: in March and April, for winter; in late July, August and September, for spring. Only in the second year does the plant go to seed. POIS. Pisum. Peas are not fussy about the quality of the soil: they are sown in clumps, or in rays, often in flowerbeds along south-facing walls: When you want to get an early crop, choose warm, sandy soil; the rays are planted about eight inches apart, and that's the distance of one foot between the holes made with the hoe, into which you throw five or six peas to form the clump; until harvest, all you have to do is hoe, weed and rake the larger species, and pinch the early ones when they have their third or fourth flower. In naturally good soils, peas should not be fertilized: fertilization makes them too vigorous, and they produce little fruit. In November and December, sow michaux and early peas along the flowerbeds; sow other early peas at the end of January, February and March, and successively the same species: prolong sowing in the open ground using the Clamar until the end of July. Pea varieties can be divided into two main sections: peas without parchment, or mange-tout; and gourmet peas, whose pods and seeds are eaten: dwarf and oar-shaped varieties can be distinguished from each other. 1. peas for shelling. DWARF PEAS. - Dwarf hátif pea. Earlier than the other dwarf varieties, from fifteen inches to two feet high, depending on the soil. Its season is that of the michaux; it flowers from the second or third node, which distinguishes it from all the others; its pod is rather small than large: it is of good quality without being striking. - Dutch dwarf. It can be used as a border plant in poor soils. - Large late sweet dwarf: large grain, very good quality, very productive; being strong, it requires more space than the other dwarfs. - Green Prussian dwarf. Both species are good and productive. 2. SHELLED PEAS. A RAMES. - Dutch michaux pea. Very early; sown at the end of February, it is sensitive to cold. - Michaux, petitpois de Paris. From Auvergne, new variety, very long, arched pod, very full of seeds (it contains up to eleven); very good quality. - Sans-pareil. - Fêve, very large and late. - Géant, even larger than the previous one. - Gros vert normand, late, with large oars, esteemed above all for its excellence for purée (1). This last species should be sown at the end of December. The Normandy pea has been perfectly successful sown at this time, as has the Auvergne pea, with a long pod. (1) These species of row peas are very productive; but they should be reserved and sheltered, because of the east wind: tossed around in the wind, when they have tender stems, it is very harmful. I won't go into more detail on a number of species that are neither known nor cultivated, but will simply mention the best ones. For some years now, pigeon peas have been almost the only cultivated species: their seed should be changed, as they are prone to bastardization, as are all plant species. 3. PARCHMENTLESS PEAS or Mance-TOUT. Early dwarf parchmentless peas. - Ordinary dwarf parchmentless. - Fan, the only one without dwarf and early parchment, quite dwarf, barely a foot high. - Without white parchment, with large pods, perhaps the best of all mange-touts: large, broad, fleshy, hooked pods; which is why it is still called ram's horns. It is long-stemmed, late, and very productive in good soils. Without parchment, it is also very productive. Turc, or crowned, name taken from the arrangement of the flowers, with large reams, very numerous pods, so tender and sweet that birds sometimes destroy a large part of them. It is said that, to protect peas from being attacked by an insect called the pea beetle, they should be sown in April for all those destined for purées: I encourage amateurs to make tests and observations on this subject. CHICK-POIS. Cicer arietinum. Annual plant, generally known. Sow in spring. POURPIER. Portulaca oleracea. Sow outdoors when cold weather is no longer a concern. Golden purslane, more esteemed than the green variety, but often degenerates as it regains its color. The seed, being very fine, is thrown clear, on well-consumed compost: it is not buried, but flattened with the hand on the ground: it is covered with moss. This method should be used for all fine seeds and delicate plants. RAIPONCE. Campanula rapunculus. Sow in March, on well-tilled and loosened soil, in a shady spot; cover very lightly with fine compost; water with a fine-hole watering can, given the fineness of the seed; cover with chopped moss, or sow radishes among, to provide shade. RAVE, Raphanus sativus oblongus, and RADIS, Raphanus sativus rotundus. These annual roots come in many varieties: long red rabe; early small rabe; rose-colored or bronce; white rabe; Le Mans tortee; early white radish; long summer gray radish; yellow radish; large Augsburg radish; horseradish or large winter black radish. Most of these varieties, especially the small long radishes, can be grown almost all year round. To obtain well-rounded radishes, the soil must be well trampled before sowing; in hot weather, plenty of water and a little shade are needed; sow little at a time, and repeat sowing often. ROQUETTE. Brassica eruca. Sow very lightly in spring, in August and September, for winter. SALSIFY, CERCIFIS. Tragopogon porrifolium. Sow broadcast, in March and April, in substantial, deeply tilled, well loosened soil that has not been newly smoked: just water often. Cultivate in the same way, and for the same purpose, as the previous plant. SPANISH SCORZONERA. Scorzonera hispanica. Its root is black; it differs from salsify in that it is commonly eaten only in its second year, except in very soft soils, where it can acquire sufficient size in its first year: in the latter case, it should be sown in February; it can also be sown in August. GARDEN SAVORY. Satureia hortensis. Annual. Small, aromatic plant, nine to ten inches tall, closely related to thyme. It multiplies on its own when introduced. EDIBLE NUTSEDGE, ALMOND-EARTH. Cyperus esculentus. From southern Europe, in Spain, and in some departments of France: the numerous tubers with which its roots are covered are used as human food, or to make a kind of very pleasant orgeat; and oil can be extracted from it. Three to four tubers are planted in March, to a depth of one inch, in preferably light, moist soil, well loosened, in clumps spaced about a foot apart, and usually swollen in water; the tubers are hoeed, weeded and watered; in October, they are removed and kept for use and for planting the following year. Spilanthus. Name of two annual plants whose pungent flavor is used in cooking as a seasoning; one is called CRESSON DE PARA, Oleracera, and the other CRESSON DU BRÉSIL: to obtain them, it is sufficient, when they are not sown by themselves, to do so in spring on a bed; then, when the plant is strong enough, it is transplanted to a southern exposure, and watered often. If you take a head of the flowers of these plants and rub it on your teeth and gums, you'll feel a little quivering in your mouth, with abundant salivation and a very pleasant freshness. TOMATO, LOVE APPLE. Solanum lycopersicon. Annual. Sown as soon as the soil warms up. A large, new species, with very high volume and excellent quality; can be grown like the previous one. JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE, EARTH PEAR. Helianthus tuberosus. It is grown like potatoes, but needs to be planted as early as February. It usually reproduces on its own, and a plot of land where Jerusalem artichokes have been grown can remain covered, so to speak, indefinitely. The taste of this tuber is similar to that of cooked artichokes. There is a variety with yellow tubers. TRIQUE -MADAME, WHITE ORPIN. Sedum album. Used as a salad ingredient. It can be propagated from seed or cuttings; it soon spreads, provided it has been placed in a warm spot. CHAPTER TWO. LARGE-SCALE CULTIVATION. THE MAIN FORAGE SPECIES. As fodder plants are now generally cultivated, I felt it necessary, in the interest of a large number of my readers, to explain the cultivation of those suited to our climate. In confining myself to the most essential notions, I shall try not to omit anything useful, and I shall avoid all scientific detail or mere curiosity. First, I'll give a few general indications on sowing artificial meadows: we must consider that success concerns not only the fodder product that we expect directly, but also the harvest of grain or other products that will follow the clearing, sometimes even several subsequent harvests. Plants that last several years, and whose roots run deep, such as alfalfa and sainfoin, require ploughing as deep and as complete as can be given; and for all forage species, with very few exceptions, the more perfect the preparation and cleaning of the land, the more successful it will be. This precaution is especially important for fine seeds and in the case of deep ploughing: when the ford is not sufficiently stale, it is advisable in certain cases to obtain this effect artificially by using a roller, or by repeated harrowing, with the harrow teeth tilted backwards. In the case of meadows to be mowed, the soil surface should be sanded, dethatched if necessary, and cleared of anything that might interfere with mowing, which is all the better the shorter it is. Applying manure to forage plants, rather than to the grains that usually follow them, is a very good method, whose advantages extend both to the current product and to the goodness and cleanness of the next harvest: I'm talking especially about annual and short-lived plants, such as vetch, clover and forage roots. New manures are generally suitable for vigorous plants with large seeds; some species, on the other hand, whose seeds are very fine, or which are delicate in their youth, such as alfalfa, carrots, etc., require consumed fertilizers, or prefer manure given a year in advance for the harvest that preceded them. Fine seeds should be sown after harrowing, rather than after the last ploughing, and should be only lightly covered; for this operation, a light harrow with short teeth is used; or the ordinary harrow, between the teeth of which thorn branches are interwoven; or only the roller: the use of this last instrument, even after harrowing, is always excellent for sowing in light soil. Forages are very often sown with oats or other cereals; or a meadow sowing is made up of large or light seeds, such as sainfoin or fromental; and others that are fine and runny, such as white or yellow clover and other grasses: in both cases, the large seeds are sown first, having been previously mixed together, if there are several kinds; this first sowing is harrowed; then the fine seeds, equally mixed, are spread over the whole field, if there are several kinds; then the seeds are again harrowed across, or rolled in the same way. I will indicate in each article the approximate quantity of seed to be used. One hectare compared to the Toulouse arpent gives 7 pugnères 4 perches; half a hectare, 3 pugnères 4 bushels 2 perches: 56 ares 90 centiares make the Toulouse arpent, or 1764 square canes, or 576 perches. There are circumstances in which it is necessary to sow more or less thickly; for example, a poor plot of land requires more seed than a good one; on a plot of land poorly prepared by unfavorable dry weather, in a situation exposed to late frosts, in all circumstances that are unfavorable to sowing, it is necessary to sow thicker than if the soil and the season favor it. I have thought it necessary to give some rough guidelines for owners who, wanting to make trials, sometimes have no data on the quantity of seed needed for the land they want to sow. FIRST CLASS. Forage plants of the grass family, AGROSTIS TRAÇANTE. Agrostis stolonifera. Trailing bentgrass can be usefully employed on peaty soils, or, as pasture, on damp badlands, where it often propagates naturally with abundance. As its seed is extremely fine, it should be barely covered, and sown at a rate of 20 pounds per acre in February or September. AGROSTIS of herd-grass and red-top-grass. An American plant that has succeeded perfectly in France on deep sandy soils, where its yield has been extraordinary, and on chalky soil that is a little cool, but not damp. Herd-grass tallies a lot, and once established becomes very vigorous and long-lasting, making it very suitable for use in permanent meadows. The extreme fineness of the seed and the slowness of the plant's first growth make it difficult to sow successfully: the young plant is choked by weeds; those who have grown it in France have preferred to sow it and transplant it. I would only recommend that, when sowing in place, the precautions necessary for the success of very fine seeds be strictly observed: its fodder is a little coarse, but very abundant. 25 pounds per acre. HIGH OAT, FROMENTAL. Avena elatior. Perennial grass, one of the largest and most productive found in France: grown extensively in the Nord department, it is very fortunately beginning to be cultivated in our departments. Fromental can be used to create natural meadows. It's not easy to create good natural meadows, because landowners don't want to sacrifice anything to obtain the seeds they need to create them: almost everywhere, we're content to collect seeds indiscriminately from the barns, which is nothing more than a mixture of all the bad seeds that exist in the old meadows: in this way, we can only create very bad meadows; such a serious disadvantage would not exist if we chose good seeds suited to our climate and our land: timothy, tall fescue, cocklebur, burnet, yellow clover, fromental; its hay, though of good quality, is a little coarse, and prone to drying out very quickly on the ground: for these reasons, fromental should be mown early, and sown thickly; it is particularly suited to high and medium meadows, and fears excess humidity. This gramen is superior to all others in forming high meadows for mowing. Fromental is often incorrectly referred to as French ryegrass. To keep avena elatior pure and free of weeds, mow young seedlings of this plant four or five times a year. The agronomist can keep the seed unmixed, and spread these seedlings sparingly. See Turf. From repeated experiments, it has been proven that we were mistaken when we fixed sufficient seed at 100 pounds per acre. Some agronomists claim that 200 pounds should be sown; as for me, I saw an acre of land on which 140 pounds of fromental had been sown: it was quite thick, and, consequently, I limit myself to recommending this quantity. Other grasses can be added, to garnish and increase the forage. Fromental, if sown thickly, has the advantage of keeping longer: we can't recommend its cultivation enough. It can be sown in September and February. I don't need to dwell on the advantages for landowners of mucking out their old meadows; they will have harvests every year for almost ten years, whether wheat, corn or oats. After reaping great benefits from these harvests, the meadows can be re-established with a mixture of 10 pounds of red clover, 10 pounds of yellow clover, and a few grasses; this combination will produce a very good meadow. I know of large landowners who use the communication paths between their various tenant farms, sowing yellow clover along the edges every five to six years, to serve as a depaissance: this process is only good for large estates. MEADOW BROME. Bromus pratensis. It can be classed as a passable species, but there are soils and circumstances where an otherwise mediocre plant can become very useful. For example, on calcareous soil, too poor even for sainfoin, and where the aim is to obtain some kind of forage, meadow brome gives more satisfactory results than any other species. It will establish itself vigorously, providing good pasture and even becoming more mowable than orchardgrass, even on very poor sands. This plant can therefore be ranked among those which, by virtue of their vigor and hardiness, are able to succeed on the poorest soils, and offer resources and means of improvement that would not be obtained from more valuable species. It lasts a long time. Meadow bromegrass, with its narrow leaves (it has some resemblance to ryegrass), has the added advantage of being suitable for forming long-lasting ornamental lawns on very chalky soils, where even ryegrass and low meadow grasses cannot survive. It requires 80 pounds of this seed per acre. MEADOW FESCUE. Festuca pratensis. Perennial plant of natural meadows, one of the best to be used for seeding low meadows, due to the abundance and quality of its product; it is a little late, and for this reason should not be combined with early-season species such as vulpine and meadow ryegrass: sown alone, it would require 120 pounds per acre. TALL FESCUE. Festuca elatior. Stronger and taller than the previous one, this plant's hay is coarse but of fairly good quality and abundant, making it one of the most useful species to cultivate in low meadows. EWE'S FESCUE. Festuca ovina. Small, with fine leaves, not very productive, but renowned for the quality of the pasture it provides for sheep, and having the advantage of growing in fine, sterile sands and on the driest slopes. Only in such soils can it be useful, and it should be sown either in September, or early in February and March; 80 pounds of this seed is enough per acre. TIMOTHY. Timothy from the English. The considerable yield of this well-known plant has led to its cultivation: it is sown separately to make mowing meadows; it is particularly suited to damp, clayey or sandy soils. As timothy is one of the latest grasses, if you use it to form the base of a natural meadow, you should avoid adding very early species to it: agrostis, meadow fescue, tall fescue, etc., are the ones that would go best with it in this respect. Timothy can also be used very advantageously for grazing, even on mediocre soils, provided they are fresh. Sow 50 pounds per acre. FRAGRANT FLUKE. Anthoxantum odoratum. A low-yielding grass, but recommended for its earliness and aromatic scent. This plant grows in a wide variety of situations and soils: it can be found in woods and on dry, high slopes, but is not uncommon in even damp meadows. On its own, it cannot make good mowing meadows: it can be sown with advantage on sandy, mediocre soils, to provide early grazing; another use for it is to be mixed in small quantities with the seeds intended for sowing a meadow: the good smell it imparts to hay makes it more appetizing for cattle. Sow 50 pounds per acre. WOOLLY COOT. Holcus lanatus. Few of the perennial grasses are better suited to the composition of a meadow base for cool ground. In the northern départements, it grows abundantly in both cool and dry soils: its flowering time, which strikes a balance between the early and late species, and its ability to remain standing for some time after maturity, without losing too much of its quality, mean that it can be combined with most other grasses; lastly, it is very good for grazing. It requires 40 pounds per acre. If mixing grasses with artificial prairie plants, and particularly with red clover seed, is a good practice, experience has shown that woolly coot would undoubtedly be one of the most suitable species for this purpose, and preferable in all respects to ryegrass and orchardgrass. FORMATION of a natural meadow per half-hectare, or per Toulouse acre, metric weight: 115 half-kilograms fromental, 4 half-kilograms yellow clover. OTHER FORMATION of natural grassland per half-hectare, or Toulouse arpent: 25 half-kilograms gramens in mixture. 70 half-kilograms fromental. 4 half-kilograms yellow clover. OTHER FORMATION of natural grassland per half-hectare, or per Toulouse arpent: 25 half-kilograms gramens by name. 70 half-kilograms fromental. 4 half-kilograms yellow clover. These various meadows have been perfectly successful. Agronomists who have formed new prairies with the gramens I describe, and by mixing in the proportion I indicate, have obtained an infinitely diverse product gramens cost something more in money than prairies remade with barnyard seed. To do this experiment economically, you need to sow half a hectare, squeeze the fodder into a separate barn, collect the seeds carefully, and sow again. IVRAIE VIVACE, RAY-GRASS from England. Lolium perenne. Of all the grasses, this is the one least used in meadows. In our départements, it could be used with advantage with red clover, in a mixture: it is a good practice, according to experience, in large-scale cultivation; the results already obtained vary infinitely, due to climate, soil and other local circumstances; it can be partially admitted in the mixture of gramens for meadows. Ryegrass is sown with a mixture of white clover. For lawns or borders, birdsfoot trefoil can be added. See also

Turf. Ryegrass should be sown thickly in February and March, September and October: sown alone, it requires 100 pounds per acre. ITALIAN VIVACE RYE, lolium perenne italicum, has only recently been introduced to trade and agriculture; if it can be acclimatized in France, there is no doubt that the great advantages of this forage, in terms of duration, high yield and usefulness, will encourage its cultivation. Preferable to alfalfa and clover, it has the advantage of being healthier than the latter, and is not harmful when fed green to all livestock: this is an invaluable advantage, because of the unfortunate events that have resulted from the short-sightedness of herdsmen in giving clover and alfalfa still soaked in dew, and which have suddenly lost oxen, cows and bulls, as these two forages are pernicious to horned animals. It will also prevent the accidents that often occur on properties covered with these two types of forage: when horned animals escape, entrusted to the care of children who are too young, they run there greedily, and die. I will agree, however, that these two forages have been a great help to agriculture, especially in our départements, where it is growing, and from where it is spreading to distant countries. Italian ryegrass can be mowed four times; it can also be grown on land that is unsuitable for other forages: This is all the more precious, as these localities cannot receive cereals, which usually perish there due to the abundance of rain, with the water staying longer; and the little harvest that escapes this first accident is washed away by the fog, which thickens with force over all the shallows; which everyone can verify as well as I can. When I say that Italian ryegrass needs moist soil, I don't mean to say or advise that it should be given soil that is continually soaked with water: that would be against common sense; but I say moist soil, shallows (1). It should be noted, however, that in our Midi climate, the most favorable season is to sow Italian ryegrass at the end of September and October; it is already foraging in December, with strong, active vegetation: It can also be sown in spring, at the end of February and throughout March; later, its vegetation is delayed by the south winds, which in April dry out the surface of the soil where the seed has been scattered, and it necessarily remains there, being very light, until a sufficiently heavy rain attaches it to the soil: for this reason, choose damp weather when sowing. Germination doesn't take long; in a few days it covers the ground. A fair assessment of the usefulness of ryegrass (1) The summers of 1833 and 1834 were very wet, which disrupted the experiments then being carried out on Italian ryegrass. It is grown at the Ecole d'Artillerie with the greatest success: it has been mowed five times and has produced a large quantity of green and dry fodder. Italian ryegrass is grown in various cuts, especially in August and September, when green fodder is in short supply. This plant can provide this resource right up to the time of sowing, if heavy frosts are delayed: its vegetation is active and continuous, which makes us fear for its duration, which is not yet well established in our climates. PANIS ÉLEVÉ, or GUINEA HERB. Panicum altissimum. There are three species of Guinea grass: the species cultivated without success are panicum altissimum and panicum virgatum. It is impossible to acclimatize panicum altissimum in our departments, because in September, when the plant has given its fodder, small tubers of about five or six lines in diameter appear on the root; unfortunately, these tubers always tend to establish themselves half in the earth, and the other half above its surface: It is from these tubers that the shoots that form the fodder should emerge in spring; but these tubers are frozen by a cold of four degrees, if they are not covered by snow: then the plant is lost; we have no resource other than the seeds, which ripen very well; but we have lost the fodder no less. We could try growing this plant in Spain and in our southern departments. Panicum virgatum withstands cold temperatures of twelve degrees; its fodder rises as much as panicum altissimum: its seed is very difficult to germinate. A distinguished agronomist, who sowed it with the greatest care, has been unable to get it to germinate: it is possible that in transporting it by sea it has spoiled and not retained its germination principle; it is to be hoped that this remarkable forage will eventually become completely acclimatized in France (1). PATURIN, or POA DES PRÉS. Poa pratensis, Paturines offer several interesting plants, from different points of view, but especially in terms of forage quality.
