The species known as meadow-grass is perhaps the most difficult to appreciate: few gramens are as common as this one, and present themselves under more different aspects: we see it small and dry on roadsides and banks (1) These observations were given by M. le chevalier de Morteaux, a zealous agronomist; but it is said that M. le comte de Mosbourg, near Cahors, has sown it in place, and it has been perfectly successful. of ditches, large and foddery in wet meadows; but everywhere extremely tractable and very early. These two characteristics often make it more harmful than useful in mixtures formed by chance, and mean that it should be used only with caution in the formation of meadows. Although its hay is considered to be of excellent quality, it is best sown on its own in wet soils, or with meadow-grass and common meadow-grass, which, although later, need to be cut at about the same time as it; in dry soils, with dactyls and meadow-grass, a little flouve and legumes, taking care, in the latter case, to mow it very early: it would require around 80 pounds per half-hectare. Common meadowgrass, Poa trivialis, is as common as the previous species, but like it grows in very different types of soil: it is abundant on dry plains, among artificial meadows, yet humidity is very unfavorable; it is often found in watery soils: it requires 80 pounds of seed per half-hectare. MEADOW VULPINE. Alopecurus pratensis. Vulpine is generally considered a valuable plant for its earliness and the abundance of its fodder: although it thrives early, its vegetation is sustained by a new production of stems; this means it can be mixed with heath and ryegrass. It can be sown early, in autumn or February, and requires 80 pounds per acre. SECOND CLASS. Forage plants of the legume family. GORSE, SEA RUSH, THORNY BROOM. Ulex europœus. Extremely thorny shrub, natural to uncultivated land, highly cultivated in the Ariège department. I'd like to mention the Mazères, Saverdun and Pamiers plains, whose very light, treeless soil is now planted with gorse, which provides a very good income for owners. In good soil, it reaches an elevation of ten feet: it provides heating for ovens; it is used to form fences, and is of great use to the poor. It would be desirable to cultivate it more widely, especially in woodless countries. All thorny trees give a brighter fire than oak and others: a hundred bundles of gorse of equal size will serve the same purpose as a hundred and fifty bundles of oak. Cut young, it can be used as fodder, especially in countries where artificial pastures are in short supply: it is fed to animals after crushing the prickles with a mallet or under a cider millstone. Gorse is considered to be a fertilizer: good harvests can be obtained from it; this is undoubtedly due to the practice of burning the stumps and roots on the ground when it is uprooted. Gorse should be cultivated in dry, arid regions, as it provides great timber resources and ashes for smoking the land: its advantages are well known; as I have already said, it is suitable for forming almost impenetrable fences: for this, after sowing it in February and March on the sides of ditches, its young shoots are defended from the teeth of cattle, which are very comfortable with it; it is also sown as a seedling in February, to be put in place in October. If you want to cover large areas permanently, broadcast it at the same times, after preparing the ground as much as possible with good ploughing: you need 10 pounds per half-hectare. The small species of gorse, Ulex nanus, common around Paris, is used by the poor to feed their livestock when it is new, and to heat their ovens in the late season. ERS ERVILLIER. Ervum ervilia. Annual forage. The ers plant is not high, but it is always good fodder, and produces a lot of seed, which is fed to pigeons, but sparingly, because it heats them up. The plant eaten green by pigs is almost fatal to them, as well as in dry grain, bran and flour. As a human foodstuff, this seed is also highly suspect, and should not be used mixed in bread. Ears in flour can be used with advantage to fatten cattle, but must be combined with potatoes. Here's how it's done: potatoes are cut into pieces with a knife (1); a pair of oxen is usually fed 130 to 150 pounds a day. (1) M. Bourcette, in Paris, has invented a potato slicer: all the roots are chopped into small slices, which do not inconvenience the cattle; a sharp S fixed to the end of a stick can also be used to cut potatoes easily: this 11- 71 After the first fortnight's feeding, we add three times a day seaweed flour, kneaded with a little water and salt; one hectoliter of this flour is enough for the entire fertilizing period. A pair of old oxen, valued at thirteen louis, which had spent 50 quintals of potatoes in thirty-five days, was sold for twenty louis. In years of abundance of this root, which is difficult to sell, it can be used to advantage in this way, which raises the price of potatoes to over 3 fr. per quintal. Ears ground into flour are excellent for cows; they produce a greater quantity of milk, and can be fed to herds mixed with bran. Sown in October, it is more successful than in February: its fodder should be given to horses in small rations and when you want to give them strength and support them for hard work: you need three quarters of a hectoliter for half a hectare. GALÉGA, or Rue de CHÈVRE. Galega officinalis. Galéga is a fodder plant with well-stocked clumps. The latter method is good for oxen, while the former is preferable for mounts. The plant is surprisingly vigorous, requiring 60 pounds of seed per hectare. BIRDSFOOT TREFOIL. Lotus corniculatus. Little known until now in cultivation, it nevertheless deserves to be: it is good for pasture, grows well on dry land, and maintains its vegetation there in summer; it is suitable for most of the uses to which little white clover is put, and would often be preferable to it, particularly for lining grass lawns, where its yellow flowers make a very pretty effect: its seed, very-difficult to harvest, is not very abundant, which keeps it at a high price. Agronomists will recognize by experience the climate that will be most favorable to it: it deserves to be cultivated for the goodness of its fodder, albeit not very high; the seed being very fine, the land must be well prepared, and tightened with the roller: 16 pounds of seed are needed per half-hectare. WHITE LUPIN. Lupinus albus. The importance of lupin as a fertilizer prompts me to give a few details on its cultivation. The roots of this plant are woody, the stems straight, and the leaves alternate: it thrives on light, sandy soils; but it fears clay, and will not grow on loamy soil: when properly sown, lupin covers the soil perfectly, and destroys all weeds: if it is to be used as fertilizer, the seed must be placed in very close rows; if the seed is to be collected, the rows must be spaced further apart, so that the intervals can be worked, much like those of lentils. White lupin, buried in flower, is recognized as a valuable soil fertilizer. Mr. Chambord, a landowner in Lunel, having sown lupin on smooth, bastard soil, obtained a product of fifteen seeds: sown on an exhausted vine, it was entirely restored, and produced many grapes; the shoots became strong, and received so much vigor, that they were 12 to 15 pans long. Lupin has been successfully sown by several agronomists; its cultivation will probably spread everywhere: I join Count Louis de Villeneuve in urging agronomists to cultivate it. Artificial meadows began the fortunes of our agriculture; add a good number of livestock to them, and you'll have manure: lupines will come to the rescue to increase them; they succeed perfectly in soft, fresh soils with depth. As a wild bean, I think it should be sown at the same time as our field beans. The seed has the advantage of staying on the ground, and you don't have to worry about it being eaten by animals, which means you don't have to pick it until it's very ripe. Lupin is sown at the first rains in September and October, so that it can produce strong vegetation, rising from 30 to 40 inches, even to 48. This plant is known for the excellent fertilizer it supplies to the soil, when buried during flowering: three quarters of a hectoliter per hectare are required. LUPULIN, KITTY. Medicago lupulina. It has the leaf and appearance of a clover, which is why it is sometimes called yellow clover or black clover, names derived from the color of its flower or its pod. For a long time, its cultivation was confined to certain cantons, but in recent years it has spread considerably throughout central France. It is biennial, and can occupy the same place in rye crops as clover in wheat crops: Its heavy weight is less abundant; it is fine, of good quality, and almost harmless to animals; moreover, grazing lupulin for sheep is perhaps even more advantageous than converting it to hay; and as it supports continuous grazing, it could be mixed with clover in a two-to-one ratio: it is sown in February and March, at a rate of 26 pounds per half-hectare. LUZERNE. Medicago sativa. The advantages of this plant are generally known, because it is widely cultivated in our department, and in many others, being the most productive of the plants used in artificial meadows. It may be useful for countries where it has not yet been introduced to give them the necessary instructions for its cultivation: it prefers good, deep, healthy soil, well cleaned of couch grass, and smoked the year before sowing; nevertheless, it succeeds in many different types of soil: in silty soils, formed from river deposits, except in those that are peaty or clayey on the surface, or extremely thin; if smoked at sowing time, it should be done with consumed fertilizers. This plant's considerable yields and long life are largely due to the ease with which its roots penetrate deep into the soil, which must be well dug out for this purpose: the most usual time to sow it is during the first rains of August and September. Sown at this time, when the ground is well prepared, it has the advantage of fortifying the plant before the first frosts, which are sometimes very early, and often late. Some growers sow it on oats, which have already been sown in February, and on top of which alfalfa seed is spread in March or April. This fodder has several cuts, and some of the most abundant. The North, much more advanced than us in agriculture, sows it in rays six inches apart; they use a rake armed with several small iron plowshares, each tracing a shallow furrow; women quickly sow the seed mixed with sand into each furrow, and gradually cover it with a light harrow, which is passed through the furrows; In this way, we have the double advantage of being able to weed alfalfa easily, and of increasing the yield by pulling up the grass, as alfalfa would be eternal with this precaution: it's not difficult to establish the truth of what I'm saying. In fields cultivated in this way, the yield will be greater than in those sown by broadcasting: this method requires a few extra expenses and meticulous care, but is amply rewarded by its long life. In February, we choose calm weather to plaster the alfalfa. You only need 6 to 7 quintals of plaster, well cooked and pulverized, to cover half a hectare. The first cut is made green, before the plant is in bloom: its height alone should indicate the moment to mow it; this cut must be consumed green, because of the difficulty at this time of drying the fodder: the second and subsequent cuts are intended for dry fodder. The second and subsequent cuts are destined for dry fodder. Choose good weather to mow it: leave it for two days without stirring it; the experience you gain should indicate the care you need to take. It is advisable to let the fodder dry out sufficiently before putting it in the barns, otherwise it ferments, heats up and becomes very pernicious for the livestock, a very serious inconvenience that is often experienced. We sow 32 pounds of alfalfa seed per acre: it is improperly called sainfoin, lauzerde. I must point out that fresh land along rivers contains a greater quantity of weeds, so it is necessary to sow more thickly: 40 to 45 pounds are needed in this case; without this precaution, seedlings will be missed, and will be choked by weeds as they become too light. Few people are unaware of the frequent accidents that result from grazing alfalfa and clover regrowth, when cattle are allowed to graze before the dew has dissipated, or after it has rained. As they are very avid of these plants, it is prudent to keep them in the crib, observing to let the fodder wither before giving it to them: without these precautions the animals bloat and perish. In this case, to prevent the animal's death, if you're within reach of a deep enough fishpond, you must take it there immediately, so that the water reaches its back: it empties immediately, and this is what brings about its recovery. SIBERIAN MELILOT. Melilotus alba. Siberian melilot is a biennial plant that grows to a considerable height. Its long life means that it can be used in crop rotation in the same way as clover; it is likely to do better on poor, gravelly soils. Regardless of how it is later judged as fodder, it has one advantage, which is now well recognized: it provides bees with abundant, successive flowers, which they eagerly seek out: 25 to 30 pounds of seed are needed per half-hectare. SAINFOIN, BURGUNDY, SPARCETTE. Hedysarum onobrichis. Sainfoin, or Esparcette, so improperly called alfalfa, is one of the best artificial forages: whether consumed green or dried, it is not harmful to livestock; and although less abundant than alfalfa and clover, it makes an excellent soil improver, both because of its duration, and because of the debris of its leaves and the hair of its roots (1). Sainfoin thrives in warm, dry, calcareous soils facing south, and even in soils sitting on a layer of marl or tufa, known as caussonels. We can insist on the usefulness of this plant and 1) In my book, I will only refer to this plant by the French name of Sainfoin-Esparcette, which is specific to it. I urge people who might ask for it to explain themselves, and not to confuse it with alfalfa. sainfoin is used to convert land into wheat land where, despite previous attempts, only rye had ever been grown; the demonstration has been so successful, and the example so influential, that, one by one, a large proportion of the land on the Lauraguais hillsides has undergone a similar transformation using the same method. When a sainfoin meadow is intended to be mown, and you want to keep it going as long as possible, you must avoid grazing the regain, especially in the first few years; but there are cases, particularly on poor soils, where it is sown expressly for the grazing of woollen animals: then it doesn't last long; but, nevertheless, it is still a great resource. It is sown in October, as soon as the weather allows rye or wheat to be sown; on fields intended for sainfoin, it is sown immediately after the grains have been covered by the plough. If the cold weather has caused some young plants to perish, don't hesitate to throw another hectoliter of seed on the same plot in March. Experience has shown that, in spring, on fields where sainfoin was sown the previous autumn, a mixture of 5 to 6 pounds of Dutch clover and the same amount of yellow clover can be spread. The following year, the sainfoin was thicker, although mixed with a certain amount of clover, but by the third year, the sainfoin had completely occupied the soil, leaving only yellow clover, which grew very well with the predominant plant. Sainfoin can also be sown on land planted with corn: shortly before harvesting, the seed is broadcast, and when the corn is harvested, it is cut on the ground. Sainfoin can be used as a fertilizer for vines. Two-cut sainfoin, or hot sainfoin, is advertised: it is more resistant to cold than that already cultivated; the plant is more vigorous, stronger and more productive than ordinary sainfoin; finally, it gives an abundant second cut where this one only produces a weak regrowth. It is to be hoped that our agronomists will introduce its use in our regions. It requires 2.5 hectolitres per half-hectare; others estimate that 3 hectolitres are needed: sowing is generally too light. HOLLAND RED CLOVER. Trifolium pratense. Of all artificial meadows, clover is the most widely cultivated in France, no doubt due to the ease with which it fits into the three-year crop rotation, which is almost always followed without disturbing the order. In this respect, this plant has been and will continue to be of great service, contributing more than any other to the elimination of the fallow year, and demonstrating that it can be replaced with advantage by a productive year. It is to be hoped, however, that this way of using clover will be replaced by another, less defective one; for land where it would be brought back several times in a row, with only one year's interval, would certainly soon tire of it. Clover prefers soils known in our départements as boulbennes (strong, soft or cold soils), terres bâtardes (bastard soils), terres lisses (smooth soils), in short, all soils composed of a high proportion of clay, sand and little limestone. Clover is sown in autumn on wheat, or on wheat in spring, or with oats or barley in February and March; it can also be sown on the second type of corn. Sown on wheat in the first days of October, clover finds loose soil, sprouts immediately, grows deep roots before winter, and can then withstand the cold: these are the advantages. The disadvantages are that, if the winter is harsh, the clover, still young, cannot withstand it; and if the spring is rainy, this plant, acquiring great vegetative strength, flowers in part, and is extremely detrimental to the wheat harvest. By sowing on wheat in spring, we don't have to fear any of the inconveniences I've just mentioned; but it's also rare that this seed succeeds perfectly: if the months of March and April are deprived of rain, the seed cannot be born; then, thrown on land that the winter rains have tightly packed, the clover seed has difficulty breaking through the crust : if, after sowing, there are heavy showers, the seed is sometimes washed into the furrows; and if the heat comes on early, the young plants perish easily: it's often said that the seed was no good. But this seed, which is hard, and alfalfa seed, though old and black, are still born: age only deteriorates them after several years. Sown with barley or oats, in March, success is almost certain; but this method has the disadvantage of not fitting in with our soils, of delaying for a year the return of wheat, such an essential crop, which is only slightly offset by that of oats, which are so successful when sown in spring. Sown on corn in the second way, the clover is in danger of perishing in the heat of July and August; moreover, we would have to give up buttering the corn plants, an operation that is nevertheless necessary, because of our strong easterly winds: only selected spots in cool valleys, sheltered from the winds, would be suitable for this crop. Having thus exposed the good and the bad of each method, I must add that, according to experience, it is preferable, as a last result, to sow clover on wheat in the first fifteen days of October: the only precaution to take is that, if the cold reaches seven degrees below zero, 8 to 10 pounds of seed per half-hectare should be sown at the end of February; in this way we are certain that the fodder will be thick enough : As for the disadvantage that clover sown in autumn has of harming the prosperity of wheat, I know of no way of remedying it: it's a chance you have to take, fortunately very rare; you can, however, obtain a sort of compensation, by having the wheat cut very high, and mowing immediately: you thus obtain a mixture of clover and straw that makes excellent fodder. If you need to sow a fairly large quantity of land with clover, it's wise to divide it partly in autumn, and partly in spring. Clover seed should be sown a little thickly, especially when sown with wheat in autumn, or on wheat in spring: from experiments, we are convinced that 15 to 16 pounds of clover are needed per half-hectare. To put an end to our old habits, which are to use the old table weight, I observe that I have put the quantity to be sown on the arpent, which corresponds roughly to half a hectare, and that I have fixed the weight at half a kilogram: it is to be hoped that sellers of this seed will adopt the new weight, and give up the old one, which is a difficulty for trade. Land intended to be sown with clover and wheat should be formed into plots. The sower begins by mixing the clover seed with five times as much dry sand; once this mixture has been made, the sower spreads it over each bed in the same way as the wheat, coming and going, and immediately after the wheat has been covered with the plough; the light harrow is then passed over, covering the clover and making the small stripes formed by the plough disappear: if the field needs to be crumbled, this operation is carried out, taking care not to step on the beds. If you lock up this forage before it is perfectly dry, you have to mix it in the barn with straw, layer by layer. Grazing dew-laden or damp clover is very dangerous, as is using it in green under the same circumstances; it should therefore only be fed to livestock properly: the same disadvantage results as for alfalfa; livestock that are inconvenienced by it should be treated as described in its article, noting that clover is even quicker to inconvenience livestock than alfalfa. Of all the fertilizers we can use to improve artificial fodder, such as alfalfa, clover, sainfoin and farrouch, gypsum is unquestionably the most valuable, both because of the property it has of doubling, so to speak, the production of fodder, and because of its great economy. It is to the discovery of this fertilizer that we owe the success of our artificial fodder, and consequently one of the greatest improvements in our agriculture. The most favorable times to spread plaster on clover and the four fodder crops indicated are November and February: the latter is preferred, in that it fixes for tenant farmers the time when they should no longer lead their herds onto artificial meadows. Start by removing the stones; then choose a very calm day, and the hour after or before sunrise, as being the time when the atmosphere is most tranquil: the people throwing the plaster must walk abreast, bent over as they spread it with their hands, in the same way as when sowing wheat, throwing the plaster as they go and return, and walking at a good pace. Sow 6 to 7 quintals of gypsum per half-hectare: stop work as soon as you realize that the wind is removing the loosest part of the gypsum; for this, the lightest wind is enough: without this precaution, a lot of gypsum will be consumed uselessly; a calm fog, a windless drizzle, are still precious moments for this operation. The clover seeds harvested in 1834 were of poor quality; this is easy to understand: weeds, and in particular dodder, were dominant because of the heavy rains. Everyone knows that dodder poisons fields, and even more so when sown mixed with clover seed, as happened this year. The dodder is in our fields; it does not appear in dry years, and when the land has been ploughed in dry weather; but it appears with force when the land has been worked too soft and too wet. When the owner plans to let his clover crop go to seed, he should visit his field when it is flowering; he will see the part dominated by dodder: he should mow this part, to give it green or wither it; by this means he has his clover pure of this mixture, and sells the seed with advantage. I carefully searched for pretty dodder-free clover seed, and I paid more for it; but you know that you run at the cheap end of the market. Unfortunately, fraud has crept into this trade, by mixing grained sand, prepared and colored with resin, which is mixed with clover seed to the extent of one third, thus increasing its weight. GRAND TRÉFLE NORMAND. This species is much taller than the common one, later, and usually yields only one cutting, but which often equals the two cuttings of ordinary clover: its fodder is fatter, the plant is more durable: it should be preferred to the ordinary species, and should encourage agronomists to experiment. I thought I should mention it as an interesting subject for trials and observations. WHITE CLOVER, LITTLE CLOVER. Trifolium repens. This species, also known as Fin-Houssy, is perennial and particularly suitable for grazing sheep; it stands up well in dry, light soils, and can be very useful: it is also used to line the bottoms of meadows and lawns sown with grasses. TRFLE INCARNAT, FARROUCH, TRFLE DU ROUSSILLON. Trifolium incarnatum. Annual forage, cultivation of which has spread to several départements. Although incarnate clover gives only one cutting, and its dry fodder is inferior in quality to that of ordinary clover, there are few species that can render such great services to agriculture, since almost without cost, without care, without disturbing the order of cultivation, one can obtain abundant harvests of fodder; it has, moreover, the merit of being very early, and of offering resources for cattle feed in spring almost before any other plant. This clover is sown in August or early September, usually on stubble, after turning it over with a very light plough: This method, or at least the loosening of the soil surface by repeated harrowing, is necessary for hulled seed, which needs to be covered with a harrow; but for podded seed, it's enough to spread it on the stubble without any prior preparation and then roll it: it almost always succeeds. It's easy to see how forage-deprived countries could improve their agricultural situation. Once the farmer has harvested this forage, either green or dry, he is still in time to raise the forages on this part of his land, and to give it all the fallow possibilities: in this way, without any disturbance, he will have obtained a large supply of forage from the land, between the harvest and the time when he would naturally have put the plough on it. Crimson clover offers a valuable resource for replenishing missed clover, simply by throwing podded or purified seed onto clearings. Almost all wheat or rye soils can be planted with red clover: we use 20 to 25 pounds of hulled seed per half-hectare, and 200 pounds of podded seed (1). I must point out that farrouch was lacking last year; this year its success is not wonderful: I will indicate the cause. I believe, as I indicated, that farrouch sown in August and at the beginning of September is sufficient; sown in July it is too early: all the seedlings sown at this time have suffered greatly. The rains of then and of August helped the seed to develop, and raised hopes of a good harvest: the drought that began at the end of August, and continued until the end of October, brought the greatest preju(1) An early and precocious incarnate clover is announced; the farrouch. of the mountain has its seed better nourished and clearer than that harvested in the plains of Lauraguais; so it has been given preference: it is the only quality sold in our stores. About thirty-five years ago, my late father stimulated our farmers, made it known and spread it with advantage. To encourage cultivation, he was obliged to advance the seed, which was only to be paid for at harvest: it was he who had it purified for shipment overseas. At that time, it was cultivated in Bayonne, following relations with a number of agricultural societies, and with M. de Villelle-Campolhac, a zealous farmer. dice to this plant: whether the seeds were made with the purified seed, or with its envelope, mixed with grass seeds that are naturally in the mixture, they all suffered greatly: the round seed is incarnate clover, its leaf is wider than that of ordinary clover. This young plant is devoured, in dry weather, by an insect called the white aphid, which hovers all night over the plant, devouring it whole: we can convince ourselves of what I'm saying, by checking the field at night; lit by fallots or tightly bound bundles of straw, the agronomist will see a swarm of these aphids rise up by the effect of the light. Loaches also devour cabbage leaves, just as the black aphid destroys cauliflower seedlings. COMMON VETCH, BLACK. Vicia sativa. Boulbennes destined to be sown with black vetches for fodder should be ploughed as soon as possible after harvest; they are loosened by several ploughings and the use of a spiked roller: if the soil is of good quality, smoking can be dispensed with; but if the soil is mediocre, half-smoking is necessary. Vetches should be sown in the first two weeks of October, at a rate of nine-tenths of a hectoliter of wheat seed: sowing a little thickly before winter is the only way to make up for the loss caused by ice. To support vetches, mix a tenth of oats on a hectoliter of vetches. On boulbennes soils, it is essential to sow this forage in large, rounded plots; to do this, cover the vetches with the ear plow, and use the harrow to level the ground. Standing water is very harmful to this forage. In strong soils, vetches can be sown before the corn is harvested: a light hoe is used to pull up the weeds and flatten the ground; the soil is lightly covered with rakes, and then the corn is harvested in dry weather, with the stalks cut off at ground level: this method is only good when the corn harvest is delayed; it's infinitely better not to sow vetches until the corn has been harvested: if the weather permits, a good ploughing is given to uproot the corn plants; they are then removed from the fields. Vetch is very good for green feeding in cowsheds, or for grazing; but with the necessary precautions for very succulent and nourishing fodder, because given too fresh, or too abundantly, it inconveniences animals no less dangerously than wet clover. The choice of black vetch is very important: the big black one is the one you get from the Montagne-Noire; it's a good idea to change the seed every four or five years. The field that is to receive the wheat harvest, which is to follow the vetch, must be well fertilized. VESCE. Vicia, Vica. A perennial vetch is found naturally in our fields and woods, and is recommended elsewhere as useful forage. It is currently eagerly sought after. The usefulness of this plant has been recognized in northern France, due to its hardiness, and the government has even encouraged its cultivation as very advantageous. It's in our woods. Why not have women collect it in August? This way, we could obtain this fodder very cheaply. We haven't yet decided how much we need per half-hectare; as its stalk is less elevated and less furrowed than common vetch, it's certain that a third more seed would be needed (1). Heligoland vetch, field vetch, horse vetch, from England, where it is highly prized. (1) Sown on its own, it is a fodder resource. Our climate is very favorable to its cultivation, and in general it could be grown with advantage. I have refrained from mentioning it in my little pamphlet: all agronomists know how useful it is, both for grain and for fertilizing the soil; I am only indicating that faba beans are useful because of their hardiness, and that they can be adopted with certainty: you need one hectoliter of faba beans per hectare. LENTILLON. Ervum Lens minor. An annual plant whose fodder is highly prized. Lentillon likes dry soils: it is sown broadcast in September, usually with a little oats to row it. One variety is sown with rye instead of oats. One hectoliter of seed. THIRD CLASS. Fodder plants from various families. WILD CHICORY. Cichorium intybus. Very productive, early, drought-resistant forage, very useful for grazing, or to be given green in the cowshed: excellent for cows. Sown with half red clover, it succeeds in strong or light soils, provided they have a little bottom. Like other forages, it is abundant when it receives a few rains to refresh its root, which provides a well-stuffed tuft of infinitely large leaves extending from the heart of the plant. When the tuft is two or three feet above ground, and the first leaves that fall to the ground turn yellow, mow immediately; they are fed green to all the animals, oxen, cows and horses, who eat this plant with avidity; let it wither like all succulent fodder, visiting the field often, so as not to let it rise. If you forget to mow it in time, a kind of reed emerges from the heart of the stem, removing the vegetation from the leaves, which naturally line up along the stem, shrinking and taking away the fodder. This plant can be mowed several times; an agronomist who has experimented with it assured me that it was impossible for him to determine the quantity he had harvested, or to calculate the product. Its cultivation has been recommended by several newspapers. Wild chicory is usually sown in February, either alone or in a mixture, at a rate of 12 pounds per acre; it can also be sown in September. Turnip chicory has long, fleshy roots like white carrots: you could feed it to pigs, who eat the roots well. It can be grown in rows, weeded and hoeed; the roots will be more beautiful. HORSE CABBAGE, COW CABBAGE. Brassica oleracea vaccina, seu procerior. Cavalier cabbage seems to be the best, at least for fertile soils, because of its considerable elevation and the use of its leaves. All cabbages like good soil, rather stronger than lighter, and well smoked. Sow the kale, and all the larger species, in a nursery in a corner of the garden, in August or September, or in March and April; replant them in place, the former in October or November, the latter in March and April, in rows spaced about three feet apart, and two or three feet apart along the line: during their vegetation, keep the soil clean and loose by ploughing or hoeing. These cabbages produce leaves until the spring of their second year, when they go to seed. Flanders caulet is similar to collards in growth habit, height and yield. It is less tall than collards, but perhaps just as productive; it is covered from the base with numerous, strong shoots, making it a very thick bushy plant. These varieties, like all kale, can be grown in the same way, and are not very sensitive to cold. For reasons of economy, they can be planted permanently on the back of the plough. KOHLRABI, TURNEPS CABBAGE, LAPLAND CABBAGE. Brassica napo-brassica. Its main product is its root, fleshy like a large turnip; one of its qualities is to withstand very great cold without deterioration. It can be sown in the field or broadcast; in all cases, thin out so that plants are 10 to 15 inches apart. It is very good for fattening livestock: a soft, sandy and slightly cool soil is suitable. It requires 4 pounds of seed per acre. RUTABAGA CABBAGE, SWEDISH TURNIP. Brassica rutabaga. This plant was introduced to France from England, where it is widely cultivated and produces an extraordinary product; it is little known here (1). Rutabaga should be sown in the field; each plant should be at the same distance as ordinary turnips: it withstands considerable cold, and can be left in the fields over winter to be pulled up only when needed. Same soil as above. CHOU-COLZA. Brassica oleracea campestris. Rapeseed is grown extensively in Flanders (2), mainly for the oil extracted from its seeds, but it is also used for fodder. After the grain harvest, the stubble is ploughed well; rapeseed is sown on this ford at a rate of 6 to 7 pounds per half-hectare: the plant spends the winter without (1) My father experimented with it: its root, good to the taste, was kept until mid-April, long after our turnips, which wood up early. Its cultivation has been neglected. (2) One of our earliest farmers, M. Hacher de Cahuzac, cultivated them extensively on his estates in the Aude department; he had a mill specially built to extract the oil, which was very good. This distinguished agronomist was one of the first to cultivate red clover. An untimely death has taken the life of this good man, who would have boosted the progress of agriculture. The clover plant is not damaged, and at the end of the season, it provides either pasture or green fodder for the cowshed, both of which are invaluable at the time they are grown. All hardy cabbages, and even better rutabaga and chounavet, can be used in this way. The above method is only suitable if you want to make green fodder from rapeseed in spring: growing it for seed requires more care. It is essential to harvest this seed as soon as most of the pods are almost fully ripe, as much could be lost by delaying harvesting. WHITE MUSTARD. Sinapis alba. This plant is used to provide green feed for livestock in autumn. It is generally sown on stubble immediately after harvest by light ploughing. The use of the seed for gastritis and similar ailments is becoming increasingly common in medicine. Approximately 10 to 12 kilos of seed are used per hectare. BLACK MUSTARD. Sinapis nigra. Like mustard, it can be used to feed livestock, but its main use consists in harvesting the seeds to make flour. PIMPRENELLE. Poterium sanguisorba. The great merit of this plant is that it provides excellent pasture on the poorest, driest soils, whether sandy or chalky: it withstands the extremes of drought and cold; above all, it offers a very valuable resource in winter for feeding flocks. A few thousand hectares abandoned and uncultivated, due to the poor quality of the soil, could, through the cultivation of burnet, bring about a significant improvement in their agricultural situation. At least 100 pounds per half-hectare are needed; it would even be prudent to increase the seed to 120 pounds. SPERGULA. Spergula arvensis. Annual forage, particularly suited to fresh sand, which provides excellent food for cows. The butter from cows fed on it is considered to be of superior quality. It is sown in summer on the stubble, after the harvest, at the beginning of September; it is consumed on the spot, or given green to the cowshed, a resource that lasts until the frosts: its dry hay loses considerably to desiccation, due to the watery nature of the plant. This very fine seed needs little covering. We sow 24 pounds per acre. Some people claim that its seed is good for poultry feed. FOURTH CLASS. Forages-Racins. BEET, SHORTAGE. Beta vulgaris campestris. All beets are good for feeding livestock, but beet is particularly cultivated for this purpose, because of its more considerable yield: its cultivation is too neglected, yet it provides a very valuable resource for working livestock, and especially for pigs, both through its leaves and its roots, which grow to a considerable size. Beet requires substantial, soft, good-quality, fresh and deep soil. At the beginning of winter, the soil should be broken up as deeply as possible, and at the end of the season, it should be ploughed again to loosen it up perfectly: the soil is smoked and harrowed to smooth it out and make it loose. At the beginning of April, we take advantage of fine weather to sow beet seeds: to do this properly, follow the steps I'm about to outline. Once the ground is well prepared, take a string, marked in color from 15 to 15 inches, and stretch it along one edge of the field, 15 inches from the ditch; you have a small wooden planter, and opposite each mark on the string you make a hole two inches deep, where you place one or two seeds, which you immediately cover; two workers are enough for this work: we replace the cord again at 15 inches, taking care to arrange the marks in a checkerboard or staggered pattern, and not sideways, along those on the previous furrow, and we sow, continuing, the plot right to the end; in this way each plant will have a greater expanse of land for its nourishment. Two intelligent children can do this sowing. After the plant has grown a little, follow all the rows exactly, leaving only one foot in each place. I should point out, for the benefit of those unfamiliar with this type of cultivation, that each seed not only produces one root, but up to five. This is why it is essential to follow all the rows and leave only one plant in place, the one with the best appearance, the strongest, the most vigorous; without this precaution, the roots will devour each other, and the hope of production will be frustrated. To carry out this operation, it is essential to choose dark weather; the soil must be fresh and less soft: it seems pointless to replace the young plants that have failed in the empty spots; this would require prompt watering, without which they would not recover. As soon as the plants have been thinned out, the roots left in place grow rapidly, and all that's needed is to keep the ground clear of weeds. Pick the leaves when the lower ones begin to wilt, detaching the rib near the collar (the root emerges from the ground in the shape of a sugar loaf), without breaking it in the middle. When collecting the leaves, cut them by pulling towards the ground, and not from above, so as not to shake the root, which would be shaken and detached from the ground: you must not leave a snag, but rather five or six leaves that rise vertically and form the eye of the plant. This first harvest is started towards the end of June, and repeated from month to month until the end of September. Removing the leaves does not harm the growth of the roots, which grow until the end of October. The roots should be harvested before frosts, which would be very harmful to them: choose a time when the soil will be a little damp, so that they can be pulled up easily; lock them up so that they are protected from frost, either in cellars, or in large pits covered with earth. Country beet roots are excellent for all kinds of livestock: horned and woollen animals, pigs, even poultry, are perfectly suited to them; they are also useful for pigs: the roots, cut into pieces and fed to oxen, do them a world of good, refreshing them while they are fed dry fodder, and protecting them from disease: they make excellent milk for cows. This root has a pink tint: cooked, it is very good in salads; its tender leaves replace spinach in cooking: the leaves, having reached an extreme size and being very large, replace chard; its root often reaches a weight of 25 to 30 pounds, if the soil is suitable. Good agronomists, even those who have been growing it for some years, do not recommend harvesting it in the country, because the east wind dries it out, deteriorates it, makes it very tough and deprives it of some of its germination. This is, moreover, the opinion of Count de Villeneuve (special observation in his Manuel d'agriculture): you need 6 to 7 pounds of this seed per half-hectare. WHITE SUGAR BEET. Its volume is much smaller than that of field beet, but the sweet and nutritious parts are much more abundant, which makes it preferred by some growers. However, its use is much less widespread than that of beet. Its root develops completely in the ground, making it much more expensive to uproot. YELLOW GLOBE BEET. This species, originally from England, has been adopted and cultivated for some years by a large number of landowners; it grows almost on the surface of the soil, which makes it particularly suited to shallow soils. CARROT. Daucus Carota. This root is an excellent feeder for all animals; it should be cultivated across the board: one of its advantages is that it doesn't need to be smoked; it prefers soft, deep, loosened soil, amended the year before sowing. Sow from March to June, depending on climate and soil, at a rate of 8 pounds per acre, broadcast or in rows; cover the seed with a light harrowing and roller: thin and hoe it, and leave it 5 to 6 inches apart, as mentioned in the vegetable garden article. The various species are red, pale red with a large head, yellow and white: there are some differences between these varieties, regardless of color; but all can be usefully employed. The yellow from Achicourt is the best of all; the large white from Breteuil is also very good and vigorous. TURNIP TURNEPS, RABIOULE, RAVE PLATE. Brassica Rapa. Turnips are a well-known source of animal feed in winter. Their roots are used in many parts of France to fertilize oxen, and to help feed cows, sheep and pigs. Turnips like soil that is light and dry, or at least healthy, rather than strong and moist, well-prepared, cleaned and, at best, smoked. The ordinary sowing season is from the end of June to the beginning of August; in some cases, it can be extended to the beginning of September, and in others, brought forward by several weeks. The usual method is to sow turnips broadcast: sowing them in rows would be preferable, as it makes weeding and hoeing easier: it is as profitable for the turnips as for the harvest that will follow, if they are thinned out, weeded and shaped. Good harvests can also be obtained from this root, by sowing them with a single light ploughing of the stubble: these sowings are successful if the season favours them. All turnip species are suitable for field cultivation. The large Limousin and Auvergne turnip, known as rabioule, which has been given the misnomer of turneps, includes several varieties: yellow turnip, yellow Scottish turnip, Alsau turnip, called long country turnip, and known as large Berlin turnip: 6 pounds of seed are used per half-hectare. All turnips and carrots prepare the soil, breaking it up, dividing it and loosening it, even for cereals, which are perfectly successful even when sown immediately after harvesting. POTATO or PARMENTIER. Solanum tuberosum. This plant needs no recommendation; its merit is appreciated and its cultivation generally known. There are various species: white, red, cultivated in large quantities in our mountains; early yellow gherkins; early large yellow gherkins; Swiss yellow gherkins, etc., etc., etc. The experiments that are being carried out will be able to determine the choice of owners. TOPINAMBOUR. Helianthus tuberosus. These tubers taste like artichokes. Jerusalem artichokes should be grown like potatoes: these tubers never freeze. This plant thrives on ordinary, mediocre soils, and resists drought well. For some time now, Jerusalem artichokes have been widely cultivated. The leaves and tubers are ideal for cattle feed, and the stalks provide good fuel. Planting is done early in the spring. 137 On the subject of ASSOLEMENTS, I will borrow the following article, based on his experiences, from the Supplément d'agriculture by M. le comte Louis de VILLENEUVE, printed in 1834: "I have seen the time when a good crop rotation was all agriculture; it seems impossible to me to give general rules: the variety of our climate, the so varied qualities of our soils, seem to me to require a crop rotation for each commune, each estate, and even for each field. The prudent agronomist must not adopt any exclusive system: the opinion of a skilled agronomist will no doubt serve to give importance to this advice. My esteemed colleague, Mr. DECAMpS-CAYRAS, in a very interesting memoir on crop rotation, expresses himself as follows: "These systems are undoubtedly followed in part of France. Does it follow from this that we can adopt them?" "Do we have such frequent rainfall?" "Are the disastrous droughts we have not unknown to them?" "Do we have," especially as in the North, "wealthy, intelligent farmers who cultivate with perseverance and accuracy?" "Do we have, finally," large combined estates? I've been involved in agriculture for thirty years," adds M. Decamps, "and it's only by dint of perseverance, patience and iron will, and by leading a very hard life, that I've managed to achieve some success. An invariable crop rotation seems to me very difficult to establish: an extraordinary winter, a drought like that of 1832, which largely destroyed artificial fodder, must necessarily upset all calculations. A crop rotation can only be a variable base on which to prepare the means of obtaining as much wheat as possible; because in our territorial position, it's wheat that we need to speculate on: it alone offers us almost certain chances of income. This principle undoubtedly has its exceptions: some localities may present a combination of soft soils, alluvial soils, easy to work in all weathers; if you combine these advantages with the talents and perseverance of my esteemed colleagues, success will be certain; but it is not to such positions that I am addressing, it is to this large number of agronomists who want to force science to give them certain results, without taking into account the climate and the countless accidents that we are likely to experience." First of all, I must point out that, in these crop rotations, the duration of sainfoin as forage is reduced to three years, instead of four: this is undoubtedly a reduction in the amendment produced by this forage; but these three years fit in better with the return of wheat and corn. In the crop rotation that I follow on my estate at Auterive, there are two consecutive years of wheat, after the clearing of sainfoin-esparcette; I was led to this change, always for the same reason, that in the Midi, wheat must be considered the first of our resources: no doubt, after clearing sainfoin, we're sure to get a good crop of corn, but as the vigor of the plant delays its maturity, it almost always happens that we can't clear the field of weeds, that sowing is delayed; and if the frosts come early, the harvest is often mediocre. This method of sowing wheat on wheat will undoubtedly be criticized as contrary to principle; here's what Mr. DOMBASLE has to say on the subject: "I think that, in modern crop rotation, the succession of two cereal crops has been put off too abruptly; there are, however, many cases where we can allow ourselves this kind of deviation in a seven, eight or nine-year crop rotation. If Mr. Dombasle allows this deviation in the North, where we have so many resources for successful spring harvests, he would make it our duty to do so in the South, where wheat and corn are almost our only resources. Perhaps we should sow more wheat and reduce corn cultivation. It will no doubt be objected that the drought of our summers makes it difficult to clear sainfoin and wheat stubble. This is undoubtedly an obstacle that can arise, as in 1832: but in ordinary years, it is very rare that a storm does not facilitate the necessary work. In this case, we use the spider plough with the pointed share, which opens up the soil slightly, and if there is another rainfall, we can give a good ploughing with the moldboard plough. Moreover, to obtain a good harvest from a forage or meadow clearing, it is not necessary to plough deeply, in order to avoid gamat disease; it is for the second wheat that it is necessary to plough deeply, in order to bring to the surface the layer of soil amended by sainfoin. Experience has shown that when clearing land of any kind, the soil should be left to rest after the first heavy rains in September, when a crust forms that gives the roots of the wheat strength. The same does not apply to boulbennes, which can be ploughed up to the time of sowing (1). The difference between these two types of soil must necessarily have led to changes in the way they are cultivated. Thus, for strong soils, ploughing with the highest heat is excellent for destroying quackgrass, but for boulbennes it has the disadvantage of diminishing the soil's vigour. It's for the same reason that, if you've smoked a field by ploughing the second way with a moldboard plow, you should only plow the rest with a spading plow, so as not to bring the fertilizer to the surface. It also follows from these different types of soil that, for boulbennes, sowing should not be delayed, so as to sow dry soil, and for terre-fort, you should wait (1) This procedure is used for all light soils until the soil is well soaked. There are, however, years when only a few light rains fall, and you have to decide to sow; but, in this case, and even if this operation is carried out in well-moistened soil, in the spring, you have to pass the heavy roller over the wheat sown on the terre-fort, and it is even useful to pass the herd quickly and tightly after the roller. In this way, once the soil has been well compacted, the disease known to farmers as gamat or grauzel can be prevented. This disease has a very simple cause: if heavy frosts have lifted the soil, and you neglect to firm it up with the roller; if an auta (south-easterly) wind, very common at this time of year, comes up in spring, just as the wheat is about to come up in tubers, the scorching air penetrates to the roots, the soil having been lifted by the frost, and you soon see the stems turn yellow and dry out. If the soil has been sown very soft, as it were kneaded, the frost cannot lift it, and the roots are sheltered. This disease is especially to be feared when clearing forage and old meadows: rye and oats do not run the same risk. SOME SPECIES AND VARIETIES OF CEREAL PLANTS. CANARY GRASS, CANARY BIRDSEED, LONG MILLET. Phalaris canariensis. Annual plant, similar to millet in cultivation and use. Its straw is good fodder for horses and horned cattle. Sow lightly, broadcast, in April and May, on good, loose, fertilized soil. Its grain is used to feed serins. AVOINE. Avena sativa. This cereal has a large number of varieties, whose respective merits are difficult to determine, given that soil and climate often have a major influence on their success and quality. To make my book as useful as possible, I'm going to list the main cereal varieties here, pointing out that it's only by testing them in your own field that you'll be able to judge which ones to give preference to. I note that we have received requests for various qualities of oats, as well as foreign wheats. I am going to indicate several species, so that agronomists who may wish to experiment with these cereals will first have a clear idea of both their qualities and their products. I will have a price list for each year, which can be consulted; and, on requests made to me, I will send to my store the articles I have on order, provided that the commissions are given in good time. The agronomists would have liked to have foreign wheat. It is very difficult to obtain the free and new qualities, I have experienced this; but I find it even more difficult to place the little I could get, given the high prices for the port of cereals, and the low price of ours. AVOINE PATATE, or AVOINE POMME DE TERRE. Avena sativa turgida. White grain, short, heavy, with fine rind, abundant in flour. This variety has become very popular in England in recent years. GEORGIAN OATS. Georgiana. Yellow-white grain, very large and heavy, with hard bark, very large panicle, broad leaf, large, high straw, soft however, and of good quality for livestock; very early maturity: it provides more chaff for threshing than any other species. JOAN OATS. Recently multiplied in the Orléans area, because of its earliness; prone to shattering, and therefore requiring cutting before perfect maturity; black grain, fairly good quality. THREE-GRAIN OATS. Trisperma. So named because its spikelets are largely composed of three grains that remain attached at their base: highly productive, and not very difficult in the field: fairly large grain, but bearded, with hard bark. BLACK BRIE OATS. One of the best and most productive varieties in good soils: short, swollen grain of very good quality. Some of the kernels do not separate when threshed, and remain attached at the base. WINTER OATS. Hyemalis. Highly cultivated and esteemed in Brittany and part of western France, but of uncertain success in cold countries: it can be adopted in our climate, which is milder and more temperate than in the North. It is very productive in terms of straw and grain, which is heavy and of excellent quality; it ripens early and is sown in September or early October: it can be very usefully employed for the first sowings in February, or even at the end of January, which, with this species, are much more assured than with March oats. Hungarian oat, RUSSIAN oat, UNILATERAL. Orientalis. Two varieties: white and black, very distinct from other oats, in that their panicle is narrow, and all the grains are attached short and hanging on one side only; this also gives them the name "cluster oats". Black oats are extremely productive in good soils; their grain is a little thin and light in weight; their high grain and straw yields give them preference in many places. White Hungarian oats are especially remarkable for the strength and height of their straw; their grain is even inferior to that of black oats. Hungarian yellow oats, mixed with black, have been very successful; this green plant is furred, its leaf wider and higher than ours; it offers an advantage when grown green; its grain yield is immense; its stalk rises to five feet; in a short time it will be widespread in the country. Beardless winter wheat. BLANC DE FLANDRE, also known as BLANC ZÉE, OR BLAZÉE. One of the most beautiful and productive wheat varieties harvested in France. WHITE WHEAT FROM HUNGARY. Remarkable for the very rounded shape of its grain. TALAVERA WHEAT. Strongly propagated for some years in England: high straw content, long ear, beautiful white grain, elongated shape. HEDGE WHEAT. With large, thick ears, whose chaff is covered with a cottony down; this wheat, cullivated in England, is a very good breed. LAMMAS WHEAT. Red, precocious, productive; wants to be sown early, and fears damp soils; prone to shattering, and for this reason needs to be cut before full maturity. Bearded winter wheat. CaUcASE WHEAT. Very long ear, hard, heavy grain; chunky straw, yet prone to spilling. This wheat is remarkable for its earliness, and can be sown in February and March, as well as in autumn: it has a sub-variety with a red ear and no beard, which differs from the bearded only in these two characteristics. All the wheats just described belong to the common wheat species, triticum sativum. POULARD BLANC, CARRÉ, OR POULARD DE BARBARIE, triticum turgidum. This wheat belongs to the race of large bearded wheats, known as poulards, whose grain is generally of a common and little-appreciated quality; but in this respect it significantly outweighs its analogues, while, like them, it has the merit of being very productive in terms of straw and seed. It is hardier than fine wheats. MIRACLE or SMYRNE WHEAT. Triticum compositum. Remarkable for its stalked ears, i.e. composed of several ears joined into a single large, enlarged head: white, very large, rounded grain. Although this wheat has been advocated at various times, and has the merit of being highly productive, its cultivation has so far been very limited, because it is rather difficult on the land, and gives a hard, coarse flour; its straw is full and very hard. MARCH WHEAT. Triticum sativum vernum. This breed of grain is not cultivated as much as it should be. If excessive rainfall, flooding, insects or the cold have destroyed or severely damaged pieces of land sown with autumn wheat, or if landowners, thwarted by a season that is too harsh, have not been able to complete their sowing, the result is a deficit, sometimes considerable, in the wheat harvest, a deficit that could be made up by March wheat, if its cultivation were more general and more extensive than it is: for this, a few acres of it would have to be sown annually on each farm. This resource could be extended all the more easily, as March wheat would succeed in many soils too light for autumn wheat. Among the varieties of this grain, I'd like to mention the following: March wheat with white ears without beards, the most widely cultivated, although it is more often mixed with the following variety; - with white ears without beards, a little earlier than the preceding variety; - red without beards, a species cultivated in the North, which appears to be very good; Sicilian square, a short, sturdy, red ear without beards; - Fellemberg wheat, with straw as high and ears as long as autumn wheat; Pictet wheat, a sub-variety of the previous one, whose grain fits better in the bale, and which seems to be equal to it and perhaps superior in other respects; - Odessa and Tangarok wheats, which, in numerous trials carried out in France, have generally succeeded well; - Cape wheat, a pretty yellow grain, hard and heavy. These wheat varieties can be sown from mid-February to mid-March. CORN, TURKISH WHEAT, INDIAN WHEAT. Zea Mais. The usefulness of this grain for humans and animals is well known. The varieties of this cereal are very numerous: there are grains of all colors; the most cultivated are either yellow or white: these two species are generally adopted in our departments. In the Landes department, we grow a beautiful white variety, with a shorter, more conical ear than the previous one, a little earlier, and of very good quality. A few years ago, we also recommended a corn from Pensylvania, which is significantly earlier than ours, and which, in this respect, is of interest. SIOUX CORN FROM THE UNITED STATES. This breed is similar to the previous one, but with much larger ears and kernels; - pearl corn, white, very small and very pretty, which ripens with difficulty in the North, and which seems especially suitable for fodder, due to the large number of stalks and leaves it produces. Among the very early varieties, I would like to mention the following two as having particular merit. QUARANTAIN CORN. Less elevated and less productive than the ordinary variety, but much earlier, to the extent that in Piedmont it ripens, sown in June and July, on the stubble of grain that has just been harvested. This quality means that it can be grown to replace corn that has been ravaged by June hail: it's still a resource. ALGERIAN CORN. Pointed cone, very tight grain, more productive than ours: its flour is equally good for human consumption and for fattening animals; but its grain, sharp and pungent, repels the animals that are usually fed it. CHICKEN CORN. This pretty breed was brought from America: it differs from the previous one in that it is smaller in all its parts, and even earlier. The smallness of its kernels was indicated by its name, as well as by the use to which it can be put. In terms of yield, this variety cannot be compared even with the quarantine variety, but it possesses to a greater degree all the advantages attached to a high earliness; and in this respect, it is truly interesting: these two corn varieties should be sown closer together than the large one. BUCKWHEAT, BUCKWHEAT, BUCKWHEAT, BUCAIL. Polygonum fagopyrum. In general, buckwheat is the resource of poor countries and sandy, cold, mediocre soils; it also offers advantages that may make it useful on more widely distributed farms. Its very abundant grain, which, as we know, is used for human consumption, is also very suitable for poultry and pigeons; it is excellent fertilizer for pigs and good for horses; its flowers provide abundant grazing for bees: Cut green, the plant makes fairly good fodder; buried in flower, it is recognized as one of the best plant fertilizers known: moreover, buckwheat's vegetation being very rapid, and enabling it to be sown late in the season, it offers a great resource as an auxiliary or intercrop. It is almost always broadcast, and when the soil is damp, it is raised in ridges beforehand, because it fears dampness. We use half a hectoliter of seed per hectare for harvesting from seed, and twice that amount for burial. The ashes from its stems contain a lot of potash. As this plant flowers for a long time, its first seeds fall before the last ones are ripe; we are therefore obliged to take a middle term between one and the other to harvest it; when it is done, we pull them into bunches, which we place upright to let them dry. In mentioning the names of a few cereals, I can't help but mention a new rye as well. MARCH RYE. Secale cereale vernum. This rye, unknown in France, has just been introduced into the Ain department. Its grain is long, clear and clean, and makes very good bread; it is yet another cereal that can be very advantageous to agriculture. Its grain should be sown light, given its high yield. TURF. Lawns being of great importance in pleasure gardens, I must speak here of how to cultivate them, and how to preserve them. No plant forms such a pleasant carpet of greenery as ryegrass, lolium perenne or perennial ryegrass. Whenever you want to form a lawn close to the view, near the front of an apartment, or on which you want to walk or sit, you need to form it with ryegrass; you can mix in strawberry or white clover, and even a little birdsfoot trefoil, but the soil must be good and substantial: If it's light or sandy, the ryegrass will perish; if it's too wet, rushes and other large, unpleasant plants will grow. Before sowing a lawn, the soil must be perfectly prepared to receive the seeds, i.e. after a good ploughing, all stones and roots must be removed, the surface must be perfectly levelled and, if necessary, amended with potting soil, which must not be buried. Sowing is done in overcast or rainy weather, by broadcasting at a rate of 120 pounds per half-hectare; the seeds are covered with a rake and harrow, and then rolled: this last operation is repeated every spring, immediately after the frosts, to firm up the soil, and after each mowing, to tidy up the plants, in order to obtain thick, uniform greenery: all care is then limited to keeping it free of all foreign plants, watering it during severe droughts, and mowing the grass at least four times a year, if not more: this should always be done before fruiting time. A well-tended lawn, carefully purged of weeds and especially fine mosses, and amended every two or three years with consumed manure, or potting soil, and better still, if moss gets in the way, with lime, plaster or ashes, can keep in all its beauty for several years. Small masses of colchicum and crocus can be placed on a carpet of greenery, creating a charming effect and flowering, the former in autumn, the latter in spring. This practice deserves to be imitated in all lawns within view, either from the windows of the dwelling or on the promenades. MAHON GRASS. Mahon grass blooms on carpets; the flowers are pink, violet and lilac: it is very pleasant in flowerbeds, as it blooms during three seasons of the year; it is mown and pruned often, because it reproduces itself by the fall of its seeds. It is sown in March, in borders, in soft, light soil, with a mixture of fine sand, because of the fineness of its seed. CALAMBOKI. MIL imported from Athens. This plant is an excellent substitute for oats; it is suitable for feeding all kinds of animals: horned beasts, horses, mules, pigs and all fowl, which eat it greedily. Its grain is full and round; its cultivation is the same as that of millet; it is sowed in the same way as broad beans, and the soil is worked at the same times. Shoots that are too numerous should be pruned, leaving only two or three per plant; any soil is suitable for its cultivation; one of the properties of this seed. One of the properties of this seed is that it provides at least twenty carts of stalks per acre, suitable for heating the oven; its stalk rises to over two meters, the size of a reed; the leaves are very wide and of a pretty green color; from the top of the stalk there forms a large tuft, eight inches long, swollen, wide, filled with such a large quantity of seeds, that there must be at least two thousand of them. This overview should demonstrate the usefulness of this plant, whose yield is incalculable; it is also reported that two bushels are enough to sow an acre or half-hectare, which should produce 40 to 50 hectoliters at least. SWEET SORGHUM. Holcus saccharatus. I won't reprint this little work without devoting a few lines to sweet sorghum, which has been much talked about in France over the last few years. I won't mention its use in the extraction of alcohol, which numerous experiments have confirmed; but the plant, which the excessive cost of alcohols in recent years has led us to recommend so highly, would soon be forgotten, if the abundance of the wine harvest continued to show itself in subsequent years as in the one that has just passed. I mention this plant here only for its use in agriculture as green fodder; the excellent results and enormous yields it has produced, the abundance and good quality of the milk it gives cows, place it in the first rank of green fodder. It can be sown at the same time as Hungarian millet and moha, and even later, as heat does nothing to damage its vegetation. When sown for fodder, 15 to 20 kilos of seeds per hectare are used. D 0a r 2 I11 - 2 A ministerial decree dated July 31, 1851 prescribes the teaching of agriculture and horticulture in elementary school. We were the first to applaud this welcome innovation, because it should, in time, lead rural populations out of the deplorable routine that still directs them in the cultivation of their fields and gardens. Our student teachers, trained in the right methods, according to the program adopted for agricultural and horticultural education, should be, as soon as they are placed in the communes, the intermediaries through whom sound ideas and good practices will spread throughout the countryside. In addition, they will greatly contribute to the success of the farm-schools which are tending to multiply more and more, under the happy impetus of the government, by preparing, for these useful establishments, pupils or apprentices who are intelligent and accustomed to work. In horticulture, their action should be even more direct, because they can all, or almost all, combine example with precept. But if they are to achieve such a desirable goal, they must HORT. be encouraged, even urged, by their immediate superiors to turn their gardens into model gardens in which their pupils can apply the precepts they learn in class, and from which their neighbors can draw useful lessons. It is therefore the duty of all those entrusted with the supervision of schools to propagate, with all their might, a taste for the horticultural art. A well-cultivated garden will increase the modest affluence of the teacher; it will provide useful recreation and an innocent means of influence. The decree we have just mentioned is already twelve years old, and one might think that schoolteachers, stimulated by several ministerial circulars, and encouraged by the departmental authorities and by the various horticultural societies, have cultivated their gardens with taste and put into practice the excellent lessons that are part of the normal courses. Unfortunately, this is not the case for the great majority of them, and most have not responded in this respect to the care with which they have been treated. If there are exceptions, they are few and far between. In fact, when it comes to gardening and arboriculture in particular, nothing is more neglected, and consequently less productive, than the gardens of our rural schoolteachers. If a few vegetables are harvested, they are rarely the object of a judicious choice. Cabbages, lettuce, carrots, beans, etc. are sown at random, without any idea that, depending on the nature of the soil, the needs of the household and the time of sowing, there is a choice to be made from the many vegetable species or varieties, the existence of which we don't even seem to suspect. Fruit trees are not the object of more intelligent care; however, now that railroads criss-cross the whole of France, and can take the finest produce from gardens and orchards to the first markets, vegetables and fruit can become a very important branch of rural industry. Anjou, Touraine, Normandy and Burgundy are making substantial profits from their fruit and preserves, to which everyone with intelligence and care has the right to aspire. The planting of trees in teachers' gardens is often poorly understood; the grafting, selection and care of fruit species are left to the crudest routine. Plants are planted haphazardly, with no concern for the quality and nature of the fruit, let alone espaliers or trellises; the most favorably exposed walls remain bare. In this respect, therefore, there is a whole revolution to be wrought in the habits of our schoolteachers; and it would not be the least good thing for the officials responsible for inspecting schools to force teachers, if not to become perfect gardeners, at least to become men capable of giving rural horticulture a better and more profitable direction. Horticulture in elementary school must be considered from two angles: it concerns both the well-being of the teachers and the prosperity of the schools themselves. A teacher can only do so much good in a commune if he or she stays there for a long time. When the head of a school has raised several generations in the holy practices of religion, in the wise teachings of morality and virtue, and in the sound notions of duty, he is a kind of patriarch in his commune, to whom people go to confide their sorrows and pains, and whom they consult in their embarrassments and in the direction of their difficult affairs; he exerts an influence all the more sure as he does not seek it, an influence which his upright sense and long experience always turn to the advantage of the general good. The most important thing, therefore, is to attach teachers to the communities in which they are placed, right from the start of their teaching career; and in our opinion, the best way to achieve this is to attach them to the soil. When a teacher is in possession of a garden he has created, in which he has planted trees that he has raised and directed in every direction, he will become attached to his land, where he will see his young plants take on, under his direction, all the most varied forms, and lavish their excellent produce on him every year, thanks to his intelligent care. His greatest fear will be to see himself forced to abandon a garden which will be his work, and in which he will have found his sweetest pleasures; he will therefore make every effort to ensure that a change does not disturb the peaceful life he has made for himself; he will neglect none of the duties of his profession, and his zeal and activity can be counted on; for he will have become what we call a good teacher. As proof of what we have just said here, we need only recount what we achieved in a district where we served for six years as inspectors of primary education. When we arrived in the arrondissement of D*, we found almost all the school gardens in a deplorable state. They were either planted with wheat, potatoes and a few rare vegetables, or used as playgrounds for the children. This almost general neglect struck us all the more, as we found everywhere soil admirably suited to market gardening and arboriculture. We began by advising the teachers to return the pieces of land attached to the schoolhouses to their true purpose. A few responded to our invitation, but they were few and far between. Most replied: "What's the point of making gardens and planting them, if we're changed, our time and effort will be wasted? But we'd reply: "As we're determined that the gardens of the res" sort should all be in good condition, if you leave a garden "well cultivated, you'll find, in your new post," one no less well tended!" Finally realizing that our friendly advice wasn't achieving all the results we wanted, we took an energetic stand, with the consent of M. l'inspecteur d'académie. At a meeting of all the teachers in the district, we formally declared that anyone who, in future, did not give his garden all the care it required, and did not make all the improvements in its cultivation of which it was susceptible, would be proposed for dispatch to a post without a garden. This threat had the best possible effect, and by the following year, all the grounds under the schoolhouses were stocked with all the vegetables needed for household consumption. It was already a conquest. But we didn't stop there: we designated the vegetable species that were important for everyone to cultivate, we urged them all to sow asparagus pits, and we required them to plant wild plants for grafting, telling them what they had to do to properly manage the young fruit trees they were raising. Today we can say that, thanks to the encouragement given to teachers by the Horticultural Society of De*, which has taken on board our views and looks to teachers as its intermediaries in bringing horticultural progress to the countryside, thanks to the all-powerful support we have found in M. the Prefect of Je*, who distributes horticultural and agricultural treatises to schoolteachers every year, for a fairly substantial sum, at the suggestion of the primary inspectors, the goal we set ourselves has been achieved in all the communes of the arrondissement, as we shall see from the details that follow. All our teachers now have a real garden, in which they harvest the finest and best-chosen vegetables. Each garden is planted with tastefully trained fruit trees that are beginning to bear fruit. And that's not all. Following in the footsteps of the schoolteachers, their neighboring landowners have taken a liking to arboriculture, and the countryside is beginning to be populated with fruit trees. In the arrondissement of D**, there are two cantons whose soil, formed by alluvial deposits, is wonderfully suited to all kinds of cultivation, but in which the inhabitants have never wanted to plant trees around their houses, under the ridiculous pretext that trees would block their view of their fields. The advice and above all the example of our teachers have transformed these two cantons; trees are now being planted and our teachers are directing their education. Many of our teachers have grafted several hundred trees over the last four years on various landowners' estates: one alone has grafted 1,800 trees in three years. His well-understood cultivation and zeal for the propagation of arboriculture and floriculture earned him a vermeil medal at the L'** exhibition. Thus, in accordance with the wishes of the higher administration, these modest civil servants contribute with all their efforts, through their advice, their example and their personal work, to the progress of the horticultural art. What's more, we've achieved another very valuable result: all the teachers in the district entrusted to us are no longer asking for changes or promotions, because their gardens are attractive enough to keep them in the communes where they work. From this we conclude that the surest way to fix a teacher in a locality, and to obtain from him the regular fulfillment of all his duties, is to attach him to the soil, by obliging him to find all his relaxation in his garden. It is therefore to this most important aspect of their mission that we call the full attention of competent men; and we cannot urge our colleagues, the primary school inspectors, too strongly to never allow themselves to be discouraged by the obstacles and difficulties they encounter when they set out to persuade their subordinates to overcome their general reluctance to work on the land. Schoolteachers are men of good sense, and when they have been shown all the advantages of the recommendations made to them, they come to understand that what is required of them is all in their interest.
