If persuasive means don't work, don't shy away from coercion. We never reproach a leader for the pleasures he brings us, even in spite of ourselves. But apart from the direct action that primary inspectors can exert on their subordinates to force them to put into practice the teachings they have received in teacher training colleges, we think it would also be useful to appeal to emulation. Emulation is what gives birth and perfects. For more than sixty years since exhibitions for the arts, industry and agriculture were instituted in France, what progress has been made in all fields! With each new exhibition, artists, workers and farmers, comparing their works or products with those of their rivals, have been driven by the desire to equal, even surpass their victors. Hence the superiority of the next exhibition over the one that preceded it. It was only later that French horticulture felt the need to enter the fray. Its beginnings were laborious with rivals such as the Belgians and the Dutch; but by dint of perseverance our horticulturists soon made up for lost time, and their success exceeded all expectations. Each new exhibition has seen the emergence of true artists who force nature to satisfy their every desire and bend to their every whim. Soon, horticultural societies were springing up everywhere, and each département had its own special exhibition to which everyone was invited, especially schoolteachers, because, working for progress in the general interest, the various societies understood from the outset that it was through schoolteachers that improvements must spread everywhere. It is easy to understand that, with the little time they have at their disposal, outside the duties of their state, with resources as limited as their own in terms of land and equipment, schoolteachers do not have the pretension of competing on the same rank, either with gardeners whose profession is horticulture, or with amateurs who have time and a lot of money at their disposal to cultivate an art which is the charm of their lives. So, while we pay tribute to the benevolence shown to exhibiting teachers by the judges of public competitions, we feel that horticultural society exhibitions only half fulfill the goal we would like to achieve. The same would not be true if, every two or three years, a general exhibition of the products of our school gardens were held in the capital of each département. In a number of départements, some of the district's primary teachers are brought together every year to attend educational conferences held at teacher training colleges. Couldn't we take advantage of this meeting, which always takes place in September, the most favorable month of the year for fruit and vegetable exhibitions, to hold a general exhibition of their produce at no cost to the teachers? There, our teachers would be in the presence of their equals; they could compare the results of their care with what would have been obtained by the efforts of their colleagues who, better versed in the horticultural art, were superior to them; they would confer among themselves, share their procedures, and soon there would be established among all the teachers of the same department an emulation that would produce the best effects. In this way, all the consequences of the decree of July 31, 1852 would be realized. But, as we have already said, schoolteachers need to be guided in their cultivation; on their own, they would produce only partial results, which would be powerless to achieve the general progress of horticulture in the countryside. It is with this in mind that we have written this little treatise entitled : Horticulture in elementary school, because it is specially designed for primary school teachers, although we have arranged it in such a way that it can be used for the management of rural gardens, which are almost all in the same conditions as those in school houses. While we pay tribute to the merits of the many works we have on horticulture, we believe that a book, if it is to become popular, must not resemble all those overly voluminous treatises whose aim is rather to make science for people of the art, than to give elements for practitioners. We would add to all that we have just said 1. that schoolteachers, by propagating a taste for agriculture and horticulture, will render immense services to their country if they can, if not entirely stop, then at least reduce the migration of the countryside to the big cities. Iammna - G AF NEIBIYAN SOMARTIOIE IMOIMI AHT UR mmammme m AA MIIROmARAE MORRRUE MEETRIIMETI AuNA D D RNRN MMIUR D muuve ebon onp golimmni' elto ene u o amoh mm OUILAHIIREDNEETI HDD NA D MERE OEU NHUINDHOO que Due a MAATENUOT NI E - mieté eux LE JARDIN DE L'INSTITUTEUR The land annexed to the school houses is intended mainly as a vegetable and fruit garden.fruit garden. The schoolteacher's first priority is to be useful rather than pleasurable. He will grow vegetables for household consumption, and raise fruit trees to make use of their produce, and to demonstrate to the people among whom he lives the benefits to be gained by choosing the right fruit species, and by carefully and intelligently managing the trees planted in his garden. Horticulture thus practised comprises two main divisions: market gardening and arboriculture. CHAPTER ONE GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF GARDENING 1. Soil study. In order to give each plant the soil it needs, we need to learn about the soils on which we work and their various properties. 1° Strong earth, with a clay base, is generally suitable for vegetable plants; it is usually yellow and sometimes gray: it is essential to mix it sufficiently with manure; 2° Soft, whitish clay earth is suitable for fruit trees; 3° Light, sandy earth is very good for bulbous plants; 4° Heather earth is used particularly in floriculture, and is generally well suited to all plants with weak, slender roots. These different soils can be modified and mixed in a number of ways, but it would be difficult to assign precise rules to these modifications. Practice is the best guide in this respect. 2. Ploughing. Ploughing comprises three operations: 1° ploughing proper, 2° ripping, 3° hoeing. 1° The purpose of plowing is: 1° to make the soil loose, loose, light and easy to penetrate by heat and humidity, the two great agents of vegetation, and to increase and maintain its fertility by putting underneath the upper parts of the soil that have been improved by the sun, and by bringing upwards the lower parts laden with salts that have precipitated there, to a depth at which the roots of plants rarely penetrate. 2° to destroy weeds by burying them, so that as they rot they provide new salts. Ploughing should be carried out at different times and in different ways, depending on the nature of the soil and the species of plants to be cultivated. Light, dry soils should be ploughed very deeply before winter, so that rain and snow can penetrate them much earlier and correct their lack of moisture. During the summer, they should only be ploughed when it rains, or if they have to be ploughed because of drought, they should be given abundant watering immediately, to bind all their parts together and make them less prone to evaporation of the little moisture they still contain. In this type of soil, which heats up easily, ploughing is less necessary to introduce heat than to allow rainwater and watering to pass through. On the contrary, strong, compact, cold and damp soils only need to be lightly ploughed towards the end of October, to straighten them out and kill weeds; but in spring, when the rainy season is over, and in summer, when the weather is driest, they must not be ploughed too deeply or too frequently, in order to break them up, divide them, let the heat penetrate and evaporate the moisture they contain too abundantly. In addition to large-scale ploughing, small-scale ploughing is often necessary to maintain the soil's loose surface, and prevent or counteract the cracks and fissures to which it is prone, and which allow the sun to penetrate to the roots of plants and trees. 2° Ripping. When taking possession of a plot of land previously used for other crops, to turn it into a vegetable garden, it is necessary, even essential, to rip it up. Ripping is nothing other than ploughing deeper than ordinary ploughing: the latter is done to a depth of Om 25 or Om 30, whereas ripping goes to Om 60. Om 80 and even 1 mềtre deep. When ripping, the worker must set aside the good soil from the surface without mixing it with the subsoil and without bringing the latter back on top. It is important that the lower layer is perfectly loosened and cleared of any stones, roots or pieces of wood that may be present. As these plant substances decompose, they become covered with underground fungi that often invade plant roots and cause them to perish. In addition to the spade, the gardener who is breaking up the soil must be equipped with a pick of the kind that earthworkers call a pick to attack the hard parts of the soil and to extract the large stones it contains. 3° Hoeing. Under this name, in gardening, we mean the superficial manners given with the help of the instrument called a hoe to the beds occupied by a more or less advanced crop, turning around the plants without disturbing them. If you hoe a bed in the vegetable garden that is more or less overgrown with weeds, this hoeing cleans the soil and at the same time produces the effect of weeding. This last operation involves hand-pulling the weeds that grow with the plants. It's an operation that needs to be carried out often, because nothing harms the garden like weeds, whose growth is always very rapid. 3. Fertilizing. When soil has been eroded by a series of productions, ploughing is insufficient to sustain and perpetuate its fertility; fertilizers must restore the salts it has been depleted of. Anything that the soil nourishes can become fertilizer. Plants, animal excrements and animals themselves, whether aquatic or terrestrial, can maintain or increase the earth's fertility when their parts, dissolved by corruption, mingle with the earth, or rather become earth, carrying back to its bosom and returning to it the salts and juices with which they were formed or nourished. Among the minerals themselves, salt, marl, lime, gypsum and all materials from which salts can detach and melt, fertilize the earth. The fertilizers best known to gardeners, and most commonly used to improve their land, are rotted and consumed manures. But what kind of manure is best suited to what kind of soil? When and how should it be used? For not only do all manures provide the soil with salts, but some also heat it up, loosen it up and give it action. Some need more salts, others less; some have enough salts and need only heat to become active. Horse manure, which, when new, contracts a heat almost equal to that of fire, is suitable for correcting the defects of compact, cold and sluggish soils: if it is not yet sufficiently effective, sheep dung should be substituted, or a certain quantity added: in this case, poudrette would be even more effective. Stable manure, which has little heat, but is fatty and unctuous, is suitable for light, warm soils whose dilated parts need to be bound together to retain freshness and moisture. Poultry, rabbit and pigeon manures can also be used to good effect in horticulture; but the last of these, known as colombine, should never be mixed with other manures: if it is not quite dry, it should be dried when collected; then ground to powder and spread by hand over vegetating plants in cold, damp soils, without ever burying it; this is the real way to make good use of it. Sheep dung should not be mixed either: it is generally used for bathing plants that do not fear heat. No horticulture is possible without an abundance of manure and compost. When you ask schoolteachers to take up horticulture, they always reply that they have no livestock, and that it's not easy for them to get enough fertilizer to feed their land properly. 1 This is not a serious objection, for the schoolteacher has all the means at his disposal to make excellent manure, without much expense. 1° The teacher has his classroom swept twice a day. Instead of scattering the rubbish from these sweepings in front of his school gate, which is always messy, if he had them deposited in a manure pit at one end of his garden, layering them in alternating beds with weeds from weeding and debris of all kinds from the dressing of vegetables, i.e., from the sort of grooming they undergo before being used, you'd get good compost. Compost made from decomposed soil and plant matter takes on all the properties of potting soil within a few months, and can be used for the same purposes as potting soil. This type of compost is particularly favorable for vegetable plants of the cruciferous family. If, moreover, schoolteachers could place their compost pit behind the pupils' urinals and provide a conduit that would carry the slurry over its alternating layers of grass and sweepings, their compost would soon acquire all the qualities of the most recommended fertilizers. 2° Every year, the toilets in elementary school are cleaned. What's to stop a teacher from using the waste from his pits to increase the fertility of his garden? The product of latrines is a very powerful fertilizer that should never be neglected. The most convenient way for the schoolteacher to prepare it is to place the liquid waste in a pit dug as far away from the house as possible, 1 meter or 1 meter 30 centimeters deep, which is only half-filled: loose earth is placed on the edge of the pit and thrown on top of the waste, scattering it as much as possible. After a while, the whole thing is emptied and made into a heap on the edge of the pit; this is used when it has sufficiently dried out to spread it more easily. This material should never be mixed with turf or other grasses, as vegetable substances decompose very-difficulty. Understandably, this operation can only be carried out in winter. All the care that needs to be taken to collect and preserve fertilizers is in no way costly, and requires only vigilance and attention; but when it does entail some expense, this should not be a reason to dispense with it for the horticulturist who knows the importance of fertilizing gardens. USE OF FERTILIZERS. - Burying manure too deeply renders it useless, and puts food beyond the reach and reach of most plant roots. Winter is the right time to fertilize land. The land is ploughed deeply, manure is spread over it, and it is left in this state until spring. After winter, we plough less deeply than before, and bury the manure. Leaving it exposed on the ground over winter, frosts and rains kill most of them, instead of keeping them in the ground, and the worms that hatch in spring wreak havoc on crops. Manures are renewed more or less often, depending on whether the land is more or less good and yields more or less crops. Land that only produces once a year doesn't need to be smoked as much or as often as it would if several species of plants followed one another every year, or if it never had a rest, like most market gardens. Some vegetables love manure, others fear it and don't do well in recently-smoked soil; others don't do as well as they should; others acquire bad qualities; all are better in manure mixed with loam. The more delicate the plant, the more compost is needed, but rarely more than half. If we've gone into fertilizers at some length, it's because manure is the main element in horticulture. When much is demanded of the soil, it must be fed in proportion to what is required of it. 4. Watering. Most plants only grow as fast and look as good as we want them to, when the soil in which they grow is kept at a suitable level of humidity, and without too long an interruption. But this proper degree can only be learned by practice, because it varies according to the seasons, exposure, soil, nature and age of each plant. We can only say that the soil and potting compost for seedlings must be kept very moist until they have sprouted, at which point less moisture is needed. If it continues to be given in abundance, the growth of the seedlings may be more rapid, but the slightest cold, a warm ray of sunshine, a gust of wind or a momentary drought can cause the plant to melt. Supposing the over-watered seedling has been preserved from these various accidents until the time it is lifted for transplanting or planting, the roots, stems and leaves of over-watered plants will break and bruise, and the plant will be in poor condition; On the other hand, a seedling that has received less water since emergence will have firmer, less delicate roots, stems and leaves; it will withstand a little cold, sun and drought without perishing, and the transplanted plant will grow more easily and be more perennial. To water bedded seedlings, as well as seedlings which, having just germinated and begun to emerge from the ground, are not yet rooted, you need to use a watering can with a very fine head, because too much rain scatters the potting soil, uncovers some seeds and buries others too deeply; it coats and mixes the young seedlings, covering them with potting soil, which is equally damaging. When watering precious seeds that have not yet emerged, you can prevent the damage caused by watering by spreading a little long straw or moss on the bed beforehand, which you remove after watering. Plants transplanted or planted in the ground should be watered often enough to ensure that the soil around the plant is sufficiently moist until it starts to grow again. It's better to give little water at a time, and more often, so that the delicate hair that forms when the plants take root can easily penetrate the soil. But when watering weak plants, avoid using watering cans with either a wide spout or a knob, which, by forcefully delivering a lot of water, tip the plant over onto the soil and cause it to stick, or even cover it with soil that prevents it from standing up. Watering cans with fine holes not far apart are needed for delicate plants that are not far apart; for plants that are far apart, a watering can with a spout should be used, which should be lifted gently so that the jet of water does not remove the soil from around the roots, and does not make a hole at the foot of the plant through which air can penetrate and dry out the foliage. A good way to obviate these inconveniences is to place a handful of layer debris at each foot, which, in addition to the advantage of preventing the water from heavy watering from washing away the soil, also prevents the soil from drying out so quickly and splitting, and shelters the roots from the sun's rays. It's easy to judge when plants need watering, because when they do, their leaves are less green, less firm, less sustained, and the tips of the stems are less upright. You can even tell when they're going to need water if you scrape the surface of the soil, or probe deeper and find the root layer dry. It is advantageous for plants to be watered only a short time before they need it, because their products will be of better quality as a result. However, as the consequences of forgetting would be very harmful, it is advisable to water often, so that the soil is always a little fresh, brown in color and easily broken up; but it should not be watered to such an extent that some time later it gives up water if squeezed in the hand, or becomes muddy or cloddy: this is called drowning the plants. In this case, the hair and often the root soften and eventually perish. An intelligent horticulturist will know how to avoid these two excesses, both of which are equally damaging to plants. There are some vegetables that require more watering at a certain age than at any other in order to yield their produce, such as cauliflowers, lettuces and cabbages, when they are due to bear fruit, but which, once they have reached a certain growth, should no longer be watered, because they would rise. It is therefore in the cultivation of each plant that we must learn what is particular to it. It makes no difference whether you water at this or that time of day: We must always seize the moment when the plant derives the most benefit from the water we give it; and for this it is important that the water is not taken away by the sun as soon as it is poured, or that the cold does not occur while it is still wet, because, in the first case, the sun hardens the earth and sometimes roasts the plant, and in the second, watering delays the growth of plants and exposes them to freezing. These watering conditions cannot be overemphasized by gardeners, who often fail to pay sufficient attention to them. From October to May, when the nights are cold and prone to frost, water only between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m.; even then, only a little water should be given at a time, so that the plants and the top of the soil are wiped clean before night returns. From May 15 to September, but especially in June, July and August, water in the evening and water abundantly, so that the water penetrates right down to the roots and is not washed away by the sun, and so that the soil does not dry out too quickly and crack. In short, there can be no profitable gardening without continuous, abundant watering. Parisian market gardeners, who have no rivals when it comes to growing vegetables, never say "water", they say "wet", which for them means giving the soil something to drink while it's thirsty. A little water given to parched soil evaporates in a short time: cultivated plants suffer more from such watering than they benefit from it. Wherever water is scarce, frequent hoeing is needed to give the roots access to the dew of spring and summer nights. 5. Sowing. Propagating plants by sowing seeds is the most natural way of propagating: by this means, you can obtain plants that are better constituted and more durable, and breeds that are better able to adapt to the climate to which you want to accustom them. This is the only way to propagate herbaceous plants, if you want to obtain interesting varieties. The main condition for successful sowing is to have good seed, and the only way to be sure of seed is to collect it yourself, with all due care and precaution. If you want vigorous plants, you need to choose seeds from the last harvest, collected from healthy, robust plants, at the time of their perfect maturity. If, on the other hand, you want to sacrifice the beauty of the plant to that of its fruit, if you want to obtain double flowers or new varieties, give preference to old seeds, provided they have not lost their germinative virtue; and they will have retained it if they have been kept in a dry place with their natural envelopes. Most seeds can be sown as they are harvested, simply by taking them out of their envelopes; but a few, which have hairs and burrs, require preparation by mixing them with ash or sand, and rubbing them in the hands until they are free of these appendages, which would prevent even sowing. You can hasten the germination of some seeds, such as peas, beans and broad beans, by soaking them in water for twenty-four hours before sowing. Seedlings should only be sown in loose, soft, clean soil. All vegetable seeds can be sown by hand, either in rows or broadcast. Row sowing should be preferred to any other method for plants that are to receive one or more subsequent hoeing operations. When broadcasting, care should be taken to level the beds with a rake, after pulverizing the soil as much as possible. Fine seeds are thrown on the ground and should only be covered with well-consumed compost; most of the others only want to be lightly buried; it's always better to bury them less than too much. The soil is then firmed up, either by hand or with a flat board, and watered if there is no hope of rain. To prevent the water from over-watering the soil, cover it with chopped straw, moss, etc. Summer seedlings are planted in the shade, and require frequent watering. In general, the finer the seeds, the less they should be buried. Some seeds need to be sown on a bed, as we shall indicate when we list the plants that must be included in the composition of a vegetable garden. Seedlings are sown on the spot, either in rays or broadcast, when the plant is not to be transplanted, and in the nursery when it is to change places before taking up permanent residence in the one where it is to grow fully. Transplanting is often confused with transplanting. Transplanting is a provisional transplant that precedes the placement of plants in their definitive position, which is usually called transplanting. Some plants require one or even two transplants before they can be put into their definitive position, while others only need to be transplanted. This is what we will indicate for each plant in its place. 6. Layers. The bed should be considered the mother of all plants. A bed should be placed at midday, so that one end faces the east and the other the west. After marking the required width with a chalk line or stakes, dig a ditch 0.20 m deep, and work backwards to pile in the manure, mixing it well with a pitchfork to make it as uniform as possible. The manure used to make the layers should be new horse manure, after it has been left in a heap for some time. If the worker is skilful, he will roll up the manure so skilfully as he makes each bed of the layer that all the straw ends are inside. Once the first bed has been made square, of the length and width decided upon, all the other beds are then made in the same way, beating them with the back of the fork or stamping on them, to make sure there are no voids so that they can be remedied immediately, the bed having to be equally packed everywhere, so that it has no part weaker than another. This work is continued until the layer is the height it should be; this height is, depending on the season, d° Om, 70 to iu and 1n,20 when it is finished; but it decreases by a good third when it has subsided. Paths 35 to 40 centimetres wide are laid around the bed, both for traffic and for placing stoves, i.e. urine-soaked manure from the stable. This manure, placed in the paths, imparts a very high level of heat to the bed. Each layer, depending on its intended use, after being well walked on, from end to end, with feet together, and especially on the edges, must be immediately loaded with good compost, which is spread, from large to large, on its surface. For the quantity of potting soil to be used, refer to what we'll say later in the article on each plant. But above all, when you finish the layer, especially in cold weather, you must be careful to put in a larger quantity than in ordinary weather, to help it warm up; you then remove the excess when you straighten it out. Layers for melons should be made in this way, as they are always sown on only 8 or 10 centimetres of compost, which in principle would not be able to set the manure in the layer in motion. In times of snow or frost, it is even advisable to cover the entire layer with warm manure, until it is thoroughly heated. Potting soil should never be stirred too much, i.e. too finely for all seeds, and the surest way to make it so is to pass it through a claie. This rack should be made of small-mesh wire, as used to be used for sideboard flaps, and should be two meters long in all directions. Before sowing or planting anything on a newly-made layer, wait seven, eight or even ten days for it to contract the heat it needs, and then, if this heat reaches too high a level, let it moderate. This decrease in heat can be recognized by the settling of the layer. A layer that is too hot will burn the seeds; a layer that is not too hot will delay germination. The layer can retain all its heat for ten or twelve days, and when you realize that it is cooling, you surround it with stoves placed in the paths, as we have said. These stoves are made with horse manure from the stable. But when renewing stoves, it's not always necessary to use new manure: quite often, it's enough to stir the old stove completely, provided it's not too rotten, to release a residue of heat that can last another seven or eight days: often, too, a third or half of new manure is added to the old stove manure to keep the layer warm. When a layer is exposed to heat loss, and the plants it contains begin to melt, after removing the old stoves and before replacing them with new ones, pull a handful of manure from the sides under each bell, ten centimetres below the soil. This vacuum forms a kind of furnace into which the heat from the stove is more easily introduced and more effectively communicated to the plant above. Layers are made from month to month: but horticulturists rarely use layers until spring, when the soil is still cold. DIVIDING A VEGETABLE GARDEN 27 In order to keep the land of a vegetable garden as unoccupied as possible, and to maintain its fertility at all times, it is essential to alternate crops; in other words, it is not advisable to cultivate plants of the same family twice in succession, in the same part of the soil. If the garden is large enough, it should be divided into eight parts, which should be managed as follows: FIRST PART. - From September to May, winter peas and lettuces; from May to July, radishes, spinach, lettuce, cucumbers, nine-week potatoes; from August to November, autumn turnips, winter cabbage and carrots. PART TWO. - Spring lettuce transplanted in March; from May to September, peas, broad beans, beans, lentils, early potatoes, early turnips, spinach, radishes, early chicory, melons, giraumons. From September onwards, this second part will become the first, i.e. it will be cultivated like the previous one, which will be cultivated like the sixth. THIRD PART. - In March, transplant cabbage, spring cauliflower, radishes, turnips, spinach, lettuce, spring onions; in May, peas, beans, potatoes: in September, this third part will become the second, taking the place of the fifth. FOURTH PART. - From March to July, peas and broad beans are sown; from July to October, summer salads, spinach, radishes and turnips are sown, cardoons and celery are transplanted; in October, green cabbages and Brussels sprouts are transplanted. In March, this fourth part will be treated in the same way as the third. PART FIVE. - In March, planting of garlic, shallots, late potatoes, onions, cabbage, scorzon seedlings, salsify and leek. This fifth part will receive seeds from the second and will be treated like it. SIXTH PART. - From March to August, radishes, spinach, lettuce: autumn cauliflower, leek and lettuce transplants. This part will become the fourth the following year. SEVENTH PART. - This part will only receive artichokes, which are planted in April and May, and last for three years. EIGHTH PART. - The eighth part will form an asparagus pit that commonly lasts from 12 to 15 years. Most of our teachers' gardens are not large enough to follow a distribution similar to the one we have just outlined. However, in a plot of 5 to 7 ares in size, as we would like the gardens to be for school houses, we can largely conform to the distribution we have just indicated. A schoolteacher should be able to find in his garden all the vegetables he needs for his annual supply: moreover, if he knows how to make the most of his land, he will have a large enough quantity of good fruit for all seasons. Although our main aim in this treatise is the cultivation of vegetables and fruit, we are not banishing flowers from the garden. Far from it, and we recommend that schoolteachers garnish their flowerbeds with selected and varied flowers. First and foremost, time should be given over to what is useful; but the pleasurable should never be neglected, when it can be obtained without interfering with ordinary occupations. Floriculture relieves the fatigue of vegetable gardening; it speaks a sweet language: it is often the occasion for charming relationships, and this branch of gardening is sometimes the source of fruitful products. We know of schoolteachers who have made considerable profits with their varieties of reinemarguerite, and others with their collections of chrysanthemums. Incidentally, we only recommend that schoolteachers grow annuals or perennials that do well in our climates. Plants grown in hot greenhouses require expenditure that teachers cannot afford, and time that they are not allowed to give. CHAPTER III ELEMENTARY NOTIONS ON THE ORGANIZATION OF PLANTS We thought it would be useful to give a few notions on the organization of plants in general. A teacher who is called upon by his position to teach horticulture to his pupils, and to give advice on this art to all those among whom he lives, must be able to define the organs of the plants he cultivates, and explain the main phenomena they present. The plant is an organized being, deprived of the sense of its existence, of voluntary movement, feeding on inorganized substances that it draws from the air or water with the help of a vital force faculty according to laws that 2. of inorganic chemistry; combinations in which carbon dominates, and which it assimilates by a veritable intussusception, always increasing from the center to the circumference, by the duplication of the parts that constitute it, and consequently being endowed only with a relative individuality. The main organs and phenomena of plants, on which we will focus as clearly and concisely as possible, are: root, stem, rhizome, bulb, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fertilization, fruit, seed, embryo and germination. 1 Roots. The root is the part of the plant that runs towards the center of the earth; it does not turn green, even in contact with light, and normally produces neither buds nor leaves. It serves to anchor the plant to the soil, and to draw the food necessary for its growth. The presence of oxygen is essential, which is why it is important to bring it into more or less direct contact with the outside air, either by ploughing and draining, or by keeping plants in pots made of porous soil. The root differs from the stem in that it has no clearly visible central pith or tracheae. (Plant lungs.) In general, plants use their roots to draw part of their nourishment from beneath the soil, and this absorption is carried out by the spongiales that terminate them. As oxygen is the gas that most activates vegetation, it is essential to distribute well-oxygenated water to plants, or water that has been subjected to the action of atmospheric air, which, as we know, contains 79 parts oxygen and 21 parts nitrogen. 2. Stem. The stem is the part of the plant axis that grows in the opposite direction to the root, at the time of germination. It branches by means of buds in the leaf axils. The stem exists in all vascular plants (i.e. those full of vessels), but sometimes it develops only slightly, and the leaves, as well as the floral branch, seem to grow from the root. The plant is then said to be acaule (stemless). The stem is perennial when it lives several years, biennial when it lives two years, annual when it lives only one year. It's called herbaceous when it's greenish, soft and easy to break: these are generally annual stems. It is woody when it forms a solid wood that persists after hardening. It is said to be sub-woody when its base alone is hard and persists above ground for several years, while the twigs and branch tips perish more or less completely and are renewed every year. The woody stem of our trees is called the trunk. D The herbaceous stem is said to be indefinite when it flowers only through the secondary axes born in the leaf axils, and when nothing puts an end to its vegetation, it can grow, so to speak, indefinitely. The stem is defined when the axes end in flowers and cannot, therefore, extend indefinitely. The stem is stoloniferous when, from the axils of its leaves, a bud is born that elongates by flowing over the ground, develops leaves at its tip, then straightens and produces fibrous roots below the tuft of leaves that terminates it, which sink into the ground. (Strawberry.) The stem is thorny when the branches, instead of developing completely, stop in their evolution and metamorphose into hard spikes. Thorns are degenerated twigs. Buds (eyes) are the rudiments of twigs, usually found in the leaf axils. Developed buds are called shoots, scions or arrows. 41 G 3. Rhizome. The name rhizome is generally given to stems which, instead of rising, crawl obliquely or horizontally below or on the surface of the ground: its front part emits fibrous roots, leaves and buds: its rear part is gradually destroyed with age (Iris). The rhizome has the same characteristics as the stem; it is indefinite when it extends into the soil with the help of a terminal bud that continues it indefinitely. 4. Bulb. The bulb is a rounded rhizome forming a thicker or thinner, more or less convex plate, which gives rise to roots in the lower part and produces leaves in the upper part; this part represents the scaly bud of any plant. This kind of reduced stem also gives rise to lateral buds (cloves) in the axils of its scales. The bulb is tunicate when the outer leaves form interlocking chains around the base of the stem (onion); it is scaly when the leaves are narrow, fleshy and interlocked in several rows (leek, hyacinth, lily); it is solid when the bases of the leaves are tightly packed, fused and welded together, so that the bulb seems to form a fleshy, starchy, homogeneous mass (colchicum). Comparing rhizomes with bulbs, it's easy to see that these two types of stock differ only in the length of the plate, and the more or less fleshy consistency of the underground leaves. The rhizome can therefore be seen as a bulb with a very long horizontal plateau, just as the bulb can be seen as a shortened rhizome with fleshy leaves. Tubers are the name given to the ends of branches that crawl under the ground and are swollen with starch (potatoes). 5. Leaf. Leaves are usually green; along with roots, they are the main organs of nutrition: they draw gaseous and liquid substances from the atmosphere, which can be used for plant growth; they also transpire and exhale substances no longer needed for vegetation. It is in their tissue that the sap absorbed by the root and transmitted by the stem is stripped of its aqueous juices and acquires all its nutritive qualities. Of all the plant's organs, leaves are the ones that contribute most energetically to plant life. They are also the ones that show the most modifications, and from which we derive the most characters for distinguishing species. The leaf is an appendage of the stem or branch bearing one or more buds in its axil. Although the leaf axil does not appear to have buds, they do exist, but in a latent state; they can develop under certain conditions. This fact is very important in horticulture: it explains tree pruning, and should always guide the gardener in a host of operations. A complete leaf has two distinct parts: 1° the tail or petiole; 2° the blade or limbus. The leaves of a tree have been aptly compared to the lungs of animals, because of their functions and the innumerable cells they contain; we might add that they also act as stomachs, digesting or elaborating the raw sap they receive from the roots. Chemically speaking, leaves contain: 1° woody substances; 2° albumin; 3° sugar or gum; 4° green matter; 5° wax; 6° fatty and resinous substances; 7° free or combined acids; 8° essential oils. The greater or lesser presence of one or other of these principles will make the leaves sought after as food, fodder, stimulant, etc. 6. Inflorescence. The term inflorescence means the arrangement of flowers on the stem. The flower supports are the pedicel, peduncle and receptacle. The pedicel refers to the tail of the flower: it is analogous to the petiole of a leaf. The peduncle designates the axis that bears the pedicel: it is the analogue of the branch, and is usually accompanied by a small sessile leaf to which we give the name of bract, and that of bracteole to the even smaller leaves that frequently accompany the pedicel. These organs are often flower-colored. The receptacle is the bottom of a flower's calyx. It is not our intention to go into great detail about inflorescence, as this would involve abstract questions that we wish to avoid in this book, 7. Flower. The flower in plants is an assembly of several rows of organs arranged one above the other in stages so close together that each of these different circles seems to be born on the same spot as the one that precedes or follows. The flower has been regarded as a true terminal bud, since this bud seems to emit foliaceous or appendicular organs that develop from the base to the top, and these organs, as they advance towards the center of the flower, lose their leafy appearance to take on other characters. Let's assume that a flower is made up of leaves that have been variously transformed in their tissue, color, consistency, odor, etc.; that they have taken on the name of calyx, corolla, stamen, pistil, depending on the rank they occupy as they move from the circumference to the center. A complete flower is therefore made up of four rows of organs. 1° The calyx. Whatever its coloring, the calyx is the outer row or lower whorl of the flower; its position alone should serve to distinguish it. It is made up of a variable number of small leaves, more or less free and independent, more or less intimately fused. The pieces making up the calyx are called sepals. 2° The corolla is the second row of organs in the flower; it is placed inside the calyx and alternates with its divisions; it is usually simple, very rarely multiple; its leaves are called petals. The corolla is usually of a color other than green; however, some plants have green petals. The corolla is single-petaled when the various parts of which it is composed are more or less completely fused together; it is polypetaled when the petals are free and independent of each other. 3° The stamens, to which we have given the name androecium, show more profound modifications than the corolla. Instead of flat, foliaceous organs, there are small bodies, usually yellow in color and ending in a small head. A complete stamen is made up of a foot or net and a kind of head, the anther, most often with a deep furrow dividing it into two equal halves; each of these halves is called a loge and has a slight suture through which, when the flowers open, a particular dust called pollen escapes. The dust (pollen) contained in the anthers, acting on the stigma or top of the pistil, helps to produce seeds. This impalpable dust, often carried great distances by the wind, is made up of small grains of a particular shape in certain plant families, but of an identical structure in the vast majority of plants. These microscopic granules are made up of two interlocking sacs, or membranes, one outer and the other inner; the latter contains a mucilaginous liquid interspersed with granules to which we have given the name fovilla, which is the essential element of pollen. 4° The pistil. We have just defined the three rows of organs that make up a perfect flower, to arrive at the central body known as the pistil. This organ occupies the center of the flower, ending, as it were, the vegetation of the floral branch. In most cases, the pistil is placed immediately on the receptacle or more or less dilated or flared top of the pedicel; most commonly, the pistil is sessile; but in some plants, its base is very elongated (carnation), either on its own (caprier), or with the stamens fused to it; in the latter two cases, the pistil and stamens are carried outside the corolla. The pistil consists essentially of two parts: the lower, usually swollen and green, ovary; the upper, papillose, whitish and often viscous, stigma. 8. Fertilization. When the flowers open, the anther lodges open and spread their pollen over the stigma, which retains this dust with the help of its viscous papillae. Once applied to the stigma, the pollen grains undergo a sort of germination, so to speak; the inner membrane of these grains herniates and exits through the small doors pierced in the outer membrane in the form of an excessively tenuous tube which insinuates itself between the papillae of the stigma, penetrates the style, whose central canal it follows, arrives in the cavity of the ovary, penetrates the ovule to connect with the embryonic cavity via the micropyle. Once there, the embryo sac receives the fovilla, and the embryo begins to appear in the form of a small globule. Everything is thus ready for this important act of plant life. Once fertilization has taken place, the ovule continues to develop to form the seed. 9. Fruit. The fruit is the fertilized, ripe pistil, containing seeds capable of germinating and reproducing the plant. This is the normal state, as we know of fruits that ripen without producing fertile seeds. If we have succeeded in making ourselves understood, it will be easy to see how fruit can sink and abort; indeed, a drop of water falling on the stigma is enough to wash it clean, sweep away the pollen, prevent fertilization and often halt the development of fruit and seed. However, it's worth noting that ovule sterility doesn't always lead to fruit drop. The fruit must always contain the seed: one is the container and the other the content. A fruit must always contain traces of the style; a seed will always contain traces of the micropyle. We shall not stop to describe the innumerable forms of fruit. In general, fruits can be divided into two groups: simple fruits and aggregated fruits, which are dry or fleshy. Among the former, we distinguish the follicle, the vegetable and the drupe; among the latter, the capsule and the berry. With these five names, we can describe all fruits; we always manage to make ourselves understood without overloading the memory with bizarre names. 1° The follicle is a dry fruit with several seeds, opening by its ventral suture, like the peony, columbine and oleander. 2° The vegetable or pod is a dry fruit usually opening in two valves, either by its ventral suture, or, more rarely, by its dorsal suture. Vegetables sometimes twist in a spiral, like alfalfa, or divide into several articles, like sainfoin, each enclosing a seed. 3° The capsule is a dry fruit with one or more chambers that open more or less completely. The fruits of purslane, chickweed and henbane have a peculiar arrangement: they split crosswise and open like soap boxes; they are called pyxides. In reseda, the fruit remains open and the seeds are exposed to the air shortly after fertilization. 4° The drupe is a fleshy fruit that doesn't open and usually contains just one seed, like the peach, plum and walnut. The berry is a fleshy fruit in which there is no stone; it differs from the capsule only in consistency. Some fruits can be called either a berry or a capsule, so to speak (e.g. chillies). 10. Seeds. Seeds are fertilized ovules suitable for germination; they contain a plant in miniature: the seedling, embryo or germ destined to reproduce the species. Every seed is covered by a tegument, which itself is usually composed of three membranes or skins more or less intimately fused together. The teguments of the seed vary infinitely; each species has, so to speak, a particular character, and this is often a good way of differentiating them. 11. Embryo. Plant seeds contain an embryo or seedling. In the vast majority of cases, the embryo has two lobes or cotyledons. Hence the name dicotyledons. Other plants have only one undivided embryo, i.e. a single cotyledon: hence the name monocotyledon. D Every dicotyledonous embryo consists of a kind of small stem (tigelle) reduced to a nipple at the tip of which corresponds the young root, and two lobes or cotyledons between which the rudiments of the bud can often be distinguished; this rudimentary bud has been given the name plumule, because of its resemblance to a small feather. The monocotyledonous embryo is usually cylindrical in shape. In general, it occupies the axis of the seed; but in grasses, it is placed, so to speak, outside and pushed back to the geometric base on one of the sides. 12. Germination. Germination is the act by which the embryo grows, sheds its integuments and eventually becomes self-sufficient, drawing its nourishment from the element in which it is placed, or even from another plant if the plant is parasitic. The free end of the tigelle, ending in the nipple or root point, is usually the first part to protrude outwards, enlarging the orifice of the micropyle to which this radicle always corresponds. The degree of heat, and the amount of oxygen a seed requires to germinate, varies for each species. The need for the seed to remain in the ground before germinating also varies widely. It's a fairly general fact that the seeds of spring annuals need a fairly long time in the ground before they can germinate. The physical phenomena of vegetation are brought about by a combination of atmospheric elements, water and certain organic substances in the soil. The action of atmospheric air on plants is divided into two perfectly distinct phases: germination and vegetation proper, which includes the development, growth and multiplication of the species by means of the organs and phenomena we have just briefly defined. It therefore follows from the foregoing: 1° That a plant, since it assimilates inorganic substances, is a living being, an intermediary between the mineral and animal kingdoms; 2° That we must not consider a tree as a simple being, such as an animal which has only one vital center, but as a true polypier, endowed with a relative individuality, formed from the particular and successive productions of all the gems or buds which have developed and succeeded one another since its origin; 3° That the common life of a plant consists in the property of all its tissues to absorb in common the inorganized substances necessary for the development of its gems; 4° That each bud produced by the plant is the center of a particular vital force, and that all these buds are the origin and natural source of new individuals. The care to be given to young plants is the domain of horticulture; the details relating to it will necessarily find their place in the various articles of this treatise. GARDENER'S CALENDAR 41 To conform to custom, we will begin our horticultural calendar with the month of January, although gardening work forms a circle that is difficult to break, and there are times when the cultivator's care must be, and indeed is, more multiplied. But we would point out with the author of Le Bon Jardinier that, for a vegetable garden, we could fix the beginning of the horticultural year at August, because it is at this time that the gardener begins to work by distant forecast, that he begins to calculate the seasons and to sow a certain number of seeds, the produce of which will only be harvested the following year. As the temperature of all years is not uniform, our indications cannot be rigorously exact; sowing will have to be brought forward or delayed, depending on whether the season is early or late. It should also be noted that our calendar is designed for the average climate of France, and can only be applied to the south or north of the empire, with the modifications required by differences in climate. JANUARY. Vegetable garden. - Work in the open ground. - Work continues on the ripping of the soil, which began in November and December. The fertilizers to be buried during the first ploughing are brought to the beds. When the weather is mild and rainy, we remove the litter or leaves covering artichokes, celery and other delicate plants. Pits are opened for planting asparagus in March and April, to give the soil at the bottom time to ripen. If the weather doesn't allow us to work outside, we make straw mats, put our tools back in order, and check the seeds to see which ones we're short of, so that we can stock up in good time. We sow, in small quantities at a time, early peas and bog beans on the coasts, on the south-facing slopes, or in well-sheltered places; towards the end of the month, we can sow onions in light soil, with the precaution of covering them with litter, in case of frost. Cauliflower seedlings sown in autumn for coastal planting, at the foot of a south-facing wall and to be used for spring planting, are sheltered under frames or, in the absence of frames, under straw mats supported by pea oars. Fruit garden. - Ripping is done more deeply here than in vegetable beds. If there are trees to be planted, the holes should have been made in autumn, if time, location and circumstances allow. All tree species, except conifers, can be planted in dry soils; but in wet, cold and rotting soils, it's best not to plant until March and April. When it's not freezing, start pruning weak apple and pear trees, and those of mediocre vigor. For those that are too vigorous, we wait until March and April. In rainy weather, we scrape the bark of old trees to remove moss and lichen, or rid them of their dead wood. Landscaping. - In general, there's little in the way of groundwork to be done in a pleasure garden in January. However, despite the cold of the season, you should find snowdrops, violets, crocuses and pink saxifrages ready to bloom in a parterre. When the weather is mild and rainy, we remove the litter from herbaceous plants, which fear rot as much as the cold. Cover them if frost returns. In soils that are not too damp, you can plant hyacinths and tulips, if you neglected to plant them in autumn. We stock up on normal or free soil, heather soil, sand and all the animal or vegetable substances that can go into the various composts, which we take care never to run out of. FEBRUARY. Vegetable garden. - Everything that could not be completed in the previous months is continued, but in February the work becomes more extensive. Ploughing is done as often as the weather permits, so as not to be behind schedule in March. Onions, early peas and broad beans are sown; after the 15th, spinach, chervil, wild chicory, prinprenelle, sorrel, parsnips, carrots, leeks to be replanted later, and parsley are planted in beds or borders. Small spring lettuces, such as gotte, are sown in the onion beds. Garlic and shallots are planted, and green romaine can be planted on good soil to be grown under cloche. Whenever the weather is mild, we remove the leaves or litter covering artichokes and celery, and cover them if there is any sign of frost. Towards the end of the month, you can replant sorrel and thyme borders. During bad weather, we make straw mats and repair tools. We continue to warm the beds planted with seedlings or plants already transplanted; we make others on which we permanently transplant cucumbers, melons, lettuces, romaine (remembering that lettuce and romaine need very little heat), and early cauliflowers; We continue to sow melons, cucumbers, radishes, head lettuces, romaine lettuces, Italian curly endive, various supplies, and lettuces for cutting while we wait for the head lettuce. We destroy the layers made in December that have yielded their produce and lost their heat, and take the unconsumed manure, which we mix with new manure to make new layers. Dwarf peas should be sown in frames, dwarf beans and broad beans in close proximity, and then transplanted to warm layers. Asparagus is planted on beds to replace asparagus that is running out, and new beds are forced into the ground, as are strawberry plants; cauliflowers and eggplants are sown, and in March will be ready to be replanted on beds or on the coast. Fruit garden. - The work indicated for the previous month continues in this one, but we must hurry to finish planting in dry, light soil. The pruning of apple and pear trees continues; the vines must be completely pruned in this month, because if they were pruned later, weeping would result. Strawberry plants are pruned back to make them branch out and produce more fruit. If, in December or January, you have not cut your supply of fruit and other tree branches and put them in the ground, with a northern exposure, to make split grafts at the end of March, in April and May, when pruning, look for the most suitable branches for grafting among those removed, and put them in the ground, each at the foot of his tree, to avoid mistakes, until they are available. After the 15th of the month, wherever the trees have been pruned, we start the general ploughing, so that it will be finished by the time the March hail arrives. If you haven't already done so, you can also cut the shoots of trees and shrubs that have taken cuttings, dividing them, species by species, into sections 0 m. 20 to 0 m. 30 long, with several eyes, and making small bundles that you bury by the large end, in fresh sand or light soil, sheltered from frost, sun and heat, until March and April, a favorable time for planting. You can also sow pear and apple seeds, as well as many seeds from trees and shrubs that don't have the bone envelope, such as chestnut, chestnut, ebony, rose, etc. Bedding. - You can sow ranunculus, anemones, thlaspis, quarantine, larkspur, poppies, poppies, immortelles, blueberries, adonides in the ground. In the open ground, you'll find helleborine, small periwinkle, perennial daisy, a few fragrant violets, perceneige, herbaceous heather, liverwort, Japanese spirea, rosemary, etc. in January. Sow wallflowers, different kinds of verbena, dahlias, bright sage, amaranth, sensitive, cobea, etc. on the bed. MARCH. Vegetable garden. - March is the month when the earth calls for all the gardener's activity. Ploughing is completed; all manures and fertilizers are buried; borders of all kinds are replanted. We start sowing various types of peas, broad beans, romaine, several types of lettuce, wild chicory in borders or beds, chervil, parsley, onions, leeks, spring onions, carrots, spinach, turnips and radishes, and most garden vegetables, except beans, which cannot withstand the slightest frost. The first early potatoes are planted. Artichokes are uncovered, started and ploughed after the 15th of the month; asparagus is ploughed and smoked; last year's seed-bearing bulbs and roots, such as celery, onions, carrots, turnips, beet, etc., are put in the ground, and to avoid the bad effects of sunstroke and light frosts, which are often felt at this time of year, seedlings and plantings are covered with a thin layer of compost or light mulch. Asparagus is planted, but in strong, cold soil, it's best to wait until the first days of April. Now is still the time to sow this plant, either in the field or in a nursery. Layers and frames. - Maintain the warmth of the beds on which first-season melons and cucumbers, cauliflowers and fine Italian chicory are permanently planted. Melons and cucumbers, cauliflowers and lettuces already grown are replanted on new beds for the second season, and the same seeds are sown for a third season; in addition, turnips, lettuces and supplies are sown to await the produce of the open ground, as well as beans, some intended to produce on the spot, others with the aim of replanting them either on beds or in a good soil with proper care. Fruit garden. - Prune espaliers and counter espaliers. All branches that are to be tied should be tied immediately after pruning, before their eyes have elongated, so that they cannot be broken or cut off during the tying operation; after removing all the removed wood, the base of the trees should be ploughed and a good mulch spread. Peach trees should not be pruned, so as not to hasten their flowering, which could be damaged by late frosts. Nursery plantings should be completed as quickly as possible, cattails and tall trees pruned, staked and ploughed. The mothers of coignassier, paradise and all shrubs propagated in this way are pickled or ridged. You can also sow apple and pear seeds and many other tree and shrub seeds in the ground or in a terrine. Towards the end of the month, if the weather is favorable, cuttings prepared in February can be planted, but they must be properly mulched. Bedding. - Sow in beds: balsamines, queen marguerites, tagetes or carnations and marigold roses, nyctages, belles-de-nuit, elegant ragworts, Chinese bumblebees, campanulas, wallflower ragworts, and in general all delicate plants. In the open ground, we have almond, thorn and nannyberry trees, mountain ash, spirea, andromeda, viburnum, iris, tulips, narcissus, primrose, bear's ear, spring cynoglossa, anemones, double-flowered poplar, arbutus, etc. APRIL. Vegetable garden. - We continue the work of the previous month: but as heavy frosts are no longer to be feared, we sow and plant all kinds of vegetables in abundance. White melons, wild chicory, Versailles and Italian lettuces are sown on beds for July; celery and kale for August, long-headed cabbage and broccoli for September. In the open ground, previous seedlings are weeded, those that are too thick are thinned out, artichokes are grommeted, and the best grommets are planted to form a new plant. We continue planting asparagus, and straw the plants to protect them from drought. Water in the morning and around mid-day, but refrain from doing so in the evening, for fear of the cold. Care should be taken to sow fast-moving plants such as turnips, radishes, spinach, chervil, lettuces, romaine, peas, etc. frequently, so as not to run out. We also sow summer chicory, celery, cardoons, savoy and Brussels sprouts. The first peas and broad beans are headed, to bring their fruit forward. Lettuces, cauliflowers and cucumbers grown on beds are planted in the open ground. Beets, beans, cucumbers and gherkins are sown in potting soil pots. Fruit garden. - We finish pruning the vigorous fruit trees that we had left last, as well as the peach trees whose flowering we had feared to bring forward by pruning too early. When the buds of trees that have been pruned into any shape have elongated from Om 020 to Om 025, all those that are useless, harmful or misplaced should be removed, leaving only those that are necessary for the fruit, beauty and harmony of the tree. During this month, late frosts often surprise the young vine buds, flowers and new shoots of some fruit trees. The damage is not irreparable, however, if you catch it in time, i.e. before the sun's rays have struck and destroyed them. You must therefore be quick to light grass or wet straw, whose thick smoke is directed by the wind onto the affected buds: this is enough to save them. As for the flowers and shoots of fruit trees, if late frosts threaten to damage and destroy them, they should be covered with canvas and straw mats, especially at sunrise, if the trees are exposed to the sun's rays. Those who don't have sheets and mats are content to water the areas affected by the cold with well or fountain water, which is sprinkled down as a fine shower using a watering can with a knob riddled with tiny holes; this method often works well for them. It's time to graft the vine. You can still plant a few trees, if you have neglected to do so at a more suitable time; but recovery will only be assured in damp soil. Bedding. - Volubilis, nasturtiums, belles-denuit, dahlias and sweet peas are sown; most perennials are transplanted. The number of flowers blooming this month is considerable, in addition to those in greenhouses. Primroses, bear's ears, anemones, narcissi, hyacinths, tulips and a large number of other lilies are in the open ground; bulbous fumitory and corydalis, their neighbors, European trolleys, lilacs, cherry trees and double-flowered cherry trees, false ebony, several cytises, etc., are also in the garden. By the first days of April, the ornamental garden should be in top shape; paths should be raked and removed; all perennials should be well cleaned, lawns mowed, beds and flowerbeds well tilled, and annuals sown on site should be in full vegetation. New plantings are visited, to encourage those that are behind schedule by watering them appropriately. Pests, especially caterpillars, are hunted down. MAY. Vegetable garden. - This month's work is so varied and numerous that it would take too long to list them all. In the first fortnight of May, plant beans, which are to be harvested dry; this does not prevent the sowing, every two weeks, of those that are to be eaten green, as well as peas and broad beans; and, as lettuces, romaine, spinach, chervil, radishes, etc., are fast-growing, sow more of them every two weeks, As lettuces, romaine, spinach, chervil, radishes, etc., grow quickly, they need to be sown often and a little at a time. We continue to sow carrots, beet, summer chicory, celery, cardoons, tetragons and gherkins. We sow savoy cabbages, large-ribbed cabbages, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, Swedish turnips and some early second-season turnips. Layered celery and cardoons are planted, as well as eggplants, tomatoes, cucumbers, gherkins and cauliflowers; tarragon is separated and replanted; finally, all the vegetables used in the country you live in are sown and planted. We make warm, muted beds for the last season's melons, for Batates if we don't plant them on mounds; we also make open-air mushroom wheels; we replant celery and cauliflowers on old beds to make them grow faster than in the ground, and we keep them in water to increase their vegetation. Now is the time to cut back old parsley and purslane, reserving the seed-bearing plants. Water indiscriminately in the morning and evening, according to the plants' needs. Fruit garden. - Trees with soft wood and thick bark, such as chestnuts, figs, walnuts and cherries, are grafted during this month, using splits and escutcheons. We begin to disbud the most vigorous. Wild shoots are removed from trees grafted the previous year, and the graft bud is attached to the tree or to a stake, to ensure that it remains upright, and to protect it from accidents that could cause it to come unstuck. Espaliers require frequent visits by the gardener, to monitor the progress of fruit development and advise on ways to encourage it. He must also pay attention to the growth of the various types of branches, so that each one achieves its intended purpose as much as possible. When a fruit-bearing branch of a peach tree has not retained any peaches, it should be cut back immediately onto the replacement branch, so that the latter gains in strength. This is also the time to remove any harmful or misplaced shoots that may have escaped disbudding the previous month. Nursery care consists in monitoring split grafts, destroying imbrications, hunting down bud cutters, reattaching trees that have become detached, and finally, carrying out the first hoeing. We start grafting with flutes and budded buds. Bedding. - Sow autumn flowers such as quarrantine, nigella, thlaspi, Venus mirror, volubilis, runner beans, carnations and wallflowers. Auricula carnations are detached and planted. The bengal, hazelnut and cinnamon roses are in full bloom, while we wait for the prodigious number of roses that will grace the gardens during the following month to come into full bloom. The other flowers are so numerous and varied that it is superfluous to name any of them. During this month, there is usually no need for

But they are always useful for receiving sick plants, either in pots or planted bare: it's a good idea to keep a few around at all times. JUNE. Kitchen garden. - Continuation of May's work. The most important thing is to ensure that none of the season's vegetables are lacking, and that those which are to produce later are in sufficient numbers and in good vegetation. From this point of view, we sow large-ribbed cabbage for replanting in August and September, early apple cabbage, kale and early cabbage in cool soil for planting in August, overwintering in the greenhouse and replanting in March; fine chicory, large curly endive, escarole, giraumons, celeriac to be replanted in cool soil and eaten until winter, pancalier cabbage and black radish for autumn and winter, wild chicory for autumn Water in the evening. Artichokes that have worn out are grilled; onions are thinned out, and the small onions removed are used to fill in the empty spaces. The most beautiful cauliflowers are selected and marked for seed-bearing. Parsley roots are thinned out. Leeks and parsley are planted for winter. Maize beans are reserved for seed. Remove rotting leaves from seed-bearing lettuces. Cover plants when the sun is too hot. Fruit garden. - We visit the espaliers to ensure that balance is maintained in all parts of each tree: if we find any disorders, we will remedy them by the means indicated for tree pruning. Early apricots are the only fruit that may need to be cut green in this month, and their branches should be trellised. As for the branches of other trees, it may be necessary to tie some and pinch others to maintain balance. In nurseries, cleanliness is maintained by weeding and hoeing; care is taken to ensure that the trees form well, and in this, they are helped merrily by pinching and removing unnecessary buds. We are still grafting stone fruit trees, particularly roses, if we have no reason to prefer blind grafting. We are starting to harvest a fairly large quantity of fruit, such as strawberries, cherries and redcurrants. At the end of the month, we see the ripening of petit-muscat, Amiré-Joannet or petit-Saint-Jean pears, and myrobolan plums. Flowerbeds. - Watering flowers and plantations is the most important task of the month: however, we must not neglect to provide good stakes for all plants that do not support themselves, such as hollyhocks, dahlias, some asters, etc., and to provide oars or stiles for those that climb. We cut off the stems of herbaceous plants whose flowers have passed, reserving only those from which we wish to collect seeds. Rosehips can be made into growing eye patches, if their wood is well nourished. This is generally the flowering time for roses. Dahlias begin to blossom, stopping only at the first frosts in October. Each of these two beautiful genera offers the most brilliant and varied flowers, and should be the object of care and admiration. As for the other flowers that bloom in this month, it would take too long to enumerate them. The beds that have been used to raise flowers are excellent for receiving languishing plants, whether placed bare or in pots. With the necessary care and well-reasoned wetting, these plants soon return to a state of perfect health. JULY. Vegetable garden. - We continue sowing and planting vegetables whose produce can be obtained in less than four months, such as lettuces and supplies, beans to be eaten green, peas and broad beans, in places where white does not take them in September; cucumbers and gherkins, black radishes, autumn cauliflowers, broccoli, kohlrabi, turnips. Celery is harvested every two weeks, so that we can always provide enough for consumption. At the end of the month, we sow apple cabbages for the following year, which we then transplant to the coast to spend the winter there, when we fear they will suffer from the cold if we plant them at the end of September. Chives are sown for winter, and leeks to succeed those sown in spring; it's worth remembering that, if the seeds sown to produce them the following spring were too new, the plants would be prone to bolting (however, the safest time to sow them is from August 10 to 15). In July, we sow white onions to be replanted in October, and scorzonera to spend the winter in the ground; we also sow red chicory for November, whose first frosts turn it white, long-shelled peas and passion lettuces. Escarole and curly endive are beginning to blanch. Finally, the gardener must not lose sight of harvesting seeds as they ripen. Garlic and shallots are harvested in this month and the next, as soon as their tops have dried out; they are left exposed to the sun for several days, then the shallots are laid out in a dry place, and the garlic is hung up in small bunches. Strawberries of the month and English strawberries are sown at sunset in very loose beds covered with a mixture of sand and earth. In general, plants are watered frequently, mainly in the evening. A Dee du ErO L Fruit garden. - Espaliers, and especially peach trees, should always be carefully tended, to ensure that the balance is maintained, or to re-establish it when it has been broken: branches that get carried away should be pinched back strictly, and weak ones pulled forward. In dry weather, in addition to the water poured at the foot of the trees, water is syringed over the fruit to soften it and give it color. Nursery work consists of raking, budding to form cattails, and grafting with a growing eye on trees whose sap lasts until the frosts, and with a dormant eye on those in which it stops earlier; but it is often safer to wait until August before grafting with a dormant eye. Bedding. - Raking, watering, mowing and pruning are the main and most expensive tasks of the month. Autumn flower nurseries are tended to, so that they can be planted in clumps in flowerbeds and along the edges of beds at the end of July or the beginning of August. Care should be taken to ensure that the taller plants don't lack stakes, so that the wind can't break them. Carnations are pickled at the end of the month or beginning of the following month. Onions and flower grafts whose leaves and stems have dried out are lifted and replanted in autumn, or even immediately, after separating the cloves and changing or modifying the soil, if you want to put them back in the same place. Among the large number of flowers in bloom are Bengal and hazelnut roses, four-season roses, king roses, Belle-Favert roses, hollyhocks, dalilias and shrubs that bloom only during hot weather. AUGUST. Kitchen garden. - You won't see an empty patch of earth in this month any more than in June and July. Strawberry plants are planted and potted to be stretched in frames. This month's strawberry plants are planted on old layers and teens, to harvest in winter. We put tiles under melons that are nearing maturity. Litter is dried to cover plants that could be damaged by heavy frosts in December. Cucumbers and gherkins need a lot of watering when it's not raining, and cauliflowers, cardoons and celery require copious watering even when it's raining a little. In addition to sowing and planting everything to be consumed within the year, we must also take care of what can survive the winter and produce the following year. So we sow white onions, leeks, salsify, scorzonera, passion lettuce, which we replant in the ground on a hillside, York and sugar loaf cabbages, which we treat in the same way, spinach, chervil, turnips and lamb's lettuce for winter, carrots for spring. The gardener must carefully study his land and his locality, in order to know the advantages and disadvantages attached to the nature of each of them. In some areas, autumn sowing must be done a fortnight earlier or a fortnight later than in others; in some, peas and broad beans can be harvested right up to the frosts, while in others they can no longer be harvested after September. All this care and work must not make us forget watering, weeding and hoeing; chicory and escarole must be tied, cardoons must be stuffed, celery must be buttered or rather stuffed, and new strawberry plants must be planted often and a little at a time. If the old ones are bald or more than two years old, replant the borders with sorrel, thyme, lavender, tarragon and so on. Winter onions usually ripen in August; if some don't drop their tops, cut them off with the back of a rake to prevent the sap from rising, so that the onion ripens better. Artichoke stalks that have ceased to produce are cut close to the ground, so that the stalk grows back better. At the end of the month, you can sow peas and beans if you can cover them with a frame just before the first frost. Fruit garden. - Up to now, we've only done partial trellising and pinching to maintain the equillibrium; now we must start to trellis completely, i.e. put all the branches in the direction they should occupy, lest later their induration gets in the way. However, if a few weak branches are still growing, which you'd like to make stronger, leave them free for a while and don't trellis them until they've hardly grown any more. If disbudding is carried out correctly in April and May, there will be few or no branches to remove. Fruits nearing maturity are carefully uncovered, to add to their flavor and color. In nurseries, we disbud trees to give them the shape we want; we make sure they are always firmly attached to their stakes; we graft all kinds of fruit trees: ornamental trees and shrubs, except perhaps the excessively vigorous almond trees, whose vegetation often lasts until the frosts. Parterre - If all the autumn annual flowers, such as balsamines, daisy queens, marigolds, etc., have not been planted in July, they should be lifted into sods and planted at the beginning of August. Maintenance, consisting of watering, raking, hoeing, cutting grass, mowing borders, etc., is much the same as in July. Carnation marcots are dried and planted in pots or in the ground. Sow quarantines for transplanting. Poppies, larkspur, immortelle, etc. are sown in place for spring flowering. Roses continue to display their beautiful flowers, accompanied by dahlias, asters, several clematis, phlox, verbenas, perennial suns, etc. SEPTEMBER. Vegetable garden. - Water in the morning; wet often and a lot at a time artichokes that are marking, and leave them only a head when the foot is not very strong. Plant wild strawberries, tarragon, sage and rosemary; place this month's strawberries on the old beds. Cut pear and virgin sorrel, to have new leaves to cut in October. Part of the parsley is cut off, for tender leaves in winter, as long as the cold doesn't destroy them. We sow radishes on their own or with chicory, chervil in rays or broadcast for the winter, spinach and parsnips in rays for spring, as well as white carrots. Serious attention is paid to piling up the manure for the time when we'll have to make layers. Celery is successively ridged, or uprooted, and replanted in deep gutters cut into the soil of the old layers. Stuff cardoons to blanch them, as well as pear corms, if you don't prefer to plant them in troughs like celery, which is simpler and better. If the winter potatoes are ripe, we dig them up. We have all kinds of vegetables, with greater ease than in the previous two months: with less heat, they don't bolt as quickly and require less watering. Asparagus berries are harvested and left to dry in the shade, then macerated in water until the seed separates easily when crushed between the fingers. The seed is washed, dried and saved for the following year's spring sowing. Fruit garden. - There is usually nothing to do to the fruit trees during this month, except for the peach trees, which are still growing, and whose balance could be disturbed by the carrying away of some branches or the weakness of others; in this case, the most vigorous ones are strictly pinched and plucked, and those which are too weak are pulled forward. We continue to uncover over-shaded fruit. The last weeding is carried out in the nurseries, and subjects whose sap was too strong in August are grafted. We visit the budded grafts made the previous month, and loosen the ligatures to prevent bulges from forming. This precaution is essential for all escutcheon grafts, in all seasons, and should be taken twenty or twenty-five days after they are taken up.
