The most beautiful bunches of grapes are wrapped in horsehair or paper bags to protect them from birds, flies and even the first frosts. The flowerbed. - We go through the garden carefully to see if the plants are fulfilling their purpose. If some are growing badly or seem to be suffering, if others are poorly placed or are not producing the desired effect, we take steps to remedy the situation at the time of the next planting; we keep an eye on the maturity of the seeds, so as to harvest them at the right time.  Everything indicated for the previous month can still be sown. Hyacinths, daffodils and tulips are planted towards the end of the month. Quarantines are sown for transplanting on the ground or in crates which are brought in when it freezes. You can also sow seeds of anemones, ranunculus or other bulbous or tuberous plants. The summer bloom is over and the autumn bloom begins, with the most beautiful and prodigious variety of flowers. HORTICULTURE. G OCTOBER. Vegetable garden. - We can only sow a little lamb's lettuce, spinach and chervil, which, if the autumn is favorable, will produce in March; but we can sow early romaine and lettuce with advantage, to replant in beds in November and December.  Young York cabbage and other cabbages sown in August can be transplanted, either in the nursery to be planted in February and March, or immediately if there is no fear of winter damage. White onions, passion lettuce and cauliflowers can also be transplanted in situ, but during severe frosts, the latter will need to be protected by cloches or frames, or at least by mats supported on slats or poles. At the end of October, asparagus stalks are cut, the pit smoked and ploughed; this is also the time to cut the last artichoke stalks, clean the base, shorten the outer leaves, and plough them to facilitate the ridging that will take place in November. We continue to blanch celery, cardoons, escarole and chicory. We pile up the new manure, which will be used extensively in the following month. We destroy the old layers, setting aside the unconsumed manure to make mulch or to bury as fertilizer. When the weather announces a few light frosts, we cover with mulch the last beds of chicory and escarole that have not yet been made, and especially those of green beans from the last season: it often happens that with this precaution taken for a few days, we secure the enjoyment of vegetables that would otherwise have been lost.  We don't make layers yet, but we can sow several vegetables on the old ones, to be replanted on new layers in December and January. Fruit garden. - During this month, trees require no care other than to be cleared of fruit, and to rest until pruning. Winter fruit should be picked in dry weather, one by one, so as not to crumple them; they are gently placed in baskets and taken to a dry room, where they are spread out and allowed to dry out for five or six days; they are then transported to the shelves of the fruit house. Towards the end of the month, if the trees have been stripped of their leaves, we can already start replanting all species of fruit trees in light, dry soils, and we can continue this operation throughout the winter, weather permitting. In cold, damp soils, where the roots could rot during the rainy, frosty and snowy seasons, it's best to wait until spring. If you have vacant land, break it up and smoke it, so that you can plant at the first favourable moment. Bedding. - The slowing down of sap and the cool nights give the leaves various hues that the horticulturist sees as the harbingers of the cold season. This news alerts the gardener that it will soon be time to bring in all the plants that must not spend the winter outside. You can still sow immortelle and other annual flowers that are resistant to the cold; plant hyacinths of all kinds, narcissi, daffodils, tulips, anemones, ranunculus, etc.; separate the marcottes of carnations better than in spring, and put them in pots to squeeze them in. The only flowers that bloom in October are Bengal roses, hazelnut roses, mus4 cades, dazzling sage, late gladioli and the many dahlias that can be considered as the backbone of a pleasure garden, if the cold doesn't attack them too early. You'll agree that all these flowers form a rather beautiful procession in a month that begins nature's sleep. NOVEMBER. Vegetable garden. - This month's work is more or less the same as the previous month's; but we start with the layers, which we take great care to protect from the cold and cold rains, and warm up from time to time. In the last fortnight, we sow snow peas, preferably at the foot of walls, with good exposure. It's still time to plough and butter the artichokes, after having shortened the longest leaves, the uprights having had to be cut as low as possible, as the fruit has been removed; we hoe celery in place and pull it out to plant it deep in old bed soil, where it whitens more quickly; we still transplant York and Cabus cabbages and winter lettuces on the hillside; we can even put some of the cabbages in place: If winter isn't too harsh, they'll benefit. Salsify and scorzonera can be silted up in case of hard frosts. Fruit garden. - You can start pruning old or weak seedling fruit trees, so that the sap doesn't needlessly rise in the buds to be removed. Worn-out trees are uprooted and the soil removed immediately, so that they can be replaced as soon as possible. Trees are cleaned of mosses, lichens, etc., which attach themselves to the bark. Nursery work consists of raising trees as they are needed, and clearing land for new plantings. Trees and shrubs that fear frost are covered with straw. Paterre. - Flowers are becoming scarce, and the only thing to be seen in gardens are Bengal roses and chrysanthemums, the varieties of which have long since been multiplied ad infinitum. We uproot annuals whose flowers have faded, and replant all kinds of perennials, so that next year they will flower better than if replanted in spring. This is also the most favorable month for planting most ornamental trees, except for resinous trees, which are best planted in spring. DECEMBER. Vegetable garden. - There's very little to do in December, unless you have to do a lot of digging. If the vegetable garden is in strong soil, and when frost is not an obstacle, the soil in the empty squares can be ploughed roughly, so that future frosts and cold weather will penetrate it and make it more crumbly: it will warm up all the better in spring, and the plantings will prosper all the more because it will have been more divided. Fertilizer and manure should be buried where they are needed. Fruit garden. - Trees need to be carefully checked for caterpillar nests, weevils and earwigs. Most apple and pear trees are pruned, and pits, pips and generally all tree seeds are stratified: to do this, a suitably large crate is prepared. First, a layer of damp sand is spread over it, then a bed of pits is placed on top, which is covered with a second, two-centimeter-thick layer of sand, a second bed of pits and so on, until the crate is full. The box is then placed in a cellar or other frost-proof place, and left until spring, when it's time to plant in the ground. Then carefully remove the pits, so as not to damage the sprout; put them in the ground and gain a year on the germination of certain seeds and on the development of the plant. Bedding. - You can still plant ranunculus, anemones, tulips and all the other onions you couldn't plant before. We no longer see flowers in the open ground, except for violets and a few chrysanthemums when the cold has not attacked them. If the open ground is not very busy during this month, the beds are very busy: they must be made successively for new seedlings and to transplant the seedlings planted in November. CHAPTER V DESCRIPTION, CULTIVATION AND PROPERTIES OF VEGETABLE PLANTS Several authors have adopted the family system for listing vegetable plants. While recognizing the superiority, in many respects, of this classification, we shall retain the alphabetical order as the most convenient for research purposes. However, so as not to deprive readers who are interested in these botanical comparisons of the advantage they could find in them, we will give at the end of this chapter the table, arranged by family, of all the vegetable species we have discussed. An. - Ordinary garlic is a bulb covered with very thin, white, purplish membranes and formed from several tubers joined together, commonly called cloves, each separately enveloped, with a very pungent flavor and a very strong odor. It throws out several fine fibers or loose threads, from which it draws its nourishing substance. Its leaves are green, oblong, full and flattened like those of quackgrass; its stem is united and bears at its tip a head wrapped in a white, pointed membrane; when this head opens, it produces lily-like flowers arranged in a bouquet, each composed of six white star-shaped florets. These flowers are followed by purpurine-colored, almost round, pea-sized fruits, which are small tubers called rocambole. Garlic multiplies through its cloves. In February or March, the cloves are planted Om, 16 apart, in beds or, better still, in borders. They can also be planted in October to produce their first products in spring. At the beginning of June, we tie a knot with the leaves and stem, to stop the sap flowing to the bulbs: when the leaves are dry, we pull out the garlic and leave it to dry out in the sun, then we tie it in bunches and hang them in a dry place. Garlic likes strong, healthy soil; if it's too damp, it'll be exposed to grease. Horse manure suits it best of all. Garlic is good for scorbutic patients, hydropics and asthmatics; it also aids digestion. Working people, such as sailors, bargemen, soldiers and peasants, who are reduced to eating coarse food or drinking unsanitary 4. water, do well to use it. In addition to ordinary garlic, there are two varieties that are not grown in France: red garlic, which is cultivated by the Gènois, and oriental garlic, which looks a little like leek. Artichant. - The root is thick and hard; the leaves are about 66 centimeters long, broad in the middle, divided into strips, cut and covered with a whitish down; its stem is 67 centimetres to 1 metre high, fluted, cottony, with branches at the top of which is a round, pointed head, more or less, depending on the species, formed of large sea-green scales, the base of which is thick, tender and whitish, good for eating; this is the only part of the plant that is used. The artichoke is propagated by eyelets, which are separated from the mother plants in spring and planted immediately, i.e. around April 15th. Artichokes have long, deep roots and require deep, cool, fertile soil. Weeding and watering are necessary when the plant is young, but it's a good idea to continue them throughout the year: with the help of the right season, and by promptly harvesting the stems, you'll get a second harvest in autumn from the strongest plants. Artichokes must be carefully protected from the cold by a cover of litter or, preferably, dry leaves: this cover must be removed as soon as possible, then ploughed, the dead or rotten leaves removed and the superfluous eyelets cut off.  This plant lasts for three years; it is warming, aperitive and very nourishing. The most remarkable varieties are: gros vert or de Laon, the best, most esteemed and most widely cultivated; gros camus, a little earlier than the preceding one, but less fleshy; De Provence, less fleshy, but earlier than the preceding ones: fears frost and is only suitable for the south of France; Rouge, a variety from the south, similar to the preceding one; Le violet, early, not very large, excellent for peppers, not so good cooked. Asparagus. - Asparagus is a perennial vegetable that plays an important role in urban diets. This appetizing, diuretic plant is very good for your health, and its cultivation is all the more profitable as it is easy to transport without deteriorating. If the soil is suitable, no vegetable garden should be without its asparagus pit; but it is above all in the garden of rural schoolteachers that this precious vegetable should occupy first place. So a teacher's first task on taking possession of his garden should be to plant the asparagus that will later bring him benefits and profits. There are two main varieties of asparagus: the green or common variety, and the large, purple or reddish-tipped Dutch variety. Asparagus multiplies by seed. It is sometimes sown in the field; more commonly, it is raised in nurseries, to establish squares with ready-made claws. The biggest disadvantage of growing asparagus is that you have to wait at least three years for the produce, but this is offset by the plant's longevity, which produces abundantly for fifteen years or more. This is the objection made by schoolteachers to whom we recommend planting asparagus: but if we demand that asparagus be grown in all school gardens, we'll have no more objections to make to advice which is all in the interest of those to whom it is given. SOWING ASPARAGUS IN A NURSERY. - Choose a patch of light soil, sandy if possible, which has been well prepared and, if necessary, amended. Sow in October, or from mid-February to the end of March, either broadcast or better, in rays spaced 20 to 25 centimetres apart; bury 15 centimetres deep; if the soil is a little hard and likely to fight on the surface, it's a good idea to top-dress. In the event of drought, either before or after emergence, water and weed the plant by weeding and hoeing. This plant is best used after the first year; this is the age at which asparagus should be preferred; however, it is customary to leave it in the nursery for two years; in this case, the same care is given in the second year as in the first.  PLANTING ASPARAGUS IN PITS. - The most important operation is to establish the plant permanently. We'll go into some lengthy details on this operation, because from our point of view, asparagus is one of the most important issues in horticulture. The methods for planting asparagus vary according to the nature of the soil. Sometimes, pits of Om, 70 to 1 metre or more are dug, from which all the soil is removed and replaced by fertilizer and other better soils. When the soil is damp, a first bed of plaster and coarse sand, heather, broom and tree twigs is placed at the bottom for drainage: Elsewhere, trenches 20 to 40 centimetres deep are dug, and manure is spaded into the bottom of the trenches; elsewhere again, only heavy smoking is used, and the whole plot is ploughed thoroughly, or just the beds where the seedlings will be planted, flat. The layout and spacing of the plants are no less variable: sometimes two, three or four rows of asparagus are planted together in a pit or bed (from Om, 80 to 1m, 60 wide); in this case, the beds are separated by paths that become ados when the soil from the dig is deposited on them; sometimes they are planted in isolated, equidistant rows, from Om, 50 to Im, 60. It cannot be said that one of these methods is absolutely and always preferable to the others, since all of them, if properly practiced and executed, produce very beautiful asparagus and long-lasting plants. Here, then, are the general principles to which we must adhere in order to operate correctly: Asparagus fears stagnant moisture at its roots, and must therefore be protected from it: this is why deep pits with bottom drainage have been devised for damp soils, and why planting on the surface, or even on raised beds, is the opposite procedure. The asparagus root reaches Om, 70 and more in length when it finds soil to its liking; it must therefore be given soil that has been added to or deeply disturbed. Sandy, permeable, soft soils are best suited to asparagus; if the bottom layer of soil is arid, thin and stubborn, it must be replaced with a better base. Consumed peat and turf, puddle and ditch muds and curings, and bedding soils can be used with advantage in these replacements. Asparagus requires a lot of food and fertilizer; whatever method is adopted, the soil must be richly fertilized. Pits should be backfilled to within 20 to 25 centimetres of soil level, and the last bed of this backfill should consist of Om, 15 of the best, softest soil possible, into which the claws are planted. Placing two or three rows of claws together in pits or beds has the advantage of making cultivation and annual replanting easier; placing the rows in isolation provides more air and food for the plants. The distance generally adopted is 40 to 50 centimetres in all directions for the large species; the common species can be a little closer. In a 1.60 m pit, you can place four rows of Om, 40 claws which, over a length of 10 meters, give 100 claws, a quantity we feel is sufficient for a teacher's garden. By planting in a checkerboard pattern, you can give the plants a uniform spacing of Om, 50. Whatever the respective dimensions observed in your planting, everything should be drawn up with a chalk line and a tape measure, and the beds marked at all four corners with good stakes. Once the pits have been prepared, it's time to plant. This is usually done from March to mid-April; the claws must be pulled out carefully, so as not to break the ends of their roots, which are very brittle, and care must be taken to leave them in the air as little as possible. Once the lines have been drawn with a chalk line, we mark the position of each plant along their length, at the set distance, with a small mound of earth taken from and around the position itself. The claws are established on this mound, with the roots carefully arranged along its sides, and then covered with 6 to 8 centimetres of soil. Once planted, it's best to cover each bed with earth. Care then consists of watering as needed, hoeing and weeding to destroy weeds. At the end of October or in November, dry stems are cut and removed, and 3 to 6 centimetres of soil or compost is added; but this is generally done in March, after light hoeing. The same care is continued for the first three years. At the third flush, you can cut some of the best asparagus, but it's better to wait until the following year, when they'll be in full production. From then on, care consists of hoeing, weeding and watering in summer, and a fall and spring treatment each year. For some, the autumn method consists simply of removing dry stems and cleaning the beds; others, on the contrary, top up immediately or at the end of December with a few centimetres of soil, compost or even short manure. The spring method is limited to light ploughing or forking with a fork, carried out with care to avoid damaging the buds, after which the soil is replenished if not done in autumn. In all cases, manuring every two or three years with short manure, at the beginning or end of winter, is essential to maintain the abundance and beauty of the produce. Depending on the quality of the asparagus being cared for, the thickness of the top-dressing will vary, but it is important to spread it evenly, so that the surface of the pit remains even. Beet. - Its roots are up to Om, 12 in diameter and 34 to 36 centimetres long; its leaves are green or violet-red, broad and flat; there are several varieties, all of which can be grown in the same way. Beet needs good, loose, deeply tilled soil, otherwise it forks and makes no profit; it is sown at the end of April in warm soils, and in mid-May in cold soils; when sown earlier, it often rises. We pull it up around All Saints' Day; remove all the tops; clean it as much as possible, even wash it if the soil is too sticky; then leave it in the air for a day to dry out, and place it in a cellar or dry greenhouse away from frosts. Nasturtium. - Nasturtiums are sown in rows in March, after the soil has been well smoked and prepared; they are then rowed, and yield more the more they are watered. The barely-formed buds and still-green seeds are preserved in vinegar and used as capers. The flower is used on salad. Cardoon. - Cardoon is sown in April in the open ground. Holes are dug one meter apart, Om, 50 wide and of equal depth; three-quarters of them are filled with earth mixed with well-consumed manure, then three or four seeds are placed in each hole, Om, 06 apart, and covered with earth mixed with manure; if all the seeds in the same hole sprout, they are pulled out so that only the most vigorous plant remains. When the cardoons are strong enough, the stalk is ridged, after having been tied into bundles; they are covered with straw and, when the ribs are white and tender, the cardoon is good to eat; it has the same nutritional properties as the artichoke. Carrot. - A biennial, indigenous plant, comprising a large number of varieties; but the red collared carrot is the best and most widely grown in our countries. Carrots are broadcast or sown in rows, with the proviso that they should be walked on a few hours after sowing, as long as the weather is fine. You lose less space by broadcasting; but, on the other hand, you can't care for the plant as easily as by raking: nevertheless, carrots grow equally well in both ways, and everyone should follow their own ideas in this respect. The key to its success is to be weeded and wetted often when young, and above all to be spaced out properly: to this end, it should be thinned out as early as possible, and left O m. 15 cent. apart in all directions from one plant to another; the further apart it is from the rest, the more food it has to enjoy. Harvest at the end of October, or during the winter following sowing. Celery. - Two species of celery are grown: common celery and celeriac. Each of these two species has given rise to several good sub-varieties. Common celery is tender and pleasant-tasting. Celery root is an excellent vegetable that deserves to be better known and more widely grown than it is: its flavor is milder than that of ribbed celery. To grow celery at different times of the year, sow from January to June. From January to March, we sow on beds and under cloches: the seed should be lightly covered and often basked. Only at the beginning of April are seedlings sown on a bed and under the same cover. Subsequent seedlings are planted in the open ground (April seedlings are planted in a sheltered spot); they are carefully thinned out, as the seedlings are to be planted without transplanting, and therefore need to gain strength in the first soil. The soil on which the plants are planted should be deeply spaded, well amended and damp or cool rather than dry. Celery should be planted in staggered rows, 20 to 25 centimetres apart, with each plant watered immediately for recovery, and moistened every two or three days if it doesn't rain. These waterings should be continued assiduously, as this plant likes water very much. When celery is strong enough, it can be blanched by tying it with three ties, in dry weather, and lining the bed with dry straw, so that only the tips of the leaves are visible; or, after tying it, mound the soil around the plant, first up to the first tie, then eight days later up to the second tie, and finally up to the third tie eight days later: this operation is called buttering. When you HORT. intend to butter your celery, you leave an interval at the time of planting equal to the width of the beds, which you plant with lettuce, chicory, etc., and whose soil is used, after the harvest of these plants, to make your mound. It is necessary to mulch or butter last season's celery before the severe frosts to which it is very susceptible. A few plants left in the ground and covered with straw can be used as seedbeds. The newest seeds are the best, although they may keep well for three or four years. Celeriac can be sown in the same way, but to obtain a soft, tender, mellow root, you need to choose deep, fresh, loose soil, or soil made soft by ploughing before winter and good topdressing. If the soil is not naturally fresh, make up for this by irrigation and frequent watering. It is planted at a distance of 40 to 50 centimetres, after having removed the large leaves and all lateral roots from the young plant chosen in the sowing. At the start of winter, we pull in some of the roots, or all of them if the soil is damp, and after cutting off the leaves, minus those in the heart, we bury it in the cellar. Celery is digestive and pectoral; it is usually eaten raw in salads; it is also served cooked in fat, and used to make aperitif broths. D Chervil. - Indigenous annual plant, sown at any time of year, either broadcast or in rows. To obtain chervil more quickly in spring, sow a few borders at the foot of well-exposed walls. The main autumn and winter sowing is done from the end of August to the beginning of October, and the last sown is the one that goes to seed last and therefore provides the longest supply. It succeeds everywhere, provided the soil is well prepared. It is eaten in salads and drunk to refresh and purify the blood. The seed ripens within the year and keeps for three years. BULBOUS CHERFEUIL, introduced into France a few years ago, has had little success: its small, starchy, slightly sweet root is somewhat similar in flavor to that of the chervis. However, as the cultivation of bulbous chervil is not very advantageous, we limit ourselves to indicating this variety, without going into further details. Chicory. - Chicory is a native plant that is much sought-after as a salad. There are several varieties, of which the main and most commonly grown are: wild chicory, curly chicory and escarole. Wild chicory is perennial: its emerging leaves produce a salad similar to baby lettuce, a little bitter, but very healthy and highly prized: it can be grown all year round by successive sowing. They can be sown very thickly, in almost any type of soil, and only require watering. The winter lettuce known as capuchin beard is obtained from this species, which is harvested in autumn and placed in alternate beds with potting soil or sand in a warm cellar. Curly endive only does well in autumn and winter; in summer, it rises easily and becomes tough. Its main merit is that it provides a lot, keeps for a long time and melts less in the fire than the others: moreover, it is a little firm and slightly bitter when eaten raw. Sow from May or June to mid-August, spacing the plants 35 to 40 centimetres apart and watering copiously during hot spells. When the plants are sufficiently full, bind them to blanch them. Escarole has a leaf as broad as that of some lettuces; it is more or less indented or elongated: it is soft and tender and of great profit, either raw or cooked, because it melts very little; its defect is that it rises easily during the summer and gets speckled by the rain. Like chicory, it should be tied only in dry weather, and then watered only with the neck of a watering can. It is grown in the same way as curly endive. COIUd de drpen d Cabbage. - The main varieties of cabbage are: white cabbage, regular cabbage, early kale, Savoy kale, savoy cabbage, large-ribbed cabbage, kohlrabi and red cabbage. The cultivation of the various cabbage species is more or less the same; they are propagated from the seed of the best species and of those that are the best eaten, which are replanted in March in the open ground. The seed of all species of apple cabbage is sown in beds at the beginning of March, or in the absence of beds, in well-smoked, well-prepared soil with good exposure; if they sprout too thickly, they need to be thinned out and watered often; whole squares are planted and tilled carefully; the more the soil is disturbed, the faster they grow. They are planted around the beginning of June, a metre apart in all directions. They should be watered and ploughed often. Seeds are sown again in mid-August, to be transplanted to a well-sheltered nursery in October and planted out the following March in well-amended, well-prepared soil. Cabbages transplanted in this way can be harvested in July, and keep well into winter. At the end of November, the remaining cabbages are removed and replanted in the nursery, bent slightly to the south-east, along the walls, protected from heavy frosts; they are covered with large, long beds: they can thus be kept well into Lent. After the cabbage harvest, the soil is left to rest until March, then ploughed to sow with onions. Cabbages should never be planted in the same place two years running. When replanting or transplanting cabbages, care should generally be taken to set them firmly in the ground, so that the eye of the plant is flush with the soil, and rather lower than higher. It's also a good idea to choose rainy weather whenever possible for this operation, because cabbages that don't wilt or recover easily are less likely to be attacked by insects. If the weather remains dry, this can be remedied by watering. If the plant is too weak, it will languish and fall prey to aphids; if it is too strong, its new roots will have difficulty penetrating the soil, it will grow little and will be exposed to climbing, knotting or hardening off. To preserve free-ranging species, it's important to keep seed-bearing plants of different species or even varieties well apart. Seeds of different cabbage species or varieties should be harvested, dried, threshed and stored separately. They retain their productive virtue for six or seven years. Cauliflower. - Cauliflower is considered to be a separate breed, although it undoubtedly originated from kale. There are three main varieties: tender or Salomon, semi-hard and hard. They have no external characteristics that clearly distinguish one from the other, but they differ significantly in their qualities. Cauliflowers need well-prepared, well-smoked, soft soil, and must be watered often. By sowing cauliflowers in September, and transplanting them to a warm exposure on ados and under cloches that are covered with straw during the cold, they can be harvested in spring: they can be put in place around March 15; until then, they should be given air whenever the weather permits. Sow in warm beds in February for late summer harvest. Cauliflowers sown in the open ground at the end of April and cultivated as above produce in August. The most common practice is to sow cauliflowers on beds in June and transplant them in July; if watered carefully, they will produce a plentiful harvest from September to November. Cauliflowers sown in autumn and overwintered under a bell, with strong, stubby stems and firm, clean, white, tightly packed heads with no inner leaves protruding, should be reserved for seedbeds. When replanting cauliflowers on loose, well-amended soil, space them 80 cm to 1 m apart. Dn mi ee min nammidide A Brussels sprout. - This variety belongs more to the Milans than to any other race: its stem is 70 centimetres to 1 metre high, producing small, tender, curly apples in the axils, which are highly prized and picked as they grow. Sown successively from mid-April to mid-June, this excellent vegetable can be enjoyed from autumn through to the end of winter, as it resists severe frost better than any of the Milans, although many of these are very hardy, especially when only half-headed. Chives. - There are two types of chives: annual and perennial. Chives grow very quickly, and can be sown from March to September. They are usually grown in borders, and all you need to do for them to grow well is to separate the clumps when they become too strong. This species, which is the perennial, does not produce seeds, and multiplies only by cloves, which are separated by bursting the clumps when planting. Annual chives multiply by seed, which is best sown in light, substantial soil in February and March, and replanted in May and April, 16 centimetres apart; the seed keeps well for two or three years. Chives are propagated by separating the cloves in March and planting them in beds or, more usually, in borders. They like good soil, warm exposure and a little watering in summer. Cucumber. - Cucumbers are sown in well-soiled soil, in April and May, in holes prepared in the same way as for melons. They need a warm exposure and plenty of water. When the stem begins to elongate, pinch it over five or six eyes and that's enough. Cucumbers are refreshing and slow down blood circulation. Gherkin is a variety of cucumber that can be sown like cucumber and requires no further care. Squash. - Originally from warm climates, squash love heat and humidity. Their seeds are germinated on a bed and under a bell in March, in pots filled with potting soil; then, after the plants have become accustomed to the air, they are removed from the soil and placed in a good exposure, from the end of April to mid-May, in the open ground, if the soil is healthy and well amended, or in small pits 40 to 50 centimetres wide and 32 centimetres deep, filled with manure and a few centimetres of potting soil on top. They can also be sown in the open ground, or in similar pits, from late April to mid-May, with two or three seeds in each hole, leaving only the strongest plant, which is watered frequently. Most species of squash are left to develop naturally and are not pruned in any way, but many gardeners do prune pumpkins. The first stem is usually cut off above the second or third eye, so that it produces as many arms. When the fruit has set, the branch carrying it is stopped 2 or 3 eyes above. Two fruits are often left on the same plant, rarely three; if you want large pumpkins, leave only one. D Ripe squash, pumpkins and pumpkins can be stored in a dry, temperate place for three or four months, or much longer in some species. There are many different types of squash, each with different qualities. But we especially recommend the following, because they do best in our temperate climates: ordinary pumpkin, giraumon, pumpkin, Ohio squash, whose flesh is easy to cook, sweet and very floury. All squashes need manuring and watering. The seeds of these vegetables keep for six to eight years; for seedlings, three- or four-year-old seeds are best. Cress. - A native perennial that, in many places, is simply collected from the banks of cool streams where it grows naturally. It can be cultivated by sowing, or by planting clumps brought from elsewhere on the banks of running waters, where it soon multiplies infinitely. The garden cress, however, is the cress alénois, an annual plant that received the name cress because of its pungent, pungent flavor. It doesn't last long, and quickly goes to seed, which means it has to be sown every fortnight, either in a row or broadcast, and in the shade in summer. There are three varieties: curly cress, broad-leaf cress and golden cress. Shallots. - Shallots can be propagated by planting bulbs, preferably small ones that are less profitable in households, and whose planting is at least as good as that of the larger ones. Good, soft, healthy soil, smoked the previous year, is needed, as shallots fear fresh fertilization as well as excessively damp soil. Plant in borders or beds almost flush with the ground, 10 centimetres apart, in February rather than March, and sometimes in October, to produce new shallots as early as June. From July to August, when the leaves are cooked, we pull them out and, after letting them dry on the ground for a few days, we take them to the attic. They must be kept dry and protected from the cold over winter. We also grow a large shallot that is less common and prone to degeneration: it is planted at 22 centimetres. Same cultivation. Spinach. - Spinach grows well everywhere; however, it produces more in light, slightly cool soil, which is especially well loosened and smoked. To grow spinach all year round, sow every twenty days from March to October. Summer seedlings should be sown in the shade, with a northern exposure, and they need a lot of watering: despite this, they are not very productive, because they go to seed almost immediately. We save for seed a plate of the first spring seedlings, or even better, of the autumn seedlings; we pull up the male individuals as soon as their flowers have passed. The seeds keep for two or three years. Spinach has a soothing effect, purifies the blood and can be used in all seasons. Spinach that appears frozen can be soaked in cold water and allowed to dry out in the open air, to regain its original appearance. Tarragon - A perennial, aromatic plant from Siberia that is propagated by bursting the stalks in April and May. Place 5 plants 30 cm apart in well-tilled soil. It's a good idea to cut off the stems at the start of winter and cover them with compost or even bedding on top, in case of heavy frosts, as the plant is a little sensitive. It can be used as a salad dressing, and makes a very pleasant vinegar. Marsh bean. - Beans are sown from the beginning of February to the end of April, and even later, in cool soil not exposed to sunlight. To get them early, sow them in December and January in beds facing south. Sow in rays or clumps. Clumps are formed by placing three or four beans in holes made with a hoe and spaced about 30 centimetres apart. Rays are planted at the same distance apart. Beans are usually hoeed twice; the second time, they are reshod, which increases their strength and yield. The blossom is much sought-after by bees; when it is completely spent, we pinch the end of the branches and stem to stop the sap and bring it to the advantage of the fruit. Many people like to eat the bean very young; when it has been harvested in this way, by cutting the stems straight away, we can hope, if the season is favourable, for a second harvest produced by the new branches that will grow from the base. Beans, especially if left in their pods, retain their germinative powers for four or five years. Strawberry. - A perennial plant with short, sub-woody stems, not very difficult to grow and requiring little heat to reach full maturity. In our climate, it's the fruit that ripens first; it's also the one that gives the longest. Strawberry cultivation has produced a large number of varieties, but there are really only three distinct species, two of European origin and one from America (see Le Bon Jardinier). Strawberries grow everywhere, but light soil suits them better than any other. Provided the sun doesn't beat down on them during hot spells, they need no care other than to be cleared of weeds. They also need to be cleared of useless runners and grommets, and old plants replaced: this is done from spring to autumn. There's no need to sow them; eyelet nets are all you need to multiply them, and this is both the quickest and easiest way. Strawberries prefer water from the gardener to rainwater and natural soil moisture. With a new plant every two years, you can be sure of always having plenty of good strawberries. The white worm is fond of strawberry roots; you'll notice that it's eating them when the leaves wither for no apparent reason; then you'll be quick to dig down and kill the worm. Beans. - Cultivation and differences in climate have given rise to a prodigious number of varieties of this excellent vegetable, but almost all are considered to belong to the common bean species. In terms of their cultivation and use, the various types of bean differ considerably, which must be taken into account when choosing the right species. Some are oars; their climbing stems need oars of between Im 50 and 3 meters to support them; others are dwarf; several are somewhere between these two dimensions. Some are particularly suitable for eating as beans, others as small green pods (green beans); a third type, called mange-tout or without parchment, can be eaten with pods and beans together almost to the point of maturity. One of these qualities does not always exclude the others. For example, the Swiss red bean, one of the best green beans, is also very good dry, and most mange-tout beans are highly prized in grain form. We'd like to give a brief introduction to the cultivation of pole and bush beans. The first beans are planted towards the end of April, weather permitting (i.e. if the weather is fine and dry); otherwise, they must wait until May, as the excessive humidity of the soil, combined with frequent rainfall, causes them to rot. The soil is first ploughed in March, then left to rest until it is time to sow the beans, at which point the soil is ploughed a second time, and the rake is used to even out the planks or squares. Runner beans are sown six or eight times on clods purposely made at a distance of Om 60 from each other, with a handful of potting soil thrown in at the bottom to ensure good growth. Dwarf beans are sown in rows only Om 07 deep, Om 12 apart, then covered with soil, dragging both feet along the sides. Beans can be sown from the end of April to the end of May only, to have them ripe, and from the beginning of June to mid-July, to have them green by the end of summer and into autumn. This vegetable is used so frequently in the kitchen, that it's arguably the most industrious in the home. It can be used in all seasons, in all conditions and for the most delicate of tastes. Dry bean seed, especially in the pod, is good for several years. As we have said, it does best in light soils; in clay soils, it needs more fertilizer and more care. Lettuce. - This vegetable has two main varieties that form two divisions: head lettuces and romaine lettuces. The former has a rounded shape; the latter is more elongated; its heart develops more easily; its flavor is much milder. The varieties of these two divisions are numerous and well enough known without needing to be enumerated. Spring lettuces can be sown in March on a small bed or in well-sheltered soil, and replanted in April; or they can be sown in the open in February and March among onions, carrots and salsify. This method is not without its disadvantages; however, it can be practiced by sowing very lightly and using only very small species. Summer lettuces can be sown in the two ways we have just described, so that their produce follows that of early lettuces; but their sowing, instead of being limited to the first spring, extends into July. After March, the plants are raised in the ground. Transplanting requires no attention other than to avoid overloading the soil around the roots, especially if the soil is strong. Lettuce sown between onion beds stays in place, after being hoeed and thinned out, and grows just as well as that transplanted. Lettuce thrives best in clean, light, substantial soil; frequent watering produces tender, soft lettuces. It is very useful, especially in dry soils, to mulch the beds before planting. Winter lettuces can be sown from mid-August to around September 10th. Replant at the end of October in the southern flowerbeds, at the foot of walls, and protect against hard frosts by covering with large beds or straw mats, which are removed as soon as the weather permits. It's a good idea to sow two seedlings a fortnight apart; sometimes the first seedlings advance too far and are liable to perish. It's always a good idea to use seeds harvested the previous year. Romaine lettuces are similar in all respects to head lettuces, but need to be tied so that they blanch and their heads fill out better. Perennial lettuce is rarely grown in gardens, but it can be cultivated with advantage: in April and May, its new shoots make an excellent salad. Lentil. - This annual plant is native to southern France: it prefers dry, warm, sandy soil. It is sown either in a garden or in the open field, in clumps or rays, and more rarely broadcast, as soon as frosts are no longer a threat, i.e. at the end of February or beginning of March. It requires no special care.  To ensure that the seed is of the best quality and most beautiful, it is threshed only as needed, either to eat it or to sow it; in this way, it is still very good in the second year. Mache. - Lamb's lettuce is a small, indigenous annual lettuce that is sown every eight or ten days from mid-August to the end of October in loose, soft, smoky soil from the previous year. Cover very lightly with a rake, and water if necessary. Lamb's lettuce should be used whole and only when young; by picking the most advanced for consumption, the plant will be sufficiently thinned out. A few plants are left to go to seed; as they ripen, the seeds fall off, so harvest several times, shaking the stalks on a cloth or cardboard. Lamb's lettuce can be harvested in the field, where it can be sown on its own, but it is always preferable to sow and harvest lamb's lettuce in the garden. This plant is refreshing and purifies the blood. Melon. - The flavor and fragrance of this fruit, which originated in Asia, have from time immemorial made it sought after and propagated in almost every part of the globe. Its varieties have multiplied to such an extent that today most of them are barely distinguishable, and every day we see those that for a time had somewhat pronounced characteristics lose them and merge with others. Melons can be divided into three main breeds: 1° common or embroidered melons, 2° cantaloupe melons, and 3° plain-peel melons. FIRST BREED. - Market garden melon, embroidered, round, sometimes a little depressed from the umbilicus to the stalk, without ribs and of medium size, very thick flesh with abundant water content, mediocre flavor. The following melons belong to this breed: sucrin de Tours, sucrin à petites graines, Sucrin à chair blanche, Ananas à chair verte. SECOND BREED (CANTALOUPE). - Cantaloup orange, noir des Carmes, prescot, petit prescot and cantaloup d'Alger. THIRD BREED. - White-fleshed Maltese melon, red-fleshed Maltese melon, United States nutmeg, white-fleshed winter melon, red-fleshed winter melon and Persian or Odessa melon. Melons in this series are referred to in many countries as watermelons, but this name should be applied more specifically to watermelons. GROWING MELONS. - Successful cultivation of early melons requires considerable equipment in terms of frames, windows and glass cloches, so that melon seeds can be sown on warm beds as early as January, and cultivation can continue until the fruit ripens on constantly warmed beds, at considerable expense. Those with limited equipment should sow at the end of April, or even better, at the beginning of May. This is what we recommend to schoolteachers, whose resources in warm manures are very limited, and who cannot hope to have ripe melons before the end of August or the first fortnight of September. For this limited crop, not layers but mounds of fresh manure are prepared at the foot of a south-facing wall around May, the time when melons can withstand the outside temperature. These mounds are rounded, flattened at the top and soon collapse in on themselves. A little potting soil mixed with light earth is spread over the top of these mounds, spaced 1.50 m apart, and four or five seeds are placed in a hole in each mound. When the plants have five or six leaves, we destroy all those that are not vigorous, keeping only the two most beautiful. As soon as the plant has grown its fourth leaf above the cotyledons, we top above the second leaf: this gives rise to two stems; if we top above the third leaf, three stems are born, from which we remove the least robust after a few days; but it's better to have only two stems, i.e. to top above the second leaf. A little later, we pinch off the two lateral stems to make them branch out; we pinch off again above the second leaf all the shoots that the first pruning has given rise to; after which we give the plant over to the natural course of vegetation, until meshes form, i.e. female flowers, which are followed by fruit. As each fruit is formed, the branch bearing it is pinched off one eye above the young fruit, and the branches with only male flowers are removed. Soon after, the number of fruits is reduced to two or at most three on each plant, choosing the liveliest, greenest and best-formed, and removing all the others. In plantations with two plants on each mound, only two melons are left on each plant. Subsequent pruning consists solely of cutting back weak, confused and overabundant branches, pinching off those that grow too long, and seeking out and destroying any fruit that appears afterwards. Watering should be very sparing, as melons are very sensitive to excess humidity, especially at the base of the plant. Water should therefore only be given during dry spells, and preferably in basins and on the sides of the mound rather than in the middle. When the melon is at the point of ripeness, and there is a fear that it may take on the taste of the earth, the fruit is placed on a piece of slate or tile; the sun's ardor then strikes it from all sides, perfecting it and bringing it to perfect ripeness. It is ripe when the stem seems to be coming off and when it gives off a strong odor; it will be good if it has a short stem, is firm under the finger and heavy in the hand. The various types of melon should not be grown too close together if they are to be kept fresh, unless they are planted at different times and do not flower at the same time. It is also advisable to keep away from melons all other plants of the Cucurbitaceae family (pumpkins, squash, giraumons, cucumbers), whose proximity could lead to accidental cross-breeding, so that after very careful cultivation, mongrel melons could be harvested that would not be edible. To obtain good seeds, we choose the most beautiful and straightforward fruit of each species, and let it ripen as much as possible. The seeds are then separated from the juice and filaments, dried thoroughly, and kept for seven to eight years, sometimes longer. Seeds from fruits eaten at their normal ripening point can also be used, even if they have been washed. Melon is an excellent fruit, very refreshing, but very indigestible. Watermelon. - Fruit usually rounded, with smooth, green, mottled or speckled rind; flesh red or white, very melting, sweet, but a little bland; seeds black or red. By sowing it early, like early melons, and then transplanting the plant into good, prepared soil with the best exposure, you can hasten its maturity and have it ready for hot weather. This type of squash can be pruned like melons and given the necessary watering. Turnip. - The turnip is an indigenous biennial plant. It has been cultivated since time immemorial, and its flavor and external characteristics are easily modified by the soil and climate. Turnips come in a large number of varieties, many of which are not very specific. Turnips are sown from mid-June to mid-August. In light soils, early varieties can be sown until the beginning of September, and seedlings sown in May and early June sometimes do well if the weather is damp and not too hot. Some gardeners risk sowing in March and April to get summer turnips, but they rarely fail to come up, even when using old seed, which should always be done. Sow on freshly-turned soil, clear and broadcast, whenever possible in rainy or overcast weather; care consists of weeding and thinning. onion. - This plant, one of the most important of the root vegetables, is perennial by nature, but is treated as a biennial in cultivation. Its many varieties change easily under the influence of soil and climate. Onion seed is sown in March in loose, light soils, and in April in clay soils. If it grows too thickly, it should be thinned out, leaving the largest plants 15 cm apart; the thinned-out plants will be used to transplant where the seed has not sprouted. Onions like substantial soil, rather light than strong, amended from the previous year, or at least before winter. They can be successfully sown in beds previously occupied by cabbage, to which good fertilizers are always given. Onion beds must be carefully cleared of weeds, and repeated watering must be kept in mind until they begin to turn, at which point watering should be discontinued unless there is a severe drought. When the onion has made its apple and reached its full size, its tops begin to yellow and fall to the sides. If, however, as autumn approaches, the onion remains green and takes too long to finish, you can force the tops to lie down by pressing lightly on them with the back of a rake, or by any other equivalent means, which speeds up ripening a little: you then pull it out and leave it in the field for a few days, then bring it in during dry weather, after peeling it and cutting off the tail 0.15m above the fruit. It is usually placed in the attic, where it is stirred from time to time to keep it in good condition. When frost approaches, it should be piled up and covered with straw and blankets to protect it from the cold, of which it is the declared enemy. Very fine onions can also be obtained by another process, which consists in sowing the seed very thickly in May, and letting it grow without watering or thinning; onions pressed in this way ripen without becoming larger than hazelnuts. As soon as they are ripe, we pull them up and keep them until the end of February; then we prepare beds, draw lines and replant these small fruits in a straight line at a distance of 16 to 18 centimetres in all directions from each other. These plants will come into their own if you give them occasional ploughing and watering when they need it: they will be earlier than seedling onions. Onions for seed are planted in February and March. They are spaced about 30 cm apart; the seed is good for two years, rarely three; it is rounded, black on the outside and white on the inside. Onions are pectoral and aperitif. D sorrel. - Several varieties of this plant are grown, including Belleville sorrel, which has broader, less acidic leaves than common sorrel; it is generally grown around Paris. It is generally grown around Paris, and is sown as a broadcast or bedding plant, or as a border plant in spring, or even better in autumn; it does well in all types of soil, although it prefers light, deep soil that is neither too dry nor too wet. It is customary to cut it flush with the ground, but market gardeners rightly prefer to pick it leaf by leaf, and always take the outer ones. Summer heat increases its acidity, so sow a bed or border in the north for that season. It can also be propagated by sprouting: this is the almost unique way of propagating and preserving the species that delicate tastes prefer, i.e. virgin sorrel, whose leaves are longer and less acidic than common sorrel. Sorrel seeds germinate for three years. Sorrel is a refreshing aperitif, particularly suited to bilious temperaments. Parsnip. - Its root is large, long, white, charming, sinewy and strong-smelling; its taste is not unpleasant in soup; it can be grown like carrots. Under the name of round parsnip or Metz parsnip, there is a spinning top-shaped variety, earlier and better suited to soils with little depth; its seed is only good for one year. Parsley. - Its seeds, which usually take a month to set, should be sown from February to August, in good, loose soil, and in autumn at the foot of a wall facing south, so as to have some early in the spring. This plant does not go to seed until the second year, and the seeds keep for two years. To grow parsley through the winter, cover it with good straw mats in times of snow and frost. Parsley is a depurative. Chili pepper. - Sow in beds in February and March, or in compost in April. Replant at the end of April or beginning of May, in a bed at midday, or in pots which are exposed in the same way or buried in a bed. Its taste and properties are similar to those of pepper; it is used in cooking, particularly for pickling gherkins. Its seeds can be kept for two years, but it's better to use new ones. Burnet. - Weans in March on beds or in flowerbeds, in sun or shade, as long as you don't let it run out of water. It can even be grown on paths, without the need for cultivation. It can also be propagated by splitting the stalks. Its seed is good for three years. Pimprenelle is used as a salad dressing; it is refreshing and an aperitif. Poirean. - Leeks require substantial soil, preferably amended the previous autumn; fresh horned cattle manure seems to be harmful to them, but they are not afraid of horse or sheep manure, especially if it is consumed; grape marc is also a good amendment for this plant, as is leached ash. - Leeks are sown in February, March and July. When it has grown to the size of a feather-pipe, we take advantage of rainy, overcast weather to carefully remove it from the ground, and immediately replant it in a bed of well loosened soil, about Om 16 apart and 10 or 12 centimetres deep, after cutting off the tips of the leaves and roots. During the summer, weed and water often, especially in dry weather. Many gardeners cut the leaves off their leeks 3, 4 or even 5 times during the summer, to make the stems grow; this practice, contrary to theory, seems justified by experience. Leeks can remain in the ground until the frosts. Around this time, they are pulled up, gathered into bunches and placed in small trenches; they are covered with litter and kept that way until May, when the best seed-bearing ones are replanted. The seed lasts for two years. Leeks are healthy and refreshing. Peas. - The many varieties of this excellent vegetable can be divided into two main sections: shelled peas, which are eaten only in the kernel, and peas without parchment or mange-tout, which are eaten in both the pod and the kernel. Both contain dwarf and paddle varieties. Peas are an annual plant that thrives in all types of soil, but they don't grow in the same place twice: they need at least three years between plantings. Peas are sown in clumps or rays, with Om 34 between each clump of five or six plants, or Om 25 between each ray if sown in rays. Care of this crop consists of hoeing, weeding and raking large species, watering when the weather is too dry and pinching early species between the third and fourth flower to make them more precocious. To obtain early plants, sow in light, sandy soil, amended with compost, at noon, in November and December. Early varieties such as Michaux peas are chosen for this purpose. Ordinary varieties can be sown as late as July. Those sown from December to March should be covered with straw during the frosts, but should be given plenty of air. D All that has just been said concerns peas to be eaten green; for dry harvesting, the usual sowing season is March and April, and even, for early species, until the beginning of June. Early pea seeds are vulnerable to attack by an insect known as the pea beetle. Late peas are much less susceptible, probably because the insect has finished laying its eggs. Peas destined for seed and mashed potato could perhaps be protected from the insect by not sowing them until April. Peas germinate for three or four years, and longer if stored in the pod. G Peas are appetizing and laxative, but not easily digested. 1★1 Chickpeas are mainly used as a puree. Potato or parmentière. - The potato is one of mankind's most useful plants, providing abundant, wholesome nourishment and yielding a starch or flour of excellent quality and in three times the proportion that would be produced by an equal quantity of land sown with wheat. ▽ INE D SI Its main varieties are: grosse blanche, spotted with red, the most vigorous of all; grosse rouge, grosse jaune, blanche longue, jaunâtre ronde flatatie ou anglaise hâtive, rouge oblongue ou vitelotte, rouge longe ou Hollande rouge, longue rouge ou corne-de-cerf, jaune de Hollande, petite, rouge longue marbrée, rouge longue ou truffe d'août, violette, petite blanche sucrée ou chinoise. Potato cultivation is based on a single principle: whatever the nature of the soil, the species or variety of potato, the soil must be made as loose as possible before planting and throughout the period of growth. The question of whether to give preference for planting to large or small tubers, to quarters or to detached eyes with or without a portion of pulp, has often been discussed. Comparative experiments seem to have shown that whole tubers, at least of medium size, give the most considerable yield, while small tubers or pieces reproduce their seed more often. So, you should prefer one or the other, depending on whether you need to be more gentle on the seed or its soil. As for the eyes or sprouts detached from the tuber, this is a very good supplementary method to use in years when potatoes are in short supply or excessively expensive, but in ordinary cases, it is far from being as good as whole or cut tubers. Finally, we have recently obtained good results from cuttings of developed and sufficiently consistent stems, planted in the course of June, to refill the lack of a room. Sowing seeds is another important means of reproduction, particularly for the renewal and improvement of breeds. Potatoes can be planted from February to May. They are planted in Om holes, 17 in each direction, staggered and 50 to 60 centimetres apart. These holes are dug with a hoe, taking care to reject the earth extracted from the edges, as some of this earth must first be used to cover the small potato planted in it with a thickness of two to three fingers. The surplus, removed from the hole, is intended to butter the plant when it reaches a height of 40 to 50 centimetres. The potato's profit lies solely in its tubers, so it's a good idea to increase their number or volume. Piling soil around the stem encourages the sprout at its base to emit a higher row of new roots, which will have grown by harvest time. The more these plants are raised, the greater their yield: this is why ridging is favourable to multiplication; it can be repeated in June or July, when the weather is favourable. In any case, we must not lose sight of the fact that the more and the better we work the potatoes, the greater their yield; so if we refrain from ridging, we must replace it with good hoeing. There is no agreement on the best method of fertilization; the method of combining the fertilizer at the bottom of the furrows or holes and placing the potato immediately on top, however, seems preyalor. In strong, clayey soils, where potatoes are of poor quality, they are improved by using new straw or other dry plant stalks as fertilizer. Potatoes are usually harvested in September, and once the soil has been removed from the tubers, they are placed in the cellar or, better still, in silos, but in any case protected from the cold. To preserve potatoes throughout the year, simply protect them from frost during the winter and, when vegetation starts to develop, place them in a dry place and cover them with dry sand, or even better, with ashes. As soon as you notice that sprouts are developing on the fruit, you visit the potatoes and break off all the shoots. Potatoes are particularly suited to field cultivation, but it's a good idea to have some idea of how to manage this plant, of which only the early varieties are usually planted in vegetable gardens. POTATO DISEASES. - The alteration of potatoes, which, for lack of knowledge of its nature, has simply been referred to as the disease, has persisted until now in several parts of France, so we think it useful to mention it here. Of all the means proposed to combat the effects of the disease, none has proved to be nearly absolutely effective; but from the mass of known experiments and observations, we can deduce a few rules, or at least a few indications, the application of which would increase the chance of obtaining healthy harvests. Excessive soil fertility, freshness and, even more so, humidity are generally considered to be conditions unfavorable to healthy harvests. For this reason, dry or at least healthy soils with little or no smoke should be chosen for planting. Harvesting as soon as the stalks have softened is also an essential precaution. The choice of varieties which, under equal conditions, are usually less affected than others, is also one of the main points to consider. These varieties, even if less productive than others, should obviously be multiplied in preference. Planting before winter (October or November), deep enough to protect the tubers from frost, is another method that has given and still gives great hope. To these various means should be added that of sowing, less direct and less rapid in its effects, but which, in the event of the disease continuing, would be one of the most effective in removing the potato from its influence. It has also been thought that a very long interval between plantings of potatoes in the same soil would bring about the complete cessation of the disease. This method, which is beginning to be tried out, promises happy results, as we have seen potatoes harvested from land that had not produced potatoes for twenty years, yielding very healthy, well-preserved fruit. Experiments will no doubt continue, and it is to be hoped that they will rid us of an evil that threatens to deprive us of one of the most precious vegetables in horticultural and agricultural crops. Several plants have been proposed to replace the potato, such as: Olluco, Glycine-Apios, Picotiane; but none of these vegetables has so far given results with which we can be satisfied. Purslane. - Purslane is very sensitive to cold; it can be sown in layers or under cloches in March; but in the open ground, it can only be sown in May, in loose, well-smoked soil. The seed is very fine and spreads lightly and freely; it needs to be very lightly covered and basked assiduously until emergence. When purslane needs it, you need to give it water and clean it of all weeds, to see it do well. It is usually eaten raw in salads, but is also very good cooked and seasoned with juice like lettuce. The variety known as golden purslane is highly prized, but often degenerates and reverts to its original green color. Another variety with large leaves has recently been introduced and is quite remarkable. Purslane seed keeps well for five or six years. Radish. - Radishes are grown for their roots, and several varieties are known: early white, ordinary white, half-long white, half-long scarlet, half-long pink, large summer, early pink, summer yellow, salmon, early violet, ordinary violet, horseradish or black winter radish. Most of these radishes, especially the small round ones, can be sown almost all year round: 1° on a bed in winter or in the first spring; 2° in the open ground in other seasons. Sow lightly and broadcast. To obtain well-rounded radishes in light soils, the soil must be heavily trampled before sowing. In hot weather, it needs plenty of water, a little shade and little sowing at a time. Horseradish is sown towards the end of May; sowing it earlier would make it prone to going to seed; thin it out when it is too thick, and leave only Om, 18 from each other, to give it good growth. Another radish variety brought to us from China is the early yellow. It is a truly garden root and one of the most beautiful autumn radishes. Rave - Used for the same purposes and cultivated in the same way as radishes, its varieties are: white, small early, pink or salmon, long red, twisted Le Mans. The latter requires soft, deep soil and needs to be sown lighter than the others. It is essential to cover turnips during frosts. Radish and turnip seeds are harvested in summer, and are good for three or four years. Rapunzel. - Sown towards the end of August on well-smoked and ploughed beds, it requires frequent watering to raise it from the ground; it is then weeded, isolating it from all weeds, and left until after winter, when it can be enjoyed from the end of February until the end of April, when its stem begins to rise. We leave in the ground the plants we want to keep for seed. - It's one of the best winter salads. salsins. - This plant needs deep, substantial, perfectly loosened soil that has been smoked for at least six months. It is broadcast from March to April and watered often, especially to help the seed set; weed, hoe and pull up the roots for consumption before the stems come up. Scorsonera. - Differs from salsify only in its black root; its cultivation and properties are the same. The seed of both plants can be kept for one or two years at most. Savory. - Cultivation of this plant is very simple; it grows easily in any kind of soil, so easily that it reproduces itself every year. It can be used until it sets seed, which keeps well for four or five years. It is particularly useful for seasoning peas and broad beans, where it enhances the taste. It is a tonic and aperitif. Tetragon. - A New Zealand plant recognized as a good antiscorbutic vegetable. It is regarded as a summer spinach, whose qualities it shares. The advantage of tetragonia is that the hotter the weather, the more it produces. It can be successfully sown in place at the end of April, in 6. soft earth and loam, spaced Om,60 apart in all directions, three or four seeds per clump to leave only the best stem. Spring sowing is sometimes capricious; autumn sowing is almost always more successful. Tomato. - An annual plant native to Mexico. Sow early on a bed or in a frame, then prick out in the garden, at midday, when frost is no longer a threat, and at a distance of 70 or 80 centimetres. When the plants have grown to around Om, 40, they are tied to a stile or trellis; they are stopped at Om, 80 or 1 meter, by pinching the top of the stems; the secondary shoots above the flowers are also pinched. When a large number of fruits have reached half-growth, we start to thin out the leaves and remove the small new shoots. At the end of the season, the leaves are completely removed, so that the fruit is fully exposed to the sun. Plenty of water in summer. Tomatoes come in several varieties: the large red, which is furrowed, is the most widely grown for cooking; the early red; the large yellow, a very beautiful sub-variety of the red; the small red, the small yellow, the pear-shaped tomato and the cherry tomato. Tomato seeds collected from the most beautiful and ripest fruits germinate for three or four years; when winter is not too harsh, tomatoes sow themselves. Tomatoes are successfully grafted onto potatoes using the herbaceous or Tschudy graft. This produces a potato crop in the ground and a tomato crop in the air. The fruit of the tomato is used to make a much-appreciated sweet and sour sauce. It's easy to digest. Jerusalem artichoke. - Multiplies by tuber, which is planted in February and March, like the potato. It does not fear frost, so it keeps perfectly well in the ground; but it is rarely planted, because once it has been grown in a garden, it is very difficult to destroy. CHAPTER VI MEDICINAL PLANTS France's average climate makes it possible to grow a fairly large number of medicinal plants, whose presence in a schoolteacher's garden is of undeniable benefit, both to the teacher and to those he or she lives among. A teacher needs to be familiar with these plants and their proven properties. We advise him to always have around his house and in his garden, i.e. at hand, all the most commonly used plants, which we will list below, indicating in each item the parts of these plants that are used medicinally. EMOLLIENT PLANTS Marshmallow. - Multiplies only by the bursting of clumps; grows everywhere. Its flowers, leaves and roots are used. Round-leaved Mallow and Wild Mallow. - Multiplies like marshmallow; leaves and flowers are used. Flax. - Only the seeds are used as an emollient. PECTORALS EMOLLIENTS Marshmallow, its flowers; Parma violet, its leaves and flowers. White broth. - Stems from Om, 70 to 1 m; blooms in July and August, in long spikes. Light, warm soil; southern exposure; multiplies from seed; used as flowers and leaves. Parietaria. - Straight stems, 35 to 65 centimeters long; full, oval, pointed leaves; small, greenish flowers. Grows in dry soil and rubble; multiplies by seed and splinters. We use the whole plant. Borage. - Can be found anywhere, and is used as fresh or dried leaves or flowers. REFRESHERS Licorice. - Its root is not widely available. Barberry. - Used as berries. We will say nothing about narcotics, which cannot be grown safely in a teacher's garden. AROMATIC EXCITANTS sage. - Leaves and flowers are used. Rosemary. - Perennial plant whose twigs, leaves and flowers are used. Lavender. - Flowering spikes and leaves. Lemon balm. - Harvested in June and September; grows in light, south-facing soil; can be propagated by sowing or sprouting; can be used as flowering spikes and leaves.
