However, we recommend that teachers explaining horticulture to their pupils describe and indicate to them all the plants of our climates whose use may present dangers. 106 CHAPTER VII DESTROYING ANIMALS HAZARDOUS TO PLANTS The best-kept gardens are often ravaged by a host of harmful animals, whose destruction requires a great deal of care and patience. The number of parasitic insects is very considerable, so we shouldn't be surprised to find them on plants. Some serve as their cradle, others as food. The gardener must therefore be particularly concerned with the care that can rid him or her of these troublesome hosts. In this chapter, we'll focus on those animals that cause the greatest damage in vegetable gardens. As with plants, we'll follow their alphabetical order. Flea beetle. - This insect, still known as the earth flea because of its ability to jump, is oval in shape, metallic blue in color and remarkable for the swelling of its two hind thighs. It is very common in certain years; it can be found on young plants, especially those belonging to the Cruciferae family, such as cabbage, rape, turnips, etc. It attacks these plants at the time when they are most susceptible to attack. It attacks these plants as they germinate, and later pierces their leaves right through. Its larva, which precedes it by almost a month, is just as harmful. The only known means of repelling this insect are decoctions of pungent plants, such as tobacco, walnut leaf and elderberry, or water laden with potash or soot. But all these methods are highly effective. Perhaps it would be better, when you have a limited amount of land, to make the sacrifice of a first sowing. When the larvae have developed, cover the surface with a layer of straw and set fire to it: in this way, the insects can be reached before they have undergone metamorphosis. Or you could sow the seeds of cruciferous plants only in heavily smoked soil, where they can develop several young leaves in a few days, in addition to their seminal leaves. The flea beetle's mandibles or jaws are too weak to attack the leaves once they have developed to a certain extent, and the insect dies of starvation. Moth. - The courtilière is one of the most feared insects by horticulturists: it is remarkable above all for its legs and the torsos of its two front feet, which are enlarged, flattened and lined with teeth that give it the shape of a hand; the other legs are nothing special; they end in two hooks. Its front legs are responsible for all the damage for which it is blamed, since it feeds on worms and insects, and by searching for them in the earth, it saws and tears up any roots in its path. In gardens, it's easy to recognize when a cricket has passed through. Plants that were beautifully green the day before fade, pale and die, and when you pull them out you find their roots truncated. It's not easy to get rid of this annoying enemy. The usual advice is to pour boiling water into the hole and oil over it. The cricket, to avoid being scalded and drowned, runs away, but on contact with the oil its stomata become blocked, and it dies of asphyxiation. Crickets can also be destroyed by placing small pots half-full of water in the ground, at Om, 04 below the level of the boards. Moths, which love humidity, fall into the water and drown. Others destroy them by spreading water dissolved in fish-mill manure on the garden beds they frequent. Criocere. - This insect attacks asparagus exclusively, laying its eggs on the surface. The only way to destroy it is to search carefully for its eggs and crush them. Ant. - The little black ant, which often invades gardens, is a most harmful insect, seeking out anything sweet. It is easily destroyed by placing honey, syrup or crushed ripe fruit mixed with corrosive sublimate in the path it usually follows. A less dangerous method, most commonly used by gardeners and very simple, is to put a little sugar water in small bottles. The ants, attracted by the sweet liquid, enter the bottles and drown. Chafer. - The cockchafer harms in all its forms: as a larva, known as a white worm, it respects no root; it is the terror of market gardeners and nurserymen alike. Larvae have been known to destroy entire fields. We are defenseless against them; their greatest enemy is the cold. Once the larva has become a beetle, it devours tree leaves, but this is also the time when it can be reached most safely by relentless hunting. Nothing is easier than catching chafer beetles: you just have to shake the trees to which the hametons have clung before going to sleep to determine their fall; you then pick them up and crush them. Be careful not to bury them alive in the ground, as not a single female perishes; they escape by digging galleries in all directions, and lay their eggs all over the garden. Earwig. - The earwig wanders and feeds at night, and hides during the day. Although it attacks vegetables, it is more likely to attack fruit, as it prefers sweet substances. To get rid of them, place hollow stems, pigs' dewclaws or broken pottery in the places they frequent: the earwigs take refuge in them as day approaches; collect and burn them. Cabbage whitefly. - The cabbage maggot is a butterfly whose larvae, along with those of the rose and turnip maggot, are the most common in our gardens. The former and the latter eat away almost entirely at the leaves of cabbages and turnips, perforating them right through and leaving only the ribs; the latter, on the other hand, attacks the center of the leaves. Although birds, when they have young, as well as toads, consume them extensively, their numbers are so considerable that it is impossible to destroy them entirely. If we observe the habits of these insects, we see that they almost all shy away from light and only come out at night to feed. If you want to avoid them, you have to hunt them by candlelight. You can crush them on the spot, or enclose them in pots to feed them to poultry, which is very fond of them. Aphids. - These insects are easily distinguished by the two horns or chelons, usually pointing upwards, which they have at the end of their abdomen. Above all, they are remarkable for their prodigious fecundity. Aphids damage the plants on which they settle in three different ways: 1° by their stings; 2° by the deformations they cause to leaves and twigs; and 3° by their exudation, which covers the surface of the leaves, causing dust and corpuscles floating in the air to stick to them, giving rise to a large number of microscopic fungi and imparting a black color to the leaves that eventually dries them out under the sun's rays. Plants can be freed from this by fumigating with tobacco. Teridion or earth spider. - The teridion attacks young seedlings, particularly carrots, biting the stem to pump out their juices. This type of spider is sometimes so numerous that it destroys entire seedlings, no matter how large. You can get rid of them by spreading an infusion of tobacco on the infected boards. The same result can be achieved with an infusion of soot, which is less costly. 1 In the mollusc class, there are still some animals that are very harmful to vegetable gardens: snails, slugs and earthworms. Snails and slugs are herbivores, and so they cause damage in vegetable gardens. Snail. - The chagrined snail is the one we encounter most often in our gardens, where it wreaks havoc. You can remove as many as you like by hand on a fine summer's day, either by looking for them under leaves, in the edges of flowerbeds, in holes in walls, or wherever you know they retreat during the day. Slugs. - The surest way to destroy these animals is to hunt them in the morning and evening during spring and autumn, when the weather is mild and especially when it rains. Quicklime, slaked in the air (powdered lime), limewater and several other caustic substances kill them, but their use by sprinkling is hardly practicable in vegetable gardens. Here's a simpler method: small piles of bran are placed at intervals; the slugs gather there, and are easily killed by sprinkling powdered lime on them. Earthworms. - Worms don't directly harm the vegetable garden, but the way they disturb the soil, even though they don't eat any plant matter, disturbs seedlings and prevents young plants from emerging. So they're an enemy you need to get rid of. This can be done by spraying with hot cattle urine, or by making infusions of walnut leaves or walnut stain, which are then sprinkled over the beds. These liquids don't actually kill them, but the odor they give off is so unpleasant that they leave the watered area when they emerge from the ground; they are then collected and fed to poultry. OBSERVATION. - Don't neglect to propagate the golden beetle, commonly known as the gardener's beetle, in your garden. This beetle wages constant war on ants and other insects, without ever attacking plants. Unfortunately, these birds are hunted or killed as a hobby, or to punish them for the slight damage they seem to commit. We have no idea of the services they render us, and we do not want to understand that the more of these birds there are in a region, the fewer insects there are. CHAPTER IX FRUIT GARDEN A schoolteacher's fruit garden consists of little more than the trees he can plant around his vegetable patches and those with which he lines the few walls at his disposal. Very few teachers have enough land to create an orchard separate from their vegetable garden. So we'll proceed on this assumption, which is the more or less general situation in our schools. In a previous chapter, we said that a schoolteacher could not, with his own resources, maintain a kitchen garden of more than 7 ares. In our reasoning, we'll take the average, 5 ares, which is a good size. Masters with land of 8 or 10 ares would have to devote part of their enclosure to creating an orchard, the size of which would depend on the size of their kitchen garden. In this case, they would plant tall trees, taking care to leave enough space between them to be able to use the orchard soil to plant field vegetables, or to sow seeds for their household needs. What is important, therefore, for the civil servants with whom we are concerned, is to deal above all with the question of the vegetable and fruit garden. When you have a large enough enclosure, you should always arrange your garden in such a way as to make squares of at least 80 centiares and no more than one acre in extent, which you arrange according to the following method for planting fruit trees. A pyramid is planted at each corner of the squares, and three spindles are placed between each pyramid at equal distances from each other. The outer beds are then planted with an indeterminate number of apple trees arranged in continuous rows. If the squares are longer than they are wide, place as many spindles or columns on each side as will fit, taking care to leave a space of 2 meters between each one. Many people prefer pyramids to espaliers, claiming that the former require less time and care than the latter. To these reasons, which seem to us to be inconclusive, we would add another which is certainly of much greater value when dealing with a schoolteacher's fruit garden, and which justifies the recommendation we make to equip gardens mainly with pyramids and spindles: this is because espaliers require considerable use of wood to support their branches and twigs, and the incessant renewal of these woods and palisades becomes expensive enough in the long run that we try to free ourselves from the expense it entails. Pyramid and spindle-shaped trees don't have the same disadvantages. However, while we recommend these last two models of fruit tree, we would still recommend that teachers erect espaliers along walls, so as to keep themselves abreast of the correct methods for pruning and directing fruit trees, whatever their shape. The following diagram applies to a 5-acre vegetable garden. 15 3 = V PV PV 4 - - NORTH. St D. PV PV 4 RV . - PV P represents pyramids. - F represents spindles. - E represents espaliers. - C represents cords. - PV represents open-air trees. A garden laid out in this way will contain eight north-facing trees, 16 pyramids, 48 spindles or columns, an indefinite number of espaliers and cords of apple trees in the three outer beds. The soil of the beds in which fruit trees are to be planted must be deeply dug up, drained if it is marshy; but if it is only damp, it should be cleaned up with a layer of 0n, 20 of house rubble, platras, which should be placed at the bottom of the dug-outs: in addition, it should be suitably amended. The most exposed walls, if any, will be lined with espaliers. These espaliers should only be made up of trees with good stems, chosen from among those whose fruit needs a lot of heat to acquire all its beauty, size and fragrance, such as peach trees, apricot trees, greengage plum trees, some cherry trees and winter pear trees. But the tree most in need of wall espaliers in our climate is the peach. If the walls are high enough, a cordon of vines can run above the espaliers. When the garden is of a suitable size, it's always a good idea to set aside part of it for a small nursery. This way, you'll never be mistaken about the kind of fruit you want to plant. It's easy to see that, with resources as limited as those of schoolteachers, only the best and most productive species should be planted. Their main concern when planting is to make a good choice between summer, autumn and winter fruits. In a special table at the end of this chapter, we will therefore indicate the species of fruit trees that are most suitable for cultivation in the fruit gardens of schoolhouses and the majority of gardens in rural communities. 7. We will divide this chapter into three parts: Multiplication, Planting and Pruning. We would point out that, in such a concise treatise as the one we are undertaking, we can only give general notions of these three arboricultural operations. However, we shall endeavor to make these notions as complete as possible, given the framework we have set ourselves, so that any teacher who wishes to follow our advice can find in our indications sufficient knowledge, not only to properly manage the trees he will be planting, but also to inculcate the principles of arboriculture in his pupils, and to help with his advice those of his neighbors who, following his example, will abandon the routine which is still perpetuated in the cultivation of country gardens, to follow the path of progress which has so notably changed the art of horticulture over the last twenty years. As for those who would like to make an in-depth study of arboriculture, we refer them to the comprehensive treatises by Messrs Hardy and Dubreuil, or to a short course recently published by an esteemed priest from Franche-Comté, Abbé Raoul. In our opinion, this treatise has the triple merit of being very simple, of resolving all arboricultural questions with great clarity, and of not costing much. We also recommend Le Bon Jardinier, which is an excellent aid for all those involved in growing vegetables, fruit and flowers. 1. multiplication. All plants multiply naturally by their seeds; but many of them reproduce naturally in our crops only by their roots, others by their stems, branches and cuttings. Propagation by seed sometimes gives rise to new breeds or varieties; propagation by roots, stems, branches and cuttings perpetuates them unaltered. Arboricultural propagation is the nurseryman's industry. But as we want teachers to raise the plants they want to populate their gardens with themselves, so as not to be misled in their choice of species, we're going to give a few notions on the art of multiplying fruit trees. PROPAGATION BY SEED. - The soil of a nursery must be well prepared by careful breaking: it is given a suitable fertilizer appropriate to its nature, and left for at least a year to any crop other than that of fruit trees, so that the delicate roots of young trees born from seed do not come into contact with fresh manure, which is very harmful to them. As a general rule, soil that is too rich and abundant is no more suitable for a nursery than soil that is poor and deprived of fertilizer. The important point is that, when they leave the nursery, plants take well wherever they are placed. Industrial nurserymen always choose a generous and very loose soil for their seedlings, because in such a soil they gain a lot for the growth. In doing so, they are only acting in their own interest, but they are doing fruit gardens a disservice, because the trees suffer enormously, and often even fail to take root when they are removed from rich soil and planted in poor-quality soil. This is why I advise schoolteachers to set up a small nursery in their own garden. Seedlings can be broadcast or combed. The pits are planted one by one at a suitable distance. Sowing is done in spring, but more often in autumn. Seedlings should be sown at Om,03 and cores at Om,06 depth. During heavy frosts, the seedlings are covered with straw or leaves, and decored in spring. In the same way, but in diflerent beds, pear, apple and quince seedlings are sown. All these seedlings produce seedlings on which we graft the species we want to cultivate mainly at the end of the autumn of their first year. All young trees, born from seed, must be uprooted and peeled, so that they can be darkened for germination. In this operation, they are subjected to a severe tringe Propagation by maromies is only used for vines and currants, which are easy to root. easily muliplie by cuttings for semi-sucking pear trees, vines, redcurrants and raspberries.
