MMITIUCAMIOY BY CRITTLE - The purpose of the gnesle operation is to force an eye or a Nion from one tree to grow on another tree, so that all deur by forming an orgamic union, become a compound individual. Cest-à- dire que de deux plantes on en fait une seule dont les branches, les fleurs et les fruits sont d'une autre espère que celles des racines et de la tige On gresle les arbres de sir mamières diflenentes - la geffc en fonie, la grefle en oparoxne, la gresse en ecman. "Om appelle muliller un sujel, netmundaer s avec la sarpe tomtes la racimes qui Seralont colatćes ce mocurtries et supprumer des hronches tomies celles qui sermient cassées ou endommmagćes. la greffe en approche, la greffe anglaise et la greffe herbacée. 1° Cleft grafting. - After choosing a healthy, vigorous subject, we take a branch from the previous year from the tree we wish to propagate, whose wood will be well seasoned, i.e. perfectly ripe. It must be at most as big as the subject or smaller. The head of the tree is cut to the required height, and a longitudinal slit is made in its upper part. The graft is bevelled on both sides, shortened so as to leave only 2 or 3 eyes, then inserted into the slit, which is held open with the tip of the pruning knife. The prerequisite for success is that the inner parts of the bark of the subject and of the graft coincide perfectly. Note that the part of the branch whose bark has been well preserved should always be turned outwards, and as far as possible, an eye should be placed above the part that has been squeezed into the slit. If the subject is large enough, several scions can be placed above it by splitting it on several sides. Ligature the grafts to hold them firmly if the individuals are weak: then protect the wounds from contact with the air with grafting wax, made up in the following way: Burgundy pitch... ... ... ... . 500 grams. Black pitch... ... ... ... ... . 125 Yellow wax ... ... ... ... ... . 100 Resin ... ... ... ... . 100 Sheep's tallow . 60 - - - - - This mixture is melted over a very low heat, and each time you want to use it, you heat it up enough to make it liquid so that you can apply it with a brush. It is essential not to use this composition too hot, as this would dry out the bark and prevent it from regrowing. 2° Crown grafting. - This type of graft is used on trees too large to be split safely. After smoothing out the horizontal cut of the tree, a small hardwood wedge is driven between the sapwood and the bark, to a depth of Om.05. The graft is trimmed to a length of 0.04 m, so that little or no wood remains at the lower end of the bevel: remove the wedge, replace it with the graft, whose denuded bevel rests against the sapwood, and press it in so as to hide the entire bevel. The same operation is performed for each of the scions, which are carefully inserted between the bark and the wood, about 0m 008 or Om 009 apart, so as to form a crown of grafts around the circumference of the stump. If the pressure of the wedge causes the bark to split, it is pulled together with a ligature when the graft is placed, then the wounds are covered with grafting wax. 3° Crested grafts. - This is very expedient, especially for small plants. It is performed in two seasons, in spring with a growing eye, and in July and August with a dormant eye. Dormant eye grafting. - Young trees are grafted in the FRUIT GARDEN. Bud grafts. 123 10 centimetres from the ground and tall stems at indeterminate heights. Choose a plain spot on the stem, make a transverse incision on the subject and a perpendicular one in the shape of a T. Using the spatula of the grafting machine, lift the lips of the bark to the right and left, then slide the prepared escutcheon underneath it from top to bottom, cutting off the part that extends beyond the transverse incision on the subject: We fold them over the escutcheon, pressing them firmly with our thumbs, and tie them with wool, taking care to leave the eye uncovered and to visit it after about three weeks to loosen the tie if necessary. In the following spring, before the serva rises, we cut off the upper part of the plant at a small distance from the escutcheon, leaving one or two call eyes above it. The buds resulting from these eyes are pinched off, when they are 12 to 15 centimetres long, in favour of the graft. Once the graft has reached a length of 50 to 40 centimetres, they are completely removed. Growing eye graft. - This is done in the same way as the previous one; only 8 to 10 days after grafting, and when the graft is taken up again, we remove the portion of the subject that exceeds the graft, leaving however a calling eye above it. The bud is pinched off when it is 12 to 15 centimetres long, and treated as we have just described for the dormant eye. Grafting or budding of fruit crops. - This graft is performed in August, when the buds have formed on the trees. A sting, stalk or twig with its impasto is removed from a tree that is abundantly supplied with these products, and placed on another tree that has little or none, absolutely like a crest, after which it is tied. This process is highly advantageous for setting fruit trees and for trimming the bare parts of structural branches. A very suitable type of ligature for bud grafting would be a wire braid prepared in the following way: seven parts of wax and one part of fat turpentine are melted together; when the substances are mixed, the braid of indeterminate length is plunged into it, and removed by pressing it with a piece of wood against the rim of the pan containing the mixture, so that it is impregnated with the substance to just the right point. When it has been used to bind the escutcheons, it would be prudent to hold it in place with a thread or a drop of grafting wax. 4° Grafting on approach. - This technique works well on all kinds of trees, provided they are close enough to touch each other in their most perennial parts. It requires the following precautions: 1° cut off part of the tree's head to encourage the sap to flow into the graft; 2° make clean wounds in the parts to be grafted, of a length and depth proportionate to the volume of the tree. To increase the chances of success, a notch is sometimes made on the subject and another in the opposite direction on the graft, so that the splinter of one enters the notch of the other; 2° join these wounds so that the barks coincide at the edges of their internal surfaces, while taking into account their external parts; 3° securely fasten these parts with ligatures or ropes made of wicker, bark or wool, depending on the size of the grafts, and if necessary with stakes; 4° protect the wounds from contact with light, air and water with the grafting wax; 5° monitor the development of the grafts to prevent nodosities, and prevent the branches from being cut by the ligatures, which are loosened if necessary: these conditions are essential for all scion grafts; 6° wean the grafts only when the parts have completely fused. Grafting is done when the sap is moving. This operation can be used to cross branches in diamond shapes, to form hedges or other fences, to change the nature of one tree into that of another, or to give two trunks instead of one to the same individual. Nature frequently performs approach grafting on its own in forests and hedges: in fact, when two branches touch and are agitated by the wind, they soon wear away at the point of contact, the bark thins, the cortical parenchyma is exposed, and then all that's needed is a few days' rest to see adhesion and mutual welding take place between the parts at the point of contact. 5° English graft. - This involves bevelling the end of the subject and the graft, so as to bring the two wounds exactly together. The operation, which can be complicated by notches in opposite directions, ends as in the approach graft. 6° Herbaceous graft. - This is a split graft performed using the still herbaceous parts of plants. It is used with great success to propagate resinous trees. The essential condition is that the part of the plant to be grafted must be herbaceous, as must the graft itself. There are several other types of graft, such as the Pontoise graft, the Faucheux graft, the connection graft, etc., all of which fall within the six types of graft we have just explained, with a few slight variations. It is therefore unnecessary to go into further detail on this subject. Preparing grafts. - Take grafts only from one-year-old wood, from healthy, fertile trees; cut the branches a month or six weeks in advance; during this interval, plug them into the ground at the foot of a wall, sinking them up to a third of the way into the northern exposure. This state of deprivation starves them and makes grafting easier. If they have been traveling and arrive tired and with wrinkled bark, soak them in water for a day or two. For scion grafting, the branch can be used immediately after cutting. 2. Planting. The success of fruit trees depends largely on the care taken when planting them, and before planting the soil must be prepared. The aim of this operation is to encourage the trees to grow as quickly and vigorously as possible. As our treatise is intended for teachers who only have a garden in which they sow vegetables at the same time as planting fruit trees, we must limit ourselves to indicating the soil preparation method best suited to the isolated plantings they are called upon to make. In an exclusively fruit-growing garden, the soil should be broken up to a depth of one meter, and drained if it is excessively moist. But in a market garden, as is usually the case in a schoolteacher's garden, it will suffice to break up and drain the beds in which the plants are to be planted, as described below. RUNNING. - Beds less than 0.80 m wide should be trenched to a depth of 1 m across their entire width. Start the trench at one end of the bed, taking care to transport the soil from the first excavation to the other end of the bed. You stand in the pit and put the soil from the trenches behind you, after dividing it up and removing any stones and roots. It's especially important to place the soil from the surface of the ground you're attacking at the bottom of the pit, and if possible, to place well-divided turf at half depth: this is an infallible way of providing your trees with rich vegetation for a long time to come. Continue in this way to the end of the flowerbed, taking care to raise it from Om, 08 to Om, 10 above the neighbouring land, with the broken earth settling down by about Om, 08. The void that remains at the end of the flowerbed is filled in with earth collected from the surface of its squares. If the subsoil of the land is watery, it can be cleaned up by breaking it up by 1m,10; this decimeter is filled in with stones or platras, so that the roots of the tree to be planted do not reach the bad subsoil. You can also avoid the disadvantages of humidity by raising your beds in mounds of Om, 20 above the garden floor. But the best thing to do when planting in damp soil is to ensure good drainage when the position of the soil allows it, and it doesn't take long to feel the happy effects. As the beds intended to receive trees in the open air (pyramids, goblets, counter-paliers) are usually close to the garden paths, it is advisable to evenly rip out the entire surface, beds and paths; the expense will not be much greater, and the tree roots will benefit from the soil in the paths. It's a good idea to do the ripping especially during the summer months, so that the soil, less humid, divides easily and is thus more suitable for vegetation. We know that soil disturbed under the influence of humidity, especially if it is a little clayey, is put in such poor condition that vegetation suffers for many years. SOIL FERTILIZATION. - As a complement to soil preparation for fruit tree planting, it is important to fertilize the soil properly. The trees will then grow more vigorously, and the desired result, the complete formation of their framework, will be achieved sooner. But for this fertilization to have the desired effect, it must be placed at a suitable depth. It is in the layer between the surface and Om, 40 deep that this fertilizer must be applied. This is done by spreading it over all the beds after breaking up the soil and immediately before planting, then burying it with a fairly deep plough. As for the type of fertilizer to be used, you'll need to make use of what you have on hand, such as actual manure, and pond or ditch silt extracted at least a year ago and stirred frequently. Slow-decomposing fertilizers, although just as energetic as the previous ones, are preferable. We include in this series: crushed bones, wool rags, wadding, manes, hairs, horn scraps, tendons, etc. Such is the care required to prepare the soil for planting fruit trees in a garden. CHOOSING THE RIGHT TREES. - Choose smooth-barked trees that have been grafted for only one year. These grafts should be healthy and vigorous, with well-conformed buds at each end where branches are needed to form the tree. These trees should have a good footing and already have good roots; care must be taken to ensure that these are healthy, free from bruising or tearing, and that the grafted branch is of good quality. Young roots should be left exposed to air as little as possible, and never to frost. When planting is delayed by a few days, the plants should be nursed in small ditches. If the roots have dried out after a long journey, soak them in water for twelve hours and plant them before they have had time to dry out. If the roots were frozen, they should be put in the cellar to thaw before being planted; just as the roots and heads of trees must be properly dressed, which is done by cutting away with the pruning knife any roots that may have been splintered or bruised during replanting, down to the healthy part; refreshing the end of the desiccated hair and roots, cutting them at a slightly elongated bevel underneath so that the wound rests directly on the earth. As for the branches, the dressing consists in removing only those that have been broken or damaged, leaving the healthy part attached to the tree. It should be noted that if too many roots are bruised, they should not be removed, as this would compromise the tree's recovery; instead, the wounds should be scraped off and smeared with grafting wax. TIME OF PLANTING. - Late autumn or vegetation is the most favorable time for planting. This is an advance, because trees planted at this time quickly sprout new shoots, and therefore grow more vigorously than those planted after winter. Nevertheless, planting can be carried out throughout the winter, from the end of October to April, whenever frosts and heavy rains do not prevent it; but care must be taken not to throw frozen soil into the trenches, or around the roots of the young plants: such soil would be poisonous to the young trees. Spring planting is preferable only for cold, damp soils that may be submerged during winter. If, however, we are unable to plant in autumn, we can do so successfully in spring by opening trenches well in advance. GROUNDING. - One of the first precautions to be taken is to set the tree at the right depth, which varies according to the nature of the soil and of the subject on which the species is grafted. In light, hot soil, it will be necessary to bury the tree a little deeper than in damp, cold soil, where it will be advantageous to keep the roots as close to the surface as possible, in order to avoid rotting and stimulate vegetation. However, the graft should be left above ground, never buried: it is always advantageous to be able to reach the roots, and therefore not to cover them too much. This makes the tree more fertile and the fruit better. When planting, we must take into account the effect of compaction of freshly disturbed soil: this is estimated at Om.08 to Om.12 per 1 metre, depending on whether the soil is light or heavy. To determine whether the tree is placed at the right height, use a large ruler placed across the hole; lay the stem along it, holding the graft at Om,07 or Om,08 above. The tree is then removed and the hole filled as follows: first, soil is thrown in so that the tree is at the required height. If you have decomposed turf, we'll put it at the bottom, dividing it well with the spade, so as not to cause too much compaction. One man holds the tree in the position indicated, taking care to align it with its neighbors if necessary, while another introduces the earth, which will be substantial, between the roots. They must all pass through the hands of the planter, who will make them take their natural direction, without constraining or forcing them. If there is a pivot and it cannot be kept vertical, it is tilted horizontally to one side. Care should be taken not to shake the tree, as is so frequently done, with the aim, it is claimed, of pushing the soil down between the roots; this habit of shaking the tree by lifting it slightly has the serious disadvantage of disturbing the roots, piling them up when they should be spread apart, and often even breaking off some of them. This practice is vicious in that, by plumbing the soil, you run the risk of breaking the roots, or at least bruising them. You only need to press lightly with your foot to hold it against the wind; rainfall is enough to pack the soil. In very late plantings, it is a good idea to wet the roots so that the soil can attach immediately, and to pour a watering can of water gently around the foot to help it settle. When planting late, or when transplanting strong trees, it's also a good idea to coat the stems and branches with St. Fiacre ointment, to protect them from sunburn and drought, and to ensure better growth. For espalier planting, the same procedure applies. Just take care to keep the stem away from the wall Om, 12 to Om, 15 (to allow it to grow bigger later) and to place it obliquely towards it so that it can be applied more easily. The roots are distributed to the right and to the left to prevent them from meeting the foundations, and care is taken not to fix the small tree to the trellis until the soil has settled. It's preferable to plant in fine weather rather than in the rain; healthy soil is better than excessively wet soil, which becomes compacted and impairs the development of the young foliage. In spring, once the planting is complete, unless the soil is too damp, a light mulch should be applied to keep the soil cool. A few hoeings and waterings during the summer, if necessary, will complete the care required. The distance to be observed between the various trees is an important factor. We are almost always in the habit of planting too close, and only see the tree when it is young, without realizing the extent and growth it is likely to take on later, and which it needs to obtain abundant, regular fruiting. Pyramid pear trees grafted on franc or coignassier should be set back 3 m in all directions in good soil, and 2.50 m in poor soil. Pear pyramids............... 2m, 66 Pear espaliers. . . . . . ..... . . ... 6m These distances may vary according to locality and soil quality. Careful examination of the vegetation in the locality will give an accurate idea of the dimensions they are likely to reach; the species and varieties that thrive best there, and whose fruit acquire all the desirable qualities, should also be noted; and it is these observations and this study, made on site, that will guide the choice of subjects and increase or decrease the distances to be established between each tree foot. When planting pyramid-shaped trees, always take care to turn the graft to the south: here's why we recommend this arrangement. The strongest winds come from the south; if the graft is turned this way, it is more resistant, as the wind presses it against the tree: otherwise, the wind would push it away from the tree, and it could come unstuck. It is also advisable to stake stemmed or pyramidal trees to prevent the wind from shaking them. 3 3. Pruning. Pruning is a combination of operations designed to: 1° to give trees, and especially espaliers, the most favorable exposure, according to the country of origin; 2° to subject them to forms recognized as suitable for good sap distribution and perfect fruit ripening; 3° to maintain this shape throughout the life of the tree, and to preserve the balance between the supporting branches, in order to prevent some of them from capturing the sap to the detriment of others; 4° to produce fruit with all the desirable qualities, and to replace fruit production that becomes exhausted or perishes. PRUNING TOOLS. - Serpette. - The pruning knife is the tool par excellence for pruning; its use is very old-fashioned; it must be well tempered and kept very clean. Handling this tool requires a great deal of practice, which only practice can provide. Here's how to cut a branch: the blade is presented obliquely to the branch opposite the eye being pruned, so that a third of the blade is engaged; the branch is held with the left hand, at Om, 03 or Om, 04 below the eye, the thumb raised in a bow, then the serpette is drawn obliquely, so that the cut ends in a point and is bevelled, at Om, 005 above the eye. A cut should be made in a single stroke, even for branches that are a little strong; in this case, the left hand exerts a slight pressure that helps the cutting action. An essential point is to know where the instrument should pass after cutting the branch, so as to direct it in that direction; failure to take this precaution would expose you to cutting and damaging neighbouring branches and, what is more serious, to injuring yourself. A bevelled cut protects the wound from humidity, as rainwater slides down the inclined part, whereas it remains on a horizontal cut where the wound is difficult to cover. Secateurs. - Pruning shears are small spring-loaded shears used for pruning trees. This tool is very injurious, and the pressure of the hook is felt on the fibers of the bark and sapwood, to such an extent that the cut closes with difficulty. These shortcomings, however, do not prevent it from being used extensively. To obtain an oblique cut, the tool should be held with the hook on top, and the hand lowered so that the tool is oblique rather than horizontal. However, the serpette is always the best tool for cutting branches against the stem where the secateurs cannot reach, and for pruning extension branches whose cut must be covered promptly. Egohine. - The egohine is a small hand saw, On.25 in length, with a hollow handle to accommodate the blade. It is used to remove large and dead branches. After sawing, the cut should always be trimmed with a serpette, to facilitate covering. TIME OF PRUNING. - The time of pruning is determined by the fall of the leaves and the rest of the vegetation; it can continue until the start of the sap, unless there are heavy frosts during which pruning is not carried out. In all cases, it is advisable to reserve stone fruit trees for the end of pruning, as they are more prone to gum and their buds are more likely to be destroyed by frost than those of other trees, especially in severe winters. We will now outline the general principles of fruit tree pruning, as we have always found it to be advantageous for fruit production and for the health, preservation and longevity of the trees. It goes without saying that pruning fruit trees requires special modifications depending on the species of trees or the shape you want to give them. For all this, we refer our readers to the masters of the art, and urge them to pick up one of the treatises by Dubreuil, Hardy, Raoul, Lachaume, etc., which deal extensively with these subjects. But we especially recommend to teachers, as we have already said, Abbé Raoul's treatise on arboriculture, to which we add Lachaume's elementary method for pruning and managing your own garden fruit trees. Both treatises are well done, and have the advantage of being clear, practical and within everyone's reach. Before starting to prune a tree, you should always assess its strength and vigor, and examine the effect of the previous pruning, in order to correct any defects. A vigorous tree can be pruned quite differently from a weak, languid one. GENERAL PRUNING PRINCIPLES. - According to Abbé Raoul, all arboriculture is encapsulated in the following four principles: 1° Air and light make a tree bear fruit; lay out your tree's symmetrical framework so that these two principles of vegetation visit it in all its parts. Don't leave it as a thick bush, a real thicket that won't give you fruit, or that will only give you fruit of poor quality and most often badly made. Space the branches so that there is Om,20 to Om,30 between them for those which are superimposed one on top of the other. 2° Let your tree, no matter what form it takes, have only the wood necessary to form its framework. It is a pyramid; it has its carpenter branches as nature has given them to it, following along and around its stem the wood eyes that must produce them; only the arboriculturist's attention must be focused on not allowing any buds to grow in the space of Om, 20 to Om, 30 that separates the ground from the lowest branch, as well as on suppressing any branch that might grow in the space of Om, 20 to Om,30 that separates a lower branch from the one vertically above it. For the same reason, only one branch should be allowed to grow from the same point, so that it has more vigour; if two are left, they will both be too weak, and the structure will be defective. This is a palmette, espalier or counter-espalier; it must have one arm on each side, 20 or 30 centimetres from the ground, on the second tier 25 or 30 centimetres from the first; a third at equal distance from the second, and so on. Any buds that appear in front of or behind the stem, as well as in the 20 or 30-centimeter space separating the first tier from the ground and the tiers between them, must be removed. This is done with a sharp instrument, when these useless buds are 10 or 12 centimetres long. These spaces of 25 or 30 centimetres between the structural branches must be observed when forming a tree, whether you want it to be full-stemmed, cylindrical or goblet-shaped. 3° All your tree's supporting branches should be lined from one end to the other with fruit-bearing products, of which there are four: the flowering bud, which will blossom the following spring, or the small bud accompanied by a rosette of two or three leaves, which still needs a year's vegetation to complete its ro8. the sting, which is 1 to 5 or 8 centimetres long, and looks like a javelin. It often takes several years to bear fruit. It is not pruned; if there are several on the same spot, only one should be left. The twig, a small, small and flexible branch 0 to 15 centimeters long, is one of the first resources for fruiting. It is easily brought to fruit by breaking off its tip. It's worth noting in passing that it's only the weaker branches that set fruit easily, while the vigorous ones usually only produce wood: hence the care that must be taken to obtain fruit, which we'll discuss later. The bursa, which is the point where the fruit or flowers are attached, is a small, fleshy, tender body with several eyes around its circumference, a precious reservoir of fruit for several years. In the midst of these four different fruit productions, any bud tending to exceed 10 centimetres in length should be pinched off. 4° In general, only remove a third of the previous year's extension or shoot in spring. You form a pyramid; this removal of a third of the growth should be carried out on all the lower branches each year, until the tree is fully formed; as for the upper branches, removing only a third of the previous summer's growth would not be enough. The cone shape of the pyramid is a guide to the length to be observed when pruning the structural branches each spring. In the same way, when you form a palmette, pruning should only remove a third of the previous summer's growth from the tier closest to the ground; the triangular shape imposed on the palmette-shaped tree will regulate the pruning of the upper tiers. For all other shapes, high stems, goblets or funnels, the principle retains all its force. In spring, remove only a third of the previous year's growth from all the supporting branches, until they are perfectly shaped. Well-meaning pruning enables you to give your trees a shape in keeping with the place you want them to occupy; it determines a wise and equal distribution of sap, and ensures that each of the main branches remains filled with fruit production to its full extent. Proper pruning also offers a tree the advantage of producing larger, better-quality fruit, because a significant proportion of the nourishing fluids that would have fed the removed parts are turned to the benefit of the fruit retained. We have said that, as a general rule, only a third of the previous summer's growth should be removed in the spring; however, this principle does admit of a few modifications, in the event of a capricious sap leaving one side of the tree to favour another. The first way to remedy the problem is to prune the branches on the strong side very short, and those on the weak side very long; As sap is known to be attracted by leaves, short-trimmed twigs will have fewer leaves, and consequently less sap, so vegetation will be reduced in this part, whereas weak twigs, having been trimmed long, will emit a greater number of leaves and be covered with more abundant vegetation, which, in the long run, will restore the balance. A second way is to incline the strong part and straighten the weak part. The vertical direction given to the weaker branches will attract sap in greater abundance, their buds will grow more vigorously, and the numerous leaves they develop will continue to attract sap during the summer, to the detriment of the strong branches that have been inclined. A third way would be to pinch the strong part very early on, and as late as possible on the weak part, or not at all, since pinching slows down vegetation in the parts where it is done. Unpinched buds will continue to draw sap from the branch carrying them. These methods can be used successively, until the balance is restored. If you need a woody branch for extension, prune short. This is the procedure used for a tree exhausted by excessive fruit production; vigor is restored by pruning short for a year. If you want to develop flower buds on a rebellious branch, or one that is to be removed later, bend it or make an annular incision, as the more the sap is hindered in its circulation, the more flower buds it will produce. If, on the other hand, you want to convert a fruit-bearing branch into a wood-bearing branch, straighten it or prune it short, to concentrate all the sap's action on one or two buds. In addition to these principles, we'd like to add a few details on various complementary pruning operations, which will provide guidance on occasion. To bend a branch back on its crown means to leave the crown, or the beginning of the branch, at least the thickness of a five-franc coin, because this is where the new shoots will be born to replace those that have been removed. These productions are born from two sub-hairs or stipular buds, which are small, slightly protruding spikes in a small cavity on either side of the base of the first ring, and half-covered by the epidermis. We also use the expression "tailler sur les sous-yeux". The advantages of this operation are great; carried out in spring, towards the top of a tree, it reduces the suction of the sap, which always tends to rise, and pushes it back into the lower parts to prepare the eyes to develop more strongly there during vegetation. Done on branches that are too heavily impastoed, this operation restores the balance of sap in a tree. Notching. - Notching consists in removing a portion of stem or branch down to the sapwood, by cutting into the latter, with the aim of temporarily interrupting the flow of sap. It can be done above or below a branch, an eye or any other production. The lower notch is made to prevent a branch from growing too much; in this case, it is made on the root ball itself, the deeper the notch, the stronger the branch; above, on the other hand, to help a bud or branch that is too weak to develop, we avoid offending the eye or the branch. The lower notch prevents too much sap from passing into the branch, weakening it; the upper one deflects this liquid into the branch or bud, forcing it to develop further. Occasionally, the bud only grows slightly, so the operation is repeated the following year. If nothing develops, there's no point in starting again in the second year. Often, to make it more fruitful, instead of making the cut horizontally, we make it obliquely in the shape of a chevron, so as to surround the eye more and make the sap flow into it more abundantly. When you want to apply it to stone fruit trees, in which it also gives good results, as they are prone to strangles, be sure to coat the wound with grafting wax. However, on peach trees, it should be done with the greatest circumspection. Incision. - Several types of incision are made in the bark, with different effects depending on the shape given. The transverse incision is a diminutive of the notch, but is only made above the eyes, at a distance of around 5 or 4 millimeters; it interrupts the sap ducts without removing the wood; it is less effective, but in many cases it is enough to ensure the development of an eye. It is mainly used on branches or twigs whose diameter is too small to withstand the notch; it is preferable to the latter for peach trees. Longitudinal incisions are made in areas where hardened bark compresses the sap canals, preventing them from allowing branches to expand to their full potential. The tip of the pruning knife is used to make a slight incision in the bark to expand it, penetrating as far as the sapwood, but without touching it. Don't make too many cuts, leaving a gap of around 5 to 4 centimetres between them, and avoid making cuts on the side facing south. This method is excellent for increasing the size of the incised parts, and is often very useful in spring; it can also be used throughout the vegetation period. It is used on peach trees to prevent gumming or to cure the tree of this disease; in this case, the incisions are more sparing and shallower. Ring incision consists of removing a circular piece of bark, using a special instrument known as ring shears, or simply with a serpette. The width of this piece varies according to the diameter of the branch on which the incision is made, but in no case should it exceed one centimeter, so that the wound can close within a year. The purpose of this operation is to bring the upper part of the branch into fruit, and to develop wood in the lower part: it also hastens the ripening of the fruit, but is somewhat detrimental to its quality. It should only be carried out on the same tree in part, and then only if it is vigorous, as it soon weakens it, especially when multiplied. A weak, already fertile tree will not withstand it. Trees with fruiting seeds, and mainly vines, are subjected to this operation; on the latter, it takes place at the moment of flowering to prevent run-off, and on the others when the sap begins to move. The incision is made immediately below the cluster, at Om,02 or Om,03, to ensure success. Seeds swell more than in the ordinary state: maturity on some species is quite suddenly advanced. Above the bunch, it gives only poor results, and the grapes hardly ripen at all. However, this procedure should be used with extreme caution, if you do not want to see the vine weaken soon. Don't wait too late, so that the wound has time to heal before the end of vegetation, otherwise the branches operated on risk perishing. Debudding. - This is the removal, at the time of pruning, of eyes deemed completely useless, and which should be removed later, during disbudding: in this way, part of the sap is used, which would have been lost if these buds had been left to grow. It should be used very sparingly. The most common case is when a fruit-bearing branch of the peach tree has been pruned long and the fruit is far from the base: all the eyes between the two closest to the heel and the fruit buds are then removed. Bending. - This consists in bending twigs and even branches into an arc or semicircle, with the end inclined towards the ground, and holding them in this position by means of a tie, with the aim of making them set fruit. The sap, whose movement is slowed down by the curve it has to follow, only develops stings and twigs, and buds are formed. This is a powerful method, but we recommend its use on terminal branches only in extreme cases, i.e. on trees so vigorous that elongated pruning and severe pinching have failed to bring them to fruition. But let's only partially bow the lateral branches taken from the strongest branches, and the twigs, taking care to remove the terminal eye. Some growers subject their entire trees to this form to make them bear fruit quickly, but we must beware of imitating them, as trees treated in this way quickly wear out and live for a short time. The fruits become small, and the sap no longer feeds them sufficiently, an inconvenience that does not occur when the arcure is only partial. When the tree is fully fruited, the arched twigs and branches will have to disappear, while the stings and lambourdes will suffice to ensure production. Disbudding. - This is useful for the training of all trees, and is essential for espaliered trees, especially peach trees and vines. More buds always develop than are necessary for the tree's existence and good conformation. Pinching only stops them from growing, while it is often useful to remove them altogether to make trellising practicable. Disbudding therefore removes all unnecessary buds, which would cause confusion and take away part of the sap, which is then reserved for those that must remain. This operation, which complements pruning, requires a certain amount of care, and should be carried out gradually rather than simultaneously: the latter would have the serious disadvantage of slowing down vegetation; you need to know which shoots to protect by training them and pinching them if necessary. It's best to start with the first shoots, mainly old trees and those that are weak and languishing. On peach trees, however, there is reason to fear that by disbudding too early, the buds destined to produce the following year's fruit will become too strong, and the fruit will be scarce; we wait a little, especially on young trees, to allow the replacement bud a sort of relative inferiority. On the same tree (peach), when triple or double eyes develop on the top of the supporting branches, keep only the weakest shoot. If it's underneath, we'll keep the strongest. When two or three buds appear at the end of an extension branch, remove the weakest and leave the strongest, as good vegetation is essential for good framework. In all cases, don't wait until the bud is more than 5 or 6 centimetres old before removing it, to make room for those that need to be trained. These should be neatly removed with a razor blade, so that the spot heals easily. If carried out too early, disbudding has the disadvantage of giving rise to false buds, which often become an embarrassment on stone-fruit trees at the time of pruning; if done too late, it disrupts vegetation by taking away outlets for the sap, which is forced to reject itself in other parts, often taking on too much strength. However, it is sometimes necessary not to disbud until late, or even not at all, but only to pinch; this is when you want to strengthen a weak branch, leaving it with a large number of buds. Misplaced shoots, such as those in front and behind, on the supporting branches of a tree in espaHORT. 9 lier, will be removed, unless they are useful for filling a gap, and even then it's better to graft. Pinching. - Pinching is an operation which consists in trimming and removing, with the thumb and forefinger nails, the top of the bud when it is still tender. The time of year is naturally determined for each locality by the temperature and the earliness of the trees to come into vegetation. It is therefore because of these two variations that it should be carried out successively, starting with the buds that absorb the most sap, and continuing gradually according to the phases of vegetation. There are circumstances where it must be delayed, as in a change of temperature with a cold wind that momentarily suspends the course of the sap, or in any other circumstance that would produce a similar effect. The effect of pinching is to 1° Stops bud elongation by suppressing the apex and forcing the sap back onto the lateral eyes, thus helping their formation; 2° Establishes a means of balance when applied to the apex of the strongest terminal buds on the lateral branches of pyramids or espaliers, by momentarily stopping the flow of sap, which then benefits the weak buds left intact; 3° To help the formation of fruit productions which, due to their position on the tree, are neglected by the sap, because of its tendency to follow a direct course. It is important to differentiate between the nature of the subject, and even between the parts of the same tree where the pinch is applied. For example, a side laden with fruit will be pinched more severely than one without. There are also species of tree where a pinch that is too short attacks the organs, such as the good winter Christian, the crassane, and generally the varieties with soft, porous wood: these are differences that you must learn to distinguish in order to produce the effect you want. In short, it's better to pinch a little long than too short, since crown pruning is used to weaken production and bring it to fruit successively. Breaking. - Breakage is an operation which consists in breaking off the lateral branches 5 centimetres from their starting point, either on pyramids or espaliers: it is carried out at the end of August, when the sap begins to slow down, so that breakage concentrates it on the fruit crops, while avoiding spoiling and aborting them. However, this sometimes happens when, after long droughts, the sap regains its strength, cancelling out and destroying the expected results. Pinching is of little importance for trees that have been well pinched; but it becomes necessary for those that have been forgotten or neglected, or for unpinched twigs left in reserve to prevent abortion of fruit production. Breakage is performed by pressing the blade of the pruning knife against the base of the twig between two leaves, squeezing it lightly with the thumb; then, turning the hand, breakage is performed. The breaking method predates pinching, and its application comes to us from the ancients, who practised it at various times of the year. The trees to which breaking is applied are pear, apple, cherry, plum and apricot, all of which are subject to the various shapes in use. Shaping trees. From the moment you plant a fruit tree, you want to give it a shape of some kind: but this shape must be subordinate to one main aim, which is to obtain, by cultivating fruit trees in a given area, the greatest possible quantity of the most beautiful fruit in the shortest possible time and with the least possible expense. This is what schoolteachers should be particularly concerned with. To achieve this, they need to use the simplest forms, the easiest to establish, and which require the least time and expense either to set up or to maintain. In addition to full-wind trees, we will reduce these forms to five, for the reasons given above. These forms are: 1° full-wind trees; 2° the pyramid; 3° the cattail; 4° spindles; and 5° cords. 1° Full wind trees. - This shape is applicable to all tree species. Trees treated in this way are best placed in orchards or along a roadside: they only take their branches from a trunk grafted onto a free-standing trunk about 2 meters high. Pruning for high-stemmed trees consists in leaving only three or rarely four of the most beautiful and best-placed branches to form the head; leaving them the first year, even before planting, for pear and apple trees, at a length of around 10 to 12 centimetres, depending on the strength of the wood. We say pear trees, because some stone trees require longer pruning, others shorter. 2° Pyramid-shaped pear trees. - Trees of this shape consist of a vertical stem topped from the top to Om, 30 from the ground by lateral branches whose length increases as they approach the ground or the base of the tree. These branches must grow in such a way that there is an interval of Om, 30 between each of those that immediately overlap, following the same direction, so that air and light can penetrate between them. They should be free of bifurcations, with only fruiting branches from top to base. Finally, they should form an angle of no more than 25 degrees with the horizon. In general, the largest diameter of the pyramid should equal one third of the tree's total height. This proportion is necessary so that the balance of vegetation is more easily maintained between the various parts of the tree. If the diameter is less than the indicated third, the inner branches, half as long and with half as many leaves, will no longer have the strength to counterbalance the tendency of the sap towards the top of the tree, and retain a sufficient quantity for their own benefit: they become increasingly languid, and eventually perish. If, on the other hand, the diameter is increased, the lower branches will absorb too much sap, to the detriment of the top. The height to be given to pyramids is proportionate to the richness of the soil and the vigor of the subjects; it varies between 5 and 9 meters. Fruit trees can only be properly framed as long as they are developing vigorously. Newly-planted young trees only show this degree of vigor once they have taken possession of the soil, i.e. once they have developed new rootlets to replace those destroyed by transplanting; for it is only then that these trees can draw abundantly from the earth the nutrients they need for their vegetation. (See for guidance, construction and pruning of pyramid-shaped pear trees. DUBREUIL, RAOUL, HARDY and LACHAUME). 3° cattail. - The cattail shape has long been confused with the pyramid shape, and is still often mistakenly so. However, it differs greatly both in layout and results. The cattail is shaped in such a way that its largest diameter is located towards the middle of the height, so that the lateral branches decrease in length as they approach the base and the top. 1 What does this shape mean? The sap is drawn towards the middle of the tree by the greater mass of branches, and abandons the branches at the base, which are then loaded with a very large quantity of flower buds and fruit, rapidly exhausting them. Despite this disadvantage, we recommend this arrangement to schoolteachers, for the trees they place between pyramids, because young trees lend themselves quite naturally to this shape, and what's more, they take less time to prune, while giving good results. Cattails can, however, be replaced by spindle-shaped trees, which are ideally suited to small vegetable gardens such as those usually found on schoolteachers' premises. 4° Spindle or columnar trees consist of a single, vertical stem, rising to an average height of 6 meters and regularly topped with fruiting branches from the base to the top. The result is a cylindrical column 0.35 m in diameter. This shape is not very graceful, but it does offer certain advantages in certain circumstances. For example, the trees that are subjected to it shade the ground much less than pyramids do, and take up much less space, enabling other products to be grown in their vicinity, and also, for the same reason, enabling a greater number of different varieties to be brought together in the same space. We also believe that the fruiting branches form more quickly, that being better lit by the sun and born directly on the stem, they are more fertile, and that the fruit is generally more beautiful. As a result, for the same surface area, a slightly greater quantity of fruit would be harvested than with pyramids. But this success can only be achieved under certain conditions. Firstly, pear and apple trees are the only two species that seem to lend themselves well to this shape. Secondly, these two trees need to be grafted, the first on quince, the second on doucin. If they were grafted on franc, they would grow too vigorously, and the pruning method applied to them would only result in the development of woody shoots. Finally, and for the same reason, these trees should be placed in warm, light, moderately fertile soil. (For this training method, see the authors already cited above, and especially Dubreuil, whose method, which we have borrowed here, seems to us the most rational). 5° Cordons. - Under this form, apple trees, which do not stand still, so to speak, generally bear fruit more quickly than under the other forms, and give more colorful fruit. In fact, this is the only form suitable for school gardens. Cords can be arranged in two different ways, but we'll concentrate on the one that best suits those for whom we're writing. HORIZONTAL OR LATERAL CORDON. - Apple trees of all varieties, one year old grafted on paradise and with a single stem, are planted at a distance of Om, 50 to Om, 40 from the edge of the path and 1m, 50 to 2 meters apart from each other, in a line along a path or all around a tile. A wire is stretched at Om, 30 or Om, 35 from the ground; a peg is planted at the foot of each tree and behind it, i.e. on the opposite side of the direction in which each inclined tree will be; it is tied loosely to this peg with a wicker, a few centimetres from the bottom of the wire, then gently inclined on to it, making it form the swan's neck, and tied to it. Later, during the winter, it is bent completely to form a perfect square. In spring, its length is reduced by pruning it close to an eye at the top, a few centimetres from its tip. When the extension branch of the first meets the second, they are grafted together by cutting the tip of the first into a triangle or, better still, into a bevel which is pushed into the elbow of the second, where a triangular or flat incision is made; they are tied together, and the ligature made over the incision is covered with a little hot grafting wax. Do the same to the others as they come together, and soon the whole is a cordon, a chain of beautiful and excellent colored fruits. The sap from the first will thus reach the second, and even the following ones: the weak will thus benefit from the health of the robust. When the cordon is welded from one end to the other, the wire is eliminated. 4 According to several reputable practitioners, it would be better not to graft apple trees together, as this would make it easier to control the sap, by letting it flow into the extension of the end, which is passed through a wicker ring under the next tree, and pruned a little each year, as is done on the ends of a finished espalier. As a result of this procedure, a distance of 2 meters should be set between each apple tree at the time of planting. exter A single cordon can form two if the subjects grow well, and this second cordon is often very useful to the lower one, in that it spends the superfluous sap and thus prevents the fruit production from going to wood. This cordon is obtained by making the first apple trees produce a bud that is raised to Om, 25 above the first cordon, and applying it to wires like the first and treating it absolutely like the latter. Fan. In addition to the above five forms, which we feel are most suitable for school gardens, we also encourage teachers to practice the management and education of a few trees, which they can form into 9. fans, palmettes, candelabras, espaliers or counter espaliers, vases and goblets. Simple palmettes. -===---- - Candelabra. It's always a pleasant distraction when you can force trees to bend to your every whim! CHAPTER X CULTIVATION OF THE PRINCIPAL FRUIT TREES In the short presentation that follows, we shall proceed as in our description of vegetable plants, i.e. in alphabetical order. Apricot tree. - This tree grows tall and fairly large; it is covered with thick, hard, greyish bark; its branches extend well; its leaves are short, broad, almost round, toothed, pointed, dark green and pungent in taste; its flowers are pale pink, each composed of five florets arranged in a pink pattern: once the flowers have fallen, they are followed by round, fleshy fruits, as large as eggs, flattened on the sides and furrowed along the length. When fully ripe, they are red on one side and yellowish on the others; their flesh is yellow, tender, melting and sweet, and contains a hard, bony, flattened stone, pointed at both ends, which contains a white, bitter almond with a pleasant taste. The apricot tree seems to be the most robust of all fruit trees, since when transplanted large enough, not only does it take well, given a few precautions, but it also often produces very fine fruit in the same year. It can be grafted to plum, almond and even peach trees, but never to other apricot trees, as the slit made to receive the graft often becomes an incurable wound. To obtain better fruit, we prefer grafting on wild black damask plum trees. Grafting onto plum trees with large or white fruit produces larger apricots, but at the expense of quality. Moreover, this tree is easy to grow, as it is content with any kind of soil that is neither too wet nor too clayey. In cold, damp soils, it should be placed to the south, but naturally it prefers a sunny exposure and warm, sandy soil, which should be deeper for trees grafted onto almond trees. Apricot trees don't like manure, and should rarely be given manure if the soil is too thin. You can dispense with pruning full-blown apricot trees, but then they bear less beautiful fruit. They should be pruned before the sap starts to move, in February, mainly to remove dead or gummy wood and greedy branches. Trees planted in espaliers require more careful pruning. They are arranged and managed in the same way as peach trees, bearing in mind that large branches must be cut off several times, lest the abundant sap turn to gum: this is what can happen to all novau fruit. It should also be noted that the sun's heat can be harmful to espalier fruit, so this disadvantage is remedied by de-spreading the branches, and holding the fruit away from the wall with a small wooden fork. You can also help them to ripen and take on a beautiful color by uncovering them before or after the rain. This operation must be carried out with care, as the fruit should only be uncovered a little at a time, and sometimes only half the leaves should be cut off. Apricot fruit is nourishing, healthy and refreshing. Cherry tree. - Most cherry trees grow to a mediocre height and medium size. The bark is hard, thick, russet or grayish, the leaves long, narrow, pointed and toothed at the edges. The flowers are white, each composed of five florets arranged in a pink pattern: the flowers are followed by round, green fruits, which gradually become red, black or white, depending on the species; they are borne on a more or less long stalk; inside, they contain a hard, bony stone, containing a small white almond, with a very pronounced bitter taste. Cherry trees do particularly well in light, deep soil. Grafting is the best and most widely used method for propagating fine varieties. If you want strong, slender trees, you can graft them to wild cherry or cherry from seed, using the "dormant eye" grafting technique. We'd like to point out that preference should be given to red-fruited cherry, as it grafts much more easily than black-fruited varieties. For medium-sized trees, graft on wild cherry or guignier scions, and for dwarf trees, graft on sour cherry. The cherry is an excellent fruit, aperitif, digestive and very healthy. Cognassier.Its gnarled, often twisted trunk sprouts many diffuse branches, with alternate, entire, etiolated, oblong, cottony and whitish leaves on top, large, white, terminal, almost sessile flowers which become fruits called quinces, pear-shaped, always covered with down, more or less large, watery and fragrant, depending on the soil that produced them; and finally greenish-yellow when ripe and good to eat, but only cooked. Quince can be propagated by seed, cuttings, offshoots and grafting, and requires no care other than the removal of greedy branches, dead wood and buds that develop at its base; this tree is not much cultivated for its fruit, but much for grafting pear trees. Walnut. - Its straight, well-spun trunk divides, at a more or less considerable height, into numerous branches that form a beautiful head. Its leaves are broad, alternate, winged, with five to nine muffled leaflets, whole sessile, elongated ovals, yellowish-green, giving off a strong odor when crumpled. The flowers, either male or female, live on the same individual: the former are arranged in long, axillary catkins, which fall after the female flowers have been fertilized. These are usually grouped in threes or fours at the tip of the young twigs, and become rounded fruits covered with an aromatic pulp, which is at first green and firm, but soon softens and takes on a dark brown tint that it communicates to everything that touches it; This is known as the brou, and surrounds a woody, very wrinkled shell, acute at the top and opening into two equal parts, revealing a kernel with solid, white flesh, divided about halfway into four parts, whose shape and taste are familiar to everyone. These fruits differ in size and quality according to variety. Walnut trees are not very fussy about the choice of land, as they thrive in a variety of soils. However, they prefer stony, sandy soils that can also retain some freshness. They are propagated from seed; young walnut trees are pruned with hooks, until the stem has reached a circumference of 0.m12, at which time they should be grafted if the quality of the fruit is more important than the beauty of the tree. Walnut trees can be grafted with a slotted eye, a ring or a flute. The latter is the most commonly used, and we feel it is the most advantageous. The following year, they can be put in place after the soil to be planted has been cleared as much as possible and well loosened. Once in place, they need no further pruning, except for the first two or three years, to form a regular head. Sin. - Left to its own devices, this tree is not likely to reach great heights, and its head is almost always sloppy and graceless, when nature alone is responsible for its adornment. But under the hand of art, it submits to all shapes, and its docile branches lend themselves to all directions. Its trunk, which only grows to a mediocre size, is made of very hard wood, covered with ash-grey bark whose epidermis, over time, rises in more or less wide, more or less thick scales, depending on the age of the tree and the stoutness it enjoyed in its youth, or the illnesses it suffered during the course of its vegetation. The bark of the young wood, colored a dull, pale green, turns a more or less dark brick-red, depending on which side the sun hits it. As it matures, its epidermis takes on a number of irregular, padded dots, advancing the maturity of the woody parts. The main branches arising from the trunk naturally take a direction closer to the perpendicular than to the horizontal, and in their early youth, their base is provided with numerous shoots or buds which follow a direction similar to that taken by their mother. Gradually, however, these buds disappear, and all the work of vegetation is carried to the ends of the branches, leaving their lower parts bare, unless art prevents or halts the effects of this tendency. Peach trees like deep, light, warm, sandy soil. It can be propagated by sowing, but only a few varieties reproduce identically and it is usually by grafting that it is multiplied. In light, warm and deep soils, hard-shelled and sweet almond trees are the most suitable for grafting; in soils lacking these qualities, especially the latter, preference should be given to black Damask and Saint-Julien plum trees, but from seed rather than suckers. Peach trees are sometimes grafted onto themselves, but in this case they are much more prone to gum. Grafting is carried out from mid-July to September, and the operation is completed by choosing the moment when the sap is not abundant enough to drown the bud, but sufficient to weld it together. If you want to grow them in the open air, place the escutcheon at a height of 1.60 or 2 meters; if you want to grow them in espaliers, place them at Om.15 from the collar. The cultivation and pruning of the peach tree require a great deal of detail, which we cannot go into here. Suffice it to say that attention should be focused on the eye, bud, shoot and woody branch of the peach tree, for these are all that make up its vegetation. Pear tree. - This is the tree that stands out most in an orchard for its elevation and the regularity of its head. Its numerous branches support each other without confusion and, in almost all varieties, present a well-rounded dome that can do without the help of art to preserve the graces of its form: in a word, it is the most beautiful and elegant of all fruit trees. Its leaves are alternate, smooth, whole, more or less oval, but always slightly elongated and pointed. The serrations along their edges are more or less deep and regular, sometimes barely perceptible. The stalks that support them are short but not too flexible, so they are always supported in an almost horizontal direction. Composed of at least five rounded petals, almost always white and concave, the flowers are gathered in clusters on a very short support, and feature a fleshy, persistent calyx, cup-shaped and divided into five long, pointed indentations. The center of the corolla is occupied by twenty or thirty awl-shaped stamens, shorter than the petals, and by a pistil whose five styles, crowned by simple stigmas, rest on an embryo that forms part of the calyx and becomes a fleshy, succulent fruit whose shape, volume, color and flavor vary according to variety, and whose center is occupied by five membranous lugs, each containing one or two pepins. All pear varieties can be propagated by scape, cleft and crown grafting: on wild pear to form large, long-lasting canopies, but only if the soil is deep enough; on quince for shallow soils and for espaliers, pyramids and cattails; on small quince for low espaliers and palmettes. Pear trees grafted onto quince set fruit sooner, but are prone to yellowing and live less long than those grafted onto sauvageon, because not all soils are suitable for quince. In general, espaliered pear trees produce much more beautiful fruit than those left in the open air, and they prefer east-facing and west-facing exposures to any other. However, there are some that can adapt to all exposures, provided the soil is suitable. Sometimes pear trees, after having been vigorous, languish and turn yellow; this is because, planted in artificial or shallow soil, they reach a depth that does not suit them; or it is because they have worn out the soil. The latter can be remedied by renewing the soil: to do this, in November, the plants are uncovered.

The roots are then immediately covered with mud collected from the streets and paths, on top of which manure is placed, which is removed in the spring and replaced with new, suitable soil. In general, melting pears and those grafted onto franc trees do best in dry soil, while fat, fresh soil is well suited to brittle pears and those grafted onto quince trees. (For pruning and management of pear trees, see Dubreuil, Raoul, Hardy and Lachaume. Apple tree. - This tree is of mediocre stature, but its half-vertical twigs give it a bushy head, which shines alternately with the brightness of its spring flowers, the suavity of its foliage, and the goodness of the fruit that crowns its annual growth. Its buds rise straight up and are covered with elliptical, elongated, alternate leaves, tapering to a point at both ends: bordered by a more or less deep serration, they are made of a strong, whitish-green, slightly hairy fabric, veined on the underside and tinted a more or less dark green on top. The flowers appear in clusters, and each is composed of a one-piece, fleshy, cup-shaped calyx, divided at the edges into two long, pointed indentations; five large, concave, rose-shaped petals, variegated with red on a white background; twenty stamens, attached to the inner walls of the calyx; and a pistil whose five fairly long styles, terminated by their stigmas, rest on an embryo that serves as the calyx's background. This embryo becomes a fleshy, rounded, conical or cylindrical fruit ending in two cavities, one of which receives the peduncle and the other contains the umbilicus. It is covered with a varnished skin adhering to the flesh, and its center is occupied by five large forms of thin, supple yet solid membranes. Each compartment contains one or, more often, two teardrop-shaped seeds, flattened on the side where they touch, and covered with a cartilaginous skin that protects a slightly bitter kernel. Apple trees thrive in all types of soil, but do best in slightly damp, oily soils. Although the roots don't prickle, it doesn't last long in shallow soil. Except for southern exposure, it can grow in all other types of soil. Like the pear tree, the apple lends itself to any shape you want to give it. Precious apple varieties can be propagated by grafting onto their own species, either in the form of a shield with a dormant eye, or in the form of a cleft or crown, but they must be chosen according to the place and shape you wish to give them. Plants raised from seedlings or burst suckers from wild apple trees or orchards are suitable for making large open-air apple trees. Small open-air trees, goblets, espaliers and cattails, spindles or pyramids can be grafted onto doucin, a smaller species than the wild apple. Lastly, cordons are grafted mainly onto paradis, a dwarf, very fertile species that imparts its qualities to grafts. Paradiso sets fruit very quickly and produces larger fruit; it also produces many root offshoots that serve as subjects. It is also more receptive to reinette, rambur and api, which are usually grafted as escutcheons. When planting apple trees, care must be taken not to bury the graft. Pruning large, full-wind apple trees consists solely of removing dead wood; funnel-shaped trees need to be hollowed out in the middle, among other things: more art is needed for espaliers, which also need to be trellised like pear trees, twice a year, at pruning and disbudding in July. Plum trees. - The plum tree is generally of medium size, with a fairly pleasant habit as long as its shoots are straight, vigorous and complete. But as it ages, its fragile wood breaks under the weight of its fruit or yields to the force of the winds, and soon these repeated mutilations cause it to lose its regularity and grace. Most of this tree's fruit hang from the branches on long, slender stalks that implant themselves at the lower end of the fruit, in a more or less deep cavity. Light, sandy soils that are not arid are suitable for this tree, which in strong soils produces too much wood and much less fruit, which ripens very late. Exposures to the east and west are the most favorable; finally, plum trees like full wind and languish when sheltered by walls or overhung by trees. Stem plums with full exposure to the wind can be grafted onto wild stone plums: pruning should be long, to prevent them from producing too much wood and very little fruit.
