CHAPTER XII HARVESTING AND PRESERVING FRUIT Harvesting begins with summer fruits, continues with autumn fruits and ends with winter fruits. Harvesting, which usually takes place in October for winter fruit, may be delayed or brought forward, depending on the local temperature and, above all, the nature of the trees, which differ in their vegetation. For example, pear trees grafted onto quince trees, whose vegetation starts early, produce fruit earlier than those grafted onto franc trees. Fruits should be harvested when the weather is fine, and as soon as you notice that some are detached from the tree without being worm-eaten. The same species of winter fruit grafted onto the franc tree should be harvested at least fifteen to twenty days later than those grafted onto the quince tree, because they retain their vegetation very late and the adherence of the peduncles to the branches protects them from gales. Harvesting can be advanced or delayed by the shape of the trees and the exposure in which they are placed; espaliered pear and apple trees ripen almost twenty days before the same species in pyramid, spindle or cattail shape. Great care must be taken when picking the fruit, to preserve the peduncle (or tail), and to avoid breaking the bursa to which they adhere, as this glues them in the future. Fruits picked about a fortnight before ripening keep longer, but this is to the detriment of their quality; more often than not, they are wrinkled and tasteless. Once the fruit has been picked and sorted into different species, it is placed in a chamber to release its water through transpiration. This transpiration, which is noticeable by the steam with which the fruit is charged, will be all the more active if the harvest has been made in fine weather, after the sun has evaporated the dew and before the cool of the evening. Before taking the fruit down to the orchard, select the most beautiful and healthiest ones that are likely to keep longer, and place them on separate shelves, keeping a small distance between them so that they don't touch. You can convert either a frost-free room or a cellar or dry cellar into a fruit store, with shelves to hold the fruit. Whichever room you choose, you need to keep it very clean, and visit the shelves often to remove spoiled fruit, as its decomposition can be harmful to others through the gases it gives off. As the fruit ripens, it loses water and its sweetness increases, due to the action of the oxygen gas in the fruit tree's air. By adjusting to this chemical combination, we can prolong or delay the ripening of part of the fruit by keeping it closed in a place deprived of air and light, at the same temperature. CHAPTER XIII DESTRUCTION OF ANIMALS HAZARDOUS TO TREES Caterpillar. - The surest way to destroy them is to comply with the law, i.e. to weed. This consists in carefully removing all caterpillar nests and egg rings from the branches, while pruning the trees, and burning them: finally, to destroy the caterpillars scattered on the plants, as well as the butterflies that come to lay their eggs. Ants. - For a long time, ants were thought to be immune to damage to fruit trees, but we now know that they devour young buds in spring, when they are first developing, and that they attack perfectly healthy fruit. It is therefore useful to think about destroying them: this is done by hanging small bottles, half-filled with honeyed water, from the branches of trees, from place to place. It doesn't take long to get rid of them completely. Wasps and hornets. - These insects sometimes cause considerable damage, especially to pear trees. To destroy them, we use the same procedure as for ants. Slugs and snails can be destroyed by the methods described in the chapter on animals harmful to plants. birds. - While some birds are a nuisance in the garden, there are some in large numbers that are undeniably useful: we therefore recommend not destroying them, but keeping them out of the garden when the fruit ripens. We have recently devised a successful method of keeping them away from fruit: small two-sided mirrors are placed above or in front of the trees and vines we wish to preserve. Tie them with a long string, so that they float in the slightest wind. Aphids. - Green and black aphids cause considerable damage to peach trees. These insects attack the underside of the youngest leaves, absorbing the fluids they contain. They can be destroyed by using tobacco as a fumigant or lotion. The woolly aphid can be recognized by the abundant white down covering it; it attacks apple trees in particular, which it promptly kills. It gets under the bark of trees, and during winter, part of it hides in the ground around the root collar. To combat it, the tree must be dug up so that it can be reached wherever it is, since it comes up again in spring. Several methods have been recommended for destroying the woolly adelgid; unfortunately, most are either inapplicable or ineffective. Only one has so far produced good results: the use of fatty substances, the most common and least expensive oils. Simply apply them with a stiff brush to all affected areas, while the vegetation is resting. Bugs or kermes. Tiger bugs. - These insects are destroyed with a mixture of quicklime, black soap and lye. HORT. 10 The soap is used in the proportion of 500 grams to 4 liters of lye, and the lime in sufficient quantity to form a sort of clear slurry. After leaf fall, apply this mixture with a brush to all infected branches and twigs of these various animals. Rats, mice, dormice and field mice. -These animals harm trees by eating fruit and sometimes gnawing twigs. They are easily destroyed before the fruit is ripe, by placing bait mixed with vomitus nut in small pots hung against the wall. Mousetraps can also be used for the same purpose. D Moles. - They disrupt the soil and fan the roots with their underground galleries. They need traps that are easy to obtain. LNGIAT NE DU BUTEERRE n avu'que av HCENTOS BERII IORMD ME MARROOEEA 4 memte n mnem OEL D CHAPTER XIV EHRAHI TREE DISEASES Gum is specific to stone fruit trees. It can be recognized by secretions that appear on the surface of twigs or branches, tearing the bark. In young trees, gum is often the result of pruning that is too short, or pinching that is too rigorous. In older trees, it is sometimes the result of impeded fluid circulation. It has been noted that gum is more frequent on trees planted in damp soils, and can also appear following sudden changes in temperature. As soon as gum appears, the deposits it forms should be scraped away to the quick, and the wounds covered with grafting wax. In the early stages of the disease, longitudinal incisions made on the branches on the opposite side to the one where the gum has formed are usually quite successful. But if the gum has vitiated the bark and sapwood around it, there is no remedy. The twig or branch must be cut off below the disease, and pruned on a vigorous dormant eye placed above it, in order to obtain a replacement twig. Blistering. - This disease is specific to peach trees, and appears on their leaves towards the end of spring. Affected leaves first take on a yellowish-green tinge; soon afterwards they thicken, tighten up, blister, turn purplish-white and yellow, and eventually fall off. The main cause of this disease seems to be sudden changes in temperature, which suddenly stop vegetation in its tracks. Experience has shown that the surest way to prevent it is to use movable coping or canopies for espaliered peach trees. If a bud is completely affected, it should be removed without hesitation, lest the disease wreak further havoc. Le Blanc, miller or leprosy. - This is a kind of whitish mold that attacks leaves, buds and fruit. As soon as it begins, to stop the disease, wet the affected leaves on a calm day at sunset and sprinkle them with sulfur flower. Repeat this operation every eight days, and the disease disappears. Chlorosis or jaundice. - Pear trees are very prone to this; leaves turn yellow, buds languish and often dry out at the tips. If it lasts throughout vegetation, it indicates soil exhaustion. If it is due to certain adverse atmospheric influences, it presents no serious danger. In the first case, fertilizers should be used to revive vegetation: if this fails, the tree should be replanted. In the second case, there's usually no need to worry about it, as jaundice ceases with the causes that produced it. As for the burning that occurs at the end of branches during droughts, simply remove the dead wood by pruning the green twig to a good eye outwards. Cankers. - All trees, especially pears and apples, are prone to cankers, which indicate poor health or exhaustion. If they are the result of accidents, such as blows, bruises, etc., they are easily cured by scraping off the affected branches with a sharp instrument, and covering the scraped areas with grafting wax. When they are due to lack of vigor, remove all the old bark, scrape it away and girdle to obtain new shoots. Mosses. - They interfere with the functions of trees and are harmful to them. Get rid of them by scraping them off in wet weather; then heat the whole tree with great care. CHAPTER XV CULTIVATION OF VINES IN GARDENS The preferred varieties are Chasselas de Fontainebleau, Chasselas rose, which takes on its pink hue only when ripe, and Franckenthal. If you want very early grapes, you can plant a black Magdeleine. Light, deep soil is best for excellent grapes. In moist, shallow soil, vines languish; in more consistent soil, their production is too strong, too watery, and their fruit is of lesser quality. In our temperate climate, vines need a warm exposure to ripen fully, and it's only along a wall, facing south or east, that they find the heat they need to ripen perfectly. Of all the methods for pruning vines, trellising them and laying them against a wall, we'll just mention the one used at Thomery, near Fontainebleau: we think it's preferable to all the others for its simplicity. The walls on which the vines are trained in Thomery are about 2.50 m high, and are finished with a projecting coping of Om.25 to Om.30. This coping protects the vines from frost and heavy rain, and prevents the upper cordon from growing too strongly. The walls are lined with trellises, the uprights of which are spaced at Om, 65 from each other and the horizontal slats only at 10. Om, 25. The first row of these is at Om, 16 from the ground. Here's how to plant the vine. The bed along the wall against which the trellis is to be planted is cleared, loosened and smoked to a width of at least 1m,60 and a depth of Om, 40 or Om, 50. If the soil is damp, the bed is sloped to keep the water away from the wall. Once this has been done, a trench 1.60 m from the wall is opened in parallel, Om.65 wide and Om.25 to Om.28 deep; then the required quantity of marcottes or crossettes is prepared, after removing the spurs and tendrils, etc... These crossettes lie crosswise in the bottom of this trench, with their heads turned towards the wall; at a distance of Om,55 from each other: when they are covered with Om,10 to 0m,14 of soil, they are compacted a little with the foot, while the end facing the wall is raised to give it a more or less vertical direction; the trench is then only two-thirds full, with the rest of the soil spread over the bed. In general, it's a good idea to spread a layer of manure Om, 08 thick in the trench, to keep it cool and prevent the soil from drying out, hardening and splitting. In March, each plant is cut at two eyes above the ground; weed, hoe and water during the summer if the heat requires it, or if the drought is prolonged, as a vine cutting must always be in a mild humidity to produce roots: we tie the shoots to a stile, encouraging their development by all known means. In the following spring, the weak shoots are pruned off, leaving only the best on each vine, which is then laid down towards the wall, as in the previous year's operation, and so on until it reaches the foot of the wall and can be planted there. These various operations usually take three years. Now it's time to form the cords. If the wall is 2.50 m high, five cords are established: the first at 0.16 m from the ground, and the other four at 0.50 m from each other, on trellis crosspieces set up in advance for this purpose. The vine destined to form the lowest cordon should be pruned just at the height of the cordon, if it has a double eye at this point; otherwise, it is important to prune on the eye immediately above the marked point; at the same time, the development of the eye placed just below is encouraged: these two eyes should form the two branches with which to form the two arms of the vine, one on the right and the other on the left: when the wood is ripe, if the upper branch rises a little above the trellis against which it is to be laid, it is gently bent so that it rests exactly on the trellis; if the other branch, on the contrary, originated a little too low, it is directed vertically up to the level of the first, and there it is also bent over the trellis on the opposite side, so that the two branches are perfectly opposite or placed on the same line and appear to come from the same point. The second cord, located at (lm, 65 from the ground, cannot be formed as soon as the first; the third will be formed even later, and so on for the others. Whatever the height the vine reaches to form the cordon, it should only be lengthened by Om, 35 to Om, 40 each year, and the lateral buds should be left to prune into spurs, in order to make it grow and produce grapes; but as soon as the cordon has reached the required height and its two arms have received the first pruning, all the spurs that would exist along the entire length of the vine should be scrupulously removed. We assume that all the vines have reached the height assigned to each one, and that their last two branches have been extended horizontally to the right and left to form the two branches of the cordon; here's how to prune these two branches until they are each 1m, 30 in length, and no longer elongate; we prune in the first year, so as to obtain three buds placed at a distance of 0m, 10 to 0*, 16 from each other; two of these buds Horizontal cordon. are converted into spurs at the next pruning; the third, on the other hand, and the furthest apart, is intended to extend the arm or cordon. During the summer, the shoots intended to form spurs are tied vertically to the trellis, while the shoot with which the cordon is to be extended is extended horizontally. At the second pruning, the two spurs are cut back to two eyes, and the terminal branch is again pruned so as to produce three buds spaced from Om, 10 to Om, 16 apart; two of these buds are trellised vertically, and the third is extended horizontally, as in the previous year, and so on, until each arm is 1.30 m long; at this point, the terminal shoot prunes itself into a spur. Each arm should have eight spurs on the upper side; this is achieved by completely removing the eyes on the underside of the cordon. It is well known that the eyes at the bottom of the buds in the vine are very small and very close together; there are at least six of them over a length of Om,005; when the bud is pruned too long, i.e. to Om,030 or Om,055, these small eyes die out and do not grow; but if you prune above them, they develop perfectly and give very beautiful bunches. Skilled gardeners are well aware of this: they always prune the spurs to 0m, 002, and sometimes less; this is why these kinds of branches never elongate in their hands. Pruning shears are much more convenient than pruning knives for trimming spurs to this length of Om, 002. If, after pruning, we see more than two buds developing on a spur, we remove the surplus, even if the shoots bear bunches; two buds with two good bunches each are better than a larger number with mediocre bunches. As young buds can easily come unstuck, you must be careful not to try to force them, when you first plant them, to suddenly take a direction opposite to the one they naturally take. Until then, simply remove tendrils and shoots without bunches, and remove and pinch the tips of those which, after flowering, seem to want to grow too much. It's a good idea, however, for the buds to extend as far as the cordon above them, but none should go beyond it: everything that goes beyond it is removed. When the grapes are close to full size, it is a good idea to sprinkle or water them with a hand pump. This softens the skin and coarsens the berry, which is then carefully uncovered by removing a few leaves, so that it can be exposed to the sun, take on color and improve its quality: if you intend to keep grapes on the trellis until the hard frosts, enclose them in paper or horsehair bags eight or ten days before they ripen. Our average climate is not conducive to vine propagation by seed. We must therefore use the only means we have used up to now for propagation, which are marcotte, cuttings and grafting. Three types of grafting are used in vineyards: 1° herbaceous grafting with and on growing shoots; 2° split grafting on wood that is one or more years old; 3° shuttle grafting. O TETNGIENIUARRE Vine disease known as Oidium tuckéri. This alteration appears in the form of a grayish-white efflorescence, first on leaves and young buds, whose development it suspends, then on the bunches themselves, whose growth it stops. The skin of the berries hardens, takes on a tawny hue, the berries split, acquire a bitter taste and corrupt before ripening. Attacked leaves and buds are covered with brown spots, the leaves fall off, and, if the disease is intense, the buds themselves are disrupted right down to their base, so that not only that year's harvest is lost, but even that of the following year; and if the vines themselves are subjected to this scourge for two or three years in succession, the vines eventually perish. Numerous methods have been tried to combat this disease, which is threatening one of our most important products, but the safest and most effective method is that employed by Mr. Rose Charmeux de Thomery, which consists of using the flower of sulfur spread dry on all the green parts of the vine. The sulfur must be spread evenly over all green parts (buds, leaves and bunches). M. Charmeux recognized, and it has since been observed everywhere, that the action of sulfur is all the greater when it is applied at the first onset of the disease, and even before it appears. It is therefore advisable to apply a first sulfur treatment before flowering; a second when the grapes are as big as small shot; a third when they have reached two-thirds of their size. Rarely is a fourth sulphur treatment necessary. Two types of instrument are used to spread the sulfur on the vines: 1° the tassel box; 2° the bellows. This concludes the task we have undertaken to popularize horticulture in the countryside. However, we do not pretend to have done a better job than our masters in the art of horticulture, the Bon Jardinier, Dubreuil, Raoul, Isabeau and Lachaume, who have been reliable guides for us in many circumstances; but what we wanted to write was a simple, clear, concise treatise, suitable for all hands, especially children. We hope to have achieved the goal we have set ourselves, and we shall consider ourselves very fortunate if we can contribute to hastening the progress of an art which is the source of much enjoyment for all those who devote themselves to it. For fifteen years I have been cultivating the land, and for fifteen years I have suffered from the absence of a special treatise which I could consult without fail and which would provide me with positive information and foolproof instructions. This treatise is intended to fill the gap. It is the fruit of long experience and can be consulted with profit. May it spare young people hardship and loss of money, may it help the memory of older workers, may it provide men of fortune with the means to take an interest in the land and receive from it all that it can give, may it inspire all friends of our beautiful soil of France with the taste and the will to increase its prosperity and wealth. And he will have obtained the fortune I dreamed of for him, and which all my efforts have tended to secure for him. Paris, 1869. 1. PONCE. CHAPTER ONE GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS To produce a lot in a small space, to provide vegetables to feed a thousand people by cultivating a plot of land whose surface area would not feed fifty if ordinary processes were applied, and if art did not know how to help nature, such is the problem posed every day to market gardening in the Paris area, And every day, the problem has its solution, although the difficulties accumulate as the vast city crosses its boundaries, erecting new shelters to house new guests, covering the formerly cultivated soil with buildings and forcing those who feed it to seek more sun and space. The horticulturalist occupies a plot of land rarely less than 7,000 meters deep and rarely more than 10,000 meters, all in one piece. They rarely own the land themselves, and pay a higher rent the closer they are to Les Halles, and therefore to the center of their business. However, it takes exceptional circumstances or a poor understanding of his profession for him not to achieve, after a certain number of years' work, a modest ease and, for intelligent people, a justly deserved and always legitimately earned fortune. Competition is a useful source of emulation among market gardeners. Vegetables sold early are excellent value; in season, they provide the grower with enough to live on and pay his expenses; late, they provide a new harvest that is productive in terms of ecus. The soil lends itself admirably to this combination of the demands of human appetite. Siliceous soils, sufficiently fertilized and mixed with a skilfully combined loam, produce early crops. Clay soils, under the same conditions, only produce late; but when the siliceous soil has produced its early crops early, and can no longer retain the moisture needed by food plants, the clay soil will begin to produce its own, and will give late crops in the middle of the hottest weather, because of its property of retaining water like a sponge and delaying the decomposition of fertilizers. The smallest plot in a market garden should not be left unoccupied for more than twenty-four hours. Any plant uprooted must be replaced immediately if the soil does not require a new way; where no plants are to be seen, the worker must be seen at work. As market gardens are always close to housing and population centers, they do not lack fertilizer, but fertilizer is insufficient to achieve the goal of this type of farming, as nature must be forced to provide spring in the middle of winter, and summer during the still short and uncertain days of spring. The soil of the market garden has no rest; although it nourishes the most exhausting plants, its master returns to it, as and when it loses, the elements it needs to comfort itself and provide vegetation with new production. Manure provides the heat, nitrogen, carbon, hydrogen, sulfur, phosphorus and calcium salts it needs. Wooden boxes covered with glass frames protect the young plants from contact with the cold air during the harsh season. A warm, humid temperature, favorable to vegetation, then reigns under these chests, as the air, heated internally by the heat of the sun and the fermentation of manure, does not cool down, experience having shown that heat does pass through the glass in the company of light, but that heat alone can no longer pass through it and remains trapped. In addition to chests, glass cloches are used to retain the heat of the sun's rays. The shape of the market garden is usually that of a more or less elongated rectangle; this is the shape that should be sought, as it is easier to supervise and divide up. The plot must be fenced off, both against marauders, animals and people, and against the wind. The best fence is a good wall; but if you can't use one, at least fence with a good chestnut trellis, against which you can apply straw mats, called windbreaks. The land should be divided into rectangles, with the longest dimension facing south. These rectangles should be set square, and those intended for frames should have a dimension of 21 meters to accommodate 15 frames, i.e. 20 meters for the frames and one meter for a pathway and two supports. They are laid out end-to-end in this way, throughout the southern exposure. When it becomes impossible to obtain a new 21-meter line, transverse lines formed in the same way are laid out at sunset. This is called making squares. A 2.34-metre rectangular board that runs the full length of the wall or windbreak established on the south side is known as the "costière"; this board is separated from a second one by a 33-centimetre path. This second board is called the counter-costiere. A new path separates the counter-costiere from the space reserved for the frames or the square. The other boards after the square are laid out in the same way as the upstand and counter-upper. The border and counter-border are repeated on the opposite side of the garden; only the second counter-border is divided into paths every 20 meters for watering. As far as possible, the grower's dwelling should be on the roadside and at the southern corner. It generally consists of a basement used as a store, a first floor and a second floor; next to this is the stable, the shed and the hangar for equipment; in front is an open space containing the well, the manege or the steam pump, the reservoir, if there is one, the tank for washing produce for sale, and the manure dump. Abundant water at one's discretion is the essential condition for market gardening. Prior to 1859, all such gardens were watered using the following system. A fulling pump driven by a manege lifted the water above ground, through a pipe, into a tank that fed a system of barrels buried at ground level, connected by terracotta tubes anointed with bitumen. These tubes do not lead directly to the barrel; a lead pipe, fitted with a stopper or swan-necked tap, runs from the buried pipe at a distance of at least 40 centimetres or 50 centimetres at most, and empties its contents into the barrel. Once the barrel is full, the pipe is plugged with the cork or tap. In some operations, the barrels are connected to each other by the pipe, so that the whole system fills up successively; this is a bad method, as the last barrel can only be filled when the others are full, whereas the system described allows water to be supplied to one, several or all the barrels at once, as desired. Buried barrels hold 2 hectoliters or more, are strapped in iron, and tarred on the outside to prevent rotting. They are placed 10 meters 66 apart, i.e. every four planks. The worker draws water from them using two copper watering cans. The author of this book has adopted, and had many of his colleagues adopt, a less primitive and much more advantageous watering system, the layout of which is his own invention. The barbaric barrel system takes a considerable amount of space away from production, and the men who do the watering are barefoot in the sodden earth all day long. Their work is very time-consuming, and is perhaps the most arduous of their profession: how many pleurisies, chest fluxions and rheumatisms have been contracted in such circumstances! - Barrels on the ground, at the crossroads of trails, have been the cause of deplorable accidents. There are hardly any years in which the newspapers don't record a few deaths of children or old people drowned in market-garden barrels, some as a result of the carelessness inherent in their age, others as a result of failing eyesight. All human motives: enjoyment, because the land watered by the new system no longer presents the muddy, odorous cesspools found around every barrel of the old system; 1. interest, because land is gained and labor saved; and finally, duty, because all danger of disease and death is eliminated for one's own and for others; all human motives, we say, must urge market gardeners to adopt the new watering system. In this system, which we shall describe in detail later, the water from the food pump, raised above the ground to a height of 5 to 6 meters, is poured into a sheet metal tank of 20 to 22 cubic meters capacity, more or less. The terracotta pipe is replaced by sandstone pipes solidly joined together by a broken ring embedded in cement, or by cast-iron or lead pipes. Barrels are eliminated. In their place, however, there is a water intake to which a 15-meter-long rubber tube is connected, fitted with a hose and a watering can head. The expensive taps of ordinary water intakes are replaced by a tubular piece of rubber, clamped to the cast-iron intake by means of a collar and closed when not in use by means of a pressure screw. The connection to the sprinkler pipe is made by means of a sleeve clamped by the elasticity of the rubber. Thanks to this system, the worker can water with dry feet, without getting wet or bending over; the lack of fatigue attaches him to this type of work, the most essential to his profession, and which was formerly performed only with bad humor due to the fatigue and dangers to which the worker was exposed. The market gardener cultivates all the food plants that grow naturally in our climate; however, if he confined himself to those that are easy to grow and require the same amount of time to develop as field crops, he wouldn't be spending his money. This is why he limits himself to plants that can be cultivated relatively quickly, and whose normal growth time he reduces by using the instruments at his disposal to obtain the temperature and humidity levels he requires. He also cultivates certain annual plants from warmer climates, which are much sought-after by Parisian appetites, and which acquire finer and more delicate qualities through this artificial cultivation. The honorable profession of market gardener counts only honest, hard-working people among its members. All of them, with the two indispensable aids of health and drive, achieve their goals. Women are in charge of sales and harvesting: women's activity is one of the first conditions for success. All the market gardener's commercial operations are cash-based. What he hasn't been able to sell during the day on the Halles square is put into the greenhouse and put back on sale the next day. In general, he has to sell at the day's price; this can sometimes be a disappointment, but the stale harvest the next day will rarely be worth more than the day before, so it's with regret that he turns to his Paris greenhouse. As we said at the start of this chapter, he has two problems to solve: arriving first for a certain product, or arriving last; in both cases there's a business to be done. The interval is just a routine trade that still pays its way, and is by no means to be scorned. A great deal of progress has been made over the last few years, and many new crops have been introduced, especially since Les Halles opened its doors to goods from the south of France brought to Paris by the railroads, which had to compete with them. This is a warning to market gardeners to try to be one step ahead and do better; the interest and honor of the trade oblige them to do so, and they will not fail. COMPOSITION OF A MARAICHER'S GARDEN We think it useful, for the intelligence of the work and the good understanding of the layout of a market gardener's garden, to describe one, such as it exists: it is that of the author of this book, who has endeavored to have an establishment without rival in the vicinity of Paris and who, self-love aside, believes he has succeeded. The cultivated surface area is 11,000 square meters. Watering is by hose, according to an economical system invented by the author of this book. The equipment includes a two-horsepower steam engine for the fulling pump when the horse is occupied, and a manege for the same service when the horse is available. - The whole is worth 1,700 francs for the pump, and 2,000 francs for the machine. The water is raised, by means of a lead pipe, to the upper part of a bolted sheet metal tank, with a capacity of 22 cubic meters. This tank is placed on a platform, 5.60 meters above ground level. A massive frame and masonry supports the whole. - The whole cost 1,300 francs. Two large lead pipes carry the water down to sandstone pipes buried 40 centimetres below ground. In these pipes, the water is subjected to a pressure that varies between one atmosphere when the tank is full and one third atmospense is 88 francs. The water mains are made up of 550 meters of sandstone pipe, to which 70 water intakes are fitted for watering purposes. Watering is by means of two rubber tubes, each 14 meters long, onto which a copper lance is mounted, ending in a watering can head. - Expenditure: 1,582 francs for the pipe, and 260 francs for the rubbers and their lance. 950 frames and their boxes, and 3,500 bells are used for the cultivation of early fruit and vegetables. 800 straw mats are used to cover the frames in times of frost during the night, and to protect the plants from the effects of the cold. - Total cost: 15,700 francs. 4 spades, 2 iron rakes, 4 iron shovels, 2 rakes, 4 planters, 2 ropes, 2 squares: this is the plowing equipment. - Value: 60 francs. In addition to the head of the establishment and the lady of the house, the staff consists of three servants, one of whom is in charge of taking the crops for sale to the Halles and bringing manure back to the farm; the rest of his time is taken up with gardening work, while his two colleagues devote all their time to it. - Annual expenditure is 1,620 francs. Two daughters, one of whom devotes her time half to sales, half to harvesting, and a day laborer during the summer, complete the staff. They are paid 600 francs a year. Using the above equipment and personnel, we produce the following per year: 24 hot layers, producing carrots, black lettuce and spinach. 12 hot-air layers, producing radishes. 40 cold beds, where parsley, sorrel, parsnips, various lettuces and cauliflower are harvested. 36 banks of romaine, some under cloches, others cold grown with carrots. Melons and tomatoes require 70 to 80 trenches, where the plants are placed under cloches, and a few trenches for early green beans. Depending on the season, the rest of the land is planted with cauliflower, apple cabbage, onions, spring onions, civet, parsley, chervil, sorrel, pink and black radishes, leeks, carrots, romaine, lettuce and spinach, all grown outdoors and cold. An establishment set up in this way provides the following average harvests per year: During the spring season: 10,800 feet of black lettuce, hot-grown. 240 bunches of spinach, obtained in the same way; average weight per bunch: 1,500 gr. 1,600 bunches of carrots, obtained in the same way; average weight per bunch: 2 kilograms. 1,000 bunches of radishes, obtained both hot and cold. 11,000 feet of Georges lettuce, cold-grown. 500 bunches of sorrel, cold-grown; average weight per bunch: 1 kilog. 500 gr. 500 bunches of parsley, cold-grown; average weight per bunch: 1 kilog. 10,500 feet of green romaine, cold-grown. 1,000 bunches of cold-grown caroites; average weight: 2 kilograms. 1,500 plants of cold-grown cauliflower. 8,000 plants of Georges and red lettuce, grown in costières. 6,000 vines of red lettuce, bedded. 3,500 feet of blond romaine in squares. 2,500 bunches of radishes, 3 handfuls each (the handful is the commercial radish bunch). 6,000 feet of cabbage-apples. 1,200 bunches of onions: average weight: 2 kilos. 1,200 bunches of seedling leeks; average weight: 2 kilos. 800 bunches of spring onions; average weight: 1 kilo. 1,200 bunches of spring onions; average weight: 1 kilo. 300 bundles of field sorrel; average weight: 1 kilo. 500. 500 callets de régence, harvested in the melon patch; average weight: 1 kilog. 1,200 bunches of carrots; average weight: 2 kilog. 200 bunches of chervil; average weight: 1 kilog. 200 bunches of civet; average weight: 400 gr. All the crops detailed above are harvested before July. The summer season begins at this time, and includes: 3,000 melon plants, on trenches with frames and cloches, and on beds with compost. 4,500 tomato plants, producing 5,000 callets of fruit for sale. 5,000 dozens of beautiful fruit. 30,000 plants of chicory, romaine and lettuce, obtained from the counter-planting of white celery. 10,000 plants of the same species, obtained from the counter-planting of escarole. 12,000 plants of escarole, also obtained in cauliflower squares by counter-planting. 120 small mannes of long pepper. 3,000 feet of autumn cauliflowers. 1,000 bunches of carrots, harvested in October. 1,000 bunches of transplanted leeks. This harvest ends in November, when the winter season begins, with crops including: 6,000 feet of celeriac, planted in June. 35,000 plants of white celery, planted in July. 600 callets of lamb's lettuce. 100 bundles of chervil. This sale ends in February, when the harvest and sale of early spring vegetables begins. It is obvious to everyone that the harvest we have just detailed can be more or less abundant, more or less good in quality, more or less productive, according to the needs and tastes of the day: the great variation in selling prices imposes absolute silence on this item. Set........ 2,500 Total annual expenses... 16,830 The dwelling comprises one floor over ground floor and cellar, with living room, dining room, bedroom, kitchen and servants' quarters. Market gardeners rarely have a living room; everything else is necessary. Some market gardeners specialize in one crop, because they have a real superiority in it, and because the product compensates them for the care they give to the plant they have specially adopted, and even provides them with a considerable profit. It's up to everyone involved in horticulture to find their own path. In any case, the trade feeds its master, and that's the main thing. When the land is walled, the walls can be planted with vines, peach trees or apricot trees, which can be used to generate income or for staff consumption. Work distribution. The head of the establishment is absent as rarely as possible: his presence is necessary to direct and supervise the work, which he almost always shares. Getting up for him and for the dorestics specially attached to the cultivation usually takes place in summer at 5 a.m.; however, some jobs require getting up between 3.30 and 4 a.m., or even spending the whole night. When rising takes place in these exceptional circumstances, or when the night has had to be devoted to work, the necessary rest takes place during the heat of the following day. The housewife gets up between one and two o'clock, depending on the distance she has to cover to get to Les Halles. The three of them set off in the carriage loaded with products to be sold. The servant's role is to drive the car, unload the produce and return after loading manure in the stables, where it is bought by the year or month. The housewife makes her sale to the fruit-growers without moving from her place, while the daughter carries the goods sold in a hood to the carriages parked some distance away, which the fruit-growers have brought with them; this is how the delivery takes place. It's easy to see why such hard work calls for a first meal; the necessary bread is brought from home, and the rest of the food can be found around Les Halles. There's something for every taste. Without going into further detail, we can say, without fear of contradiction, that market gardeners feed their staff well, a necessary condition for the hard work and exceptional fatigue of their profession. For workers who stay at home, the first meal is at six o'clock in the morning, and generally consists of bread at discretion and 20 centilitres of wine. The second meal takes place at nine o'clock, when the entire staff is assembled. Immediately afterwards, the women and servants in charge of the Halle take a two-hour rest and then get down to work. The third meal takes place at two o'clock. This is immediately followed by cultivation work by all the men, and harvesting work by all the women. At seven o'clock, the next day's sale has to be prepared, so all the staff are busy loading, which is immediately followed by the fourth meal or supper, which immediately precedes bedtime. It's hardly before nine o'clock that the market gardener and his staff can take their well-earned rest. It's clear from the above that, in this profession, the woman's activity and intelligence is the first condition for success. In charge of sales, she must not only apply herself to getting a good product from what she brings, but also guess what the needs are and indicate to her husband the species of plant that is lacking on the market and whose cultivation would be advantageous. She must adorn her merchandise, that is, give it that coquettish look without which the most beautiful products go unnoticed, be affable with the customer and willingly lend herself to any services he may require to help with transport. On the way back, she thinks about the day's provisions for meals and other family needs. No sooner has she taken a few moments' rest than she has to supervise the kitchen, take care of the dishes and laundry, then preside over the making of the boots, mantles and callets for the merchandise, examining them one by one to see if her prescriptions have been well understood, the washing well done, the measure properly filled. All this may seem very difficult to accomplish, but it's all done every day, and households where the woman's activity and intelligence are lacking are the exception. In the establishment we have just reviewed, the new watering method is being put into practice. As a point of comparison, we'd like to give you the cost of the barrels if we'd stuck to the old system. It would still have required 550 meters of pipe. 1 large barrel................ 15 1 large stopcock.......... 30 70 barrels, supply and installation... 840 70 taps................... 700 70 meters of lead pipe... 210 4 pairs of watering cans............ 120 Total costs..... 2,465 fr. The sprinkler system for the same plot costs 2,540 fr. The difference is therefore the tiny sum of 75 francs, which is well repaid by 70 meters of land returned to cultivation, not to mention the savings in labor. Anyone intending to become a market gardener must complete an apprenticeship of at least four or five years; he must remain single until he feels ready to establish himself, and work for others during this time; his establishment as an owner dates from his marriage. It's not a matter of taking a wife from an indeterminate class of society; the first condition of success is that the woman he takes should be familiar with work and sales: so it's from among his daily workmates that the aspiring market gardener chooses his fiancée. This habit, which has perpetuated the customs of the old guilds among our class of workers, is one of the first necessities of the trade. The difference in the work of each of the spouses is so clear-cut that they cannot work without the other, and the death of one of the spouses almost always leads fatally to the disastrous sale of the business when this cruel separation comes too soon. To the husband: production; to the wife: selling the products and forecasting needs, in conditions that early experience must have prepared her for. Exposed from two o'clock in the morning to all the inclemencies of the seasons, forced to be constantly on guard against the tricks of the not always very scrupulous buyers at the Halles, obliged to think about and provide for the needs of the household before enjoying a few hours of well-earned rest, the market gardener's wife has no other satisfaction than to see her savings accumulate little by little and protect her family from need. She is the strong woman of Scripture: she reigns in the interior of her home, surrounded by the love of her family and the respect of those she occupies. What a hard life, even compared to that of simple workers in other professions! But what a difference in results! The market gardeners were right to preserve the esprit de corps that ensures daily life and prosperity for all their members. However, market gardeners' wives and daughters also have their days of coquetry and festivity. Saint-Fiacre's Day, always religiously celebrated, and wedding feasts provide opportunities to adorn themselves in pompous finery. It's then, after a hearty meal seasoned with good appetite and open merriment, that the ties that will later become the solid knots of a matched marige begin. It should be added that, as a result of this corporate structure, with all market gardeners forming a single family, marriages are made with full knowledge of the facts, and none of the spouses can be fooled by the illusions so common in unions contracted among other members of society. Once the marriage has been decided, it's time to find a suitable plot of land. If the couple is wealthy, they will do well to buy the land and equipment of a market gardener who is going out of business. It's true that this will put them into debt, but they'll only have one creditor to wait on. What's more, the equipment and manure will enable him to produce immediately, and therefore make money. If, in such a case, you wanted to buy new land, you'd have to buy the necessary equipment and manure at short notice, and you'd have to make large payments before you had a single product to sell: you'd be courting ruin. When it comes to buying land, you need to consult your means and balance them in such a way that the commitments you make do not exceed three quarters of the income less anticipated needs, the other quarter being intended as a reserve against unforeseen circumstances. New plots of land are only suitable for market gardeners with their own equipment and a sufficient quantity of manure and potting soil to immediately bring their gardens into production. To put things in perspective, we can say that funds below 5,000 francs and above 30,000 francs are rare. FERTILIZERS AND LAND WORKING The only fertilizer used for market gardening is manure from stables, or failing that, from cowsheds. Anything else would only imperfectly fulfil the purpose: the first condition, in fact, is to develop heat, the second to nourish the plants. Artificial fertilizers overloaded with nitrogen cannot fulfill the first condition, as the heat produced by their decomposition is insignificant due to their small volume. Market gardeners obtain manure from stables by means of subscriptions with transport contractors, omnibus and small carriage admistrations, cavalry regiment barracks, etc. The subscription is for a fee. Subscriptions are concluded for a fixed sum of so much per month and per horse, depending on the market price on the day of the contract and the quantity of manure. Police regulations prohibit horse owners from maintaining manure heaps in their yards beyond the quantity supplied daily by the stables, when this manure is not at a regulated distance from neighboring properties. Stable manure is supplied by feeders. Stable manure is colder than stable manure and decomposes more slowly, making it particularly suitable for siliceous soils, whereas stable manure is an indispensable ingredient for clay soils. The two manures should therefore be mixed in proportion to the amount of clay and silica in the soil. If you have enough stable manure, you can do without it, and it's even preferable to do without. As the soil is expensive and must produce as much as possible, the market gardener's manure bin, although containing a considerable quantity of this fertilizer, must take up as little space as possible, so it gains in height what it is denied in surface area. It is shaped like a quadrilateral, placed on a flat surface that is as impermeable as possible. In general, the length is no more than twice the width, and the height no more than two-thirds the length. Manure is piled up with a fork and trodden down with the foot as it is unloaded. A sort of chimney is built into the center of the heap, into which other horizontal ducts lead on all sides, so that fresh air penetrates the heap and neutralizes the excess heat produced by fermentation, which can go so far as to ignite the mass. All too often, this precaution is neglected, and fire breaks out in these fertilizers, which can only be extinguished by spreading out the heap; for water, which cannot penetrate the incandescent center, is little help against this kind of fire. In such cases, a season's harvest is lost, both through the loss of the manure itself and through the spreading. As market gardening establishments are located in the middle of homes or similar establishments, manure is spread at the expense of the premises where the fire occurs, and on land in full cultivation. By delaying decomposition, he preserves gas and heat for his crops, which would otherwise be lost to the atmosphere, to his detriment and that of his neighbors. This fire hazard means that manure piles should be kept away from dwellings. We place it at least 10 meters from the premises inhabited by the market gardener, so as to monitor it more easily and to quickly multiply the air holes if we feel the need. It should also be placed close to the well, so that help can be provided more effectively in the event of a disaster. As humidity encourages decomposition, and abundant water carries away soluble parts, it should be protected as much as possible from rainwater. To this end, we make it as wide as possible from base to top, slope the edges and line the top with the longest straw least penetrated by urine and excrement. The manure heap thus constructed contains fresh manure at the top, which will produce a lot of heat as soon as it is buried and wet, but will not become fertilizer until some time after burial, at least eight days. The second, intermediate part between the top and the bottom, contains half-hot, half-fertilized manure, which is ideal for planting delicate plants requiring both abundant warmth and nourishment. The other third is made up of manure, suitable for robust plants that require nothing more than nourishment. year on a small surface such as that of a market gardener's garden leaves behind a thick layer of humus known as compost. Potting soil is composed almost entirely of carbon, with a few particles of silica and clay; repeated watering has removed the most soluble parts. Used on its own, it is unsuitable for crops intended to be grown quickly, but mixed with soil it is an excellent fertilizer for cold crops. It is also a sales product for other crops. Manufacturers of artificial fertilizers, notably poudrette, buy potting soil, which acts both as an absorbent and as a disinfectant for faecal matter, thanks to the carbon it contains, and which finds new soluble combinations in this addition, once again becoming a powerful fertilizer for field crops. Flower growers also use it to make the compost known as "terre de bruyère"; to increase its fertility, they add colombine or poulaite. Finally, in ornamental gardens, the soil in baskets and flowerbeds is covered with it, to keep the soil fresh and to bring out the greenness of the foliage and the brightness of the flowers against the velvety black background. The market gardener retains only as much compost as he needs to cover his fertilizers and form a layer of topsoil in which his produce can take root. When the frames are moved, after the crops have been harvested in layers, we find, in addition to the compost, patches of straw that have not been completely destroyed and still contain soluble parts. This is known as "fond de couches" or mulch, and is a fertilizer that market gardeners often use and keep. This light, cold manure is used as a cover for spring seedlings; it keeps the young plant moist and protects it from the scorching spring sun and the night frosts of the same period. A few trials have been carried out in order to avoid the immense quantity of manure required for early crops. Layers without manure were created, heated in the same way as greenhouse tarpaulins, using a thermosiphon, i.e. a hot-water circulation system. The soil in the tarpaulin was then fertilized with a powerful fertilizer such as guano, colombine or poulaite. These trials produced results, but they were costly in terms of fuel and, above all, manpower; a worker was needed to accomplish the task that manure does on its own and at no cost. What's more, neither potting soil nor mulch could be produced for cold cultivation. These disadvantages led to the abandonment of these trials. The first condition for the existence of a market garden is a good supply of manure. The second is the intelligent use of this resource, which will be the subject of the following chapters. Preparatory work and ploughing for cold and hot cultivation. In discussing how to lay out a market garden, we said that it was divided into plots 21 meters long and 2.34 meters wide. Now let's suppose we have a new plot of land, and we'll prepare it for its intended use as follows. The land will be chosen in such a way as to have a well that is not too deep and that provides water at all times; if this condition cannot be easily met, a tube will be drilled and sunk deep enough to reach a good underground water table. The land will be levelled, if it is not already, and first ploughed to the depth of a spade-head. During this operation, all roots and weeds will be removed, and only then will the garden be laid out, starting with the hillside and counter-hillside as mentioned above. All the paths will be cordoned off, and the soil will be kept higher than that of the planks, so that the water from the moorings runs off well into the planks and not into the paths, where it would only make mud without profit. Once the first ploughing has been completed and the beds and frame squares have been laid out, the first cold harvest can be obtained in new soil, taking care to protect the surface of the soil with a good cover of half-consumed manure in spring, and compost at any other time. To this end, the necessary quantity of manure (5 to 10 centimetres thick) is brought to the smoking bed with a hood. The plank is spaded at one end and the earth is thrown away at the other. A first trench is thus opened, and a layer of manure is buried in it, to be covered by the earth removed with the spade for the second trench. The second trench is then filled with manure and covered by the soil from the third, and so on until the end. This ploughing method is only used for cold cultivation; the manure used comes from the bottom of the layers mixed with soil from the same source. After ploughing, the clods are broken up with a rake and the soil is levelled, taking care to remove any stones, roots or weeds found. This precaution is essential, especially in the case of mercurial and common spurge, commonly known as "foirolle" and "réveil-matin", plants which invade new land in surprising numbers. After this, the land is ready to receive the seedlings or plantations it is to receive. The choice of manure is not a matter of indifference, because if you put new manure in cold crops, you will have too much heat and the plant will grow too fast, then wither or even perish immediately without having vegetated; moreover, this method will make the weeds grow back whose seeds have not yet been destroyed by the fermentation of the manure. When potting soil is lacking, we make a floor from a light layer of manure, which we water abundantly to help it decompose rapidly. It is then used as mulch and cover. As soon as a bed is empty, it is ploughed again and fertilized in the same way. It's said that it takes three years to make a good marsh; this is true, but you shouldn't imagine that the land remains unproductive during this time; it simply means that after three years, there will be too much fertilizer and the market gardener will have potting soil to sell. If fertilizer is lacking, it will take twice as long. To make a hot layer, the soil is first ploughed with a spade, then levelled. On a bed 20 metres long and 1m 66 wide, a 40-centimetre-thick bed of old, dry horse manure is laid, well handled and stirred with a fork. This layer of manure is tamped down to bind and even it out, then covered 2. with a 25-centimeter-thick bed of potting soil. Continue the same work as many times as you want to make layers, but if you make only one layer, it must be at least two meters wide, including paths and shoulders. The paths are taken at the expense of the manure layer, and the shoulders are the manure accumulated at each end of the layer. To cultivate melons, we make what we call melon trenches; the bed is broken up with a spade and all the earth removed with a hood: we thus have a trench 20 meters long by 1m 66 wide, and Om 40 deep. This trench is filled with old, dry horse manure, or, if there's a shortage, with fresh manure mixed with half mulch and half potting soil: the latter method has the disadvantage of heating unevenly and, in places, giving off blasts of fire that destroy the plants by burning the roots. The whole, well watered and trampled, is covered with 20 centimetres of soil. Before laying the soil, a series of wooden boxes lined up end to end were placed on the trench, to be covered by fifteen glass frames. These boxes are fitted with feet at each of the four corners, and with crosspieces to maintain their spacing; their cross-section across the width is a right-angled trapezoid, with the large base facing north and the small base facing south. Each trench is covered by five trunks, each closed by three frames. These are oak frames, divided into three parts by small iron bars, to which the glazing is applied with pins and putty. Each sash is fitted with two handles to lift it; it is opened to the north and south by means of a rack generally cut from a flat piece of wood such as a piece of planking; the edge of the sash bears on one of the teeth of the rack, which rests on the edge of the box. This is called giving air. The temperature of a layer can be judged by plunging your hand into the ground. It can be determined using a thermometer. The space between two rows of frames is filled with manure, known as a pathway. New manure is used for hot cultivation, and is called "rechauds". Ados are boards sloping towards the south, on which spring and autumn seedlings are sown under cloches at a time when it is prudent to be wary of the north wind. Each ados is designed to receive three rows of cloches placed in staggered rows, after a provisional sowing of radishes or other plants. To make an ados, a chalk line is stretched in the direction in which it should slope, i.e. from sunrise to sunset, over a length of 20 meters. Beginning at one end of the chord, spade the soil to the distance of a spade shoe, and throw it back onto the bare part. This creates the beginning of an embankment. Once the first row has been completed, the second is started by throwing the soil back onto the first slope. We continue in this way until we have a sloping board 1.83 m wide and with a slope height of Om 33. As we have said, the slopes are designed to receive cloches, glass vases Om 33 in diameter and the same height, which owe their name to their particular shape. Cloches are used for seedlings and transplants in nurseries. The ados are laid out in such a way that they receive sun all day long on the shortest days, while their steep slope protects them from cold north winds and exposes them to hot south winds. Frames and ados should be fitted with a sufficient number of doormats to cover the glass during frosty periods at night. These permanently installed mats are rolled to the top of the slopes, so that they can be quickly unrolled as shade, and consequently frost, gains the board they are intended to cover. When a recent layer ceases to give heat, it's because it's too dry; a slight dampening soon brings the temperature back to the desired point by reviving the fermentation of the manure. Experience is the best guide in such cases. Harrowing in market gardens is almost always carried out with a three-pronged fork that is very close together; some practitioners use an instrument called a harrow, which we feel works less perfectly. Sowing is done either broadcast or in rows for all plants that must remain in place. To broadcast seed, the gardener holds a light handful of seed in his hand and lets it pass between his fingers, swinging his arm back and forth. A bed is usually sown with two handles, dividing the width in two. When the seed is very fine, there is a risk of sowing too thickly. This is avoided by mixing the seed with very dry compost. After sowing, the seed is harrowed with a fork, then the bed is tamped, an operation also known as ploughing. The edges of the bed are then covered with soil using a rake, and covered with a light layer of fine compost. If the weather is dry, the operation is finished off with a basining. lument in the same way. Row sowing is used for supplies. The line is drawn with a hoe or foot along a string. The seed is carefully scattered along the line; the soil is brought back to the furrow with both feet, then raked in; the potting soil is spread and basined as in the previous case. Nursery sowing is used for plants that cannot be sown in situ, such as lettuces and romaine. Under a frame, it's a simple broadcast sowing; under cloches, a pinch of seeds is sown; on ados, in the circumference traced by a bell that has first been placed there. As soon as the young plant has developed two leaves, pull out the seedling and prick it out with your finger, under a frame, five centimetres apart and staggered. Twenty to forty young plants are placed in the same way under a bell jar. As the young plants grow and get in each other's way, the distance between them is doubled. At the end of the transplanting process, no more than five and no less than three plants should remain under each bell, and no more than thirty and no less than twenty plants under each frame. Very young seedlings are transplanted with the finger, large seedlings with the planter; in all cases, the soil must be firmly pressed against the roots with the hand or planter. In market gardens, weeding is done by hand to avoid injuring plants close to the weeds to be removed. Hoeing is carried out as often as the soil hardens. Experience shows when and how it should be done. We call edging the operation that consists in raising a bank around the bells to support the soil with which they are loaded. The kerbstone is a plank applied along these embankments, which is tamped down to bind and solidify the soil. The muted layers are laid in trenches half as wide as the ordinary layers, they receive the same thickness of manure and are covered with a bed of earth. In very cold weather, hot cultivation layers need to be reheated. Ordinary paths and bunds are replaced with new manure, which is forked in every week, and new manure is added as soon as it becomes apparent that the heat is dropping. It's at the time of ploughing and bed reshuffling that you need to destroy the larvae of white grubs, moths, the larvae of earwigs known as fiddleheads, which destroy a good number of lettuce plants in spring, and the earwig, which destroys cauliflowers. Many ways have been suggested to destroy these enemies of plantations, the best of which is to pick them up by hand and kill them. Slugs and snails are another scourge. They are hunted down every day, as are caterpillars. Ants rarely establish themselves in marshes, and are rarely seen except in new fields. CULTIVATION TOOLS AND INSTRUMENTS MEANS OF MAINTAINING AND PRESERVING THEM Everyone is familiar with the spade; there are several shapes; the one we prefer is 36 centimetres high, 22 centimetres wide at the top, and 18 centimetres at the tip: it is attached to the handle by a socket, and the blade is very lightly girdled. The hoe, iron rake, rake, chalk line and planter deserve no special mention. The loader is a kind of horizontal T mounted on three 80-centimeter-high legs. The longest leg of the T carries two horn-shaped pieces of wood spaced apart. The loader is used to support hoods loaded with manure or vegetables. Carriages known as jardinières belong to the tapissière family; they are suspended on two wheels. For transporting manure, a cart is used which is suspended when it is used for two purposes, i.e. when it has to carry manure back from the hall. If it's used only for manure, no springs are used. Mechanically-made doormats are now more regular, more convenient and just as inexpensive as the doormats that used to be made by hand; however, for people who are far from manufacturing centers, it's a good idea to know how to make doormats yourself. For this purpose, we use a wooden frame 2 meters long and 1.33 meters wide. Three pegs are fixed to each end bar. With the frame thus laid out, we stretch a string from bottom to top over each corresponding peg; the top string being stopped on the peg by a slipknot, we leave it an excess length equal to twice the length of the frame. Once this is done, we spread a very even layer of rye straw over the frame, then a second layer of the same straw, with the ears pointing in the opposite direction to those of the first; we take the string holding the middle peg, and wind it onto a piece of wood which serves as a shuttle. Separate a pinch of straw by passing the shuttle from right to left over the straw and under the string, then pass it back into the loop formed earlier, and tighten the knot by flattening it between thumb and forefinger, and so on to the end where the string is stopped by a knot. The same procedure is followed for the two rows at the ends, and when the doormat is finished, the ears of corn are cut on each side to even out the edges. Doormats are made on rainy days and winter evenings, when it's impossible to attend to outside work. There are two types of sash boxes: they can either be made in one piece, or they can be dismantled. The former are made as follows: Take four pieces of 8-centimeter squared oak, cut two to 35-centimeter lengths, and the other two to 30-centimeter lengths. On the first two pieces, nail the two ends of a 30-centimeter-wide by 3.90-meter-long plank, leaving 5 centimeters of foot space for the oak pieces. On the other two pieces, we nail a plank 25 centimetres wide and 'm 90 long, leaving a further 5 centimetres free. The first board and its two feet form the back of the trunk, while the second board and its feet form the front. To close the trunk, we join them together by nailing a plank to each end, so that with all four feet in the same place, the upper part should slope 5 centimetres over a length of 1m 40. Since the quadrilateral thus formed is to accommodate three frames and a heavy load of soil, it's clear that these boards would warp if they weren't prevented by two bars, dividing the trunk into three equal parts, each of which is intended to be covered by a frame. These bars are cut into dovetails at each end, which fit into notches made in the boards for this purpose. When not in use, these chests are kept in the garden in the shade, and along a wall as far as possible; they are stacked dozens or dozens on top of each other, and last for five or six years. The short lifespan of fixed boxes, and the inconvenience of having to leave them unprotected after they have been in use, has led to the adoption of boxes that can be dismantled, and which, although initially requiring a larger outlay of capital, actually cost less, since they take up less space when not in use, and can be sheltered from the inclemency of the seasons. Market gardeners use two types: gambrel boxes and crutch boxes. The gambille consists of a 1.40-meter oak crossbeam nailed to two unequal legs, one 30 to 35 centimeters long, the other 20 to 25. Each of the legs carries an iron staple or hook on the outside, and the boards of the trunk engage in this staple by means of two notches. To cover a layer of fifteen frames, you need four gambilles and two heads for each end. These heads each consist of a plank, cut to match the slope, and mounted on two legs, each bearing a hook. The crutch is the essential part of the sliding chest. It's a 1.40 m long oak crosspiece nailed at each end to two solid legs of unequal length. These legs are notched, the front leg 11 centimeters deep, the rear 16 centimeters. These notches are the same thickness as the boards they are designed to accommodate. Two strong legs join each crutch to its two feet. Two plank ends are joined in the notch, and the planks are notched so that they fit snugly together. Ten boards are needed for each layer of fifteen frames. The heads are nailed to two notched feet like those of the crutch. The crutch trunk is superior to the gambrel trunk because of its simplicity and ease of repair; it is also less expensive and easier to assemble and disassemble, as the parts have less adherence to each other. The main disadvantage of the gambrel chest is that the wood has swollen with humidity, and the iron parts hold them so tightly together that they cannot be dismantled without damaging some of them; crutch chests, being made entirely of the same material, do not have this disadvantage. The bar is one of the most important parts of the chest, and it is generally at the point where the bars are assembled that the rotting of the chest boards begins. The tail bar, which requires a deep notch, must therefore be rejected; it has been replaced by the staple bar, fitted at each end with a right-angled iron plate attached Chassis Barre à queue Tête de Coffre à Gambilles Barre à Agrafe FI Tête de Coffre à Béquilles 4 Barre à Crochet R4II Mear A Lagnon. Lopont " D D D G G D D D D D D D D D . D D D D D D G D 1 the bar with two screws. The board is only notched a few millimeters thick, i.e. the thickness of the small iron plate. The use of the staple bar is obviously an improvement, but it does have its drawbacks: the staple is too weak to bear a heavy load, and after a few years, the screws play into the wood and the plate comes loose without the bar being able to be used again. The author of this book has invented a system of hooked bars, which he has been using with advantage for some time now. It consists of counter-soldering an iron plate in such a way that the hook screws are applied from underneath the bar. The plate is applied to the standing wood by a first right-angled bend, a second brings it back in the direction of the bar, and finally a third completes the hook. This system enables the bar to withstand heavy loads without inconvenience. Each hook costs just 12 to 15 centimes. You can do it yourself, but you need to take precautions, as strip iron is very brittle. You can be sure of success by reddening the iron and bending it onto a specially-made core. Market gardening frames all have the same shape and dimensions: they are rectangles measuring 1.40 m long by 30 m wide. They are glazed with twelve equal panes and four half-panes of half-double glass at the bottom, and have a handle on each opposite bar along the length. The oldest model is made entirely of oak and costs 12 or 1,300 francs with its box. It provides good service, and well-maintained paintwork lasts from fifteen to twenty years. Preference is given to an oak-framed sash, the small timbers of which are replaced by T-iron bars. One hundred frames of this model cost 1,400 to 1,500 francs with their boxes. They have the advantage over their predecessors of being less shady in the trunks and of lasting a few years longer. A third type of frame has three oak bars and the fourth, lowest bar is made of double-T iron. One hundred frames of this model are worth 1,600 to 1,700 francs. It is superior to the previous models in that the bottom bar, which is most exposed to humidity, rots very quickly in wooden-framed sashes. It therefore requires fewer repairs and lasts longer. Frames made entirely of iron are not used for market gardening: their high price, their weight, which makes them difficult to maneuver, and the conductivity of iron, which causes too much heat in the sun and heat loss in the dark, all combine to make market gardeners reject this type of frame. Before the tiles are laid, the frames are given two coats of ceruse white, crushed with linseed oil and petrol, and the brilliance of the white is extinguished with a little lampblack. The glazing putty is applied in the same shade with linseed oil and Spanish white mixed with black. A third coat is applied to the top after this putty has been applied. The frames should be returned to the shed as soon as the glass is no longer needed, i.e. as soon as the plants grown under them no longer fear the cold of the night. Beforehand, we take care to accustom them to the outside temperature by giving them plenty of air. Under the sheds, stacks of fifty frames are formed, sometimes more, depending on the height of the shelter and the space available, but the lower the stacks, the more manageable they are. The chests are left on the ground for a while, then stacked in the open air in the shade. Ten to twelve chests are stacked one on top of the other; if any can be dismantled, they are stored in the shed whenever possible, otherwise they are piled outside with their accessories, and secured with a layer of bedding. When the rains give us time to spare, we iron the frames one by one, replacing any missing glass or putty, as the market gardener needs to know how to use a diamond like a glazier; a coat of oil paint on top and underneath completes the maintenance work. It is customary, when removing bells before tightening them, to put one inside the other. This is a bad habit, because the inside of the bells is more or less damp, and this is enough to make the two touching glass surfaces stick together, and cause breakage when you try to free them. It's a good idea to set the bells upright one on top of the other; a small wooden cube is placed on top of the first, which is removed, and the edges of the second, which is placed on top, cannot touch those of the first; a new cube is placed on top of the second, so it can receive a third bell. All must be placed on the wooden cube in such a way that they can rotate freely without touching the glass of the bell below. Before clamping them permanently, they are washed one by one, and placed, as we have just described, in a shed or even in the open air, they are covered with litter and old mats to prevent shocks which could break them. A broken bell is discarded only when it cannot be repaired. 4. Bells that have been broken into several large pieces are repaired when these juxtaposed pieces only form cracks that need to be reattached in a solid manner. For this purpose, pieces of glass are cut into small squares, called pins, and white ceruse ground in oil is added to a little minium to speed up drying; one side of each pin is coated with this preparation and applied externally across the crack; the whole length of the crack is thus lined with pins from distance to distance. The preparation is left to dry thoroughly before the bell is stirred, making it as strong and usable as a new one. Doormats are returned to the shed as soon as the season allows their use to be discontinued. Care should be taken to expose them first to dry air, and to ensure that they are no longer damp. Sprinkle them with fine ash to absorb any remaining water and protect them from insect attack; then roll or stack them until they are needed again. Temperature is an essential thing to know; our senses can deceive us, but the thermometer never does. We have the bad habit of hanging the thermometer along a wall and using the primitive thermometer fixed on a wooden board. The only admissible instrument that gives accurate readings is the glass thermometer, which can be suspended from its top so that the air envelops it completely. Observations should be made in the middle of the garden, in the prevailing wind, one in the shade, the other in the sun. This thermometer is suspended by a cord from the end of a small gallows. There's no need to keep it stationary, and it can be used for other useful indications. To judge the temperature of a layer, the grower usually uses his hand, and this is sufficient in practice. However, as it may sometimes be useful to determine a constant temperature for certain crops, it would be a good idea, in experiments intended for publication, to use the very thermometer whose use we recommend. Almost all market gardeners have at home, and with good reason, the Vidi dial barometer, which indicates atmospheric pressure and depression with sufficient accuracy for their needs. However, the bad habit of striking the dial to set the needle in motion should be avoided, as this causes mercury to escape from the bowl, thereby destroying the correspondence between the needle's position and the barometric height. A more convenient barometer is the Bourdon. It takes up less space, is more sensitive and, as it contains no mercury, can be set in any position without being disturbed. An equally useful instrument is the hygrometer, which indicates the degree of dryness and humidity in the atmosphere. It's a simple fixed point, wound around a movable pulley and terminated by a small weight. A needle is attached to the pulley shaft. Air saturated with water vapour causes the rope to stretch, absorbing its moisture; dry air, on the other hand, causes it to shrink, evaporating the water vapour it contained. The needle moves in one direction or the other as the rope lengthens or shrinks. The two extreme points indicate maximum and minimum air humidity. Commercially, the support for this device is shaped like a capuchin, with a movable cap serving as a needle. The cap covers the head when the string lengthens, meaning rain or thaw; it uncovers the head when the string narrows, meaning drought, heat or frost. CULTIVATION Seventeen families of plants provide the vegetables strictly necessary to supply the market halls with this branch of industry. 1° Liliaceae provide garlic, asparagus, spring onions, civets, shallots, onions and leeks. 2° Polygonaceae provide sorrel and rhubarb. 3° Chenopodaceae provide spinach, pear, arrowroot and beet. 4° Solanaceae supply tomatoes, chillies, eggplants and potatoes. 5° Labiatae supply basil, savory and thyme. 6° Borraginaceae supply borage. 7° Companulaceae supply raiponium. 8° Compositae supply artichokes, cardoons, lettuces, chicories, escarole, romaine, dandelions, salsify and scorzonera. 9° Valerian plants provide lamb's lettuce and regency. 10° Umbellifers provide carrots, celery, parsnips, chervil and parsley. 11° Crucifers provide cabbages, cauliflowers, watercress, mustard, turnips, radishes and turnips. 12° Tropaeolae provide nasturtiums. 13° Portulaceae provide purslane. 14° Ficoides provide tetragonia. 15° Rosaceae supply strawberries and burnet. 16° Legumes include beans, lentils, peas and broad beans. 17° Cucurbits include melons, cucumbers, gherkins, squash and pumpkins. To these families can be added a grass, maize; a bromeliad, pineapple; a convolvulaceous, sweet potato; a dioscorea, Chinese yam; an oxalid, crenellated oxalis; and finally, a fungus of the agaric genus, the mushroom.
