N°53 A CUCNYLAGARENNE 4 LPONCE RPœ n Lai Mortieulteur Maraicba Gracaux Ou licio d Jllats. Rérolte. P.278. 8 51 bes a- land for ados, celery, melons, tomatoes, cucumbers, beans. The manure is used to make the beds for these plants. If the manure is dry, it is used to make well-manicured beds, which are wetted for a few days before use. If not, chains are made immediately, and the beds continue to be earthworked and the old trenches emptied. Sowing. - March is sowing month. Each part of the garden gets its own seedbed. Pink and red radishes, carrots, leeks, spring onions, spinach, asparagus and arrowroot are sown in full squares and other seedbeds. In warm conditions, sow eggplants, basil, borage, baselle, white celery, Rouen chicory, flageolet beans, melons, chillies and potatoes. - Sow beans in cold frames. Old bed: beans, white mustard. In open ground: strawberries, fennel, chervil, bulbous chervil, savoy, quintal, Bonneuil, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, broccoli, crambe cabbage, turnips, red onions, sorrel, salad burnet, dandelions, leeks, peas, purslane, salsify, scorzonera, savory, tetragona, tomato, thyme. Artichokes are propagated by suckers, and oxalis by cuttings. Planting, transplanting and disadvantages. - All plants sown during the previous month are transplanted by cuttings: melons, cucumbers, eggplants and others. Blonde romaines, grey and red lettuces are planted in full squares; Rouen chicory, melons, cucumbers and beans are bedded. Cauliflower is counter-planted on layers, cold bays and soil. We plant garlic, shallots and leeks on layers, civets, asparagus, tarragon, potatoes in good shelter; we multiply Chinese yams by their bulbils. Care for growing crops. - If the season continues to be rigorous, we give the same care to beds and forced crops as in previous months. Air beds should be fitted with mats. When the sun is too hot, cover all new plantings for a few days from 11 a.m. to 2 a.m.. The plantations are given a few drops of water. Watering starts at the end of the month if the weather is hot and dry, and is carried out under cover when necessary. Harvesting. - See previous month, and add purslane and potatoes to the new Special Observations. - The air layers of the plan would become cucumber layers, those with frames cloche layers and vice versa. Lettuces would be replaced by melons, tomatoes by beans, melons would be replaced by onions, apple cabbages, lamb's lettuce, raipons, civets and apple cabbages by preparations for melons; spring onions by blond romaines and cauliflowers; white onions by sedges or romaines, cauliflowers, radishes and spinach. All costières would be planted with green romaine or lettuce. VII Work in April All the equipment has to change places, with frames and cloches reserved for melons, cucumbers, beans and tomatoes. Work on the beds and trenches is in full swing, with ploughing and manuring completed. Mushroom millstones begin to be shredded for mulch. Seedlings. - Arrochokes, eggplants and basil on old layers, nasturtiums at the foot of the walls, borage, baselle, carrots, white celery, cardoons on old layers and on soil at the 25th, chervil, wild chicory, curly endive, Milan cabbage, Vertus cabbage, broccoli, spring onions, yellow cucumbers, pumpkins on old layers, watercress and perennials on soil, spinach in other seflageolets on soil in good exposure. Layered melons, white mustard, turnips, parsnips, parsley, layered chillies, salad burnet, leeks, leeks, peas, potatoes, purslane, pink and red radishes; in other seeds, salsify, scorzonera, savory, layered tomatoes, old corn. Planting, transplanting and disadvantages. - All the previous month's seedlings are transplanted into the nursery. Asparagus and eggplant are planted in hot cloches. We start planting cold chicory in trays and cloches. Bonneuil cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli are counter-planted with romaine and lettuce. We plant ordinary savoy cabbages, quintal cabbages, Brussels sprouts, cucumbers on layers, cold flageolet beans under frames and cloches, romaine, lettuces, melons on layers or trenches, leeks, tomatoes on trenches under frames and cloches as well as on soil under frames and cloches. Thyme borders, tarragon 16. clumps and Chinese yam bulblets can be propagated. Care for growing crops. - Care should be taken to weed, ventilate the frames and cloches, and cover them with mulch or light mulch when the sun is hot. All plantings under glass require constant care during this month. Plants are wetted immediately after planting. If the weather is dry, start watering carrot beds, cauliflowers, onions and apple cabbages. Salads should be watered moderately, mainly in the morning if the weather is dry and warm. If it's cold, they'll rust. Radishes need plenty of water. Layers and trenches for melons should be made of well-wetted manure. Start pruning and topping young melon and cucumber plants. Harvesting. - Early crops are beginning to produce. We finish harvesting white and green asparagus, and start cutting open-ground asparagus in good exposure. The same is true of artichokes under chassis and those with good exposure. We harvest bedding carrots, new chervil, early apple cabbage, new cauliflower at the end of the month, green cucumbers, spring onions, civets, watercress, spinach, tarragon, broad beans, forced strawberries, beans, lettuces, romaine, lamb's lettuce, regency, white mustard, turnips, white onions towards the end of the month, sorrel, parsnips, parsley, leeks, peas, new potatoes, purslane, pink and red radishes, raiponce, salsify, scorzonera, sea cabbage. Special remarks. - Tomatoes can be replaced by carrots, cauliflower by carrots, and cloche layers by tomatoes, which would also replace romaine and cold lettuces. Tomatoes would be replaced by melons, the latter by cold-grown chicory and beans. Cabbages would be replaced by cucumbers, chives by chervil, and vice versa. Apple cabbages would take the place of white onions, red lettuces that of romaine; blondes, and the costières would be occupied by early apple cabbages or onions. VIII Work in May. All the glass is out and used. There must not be a single unoccupied spot in the field. Frame and bell trenches are completed. The sash layers are turned over, a job to be done during the month. The horse harnesses are repaired or replaced, the carriage repaired or repainted, or a new one purchased. Doormats are brought into the shed, repaired if necessary and sprinkled with ash. Sowing. - Most of this month's planting is done in the ground. We sow arroche in other seedbeds, eggplant in old beds, beets, borage, cardoons, in old beds or in the ground, carrots, white celery up to the 4th, - chervil, curly endive and Rouennaise endive hot, early savoy cabbage, Vertus savoy cabbage, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi; kohlrabi, cauliflower, broccoli, spring onions, cucumbers and gherkins on old layers; pumpkins, squash, giraumons, watercress and spinach in other seedbeds; broad beans, fennel, beans of all kinds, lettuces, romaine, hot escarole, hot melons, white mustard, turnips, oxalis multiplied by cuttings, parsnips, parsley, chili pepper, salad burnet, leeks, peas, potatoes, purslane, radishes in other seedbeds, periwinkle, salsify, scorzonera, tomatoes, corn. Planting, transplanting and counter-planting. - The previous month's 16. seedlings are transplanted into the nursery. By adding manure, we plant melons on soil and on old layers, we plant them on new trenches with frames and cloches, we plant cucumbers, gherkins, eggplants and cardoons on old carrot layers without turning them over. We transplant beet, white and celeriac in nurseries; we plant Milan des Vertus cabbage, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower as counterplants to chicory, romaine and lettuce. Pumpkins are planted in holes or trenches, while beans are planted in pots with lettuce, romaine and curly endive. Scarole counterplanting takes place in lettuces and romaine: On old beds and in costières, piment̂s and tomatoes are planted. Corn is transplanted. Care for vegetating plants. - When the weather is dry, water abundantly in the morning and evening, preferably during daylight hours. Great care should be taken when removing plants from among the others. All new plantings should be wetted first, then watered for a few days. Planting plots should be well mulched and wet before planting. Young plants should be watered sparingly. Only water plants that are three-quarters mature should be watered abundantly. Never wet romaine, lettuce, spinach, chicory or escarole in the sun, as this heats up the plants and exposes them to rot. The strongest under-frame melons are bathed until the fruit has stopped. Cucumbers and gherkins need very little water during harvesting, and only need to be basked. Melons are pruned morning and evening, which is the most favorable time, as are cucumbers, eggplants and tomatoes. Tomatoes are potted. As in the previous month, care must be taken with planting under glass. While the sun is shining, the windows are covered with a light mulch or Spanish white washed down with water, and frequent weeding and raking are carried out in plantations where there are no seedlings. A weed-free garden is every gardener's badge of excellence. Harvesting. - This is the best time to harvest. Here's an approximate list: Asparagus, artichokes, belles-dames, eggplants, borage, carrots, chervil, cellar and quarry mushrooms, chicory, kale, cauliflower, spring onions, civet, cucumbers, watercress, spinach, tarragon, broad beans, strawberries, spinach, tarragon, broad beans, green beans, lettuces, romaine, melons, white mustard, turnips, white onions, parsnips, parsley, burnet, leeks, peas, pears, parsnips, parsnip, red and pink radishes, rhubarb, savory, thyme, strawberries. Special remarks. - Tomato beds can be replaced by cloaked melons, as can carrots. Tomatoes in cloches can be replaced by cucumbers and eggplants, cauliflowers by melons in trenches, and tomatoes in frames by beans. Melons would be replaced by tomatoes, seed radishes by carrots and seed onions, spring onions by apple cabbage, apple cabbage by carrots, romaine or lettuce, white onions by chicory or cauliflower. The romaines would receive lettuces, chervil, civet, spring onions and leeks. The costières would receive cauliflower, beans or marjoram potatoes. IX Work in June. Glass is becoming less useful. From the 15th, the frames covering the already large melons are removed. As the melons are sold, the frames are transferred to melons with bells that have been prepared for this crop. Frames that are not intended for this purpose are taken into the shed and placed in stacks of fifty. Care should be taken to leave a space between the rows for any repairs that need to be made. As for the bells, don't leave them three inside each other, as is the bad habit when removing them. It's better to prepare a stretcher and stack them six high, separated by a small cleat at the top of each one. They are then transported to the place where they are to be kept. Care should be taken to remove the forks at the same time and put them under cover, and the same precaution should be taken for the cleats to give air to the frames: there is no small saving. The trunks remain on the ground until July. The empty cabbage and onion beds are ploughed, and smoked if necessary, but it's best to have taken this precaution in spring or autumn. We finish turning over the cloches for the last melons. Sowing. - All this month's seedlings are sown in the open ground, but it's safer to sow on an average turned-over bed. Seedlings include : arrowroot, carrots, chervil, chicory, escarole, savoy, Vertus, Brussels, cabbage, kohlrabi, kohlrabi kohlrabi, cauliflower up to the 10th, spring onions, watercress, perennial watercress, spinach, green and dry beans, lettuces, romaine, white mustard, turnips, sorrel, parsnips, leeks, peas, purslane, pink and red radishes in other seedlings, black radishes, raiponce, rhubarb. Planting and disadvantages. - In the first days of the month, we finish planting melons on old layers turned over from cucumbers and gherkins, we plant eggplants and long pepper on old layers and in costières, we do the same for cardoons. White celery is counter-planted in chicory, lettuce and romaine, celeriac in carrots and escarole, and chicory in land emptied by apple cabbage and onions. Milan, Brussels and broccoli sprouts are planted. We continue to counterplant cauliflower with melons, romaine, lettuces, chicory and escarole. Finally, lettuces, romaine, leeks and the last tomatoes are planted. Care for growing crops. - Melons should be pruned and drenched morning and evening if the weather is dry. All plants at three-quarters of their growth need plenty of water. Tomatoes await pruning and trellising, which should not be neglected; the same applies to cucumbers and eggplants. Gherkins need to be spread out properly. Melons still in frames and cloches require a great deal of care; during the heat of the sun, they must be given plenty of air. All new plantings require a lot of water, and others need frequent watering, especially when the sun is hot. Weed frequently, cover cauliflower heads with healthy leaves torn from the mother plant, mulch plants intended for planting, prune and pick pumpkins. Harvesting. - These consist of field asparagus, arugula, eggplant, basil, borage, nasturtium, carrot, cerfiul, quarry mushroom, chicory, escarole, apple cabbage, cauliflower, spring onion, civet, cucumber, garden cress, perennial cress, watercress, spinach, tarragon, broad bean, strawberries, green beans, lettuces, romaine, melons, white mustard, turnips, white onions, sorrel, parsnips, potatoes, stonewort, parsley, salad burnet, pepper, pear, pear, peas, potatoes, purslane, pink and red radishes, rhubarb, savory, tetragona, tomatoes, bulbous chervil. Special remarks. - Tomatoes can be replaced by long pepper squares; gherkins by melons, eggplants and cucumbers; cauliflowers and carrots by melon squares. Tomatoes can be replaced by chicory and melons by tomatoes and beans; cabbages by celeriac, spring onions by escarole, seedlings by long pepper, chicory and romaine by carrots, leeks by escarole, chico18 rées or cauliflower, and tomatoes, eggplants or gherkins can be planted in the costières. 8 Work in July. All equipment must be stored in the shed, the frames stacked as previously mentioned, the bins packed and covered with old straw mats or litter. Those that are broken and can be repaired are set aside. All broken glass is collected in a barrel and sold when out of use. Only glass used to make pins should be kept. All trunks must be removed; those on foot are stacked outside. It would be a good idea to cover them with litter or canvas intended for this purpose; those that can be dismantled are put under the shed piece by piece, or in piles outside, with the same precautions as for the former. S 2 :ag A FIFIEFIZI time to make repairs or set aside those that need them so that they can be done as soon as possible. If there's time, it's a good idea to scrape the frames before painting them, remasking them, and replacing broken windows, as it's useful to be ahead on these jobs. Loaders, stretchers and other tools and utensils not currently needed should also be inspected, repaired and sheltered. Empty plots of Bonneuil cabbage and cauliflower are ploughed. If they are to be smoked, only very good manure should be used, the clods should be broken up well, and even moistened if necessary before ploughing. If there is too much drought, all the trouble caused by this can be regained. Ploughing should be done early in the morning, so that you can rest during the heat of the day. Sowing. - You can sow arroche in other plants or crops, carrots, chervil, curly endive, escarole, spring onion, watercress, spinach in other plants; lettuces, romaine, white mustard, turnips, parsnips, leeks, peas, purslane, pink and red radishes in other plants, or on their own, black radishes, raipons. Planting and disadvantages. - The last cardoons are planted, white celery is counter-planted with chicory, lettuce and romaine, and the last celeriac is counter-planted with melons in trenches and potting soil. Curly endive and escarole are planted, cauliflowers are counter-planted in trenches and salads, and melons, gherkins and cucumbers are grown on soil. Milan, Vertus and other large-ribbed cabbages, kohlrabi and turnip cabbages, broccoli, strawberry plants transplanted in May and leeks can all be planted in the ground at this time. Care for growing crops. - Finish pruning melons, cucumbers and pumpkins. Depending on how dry the atmosphere is, they are wetted. Weeds are destroyed, caterpillars attacking all varieties of cabbage are hunted down; the ground is covered with growing plants, and watering is the main care they require. Cucurbits need a lot of water; pumpkins, squash and giraumonts are pruned and pickled. Tomato pruning and trellising is one of the month's major occupations. Harvesting. - Arrochokes, artichokes, basil, borage, nasturtiums, carrots, chervil, quarry mushrooms, curly endive, escarole, Bonneuil cabbage, ordinary Milan cabbage, cauliflower, spring onion, civet, cucumbers, gherkins, watercress, watercress, shallots, spinach, tarragon, broad beans, bulbous chervil, lettuces, romaine, melons, white mustard, turnips, white onions, parsnips, potatoes, stonewort, parsley, long and square peppers, salad burnet, leeks, periwinkle, peas, potatoes, purslane, pink and red radishes, tetragona, strawberries, spinach, tomatoes. Seeds are starting to be harvested, so now is the time to look after seed carriers. Special observations. - Tomato beds will be replaced by eggplants; melons will be replaced by gherkins, cucumbers or white celery; tomatoes will replace key melons; escarole, cauliflower and carrots. Melons would give way to cauliflower and carder-pear; chicory and romaine, to carrots and leeks; civet, to pear; seed radishes, to chervil; seedlings, to tomatoes; chicory and white celery, to Bonneuil and red cabbages; escarole and chicory, to toma es; costières would receive chicory, escarole and carrots. XI Work in August. Repairs to frames and bells continue. The land is largely occupied, so there is little plowing to be done. The drought requires some wetting, but this is nothing compared to the previous month. We empty the melon trenches as soon as the fruit is sold, if we don't counter-plant in them. Sowing. - Sowing is infrequent. They are limited to arrowroot, chervil, spring onion, spinach, lettuce, romaine and lamb's lettuce from the 15th; turnips, leeks and late peas, which you can't be sure of harvesting; pink and red radishes, and white onions in nurseries, from the 10th. Planting and disadvantages. - White celery is still planted with radish and spinach seedlings. We counter-plant chicory and escarole, lettuce, romaine and cauliflower. Leeks and watercress are planted with cuttings; escarole and chicory are transplanted with plugs in September. Care for growing crops. - Watering continues; in fact, it is very necessary, as the soil has suffered from the drought. Melon pruning is nearing completion, with only one fruit left. Tomato trellising and pruning require great care. Weeding must be repeated. Plenty of water must be applied when planting, and young plants must be supported by frequent basking. Pumpkins and cauliflowers need to be pruned and wetted every other day, and caterpillars need to be kept at bay. Harvesting. - Arrochokes, artichokes, eggplants, basil, borage, baselle, nasturtiums, carrots, white celery, chervil, bulbous chervil, quarry mushrooms, curly endive, escarole, Bonneuil cabbage, red cabbage, ordinary Milan cabbage, spring onions, pumpkins, cucumbers, gherkins, watercress, perennial and watercress, shallots, garlic, tarragon, broad beans, green and shelled beans, lettuces, romaine, corn, melons, white mustard, turnips, red and yellow onions, sorrel, burnet, leeks, peas, potatoes, purslane, pink and red radishes, tomatoes, thyme. - Most seeds are harvested during this month. Special observations. - Tomato, melon and gherkin beds will contain cardoons and cauliflowers; 8 5. P. 297. 3 S aco 29 A escarole and romaine will be replaced by celeriac and the latter by carrots. - Tomatoes will be replaced by chicory and melons by white celery; cauliflowers by melons, seeded spring onions by chervil, seeded radishes by spring onions, burnet or cress, white celery by red and Bonneuil cabbage, escarole and leeks, the latter by chicory, chervil or lamb's lettuce. Chili will be replaced by tomatoes, white celery by escarole, chicory and cauliflower, the latter by leeks; all costières will contain only white celery, escarole or chicory. XII Work in September. We are finishing repairs to the frames, chests and bells, which are due to come into use the following month. There is almost 17. no plowing to be done, as the garden should be fully occupied or nearly so. Sowing. - This is the month when we do the least. We still sow chervil and borage to have them available at all times, bulbous chervil, Rouen chicory and escarole for replanting under frames, apple and beef cabbage for spring, cauliflower, spring onions, spinach and black lettuce in the first few days of the month and later for cold work under frames or cloches, and at the end of the month for hot work. Lamb's lettuce, turnips, pink and red radishes and stone drills are also sown in the early days. Planting and counter-planting. - Almost everything is finished by the previous month. Rouen chicory is transplanted under cloches, to be put under frames the following month at the same time as escarole. We plant strawberry plants from nets and prepare well-smoked ground for planting seedlings to be put under frames over winter. At the end of the month, black lettuces are transplanted cold or placed indoors. Leeks, escarole and lump chicory are planted in empty plots. Start transplanting white onions and sow them in the first few days to keep them in place. Care for growing crops. - Give celery and cauliflower abundant watering, weed frequently and rigorously hunt for caterpillars, cover cauliflower with a leaf from the mother plant, cut down manure to make mushroom wheels, wet the manure, make a floor of it, and reshuffle it. Cover celery to blanch it, stuff the oldest cardoons planted for the same purpose. Harvesting. - Garlic, arrowroot, artichokes, eggplants, borage, nasturtiums, carrots, white celery, celeriac, chervil, bulbous chervil, quarry mushrooms, curly endive, escarole, red cabbage, savoy cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, spring onions, the last cucumbers and gherkins, pumpkins, watercress, watercress, shallots, spinach, tarragon, broad beans, strawberries, green, shelled and dried beans, lettuces, romaine, lamb's lettuce, melons, white mustard, turnips, red and yellow onions, sorrel, parsnips, potatoes, stonewort, parsley, pepper, salad burnet, leeks, peas, potatoes, purslane, pink and red radishes, tomatoes, thyme. Special observations. - White celery and cabbage can be replaced by carrots and celeriac; escarole by parsley and sorrel; white celery by chicory or the last of the bell melons. Tomatoes would replace celeriac and celery root; lamb's lettuce, chervil; spring onions and civets would be replaced by spinach, radishes, celery and cardoons; escarole by cauliflower, peppers by escarole, the rest of the celery by transplanted onions and lamb's lettuce. In the costières, there would be chicory, escarole, lamb's lettuce and chervil. VEGETABLE GROWING. Under this heading, we understand the cultivation of vegetables that people outside the profession can grow for their own personal use; we will not describe again the methods set out in this book, we refer to the special chapters for details: we will only give here the distribution of the soil and the advice necessary for success. The average family is made up of 5 or 6 people. If this family lives in the country, and if one of its members can devote an hour a day to cultivating a garden of 400 to 500 meters, this family can be sure of having vegetables for its consumption throughout the year, by putting into practice the rules we are about to explain. Similarly, a teacher training college, a seminary, a college, a community of 50 to 60 people will find its vegetable consumption on an area ten times larger, i.e. 4 to 5,000 surface meters. To achieve this, it's absolutely essential to ban all open-air fruit trees from the kitchen garden, and to plant only espaliers. - Cordon or cattail trees should also be banned; only then will you be able to grow good, beautiful vegetables. - Manure and potting soil must be available in sufficient quantities for the area to be cultivated. In the absence of pure horse manure, cow, chicken, rabbit, pig and other types of manure can be used, mixed with sweepings, peelings and weeding residues to form a compost; shrub leaves and any decomposing organic products that may be available can also be added. However, to make the layers, you'll always need a supply of horse manure, a supply of potting soil for spring sowing and planting, and a supply of mulch for summer covering. A vegetable garden for 5 or 6 people requires 7 frames and 50 bells, which, with tools, requires an expenditure of around 200 francs. For a gathering of 50 or 60 people, you'll need 70 frames and 500 bells, the cost of which, combined with the rest of the equipment, comes to around 1,250 francs. In such cases, it's a good idea to adopt the watering system we've described. The cost can be appreciated by the following estimate, made for the model of vegetable garden whose plan we present to our readers: A manege pump........ 1,200 fr. 300 meters of lead pipes. 1,000 42 water outlets or taps.... 15,000-liter tank, 3-millimeter sheet metal....... Tank assembly......... 14 meters of rubber and lance..................... 1 stopcock...........- 500 600 400 160 30 A small steam engine... 2,000 Total................ 5,890 It would be a good idea to obtain 300 meters of potting soil in the first year, at an estimated cost of 1,200 francs, excluding transport costs. It is essential to secure manure for a stable of 15 to 20 horses, which costs an average of 3 francs per month per horse. There's nothing frightening about these figures if you consider that, in a house of this kind, the steam engine and the water from the reservoir can meet needs other than watering the vegetable garden, that the initial costs are quickly reimbursed by the savings resulting from the abundant vegetables harvested, and that the permanent expense is reduced after a short time to an annual sum of 600 to 700 francs for the purchase of manure. With this in mind, we'll now give a table of the plants to be grown for the two potacers we've taken as types, asking the reader to look up the details of their cultivation in chapters V, VI and VII. MSTORY OF MARKET GARDENING, ITS PROGRESS AND IMPROVEMENTS. Until the sixteenth century, we know nothing precise about market gardening; vegetables native to France or long-acclimatized there were grown only on soil or on beds in the open air. 16th century. Rabelais sends the first lettuce and romaine seeds from Rome to Cardinal d'Estrées (1540). 17th century. Work on vegetable plants by Dr. Mizauld. (1605.) First mention of the use of bells by Olivier de Serres. (1623.) Cultivation of melons using rolling boxes retracted into the greenhouse during frost and at night: Olivier de Serres. (1623.) Cultivation of melons on beds and cauliflowers; Théâtre du Jardinier, by Claude Mollet, gardener to Louis XIII. (1643.) Cultivation of early vegetables, use of frames by La Quintinye, head gardener of the Versailles kitchen garden. (1688.) 18th century. Cultivation of pineapples and potatoes using hot greenhouses by Gondoin, gardener at the Château de Choisy-le-Roi under Louis XV. First greengrocers: - Tassère, gardener to the Régent in Bagnolet. - Debille, Ébrard, Valette, François, Fournier, Heude, Jaulin, Marie, market gardeners in Paris, start using frames for industrial cultivation. (1780 to 1800.) Forced strawberry plants, by Legrand (1776). - Hot cultivation of peas, beans and carrots, by Decouflé. (1788.) - Hot cultivation of curly endive, by Stainville, (1791.) - Invention of the watering crank, first use, by Bourgeois, market gardener in Grenelle. (1792.) Heated white asparagus, by Quentin. (1792.) Green asparagus, by Marie. (1800.) 19th century. Hot cauliflower, by Besnard. (1811.) Cold Romaines under cloches: Dulac, Chemin, Fanfan Quentin. (1812.) Founding of the Horticultural Society. (1827.) Adoption of the fulling pump. (1836.) Adoption of lance watering, by 1. Ponce (1859. END. PagesPREFACE.............................................. CHAPTER ONE ESTABLISHING A VEGETABLE GARDEN When you want to set up a vegetable garden, choose a plot of land a short distance from your home, so that you can pick up vegetables for immediate consumption at any time. However, the land should not be so close that you have to worry about the odors given off by the manure from the beds. It is essential to have water available in the garden itself, as the cultivation of vegetable plants requires frequent watering: in mediocre soil, but well supplied with water, vegetables can always be grown, whereas in top-quality soil that cannot be watered, it is almost impossible to grow them. To allow rainwater to run off, it's a good idea for the soil in the vegetable garden to be slightly sloping; let's add that, as the soil is constantly being stirred up in one or other of its parts, and the vegetable beds don't always have the most pleasing appearance, it's not a bad idea to hide the view a little, which is done by means of the fences we'll talk about shortly. There are no hard and fast rules for determining the exposure of a vegetable garden; indeed, it's easy to see that its location must vary not only with the climatic conditions of the place where it's set up, but also with the plants grown there. In any case, we'd say that in the north and center of France, southern exposure is often the best; in a dry, hot climate, such as that of the Midi, for example, you should prefer exposure that gives plants the shade they need to prevent them from being scorched by too much hot sun. In some provinces, it is customary to place fruit trees next to vegetables. This method, excellent for southern regions, is far from advantageous for more northerly climates, where the trees in the vegetable garden prevent the crops placed at their foot from receiving direct sunlight. In this case, fruit trees should not be planted in the vegetable garden, unless they are espaliered! Fences. The most perfect fences are undoubtedly walls, which break the wind, allow espaliers to be formed and are an excellent means of protection. They are generally raised to a height of 2 meters, and are white in color, the color that best reflects the sun's heat. Their main drawback is the relatively high cost of their construction. They give shelter to numerous insects and pests, which are very difficult to avoid, and, 1. For espalier training, see Arboriculture pratique, by Troncet and Deliège (same bookshop). also, as they borrow nutrients from the soil, the latter yields little in the way of produce in their vicinity. What's more, they are often damaged by domestic animals during the first few years of their formation, and don't provide sufficient protection for the vegetable garden. Wooden fences and galvanized wire trellises are frequently used, although they offer little resistance to wind action; they can be supplemented with windbreaks, as some horticulturists do. These windbreaks, which are given a height of around 1.50 m, are generally made of rye straw. Windbreaks. Soil type. The most suitable soil for growing vegetables is one in which the various elements are mixed in the right proportions; it is then easy to work and is known as loose soil. Soil is of inferior quality when one of the elements is in excess; it is said to be strong if clay is in excess; it is said to be light if the limestone or silica element dominates. Clay soils are often very difficult to work, and almost always retain far too much moisture. However, they are preferable to siliceous soils, which are easier to plow but dry out relatively quickly. 1. The building blocks of soil are clay, silica and limestone. Humus or loam comes from the decomposition of plant and animal matter. However, both have their advantages: the former are suitable for growing large vegetables, such as cauliflower, artichoke and cardoon; calcareous or siliceous soils can be sown early, as they warm up in the first days of spring. In summer, heavy soils should be hoeed frequently, while light soils should be watered abundantly. If one of the elements is in too high a proportion, the soil must be amended by adding a certain quantity of the missing element: sand, for example, to clay soils, marl to siliceous soils, clay to calcareous soils. Soil conditioners made from organic matter are also frequently used; we'll come back to this subject in a later section on fertilizers. Preparatory work. When a new plot of land is to be cultivated, a number of important operations need to be carried out beforehand. Raking, the most difficult and costly of these operations, is designed to loosen the soil to a great depth. If necessary, dry grasses are pulled up and burned beforehand; their ashes spread over the soil will provide an excellent amendment. A trench 1.50 to 2 metres wide and 60 to 80 centimetres deep is dug with a pickaxe at one end of the plot, and the soil removed is carried to the opposite end of the garden. A second trench is then dug next to the first, and the earth used to fill this one, and so on, until the last trench is reached, which is filled with the earth removed from the first. During this work, the stones are set aside to be used to form the paths. After trenching, the clods are broken up and the top soil levelled. It goes without saying that when the subsoil is of poor composition, it should not be brought to the surface. When it is not deemed necessary to break up the soil, it should at least be turned over with a spade to a depth of 20 to 30 centimetres. Once the soil has been well loosened by ripping followed by ploughing, or by simple ploughing with a spade, it needs to be suitably distributed. As the garden almost always has a regular shape, this operation is relatively easy. It can be divided into two equal parts by a main path 1.50 to 2 meters wide, laid out in a straight line using a chalk line. In the same way, a driveway 60 centimetres to 1 metre wide, running all the way around the enclosure, can be set at a distance of around 2 mềtres from the fences, leaving strips of land on the edges, known as coastal strips. In northern regions, the coastal strips along the well-exposed walls should be wider, so that first-season vegetables can be grown there. The next step is to form the beds, which can be 1.50 to 2 meters wide. To do this, paths perpendicular to the main aisle are laid out at the required distance, always using a chalk line, and given a width of 30 to 40 centimetres. The paths are stone-covered and compacted, then covered with a 3 to 4 centimetre layer of sand. CHAPTER II FERTILIZERS Whatever the nature of the soil in which the vegetable garden is established, it is necessary to provide it with fertilizing materials, in other words, fertilizers, in order to obtain vigorous, high-quality vegetables. The fertilizers used are manure, mulch, potting soil and chemical fertilizers, which we will examine in turn. Manure. Manure is formed mainly from the excrement of domestic animals. The most suitable for vegetable cultivation is cow manure; but horse manure, half-consumed, is also an excellent fertilizer: it is used above all for the cultivation of early vegetables, as it releases a certain amount of heat during fermentation, which is put to good use. Sheep manure, hen manure, pigeon manure and guano are also very effective; city mud, sea plants such as kelp, bone meal, rapeseed cake and all organic residues can also be used to improve soil. Human manure itself gives very good results; unfortunately, it is not used as often as it could be, as some gardeners are averse to this fertilizer. Before use, it can be disinfected with powdered charcoal, sawdust, horse dung or iron sulfate at a rate of 2 kilograms per cubic meter. Cattle manure is generally applied to the soil in late autumn or early winter. Each year, around 300 kilograms of manure per acre are used for this operation. In bedded gardens, the manure from the beds, half used up, can be used as fertilizer for other parts of the garden. Human manure, if dried out, is called poudrette and mixed with the soil like animal manure; if not, it is called Flemish manure, and is spread by sprinkling after being left to ferment for some time; guano, poulinée and colombine are diluted in water and then spread in the same way; liquid manure, poured over flowerbeds, almost always produces good results. TERREAU. Mulch. Mulch is a layer of short, half-consumed manure spread on the surface of the soil, either to promote seed emergence, or to maintain a certain freshness in soils that require frequent watering. The mulch, which is given a thickness of 4 to 5 centimetres, is often formed with manure from the beds. It is applied only from the end of April onwards, on cultivated beds; placed earlier, it retains excess moisture in the soil, which could lead to frost. In autumn, when the mulch is buried by ploughing, it acts as a fertilizer. Potting soil. When manure has reached its final stage of decomposition, it is called compost. Manure heaps, left to their own devices, always reach this state, but the potting soil used in vegetable growing usually comes from old layers. Many growers, however, set aside a small area in the corner of the vegetable garden where vegetable peelings, old leaves, dried grasses and even rags are thrown, with the aim of converting them into potting soil. These are watered with household water, and when the whole is sufficiently decomposed, it can be used as a soil improver; its action is one of the best on crops; it makes compacted soils looser and lighter. It should be noted here that plants with mature seeds and those suffering from cryptogamic diseases should not be thrown onto the manure. The former would needlessly give birth to seedlings that would borrow their nourishment from the soil; the latter would alter the whole mass, which would quickly become a source of contamination. Plants in either of these conditions should therefore be burnt, and their ashes thrown onto the compost. Chemical fertilizers. If the nutrients removed by cultivation are not returned to the soil, it will soon become impoverished. To maintain its fertility, therefore, it is essential to supply sufficient fertilizers. Organic fertilizers can certainly contribute to a certain extent to making exhausted soils productive again, but as manure is often lacking, complementary fertilizers, i.e. mineral fertilizers also known as chemical fertilizers, are used to supplement the action of animal and vegetable fertilizers. The nutrients required by plants are of several kinds; there are four main ones: nitrogen, phosphoric acid, potash and lime; hence four types of mineral fertilizers: nitrogen fertilizers, phosphate fertilizers, potash fertilizers and lime fertilizers. The most commonly used nitrogen fertilizers are : Ammonium sulfate, which usually contains 19 to 20 percent nitrogen; it is usually extracted from sewage or water used to purify lighting gas; Sodium nitrate or azotate, containing 15 to 16 percent nitrogen, which is usually imported from Chile; Potassium nitrate or azotate, which is what we usually call saltpeter; it gives only 13% nitrogen, but contains potassium in the proportion of 44%, which also places it among the potassium fertilizers. The main phosphate fertilizers are : Lime phosphate, obtained from bones and mineral phosphates; the latter are almost always insoluble, and only become soluble when treated with sulfuric acid, when they are called superphosphates or acid lime phosphates. Bone powder, bones from which gelatin is obtained, and animal black used to refine sugar are also very active phosphate and nitrogen fertilizers. The most commonly used potassium fertilizers are : Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate, often mixed together and containing 25 to 50 percent potash; these are supplied in large quantities from Germany; Plant ash, long used, but containing fewer fertilizing principles; Residues from sugar manufacturing and beet distillation. The main calcareous fertilizers are: Lime, which should not be mixed with manure, as it releases the ammonia it contains; it is spread in small heaps, which are then covered with soil; marl, a mixture of carbonate of lime or chalk and clay, which is used like lime; finally, plaster or lime sulfate, which is widely used. The soil must contain the four nutrients in the right proportions: nitrogen, phosphoric acid, limestone and lime. To supply them to exhausted soils, we can use a mixture made up of 100 grams per square meter: soda nitrate 2 to 4 parts, lime superphosphate 3, potassium chloride 1, gypsum 4, iron sulfate 1 per 100 of the mixture. The following mixture, recommended by M. Grandeau, is used after being dissolved in water at a rate of 1 gram per liter: ammonia phosphate 30 grams, potassium nitrate 45, sodium nitrate 15, ammonia sulfate 10. CHEMICAL FERTILIZERS. CHAPTER III GARDENING INSTRUMENTS We shall not deal here with the many instruments that have been devised to facilitate horticultural work, most of which require a certain skill to be usefully employed, a skill that can only be acquired through practice. We will confine ourselves to examining in turn the various tools that are easy to handle and commonly used. Watering cans can be made of zinc, tin, yellow copper or red copper. Red copper watering cans are usually preferred, as they are the most durable. Watering cans have a capacity of around 10 liters, and are fitted with a movable spout pierced by a large number of small holes. The spade, whose shape and dimensions vary from region to region, is used for ploughing. It consists of a flat blade of hardened steel, fitted with a socket into which the handle is inserted. The pickaxe is used for ripping and deep ploughing, and is very useful for working hard or stony soils that cannot be cut with any other instrument. The hoe is used to stir up the soil and cut weeds. It consists of a broad blade with a socket into which the handle penetrates. The hoe, which can take several forms, is used like the hoe to slice weeds and stir the soil, to loosen the surface and allow air to penetrate; it has a sharp blade on one side and two long teeth on the other. The serfouette is a kind of small hoe, with a blade sharp on one side and a single tooth broadened towards the middle on the other; it is used for hoeing and for tracing the radii and boundaries of paths following the line indicated by the chalk line. GARDENING TOOLS. 17 Bèche Pioche L Houe Binette Serfouette fourche à dents platee fourche ordinaire Ratissoire Pelle 4 Brouette à coffre d LE POTAGER. Rake Watering can E B H Stretcher wheelbarrow 2 The flat-tined fork is used for ploughing, like the spade, but it is mainly used for more specific tasks, such as stirring up the soil at the foot of trees, which the spade cannot do without damaging the roots. There are two or three tines. The ordinary fork is made up of two or three large, slightly curved tines joined to a handle by a socket; it is used for loading manure, making layers, breaking up clods of earth, harrowing seedlings, and so on. The rake is used for dethatching, cleaning paths, smoothing the soil after ploughing and harrowing seedlings. The rake can be made of wood with iron tines, or entirely of iron. Rakes, used for weeding and raking alleys, come in two types: push rakes and pull rakes; the latter's socket is curved to allow the instrument to be pulled back while working. Shovels come in a variety of shapes and sizes; they can be made of wood or iron, and are used for loading and unloading earth, manure, etc. Wheelbarrows come in a variety of shapes. There are two types of wheelbarrow: trunk wheelbarrows with two sides to hold the load, and stretcher wheelbarrows with crossbars at the bottom. The former are used to transport soil and fertilizers; the latter can carry more cumbersome loads, such as straw, straw mats, watering cans filled with water, etc. The trowel essentially consists of a wide blade curved in the shape of a half-cylinder; it is used to pull young plants out of the ground for transplanting, without crushing the roots. The planter, frequently used for seedlings and transplants, is a simple spindle-shaped piece of wood 20 to 30 centimetres long. Its end can be lined with iron or copper. The chalk line is mainly used to mark out paths and alleys, and to draw the radii of seedlings. You can easily build your own by tying the ends of a forty-meter-long rope to two stakes. The frames, designed to encourage the growth of vegetables that would only come into the open later, are made up of GARDENING INSTRUMENTS. ~~ 3 m Frame M 664-4.7 imi Faceted bell String 2 Planter Doormat 18 Vegetable bell and Rack Planter 2 two main parts: the box and the panels. The trunk is a bottomless box that supports the glazed panels, so that they are slightly inclined. The most common model has three panels, a length of 4 meters, a width of 1.33 meters and a height of 33 centimeters at the back and 26 centimeters at the front. The panels are wooden or iron frames, 1.33 m wide by 1.36 m long, divided by the crosspieces to which the panes are attached. The mats, made of rye straw, are generally a little larger than the frames on which they are laid. Many growers build them themselves. Placed directly on the ground, they protect seeds and young plants from frost. Cloches are used for the same purpose as frames; a distinction is made between verrines or faceted cloches and cloches maraîchères, the most commonly used today. The former consist of a small iron frame with flat glass panes; they are much more expensive than the latter, and allow less heat and light to reach the plant. The most commonly used market gardening cloches are made of colorless glass and measure 40 centimeters in diameter; when they crack without becoming unusable, you can try repairing them with ceruse white. When you don't want to use them any more, place them one inside the other, interspersed with a bit of straw. The rack is formed by a slat with a certain number of notches; it serves to support the edge of the bell above the ground, so that air can penetrate to the plant. When the bell is to be raised on all sides, it is held in place by three racks. CURRENT WORK 21 When the gardener sows or plants vegetables at the usual times to cultivate them in the open air, without any care other than that which is normally essential for their growth, he is practicing natural cultivation; when he seeks to hasten their development by the use of layers, frames, cloches, etc., he is practicing early cultivation; when he seeks to hasten their development by the use of layers, frames, cloches, etc., he is practicing early cultivation, When, finally, vegetables are grown out of season, either on beds and under frames, or in a greenhouse, with the aid of artificial heat, the cultivation method used is called forced cultivation. In greenhouses, heat is generally produced by heating with hot water using the thermosiphon. Among the various gardening tasks, some are common to all three cultivation methods, such as sowing and transplanting; others, such as assembling layers, are specific to early cultivation and forced cultivation. We will look at these various operations in turn, starting with the most general. Ploughing. In vegetable cultivation, ploughing is mostly carried out with a spade; for it to be done properly, the instrument must penetrate to a depth of between 15 and 30 centimetres, and the soil removed must be turned over so that the deep layer is brought to the surface. Whenever we want to sow or transplant a plot of land, it must be ploughed; during this operation, we bury all weeds that cannot multiply by sprouting, but take care to remove those that could reproduce in this way. In late autumn and early winter, when ploughing is carried out to bury fertilizers, they must not be buried too deeply, as if the roots of the vegetables could not reach the fertilized area, the amendments would have no effect. Ploughing should be avoided after a frost, as the hardened soil could only be imperfectly divided; immediately after a heavy rain, the soggy earth, forming a compact mass, would only be worked with difficulty. Sowing. Sowing is the most common method of propagating vegetable plants. Sowing can take place as early as the end of February, if the winter is not too cold, but this is not a strict rule, as some vegetables, such as the early St Catherine's pea, can be sown at the beginning of winter. Sowing will alternate with harvesting, but rarely later than July for vegetables to be harvested the same year. When seeds that should be sown in spring take a long time to germinate, they can be planted as early as December of the previous year. If sown earlier, they will germinate before winter, and the first frosts will destroy the young plants. The smaller the seedlings, the less soil they should be covered with; in some cases, it's enough to sprinkle a little potting soil over the seedlings. If, for one reason or another, you want the seeds to emerge quickly, you can put them in a canvas bag and soak them in water for a while before sowing. Broadcast sowing. - Sowing can be done in a number of ways, the simplest of which is to take the seeds in your hand and throw them as evenly as possible over the chosen area. This is known as broadcast sowing. This operation is usually carried out in two stages, i.e. on two opposite edges of the sowing bed, so as to cover half of it each time: this avoids throwing the seeds into the paths. When you're sure of the quality of the seeds, sow them lightly to obtain plants that are as strong as possible. If, despite this, the emergence is too thick, you'll have to thin them out, i.e. pull out the weakest plants to allow the others to grow freely. We usually avoid sowing too thickly by mixing a little fine sand with the seed. After sowing, harrow with a rake or fork, then plow, i.e. tamp down the soil, either with a board or with the back of a shovel or rake. Water if necessary. Ray sowing. - Ray sowing consists in opening small furrows with a serfouette, following a line determined by a chalk line, into which the seeds are deposited, then covered by harrowing the seedbed; later hoeing will be easier. A modification of ray sowing, poguet sowing, is carried out by making small holes with a serfouette, into which the large seeds, such as bean seeds, are placed in numbers of two to five. Transplanting. Transplanting is an operation whose effect is to make plants produce abundant hairs, thus making them more robust and delaying their going to seed. It consists in changing the soil of vegetables when they have reached a certain size and could harm each other. To do this, you must not wait until they are too developed, as transplanting would then offer little chance of success. The soil in which the plants are to be transplanted must have been ploughed, mulched and watered if the weather is dry. Transplanting is done in lines, spaced according to the volume the vegetables can reach. Holes are made with the planter, into which the plant roots are placed, then filled in with soil. Each plant is then watered, compacting the soil around the roots. Transplanting can also be carried out in a small space, in pots, on a bed, etc., for plants whose vegetation is long-lasting and which need to be sheltered at the start of their growth. Weeding. Weeding is one of the most important operations in vegetable growing; its purpose is to prevent weeds from growing alongside vegetables, whose development they would otherwise hinder. Weeding consists of pulling out these weeds either by hand or with an implement, and should be repeated as often as necessary, especially when the plants are still young. In alleys and paths, weeding is done with a rake; in flowerbeds, it is mostly done by hand; but as it would be difficult if the soil were dry, it should preferably be done after rain or watering, so as not to raise the soil, which could disturb or expose the roots of the plants to be preserved. Hoeing. Like weeding, hoeing is an operation that should not be neglected; it is especially useful when the soil has been hardened by rain or watering. Depending on the situation, hoeing can be carried out with a hoe, a flail or even a hoe. It should not be too deep, for fear of damaging the plant roots, but deep enough to allow air to reach them. It also makes it easier for water to reach the deeper parts of the soil, so that evaporation is greatly reduced and the soil stays moist longer. Hoeing can take the place of weeding when care is taken to destroy all noxious plants at the same time; it must be repeated more often in compact soils than in light soils; it becomes less necessary when the soil is covered with mulch. Watering. It's a well-known fact that frequent watering is essential to ensure rapid, vigorous vegetable growth. In our gardens, watering is done with watering cans. Sometimes, to make the work easier, there are several reservoirs in the same vegetable garden; these reservoirs often consist of barrels sunk into the ground and connected by pipes; as they are also connected to a pump, they can all be filled at will. The gardener doesn't always have such a system at his disposal; sometimes he draws his water from a well or a stream; but as most of the time it's impossible to do otherwise, he uses whatever water is within his reach. We would point out, however, that rainwater is the best for watering, followed by running river water, spring water, well water, pump water and finally pond water. Before using well water, it's a good idea to leave it in the open air for a while, so that it can take on the temperature of the atmosphere and become sufficiently aerated. The time of day to water varies with the season. In summer, it's preferable to water in the evening, as the water evaporates less at night, so the vegetables are under its influence for longer; on the other hand, in autumn and spring, watering should take place in the morning, as if the water were poured on in the evening, its freshness could be harmful to the plants. When watering large vegetables, such as cabbages, we often remove the head of the watering can, allowing us to pour the necessary amount of water more quickly. Light watering without removing the head is known as "bassinage". Layering. Layers are piles of manure which, through fermentation, can release the heat necessary for early vegetable cultivation. Most often, layers are made from horse manure mixed with tree leaves, such as chestnut, beech or oak. For them to produce good results, they need to be at about the temperature at which vegetables grow best naturally. There are several types of layer, depending on their degree of heat and the shape they take. We'll look successively at floor layers and trench layers. Floor layers. - They are rectangular in shape, and their dimensions vary according to the number of frames or bells you wish to cover them with. However, their width is almost always between 1.33 and 1.70 meters. When new, unfermented manure is used to build them, the heat produced is considerable and the layers are said to be hot. When layers are built with a mixture of new manure and manure that has already fermented, or annealed manure, the heat developed is less and the layers are lukewarm; construction of the latter generally begins in November. Before building a layer, the location is first determined using four stakes around which a chalk line is stretched; the new manure is then mixed with the annealed manure, and the mixture is placed in the chosen spot using a fork, taking care to tamp it down as you go along, to maintain the same level throughout, and to raise the lateral edges of the layer vertically, which can vary in thickness from 40 to 65 centimetres. If the layers are intended to carry bells, they are filled with about 20 centimetres of potting soil, then carefully edged. If the manure is not sufficiently moist, it is watered to facilitate fermentation. At first, the temperature rises rapidly, reaching 65 degrees (the so-called "coup de feu"), but soon drops to around 25 to 30 degrees. Sowing generally begins at this point. Trench beds. - Trench beds are mainly used for growing melons; they differ from floor beds only in that they are raised on the bottom of a pit, so the height above ground is less. Trenches are generally 1 meter wide and 33 centimeters deep, with an average total layer thickness of 65 centimeters. Some of the annealed manure used comes from the old layers. Trench layers in which annealed manure is almost the only material used are known as deaf layers; the width of the pit is usually 55 to 60 centimeters, and the depth 25 to 30 centimeters. The upper part is filled with potting soil and covered with long manure. During the winter, it's necessary to protect the layers from the cold, and this is achieved with the help of "accots" and "réchauds". Accots are piles of old manure which surround the layers or frames; rechauds differ from accots in that only new manure is used in their composition; they are preferable to the former, as the heat they give off can prevent the layers from cooling down. CHAPTER V ASSOLEMENTS Once the crops to be grown in a vegetable garden have been chosen, and a suitable location assigned to each one, it seems at first sight as if this arrangement could be adhered to at all times; this would certainly be the simplest and most convenient way of doing things, were it not for the disadvantages that have long been recognized. This is because the plant borrows elements from the soil that are always the same, so that the soil ends up lacking the nutrients it requires; but it does contain others that are suitable for species which, thanks to their root systems, can draw their nourishment from different layers of the soil. This observation has led growers to alternate their various crops on the same site. This alternation is called crop rotation. Vegetables are not chosen at random. Experience has given us some general rules on this subject: the most exhausting crops are replaced by less exhausting ones; deep-rooted plants are replaced by shallow-rooted ones, etc. When several harvests or seasons are grown on the same planting bed in a single year, care is taken not to use the same crop for two consecutive seasons, so as to always have good-quality produce. It's easy to understand the advantages of a good crop rotation; like Mr. André Thouin, we can say that it's "the art of alternating crops on the same piece of land, to constantly produce the best products at the lowest possible cost". Choosing a crop rotation is quite a difficult task, as the grower must take into account not only the needs of the plants grown, but also the elements contained in the soil. It is therefore very difficult to give a system that is suitable for all cases; however, we will quote a model that we have borrowed from M. Courtois-Gérard. It shows the distribution of land for a 15-acre garden, and indicates the successive crops to be grown in each bed for the harvests of the same year. The horticulturist will make any modifications he deems necessary, and will ensure that a crop is brought back to the same bed only every five or six years. There is no room for parsley, chervil, sorrel, wild chicory, watercress or shallots, which are usually grown on the borders. The horticulturist will judge whether his garden is in the right conditions to produce them, and if necessary, he will substitute them for others less interesting to him. In any case, some vegetables will be sacrificed, as it is impossible to grow all species in a small vegetable garden. 31 SEEDS The vegetable varieties we grow have often been obtained by successive improvements of wild types. These improvements could only be fixed by selection, i.e. by always looking for subjects with the highest degree of the desired qualities for the production of seeds for future sowing, and by surrounding them with the most attentive care to prevent them from suffering the action of surrounding plants of lesser value. Improved plants all have a natural tendency to revert to the wild type from which they originate (the law of atavism); selection is therefore an absolute necessity to perpetuate breeds. Most of the time, gardeners cultivate varieties of the same species in beds far enough apart from each other; but this precaution is often insufficient, as insects can, in spite of this, fertilize one subject by means of pollen taken from another located at a certain distance from the first. The most effective method is to cover the seed-bearing vegetables with gauze when they flower, and uncover them once fertilization has taken place. It's preferable to collect the seeds you want to sow yourself, as this way you can be more sure of their quality. In the article devoted to each crop, we'll explain the special care to be taken with seed carriers. If, despite the precautions we have indicated, new varieties should appear, it will be up to the grower to judge whether or not they should be kept in the garden. Some seeds need to be sown fresh to produce good results, but almost all can retain their germination capacity for several years. In the table below, we give a few notes on the seeds of the main vegetables, taken from MM. Vilmorin-Andrieux et Cie's book on vegetable plants; the gardener will find this information useful. These indications should not exempt the gardener from seeking more detailed information in the articles devoted to each crop; their sole purpose is to provide a reminder of the work to be carried out at particular times of the year. As they relate to the climate of Paris, the horticulturist will be able to modify them according to circumstances. January. The work carried out during this month is mainly related to forced cultivation. The horticulturist must set up new beds and care for those previously sown: he reshuffles the stoves and aerates the plants from time to time, transplanting those that are vigorous enough, and harvesting vegetables fit for consumption. He can also sow asparagus, carrots and other early vegetables; asparagus, early carrots, chervil, some varieties of chicory such as summer chicory, as well as some wild chicories for cutting, early cabbage and early savoy cabbage, early cauliflower, crambe, Alen cress, spinach, early broad beans, strawberries, the earliest varieties of beans, lettuce, cucumbers and melons. For the latter, we prefer the very early Cantaloup Prescott frame melon and the black Cantaloup des Carmes melon. Sow the earliest varieties of turnips, onions, leeks, peas, radishes and tomatoes, and plant potatoes. In the cellar, mushroom stacks can be larded. The only things that can be sown in the open ground are ordinary garlic, bulbous chervil, onions, parsnips, parsley, broad beans and early peas. For the latter two vegetables in particular, sowing must be done in good exposure. February. The general work carried out in February is a continuation of that done in January. The layers that have already produced are turned over and raised again, adding a certain quantity of new manure. Early crops are sown in the same way as in the previous month. Crops grown in the open are quite numerous. This is the time for planting asparagus claws, asparagus seedlings, early carrots, baby celery, wild chicory, cabbage, spring onions and chives, watercress and Alen cress, spinach, spring lettuces and romaine, leeks, early radishes and scorzonera; planting of shallot bulbs, crosne tubers and Jerusalem artichokes. March. From March onwards, bedding out gradually loses its importance, giving way to natural cultivation. Nevertheless, a number of vegetables can be sown under frame: artichokes, eggplants, cardoons, celery, chicories, cabbages and cauliflowers, squash, cucumbers, strawberries, beans, lettuces and romaine, melons, turnips, dandelions, leeks, potatoes, radishes, tetragonia and tomatoes. In the cellar, the mushroom stacks are larded. Towards the end of the month, you can uncover a number of vegetables, such as artichokes, which have been sheltered until now and will now be able to withstand the outside temperature. Almost all vegetables can already be sown or planted in the open ground. We'll mention just a few: ait, arroche, asparagus, carrots, chervil, chicory, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kohlrabi, spring onions, chives, cress, crosne, shallots, spinach, broad beans, strawberries, yams, head and romaine lettuces, lentils, turnips, onions, sorrel, parsnips, parsley, dandelions, leeks, peas, potatoes, radishes, horseradish, salsify, scorzonera, tetragon and Jerusalem artichokes. April. In April, frosts are usually no longer to be feared, so plants grown on beds can be given frequent airing. Some eggplant, cardoon, chicory, cucumber, squash, bean, melon, pepper and tomato seedlings are still sown in frames and on beds. Plants vigorous enough to withstand this operation continue to be transplanted; cucumbers, squash and melons are pruned. Mushroom wheels can be larded in the cellar. Field work consists of thinning, hoeing, weeding and watering. Vegetables sown in the open ground are transplanted; artichoke eyelets, asparagus claws, crosne and potato tubers and tarragon are planted; a number of vegetables are sown: arugula, beet, carrots, celery, celeriac, chervil, chicory, cabbage, cauliflower, kohlrabi, turnip cabbage, chives, civets, watercress, spinach, broad beans, strawberries, beans with good exposure, yams, lettuces, lentils, white mustard, turnips, onions, sorrel, parsnips, parsley, dandelions, leeks, peas, potatoes, radishes, horseradish, rutabagas, salsify, scorzonera, tetragonia, thyme, tomatoes. Care must be taken to destroy all harmful insects. 37 In this month, beds are used only for planting potatoes, cucumbers, melons and chicory, the latter not needing to be sheltered by frames. The horticulturist is mainly occupied with outdoor work. He plants artichoke eyelets, tarragon stalks and potato tubers; He sows arroche, asparagus, beet, cardoons, celery, celeriac, chervil, summer chicory, escarole, large-root wild chicory, chicory for capuchin and witloof beards, improved chicory, cabbage, cauliflower, kohlrabi, kohlrabi, spring onions, cucumbers, watercress, spinach, strawberries, beans, head and romaine lettuces, lentils, melons, turnips, sorrel, parsley, dandelions, leeks, peas, purslane, spring, summer and winter radishes, salsify, scorzonera, tetragonia, thyme. Juim. In June, the only plants that occupy the beds are eggplants, melons, potatoes and mushrooms in the cellar. Watering, in particular, must be repeated often, as the heat quickly evaporates the water; the soil, hardened by successive waterings, must itself be hoeed from time to time. There are still a relatively large number of seedlings to be sown at this time of year; beets, cardoons, carrots, ribbed celery, chervil, summer chicory and escarole, various types of chicory with large roots, cabbages, cauliflowers, broccoli, kohlrabi, spring onions, cucumbers, squash, cress, spinach, strawberries, beans, head, romaine and leaf lettuces, lentils, lamb's lettuce, turnips, sorrel, parsley, dandelions, leeks, peas, purslane, radishes, radish, rutabaga, salsify, scorzonera, thyme. July. Vegetables require the same care in July as they did in June, but need even more watering, as the heat is generally stronger. Carrots, chervil, endive and wild chicory, cabbages to be harvested the following year, broccoli, kohlrabi, kohlrabi, spring onions, cucumbers, cress, spinach, strawberries, beans, lettuce, lamb's lettuce, turnips, onions, sorrel, parsley, dandelions, leeks, peas, purslane, summer and autumn radishes, radish, scorzonera and thyme. August. Growing operations in August are absolutely the same as in previous months, but if the temperature is lower than in July, watering will be less frequent. As always, mushroom wheels can be larded in the cellar. There are fewer open-ground seedlings; carrots, chervil, bulbous chervil, chicory, cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli, spring onions, watercress, spinach and strawberries, winter and spring lettuces, lamb's lettuce, turnips, onions, sorrel, parsley, dandelions, leeks, periwinkle, purslane, winter radish, raiponium and scorzonera. 39 From September onwards, a smaller number of vegetables are sown in the open ground. Weeding, hoeing and watering are still the same general procedures for those still in vegetation. We are still sowing carrots, ordinary and bulbous chervil, chicory endives (which will be sheltered by frames when the cold comes), cabbages, cauliflowers, cress alénois, spinach, lamb's lettuce, turnips, early onions, sorrel, parsley, leeks, radishes; we are planting strawberry plants and trimming mushroom wheels. October. In October, a few more vegetables are sown in the ground. These include: ordinary chervil, bulbous chervil, cauliflower, watercress, spinach, strawberries, lettuce (which needs to be sheltered with a frame), sorrel, parsley, dwarf peas (which need to be protected from frost with chests) and radishes. Garlic and shallot bulbs are planted, mushroom wheels are trimmed, celery is mounded and cardoons are stuffed for blanching. November. In November, bedding becomes more necessary. Carrots, chervil, wild chicory, cauliflower, watercress, spinach, lettuce, peas and radishes are sown for forcing. In the open ground, plant garlic and shallot bulbs, common chervil, bulbous chervil, broad beans, lettuces and peas. For pea seedlings, Michaux peas are preferred. Mushroom grasses can be larded. Special care includes buttering artichokes, blanching celery and tying escarole and chicory. Celeriac and head cabbage are also trimmed; cardoons are stuffed and placed in the vegetable greenhouse if the weather is cold; cauliflower is placed in the greenhouse; asparagus is smoked; root vegetables that fear low temperatures are placed in the greenhouse. December. December is the most important month for forced cultivation: the gardener puts up layers for new seedlings, and from time to time aerates young plants in vegetation. Every evening, he covers his trays with straw mats, which he removes in the morning. The seedlings that can be sown on beds at this time, in addition to mushroom sowing, are carrots, chervil, wild chicory, cucumbers, broad beans, early beans, lettuces for cutting, melons, leeks, early dwarf peas and early radishes. You can also plant early Marjolin potatoes. Vegetables that are to overwinter in the garden must be covered with bedding; seedlings are entirely suspended. CHAPTER ONE THE POTATO The potato, regarded today as the best of our vegetables, is an annual plant with a herbaceous stem, whose underground parts are lined with swellings called tubers. We won't go into the history of the potato here; we know the difficulties it encountered when first introduced to France, and how Parmentier, by dint of perseverance, succeeded in making it accepted by his compatriots. The potato can grow in all types of soil, and almost always yields abundant harvests when the soil is thoroughly fertilized before planting. However, strong, damp soils are less suitable than light, chalky ones; in any case, the potato plays an important role in most vegetable gardens, due to its nutritional value and the variety of ways in which it can be used. Propagation. Potatoes can be propagated by sowing, but this is rarely done, unless new varieties are desired. The fruits containing the seed are small, unpalatable berries, generally smaller than a walnut. Reproduction is usually carried out with the help of the tubers themselves, which, when placed in the ground, soon produce stems whose first food is drawn from the material they contain. Once the potatoes have been dug up, it's a good idea to leave those intended for the propagation of the species in the ground for a while, before bringing them in. To do this, choose tubers with the most pronounced characteristics of the varieties you want to reproduce. When they have taken on a greenish hue, they are brought in and, some time before planting, placed on racks or, as some horticulturists recommend, in oyster baskets, so that they can begin to grow. For varieties that produce few sprouts, only one layer of potatoes should be placed on the tray or in each crate; for ordinary varieties, several layers should be stacked on top of each other. The tubers should also be exposed to air and light from time to time, simply by opening the windows when the outside temperature is not too cold. Thus prepared, potatoes can be harvested earlier than if they had been planted without any care. Natural cultivation. Soil intended for natural potato cultivation must be ploughed and smoked before planting, which usually takes place in April. Holes, 50 centimetres apart in either direction, are opened with a hoe, 10 to 15 centimetres deep. A tuber is placed at the bottom of each hole, then covered with soil. A few days after emergence, when the plants can be easily distinguished, the first hoeing is carried out, which has the advantage of removing weeds. When the stems are 20 centimetres high, they are ridged, i.e. the soil is lifted around each plant, either with a hand hoe, or with a ridging tool for large-scale cultivation. It is easy to see that varieties whose tubers are deep in the soil should not be ridged as hard as those whose tubers are a few centimetres above the surface, and that if the soil is clayey, ridging should be weaker than if it is siliceous or chalky. When planting takes place, as we said earlier, in the course of April, we can obtain, with the early varieties, a harvest of new potatoes at the beginning of July. Tubers that are to be consumed throughout the following year should not be pulled until the tops have dried out. This can be done with a hoe or a flat-tined fork. Leave the potatoes to dry out on the ground for a few days, then store them in a dry place. To prevent sprouting and preserve potatoes over winter, simply remove the eyes with a knife or small gouge, notching the tuber to a thickness of 2 to 3 millimetres. For large supplies, the procedure described by Mr. Schribaux can be used, which consists of immersing the tubers for ten to twelve hours in a solution of 1 hectoliter of water and 1 to 2 liters of commercial sulfuric acid, at 66 degrees Baumé. The solution is placed in a wooden container, and the tubers are washed thoroughly before treatment. This operation should be carried out in March or April, when the sprouts are visible. Forced cultivation. Forced cultivation of potatoes is carried out on beds covered with frames. The layers are generally 60 centimetres thick. They can be planted from the beginning of January, for harvesting in March. During the day, when the temperature eases and the sun falls on the frame, the plants can be uncovered; in the evening, don't forget to place mats over the panels. Gardeners who grow potatoes on trays generally use them for two successive seasons; the second, when the temperature is higher, naturally requires less care. For the night, it is sufficient to cover the young plants with straw mats and to support them above the layers with stakes, when bad weather sets in. Varieties. The varieties of potato known today are very numerous, so we'll limit ourselves to mentioning those generally considered to be the best or most productive. Round yellow potatoes. - Among the round yellow potatoes we'll mention the following: The Bonne Wilhelmine potato, widely grown as an early crop, as its tubers form quickly; The Chardon potato, which ripens in the first half of October; it is very productive, and, as its flesh is not of superior quality, it is often used for animal feed; it can nevertheless be eaten on the table at the end of winter; at this time it is better than immediately after harvesting; The Snowflake potato, one of the best American varieties, quite productive, which ripens around the middle of July; The Shaw potato, widely grown around Paris, whose flesh is mealy; it can be harvested in the first̀re fortnight of August; The Segonzac potato which, like the previous one, is often grown around Paris, and whose ripening takes place at the beginning of August. .P - Quarantaine de Noisy potato. Vitelotte red potato. 45 Long yellow potatoes. - Long yellow potatoes include The Marjolin or Quarantaine potato, now widespread, which ripens in the first fortnight of July; this excellent variety is the most widely grown on beds; it is planted when sprouted; The Quarantaine de Noisy or late Marjolin potato, a superior variety now much sought after; It is very productive and ripens at the beginning of August; The Marjolin tetard potato, productive, early and of good quality; The Joseph Rigault potato, a semi-early variety, productive and of good quality; The Magnum bonum potato, semi-late, productive and of good quality: The Royale or early English potato, an excellent variety, as early as the early Marjolin.
