Purple potatoes. - Purple varieties are less numerous and less sought-after than yellow and red varieties. Here are a few examples: The round Violette potato, fairly productive, which can be harvested in the first half of September; The late Violette potato, grown especially in Brittany, which ripens in early September; it keeps well. Enemies. Like most vegetables, the potato is subject to attack by a number of insects, such as the white grub, the cricket and the moth; but it is also attacked by a disease that alters its tubers and makes them unfit for food. The disease is caused by a microscopic fungus called peronospora infestans. Peronospora attacks begin on the leaves, which turn yellow and become covered with brown spots. Gradually, the disease spreads from person to person, and usually reaches the tubers two or three days later. Some horticulturists have advised cutting off the leaves and stems as soon as the first symptoms of the disease appear: this over-aggressive procedure has the disadvantage of compromising the plant's vegetation later on. Others have claimed that the use of sulphur flower gives good results; we don't think this method is the most effective. In our opinion, the most effective treatment consists in immediately spraying affected stems and leaves with a liquid called Bordeaux mixture, composed of 88% water, 6% copper sulfate and 6% lime. In an experiment carried out in Joinville-le-Pont by Mr. Prillieux, Inspector General of Agriculture, not a single tuber was found to be affected on nine treated plants, while seventeen tubers were found to have been altered on six untreated plants, which had been set aside for comparison. PATATO, IGNAME, CROSNE, TOPINAMBOUR, OXALIS Potato. 49 Like the potato, the potato is a tuberous plant. It does well in the south of France, but requires more care in the Paris climate. In warmer countries, they often replace the potato, because, like the potato, they can be prepared in many different ways. Its floury flesh has a sweet flavor and a fragrance rather reminiscent of violets. In the south of France, potato cultivation requires little more care than that of the potato, and for the same surface area, it produces much greater yields. In spring, the tuber is planted in loose soil, which is soon covered by the creeping stems that develop on its surface. The main care consists of frequent watering via irrigation channels. In central and northern France, potatoes are grown in layers. In January, the best-preserved tubers are planted on a warm bed, covered with a frame and covered with mats for the night. When the shoots have developed, we detach them, keeping a fragment of the tuber with them, then plant them in small pots which we push into the bed and cover with a bell. At the beginning of March, they are transplanted onto a second layer of dry leaves covered with around 15 cm of potting soil; once this is done, the young shoots are sheltered by a frame. Around mid-April, the air is gradually allowed to penetrate under the panels, and later, when the outside temperature has become sufficiently warm, they are removed permanently. Sometimes, as they develop, the potatoes appear on the surface of the soil; in this case, they must be covered with soil. Harvesting takes place as late as possible, so that the vegetables have time to develop sufficiently; but as soon as the frost has reached the tops of the tubers, they must be uprooted, as the insufficiently protected tubers will themselves be attacked and rot quickly. When pulling potatoes, care must be taken, as those that are crumpled or injured will spoil immediately. When they have dried well on the ground, they are placed in layers in baskets, with a bed of tannin or heather that has been dried beforehand, and then placed in a place where the temperature does not fall below 8 to 10 degrees. There are many varieties of potato, the main ones being: the yam potato, with its grayish skin; the yellow potato, with its elongated, thin tuber, smooth skin and very fine flesh; the pink Malaga potato, also known as the red Algiers potato, one of the earliest; and the white potato, inferior to the above in every respect. M 41 t21 Malaga pink potato. Chinese yam. The yam is a tuber introduced to France in 1848 by M. de Montigny, consul in Chang-Haï. Much larger than the potato, yams can reach up to 1 meter in length; their taste is reminiscent of that of the potato, so most of the preparations suitable for potatoes can be applied to yams. Yam is a perennial plant that is sometimes left in the ground for two years before being harvested; it is easy to store; its annual stems are voluble, i.e. they can curl up like those of bindweed; they can be left to crawl on the ground; they then grow less, but make hoeing difficult. Yam can be propagated in a variety of ways: each of the little buds on the tuber can give rise to a plant; bulblets from the leaf axils can also be used for propagation. The best method is to plant unbroken tubers no more than 10 cm long in March. Stems are sometimes given long stakes around which they wrap as they grow, making routine gardening easier. When yams are propagated by bulbing, the first year's harvest is often minimal, but by the second year it has increased considerably. 40 8 Chinese yam. But the main obstacle to large-scale cultivation of Chinese yam is the difficulty of digging it up, which is generally done in November of the first year; it is often necessary to dig 80 centimetres or even 1 metre deep to obtain the tubers without damaging them; as a result, cultivation costs are very high. In the past, yams were grown as a forage crop to replace potatoes, given their much higher yield. However, the cost of harvesting them had to be borne in mind, and today yams are grown only as a vegetable, mainly as a curiosity. The genus Igname (Dioscorea) includes a considerable number of species and varieties that play a major role in the diets of populations in certain parts of the world. Crosne or Stachys affinis. The Japanese crosne is an excellent vegetable originating in China, which appeared in France in 1882, and whose cultivation is spreading more and more. It is now widely consumed in France, thanks to the perseverance and efforts of Messrs. Paillieux and Bois, who have done their utmost to propagate it in France. Crosne is easy to grow; it thrives in all types of soil. However, for easier harvesting, it's best not to grow it in compacted soil. In February, in holes 20 centimetres deep and 40 centimetres apart in both directions, crosnes are placed, usually three in each hole. Hoeing is done frequently, but rarely after the end of September, when tubers at shallow depths run a high risk of 1. This can be seen in the article devoted to this genus by Messrs Paillieux and Bois in their Potager d'un Curieux. Crosne du Japon. to be damaged. Each plant can be lightly butted when the last hoeing is done. Weeding should not take place before the beginning of December: it is often only at this time that the tubers are fully developed. As crosne does not fear frost, harvesting can be carried out at any time. To preserve crosne, it should not be left in the open air, where it will quickly wither; it should be placed in sand and kept in a cool, dry place. Crosne is a vegetable which, because of the care required to harvest it, is only suitable for small-scale cultivation; despite all the precautions taken to uproot it, a fairly large number of shoots generally appear around May, which, if left in place, would produce nothing. On the contrary, if you transplant them, you can obtain an abundant harvest. Crosne can be prepared in a variety of ways. In general, all the preparations suitable for potatoes can be applied to it; it is not peeled, but simply washed before cooking, which lasts twelve to fifteen minutes. Its pleasant flavor is reminiscent of potato, salsify and artichoke. Crosne is attacked by only one enemy: the white grub of the chafer. Jerusalem artichoke. The Jerusalem artichoke is a plant native to North America, with reddish-purple tubers about the size of potatoes. Mainly used as a fodder plant, Jerusalem artichokes are sometimes grown in the vegetable garden; their sweet taste is not unpleasant, but the quality of the flesh is inferior to that of most of our tuberous vegetables. Jerusalem artichokes require little labor to grow, and yield quite a lot. On the other hand, cattle can be fed on the aerial part of the plant; but it is necessary to wait 4 2 A 9 9 I EI Topinambour. before cutting the stems and leaves, until the tubers are sufficiently developed for them not to suffer. Some growers have claimed that it is more advantageous to leave Jerusalem artichokes to vegetate for two consecutive years than to harvest them in the first year. However, several experiments carried out by M. Joigneaux show that the harvest obtained in the first case is much lower than the product of two annual harvests. Jerusalem artichokes thrive in all soils, no matter how arid; when in the ground, they have little fear of frost; they are reproduced in spring by planting tubers; they are uprooted when the tops have died. The tuber is easy to preserve. Jerusalem artichokes can be reproduced by sowing, but the results obtained in this way are generally unsatisfactory. However, progress has been made in terms of flesh quality. The yellow tuber variety has a more delicate flavor than the ordinary variety, but is much less productive. Oxalis. Oxalis is a little-cultivated vegetable, as its yield is extremely low. Two main species of oxalis are grown: crenellated oxalis and Deppe's oxalis; the former is the more palatable and widespread variety, and is a tuber native to Peru with fairly deep notches; its shape is elongated and its volume slightly larger than that of a walnut. The crenellated oxalis, whose smooth skin can be red, yellow or white, reproduces by planting its tubers in May in holes spaced about Om, 80 apart in both directions; this spacing is necessary to allow the stems to develop freely. To stimulate tuber growth, they are often planted in March on warm beds, for transplanting in May in loose soil. As the stems develop, they should be covered with soil, although leaving around 20 cm of their terminal part in the open air, to encourage tuber formation on buried shoots. At this stage, crenellated oxalis has a pronounced acid taste. "In South America, say Oxalis crénelée. MM. Vilmorin-Andrieux et Cie, this acidity is eliminated by exposing tubers enclosed in woollen cloth bags to the sun. After a few days, they become floury and sweet; if this treatment is applied for several weeks, they dry out, wrinkle and take on a flavor somewhat analogous to that of dried figs". Red or yellow oxalis are the best for eating. The edible part of Deppe's oxalis, native to Brazil, is formed by the bulging roots, which are similar in shape to carrots. This species is generally propagated by bulblets or eyelets, which develop in the region of the root collar; they are planted in April in holes spaced about 35 centimetres apart in both directions; they are watered when dryness sets in. As mentioned above, the roots of Deppe's oxalis are inferior to the tubers of crenellated oxalis. The leaves of both plants can be used as a vegetable, and are eaten in the same way as sorrel. CHAPTER III RAVES AND TURNS, CHOUX-NAVETS AND RUTABAGAS CHOUX-RAVES, RADISHES, WILD RAIFORT Raves and turnips. In turnips and rabe, the food part is formed by the root, which is quite bulky and varies in shape from one variety to another. The color itself varies, with black, violet, orange, yellow and white varieties, as does the flavor, which is generally sweet. The words "rabe" and "turnip" are often used synonymously; however, the former has a slight difference from the latter: its root is more globular. Multiplication. - Turnips and rabe are generally propagated by sowing, which, depending on the earliness of the variety, takes place from the end of June to the beginning of September. Sowing can be done either broadcast or in rows; we recommend the latter, which makes gardening much easier. These seedlings are usually sown indoors. Cultivation. - When turnips and turnips are well advanced, you can light them so that the plants don't get in each other's way later on. On the other hand, the drier they are, the more frequent and abundant the watering should be. Some hoeing and weeding is also necessary. Turnips are uprooted when they have developed enough to be eaten; we rarely wait until they have reached their maximum volume, as they are tastier when they are young than when growth has stopped for good. If care is taken to sow several times, one or two weeks apart, turnips can be harvested for a good part of the year. Varieties. - Among the many varieties of turnips and rabe, we'd like to mention the following: Le navet long des Vertus, white in color, with sweet, tender flesh of good quality; it is widely grown around Paris; Le navet long des Vertus, Marteau race, the most renowned of turnips; its shape differs from that of the preceding one in that the end is rounded instead of conical; it's almost the only one used for forced cultivation; the Freneuse turnip, which adapts well to poor soils; its skin is grayish and its flesh white; the long Meaux turnip, whose elongated root is often deformed; It's also known as the "corne-de-bœuf" turnip; The yellow "boule d'or" turnip with a spherical root; this variety, with its yellow epidermis, is highly prized; The early flat white turnip, which is highly prized and in which the edible part is almost entirely out of the ground; The early flat red turnip, which differs from the previous one only in color; it is well suited to forced cultivation; The late Auvergne turnip, which is grown extensively in the Me Navet des Vertus, Marteau breed. Navet jaune boule d'or. FF Navet long de Meaux. central France, for animals, but can also be used as a vegetable. Seed carrier. - At harvest time, the horticulturist must choose plants with all the characteristics he wishes to obtain, in order to make them produce seed. These plants can be left in place, or planted in another location where they will occupy less surface area and remain Altise. until fruiting has taken place. The seeds harvested are very small and brown in color. The insect that causes most damage to turnip plantations is the flea beetle, also known as the ground flea. Flea beetles attack mainly young plants, sometimes forcing the gardener to repeat the sowing several times. We try to combat this insect by repeated drenching, and by adding tobacco juice to water. 58 Kohlrabi and rutabagas are similar to turnips in taste and root shape. Sensitive to hot weather, they are unaffected by cold, so are widely grown in northern France. They are generally sown in May and June, either broadcast or in rows, and later thinned so that the plants are about 40 cm apart. The only care required is some hoeing and, during drought, some watering. Vegetables are generally uprooted in late autumn and stored in a cellar over winter, after slicing off the leaves. Kohlrabi and rutabaga are often used for large-scale cultivation; in this case, the latter is generally preferred, because of the ease with which it can be uprooted; for vegetable cultivation, on the other hand, the former is more commonly used: white kohlrabi, white kohlrabi with red collar, smooth white kohlrabi with short leaf, rutabaga with green collar, rutabaga with purple or red collar, early flat yellow rutabaga, oval rutabaga. This part bears leaves; its flavor is similar to that of kohlrabi. Kohlrabi can be sown from March to June. Large round winter black radish. Winter long black radish. Radishes are one of the vegetables that require the least care to prepare, so consumption is considerable. They are propagated by sowing, at different times of the year, depending on whether you are growing all-month radishes, summer radishes, autumn radishes or winter radishes. All-month radishes. - All-month radishes can be sown from the beginning of January on a bed, and from March to November in the open ground; their growth is very rapid: they require barely a month of vegetation to be fit for consumption; as their cultivation requires only a small plot, they can be broadcast among the other vegetables. If you force them under a frame, don't forget to give them air from time to time. Radishes need to be thinned out after sowing, then weeded and watered frequently throughout the summer. Radish varieties for all months include: round pink radish, half-long pink radish, half-long pink radish with white tip, half-long scarlet radish, half-long scarlet radish with white tip, half-long white radish, long pink or salmon radish, long pink radish, Vienna radish. Summer and autumn radishes. - Summer and autumn radishes also include larger varieties that grow more slowly and require stronger soil than ordinary varieties; they are best sown once in the vegetable garden, in rays about 15 cm apart, in May or June, sown very lightly. In calcareous, siliceous soil, water often. Don't wait until the roots are fully developed before pulling them out; they are almost always eaten when they are about halfway through their growth; later they will be less tender and of much poorer quality. We'd like to mention a few varieties of summer and autumn radishes: the round Dlanc summer radish, the giant white Stuttgard radish, the yellow or red summer radish, the round gray summer radish, the round black summer radish, the half-long white Strasbourg radish. Winter radish. - Winter radishes, also known as horseradish, are even slower-growing than their predecessors; most are very large, reaching the size of an ordinary turnip. They require fairly substantial soil; they can be sown in rows 25 to 30 centimetres apart, from May to August; weeded and hoeed from time to time; watered abundantly during the summer and harvested after three months. Winter radishes buried in sand keep well in a cool place; other varieties should be eaten immediately. We recommend the following winter radishes: Large round black winter radish, large purple winter radish, long black winter radish, large white Augsburg radish, white Russian radish, gray winter Laon radish, pink winter Chinese radish. Young radishes are often attacked by flea beetles; we have already indicated the remedies generally used. Horseradish. Wild horseradish, also known as cran de Bretagne, cranson rustique or capucin mustard, grows on the coast, particularly in Brittany. It is a perennial plant with a strong, pungent flavor, similar to that of mustard. It can be propagated by sowing seeds in spring, but is more often reproduced by planting root fragments in autumn. These fragments emit adventitious roots that grow vertically and deeply into the soil; they are placed permanently using a planter. The only care required in growing this vegetable is hoeing and weeding. Harvesting takes place after three years of cultivation. Placed in a cellar and buried in sand, horseradish keeps very well. After grating the skin, it is used as a condiment. Horseradish. BETTERAVE, CARROT, PANAIS, CÉLERI-RAVE CERFEUIL BULBEUX, PERSIL A GROSSE RACINE Beetroot. 65 Beetroot can be grown as a vegetable, sugar or fodder crop. We will deal here only with the cultivation of beet, a vegetable used mainly in salads as a dressing. Beet requires deeply tilled, well-smoked soil, rich especially in potassium fertilizers. It is harvested in April or May, either broadcast or in rays 35 to 40 centimetres apart. Thinning takes place once the plants have emerged; later, weeding and hoeing are carried out; harvesting generally takes place in July or August. Roots you want to keep Beetroot from Castelnaudine. The main varieties of beet are: POTAGER. Red beet, Castelnaudary red beet, dwarf red beet, long red beet, long yellow beet, Castelnaudary yellow beet. Carrot. Like beet, carrot requires soil that has been deeply disturbed by ploughing and that has received a certain amount of fertilizer during the year preceding its cultivation. It thrives best in light soils, and does admirably in cool, siliceous soils. It can be grown in the ground or in beds. Natural cultivation. - Carrots are generally sown in a bed facing south or east. Very early varieties can be sown in September; carrots covered with mats when it freezes can be harvested in May. Sowing can be done either broadcast or in rows; after September, others can be done in February, March, April, May or June, depending on the variety. After emergence, carrots are thinned out; during the growing season, they are hoeed, weeded and watered. In winter, carrots can be stored in straw or fine sand, after removing the leaves. Forced cultivation. - When growing on a bed, a bed producing a temperature of around 15 degrees is generally put up at the beginning of December, and loaded with a 20-centimeter-thick bed of terra-cotta. Once the desired temperature has been reached, the seed is sown; in January, unconsumed manure is added to the stoves, to raise the heat of the layer a little.

When the weather is dry, the plants can be lightly soaked in water. With this cultivation method, carrots fit for consumption can be harvested as early as April. Varieties. - The most popular carrot varieties are : Red carrots: Altringham long red, Vilmorin long red, pointed half-long red, obtuse half-long red, Nantaise half-long red, early short red, very short red with frame. Yellow carrots include: jaune lonque, jaune courte. Finally, let's mention a variety that is actually more curious than useful: the violet carrot. Seed carriers - Carrots from which seed is to be obtained are selected at harvest time from among the best varieties, and then placed in gauges. This is usually done by transporting the plants to a trench dug with a northern exposure, and covering them with thick litter. In spring, they are replanted in rows, 50 cm apart in both directions. The seeds are ready for harvesting in August. Don't forget to cover each plant with gauze at the time of fertilization, if the different varieties are not far enough apart. Pests. - Carrots are prone to attack by a variety of insects; the most feared for young plants is the spider mite 4 1 E mm Altringham long red carrot. Red semi-long pointed carrot. Red half-long Nantaise carrot. Long yellow carrot. red, which ravages plants as soon as they emerge. This insect is combated by frequent drenching. Parsnip. The shape of the parsnip is quite similar to that of the carrot; it is white and is mainly used to give broth a pleasant flavor. However, it is also used for animal feed and, in some regions, for human consumption. As parsnip cultivation is absolutely identical to that of the carrot, we won't go back over the various operations involved. Parsnips are not very sensitive to frost, so they can be dug up very late in the season; in some areas, they are even left in the ground throughout the winter; the plants are removed from the ground when they are to be used immediately. Seedlings should be left in the ground during the coldest weather; they will continue to grow the following spring. The main varieties of parsnip are Round hatif parsnip. Long parsnip, improved Brest parsnip, long Guernsey parsnip, early round parsnip. Celeriac. Celeriac is a vegetable whose root has been mo25 dified by cultivation. It thrives in loose, fresh, fertilizer-rich soil, and can be propagated by sowing, either in the ground or on a bed. Sowing in the open ground takes place towards the end of March; when the plant is sufficiently developed, it is pricked out, then planted out in May. By October, the root is generally large enough to be delivered for consumption. For bedding plants, sowing usually takes place in February. In addition to transplanting and planting, celeriac requires abundant watering. To encourage growth, we usually cut off the side roots and lightly butter the plant. The main varieties of celeriac are : Ordinary celeriac, smooth Paris celeriac, Erfurt celeriac, small-leaf apple celeriac. Bulbous chervil. Introduced to France in 1826, bulbous or tuberous chervil is now quite sought-after. Its root, which is only small, is roughly carrot-shaped, gray in color, with white flesh and a flavor reminiscent of chestnuts. It is eaten like potatoes. Bulbous chervil can grow in any soil. It is usually sown as a broadcast crop in autumn, with very little covering; most of the time, it's enough to lead the seed. As the seed is not expected to emerge until spring of the following year, it is important not to let weeds encroach on the planting bed. Water frequently as the plant grows. By stratifying the seeds, i.e. depositing them in small containers in which a layer of seed alternates with a layer of sand, and watering the preparation, it is possible to sow only in the spring of the year of harvest. When the stem and leaves have dried out, bulbous chervil can be harvested, but it's a good idea to wait a while before eating it, as its taste is then more delicate; bulbous chervil is also easy to store. TI Parsley with a large root, highly renowned in various countries, is less appreciated in France. The root, which is the part used here, is roughly shaped like a long carrot; its color is that of parsnips, i.e. grayish white. Its cultivation is no different from that of parsnips. Big-rooted parsley is sown in spring, in well-tilled soil; as it is very hardy, it can remain in the ground through the winter; however, it is sometimes put in gauges to be replanted as spring approaches. The root is pleasantly flavored, somewhat reminiscent of celery root; it can be used in the same preparations, but can also be eaten after cooking in ash, or sliced and mixed into salads. The leaves, similar to those of common parsley, can be used for the same purposes, but it is preferable to leave them on the plant if the roots are to develop fully. However delicate the flavor of large-rooted parsley may be, we all agree that it has one rather serious drawback: the food part is too small to pay for the work it requires; however, in home gardens, where it is not the object of speculation, this drawback loses its importance. There are two main varieties of parsley with a large root: the tardice variety, more elongated, and the hâtive variety, swollen near the neck. CHAPTER V SALSIFIS, SCORSONERE, RAIPONCE, SCOLYME Salsify. Salsify is a vegetable with an elongated root up to 20 cm long; the skin is yellowish; the flesh is white; it has a slightly pungent flavor without being acidic. Salsify can be grown in well-tilled soil, as its taproot digs fairly deeply into the soil. It can be propagated by sowing, in spring, in rows about 25 centimeters apart. After emergence, the plants are thinned out so that they are 10 to 15 centimetres apart. Weed and water when necessary; in October, white salsify can be uprooted and removed from the ground as needed, often harvesting well into winter. Subjects intended to serve as seedbeds should be moved to a different location in the spring; several experiments have shown that the best-rooted seeds come from subjects that have flowered in the second year, in a different location from where they spent their first year of vegetation. 73 The importance of growing white salsify has diminished considerably since the introduction of scorzonera into most vegetable gardens. The latter has all the qualities of the former, to which it adds greater hardiness. In fact, scorzonera can grow at more northerly latitudes than white salsify. The taste and shape of scorsonera are absolutely the same as those of salsify; it differs, however, in the leaves, which are larger, and the root epidermis, which is black instead of white. Cultivation is absolutely the same, but scorsonera doesn't necessarily have to be pulled out of the ground in winter; later, during the second year, the vegetable, while developing, remains tender and therefore fit for consumption; it can even be eaten after fertilization and seed production, without losing any of its flavor. 3 Rapunzel. Rapunzel. The raiponce, now little cultivated, is reminiscent of the long turnip in the shape and color of its root; it hardly exceeds 12 to 15 centimeters in length; its flesh is firm and sweet to the taste. It is usually eaten raw, mixed with lamb's lettuce. Riponce is sown in June, either broadcast or in rays 15 to 20 centimeters apart; a little sand is mixed in with the seed to make sowing more uniform. Prefer soil that has not been smoked too recently. After sowing, press the soil down and lightly baste to avoid carrying away the extremely small seed. After emergence, thin out; harvesting can begin in October or November; during winter, uproot as needed. Scolyma. Scolyma, like raiponce, is little cultivated in vegetable gardens; its root can be used like that of salsify and scorsonera. In the southern provinces of France, it grows spontaneously in uncultivated land, where it is often simply harvested. In northern France, on the other hand, it is widely cultivated, as it requires no care. Scolymes can be broadcast or sown in rows in March or April. To prevent food plants from flowering, the stems are pinched off as they develop. Harvesting begins in October. Before delivering them for consumption, the scolyme roots are split lengthwise to remove the fibrous middle part. If the whole root is tender, as can be seen by detaching a small section at the lower end, it can be kept to produce seed. In this way, it may be possible to obtain bark beetles whose entire root is edible. It thrives best in substantial soil that has been carefully fertilized during the year preceding its cultivation. ) N ATIF DE PARIS Although it is biennial, it is generally left to develop for only one year. Cultivation. - The most common method of reproduction is sowing; however, some varieties produce bulblets which are also used to propagate the species. Sowing takes place in March, in well-tilled soil; it is broadcast, then lightly harrowed with a rake; it is then planted and, if necessary, watered a little. Some time after germination, the plants are thinned out; later, cultivation is limited to a few waterings, if drought makes them necessary, and to a few hoeings, which are carried out from time to time, when the usefulness is recognized. Another cultivation method is used in regions with mild winters: sowing from August to October, for planting in late autumn or early winter; this produces large varieties that are harvested in May. A third process, recommended by Messrs Lebrun and Nouvellon, involves replanting small onions, slightly larger than hazelnuts, which have been sown very tightly in March or April of the previous year. These onions develop in a short space of time and produce very fine products in the second year. Varieties. - There are many varieties of onion; the most commonly grown are : The early white Paris onion, of medium size, which keeps well; the large white onion, fairly voluminous, but late, of mild flavor, which keeps rather poorly; the Danvers onion, reddish yellow, early, which is not sown in autumn; the straw-yellow Vertus onion, early and easy to keep; the Cambrai or Mulhouse onion, reddish yellow, early, which keeps well; The yellow sulfur onion from Spain, a little late, but of good quality and easy to keep; The pale red onion from Niort, early, highly prized, easy to keep; The black red onion from Brunswick, purplish red in color, very easy to keep; The round, very large Madeira onion, prized for its flavor, very difficult to keep: The flat Madeira onion, very voluminous, which differs from the previous one only in shape; Sulfur yellow Spanish onion. Round Madeira onion. OGNONS. Mulhouse onion ( ) Niort pale red onion. Flat Madeira onion. 7 Piriform onion, late, easy to preserve; Egyptian onion or Rocambole, red, reproduced by bulblets, which replace the fruit; Potato onion or potato onion, propagated by cloves; generally planted in February; mounded to encourage the development of individuals growing in groups around the cloves planted. The method for preserving onions is simple: just bind them together in bundles using the stems, which are then turned on themselves to bind them together and hang them in a dry place. Seed holders. - Onions destined to supply the seed are replanted in February or March at a distance of 35 to 40 centimetres from each other; the stems are cut after fruiting; they are tied together and hung in a dry place where ripening is completed. Enemies. - The main enemy of the onion is the small white worm, which penetrates the bulb and stops its growth; there is no preservative against this insect, whose attacks have so far been impossible to avoid. Onions are also subject to a disease called rot, which affects young plants in particular. There is no known cure. Leeks. Like many of our vegetables, the leek is a biennial plant, which is cultivated as if it had only been growing for one year. The part used in cooking is the part that is sunk into the ground; it is white in color, contrasting with the green of the leaves. Cultivation. - Leeks thrive best in cool, damp soil, smoked with consumed manure. It is propagated from seed, which is usually broadcast at the end of February or beginning of March; after the seeds have developed, they are thinned out; in May, they are usually transplanted with a planter, deep enough to increase the length of the useful part, leaving a distance of about 25 cm between the plants in both directions, then watered abundantly. The main care required during cultivation is hoeing, weeding and watering. You can start harvesting in August, but if you take care to sow on a bed in February, you can obtain leeks as early as June. The bed used for this cultivation should be about 40 centimetres thick and produce a heat of 15 degrees. Transplanting takes place on 4 June. Poireau monstrueux de Carentan. seedlings are sown in the ground at the end of February; the work is then the same as for cultivation in the ground. Varieties. - The main leek varieties are : Le poireau long, which fears little cold and has a relatively long blanched part; it is often lightly ridged to increase its length; Le poireau gros court, which is early and not very frost-resistant; Le poireau jaune du Poitou, which is early and develops rapidly; Le poireau très gros de Rouen, which is short but quite voluminous, hardy and of good quality; and finally Le poireau monstrueux de Carentan, a highly recommended variety. Seed carriers. - The leeks that are to provide the seed are sown in July and transplanted in September. In winter, they are protected from frost by bedding; by the following September, the seeds are generally ripe. The stems are then detached, tied together and hung in a dry place. The enemies of leeks are the same as those mentioned above for onions. Garlic. Garlic is used extensively in the southern provinces of France, as a seasoning in food preparation. Its strong flavor has made it sought-after since ancient times, and it is widely cultivated. Garlic can grow in all types of soil, but produces its best results in light, substantial soils. It is reproduced by its cloves, which are planted at different times depending on the climate. In the south of France, this is the garlic moth (very enlarged and natural size). In central and northern France, it is more usual to plant the cloves in the early spring. When the stem is sufficiently developed, it can be twisted on itself and held in this position by tying. This facilitates bulb growth. Garlic planted in February or March is harvested in August. Garlic varieties include ordinary garlic, early pink garlic, Rocambole or Spanish garlic, and Oriental garlic. Garlic is sometimes attacked by larvae of the garlic moth, also known as the leek moth; like onions, it is prone to rot. Shallot. Shallots, like garlic, multiply by their cloves; they thrive best in light soil that has been thoroughly fertilized the previous year. If this has not been done, it is preferable to give this vegetable well-consumed manure rather than fresh manure. The cloves are planted in February or March, about 10 cm apart and shallowly; they are hoeed and weeded from time to time during the summer. Harvest around July. The most widely grown varieties of shallot are: Noisy shallot, Jersey shallot, earlier than the above. The insects we mentioned when talking about onions, leeks and garlic sometimes attack shallots, which, like these vegetables, are prone to rot. THE POTAGER. Chives. Although the chive is considered a herbaceous vegetable rather than a root vegetable, we place it alongside the onion, garlic and shallot, with which it has many similarities. Chives usually multiply by means of their seeds, which they produce in fairly large quantities. It is sown indoors and broadcast in February-March and even April and May. For most of the summer, the leaves are harvested and used as seasoning; the only cultivation care required is hoeing and watering. At the beginning of December, the remaining vines can be gauged for use during the winter. The main varieties of spring onion are : Common chives and early white chives. As the chive is a perennial plant, the plants destined to produce seeds can produce them for several consecutive years. Chives or civets, which have the same uses as chives, are propagated with the help of their cloves, which are planted in February or March. As a perennial, it can be preserved over winter by cutting the stems at ground level and covering them with a light layer of compost. It is often grown as a border plant. Ciboule. A Ciboulette. As it is a perennial vegetable, it can be planted in the vegetable garden in such a way as to provide for a family's needs for several years. The only soils where asparagus will not grow well are impermeable ones. The edible part of the asparagus plant is formed by the shoots that emerge each year from the underground part or claw. These shoots, as we know, have a delicate flavor that makes them much appreciated. Natural cultivation. When you want to establish an asparagus plant in your garden, you can either buy seedlings and transplant them, or sow them from seed in March-April, either broadcast or in rays, in soil that has been smoked and ploughed in autumn; then cover with a light layer of potting soil, and lightly baste. Once the seedling has developed, thin it out so that the remaining plants are 7 to 8 centimetres apart. Water occasionally and hoe lightly, taking care not to injure the young plants. The following spring, the plants are planted out, as far as possible in one of the healthiest parts of the garden. Planting can be done in a single row, but most of the time it's done in beds. Whichever way you do it, the growing process is pretty much the same. In February or March, the soil is prepared, having already been fertilized and ploughed in autumn. Pits are dug about 50 centimetres wide, 70 centimetres apart and 15 centimetres deep, into which fertilizer is placed; the location of the claws is then determined, at a distance of 40 to 45 centimetres, so that small mounds of potting soil about 5 centimetres high can be raised, on which a seedling is placed; a layer of potting soil or even compost is then thrown on top; the soil is then brought back to its original level by covering with some of the soil removed. The remainder will be used later for ridging the plants; in the meantime, it is left on the paths. At the end of autumn or the beginning of winter, the stems are cut back to 10 or 20 centimetres from the ground: the remaining part indicates the place of each plant. After hoeing, or rather shallow digging, each plant is given a light layer of natural manure mixed with chemical fertilizers, which is mixed with the soil in spring. The same care continues into the following year. In autumn, dead stems are cut off and, if desired, the location of the claws is marked with a small stick stuck in the ground. Fertilizers are always applied in the same way. In the third year, asparagus can be harvested for consumption, but it is preferable to wait four years before harvesting. In the third year, asparagus is ridged, bringing back the soil that had been left when the plants were planted. Ridging is usually done in April. The mounds of earth formed are 25 to 30 centimetres high. When harvesting asparagus, some horticulturists advise not to cut them under the soil, as is too often done: they believe that the best method would be to spread the soil around the spear and break it by hand, then replace the soil that has been removed. Harvesting begins when the first asparagus shoots are a few centimetres above the surface of the soil, generally in April, and is completed in the first fortnight of June. In subsequent years, cultivation is carried out in exactly the same way; however, after the sixth year, asparagus is usually only fertilized every two years, although annual fertilization is preferable. An asparagus plantation thus established can produce for more than ten years. Although the above-mentioned method is still the most widely used for growing asparagus, there is another method that also gives excellent results. In Argenteuil, the center of asparagus production, different methods are used. Most gardeners there agree that the vegetable should be buried shallowly in the soil, to benefit from the influence of the air, and their various cultivation operations are geared to the application of this principle. They also claim that, with the ordinary method, the fertilizers supplied are placed at too great a distance from the plant's roots, and they try to obviate this inconvenience. Here's how they do it: at the time of planting, the claws are placed only about 15 centimetres below ground level. Every year, at the start of winter, they dig up the soil around each plant to check the condition of the roots and place the fertilizer needed for vegetation. This method seems to us to have a few advantages, but both methods can produce some very fine products. Forced cultivation. Forced cultivation of asparagus is so common today that we can't resist saying a few words about it. M. Courtois-Gérard, in his Manuel pratique de culture maraîchère, discusses the subject at some length. We will outline the procedures he recommends. The first method consists in forcing the plant on the spot where the asparagus is to be grown; the second, in planting the plant in layers once it has reached a certain stage of development. The former produces white asparagus, the latter green. When forcing white asparagus, we plant as we have indicated for ordinary cultivation, and only start forcing in the first fortnight of November of the third year of planting. To do this, the trunks are placed in position, then a layer of potting soil is spread on the boards; the paths are then dug to a depth of around 50 centimetres; the soil removed and placed on the boards will raise them by around 30 centimetres, and by this means, you will obtain shoots of greater length than by the ordinary methods. In the paths, stoves of unconsumed manure are set up and raised to the height of the frame panels. Mulch is spread over the boards, and removed as the asparagus emerges from the soil. The panels are then lowered, kept closed at all times, and covered with mulch every evening. Every fortnight or so, the stoves, which have lost their heat, are replenished; a certain quantity of old manure is removed and replaced by fresh manure. The temperature under the frames should, as far as possible, be no lower than 15 degrees and no higher than 25. Twenty or twenty-five days after placing the boxes, we start harvesting the asparagus, which can be picked every two or three days. Green asparagus is foraged in layers 60 to 80 centimetres high, at a temperature of 20 to 25 degrees Celsius. To form these layers, we use a mixture of consumed manure, fresh horse manure and cow manure; we spread a light layer of potting soil on the surface, then place the boxes. A few days later, they are lightly covered with potting soil, and stoves are set up, to be changed every time the temperature drops. The frames are covered every evening with straw mats, and when the asparagus begin to show, the panels are lifted from time to time to allow the air to penetrate. Fifteen days later, the asparagus is ready to pick. Harvesting can be carried out over a period of about three months. Once the claws have stopped producing, they must be pulled out, as they can no longer be used. Varieties. There are quite a few varieties of asparagus, but we'll just mention a few that are of some importance in vegetable growing: Green asparagus, whose tips quickly take on a rather pronounced green hue; it's worth pointing out here that it's not this variety alone that produces the vegetables we sell under this name; all asparagus can become green by the cultivation process we indicated earlier; Violet asparagus from Holland, which is very commonly grown; White asparagus from Germany, which is often confused with Dutch asparagus, but which is a little earlier than the latter; Early Argenteuil asparagus, which has a pointed tip and relatively large shoots; Late Argenteuil asparagus, which is more productive for longer than the previous variety. Seedstocks. The choice of rootstocks has a major influence on the quality of the produce harvested, so great care must be taken in selecting them. The general rule is to keep isolated, during flowering and fertilization, those plants which have been designated in advance to be used for the propagation of the species. All too often, gardeners neglect these precautions, and hybridization, which is the consequence of this lack of care, leads to the degeneration of the best varieties. In addition, the grower must not harvest from the claws intended for propagation, as it is necessary to preserve their full strength so that their seeds produce vigorous, good-quality products. By following these instructions, you will not only be able to keep good varieties healthy, but also improve them from time to time. Sowing. In addition to white grubs and cricket beetles, which cause considerable damage to the claws, asparagus is attacked by the asparagus beetle and the twelve-spotted beetle, which infest the stems and branches of the plant. To destroy them, the stems are shaken over a container of soap water; the larvae detached from the plant fall into 2 A Asparagus beetle Larva of the asparagus beetle. Twelve-spotted beetle. These insects are shown enlarged on the first line and in natural size on the second. the vase. Another method of getting rid of the beetle is to place wood ashes at the foot of each plant; by shaking the stalks as described above, the larvae fall to the ground, where they are burned by the ashes. Asparagus plantations are sometimes ravaged by a disease that rages especially when the soil where the asparagus plantation is located is too damp: we're talking about rust, caused by a microscopic fungus that develops on the stalks. CHAPTER II Cabbages Cabbages are one of the most useful vegetables in our diet. We will look successively at ordinary or cultivated cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower and broccoli. We won't go back over kohlrabi or turnip cabbage, which were discussed in the second part of this volume. Cultivated cabbage. Cabbage is considered to be native to Europe; it grows spontaneously near the sea; it is perennial, but is almost always cultivated in our gardens as an annual or biennial vegetable. Cultivation. - The cultivation of cabbage varies according to whether we have spring, summer, autumn or winter varieties; all, however, do well in well loosened soils, rather moist than dry, and fertilized with consumed manure. Cabbages are propagated by sowing, usually by broadcasting, lightly harrowing the soil and covering it with a light layer of compost, then watering with an apple. Spring varieties are sown in late August or early September, in the open ground; summer varieties are sown in January or February; autumn and winter varieties are sown in April, May or even early June, in the open ground. When the plants have reached a certain stage of development, for example, when they have two or three leaves, they are transplanted. Transplanting is carried out in rows about 10 centimetres apart; the distance to be left between two plants on the same line is also 10 centimetres. Transplanting is carried out using a planter. If there are any plants lacking the terminal bud, these must be carefully removed, as they will not grow after transplanting. Transplanting, essential for spring varieties, is not compulsory for U DE MILAN ORDINAI summer cabbages. It is never used for autumn and winter cabbages. Planting, like transplanting, is done with a planter, in rays spaced at around 30 centimetres apart, a distance that can vary according to the volume of the varieties being grown. After planting, the cabbages receive abundant watering, which can be done at the spout to save time. Spring varieties can be planted in November; summer, autumn and winter varieties a month or a month and a half after sowing. During the cultivation period, the cabbages are hoeed and watered from time to time. Spring cabbages can be buttered three or four months after planting, for harvesting in March or April. Summer cabbages are delivered for consumption throughout this season; autumn cabbages are harvested throughout the fall, and winter cabbages generally at the end of November. The most common method of storing cabbages over winter is to turn them upside down after harvesting, i.e. place the head on the ground, with the roots in the air. They can also be placed in a gauge in this position, and covered with about 15 cm of soil. Varieties. - As we said earlier, there are spring, summer, autumn and winter varieties. Some of these are smooth-leafed: these are mainly smooth-leafed cabbages; others are curly-leafed: these are mainly savoy cabbages. The best spring cabbage varieties are: small Yorh cabbage, large York cabbage, small Coeur-de-bœuf cabbage, medium Coeur-de-bœuf cabbage, large Coeur-de-bœuf cabbage, Joanet or Nantais cabbage, early Milan Ulm cabbage, early Milan Saint-Jean cabbage. Among the varieties that can be grown in summer are: Ulm early savoy cabbage, St. John early savoy cabbage, Vertus large savoy cabbage, Étampes early savoy cabbage and red cabbage. The most esteemed varieties of autumn cabbage are : Bonneuil or Saint-Denis cabbage, Schweinfurt cabbage, Winnigstadt pointed cabbage and Pomeranian conical cabbage. Among the most recommendable varieties of winter cabbage are: ordinary Savoy cabbage, Norwegian Savoy cabbage, Vaugirard green cabbage, which keeps well, Quintal cabbage or large German cabbage, and blond cabbage with a large rib or Meaux cabbage. Seed carriers. - Cabbages from which we want to obtain seeds have had their heads removed like the others, but we use Joanet cabbage or Nantais cabbage. CHOUX. Medium beef cabbage.
