It's a good idea to cover each plant with gauze, as this not only ensures seed production by flowers from the same individual, but also protects the seeds from birds, which often feed on them. You can hasten the fertilization of some late-flowering varieties by cutting off the ends of the stems as they begin to produce flowers. Spring cabbages are naturally left to set seed. Enemies. - Cabbage is attacked by many insects. Foremost among these is the flea beetle, which wreaks havoc on young plants. Several types of caterpillar are also to be feared. These include the cabbage whitefly, the harvest moth and the cabbage moth, which can be destroyed by adding water to tobacco juice. Aphids are destroyed in the same way. Cabbage is also subject to a disease known as cabbage hernia, caused by a microscopic fungus that spreads on the roots, which soon develop numerous blisters. Affected plants should be burned. Brussels sprouts. Brussels sprouts are very similar to savoy cabbage. It differs in that its stem is higher and its top does not have the same layout. The edible part consists of small apples, about the size of walnuts, attached along the entire length of the stem. Brussels sprouts are propagated by sowing, preferably in cool, substantial soil, from March to June, so that they can be harvested throughout the winter. When the plants have reached a certain level of development, they are transplanted. To do this, they are placed in rows 40 to 50 centimetres apart, depending on whether you are transplanting ordinary or dwarf Brussels sprouts; the distance of 40 to 50 centimetres is maintained between two plants in the same row. Cultivation care is no different from that for cultivated cabbage. The first Brussels sprouts can be picked in October. There are several varieties of Brussels sprouts: ordinary Brussels sprouts or large Brussels sprouts, which are the most commonly grown and produce the most highly-prized products; semi-dwarf Brussels sprouts; dwarf Brussels sprouts, which are less tall than the preceding varieties, but have larger sprouts that can be harvested earlier. We won't add anything to what we've said about the rootstocks of cultivated cabbages; the same care should be applied to Brussels sprouts. Cauliflower. In cauliflower, it is no longer the leaves that are sought after for consumption, but the hypertrophied flowering shoots that are eaten, providing a healthy, nutritious food. Cultivation. - Cauliflower can be grown in several ways, depending on when it is sown. It can be sown in late summer or early autumn, or in late autumn or spring. In the first case, seed is sown around the beginning of September on a bed that has been given a certain amount of potting soil, or even on a dull layer. In October, the seedling is transplanted and sheltered by a frame; then, in the following January, it is transplanted onto a warm layer covered with frames, on which straw mats are placed to protect the seedlings overnight. Water when necessary and lift the panels when the outside temperature is not too severe. At the end of April, you can start harvesting cauliflowers. Consumption can continue well into May. When sowing is carried out in late autumn or early winter, it is done on a warm bed; transplanting is also done on a bed where the young cabbages are carefully sheltered by frames. When spring comes, they are uncovered more frequently and, in the first days of April, they are placed in the open ground where they conti5 Lenormand short-stalked cauliflower. Sicilian black cauliflower. vegetation. The most advanced can be harvested at the beginning of July. When seedlings are finally sown in May or June, they are always grown in the open ground. Transplanting is not practiced, and the plants are planted permanently in July. Care should be taken to water abundantly during hot spells, as drought can be very damaging to young plants: they are often placed in a shady spot where they have nothing to fear from the scorching sun. To preserve cauliflowers, we hang them upside down, after removing the leaves. When you want to use them, leave them to soak in water for a while before serving, so that they regain their volume, which is usually considerably reduced by evaporation. THE POTAGER. (Cenges -* Varieties. - The most esteemed cauliflower varieties are: Tender Paris or Petit Salomon cauliflower, whose head forms fairly quickly, but which is difficult to preserve: Semi-hard cauliflower or gros Salomon, early, with a dense head that is easy to store; Hard Paris cauliflower, less early than the preceding varieties. Lenormand short-stalked cauliflower, now widely cultivated thanks to its hardiness and the various qualities it combines; Holland hard cauliflower, fairly large, late and easily adapted to strong soil; English hard cauliflower, hardy and late; it is one of the most popular varieties to sow in April or May; Sicilian black cauliflower, with a violet-colored head; it is an early variety, with large, tightly packed seeds. - Cauliflower rootstocks are sown at the end of September and protected under a frame over winter. They are usually transplanted in March, and the most beautiful individuals are chosen to produce seeds. They need to be watered abundantly while they are growing, and the stems and branches pinched off to increase seed production, which usually ripens in September or October. Enemies. - In addition to the enemies we've mentioned for cultivated cabbage, cauliflower can also suffer from a disease that sometimes affects seed-bearing plants. We're talking about powdery mildew, caused by a small fungus whose effects have so far been unstoppable. Broccoli. Broccoli may be considered a type of cauliflower, but in reality it differs very little from cauliflower. Growing broccoli is very easy, as it is fairly cold-resistant; it is a good idea, however, to shelter it during the winter with a layer of litter a few centimetres thick. Broccoli can be sown from March to May; the earliest varieties are sown first. Transplanting takes place in the nursery when the plant has developed sufficiently, and permanent planting takes place four to five weeks later, in rays spaced 60 to 70 centimetres apart in both directions. Cultivation is absolutely the same as for cauliflower, and if care is taken to sow the plants successively, they can be harvested in autumn, throughout the winter and at the beginning of spring. The main broccoli varieties are: early white broccoli and Mammoth broccoli. White broccoli Mammoth. ba CHAPTER III CRAMBUS, PEAR, CARDON, RHUBARBUS, FENNEL Crambé. Crambé or sea cabbage is an excellent vegetable whose young leaves, blanched, are used for consumption. It is very easy to grow, yet not very common. Crambé thrives in light soil, previously smoked with consumed manure; it is perennial; a plantation can produce for ten consecutive years. Crambe is propagated in two ways: by sowing and by root cuttings. Sowing can be done in situ, but it is preferable to prick out the seedlings; we therefore recommend sowing in a well-soiled bed, where vegetation will begin. Sow the seeds in rays about 30 centimetres apart, then cover with a few centimetres of potting soil. After thinning, plants on the same line should be 15 centimetres apart. Later, water and hoe as required. Planting takes place in February or March, in troughs spaced 60 to 70 centimetres apart in one direction, and 50 to 60 in the other. Every year, dead leaves are removed in autumn, and mulch is applied to the plantation after hoeing. The leaves can be harvested as early as the second year, but to avoid weakening the plants prematurely, it's a good idea to wait three years before releasing them for consumption. To whiten the leaves, a ridging is usually done at the end of January. In order to harvest gradually and over a longer period, a certain number of plants are ridged first; the others are only ridged a fortnight later. Here's how it's done: the plants are surrounded by a small mound of potting soil about 15 cm high, on top of which a layer of manure or dry leaves is laid. When you see the leaves emerging from the soil, cut them off near the collar, leaving the eyes around it. This section will trigger the development of a number of buds, of which only four or five will remain. When a first crop has been harvested, a second one is dug up to obtain a second crop, after which the soil used for this dug-up is poured into the soil. There's a second method for blanching leaves: cover each plant with an opaque vase or cloche. When the leaves have reached 15 cm in length, they are cut off as before. To propagate crambe by cuttings, dig up old plants in March and divide their roots into 10-centimeter-long fragments. If the roots are about 1 centimetre in diameter, the fragments can be placed directly in the ground, where they produce buds, of which only the three most vigorous are kept. If the roots are not large enough to produce cuttings that can be planted immediately, the pieces are planted in Crambé rays, 20 centimetres apart in both directions, and not planted permanently until the following year. Root cuttings are widely used for propagation, often producing excellent harvests. In England, where crambe is much more widespread than in France, this vegetable is the object of forced cultivation. The plants to be forced are watered in autumn and planted on beds; the plantations are covered with frames on which straw mats are laid to intercept the light. Crambé is subject to flea beetle attack. Pear. Pear is very similar to beet, but whereas in beetroot it is mainly the root that is developed through cultivation, in pear it is only the leaves that are developed. Depending on the harvesting season, seedlings can be sown from March to June. Some growers even sow at the end of July to harvest the following spring. Seedlings are sown either in the field or in nurseries, in rays spaced 40 centimetres apart. During the growing season, pear need only be hoeed and watered. When sown in July, the plants are ridged over winter and sheltered with bedding. Harvesting is carried out by removing the leaves to be used immediately; to have some in the winter, pears are protected by frames placed on the boards, and surrounded by a stove. Whenever the weather permits, air is allowed to penetrate the panels. Two main varieties of pear are grown: the common pear or blond pear, which lends itself to the same uses as spinach and can produce about a month and a half after sowing; and the chard pear, whose stalk, commonly known as the tail of the leaf, is very well developed; chard pears are sown mainly in June, and harvested at the end of April. Plants intended to produce seed are wintered under glass; the seed usually ripens the following September. Cardom. Cardoons are botanically similar to artichokes. The edible part is the leaf stalk, which has been developed by cultivation. Cardoon can grow in any soil and almost always gives satisfactory results. It is propagated by sowing, either on a bed in April, or in the open ground in May, in the position it will occupy throughout its growth. Sowing is done in bunches, 1 m apart in both directions. Two or three seeds are placed in each hole, with a little potting soil thrown in at the bottom. After emergence, the most vigorous of the plants sown in the same hole is selected, and the others are removed. During the summer, weed and water abundantly. In September, the plant is blanched. This is done by wrapping the entire plant in straw, then tying it up, leaving only the upper tips of the leaves sticking out. Cardoon is left in this state for around three weeks, after which it must be used immediately, otherwise it will rot. To extend the consumption period, cardoons are gradually stuffed. As cardoons are very sensitive to frost, some time before winter we pull up all the plants and put them in a sheltered place, such as a vegetable greenhouse, where they will naturally turn white; we take care to remove any leaves that start to rot. Cardoon varieties are few and far between. The most widely grown are: Toure cardoon, which is generally very popular; inerme full cardoon, which has no prickles; Spanish cardoon, which is widely grown in the south of France; Puvis cardoon or artichoke-leaf cardoon. The seed heads are covered during the cold season, and are uncovered as spring approaches. In September, the cardoons are ready to set seed, which they do for several consecutive years. Young cardoon plants are subject to attack by grubs and crickets. 5 Cardon de Tours. Rhubarb. Rhubarb has been cultivated in Europe for no more than two centuries. As with cardoon, it is the leaf stalk that is edible. In England, rhubarb is much more widely cultivated than in France. Rhubarb thrives in sandy soil. It is propagated by sowing, but also, and above all, by planting fragments. Sowing should be done as soon as the seeds have reached maturity. When dividing plants, this should be done in spring. Each part to be planted should bear a bud. Permanent planting is generally carried out in spring, in soil that has been fertilized with manure. Plants are planted 70 centimetres apart in one direction and 1 metre apart in the other. Harvesting does not begin until spring of the following year. To do this, take care to detach the leaves by pulling them, not by slicing them with a knife, as is too often done. A rhubarb plant can produce for eight years, but it must not be allowed to 4 American Wavy Rhubarb. flower, so the stems are cut off as soon as they appear, to preserve the plant's vigor. The best rhubarb varieties are : Victoria rhubarb, Michell's royal Albert rhubarb, Nepaul rhubarb, Monarque rhubarb and finally American wavy rhubarb. The flower stalks of plants destined to produce seed are kept; seed usually ripens in April. Florence fennel. Florence fennel is an annual vegetable that can reach 60 to 70 centimeters. The most sought-after part is the base of the stalks, which swell to form a sort of whitish apple above the collar of the plant. Florence fennel is sown in April, in rays about 45 centimetres apart. After emergence, the plant is thinned out and care is limited to weeding and frequent watering. When the plant has reached a height of 25 centimetres, it is mounded so that the swelling formed is half covered with soil. Harvesting can begin ten or fifteen days after ridging. Fennel is eaten after cooking; its flavor is reminiscent of celery, with a sweetness that celery lacks. This very delicate vegetable is rarely grown in France. It is most widely grown in Italy. Florence fennel. ARTICHUT 107 The artichoke is one of the most widely cultivated perennials, both by market gardeners and hobbyists. It is found throughout France. However, as not all varieties would thrive equally well everywhere, each region cultivates the breeds best suited to its soil. Reproduction methods. Artichokes prefer substantial, moist soils that are compact rather than light. It can be propagated either by sowing or by the eyelets it produces in abundance. The second propagation method is preferable to the first, as it reproduces more faithfully the varieties grown. Sowing is done in flower pots filled with soil and placed in a warm layer. In February, plant four or five seeds in each pot; after emergence, keep only the two most vigorous plants in each pot, and plant them in clumps in May, in rays about 80 cm apart in both directions. You can also sow in the open ground in May. In this case, sowing is done in bunches: four or five seeds are placed in each hole and, as before, only two plants per bunch are kept, to be planted permanently when they have developed sufficiently. The eyelet propagation method is the most widely used. Each plant produces a certain number of eyelets, which must be removed if it is not to be exhausted. Only two are left, to ensure the following year's harvest. Separation of the eyelets, or œilletonnage, takes place in April. First, the plant is dethatched, exposing the part where the eyelets are attached to the main plant. Using the tip of a knife, the eyelets are detached, but care is taken to remove with them a small piece of the root of the old plant, without injuring it too much. Once this has been done, the soil is brought back around the plant. Before planting, the eyelets are pruned with a serpette, i.e. the leaves are shortened with this instrument, so that the remaining part is about 20 centimetres long, then planted in rays, about 80 centimetres apart in both directions. Planting is done using the planter in holes 8 to 10 centimetres deep. Lightly press the soil around each plant, then water with a spout. Cultivation. After planting, hoe and water frequently. Many plants will produce artichokes the same year they are planted. Once harvested, cut the stems that have produced at ground level, then shorten the leaves. At the start of winter, we spade the soil between the plants, which we then butter to protect them from frost. In northern regions, where these precautions would be insufficient, we'll shelter the plants with litter. In winter, when temperatures are mild enough, the mound can be uncovered to allow air to circulate around the plant. The following spring, cut down the mounds, plough and smoke the soil, then proceed again with eyeletting, as it's a good idea each year to replace some of the plants with young ones. The same plant should not be kept for more than four years. If you only want to harvest in spring, plant the carnations in July. Some growers force artichokes into trays, placing them in November on a bed surrounded by a stove. The frames are covered with straw mats at night. During the day, the panels are lifted whenever the temperature permits. Varieties. There are many varieties of artichoke. Here are some of the most recommended. Artichoke gros vert de Laon. Artichoke violet hátif. The large green Laon artichoke is the most widely grown artichoke on the Paris market. It multiplies well by sowing; the receptacle is very large and fleshy. The artichaut vert de Provence, or artichaut pointu précoce d'Alger, is less voluminous than the artichaut de Laon. The head is generally eaten raw, with pepper. The artichaut camus de Bretagne is an early variety. It is grown mainly in western France. The scales are green in the middle, with brownish edges. The purple artichoke is grown mainly in the south of France. It is an early variety, with a relatively small head. It is eaten fried or peppered. Gray artichokes are often found near Narbonne, from where they are shipped in large quantities to Paris during the winter. Enemies. Artichokes are often ravaged by the field moth, a quadruped that damages many vegetables. Among the 2* - -3 Mulot. . - a. 2 insects, the white grub and cricket are the most damaging. To keep them at bay, simply grow lettuces between the artichoke rows. As for aphids, which often get into the heads, we have to leave them there, as tobacco juice with water added to get rid of them would give the artichoke an unpleasant taste. SPINACH, TETRAGON, ARROCH, CUCUMBER Spinach. 111 Spinach can be propagated by sowing, starting in March. By staggering sowings from two weeks to two weeks, this vegetable can be harvested for a long time, and can be sown as late as the end of August. Spinach should be permanently sown in rows 25 to 30 centimetres apart. During vegetation, water frequently and abundantly. Spinach sets seed very quickly, but fruiting is slower if sown late in the year. It is harvested about six weeks after sowing, by cutting off the most advanced leaves with the fingernail, which are eaten in the same way as sorrel. The best spinach varieties are : Ordinary spinach, which is closest to the wild type, with prickly seeds; English spinach, also with prickly seeds; Dutch spinach, with round, seedless seeds; Viroflay monster spinach, with very broad leaves; sorrel-leaf spinach; lettuce-leaf spinach, and finally slow-rising spinach. The plants you want to sow should be sown in September. By the following July, fruiting is complete and the seed can be harvested. As male and female flowers are borne on different plants, care should be taken to leave a few plants with male organs next to the female plants. Noctuid moths and cutworms are two dangerous enemies, sometimes destroying a large part of a spinach plantation. Two diseases are to be feared: jaundice, due to excessive heat, which can be fought by abundant watering, and damping-off or rot, due to soil humidity. Tetragonia. Originally from New Zealand, tetragonia is very similar to spinach; it is used in summer for the same Q purposes, and has the advantage of being less sensitive to heat and of not going to seed as quickly; it is still called summer spinach. Tetragonia can grow in arid areas, where growing spinach would be more difficult. It can be propagated by sowing, either on a bed in February or March, with seeds that have been left to soak in water for some time, and then transplanted in rays spaced about 60 cm apart, or immediately in the field in May. Growing tetragonia requires almost no care. Most of the time, the plant is left to reproduce on its own by its seeds, which fall to the ground in autumn and sprout in spring; it is then transplanted when the plants have acquired sufficient vigor. "Tetragonia. Little cultivated in northern France, tetragonia is more widespread in the southern provinces, as this plant requires little water to produce excellent products. It has a pleasant flavor. Arroche. Arroche has long since taken its place in vegetable gardens. It is an annual plant similar to spinach. It is generally sown in rows and rows in March. Like tetragonia, it produces in summer and has little fear of heat. After emergence, it is thinned out and watered from time to time. Arrowroot bears fruit very quickly, so to prolong consumption, sow several times, a few days apart, from March to September. Garden orache is an excellent vegetable that deserves to be more widely grown. The most widely grown varieties today are: Blonde arroche, dark red arroche and green arroche. These three varieties differ mainly in leaf color. Arrowroot is generally mixed with sorrel, softening its acidic flavor. It can also be mixed with spinach, or even eaten on its own. To harvest the seeds of this plant, cut the stems in September before they are fully ripe, then leave them to mature in a dry place. Sorrel. Arroené blonde. Sorrel can be propagated by sowing or by dividing clumps. Sow in rays, from March to July. Spread a light layer of compost over the seed, then water with an apple. POTTING. The young plants are later thinned out, and two or two and a half months after sowing, harvesting can begin, by hand-pulling the most advanced leaves. The second harvest takes place at the end of October, when the soil is lightly hoeed and mulched. Growing sorrel requires frequent watering. When propagating by dividing clumps, this operation is carried out at the beginning of April. This method is particularly useful when you want to create a border of mainly male-flowered sorrel. In this case, as fertilization does not occur, the plants retain their vigor and produce beautiful products. The same plant may produce leaves for three or four consecutive years. When some plants are completely exhausted, they can be replaced by others, by separating the clumps or sowing them anew. Sorrel can also be force-fed. To do this, plant in November on a warm layer with a few centimetres of potting soil. Air is supplied as often as possible. At night, we cover the panels with straw mats. The main varieties of sorrel are: Belleville sorrel, which is widespread around Paris; virgin sorrel, which goes to seed quickly; round sorrel, which is very acidic; and spinach or patience sorrel, which is very productive and not acidic. Seedlings are sown in July; the following year, at the same time, seed can be harvested. Sorrel sometimes suffers from attack by various kinds of caterpillars. To get rid of them, add tobacco juice to four times its volume of water, or soap water. Belleville sorrel. LETTUCE, CHICORICE, CELERY Lettuce. 115 Lettuce is one of the most highly esteemed lettuces. Two main species are grown: head lettuce and romaine lettuce or chicon, both of which contain a considerable number of varieties. These varieties are classified according to when they are eaten. We'll look successively at winter, spring and summer lettuces, followed by a fourth group of lettuces for cutting, which can be grown at any time of year. Winter lettuces. - Winter lettuces are sown during the second half of August and the first half of September. At the end of October, they are planted in a well-exposed bed sheltered from the wind by a wall. During cold spells, the plants are covered with bedding and allowed to breathe as often as is safe for the vegetation. These varieties generally have little fear of snow, so they can be left in place without risk of loss. Their growth, halted for some time by the bad season, resumes with renewed vigor as soon as the cold has ceased. Towards the end of April, the first plants can be harvested. Harvesting can continue for five or six weeks. Among the winter lettuces, we'd like to mention: Passion lettuce, very hardy, but only used for winter sowing, as it sets seed quickly during the summer; Morin lettuce, not very bulky, but quite hardy and highly esteemed; Brown winter lettuce, very hardy, but which has the disadvantage of setting seed quickly; Red winter lettuce, an early and very productive variety. Among the winter romaine varieties, we'd like to mention those whose cultivation is identical to that of head lettuces: Green winter romaine, hardy and very productive; romaines that rarely head on their own are usually tied, to allow the inner leaves to turn white; this precaution is unnecessary for this variety; Royal green romaine, quite similar to the previous one, but wider and less dark green; Red winter romaine, hardy and productive, slow to bolt and head naturally. Spring lettuces. - Spring lettuces are grown differently from summer lettuces. In March, they are sown in warm soil or in well-exposed potting soil. Transplanting takes place in April, and harvesting begins in early June. Spring lettuces are also used for forced cultivation. In this case, they are sown in October on a bed and grow entirely under a frame. We recommend crepe and gotte lettuces for forced cultivation. The most popular spring lettuces are : Early, black-seeded crepe lettuce, ideally suited to under-frame cultivation; also known as little black lettuce; White-seeded gotte lettuce or gau lettuce, very productive and hardy; as it takes up little space, it can be planted with narrower spacing than the other varieties; Slow-rising gotte lettuce, early and productive, with a tight head and excellent quality; Red-edged lettuce, slow-growing but most productive. The most widely grown spring romaines are : Market-garden green romaine, highly esteemed and fast-growing; LETTUCE. e Crepe lettuce. Red winter romaine. Moraine lettuce. O ca-é o Palatine lettuce. - S.a. Romaine blonde maraichère. 117 Romaine blonde maraîchère, which is sometimes subjected to forced cultivation; it is very bulky, but a little less early than the preceding variety. Summer lettuces. - Summer lettuces are easy to grow. They can be sown in nurseries from March to July. When the plants can withstand transplanting, they are pricked out and later set out. During the development of summer lettuces, water frequently and abundantly. To reduce water evaporation, cover the soil with mulch. Among the varieties of summer head lettuce, we'd like to mention: Blonde summer lettuce, widely grown, small but productive; it's fairly early; Blonde Versailles lettuce, larger than the previous one, of roughly equal quality; Large lazy blond lettuce, highly developed and very productive, which succeeds almost everywhere; its very tender head is of excellent quality; Palatine lettuce, productive and requiring little care; its cultivation is very advantageous; Blonde Batavia lettuce, whose head is relatively large. The most popular summer romaines are : White-seeded Romaine Alphange, which is very bulky, but has difficulty forming its head; Black-seeded Romaine Alphange, which, like the previous variety, needs to be tied in order to peel; White-seeded English Brown Romaine, whose outer leaves have a bronze tint; It is very hardy; English brown romaine with black seed, which differs from the previous variety only in the color of its seed; variegated romaine with white seed, whose leaves have red spots; the head is difficult to form, so it must be carefully tied. Cutting lettuces. - Cutting lettuces are picked young, before the heads have fully formed. They are grown in all seasons, from March to November, often among other vegetables. Special breeds are not used for this type of cultivation, but early varieties such as gotte and crepe lettuces. The lettuces to be sown are chosen from among those with the most beautiful heads. They can be left in place or transplanted. Once the stems have developed, they are held in place with a stake. During fertilization, follow the general rules we have outlined (page 31). Stems are cut before full maturity, usually at the beginning of August, and when dry, beaten to remove the seeds. Lettuces are susceptible to snails and slugs, which the grower must destroy whenever they are encountered. Many aphids are also very dangerous. Repeated watering helps to destroy them. To get rid of them, syringe with tobacco juice and four times its volume of water, or with water in which black soap has been dissolved. Powdery mildew, caused by a microscopic stinging fungus, is also a formidable enemy of lettuces; we have not yet found a way to prevent it. Chicory. There are several species of chicory in cultivation. We will look successively at endive chicory, which includes curly endive and escarole chicory, then wild chicory, which produces nasturtium, large-root or coffee chicory, F'itloof chicory and slicing chicory. Chicory endive. - Chicory is fairly easy to grow. The plant grows quickly, so you can grow it several seasons in the same year. Chicory is propagated by broadcasting seedlings in the ground, from April to September. Later, in September and October, chicory is sown under a bell, then on a bed. When the young plants have acquired sufficient strength, they are transplanted in rays 30 to 35 centimetres apart, and watered frequently during their growth. By the end of July, April sowings can produce vegetables fit for consumption. To make chicories more tender and delicate, they are blanched when they are almost fully grown. To do this, the leaves are lifted and tied together with a straw or wicker twine. After this operation, watering is carried out at the neck, so as not to allow water to enter the leaves, where it could cause rotting. Salads can be used a fortnight or three weeks after blanching. In some provinces in the south of France, chicory is blanched by covering it with soil, a process we do not recommend. When blanching during cold weather, chicory should be covered with straw mats, transported to the vegetable greenhouse and planted in damp sand. When sowing under a bell, transplanting is also done under a bell, but permanent planting takes place under a frame. During forcing, the panels are lifted as often as possible without S Fine summer chicory. Meaux curly chicory. Scarole en cornet. 2 2 Scarole blonde compromise the operation. Chicory sown in September or October finishes growing in January or February. When growing under a frame and on a bed, the temperature of the bed should be around 25 degrees. The layer is about 50 centimetres thick and covered with 15 centimetres of potting soil. Once the seedling has been sown, it is simply plumbed in without covering it with soil. The developed plant is transplanted onto a layer of lesser heat. Harvesting can begin in late April. Towards the end of March, the plants that are still growing are transplanted into the open ground, still sheltered by cloches or frames. Later on, all shelter is removed. To preserve chicory plants that have developed before winter, they can be uprooted in November, leaving the soil adhering to their roots. Placed upside down in the vegetable greenhouse, they will blanch naturally. If you only have a small number, you can shelter them in frames on the ground, or cover them with straw mats. The best varieties of chicory are curly endive: Fine summer chicory, also known as Italian chicory, which is suitable for both outdoor and forced cultivation; it is very widespread: Meaux curly endive, which is very hardy and makes an excellent autumn salad; Picpus curly endive, which is mainly used for outdoor cultivation; it is hardy and its leaves are very tender; Rouen curly endive or corne-de-cerf chicory, which is also very hardy and admirably suited to outdoor cultivation; Mousse chicory, very productive in a small volume; often grown under cloche; Ruffec curly chicory, which is bushy, very hardy and highly recommended for outdoor cultivation; ever-white chicory with very pale green foliage; also known as golden curly chicory. Among escarole chicories, we'd like to mention: Round escarole, which, like other types of escarole, is grown mainly for autumn consumption; it is usually sown in June; Pale-green, blond escarole, which is highly prized; Horn-shaped escarole, whose leaves are actually horn-shaped. Wild chicory. - As we have said, wild chicory has given rise to chicory beard, coffee chicory, Witloof chicory and chopped chicory. The usual way to grow wild chicory is to sow it in spring, very thickly, indoors and in rows, in deeply loosened soil that has been smoked for some time. After development, the most advanced leaves are cut off with a knife. The same plants can produce several harvests in the same year. New seedlings are sown every year. Magdeburg chicory. Nasturtium beard. When you want to grow Magdeburg chicory, you use wild chicory seedlings that have been sown in the open ground in June. These plants are dug up as winter approaches; their leaves are sliced off to within 1 cm of the collar, then the roots are bundled. Forcing is carried out in a dark place, such as a cellar. A layer of horse manure about 35 centimetres thick is laid down, and when the temperature has dropped to 20 degrees, the bunches are placed side by side, upright and about a third deep in the layer. On average, we baste twice a day, and when the leaves have reached a sufficient length, we cut them for consumption. Many growers use the simpler method of placing bunches of chicory on a layer of damp sand, which is admittedly slower-growing, but produces a product of just as good quality. In the case of large-root chicory or coffee chicory, it's the Witloof. root that's most often used. By dividing the root into small pieces, which are then roasted, a product is obtained which, when mixed with coffee, gives it a pleasant flavor. Two main varieties of wild chicory are grown: the highly productive Brunswich chicory and the Magdeburg chicory. Big-root chicory varieties are also used to produce cappuccino beard. One of these, Brussels endive, which is actually a sub-variety of Magdeburg endive, is grown to produce a salad called Witloof. Witloof is obtained by forcing this variety, whose leaves take the shape of an apple which, blanched, makes an excellent food. Brussels sprout chicory is sown in the open ground in June, in rays about 30 cm apart. After emergence, the plants are thinned out to 15 cm apart on the same line. As the plant develops, water abundantly and hoe when necessary. At the end of autumn, all the plants are uprooted; only those with a diameter of at least 3 centimetres are used, with the leaves removed a few centimetres from the collar. The roots themselves are dressed, i.e. the rootlets are detached and the tip of the pivot cut off, so that the remaining part is about 25 centimetres long. Once this has been done, we dig a pit about 35 centimetres deep and 70 to 80 centimetres wide, at the bottom of which we plant the roots vertically, pushing them in 8 or 10 centimetres and leaving an interval of 4 to 5 centimetres between them. The trench is then filled with potting soil, and covered with a thick layer of litter or about 40 centimetres of unconsumed manure. This last method generally produces excellent-quality white shoots within a month, which are harvested by digging up to the crown and slicing off the base of the head. Cutting chicory is by no means the least esteemed of all lettuces. It is sown in spring in rays 25 centimetres apart. It is thinned out, weeded, hoeed and watered from time to time during vegetation. During the winter, we remove the dead leaves, then cover each bed with a layer of potting soil, so as to hide the leaves completely. Twenty or twenty-five days after this operation, harvesting can begin. The most popular varieties of chicory for cutting are : Improved wild chicory, derived from the wild type that grows spontaneously in France; its leaves are curled into a cone shape; variegated improved wild chicory, a variety similar to the previous one, but whose leaves are spotted brown; curly improved wild chicory, whose leaves are finely cut and slightly blistered; of all the wild varieties, it is the one that most closely resembles endive chicory. Improved wild chicory. Chicory seeds are obtained by beating the flower stalks, which have been cut a little before maturity. Harvest cutworms sometimes devastate plantations. Look for it and destroy it. Celery. The stalks of celery leaves, and sometimes the leaves themselves, provide a highly appreciated seasoning and salad. Hollow celery. We won't go into the celeriac we dealt with earlier. We will only describe the cultivation of the varieties whose ribs are used. Celery requires fresh, substantial soil. It is propagated by sowing from February to June, first on bedding to transplant on bedding and plant in the ground, then from April directly in the ground, but never in situ. Permanent planting is done in rays 25 cm apart in both directions. To facilitate growth, weed and water frequently. Before delivering them for consumption, we usually blanch the petioles, which is done by mounding. First, all the leaves are tied with a twine of straw, then the soil is brought up around each plant, once to a third of its height; after eight days, the mound is raised to two-thirds of its height, and finally, eight days later, the operation is completed, leaving only the tips of the largest leaves to emerge. Among the varieties of celery we'd like to mention: Golden-white celery, an excellent breed with well-developed ribs; Turkish celery, which is less and less cultivated, despite its quality; Short white celery, less vigorous than the preceding varieties; its leaves are numerous; it can be buttered without binding; Violet de Tours celery, whose ribs have a purplish tint; it is very hardy and highly esteemed; Small celery or hollow celery, this last name comes from the fact that its ribs are hollow; its leaves are also used. The seedbeds, removed in November, are planted in rootballs 55 to 60 centimetres apart. They are firmly planted and covered with a thick layer of litter, so that they can survive the winter without fear of the cold. The seeds can be harvested at the beginning of September of the following year. CHAPTER VII DANDELION, MACHE, POURPIER, CRESSON Dandelion. Dandelion grows spontaneously in almost all of France, and is rarely cultivated in the kitchen garden; we are often content to pick it in the meadows, where it is sometimes found in large quantities. The dandelion is a perennial plant that does not suffer from extreme heat or low temperatures. It reproduces by seed, which can be sown from late February to mid-June. However, it's best not to sow seeds until June, as the plants will not flower the same year. Sowing can be done either in the nursery or in the field. In the former case, seed is broadcast on well-tilled soil, then covered with a light layer of compost. When the plants are sufficiently vigorous, they are planted in rows 10 cm apart in both directions. Picked in meadows, dandelion leaves make an excellent salad, but to eat them with their full flavor, 68 they need to be blanched; in gardens, this is done by covering each plant with soil in November; deprived of light, the leaves quickly lose their green color. Two varieties of dandelion are usually grown: the full-hearted dandelion and the moss-enhanced dandelion. The latter is the more popular. The few plants set aside to bear seeds are not blanched; at the end of May of the second year, the seed can be harvested. Lamb's lettuce. Lamb's lettuce grows naturally throughout France and much of Europe. It is an annual vegetable, highly prized as a salad. Lamb's lettuce is reproduced by sowing in August, very lightly and broadcast, in soil that has been well loosened by ploughing. After sowing, the soil is harrowed with a fork, then a small layer of compost is spread over the surface. Water from time to time during the germination period. During its growth, lamb's lettuce requires frequent weeding. Sown in August, it is generally ready for consumption in October. If you want to ensure winter production, you can sow it in September, but in this case, during the cold season, it's best to keep it in the garden. Round-leaf lamb's lettuce. the plants must be sheltered by a heavy bedding. The same applies to spring lamb's lettuce, sown in October. It is not essential for lamb's lettuce to be grown in land specially set aside for it. It can be sown very lightly among other vegetables such as cauliflower and chicory, which it will not harm in any way. Several varieties of lamb's lettuce are grown, including round-leaf lamb's lettuce and Étampes green lamb's lettuce. A third variety, mâche régence, is more voluminous, but also later-ripening than the previous ones. It is grown in the same way, but is sown lighter and preferably in October. A few plants from the autumn sowing are left to carry the seed. It flowers in May, and can be harvested in June. Purslane. Purslane is a relatively uncultivated plant, used only as a garnish for salads. All varieties of purslane are edible, but only one is grown in the vegetable garden: golden purslane, whose leaves and shoots are eaten when still young. When you want to plant purslane in a corner of the garden, sow the seed in well loosened soil. A rake is then used to harrow the soil, followed by a very light layer of compost. Sowing can take place from the beginning of May to the end of July. If sowing is carried out during a drought, it is necessary to water from time to time, firstly to help the seed germinate, and later to encourage the plant's growth. These waterings will help to make the vegetables tender and tasty. When you take the precaution of sowing very lightly, the leaves develop more than when you sow them thickly and, what's more, you have the advantage of being able to harvest them twice. Once you've established a few vines of purslane in a bed, you don't need to resow every year. The plant multiplies on its own, and some growers claim that it is more vigorous under these conditions than when you have taken the trouble to sow it. Cress. Two main species of cress are grown today, differing greatly in cultivation and botanical characteristics: Alenois cress and watercress. Alenois cress. - The Alenois cress is an annual; it reproduces by sowing in the open ground and in rays, at the end of April or beginning of May. The seed is then covered with a thin layer of compost. Harvest when the leaves have reached a length of 8 to 10 centimetres. The same plants can be harvested twice in succession. When sowing is staggered from fortnight to fortnight, the harvest lasts for several months. Today, three main varieties of watercress are grown: common watercress, curly watercress and broad-leaf watercress. After the second harvest of leaves, watercress quickly produces seeds: leave it in place if you want to obtain some. Watercress. - Watercress, the most esteemed of cresses, is a perennial aquatic plant. It grows wild in all parts of France. It can be found on the banks of flowing waters, the presence of a watercourse being an essential condition for its growth. Watercress is a perennial vegetable that can be used either as a garnish for meat or as a salad. A very healthy and refreshing food, it is now widely cultivated, but it is a specialty and not within the reach of all growers. To establish a watercress bed, you need a site where you can bring in water at will, and from which it can drain without impediment. When these conditions are met, a pit is dug to the length of the available space, with a width varying between 1 and 2 meters. It should be 35 centimetres deep, and the bottom of the trench should slope in the direction of the water current. The bottom of the trench should be ploughed, then fertilized with consumed manure; once this has been done, water should be left for one or two days before planting. Watercress is propagated in August using cuttings, or rather rooted seedlings, which are placed in damp soil after letting the water run off completely. At the bottom of the pit, holes 8 to 10 centimetres apart are planted in either direction. Three or four cuttings are placed in each hole, taking care not to bury them too deeply. To facilitate recovery, use a windbreak to shade the cress bed. After a few days, you can start to slowly circulate the water, keeping it at a height of 3 or 4 centimetres in the pit; the speed is increased a few days later, until the cress is entirely under water. Harvest as the cress develops, but make sure that aquatic plants do not interfere with its growth. To prevent watercress from freezing in winter, the water that submerges it must run off fairly quickly. It's a good idea not to pick cress when it's cold. Cress can also be propagated from seed; we won't go into detail on this method of propagation, which is rarely used today. When cress production weakens, a new planting should be made, which can be done in the same pit, taking care to renew the fertilizers. CHAPTER VIII PARSLEY, PERFEUIL, PERCE-PIERRE, MOUTARDE, BASILIC THYME, ESTRAGON Parsley. Parsley can be propagated by sowing in the garden from March to the end of August. Parsley is often sown in borders, as the quantity required to feed a family is not very large. However, gardeners sometimes grow it in beds, in which case they sow it in rays 25 cm apart. Emergence takes place after a month or so; the plants are thinned out, then weeded and watered as they grow. Three months after sowing, you can start picking the most advanced leaves. Parsley fears low temperatures, so if you want to have some during the bad season, take care to shelter the plants under a frame or transplant them to a bed. In this way, production will continue throughout the winter. Some growers are content to shelter the plants with bedding and straw mats, but this is often ineffective. Several varieties of parsley are grown: Common parsley, large Naples parsley, curly parsley, very curly dwarf parsley and fern-leaf parsley. Seedlings are sown in June. They are left in place over winter, sheltered by frames or other means of protection. Seeds mature in September of the second year. Chervil. Chervil thrives best in shady areas, but can be grown in all soils and climates. It can be sown from early March to late October, either broadcast or in rows 25 cm apart. To have chervil throughout the year, sowing is staggered from fortnight to fortnight, as chervil rises very quickly in summer. Curly chervil seedlings. Chervil in flower. in spring or summer usually produce a single harvest, but those sown in autumn can produce for longer. Among the best varieties of chervil are: common chervil, the most widespread and one of the most highly esteemed; curly chervil, which grows earlier than the previous variety and has all its qualities; its leaves are thin and slightly blistered; musky chervil, a large perennial plant very different from the previous varieties, with a fragrance reminiscent of aniseed. The seed of this variety needs to be sown as soon as it ripens, as it retains its germinative properties poorly; if sown in autumn, the seed sprouts in spring; if sown in spring, the seed does not develop until the following year. Chervil and curly chervil seedlings are usually selected from autumn sowings. Their leaves are not harvested, so that they retain all their vigor. Seeds mature around June. Perce-pierre. Stonewort is a plant that grows spontaneously on our coasts. In the kitchen garden, it is sown in September; it can also be sown in March, but it has been found that autumn sowing gives better results. Sowing takes place in light, substantial soil, with good exposure wherever possible, and with seed that has just reached maturity. Over winter, the seedlings are covered with litter. Stonewort leaves are used as a condiment after being preserved in vinegar. 3 Stonewort Mustard. Mustard is rarely grown in the kitchen garden, as it is mainly cultivated in large quantities; it is a very hardy plant that requires little care. There are two main species: white mustard and black mustard. White mustard is used when very young, generally after eight days' cultivation; its leaves are eaten as a salad, especially in England, where it is mixed with lettuce and watercress. The seed is also used in the preparation of the condiment known as mustard, but it is mainly the seeds of black mustard that are used for this purpose. In the garden, black mustard is sown in rows. It requires almost no care. Basil. Mustard. Basil is a highly regarded condiment today, although it is still relatively little cultivated. It is propagated by sowing in the months of March and April. Transplanting takes place when the plants have grown several leaves; it can be done on a bed or even in a nursery. Plants are planted out in the open ground around the middle of May. Care should be taken to water abundantly during the summer. Two main species of basil are grown: large basil and small basil. Both have the same aniseed flavour and can be used in the same way; but, while the stem of the former can reach up to 40 centimetres, that of the latter rarely exceeds 20 centimetres, which means it can be grown in pots. Basil. Thyme. Common thyme is best grown as a border plant. Placed in a good spot, it thrives in all types of soil. It can be propagated in a variety of ways, either by cuttings, by dividing clumps, or by sowing; in most cases, it is reproduced in the latter way, which is preferable in every respect. Sowing takes place in April, usually directly in the ground. If you prefer to grow it in a nursery, you can plant it in June or July. All you need to do is grow a few vines of

thyme, renewed every three or four years. Thyni. Tarragon. As tarragon does not produce seeds, it must be propagated by dividing clumps or taking cuttings, which are planted from mid-July to the end of August. The work involved in growing this plant is insignificant. At the start of winter, cut off the stems and cover with a little soil or litter. In the Paris area, however, some market gardeners grow tarragon under frames to keep it in season. In gardens, tarragon is grown naturally. Tarragon is used as a condiment in salads, and above all to flavor vinegar. Yo Tarragon. R CHAPTER I Squash, cucumbers Squash. Squash is one of the most widely used vegetables in our diet. Although there are countless varieties, they can all be grown in much the same way. In squash, as in the plants we're going to look at, the edible part is provided by the fruit. Cultivation. - Squashes are propagated by sowing, which can hardly be done in the open ground before May. To facilitate growth, they are sown in deep holes 50 centimetres long and of variable width, filled with manure and covered with 20 centimetres of compost. Two or three seeds are placed in each hole. Sowing, which is done in the open ground when natural cultivation is applied, can be done on a bed if you want to hasten the ripening of the fruit. In this case, the seedlings are transplanted to the bed, buried up to the cotyledons and then planted in the open ground. Alternatively, seedlings can be sown in pots filled with potting soil, which are then pushed into the bed up to the rim. Leave them there until the plants have gained sufficient strength, and the outside temperature has become mild enough to allow safe transplanting. After transplanting, the young plants are sheltered from the hot sun for the first few days. When growing varieties with non-running stems, transplanting can be carried out in furrows 1.50 m apart. Once the main stem has grown a few leaves, it is useful to prune it above the second leaf to facilitate the development of two second-order branches which, once they have grown, are themselves pruned above the sixth leaf. In this way, the stems won't use the nutrients to develop, which must be used by the fruit. It's on the third-order branches that the flowers are formed, followed by the gourds. If you want to obtain very large fruits, it's a good idea to keep only two or three per plant. After fertilization, select the best-knotted ones, then prune the branch to which they are attached above the second leaf beyond the fruit. Stems can also be "marcotted", i.e. the parts with knots are placed in the ground, so that they emit adventitious roots. In this way, the squash will benefit from the surplus food provided by the new roots. If watered in times of drought, all these methods combined will produce fruit of considerable volume and excellent flesh. Varieties. - M. Charles Naudin was the first to establish a classification system that reduced to a few main types the infinite number of squash varieties which, until then, had been grouped together and considered as originating from several distinct species. Mr. Naudin has shown the links that exist between apparently very dissimilar varieties, and today his simple classification is universally adopted. We therefore report, with Mr. Charles Naudin, on the various Potiron rouge vif d'Étampes. aros E Courge cou tors du Canada. Giraumon. Boulogne grey pumpkin. 141 U S Marrow squash. The larger varieties are mainly grown by market gardeners, who always find an outlet in the big cities. In home gardens, the smaller varieties are usually grown, as the larger fruits cannot be eaten all at once, and spoil when opened. In fact, it's easy to obtain medium-sized fruit from large breeds: just keep four or five per plant instead of just one. The seed for squash seedlings should only be taken from fruits that show all the characteristics you want to obtain. Cucumbers. Cultivation. - In our climate, cucumbers can be grown in the ground. This is the simplest and most widespread method. They are propagated by sowing seeds, which is done in May, directly in situ, in rows and generally in a single row. Leave a distance of 1.35 m between two plants, then mulch. Water frequently to facilitate growth. When the main stem has given birth to five or six leaves, it is pruned above the second; later, the two lateral branches undergo the same treatment above the fifth or sixth; when the first fruits are set, the branches bearing those you wish to keep are cut to two leaves above them. This operation, which is carried out when the fruit has reached half its size, continues as the cucumbers are produced. In this way, a dozen cucumbers per plant can be preserved. If gherkin cucumbers are grown, the plants are left to produce as much as they can, and the fruit is picked young, when it has reached 6 to 10 centimetres in length. Other varieties are harvested in August or September, from plants sown in May. CONCOMBRE RNICHON VERT PETIT DE PANS When you want to use forced cultivation, sow on a warm bed and under a frame from the beginning of February; when the plants have grown a few leaves, transplant them to a second bed. After two or three weeks, the plants are planted out by removing the rootballs and planting them again on a bed. Four plants are placed under the same frame, mulched and watered to help them take root. As they develop, the stems are pruned as described above. Thereafter, the only cultivation care consists of providing air whenever possible, and watering from time to time. By the end of April, most of the fruit has ripened and can be harvested. We have not yet managed to stop its ravages. MELON 147 The melon is a vegetable that needs warm, fertile soil to thrive, which is why, in most of France, it is grown on a bed. We will, however, say a few words about natural cultivation, which, although rarely practiced, is of some interest in the southern provinces. Natural cultivation. In natural cultivation, the seeds are sown on the bed in April, but in May, they are placed in holes that have been filled with 25 to 30 centimeters of manure, over which a layer of compost has been spread. Transplants are planted in rows at varying distances from each other, depending on the varieties grown; the plants transplanted in this way have previously been pruned above the second leaf. To facilitate recovery, they are sheltered by cloches for the first few days, then, when they continue to grow and the temperature is high enough for them to be safe, the cloches are removed for good. As vegetation continues, two branches develop, which are pruned above the sixth leaf. When a fruit begins to form, the branch bearing it is cut off above the second leaf, located beyond the point of attachment. Some growers prune differently, while others don't prune at all. In any case, the system we have adopted has many supporters, and the results are almost always satisfactory. It should be noted, however, that pruning is not indispensable in natural cultivation. An important question for the gardener is to know when melons need to be picked in order to get their full flavour and aroma. There are several signs that a melon has reached maturity. Most commonly, small cracks appear around the stem; the stalk seems to want to detach itself entirely; the fragrance of the fruit becomes more penetrating; the color of the rind is lighter; the part next to the eye is softer. When the melon has reached this stage of development, it can be picked by slicing the stalk 8 or 10 centimetres from the point of attachment. It can then be taken to the fruit orchard, where it will remain for a few days to complete ripening before being eaten. Although many varieties show their ripeness through all these characteristics, it should not be forgotten that some show it through only one or other of these signs. In fact, a single sign may suffice to guide the horticulturist. Forced cultivation. In forced cultivation, melon seeds are sown from mid-January on a bed with a temperature of around 25 degrees. A furrow is opened on the surface, into which the seed is placed, then covered with a little potting soil. Once this is done, the frames are put in place, surrounded by a stove. At night, they are covered with straw mats. Once the plants have broken through the surface of the soil, they can be given some air. Once the plants have grown a terminal bud, they are ready for transplanting. Transplanting can be done on the same layer, if it has retained sufficient heat. The best way is to plant out in pots, which are pushed right up to the edge of the bed, so that when the bed's temperature drops, the plants can be transported on a 2 Melon Cantaloup Prescott fond blant de Paris. Melon de Honfleur. Melon Cantaloup noir des Carmes. Melon Cantaloup Prescott hâtif à chässis. Melon maraîcher rond de Paris. 149 seconds without any break in vegetation. To encourage the plants to put out more roots, we bury them up to the cotyledons; they are then lightly bashed. To facilitate recovery, the frames are covered with straw mats for two or three days; air is then allowed to penetrate from time to time, but only when the temperature is above zero. Fifteen or twenty days before transplanting, we proceed with planting. Planting is usually done on a trench bed. Two plants are planted in the same frame. These plants should be pruned as described above. The cultivation method we have just described applies to early varieties, which we want to produce in May or June, and which are therefore sown in January or February. Those sown at the beginning of April are much less demanding. Sowing is done as before, on a bed and under frames or cloches. Sow on a second layer, 60 to 65 centimetres apart; plant in a single row and place the bells, which are lifted with racks whenever you feel they are useful; remove them completely when they are no longer needed. Varieties. We classify melons into two categories, which include almost all our cultivated varieties: Cantaloupes and brodés melons. Cantaloupe varieties include The Cantaloup d'Alger melon, highly esteemed both for its hardiness and the sweetness of its flesh; The Cantaloup noir des Carmes melon, with a very dark green rind; the bright red flesh is of the highest quality; The Cantaloup Prescott fond blanc de Paris melon, with deeply marked ribs; The Cantaloup Prescott silver-white melon, widely grown around Paris; The Cantaloup Prescott petit hâtif à châssis, one of our best melons, admirably suited to forced cultivation; The Cantaloup sucrin green-fleshed melon, with the most delicate flavor. Among the embroidered melons, we should mention: The pineapple melon, small in volume but very productive; its sweet flesh has a pleasant aroma; The maraicher melon, spherical in shape; the rind is almost entirely covered with fine intertwined lines that make up the embroidery; The Honfleur melon, very voluminous; it is hardy and of good quality; it is one of the most frequently used for outdoor cultivation; The red-fleshed Cavaillon melon, generally highly appreciated; The sucrin de Tours melon; the rind is covered with coarse embroidery; the flesh is of good quality; The green row melon, an excellent variety that is generally grown by guiding the stems on a trellis; it is not very large, but its flesh has a very spicy flavor. -=- O 4 4 En 9 O Melon seeds should be selected from varieties that best combine the desired qualities. Hybridization between different breeds should always be avoided. Enemies. Melons can be attacked by many kinds of insects. In addition to grubs and crickets, the gray moth, which we have already mentioned, is all the more formidable in that there is no way to combat it. Aphids are much less dangerous, as their ravages can always be stopped. A disease that sometimes occurs in melons is canker, which attacks the branches. To stop its effects, the affected parts are removed with a sharp instrument. Jaundice, which manifests itself in the yellowish hue of leaves and stems, is caused by a general weakness of the plant.  GE RN Green climbing melon. TOMATO, AUBERGINE, PIMENT Tomato. 153 As tomatoes are native to South America, they require a great deal of heat to produce abundantly. In the southern provinces of France, it is always grown in the open ground, but in the climate of Paris, the plants are always raised on a warm bed. Cultivation. - Tomatoes are usually sown towards the end of March; transplanting is done three or four weeks after sowing; a month later, the plants are pruned 50 to 60 centimetres apart. When the plants have reached a certain height, it's a good idea to give them a stake or even fix them to a trellis; this procedure has the advantage of preventing the fruit from coming into direct contact with the soil, which could lead to rotting. It's even better to grow them close to a wall, which will shelter and reflect the sun's heat. To fully expose the fruit to the sun, thin out the leaves when they are half their size. Water frequently and abundantly. To regulate production, we usually prune the branches. The main stem is cut above the fourth branch. Each of these secondary branches is allowed to produce four bunches of flowers. You can prune in different ways; any system that fulfils your purpose should naturally be considered good. Tomatoes sown at the end of March can produce in August, but forced cultivation will produce fruit much earlier. For this reason, sowing can start in September, although in most cases not until January. Transplanting and planting are done on a bed sheltered by a stove, and always under a frame. Only two branches are left on the forced plants, which are attached to a wire held in place by small stakes. When a sufficient number of flowers have been produced, the stems are cut to stop their growth. If sown at the beginning of January, the crop can be harvested in May. If sown in September, harvesting is accelerated by several months. Varieties. - The best tomato varieties are: The large red tomato, quite productive, which is grown on E 7 V all over the Midi region, as it is a little late; The early large red tomato, widely grown in central and northern France; The early dwarf red tomato, a good small variety, very suitable for under-frame cultivation; The smooth large red tomato, remarkable for its volume; the latter has no ribs. Tomato seeds should be taken from fully ripe fruit, crushed and removed. They are then carefully washed and left to dry. Tomatoes, like potatoes, are attacked by peronospora infestans, which can be treated with Bordeaux mixture. 2 2~~ 5- Early dwarf red tomato. 155 Cultivation. - In our climate, eggplant is almost always sown in the soil. They are generally sown at the beginning of March; three or four weeks later, the plants are ready for transplanting; they are placed in pots filled with potting soil, which is then pressed into the bed. Transplanting takes place in the open ground; the young plants are removed from their rootballs and planted in rays 45 to 50 centimetres apart, as far as possible in a well-exposed bed. During growth, water frequently and take care not to let any weeds grow. Harvesting can begin in early September. The very early dwarf violet eggplant, small in size but relatively very productive; The very early Barbentane eggplant, a new variety, long, violet in color, very early. These are: The long red pepper, the long yellow pepper, the Chile pepper, the cherry pepper, the tomato pepper, the monstrous pepper, the sweet pepper or large square pepper. The pungent, hot flavor of chili peppers makes them sought-after by only a small number of enthusiasts, which is why they are not widely cultivated. BEANS, PEAS, BEANS, LENTILLES Beans. 157 Beans are one of the most important food crops. The seeds are used in shelling and parchment varieties. In mange-tout varieties, the whole fruit is used for consumption. Cultivation. - When cultivating beans in the open ground, it is important to keep the soil substantial and light, ivory butter beans. Giant white bean. Val d'Isère bean. Haricot zébré. Émile bean. moderately humid, with good exposure. Sow when frosts are no longer a threat, generally in May for the Paris climate. Sowing is often done in rows 40 to 45 centimeters apart and 5 centimeters deep. Holes are made 15 to 20 centimetres apart on the same line: a bean is placed in each hole, then the furrows are closed and lightly basked if necessary. If sowing in clumps, place four or five seeds per hole. Once the plants have grown a few leaves, hoe them, then weed and water. Some horticulturists hoe the young plants, which seems to have a positive effect on vegetation. Several seedlings are usually sown over the course of a year, enabling harvesting as late as October. When growing snap beans, which require less time to develop, they can be sown later than other beans. String beans, on the other hand, should be sown at the beginning of the season. When the stems of pole beans have reached a height of 30 to 35 centimetres, they need to be rowed, i.e. provided with stakes or rods to support their growth. These can be rods or even simple reeds. Dwarf beans have the advantage over pole beans of being self-supporting throughout their development. When the pods of snap beans have reached a sufficient size, they should be picked as soon as possible, because if you waited until they had developed further, they would be less tender and the threads in their pods would be detrimental to their quality. Beans that are to be eaten fresh are picked a little before full maturity. In this case, they can be harvested every two or three days. As beans are very sensitive to frost, late sowings must be sheltered from the cold. Although dry beans can be eaten constantly, it has been found useful to force-feed this vegetable. Seedlings are sown around mid-January, on a warm bed. They are sheltered by frames which are lifted whenever possible during development, and any leaves in poor condition are removed from the plants. It goes without saying that only dwarf varieties are used for forced cultivation, as the others cannot restrict their development to occupy only the space reserved under a frame. The dwarf Dutch bean is usually preferred, and four rays 15 cm apart are planted under the same box. Water from time to time during growth, and place mats over the panels at night. In April, fresh beans can be picked. If several successive sowings have been carried out, they can be harvested until the products of natural cultivation replace those of forced cultivation. Varieties. - We group bean varieties into pole beans and bush beans. In these two categories, we'll talk successively about shelling beans and beans without parchment. The best varieties of string beans for shelling are : The Soissons bean, which is best eaten dry; it is widely grown around Paris; The Liancourt bean, hardy and productive; it is a much-appreciated variety; The rice bean, whose very small bean is of good quality; The sabre bean, a little late, but very productive; its stalk can reach 3 meters in height, and its very large pod contains a top-quality white bean. Peas. Cultivation. - Pea cultivation is one of the simplest. To be successful, it must be grown in loose soil with plenty of water. Green pea. Pois sabre. Clamart pea. Ram's-horn pea. Green dwarf pea. However, peas can be grown successfully in almost any soil. Peas are sown in rays, at times that vary with the climate. 11 with the climate, from late November in the Midi, to February in the North; they continue throughout the spring. We often sow in clumps, spacing the rows more or less according to the size of the varieties we're growing. When the larger varieties have reached 30 or 40 centimetres, it is necessary, as with beans, to support them with oars that are always slightly inclined towards the middle of the bed; the ends of the stems can also be cut off above the third and fourth flowers. In this way, you can speed up production and dispense with the need for oars. When the pods are ready to be picked, cut off the stalk with the fingernail; pulling them off could injure the feet. Like beans, peas have been subjected to forced cultivation, for which we prefer to use the very early dwarf pea with a frame. In this case, it is not essential to use layers. You can also sow in a sheltered, well-exposed bed, protecting the plants with frames. Sowing then takes place in November. At the time of frost, it is sufficient to surround the boxes with a brace. When using varieties other than the very early chassis dwarf pea, it is necessary to lay the stems on the ground when they have reached a height of around twenty centimetres, so that they can continue their development unhindered. November sowings produce in April. Varieties - Like beans, peas are classified into pole and bush peas. Each of these groups includes hulling and non-hulling varieties. Among the string peas for shelling, we'll mention : Prince Albert pea, an early and very popular variety, sometimes used for forced cultivation; Dutch Michaux pea, generally 1 meter high, hardy and productive; Ordinary Michaux pea, also known as St. Catherine pea, sown mainly in November, hardy and fairly productive: The round-grained William pea, whose pods are slightly curved; it is early and productive; The Auvergne pea; its pods are curved; it is a highly appreciated vegetable that requires little care; The sabre pea, less cultivated than most of the preceding ones, but nevertheless a good variety; The Clamart pea, late, but nevertheless highly esteemed; The Knight pea, with wrinkled grain, which is cultivated especially for late summer. The best breeds of peas without parchment are : Corne-debélier pea, which is hardy and productive; POIS PRINCE ALBERT Butter pea, which is less widespread than the previous one. The most recommended varieties of dwarf shelled peas are : The very early chassis dwarf pea, remarkable for its earliness and small size; The Dutch dwarf pea or ordinary dwarf pea, one of the best dwarf varieties; The very dwarf Brittany pea, widespread especially in England; The large green dwarf pea, its round seeds are quite developed; The American marvel pea, with wrinkled seeds, whose cultivation has made notable progress in recent times.
