The first, most famous and tireless of all plant researchers in Pannonia and Austria (1), Charles Clusius, offered the learned world a Notice on this plant; it is not inappropriate to reproduce his entire description here. He wrote "This plant, whose root is very thick and very long, is not commonly found; in fact, I remember having received some the size of an arm and the length of a cubit, and some larger, from the illustrious Lord Balthasar of Bathyan, who, in my favor, ordered me to bring some from Transdanubian Hungary (2) so that I could import them into the garden in Vienna. It produced leaves that differed little from those of Rave (3) in their incisions and cut-outs, but were shorter, more like the leaves of Panax Heracleum, covered with a rough, bristly down, contrasting with the greenery in their paleness (4); others, divided by slightly shallower, equally rough cut-outs, from the middle of which emerge (1) Stirpium pannonicarum austriarumque. (2) Ungaria transdanubiana. (3) Rapi. (4) Ex viridi pallentia. ge a stem a cubit or more high, an inch thick, ridged, concave and knotty, rough like the leaves; it is embraced by means of a wide pedicel by small, multifid leaves, equally rough thanks to the down that covers them. The stem ends in an umbel, similar to the umbels of Panax Heracleum, in which the flowers are similar in shape and color (1). Faded flowers were followed by rare (because some flowers are not fertilized), very thick fruit, rather similar to the large, ridged fruit of Libanotis cachryfera. "I cultivated these roots for two years, before a single one produced a stem, flowers and seed; then they rotted and gave off such a foul smell that they were thrown out of the garden. "The Hungarians neighboring Erlau (2), as well as those living immediately beyond the borders of Dacia, feed on them in years of famine and misery, instead of bread; this was assured to me not only by this illustrious man (3), but by other distinguished men who lived in this province. The result was that I was left in doubt as to whether it was identical with the Baltracan born in Tartary (4), as recalled by Josaphat Barbarus, a Venetian pratrician, in a letter to Peter Barocci, bishop of Padua, added at the end of the last chapter of his narrative published on his departure for Persia. "(1) Summus caulis in umbellam desinebat, Panacis Heraclei umbellis similem, in quibus flores et forma pares et colore. (2) Agriæ vicini. (3) Heros ille illustris ? (4) An eadem esset cum Baltracan in Tartaria nascente. name of Tartaria; indeed, like the Germans, they commonly name Tatars those we call Tartars. "Thus concludes Clusius; Jean Bauhin copied him in his Histoire des Plantes; but it is to be believed that neither he, nor any other author of those he cited, except Clusius, saw Hungarian Tartaria (1). "All of them, imitating Clusius, wrongly classified it among the Umbelliferae. It must be admitted that, in the first month of stem growth, as long as the plant still bears its curled, folded leaves (2) and its flowers closed and clustered on the ramuscules, it resembles, in a way, a Heracleum, in such a way as to be able to impose it on a botanist; but it differs greatly from it after its blossoming, so much so that I cannot wonder enough that Clusius, the most exact man besides, could have confused a cruciform plant (3) with an Umbellifera. "Indeed, we find no mention of it in his Histoire des Plantes de Pannonie et d'Autriche, published in 1583, and, before his return, he died in Vienna in 1587. It may well follow that this description was less well elaborated by him; perhaps it was from memory that he entrusted it to paper after the plant's death; what seems likely to corroborate this conjecture is that he did not depict such a rare plant and that, contrary to his habit, Clusius said nothing of its (1) Sed nec hunc, nec præter Clusium auctorem alium ex citatis ullum Tatariam ungaricam vidisse, credibile est. (2) Dum planta folia adhucdum sua rugose complicata... gerit. (3) This was Tournefort's name for the plants that made up the fifth class of his system. "For a long time now, Jacquin's illustrious professor had been possessed by the desire to see and examine the plant he knew from Clusius; an opportunity soon presented itself: The famous imperial astronomer Maximilien Hell was leaving for Agria (the Erlau of the Germans, the Eger of the Hungarians), a town in the county of Hevesch (1), in Hungary; Jacquin asked him, if he came across the plant called Tataria by the locals, to be so kind as to bring it back to him on his return, or to send it to him. "This distinguished man took care to transport to Vienna two roots which he had had dug up; he brought back dried samples of the flowering plant himself, and, on the way back, took care of the roots which, after a six-week journey in summer, arrived putrefied and fetid. One of them was four feet long and, though truncated, almost as thick as a leg. The dried samples indicated, against all expectations, a cruciform plant. "The very learned and skilful surgeon of the Caramellia regiment, H. Engelsdorfer, also carried out this mission, and more happily, in 1777; he sent to the Botanical Garden, at the request of the illustrious professor, several roots that he had been able to collect that were shorter and thinner; they recovered very well and produced ripe flowers and fruit every year. "He answered several questions (although he was unable to answer the others because of his sudden departure for the Bohemian army): 1° that the plant was now called Tataria by the locals; 2° that it (2) Comitatus Hevessiensis in Hungaria... grew in the fields, in the middle of the harvest, in a soil composed of fertile, black earth, one foot deep, under which lay a three-foot layer of yellowish clay, then, finally, and below, sand; that the root of the adult plant penetrated to this depth; that because of this, it was difficult to remove it whole, because the hole, as soon as you reached the sand, filled abundantly with gushing water: 3° that every year, the roots were torn up and cut by the plough, and that, even when thus wounded, they still grew back; 4° that nowhere around Erlau did he discover that they were consumed, except by children who ate the cooked root because of its sweet taste (1); 5° that some were eaten by hares, which are very numerous in this area. "It grows not only around Erlau, but also in other parts of Hungary. The servant of a very learned professor, who was of Hungarian nationality, having seen some brought in, immediately recognized it, referred to it by the Hungarian word: Tatar-Kenyér, or Tartarian Bread, and declared that he had eaten some in Debrezin. On his suggestion, we made a salad from the fresh, raw root, peeling it, cutting it crosswise into thin slices and seasoning it with oil, vinegar and salt; it pleased everyone. "A pleasant taste is also obtained by cooking the still tender stem, before the flowers have developed, and preparing it in the same way as cauliflower (2). Its use is not, however, very convenient, unless you take care to remove the bark fibers, which are numerous, tough and difficult to chew. (1) Ob dulcedinem. (2) Brassicæ caulifloræ adinstar... "At the same time, the Reverend Norbert Boccius, superior of the Order of St. John of God in Feldsperg and a tireless researcher of Moravian plants, also made known this plant discovered by him and a learned professor in that country. He found it growing abundantly in vines, in clay soil, near the village of Hurtau, near Aussitz; it is known there, he says, as Hieronymus-Würzel (1), or St. Jerome's root, and is carried to Bohemia, where farmers give it to cows to increase their milk. ." Clusius' conjecture that our plant is identical with the Batracan of the Tartars is destroyed by this: Josaphat Barbarus split the bark of the Batracan at the moment of ripening, separated it from the woody part (hence the conclusion that the stem appears to be perennial and frutescente) and added that the seed was of a strong odor, but nevertheless of a pleasant flavor; none of this relates to our plant. "I think it far more worthy of attention that Clusius says, according to others it's true, that in certain parts of Hungary, the inhabitants feed on this root in times of famine and misery. In any case, the root's long lifespan, its volume in the adult state, its resistance even to deep lesions, its resistance to the cold of our winters, etc., all encourage its cultivation, or at least its preservation, (1) Racine de Saint-Jérôme (St. Jerome's Root) seems to me to be the correct translation; the word saint is often neglected by Germans, who give the fruit of the Carob tree, commonly known as Pain de Saint-Jean (St. John's Bread), the name Johannisbrod. Nowhere does it extend beyond the 51st degree of north latitude. It likes dry soils, as well as loamy (provided it's not salty), sandy and humus-rich soils. However, it prefers the depressions found in arid plains, varying in size but never reaching, in dry terrain, the size of the drawing transmitted to me. In succulent soils near rivers, where it also spreads, it produces the largest, most pungent-tasting roots. "Here is a description of the plant, based on live specimens in the Garden, and others dried from the forests (3), as well as on sketches: "Perennial root, long fusiform, as thick as the arm and thicker in the adult state, two to four feet long, cylindrical, simple or divided inferiorly into limb-like forms (4); it blackens in the air; fresh, it is even black; washed and dried, it is rather grayish; it emits few fibrils throughout its extent. Inside, it is clearly fleshy, whitish with a slight dirty-yellow tinge, with irregular radiating lines; the flavor is mild, with no real pungency. Kept in the air, it gradually shrinks, becomes rough and covered with protrusions, hardens, ceases to be like itself (5) and becomes useless. "The radical leaves that first appear are often small and entire; then they themselves, as well as the stem leaves and those of the lower branches (6) are variously and irregularly multifid, sometimes very ample, pinnatifid, of decomposed form or (1) Meloe syriaca. (2) Meloe vesicatoria. (3) Instead of forests, we should always understand, no doubt, the state of nature. (4) ... Aut inferne incrura divisa. (5) Fitque sui dissimilis... (6) Et caulina atque ramea inferiora. overdecomposed (1), sometimes divided into oblong, toothed and acute strips, of a slightly glaucous green, glabrous on both sides; the upper leaves of the stem and branches are simple and oblong. The angular petioles are glabrous in the larger leaves, but the petioles of the smaller ones, like the ribs, are very thick and prominent, and the veins are bristling with white hairs. However, this hispidity and the shape of the leaves not only vary in the different plants, but also in the different parts of each plant, so that a description that would suit each and every one would be in vain applicable here. "The flowers, which are very numerous, spread out in terminal, stalked corymbs, exude a strong, pleasant honeyed odor, so much so that it is as if you were approaching the nostrils of a bee's comb; The calyx is greenish-yellow, the petals milky-white, the anthers greenish, the ovaries green, the stigma yellow, the fruit pea-sized, consisting of a shiny green fleshy envelope, but dry, rough and poorly colored when ripe, and a seed with a blackish envelope and a pale yellow embryo (2), with a slightly acrid and unpleasant taste. It begins to flower in mid-April. The fruit ripens in June, but only a few reach the desired stage of development; most remain small and unripe (3). Considerations relating to fruiting (4) must be accepted as such. (1)... Decomposite vel supra decomposite pinnatifida (2)... Nucleo... (3) Steriles perstant. (4) In fructificatione character observatur nune subjungendus. "Calyx tetraphyllous, leaflets oblong, obtuse, concave, canaliculate, spreading, deciduous. "Corolla with four petals, oval-faced, very obtuse, flat, almost twice the length of the calyx, inserted on a short, erect tab. "Stamens. Six thick, erect threads, two of which are opposite, the same length as the calyx and simple; the other four are longer than the first and bifurcated at the apex, one branch of this bifurcation directed towards the ovary and sterile, the other slightly inclined outwards and antheriferous. Incumbent anthers. "A green glandula alternates with the threads belonging to the large stamens. "Ovary ovate, style absent, stigma capitate. "Fruit globose, unilocular, indehiscent. "Against all expectations, analysis of the root, treated by distillation, produced results quite different from those usually obtained with cruciform plants. It yielded an aqueous mucus, an acidic spirit (2), an empyreumatic oil; having obtained the above, it was treated in a new vessel and at a higher temperature; a small quantity of a volatile alzaline spirit was obtained, just as with other plants an acidic spirit is abundantly obtained. By incineration, the residue yields fixed vegetable alkaline salt in great abundance. C. Tataria seeds are difficult to obtain. We asked in vain for them in Pesth and Vienna; they finally came to us from Saint Petersburg, thanks to the benevolent enterprise of MM. Vilmorin, who obtained them for us from M. Regel. But the learned director of the Bolanic Garden in St. Petersburg was unable to provide us with the information we wanted on the plant's cultivation and uses. To the two questions put to him on our behalf by Dr. Bretschneider, with the kindness he always shows us, Mr. Regel replied that Crambe Tataria grows wild in southern Russia; that it is not cultivated(1).... As you can see, we have made very little progress in the experimental cultivation of C. Tataria. We doubt very much whether it will ever be a vegetable to be introduced into our kitchen gardens, but it does interest us a great deal, and we'll tell you why. In France, little use is made of these light, easily digested starches, particularly suitable for feeding children and convalescents, of which considerable quantities are imported from England under the name of Arrow-root (see the chapters on Maranta arundinacea and Canna). The name Arrow-root is wrongly given to the starch obtained from various Canna, Tacca pinnatifida and, according to Simmonds, a few other plants. The real Arrowroot comes from M. arundinacea, but we can't say whether this is superior to the similar starches often substituted. Liuto's Chuno is another type of Arrowroot (see the chapter on Alstrœmère Ligtu). Leaving aside Sago, Salep and Tapioca (Manioc), this brings the number of plants from which beneficial starch is extracted to four main species: Maranta arundinacea; Canna; Tacca pinnatifida; Liuto (Alstrœmeria Ligtue). However, we are inclined to believe that the roots of C. Tataria are also suitable for the produclior of an Arrow-root. C. Tataria is classified as a food plant by the ancients. "Crambe Tataria Jacq., a plant from Hungary, appears to be the Chara whose roots fed Caesar's soldiers in Albania (Caes., B. C., 3, 48); Hungarians still make bread from it in times of famine (1)." Crambe cordifolia Steven, from Persia and the Caucasus to Thibet and the Himalayas, at altitudes of up to 14,000 feet, is a beautiful perennial, very hardy in our climate and extremely easy to grow. Its roots and leaves are edible. Harvested as they begin to develop, the leaves are tender and can replace cabbage, but their flavor is milder. PARA SPILANTHES OLERACEA L. Compositae family. Annual plant, native to South America, which, along with its fusca variety (S. fusca Desf.), is cultivated in our gardens as an odontalgic. According to P. Joigneaux (2), the leaves of Para cress have a very penetrating flavor that provokes salivation and hence digestion. Its flowers (1) Les plantes alimentaires des anciens, by Édouard Martens. It is a very energetic antiscorbutic, and highly esteemed in tropical regions, where it advantageously replaces Cochlearia, which would not grow there. It is an ingredient in many toothpastes. Rousseau, Histoire naturelle et médicale du Cresson de Para, 1825, has highlighted the merits of this plant, which is extremely easy to grow, even in our climate. The hot, peppery flavor of Para watercress makes it highly sought-after as a condiment in hot countries. It is used in small quantities and well chopped, in combination with salads. R. P. Bull. Soc. d'Accl., 1887, p. 394. Fam. des Labiées Synonyms: English: Chinese Artichoke; German! Knollenziest; Italian: Tuberina (1). DESCRIPTION. - MORPHOLOGY Perennial plant. Stump emitting numerous underground, tuberous rhizomes. Tubers formed by a succession of nodules, rather resembling the swollen root collars of rosary oats (Ar(1) G.-S. Bullo, Raccoglitore Anno, XIII, series III. 10 LE POTAGER D'UN CURIEUX Fig. 27 - Crosne (Stachys affinis), Iubercules. V CROSNE Fig. 28 - Crosne (Stachys "ffinis), flowering branch. 147 rhenatherum elatius, var. bulbosum Gaud.; Avena precatoria Thuill.) Stem simple or stalked, erect or flattened at base, quadrangular, 25 to 40 cm high, hispid at corners. Leaves opposite, petiolate, rough, hispid, cordate at base, acuminate, crenate-toothed; lower ones ovate-oblong, gradually smaller as they grow higher. Flowers sessile, grouped 6-4 in distinct false whorls. The flower consists of a subcampanulate or infundibuliform calyx, obconical, with equal, acute teeth. Corolla 10 to 24 millimeters long, purpurine, with exserted tube, before a ring of hairs inside. "Tubers have the same morphological value as those of the potato. They are swollen twigs, tuberculated under the influence of the underground station. As they swell, each internode of the modified branch loses, so to speak, in length what it gains in diameter. "On a cross-section of one of these swollen, perfectly round internodes, we find, as in the aerial branch, four libero-ligneous bundles occupying the place of the rounded angles. The bark is not very thick, while the medullary tissues develop considerably, forming almost the entire mass of the tuber. Lateral roots, arising directly from the node, form on either side of the angular libero-ligneous bundle, so that there are eight roots at the same level, a little above the emergence of the leaves. Other lateral roots may form above these, always in the same way. When the tuber is planted, the buds that develop into twigs and stems are those closest to the upper end (1). Habitat. - Denominations. "In a memoir entitled Fragmenta floræ orientalis (Bulletin de la Société impériate des naturalistes de Moscou), vol. 54, no. 4, M. de Maximowicz, a learned Russian botanist and himself a well-known explorer of eastern Asia, has given brief but precise information on the Labiatae in question, concerning its history, homeland, synonymy and, I might add, dietary characteristics. In the above-mentioned memoir, it is stated in substance: Stachys affinis Bunge, Enum. pl. ch. bor. n° 289. S. Sieboldi Miq, Prolusio, p. 44 (description follows). Hab. - Northern China to Kantaï (Bunge); Peking (Tatarinow), where the plant is cultivated under the name Kan-lu, because of its fleshy root, edible according to Skatschkow and Dr. Bretschneider, who found it on Mount Po-hua-shan. In Japan, the plant has been observed in Yedo, where it is rarely cultivated under the name Daima Gik (Siebold). The Japanese botanist Tchonowski observed it in the principality of Nambu (M. de Maximowicz does not say whether it is cultivated or spontaneous)... Stachys affinis Bunge is known to be cultivated in several Chinese provinces. It is discussed at some length in volume IV (vegetable plants) of the great Chinese encyclopedia entitled Tchi wou ming chi thou Kuo, where the plant is (1) P. Maury, Association française pour l'avancement des sciences; Oran, 1888. skilfully illustrated as Tsao che tsan (silkworm stone plant). I am indebted to the kindness of a priest of the Missions étrangères, the R. P. Mutel, a learned sinologist, for this information. Mutel, a learned sinologist, the translation of the article concerning the Stachys affinis, and I give it here, deleting the passages unnecessary to the subject: "The Tsao che tsan was revealed and mentioned for the first time in the great Flora called Pen-tsao-hou-eipien: it is the Kan-lu (sweet dew); its stem and flowers resemble those of the aquatic thyme (Lophantus?); the root has unions (united pearls). In northern lands, it is grown "extensively as a vegetable. Tou-peu-Tsucun (a poet of some sort) says this in his poem "du Ta-houah-tsai" (vegetable from Jede's ring): the plant "called Kan-lu, what does it produce? At its decline, it bears "Jade rings, bound together and yet mobile, ind" hanging from each other. These rings are precisely the "vegetable" we're talking about. The above passage from the Chinese encyclopaedia describes the Kan-lu in an entirely oriental manner, i.e. by comparison with objects we can actually see. Nevertheless, it shows that it is cultivated mainly in the northern provinces, and that the describer's imagination was particularly struck by the pearly, jade-like appearance of its rhizomes. Elsewhere, it is said that Kan-lu holds a place among the food plants listed in the Kiou-Hung-Pentza (Flora of the Salvation from Dearth), a work often cited in Chinese books. In this respect, Kan-lu deserves attention, and the multiplicity of its rhizomes, combined with their nutritional qualities, indicates that its cultivation can, to a certain extent, offer a resource not to be scorned. Very recently, Mr. Delavay, a missionary in Yunnan, sent the Museum Herbarium some fine specimens of Stachys affinis in flower and fruit; they were accompanied by the following label: "N° 3079. Red flowers. Cultivated for its edible root; small tubers in rosaries. Chinese name: Tignou-tze (earth button). Harvested at Tcheou-choui, near Tapin-tze, September 23, 1887." Another label reads: "The woods at Talong-tan, near Tapin-tze." This shows that the plant is not only cullivated in northern China, but also in the Austro-Western provinces of the empire, where the name given to it is not that of Kan-lu, no doubt due to a particular dialect, but which nonetheless offers a meaning analogous to that of: united pearls, ring of jade, which, as I said above, serves elsewhere as a term of comparison for the rhizomes of the plant. Siebold received Stachys affinis from the Decima Garden in Japan, but he seems to have been unaware that it was a food plant and gave it no name. For his part, M. de Maximowicz saw it in Yédo, in the gardens, where, he says, it is rarely cultivated and where Dr. Savatier collected a single specimen. Miquel, Prolusio, p. 44, had given Siebold's plant the name Stachys Sieboldi; but, with the help of the extensive material he obtained, Maximowicz demonstrated that it did not differ from Stachys affinis. Finally, more recently, M. Faurie, a missionary in Japan, sent us a specimen of this species, with this note: "Aomori (prov. sept. de Nippon); the plant is cultivated there for its root. It is also shown under the name Tsyo rogi, Chorogi, in CROSNE, volume XI, plate 13, of the Japanese collection entitled Somokou dusets (1)". INTRODUCTION IN FRANCE - CULTIVATION AND YIELD In the spring of 1882, we received from the Société nationale d'Acclimatation a box containing rhizomes of Stachys affinis, a plant that had long been on our desiderata lists. The rhizomes had been sent by Dr. Bretschneider, physician to the Russian Legation in Peking, who was kind enough to respond to a request for useful plants from China addressed to our Minister in Peking, Mr. Bourée, by the Société nationale d'Acclimatation. All but five or six of these rhizomes had rotted during the trip, but the plant's power to multiply is such that the loss of most of them left us with no regrets. In the first year, every tuber planted on an old bed gave us a satisfactory harvest, and by the end of the second year, the clumps left in place gave us two to three hundred to one. On January 4 1888, M. Paillieux presented the following note to the members of the plant section of the Société nationale d'Acclimatation: "Gentlemen, if you will allow me, I will speak to you again today about Stachys. It will probably be the last time. "You know that, for three years, I have offered and given to everyone, in and outside Paris, seedlings of our new vegetable. Last spring, however, I predicted that it would not be offered on the market again this winter, and that it would only be grown in a few amateur (1) A. Franchet, Le Jardin, 1889. gardens. It was impossible to predict when the plant would be adopted by growers and enter general consumption. "Now, I'm loaded with years and in a hurry to act before age forbids any work. "I knew that bulbous chervil, introduced into Western Europe in 1726, had only been known in France for fifty years, and was still not widely grown today. "If I consulted my memories, they would tell me that, in the space of a hundred years, only two new vegetables had been introduced to France: the Chinese yam, which has almost been abandoned, and the bulbous chervil, which I mentioned earlier. "I wanted to spare Stachys the long incubation period undergone by previously introduced plants. I wanted to try to achieve in three months the propagation of the excellent vegetable that our Society has introduced, and which, in my opinion, is destined to occupy a large place in general consumption. "I thought I could only achieve my goal by immediately becoming a producer and seller. The foregoing considerations led me to this decision. "I rented some land around my garden and planted Stachys, thus securing a harvest which is not yet complete and which will give me around 3,000 kilograms of tubers. "Convinced that the words Stachys affinis could not be pronounced by our cooks, I named the tubers Crosnes, which is the name of my village. "I had three thousand prospectus cards printed to publicize the vegetable, which have been a great help to me. I distributed some of them to the members present at the January 4 meeting, and I'm making some available to you again today. "From the last days of November, I've been making room, looking for buyers, rejected by most, welcomed by a few. "At the moment, I have ten buyers in Paris whose sales are increasing daily. I ship our vegetable to Lille, Roubaix, Amiens, Reims and even Brussels. I'm expecting requests from a few other towns. "I have the satisfaction of seeing that purchases are constantly being renewed. Our success is not a flash in the pan; it's a fire that won't go out. "I had my tubers tasted by Brébant, the friendly and renowned restaurateur you all know. He recognized their merit, put them on his daily menu, and included them in the Japanese salad, the fashionable dish whose recipe is pleasantly given in Francillon, and the author is now familiar with Stachys. "MM. X..., from Paris, have used 100 kilograms of Stachys to make their Pickles. They are sending some to a house in the provinces, and wrote to me on January 30th: "Yesterday, Saturday, the courier gave us a case of Stachys on your behalf. Please send us more: "30 kilograms next Tuesday; "30 kilograms next Saturday. "In case your crop runs out, please reserve about 100 kilograms for us. These Stachys are all shipped to the provinces and eaten as fresh vegetables. Success seems assured, and we believe that next year you can produce them without fear. "L'Art culinaire of January 30 contains a small note on Crosnes, with a very exact figure of the tuber: "Under the name Crosnes du Japon, the Société nationale d'Acclimatation has just introduced and wants to propagate this new vegetable. We can only applaud this attempt. "Appearing only in winter, when our excellent French products are in very short supply, this vegetable can be of real use in culinary service. Its shape is original and graceful; its taste is reminiscent of the artichoke. It is very easy and quick to cook, and can be used in a variety of ways. "To spread the use of our vegetable more and more, I have just made an agreement with an active and intelligent young man who will continue the work begun. "Unfortunately, it is doubtful whether my harvest will meet demand during the month of February. I couldn't possibly undertake a more extensive cultivation. "As soon as Stachys appears at Les Halles, do I need to tell you that your colleague will disappear as a salesman and return purely and simply to being the researcher of new plants to whom you have always given your sympathy and encouragement? Success was thus assured from the start of 1887. It grew steadily. Mr. Paillieux was overwhelmed with requests, which he met to the best of his ability. Hundreds of publications, in France and abroad, special journals, bulletins of horticultural societies, scientific bulletins of major newspapers, celebrated the new plant. As early as 1891, commission agents at Les Halles received and sold large quantities of tubers. Our vegetable could be seen in almost every fruit store in the capital; it even made an appearance in the small cars of four-season merchants. It's now a household name. The price has dropped considerably. Consumption will be widespread. It's a given, a definitive conquest. In Le Potager d'un curieux, 1st edition (1885), p. 88, we were the first to mention the cultivation of Stachys, twelve years ago. We publish hereafter all the information we have gathered since then, indicating, where appropriate, the sources from which we drew it. The plant is hardy. Since 1882-83, it has withstood our winters without suffering. It will certainly withstand the coldest weather. We've been growing Crosne for fifteen years, which allows us to indicate a very simple cultivation procedure. The tubers should be planted in February, after which they would begin to vegetate. They are very willing to come out of their rest. If a plantation is covered with manure so that frost or snow do not interrupt the uprooting, the rhizomes germinate immediately. We can't say which soil Crosne prefers. All soils are suitable, but it seems to us that in a compact, clay soil, digging would be very laborious and too often interrupted by frost, snow or rain. We therefore recommend choosing soil that is a little sandy, or in any case well loosened. We plant in holes 20 centimetres deep, spaced 40 centimetres apart in all directions, with three tubers per hole. We repeat the hoeing until October 1, to keep the soil perfectly clean. When we do the last hoeing, we think it's a good idea to lightly butter the clumps. We don't hoe after October 1, because the tool would cut the rhizomes that extend horizontally. In the Paris climate, we believe it's wise not to start uprooting before December 1st. Tubers are not perfect until then. They begin to vegetate again on March 1st. In home gardens, we pull as the table requires. There's no need to worry about frost. In the field, large quantities are harvested at a time for sale. Tubers can be stored in sand, in a dry place. They do not fear the cold, but when exposed to the air, they wither and are no longer presentable after twelve or fifteen days. Yield, as always, is more or less considerable, depending on the fertilization and the care given to the crop. We dare not say what it might be in a garden, but we have seen that it always exceeds expectations. In large-scale cultivation, we think that we could count on 12,000 kilograms per hectare; but the plant is above all, and can be exclusively, destined for small-scale cultivation, because of the difficulties of uprooting and preserving the produce. No matter how much care is taken in uprooting, a host of offshoots appear in May. This plant can be transplanted and produce a harvest equal to that produced by the tubers; but if left in place, it is unpleasantly surprised, when winter comes, to have almost no harvest at all, as the plant quickly exhausts the soil. Exposure to too much heat is not without danger. It's true that we've only once lost a plantation to sunburn, and we've always feared that this accident would happen again. In the south of France, Stachys must be grown in the shade, and requires frequent, moderate watering. Dr. Louis Planchon, who has experimented with growing this plant in Montpellier, tells us that he has obtained good results only thanks to these conditions; he adds, moreover, that nowhere in the region has Stachys flowered. We know of no other enemy to Crosne than the white grub. It takes around 600 tubers to make 1 kilogram. INTRODUCTION IN OTHER PARTS OF EUROPE Crosne has spread from France to England, where it is known as Chinese Artichoke. Numerous cultivation trials have been carried out, as evidenced by articles published in horticultural journals such as The Gardeners' Chronicle, The Garden, etc.; however, we do not know whether the plant is widely cultivated in this country, or whether it has definitively entered the consumer market. In Belgium, it was cultivated soon after its introduction, and success was at least as complete as in France. In Germany, where the plant is known as Knollenziest, Crosne is cultivated only by a few horticultural enthusiasts, but efforts are being made to spread it. According to Villkomm, attempts made in Austria suggest that Crosne can thrive in open fields in all parts of the empire, and that it would be worthwhile extending its cultivation. In Italy, as early as 1887, Messrs Ingegnoli frères of Milan recommended its cultivation; the plant, which they had been experimenting with for some time, had given very good results, and they wrote that it "deserved one of the best places in vegetable gardens". The Italian newspaper Raccoglitore had written about it in 1886; in 1887, various cultivation experiments were carried out in the province of Padua and in the Royal potager agraire, thanks to the active president of the Comice agraire de Padoue, Professor Keller. Mr. Bullo, in agreement with Professor Saccardo, proposed the name Tuberina for the plant, which has the merit of being easy and brief. He published in the Raccoglitore, vol. XIII, ser. III, a long note on the history, uses and cultivation of this new vegetable. We have extracted some interesting information on the introduction of Crosne in Italy. "In Lombardy, several individuals grow Stachys affinis; however, it has not yet appeared on the Milan market. On the contrary, in Monza, near Milan, it is very much in vogue: we started growing it in the Royal Park, and, having pleased the court, all the city's families wanted to grow it. It is sometimes seen on the Monza market and, in memory of the protection given to this vegetable, it is called Pomme de terre de la Reine (Pomo di terra della Regina). I would have really liked to keep this name," he says, "but thinking that it is too long to become popular quickly, and that there are already other plants with almost similar names, I decided to propose the name Tuberina, which is shorter and easier, and which cannot be confused with others. "I was supported in this idea by competent people who encouraged me to make the proposal. "In Piedmont, Stachys is known by name only; we hope soon to see it cultivated there too, at least on a trial basis. "In the southern provinces, it is still unknown; the Société d'Acclimatation in Palermo is currently trying to make it known in Sicily, and the Dammann house in Saint-Giovianni di Teduccio has been experimenting, but, to tell the truth, with unsatisfactory results, obviously due to the too-high summer temperature. "Italo Mazzon, the excellent poultry farmer from Padua and lover of all that is new and useful, cultivated it as early as 1887, and this is what he wrote to me on the subject: "Stachys affinis is a plant that deserves to be cultivated on a large scale, especially in sandy soils. The tests I have carried out have convinced me that, in clay soils, although quite productive, it would not be to be recommended, because the rather fragile roots would tend to lengthen and the nodes to enlarge. A tuber of any size, planted in suitable soil, yields about 1.5 kilograms of product, and many other tubers about the size of a finger. "I was already convinced that Stachys must give a large product, but experiments made at the Royal potager agraire have never given the product noted by Mazzon, and this must depend absolutely on the quality of the soil where the experiment was made. "Mazzon sent Stachys tubers to the Treviso exhibition in 1888 and won a medal. CHEMICAL COMPOSITION OF TUBERCULES (1) "Of particular interest are the tubers known in the trade as "Crosne", which are formed by the swollen internodes of the underground branches of a Labiatae (Stachys affinis)(1) A. de Planta. This work was carried out at the agricultural chemistry laboratory of the Zurich Polytechnicum, directed by Professor E. Schultze Revue générale de botanique, February 15 1889, p. 85. These tubers, which are being used more and more every day in France, England and Switzerland, are indeed a first-rate foodstuff, and the nature of the substances they contain was known only very inaccurately. "I shall not insist here on the details of the procedures I used for the chemical analysis of tubers (1), and I shall leave aside their morphological development. "It can be seen that nitrogenous substances are found in significant proportion in this food, and that carbohydrates, in very high quantities, are represented above all by galactan, a substance discovered in 1886 (1) See the article I published in Nobbe's Versuchestationen, 1888. 11 by Messrs. E. Schultze and Steiger, in the seeds of Lupin (Lupinus luteus). "Galactan, this new substance, is intermediate between starch and sugar; it is a material analogous to dextrin, but is very clearly characterized. The proportion of galactan in tubers is around 75%. 100% of galactan in Stachys affinis tubers is quite remarkable, and no plant is known to contain a similar proportion of this substance at any stage of its development. Sugars are found only in trace amounts in these tubers, and even then their presence is not certain, as glucose is formed after the interversion of galactan by extended hydrochloric acid. "I would add that, among the nitrogenous substances, I was also able to isolate glutamine and tyrosine. "The richness in non-nitrogenous substances, and especially in galactan, which is a very easily assimilated substance, shows that crosnes are a precious food in many cases for the sick and for all those who suffer from a delicate stomach. "The only analysis of these tubers that I could find in my bibliographical research was published by M. Carrière, in the Revue horticole, in 1885. "The chemist who carried out this analysis found 68.96 O/0 starch, and the tubers I analyzed in February contained no trace of it (1). "It is true, as M. Dufour (from Lausanne) has noted, that traces can sometimes be found (1) The analysis published by M. Carrière gives only 17.88 e/, of starch and non-nitrogenous substances. Revue horticole, 1885, p. 236 - P. et B. d'amidon dans les tubercules de Stachys affinis récoltés en automne, mais ce n'est là que de l'amidon transitoire qui, selon toute apparence, se transforme en galactane pendant l'hiver. This interesting fact shows that a chemical study of these tubers at various stages of development could yield remarkable results. "In any case, it is not this transitory starch (existing only in trace amounts) that may have been found in the analysis I have just quoted. It is, without doubt, galactan that has been counted as starch, and the difference between these two bodies is important enough from the physiological point of view, as well as from the dietary point of view, to deserve to be pointed out." Messrs. Planta and Schulze discovered a new substance in Crosne, which they named Stachyose and described in two memoirs summarized below: STACHYOSE. - Extracted from the juice obtained by pressing Stachus affinis using a series of treatments with lead acetate, hydrogen sulfide and alcohol. Slowly crystallizes by careful addition of alcohol to its aqueous solutions in the form of shiny crystals adhering to the walls of the vases in which they are deposited. Weakly sweet, highly soluble in water, strongly dextrorotatory; reduces Fehling's liquor only after boiling with acids, like cane sugar; gives by oxidation with azotic acid about the same quantity of mucic acid as milk sugar. Its formula is CISH32 OIe - 3 Ha O. Stachyose resembles tactosine, which Meyer extracted from the Caryophylae, but differs in its rotatory power, which is lower than that of lactosine (1). When boiled with extended acids, Stachyose gives a (1) See Planta and Schulze, Berichte der deutschen chemischen Gesellschaft, t. 23, p. 1692. mixture of reducing sugars containing half its weight in galactose, the other half being a mixture of glucose and levulose. In this respect, it can be compared with raffinose from beet or cotton cake, which gives the same reducing sugars in the same circumstances, but in equal proportions. It is therefore possible that the formula for Stachyose should be doubled and written as C38 Het O3* (1). In the two memoirs we have just summarized, the authors do not indicate the quantity of Stachyose supplied by tubers. Just as starch and inulin give glucose and levulose when heated with acidulated water, so Stachyose treated in the same way gives galactose, but at the same time as glucose and levulose: CE H32018 - 2H2O stachyose CHROS Ce He 9e glucose T levulose C HOU galactose FOOD USES Crosnes are all the better for being freshly plucked. They don't need to be peeled; simply wash them carefully so that no earth or sand remains in the internodes. They cook in twelve to fifteen minutes; if left too long on the fire, the water will penetrate them and they will become mushy and bland. Cooks have given the newcomer a warm welcome; indeed, there's no other vegetable that's so quick and easy to prepare. This one (1) See Planta and Schukze, same collection, t. 24, p. 2705. therefore met with no resistance and immediately became a regular, a friend of the house. Its flavor is pleasant, but weak. It has to be cooked in saltier water than usual. We don't know how the Chinese prepare it for the table, but here it accepts all the preparations with which we are familiar, and that's enough. It is likely that the Japanese prepare it with their excellent and inevitable sauce, "Shoyu"; but we really have no information on its use in Japan other than this: Choro-gi has tuberous, caterpillar-like roots, which are preserved in plum vinegar for eating (1). In France, crosnes are usually served as fresh flageolet beans, with or without chopped parsley. They are delicious as a garnish for veal stew, and in this state, the farmers in our village are crazy about them. They are also excellent fried. One enthusiast recommends cooking them the day before and frying them, cold and firm, the next day. They can also be eaten au gratin. They are perfect in salads, simple or mixed. Potel & Chabot sometimes cook them in stock beforehand. Lastly, they are very good in vinegar preserves, combined with gherkins, Catawissa onions and so on. As you can see, all our preparations (1) Le Japon à l'Exposition universelle de 1878, Paris. A la Commission impériale du Japon, 15, avenue de Matignon, 1878. are applicable to them, and the hostess is spoilt for choice. In recent years, marsh marigold (Stachys palustris) has been advocated as being able to provide the same services as Crosne. Some authors have even argued that these two Stachys are identical, and that there's no reason to grow a Chinese plant when we have its analogue in France. We have grown both species side by side for several years. It never occurred to us that they could be confused. In Stachys palustris, the leaves are sessile, lanceolate, whereas in S. affinis they are petiolate, oval, attenuated at the apex and cordate at the base. The former species flowers abundantly every year, while the latter only very exceptionally (1). Finally, and most importantly, the rhizomes of marsh milkweed are very elongated; they can reach 15 to 20 centimetres in length; they are acrid and bitter, almost inedible. To consider using them, we'd have to start by creating an improved breed, as suggested by the ancient authors who wrote about their edibility. Mr. Chappellier, of the Société nationale d'Acclimatation, is undertaking trials to this end, by hybridizing the two species. We hope his efforts will be crowned with success. (1) Stachys affinis has a rare peculiarity, but there are other examples. The abundance of rhizome production is such that the plant doesn't need to form seeds to reproduce. Flower buds appear, but remain small and do not bloom. The first flowers observed in France with any certainty were seen by one of us, in Mr. Le Tourneur's garden, at Roche-Gauthier, near Granville (Manche) (See Revue Horticole, 1891, page 463). On March 24 1892, M. Chappellier presented to the Société Nationale d'Horticulture de France (see Journal de la Société Nationale d'Horticulture, 1892, p. 137), tubers of Stachys floridana Shultlew, (native to Florida), which had been sent to him from the USA under the name Florida Artichoke. The presenter was unable to give any information on the use to which these tubers might be put, but he thought that the vulgar name under which he had received them suggested that they were edible. M. Chappellier has cultivated Stachys floridana, and we were able to see a few plants in flower in his garden at Boissy-Saint-Léger (Seine-et-Oise) (see Revue Horticole, 1893, page 17). The plant resembles Stachys affinis, but is less developed and less vigorous. The tubers are more elongated, reminiscent in shape and volume of the rhizomes of Stachys palustris; they have a pronounced unpleasant flavor that makes them inedible. Mr. Chappellier continues to cultivate Stachys floridana in the hope of one day obtaining a hybrid between this species and Stachys affinis. In the meantime, there is no doubt that, through selection, we can increase the volume of Crosne tubers, if we judge that it is in our interest to have them larger. CYCLANTHERA PEDATA Schrad. Cucurbitaceae family. Annual plant, with climbing, glabrous stems; bifid tendrils; alternate, petiolate leaves; in July-September, small, axillary green flowers, the males in long-stalked corymbs, the females solitary, sessile at the base of the male flowers. Pediaria is native to Mexico. It is a trailing or climbing plant of extraordinary fecundity. We won't dwell on its cultivation, which is that of the Gourdes. We left the stems lying around, and for several months they produced flowers and fruit in abundance. Supported by a trellis, these stems reach up to 4 meters in height. The leaves resemble those of the Virginia creeper and are very filling. Fruit should be picked daily. If they are to be used, they must not be larger than olives, as they soon become soft and spongy. Harvested at the right time, they can be candied like gherkins. Their defect is that they are not crunchy. They have a strong Cucumber smell, which they give up to take on the taste of the vinegar in which they are immersed. The same is true of almost all the vegetables we associate with Gherkins. Cyclanthers are no better or worse than others. They're pretty little vinegar sponges. The seed is black and curious. The plant is hardier than the Cornichon de Paris. COMESTIBLE CYCLANTHERA CYCLANTHERA EDULIS Ndn. Pepino de comer of the South American Spaniards, who eat the fruit in a variety of ways. The plant differs from C. pedata only in its larger size and in the size of the fruit, which is six to seven times the volume of C. pedata and retains its shape, but is smoother. Strong, climbing annual plant with broad, pale-green leaves; female flowers usually solitary and subsessile in the leaf axils; spongy flesh before ripening, with a strong cucumber odor. Rapid growth. Very rambaceous, very fertile plant (Catalogue of Ch. Huber et Cle, horticulturists, Hyères). Cyclanthera edulis appears to be native to Colombia and, if memory serves, Mr. Triana tells us that its fruits are usually eaten halved and stuffed like cucumbers and eggplants. The fruits prepared in this way are therefore, to all appearances, much larger than those of C. pedata, and this is in fact what the Catalogue of Messrs Huber et Cie, quoted above, says; but it is a fact that we have not been able to verify. We received the seeds listed in their catalog from these gentlemen, and gave half of them to a skilled gardener in our neighborhood. We sowed them in trays and on beds and obtained very strong plants, similar to C. pedata, with flowers, but no fruit. Our neighbor obtained flowers and fruits, but these were hardly larger than those of C. pedata. This is what Mr. Naudin reports about C. edulis: "We received from New Grenada, under the name of Pepino de comer, through the intermediary of Mr. de Geoffroy, French consul in Bogota, the seeds of a Cyclanthera which, if it is not identical with C. pedata, as I am tempted to believe, is extremely close to it. We cultivated it at the Muséum in 1858; but, owing to various accidents, the three or four living individuals we had were so retarded that they only flowered in the late season and did not set a single fruit. The ovaries were perfectly smooth, and this is about the only difference I found between them and C. pedata, where they are somewhat mature. "According to what M. de Geoffroy told us, the fruits are edible before they are ripe, and can be eaten cooked. This species is probably the Momordica pedata pomis striatis of P. Feuillée..." We have also cultivated the Cyclanthera explodens Schrader, which can be found in botanical gardens and requires no more care than the C. pedata. Its fruits are shorter and smaller than those of C. pedata; too soft to be used as pickles, they have the peculiarity of exploding when ripe, spitting their seeds violently in the face of any indiscreet person who touches them. CYPHIA TORTILIS N.-E. Brown. Family Campanulaceae, tribe Cyphiaceae. In February 1894, Professor Mac Owan, government botanist at the Cape of Good Hope, sent us tubers of a plant which, he told us, was related to the Bosch Barroe (Cyphia sylvatica Eckl.), but nevertheless distinct, tubers which are eaten after being roasted in the ashes of the fire made by outspanned? travelers, but which could not be recommended as having first-rate eating qualities. We planted these tubers under a frame, in the open ground, and, in the course of the year, we observed the flowering of most of the plants grown. This same species had also been sent to Kew Gardens, and in the October 1894 issue, p. 356, Mr. N.-E. Brown described it as new. In the autumn, we harvested these tubers, which had not multiplied and had not grown appreciably. We cooked some of them and offered the others to the Museum, the tasting having made us recognize the futility of continuing to cultivate them as a food plant. Japanese radish. 173 RAPHANUS SATIVUS L., var. Cruciferae family. Although Daikons have been described by Henri Rivière as belonging to a particular species, we do not believe we should adopt this view. These plants, like the varieties of Radish we grow in France, vary infinitely, both in the shape of their leaves and their roots, and should be attached to Linné's Raphanus sativus. We had a large collection of Daikons presented to the Société nationale d'Horticulture by gardener Henri Véniat. If we're not mistaken, this was the first time that several varieties of this little-known plant had been presented to the Society. Until then, we'd confined ourselves to showing off a specimen of some kind and saying: here's the Daikon, without considering that this vegetable, like so many others, has properties, qualities and even defects, which vary infinitely, depending on the variety we've grown. Our Radishes are of Chinese origin, but we've obtained countless varieties that appear in the catalogs of grain merchants. Round and short, long and half-long, early and late, white, pink, red, violet, yellow, grey, black, small or huge; it's enough to make you get lost. The same applies to daikons. Some are sown in spring, others, more numerous, are sown in August and used throughout the winter. One is very fast-growing and must be used after a few weeks' sowing, otherwise it will be eaten hollow. Some are inordinately long and require ploughing with two spades; others are short or half-long and require only ordinary ploughing. All the varieties we have are white. Some are said to be red inside and out, and would be the best. We asked in vain for them in Japan; all we received was a degenerate pink winter radish from China. In June 1878, we received three varieties highly esteemed in their country of origin: Sakurashima, Tsuri and Nerima Daïkon. We sowed them immediately; these plants went to seed so quickly that they did not form usable roots, but we knew from then on that we had to sow late. In 1881, we received new seeds, which we sowed on August 1. The result was very satisfactory, and the horticulturists of the Société d'Horticulture de Montreuil can recall a presentation of very fine roots made to them by Henri Véniat. This variety, to which 12 the Japanese author quoted above gives the name Natsu Daïkon, i.e. Summer Daïkon, was part of a collection of forty-two seed packets collected by the intrepid traveller Mr. Colteau, a collection which had come to us through the kindness of Dr. Paul Sagot. Sow in rows and, if you want to obtain well-developed plants, thin to at least 15 cm. As for fertilization, we'll quote what Count de Castillon said in Volume IV, page 519, 3rd series of the Bulletin de la Société d'Acclimatation, to challenge certain points: "Struck by the negative results obtained in France in growing Daikon, I wanted to find the cause. To do this, I thought I could do no better than to consult the Japanese work entitled: Só moku so date gusa; here is what it says about Daïkon, which would be more than enough to show the reasons for the lack of success that is generally complained of: in spring" and summer, the ground is dug up extensively; a mixture of ash and pou" drette is "carefully incorporated, and sown from the first to the tenth day of" autumn (late September), in rows and on ridges. There are also daikons that are entirely red, not only on the outside but also on the inside; they are very tender and have a delicate taste. "Japanese cultivation can be summed up in the following three points: 1° deep cultivation; 2° highly active, rapidly assimilable powdered fertilizers; 3° (and this is a crucial point) autumn sowing. It's obvious that the Japanese don't sow Daikon in spring, because they've recognized that seedlings sown at this time go to seed very easily, without producing large roots. Something similar happens with certain plants, such as turnips. "It should also be noted that the variety of Daikon "most esteemed in Japan for its edible qualities" is red Daikon. It is therefore on this variety that "the next trials should preferably focus". We have no doubt that a very good result can be obtained by digging deep into the soil, amending it with ashes, and smoking it with poudrette; but we do not consider these practices necessary. Daikons are extremely hardy and thrive in good garden soil. They sprout spontaneously, and the seeds that spread from side to side give rise to superb plants. We confess to being at a loss to understand the difficulties the first experimenters seem to have encountered. We would like to draw your attention to the comment made by M. Its "nutritional qualities, invaluable for dairy cows, which are very fond of it, seem to place it "between the green-necked carrot and beet. "Daikon is also likely to play a major role as a catch crop. Sown in the second half of July, the plant can be harvested in October, so it takes up very little land and is doubly valuable. The way we use Daikon is completely different from that of the Japanese. They eat all varieties, cooked or salted; they also use it as a condiment, grating it when fresh, or drying it. They also eat the leaves prepared in the same way as the roots. Here, however, it's a different matter. We gauge the roots in November and take them fresh as and when we need them. They are tender, full of vegetative water, and less pungent than black radish and even Chinese pink winter radish. They are infinitely pleasing to the people in our families and to the edible merchants to whom we let them taste. Cooked, we find them inferior to turnips. We have yet to experiment with Daikon as a fodder plant, in catch crop. It's not up to us to resolve this important question. Satzouma daikon This variety deserves a special mention. "The Dolic bulbous belongs to the Diadelphia decandria and is a member of the Leguminosae family. It is closely related to the bean genus and, like it, grows sarmentose, creeping stems; it produces a taproot, similar in shape and size to the European sweet turnip (Brassica napus maxima), but more nutritious and softer than it. The Malays and the inhabitants of the Philippine Islands delight in it, eating it raw or boiled like potatoes. It can be found on the best tables, prepared in a variety of ways, making it both a healthy and tasty dish. The rural landowner, when he gathers a lot of it, feeds it to his domestic animals; I've noticed that they eat it greedily and that it fattens them up in no time, especially the pigs. "It seems to me of the utmost importance to recommend the cultivation and multiplication of this bulbous plant to the inhabitants of the French colonies, especially as it can, at any time, provide them, without any preparation, with healthy and abundant food. Weddell, published in this volume, under the article Poire de terre). The above-mentioned learned botanist observed the plant in La Paz; having been unable to collect more than incomplete samples, he was unable to determine it with any certainty. For many years afterwards, no further samples were obtained, and no one knew to which botanical species Ahipa could be attached. In 1886, Dr Ernst from Caracas sent Kew samples of a plant cultivated in Merida, which he said corresponded exactly to Weddell's description of Ahipa, and which he believed to be Dolichos tuberosus Lamk. There were several specimens of Dolichos tuberosus in the Kew herbarium, including those collected at Tarapota by Spruce. Professor Oliver found this plant distinct from Pachyrrhizus angulatus. Mr. Bentham considered Spruce's samples to belong to the latter species. Finally, Dr Morris thought it might well be a variety produced by cultivation, but marked enough to require a distinct name for cultivation. He published a series of notes on both plants in the Bulletin of miscellaneous information of the Royal Garden of Kew, with a view to making their merits known, accompanied by two good figures enabling the distinctive characters of these species to be easily seen. According to him, Pachyrrhizus tuberosus differs from P. angulatus in its leaves, which are rounded rather than toothed, its flowers, which are white rather than violet, its pods, which are much wider, and perhaps also its seeds, which are kidney-shaped, white, black or variegated. Like the Bulbous Dolic, the Tuberous Dolic is a most valuable food plant for hot countries; but it is curious to note that its seeds, as well as those of several other Phaseolae, possess toxic properties. According to Dr. Ernst, these seeds are used in Merida (Venezuela), either as a decoction or in powder form, to destroy vermin. One of his students wrote to him from the state of Tachira that he had seen a case of poisoning with a type of bean called Tapiramo (a species of Dolichos); cooks therefore usually throw away the first water in which Tapiramo is cooked. For the uses of this plant, we believe we can do no better than reproduce what Macfadyen says about it in Flora of Jamaica, page 285: "Its root is formed of a number of ramifications several feet long, running under the surface of the ground, emitting in their course a succession of tubers. Its seeds are poisonous, but the root yields abundant and very healthy food. The product of three plants is generally enough to fill a bushel. "The tubers, after being boiled, can be eaten like yams and other common roots; they would also produce an excellent substitute for Arrow-root. The starch is pure white and equal in all respects to the latter product. It is very pleasant to the taste and easy to digest. It is used to make custards and puddings. The waste obtained after extraction of the starch, which is unusable in Arrow-root, can be dried to produce a good, healthy flour. A delicious flour can also be obtained by cutting the tubers, drying them in the sun and then reducing them to powder. The plant certainly deserves to be much more widely cultivated than it has been up to now. It should, with great advantage, replace Arrow-root in crops. "It can be planted at any season of the year, and the roots are ready to be pulled up after four to five months. Its production is much greater than that of Arrow-root, and the proportion of starch is also more considerable, so that its low price could put it on the market, even for use by cloth printers, in place of starch, which is usually used. Yam-Bean has been cultivated for many years in Jamaica. It is said to have been introduced from Martinique. SWEET FENNEL FOENICULUM DULCE C. Bauh; Anethum dulce DC. Umbelliferae family. Stems a little compressed at the base, 1.30 m high. Leaves radical, almost distichous, with elongated, capillary segments; umbels with 7-8 rays. Italian sweet fennel is an annual plant. It is said to be native to Italy. Miller, in his Dictionnaire des jardiniers, makes no such claims. It is believed, he says, to have been imported from the Azores. He gives it the name Fœniculum azoricum. Abbé Rozier, in his Cours complet d'Agriculture, confines himself to saying that the sweet fennel of Italy, as reported by travelers, is much less sweet than that of the Azores. He cites the coasts of Attica as one of the most renowned countries for this plant. Sweet fennel is sown in February and March, in nurseries, under frames; later, in the open ground, until the end of July. In Italy, it is still sown in August. As soon as the plant is ready, it is planted at Om, 35 in all directions. This spacing facilitates ridging, which is carried out once or twice. Since the part of the plant you want to obtain is white and tender, and hardly Fig. 32. - Sweet fennel. more than Om, 10 high, it is rarely necessary to ridge more than twice. Fennel needs a light, loamy soil. For several years now, we've been culling it on an old layer, and we get superb plants. It's important to hoe in good time and water abundantly. Thanks to this care, the petioles agglomerated above the plant's collar form a thick, flattened apple, the only one used for the table, to the exclusion of stems and leaves (1). Fennel goes to seed too quickly in summer, and rot often sets in. Keep an eye on it and pull it out in good time. It keeps for quite a long time (1) Les Plantes potagères. Vilmorin-Andrieux et Cre. 13 out of the ground. Besides, it's better to have less beautiful apples than to risk losing everything. Sowing at the end of July is the most important. It's the one that will provide Fennel for the table until January. The plant is placed in three rows in September, so that it can be covered with a frame when winter approaches. All that's needed for the plant to continue to vegetate and develop is for the temperature not to fall below zero. So, as is customary in such cases, straw or leaves are placed around the boxes and straw mats on the frames, and air is let in whenever the weather permits. When the fennel has formed its head, we keep it under the frame, or pull it out and put it in the vegetable greenhouse. It's easy to reach the month of January, and we think it's easy to go beyond that. Fennel seed degenerates quickly, and all horticultural treatises agree on this point. It has to be brought in from Italy every year. We prepare sweet fennel in three equally satisfying ways. We prepare it with cream, juice or parmesan. This last recipe was supplied to us by Le Bon Jardinier, 1873, from which we reproduce the following information: "Fennel is consumed in large quantities in Italy. It is eaten raw, like artichokes à la poivrade, generally without seasoning. It is very good as a garnish for poultry or large meat stews; in white sauce, au jus, au gratin or macaroni. For the last three, it is cooked in water beforehand. To prepare 'au gratin' or macaroni, take a saucepan, put some butter in it, then a bed of already cooked and drained Fennel, cut into quarters; salt and pepper lightly; sprinkle with grated Parma cheese and small pieces of butter, and continue until the saucepan is full. Cook over a moderate heat, covering the pan with its lid, which should be topped with coals. During a trip to Italy, Mr. Audot gathered new information that we are now presenting as a complement to the above. In Naples, especially in the Roman Elats, and even further afield in Venice, Fennel is so widely used that you can't take a step into a town or cross a village without encountering it. There is not a table where it is not served, from January to June. To our heaviness, we'll quote M. Audot: "Like Celery, Fennel is served in blond sauce and salad, or in soup, like Cabbage; but the most general custom is to serve it for dessert with fruit; it then decorates the lable, planted in the water of a glass bowl and raising its fine, elegant foliage like plumes; it is also eaten unseasoned. At first, I laughed at this custom, which reminded me of the English practice of serving Radishes for dessert, and even of carrying some in one's pocket to eat when out and about; but it wasn't long before I got used to Fennel, whose mild flavor and pleasant taste appealed to me; only, I preferred it as an appetizer, like Radishes and baby Artichokes (1)". 11) Extract from Notes sur les jardins du sud de l'Italie, recueillies pendant un voyage en 1839-1840 et lucs à la Société royale d'Horti faveur than in Italy, and it is in vain that most horticultural treatises present Fennel to amateurs as an excellent vegetable to introduce into their gardens. We believe that it has always been grown in France, but has never been widely used. The obstacle is undoubtedly its slight anise flavor. However, we accept this flavor in anisette, gingerbread, croquets and so on. We accept sweet fennel seeds converted into small sugared almonds. Fennel apples, candied like Angelica, are excellent. A tin of candied Fennel was part of the lot exhibited by gardener Henri Véniat (Société d'Horticulture) in October 1877. This preparation was very favorably appreciated by all who tasted it. Our fathers sought out Spanish chervil, which they blanched. It had a pronounced anise flavor. The Germans make great use of Cumin, whose taste is very close to that of Anise; they melt it into bread. The English and Arabs use it as a condiment. The Russians make a liqueur called kümmel. The Dutch are said to use it in their cheeses. The Italians can't do without their fennel. Fennel and bread! they say. In the province of Venice, it's used in bread, just as Cumin is used in Germany. Italian gourmets use the tubular stalk of the Fennel plant as a blowtorch to sniff the culture of Paris, by M. Audot, editor of Le Bon Jardinier (Revue horticole, vol. V (1844-1844), p. 16). and the liqueur acquires an exquisite aroma in the process. In Spain, on the African coast and in the Azores, Fennel is not sought after. It seems to us that the flavor of Anise, which is common to Cumin and Fennel, is considered excellent throughout Europe. In France, it is not yet universally accepted in this vegetable, which is easy to grow and available in all seasons: it's a question of habit and taste education. Abbé Rozier, in his Cours complet d'Agriculture (1786), tells us that sweet fennel is grown in gardens in the north of the kingdom. What was done in the past will undoubtedly be done again. In spite of its slight anise flavor, we say, because of this flavor, say the Italians, sweet fennel is, in our opinion, an excellent vegetable. We recommend it to connoisseurs. FUKI PETASITES JAPONICUS F. Schmidt. Family Compositae. This plant is native to Japan, where it bears the name Fuki; it is the Korokoni of the Ainos, who use it extensively for their food. According to Messrs Balchelor and Miyabe, Ainu Economicplants (Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japon, p. 222), the Ainos eat mainly the petioles, but also the flower, called Makayo. The petioles are often roasted over the fire, then peeled and eaten; more generally, they are boiled (stewed); they are also made into Pickles or preserves, by salting them after boiling, and mixing them with Ikokuttara leaves (Polygonum sacchalinense), which give them a reddish tint; sometimes no salt is added. The Catalogue of Japanese products at the 1889 Exhibition says of Fuki: "To use the flowers of this plant, collect those that grow on the ground before the leaves; their taste is a little bitter; the pleasant smell is similar to that of Jamasó (Hops); they are used when their length is about thirty centimetres". We received a few Fuki plants from Japan, which we planted in the Crosne garden in 1896, and sheltered with glass boxes during the winter. In March 1897, inflorescences developed, preceding the leaves as happens in the various species of the Petasites genus. The leaves then developed, very large and numerous, reaching a height of seventy-five centimetres. The plant's rhizomes had passed under the glass trunk and invaded all the surrounding parts of the flowerbed. We picked a few leaves and peeled and cooked the long, fleshy petioles. The tasting was not favorable. Fuki may be acceptable as a pickle, but we found it to have such a pronounced aromatic and bitter flavor that we cannot recommend it in any capacity. GLACIAL Ice herb, Crystalline Ficoid. MESEMBRYANTHEMUM CRYSTALLINUM L. De Candolle, Plantes grasses, pl. 128. Family Mesembryanthemata. Annual plant, native to the Cape, Canaries, etc., imported, according to Miller, from the Cape of Good Hope; long cultivated for ornamental purposes. Flat-lying, fleshy herb, covered on all sides with transparent vesicles full of water, giving the impression of being covered in ice. In July-October, white, insignificant flowers. According to Duchesne (Répertoire des plantes utiles), Glaciale leaves are often eaten as a vegetable in Bourbon. In a letter to Messrs Vilmorin-Andrieux and Cle (1), Mr Picard of Saint-Quentin recommends using this Ficoïde as a spinach. Cultivation: Sow in March-April in a well-exposed spot, or preferably on a bed. Transplant to a well-soil bed as soon as the plant has a few leaves, at 0.60 m in all directions; do not neglect watering. The plant (1) Revue Horticole, 1859, p. 72. soon takes on extraordinary growth and can be picked throughout the summer. The Glaciale has its rightful place in the vegetable gardens of the curious. It is both beautiful and useful. There's no one who hasn't admired, on a fine winter's morning, the marvellous effect of sunlight on frost-covered trees. This is the spectacle offered by the Glaciale in midsummer. Unfortunately, it's spread out on the ground, so you have to bend down to admire it properly. It's not exactly an ornamental plant, and that's not why it belongs in this book. We consider it a highly esteemed vegetable, similar to Tetragona in cultivation and use. We pick its tender leaves and the tips of its stems. We prepare them in the same way as spinach, and everyone we've tried them on has agreed that Glaciale is a good vegetable with a distinctive flavor, a sui generis dish that's highly recommendable. Mme Henriette Davidis, whom we like to quote when talking about vegetables that are unusual in France, has this to say about this Ficoïde: "Glaciale is an admirable ornamental plant for gardens, and at the same time provides a delicate vegetable in summer. Its leaves and stems, as long as they are tender, should not be chopped, but only cooked, with breadcrumbs slightly browned in fresh butter, seasoned with salt, nutmeg or nutmeg flower and served with potatoes. Cooking time: barely a quarter of an hour". We give this recipe for what it may be worth; but, in recommending Glaciale as a vegetable, we also take our cue from a note by M. Siroy to be found in the Journal de la Société d'Horticulture de France, 2e série, tome XI, page 525. We believe that the Glaciale should be cultivated, admired and eaten. Our attention was drawn to it by a note from M. H. Lecoq, Revue Horticole, 1869, p. 207: Ficoïde à feuille en cœur (Mesembryanthemum cordifolium L.). Perennial plant, native to the Cape of Good Hope, from where it was brought by M. Bruyère. Although vigorous, it is not nearly as productive as its predecessor. Its flavor is also less pleasant. However, it deserves to be classed as a substitute for Spinach, or better still, Chicory, with which it is slightly bitter. Multiplication by cuttings taken in autumn, overwintered in a greenhouse and planted in spring, or by seedlings as described for Glaciale. The plant is very leafy. It spreads widely, so you need to give it about 2 meters of space. Five or six plants, planted in good soil in May and liberally watered, are enough for table service. Mesembryanthemum angulatum Thunb. from southern Africa, a species closely related to M. crystallinum, can also be used as a spinach substitute. Mr. Mac Owan, government botanist at the Cape of Good Hope, writes that he finds this vegetable comparable to New Zealand Tetragon, but a little more glutinous. GOMBO, KETMIE COMESTIBLE HIBISCUS ESCULENTUS L. Fam. Malvaceae. Annual plant. Stem 6-7 decimeters, simple; leaves cordate, 5-lobed, obtuse, toothed; petioles Fig. 33. - Long-fruited okra. longer than flowers; in June-July, yellowish-sulfur flowers, with purple centers, solitary, axillary; capsule pyramidal or conical; calicle of ten deciduous leaflets; calyx tearing longitudinally. South America. We wouldn't go too far if we said that okra is one of the most precious vegetables known to us. It is used daily in Egypt, Syria, Greece, Turkey, India, Louisiana, the West Indies and throughout South America. Its various culinary applications, as well as its properties as a substitute for coffee and cocoa, are described below. Its cultivation is scarcely known in the Paris region, where the climate is unfavorable: sow the seeds on a bed in February, prick out the young plants also on a bed, and wait until the last days of May to place them permanently on a new bed, under a high frame or on a well-sheltered hillside, in light, well-smoked soil. When the summer is hot, you can succeed by planting on June 1 on an old bed. Harvesting is then later. It is necessary to water abundantly during hot spells. In our climate, okra will never be more than an amateur plant, not very productive, and market gardeners will not grow it. Its capsules travel well without spoiling, and if they were in demand in Paris, Provence, which already sends us some, could produce and sell them, at low prices, in quantities equal to demand. We know of French people living in the colonies who declare Gombo to be excellent; however, there is nothing to suggest that it will soon be a success. Foreigners living in Paris are so far the only ones to buy it when it goes on sale. We do, however, see it occupying an honorable place in a good house, very Parisian and very distinguished. It is frequently served on the table, and the cordon bleu chef who prepares it has kindly shared his recipe with us. Gombo seems to be only an accessory to the dishes of which it is a part, but it is not; it is essential and, without it, these dishes would not exist. Interesting information on okra can be found in the following publications: Flore des Antilles, by Descourtilz, vol. IV, p. 169; Note by Dr Sagot (Journal de la Société nationale d'Horticulture de France, 1872, p. 545); Manual of Gardening for Bengal and upper India. by Thomas A. C. Firminger; Agricultural botany, by William Darlington; Note by Léon Rattier (Revue horticole, 1854, p. 171). From this last, very extensive and instructive note, we feel we must extract a few passages: "During my travels in the East, I almost always heard it called by the Greeks Grekika kerata (Greek horns), and by the Turks Bamieh. The latter name seems to have been adopted in Egypt, according to M. Bové (Observations sur les cultures de l'Egypte, extractes des Annales de l'Institut horticole de Fromont, t. VI, avril 1834)... Wherever the plant is cultivated, it provides an important resource for food and medicine. In the West Indies, the natives eat it boiled in salted water or raw in salads. It forms the basis of Calalou, highly esteemed by the natives and popularly used. Nor do we disdain serving its various preparations on the most sumptuous tables; but then, almost always, it is combined with foods or seasonings of high taste, to spice up its somewhat bland flavor; it becomes a very pleasant dish, but no longer possesses the qualities that make it sought after for medicinal use...". "M. Bové says that in Egypt, Ketmie is one of the country's most common vegetables; that it is highly esteemed in the various regions where it is grown, and that Europeans consume it extensively for seven or eight months of the year. "Nafé paste and syrup, prepared in Paris with the mucilage of edible Ketmie, have given good therapeutic results. "Finally, the infusion of roasted Ketmie seeds has been recommended as a substitute for coffee, and M. Vilmorin, in the latest edition of Le Bon Jardinier, mentions this preparation as one of the least bad of those that have been substituted for mocha. "I doubt that M. Vilmorin has experimented with it himself, for I myself have drunk the infusion of Ketmie seeds in the East, often prepared with more than carelessness, and it has always seemed to me a very pleasant drink, offering a marked superiority over the inferior qualities of coffee and sometimes almost equaling mocha. But to obtain this result, it is necessary to use well-chosen seeds, perfectly ripe and roasted with great care. The process I've found most successful is to place the seeds in a wedge-burner and heat for as long as the crackling sound lasts. As soon as the crackling stops, place them on a marble table, or on any other object that will cool them quickly. Stack and filter. "I have tried to roast only to a degree sufficient to color the inside of the seed a light hazelnut; then the starch it contains remains soluble. After reducing it to a fine powder and passing it through a sieve, we mix it with milk or sugar water; if we then proceed as when we want to obliterate a flour porridge, we obtain a product quite similar to chocolate, very pleasant to the taste, and retaining much of the special aroma that distinguishes the seed...".
