KETMIE ACIDE Guinea sorrel. HIBISCUS SABDARIFFA L. Fam. Malvaceae. Annual plant. Stems 7 to 8 decimeters long, glabrous, reddish, twiggy. Leaves toothed, lower ones oval, upper ones with three wedge-shaped lobes. In June-September, flowers yellow, purple-ground, solitary, axillary, almost sessile. Twelve-toothed calicule. East Indies. We have cultivated Guinea sorrel under a frame, and have obtained flowers and seeds without difficulty; but we cannot conceal from ourselves that this culture will never be profitable in the Paris region. It may find a place in the kitchen garden of the curious, but it won't make it out of there. It's an amateur plant. "After flowering, the calyx lengthens, becoming thick, fleshy, dark red and acidic in flavor. In the West Indies, this acidity has led to it being substituted for sorrel, whose properties it shares. According to the nature of their respective functions, cooks and chefs use it in coulis and butter, and make good use of its calyxes and leaves for glazed stuffings, on which different meats are to appear; confectioners reserve a more distinguished use for the same parts, and make preserves and jams with a pleasant, refreshing acidity. "Acid Ketmia grows naturally in Guinea, the West Indies and all of southern America..." (Descourtilz, Flore des Antilles). Another note from A Manual of Gardening for Bengal and upper India, by Thomas A. C. Firminger: "Roselle-Indian Sorrel. Annual plant, native to the West Indies, but now cultivated in most gardens in India. "The part of the plant that is used is not the fruit itself, but the calyx, whose large, thick, succulent sepals are used to make delicious pies and puddings, as well as a remarkably beautiful jelly, which differs only slightly from red currant jelly, of which it is, in many respects, an excellent substitute. "There are two kinds of Indian sorrel, one red and the other white, which are very similar, except that the white one seems a little less acidic...". The Hindostani name for the plant is Patwa. We bought some Guinea sorrel jam from M. Hédiard, which we tasted and found pleasant. The formula was sent to us by an inhabitant of Pointe-à-Pître: Confitures de Groseille-pays. (Letter from Mr. BrEr.) " Once the fruit has been picked, the red petaloid calyx must first be separated from the green receptacle to which it adheres. Here, where the acidity of the fruit is feared, on the pretext that it is safe, and where, on the other hand, ripe fruit is disliked, saying that it is past its prime, here, I say, we begin by throwing boiling water on these quasi-flowers, to remove their excess sourness, and we don't use this first infusion. In a second operation, the red calyxes are cooked in water and the sugar melted. The proportions of sugar are at least those used to prepare all acid fruit syrups, without taking into account the pectin that the juice may contain; for it sometimes happens that the jams we eat are almost set in jelly, and, at other times, that they remain in syrup... It remains to be seen whether it is appropriate to use the first water, which is rejected here because of its excess acidity. Is there not a risk that this water will carry away all or part of the pectin along with the acid? In either case, one principle is sacrificed for the other. So it's up to you to decide which you prefer to keep. "I think we could perhaps make a first concentrated infusion, intended to prepare the acid jelly, and, with the same fruit, prepare a jam that would still be sufficiently sour. Another species of Hibiscus, H. cannabicus L., is often cultivated in tropical regions. Its acidic leaves are eaten like sorrel. KITESH or KEN HIRUGAWO CALYSTEGIA JAPONICA CHOISY (SYN. CONVOLVULUS JAPONICUS THUNB.). Family Convolvulaceae. This plant has some analogy with our great hedge bindweed (Calystegia sepium): the stems are voluble and can reach several meters in height; the rhizomes are extremely abundant and absolutely comparable to those of its European congeners. Batchelor and Kingo Miyabe: Ainu Economic plants (Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan, p. 226), say that the long, fat roots of this plant are dug up in spring by the Ainos, for whom they serve as food. They eat them roasted or boiled, alone or with other foods such as rice or millet. We received the plant from Japan and it proved absolutely hardy in the Crosnes garden, where it quickly invaded the flowerbed dedicated to it. We tasted a few of the many roots harvested: fried, they proved stringy; cooked in water and pureed, we obtained a mild-tasting starch, pleasant enough, but of no particular merit. Among the other food plants sought after by the Ainos and cited by Messrs Batchelor and Miyabe (loc. cit.), but which we have not cultivated, we would point out: 1° Anemone flaccida Fr. Schm. (Pukusa. Kina, Gajo-so or Fukubero, whose leaves and stems are eaten by the Aïnos. The people harvest large quantities in spring, when it is in flower; they dry it for the winter, although they eat a little green. They eat it boiled with fish or sometimes in soup; the 2° Corydalis ambigua Cham. et Schlcht. (Toma, Engosaku). The Ainos eat large quantities of this plant's tubers, especially those from the Ishikari valley of Saghalien and the southern Kuriles. The tuber has a slight bitterness, which is removed by boiling it in water several times. In Etorup, the Ainos boil them with some earth to remove their bitterness. They are eaten either simply boiled or mixed with rice. In Saghalien, they are generally cooked with seal fat. Il, p. 213; Conophallus Konjak Schott, ex Miq, Prolusio flor. jap. p. 134; Amorphophallus Konjac C. Koch, in Berl. Allg. Gartenz. 1858, p. 166; Arisæma Conjac Sieb. Fam. des Aroïdées. M. le Dr Vidal has published, in the Bulletin de la Société d'Acclimatation (July 1877 issue), a memoir of the highest interest on the Konniyakou. This memoir occupies fifteen pages, and its length does not allow us to reproduce it in extenso; but we believe we must extract the essential parts and advise growers to have recourse to the memoir itself, when they undertake the cultivation of the plant. Extracts from Dr. J. Vidal's memoir. Dr. Vidal witnessed the great consumption of Conophallus Konjak tubers by the Japanese population. He was able to study its cultivation methods, as well as the type of preparation the tuber undergoes for use as food. "The specific name Konjak, given to the plant by the botanist Schott, is obviously a poor transcription of the native word Konniyakou, because the y is generally replaced by the j in the spelling of Japanese deposits, adopted by the Dutch and Germans. 18 DESCRIPTION "Konniyakou is a perennial aroid with a tuberous root. Its stem is a fairly light-green spike, speckled with brown and blackish spots, which can Fig. 40. - Amorphophallus Rivieri. reach a height of around 1 meter, with a circumference of Om, 70 to 0m, 80 at the base; it ends by giving rise to three large leaves (1) which spread obliquely, forming equal angles with each other and with the axis of the stem; the blade of these leaves is deeply and somewhat irregularly cut, so that (1) What Dr. Vidal refers to as stem and leaves is actually a single leaf whose petiole arises directly from the tuber and whose blade is trisected. They are almost pinnate; the main midrib is accompanied on each side by a band of leaf blade, which continues with that surrounding the secondary veins of the leaflets. At a depth of 3 or 4 inches below ground, the stem is implanted on the middle of the upper surface of a tuber, more or less developed according to the age of the subject; this tuber, which is more or less hemispherical, represents quite exactly the ties égales; and it is in the middle of the slightly concave plane of section that the neck of the plant is formed; as for the convex surface of the tuber, which is the largest, it gives attachment to a few rootlets and is provided with eyes, in the manner of Potatoes." The doctor did not see the flowering and fruiting organs of the Konniyakou, which, he was told, only flowers every two years and probably does not flower in the central provinces of Japan. It is therefore probably native to the southern provinces. According to the information provided to the author of this report, the Konniyakou flower has a spadix with male flowers at the top and female flowers below, surrounded by a large, red, lanceolate, acute spathe which curves at right angles through its middle, so that its upper half, now horizontal, rests on the tip of the spadix. The fruit consists of a large number of small red berries implanted on the corresponding, strongly swollen part of the spadix. CULTIVATION "Konniyakou cultivation is one of the simplest and most economical, and this is how the doctor saw it practiced in one of the most successful districts, some thirty leagues north-west of Yedo, in the province of Jo-chiou. "In this mountainous country, farmers prefer to plant Konniyakou on arid, non-irrigable land, unsuitable for growing cereals, and most often located on a more or less steep mountain slope; Holes 4 to 5 inches deep are then spaded, about 2 feet apart; a tuber is placed in each hole, and simply covered with soil; no fertilizer is ever added, and watering is also unnecessary. The tubers are planted in the spring, at the end of March or beginning of April, taking care to use only medium-sized tubers, i.e. those no more than one or two years old, as large tubers are said to be less successful. "Once the plantation has been established, little more attention is paid to it, and the tubers multiply in the following way: As the stem emerges from the ground, a certain number of underground branches or stolons of varying size emerge from the eyes on the convexity of the tuber, and when they have reached a length of a few inches, they swell into a mass that is the beginning of a young tuber; this develops rapidly, in turn supplying rootlets and producing an aerial stem that soon emerges from the ground shortly after the one that came from the first tubers planted. Each of these tubers gives rise to around fifteen new tubers within a radius of around 1 foot. "Harvesting takes place regularly every year, in autumn, in the last fortnight of October and in November. It simply consists in pulling out the tubers, exactly as if they were potatoes, sweet potatoes, etc., and then levelling them. All that's left to do is to roughly level the land, and use the harvested produce for other purposes. If the tubers are not to be used until some time in the future, it is essential to remove as much earth as possible from them, and to store them in a dry, well-ventilated place, on a floor as far as possible. "One might think that after a first harvest of Konniyakou, it would be necessary, as is usually the case in Europe, to plant a new crop in order to obtain a second one; but this is not the case, and the Japanese don't take this trouble; and, something which, while seeming strange, is no less real, they obtain every year, without any new expense or work, a harvest as large as that of the previous year. The Japanese explain this fact by saying that, firstly, it's very difficult not to leave a few unnoticed tubers in the ground when digging them up; and secondly, a certain number of those that appear too small are deliberately neglected. As a result, there are always enough tubers left in the ground to produce a normal harvest the following year. "During the winter, the Konniyakou stem withers, dries out and dies: it is replaced the following spring by a new stem emerging from the collar, immediately next to the place occupied by the previous one on the same tuber. "This brief description shows that nothing is simpler and less costly than cultivating this Aroidea; and, in fact, it's hardly possible to apply the name of cultivation to such simple procedures. There is no difficulty in choosing the land, since it is precisely the most ungrateful soils that are preferred by the Japanese; nor is there any expense, either in terms of fertilizers, which are never used, or in terms of labor, which is reduced to planting once and for all, and then simply uprooting. "However, given that the Japanese devote only their least fertile and even arid soils to this type of cultivation, we should not conclude that these types of soils are necessary for the success of the operation; This would be a mistake, as I've found that Konniyakou are even more successful when they are grown in better conditions, for example, when they happen to grow on good soil in the vicinity of farms, and can benefit from the fertilizers and watering given to the other crops they grow in. The Japanese have told me that they plant Konniyakou in poor soils only to make use of soil that is unsuitable for any other crop, and this is why it is only grown in mountainous districts; indeed, wherever the soil in the plains and valleys is of better quality or can be irrigated, it is always devoted to growing cereals, especially rice, which is by far the most important crop for the Japanese people. Nevertheless, in the sericulture districts, where plantations are often laid out around the edges of fields, rows of Konniyakou are also planted along the edges, sheltered by these same Mulberry trees. And on this subject, it should be said that, although this plant is very hardy, it should be avoided, if possible, if it is to be exposed too directly to the sun's rays; at least in slightly hot countries; for it should not be forgotten that it belongs to the Aroidae family, and that most plants in this family thrive in damp, shady places; so I have often seen plantations of Konniyakou in the vicinity of either Mulberry trees or Tea bushes; but any tree or shrub could perform the same protective function just as well, with the exception of resinous trees. "It has already been said that each tuber planted gives rise, on average, to about fifteen new tubers in the first year; this is enough to give an idea of the yield of a plantation; moreover, as the plant is perennial, the tubers can be left to grow for several years; but for food use, the Japanese only make their preparations with those from the first or second year, because those that are older lose in quality what they have gained in size. The weight and volume of the tubers vary greatly according to their age; those of the first year weigh, on average, from 75 to 100 grams, also having, on average, a circumference of Om, 18 to 0m, 20. I found that the weight of a third-year tuber was 1 kilogr. 700; with a circumference of Om, 56. These tubers are covered with a thin, brownish skin; their mass is formed of a white, resistant parenchyma, which, when cut, recalls the appearance of Turnip or Rave; they give off a strong, characteristic, unpleasant odor, which they do not lose by cooking in water; when cooked and simply divided with the fingers, they present a gritty, starchy appearance. Their flavor is strong, pungent and acrid, giving the mouth and back of the throat a tingling, burning sensation that can last for hours. "Fortunately, a simple and inexpensive treatment is all that is needed to transform it into a healthy and pleasant food. The secret of the operation consists in subjecting it to the action of a little milk of lime, by means of processes that the author has seen used by the Japanese, who prepare large quantities of it. "The Japanese use the Konniyakou tuber as a foodstuff in three different forms; but the basic preparation is the same, and it is only the handling that differs a little, as well as the form given to the manufactured product. Thus, they prepare a kind of vermicelli which they call Chira tahe, a wafer called simply Konniyahou and finally a kind of dry cake known as Chiro Ro." The author describes the processes used to make Chira take. He even gives two drawings showing the apparatus used. The product has the appearance of a large white vermicelli and is a healthy food with a fairly good taste. The doctor uses it in the same way as Italian pasta is used in Europe. The patties known as Konniyahou are slightly inferior to Chira take. The memoir describes how they are made, as well as Chira ko. Whatever form you give to the dough obtained from the Konniyahou pulp, the basis of the preparation is the same, and it always consists of adding a small quantity of milk of lime to the pulp. One thing is certain, and this has been demonstrated by centuries of Japanese experience: Konniyakou tubers, prepared as described by the author, are perfectly safe and wholesome. The memoir we have just read had been published for several years when we received a leaflet, translated for the first time from Japanese, which its translator, Count de Castillon, kindly sent us. The leaflet includes: 1° a brief history of Konniyakou; 2° its botanical description; 3° the methods used to cultivate it; 4° those employed in the manufacture of the food products it supplies; 5° finally, it describes the plant's uses other than for food. This document is of considerable interest. It confirms the information provided by Dr. Vidal on a number of points, but says nothing about these harvests which, according to him, would continue without new planting or fertilizers. It is likely, therefore, that the simple, economical cultivation methods described by the author of this report are only successful in the province he mentions. We will now read a description of Konniyakou cultivation, extracted from the notice translated by Count de Castillon, whose precision and clarity leave nothing to be desired. "After the spring equinox, the tubers saved for seed are dug up and planted in ridges of the same width as the Sato imo (Colocasia antiguorum). Although the price of seed varies from place to place, in general a weight of 24 kuwan me (90 kilograms) is worth around 2 yen (10 fr. 50). Although the shady, dry soils on the mountain slopes are ideal for growing this plant, it is prone to rot in very shady areas. Places under the cover of trees, where the sun only shines from ten o'clock to noon, are excellent. For fertilizer, we use horse litter, which decomposes and serves as manure. It also serves to intercept the sun's scorching rays during the hot season. At the end of autumn, when the stems are slightly wilted by the first white frosts, a general uprooting is carried out. The small tubers that have formed around the roots are detached. The large ones are converted into Konniyakou, and the small ones, destined to be used as seed the following year, are buried as if they were Sato imo tubers, in warm soil, in a pit covered with planks and then with earth, forming a small mound opposite the north and facing south, where they will be sheltered from the cold, rain and dew. "Although the yield varies according to the year's conditions, in good conditions 1 tan (9 ares 91 centiares) can yield 70 tawara (1) of tubers, just as they come out of the ground, i.e. unwashed. The cultivation rules we have just described (1) Tawara. In the wholesale of Imo, etc., one tawara represents a weight of 16 kuwan me, net, in Tokio and 20 kuwan me in Kioto. 1 kuwan me - 1000 me (3 kilogr. 750). pose vary slightly, depending on whether the soil is cold or hot. In warm soils, we cultivate on ridges in hata, hillside fields, and harvest in the course of the same year. In cold soils, the tubers are dug up and buried in silos. The following spring, they are replanted in hata. Silage is made as we have already mentioned." USES OTHER THAN FOR CULINARY PURPOSES "When rats cause damage, we keep them away by spreading this raw root, cut into slices, as if we wanted to make a plaster. "These tubers, also raw, are used to make a paper glue that sticks so well that it cannot be peeled off, and is also used to make snacks. "It is said that the decoction of this root is good against the winds. KON NIYAKU D'II NUMA "In the village of li Numa, Umi-Gami district, Simosa province, there's a plant called Kon niyaku d'li Numa; but it's not the one we've just been talking about, it's Tsuno mata (Gymnogongrus pinnulatus), which, when boiled, resembles the true Kon niyaku in consistency, hence its name. It is cooked with Shô yu, or eaten after being preserved in miso." After reading Dr. Vidal's memoir, which made a deep impression on us, we asked for Koniaku tubers in Yokohama, which we received and planted. Our personal observations seem to justify the author's assertions regarding the hardiness of this Aroidée, whose importance increased singularly in our eyes when we received the notice from M. le comte de Castillon. Koniaku is not a vegetable plant; it belongs not to horticulture, but to agriculture, whose domain is not ours; but, when we come across a plant of such interest, we cannot resign ourselves to ignoring it. In his Nouveaux Mémoires sur l'état de la Chine (1696, Paris, 2 vols.), Louis Le Comte reports that, in addition to cotton, the Chinese wear fabrics in summer made from nettle and another species they call Ko pou, which they highly esteem. The latter is supplied in Fokien by a plant called Ko, a creeping shrub that they let grow in the fields and which is often extremely long. It has rounded leaves, larger than those of Ivy. They are soft, green above and covered with white down below. The stem is as thick as a finger. To obtain textile fibers, the stems are immersed in water, as we do for flax, and, after stripping them of their outer bark, the fibers of the second bark are used to make a fabric that is very beautiful, transparent and fresh (I, 242). Information on the seeds of a textile plant sent from China by a French missionary (1): "The Ko plant is also called Hoang-kin, Lan-ho and Khithsi. It can be found everywhere, but especially in the provinces of Tche-Kiang and Kiang-nan. It grows just as well in uncultivated areas as in cultivated fields. It starts to grow in spring and extends its purple stem to a length of 1 me 2 tchang (3 to 6 meters). The stems are harvested and, after suitable preparation, textile filaments are obtained. The root is violet on the outside and white on the inside; it grows to the size of an arm and 2 to 3 meters long. Its leaves are three-lobed, like those of the Fong tree, but longer, with a green surface and pale underside. In the seventh month, this plant produces reddish-purple flowers in clusters. After drying in the sun, they can be boiled in water to make stock. "The fruits of this plant resemble small yellow beans. They should be picked in the seventh or eighth month. HARVESTING " The stems of the Ko plant are usually ripe in summer, which is when they are harvested. Those that are still green and short are left. Those about 3 meters long are harvested with the root, which, according to some authors, yields a nourishing starch. They are called Theou-ko, or Ko stems (1) Industries anciennes et modernes de l'Empire chinois, by MM.Stanislas Julien and Paul Champion. Paris, Eugène Lacroix, libraire-éditeur, 1869. of the highest quality. When the stems are extraordinarily long, with white spots near the root, they are good for nothing. As for those without white spots, 2 or 3 meters of each stem are cut off; these are called eulko, i.e. second-quality Ko stems. PREPARATION " Once the stems have been collected, they are boiled in water over a hot fire. The filaments are removed with the fingernail; they are as white as those of Hemp, but are not adherent to the green part of the plant. Once the filaments have been plucked, they are washed in running water, beaten and, after being thoroughly cleaned, dried in the open air. Their whiteness increases if they are exposed to the dew for one or two nights. After that, they should be placed in the shade, as they fear the sun's rays. Abel de Rémusat; Arbutus, according to P. d'Entrecolles), they will remain reeking all summer long. Some people wash them in a porcelain basin with boiling water, in which they have crushed Meï leaves. It's essential not to use a wooden tub, otherwise Ko's clothes will turn black. Kudzu in Japan In the book Le Japon à l'Exposition universelle de 1878, we read: "Kudzu (Pueraria Thunbergiana) is a wild plant whose roots yield starch. Its leaves are used to feed cattle, and its fibers to make cloth. We are indebted to the kindness of Count de Castillon for two notes he has translated from Japanese, which describe in the most instructive and comprehensive detail the use made in Japan of Kudzu roots and fibers. The one we're about to read describes the process used to extract the starch. The other, published in the Mémoires de la Société des Etudes japonaises, 1878-1879, describes the manufacture of Kudzu cloth. It and the foreword that precedes it can be found at the end of this chapter. KUDZU KO (Kudzu starch) (Extract from the Notice sur les pluntes à fécule du Japon) "Kudzu (Pueraria Thunbergiana) is a climbing plant that grows wild in mountains and wastelands. In spring, young shoots emerge from the old stem. Each petiole bears three leaves similar to those of Ingem mame (Phaseolus vul20 garis); leaves and petioles are covered with hairs. In autumn, clusters of wine-purple flowers similar to those of Mame (Leguminosae) emerge from the leaf axils, producing pods. From the ninth and tenth months until the twelfth, when the eyes start to develop, these roots are pulled out with an iron pick or hoe. They are washed to remove the soil, and carefully crushed on a flat stone with a wooden or metal mallet. A tub is filled with water, in which the roots are kneaded to extract the soluble parts. The pulp is filtered and placed in a hemp canvas bag, which is then pressed. The residue is discarded. Immediately afterwards, filter through a cotton cloth bag. Leave to stand for one day. Decant the top water and dry the deposit, which is divided with a cleaver. The black starch underneath is scraped off and discarded. Place a second time in the sumasi-ohe (washing tub) with a large quantity of water, and stir while swirling. As the deposit precipitates, the falsetto is successively removed from the superimposed cinnamons, starting with those at the top, to draw off the water from the upper part. This process is repeated two or three times. After the precipitate has dried, it is removed with a small trowel and placed in the sara-si (flat box), lined with a cloth sprinkled with ash, to dry in the sun. Kaï-Kudzu (Ashen Kudzu, Grey Kudzu) is then obtained, and to make this starch perfectly white, a suitable proportion is placed in a tub and stirred circularly in water as before. Filter through a tightly woven sack; leave to stand for a day, after which it is decanted; change the water a third time, leave the deposit to precipitate, and, by repeating this operation seven or eight times, remove all soluble parts. When the starch is dry, we place it in a sara-si stretched with thick paper, and, by putting it to dry every day in the sun, it forms perfectly white lumps, and we then have Kudzu ko (Kudzu starch)." In 1879, we sowed seeds we had received from Dr. Hénon against a wall facing south. They produced vigorous stems that soon reached the wall coping. They didn't flower, and when winter came, they froze. The stump did not suffer. In 1880, the stems were stronger than those the seedling had produced, and 30 degrees of cold froze only those parts that exceeded 1".50 in height. The lower parts, which had become woody, therefore withstood the severe winter; they had not flowered. In 1881, the full height of the stems survived the winter well. The plant did not flower. Since then, the plant has flowered every year at the end of September. We have therefore observed that the Kudzu is absolutely hardy, with luxuriant vegetation, but at the same time, in the Paris climate, it is completely sterile, making it impossible to multiply the plant by sowing. At the Muséum, where a few plants of Kudzu exist, the plants have, like ours, withstood the winters; it is true that they are placed in the part of the garden known as the layers, i.e. in the best sheltered spot. We tried taking cuttings, but failed. Laying down stems gave better results. Then, the mother plant having acquired extraordinary vigor and development, we were able to lay down some twenty stems, which gave us as many new plants. Multiplication is therefore easy and unlimited. This is a crucial point, as the plant does not produce seeds in the Paris climate. We have seen that the Kudzu stump provides a valuable starch and that its leaves are sought after by livestock; but Pueraria Thunbergiana is first and foremost a textile plant. In Japan, however, it does not seem to be cultivated for its fibers as widely as in China. When asked about this, Dr. Hénon wrote on July 29 1883: "If I have not spoken to you about the uses of Kudzu as a textile plant, it is because I have never seen it put to this use. In the part of Japan I lived in, Kudzu grows everywhere in coppices; it vegetates there with great power, grows stems 8 to 10 meters long, flowers very abundantly and is covered with pods, which, to tell the truth, contain few seeds. It is not cultivated, but in winter, poor people pull out the roots, not without difficulty, and an excellent starch is made. The starch obtained from this starch is much better, more resistant, without being brittle, than that from rice or wheat. This starch is sometimes used as a food starch and in cakes. Kudzu is therefore cultivated for two purposes: firstly, an excellent starch is extracted from its roots, and secondly, it provides material for the manufacture of fabrics, the industrial importance of which was pointed out to us a few years ago by Mr. Eugène Simon, former French consul. The stems of Pueraria Thunbergiana emit such long, numerous and fibrous sprays that one cannot doubt the profit that would be made if the plant were naturalized or cullivated in France. We believe in the accuracy of the information that presents its fabric as remarkably beautiful. It seems to us that Kudzu or Ko seeds should be imported from its native countries. It is so hardy that it can be grown anywhere by letting it crawl along the ground. Indeed, it would be impossible to provide high enough supports for a plant whose stems reach 8 to 10 meters in length. So we have to let it crawl, as the Chinese and Japanese do. In a letter dated August 16 1883, Count de Castillon wrote: "In the San kaï meï San dzu ye, Kudzu is shown as a plant crawling on the ground, and the drawing shows Japanese peasants extracting it. There is therefore no need to climb it. Kudzu or Ko could therefore be grown by letting its stems spread out over the field, and its stumps would yield abundant, inexpensive harvests for an indeterminate period of time. A perennial, textile and extraordinarily productive plant deserves serious and decisive experimentation. As for us, we thought we could take advantage of its nutritional properties to talk about it at length, as we have just done. LA TOILE DU KUDZU Notice translated for the first time from Japanese by M. le comte de Castillon (see Mémoires de la Société des études japonaises, 1878-1879). Kudzu (Pueraria Thunbergiana) is an extremely valuable food and industrial plant. It is also an ornamental plant, and its spirited growth combined with its extensive foliage make it ideal for lining walls and cradles. It also has medicinal properties that merit serious study. Its roots, flowers and pods are used as a remedy in China and Japan. In the latter country, its leaves are used as fodder, and its long, thin, very resistant twigs are used as string. The starch provided in abundance by its long, voluminous roots, which can reach a length of 3 meters and a diameter of Om, 10 to Om, 12, is of an exceptional quality. Its finesse, brilliant whiteness and pleasant flavor make it the best of its kind. Dr. Filhol, the learned chemist from Toulouse (1), has recognized the nutritive power of this root as equal to that of the potato. The only plant of this species that exists, we believe, in Europe, was introduced by us three and a half years ago, in the spring of 1875. (See Annales de la Société d'Horticulture de la Haute-Garonne, 1875.) Everything leads us to believe that this precious plant will adapt perfectly to our climate. Moreover, it requires no cultivation care. Finally, its climbing stem provides a fabric with special properties, but manufactured by processes that our industry will probably find ways to simplify. This is what we will be able to judge after hearing the Japanese author, to whom we leave the floor: "Kudzu (Pueraria Thunbergiana), a perennial plant of the Leguminosae family, closely resembles Fudzi mame (Dolichos cultratus Thunb.) and Ingen mame (Phaseolus vulgaris L.); but its stem and leaves are covered with hairs; its sarmentose stem is extraordinarily vigorous; its seeds are inedible. "This plant grows spontaneously in the various provinces, on mountains or in wasteland, depending on the place. Everywhere, a starch called Kudzu ko is prepared from its roots, and at the Kake gava relay station, in Yen siu (Totoini province), a thread is extracted from its stem, with which a fabric of the highest reputation is woven. This Kudzu comes from the mountains and wastelands of the village of Kura-ma, to the north-east of the aforementioned post house, from the localities of Matsu-ba and Oho zawa, and from the village of Tomi-da, located south of Naka-yama, Koya, etc. It is considered to be of the highest quality. It is especially considered to be of superior quality if it grows on the mountains of the village of Musi-bu, which faces the north side of Mari-matsi, in the Sudzi district, and on those of the village of No-be. "If now we investigate how long ago Kudzu began to be exploited, although this point is not yet elucidated, as we possess a song composed by His Exc. Tameal (1) on the Kudzu cloth of celieu, it is today something like more than 680 years since this fabric must have been made. "We will now give a general description of the manufacture of this fabric. As for Kudzu starch, it will be dealt with separately when we talk about this type of food. "Although Kudzu stalks are found to have reached a length of 2 to 3 zyau (3 to 9 meters) and beyond by the time autumn arrives, they must be cut for a period of about fifty days from the first fortnight of the fifth month (June 5-21) to make thread. Their length, which at this time is only 7 syaku (2m, 10), reaches 9 syaku (2m, 70) in the middle of this period, to reach 1 and 2 zyau (3 to 6 meters) in the last days. But as the 3 or 4 syaku (Om, 90 to 1°, 20) above the roots are of poor quality, they have to be left, which reduces the harvested length from around 3-4 to 6-7 syaku (Om, 90-1m, 20 to 1m, 80-2m, 10). "On the same day as this operation, they must be plunged into a boiler full of boiling water. They are shaken in all directions for a very short time (2 and a half seconds, 5 of our European seconds). After stirring, they are returned to the water for the same number of seconds, then removed. "They are then soaked in running water, where they are left for a day and a night. A doormat is spread on the ground, on which they are piled; another is laid on top as a blanket, and they are left wrapped in this way for two days and two nights, and, when they are uncovered, the fermenting stalks give off vapours; they are watered, which puts an end to this fermentation. This is called naha midzu (middle water, second water). "The mats are replaced as before, and the stems remain in this state for a day and a night. "They are then put to soak in shallow running water, where they are trodden on with the feet; the bark is then removed and the stem core discarded. The strips of bark are equalized in length, and placed in bundles of thirty; then, taking two of these strips at a time, with one hand, they are inserted between the branches of a small fork 2 tan (Om, 06) long, which is held with the other. "When they have turned white, they are hung on a horizontal bamboo pole to dry in the sun. Before drying is complete, they are removed and, by shaking them briskly, the bark fibers separate by rubbing against each other, thus obtaining the filasse, which is then left to dry completely before being converted into Kudzu wo (Kudzu thread). "To make Kudzu wo, we choose the best strands from the tow; with thumb and forefinger, we tear them apart as finely as possible; then we add them end to end, knotting them tightly. Scissors are used to cut off the ends of the threads that extend beyond the knots. The threads whose knots have been sheared off in this way are called tsuguri. They are then rolled up in the wo oke (a round yarn box with a louvered bottom), which is then placed in a basket of the same shape and immersed in water. "Then, by interlacing the threads in the shape of an 8 around the thumb and little finger (literally: as in the game children call aya, cat's cradle), small hanks are formed, and they are ready to be used for the weft. As this is their only use, silk, hemp or cotton threads must necessarily be used for the warp. "The loom does not differ in any way from the ordinary loom; only that the weft thread is wetted with water before being placed in the shuttle, and as it passes the reed, the knots are lifted out, which are trimmed with scissors when the weaving is complete. The fabric is then rinsed with clean water, dried, then re-wetted; it is wound onto the maki ginuta (fulling cylinder) and slowly beaten with small strokes, which gives the fabric a sheen, which is then dyed in various shades, after which it is stretched by means of the sii-si (1), and a coat of nori, a primer composed of 10 momme (37 gr. 50) of Kudzu ko (Kudzu starch) and 400 me (1 kil. 500) of water, then the Kudzu cloth is finished. (1) A dyeing instrument designed to remove wrinkles from a fabric; it consists of several bows of elastic bamboo that hold the fabric taut across its width. This instrument is also known as a mogari (thief). The bamboo generally used for this purpose is ma-daké (B. Quilioi), which has earned it the syuonym mogari take. "This fabric does not soften under the action of water; and, as once wet, it dries quickly, it is used for kappa (1), kakama (2), etc. The pieces being woven in large widths, it is easy to weave them. The pieces, woven in large widths, are also used for fusuma (3) interlinings, and this type of production has developed considerably in recent years. "The first manufacturer of Kudzu yarn at the Kake gava post house is Sudzuki gen pe. The main manufacturers of this fabric in the same place are Naru hira Kiu meï, Sató Kuni yosi, Matsu moto yosi naga, etc. The main house for Kudzu cloth is Sató Kuni yosi. The main manufacturer of Kudzu cloth is Hyo-do, in the village of Taka-mura. "A total of 60,000 tan (a tan is worth 8m, 50) of this cloth (500,000 meters), with a gold value of 49,200 yen (263,809 fr. 65), is manufactured in the places we have mentioned, in equal quantities in the three types, upper, middle and lower." KUMARA (1) BATATAS EDULIS Chois. var; Ipomxa Batatas Poir. var; Ipomæa chrysorrhiza Hook. f. Family Convolvulaceae. Closely related to the common potato, Ipomxa Batatas Lamk. of which it is merely a variety; cullivated since ancient times by the Maoris of New Zealand. In 1884, Messrs Vilmorin-Andrieux and Cte received Kumara tubers from Mr. J. Hooker, harvested at Kew. Unfortunately, these tubers arrived in such a state of decomposition that it was impossible to plant them. This is a very unfortunate accident; as the climate of New Zealand is more or less the same as that of central France, the Kumara would have been a great potato for us. There are between twenty and thirty varieties of this Ipomoea. (1) Notes taken almost entirely from a report published by Mr. Schomburgk, Director of the Adelaide Botanical Garden in South Australia.) Its tubers differ from one another like those of our potatoes; some have red skin, others purple, others white. Some are smooth and cylindrical, others deeply furrowed or regularly fluted; others are short and thick, obtuse at the tip; but there is never any mixing between these varieties. All reproduce exactly the types planted. The only sign of degeneration, caused by soil or drought, is in the volume of the tuber. All the varieties are ancient and have been perpetuated by the perfect preservation of the tubers. In the memoirs of the New Zealand Institute, Mr. W. Colenso gives a very interesting report on this favorite vegetable of the Maoris: "They have been using it," he says, "since prehistoric times, as many legends show. "When the seasons and soil are favorable, its yield is considerable. However, it has a powerful insect enemy in the form of a large larva, which devours the leaves of young plants long before the roots or tubers have developed. "Each plant is visited by elderly women, using a planter or pointed instrument, to select and pull out some of the season's most beautiful new tubers. The soil is loosened around the plants, and then mounded again, not unlike the hoeing of potatoes, but with much greater care. "The young tubers from this first uprooting are scraped and half-dried in the sun on clean mats, carefully protected from the dew. When dry, they are either eaten or stored in baskets as a kind of candy or candied tuber. They are held in high esteem by the Maoris and eaten raw, or soaked and crushed in a little hot water. "During the general uprooting, which takes place late in autumn, but always before the frost, great care is taken to collect the roots. They are carefully sorted according to volume. Any that are bruised, broken or slightly injured are set aside for prompt consumption. The rest are collected in large flat baskets, always new, and placed in good time in suitable stores, taking great care not to do so

Colenso says, "In my opinion, one of the most remarkable things about this useful tuber is how the first varieties were obtained. Mr. Colenso further says: "In my opinion, one of the most remarkable things about this useful tuber is still to be noted: how were the first varieties obtained?" On this subject, he could learn nothing to his satisfaction from the Maoris themselves, except that all the varieties came to them from their ancestors. He tried to find out if the old Maoris had ever seen the Kumara in flower. "No, they had never known anything like it," he said, and they never brought in their crops until the leaves had dried out. Mr. Colenso also often wanted to know if any new kind or variety had recently been obtained by the Maoris or their immediate ancestors; to which they also replied: "No." "Is it not possible," says Mr. Colenso, "that in remote times the plant flowered and that ancient cultivators, voluntarily or accidentally, obtained roots from sown seeds? Is it not also possible that the plant, after artificial, persevering, assiduous cultivation, tending to obtain early varieties, and continued for centuries, came to flower definitively, as happened in England with potato varieties, after repeated cultivation? The earliest varieties give neither flowers nor seeds. Professor Kirk of Wellington, New Zealand, has twice sent Kumara tubers to Mr. Schomburgk, and has enclosed the most interesting information: "The Maoris," he writes, "cultivate about twenty varieties, all of which are said to have been brought to them by the mystic 'Hawaiki'. "The one with the most delicate taste is a small pink-fleshed variety. Its cultivation is almost abandoned, but it deserves to be grown as a delicacy. I haven't seen it for twelve or thirteen years, but I'll try to send it to you next spring with other varieties. I intend to visit the north, and there I'll be able to make arrangements. Mr. Kirk continues: "I have written to a Maori friend of mine, asking for information on the vegetation, cultivation and cooking of Kumara, and will send it to you when I receive his reply. For the moment, I'll limit myself to saying that Kumara is planted on small mounds arranged in staggered rows, about 18 inches apart. The soil should be light rather than compact and rich. Once the piece of land has been planted, it is strictly forbidden to women. When ripe, the crop is harvested with great ceremony. It's best baked in the oven, in the Maori way. The planting season begins in October and continues until December. The soil is ploughed or spaded, and small mounds are formed after finely breaking up the clods. The mounds are 8 to 10 inches high, and a tuber is planted in each one, barely covered with soil. The plantation then requires no further care other than careful weeding. Harvesting takes place in March and April, with the crop ripening around mid-March. To preserve the tubers, we use the Maori rua method. The rua is a shallow pit, dug in an easily drained area and in soil of sufficient consistency, the excavated earth being used to raise the sides and cover the tubers to form the roof. The sides of the rua are built without using water, the earth simply being beaten with the hand. A post is placed at each end of the pit, and these posts support a ridge from which fascines and pieces of wood are stretched to the wall, tightly packed together and covered with earth. Tubers are also kept in shallow pits with a good layer of branches at the bottom and a good covering of the same nature at the top, before the soil is thrown on top. If they are exposed to the air for long periods, they are lost. They are removed with sharp-tipped sticks, about a foot long, a job that must be done with care to avoid injuring them, as those damaged will soon perish. If the tubers are left in the ground, they quickly rot during the winter rains. The Maoris prefer to cook them in their ovens, although they often boil them like potatoes. Some types of Kumara are quite watery. These are not good boiled, as this method of cooking makes them even more watery. All are even better when baked or roasted. It will be noted that Mr. Colenso, speaking of an initial uprooting, says that it is done by elderly women, whereas Professor Kirk says that women are absolutely forbidden to enter Kumara plantations; but there is no contradiction here. This is obviously a belief shared by many of our gardeners, who at certain times attribute a pernicious influence to the presence of women, particularly on Melons and Mushrooms. In 1884, the Kumara had not yet been fully acclimatized in South Australia, but its cultivation seemed likely to succeed, and Mr. Schomburgk hoped to distribute tubers in 1885. The plant had recently been introduced to the East Indies. It had produced first-rate harvests there. Mr. Duthie, Director of the Saharanpur Botanical Gardens, said in his last report: "I consider Kumara a very valuable addition to our vegetable varieties. In his work entitled Origine des plantes cultivées, M. Alph. de Candolle, in his search for the potato's native country, states that considerations of roughly equal value would allow either America or the East Indies to be attributed the plant's paternity. However, the Kumara, which is certainly only a variety of the Potato, is found neither in America, where it does not yet appear to exist, nor in the East Indies, which recently received it from New Zealand. According to this hypothesis, this primitive type of Potato should have been carried from America or India to Oceania, where it would have been modified to form a distinct race. Moreover, this introduction would have had to go back a very long way, since the plant seems to have existed among the Maoris since prehistoric times. In addition, Alph. de Candolle states: "The plant is cultivated in Taïli, the neighboring islands and New Zealand under the names : Umarra, Gumarra and Gumalla, described by Forster as Convolvulus chrysorrhizus, is Batate according to Sir Joseph Hooker. Seeman points out that these names resemble the Quichuen name for Batate in America, which, he says, is Cumar." Canadian bitter root. White Lewisia. Bitter Root. Mountain rose. LEWISIA REDIVIVA Pursh. Fam. Portulaceae. Our attention was drawn to this plant by a report from the Commissioner of Agriculture (1), which states: The California Indians give Lewisia the name "Spatulum". Its root is compact and fusiform, dark on the outside, white and mealy on the inside. It provides an abundant supply of concentrated food, of which a single ounce is enough for a meal. The plant is worth cultivating." We'll say later what we think of the extraordinary nutritional value attributed by the report to Lewisia and affirmed successively by several botanists, who seem to have repeated, without further examination, what their predecessors had said; but this is not the only merit of the plant: it is also very ornamental, and, with its spring flowers, pink and relatively large, is quite worthy of taking its place in our gardens. And that's not all: its vitality is quite astonishing, making it a real plant curiosity. We are going to present the information we (1) Report of the Commissionner of Agriculture for the year 1870. Food products of the North American Indians, Washington; Printing office, 1871. on its habitat, its nutritional properties, its vitality and its hitherto little-known cultivation as a decorative plant. HABITAT "The plant is found on the summit of Mount Diablo, looking north to Colombia, east to Montana, Utah and Arizona (1)." "It is found everywhere in Oregon, near mountains, in arid prairies, along rivers (2), among them the Lewis and Têteplate rivers (3), as well as on the banks of Clark's river (4)." FOOD PROPERTIES "The natives use it extensively as a food. Stripped of its bark, the inner white part of the root is boiled in water to produce a substance similar to boiled Salep or Arrow-root. The dried root is almost converted to starch by maceration in cold water (5). "It is a favorite food among aborigines. With the bark removed, a handful of roots, boiled with meat, forms a considerable quantity of nutritious mucilage. VITALITY "The roots of Lewisia have such vital energy that the specimen in Lewis's herbarium, as Pursh notes, showing some signs of vegetation, was planted in a garden in Philadelphia, where it lived for a year; and Douglas's specimens, in the same conditions, vegetated for some time in the garden of the Horticultural Society in London (2)." "In June 1826, Douglas had collected specimens in flower, but they had fallen from the boat into the water while descending a rapid; in March 1827, those that recovered to live, after having been compressed in the herbarium, were planted as said above (3)." "We have had desiccated specimens, kept for two years, or more, which still gave fresh harvests of leaves. "The specimen on which our figure was taken at Kew, collected in English Columbia, to be preserved in the herbarium, by Mr. Lyall, R. N. of the delimitation expedition, had been plunged into boiling water because of its well-known obstinate vitality. A very remarkable and beautiful rock garden plant, resembling Purslane. "It is very dwarfed, only about an inch high, and has two small tufts of narrow leaves, from the center of which rise flowering stems. "The flowers are large relative to the dimensions of the plant, measuring from 1 inch to 2 1/2 inches in diameter, and varying from dark pink to white. The roots are succulent and have the property of retaining their vile principle under the most unfavorable conditions. "It sometimes fails to develop its annual leaves, with the result that it is often thought to be dead and difficult to treat, although this is not the case. "When grown in pots, it should be planted in broken stones and its roots plunged into a light, sandy loam (2) with peat. "After flowering, the plant curls up and looks like a heap of dried-out, twisted bits of string; but such is the nature of the plant and hence its name (3)." (1) Botanical Magazine, pl. 5395. Our drawing is taken from the colored figure published in this work. (2) English loam is an excellent quality free soil. (3) Robinson, The English flouer garden, London, 1883. Our kind and learned correspondent, Mr. Havard, United States Army Surgeon, wrote to us on June 14 1888: "I have mailed you a small Fig. 42. - Lewisia rediviva. packet of roots of Lewisia rediviva (Portulaceae), one of the most sought-after native plants of the Oregon Indians. I received these roots from one of my correspondents and it is quite likely that, if you wish, I can send you another package. "The plant was in full bloom at the time of removal, which probably explains the thinness of the roots. They must be much fleshier in spring, when the first leaves sprout, which is when the Indians pull them out. It's a very hardy plant, as its name suggests, and so I hope that, despite the adverse circumstances, the roots will retain their vitality until you can get them into the ground." We planted these roots at the reception, and by autumn, although absolutely deprived of water, they were showing budding leaves. They gave us flowers in May. Another letter from Mr. Havard, dated September 1st: "I will answer as many of your questions about Lewisia rediviva as I can. The Indians do not cultivate this plant; they pull it from uncultivated land in spring (April), as soon as the first rosette of leaves allows them to recognize it, i.e. before it flowers. They eat the root dried or baked in an oven, which simply consists of an earthen hole lined with stones. The result, after removal of the bark, is what you see in the enclosed small package received from Washington territory. These cooked roots will give you the answer to your question about their maximum size. Of all the samples I have received, I have not seen any larger. The Indians eat them as they are, or make flour from them, which they eat either as bread or in soup. "No one has ever ventured to sow Lewisia seeds. Although a perennial plant, it is more than likely that medium-sized roots would be produced in the first year. It remains to be seen whether the starch, which forms the main part of these roots, would be accumulated in sufficient quantities to make them excellent. "Does the plant have divisible stumps? I believe that the many branches of the mother stock could be separated without their vitality suffering. "The whites of Oregon and Washington territory are not fond of it; it is not an ordinary article of their cuisine. "In short, these roots are nourishing, but their mealy flavor has nothing to recommend them in any special way, and they seem far too small to be profitably cultivated, unless cultivation can modify them, which is quite possible. "If Lewisia is a disappointment as a vegetable plant, it deserves to be grown as an ornamental. I expect to receive a parcel of it before long, so that I can send you a few more roots and probably some seeds too." We received this package; it contained seeds which were sown immediately. Wishing to ascertain the nutritional properties of Lewisia, we used the cooked roots we received for this purpose, and gave them to Mr. Arnaud, chemist at the Muséum (1), who very kindly offered to examine them. We didn't put enough roots at his disposal for him to make a quantitative analysis, but enough for him to give us this (1) Chevreul's successor as Professor of Norganic Chemistry. reply: "The root of Lewisia rediviva contains no nitrogenous matter and, consequently, no albuminoids or alkaloids whose presence could explain the nutritional value attributed to it. It can therefore only be considered as a starchy material, analogous to many other roots or tubers. As we have just said, Mr. Arnaud did not have a large enough quantity of roots to make a complete analysis; but we have since received from Mr. Havard the following analysis, published by Mr. H. Trimble, Professor at the College of Pharmacy, Philadelphia: Fatty matter, resin and wax............ 4.98 Mucilage gum.................... 14.80 Albuminoids.......................... 3.58 Starch.............................. 8.57 Water................................... 12.17 Ash............................. 2.53 Woody fiber and indeterminate matter.. 53.37 100.00 and the American chemist accompanies his analysis with the following observation, approved by M. Arnaud: "The quantity of starch found may seem low when one considers the use made of the Lewisia root, but the large quantity of gum and mucilage makes up for what is lacking. We can therefore believe, without taking on the task of resolving the question, that the Indians really feel nourished by the "spatulum" and that the nutritional power they attribute to it is not imaginary. We conclude by recommending the cultivation of Lewisia, made easy by its extraordinary vitality, either with the aim of obtaining larger roots than the wild plant, or to add a very pretty flower to the current riches of our gardens. LIS COMESTIBLES La Flore des serres et des jardins de l'Europe published (vol. VI, 1850-1851, p. 145) a very interesting note by the learned botanist Fischer, as follows: "Sur les Liliacées alimentaires de la Sibérie. The disaster that has struck the potato harvest in recent years has focused the attention of botanists and farmers on plants that are supposed to be able to replace, in some way, this precious plant. Unfortunately, none of the species proposed to growers combines all the valuable qualities of the potato: ease of cultivation, rapid and fertile multiplication, abundance of nutritive matter, pleasant flavour, easy digestion. Yam, Batate douce and Manioc require tropical temperatures, and their cultivation, which alone could be on a par with that of the Solanée, is strictly excluded from northern latitudes. "Tuberous nasturtiums have too strong a taste; Topinambur, whose merit in other respects is indisputable, and Oxalis are too watery; Apios requires a large area for cultivation, and soon becomes hard and inedible; Psoralea esculenta scarcely lives up to the expectations we had of it; Camassia esculenta has perhaps more right to the protection of agriculture than the last two of these plants, if, however, its multiplication is prompt and easy. It is the only one of all the plants mentioned that can be compared with the Liliaceae of Siberia, which have always served as food for the inhabitants and which deserve to be better known in this respect. "Erythronium Dens-canis, the beautiful large-flowered variety of which is widespread in the south of western Siberia, is sought after and harvested there as an excellent food, of which a certain supply used to be sent annually to the court of St. Petersburg. Propagation by seed is very reliable, and the plant produces many of them; sown as soon as they are ripe, these seeds all sprout, but it takes three years for the bulb to reach its normal size. The local name is Kandyk. "In Siberia, lilies are known as Sarana, and Lilium tenuifolium L. and Sarana kamtschatica Fisch (Lilium kamtschaticum, Fritillaria kamtschatica by the authors) are the edible species par excellence. L. spectabile Fisch. is also used as food. These three plants multiply with extraordinary ease: L. tenuifolium L. reproduces almost exclusively by seed, but also, like the other two, by cloves, and it seems that each of the bulb scales, elongated and pointed in L. spectabile, large, short and rounded in the shape of a tuber in the Kamtschatha Sarana, forms a new plant; this mode of propagation is even essential for the Kamtschatka Sarana, as it rarely bears seed, a large number of flowers becoming sterile through abortion of the pistil. In Kamtschatka, there is a lily very similar to L. canadense, which I call L. avenaceum, after the name it goes by in the country and because of the shape of the bulb scales, which resemble large oat seeds; this species has not yet been introduced into our gardens; in its native country, it is eaten like the ordinary Sarana, which is nevertheless preferred. "Nowhere in Siberia are these useful plants cultivated; everywhere, it is the bulb of the wild plant that is harvested, and harvested in abundance. Lilium tenuifolium and Lilium spectabile are found in the eastern part of the Tomsk government and are widespread around Baikal and throughout trans-Baikal Siberia (Daury), as far as the eastern ocean. The Kamtschatka Sarana can be found along the Eastern Ocean coastline, in Kamtschatka itself and on the islands off the west coast of America. "It is not impossible that, when cultivation, and especially careful cultivation, ad hoc cultivation is involved, satisfactory results of improvement will be obtained. (2) Phonzo-Zoufou (Botanical treatise with plates), by Iwasaki Tsounemassa; Yédo, 1828. Somoku-Dusets under the names Shiratama-Yuri, Okina-Yuri and Kanoho-Yuri. Phonzo-Zoufoule marks under the names Liu-Kiu-Yuri and KanokoYuri. "Lilium Thunbergianum Rœmer et Schultes is referred to in the Somoku-Dusets as NatsuSukashi-Yuri, Haru-Suhashi-Yuri and HiratoriYuri, and in the Phonzo-Zoufou as Skachi and Hogaku. It can be found in fields, mainly on Parry Island. It is also found on Nippon Island and is common around the city of Yokohama, where its edible bulbs are used in Japanese food. "Lilium tigrinum Gawler, classified in SomokuDusets and Phonzo-Zoufou as Oni-Yuri. Very common on the islands of Nippon and Yeso. The edible bulbs of the Tiger Lily are eaten by the Japanese, cooked, boiled and candied. "Lilium callosum Sieb. et Zucc. Hime-Yuri or L. pomponium Thunb. According to Kæmpfer and Siebold, this species is common, in the wild, in the sparsely wooded mountainous regions of Japan, at an altitude of 165 to 650 meters. Mr. Maximowicz says it is commonly cultivated on the island of Kiusiu, near the city of Nagasaki. The Japanese use the edible bulbs of L. callosum in their food, and eat them cooked, boiled and candied. They extract a white starch from these bulbs, which was represented at the 1878 World's Fair, class 69 (Cereals, floury products from Iwaté prefecture, Rikuchiu province). This species is also called Yama-Yuri by the Japanese". Dr. Mène also cites the following Japanese Liliaceae: "Erythronium grandiflorum (which is only a variety of E. According to Dr. Kramer and Dr. Savatier, it is found in the wooded hills of the northern provinces of Nippon Island. The Japanese botanist Keiske marked it as existing on the island of Yeso. The bulbs contain a starch that is used in Japanese food. Flasks of this starch were on display at the World's Fair.
