It is usually grown as an ornamental plant, but its bulbs are also used in cooking. They have an excellent taste, so some growers cultivate them specially. There are over twenty varieties of the lily, but only two or three whose bulbs are used. Lilies are planted around the farm, and the bulbs are harvested after two or three years. Some bulbs have a circumference of almost 33 centimeters. The lily flowers are sold to flower merchants. As for the bulbs that we like to taste, growers reserve them for themselves, either to eat or to sell". In 1878, Dr. H*** sent us bulbs of Yama-Yuri (Lilium callosum) and Wasei-Yuri, with the following note: "Yama-Yuri is the species of Lily most cultivated as a vegetable in Japan, at least in the center and south. I believe that in the north, L. auratum is grown as a food plant, but I'm not sure, as I haven't travelled there. "The Japanese name for Wasei-Yuri means early lily; it is grown less than the other; in Japan, it is planted in autumn and Yama-Yuri in spring. On several occasions, our kind correspondent has given us interesting information on Japanese edible lilies. We reproduce them below: "Most Japanese lilies are edible, but 22 not all. In the part of Japan I lived in, only Yama-Yuri and WaseiYuri are grown for the table. Both are very good; I ate them all winter, once or twice a week, and they really are a very good vegetable. "The poor people gather from the wild the bulbs of L. japonicum Thunb. (in Japanese SassaYuri, i.e. with a small Bamboo leaf), very common in the mountains; it's a mediocre eater. "They also sometimes eat L. tigrinum (OniYuri, i.e. Devil's Lily), but this is a detestable, extremely bitter food. It is, however, quite abundant in Japanese markets, at least in Yedo and Yokohama. While I was in Japan, I grew L. tigrinum in my garden and, despite the protests of my Japanese cook, who told me it wasn't good for a rich man like me, I wanted to try it. It's very bad and frankly bitter, despite having been blanched twice in boiling water beforehand. I'm not suspected of being too severe about this dish, as I declare L. callosum an excellent floury vegetable, equal to our best. "In the far south, in the Liou Kiou islands, we are said to eat the bulbs of L. longiflorum, which grows wild there; but I can only speak of it by hearsay. "The preparation of lily bulbs for the table is very simple. They are separated scale by scale, then carefully washed and lightly blanched in boiling salted water. They are then served either sautéed in fresh butter, in a red sauce with meat juice, or in a white sauce. Now that's European-Japanese cuisine. "The true Japanese recipe is as follows: after blanching them as above, they are cooked for a few minutes in a sauce composed solely of water, Shoyou and a little grated dry fish. They are quite tasty this way; but at first sight, a European palate finds fat-free sauces strange." In the Bulletin of micellaneous information from the Royal Garden of Kew, 1889, page 116, we find the following additional details on lily flowers and bulbs used as food: "It is well known that, in countries where lilies are indigenous and abundant, they are sometimes used as food plants. For some years, the dried flowers of certain Lilies have been an important article of trade in China, and in the consular report on Chinkiang trade for the year 1886, page 10, it is stated: "The export of Lily flowers has increased from 7,033,000 pounds to 7,677,622 pounds; this is the most considerable export of many years. The harvest was very good, and prices were remunerative for most of the year. No more than two-tenths is consumed here; the rest goes south, where it is used to flavour soup. The cultivation of this plant increases annually in the north of this province." In a letter to Kew from Mr. Pelham L. Warren, Consul in Taiwan, dated August 16, 1883, the following indicalions are given, relating to the provenance of the lily flowers used in China: "The lily flowers mentioned in Mr. Watter's consular report, about which you ask for information, are the dried flowers of Hemerocallis graminea and Lilium bulbiferum. They are used by the Chinese to flavor soup; they also eat them as a vegetable. Lily flowers are also said to be effective for lung ailments, and to have tonic properties. Enclosed is a small sample of those imported here. Hankow is China's leading export city; large quantities also come from Japan." The sample sent by Mr. Warren was evidently a Hemerocallis flower, and Mr. Baker said that it could indeed be H. graminea Andr. (H. minor Mill.), the Asphodete Lily. There were no samples of Lilium bulbiferum flowers. The Japanese make much use of lilies as food, according to Professor Penhallow, who gives the following interesting account of their use in the American Naturalist, volume XVI, page 119: "Various species of Lilium abound in the forests and are used as a source of floury food. At the beginning of autumn, women can be seen returning to their villages, laden with bulbs. They are completely crushed in a large wooden mortar, after which the starch is separated from the cell mass by repeated washing. The starch is then hung up in sacks for winter use, while the cell mass is dried in round, perforated cakes, somewhat resembling miniature millstones, and hung up to dry." Efforts were made by Kew's Museum of Applied Botany to obtain lily cakes from Japan. Here is a copy of a letter addressed to this establishment by Mr. Power Le Poer Trench, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Tokio: "I have made the utmost efforts to obtain, for the Director of the Royal Garden, Kew, samples of lily bulb cakes, said to be used as food by the Japanese; but, in spite of all the researches I have made, I have not been able to find any in Tokio or Yokohama. "However, Mr. Wooley, who was passing through Yokohama last December on his way back to his post, took it upon himself to inquire whether any could be obtained in any village or town in the northern part of Japan, and, the month before last, he wrote that he could not get any in Hokodate, and that the Japanese said they had never seen any. "He was inclined to believe that Professor Penhallow had confused them with Fu cakes, which are made from wheat and hung up in stores to be sold, and that the ones he refers to are found only in the Aïno region. He had, however, written to Mr. Brooks, botanist attached to the Agriculturau College, Sapporo, and asked him to try to obtain the requested samples. "Later, I received another letter from Mr. Wooley, saying that he had at last succeeded in obtaining the requested cakes, and he sent me a small package containing a specimen of the smallest kind, the larger ones being, he said, of an awkward size for transport and running a greater risk of being broken." Here is the description of the samples explaining the economic use of Lilium cordifolium bulbs: Uba-Yuri (Japanese name), Kiu (Aino-name), sent to the Royal Garden Museum, Kew: "1° Fibre from which the starch has been partly extracted. "After the bulbs have been thoroughly washed and soaked in water for two days and two nights, they are pounded in a wooden mortar, then transferred to a vat filled with water. The whole mass is kneaded with the hands, and left to rest overnight to allow the starch to settle, after which the cell mass is removed and dried. "2° Cakes are made from the above fibers, by pounding them in a mortar with a little water, then kneading the mass and shaping it with the hands. The cakes are hung to dry in the Ainos' huts. The coloring is caused by smoke. The cakes are not eaten by the Japanese. The Ainos boil them and eat them, either plain or mixed with rice (the cakes vary in size, the largest being over a foot in diameter). "3° Starch made by the Japanese from UbaYuri bulbs. The starch made by the Ainos is similar, but coarser. "4° Uba-Yuri confectionery made by the Japanese. Of the various species of edible lily reviewed in the course of this study, Lilium tigrinum is the only one that grows vigorously in our gardens, and we might even add that it stands up perfectly to our harshest winters. But, as we have seen from the information supplied by our correspondent Dr. H***, its bulbs are only a mediocre source of food. Even if it were otherwise, its cultivation as a food plant could only be recommended as a curiosity. It takes far too long to obtain Lis bulbs that are sufficiently developed to be used. The same observation applies to Erythronium grandiflorum, Sarana kamtschatica and a large number of other bulbous plants, some of which offer considerable resources in regions where they grow naturally and can be harvested abundantly around the home. We thought it would be interesting to show that, nonetheless, certain Lilies, which we generally only know to be of high value for the decoration of our flowerbeds, could, in a pinch, provide us with a vegetable that would not be to be scorned. MACA (Native name in Quichua language.) LEPIDIUM MEYENH WALPERS. Cruciferae family. In September 1893, Messrs Vilmorin-Andrieux and Cit kindly associated us with the trial they were about to carry out on a new food plant: "One of our customers has come to offer us," they wrote, "seeds of a plant cultivated and indigenous to Upper Peru, called Maca in the old Peruvian dialect (Quichua language), and which would be used for human nutrition. It is said to produce an edible tuberous root, similar in shape to the turnip and in taste to the potato. "Just looking at the seed and tasting it, we think it's a cruciferous plant, and that the seed is shaped like that of the Alen cress; but what it really is, we'll have to find out in a trial. "We think it would be of interest to you to do the same, and to this end we enclose a sample of these seeds. Please keep us informed of the results you obtain. Shortly afterwards, Messrs Vilmorin-Andrieux and Cle received a letter from the same person, providing them with valuable information: "A few days ago, we gave you a packet of Peruvian Maca seeds. "We have just received some information about this plant and how to grow it. "Maca: Quichua name. "This plant belongs to the Cruciferae family. It has many points of resemblance with the Cresson alénois, grown in our gardens. Its leaves are cut and give off a strong odor. "The stem does not rise when flowering, but branches out and spreads over the surface of the soil. "The taproot is fleshy and sweet. It is used as food by the Indians of the high plateaus of the Andes. "The seeds were harvested in the Pampa de Junin, at altitudes ranging from 4,000 to 4,100 metres above sea level, where it freezes like in France. "The Indians grow Maca in blackish, peaty soil, which must not contain limestone. In France, this soil is replaced by a mixture of loam and heather. The plant is grown on humpback lines. It is thought that this procedure is necessary over there, because the soil is peaty and at the same time very marshy. If the roots are raised above the ground, it's probably to protect them from humidity. "We sowed some in Dauphiné, in August 1885, and the harvest would have been satisfactory, had this crop not been neglected at the onset of winter. "The Indians say that the roots should be left in the ground for two years. This was not the simplest of trials. The letter does not say when the Indians sow Maca; the seasons in the Andes are reversed relative to ours; our altitude above sea level is insignificant; the soil around Paris is neither peaty nor humid. We first sowed under glass, cold, in October 1893. The seeds germinated quickly and produced small, spindly plants, most of which resisted the frosts, albeit with little protection. In spring, these plants developed little. spread out on the ground, flowered early and gave fertile seeds, but their roots were so tenuous that they were not usable. In 1894, we sowed seeds from our harvest and the result was the same: some plants had a slightly thicker stump, about the size of a walnut, but too hard to be eaten. In 1895, new seedlings were sown in the open air. The plants stood up perfectly to the rigors of winter; although they were partly eaten by flea beetles, they flowered in spring and disappeared after ripening their seeds, without giving us the results we had hoped for in the letter reproduced above. We attribute our failure to invasions of flea beetles, which make it almost impossible to grow crucifers in the Crosnes garden. Maca seems perfectly suited to our climate. TWO-HORNED MACRA Ling-Kio. TRAPA BICORNIS L. fil. Family Onagrariaceae. Annual aquatic plant. Slender stem; leaves, some submerged, reduced to linear strips, others in rosettes floating on the surface of the water, with fairly long petioles, cylindrical at first, then vesicular towards their middle, at flowering time, with diamond-shaped blades, entire or only slightly toothed. Flowers white, small, briefly pedunculate, set in the axils of the upper leaves; calyx with two accrescent divisions, later becoming the horns of the fruit; corolla with four petals; stamens four; style small, ending in a captive stigma. Fruit woody, with two opposite, thick, obtuse horns, curved at the top. "The great Lake Talo is famous for its Linkio aquatic fruit. This fruit resembles the Tribulus "ad instar triangularis pyramidis undequaque prominens". Its rind is green, thick and reddish at the tips, turning black as it dries. Its subsFig. 45. - Trapa bicornis. inside is very white; its flavor is that of the Chestnut "magnitudine tres quatuorve castaneas xquat". The plant is cultivated in stagnant waters throughout China." (Martini, Novus atlas sinensis, 1655). "It has small leaves that float on the surface of the water, at the end of very long stems. The numerous fruits remain hidden underwater. Cultivated on a large scale in the lakes and rivers of northern China." (Roxburgh, Flora indica). Robert Fortune reports that he saw Ling-Kio fruit being harvested: "Having returned for some time to Shanghal, I resolved to penetrate, if possible, into the district of Kwey-chow-Foo. Going up the river in a south-westerly direction, I arrived, shortly after passing Kea-Hing-Fo, a city of some 270,000 inhabitants, at an immense pond which, I presume, communicates with the famous Taï-Ko. The water was very shallow and covered with Trapa bicornis, which the Chinese call Ling, and whose fruit, of rather bizarre shape, as is well known, resembling an ox's head armed with its two horns, is highly prized in China. I observed three very distinct varieties, one of which produces fruit of a beautiful red color. "A large number of women and children, in small circular boats much like our laundry tubs, were busy fishing the Ling. In fact, nothing could be more suitable for this kind of work than these singular boats, which, large enough to hold the fisherman and all the catch, steer gently through all the plants without breaking them. The sight of this immense quantity of individuals thus navigating this marsh, each in his own vat, formed for me a most entertaining sight." The Trapa bicornis," says another traveller, M. Marchal, from Lunéville (1), "is highly esteemed in China. It forms the food of populations where the rice harvest is insufficient. Harvesting them is reminiscent of the grape harvest in France. Ling is sown at the end of autumn, in those parts of ponds where the water is shallow and clear, and in those places most exposed to the south. (1) See De l'amidon du Marron d'Inde, Ad. Thibierge et Dr Remilly, 1857. The Chinese claim that this crop absorbs the putrid emanations rising from the surface of stagnant water. If the harvest is very abundant, Trapa is fed to barnyard birds, which quickly fatten and acquire an exquisite taste. A hundred years have passed since Abbé Grosier, whom we quote below on the subject of the Pitsi, Heleocharis tuberosa, to which, like Duncan, he gave the name of Water Chestnut, recommended the cultivation of Ling-Kio (Trapa bicornis). We have and we neglect," he said, "in some provinces of France, a species of water chestnut that the Latins have named Tribulus. The missionaries believe that this plant could be the one the Chinese call Ling-Kio, from which they derive great benefit; if this identity were confirmed, it would be easy to extend its cultivation everywhere, which would offer a new resource in times of shortage: "1° This other water chestnut, Ling-Kio, is a refreshing fruit, pleasant in summer. When it is green, it is sold in Peking, on the markets, like hazelnuts in Europe; " 2° Dried and ground into flour, it makes a very good porridge, especially when a little wheat flour is added; you can even mix a third of it into the flour used to make bread; " 3° Baked in the oven, candied with sugar or honey, it becomes a healthy and pleasant food; " 4° It provides a suitable food for geese, ducks and other farmyard birds. "The cultivation of Ling-Kio requires no care. The plant reproduces itself wherever it is found. When you want to throw it into a pond or stream, throw the seed in late autumn into the part of the pond where the water is shallow. Choose a spot where the water is clear and the shore faces south. The more heat the Ling-Kio receives, the healthier and tastier it is, and the more fruit it produces. TWO-PINTED MACKER Singhara. TRAPA BISPINOSA Roxb, Pl. of the Coast of Coromandel, pl. 234. This species differs from the previous one in having a fruit with straight, sharp-pointed horns and toothed leaves. It grows in central and southern Asia, where it is Fig. 46. - Trapa bispinosa. called Singhara, as far as Ceylon and Japan; it is also found in southern Africa, as far as Zambezia. Its fruits are often converted into starch, and can be used to make excellent-tasting cakes and soups, or stored and preserved as food. Production is abundant and economical, as the plant reseeds itself spontaneously. It lives for several years. In some regions, such as Kashmir, Trapa fruit is an important food source for the local population. This species probably includes Trapa cochinchinensis Lour. and Trapa incisa Sieb. et Zucc. M. L. Bouley, director of the gardens of the Maharadja of Kashmir, in Srinagar, published the following interesting note in the Revue horticole (March 16, 1884): "Trapa natans and bicornis (1) are so abundant in the lakes of Kashmir, and grow there with such vigor, that the parts where these plants are found look more like immense meadows than lakes; it is therefore impossible to navigate there, even with the frailest boat. "The products of these two plants are considerable; in autumn, the harvest occupies thousands of people. "Before being delivered for consumption, the chestnuts are crushed to remove their woody, pungent husks, and then ground. The coarse flour obtained is eaten as porridge. "This flour is sold very cheaply, which can be explained by the absence of cultivation costs, and its consumption throughout the winter is enormous. Every day, large ships loaded with Trapa fruit arrive in Srinagar. Mr. Ermens, Mr. Bouley's predecessor in the position of (1) This must be Trapa bispinosa. the Maharadja's Director of Cultivation and a long-time resident of Kashmir, has kindly provided us with the following additional details on Singhara cultivation: "After a great famine, the governor of the district in which the Woorlake is located introduced Trapa cultivation. This lake, which measures at least 2,000 hectares, is so full of it that navigation is impossible. The fruit is harvested by the boatload, and the governor profits greatly from it, as each grower pays him a royalty. It is widely consumed, and in the recent famines, this harvest saved the lives of a large number of inhabitants. "Fresh Trapa fruit is eaten like walnuts, cooked in water; it is a common food. It is very indigestible, and the Hindus, to obviate this inconvenience, place on their stomachs a heater called a kangreiï, which, according to the country's doctors, facilitates digestion; hence it follows that their stomachs are blackened and as if smoked by this process." The preceding notes were published by us, in 1888, in the Bulletin de la Société nationale d'Acclimatation; shortly afterwards, Mr. P.-L. Simmonds, F. L. S., whose name is known to all those concerned with applied botany, sent us a copy of the Journal of the Society of the Arts, issue of August 31, 1888, containing an article signed by him and entitled: Edible aquatic plants. In it, we found some details that we think it would be useful to reproduce: "In the last issue of the Bulletin de la Société d'Acclimatation de Paris, an article appeared on aquatic food plants, which deserves attention for the novelty of the information it provides, and to which, while taking one or two passages, I can add a few additional details that will be of interest. "It is said that Trapa natans formed a large part of the diet of the ancient Thracians, just as Trapa bispinosa does for the inhabitants of Kashmir and T. bicornis for the Chinese. Dr. Royle says that the former produced up to 12,000 pounds a year in revenue to the Runje Singh government, the tax being levied on 96,000 to 128, 000 donkey loads, from the great lake of Oaller..... " In Gugerat, its fruits form an important food item. On feast days, it is made into a red tincture, which is mixed with a yellow color derived from the flowers of the Butea frondosa. "Colonel Sleeman gave the following interesting account of Trapa bispinosa in his Travels in the South-West Provinces: "Here, as in most other parts of India, the reservoirs are spoiled by the Water Chestnut (Singhara), which is everywhere planted and cultivated in water-covered fields of great extent, as regularly as Wheat or Barley is on dry plains. It is cultivated by a class of men called "Dheemurs", who are everywhere fishermen and palanquin bearers. They have boats to plant, weed and harvest Singhara. The tenures of each cultivator are carefully indicated by long Bamboos driven into the water, and they pay so much per acre for the part they cultivate. "The long stems of the plant reach the surface of the water, over which their green leaves float, and their pure white flowers bloom pleasantly in their midst in the latter part of the afternoon. The nuts grow underwater, after the flowers have wilted. They are triangular in shape and covered with a coarse, brown tegument, adhering strongly to the kernel, which is white, edible and of a fine, tight texture. "These nuts are highly prized. They are carried to market on the backs of oxen, often 200 or 300 miles away. They ripen at the end of the September rains and can be eaten until the end of November. "The rent paid for an ordinary tank is about 100 rupees (L. 10) a year. I have known of a very large one for which 200 rupees and even 300 (L. 30) a year were paid; but the silt grows so rapidly by cultivation, that it promptly destroys any tank in which it is allowed; and, where it is thought desirable to conserve the tank for use of the water, it must be expressly prohibited." Necklaces made from Singhara nuts are sold in Benares and considered sacred. "A few years ago, Captain J.-P. Pogson of Simla advocated more extensive cultivation and use of this plant: "Having the example of Kashmir before our eyes," he says, "it is very singular that the much-vaunted reservoirs, the great lakes and the inland sea of fresh water of the Madras Presidency, and also the immense 'Vheels' of the north-west and west provinces, are not regularly employed in a more profitable manner by the cultivation of Singhara. The dried nuts would keep, I believe, for many years, and would still be sold in England as Arrow-root or Singhara starch, for food or industrial uses. Any old Singhara store could be processed and sold in this way. "Like Wheat grain, Singhara kernels can sustain human life for a definite time and are pleasant to the taste, seasoned with salt and pepper, or in soup (porridge) with sugar, "ghoor or jaggery" (1). If the almonds are broken into small pieces, they can be ground into flour using a hand mill, and the product kneaded into a dough for making small "chuppaties" or cakes. "By soaking almonds overnight in cold water, they can be boiled the following morning to make food. Steaming them might be just as good, maybe better, but I've only tried soaked almonds boiled. A few years ago, I ate a "Hulwa" made with Singhara flour, and it was more pleasant than the one made with wheat flour flowers. "The Madras Presidency boasts some ancient and magnificent hydraulic works: the Viranum reservoir (2), 35 square miles in extent, with 12 miles of dikes; the Cauverypank reservoir, whose 4-mile dikes are consolidated with stones throughout their length; the Chembrumhankam reservoir, similar to a picturesque inland sea, a work whose execution dates back to unknown times. The first of these artificial lakes has a surface area of 22,400 acres, and the third, compared to an inland sea, is ten times as large. (1) "Ghoor" is the sugar residue of India; "jaggery" is the sugar residue of China. (2) The English word tank can only be translated by reservoir, which however is not applicable, in French, to ponds, lakes, inland seas, i.e. the vast bodies of water referred to here. However, we know that in Kashmir 30,000 human creatures feed on the Singhara nut for five months of the year, and if the picturesque inland sea we're talking about deserves its name, its bed and water surface could be put to profitable use by Singhara cultivation. The 35-square-mile reservoir could become a first-class nursery to supply Madras with nuts for seed. "The yield of the Water Nut, per acre, is, as yet, unknown; but, assuming the harvest of 4 quarters (480 pounds) each of walnut kernels per acre, the 22,400 acres would yield 43,800,000 pounds of food, and, reckoning 60 pounds per adult per month, the above quantity would suffice to feed 716, 800 people for one month, or 143,360 for five months. "The cost of this abundant and permanent food supply would be insignificant. There are 4,000 square yards in an acre, and by allowing one nut of seed per yard, the price of nuts and rail transport could easily be calculated. The first year's harvest would more than cover the costs, and we would then have a harvest in perpetuity that would only have to cover the costs of supervision, care and harvesting. "As the harvest belongs to the State, a considerable income would be obtained from the sale of the nuts, even if the almonds were only sold at half the price of rice or another grain. "In good years, the farming population would make ample use of this nourishing and economical food, and sell and export their harvests of Rice, etc., and in bad years of famine, the walnut harvest would be a resource; finally, their presence would have a great influence in preventing the artificial production of local famine. "Walnuts, once sown, resow themselves, so that the square yard could soon produce nine plants or more. The inland sea, when covered with these nuts, will be a source of wealth for the state and profit for the public. As the annual, spontaneous or artificial exlension of the crop is a very simple thing, the government of Madras would in a few years find itself the owner of a Singhara plantation of great value." Captain Pogson, writing from Simla, goes on to say: "The Singhara Nut of India and Europe being a perennial aquatic plant, the old roots bear fruit annually. If they grow in water 2 feet deep, we enter it to collect them, going from one to the other, and deposit them in a floating container, such as, for example, a 5-gallon barrel. If the water is deeper, we'll have to use any raft or canoe and pick the nuts." "In this country (India), they are gathered several times during the season, and the last ones to be harvested, i.e. those that are the largest and have hard kernels, are eaten boiled. Others are peeled, dried and ground into flour, while others are buried whole, to be used as seed the following year. For example, the pond or depression in the ground which has provided a crop of walnuts may dry out in hot weather; at the start of the rains, this place will become a pond again; the walnuts for seed will then be dug up and sown 12 inches apart in the still slightly deep water, placing each walnut about 2 inches deep in the submerged soil, and sowing is continued in this way every day, as the waters rise. The nuts will germinate in due course and provide the year's harvest. "Naturally, if the water didn't dry up, the old roots would live and, within the season, give a new shoot of stems that would bear fruit as usual. It follows that, when a perpetual harvest is desired, the nuts should be sown in the bed of a shallow, freshwater pond that never dries out." MACRE VERBANAISE (1) Lagana. TRAPA NATANS L., var. verbanensis Jaggi. Under the name Trapa verbanensis, De Notaris described a plant that grows in Lake Maggiore and whose fruit has only two obtuse, unbarbed horns. Mr. Jaggi, in a note he has published on Macres (2), makes it very clear that this is simply a variety of Trapa natans with aborted median horns. (1) We presented the fruits of this species at one of the meetings of the Société botanique de France (Bull. Soc. Bot., 1888), in comparison with fruits of Trapa natans with only three horns. 6) Die Vassernus (Trana notms L.) und der Tribadues der Allen Zurich, 1883. We can't reproduce here all the reasons he gives in support of his thesis, but one of the most convincing is certainly the fact that in the same lake, fruit with two or three horns can be found mixed with the four-horned Trapa natans. All gradations of abortion are thus to be found. Fig. 47 - Trapa verbanensis. Professor Gibelli of Bologna, who transplanted T. verbanensis to Modena, obtained fruit with two or three horns. Leysser, Mertens and Koch, in their flora of Halle; Boehling, in his flora of Germany, say that Trapa natans sometimes has two-horned fruits. They did not think there was any reason to create a species of this variety. The fact that the horns are obtuse is also of little importance, as we sometimes find Macres with four horns that are more or less rounded at the top. Cultivation trials carried out in Modena prove that the Fig. 48. - Trapa verbanensis. Leaf seen from below, and young fruit, natural size. Trapa verbanensis reproduces at least for some time. Here is the information we have gathered on this variety. We are indebted to Mr. Rovelli, President of the Verban Horticultural Society of Pallanza; to Mr. D. Lampertico, Secretary of the Vicenza Agricultural Show, who was kind enough to consult Professor Saccardo, of the University of Padua, and to Dr. Mattirolo, of the University of Turin. Trapa verbanensis is known as Lagana on Lake Maggiore and Lake Varese, and is also commonly known as Castagna del lago and Castagna d'acqua. It is found in large quantities in the Bay of Angera, Lake Maggiore, where the bottom is visible. It vegetates admirably without any care in botanical jardius; it is a little less productive than Trapa natans. Its fruit ripens at the end of October, a time when it is easy to obtain. They are eaten either green, like hazelnuts, or cooked, requiring a fairly long cooking time. They are not much sought-after, and are rarely seen on the market. The same fruit is used to make rosaries, which are frequently sold in Arona, Varese and other towns. We immersed some rooted Verbanese mackerel plants in a pond, as a gift from Mr. Latour-Marliac of Temple-sur-Lot. They vegetated well and gave us a few green fruits on September 15, the time when M. Latour-Marliac obtained his first green fruit. Latour-Marliac, for his part, obtained a certain quantity of ripe fruit. Trapa verbanensis has larger leaves than T. natans, which is well known in our western regions. Its petioles are red; the variety is more beautiful than the type. There is another variety of Trapa natans that Areschoug has named T. natans, var conocarpa (1). It originates from Lake Immeln, in Shonen, Sweden, and differs from the type in the way the horns are inserted, which are not very coherent, the lateral ones detaching from the fruit at mid-height, the median ones at the lower quarter: the fruit is therefore naked over a large part of its height. XANTHOSOMA SAGITTIFOLIUM Schott. Bot. Mag. tab. 4989; Engler, Flora brasiliensis, p. 191; Arum sagittifolium L.; Descourtilz, Flore des Antilles, 8, t. 553; Arum xanthorrhizon Jacq, Hort. Vindob, 11, 73, tab. 157; Hortus Schœnbr, 11, 32, tab. 188; Caladium xanthorrhizon Willd; Caladium sagittæfolium Vent; Caladium utile Hort; Yanthosoma utile C. Koch et Bouché; Yanthosoma xanthorrhizon C. Koch (Engler, Monographiæ phanerogamarum, vol. II, Araceæ, p. 469). Aroidae family. At the request of the Société nationale d'Acclimatation, M. D. Albuquerque has kindly sent us (1) Mémoires de l'Académie royale des Sciences de Stoekholm, 1874. tubers of Mangareto branco, with a promise to research the violet variety for our use. Vigneron-Jousserandier cites Mangaride as being cultivated in Brazil and yielding from twenty to thirty small tubers, and V.-L. Baril, comte de Lahure, in a work entitled L'Empire du Brésil, has this to say about it: "The Aroidea called Mangareto branco grows in small clumps. The main tuber is about the size of an apple. It is surrounded by several other small tubers as big as Walnuts, and often smaller. It is these small tubers that are edible. They have a pleasant taste and are floury, though less so than potatoes. Mangareto branco is one of the varieties of Xanthosoma sagittifolium, an aroidea which, in tropical America, plays the same role, but to a much lesser degree, as Taros (Colocasia) in India, Egypt, and mainly in Oceania. In warmer regions, the plant is easy to grow, but not very productive; it has been cultivated by the indigenous Indians from time immemorial. In the Journal de la Société nationale d'Horticulture, 1871, pages 506-514, Dr. P. Sagot published a note on Tayes or Tayoves in French Guiana, from which we extract the following: "The American species (Xanthosoma) are distinguished by their milky juice and by the fact that the petiole is inserted at the edge of the leaf and not inside the leaf blade, from below the leaf, at a certain distance from the lower edge. "In the Asian and Oceanian species (Colocasia antiquorum and C. esculenta), Kouchou (India), Kulcas (Egypt), Alcolcalz (southern Spain), Tallus (Java), Tallo, Taro (Oceania), the juice is limpid and the leaves are pellate, i.e. borne by a petiole that is inserted from below, inside the leaf blade. "The varieties grown in French Guiana are : Taye banana, Taye white, Taye violet, Touca, Grande Tayove. "There may be other races in French Guiana, which I have not seen; but, in general, I think I can say that Tayes are inferior, in abundance and quality, to the products of the Taros. "The tubers, of good quality, boiled and cooked, are healthy and pleasant. They are considered more nutritious than other floury roots. The most delicate are those that are young and have grown well hidden underground: for example, the lateral tubers of the rhizome, which form rounded outgrowths around the main root. "The leaves, chosen young and tender, blanched and cooked in boiling water, are good to eat, but have little taste. A few are often added to various dishes frequently used in the colonies. I confess, however, that this way of using them seems to me only a very incomplete justification for the pretentious name of Caribbean cabbage, which has been given to these plants". In the first days of April, we planted the Mangareto branco tubers sent by Mr. Albuquerque, on a bed and under glass. The plants vegetated vigorously, were abundantly watered throughout the season, which was quite warm, and were only uprooted on October 6, after a heavy white frost. We only found a small number of tubers, as big as peas. Cultivation of the American Aroidea is therefore impossible in the Paris climate, even with the help of layers and frames. We were similarly unsuccessful with all the Taros from New Caledonia and India, of which we had received numerous varieties, differing in quality, tuber shape, fertility and earliness, some requiring flooded soils, others being able to be planted in dry soil. However, it seems that the tubers harvested would have reached their full development under the influence of one more month of heat. MARANTA ARUNDINACÉ (HERBE A LA FLÈCHE) MARANTA ARUNDINACEA L., Redouté, Liliac, I, tab. 57; Bot. Mag., tab. 2307; Maranta indica Tussac, Flore des Antilles, I, tab. 26. Scitaminaceae family. Stump producing underground, fleshy, cylindrical, scaly suckers, about 30 cm long and 2 to 3 cm in diameter. Stems about 1 metre high. Leaves glabrous, oval-lanceolate, sheathing petiole. Loose panicle; white flowers. According to Tussac, this species was introduced from India to the West Indies, where it is widely cultivated as a food plant. The starch known as Arrow-root is extracted from its fleshy suckers. These suckers can also be eaten plain, either boiled or prepared in a variety of ways. Arrow-root starch from Maranta arundinacea is also known as A. de la Jamaïgue, A. des Antilles, A. des Bermudes, A. de Saint-Vincent. This starchy product comes to us mainly from America; it is also widely cultivated in India and in certain parts of Africa, notably on Bourbon Island or Reunion Island. Its name derives from its use by the natives to heal arrow wounds. M. arundinacea is the Toulola of the Caribbean. It is grown in the West Indies in Jamaica, in South America where it is called Anvert, in Guadeloupe, Reunion, Guyana and India. The starch contained in its rhizome is known as West Indian Arrowroot. This starch exists there in the proportion of 22 0/0. There are two varieties of Maranta in Brazil and Jamaica: one called White Anvert and the other Red Anvert. In Brazil, the elongated-root variety is more highly regarded in the province of Para than the rounded-rhizome variety. In French Guiana, the Caribs eat the root after cooking it under ashes. The rhizomes are acrid and rubefacient, but cooking makes them edible. Marantas require deep soil that is always cool but not damp. They can be propagated using their creeping, perennial rhizomes. Sections should be planted on divided, stony ground. They should be spaced 1 m to 1.20 m apart. During their growth, these plants only require hoeing, and their rhizomes are removed at the end of the first or second year. An average hectare yields 500 to 600 kilograms of arrowroot and 1,500 to 2,000 kilograms of couac or pulpy residue. Arrowroot is a light, nutritious food. It is especially suitable for delicate people and children. In Cuba, Maranta starch is used to make excellent creams that keep for a long time in bottles. In England, large quantities of arrowroot are imported every year from Ceylon, Hindustan, the West Indies, Bermuda, Nicaragua and Melanesia. Couac, or coarse flour, is used to feed domestic animals. In Botanical Magazine, loc. cit. Maranta arundinacea is a plant of considerable interest, furnishing for the table a distinguished food, sold under the name of Arrow-root of India, extracted from its roots, not as has been said by drying and grinding them, but by macerating them in water, in the same manner as starch is extracted from Wheat, Potato and other starchy substances. "In recent years, Maranta starch has been imported in large quantities from the West Indies to England, and recommended as a food for young children, and as light nourishment for the sick. "The plant is native to South America and is grown in all the islands of the West Indies. Here, it must be kept in greenhouses, where in July and August it produces its flowers, which fade very quickly." Introduced by Dr. William Houston, before 1732. We have tried unsuccessfully to grow Maranta arundinacea. MARGOSE A PIQUANTS Pandipane, Gatole, Caïqua du Pérou, Momordique à feuilles de Vigue. Momordique Papareh, Papareh Herya, Melon de San-Gaëtano. Karela (Hindostani), Karala (Bengali), Khu qua (China). MOMORDICA CHARANTIA L., Spec. ed. 1, p. 1009. DC, Prodr. III, p. 331; Naud, Ann. se. nat. ser. 4, vol. XII, p. 131; Revue hort. 1859, p. 620, figs. 134 and 135; Flore des serres, X, p. 193, tab. 1047; The Garden, XII, p. 161; Cogniaux, CUCURBIT, Monogr. Koch, Belgique horticole, XI, p. 92. Family Cucurbitaceae. Plant native to Asia and Africa, naturalized in tropical regions of both worlds; annual, with spindly, climbing stems, up to 2 meters high, twining, hairy, with usually simple tendrils. Leaves alternate, deeply 5-7-lobed, dark green above, pale green below, sometimes almost glabrous except at the veins, more often pubescent on both sides; lobes oval, acute, toothed. Flowers yellowish, monoecious, borne on equally long, deflexed peduncles; male flower peduncles bearing a heart-shaped, entire bract inserted towards their middle or at the base; female flower peduncles hanging after anthesis. Male flowers grouped or solitary, larger than females; calyx with five divisions half as short as those of the corolla. Female flowers solitary, with slightly shorter pedicel, quite large, pale yellow. Fruit pendant, oblong, 10 to 15 cm long, thinned at both ends. PETITE MARGOSE A PIQUANTS MOMORDICA CHARANTIA L., var. abbreviata Ser. in DC, Prodr. III, p. 311; M. zeylanica Miller, Dict. des jardiniers, n° 3; M. senegalensis Lamk, Encyclop. méth. Charantia, var. muricata Griseb, Fl. Brit. W. ind. isl. p. 287. This plant is a simple variety of the preceding one, from which it differs only in that it is a little smaller in all its parts. It is native to the same regions. M. Charantia is a vegetable plant cultivated under various names in China, Cochinchina, Malabar, Peru, Mauritius, Reunion, etc. It is known in Reunion under the name M. Charantia. It is known in Réunion under the name of Margose, and is mainly cultivated there in the small-volume variety named by M. Naudin M. Charuntia, var. minor. It is grown in the same way as the Melon de châssis, except for pruning; however, when a large number of fruits have formed, the stems should be pinched, part of the leaves cut off to aerate the plant, and watering should be moderated to avoid rotting. Margose vegetation is very active, and fruiting, right up to the end of the season, is all the more abundant as the fruit is never left to ripen and is used green. In a pinch, after having raised the seeds in a frame, the plant can be placed in the open air, around June 1st, near a wall facing south; but the fruit obtained is often short and misshapen. We cannot recommend outdoor cultivation in the Paris climate. M. Charantia is sometimes grown in France as a curious plant. Its ripe fruits are a beautiful yellow-orange, open on their own and reveal rows of seeds wrapped in a very appetizing cherry-red pulp. This is undoubtedly a wonderful dessert dish, and the seeds are happily sucked; unfortunately, the pulp that covers them is sparse and tasteless. The use made of Margoses in warmer countries is quite different and much more interesting. We do not know how they are prepared for the table in China, Peru, etc.; but we owe to the kindness of Mr. Édouard Wilmann, member of the Société des Botanistes français, precise information on their use in Réunion: "This fruit, which reaches an average length of Om, 07 to Om, 10, is always picked and used before maturity. Once ripe, it is worthless for culinary purposes. Some like it very tender, others prefer it when it has already reached a certain consistency; it is, in any case, excellent until ripe. "For the table, it is prepared: "As achards: Simply remove the seeds and place the fruit, split in half lengthwise, in the sauce prepared for this purpose: vinegar, olive oil, ginger, garlic, chili pepper, salt, etc. It is usually added: cucumber, garlic, garlic, salt, etc. Cucumbers, cabbages, carrots, mangoes, etc. are usually added; "In rougaille: the fruit is cut into rougaille pieces, always after removing the seeds, and seasoned with lemon juice, chili pepper, ginger, etc.; "In curry: the fruit is cooked, halved, with fresh or salted bacon, fresh or salted fish; with or without curry powder, but with the ordinary condiments of Creole cuisine. In India, the fruit is eaten sliced and fried, but must first be cooked in water to remove all its bitterness. We have to say that we have tried unsuccessfully to introduce the fruit of the little prickly Margose into our Pickles. Their extreme bitterness makes them unsuitable for this use. MATAMBALA PLECTRANTHUS TERNATUS Sims; Botanical Magazine, tab. 2460; Bojer, Hort, maurit. p. 253; DC. Prodr. XII, p. 65. Labiatae family. On July 15, 1884, our correspondent in the Transvaal, Mr. Mingard, wrote to us: "With this letter, I am sending you some tubers of the Potato fade or wild, called by the Magwamba: Matambala. It has the same cultivation and uses as the ordinary potato. The natives appreciate it very much and prefer it to any other tuber. They keep the seeds (1) in the sand, or hanging in their huts. They plant it at the same time as corn. On October 20 1884, Mr. Mingard wrote again: "I'm sending a small bag of Matambala to the post office. These will be the last ones I can send you. The natives planted them a fortnight ago. It likes light soils, has the same vegetation period as the Potato, but the stems are noticeably different; they widen as soon as they are born. (1) Read tubers. The flower is small, yellow or blue (1). A tuber planted in its entirety yields from ten to twenty to one. Matambala is prepared like potatoes. No flavor. "I delivered the letter and package to the post office on October 29th. The tubers are starting to sprout. According to your advice, I chose the ripest and hardest. However, the tubers from this last shipment rotted on the way; but, fortunately, those sent to us the previous July preserved well in the sand, and we were able to plant four of them on a bed and under glass, on the following March 15th. Three plants thrived admirably; only one died at the end of June. We pulled it out on July 1, and found, to our great surprise, a dozen small tubers forming a tight cluster immediately below the plant's collar. These tubers appeared to be ripe and preserved well in the sand. The other three plants vegetated vigorously, spreading out their numerous stems on the ground, which marcelled spontaneously, and filled the trunk in which they were planted; but, when we pulled them out in autumn, they gave us only an almost insignificant harvest. The plant recovers very easily from cuttings, which has enabled us to obtain a large number of plants that have been distributed to the Muséum and to various per(1) M. Mingard has certainly confused the flowers of several species. In fact, on the east coast of Africa, there are several Coleus and Plectranthus with edible tubers, some with blue flowers, others with yellow. The one we collected had blue flowers. sonnes. They flowered the following winter in the greenhouses of the Muséum and the Jardin Bolanique of the École Vétérinaire d'Alfort. Dr Sagot, in his Manuel des cultures tropicales, p. 84, says he saw Matambala in Mr Paillieux's garden at Crosnes, but only in leaf. It was after examining a flowering specimen, which we showed him the year after his visit to Crosnes, that he applied the name Solenostemon den siflorus Benth. to it, a name written in Bentham's own hand on the label accompanying a specimen kept in the Muséum herbarium, and which he considered to be comparable in every way to our plant. The Museum specimen appeared to us to be merely a compact inflorescence form of Coleus tuberosus, the name by which we referred to Matambala in the second edition of Potager d'un Curieux, and which we now rectify after comparing our plant with live specimens of Plectranthus ternatus grown in the Museum's glasshouses and the figure of this plant published in Botanical Magazine, plate 2460. Plectranthus ternatus is native to the Comoros Islands and Madagascar, from where it was introduced to Mauritius and probably to other countries, since Mr. Mingard sent it to us from the Transvaal. Mr. Daruty de Grandpré, President of the Mauritius Acclimatization Society, wrote to us from Port-Louis: "I read with great interest your notes in the Potager d'un Curieux. I did not see any mention of a plant in which I am interested because of its edible qualities. I'm referring to Plectranethus madagascariensis, known here as Oumime (1). "Oumime produces a tuber that we eat in exactly the same way as potatoes, although it has a distinctive taste that may not appeal at first to European palates. However, I'm sure that it would be easy, through cultivation, to completely remove this particular taste, at the same time as increasing the volume of the tubers. "I'm mailing you some Oumime tubers, so that you can try growing them in France. In his Histoire de la grande Isle de Madagascar, De Flacourt speaks of Houmimes or Voamitza: "These are," he says, "small roots as big as octopus, which multiply extremely, for from one plant more than two hundred will grow". Matambala requires too much heat for it to be cultivated profitably in our climate. But if our kind correspondent's shipment has not produced any useful results for France proper, it has provided our colony of Gabon-Congo with an excellent and much-appreciated vegetable, which will spread from there to all regions with a similar climate. (1) Mr. N.-E. Brown, author of a note entitled: Tuberous Labiatæ, published in the Kew Bulletin, January 1894 issue, establishes that the Oumime is not the Plectranthus madagascariensis, but the P. ternatus Sims. The name applied by Mr. Daruty de Grandpré refers to the Oumime bá̂tard or wild Oumime, which does not produce tubers. The tubers we had donated to the Muséum were multiplied, and two of them were given by Professor Max Cornu to Mr. Pierre, who was leaving to take up the post of Director of the Colonial Garden in Libreville (Gabon-Congo). Mr. Pierre cultivated Matambala, and was so successful that he actively propagated the plant in the colony. He gave some tubers to Mr. Thollou, attached to the Brazza mission, who transported them to Brazzaville, where they multiplied and spread rapidly. During a trip to Paris, Mr. Thollon gave us the following information on our Labiatae: "Matambala grows extremely vigorously during the rainy season. During the dry season (June to October), the plant vegetates, but needs watering to produce tubers. It is during this period that the flowers appear. "Harvesting takes place from December to January. Each clump produces a dozen tubers the size of walnuts, and many smaller ones. "To date, the plant has not been subjected to rational cultivation. We are content to detach twigs which, when placed in the ground, take root with the greatest of ease and which, left to their own devices, without any care, nevertheless give the result indicated above." Mr. Thollon considers the Matambala to be one of the most useful vegetables to propagate in our equatorial African possessions; it would take the place of the potato, whose cultivation is impracticable, the yield being almost nil. He fed it to a large number of travelers, who were extremely pleased, as its flavor is so similar to that of the precious Solanée, that they thought they were back to their favorite vegetable, the absence of which in tropical regions is one of the harshest hardships for Europeans. Finally, here's some new information that Mr. Pierre sent to one of us: "Back from a trip to the interior and south of Loango, I've just found your letter, which has followed me here. "It was in 1887 that I brought to the colony two Matambala tubers, as big as large peas, which Mr. Cornu had entrusted to me. I gave one to Mr. Thollon, who transported it to the interior of the Ogoué, in Brazzaville. There are now some in the Oubanghi at latitude 6° north and longitude 17° east. The plant has spread in these countries with extraordinary rapidity. "The Crampel mission, which is said to have found some around 4° north latitude, has eaten the tubers and may import it as far as Lake Chad. When he left Gabon, I gave Mr. Crampel some Basella alba seeds, a plant that will also be imported into central Africa. "Matambala also exists in Loango, where Mgr Carrie introduced it from Brazzaville. "The plant has improved in the interior. We've obtained tubers as big as Walnuts, and I'm certain that, if cultivation were better done, we'd obtain even better results. Plant in well-prepared, not too dry, moist soil, and above all leave more distance between plants. "The taste of the tuber is very similar to that of the potato. It's a plant of the future, especially in the interior of our colony. In Libreville, where we are 5° further north, I have obtained only mediocre results. "The plant is known throughout the interior and on the coast by the name Pomme de terre de Madagascar, which must have been given to it by M. Thollon. As this name is inappropriate, I am doing my utmost to combat it. Its fleshy tubers are quite similar to those of the potato, not only in shape but also in flavor. This plant was sent from Japan to the Museum by Abbé Faurie, and Mr. Maxime Cornu was kind enough to offer us a seedling. The tuberous rhizomes grow up to 20 centimetres long and 1? to 2 centimetres in diameter, and are quite reminiscent of those of Stachys palustris, whose cultivation Mr. Chappellier has sought to propagate as a food plant; but, although their flavour is better, and they are produced in large numbers, there is no reason to recommend their use, as their fibrous consistency makes them unpalatable. Lycopus lucidus has proven to be absolutely hardy in our climate; it is regrettable that we cannot make better use of it. Decaisne, who considered them to belong to the Cucumis Dudaïm. We harvested fruit of the shape and volume of a large orange, with smooth rind, streaked with ten dark-green stripes against a yellow-orange background, running from the stalk to the umbilicus. Fruit height, approx. Om,8; width of stripes varying from Om,01 and 0m,015 to Om,02; average weight, 310 grams. The small volume of the fruit would make it one of those portable melons to which we have given the name of Pocket Melon or Hunter Melon, if it could have the same use; but it lacks sugar and can only be eaten for dessert. In China, it is tasty, sweet and fragrant. M. Naudin acknowledges that it can be used as a dessert garnish. He tells us that it is highly prized in most Muslim countries, that it abounds in Persia, Egypt and the whole of North Africa; that he has found it on the markets of Algeria; that it has long existed in the Spanish colonies of America. So it's not inedible. Its flesh is white, juicy and fragrant when very ripe. We suggest using it as follows: For a table of twenty place settings, arrange twelve to fifteen pieces of fruit in a pyramid or basket, forming a beautiful middle course that will charm the eyes of the guests. For dessert, the maître d'hôlel will remove the dish, cut the fruit in half, quickly replace the seeds with powdered sugar and serve each person half a fruit in the shape of a cup, to be eaten with a spoon like an ice cream. This dessert will be good and very elegant; we've made sure of that. One of our correspondents confirms our assessment. He writes us from Setubal (Portugal): "Yesterday, I got my hands on a Melon zébré de Chine, which I had been displaying for a fortnight on a shelf; it had turned almost all yellow, even in its green part, which had taken on this hue: it was just right for what I wanted to do with it. I divided it up, tasted it and found that it tasted a little like pineapple. I ate half of it, thinking that it could be used for something else. Continuing the experiment, I emptied the other half of its seeds, and, in this empty space, I put sugar, then a very good liqueur wine, called bastardo here. I left it to infuse for a quarter of an hour, and then, using a teaspoon, I started to make it like ice-cream, and the paste looked very much like it. It was delicious. It occurred to me that these melon halves could be glazed in a variety of ways. "I'll give you my test; it's by these random means that discoveries are made. I'm a convert, and I hasten to confess it. If only to eat this little melon, I'll grow it. The C. Dudaim produces only twelve to fifteen fruits per panel; its price would still be quite high. Cucurbitaceae family. By way of description, this melon bears a striking resemblance to the large white Paris cucumber. We've been growing it for several years under glass. We don't prune it, for fear of deforming it by making it bigger. In fact, its shape lends itself perfectly to the use we make of it. We pick them when they are very ripe, when they are pleasantly fragrant. Unfortunately, it lacks sugar, like all the melons we have received from China and Japan; but when cut into thin slices, dipped in doughnut batter, fried by a skilled hand and liberally sprinkled with sugar, it makes an excellent dessert, which retains a light pineapple flavour and is very well received by everyone. This is not the only use for Shiro uri. In 1879, at the Horticultural Exhibition in Brie-Comte-Robert, gardener Veniat presented this melon, which he had been growing for two years under glass, in the same way as the Cantaloupe, except for pruning. Fruit small, pear-shaped, with smooth, apple-green rind, divided into ten ribs barely indicated by lines darker green than the rind. This melon is one of the best we have received from the Far East. The seeds were sent to Mr. A. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire by Dr. E. Bretschneider, without any particular mention. Cultivated under a frame, they have successively given us a dozen ruits, on which we will make our opinion known. These melons from China and Japan have a special flavor, which can in no way be compared to that of melons grown in Europe. We wouldn't accept them in France, after soup, like Cantaloups, Sucrins, etc. We can't, in our opinion, accept them in the same way. In our opinion, they can only be eaten for dessert. Melon Chayole should be picked very ripe, and only eaten when it has softened a little and yields to finger pressure. Then, for dessert, after having been peeled like a pear and cut into two or four parts, it is eaten with a generous sprinkling of sugar. Presented in this way, it looks like a bouquet to many people, but it should be considered as a fruit in its own right, forgetting that it's called a melon, and not wishing at all costs, as is commonly done, that it resemble what we already have. Oriental melons lend themselves better to confectionery than our own, which are watery. Nevertheless, with the possible exception of the Japanese Shiro uri, they are amateur plants that require as much care as the finest Cantaloupes. They are therefore not generally cultivated. Their singular shape may give rise to hybridization trials. MELON DE NOUMÉA OU DE LA DUMBÉA CUCUMIS PANCHERIANUS Ndn, Ann. des se. nat. ser. 4, vol. XII, p. 112, tab. 8, and ser. 5, vol. MELOTHRIA PENDULA L., Pluk, tab. 85, fig. 5. Fam. Cucurbitaceae. Annual, climbing plant, common in parts of North America, reported even in Guiana and Brazil by travelers who have visited these countries. Also found in China. M. Fontanier, French consul in Macao, sent some seeds to the Museum. This plant reaches 3 to 4 feet in height; its leaves are cordate, five-lobed or angular, and scabrous. The fertile (hermaphrodite) flowers are borne on simple, thread-like, pendulous stalks that are longer than the leaves. Male flowers are borne in clusters on peduncles about 6 cm long. The calyx teeth are tubular. Petals are obovate, deeply indented. The fruit is green, hairless, ellipsoidal and olive-shaped. Sloane says that the inhabitants of the regions where this plant grows sometimes pickle its fruits while they are still green. We have cultivated Melothrie pendante with complete success. We sowed it on a bed and under a frame, and put it in place at the end of May. Set up on a coarse, very wide-meshed trellis, it covered itself with abundant foliage and a multitude of pretty white-dotted fruits, the color, shape and volume of an Olive. We have put these fruits in vinegar, like gherkins; but we cannot recommend them for this use. Only more or less crunchy fruits should be used in pickles. Melothrie fruits are hollow and soft. They are pleasing in shape, color and abundance, but are of no real use. Mélothrie is an amateur plant. MIOGA ZINGIBER MIOGA ROSC. - Amonum Mioga Kæmpfer. Family Zingiberaceae. Perennial plant. Scaly, horizontally spreading rhizomes. Annual aerial stems, Om 50 to 0m, 60 high, simple, covered by leaf sheaths. Stem leaves alternate, distichous, simple, about Om, 20 long and Om, 5 to Om, 6 wide, lanceolate acuminate, light green, scarcely petiolate, ligulate; lateral veins extend from the median rib of the leaf blade. Peduncle arising from the stump, rising subterraneously, bearing an ovoid inflorescence composed of overlapping bracts, dotted with reddish-brown, unfolding five or six flowers at ground level; calyx tubular, split on one side and transparent; corolla with short tube, formed of three equal, lanceolate outer lobes, about Om, 3 long; labellum three-lobed, obovate, Om, 2 1/2 long. Mioga is native to Japan. It was described by Kæmpter in his book Amænitatum exoticarum..... fascicule V, page 826. It was collected by Thunberg, Siebold, Buerger and Mohnike (1), near Nangasaki. It grows spontaneously, but is generally cultivated. (1) Thunberg, Flora japonica, p. 24; Miquel, Prolusio Roræ Japonicæ, p. 304. In the book Le Japon à l'Exposition universelle de 1878, we read: "Mioga is a plant whose young stems and flowers are eaten. The fibers of its stems can also be used to make ropes". Fig. 52 - Zingiber Mioga. In the Note explicative des objets exposés par l'École agricole de Komaba, à l'Exposition universelle de 1889, (Ministère de l'Agriculture et du Commerce, Tokio, Japon) we find the following details: "Le Mioga (Amomum Mioga). Mioga flowers are harvested from the roots on the ground around June or July; they are shaped like spinning pins. The young stems, brewed in spring, are tender and taste just like the flowers". Dr. H*** wrote to us on April 11, 1879: "I am sending you a small root of a species of ginger called Mioga in Japan, and Amonum Mioga by Thunberg. The inflorescences are eaten before the flowers bloom; it's quite good. Although all Zingiberaceae are considered to be greenhouse plants, this plant has spent the winters perfectly at my place for the last three years, in the open ground, planted 0.10 m deep and covered in winter with a few dry leaves. It flowered well last summer. If the piece I'm sending you is a little small, it's because I haven't multiplied it much yet. The doctor wrote again on June 7 of the same year: "My Mioga plants have spent the winter perfectly in the open ground and are growing on all sides. If the too-small plant I sent you did not grow, I could send you as many as you would like next winter." We did not ask our kind correspondent for a second shipment. The section he had sent us had vegetated so well that we could plant it the following spring. As we can see from the date we received it, our Mioga withstood the harsh winter. It was, it must be said, protected by a thick blanket of snow; but in 1891, nothing defended it against the cold. We believe there is no plant hardier than the Mioga, nor one that multiplies more rapidly. We have not seen it affected by any disease, or attacked by any insect. We plant the rhizome sections in a garden bed 1.30 m wide, in two parallel lines, Om.50 apart, leaving a space of Om.40 between the lines and the paths, which does not prevent the plants from bearing their stems and inflorescences under them. There are very few weeds in the bed, and a hoeing or two does justice. Watering optional. Do not hoe after July 31st: you risk cutting off shoots and inflorescences. Weeding can be done by hand. Harvesting begins around August 15. Planting is monitored in the same way as for Asparagus; like Asparagus shoots, we cut close to the rhizome, as soon as the inflorescence shows its sharp tip on the surface of the soil. We've never cut off the shoots, except for a few to taste them, for fear of reducing propagation. They are harvested like the inflorescences, and we have found no appreciable difference between the flavor of one and the other. We assume that you should wait two years before harvesting shoots from a plantation, and only cut them in spring, although they are also produced in autumn. We would therefore regularly harvest inflorescences from August to September, and shoots from late April to late May. It would probably not be wise to extend the cutting beyond this period. We won't insist on Mioga's hardiness and rapid multiplication. We will talk about the uses to which its shoots and inflorescences can be put. Our correspondent wrote to us on August 18, 1880: "If you want to try tasting these Miogas, wash them carefully to remove any dust or earth that may have remained between the bracts, blanch them in boiling water with a little salt, pass them through cold water, then cook them for a moment in a sauce au jus, like onions, leeks or celery. It tastes very different from what we're used to eating; but, in my opinion at least, it's not bad." We tasted Mioga inflorescences prepared au gratin like macaroni, with alternating layers of vegetable and grated Parmesan: it's quite good. We ate them as a salad, after simply blanching them in boiling water. We found them very tasty. A slight resinous taste disappears after the second or third bite, and the slightly spicy flavor of the vegetable blends quite well with that of the oil. Finally, to make pickles, we combined Mioga inflorescences with West Indian Angouries, Catawissa Onion bulbs and Spanish Sweet Peppers. We were delighted with the result, and particularly recommend this use. We hope that people will persevere in trying out various culinary preparations; there's still a lot to do. To those who ask us if our vegetable resembles any of the others we use, we say: No, Mioga doesn't taste like cabbage, cardoon, artichoke or any of our other vegetables... it tastes like Mioga. 401 CRYPTOTÆNIA CANADENSIS DC; Chœrophyllum canadense Pers; Myrrhis canadensis Moris; Sium canadense Lamk; Conopodium canadense Koch. Solanaceae family. 403 The correspondence relating to the Fiji Islands, presented to both Houses of the English Parliament by order of His Majesty, in May 1862, is accompanied by an interesting appendix, consisting of a report by Doctor Seeman on the vegetable productions and resources of the Viti or Fiji Islands, in which a chapter, on page 58, is devoted to vegetables eaten with human flesh, a report from which we give the following extract: "Since, thanks to the influence of trade, Christian teaching and the presence of a British consul, cannibalism survives in only a small number of localities and is becoming every day, and more and more, a mere historical subject, it may be important to know this: human flesh, Fijians have repeatedly assured me, is extremely difficult to digest, and the healthiest men suffer for two or three days after eating it. No doubt to aid digestion, bokola, the technical name given to the flesh of the dead man, is always eaten with added vegetables. There are three main types of vegetable that Fijians believe should accompany bokola: Malawari leaves (Trophis anthropophagorum Seem.), Tudana (Omalanthus pedicellatus Benth.) and Borodina (Solanum anthropophagorum Seem.). The first two are medium-sized trees, growing spontaneously in many parts of the archipelago; but the Borodina is cultivated, and there are usually several large clumps near each "buré" (or foreigners' house), where the bodies of men killed in battle are always carried. "Borodina is a bushy shrub, rarely more than 6 feet tall, with dark, glossy foliage and berries the shape and color of tomatoes. This fruit has a slight aromatic odor and is accidentally prepared as Tomato sauce. The leaves of these three plants are rolled around the bokola, like those of Taro around pork, and cooked with it on heated stones. Salt is not forgotten. "While all other kinds of vegetables and meat are eaten with the fingers, cannibals' food is only touched with forks, generally made from the wood of the Nokonoko (Casuarina equisetifolia) or the Vesi (Afzelia bijuga A. Gray), bearing curious names and having three or four long tines. The reason given for this departure from the usual way of eating is the widespread belief that fingers that have touched the bokola can cause skin diseases when in contact with the delicate skin of children, and, as Fijians love their offspring dearly, they scrupulously make use of forks on the occasions indicated. "The Borodina mentioned above is the subject of today's plate (1). Our plants were obtained(1) Botanical Magazine, 3rd ser. t. XX, p. 5424. from seeds brought back by Dr. Seeman, and flowered in the greenhouse of the Royal Gardens in July. Except when bearing fruit, this species of Solanum has nothing to encourage cultivation. It is only of historical interest, linked to a practice that is falling further and further into disuse with each passing year". In 1878, we sowed Solanum anthropophagorum on a bed and under a frame. On June 2, we planted it outdoors on an old bed. At the beginning of September, quite a few fruits began to turn red. In October, these fruits not being ripe, we enclosed the plant in a glass cage, and shortly afterwards harvested its berries. They were dry, or at least not juicy enough to make a tomato-like sauce out of them. Annual plant, native to southern America, reaching about 1 meter in height, hairy, glandular, bearing yellowish spines on all parts. Stem woody at base. Leaves pinnatifid, five- or seven-lobed, irregularly toothed, bristling with coarse hairs, very thorny, decurrent.
