What we have to say about Morelle de Balbis will take up less space than its description and synonyms. The plant is more ornamental than edible and should not detain us for long. It acquires great proportions in rich soil. We obtained plants bearing both blue and white flowers, and it seemed to us that the fruits following the blue flowers were of a more beautiful red than those of the white-flowered plants. We measured the diameter and circumference of one planted on an old bed, and we regret not having kept the figures; the dimensions were enormous. The cultivation of S. Balbisii is the same as for tomatoes. It is sown in trays and under beds, planted at the end of May and ripens in September and October. Harvesting is difficult. The plant is equipped with innumerable thorns, which defend its approaches. We try to pick its pretty red berries, but usually give up. We do remember, however, seeing a Morelle de Balbis plant near the Museum's greenhouses, stripped of its fruit by passers-by as it ripened; but surely this innocent petty theft was not accomplished without spilling blood. The taste of S. Balbisii are quite insignificant. They could be preserved in caramel and fondant, like those of Physalis peruviana, which are much better; what we can say is that the plant is very beautiful and worthy of the attention of connoisseurs. MORELLE DE SALTA Small Salta Tomato. Under the name of Petite Tomate de Salta, Dr. Weber has given us seeds of a variety of Morelle de Balbis (Solanum sisymbriifolium). The description we have given of the latter is in every way applicable to the Petite Tomate de Salta. Its fruits are smaller and less abundant, but its leaves are more finely cut and of a brighter green. It's easy to grow, and its development is such that three plants are enough to form a large basket. It should therefore be grown exclusively as an ornamental plant. In this respect, we would prefer it to Morelle de Balbis; we thank Dr. Weber for introducing us to it. BIRD'S MORELLE SOLANUM AVICULARE Forst. (Syn.: S. laciniatum Ait.) Solanaceae family. This species is native to Australia and New Zealand. It is a shrub that can reach 3 meters in height and is cultivated in our European gardens for its ample, laciniated, highly ornamental foliage, as well as for its rather large, purplish-blue flowers. Dr. Kirk, from Wellington, New Zealand, author of important publications on the flora of New Zealand, was kind enough to send us seeds of this plant, which, he told us, the Maoris cultivate to eat the large berries, yellow, orange or violet in color, depending on the variety. Our kind correspondent also told us that these fruits are eaten either raw or cooked, but mostly in the first state. We have grown the plant in Crosnes, but have only harvested a very small number of fruits, absolutely comparable, incidentally, to those of Solanum laciniatum, which our gardeners use to form baskets in the gardens. The flavor of these fruits is nil. Morelle des Oiseaux deserves to be recommended as an ornamental plant, but does not seem to us to be of any interest as a food plant. MORELLE NODIFLORE SOLANUM NODIFLORUM Jacq. Icones rar. 2, tab. 326; Dunal, in DC. Prodr., XIII, 46; S. nigrum, var. patulum Lin. Solanaceae family. Very widespread in Mauritius and Rodriguez, and cultivated in vegetable gardens. Found throughout the tropics. Brède malgache (Flora of Mauritius and the Seychelles, Baker.) Annual plant, reaching 6 to 7 decimeters in height, with sub-frulescent, stalked, almost cylindrical, glabrous stems, with thickened nodes; leaves alternate, petiolate, ovate, acute, a little decurrent on the petioles, entire, glabrous and green on both sides; peduncle simple at the base, dividing at the top to form a kind of umbel composed of five or six flowers, small, whitish, with obtuse sepals; corolla deeply divided, lanceolate, acute, very open; berry round, small, black, shiny; seeds white. Grows in all tropical parts of the old and new continents. Morelle nodiflore seeds were brought to us from Nouméa by our correspondent, Mr. V. Perret. Sown in trays and planted in the ground in mid-May, they produce the most vigorous vegetation. The tops of the plant are edible, but we believe it prudent not to eat the fruit; several Solanum plants in this section have poisonous fruit. Is Solanum nodiflorum spontaneous or introduced to New Caledonia? We can't say, but it is found in the parts of the island furthest from the points occupied by Europeans. The plant is widely used in tropical regions, where it is used in calalou and vegetable soups. Several species of Solanum, such as S. oleraceum Dunal and S. nigrum L., are used in the same way. We tasted Nodiflora nightshade, chopped and prepared like spinach. We didn't like it; it had no flavor other than a slight bitterness. We're too rich in edible herbs - Spinach, Tetragona, Glacial, etc. - to recommend a plant that, in our opinion, is inferior. We felt, however, that a morello that is universally esteemed in warmer countries and easy to cultivate in our climate deserved a place in a curious gardener's kitchen garden. Our taste is not the law. MORELLE DE WALLIS Guayavo, Pepino, Melon Pear, Melon Shrub. SOLANUM MURICATUM Ait, var; S. Wallisii Carr; S. quatemalense Eisen. Solanaceae family. "Plant of great vigor, bushy, compact and very branched from its base, which becomes subfrutescent or even subligneous, nigrescent or better black in all its branches; branches and twigs numerous, slightly angular or subaligned. Leaves very long lanceolate, entire, very rarely and slightly lobed, about 12 centimeters long, 4 centimeters wide, regularly attenuated at the tip; petioles 5-7 centimeters long, purple-black, as are the veins. Flowers gathered in a kind of scorpioid corymb, solitary on a pedicel of about 15-20 millimeters, black, strongly villeinous. Calyx with short oval divisions, very long-lasting. Corolla spreading, 25-30 millimeters wide, glossy dark violet, divisions abruptly narrowed and acuminate at the tip; stamens included, with threads shorter than the anthers. Fruits elongated, heart-shaped, reaching about 6 cm long by 4 cm, sometimes more, in Fig. 53 - Wallis nightshade. diameter, regularly attenuated at the apex, which is abruptly rounded, slightly narrowed at the base, on which the calyx divisions are applied; skin smooth and very plain, shiny, of a very beautiful mottled violet, dotted, often here and there banded or widely spotted. Flesh yellowish-white, thick, melting, very juicy, slightly pungent flavor, reminiscent of melon, slightly sweet, but with a peppery, pungent aftertaste. Seeds borne on a sort of fleshy central placenta, erect in the center of the fruit". E.-A. Carrière (1). After giving this description, Mr. Carrière continues: "The qualities we have just mentioned are those we have observed in fruit that ripened in our greenhouse, and which consequently could not reach the perfection they should acquire in equatorial climates. In Nice, the fruit already appears to be of superior quality, judging by what Mr. Ch. Huber has told us. In a letter from Nice, dated January 13 1877, he says: "I have just eaten another Solanum Wallisii fruit, and I am extremely satisfied with its good taste; the flesh, very melting, yellow in color, like that of a Prune ReineClaude, is very sweet. For the fruit to acquire this quality, you need to wait until it has reached a tender consistency, leave it to rest and avoid squeezing it by hand, as is often done, which detracts from the good taste. The plants I left in the ground did not suffer from the cold of December, and are growing as well as if they were in a greenhouse. For northern countries, I think a cold greenhouse will suffice to overwinter them... I also made some (] Note on the S. Wallisit, colored figure (Revue horticole, 1877). p. 291). prepare them cooked, and I have found that they make a delicious dish". The Wallis nightshade was introduced to Europe by Mr. Wallis, who bought the fruit at the market in Guayaquil (Ecuador), where it is sold under the name of Guayavos. The fruit is highly prized by the locals, who eat it raw or cooked. Mr. Ch. Huber received the seeds from Mr. Ortgies, sowed them on December 12 1875, and, provided with numerous plants, put the plant on the market. We then tried its cultivation, and one of us, in a letter of which we reproduce a part, informed M. Carrière of the results he had obtained: "Cuttings of Morelle de Wallis are taken outdoors as easily as those of Pelargoniums, and the plant provides them abundantly. I took a good number of them last August; they spent the winter under glass, side by side with the Pelargoniums. Only the mother plant died. "When spring came, I kept eight of them, four of which were kept in pots. The other four were planted in the ground, poorly protected by a frame that was constantly raised 25 or 30 centimetres above the trunk. This allowed air to circulate under the trunk. It had to be lifted to straighten the plant, which doesn't rise much, but whose stems I didn't want to drag along the ground, as they would have immediately taken root, which I wanted to avoid. "The plants vegetated vigorously, and were constantly disbudded. Only three or four branches were retained, and they were continually crowned with charming bouquets of flowers. Cuttings kept in pots, also placed under a well-ventilated frame, produced many flowers, but did not set a single fruit. "Of the four plants planted in the open ground, only one set three fruits. Two of these fruits are already much larger than the one shown in our Revue; the third is still growing and looks set to reach the same size. These fruits are of rare beauty. They have been tied since July 1st (1). "The details I've just gone into make it clear where I went wrong. The season having been colder than usual, I should have given my plants a little more warmth. I didn't, and I was wrong. Now let's look to the future. "Wallis nightshade is extremely hardy, in the sense that its cuttings take root in the open air, that its vegetation is always very active, and that no disease or insect seems to be able to compromise its cultivation. "What does it need? A little more heat than I've been giving it. This is no problem for gardeners or market gardeners. Take cuttings in August, keep them over winter in a frame, bring them forward a little in spring on a warm bed, disbud them carefully, remove half the flowers from each bunch - these are the tips I can give today. We are convinced that Wallis nightshade can be grown without difficulty. However, it (1) One of these fruits, fully ripe on September 2, measured 9 centimetres in height and 27 in circumference. Its shape was reminiscent of an unflattened ox heart; its smooth, shiny skin was marbled with violet pink; it was indeed of rare beauty (Rédaction de la Revue horticole). will always require more care in our climate than it deserves. We tasted the fruit we obtained. They were superb, perfectly ripe, fleshy, juicy and appetizing. We were full of illusions about the result. The curious will understand the bitterness of our disappointment; our fruit tasted like cucumbers and left an unpleasant tingle on the tongue. We put them in compote, and they were no better. So why did we just talk about them at length? It's because these beautiful fruits, certainly very good in Guayaquil, could be a useful acquisition for the Mediterranean coast and for Algeria; it's because, after all, we don't just write for the outskirts of Paris. MOTSIJI BIDENS PILOSA Lin; Ceratocephalus pilosus Rich; Kerneria dubia Coss; Kerneria tetragona Mœnch. Family Compositae. Egyptian bean, Egyptian pink lily. Pytagorian Bean. NELUMBIUM SPECIOSUM Willd. ; Nelumbo nucifera Gærtn. Family Nelombonaceae. 423 Perennial aquatic plant, native to southern Asia, once widespread in Egypt, where it was introduced and from which it has long since disappeared. It was one of the Lotus species of the Nile; the Egyptians deified it and depicted its flowers and fruits on most of their monuments. Later, they searched in vain for it in the waters of the Nile, and for a long time it was known only from medals and hieroglyphics. The descriptions given of it were all imaginary and erroneous, and only served to confuse the question of its identification. In 1602, the plant was finally discovered in its native India, and the learned botanist Lécluse (Clusius) was able to recognize that Nelumbo and the famous Egyptian plant belonged to one and the same species. This aquatic plant, one of the most beautiful known, is composed of a tracer rhizome, underground, more or less branched, equipped with swellings or nodosities from which the leaves are born, with cylindrical, needled petioles; some with a floating, peeled, flat blade; others rising up to 75 centimetres above the surface of the water, orbicular, with cup-shaped raised edges, about 25 centimetres wide. The upper surface of the leaves is rough, and water rolls over them like crystal globules. The flower blooms in July-August. It rises on a peduncle that starts on the stump and reaches or even exceeds the highest leaves. It is around 25 centimetres wide, with some twenty petals, whitish at the base and pink at the top. The stamens are numerous and have Fig. 56 - Indian Nelumbo (Nelumbium speciosum). extrinsic anthers, whereas in the Nymphaea they are introrsic. The fruit, shaped like an inverted cone, has a flat upper surface with some twenty cells, each containing a seed the size of a small hazelnut. The fruit resembles a watering can apple with large holes. This is the most famous and beautiful of all aquatic food plants. It could have been the subject of a long and interesting article, if, fortunately for the reader, we hadn't been pre-empted by the Bulletin de la Société nationale d'Acclimatation. In his work entitled Les Productions végétales du Japon, Dr. Mène says it all, without prolixity or omission, about Nelumbo nucifera. On pages 376 et seq. of the separate edition, you'll find all you need to know about the plant's nutritional and medicinal uses. The author reminds us that, among the Egyptians, the Nelumbo flower, under the name Lotus, was a sacred flower, and that today it still occupies the same rank in India, China, Japan, etc. We recommend reading the entire chapter devoted to Nelumbo, borrowing only what the author has to say about its food uses: "Its rhizomes and seeds are used in Japanese cuisine. Mounds of Lotus rhizomes, known as Hasu-none, can be found on the markets of Japan, as well as in China, Cochinchina and the kingdom of Siam. The taste of these rhizomes, when cooked, is reminiscent of that of turnip, cardoon and celery; they are eaten raw, boiled in water and ashes, boiled or fried like salsify; they are also ground to a powder, dried and used especially in soups; they yield a pinkish-white starch, which was featured in the Japanese section of the World's Fair and is used in soups. "As for the seeds, which taste a little like hazelnuts and sweet almonds, they are edible and the Japanese eat them with their meals as sweet dishes; they are used to make cakes and pastries. Dr. E. Bretschneider wrote to us on June 7, 1887: "The Chinese eat the rhizomes of this plant raw or cooked, but a starch is prepared from them which is an excellent food for small children; it makes a good porridge in water and milk. Rhizomes are harvested in autumn, when they are very rich in starch. It is widely consumed in China, and tastes excellent. "Nelumbium seeds are eaten both green and ripe, but taste better when green. They are also eaten toasted, and are widely used in China. "The starch is sold everywhere under the name Ngeonfen. R. P. David, for his part, gives information that shows the usefulness of Nelumbo: "I have seen that, throughout China, the magnificent Nelombonée with its large purpurinous flowers, known as Nelumbium speciosum, is highly esteemed, not only for its beauty, but as a food and medicinal plant. But until now, I've only seen the roots and seeds used as they are, or seasoned with sugar. In Tzitan, and perhaps elsewhere, we know how to extract a white starch from this large root, which is said to be very corroborating. To prepare a bowl, a single spoonful of this flour is placed at the bottom of the vase, and boiling water is poured over it, while a small stick is used to shake it rapidly. "This white material loses its color almost immediately, to resemble gelatin, and all the water in the bowl is transformed into a beautiful, transparent, consistent mass, but on cooling it becomes brown and solid. Mixed with a little sugar, Ngeon-fen is excellent for those who are ill, and also for those who are not." When in bloom, Nelumbium speciosum forms one of the most beautiful adornments of the Srinagar lake (Kashmir); its cheerful green foliage completely covers the waters, and from this green surface emerge myriads of peduncles terminating in enormous pink flowers reminiscent of our most beautiful Peonies. These flowers of a sacred plant are placed in temples and in the private oratories of the Hindus and renewed every morning for the duration of the flowering period. The leaves, which are of a very strong fabric, measure 45 centimetres or more in diameter. In the edge of these leaves, a rush is passed which serves as a lace and is intended to raise them so as to hold liquid food. This type of vegetable crockery, unknown in France, is then placed in the shade to dry. It is on these leaves that the great lords of Kashmir have their food served, and as these improvised vessels are only used once, they are assured that their dishes are always clean. Nelumbium seed is very good when fresh, and its taste is reminiscent of hazelnut. Consumption is low, as the flowers are cut to decorate temples. In autumn, when vegetation ceases, the young, undeveloped leaves forming a kind of turion are harvested by the natives, bundled and sold on the Srinagar market. These shoots have the length and appearance of beautiful asparagus and are called Nadrou. The natives, who are very fond of them, eat them cooked. Europeans make no use of them; however, Mr. L. Bouley, Director of Cultivation for H.H. the Maharadja of Kashmir, has eaten them with kari, and assures us that this dish is not to be despised. We have gathered the above curious information from the dictation of Mr. Ermens, the Maharadja's former Director of Cultivation, and from an article by his successor, Mr. L. Bouley, published in the Revue Horticole, March 16 1884. In August 1835, Raffeneau-Delile, Professor of Botany at the Montpellier Academy of Medicine and Director of the Jardin des Plantes, published a paper in the Bulletin de la Société d'Agriculture du département de l'Hérault, entitled: Acclimatization du Nelumbium speciosum dans le midi de la France. In it, he dwelt on the plant's historical interest and its uses as an architectural ornament and religious attribute, but made light of its nutritional properties: "The Lotus of ancient Egypt," he said, "grew in lakes on which people sailed in boats. Its broad leaves rose out of the water enough to shelter the boats, or perhaps to cover them. They were the size of Thessalian hats and conveniently served as dishes and cups, so that Alexandria's stores were well stocked with them...". He reported on the culling processes he had applied to the Nélumbo and the happy results he had obtained. He concluded by saying: "Our plant, because of its rarity, had the privilege of being much visited and much admired, attracting a number of people who learned with interest that it is useful for its seeds and roots, which are good for food in India; but this quality of food is base, without merit, in comparison with the elegance, color and pleasantly aniseed fragrance of its flowers". At the time, Nélumbo was being cultivated for the first time in the open air, and Raffeneau-Delile took infinite precautions to ensure its success; but today this cultivation is well known and no longer presents any difficulties. M. Planchon, professor of botany and director of the Jardin des plantes de Montpellier, wrote to us: "We didn't need to hybridize Nelumbium to cultivate these beautiful plants in the Midi and even in central France. The rough-leaved form, called by Delile asperifolium, can withstand our harshest winters here. It's probably the same variety that flourished, before 1880, in a large pond in the Parc de Baleine, in the Allier region, then belonging to the uncle of Mr. Doumet-Adanson, the current owner. "All the plants were killed by the exceptional winter of 1880. I suppose you could also grow the plant at Crosnes; but I fear that, for want of light, even more than heat, these splendid plants will not flower as easily as they do under our sun." In 1887, we immersed a few Nelumbium plants in Crosnes. They soon disappeared. M. Planchon's letter shows that Lotus cultivation is easy in the south of France and practical in central France. Farther north, however, it would be pointless to try it with the aim of harvesting rhizomes and seeds; this would be a luxury crop, the procedures for which have been known for a long time. In this respect, Nelumbium cannot be grown in the Paris climate. NUPHAR AUVENUM Ait. Ta-wah-pah. Northern American species. Its roots grow 4 or 5 feet deep in water, and Indian women pull them up and collect large quantities. The roots are 1 to 2 feet long, porous, sweet-tasting and glutinous; they are usually eaten boiled with wild birds, but often roasted. Large quantities of these roots are kept in homes as winter provisions. The plant is called Ta-wah-pah by the Dakota Indians. The seeds are an important foodstuff for the Klamath Indians of California, who pulverize them to make bread; they are also eaten toasted (1). NUPHAR MULTISEPALUM Engelm. Fam. des Solanées Perennial plant, with spindly, sarmentose or recumbent stems, the lower ones radicating; leaves small, unequal, petiolate; flowers white, solitary, rarely geminate, pendant. Calyx 2 to 3 millimeters in diameter, cupuliform, with five narrow divisions that persist at the base of the fruit; corolla tubular, white, 2 to 3 1/2 millimeters long by 2 to 3 wide, glabrous, with oblong linear divisions having their tips curved; berry oblong oval, 2 to 3 centimeters long by 1 centimeter wide, first green, then white, finally rust-colored near the stalk. This plant is found in Magella, in the pampas of Buenos-Ayres, Montevideo, southern Brazil. According to Dombey, the fruit is sour and can be eaten. Mr. Charles Barbier harvested the plant in the Buenos-Ayres pampas and was kind enough to give us the seed. Here is the information he gave us: "The fruits of the plant are perfectly edible. In La Plata, children seek them out and Fig. 57. - Rooster eggs (Salpichroa rhomboidea.) are feasted on. They are also made into a popular household jam, with the addition of sugar and herbs to make them more tasty. I enjoyed eating it. This plant is very hardy and productive. It's worth trying to improve it. The plant has long existed at the Muséum, but does not bear fruit there. To obtain fruit, it must be trellised against a wall at midday; it is then covered with thousands of small white berries resembling swallow eggs. Perennial because of its roots, it grows back each spring, and it's quite difficult to clear the soil of it. In August 1877, we presented Oufs de Coq to the Société d'Horticulture, under the name Withania origanifolia (1); in October of the same year, we exhibited (Henri Véniat, gardener) a Salpichroa plant laden with a multitude of its pretty white berries, and jams made from these fruits. Here's the recipe for these jams (Mamoz): "Cook the fruit in as many liters of water as kilograms of fruit, boiling for fifteen or twenty minutes. "Remove, strain through cheesecloth while hot; weigh and add equal weight of sugar, set on fire. "Add 20 to 50 grams of Japanese glue, depending on the consistency you wish to give the jam. "Cook until a drop placed on a plate holds together halfway. (1) This is the name under which the plant was cultivated in the botanical garden of the Muséum at the time. "The grating of a Lemon is enough for 5 pounds of fruit; it is obtained by rubbing sugar on the Lemon: the sugar is then crushed, dissolved in a spoonful of water, which is poured over the jam at the last moment. It's important that the lemon doesn't cook. In our opinion, Rooster Eggs are more of a curiosity than a useful plant. This is also the conclusion of the notes published on this plant by Mr. Ed. Zuccagnianum, 1 m to 1r.50 high, non-spiny, with cylindrical, green, slightly rough stems, branched from the base; leaves oval, attenuated at both ends, with petiole about 3 cm long; blade 10 to 12 cm long by 5 to 6 cm wide, with uneven base, sinuous margins, covered over all its parts with star-shaped hairs. The seeds were given to us by Mr. Pobéguin, attached to the Brazza mission, who told us that the fruits are eaten like peppers in the Congo. For us, the Olivaire is of no interest from a food point of view. OLLUCO Ulluco, Melloco, Papa lisa; Uyuca or Rouba (Venezuela). ULLUCUS TUBEROSUS Lozano. Chenopoda family. Perennial plant. Tubers rounded, hardly exceeding, in our climate, the volume of a large Walnut, pink, very smooth, with yellowish flesh, mucilaginous or starchy when the tuber reaches full maturity, developing on rhizomes which originate at the base of the stems; these, branched and creeping, take root at every point where they touch the ground; the leaves are alternate, thick, spatulate, shiny green, with a fairly long, reddish petiole. Flowers are small, greenish, axillary and do not ripen their seeds in our climate. Native to the Andes. It is with regret that we devote a chapter of this book to a plant whose cultivation has been experimented for three years, with great care, at the Muséum, by M. Louis Vilmorin, in the garden of the Société nationale d'Horticulture, etc., and whose rare tubers have been unanimously declared inedible. But Ulluco belongs to the history of attempts to introduce exotic food plants, and it is for this reason alone that it has a place here. We shall therefore limit ourselves to indicating the sources from which we can, if the desire arises, draw all possible information on the Chilean Chenopodea. Mr. Ed. André has kindly sent us the following note on the plant he observed at the Pasto market (New Granada): "Ollocos (Ullucus tuberosus). This vegetable, generally detestable, is represented here by several varieties: violet, white, yellow, green and salmon pink, among which several are really not bad and can almost equal Ocas." In 1895, Messrs Vilmorin-Andrieux and Cte sent us tubers of a plant they had received from Mr. Bourgoin, of Merida (Venezuela), under the name Uyuca or Rouba, accompanied by the following letter: "I have the pleasure of sending you some tubers of Uyuca or Rouba. These tubers are edible and, when cultivated, quite floury; they taste more or less like potatoes, but the family to which they belong is different; it's an Oxalidae. They are mainly used candied in vinegar with chillies. "I believe that this crop would be perfectly successful in France, as the plant is only found here on the high mountains, in what we call the cold country (average temperature of -10 to 12°)". We planted these tubers in the spring of 1896, and they developed leafy stems which enabled us to recognize them as Olluco. The tubers were so much larger and of such a different shape to those we had grown up until then, that we had not had the idea of attaching them to this plant when they came to us. GABON OLOMBE SOLANUM PIERREANUM Paill. et Bois. Solanaceae family. Annual plant, erect, about 1 meter high, completely inert, covered with white starry hairs on all parts: stems, leaves, peduncles, calyx, outer part of corolla. Stem cylindrical, branched, blackish-purple. Leaves alternate, first purple, then green, except for the veins, which retain their primilive color; petiole about 5 centimeters long; blade oval, acuminate, 10 to 15 centimeters long, measuring 6 to 8 centimeters at its widest point, almost entire or sinewy, with very prominent veins on the underside. Peduncles opposite the leaves or most often arising from the internodes, about 2 centimeters long, sometimes uniflorous, usually bifurcated and bearing two flowers, rarely triflores. Calyx campanulate, 7 to 8 millimeters long, with 5 or 6 shallow, triangular divisions, accrescent after anthesis; corolla about 2 centimeters in diameter, with 5 or 6 spreading, slightly purplish-white divisions; stamens with very short threads, linear anthers, opening at the apex with two pores, about two-thirds the length of the corolla; pistil the same length as the stamens, with a straight style ending in an obliquely inserted stigma. Fruits sometimes solitary, more often geminate, rarely grouped in threes, borne on swollen pedicels Fig. 59. - Olombé from Gabon (Solanum Pierreanum) conical, pendulous, ribbed like those of S. Gilo Raddi, spherical, depressed at the bottom and top, 3 to 4 centimeters in diameter and 2 to 2 1/2 centimeters thick, colored greenish-red and flamed purple-brown. Olombé seeds were sent to the Museum by Mr. Pierre, Director of the Colonial Garden in Libreville (Gabon). They have been sent to us by Mr. Maxime Cornu. The fruits of this Solanum are apparently eaten by the Pahouins. In 1888, we first sowed the plants in March, under a frame. The plants vegetated well, flowered abundantly, but did not set fruit. In 1889, we sowed again, under the same conditions, but transplanted most of the plants outdoors. This time we obtained a few bright red fruits, flamed black, which we tasted and which did not seem usable to us; but we must say that the plant, sent by us to Mr. Latour-Marliac, of Temple-sur-Lot, was covered at his place with pretty fruits and showed itself, under the climate of Lot-et-Garonne, decidedly ornamental. Olombé is a new Solanum that will be cultivated beyond the Loire, if not for the table, at least for garden decoration. RUMEX ABYSSINICUS Jacq. ? Fam. Polygonaceae. 445 The seeds of this plant were entrusted to us by Mr. Maxime Cornu, professor-administrator at the Muséum, who had received them from Mr. Blaise, a ship's lieutenant, with the following indication: "Oseille Pahouine. Large size. Excellent for eating. From around Donguilah (Gabon)". M. Cornu presented four plants to the Sociélé nationale d'Horticulture de France on July 2, 1896. We sowed these seeds under a frame in the spring of 1896. The resulting young plants were planted outdoors in the first days of June. They grew vigorously, so much so that by autumn they had reached over 1 metre in height and produced abundant, ample, tender, slightly acidic leaves. The plants were ready to bloom, but the first cold spells came before the flower stems could develop. By this time, the clumps had become very large. We lifted some of them into pots to overwinter under glass; unfortunately, they died before the warm weather returned. In 1897, Mr Grosdemange, head of the nursery and vegetable garden, took cuttings from them, which took root without difficulty. Pahouine sorrel is a plant which, thanks to its abundant production of leaves that can be used like ordinary sorrel, is destined to be of great service in hot climates. It is particularly worthy of our colonists' attention. We cannot guarantee the specific identification of this plant, of which we have only been able to observe the leaves and seed. However, from what we have been able to see, Pahouine sorrel is, if not Rumex abyssinicus, at least a very close relative. R. abyssinicus Jacq. (R. arifolius Ait.) is native to Abyssinia, but exists, naturalized (?) in Réunion; according to M. Cordemoy (Flore de la Réunion, p. 285), it abounds in the Plaine des Palmistes and is common in the middle region. On Reunion Island, the plant is known as Oseille sauvage, and its leaves are used as a vegetable. Canaigre sorrel RUMEX HYMENOSEPALUS Torr. Another species of sorrel, Canaigre (Rumex hymenosepalus Torr.), deserves the attention of growers in the Mediterranean region. Dr. Trabut, Government Botanist, Algiers, has published a note on this plant in the Journal de la Société nationale d'Horticulture de France, 1896, p. 383, in which he highlights its industrial and nutritional merits. Canaigre is a Patience native to southern California, Arizona and northern Texas. In these regions, this large sorrel covers immense areas; it vegetates during the winter, then disappears during the dry season. Its tuberous root is reminiscent of that of the Dahlia; it contains very high proportions of tannin, and factories are already preparing highly esteemed tannin extracts on the spot. Mr. Trabut has continued to study the acclimatization of Canaigre in Algeria, where this Polygonaea seems to have found a suitable climate. Struck by the extent of the plant's foliage and its abundance, he had the leaves prepared in the manner of sorrel and, he says, obtained a very acceptable dish, reminiscent of ordinary Patience (Rumex Patientia), which, in his opinion, is too little used. I don't think," he adds, "that this new vegetable is destined to take a major place in consumption, but it should be mentioned; and, because of its hardiness, it deserves a place in the gardens of growers in southern countries. Canaigre is slightly laxative; in this respect, it can be sought after as a hygienic food. Canaigre is grown at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle, where it flowered and fructified in 1897. Root perennial, long, fleshy, thick; stems numerous, herbaceous, often reaching over I meter in height, adults glabrous, young pubescent; petioles sheathing, with dilated, gutter-shaped base; compound leaves, with oval or heart-shaped, acuminate, saw-toothed, pubescent leaflets; small, greenish flowers in globose umbels with a small oligophyll involucre, arranged in a compound cluster. Calyx adherent to ovary, with very short, 5-toothed blade; corolla with 5 petals; 5 stamens; ovary inferere, with 5-10 lodges; 5 divergent styles; fruit drupaceous, blackish-brown, crowned by calyx and styles, with 5-10 monosperm pits. "Udô flowers in August; its fruit ripens in November. Its herbaceous stems perish with the first frosts of winter. "This plant probably comes from China, where it is used as a sudorific remedy; it is cultivated throughout Japan, in gardens and fields. "It is mainly cultivated for its root, which has a pleasant, aromatic and bitter taste, and is eaten in winter seasoned in the manner of our Scorsonères. The young stems serve as a delicious vegetable. "As the plant thrives throughout Japan, it would acclimatize just as well in our gardens; it would therefore be desirable that, cultivated here, it should increase the number of our vegetable foods by a pleasant, fine and nourishing dish". (Siebold and Zuccarini, Flora Japonica, I, p. 57). In the Note explicative des objets exposés par l'École agricole et forestière de Komaba à l'Exposition universelle de 1889 (Ministry of Agriculture and Trade, Tokio, Japan), we read: "Oudô (Aralia cordata). To cultivate it, we make pits and put its roots in them, after having given the fertilizer of horse dung, spread on the surface of the earth. This operation takes place during the very cold season. The roots sprout white buds. It's a vegetable with a delicate taste and a pleasant smell." Our excellent correspondent, Dr. H***, wrote to us on April 25 1879: "The only vegetable I regret not having brought with me is an Araliaceae called Oudô, Aralia cordata de Thunberg, in Japan. The young shoots are harvested wild in spring and eaten cooked, just as we eat celery and cardoons. It is very strong and very bad, as is unbleached Celery; but Oudô, cultivated and blanched under leaves or litter, is very good, and is eaten in the spring." It will be noted that our correspondent does not mention, as Siebold did, the use of Oudo roots in cooking. 28 As early as 1879, we asked Japan for Aralia cordata seedlings. We received seeds, not plants, in the spring of 1883; but to obtain germination of Aralia seeds, they must be sown immediately after the harvest, so ours did not germinate. Thanks to the kind assistance of MM. Vilmorin-Andrieux et Cie, we received, a few years later, ten perfectly healthy plants of the Japanese variety. The Oudò thrived perfectly at Crosnes, proving just as hardy and easy to grow as the North American Aralia racemosa, from which it hardly differs, grown in all botanical gardens, where it is so invasive that it is difficult to keep clumps to a minimum. We stretched the plant, and the shoots obtained had the appearance of medium-sized asparagus; they were white and very appetizing. Unfortunately, the tasting was not favorable; we found them to have a turpentine flavor, admittedly weak, but too pronounced for this vegetable to be adopted in Europe. This failure is all the more regrettable as the plant is very productive and would come to our gardens almost care-free. Chopped and cooked young leaves have given us an acceptable aromatic vegetable, but of no particular merit. Another Araliaceae, Stilbocarpa polaris Decaisne et Planchon (Aralia polaris Hombron et Jacquinot), deserves experimental cultivation in our climate. This perennial plant is native to New Zealand and the Auckland and Campbell Islands. Its long rhizomes are fleshy, sweet and edible. Information on this plant can be found in Flore de la Nouvelle-Zélande, by Hooker f., vol. I, p. 95, and Mueller, Select extra-tropical Plants, p. 324. OXALIS CRENATA Jacq. Family Oxalidae. Perennial; roots tuberous, the shape and diameter of a large walnut; stems ascending, succulent, twining; leaves trifoliate, with obovate leaflets, a little thick; in May-September, flowers large, Fig. 60 - Crenellated Oxalis (Oxalis crenata). yellow, in umbels longer than the leaves; petals crenate. Oxalis crenata was imported from Lima to England around 1829, from where it soon spread to France. In Peru, it is known as Oca. In 1850, Mr. Boursier, French consul in Quito, sent the Museum the red Oca, a variety considered in Peru to be much preferable to the yellow Oca. We remember growing Oxalis crenata in the Landes department of France, and obtaining very good harvests without difficulty. We punctually followed the instructions provided to us by the Maison rustique and by Le Bon Jardinier. We have borrowed from the latter the cultivation methods that have worked well for us: "When properly cultivated, the plant produces a quantity of small yellow tubers that rarely reach the volume of a hen's egg, but whose number is sometimes enormous. This large-scale multiplication is achieved by ridging, or rather by continuous layering, as we'll explain shortly. The tubers contain 10 to 12% starch, but differ essentially in quality from those of the potato, to which Oxalis has been inappropriately compared; they are easy to cook and provide a healthy, light, fairly pleasant food, with a slightly acid taste, which can be removed by cooking them three-quarters of the way through in water. The leaves and tops of the shoots can be used in place of sorrel, of which they have the same flavor; in Lima, they are also eaten in salads. Cultivation is not difficult; the tubers can be brought forward in layers in March, for planting at the beginning of May, or planted permanently around mid-April, or planted by cuttings, which take root with great ease. Soft, light, well-amended soil is best. The distance between plants should be around 1 metre; a single row in a 1n.30 bed is enough to fill the soil at the end of the season. According to Mr. Guesnet, you should start buttering as soon as the shoots are Om, 08 to Om, 10 in length; you first mound in the center, spreading them apart, to force them into a horizontal direction; then, as they lengthen, you refill them moderately with new soil and continue regularly until September, when the tubers start to form.The tubers are pulled out as late as possible, when the stems have been destroyed by frost; the tops can then be cut off and the clumps covered with dry leaves; the tubers keep and even thrive under this covering, as M. Redouté has found. Torn up, they keep very well through the winter, kept in a healthy place and buried in very dry sand. "The red Oca, received by the Museum in 1850 from Mr. Boursier, French consul in Quito, is a variety of Oxalis crenata, from which it differs in the color of the tuber, whose skin is a bright carmine red, and in its slightly spindlier stems, colored reddish purple and remarkable for their extreme flexibility. Its tubers seem to us to be neither larger nor more abundant than those of the old yellow variety, although, according to M. Boursier, the red Oca is considered in Peru to be far superior to the yellow Oca". We have said that we have grown Oxalis crenata in the Landes department, and that we have done so with great success. We must add that the tasting had not been favorable to it and that we had given up its cultivation; but we had tried it in 1849, and Weddell's Note, which is of such keen interest and which we are going to reproduce, had not yet appeared. We therefore absolutely reserve our opinion. Weddell's note (1). - I hasten to say that, to my taste, this vegetable is almost the equal of the potato when properly prepared. The way to grow Oxalis is well known, so I'll deal without preamble with the question of the treatment the tubers require to become edible: "When Ocas are pulled, they are always more or less acidic; however, their degree of acidity differs with the varieties. As a general rule, white varieties are much less acidic than red varieties. Whatever the variety in question, sufficiently prolonged exposure to the sun constantly leads to the disappearance or more or less complete metamorphosis of its acidic principle. In a word, something quite analogous to the ripening of fruit takes place. A white Oca (Oca bianca) treated in this way no longer retains any trace of acidity, and is in no way inferior to a good potato. "Exposure to the sun, whose sole purpose is to destroy the acidic principle of Ocas, should last from six to ten days, and even a little longer, depending on the variety of Oca. The operation is best performed in large woolen bags. The changes that take place in the tissue of the tubers seem to be facilitated by this means, and they can be turned over more conveniently; but the bag must contain few enough tubers that, when spread out on the ground, they form only a very thin layer under their envelope. (1) Remarks on some edible tubers, by M. Weddell, assistant naturalist at the Muséum (Revue horticole, 1852, p. 148). "When exposure to the sun is prolonged much longer, for several months for example, tuber ripening goes much further. The Oca then loses most of its juices and takes on the consistency of a prune, while acquiring a very pronounced sweet taste; this is what is known as Caui." I don't need to tell you that, in the two preparations just mentioned, you must be careful not to let the tubers freeze. "On the contrary, jelly is the main agent in the preparation known as Caia, which I'd like to talk about. Caia or Chuno de Oca is made in the same way as Chuno blanc des Pommes de terre, with the difference that after the tubers have been frozen, they are not macerated in running water, but in still water. Under these circumstances, the Oca becomes partially corrupted and, when dried out, retains an odor and taste that I will simply compare to those of some cheeses. The Indians consume a great deal of Caia, which they no doubt find very tasty. As for me, I can in no way recommend it. I've already stated my opinion on the other forms of Oca, and I won't go into them again. However, I think it useful to point out that in Bolivia, the tubers of this Oxalis, in addition to their intrinsic qualities, have another which is of no small importance: they are multiplied more abundantly than potatoes themselves in La Paz; they cost at most half as much as potatoes. On the one hand, in the Paris climate, Oralis crenata can only be harvested in October, and its tubers are unpleasantly acidic. On the other hand, the only way we are taught to eliminate this acidity is to expose the crop to the sun for at least six to ten days. How can we count on good weather and sufficient warmth in October? It seems clear to us that the experiment should have been carried out on the Mediterranean coast and not elsewhere, and that time and effort were wasted in carrying it out on the outskirts of Paris. It's true that in 1835 we learned that a skilled English gardener named Pringle had found a cultivation method that enabled Oxalis to be harvested in August, and Poiteau, the eminent gardener, botanist and painter, not concealing the jealousy he felt as a French horticulturist, exclaimed: "As for me, I won't sleep again until I've found Mr. Pringle's secret, or at least obtained a result similar to his". What has become of gardener Pringle's discovery? Do the English accept the acidity of Oxalis? The English sun, whose reputation is well established, certainly can't make it go away. Mr. Ed. André, on his trip to New Granada, collected some interesting information on Oxalis crenata. He kindly shared with us the following lines from his travel notes: "Ocas de Pasto are widely cultivated and consumed in these cold regions, and there are more than ten varieties. They should be cultivated more seriously here than is usually the case; don't forget to dry them in the sun to develop their sweetness. Cooked in water, they are very good; they are peeled by turning them by hand in a servielte. Their starch is very fine and they have a pleasant, tangy taste. Varieties are round or long, pink, white, violet, yellow, wine-red, etc. ". Every year, a few tubers of crenellated Oxalis can be seen on the shelves of exotic produce retailers and a few grocers. The red variety is offered as an excellent vegetable. One of us saw some beautiful red tubers on the market in Pau. In the country, they are eaten simply boiled or fried whole in the pan. We don't expect the sale of Oxalis to expand much in Paris. The price will always be too high for its merit. We have read what Messrs. Weddell and Ed. André have to say about sun-drying Oxalis tubers. In our trials, instead of the sun, we used the oven, as is done for prunes. We ate Oxalide fresh, in compote and cooked salad; then, dry, in the same two ways. We found no appreciable difference. If pruned tubers are soaked in water for a few hours, they regain their original volume. They can then be used in compote with wine and sugar, like Prunes, which they taste a little like; or in salad, with a slightly spicy seasoning. In both cases, they are absolutely tender. OXALIDE DE DEPPE OXALIS TETRAPHYLLA Cav. var. Deppei; O. Deppei Sweet. Family Oxalidae. Perennial plant. Root tuberous, napiform, surmounted by small bulbiform buds; petioles 12 to 15 cm long, pubescent in youth, glabrous thereafter, bearing four wedge-shaped, obcordate leaflets, 3 R Fig. Gl. - Deppe's Oxalid. sessile, ciliate, glabrous and purple-zoned above, pubescent below; from May to September, umbels of eight to ten cherry-red flowers, whereas they are purplish pink in the species type, higher than the leaves; petals rounded at the apex. Deppe's Oxalis is native to Mexico. It was brought to England in 1827 by Mr. Barclay, and six years later, towards the end of 1833, Mr. Jacquin aîné introduced it to France, seeing it flower for the first time in 1834. Growing it is not difficult. According to Le Bon Jardinier, it requires rich, well-tilled soil; it multiplies easily, producing bulblets in large numbers around the root collar, which, when planted in April in light soil, become new individuals. We have cultivated Deppe's Oxali le on the assumption that it could be considered a useful vegetable plant, but from this point of view, it seems worthless. The roots are barely edible. We have prepared the leaves as sorrel, and, if this distinction is possible, we have found them to be rather sour than acidic, and in short not very pleasant; but you will see, from the extracts we are about to read from a letter from Mr. Morren, director of the garden at the University of Liège, dated January 10, 1845, to what extent we can differ in opinion. For eight years now," says Mr. Morren, "Deppe's Oxalis has appeared with honor on our tables in more than one form... We use its leaves in sorrel, its flowers in salads and its roots in asparagus. "The young leaves, taken from the center of the clumps, make excellent sorrel, with a pure taste and no crackling of calcareous salts (lime oxalate); their use in soups and sauces cannot be faulted by the most discerning palate. When mixed with lettuce, the cut flowers, even with the tips of their stems, make a substitute for vinegar, with a more exquisite and frank acidity that is even preferred by a delicate palate; this is for the use of the plant during the summer. "Around mid-October, or even in November, we remove the plant from the ground and find around sixty bulbils at its collar, which, when stored, serve to propagate Oxalis; below these bulbils, we discover two to four large roots, 10 to 20 centimetres long and varying from 2 to 5 in diameter. These roots, fusiform like young carrots, have a certain transparency that brings to mind the Salep of the Turks. I cannot share the opinion that these roots are similar to Topinambours and Scorsonères; but, in these matters, it is very difficult to agree: de gustibus non est disputandum. Oxalis is similar to asparagus and young white carrots, but the taste is more delicate and, if you'll pardon the expression, a little oriental. We cook these roots in water and salt, and eat them Dutch-style, with a sauce of fresh melted butter and egg yolks. Friends of mine have assured me that these roots have had a similar effect on their bodies to that experienced when Salep is taken after a debilitating diet. I can assure you, moreover, that I have always found myself enjoying the use of this excellent plant at all my meals. Faced with these assertions, made with such assurance and conviction, one remains disconcerted and can only repeat the de gustibus that the author of the letter opposes in advance to his contradicts. Enthusiasts will appreciate. We have no hesitation in recommending the cultivation of Deppe's Oxalis as a border plant. The plant will be right at home in the gardens of the curious. Pépin, head gardener of the botanical school at the Muséum, published a fairly extensive memoir on the cultivation and use of Pé-tsai, in which he reports on the results of his multiplied seedlings grown under various conditions. He reports on the opinion he formed of the plant, considered as a vegetable, through repeated tastings. Fig. 62 - Pe-tsai (Chinese cabbage). This memoir was presented by its author to the Société d'Horticulture. We refer the reader to it, and reproduce only a small part of it: "It was some twenty years ago," says M. Pépin, "that Pé-tsai was known under the name Brassica sinensis in botanical gardens, and was considered a simple collector's plant; but for the last three years that M. l'abbé Voisin, a specialist in the cultivation of Chinese cabbage, has been working on it. Abbé Voisin, Attorney General for Foreign Missions, has informed us that this species of cabbage is highly cultivated and esteemed in China, its 30 reputation as a culinary plant has been rehabilitated in France, and M. Ducros de Sixt, lawyer at the Royal Court of Paris, was the first to give us some details on Pé-tsai, its cultivation and uses in China. We believe this to be an error, and that our missionaries had been publicizing the importance of Pe-tsai cultivation in the Chinese empire for over a hundred years. Fig. 63. - Pak-choi, a variety of Pé-tsai. Mr. Pépin goes on to say: "In the spring of 1838, a large number of seedlings were sown, and I know from many people who were interested in studying this new cruciferous plant that, in general, they were not very satisfied, and that nowhere did Pé-tsai peel, a quality that is said to be constant in China". Here, the error is serious, and the results obtained by the author of the memoir must have made him despair by enlightening him. Indeed, the Pé-tsai does not apple, nor does it show any inclination to do so, either in China or in France. In his work entitled Description de l'empire de la Chine, published in 1735, Father J.-B. du Halde pointed out, as a peculiarity of Chinese cabbage, that it does not form an apple like European cabbage. Mr. Pépin goes on to say: "As spring sowing did not give me any different results from those I had already obtained in previous attempts to grow Pe-tsai, I thought I should try autumn sowing; only, this first attempt had already shown me that Pe-tsai is annual and not biennial, and even less perennial, as it is said to be in China". As we can see, the author's information on Pe-tsai was highly inaccurate, which in no way detracts from the experimenter's merit. Shortly after the publication of the above-mentioned memoir, an unsigned note appeared in the Revue Horticole, volume IV, 1838-41, page 112, which we believe must be attributed to Poiteau, then editor-in-chief of the Revue. This note is so complete, so interesting and so probably forgotten today, that we have no hesitation in reproducing most of it: ".... Mme Bréon, wife of M. Bréon, horticulturist-grain grower, who lived on Bourbon Island, where Pé-tsai is grown, told us that it was a resource during the hot, dry season, which it withstood more easily than other plants of the same use. During the rest of the year, Pé-tsai is used, not because it is preferable to other plants, but simply as a change of food, even when its quality is inferior. In Bourbon, you'll never see it eaten. "On the subject of Chinese cabbage, we have researched and read extensively in works on China; we will report what we have found most explicit on this subject in the writings of missionaries and travelers. "Rice, cabbage and a little garlic or onion instead of meat, with a common tea beverage, are often all that make up the meals of Chinese peasants and workers. Although our Lettuces and Romaines are well known to them, preference is given to Pe-tsai, which holds a distinguished place among Chinese vegetables. "The best Pe-tsai are found in the northern province, where the first frosts make them very tender; their abundance is almost unbelievable. During the months of October and November, in the morning, it is sometimes difficult to pass through the immense number of small carts and wheelbarrows loaded with them, which crowd the gates of Peking and Hang-tchou-fou. The Chinese custom is to preserve them in salt, or to marinate them and cook them with Rice, which is naturally fortinsipid. "There are three types of Pé-tsai (1): 1° Pé-tsai, with white, thin, very tender leaves, which tingle like Roman lettuces when a little help is given; 2° Nisontou, i.e. beef strawberry, because its leaves are crenate, very large, fleshy, full of juice and quite mild; 3° Purplish, whose leaves are very loose, smooth, very tender and of a pleasant taste, but mixed with a hint of bitterness, like some species of Lettuce. Among these three species, we also distinguish those (1) This is a missionary speaking. whose leaves are elongated like a snake's tongue, or rounded, cut or plain, with flat ribs like Beets (Poirées), blond or with rounded ribs like Lettuces, etc. (1). We won't insist on the details of these differences. Our cabbages, chicories and so many other vegetable plants long ago taught us in the West that the same plant appears in a prodigious number of forms, sometimes changing beyond recognition. It is inevitable that Pétsai, being grown in such a vast empire and cultivated so diversely, should change from place to place and take on different forms. "The climate, the season and the nature of the land make a big difference between Pé-tsai and Pé-tsai in terms of taste, quality and size. Some always taste bland and almost insipid, while others have a very pleasant taste and a kind of natural perfume. Some are healthy and wholesome, while others are not. In some places, they cannot be eaten young, or even before the first frost, while in others, they can be eaten at any time, depending on how long you want to wait for them. The most careful cultivation always leaves them mediocre in some cantons, whereas in others they come into their own. They grow visibly and swell to weigh from 10 to 12 pounds, to 18 and 20. (1) Pé means white, tsai means vegetable; thus, Pé-tsai is a white vegetable. Of the three species of Pé-tsai cited in the leaflet, two are not worth accepting. The third differs from our Cardes-Poirées only in that the Chinese variety is more tender and less bland, wider and longer than ours. This species has been successful in France; the other two would be equally successful if they were worth trying to cultivate. (These observations are not ours. - P. B.). "The Pé-tsai most esteemed in Peking are those from the area around the small town of Ngan-sun; they are, in fact, the ones preferred for the table of the emperor and his entire family. European gourmets would like to cook and season cabbage in a way that would flatter their delicacy; Chinese gourmets, on the other hand, either through prejudice or finesse of taste, reason about Pe-tsai as they do about venison and game, claiming that the more seasoning you give them, the more they lose their own flavour. We will candidly confess our profound incapacity and ignorance on this serious subject, and confine ourselves to recounting that, while on duty at the palace, we found Ngan-sun's Pé-tsai very good and very delicate, cooked simply in broth and with no seasoning other than salt. Our testimony will undoubtedly prove nothing, but we give it for what it is worth. "Our Europeans in Canton call Pé-tsai Chinese cabbage. Let them say why. It seems to us that it requires less smoky soil than our cabbages. When you want to grow good Pé-tsai rather than big Pé-tsai, and to grow them in their own time rather than pushing their growth, you need to choose an uncovered soil that's damp rather than dry. Low-lying soils that are not too swampy are very favorable. When it comes to choosing fertilizers, ashes of various grasses and powder are best suited to them. "Pé-tsai trees only set seed the year after they are planted. The Chinese take the same precautions to obtain seeds as we do for cabbages. They keep a few selected plants in a greenhouse or other sheltered spot, and when spring comes, they replant them in a sunny spot, watering them until they bloom and set seed. The seed is usually ripe by June or July. Gardeners here are divided on what to sow. Some want the new seed to produce stronger, more vigorous and easier-to-grow Pétsai; others claim that those sown from the previous year's seed, well preserved in the air, in an open, north-facing spot, produce more tender, more delicate Pé-tsai that are easier to peel (1). "In the southern provinces, we sow Pétsai in all seasons, and they come in well. When you want to have them in late spring, summer and all autumn, you need to choose well-watered soil and, as far as possible, an eastern exposure. In the northern provinces, such as Chan-tong and Pétché-li, where they are incomparably better and more delicate, they are sown on a bed in mid-July or August, in the same way as cabbages. Once the heat wave has passed, they are transplanted with a string into holes made with a large planter, so that a little poudrette can be added. Those who are only interested in profit plant them in a checkerboard pattern, 7 or 8 inches apart, because Pé-Isai can be eaten at any period of growth. They split the rows as they grow, choosing those they want to leave behind and keeping only those they see are well on the way to reaching their best size. Those who only want to have beautiful Pe-tsai plant them, as we do cabbages, 1 1/2 feet apart. Whichever way they are planted, they should be watered as soon as possible to bind the roots and facilitate recovery. (1) This probably involves binding the leaves, a rather delicate operation due to their extreme fragility. - P. B. then plough, weed and boot them until they are in full flood and have reached the dews and cool nights of autumn. Autumn is admirable here (1) and almost as beautiful as in our Béarn region. The fine, mild weather is undoubtedly the main cause of the charming way in which the Pé-tsai grow at this time, as if at a glance; as long as the soil is not too parched, we don't bother watering them, and this does them no harm; however faded and withered they may appear in the high noon, the next morning we find their leaves erect, fresh and full of vigor, but they remain green or at most blond until the first cold. "On the other hand, when the first cold weather arrives, their broad ribs soften, and the rest of the leaf gradually turns a perfect white. "Some people tie their Pé-Isai like our Roman lettuces, to obtain a larger head and softer leaf ribs; but others leave them to their own devices and claim that Pé-tsai thereby lose in flavor, taste and fragrance what they gain in whiteness and tenderness. The truth is that in Ngan-sun and other places where they are so good, so tender and so excellent, they are not bound at all. "When the Pé-tsai are fully grown, they are from 2 to 3 feet high, and weigh, as we said, from 15 to 20 pounds. We wait until the frosts have macerated them a little before harvesting. Their first outer leaves suffer a little, but we don't worry about that, as they must remain in the field to form compost. (1) In Peking, no doubt. "As the Chinese are great herb eaters, Pé-tsai are a real harvest, especially for the northern provinces; for, although more southerly than Provence, the cold is so rigorous that gardening there is absolutely closed from mid-November to mid-February; free to our physicists to explain as they see fit, much more closed than in the most northerly parts of France. "We have found several ways of preserving the Pé-tsai harvest and making it last throughout the winter; some preserve them in salt and vinegar; others cook them halfway in the steam of boiling water or wilt them in the cold northern air, after removing the leaves, then pass them through mustard or ginger water, cutting them into pieces. "However, as these sparing or household inventions, which are perhaps not sufficiently well known in our countryside, always take away something of the good taste of Pé-tsai, a large quantity is kept fresh until spring. "There are two ways of doing this: the first is to expose them to the sun for a while to remove any excess moisture that might cause them to turn yellow, and then pile them up in a greenhouse or in specially dug ditches; the second is to plant them en masse in damp river sand, at the bottom of a greenhouse. Those who don't want to keep them that long lay them flat on soil that's neither too dry nor too damp, and, after throwing a bit of chopped straw over them, cover them with a foot of dry earth; those who have a convenient place for it hang them by the foot, like cabbages, and as close together as possible. Moreover, the industry benefits so well from all these ways of preserving Pe-tsai, that they are available in Peking all winter, and at good prices. Consumption is so prodigious in this immense city that we don't dare say what the total must be. We will now say what we think of Pétsai. Our personal experiments have not given us satisfactory results, but they have served to form our opinion. First of all, we shall rule out any summer cultivation. The rapidity with which the plant goes to seed before it is fully developed, the heat of the sun which prevents its ribs and leaves from becoming tender and white, the abundance of fresh vegetables preferable to Chinese cabbage, these various causes would make it unsuccessful to grow Pé-tsai during the summer. The obstacles are different, but equally serious, if you sow in August, to harvest in winter. From the end of September, vegetation and plant development slow down, and the cold soon comes to a complete halt. However, Pé-tsai should be sown at the end of summer, but it must be able to vegetate for a long time, and frosts must not prevent it from reaching the extraordinary size it acquires in China before winter. Roscoff, Cavaillon and Hyères all seem to lend themselves to winter cultivation of Chinese cabbage. We are inclined to believe that Roscoff and the whole of the region where the Gulf stream draws the temperature down would be particularly favorable. In this privileged, truly temperate region, the grower fears neither sunlight nor the rigors of winter. Pé-tsai would develop slowly and widely, and perhaps take an important place in the Paris consumer market. Our streets are often clogged with the immense quantity of cauliflowers sent to us from Finistère; but these, with their strong flavor and difficult digestion, are not suitable for everyone, and would often give way to the milder and lighter Pé-tsai. It would be desirable for the cultivation of the latter vegetable to be seriously experimented with in Brittany. According to Messrs Sagot and Raoul, Manuel des cultures tropicales, Pé-tsai could be of great service in hot countries, where it produces tender leaves that are a valuable resource. Various varieties of Chinese cabbage are said to have been introduced into the English and Dutch colonies in China and the Malay Archipelago. In his interesting 1875 publication, Mémoires de la Société des sciences naturelles de Cherbourg, tome XIX, of which he kindly gave us one of the reprinted copies, Captain Jouan cites Physalis peruviana L. among the medicinal plants. Our Physalis is called Konini in the Marquesas Islands, and, according to Jardin, is used by the natives in compresses against headaches. But it is as an edible fruit, suitable for making pies, syrups, jams and various confectionery items, that the berries of P. peruviana are sought after and that the plant that produces them is cultivated in Peru, Cape Town, India, etc.. In a memoir entitled: Enumeracion de los generos y especes de plantas, etc., M. Martinet, professor of natural history in Lima, says: "We eat the fragrant fruits of Physalis peruviana". In the Manuel de jardinage pour le Bengale, which we sometimes quote, we find a chapter devoted to our plant, which we reproduce in full. Physalis peruviana is known in English as Peruvian cherry, Cape gooseberry. The manual states: "A perennial herbaceous plant native to Peru, naturalized in Cape Town and widely cultivated there. "The fruit, which exactly resembles that of the Alkekenge of English gardens, of which it is undoubtedly the closest relative, is enclosed in an appendix of dry leaves (1). "It is of a light amber color, of the exact volume and shape of the Cherry, and as delicious and useful as any of the products of the countryside. There is perhaps no fruit in the world that provides a more exquisite jam. "The seeds should be sown in May or June, and the plant put in place, in the open ground, in lines (1) The calyx develops at the same time as the fruit, covering it entirely and drying out before harvest. 4 feet apart and 2 feet apart. "The plants can thrive in ordinary garden soil, but preferably in soil that has received a little fertilizer. When they are about 8 inches tall, they should be buttressed at half their height. When they flower, it's a good idea to pinch the tips of the sprays so they don't spread out too much, and also to provide more food for the fruit. "The berries ripen in January and February. Although perennial, Physalis should be grown as an annual, and old plants, after bearing fruit once, should be uprooted and discarded. When the season is ripe, seed should be sown to make a new plantation. "The plant is delicate and doesn't tolerate much cold. I tried several times to grow it at Ferozepore, but without success. It grew vigorously throughout the warm season, but the cold would destroy my abundant harvest before it was ripe." The last paragraph of the English author's book is applicable to Physalis cultivation in the Paris climate, and just recently, a plantation that promised us 80-100,000 fruits gave us only 2,000 perfectly ripe. All the rest were destroyed by a 2-degree frost. It's in the South of France that Physalis cultivation will be most fruitful. If growers on the Mediterranean coast would be so kind, they could, with a few precautions, preserve the fruit throughout the winter, ship it to Paris in unlimited quantities and obtain a handsome price. Berries picked on March 7th in Antibes were sent to a member of the Société d'Acclimatation, who gave them to us. Their ripeness and freshness were impeccable. We'll briefly describe our cultivation methods. It should be noted that they are specific to the climate around Paris, and will have to be modified to the north and south of this region: We sow in March on a bed and under a frame. When the plant is ready, we put it into cups, still on a bed and under a frame, one plant per cup. Towards the end of May, we plant in the ground, 1.10 m apart in all directions. The plantation is hoeed twice during the season. We remove all the lower buds and keep only the upper shoots. We pinch off the shoots as soon as they start to flower. Harvesting begins in September and continues until the frosts. The fruit is not ripe until the calyx enveloping it has completely dried out. In our northern departments, Physalis peruviana cuttings should be taken at the same time as Pelargonium cuttings, overwintered alongside the latter and planted at the same time, when there are no more frosts to worry about. South of the Loire, they can be sown in nurseries in the open ground. On the Mediterranean coast, harvest throughout the winter, protecting the plants from frost. Harvested berries should be stored in a cool, dry place. They keep perfectly well for four months. Harvested in the South of France at the end of October, they will provide the basis for a very lucrative trade until March; we say very lucrative, because a good price will always be obtained for a fruit that keeps fresh throughout the winter. Physalis peruviana is extremely productive; we have seen vines loaded with over a hundred fruits. We are not exaggerating when we estimate that 400,000 berries will be produced per hectare in the Alpes-Maritimes, Var, Bouches-du-Rhône and Hérault departments. These berries travel well and arrive in Paris in perfect condition. Confectioners and confectioners will buy them, and once the competition has lowered prices, the working-class population, always eager for fruit, will take their turn. The ripe berries of P. peruviana, eaten in their natural state, are pleasant, but inferior to strawberries, cherries, etc. They are good in compotes. They are good in compotes, but the confectioner's and confectioner's industry makes them excellent. The confectioner prepares them with fondant and caramel. They make exquisite jams and syrups. The confectioner uses them to make flans and tarts. The T... house has made jams and syrup that are second to none in Paris. Maison B... sold 30,000 berries candied in fondant and caramel in the space of a season. The fruit used by these houses had been delivered to them by a friend of ours, an enlightened horticultural enthusiast, to whom we had supplied seeds. As we finish preparing the third edition of Potager d'un curieux, they continue to be sought after by confectioners, who run out every winter. 31 We believe that Physalis peruviana should be cultivated and propagated, and we are happy to see that our efforts to bring it into consumption have not been in vain. The calyx, which is accrescent as in all other Physalis, becomes, at maturity, large, almost spherical, hanging, salc-green, as if varnished; it bears 10 violet streaks running from the base, which is completely saturated with violet, to the apex. The berry is highly developed, almost as large as a Prune de Monsieur (1), filling the entire calyx and often tearing it open when it cannot contain it; it is almost round, hairless and blackish-green. The seeds are yellow. Mr. Carrière has indicated with great precision the cultivation method applicable to the violet Physalis. In the Midi, on the other hand, the yield from a plantation of Physalis violet would be enormous. We'd now like to talk about the uses to which the plant's berries can be put. In their raw state, they are slightly acidic, with little or no fragrance of their own. We find them insignificant. In fritters, they are extremely acidic and unpleasant. In green sauce, after prolonged cooking, they are acidic but not excessively so, and as they can easily be kept on the board until January, and even well beyond, they could, during the winter, replace the tomato, which they are far from being worth. The Mexicans are said to make an excellent syrup from them, which they use against diseases of the respiratory tract. M. Balarce gave the formula to M. Bossin, after having experimented with it successfully (Bull. Soc. d'Acclimat., 1875, vol. Il, p. 69). In the Paris climate, the Petite Tomate du Mexique can only be found in the gardens of the curious. PHYSALIS DU COSTA-RICA PHYSALIS LAFONII Paill. et Bois. Solanaceae family. Annual plant, from Om40 to 0m50 centimeters high, covered on all its parts with a grayish pubescence formed of numerous, simple, short hairs. Stem erect, strongly angled, twiggy. Leaves alternate, sometimes opposite, very variable in shape, sometimes broadly oval, with a truncated or rounded base, sometimes obovate, more or less long attenuated, entire, irregularly denticulate or slightly sinuous at the edges, those of the main branches varying from 15 to 18 centimeters long by 10 to 12 wide, those of the secondary branches smaller; petioles 4 or 5 centimeters long. Perennial, 2 to 3 meters high, with thick, fleshy roots, cylindrical, glabrous, furrowed stems; broad, oval-lanceolate, acute, barely mucronate, soft leaves. In August-September, flowers are first white, then purple, arranged in fairly long clusters, longer than the leaves; pedicels twice as long as the calyx, which has 5 deep divisions; stamens 10; single ovary, surmounted by 10 styles; fleshy fruit, often with 10 ribs. "The word Phytolacca, given by Linné to this plant, derives from a Greek word meaning plant, and from lacca, lacquer; and, indeed, all species of this genus have a red tint. Their leaves become red in the late season, as do their fruits, which are then full of a lacquer-red juice that dyers can fix to a certain extent with alumina sulfate and liquid ammonia. It is grown in Europe... D. °... It is native to North America, particularly Virginia. It has become naturalized in the southern parts of Europe, and even in France, in the West Indies, in the colonies of Martinique and Guadeloupe, in Santo Domingo (Haiti), and so on. "Spinach is eaten in place of Phytolacca, which Creole ladies seek out for their calalous. Some fraudsters color wine with the juice of its berries, which gives it a sharp, unpleasant taste (1)." Descourtilz is not the only one to present Phytolacca as a common food plant. William Darlington, in his Agricultural Botany (Philadelphia 1847), tells us that the young shoots of Phytolacca are a good substitute for Asparagus; that its ripe berries have even been used by confectioners to make pies of dubious merit. He adds, however, that the plant is treated as a weed by careful farmers. Pépin, in the Revue horticole, 1847, volume IX, page 218, claims that during the months of January and March, several Paris edible merchants sold bleached Phytolacca decandra stems. These stems, quite similar to Asparagus, are sold," he says, "in large quantities in the markets of the United States, where this plant has long been regarded as edible. M. Lakanal, who lived in Kentucky for over twenty years, assured him that it was considered an excellent vegetable (2). (1) Descourtilz, Flore des Antilles, vol. V, p. 32. (2) According to Nuttall, The genera of North America, t. I, p. 293, "the young shoots of the Thytotacca, previously boiled, are edible." "Several people in Paris have experimented with it, and have not found the dish to their taste; but it seems that this opinion is not general, since Phytolacca has become, momentarily at least, a culinary plant among our leading restaurateurs." In the Revue horticole, 1868, page 440, Mr. Jean Sisley published a note translated from the American Agriculturist, same year: "The sight of the long clusters of blackish-purple berries on this beautiful plant, ripening at the moment, reminds us of the excellence of its spring shoots. They are numerous, the size of a finger, with undeveloped leaves. These shoots, cut while still young and cooked like asparagus, are so delicate that anyone who has tasted them wants to eat more. "Since the shoots are good, taken from plants growing on the edges of paths and hedges, without cultivation, it is likely that they will be better when the plant is grown in gardens. We therefore recommend that instead of treating it as a weed, we cultivate it with care, and advise those who would like to try it out to transplant the roots in autumn, divide the large clumps and plant them 1 meter apart in well-tilled, smoked soil. "We are well aware that this plant is reputed for its medicinal qualities; but, in any case, the young shoots lose their medicinal properties when cooked, and we know a good number of people who have been eating them for years without the slightest inconvenience."
