Braconnot, from Nancy, has carried out experiments on P. decandra. He concluded from his experiments: "l° that potash exists in enormous proportions in this plant; 2° that its molten ashes can be used commercially as a fairly rich alkali; 3° that potash is saturated in the plant by an acid analogous to malic acid, but which differs in some respects; 4° that the berries can be fermented and distilled to produce a certain quantity of alcohol; 5° that the coloring matter can be used as a reagent; 6° that the lees can be used as food; 7° that the cultivation of Phytolakia can become a branch of industry for the production of potash. 100 pounds of ashes out provided 66 pounds 10 ounces 5 coarse of dried salt, containing 42 pounds of pure, caustic potash." (Annales de chimie, t. LXII, p. 71 ff.) After reproducing what our predecessors have said about P. decandra, we will briefly discuss our personal experiences. The plant is hardy. It is sown in nurseries and planted out when the young plants are mature. The clumps are divided in autumn, and planted 1 metre apart in all directions. In spring, when vegetation begins, place upside-down pots over the plants, after having blinded the holes, and harvest the shoots as soon as they have reached 15 to 20 centimetres in height. Cooked and served like asparagus, they are fleshy and tender, but bland. We ate them, albeit in small quantities, with no ill effects. The red juice of the Phytolacae berry is a popular purgative in the United States, but used in very small quantities, it is completely harmless. In our village, it has sometimes been used to give wine an artificial color. It is used in the same way in various countries. In Germany, it is used to make a preservable syrup for coloring various dishes. According to Madame Davidis, this syrup is prepared as follows (1): "The bunches of ripe Phytolacus berries, the cultivation of which is described in my Vegetable and Florist Garden (2), in the ornamental shrubs section, contain this admirable red juice which is sold as an expensive commodity in Berlin and other large cities, to color frothy sauces, white jellies and milk dishes, and which is prepared as follows: in late autumn, when the bunches have ripened to a glossy black, they are de-stemmed and pressed. To clarify the juice, it is left to stand for six to twelve hours in a narrow porcelain vase, then drawn off. Then put it in an earthenware pot that has contained no fat, with a third of its weight in crushed sugar, and let it boil a few times, while skimming, since longer cooking would turn its beautiful red color brown. (2) Ouvrage de Mme Davidis. cold, it is poured into properly washed, dried and sulphured medicine bottles, corked, sealed and kept in a cool place. PIPENGAIL LUFFA ACUTANGULA Seringe. Cucurbitaceae family. The plant is usually cultivated in tropical regions; it is native to India, where it bears the names Torui (Hindustan), Jhinga (Bengalese). According to Roxburgh, the fruit, half-developed, boiled and prepared with butter and salt, is not inferior to green peas. It is also considered a foodstuff on the west coast of Africa. Mr. Pierre, director of the Colonial Garden in Libreville, has sent us some seeds under the name Long Okra, which is given to him in Sierra Leone and Liberia. The plant is called M'Counive in Gabon. We received seeds from our colleague Mr. E. Harel, and from Dr. de Cordemoy. We sowed it on March 15 on a bed and under a frame, and kept only one plant in a single-panel box. The plant filled the box well and its stems spread outwards. We then raised them on large poles and we believe they would have easily reached a height of 4 meters, if we had been able to provide them with supports of that size. The first fruit appeared on July 18, four months after sowing, and many more followed until September 10, when a strong wind destroyed everything. We believe that four feet of Pipengaille, properly cared for, would be enough to provide a weekly dish for a family's table. We had some difficulty in getting the vegetable properly prepared, although Dr de Cordemoy had kindly given us the following recipe, which is in use in Réunion: "Peel the fruit. "Leave or remove the seeds, depending on how hard they are. "Brown half an onion, then fry everything together. "If necessary, add a dash of vinegar at the end. Three times, when we followed this recipe, we found that the cook had used too much onion and too much butter. It was only by successively reducing the quantity of these two ingredients that we arrived at a satisfactory result. We harvested the fruit at half size, and cut it into one-inch-thick slices. We omitted the vinegar drizzle. Pipengaille is a highly sought-after vegetable in Réunion, and would be very useful in our Midi and in those of our colonies that do not yet have it. It's good, delicate, but weak in flavor. It would travel unaltered between Provence and Paris. It could even be shipped from our African colony. 6 Fig. 67. - Luffa acutangula. Cyperaceae family. A tuberous form of Eleocharis plantaginea Retz. Aquatic plant, perennial, native to the Far East. Fibrous, stoloniferous root produces rounded tubers the size of small walnuts. Stem erect, gnarled, aphyllous, with one or two short sheaths at the base. Flowers in terminal, solitary, cylindrical spikes. Scales oblong, membranous, margined. 3 stamens. Style trifid, rarely bifid, thickened at base, compressed. Achains obcordiform, surrounded by small curved bristles. Around 1655, Martinus Martini, in his Novus Atlas sinensis, wrote: "City of Kia-hing (Prov. Che Kiang). The Chinese call Pe ci a plant with round fruits (1) that grows in stagnant waters throughout this region. The volume of these fruits hardly exceeds that of a chestnut. The kernel is covered with a very thin, brown skin, and the pulp is pure white, full of juice, with a pleasant flavor, harsher than that of ordinary fruit and somewhat acidic. If, at the same time as the fruit, you put a copper coin in your mouth, you will break it with your teeth as easily as the fruit, and you will reduce it to edible pulp by a marvellous force of nature, which I have often experienced myself." In 1696, the R. P. Louis Le Comte, in his Nouveaux mémoires sur l'état de la Chine, speaking of the Pe ci, reported what Martini had said, that, when these fruits are chewed at the same time as a copper coin, the latter is easily crushed with the teeth, a tale also found in Chinese books; but Le Comte refutes this assertion by invoking his own experience (Notes taken from the work entitled: Early European researches in to the Flora of China, by E. Bretschneider, D. M. London, 1881). Dr. Bretschneider wrote to us from Saint-Péters(1) Les misionnaires ont eru voir un fruit dans ce qui m'etait qu'on tubercule. - P. B. bourg, November 20 1885: "The Chinese name for Eleocharis tuberosa is Pi t'si. The plant is cultivated all over China, in Peking as well as in Shang-Hai, Canton, etc. "I have sent some tubers of it to you. "I sent tubers the size of chestnuts to the late Mr. Decaisne, but they did not arrive in good condition. Eleocharis tuberosa would be a good acquisition for our crops, because its tubers are very good to eat. To send them from China to France, we'd have to put them in a pot filled with vase and water. Someone would have to take care of this pot on the boat and renew the water that evaporates. In this way, young plants would be brought to Marseille. "The plant is grown in water, like rice. I'm not in a position to point you in the right direction in China, but I would advise you to go and see my friend Mr. Dévéria, first Chinese interpreter at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he will tell you what to do." Our learned correspondent wrote again, dated June 7 1887: "The plant is widely cultivated around Peking, in submerged areas. It never flowers. It is grown for its tubers, which do not form until very late in the autumn. They are harvested in spring and eaten raw or cooked, or candied in vinegar. Europeans don't eat much Pi t'si; however, it has a rather pleasant taste. There is no need, as we have been told, to reject the residue after chewing the tuber." In the same letter, the doctor renewed his recommendations for transporting chi noises aquatic plants. We read in Roxburgh, Flora indica, volume I, page 210: "The plant is cited by Abbé Grosier under the name Pi t'si. Under the names Maatai, Pu-tsai or Pe t'si, or Chinese water chestnut. Mr. Duncan, in compliance with the Governor General's wishes, sent it from Canton to the Company's Botanical Garden in Calcutta, where it flowers towards the end of the rains, in September. "For the economic uses of its tuberous roots, I beg permission," says Roxburgh, "to refer, on the one hand, to Abbé Grosier and other historians who have had occasion to observe how they are employed by the Chinese, and, on the other, to the following extract from Mr. Duncan's letter which accompanied the plants: 'Maa tai, Pu tsai or Pi t'si, according to Abbé Grosier, Châtaigne d'eau. Cullive in tanks that are smoked for planting, towards the end of March. The water in the tank is then drained, and small cavities are made in the bottom, filled with human fertilizer and left exposed to the sun for two weeks. Their contents are soon mixed with the muddy bottom of the reservoir, and the splinters or roots are deposited. The water is then returned, and the new crop reaches perfection on September 1st. This nut is highly esteemed by Chinese of all classes, not only as a root for the pot, but also as a remedy. It is eaten boiled or raw. I wouldn't vouch for the singular virtues attributed to Maatai, but I'll just mention one of the most plausible. Children here play with coins in their mouths, which sometimes slip into their stomachs and cause alarming symptoms. The nut, raw or boiled, is then immediately given to them in quantity; it never fails to relieve them and is always considered a specific. It is claimed to decompose metal." We could, like Roxburgh, refer to the Description générale de la Chine, Paris, 1785, by Abbé Grosier, but this work is not available to everyone, and the reader would be deprived of the information it contains, which is most interesting. We therefore reproduce here the passages relating to aquatic edible plants: "In Europe, people have dared to suggest that the Chinese leave part of their land uncultivated; they were unaware, no doubt, that they cultivate the very bottom of waters and that the soil of lakes, ponds and streams provides them with harvests that are still unknown to us. Their industriousness has led them to find resources in a large number of aquatic plants, many of which, such as Pi t'si and Lien hoa, are the delights of the best Chinese tables. "In order to give the people an example of this culture, the government takes care to have them planted in ponds, in bodies of water and in all waters belonging to the State. The emperor himself has them planted in the ponds that adorn his gardens, and almost all his palace moats are filled with them. The flowers and greenery of these useful plants also almost entirely cover the two immense bodies of water in the center of Peking, which are separated only by a single bridge where everyone passes and from which the magnificent gardens of the emperor's palace can be seen. The Pi t'si or true Water Chestnut (1) (1) For us, the Trapa natans is the true Water Chestnut, and grows only in the southern provinces of China; it withers away in Peking. Its leaves are long like those of the Joncus, but hollow and tubular like those of the Chives. The extraordinary thing about this plant is that its fruit is enclosed in an envelope formed by its roots, like a chestnut in its thorny shell; this shell can be broken and the fruit removed without damaging the plant. This water chestnut is very healthy and has a very delicate taste; it is given to sick people to chew on to refresh their mouths". So far, we have made vain efforts to obtain Pi t'si. We received several tubers of Eleocharis tuberosa from R. P. Heude, of Shang-Haï, which arrived in Paris too tired from the journey for us to be able to vegetate them. Dr Bretschneider tells us what to do, but where can we find a complaisant traveller who will agree to transport the roots, give them the necessary water, and add the precious pot to his travel impedimenta? We're not discouraged, but we are extremely embarrassed. What may console enthusiasts in the Paris area is that the climate there would not allow cultivation of Pi t'si; not because it has anything to fear from the cold under the water with which it would be covered, but because the harvest of its tubers takes place late in autumn, and we don't have, as in Peking, after winters where the Pi t'si is the only one; but the Chinese have the Pi tst and the Ling io, and, for them, the piv'est is the true water Châtrigne. thermometer falls to 20°, six months of tropical heat. Abbé David observed 40° in the shade as early as May. The Chinese water chestnut is therefore confined to a few of our southernmost départements. This is the place to mention two Eleocharis, neighbors of the Pi t'si. To our great regret, we have so far been unable to obtain them, and cannot therefore devote a separate article to them. We would be grateful if anyone receiving tubers of these plants would inform us: ELEOCHARIS ESCULENTA Vieillard (Herb. de la Nouvelle-Calédonie, n° 1456). Herbaceous, bushy, stoloniferous plant; stolons with mealy tubers, closely resembling those of Cyperus esculentus L.; stems erect, aphyllic, 40 to 50 cm high, jonciform, smooth, green, divided internally by numerous diaphragms that are barely visible when fresh; pellucid sheaths, membranous, short, terminated by an acute triangular ligule. Flowers in elongated spikes, greenish, hermaphrodite, the lower ones sterile; scales greenish, membranous, broad, concave, scarious at the edges, striate in the center; perigone silky; bristles 8, unequal, white and scabrous; stamens 3; anthers elongated, mucronate, twice as long as the netting; ovary compressed, surmounted by a persistent style; seed black, shiny. This Cyperaceae is very common in flooded areas; its tubers are edible and quite sought-after (1). In the light of the above description and its accompanying indications, we thought it would be easy to find Eleocharis esculenta. We have written to our correspondent on several occasions. We pointed out to him the marshes around Balade as the plant's definite habitat; we tired him with our repeated requests. He always replied that Eleocharis esculenta could not be found. Notice sur l'Ahipa et l'Aricoma, plantes alimentaires du haut Pérou, by A. Weddell (Ann. des se. nat., loc. cit.): "Few countries offer as great a diversity of climates as Bolivia or high Peru; some points of their territory are even situated in such a special way that the inhabitants, on leaving their temperate skies, can reach in a few hours and at will the zone of perpetual snow or that of tropical vegetation. Such, in particular, is the position of the city of La Paz, built at the bottom of a ravine that connects it, on the one hand, with the tropical valleys of the eastern slopes of the Andes and, on the other, with the glaciers of the great Cordillera that rise majestically above it. It's easy to understand the advantages of such a location in terms of plant foodstuffs, which must almost inevitably be far more varied than in less favourably-placed locations. This is indeed the case; so when, on my last trip to America, I wanted to take stock of the edible plants on sale at the La Paz market, I was not surprised to find, alongside Strawberries, Apples and Peaches, Bananas, Pomegranates and Pineapples; But the products that particularly attracted my attention were those that seemed to have some analogy with the potato, for which a substitute was being sought at the time, and I was all the more interested in this examination as, alongside the tubers of Oxalis tuberosa, Ullucus and Tropxolum tuberosum, which were much talked about in Europe, I noticed two others that were still unknown to me and which had more or less the same appearance as the swollen roots of the Dahlia. However, like the Dahlia and the Potato, they were no longer products of the temperate or cold parts of the Andes, since they both originated from the subtropical zone, and as such, they could be seen in the company of the starchy roots or tubers of Manioc, Arracacha, Canna edulis or Colocasia esculenta. "One of these tubers, 10 to 15 centimeters long, tapering at both ends and yellowish in color, is known in La Paz as Ahipa (or Ajipa); the other, larger, stockier and darker in color, is known there as Yacon or Aricoma. Both are brought in considerable quantities from the warmer parts of the ravine, where they appear to have been cultivated since time immemorial. "At the time of my visit, the season was unfortunately too advanced for me to obtain the materials that would have enabled me to learn about their botanical origins; I therefore regretted leaving the country without having been able to satisfy my curiosity; and, despite numerous requests, it is only recently that I have obtained samples (1) that enable me to shed light on the question. "Now, those I received from the plant that provides the first of these tubers, Ahipa, although devoid of flowers and fruit, nevertheless allow me to affirm that it belongs to the Leguminosae family and the Phaseolae tribe, and I thought at first that it must be a species of Dolichos, perhaps the Dolichos tuberosus Lamk, which is claimed (Lamk.. Encycl, Encycl., Il, 295) to have been brought from South America to the West Indies by the Caribs. "In order to compare these two plants, I assumed that they belonged to the same genus, which has not yet been demonstrated; I would even add that Mr. Bentham, to whom I sent some of the leaves I had just received from Bolivia, told me that they could very well be those of a species of Stenolobium. It was also suggested that my plant might be one of the Rhynchosia species, which are currently cultivated in India for their tuberous roots. "Samples of the plant that produces the second tuber, the one known in La Paz as Yacon or Aricoma, are much more complete than those of Ahipa, so I had no difficulty in recognizing a completely new species. As I said, the tubers are generally more voluminous and stockier than those of the preceding plant; like them and like those of Dahlia, they result from a particular development of the roots, and they are all the more comparable to the latter as they are the product of a plant of the same family. This plant is a species of the genus Polymnia, for which I propose the name P. edulis, and which I will describe as follows: "It grows spontaneously near Quitame, on the eastern slopes of the Audes de Bogola, at an altitude of 2,000 meters (Triana). It is cultivated in the subtropical region of Peru and New Granada, where, according to Triana, it goes by the names of Jiquima and Jiguimilla. "The tubers I saw for sale at the La Paz market averaged about the size of a fist, but I was assured that some weighed close to 2 kilograms; each strain produced an average of (1) More complete samples were recently sent by Dr. Ernst and established that Ahipa is nothing other than Dolichos tuberosus Lamk. To complete what I have to say about these two vegetables, it remains for me to talk about their nutritional qualities and flavor. We'll start by saying that both are eaten raw like apples, and that they are held in the same high esteem as apples by the lower classes of the population. Should we conclude from this that their flavor is just as pleasant? "The Aricoma, which I prefer, seems to me more like a bad pear in this respect. Moreover, it contains only a very small amount of starch, whereas Ahipa contains a fairly significant proportion and could be compared, in terms of its nutritional properties, to the tuber of Ullucus tuberosus, while Aricoma would be the analogue of Topinambour, from which it differs, however, by a much higher proportion of sugar. "To sum up, what I have seen of these two tubers has convinced me that, if there could be any advantage in trying to introduce them into our crops - and I have no doubt that they would thrive in Algeria's climate - it would not be as food plants for man, but rather as industrial plants, intended for use either in the manufacture of 'alcohol, or as cattle feed; In both respects, Polymnia edulis would undoubtedly be the preferred plant, both because of the greater quantity of saccharine matter in its lubercules and because of its high yield. I would add that this plant, considered as a successor to the Topinambour, would have one advantage over the latter, namely that it doesn't stalk and is therefore much easier to eradicate from the land where it is grown. Its green parts are, moreover, even more abundant and, above all, more tender than those of the Topinambour and, for this reason, would undoubtedly be more sought-after by livestock. Cultivation of Polymnia edulis failed to produce any useful results, and the plant joined the list of dismal failures in the quest to eventually replace the potato. However, as the story of the discovery of two new food plants is not without interest, we think it will meet with approval to have reproduced Mr. Weddell's note in extenso. We sowed the seeds we received in buckets, under a cold frame. We obtained only a small number of plants, which we put in place, in the open air, on a piece of old bedding. We could certainly have planted in sand, but our main aim was to have vigorous plants and to harvest the seeds, even if the tubers were less developed. We didn't stick to sowing, and as soon as we had strong enough plants, we took cuttings, all of which sprouted easily. This means that both sowing and taking cuttings can be practised, but mainly taking cuttings. We had hoped to obtain tubers which we had planted and which we assumed would give us stronger plants and an earlier, more abundant harvest. This was not the case; after six consecutive years of careful cultivation, we were no further ahead than the first day. We have only obtained tubers that are insignificant in number and volume. The harshness of our winters, however, is no obstacle to the cultivation of Purslane, since it is an annual and summer crop; the habitat of the spontaneous plant is not free of frosts, and the thermometer sometimes falls to 6 or 7 degrees below zero. Since we are concerned exclusively with vegetable plants, we have said nothing about the Purslane flower, which is the subject of this chapter. It is very large, with a warm, vivid purplish-pink color, close to violet. Enthusiasts who have seen it agree that it is larger than in any other variety of large-flowered Purslane. PROVATZA STATICE SINUATA L. Fam. Plumbaginea. Statice sinuata is a perennial that grows wild throughout the Mediterranean region, but in France is found only on the Hyères islands. The stem reaches 10 to 30 centimetres in height. The radical, rosette-shaped leaves are cut into rounded lobes and bear sparse hairs. The flowers, in dense, terminal clusters, are large, blue, with pale yellow petals. This species was brought to our attention by Dr. de Heldreich, Director of the Botanical Garden of Athens, on the occasion of the publication of the second edition of Potager d'un Curieux. In a letter received on June 10 1892, he wrote: "If I had known you were preparing a new edition of your interesting work, I would have been able to offer you some more material from this country, in particular Provatza (a young plant of Statice sinuata, excellent in cooked salads)." We cultivated Statice sinuata, sowing it thickly in autumn; the following summer, we obtained abundant, very tender leaves, with an excellent cooked flavor. Raw, in salads, the young leaves are very acceptable. The flavor is mild and pleasant. PSORALEA COMESTIBLE, PICOTIANE Tipsina of the Iowa Indians; Taagu of the Osages, according to M. Trécul. PSORALEA ESCULENTA Pursh. Family Papilionaceae. Perennial, hairy, tuberous-rooted, simple, edible; stem from Om, 30 to Om, 35; palmate leaves, with 5 elliptical oval leaflets, glabrous below; in June-July, blue flowers, in axillary spikes, pedunculated; corolla the length of the calyx. We know that the same was true of all the plants we had imagined replacing the potato, if the latter had succumbed to the disease it was suffering from. Trials of this kind are always interesting, as much for their own sake as for the purpose to which they may lead; but they may have to be followed for a long time before bringing about a result, which itself remains doubtful; so that they should be recommended, in the present state of the question, rather to public educational establishments and experimenters, than to growers themselves." Family Salsolaceae. 323 Annual plant. Stem straight, twiggy, 1m, 80 high: leaves alternate, triangular, with two sagittate extensions at the base, cut by very obtuse teeth, blond-green, pulverulent when young; flowers whitish, very small, in tight, compact clusters. Compressed, yellowish-white seeds. There are varieties with green, reddish or reddish stems and leaves. Quinoa has been much talked about in the past, but is now forgotten. We are familiar with all the published notes on this plant, which we have grown ourselves. They all agree on the benefits of growing it in France as a successor to spinach. It is in this capacity that it appears in the 1839 issue of Le Bon Jardinier, where it is the subject of a note by M. Vilmorin, instructive and complete enough that, having reproduced it, we have nothing left to say: "In 1836, trials multiplied; everywhere Quinoa succeeded well. The plant is very vigorous, almost impervious to the cold; it produces, in good soil, an extraordinary abundance of seeds, but the seed has so far not been used in a satisfactory way; either it does not acquire in France the same quality as in America, or, more probably, our palates are not shaped to its strange flavor; few people have found it to their taste. It has the real disadvantage of being quite bitter and pungent, which can only be removed by repeated washing. With repeated care, I can make very good cakes and passable soups from it, but preparation is a tricky business; the seed is very small and requires a long cooking time, so it won't meet with the approval of cooks. As for the mistresses of the house, perhaps some of them will judge it like the ladies of Lima, for whom, it is said, Quinoa is a favorite dish; in this case, it would be classified, in France, among those secondary products of which one wants a little for the variety, but not, as in America, among the economic plants of first utility. This would only happen if we could find a way of preparing the seed that would make it easy to use and pleasant tasting for the greatest number of people. "As a vegetable crop, Quinoa will be more readily adopted, because it is a good summer substitute for spinach. "If you want to harvest it as grain, you can sow it either on a bed in March, or even in a sheltered bed, and plant it in April or early May, or in the open ground, in rows, during April. As the plants become very large and strong, they should be spaced about 50 centimetres apart. They require fertile, light rather than compact soil, and exposure to full sun if they are to be harvested for seed. On a plantation that looks able, you can cut off the secondary shoots, which develop in large numbers, to take the leaves; but if you are only thinking of this last product, you should sow in closer rows and cut the stem at the time of the first harvest, to make it branch out. "A Quinoa bed established in this way will provide a succession of constantly renewed products throughout the summer, if watered regularly. In our opinion, Quinoa is a good substitute for Spinach. Enthusiasts will do well, however, to try the other substitutes for this vegetable, which we lack during the summer, i.e. Tetragona, Claytone, Safflower...".

Two other Salsolaceae are particularly sought-after in the deserts of Central Asia, for their edible seeds. These are Agriophyllum gobicum and arenarium. Prjevalski mentions them in the relabon of his third voyage (in Russian), and we reproduce below the translation (1) of the passages that the learned Russian traveler devoted to them: "Soulhhir is a Chenopodea (Salsolaceae). frequent in the whole of Central Asia, up to 48° degrees of northern latitude. It grows only on bare sand. There are two species: Agriophyllum gobicum and A. arenarium. "The former dominates the Ala-Chan, Ordos and, in general, the southern and eastern parts of the Gobi Desert; the latter occupies the western region and grows as far as Turkestan and the Caspian Sea. "Soulkhir is also found in the upper KhouanKhe (river) and in the Tzaidamme (I spent the winter there: I was unable to pick any of the plants, and therefore cannot say which of the two species it was). This plant is absent from northern Thibet. "I said earlier that Soulhhir grows on bare sand. Like other local plants, it makes do with rainwater, which filters through the sand and then (. We owe this translation to Tobhigeance by M. Vilbouche- vitch. rises to the upper layers through evaporation. "To take advantage of this moisture, the Soulkhir has incredibly long roots, as do all plants growing in the same conditions; they are able to draw water from a considerable depth. It goes without saying that sand vegetation is all the richer the more abundant the rainfall. "Soulkhir is an annual plant. In the Ala-Chan region, it grows up to 1 metre in height in good conditions, and its stem can be up to 5 centimetres (?) thick; on average, however, these dimensions are half that. "Not only is Soulkhir superb fodder for Mongolian livestock, but its seeds, which are as small as those of the poppy, are an essential food for the indigenous population. "The saying, 'You have to have sown to reap', does not hold true in Ala-Chan; every year, at the end of September and especially in rainy years, they reap an abundant harvest of Soulkhir from their sands. "The exposed areas of loess clay subsoil are used as threshing floors; the seeds are then roasted and ground to flour using hand mills. "Birds from the northern Gobi that winter in the Tingueri sands also feed on them. Prjevalski gives the following details of the Tungueri sands in the Ala-Chan desert, where these plants grow. They give an exact idea of the environment in which they thrive. "These sands present a sea of mounds, reaching from 10 to 20, rarely up to 30 meters high; they are arranged in complete disorder; long sand ribs divide the mounds. "The mounds themselves are strongly compressed by the wind on one of their slopes, so that the foot does not sink deep into them. The opposite slope, on the other hand, is very steep, and the sand has no consistency. "Between the mounds of sand there are funnel-shaped holes or valleys that often expose the very bottom of the plain, which is, as in most of these sandy deserts, salty clay, smooth and hard as a parquet floor. Water is generally lacking. It is rare to find a spring. "There are also few places where bad salt water can be obtained, by digging 3-4 feet into the loamy subsoil of the sands. "As a general rule, the sands are bare and some vegetation only appears on the edges of sandy places and, from time to time, on the bottoms of the above-mentioned valleys and funnels; the desert flora is, moreover, quite varied in these parts; we collected seventeen species in the Tungueri sands, which had not yet appeared in the year's herbarium. MONSTER RED RADISH FROM KASHGAR BAN-TCHOUNG-TSI FROM KASHGAR. In the spring of 1890, Mr. N. Zolotnitski, president of the botanical section of the Imperial Acclimatization Society of Russia, based in Moscow, sent us a large collection of seeds from Kashgaria and Pamir. Included in this collection were seeds of Ban-tchoung-tsi, Kashgar's monstrous red radish. We applied to this species the cultivation required by the extraordinary development of its roots. The seeds were sown in rows, and the plant was thinned out to give each plant fifty centimetres of space in all directions. We'll mention the Radishes we obtained in 1893. They were enormous. The largest weighed 3 kilos 700 grams. Given by our gardener to a Paris delicatessen, it appeared in the display under the name of Russian Radish. After attracting the admiration of passers-by, it was served in slices to the establishment's customers, who were very satisfied. We have given many Kashgar Radishes to friends and neighbors; they have been declared excellent. The flesh is crisp without being hard, and piquant without excess. Its fault is that it's too big to be served whole, which is a pity, because it's a splendid root. It sets seed quickly, and we have found that in the Paris climate, it should not be sown before July. M. Edouard Blanc gave the Muséum the seeds of a voluminous Radish he brought back from a trip to Turkestan, which we consider identical to ours. Professor Maxime Cornu, rightly believing that it could be used by farmers, presented some fine specimens to the Société nationale d'agriculture. From this point of view, we won't deal with it here. We must say, however, that in 1891 and 1892, we received from Moscow, under the name Dong-la-bout (?), a variety of long, red, monstrous Radish from Kashgar, which we feel could be presented to growers. Like the Japanese Daikon, its flesh is almost tasteless, but its skin is excessively pungent and could doubtless be served on its own as an appetizer. RAPHANUS CAUDATUS L. Cruciferae family. Annual herb, cullivated in Java, where it is probably spontaneous and its candied siliques, known as Mougri, are eaten. It is also cultivated in the Punjab and in western and northern India. Fusiform root, from which rises a stem the size of a goose feather, from Om, 33 to Om, 50 high, sparsely branched, initially straight and eventually receding; the leaves, alternate, very spreading, with two short petioles, are divided, up to the middle, into a small number of triangular lobes, acute and saw-toothed, as is the terminal lobe, which is larger and ovalelanceolate; as they rise on the plant, their shape simplifies, but even the tallest of them is sinuous rather than simply toothed; flowers gathered in small numbers in leafy terminal clusters, each emerging (according to the figure given by Linné fils) from the axil of a floral leaf; white petals, four in number, with purple veins and an inverted heart-shaped blade; siliques 4 to 5 feet long (1.33 to 1.65 m), thicker than a thumb at the bottom, gradually narrowing from base to tip, more or less curved, reddish in color, roughly rounded in cross-section and containing numerous, oblong, purple seeds in their single chamber. We find the above description in a Note by M. P. Duchartre (1869), made necessary by the confusion that tended to arise between Linnaeus' Raphahauscer 112 2- "Orenine Fig. 70. - Snake Radish (Raphanus caudatus). nus caudatus and a plant from India, called Madras Radish, which M. Courtois-Gérard had encountered in the Botanical Garden of Edinburgh, and from which he had brought seeds to France (1). Seven years later, M. Ed. André published, with figures, in the Revue Horticole, an extensive and most interesting Note, to which we refer the reader (2). Growing Raphanus caudatus is like growing any other large radish, and requires no description. It is as simple and easy as can be. The plant is distinguished from all the other Radishes we have by the extraordinary size of its siliques. Although degenerated, a few years ago it was still producing siliques in our garden that were 40 to 50 centimetres long, alongside others that were shorter; in other words, some of the siliques were longer than the whole plant, as Linnaeus pointed out, and when they reached the ground they spread out in sinuosities, like a snake. Our cultivation was considerably hampered by the ravages wrought by flea beetles and a large grey aphid. The latter, which would certainly not have resisted a spray of labac juice, devoured our plants in a matter of days. Its stalk reaches a height of 50 centimetres, and the edible part, reduced to around 30 centimetres, stripped of its bark and cooked for half an hour in a light juice, makes an excellent-looking and tasty vegetable dish. In our families, it's customary simply to cook the stems in stock, leaving the vegetable its natural flavor. Nothing could be easier, as you can see, but the cordon bleu cooks of our village don't stop there, and one of their most successful preparations is with cream and cheese. Note from M. Chappellier: "The crate in which these bulbs made the journey from Persia to Paris remained en route during the autumn of 1881 and the winter of 1881-1882; they came into vegetation and flowered there. "As far as the abnormal condition of these specimens allows me to judge, I am inclined to believe that this Crocus belongs to the C. cancellatus group. "Under the type cancellatus, created by Herbert, authors have grouped the following subtypes, considered by some as species, by others as varieties or synonyms: "C. cancellatus Herb; "C. Schimperi Gay; syn. C. Spruneri Boiss. et Held. "C. damascenus Herb; syn. C. edulis Boiss. et Blanche. " C. Kotschyanus Herb; C. cilicicus Kotschy; C. pylarum Gay; C. mazziaricus Herb. "Here are the main characteristics of C. cancellatus that I found in the Persian Crocus: " Autumn flowering; " Yellow pollen; " Multifid style; " Synanthous leaf; " No involucre (at the scape); " Bivalve bract (at the ovary); " Strongly reticulated tunics, with persistent star at the base; perianth varying from lilac-white to violet. "In C. cancellatus, the throat is yellowish-white or yellow; in Crocus persan, it is lilac-white or violet. "In the latter, I've also noticed a disproportionately long scape. I don't think these peculiarities are due to abnormal flowering in closed, dry boxes. "The geographical distribution of the varieties of C. cancellatus known to date extends from the Ionian Islands to Syria, where C. edulis grows, and Armenia. "M. Pissard's Crocus was collected at an altitude of around 1,300 meters, in the plains and hills of a locality called Sultabatt, in the province of IrathFérahan, southeast of Amadan, about 120 kilometers from Teheran. "Until now, only C. speciosus had been found in Persia. "Here is the information Mr. Pissard gives on the use of this plant. "The onion is edible; it tastes like chestnuts; the natives eat a lot of it. "In July 1881, these onions, boiled and grilled, were presented at an official dinner at the home of the Minister of Telegraphs; several Europeans attending the meal found them exquisite, and the Shah of Persia ordered a large supply for his table. "Until a new contribution from the place of origin or a normal flowering of the recently introduced bulbs allows a more mature examination, I think that it is with the C. edulis Boiss. et Blanche, subtype of the C. cancellatus Herb. that the new Persian Crocus has the most analogy, and I propose to annex it to the cancellatus type, under the name of C. posrieus" (Paris, April 2, 1882). SAGITTARIA SAGITTÆFOLIA L., var, diversifolia Micheli, Monogr. phanerog., vol. III, p. 67; S. sinensis Sims, Bot. Mag. tab. 1631; S. macrophylla Bunge; S. alpina Willd.; S. hirundacea Blume; S. hastata Don; S. porriana Sweet; S. heterophylla Miller; S. acuminata Smith; S. natans Pallas; S. obtusa Thunb. Family Alismaceae. This plant grows in stagnant waters and on the banks of rivers and lakes in the temperate regions of Europe and Asia. Its shape and leaf volume vary according to whether the water is stagnant or running, or more or less abundant and deep. Authors have made species of the various forms it presents; but it is quite certain that these are merely modifications due to the influence of the environment, as one and the same plant may present wider or narrower, acute or obtuse, sagittate or entire leaves, etc. In the typical form, the leaf is flattened, and in the typical form, the leaf is flattened. In the typical form, the leaf is sagittate, with a variable blade, sometimes narrow, sometimes acute, with divided base lobes, sometimes broader, sometimes with obtuse middle lobes, those at the base almost straight. In running water, stems and petioles are spindly and sinuous; the leaf is oblong, with a rounded, emarginate base, more rarely briefly lobed, with divergent, acute lobes (S. alpina Willd.), or the leaf is limbless, translucent, weakly membranous, up to 2 meters long (S. sagit- tæfolia, var. valisneriïfolia Coss. et Germ.; Vallisneria bulbosa Poir.). Radical leaves oblong, usually mottled pale green on a dark green background, very thorny, narrowed at the base to form a stalk; stem very stalky, reaching about 60 to 80 centimetres in height, lined with sessile, decurrent, very thorny leaves; flowers in sessile heads, grouped in twos or threes, with bright yellow florets. When we come across an article in a little-known publication, almost impossible to find for most of our readers, written in perfect agreement with our opinion on the cultivation and merit Fig. 75. - Scolyme d'Espagne. of one of the plants in our kitchen garden, we have no hesitation in reproducing it in full. This is what we'll do for the Scolyme d'Espagne. In the Bulletin de la Société d'Horticulture de l'Aube, Volume I, page 217: Culture du Scolyme d'Espagne. "If there is one vegetable that deserves to be cullivated with care and which is, on the contrary, neglected and almost abandoned in certain localities, it is certainly the Scolyme. No vegetable, old or new, seems to me to possess as many qualities as this one. Its delicate taste, long shelf life, rapid growth and the time it appears on our tables mean that it can compete without too much disadvantage, not with Scorsonera or Salsify, with which it is most closely related, but with Cardoons and Cauliflowers, the vegetables to which gardeners devote all their care; But, unfortunately, Scolyma doesn't always succeed when left to its own devices, and its seeds, whether poorly chosen or preserved, or sown in unfavorable conditions, don't always grow very well. I will indicate, as best I can, the procedures that I have found suitable up to now, and which have been fairly successful. I do not claim to have brought cultivation to any great perfection, but I am convinced that amateurs who have succeeded and appreciated the value of this vegetable once will not abandon it, despite the occasional setbacks they may experience. "The Scolyma seed is small and enclosed in a membranous or foliaceous envelope. This envelope, which hides it from the eye of the examiner, makes it very difficult for him to appreciate its quality by sight. "It is sown from June 20 to July 15; earlier, the plants rise, flower and produce roots that are perhaps a little larger, but which lack the qualities of those that have not flowered. Sown later, the yield may be low. The seeds are placed in furrows 4 to 5 centimetres deep, about 20 centimetres apart. Don't be afraid of sowing a little too thickly in the furrow. "At this time of year, the soil is usually dry, and when worked, it dries out quickly to the depth where the seeds go. Watering, unless excessively abundant, is not always a remedy. To remedy this dryness of the soil, when the furrows that are to receive the seeds are made, they are watered to the point of becoming almost muddy; we sow on this wet ground and cover with the soil from the edges of the furrow, which has also been wet. "This moisture in the soil is maintained fairly well, and a few sprinklings, if the temperature is too dry, are enough to make the seeds stand up; because with this cultivation method, it will rarely happen that the seeds don't stand up in sufficient quantity. In general, summer sowings are not very successful, because the seeds may be a little dried out by the high temperature of the season, and because the soil contains much less moisture than in spring and autumn. If, to these differences in germination conditions, we add the separation of the soil from the seed by the membranous envelope that surrounds the latter, we will understand perfectly why this seed often lifts very poorly, and it is, I believe, this disadvantage that makes it abandon cultivation. "The leaves of this plant, with the exception of the seminal ones, bear a strong resemblance to a thistle. "When all the seeds have risen and the plants have already gained some strength (four to five leaves, not including the seminals), thin them out, leaving a distance of about 10 centimetres between the plants in the furrow. Plants that have been carefully removed can be permanently replanted. I say carefully uprooted; as far as possible, the root tip, which is not long at this time of year, should not be broken, and care should be taken when replanting not to go around it or crumple it. Once the plant has been transplanted, the soil must be kept wet to help it recover. "The rest of the work, during the year, consists of keeping the soil clean and weeding it once or twice, and above all watering it well if the weather is dry. A little manure water, not too strong so as not to burn the leaves, sprinkled on these vegetables will give them rapid growth and ensure a beautiful, good product. Very often, Scolymes don't reach full growth until the end of September and during October. "Scolymes are good to eat from late October or early November. The root is the only part of this vegetable that has so far been recognized as worthy of appearing on the table. In the middle of each root is a hard, woody part; this center, which its hardness prevents from being good to eat, only separates from the edible part when they have been cooked for preparation. This separation is easy to achieve. As far as I know, cultivation trials have not yet succeeded in making this woody part softer that it does not need to be removed for preparation. However, some people believe that this is the result that market gardening can achieve. "When winters are mild, Scolymes can remain in the garden until spring, when they will grow again; but when we fear that they will start growing again, we pull them out, cut off the upper part of the root that holds the leaves and bury them in sand in the cellar. They keep well until June, but in general, when winter approaches, it's a good idea to pull some of them out, prepare them as I've said, take them down to the cellar and cover the plants left in the garden with straw or straw mats. Although the cold only seems to kill the top of the root, the damage is always greater than it seems, because the frozen part causes the part that touches it to rot when it thaws. When weeding, either in spring or autumn, we choose the prettiest plants to bear seed. Place them in spring, 30 or 40 centimetres apart, in a good, well-ventilated spot away from the garden. "In June and July, the plants come up and give yellow flowers; but these flowers, which are born in the leaf axils, follow one another incessantly, and some have already ripened their seeds when the others bloom. "If the plants were not bristling with leaves more prickly than those of the Holly, one could try to collect the seeds as they ripen; I don't know of any amateur zealous enough to have wanted to do this. You seize the moment when the plants seem to have the greatest quantity of ripe seeds; you cut them, then place them on a cloth, in a basket, in a very dry place. After a few days, they are threshed and the seeds collected, which need to be winnowed in order to separate the bad ones. This operation must be carried out with care; many seeds that seem incapable of germinating do, however, germinate very well, as I was able to ascertain by winnowing them one year, in spring, before sowing them. Seeds which had fallen, as bad, in a position not very favorable to their germination have however risen well and in quantity." The note we have just read teaches us everything we need to know about growing Scolyme d'Espagne. It attributes, probably with good reason, the neglect in which this vegetable has remained to the irregularity of seed germination, and indicates the means to overcome this difficulty. But it may not be the only reason. One of the main obstacles to the success of a vegetable, however good it may be, comes from cooks and their routine habits. They probably reject Scolyma because, after cooking in salt water, they have to remove the central part of the roots, which is almost always woody and inedible. However, all vegetables give them at least as much trouble. Don't you have to remove the hay from artichokes, strain purees, shell broad beans, peas, beans, chop spinach, etc.? What's more laborious than removing the Scolyma cord? We hope that housewives, having recognized the superiority of the Scolyma root over all similar roots, will succeed in overcoming the resistance of their blue cords. Scolyme, once up, is a hardy plant. It occupies the soil for only three and a half months; the flavor of its roots is, in our opinion, infinitely more pleasant than that of Scorsonères and Salsifis, which occupy the soil two and three times longer. We can't recommend its cultivation enough. 36 In Spain, Scolyme is used differently from France, where only its roots are eaten. We didn't know this until we read a note by E. Bourgeau, botanist and traveler. Bourgeau, botanist-traveler, inserted in the Revue horticole, year 1852, page 60, a note which we feel we must reproduce: "Edible plant, vegetable, spontaneous in the southern part of Spain, which means that it is hardly cultivated there; but it is not the same in the vicinity of Madrid. It is the petioles and the middle rib of the leaf that are used in Spanish cooking, either in small packets put into stews, or prepared in different ways and combined with meat, or added to eggs, omelettes, etc. "Around January 1st, the fields are harvested, and the leaves are used for cooking. "Around January 1st, fields are almost universally covered with rosettes of leaves, which farmers harvest in the manner of dandelion, i.e. 1 or 2 inches from the taproot. The leaf blade is removed, leaving only the entire length of the rib, which is joined together and tied like a Romaine lettuce. Everyone prepares this vegetable as they see fit, either retaining a little of the root or eliminating it altogether. In January and February, a dozen are sold at the market for 30 centimes; in March and April, a dozen are only worth 15 centimes. "The markets are covered with it for five months of the year, and because it is so widely consumed in the country, the plant produces a fairly good income for country people every year. Sales end in May, by which time the leaves have become too hard and prickly to eat. "Scolyme's long, fleshy root is used as a vegetable in Provence and Languedoc, where the plant grows abundantly; in Montpellier, it's called Cardouille. It is not cultivated there; it is gathered wild in the fields, and, as the central axis is usually woody, the root is split longitudinally, removed, and it is the cortical part, bound in small bundles, that is sold" (1). In closing, we reiterate our advice to grow Scolyme d'Espagne. SCORZONERA DELICIOSA Gussone. Index seminum horto Boccadifalco, 1825, p. 11; Floræ siculæ synopsis, II, p. 389; DC. Prodr. VII, p. 118. Compositae family. Sicily. Tuberous-rooted perennial, cylindrical, oblong or almost globose, brown on the outside, white on the inside; stem simple, rarely twining at the base; leaves linear lanceolate, acuminate, flat, glabrous, a little tomentose at the base; capitula solitary at the tip of the twigs; involucral scales glabrous, acute, the outer ones lanceolate, ending in an acute point. Purple flowers. Here's what Gussone says about Scorsonera délicieuse: "The roots of this species are used (1) Le Bon Jardinier. in Sicily, candied in sugar, then dissolved in cold water; they are also used to make refreshing sorbets, iced and perfumed with large-flowered Jasmine, an aromatic that makes them very pleasant; finally, they are classified among those that provide refreshing decoctions." This plant does not seem to us to justify the ambitious qualification given to it by the Italian botanist. We received it from Mr. E. Morelli, engineer, and from Mr. Todaro, our colleague, eminent jurisconsult and director of the Palermo Botanical Garden. The latter wrote to us on April 27 1886: "With regard to the four plants requested, the Scorsonère délicieuse is the only one of them that we have in the garden and that grows spontaneously in the Palermo area... This species, which is widely used in Sicily, either in decoctions, juleps or sorbets, cultivated in pots, perishes if watered after flowering." In the course of the same year, we received several letters from Mr. E. Morelli, from which we extract the following: "I have never heard of Scorzonera outside Sicily, and even there it is only used by confectioners, who make a syrup that is consumed either as a drink in the same way as orgeat, lemon or other syrups, or for making ice cream... " ... In Sicily, plants are not sown, but propagated by simply separating the roots, which is done in October and November. As the plant is completely wild, no care is taken. The roots, which are the only part of the plant that is used, can be harvested at any time by pulling them up as soon as they have reached their normal size. "To use them, we crush them as best we can, then throw them into an aqueous sugar syrup, boil until concentrated and strain through a cloth. They can also be candied in the syrup, taking care to boil them first to remove the rind... " ... In Palermo, they are used to make refreshing decoctions, syrup and jam. The syrup is sold by the best confectioner in the area for 1 fr. 10 per bottle of about 400 grams, the jam for 3 fr. 20 per kilogram; both contain enough, even too much sugar, so there's nothing to fear from the journey. "The plant tolerates the cold perfectly. In Sicily, it is even found on mountains, where it overwinters under the snow. "My gardener claims that some of the roots are harvested when the leaves start to wilt, i.e. around the middle of August; some are left to avoid destroying the plants, which is all the more important as, in a new plantation, you can only harvest in the second year, whereas once the plants are well established you can pull out roots every year. "In fact, however, this plant is not cultivated here; it grows spontaneously in the mountains, without any care. It is therefore probable that, in cultivated land, it could produce more abundantly. The same observation applies to the question of whether the roots can be eaten as a vegetable. Here, the fiber is very hard; to use it to prepare herbal teas, it is grated after being scalded to remove the outer shell. It is not unlikely that, in your climate and in better soil, it will be softer. We have little to add to the information provided by the letters from which we have just given extracts. We can hardly expect the roots of Scorzonera deliciosa to become tender enough to be used as a vegetable. That they make refreshing decoctions; that they provide the material for syrups, jams and frozen sorbets, is a given, since, in these various forms, they are in general use in Sicily; but we are obliged to contradict the learned Dr. Baron von Mueller, who, in his Select extra tropical Plants, presents Scorzonera deliciosa as a purple-flowered species, equal, if not superior in its culinary uses, to Salsify, to which it is closely related. We planted Scorzonera deliciosa roots in the ground, and they thrived. We covered them for the winter with frames and leaves. Although they overwinter under the snow in the mountains of Sicily, this fact does not allow us to believe that they can withstand the cold in the vicinity of Paris; precautions are necessary. Mr. E. Morelli sent us syrup and jams from Scorzonera. The latter arrived in the most unfortunate condition. All the liquid had drained out of the crate in which they were stored, and all that remained in the jars was a tasteless paste. The syrup was excellent. 567 MALaBaila SEKAKUL Russell; Alepp. II, p. 249 (Syn.: M. platyptera Boiss; Pastinaca dissecta Vent; Pastinaca Sekakul Rauw; Leiotulus alexandrinus Ehrenb.). Umbelliferae family. Perennial, indigenous and cultivated in Anatolia, Armenia, Svrie, Palestine, etc. (Boissier, Flora orientalis, vol. 2, p. 1057). The root is tuberous and oblong; the leaves are bipinnate, with toothed or incised segments. The whole plant reaches 30 centimetres in height or a little more. In a note published in the Journal de l'Académie d'Horticulture, 2nd edition, tome I (1831), p. 134, De Candolle regrets that the cultivation of this Oriental umbellifer has not been given more attention in Europe. Its root, says Rauwolf (Travels, vol. I, p. 66, ed. Rai, London 1693), is cylindrical, swiveling, grayish on the outside, white on the inside, of delicate consistency and as if medullary, an inch thick and an inch and a half long. Instead of fibrils, it has wart-like nodules. Its flavor is mild and not unlike that of the carrot. Jean Bauhin and Morison gave crude figures of it, and from then on the plant was almost forgotten by European naturalists. Miller mentioned it briefly in his dictionary under the inaccurate name of Tordylium Sekakul. Russell, in the report of his trip to Aleppo, vol. II, p. 249, refers to it as Pastinaca Sekakut, praising it as a food plant. Olivier and Bruguières harvested it near Aleppo and sent seeds to Cels. The resulting plants were described and illustrated by Ventenat, Jardin de Cels, tab. 78, under the name Pastinaca dissecta. Sekakul is reminiscent of parsnip in its yellow flowers and fruit, but is easily distinguished at first glance by its sharply dissected leaves with toothed lobes. In the note we quote, published over sixty years ago, De Candolle said: "The root seems to me to have more in common with the parsnip than with the carrot, and if to the delicacy of the former, it joins the flavor of the latter, it would seem to deserve to be introduced into our vegetable gardens." In our research into experiments to cultivate new food plants in European gardens, we have found no trace of trials with Sekakul. We regret to add that, despite the requests we have made in the East, it has not yet been possible to obtain seeds of this Umbelliferous plant, the value of which we would nevertheless have liked to know. We would also like to mention another Umbellifera that we were keen to cultivate, but were unable to obtain; this is Sium Helenianum Hook. f., Icones plantarum, pl. 1032, a plant native to the island of St. Helena, whose green stems are sold in markets under the name Jellico, and eaten raw (Official guide of the Museums of Economic Botany (Dicotyledons aud Gymnosperms), 2nd ed. 1886, p. 83). SERI Panturasee (Bengalese.) OENANTHE STOLONIFERA DC. Phellandrium stoloniferum Roxb; Dasycoma subpinnatum Miq. Umbelliferae family. Perennial, native to marshy areas of Japan, China and India. "This marsh herb is used as a spinach. (Mueller, Select, etc.). "Seri or Œnanthe stolonifera grows wild in wetlands and marshes; however, that which is sold commercially is the result of cultivation and is eaten cooked." (Le Japon à l'Exposition universelle de 1878, vol. Il, p. 137). "According to the Japanese Commission, Seri is frequently cultivated, used in food and eaten boiled and salted". (Dr Mène, Des productions végétales du Japon). A note kindly sent to us illustrates the cultivation method used in Japan. It is dated Yokohama, October 22 1886. "The plant does not reproduce by seed; it reproduces in the following way: the soil must be muddy and constantly covered with water. The rice fields here are very suitable for growing Seri. First, the soil is stirred well to obtain a liquid, even mud, which is left to stand for about a week. Then take the roots, cut into small pieces of about 2 cm, and sow them in prepared soil. The seedbed should be fairly light. The roots are then pressed lightly into the mud. After four or five days, you'll start to see the leaves grow. It's a good idea then, as far as possible, to increase the quantity of water in proportion to the plant's growth, but always leaving the leaves above the water. "This culture can be tried out in a crate, provided the bottom of the vase is 8 to 10 centimetres deep. The above-mentioned note accompanied a shipment of well-packed Seri plants, which, according to the experienced Japanese shipping agent, were due to arrive safely in Paris; however, the plants had died during the journey, and a new request was sent to Yokohama. OENANTHE SARMENTOSA Nutt. We have cultivated this species, which was sent to us from North America. Its young stems and leaves are eaten by the Oregon Indians. The plant has grown vigorously in our basins, and its long, creeping stems have spread out in all directions. But, as the genus Œnanthe contains a good number of poisonous species, we didn't want to taste the American herb until we were sure it was harmless. To this end, we turned to Dr. Gréhant, director of the physiology laboratory at the Muséum, who injected guinea pigs with a concentrated extract. The experiment having been favorable, we had a dish of Œnanthe sarmentosa prepared; but we must declare that, apart from a slight aromatic flavor, analogous to that of Celery, it seemed to us to have no particular merit. COMESTIBLE SOUCHET Souchet Sultan. Ground almond. CYPERUS ESCULENTUS L. Family Cyperaceae. Creeping plant. Rhizomes producing slender fibers, each ending in an ovoid tuber, marked with circular impressions, yellowish-brown on the outside, white on the inside, with a pleasant, sweet flavor. Stem triqueterous, glabrous, leafy at the bottom; leaves as long as or longer than the stem, flat, canaliculate and keeled, rough towards their tips on the margins and keel. Umbel simple or compound, with 7-10 unequal rays, the longest of which branch at the apex, with an involucre of 4-6 leaves longer than the inflorescence; on each ray attach 10-14 lanceolate or linear spikes, compressed, with 10-18 flowers; the scales are elliptical, almost obovate, keeled-navicular, 7-9-veined, yellowish-brown, with a green midline. Yellow nutsedge grows spontaneously in southern Europe, the Orient and northern Africa. Its rhizomes are lined with tubers the size of hazelnuts, with a pleasant, sweet flavor reminiscent of chestnuts. Fig. 76. - Yellow nutsedge (Cyperus esculentus). Easy to grow. Tubers are planted on May 1st, in clumps spaced 25 to 30 centimetres apart in all directions, and first soaked in water. A forty-eight-hour immersion is necessary. If the season is warm, vegetation is very active. The single culm clumps, produced by just five or six tubers, give rise to a multitude of new shoots, spread out and join together, turning the plantation into a meadow. Weed by hand, if possible, to avoid cutting the young shoots; water abundantly when the weather is hot and refrain from doing so when it's cold. Not watering does not compromise the harvest, but it is much less. In Spain, we irrigate the plantation as soon as it is established, and repeat every eight to ten days. Harvesting takes place in October. If it doesn't freeze, we can wait until the first days of November. Valencian growers cut the stems before flowering to encourage the development of the roots and tubers; but in the Paris climate, you don't get flowers, and we remember growing Souchet, not without success, in the Landes department, without our plantation having produced a single flower. Moreover, Souchet is grown in Spain not by sowing seeds, but by planting tubers. Harvesting is carried out by pulling up the clumps, which are knocked against a reed rack over a wicker sieve to separate the tubers from the roots. The tubers are then carefully washed and, when clean, laid out on mats in the sun to dry and preserve them. In this process, they lose around a third of their weight (1). Dried tubers retain their germanative properties for a full year. Chufa, the Spaniards' favorite refreshment, is made with tubers from the last harvest, not from the current crop. Chufa (1) Bulletin de la Société impériale d'Acclimatation, t. X, n° 12. Note presented by Mr. Ch. Barbier, civil engineer. is an orgeat that lends itself admirably to making ice creams, which are widely consumed in Madrid. To prove its merit, we ourselves served it to a gathering of twenty people, who found it very good. Here's the recipe for Chufa: Soak 250 grams of tubers for 48 hours; grind; add 1 liter of water and 150 grams of sugar; strain. Serve as orgeat, or use to make ice cream. It cannot be preserved. We didn't stick to this recipe, and knowing that the Israelites of Oran make Souchet cakes, we managed to have some made that were not significantly inferior in quality to ordinary almond cakes (1). However, we would like to point out a few precautions to be taken. The skin of ordinary almonds is easily removed with boiling water; but the tuber of the Souchet resists, and it is impossible to remove the film that envelops it. This film is so thin that, after careful grinding, there is absolutely nothing left of it; but there is a sort of callus at the point where the tuber attaches to the rhizome, and, to get rid of it, the ground almonds must be placed in a sieve of suitable fineness. The calluses remain there. There is no need to give a recipe for these cakes here. Proceed as for ordinary almond cakes. Instead of bitter almonds (1) Journal de la Société centrale d'Horticulture, 1877, t. XI, p. 40. you can add a little cinnamon to enhance the taste. Yellow nutsedge makes an excellent oil and a good brandy, but we would be going too far if we were to consider it as an economic plant. In this respect, however, we consider it to be extremely important, and recommend to those of our readers who are concerned with agriculture and industrial plants, the Note we published in the Journal de la Société centrale d'Horticulture, 1878, tome XII, 2nd series, page 341. As a limited-use vegetable plant, Yellow Nutsedge nevertheless has a marked place in amateur gardens. SOYA (1) Mame and Daizu, in Japan; Yeou-teou in China. GLYCINE SOIA Sieb. et Zucc; Dolichos Soja L.; Soja hispida Mœnch; Glycine hispida Miquel. Legume family. Paillieux; Paris, Librairie agricole, 26, rue lacob. -- in the Kingdom of Siam, Cochinchina, Tonkin and especially in China, Thibet, Mongolia and the provinces of Honan, Shengking, Shangtung and Chan-si. 4 Fig. 77. - Soya (Glycine Soja). Kæmpfer describes the plant in his Amœnitatum exoticarum politico-physico-medicarum, fascicule V, 1792: "Sorte de Haricot à pods velues comme celles du Lupin, à graines arronées et blanches comme celles du Pois; haut d'environ 4 pieds. "It has a hairy, unevenly round stem. "Its leaves resemble those of the common bean, but with coarser hairs on the underside. In August, in the leaf axils, it blooms bluish-white, very small flowers on a common stalk, similar to those of the Lentil, with straight, barely spread out standards and wings, followed by numerous pods, barely 2 inches long, covered with rough, long hair, similar to Lupin pods with yellow flowers, containing two seeds, rarely three, similar in shape and flavor to Garden Pea, a little compressed though, with brown umbilicus. " Kæmpfer seems to have known only one type of Soya, with white seeds and a brown umbilicus; but we know that there are at least thirty varieties with yellow, black, white, grey with white spots, greenish, red or variegated red seeds, some with a white hilum and others with a red hilum. In addition, depending on the variety, the leaflets may be rounded or lanceolate, barely hispid or very hispid; the flowers may be blue, white or purple; and the fruits, round or flattened, may contain 5 or 6 seeds. The quality of these seeds is mainly due to their high nitrogen content and the large quantity of oil they contain. Soya is one of the most widely used plants in China and Japan, for both food and industrial purposes. 37 I. - Soya in Japan. The famous traveller and naturalist Kæmpfer (1) was one of the first, if not the first, to make known the plant we are concerned with. We cannot resist recounting the journey during which he saw Soya and was taught its uses. Kæmpfer arrived in Batavia in September 1689, which he left the following May, and embarked as physician to the embassy which the Dutch Company sent to Japan every year. He obtained permission to go on board the ship that was to reach Siam, and finally, on September 25, he went ashore in the small town of Desima, near Nangasaki. By the services he rendered the Japanese, by his complaisance, by his liberality, he insinuated himself into the friendship and familiarity of the interpreters and officers, and won them over so well that they refused to answer any of his questions and, when he was alone with them, revealed to him even those things about which they are bound to inviolable secrecy. A young man who had been given to him for service, and at the same time to study medicine and surgery under him, having successfully treated Desima's principal officer under his direction, received permission not to leave Kæmpfer's side. Kæmpfer taught Dutch to his pupil, who, out of gratitude, brought him all the books he could wish for. So, despite the jealousy and mistrust of the Japanese government, Kæmpfer was able to (1) Kæmpfer Engelbert, physician and famous traveler, born September 16, 1651, at Lemgo, in the county of Lippe, Westphalia; died November 2, 1716. satisfy his curiosity on most of the points he wished to know. When the director of Dutch trade left for Yedo on February 10, 1691, Kæmpfer accompanied him, and thus had the opportunity to see the interior of the empire. The following year, he made the same trip with another director. He left Nangasaki on October 31. Following these trips, he published his Histoire naturelle du Japon. Miso, according to Kæmpfer. "To obtain Miso, we take a measure of Mame or Daeds beans (Soya), which we cook for a very long time in water, until completely softened, and which we reduce to a soft pulp by crushing them. This method of crushing is continued to mix the pulp with four measures of salt in summer, a number reduced to three in winter, as the product is all the more irreproachable the less salt is added; I would add, however, that it keeps less long. "We then add and mix in a measure (of volume equal to that of the beans) of Koos or husked rice, slightly steamed with fresh water; then, after cooling, we place in a warm cellar for twenty-four and forty-eight hours, until it cools and contracts. "This mixture, which has the consistency of porridge, is introduced into a wooden vase that has contained the beer commonly known as Sacki. Before use, this product is kept for one or two months. "Koos gives the pulp a sweet flavor, and its manufacture requires, like the Italians' polenta, the skill of a master. For this reason, there are those who only prepare it, and then purify the resulting product. SOOJU, according to Kæmpfer. "To make Sooju, we take Daeds beans cooked to the same point and an equal quantity of Muggi, or Wheat, and as much roughly pulverized Barley or Rye; the latter seed gives a blacker product. In short, one measure of each substance is used. The beans are mixed with the crushed wheat, covered with a cloth and left to ferment for twenty-four hours. The mixture is then covered with the prescribed salt and placed in a clay pot, where two measures of ordinary water are mixed with half the dose. The next day, the mixture is stirred with a spatula, covered and stirred several days in a row, at least once and preferably two or three times. "After three months' preparation, the mass is filtered and the liqueur is expressed and stored in wooden vases; the clarity and quality of this liqueur are in keeping with its age. Nothing has changed in the last two hundred years in the way Miso and Shoyu are made, and their consumption has not diminished. In Japan, these products are still an absolute necessity. The information we receive from those of our nationals who visit or live in Japan does not differ appreciably from that collected by Kæmpfer in 1689; but the learned traveler said nothing about To-fu (Daizu), a cheese made from Soya seeds; we have to fill this gap. He paid particular attention to the species used to make Miso and Shoyu, citing only three or four varieties, whereas there are probably some thirty. Among these varieties, some are early, others late. The latter cannot be usefully cultivated in central France. Some are used as vegetables for direct human consumption, such as beans, broad beans, peas, lentils, etc., etc.; others are prepared in more or less complicated ways, making them veritable industrial plants. The choice to be made among these varieties is impracticable by far. You would have to take them all in, grow them all, taste them all, and only reject those that should not be kept after complete experience. Mame no. 9 on our list is not without merit: "Ordinary Soyas," we write, "at least the yellowish-white variety, most commonly used to make Shoyu, To-fu and Miso, are not usually eaten in the wild. Black and green Soyas are sometimes eaten in the same way as dried beans. A variety with large green beans is eaten quite often in Japan after being roasted, ground and mixed with sugar. Children love this kind of racahout or revalescière and eat it by the handful. As far as I know, no pastry or cake is made from soybeans. Mame tea is also eaten plain. It's likely that several other varieties are eaten the same way, but we don't know. What we can say is that all Mame can be used to make Miso, Shoyu and To-fu. Our kind correspondent, Dr. H***, brought us a large, yellowish-white Mame, the most widely grown for making Miso, Shoyu and To-fu (2), but unfortunately too late for our country, where summer is too short, and he had to stick to growing the small, round-grained, yellowish Chinese Mame. The latter is much less beautiful, but ripens perfectly. This is the variety most cultivated in France, and to which we have given the name Soya d'Étampes. Mame is grown in Japan in the same way as beans, but the plants need to be spaced much farther apart and are more resistant to autumn frosts. The Japanese don't make Soya oil. They use only sesame oil for cooking and rapeseed oil for lighting. Other oils, extracted from the fruits of different trees, are used for industrial purposes. In the part of Japan where our correspondent lived, Soya straw was fed to animals. In Satsouma, in the far south, fine horses were given rations of Daizu seeds, which were said to be a much better, but more expensive, food than naked barley. Horses eat Daizu very well, both raw and cooked. According to Krasnow (1), early Soyas, sown in early to mid-May, require between 2,300 and 3,000 degrees of heat, but most perish as soon as the thermometer drops to 2 degrees below zero. It was Eurotium Orizæ, the fermenting agent in Saké or rice brandy, that determined the fermentation process in the making of Shoyu. Here's what the book Le Japon à l'Exposition universelle de 1878 has to say about Mame: (1) Krasnow, Les régions théières de l'Asie subtropicale (1er vol., Japon), St. Petersburg 1897, (in Russian). "Mame has many uses, as it can not only be eaten cooked and ground into flour, but also used to make Shoyu, Miso and To-fu. Mame, its husk, leaves and stalk are used to feed horses; they have also been used recently, on a trial basis, to feed sheep, and the results obtained have proved that they are the best food that can be given to them. "To-fu is made from two types of boiled mame (1): Shiro mame and Ki mame; once pressed and hardened, it can be kept for a long time. Yuba is a similar paste (2), made with the same ingredients." He does, however, give us a recipe for its preparation, which we reproduce because it is very simple and does not, like Kæmpfer's, prescribe the use of Koos, or husked rice mixed with Daizu. Miso," he says, "is a more or less fermented paste made with Daizu (Soya). It's used to make a kind of soup, which is almost every Japanese person's lunch. It's very bad, and I've eaten some on my travels, not having anything else to hand, but it's by no means a desirable acquisition. As for making Miso, it's very simple.
