If the vegetable garden is large enough, look for a place outside the crop rotation to create an asparagus plan; divide the four squares subject to crop rotation into equal parts, and orient the square beds from north to south, and make alleys around and in the middle of the garden wide enough for wheelbarrows to circulate easily. When the plan has been sufficiently worked out on paper, the layout is laid out on the ground as follows: first, the beds and squares are marked out with a chalk line; at each corner, a sturdy stake is driven in at least 60 centimetres to find the reference points; all the measurements are checked; the paths are then emptied to a depth of about 20 centimetres, with the soil thrown back onto the beds and squares so that the layout does not fade, and the soil is prepared. DISEESOE GO LEVELLING, AMENDMENT AND RIPPING. Once the layout has been laid out on the ground, and the stakes placed at each corner for easy retrieval, we proceed to levelling. But first, the ground must be carefully examined to level it, if it is not well levelled, which is the first condition to make watering profitable for the plants. Levelling should be carried out at the same time as ripping, by the diggers who perform it, and without any great increase in cost. It's easy for them to do when their work is well prepared, and costs them little more trouble, which is a great saving for the owner. Levelling by the day, before or after ripping, is often more expensive than ripping, and has the disadvantage of damaging the soil, especially after ripping. However, if the ground is covered with mounds of earth, or has a very steep slope, it should be roughly levelled before scribing. In all other cases, proceed as follows: Take three levelers (pl. 3, fig. 1), or better still four, for each side of the square to be levelled, i.e. twelve for a square we assume to have 18 metres on each side. The first leveller is placed not quite at the corner of the square, but 20 centimetres from this corner, in the driveway, so as to drive levelling pegs all around the square, so that the diggers don't disturb them while digging and use them for levelling. With the first leveller placed at a height of around 80 centimetres, a second is driven in 6 metres from the first, and at the same height; then the third is placed 6 metres from the second, all three are aligned one on top of the other, and the fourth is placed at the other corner. Then, as we've just done, we place three levelers, 6 meters apart, on each of the two faces adjoining the one already levelled, and two on the fourth, to determine a perfectly horizontal line all around the square. Once this has been done, a levelling rod (pl. 3, fig. 2) is adjusted to the length of a leveller of average height, which is the height the ground should have, and a peg is driven in between each leveller with a mallet, adjusting its height with the levelling rod. In addition, when placing the levelling pegs, you must take into account the overrun of the excavated earth, which is about one tenth: thus, when excavating to a depth of one metre, you must count on ten centimetres of overrun, and place the pegs ten centimetres higher than the actual level. Once the stakes have been driven in, the levellers are removed one by one, and a stake adjusted with the levelling rod is placed in their hole, and if necessary with two rods when there are not enough levellers left. The head of each stake represents the exact height the ground should be; these stakes, placed three meters apart at the edge of the path, are a sure guide for the diggers, and make it easy to check the levelling at any time, with a rod placed on the stakes at each end, and a third placed on the ground. A bonus of five or ten francs, depending on the size of the garden, will sufficiently compensate the diggers for the time they have wasted checking their levelling with a levelling rod. The same stakes will be used to level the paths once they have been levelled. It is useful to give them a general slope, almost imperceptible to the eye, but necessary to facilitate water run-off during rainstorms. A slope of two millimeters per meter is sufficient; let's take as an example our 18-meter square, with seven stakes on each side. These stakes are placed three meters apart, and the overall slope is 36 millimeters. The stakes must therefore be driven in as follows: the first will not be touched; the second will be driven in by 6 millimeters; the third by 12; the fourth by 18; the fifth by 24; the sixth by 30, and the seventh by 36. All that remains to be done is to put soil up to the head of the stakes, and the slope will be adjusted with great accuracy, without pain or unnecessary expense. Alleys should not be levelled until at least three weeks after breaking, when the earth has regained its plumbness, and the levelling has been checked and found to be accurate; but, I cannot recommend it strongly enough, the levelling stakes should not be disturbed until the broken ground has been completely settled. Once the levelling stakes have been placed, we proceed with the general ripping. There are three ways to break up the soil, depending on its quality and depth: 1° WITH OPEN GAUGE. If the soil is of the same quality down to a depth of one meter, and if there are no amendments to be introduced, all that needs to be done is to break up the soil, at the following depths: 80 centimeters in clayey soils, 1 meter in medium-consistency soils, and 1 meter 10 centimeters in sandy soils. This work is paid by the job: 25 to 30 centimes per metre in clay soils, depending on their tenacity, and 20 centimes in medium-consistency soils and in sands. In all cases, whether for planting trees or for vegetable garden beds, smoking must never be allowed while ripping. This is what is most often done: in this case, manure buried very deeply, and therefore placed beyond the reach of the roots, is entirely lost. Ripping must always be done by the company or by the job: only then can it be done at the prices I have indicated. Whenever an owner tries to have them done by the day, no matter how cheaply he pays the workers, the work is poorly done and comes back at an exorbitant price. A good digger does an average of 20 meters of digging in a day; he always asks to work by the job; he prefers to take the trouble and earn the money. A poor day laborer, on the other hand, does barely four meters a day, and constantly repeats that ripping is an impossible job. In this case, if the owner lives in a country where the workers are too soft to undertake the task, i.e. are not willing to go to a little trouble to earn h to 5 francs a day, he will have a great advantage in bringing in diggers and paying them for their trip there and back. I sent some to Berry and Touraine, the owners were delighted, and the local workers considered them fantastic workers. Ripping should never be done with a spade, but always with a pick and shovel. Breaking up with a spade is disastrous for the landowner, in that the soil is turned upside down, with the good soil at the bottom and the bad soil on top, and can remain completely infertile for several years, and ruinous for the workman, because he makes no progress, and earns pitiful days with great difficulty. Both would do well to keep quiet. Raking with a pickaxe is the only way to benefit the owners, and the only way to benefit the worker, especially if he knows how to avoid transporting earth: Let's say we have to break up four vegetable garden squares separated by a cross-shaped path (pl. 3, fig. 3). We'll have all four squares dug without rolling a single wheelbarrow of earth. We'll open the trench at the corner of the first square facing the middle alley (A pl. 3, fig. 3). This trench will be four meters wide and two meters long, so that three men can work in it abreast without getting in each other's way. The earth from the trench opening will be thrown into the alley next to its opening (B pl. 3, fig. 3). Six men will go down into the trench and work in threes abreast: three to pick and three to shovel, taking turns. The first three will cut the soil at the bottom of the trench, in 30 to h0 centimetre thick slices, to the required depth; the second three will pick up the soil with their shovels as it falls under the pickaxe, and mix it again by throwing it behind them, up to the height of the levelling stakes. In this way, the soil will be perfectly mixed, giving one meter of ford of excellent soil of the same consistency. This soil will always be fresh, remarkably fertile and, thanks to its natural freshness, will save half on watering. The trench has been opened at the left-hand corner of the first square; the trenching will be carried out in such a way as to end at the opposite corner, the right-hand corner at the bottom of the square, where there will be a void equal to the soil removed and left in reserve in the alley (C pl. 3, fig. 3); this void will be filled with the soil from the opening of the trench at the right-hand corner of the second square; this soil will be shovelled over the alley (D pl. 3, fig. 3). The second square will be ripped out like the first and finished with the left-hand corner at the bottom (E pl. 3, fig. 3); this new void will be filled by opening the trench of the third square at the corner facing the void (Fpl. 3, fig. 3); this square will be ripped out like the previous two and finished with one of the corners bordering the transverse aisle (Gpl. 3, fig. 3); the void will be filled by opening the trench of the fourth square (H pl. 3, fig. 3), which the diggers will end at the right angle, at the top, where the earth reserve from the opening of the first trench is located (I pl. 3, fig. 3). All that's left to do is shovel it in to fill the final void. In all trenching operations, it is essential to mix the top, middle and bottom layers of soil together; to remove stones and roots with the utmost care, to break up any clods of soil, and to bury quackgrass very deeply if there is any; it never grows back when buried more than 60 centimetres deep. The soil in a vegetable garden that has been broken up must be completely cleaned. This is a one-off operation, but it must be done properly if it is to be profitable. 2° DEFONCEMENT WITH AMENDMENT is done at the same depth as the previous operation, and is carried out in the same way, with a shovel and a pickaxe, so that the mixture of soil and amendment is perfect. If the soil is clayey, it's best to use as much topsoil as possible. Soil from the surface of the alleys should be removed to the depth of a spade shoe, and thrown into the flowerbeds, to be replaced in the alleys by soil from the bottom of the trench. Surface soil, exposed to the influence of atmospheric agents, is always loose, whereas bottom soil is excessively plastic. When an amendment is added to the soil, such as platras, sand or coal ash, it is spread evenly over the square to be trenched; the soil from the alleys is thrown on top; the whole is mixed well while trenching, and the soil from the bottom is thrown into the alleys to replace that removed. The price for this breaking down is the same as for the previous one, but with the difference that the earth taken from the paths is paid to the earthworkers at 10 cents per metre of surface area. When the amendments are applied to siliceous soils, and it is not necessary to take 8 soil from the alleys, ripping is paid for at the same price as open-gauge ripping. Only the spreading of the amendment is paid for separately, by the day. 3° DEFONCEMENTS WITH CHANGED SOIL are the longest and most expensive, and are carried out in shallow soils whose subsoil is unsuitable for cultivation, when it is composed of clay, marl or tuff. We start by taking all the topsoil from the alleys, and throwing it onto the squares; we open the trench as I mentioned earlier, mix in all the good soil, and throw the subsoil back into the alleys. When there are 50 or 60 centimetres of good soil, the work isn't enormous, and it's quite easy to make a metre of excellent soil, without too much ploughing. In this case, you pay an extra five centimes for breaking up the soil; the paths count as breaking up the soil; the diggers graze the earth and level the paths. But when there is only 20 or 40 centimetres of good soil, the operation becomes more difficult and more expensive. In this case, there's no room for hesitation: create deep, rich soil where none exists. Despite the apparent difficulties involved, it is no more costly, when done properly, than a poorly executed rip in good soil. The first thing to do is to take all the topsoil that can be found in the alleys and throw it onto the squares. Once the trench has been opened, all the good earth is used; the bad earth is then extracted and used to fill the voids in the alleys, and the excess is taken away, to be replaced by good earth, strong or light, depending on the consistency of the soil, taken from elsewhere, and used lastly to recharge the trench and complete the levelling. These extremes are rare and exceptional. Most of the time, the subsoil can be partially mixed with the soil from the squares and alleys, without having to resort to costly ploughing. However, when it comes down to it, and a vegetable garden is essential, it should be created as small as possible, but done properly: such an operation, if poorly executed, would be quite costly and give only poor results. In this case, the cost of clearing is ten centimes more per metre than the current price; the driveways count as clearing; the earthworkers level them and load the cars with bad earth extracted from the ground, and they are paid extra, by the day, for spreading the earth brought in. Before concluding on the subject of ripping, it should always be done in advance, and in dry weather, especially in clay soils. As far as possible, they should be done in autumn or early winter, so that the garden can be cultivated in spring. Creating a garden is a serious matter, if you want to do it well and achieve profitable results. It requires the intervention of a special man, for the plan and arrangements to be made, and the indications to be given for execution. This man, almost always overloaded with work, needs the time to study the necessary arrangements in all their details, and also, for the workers, the indispensable time to carry out their work in good conditions; if haste is harmful in almost all the circumstances of our lives, I could say that it is the worst of all things in the creation of a garden. DIEEEGE GO ASSOLEMENT, FERTILIZER DISTRIBUTION, LAYERS. Crop rotation! It's the key to fertility, the basis of production in the vegetable garden and in field crops. And who doubts, in this day and age, among the majority of gardeners, and even among some doctors of horticulture, that a well-understood rotation of the vegetable garden is the first element of success, a sure guarantee of both richness and economy in production? Rational crop rotation is the basis of the soil's fertility, and the key to the vegetable garden's wealth, because crop rotation contains: 1° RESPECT FOR THE LAW OF ALTERNATION. This law means that the same product, however abundantly smoked and well cultivated, rarely yields a maximum crop two years running in the same plot. Old practitioners, measuring their knowledge not by experiments, which they refuse even to indulge in, but by their dexterity in handling the spade and rake, will say from the outset, and without any circumlocution whatsoever: This is all nonsense, I sow peas and onions too, for four, five years, in the same plot, and I still get some! Some go so far as to ask us in all seriousness whether we invented peas and onions, and then dare to hold it against them, who sowed them before we were born! We hasten to decline the honor of inventing peas and onions, and even go so far as to confess, in all humility, that we still harvest them by sowing ten years in a row in the same soil; But on the strength of our studies, our observations and our experience, we affirm that from the second year onwards, there is a decrease in the product; in the third, degeneration, tardiness and a very noticeable decrease in the harvest, and I would even go so far as to assert that the longer successive sowings are in the same soil, the greater the degeneration. What's more, I'm deeply convinced that the bastardized vegetable varieties, barely fit to feed animals, found in almost all regions of France where vegetable growing has been entirely localized, have only reached this state of degeneration and tardiness as a result of successive sowings in the same beds. I would go even further and say to those who want to propagate routine varieties: Take your seeds of varieties that have returned almost 4 to the original type through promiscuity; sow them for five or six years, and every year the new seeds in new soil, and you will succeed, if not in recovering the primitive variety, at least in appreciably improving the one you have sown. Neither you nor I made this law, it emanates from God, your greater or lesser skill in handling the spade and rake will not destroy it, and routine is powerless to ward off its effects. So let's put all false pride aside and sow our vegetable garden for four years, so that the same species only returns to the same patch every four years. In this way, we'll not only be assured of maximum harvests, but also of keeping pure the precious varieties that will replace your woody vegetables. I'm not calling for the upheaval of everything that exists in order to create something new. Far from it, knowing how great the force of habit is, I will say here, as in my courses, to all those who hesitate: Before destroying, experiment; make comparative tests, they alone can enlighten you in a certain way. If you have a vegetable garden made up of four squares cultivated in the local fashion, continue your usual cultivation in three; try the one taught in this book in the fourth, and when you have seen the results and compared the expenses and produce of the two crops, adopt frankly and without second thoughts, the one that will have given you the best and most abundant produce, with the least expense, 2° THE ECONOMY OF FERTILIZERS THROUGH THEIR REASONED DISTRIBUTION. I posit that the same quantity of fertilizer, used with discernment over a given area, will produce six, when the same quantity, and even a greater quantity, distributed wrongly over the same area, will produce barely one, with the same amount of labor. Let's suppose a vegetable garden of twenty-four ares, divided into four equal parts, spending annually twenty cars of manure. If this vegetable garden is not subject to crop rotation, these twenty cars of manure will be equally distributed over the twenty-four ares. In this case, the four squares will receive insufficient manure, and especially if it has been buried before it has entered a state of decomposition, as is done almost everywhere, under the pretext of warming the soil, here is what will happen almost infallibly: Artichokes, potatoes, cabbages, leeks, etc., etc., lacking sufficient nourishment, will give stunted, hard, stringy, stunted, in a word inedible products, which will take twice as long to complete their pitiful vegetation, as these same prime products would have required, with sufficient nourishment. Roots, strawberries, lettuces, etc. etc., will sprout leaves and go to seed on their fresh manure, before they have produced a passable root, a succulent fruit or a presentable apple. Poorly applied fresh manure, sufficient to destroy the first crop, will be almost totally absorbed by it, and the following crop will be nil. Peas, beans, etc., etc., on a quarter of fresh manure, will produce gigantic stalks and no grains. The owner and gardener will watch them grow every day, hoping for fruit when they stop growing. Finally, when they've smothered everything, the fruit appears so scarce that it's decided to uproot them to save the other crops, and the gardener says as he loads up a car with fodder: the land is worthless for vegetables, nothing succeeds! The soil is excellent, most of the time, the crop alone is bad. The twenty-four-acre vegetable garden, smoked in this way, has yielded nothing but pitiful produce: not a single melon, not the slightest early crop. If we sow this same vegetable garden with an equal quantity of manure for four years, we'll obtain maximum crops of open ground everywhere, and a good supply of melons and early vegetables, a huge advantage of crop rotation; 3° THE POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING AN ABUNDANT PRODUCTION OF EARLY VEGETABLES AS AN ADDITIONAL CROP, NOT ONLY WITHOUT ANY INCREASE IN FERTILIZER EXPENDITURE, BUT ALSO BY IMPROVING FERTILIZERS AND MAKING THEM MORE SUITABLE FOR BURIAL! Fertilizers can only be assimilated in a liquid or gaseous state; in other words, plants can only absorb the nutrients they contain once they have decomposed. Once it has been proven that decomposed fertilizers have an immediate and more energetic effect on plants than fresh manure, it is to our advantage to decompose our fertilizers before burying them. The most economical and profitable way to decompose fertilizers is in layers. These layers will give us all the primeurs we want, at no cost other than the initial purchase of a few frames and bells. The savings in manpower that would have been needed to handle the manures will more than cover the cost of maintaining the frames and bells, and the annual harvest will only be burdened by the initial purchase of the equipment. In the past, the installation of a bed was considered difficult, expensive and even ruinous. It's a mistake we're beginning to come round to, and let's face it, when the use of diapers is popularized, and their usefulness is generally recognized, open-ground crops will double their output, and the smallest garden, while doubling its production, will yield melons and early fruit without any expense whatsoever; there won't be a village, a hamlet, where the parish priest or the schoolteacher can't harvest in quantity if they want to take the trouble. We are assured of the praiseworthy zeal of the country parish priests. We have seen them at work in several départements, and we know how enthusiastically they have welcomed our arboriculture lessons, and how devotedly they continue to teach them to their parishioners, in their own interest, and in that of public wealth. They eagerly await the modern Potager to complete their work, all charity and devotion. I would like to take this opportunity to express my gratitude to the clergy, especially those of the Oise department, for the special care they have shown me, and for their noble zeal in bringing light to the most backward regions. Thank you for having so helpfully assisted me in my work; thank you to the clergy, thank you for the country, thank you again to the Brothers of the Christian Doctrine for their praiseworthy eagerness, and their tireless zeal to teach the true principles of cultivation and arboriculture to children. Their noble efforts will be crowned with success, and soon their dedication will bear fruit in bringing light, ease and progress to small farmers. Thanks to the initiative of several prefects, and their particular benevolence for agricultural interests, primary school teachers are rendering important services by teaching cultivation and horticulture to the children of rural populations deprived of the courses given in the towns. This useful and praiseworthy teaching is already bearing fruit in certain areas, especially in the department of Oise, where primary school teachers, encouraged and stimulated by higher authority, are competing in zeal not only for teaching, but also for horticultural practice. The teachers of the Oise department, authorized by the Prefect to give their pupils time off to attend arboriculture lessons, have already achieved brilliant results in arboriculture, and are also waiting for the Potager Moderne to teach and practice vegetable growing, which is so useful and profitable for rural populations who are unaware of it, and can derive definite benefits from it. Assured of the intelligent and devoted support of the clergy, schoolteachers and a good number of landowners, I close my ears to the cries of routine and actively pursue a project which, I am convinced, will render important services by creating new wealth in regions deprived of horticultural education. Layers are, in fact, the factory of assimilable manure and fertilizer par excellence, and it is in the grower's interest to establish as many of them as possible, in order to increase both the crops grown in the open ground and the products from frames and bells, which are always very expensive, and cost nothing when layers are included in the vegetable garden rotation. It's easy to build up a large number of layers with a great saving in fertilizers, frames and bells, by using horse manure mixed with leaves for warm layers; cow manure mixed with leaves, mosses, etc., for warm layers, and herbaceous matter mixed with a little manure for dull layers, and by using economical shelters for certain products instead of frames and bells. In this way, we can considerably increase the mass of fertilizers and potting soils, so useful for certain vegetable plants and for flower breeding, and obtain everything we could possibly want with the greatest economy, while at the same time improving fertilizers. I shall devote a special chapter to the manufacture of hot, warm and muted layers, and to the shelters designed to cover them. I shall also devote a chapter to the rotation of each of the gardens I deal with: those of the owner, the tenant, the farmer, the presbytery, the communities and boarding houses, the teachers, the railroads and the camps, each of which requires a special cultivation and rotation. I'm only dealing here with the four-year vegetable garden rotation in principle, and reserving the right to modify it for each of the gardens I've mentioned. In the kitchen garden, we grow vegetables that require very copious manuring to give good results; these are artichokes, potatoes, cabbages, leeks, etc., etc.; others that require a large quantity of humus in the soil, and do not do well on fresh manure; these are roots, strawberries, lettuces, etc., etc.; still others that require a large quantity of humus in the soil, and do not do well on fresh manure; these are roots, strawberries, lettuces, etc., etc.; still others that require a large quantity of humus in the soil, and do not do well on fresh manure, etc.; still others produce only stems on fresh manure, and require a certain quantity of potash instead of fertilizer in order to bear fruit, such as peas, beans, etc., etc. We have seen the results of these various crops on a quarter, and even a third, of fresh manure, results that are unfortunately all too frequent in the many gardens we visit during our excursions in the départements; let's now look at those obtained in the vegetable garden subjected to four-year crop rotation. Let's assume a vegetable garden of twenty-four ares, divided into four equal parts, and with twenty cars of manure to spend annually. If we don't let anything go to waste, and if we carefully make our composts, we'll make twenty cars with five of manure. In the first year, we'll spread the twenty cars of compost on square n°1, to which we'll mix the most active manure from the demolition of the layers, and we'll bury the whole thing in this square, destined to receive all the vegetables requiring very abundant nourishment, then we'll reserve the most decomposed compost and manure from the demolition of the layers, to mulch and top-dress the vegetables in square n°2. The previous year, square n° 2 received the same amount of manure as square n° 1, and produced a maximum harvest of hearty vegetables. The composts and bedding manure are fully decomposed, and despite the abundant production of the previous year, the soil is saturated with humus, thanks to the maximum manuring given. This same year, we'll be growing roots, strawberries, tomatoes, lettuces, etc., in plot no. 2, without fertilizer, as these plants dread fresh fertilizer; a topdressing and mulches applied with our layer residues, which have been set aside, will be sufficient to obtain a maximum harvest in this plot. Two years ago, square no. 3 was fertilized in the same way as square no. 1, and the previous year with the same topdressing and mulch as square no. 2. This unfertilized, but abundantly ashed square will be devoted to the cultivation of vegetables with dried fruits, such as peas, beans, etc., which will still give a maximum harvest, in soil depleted of fertilizer, but provided with ashes, the only condition in which they can fructify abundantly. Finally, square No. L, which was fertilized three years ago, top-dressed and mulched two years ago, and ashed the previous year, will be destined to receive : 1 The beds we will build there with our reserve of fifteen cars of horse manure, with added leaves, for the warm and hot beds, and herbaceous matter for the dull beds; 2° Without any manuring, all the flower and vegetable seed crops, which will give the best results in a soil exhausted of fertilizer and still well ashed; 3° An early pea crop, without fertilizer and with partial ashing, and even a green bean crop if required; 4° Flower and vegetable nurseries with topdressing and even maximum fertilization, ending the rotation and starting it again the following year with full fertilization. So, after harvesting peas and green beans, it's easy to use the compost or manure from the first layers to establish the vegetable nurseries so necessary in the kitchen garden. Four-year crop rotation offers the following advantages over other crops: 1° To produce maximum harvests on each sole, the land being in the state of cultivation and fertilization that is most favorable to the plants it supports; 2° To spend no more on fertilizers or labor than crops with much lower yields; 3° To enable the grower to produce an abundant crop of early vegetables, with almost no additional expense; 5° To regularize the fertility of all parts of the garden, through regular fertilization and cultivation; 6° To further increase fertility, by introducing into the soil, at regular times, a stimulant (ash) that powerfully activates the action of fertilizers. Having set out these principles, let's look at the most suitable rotation for each of the gardens I'm working on, according to the fertilizer resources available, the means of producing the greatest quantity, and the vegetable varieties specific to each garden. 19 FERTILIZERS, CROP ROTATION, VARIETIES OF VEGETABLES TO BE GROWN. I have purposely excluded from this book the kitchen garden of a château that always has a skilled gardener. By owner's vegetable garden, I mean that of a house with a fortune of ten to twenty-five thousand francs, large enough to provide vegetables for the countryside during the summer, and for the town throughout the winter. FERTILIZER SERVICE. First and foremost, we need to organize the fertilizer service and production. Let's assume that the house has two horses, two cows, a pig and a farmyard, and that with the fertilizers from these animals we have to meet Siuseg G the needs of a park adorned with flower baskets, the fruit garden and the vegetable garden. This is possible if we take the trouble to make our fertilizers properly, and don't let anything go to waste. The first thing to do is to organize the fertilizer factory. We'll choose a northern location, sheltered by tall trees, where the sun doesn't easily penetrate; we'll set up two platforms, about 30 centimetres above ground level, and both inclined towards the center (A pl. 3, fig. 4), so that all the liquid parts fall into a pit that we'll establish there. LIQUID FERTILIZERS. The liquid fertilizer pit will cut the platforms in half along their entire length (B pl. 3, fig. A); it should be wide enough and deep enough to hold twenty to thirty bariques of liquid. This pit must be perfectly watertight; the best way to do this is to build it in bricks macerated with cement, and to line the inside with a good cement plaster, which is the most solid and perhaps the most economical. The liquid fertilizer factory should be all the more active as it is intended not only to supply the needs of vegetable and fruit gardens, but also to contribute to the manufacture of a large quantity of excellent compost. We'll put in this pit all the liquid manure from the stables and cowsheds, the urine from the house, the water from 8 dishes, soap, washing powder, in short, all the liquids we can get our hands on. Nothing could be easier than to collect the liquid manure and all the household wastewater in a receptacle of some kind, and carry it to the pit every day, or to install very economical underground pipes, with cement-welded drainpipes, which will carry the liquid manure from the stable and barn, and the household wastewater from the dwelling house, to the liquid fertilizer pit. In addition to the liquids brought into the pit, we'll add all the manure from the pigeon houses and hen houses, which must be carefully cleaned every week. This is an infallible way of ensuring that we don't lose the pigeons, keeping the poultry healthy and ridding them of the insects that devour them. Latrines with a movable barrel will be set up for servants and workers; all faecal matter from them will also be disposed of in the liquid fertilizer pit. If it is possible to set up mobile barrels, as is done in many places, for the masters, this should be done as a matter of urgency, and the product added to the liquid fertilizer. A few kilograms of iron sulfate thrown into the pit immediately neutralizes the odor. If it were not possible to collect the faeces, it would be necessary to buy

In all cases, liquid fertilizers should be disinfected, firstly in the interests of health, secondly to remove workers' reluctance to use them, and thirdly because iron sulfate, while disinfecting, also increases the value of the fertilizer. With twenty-five or thirty barrels of liquid fertilizer composed in this way, together with manure from cows, pigs, rabbits and the farmyard, it will be easy to make a very large quantity of excellent compost that will ensure the fertility of the vegetable garden. MANURE. Horse manure can be stored in reserve for making diapers. Simply place it in a dry heap, sheltered from rain, and store it for as long as you like. Horse manure has the property of keeping indefinitely when dry, and of fermenting and developing its full caloric action as soon as it is wetted. The mass of layers can be increased by mixing horse manure, which has been set aside for this purpose, with leaves from the park and, if necessary, those collected in the woods. Some cow manure, mixed with leaves, can also be used in the spring for warm, muted layers. Now that we've secured our layer service, let's get back to making fertilizer. With the pit filled, as we've just indicated, with liquid fertilizer made from liquid manure, urine and all household water, plus columbine and faecal matter collected in the house, and in their absence of poudrette, we need to think about increasing the mass of fertilizer, with composts of herbaceous matter, which are most often left to waste. Here's how it works: COMPOST. Start by making a heap of all the detritus from the vegetable garden; herbs from weeding and hoeing: stalks from vegetables, asparagus, artichokes, peas, beans, cabbage cores, lettuce, etc., etc.; in a word, all the vegetable matter you can get your hands on; all is good, provided it is used fresh and never left to dry out. To avoid weed production, it's a good idea to use only plants before they flower, or even in flower, but never in seed. This would have the disadvantage of filling composts with seeds that would soon germinate and, if not suffocate crops, at least cause enormous weeding labor. Any defoliated grass should be set aside for burning, and the ash added to the compost. Depending on your resources and the size of the property, you can considerably increase the compost mass by adding broom, gorse, heather, reeds, leaves, marsh and ditch grasses, seaweed, kelp, hedge and lawn clippings, etc., etc., etc... If the property contains a certain quantity of brambles and thistles, they should be cut back as a matter of urgency to prevent them from multiplying, and burning them produces excellent ashes that add to the quality of the fertilizer. 8 Sawdust and shavings left to rot in the woods for most of the year will provide valuable ashes, which will also bring their share of fertility to the vegetable garden, especially in regions where the soil is devoid of limestone, such as Brittany and Sologne. You can't make too much of ashes in these regions, where they're more valuable than fertilizers. Once the plant matter has been brought together, a first bed, thirty to forty centimetres thick, is formed on one of the platforms; this bed is covered with manure, then watered copiously, every two or three days, with the liquid fertilizer contained in the pit. This is done with a scoop when the pile is not too high, and with a liquid manure pump when it is higher. A few days later, the heap is covered with a new bed of herbaceous matter, which is then topped up with another bed of manure. Every day, all kitchen scraps are thrown onto the compost heap: vegetable peelings, eggshells, scraps, feathers and blood from poultry and game; soot from chimneys, house and yard sweepings, etc., etc.; ashes from the compost heap are also thrown on, (Wood ashes from fireplaces will be set aside and kept for pea and bean seedlings, etc.), etc.) Continue to build up the compost heap, alternating with a bed of herbaceous matter, manure and kitchen waste, until it reaches a height of two meters, taking care to water it every two days with the liquid fertilizer contained in the pit (C pl. 3, fig. 4). If this is done as I've indicated, fermentation starts immediately, and the plant matter rapidly decomposes. When the heap has reached a height of two meters, dismantle it by cutting it into vertical slices (D pl. 3, fig. 4), mix all the decomposed herbs with the manure, and form a heap next to the first (E pl. 3, fig. 3; water five or six more times with the liquid fertilizer, copiously enough for the liquid, filtering through, to animate all the herbaceous parts, then break up this compost heap a second time, mix all the parts well together again, and put it in reserve on the other side of the platform (F pl. 3, fig. 4). In this state, it's one of the best fertilizers, and perhaps one of the most powerful you can use. With a good supply of liquid fertilizer, it's easy to make masses of compost, and considerably increase the fertility of the vegetable garden, with no other expense than a little effort and activity to collect, gather and mix together all the fertilizing substances that are most often left to waste on the public highway, to the detriment of everyone's health. The manure factory should be set up in one of the reserve yards I mentioned when creating the kitchen garden, within easy reach of the gardener. The first platform is dedicated to manufacturing, the second to storage, i.e. to the manufactured fertilizers. So, as soon as the first compost heap is dismantled and rebuilt next to it, to receive a few more sprinklings of liquid fertilizer, a new one must be built in the place it occupied; as soon as the first has been reworked a second time and transported to the reserve on the other platform, the second, dismantled in its turn, takes its place, and a third is built. Pond silt, like aquatic grasses, is excellent in composts, but it is urgent to add a little quicklime before mixing it into composts. I insist on this lime mixture, because I've often seen these vases and herbs used fresh, and when they are, very poor results are obtained. Most often, they are left to air-macerate for a year, and are used with no other disadvantage than that of having piles of sludge spread out in a park, and this is one that can easily be avoided with the addition of quicklime, by leaving the vases to drain for only eight or fifteen days, and mixing them with the composts. When the manufactured composts remain in reserve for a long time, on the second platform, it is a good idea to water them, from time to time, with the liquid fertilizer from the pit, especially with the bottom, which is always thicker. I cannot overemphasize to owners and gardeners the importance of making composts; you need to have made fertilizers yourself, and had as many made as I did for others, to get a fair idea of the immense resources to be found in a host of objects that are allowed to go to waste, almost everywhere, to the detriment of cultivation. The manufacture and economy of fertilizers is an important question, not only from the point of view of the fraction of cultivation which is the subject of this book, but from the point of view of general production. Large-scale cultivation, which possesses a high level of capital and knows the value of fertilizers, not only lets nothing go to waste, but also buys artificial fertilizers for large sums, and makes considerable profits. Small-scale farmers, with little capital and no knowledge of the value of fertilizers, let their manure run through village streets, and sow their fields with weeds and crop failure, instead of increasing the mass of fertilizing substances. Small-scale farmers support themselves through hard work, and if I may put it this way, excessive hard work partly compensates for the lack of fertilizers. But if we could prove to him that, by wasting manure and a host of other fertilizing substances, he is wasting whole loaves of bread, we would quickly improve his position and significantly increase overall production. Many mayor-cultivators have issued by-laws to prevent the discharge of liquid manure onto the public highway; we congratulate them on this, as it is bread that they are giving to the peasant without him even suspecting it. If this measure, which is as wise as it is healthy, were taken everywhere, the mass of fertilizers would be significantly increased, and general production would rise, in proportion to the quantity of fertilizing materials introduced into the soil. The Emperor's powerful protection, and the very special care with which he surrounded cultivation, drove agricultural progress forward by leaps and bounds. Several prefects, faithful interpreters of the thought of the Head of State, have encouraged agricultural education; their efforts are tending to spread it in the countryside, and we are happy to note that primary school teachers, encouraged in this way, are competing with zeal to spread the first notions of agriculture and horticulture. I appeal here to those who have heard me so often; let them prove, in their lessons, to the children of the countryside, that it is as reprehensible to lose fertilizer as a piece of bread; they will have accomplished a great work, and contributed, more powerfully than they perhaps suppose, to the increase in public wealth. FOUR-YEAR CROP ROTATION. The most advantageous rotation for the owner's vegetable garden is the four-year rotation; but as it is urgent for the owner to be abundantly supplied with everything, it will be useful to reserve, outside the rotation, the space necessary to create an asparagus plan and an artichoke square. These two crops should each occupy a space equal to one of the four squares sown every four years. 0 Will that be a lot of asparagus and artichokes? It's true, but to have enough, you often have to grow too much, to prepare for bad years. VEGETABLE SALES. Asparagus and artichokes are vegetables par excellence, first for the home, then for sale; they can be transported, and always have a well-established value on all markets. If there are too many in good years, nothing is easier than to send them to market, and even to Paris, if the local market price is not sufficiently lucrative. In the past, it was difficult for the owner to sell excess produce, as commercial bad faith was an insurmountable obstacle. The owner was offered 25 centimes of what was worth three or four francs. In such cases, it was preferable to give the surplus to the animals after everyone had had their fill. Today, thanks to the fruit and vegetable factors set up by the City of Paris, the owner can still sell excess produce at the going market price, for a commission of 5 p. O/0, without having to deal with buyers. To sell whatever you want, all you have to do is ask M. Langlois, fruit and early produce letter carrier, rue des Halles-Centrales, Paris, for a few rubber-stamped addresses. You put your produce in a basket, stick the gummed address on it, put it on the railroad without franking, and the next day you receive your sales account and your money. Everything is sold by auction; and the bond paid by the factors, as much as strict inspections, vouch for their good management. The asparagus plant can last from 25 to 30 years, if well cared for. Artichoke patches, on the other hand, will only remain in place for four years to produce good products. Its size being equal to that of the crop rotation squares, and the artichokes having been fertilized four times in four years, we'll move them to crop rotation square no. 1, and place the crops intended for square no. 1 in the old artichoke square, without changing our crop rotation. Four years later, we'll put our artichokes back in the next square, and have them successively occupy all the squares in the rotation. In this way, the artichokes will only return to the same square every twenty years, so to speak, in new land for this crop, where they will always produce superb and abundant produce. When the asparagus is exhausted, we'll also have to create a new plan in another square, and subject the one that used to grow it to crop rotation. Crop rotation, I can't repeat enough, is the key to the richness of the vegetable garden, and it's only through it, with its manuring, its cendrages and its regular harvests, that we can be sure of producing abundantly, without more labor and without more fertilizers. But to achieve these results, crop rotation must be applied to the letter, not just about. Many gardeners, unaware of its importance, said to us when we introduced it into their gardens: "I do pretty much that, only I give less manure to square n° 1, and I give a little to all the others, that's better! They'll be able to cultivate in this way for many years, without having to bring their land to a state of cultivation. That is, to saturate it thoroughly and regularly enough with humus, to bring it to the highest degree of potency and fertility, in all parts of the garden. Almost everywhere, the same products, especially those that require a lot of fertilizer, come back every year on the same beds, especially in the flowerbeds, for which the gardener has a particular predilection, because he claims they are well greased. And every year he loads these beds with the same exhausting crops, and gives them half a manure, and since most of the time he doesn't make composts or layers, he misses the fertilizers and the rest of the garden goes without. The gardener then says: I've greased my beds well, I don't need manure to grow potatoes, beans, etc., etc., and he gets the results everyone knows about. We had great difficulty in introducing a regular crop rotation in certain vegetable gardens, where the owners had asked us to guide their gardeners. This regularity of cultivation offended received habits, disturbed the way things were done; changing the layers seemed monstrous. The owners wanted it, we persevered, and I'm happy to say today, after seven years of application, that the gardeners most opposed in principle to rotation, those on whom we imposed it, are now its strongest supporters. They say that no garden can compare with theirs, and that cultivation there takes care of itself. This is true up to a point; they complete the second rotation, their garden is in what we call a cultivated state in all its parts, and fertility, far from diminishing, can only increase with each rotation. If the owner's house is of a certain size, if he lives in the country in summer, in the city in winter, and if he wants to be supplied all year round by his vegetable garden, he should apply, to the letter, the four-year rotation as I have indicated, and establish six squares of equal size in the vegetable garden: four will be dedicated to the rotation, the other two: one to asparagus, the other to artichokes, and will return to the rotation when these two crops have been moved to occupy all the squares in succession. Artichokes will be moved every four years, asparagus every fifteen or twenty. As it takes three years before asparagus can be harvested, as soon as production begins to decline, half of an asparagus square should be created first, and half of the existing square destroyed; in other words, only what is needed to supply the house should be kept, and sales eliminated, so as not to hinder the other crops and give them the same amount of land. As soon as half the newly planted square is in a position to yield, the other half is planted, and the old square is completely destroyed and returned to the crop rotation. We create squares of asparagus that are a little too large to be able to replant half of them in another square, so as never to be deprived of this precious vegetable, to have enough with half a square, and to find a fairly high indemnity in the sale of the other half, when the whole square is in yield. By adopting this crop rotation to the letter, and with the quantity of layers that I have indicated, the landowner will always be abundantly supplied with all kinds of vegetables and early crops, throughout the year, and if the crop rotation is strictly applied, far from decreasing, the produce will only increase with each rotation, i.e. with each four-year period when the crop rotation starts again. Some landowners, out of a misguided sense of economy, and perhaps also under the influence of the prejudice that layers are ruinous, will want to apply crop rotation without layers. It will be a ruinous economy for them, and I'm going to prove it to them. Let's take a look at the expense of layers. If the park is a little large, and has a certain number of baskets, the flowers will first have to be cared for, and this is the job of the head gardener, who carries out this task in the same way as he does the kitchen garden; in addition, the paths have to be raked once a week, the borders mowed, and the heavy work in the kitchen garden carried out, which is the job of the gardener's assistant. A gardener's helper is indispensable for a property of any size, and costs an average of six hundred francs a year. If the owner wants to make a false economy, dispense with this gardener's helper and replace him with day laborers, on the pretext that he only lives in the country from May to November, this is what will happen. Day laborers are rare in the countryside, and during the summer they cost the farm 3 fr. a day; but as soon as they have to go and work for a rich bourgeois, they will demand 3 fr. 50 c. and even 4 fr. a day. A day laborer at 3.50 c. a day from May 1 to October 31 will cost the owner 649 fr. For this sum, he'll be giving his gardener a poor helper, incapable of doing any gardening work at all; he'll be more of a driving force than a helper, and even then, the gardener won't have the driving force he needs when he needs it most, because he's hired by the day. For example, during the scorching heat of July and August, when the vegetable garden needs to be watered twice a day, the gardener will be alone in the morning to do this work, which is materially impossible; he will have nothing to ask of his helper, who will show him the clock marking five o'clock. That's when the day begins, and the gardener has been watering for three hours. In the evening, the helper leaves at seven o'clock - that's the time, there's nothing to say about that - and the gardener waters until nine and sometimes until ten. This helper costs 49 fr. more than a boy who works hard, because he's learning a trade, and is always next to the gardener who gets him up at the same time as him, and only sends him to bed when he goes himself. The owner, who is the gardener's enemy, will say to me: "But in winter, what will I do with this boy whom I also pay? To which I reply: "Sir, your boy costs you 19 francs less than a day laborer who hasn't done half his work. I must admit that if you don't have diapers, frames and bells, it will happen quite often, when the winter planting and ploughing are finished, that your gardener's boy won't get much done, and your gardener will have to rest completely from his summer fatigue. You like activity, Monsieur, and you're right; give your two men frames and bells, let them do diapers, they'll send you to town, all winter long, salads, peas, green beans, melons, tomatoes, etc., etc., etc. You'll have the satisfaction of having early crops that cost you only the purchase of the glass, and their cultivation will keep your gardeners busy, who, while giving you great satisfaction, will also improve the manure destined for landfill by making the layers. It has been proven that manure used to make layers, and which has produced a harvest of early crops free of charge for labor and purchase, is preferable for landfill. So far, we've made a profit of 8. Let's see what glass costs. One-meter iron frames cost 8 francs. Single glass is 3.50 c. a meter, and double glass 7 francs. You won't take single glass, because you'd break windows all the time; double glass is as solid as stone, so you'll choose that one, it's the cheapest. Give your gardener 25 iron frame panels, glazed in double glass, at 15 fr. 375 " 150 button bells at 1 fr. . . . . 150 " Total... ... . 525 "This equipment is sufficient to obtain all the early fruit and melons you want, and will last for twenty years; so you have to spend 26 fr. 25 c. each year on your melons and early fruit. Sell fifteen melons for 2 francs, they're available everywhere at that price, and you'll have melons and early fruit for nothing, and what's more, you'll have improved your manure at a profit. To finish convincing the enemies of layers, should I tell them the account I give daily to the owners who come to visit my garden, and say to me on seeing my melons and vegetables: what a production! it's superb! but how expensive it must be! to which I reply: every year, in January, I buy two cars of manure to build up a warm layer on which I sow my melons and some 3 spring vegetables. In February, I buy about three cars of inn manure, the best of all, with which I build up a second warm layer, which I use to transplant my melons in the nursery, and in April, I buy another three cars of the same manure, which, mixed with leaves or moss, is used to make warm layers, on which I place, under cloche, the melons of the last season. Total, eight cars of good inn manure at 5 fr. .. .. . A0 fr. Plus, about three meters of manure, picked up by old men and children, at 5 fr. . . . . . . . . . .. . . . . .  55fr. With the three meters of horse manure, and the household water, I make about ten cars of excellent compost, mixing it with the detritus from the vegetable garden, the fruit garden and the kitchen. My composts, together with the manure from the demolition of the diapers, are more than enough to smoke my vegetable garden to the max. Every year, I mulch the fruit garden with my excess manure; in addition, the layers give me considerable quantities of potting soil. My total expenditure on fertilizer is 55 francs a year. I have about twelve ares of vegetable garden, the land is in perfect condition for cultivation, and these twelve ares, cultivated when we have the time, produce the following annually: 1° Two hundred first-quality melons; 19 2° All the vegetables I could possibly want for my household, consisting of three masters and two servants; 3° The complete supply for my gardener and his family, consisting of six people; 4° The surplus of certain harvests, so abundant that it is impossible to eat them, such as peas, artichokes, beans, etc., these are sold for around 80 francs a year. I must say, as a tribute to the truth, that my vegetable garden is cultivated in the worst possible conditions. During the winter, I use it to temporarily bury trees destined for expeditions and the creation of fruit gardens. I often have to keep a supply of trees until March, and even April. It's only towards the end of this month, and when my pupils are not too busy with work outside, that I put my vegetable garden fully into cultivation; and in these deplorable conditions, twelve ares that I fertilize with an expense of 55 francs produce for me annually: 1° 200 melons; 2° Vegetables for eleven people; 3° A silver product of 80 fr. I haven't taken labor into account.
