Weed, thin and water as needed, as with other broadcast seedlings. Three crops of lettuce can be grown after summer parsnips, and winter parsnips can be sown after a crop of onions. Parsnips do not fear frost, and July seedlings can be kept in the ground throughout the winter without any inconvenience. PATATO. The potato is not as good as the potato, but as it is more difficult to grow in our climate, and as it is a vegetable belonging to the do8 maine of fantasy, it is a good idea to have a few plants in the vegetable garden. I attach too little importance to the potato to grow it as an early crop, and clutter up the frames with it, so we'll be content to grow it on a deaf bed, and harvest it around August. In April, potatoes are planted in warm soil. As soon as they have produced shoots eight to ten centimetres long, they are removed with a small piece of the tuber, and planted permanently, in the middle of a deaf layer, at a distance of 60 centimetres. Cover with cloches, and shade for a few days to ensure recovery. Ventilate whenever the temperature permits, and replace the bells at night, as long as frosts are to be feared; the potato is very sensitive to them. Watering is useful, but only moderately. Potatoes don't like excess humidity, so only wet them thoroughly during hot spells. When frost is no longer an issue, remove the cloches completely. Tubers can be harvested as they form, if desired. This is easily done by digging into the bed with your fingers; they are detached when ripe, and the root is immediately covered. The whole crop is harvested in September. Potatoes are quite difficult to preserve; they are very sensitive to cold, and rot when 24 9 bruised. It should be harvested with as much care as the most delicate fruits, and stored in a warm, dry place, buried in ash or heather soil, completely dry, bed by bed, and placed far enough apart so that they do not touch. PARSLEY. Parsley is a must in any well-kept garden. Sow it in the borders of squares no. 2 and no. 3 in spring and August, so that it is always in full bloom. Sow parsley in pots in August for winter supply. The pots are completely buried in the ground, and as frost approaches, they are moved into the orangery, or if there is no orangery, into a cold frame. With twenty pots of parsley, there's never a shortage during the winter. When the cold becomes severe, bury two pots in the compost of a warm layer, and replace them with two others when the parsley has grown enough to be picked. CHILI. Chillies ripen only imperfectly in the vineyards. Its main use is for preserving before ripening. It is sown on a warm bed under a frame in February or March, for transplanting to nurseries under a frame as soon as the plant has four or five leaves, and for setting out on a warm or 18-deaf bed in May. The Spanish sweet pepper is the variety that ripens best in France. It can be counter-planted on a melon bed, or between cucumbers. PIMPRENELLE. PIMPRENELLE is sometimes used in the kitchen, as a vegetable. It's a poor plant for the vegetable garden, but a precious fodder for animals. The burnet comes from everywhere, and succeeds everywhere. It is usually sown in the borders, in March, in squares n° 3 and n° h, for kitchen use, but when there are a certain number of animals in the house, and the vegetable garden is large, it is worth growing it as fodder. In this case, sow in February, in square no. h, in rows 30 centimetres apart. The soil can be turned over and a buckwheat plant sown, which will provide abundant seed for poultry, especially if it is vigorously ashy. If there are a certain number of animals, we surround the whole square n° 3 with borders of burnet, and we keep them for two years, to destroy them when the square in which we sowed becomes n° 1, then we resow the borders of square n° 3, for two years, and so on. LEEK. Leeks require substantial, slightly clayey soil; they like slightly decom8 posed fertilizers. We sow it at two times of the year to make two seasons, which is enough to ensure that we never run out. Leeks are sown in March and July, in plot no. 2. The March seedlings are transplanted when the plant has grown to the size of a feather pipe. The root tips and largest leaves are cut off and transplanted in beds, or counterplanted in other crops. To obtain very white leeks, transplant at a depth of 10 or 12 centimetres. When you need a large quantity of leeks, you transplant in beds in plot no. 2, after a harvest of lettuces or large strawberries: the bed is ploughed deeply, with edges to retain water from watering; stakes are placed 20 centimetres apart and 10 centimetres from the edges. Place the string on these stakes, and trace the lines with the spiked trowel. Stagger the leeks on these lines, 10 centimetres apart. Hoe often and water copiously. Leeks planted in rows in May can be harvested in summer and autumn. If you don't need to use a large quantity of leeks, you can counter-plant them in squares n° 1 and n° 2. In square n° 1, between cauliflowers, autumn artichokes etc., etc., etc. In square 2, between strawberry plants, lettuces etc., etc. July seedlings are planted in September, in beds, in plot no. 1, for harvesting in winter and spring, or are counter-planted in plot no. 1, in strawberry beds, between last-season cabbages etc., etc. PEAS. Peas are an excellent vegetable. It should be given a large place in the vegetable garden, and harvested as long as possible. Peas like light, medium-consistency soils; they do poorly in clay soils, but do best in new, fertilizer-free soils. Fresh fertilizers are harmful to it, and it grows huge stalks without producing grain. Peas, like all pulses, need a certain amount of potash to bear fruit abundantly, and give pitiful results when sown two years in a row in the same bed. It needs new soil, or at least soil that hasn't produced peas for two years. Many authors have claimed that the law of alternation should not be respected for vegetables, except for peas, which reduce their production by more than half when sown two years in a row in the same bed. The excuse given for violating the first of nature's laws was the amount of fertilizer buried in the garden. All vegetables seemed to agree with this error, but only the pea protested. It is indisputable that many vegetables 18 produce fairly satisfactory yields when grown for several years in succession on the same bed, but it is at least as indisputable that these vegetables produce almost double the yield when they are grown only every three or four years on the same bed. This, at least, is what our experience of vegetable rotation has shown us over the last ten years. A hardy species will tolerate a poor crop, but if given a good one, it will produce twice as much. It was experience gained through observation that led us to adopt a four-year rotation, with layers, and, thanks to this rotation, the right distribution of fertilizers, and respect for the law of alternation, we obtain double produce without further expense. You never know where to put peas in a garden that is not subject to rotation. In our kitchen garden, we'll grow them in plot no. 3, where they'll find soil that is no longer loaded with fertilizer, has been resting for three years from pea production, and is abundantly ashed, the last condition for obtaining large quantities of good-quality grain. We'll be growing just one variety under a frame: the very-dwarf pea under a frame; early cultivation differs essentially from that in the open ground, and we'll be giving it the honors of primacy. In November, we sow very young peas on a warm layer under a frame, in rows 15 centimeters apart, with the peas side by side in the furrow. Cover at night with straw mats, and provide air whenever possible. In the first fortnight of December, peas are unfolded and transplanted by two or three feet together, on a warm bed under a frame, in rows 15 to 18 centimetres apart, with the clumps staggered at 10 centimetres on the rows. The practice of transplanting is excellent for peas, especially for frame peas. Transplanted peas grow less stemmed and bear fruit more quickly than those sown in the field. As soon as transplanting is complete, spread a little wood ash between the rows. Cover with straw mats for two days, to help the plants take root. As soon as it is well established, we bury the ash by lightly hoeing with a weeder; we give as much air and light as the temperature allows, and we control the stoves so as to regularly obtain a heat of 15 to 18 degrees under the frames. When the peas have formed three or at most four flower stages, we pinch the main stem to stop it elongating and concentrate the action of the sap on the knotted fruit. We turn up the heat on the stoves a little, and a few days later we start picking peas. Chassis peas should only be grown when far from Paris, where in December, January and February, peas harvested in Algiers are sold at low prices. According to an ancient custom, peas are sown in sheltered beds on St Catherine's Day, November 25. These peas are quite early, it's true, but even greater earliness can be obtained, with less trouble, by sowing under a frame and transplanting in the open ground. For this purpose, we sow the very dense Dutch dwarf, in rows 15 centimeters apart, on a warm bed and under a frame, in January or February, to be planted out in the open ground in April. Choose a bed against a south-facing wall; plough well; place stakes 25 centimetres apart at each end of the bed; lay down the chalk line, and after tracing the lines with a pointed trowel, transplant the peas in staggered rows, 25 centimetres apart. We shelter them from the sun with straw mats for two days to ensure a good start, then spread ash between the lines and lightly hoe it in. Four or five stems are placed in each hole. Water very sparingly to avoid damaging fruiting, and cover at night with straw mats if frost is to be feared. When there are four stages of flowers, pinch off the main stem to stop vegetation and make the fruit grow, and harvest as you go along. Peas grown in this way require little more care than those sown at St Catherine's Day, and ripen a month earlier. I admit to growing in clumps only for early peas that will be transplanted. For all open-ground crops, without exception, we will adopt row sowing, which gives triple the results of clump sowing. The Michaud de Hollande pea produces its first pods almost at the same time as the Ste-Catherine peas, if sown early. This is the pea par excellence, in terms of quality, earliness and fertility: there can never be too many in the vegetable garden. The Michaud de Hollande pea, sown in February, bears fruit at the same time as the Ste-Catherine peas, when properly cultivated. It is sown in square no. 3, in rows at least one metre apart, but in a single row dug with a spiked trowel, at the bottom of which it is sown very thickly (pl. 10, fig. 1). I insist because people who don't usually sow peas in rows never want to sow them thick enough, and place the rows far enough apart. The distance between rows is one meter for Michaud de Hollande; one meter 10 cent. for Ruelle and Michaux peas, and one meter 20 cent. for Clamart. No less seed should be planted than is available (fig. 1, pl. 10). Furrows should be five to six centimetres deep, and oriented north to south. As soon as the seed is sown, it is covered, taking care to break up the clods; then a rough rake is used to remove the largest stones, and a layer of ash is spread over all the lines, about 30 centimetres wide, one centimetre thick on the line and five millimetres on the edges. The fine rake is used to attach the ash to the soil, without burying it, and to remove any foreign matter. When the peas have risen well, i.e. when they are about three centimetres high, we give them a vigorous hoeing, amalgamating the ash left on the surface with the soil. When the peas are twelve to fifteen centimetres high, hoe them a second time and row them in. It's very important to row on time, and, I repeat, the peas must not be more than 15 centimetres high, or the harvest will be significantly reduced. To row the peas, don't use twisted, branched branches, but straight, unbranched sticks. Two rows of oars are placed at each row of peas, and the oars are driven into the ground as follows: one row of rods at a distance of twenty-five centimetres, driven firmly into the ground, inclined to the same side (A, pl. 10, fig. 3). A second row of rods is then placed, driven in the opposite direction to the first (B, same figure), and crossed at points C, for added strength. The rods thus laid form a very solid trellis with regular lozanges. Two lines of trellis are constructed for each line of peas, one on each side, leaving a spacing of 25 to 28 centimetres between the two lines (pl. 10, fig. A). The line of peas is trapped between two trellises; the tendrils cling to the oars on either side, and when the peas are large, they form a hedge as straight and strong as a well-stocked and carefully mown thorn hedge (pl. 10, fig. 5). Paddles should be set at the following heights: 1 m for Michaud de Hollande; 1 m 20 cent. for Ruelle, Michaux and Clamart peas. All rods must be driven in so as to be at the same height, and to form a regular trellis. This method of rowing peas requires more wood, and also much more time than the one commonly used: this is undeniable, but wood and labor, even if they cost five times what they are worth, the owner will still benefit immensely from rowing as we indicate. You can row rows of peas with ten or twelve bundles of oars, and one or two days' work for the woman; the expense is almost nil, the garden will be much more regular and you'll get the following benefits: 1° A harvest at least twenty times greater than that of peas sown in bunches, or in rows that are too tightly packed and poorly rowed. This is easy to understand: our spaced rows, aerated and evenly lit on both sides, are remarkably fertile, whereas the pods can't form in the shade, in the middle of the clutter we see all too often in gardens; 2° An enormous time saving when picking the peas. All the pods hang outside on either side, so you don't have to look for them, just pick them. It's much quicker to pick a large basket 3 of peas on our rows than a handful in our seedbeds, and even picking this handful means breaking a large number of stems. The time saved in harvesting far exceeds that used in rowing; 3° Harvesting more than a fortnight earlier. This precocity is due to light, which is the most powerful agent of fruiting. Earliness is always very profitable if the crop is sold, and even if it is consumed, as it allows you to harvest one more crop in the year, while giving yourself the satisfaction of primacy. I recommend the pea cultivation I have indicated, to the exclusion of all others; both for the owner and for the speculator, since the yield is so much higher than that obtained by other cultivation methods. It's easy to convince yourself of this by making a comparative test. The landowner who sows in bunches, and devotes two ares to this crop, should continue it on one are, cultivating the other as I have indicated, and should take into account the time spent on each of the crops and their yields. This is the best way to cut short all objections, and reverse vicious habits in favor of a fruitful crop. When peas have formed five or six tiers of flowers, they are pinched off, i.e. the end of the main stem is removed. This operation is of great importance; it hastens the harvest and considerably favors the development of the fruits, by concentrating all the action of the sap on them. Nothing is lost by pinching; on the contrary, a few flowers are removed from the end of the stem, but these flowers, which would only have produced a few bad pods containing two or three seeds, would have delayed the ripening of the lower pods by more than a fortnight, and would have hindered their development. Once the peas have been pinched, all that's left to do is to hoe them from time to time, to destroy the grass growing between the rows, and to pick them as they ripen. It's urgent to sow peas often, every fortnight or three weeks, so as never to run out. Once you've picked four rows of peas, you're ready to pull them out. So you have to sow a few at a time, but very often, so you never run out. Michaud de Hollande, Ruelle and Michaux peas are sown from February to May, and Clamart from April to July. When harvesting peas for seed, be careful not to do so from a crop that has already been picked. The first pods provide the best seed, and by letting the last pods ripen, you only obtain waste seed that is prone to degeneration. What's more, you have to tie up one or two beds for a long time to harvest one liter of peas, and it would be better to buy it than to deprive yourself of a harvest. When you want to harvest seed, you make a special sowing in square n° A; you pinch early, and let everything dry without picking anything, it's the only way to get good seed. 25 POTATOES. Potatoes are extremely easy to grow, both as an early and seasonal crop. They are an indispensable vegetable, and you should never be short of them. It is therefore necessary to grow early varieties in trays and in the open ground, and then in the open ground a few good seasonal varieties chosen from the various kitchen gardens of the owner, tenant, etc., etc. The early Kidney or Marjolin potato is an excellent early variety, which benefits from being grown as an early crop, both indoors and outdoors. It is planted on a warm bed from December to February. Four rows are planted per frame panel, staggered 32-35 cm apart. In the early stages, we counter-plant with various nursery vegetables. Warmth of 15 to 20 degrees is maintained under the trays, with the help of stoves; air is given whenever the weather permits, the soil is covered at night with straw mats, and watered moderately to keep the layer moist. Potatoes are harvested as they come up, by digging at the base, and immediately covered with potting soil. If you have a temperate greenhouse at your disposal, plant a few potatoes in large pots and place them in the greenhouse. This is the easiest growing method, requiring only a few waterings. Harvesting is done in the same 8 way, as the tubers develop, by carefully digging at the base. You can still obtain very early potatoes with Kidney, by planting it in the open ground in plot no. 1, in the second half of February. To save time, germinate the potatoes under a frame, or, even simpler, in a warm place, in a greenhouse, or even in the gardener's bedroom. Four rows of holes, 25 to 30 centimetres deep, are made in each board, staggered 50 centimetres apart in all directions. The sprouted potatoes are placed at the bottom of the holes; they are covered with five to six centimetres of soil, and a small reserve of bedding is placed in the alleys to cover them in case of frost. When the potatoes are well established, we give them a vigorous hoeing, filling the holes completely, hoeing them from time to time, and harvesting them in the first days of June. We grow the seasonal varieties in squares in plot no. 1. We plant in March in holes staggered 70 centimetres apart in all directions. The plant is hoeed several times and lightly ridged to encourage tuber development. Potatoes can be counter-planted with garlic, leeks, etc., in the first period of their vegetation, and with winter cabbage in the last. 8 PUMPKIN. Pumpkins are sown on a warm bed in March, to be transplanted in a nursery between other plants in April. Alternatively, they could be sown on a dull bed and covered with cloches, or, if precocity is not a priority, they could be sown on a warm bed in April and transplanted in May; Whether the seedling is transplanted onto a warm bed and placed in a frame, or sown a month later, it cannot be placed under cover before May. They can still be sown in April, but with a cloche or at least a flowerpot for shelter. Pumpkins are sensitive to the cold, but once frosts are no longer a threat, they can be grown in the ground. Around May, round holes 50 centimetres deep and one metre in diameter are dug about two metres apart. These are filled with well-tilled and sufficiently watered manure, covered with 20 to 25 centimetres of good soil mixed with loam, and the pumpkins are planted in clods in the center of these small layers. When pumpkins are planted before May 15, it's a good idea to shelter them at night with a glass bell, an economy bell, or at least an upside-down flowerpot, to protect them from the white frosts that destroy them. When planted, they should be sheltered for at least two days to ensure a good start. 16 Pumpkins require a great deal of water; you must not spare watering if you want them to grow early and in good volume. The more you water it, the fatter and tastier it becomes; pumpkins don't mind two or even three thorough waterings when the season is dry. Pruning a pumpkin is very simple. The main stem is allowed to grow to a length of 1.5 meters for the large yellow pumpkin, and 1 meter for the Spanish pumpkin. Pinch to develop the branches on which the meshes (female flowers) appear. If you want monstrous pumpkins, leave only one fruit on the large yellow, or two if you don't want monsters. You can leave two or even three on the more delicate but much smaller Spanish pumpkin. Once the fruit is set, choose the best-formed and most advantageously placed to preserve them, and sacrifice all the others. The fruit-bearing branch is pruned two eyes above the pumpkin, so that it can benefit from the full action of the sap, and care is taken to ensure that no new branches develop that are too vigorous. If they do, remove them. Water copiously, but not excessively, until the fruit has formed, then increase watering as soon as it has, as the plant can never have too much water. There's a very simple way for everyone to increase fruit volume considerably, and that's to pickle the stem 50 centimetres above the fruit's attachment. Make a hole 25 centimetres wide, 50 centimetres long and 30 centimetres deep. Put about 15 centimetres of consumed manure in the bottom; cover with a centimetre of earth, on which you fix the pumpkin branch with two hooks, and cover completely with earth. A few days later, the buried part of the branch has sprouted roots, and this new root system gives the fruit all its sap, considerably increasing its volume. Marcotage makes it possible to keep one more fruit per plant, thanks to the root systems created. Pumpkins can be counter-planted with a few lettuces, if done in small quantities. But in vegetable gardens where an entire square is planted with pumpkins, they can be sown with green beans and harvested before the pumpkins have invaded the field. This harvest costs nothing, but should be removed as soon as it gets in the way of the pumpkins. RADISHES. We sow radishes all year round on beds, and in the ground, a little at a time and very often, so as never to run out. But as we only need a very small quantity of radishes at a time, we only sow them in counter-planting, on beds and in the ground, i.e. between other harvests. Layered radishes are sown in December, January and February, between lettuces, melons, cauliflowers, etc.; from March to August, in the garden, 9 in plot no. 1, between cabbages, artichokes, etc., etc. Radishes require a lot of water; they should be watered at least twice a day in summer to keep them tender and not too pungent. When sowing radishes in the ground, it's a good idea to beat the soil a little with the back of the spade; they are always rounder and better formed when the soil has been lightly beaten. RAVE. Cultivation is the same as for radishes. RAIPONCE. An excellent small salad, invaluable for those lacking layers and frames, in that it is harvested in the open ground during winter. Ruiponce is broadcast in square 2, in lettuce beds, as a counter-planting, and in special beds around June. The very fine seed should be mixed with twenty times its volume of soil, so as to sow fairly lightly. Cover the seed with a little top soil, and water assiduously until emergence. We start by harvesting the raiponces that have been sown in counter-planting, and keep those that have been sown in beds for harvesting at frost time. All you have to do is cover the beds with litter as soon as it freezes. Lift the cover, and harvest as needed. 3 Riponce is little cultivated, and wrongly so, as it is a precious resource for tenants, farmers, teachers and small landowners. RHUBARB. Rhubarb can be propagated by sowing it in seedbeds or in the ground, in rows, around March, or by splitting it off. Transplant to nurseries at a distance of 50 centimetres in all directions, whether the plant comes from seed or from cuttings. Hoe and water thoroughly throughout the summer. The following spring, place the plants in square No. 1, staggered one metre apart in all directions. Water often and thoroughly. Harvesting of the petioles begins in summer and continues the following year. SALSIFIS. Sow salsify and scorzonera in squares 2 and 3, in rows 25 to 30 centimeters apart, around March, to harvest the roots in autumn and winter. A little watering to ensure that the young plant emerges and grows well, and occasional hoeing to loosen the soil, is all that salsify needs. They can be left to overwinter in the ground without suffering, as they don't freeze. If you want to eat them over winter, it's a good idea to pull them up at frost time and store them in the cellar, or cover a few beds with bedding so you can pull them up when it freezes. 18 MI Aromatic plant essential for cooking. It is sown in spring, in borders, in plot no. 3 or plot no. h. We use it green throughout the summer, and pull it up in autumn to dry it and keep it all winter. Dried savory retains its aroma. THYM. To be grown in borders in squares 3 and 4, by splinters of plants, planted in spring. TOMATO. The tomato is one of the best condiments we have; its use has become more popular in recent years, thanks to advances in horticulture; its yield exceeds that of the potato. Nothing is easier than growing tomatoes in the open ground; early cultivation, under frames, is more difficult, but nevertheless accessible to gardeners of very average strength. To obtain early tomatoes, we sow in December and January, on a warm bed and under a frame, then transplant to a nursery on a slightly cooler bed, and even transplant to a nursery at a greater distance, on a third bed, before planting. These successive transplantings are intended to prevent the plant from growing too many leaves and to hasten fruiting; they are necessary, especially for tomatoes destined to ripen under chassis, as they always have a great tendency to grow too vigorously. Around February, tomatoes grown in nurseries under warm conditions are counter-planted with first-season green beans or other crops soon to be removed. Four tomato plants are planted under each panel. They are covered at night with straw mats, given air during the day whenever the temperature permits, and watered with care. The tomato plants are planted on two branches attached horizontally to small stakes or, more simply, to transverse wires. As soon as the two reserved branches are full of flowers, pinch off the ends and remove any new shoots that appear. As soon as they start to turn red, remove all the leaves covering them to speed up ripening. Tomatoes can be harvested in the first days of April. Tomatoes can also be harvested very early, by planting them at the edge of the in-season melon beds, on the north side; they provide shelter for the melons, keep insects away with their smell, and bear fruit well before tomatoes planted in the ground. Stakes one metre high are placed every two metres, and this one-metre height is divided into three. The stakes are linked together by three wires twisted around each stake, arranged as follows: the first 30 centimetres from the ground; the second 30 centimetres from the first, and the third 30 centimetres from the second (pl. 10, fig. 6). These wires are hand-tightened as much as possible, and a tomato plant is planted every 80 centimetres along the fence. As they grow, we tie the tomatoes to the wires, like a vine, taking care to leave a certain distance between the branches, and to remove any that might obstruct the light. As soon as a certain quantity of fruit has set, all the branches on the wires are severely pinched, without exception, and all new shoots are ruthlessly removed. We water very copiously when the fruits are well formed, and remove the leaves when they start to turn red. This palisade shelters the melons from the northern gales, and is literally covered with tomatoes by July. Tomatoes are only planted in the open air in May, when frosts are no longer to be feared, or if they are planted in April, they are sheltered at night with a bell until May. For open-ground cultivation, three wires are also laid on stakes, with the rows 1 metre apart, and the tomatoes are staggered at 80 centimetres, around May 15. Water copiously for recovery, suspending watering a little at flowering time and doubling it when the fruit has reached the size of a hazelnut. Pruning is the same as above, and must be carried out energetically if you want to harvest a lot, i.e. spend all the sap on the fruits by removing all the new shoots, and bring forward their ripening by exposing them to the action of the sun's rays, i.e. by cutting off all the leaves that shade them as soon as the fruits have reached their full size. A certain amount of green fruit always remains on field tomatoes as frost approaches. Pick them carefully, and place them on dry straw in a room where it won't freeze. Tomatoes are planted in square No. 2, and when a special bed is made, it is carefully mulched; tomatoes can be counter-planted with lettuces. You can also counter-plant salad beds already mulched with tomatoes. TRUFFLES. I won't go into the subject of truffle cultivation, since the means of reproduction are not yet known. What I have said about Etampes truffles has stirred up the whole Périgourdine community, and given rise to a host of articles to which I have not wished to reply, as I have other things to do than to write slogans in favor of the Périgourdins. The town of Etampes supplies excellent truffles, and harvests considerable quantities every year; moreover, Etampes produces truffes à la reine, a variety much appreciated by gourmets. These are the facts in all their brutality. Everyone can verify them by passing through Etampes, and this is my only answer to the Périgourdins: Périgord truffles have lost none of their value, because Etampes produces excellent ones. Why deny it? DISEESCQO There's no medal that doesn't have its reverse side; gardening has its own; they are numerous, that's undeniable; but we mustn't exaggerate them. I would be failing in my self-imposed mission if, after indicating all the means of action, and pointing out the successes that are easy to achieve, I were to pass over the setbacks in silence. But before we get discouraged and repeat in chorus with the unintelligent and mediocrely hard-working masses: we're out of luck! or the soil is worthless! let's look for the cause of most of these failures. Let's start with those of large-scale cultivation. Alas! how many stars we have seen spinning! Why? because most of the time, highly intelligent men with a certain amount of capital, but who knew nothing about cultivation and didn't want to take the trouble to study it, threw themselves like madmen into clearing land, and spent their fortune and their intelligence on it. These men forgot that cultivation is a science, that it is necessary not only to know, but also to know how to do it; they unfortunately ruined themselves, and the irrefutable setbacks and obvious failures that have befallen so many families. Does this mean that large-scale cultivation is bad speculation? Obviously not, since the operations begun by these agricultural madmen, and continued by farmers, have produced the most brilliant results, and created more fortunes than they have ruined! Back to the vegetable garden! I've said that it's not just a question of knowing how to do things, but also of knowing how to do them. Most of the time, we fail at the easiest things, because we don't know how to do them, and we know even less how to do them. There's a very simple remedy to this state of affairs, and that's to learn; it's easy with a little intelligence, a lot of goodwill, and putting all false pride aside. You can't blame a man for not knowing something he wasn't able to learn; you can only pity him for not having been able to learn, especially when he's intelligent. Having said that, let's look at the causes of the main setbacks in vegetable growing, and try to avoid them. We have to constantly fear, and constantly fight, three causes of ruin for the plants we cultivate: 1° Atmospheric influences; 2° Diseases; 3° Insects. Humidity, frost, wind and storms are all enemies to be dreaded, but by fighting them with perseverance and energy, we manage to ward off their disastrous effects. Humidity is particularly pernicious for crops grown in trays and cloches; in the absence of sunlight, it causes plants to rot. That's when you need to redouble your efforts: carefully wipe the inside of glass panes and cloches, give as much air as possible to evaporate it, and make sure that no clutter forms under shelters; in other words, that plants don't get tangled up together; that they lack neither air nor light. Frost destroys everything if you can't fight it and let it surprise you. As early as October, you should prepare all your blankets, mats, litter, etc., to be used at the first sign of frost: when wild ducks and geese pass in flocks, heading from north-east to south-west, it's a sure sign of frost a few days later, just as their passage from south-west to north-east is a sure sign of thaw; thick, continuous fog almost always precedes frost: When, at the onset of winter, the wind stays to the north-east, the weather clears, and the stars shine brightly, we can expect a hard, continuous frost. We must be ready to cover everything as soon as these conditions appear; we must uncover with the same eagerness, as soon as the thaw comes, but keeping the shelters within reach if there is a recurrence of cold. Violent winds also cause great damage. You have to anticipate them, tie everything down and secure everything to avoid their ravages. When the wind is very still and uncertain, and the sunset is very red, it's a sign of a storm. Thunderstorms also cause great damage, as they are often accompanied by hailstorms and sometimes hail. You need to prepare everything when you see it coming: close the frames, take down the bells, and keep straw mats ready to cover melons and seedlings in case of hail. Diseases affecting vegetable plants can sometimes wreak havoc. In principle, however, diseases only affect weak plants that lack food and are placed in poor conditions. We never see diseased plants in the Paris marshes, which are typical of vegetable cultivation. When vegetables are cultivated in a more rational way, provided with the right fertilizers, and the soil is given the necessary care, diseases will disappear, as they are most often only an effect of poor cultivation. The same cannot be said of insects, which sometimes suddenly invade our crops and wreak havoc. Spider mites cause serious damage to seedlings, particularly carrots. They pierce the stem, usually killing the young plants. They can be destroyed by spreading ash or quicklime in the pathways, and at the same time drenching the seedlings with a decoction of soot or a solution of black soap. Caterpillars of all families cause great havoc, especially in cabbage plantations. They can be destroyed fairly quickly by spraying the affected plants with a black soap solution. A mixture of water, oil and ammonia would achieve a more rapid result, but the oil clogs the leaf stomata and impedes vegetation, whereas the black soap stimulates it. Courtillères cause real havoc in beds and seedlings. They are very difficult to destroy, but some can be killed by pouring soap water into their holes, or by pouring a few drops of oil and water over them. Ants are rare in well-watered vegetable gardens, as they fear excess humidity. When an ant-hole is discovered, it should be dug out with a pickaxe and boiling water poured over it. Slugs are formidable enemies, eating everything. You can destroy some of them by spreading ash around the boards they visit. They can also be hunted early in the morning, when there are plenty of them, but when there are many, and the garden is walled, the easiest thing to do is to get two or three hedgehogs and let them roam free. In just a few days, they'll devour all the slugs, without ever touching the plants. The flea beetle is very damaging to cabbage seedlings, which it sometimes destroys. When infested, we sacrifice the seedling to destroy them, by covering it with fine, dry grass and setting fire to it. Aphids are easily destroyed with two or three syringes of black soap water. White grubs are the scourge of the vegetable garden, and unfortunately we have no effective means of destroying them, as it is impossible to reach them underground. Their ravages will only diminish appreciably when the beetles are properly controlled, as is the case in some départements. They mainly attack the roots of strawberry and salad plants; as soon as you see one of these plants wilting, you dig around it and kill the worms. When there is a large quantity of worms in a bed, it is worth sacrificing the harvest and ploughing it very deeply, as this destroys many of them. In any case, it's always a good idea to have a few tame ducks, which you can train to eat the worms when you're ploughing. Nothing is simpler than training ducks to do this. All you need is for them not to be wild, and to follow you when you need them, which is easy if you throw them a bit of bread. As soon as they see soil moving, they'll place themselves in front of the ploughmen, and not a worm will escape them. When ducks have been to the plough once or twice, you only have to show them a spade to take them a league away; they follow with the greatest alacrity, place themselves in front of the ploughmen and never leave the top of the gauge, so impatiently are they waiting for the shovelful of earth that will provide them with a worm. I've noticed that in vegetable gardens with regular crop rotation, square No. 3, the ashy one, is always less attacked by grubs. The causticised ash keeps them away, if it doesn't destroy them. Another excellent measure is to have your chickens weed your gardens. Leave them free in the vegetable garden for part of the winter, when there's nothing to eat, as they're almost as fond of greenery as they are of insects. Or, better still, have 2-metre-square racks made, and when there are a lot of insects, park them with the racks, like sheep, in the most infested part, after removing the crop and giving it a light ploughing. Ten hens devour more insects in an hour than a man can destroy in a year. Small chickens are also excellent caterpillar destroyers for part of the summer. From birth until they are six weeks or two months old, they don't scratch, or not enough to do any damage. So when a cabbage patch is lost to caterpillars, it's difficult to destroy them because you only have the resource of picking them up by hand. Take a hen with her chicks; place the hen under a chicken cage in the middle of the square, leaving an opening big enough for the little chickens to get in and out. The chicks will spend their whole day eating caterpillars, and will refuse any other food as long as they can find it. The cage is changed every day, and when it has gone all the way round the square, it is purged of caterpillars. SUMMARY OF WORK IN THE VEGETABLE GARDEN, SORTED BY MONTH. The horticultural year really begins in August. This is the time when all seasonal crops are planted, and when work begins on those for the following winter, spring and summer. In August, there's still time to collect enough manure and leaves to build up the layers, and to make enough compost to start a regular crop rotation the following spring, with or without layers, and thus considerably increase the production of the vegetable garden. The summary of work I have given here is intended to remind the gardener of the main tasks to be carried out each month of the year, and to make it easier for the owner to direct and supervise this work: AUGUST. All outdoor plants are watered according to their needs; the loose soil, 14 in all crops, is maintained by frequent hoeing. Weeds resulting from hoeing are collected and mixed with the compost heaps in the factory. In August, we sow early white onions for transplanting in October; Yorck and oxheart cabbages for nurseries in September and October; short red Dutch carrots for harvesting before the frosts; leeks for counter-planting in spring; salsify, spinach, turnips and lamb's lettuce for winter, and passion lettuce for late winter. The last plantings of celery, chicory, etc. are made in the open ground. Beans are sown to eat green, and sometimes green beans, if the late season is mild. This is also the month to visit the borders, and replant them if they are in poor condition. Layers are no longer in use; the last melons are harvested, into which cauliflowers have been counter-planted. Unnecessary layers are demolished, and their products mixed into the compost mass. SEPTEMBER. Now that the heat is over and watering has subsided a little, it's time to activate all the field crops and prepare for winter and the following year. Early carrots, turnips, spinach and lamb's lettuce are still sown in the open ground. The previous month's seedlings are transplanted into nurseries. 8 Cauliflower, Yorck cabbage, gotte lettuce, chicory for winter and spring, and leeks for transplanting are also sown. Celery is being ridged, cardoons are being stuffed for blanching, and strawberry plants are being planted. We keep a few old beds on which to transplant lettuces sown in the open ground, and carefully collect all the manure needed to build up the beds as winter approaches. We grind the horse manure and mix the others with the composts. OCTOBER. Everything that can be removed is gradually brought in. Field harvests yield a quantity of leaves and herbaceous matter that are carefully collected to increase the mass of the composts. Never lose sight of the vegetable garden's rotation, and constantly think about what manure and leaves are needed for the beds, what composts are needed for plot no. 1, what potting soil is needed for plot no. 2, and what ashes are needed for plot no. 3. The month of October provides plenty of fertilizer, and nothing should be wasted. We are still sowing lamb's lettuce, spinach, chervil and radishes. All seedlings from the previous two months are transplanted into nurseries. We demolish the useless layers, those that have lost all their heat; some of the manure from these layers, that which has not been excessively consumed, is mixed with the herbaceous matter; the most decomposed is piled 9 separately to make new compost for the layers, and the old compost from the layers is reserved for the composting of square no. 2. Transplanting is carried out on muted layers that have produced melons, chicory, crepe lettuce, romaine, cauliflower, etc. We also sow on muted beds and under cloches: gottes, small black and romaine lettuces, to harvest during the winter. On rainy days, we repair all our shelter equipment, so as not to be surprised by frosts. We also start collecting leaves, and pile them up for diapers and composts. NOVEMBER. All shelters, frames, cloches and straw mats must be in good condition. We must have a certain quantity of bedding ready to cover field crops at the first threat of frost. Asparagus stalks are cut to a height of 40 centimeters, to mark the place of the base, and the mound made in spring is cut down to leave only 10 centimeters of soil on the crown, so that the asparagus can breathe. Carefully cut off any remaining artichoke stems, remove the largest leaves and start buttering. Artichokes grown annually are pulled out and returned to the cellar or vegetable greenhouse. All that's left to do is harvest and bring in the field crops, and protect what's left from frost. 3 Collect leaves in the garden, the park and even the woods, and stock up on broom, gorse and heather to mix into compost. In the woods, you'll also find very fine, fairly long grass that has dried on the ground and is excellent for making litter. Pond and ditch curings and pond grasses are also collected, as well as as ashes from lime kilns, factories, locomotives, etc. All of this should be done while the plants are growing. All this should be done while the field crops are resting; this resting time is used to activate the fertilizer factory. We can start smoking as much as we can a few planks of plot no. h, which will become no. 1 the following year, and put in Yorck and beefheart cabbages. We start to build up a few warm layers to sow peas and beans to eat green, and to set out lettuces, chicory, cauliflower, etc., between which we can place a few tufts of sorrel. As new layers are built up, the old ones are demolished, and the manure from them is distributed as we have indicated. Keep an active watch, and observe the weather more than ever; increase straw mat coverings at night, and apply stoves if frost is felt. DECEMBER. The fertilizer factory should be working as hard as possible, as it does during the whole of time 26, when field crops take up very little space, in order to meet the needs of spring. When the weather is mild, we uncover the artichokes and plow all the free beds. If it's freezing, on the other hand, manure is hauled in to clear the beds, and once everything has been transported, it is buried as soon as the thaw sets in. If the frost persists, we increase our supplies of leaves, broom, gorse and moss, which we fetch from the woods, and we cover whatever remains in the ground. When the weather is mild, early cabbages can be planted in square No. 1. Layering requires a great deal of activity in this month. New warm layers are put up for sowing melons, tomatoes, etc., and a few warm layers for sowing carrots and radishes, and putting peas, beans, etc. into place. We apply stoves wherever needed, depending on the temperature; we cover the frames at night with straw mats, and the bells with litter. If it snows, cover all the layers with straw mats and bedding, and carefully remove any snow remaining on and around the layers as soon as it has stopped falling. Air is given whenever the weather permits, in full sun, and when the thermometer is above zero. If some plants, poorly covered at night, are affected by frost, we must be careful not to uncover them; on the contrary, we double-cover them to let them thaw slowly, in the shade, which is the only way to preserve them. JANUARY. The manure for plot no. 1, the compost for plot no. 2, and the ashes for plot no. 3 should be transported to the site, so that we can take advantage of the mild weather to deep-till the fertilizer for plot no. 1; plow plot no. 2, and throw the compost into the beds as needed after plowing; plot no. 3 should also be plowed and ashed in January, or by February 10 at the latest. The soil is cleared of the last crops left in the ground or under the bedding; artichokes are kept in good condition; asparagus is smoked under cover, without being replanted, and if the weather is mild, early cabbages are planted, which can be counter-planted with leeks. In January, we increase the number of warm and hot layers, to set out melons, and nursery all early seedlings. Air is provided when the weather is mild; stoves and blankets are increased when it's freezing. Asparagus is heated; cucumbers, melons, tomatoes, chicory, etc., etc., are sown under frames. We also sow cauliflower, broad beans, beans, etc., etc., for transplanting in nurseries. Early carrots are sown, early potatoes are planted, and strawberry plants are started. Finally, we organize all the winter crops; we raise the seedlings that will be planted in the open ground two months later, we sow and counter-plant lettuces in the middle of all this, so that we never run out of them. FEBRUARY. We take advantage of the fine weather to sow onions, carrots, leeks, parsnips, etc., etc., in the open ground, in plot no. 2. Spinach can be sown between the early cabbages. The first peas and broad beans are sown in plot 3. The beds still require continuous care throughout February. All the plants sown in warm layers and transplanted in trays are placed in warm layers. Melons, cucumbers, tomatoes, cauliflower, savoy cabbage, celery, lettuces, chicory, romaine, radishes, etc., etc., are constantly sown and transplanted under glass. Air is provided as often as possible, shelter is provided at night, and the layers are kept warm with stoves. MARCH. Work in the open ground resumes in full swing. Carrots, onions, radishes, lettuces, sorrel, spinach, second-season peas, lentils, etc., etc., are sown in the open ground. All plants that can withstand full soil are planted: cabbages, lettuces, etc., and counter-planted as described in the general and special crops section. Strawberries, shallots, garlic, civet, all roots for seed, etc., etc., etc., are planted. 8 The beds require a fair amount of supervision in March; frost is hardly to be feared any more, but in exchange the sun gains strength, and sunburn is to be feared, especially when the plants, raised under glass, have not had all the air and light it was possible to give them. Shade is needed for the first few days, to gradually accustom the plants to very bright light. Melons, cucumbers, etc. are planted on warm, muted beds, and anything that can do without shelter is transplanted into the ground. APRIL. Asparagus is given a good ploughing, and mounded as I have indicated. We demolish the mounds of permanent artichokes, and spread the manure that covered them; we plow deeply and grommet at the same time. Artichokes kept in pots for annual cultivation are planted in plot no. 1, as are those kept in the cellar for the second season. All transplants grown under glass are planted in the open ground; cabbages, lettuces, etc. begin to be sown in the open ground. Pot-raised beans are transplanted, and all the bean varieties you want to grow are sown in the open ground. Layers no longer need heaters, as the sun takes their place; tender plants need to be shaded, and well covered at night. Various vegetables are still sown on the beds, to be transplanted in nurseries or in the open ground. MAY. The first harvests begin; they are immediately replaced by new seedlings and new plantings, so as to have everything throughout the summer. All harvests must be counter-planted to increase yields. We hoe, weed and water as needed. The fertilizer factory, depleted by the spring crops, must also be kept in mind. We demolish the first layers to mix the product with herbaceous debris from the vegetable garden. Carrots, turnips, cabbages, lettuces, romaine, chicory, cardoons, etc., etc., continue to be sown; nurseries are created to counter-plant and replace, as and when necessary, all that is removed. We sow beans to eat green, especially flageolets. The beds are easy to manage; air is given as often as possible; even the frames and bells are completely removed, and covered in the evening and at night. JUNE. We continue sowing in the open ground, so as never to run out of produce. We sow little and often everything, so as to always have well-stocked nurseries to fill the gaps which are frequent at this time of year, when the vegetable garden is in full production. Water as needed. The beds have produced the first melons, and we counter-plant them with cauliflowers, or replace them with other plants. JULY. The harvest is in full swing. Removed crops are replaced by nursery produce. Unnecessary layers are demolished to provide fertilizer for the mass, and everything that can be harvested before the frosts is sown. Clamart peas and beans can still be sown for harvesting in the late season. Cucumbers and melons are counter-planted with cauliflowers. END. Diuee ( 3 BEESGE COOgle FIRST PART. L'ÉCOLE DU JARDIN POTAGER. CHAPTER XXVII. Description of the CIBOULE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. THIS plant is an annual; there are three species, the common, the S. Jacques, and the perennial. The root of the first is an assembly of several bulbs joined together and aligned, forming a single bundle of hairy, white roots; its leaves are small, eight to ten inches long, cylindrical, sistulous and pointed, with a pungent taste; its stem is naked, straight, two to three feet high, M731699 A 3 1 swollen in the middle, bearing at the top a head shaped like that of the onion, but smaller, composed of white lily-like flowers, each with six small stamens and a pistil that turns into a rounded fruit divided into three chambers filled with rounded, angular, black seeds. The second differs in that its leaves are shorter, more swollen in the middle and more upturned on the ground; its flavor is stronger; but in all other respects the same. The third species, which is perennial, resembles the first in every way. All three species are used indiscriminately in most stews, both fatty and lean, eggs and vegetables of all kinds. It is also eaten in salads with lettuce when young, and is one of the most necessary plants for cooking. In medicine, it is used for the same purposes as onion, for which it is sometimes substituted, as it has much the same qualities and properties. The first species, which is the most widely cultivated, is sown from the end of February to August, and the newer it is, the more delicate it is; this is why it is sown in every month during the summer season: those sown in July and August are very prone to perish if not covered; on the other hand, once they have withstood the frosts, they have the advantage of keeping well into the spring much longer than the first seeds, which go to seed very quickly. The best way to preserve it and make it more profitable for the winter is to replant it in June from the first seed; when it is replanted later, the worm destroys a lot of it: When planted later, the worm destroys a lot of it, so we erect boards and trace small spokes eight inches apart; we join three or four feet of them together, and space the clumps half a foot apart, four good inches apart: these little clumps grow considerably, and provide abundantly until spring; they even make up for the lack of onions, when we run out. When frost approaches, we pull up a certain quantity and carry it to the greenhouse, or if there is no greenhouse, we make a trench seven or eight inches deep in the garden, and bury it close to the ground, covering it with dry litter in such quantities that frost cannot penetrate it, and we can always remove it if necessary. Market gardeners replant chicory in the same beds where they sow their spring onions during the months of June and July; and as the chicory is removed six weeks after being planted, it does almost no harm to the spring onions, and they thus make a double harvest in the same land; those for whom the land is precious can practice the same thing. Cultivation of this plant is quite straightforward, and any kind of soil is suitable, provided it is well prepared: If the soil is hard, cover the bed with an inch of potting soil, wet it if necessary and weed it. There is no need to take any other precaution, as it sometimes wilts or is eaten by worms. Replanted spring onions are the best for seed, because they have more body, and their heads are larger and better nourished; consequently, you need to keep a bed of them in place, which you let grow in spring; when the stem is fully formed, it is supported either with running laths, or with stilts to which several nipples are tied together, and in the absence of laths and stilts, they are tied with the month of August when the seed begins to uncover and emerge from its lodge, We leave it to dry in the sun for a few days on a sheet, then rub it with our hands, winnow it and lock it up, but it's better to leave it in its stuffing until it's needed, as it keeps better there and lasts four years, whereas winnowed it's only good for two years; It differs from onions only in size, which is slightly smaller. Once the seed has been harvested, if you don't need the space, cut off the stalk and all the foliage at ground level. The plant sprouts new shoots and produces seed again the following year, sometimes even three years later; that's what I've found. The S. Jacques has an advantage over the common one, in that the worm does not get into it, and that one foot is as effective in food as twice the size of the other; it is also not subject to winterkill, whatever the severity of the weather; I'm referring to the foot of the plant, as its leaves dry up and disappear in August, and it's only in the following spring that it comes back to life; then you can see it grow at a glance, forming extraordinarily large tufts that supply abundantly, and which are later to go to seed than the other species: It is not cultivated differently from the first, except that there is only one season to sow it, which is spring. Perennial chives bear no seeds, and multiply only from offshoots, which are detached from old clumps and replanted in the same way in spring and autumn. They keep well for ten years, and are planted 7 or 8 inches apart in all directions in prepared beds: A single plant is sufficient and produces 110 to 12 in the course of the year, which are detached little by little as needed, without destroying the whole clump; the few that are left reproduce again, and supply from year to year during its life; if, however, you prefer to replant new ones every year, it's all the same. In addition to this merit, it grows more rapidly than the other variety in spring, even though it is stripped in winter; during most of the summer, its hay dries out just the same if it is not wetted exactly; but in autumn, it greenens up again, and resists all the bad weather of the seasons, and will supply without interruption all year round if some care is taken to maintain its vigor; These advantages make it preferable to the other, and keep those who know it attached to it; our market gardeners, however, hardly cultivate it, and give as their reason that it is harder than the other; but the fact is that they want the same bed to yield them three or four different things every year, which the nature of this plant does not allow; its cultivation has nothing different from the other: We crimp it from time to time, and clean it of its bad leaves, particularly at the beginning of spring; those who have only this species, pull it up when frost approaches, and put it under cover either in the greenhouse or in a trench, as I explained for the other. There is a second species that is almost unknown in France, but is fairly common in Holland and Germany; it multiplies like the shallot, and forms an assembly of small bulbs numbering 60 or 80 very distinct from each other, which are used for the same purposes as ordinary onions: a single bulb forms this quantity from the month of November, when it is placed in the ground, until the month of August, when it is pulled out; it is left to dry like the shallot, and is locked up dry; it keeps all winter, and is no longer used as a spring onion; after the month of June, the stalk begins to turn into an onion. This species can be considered as much an onion as a spring onion. CHAPTER XXVIII. Description of CITROVILLE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Of all plants, this is the one that takes up the most space; it crawls like a cucumber or a melon, and its stalks extend up to 3 or 4 toises from its base. Its roots are small, straight, fibrous and hairy; it grows large, hollow, fragile, hairy sarmens on the ground, lined with large, deeply-cut, rough, bristly leaves; from the axils of these leaves, tendrils and pedicles emerge, bearing yellow, bell-shaped, flared flowers, divided into five parts, some sterile and others fertile, resting on an embryo that turns into a rounded fruit; The flesh is white, firm and sweet-tasting; the seed is contained in a fungus-like substance in the middle of the fruit; it is oblong, broad, flattened, cleanly rimmed all around, and lined with a slightly rough rind, under which is a white almond, pleasant to the taste. This species, as I describe it, is the most remarkable of all those cultivated in France; but there are an infinite number of others that vary either in the shape and size of the fruit, or in its external color, which can be green, white, yellow, mottled or striped in several ways; Suffice it to say that the quality of the fruit is always more or less the same, and there is no marked difference except in the species grown around Paris, known as Potiron. The bulk of the plant is quite similar to the previous one, but the leaf is almost round, without a cut, preceded by an extremely long and concave tail, about the size of a thumb; the fruit, in shape, is also quite similar; but it surpasses the pumpkin in size, as I have seen some weighing around 170 lb. It is usually a little flattened, especially on the head side, but chance produces some that are more or less elongated, and in general, they have many inequalities in their circumference; some are even marked with ribs, the skin is smooth, orange-colored, and the flesh the previous yellow; it melts less than all the other pumpkin species, and its flesh has more taste, but it still has the blandness of the others: however, cooked and mixed with milk, it can be served as a soup, and has its fans; this is also the only way to eat it that is bearable for people of a certain kind: country folk and craftsmen fricassee it with onion and in several other ways; but this stew can be abandoned to them, for on the whole, it's a tasteless dish and bad food, especially for cold temperaments; nevertheless, as it is an economical resource for people whose stomachs suffer everything, and for the peasant in particular who cannot feed on expensive food, it is appropriate for those who have country possessions, or who are burdened with children and servants who must be supported at a fair price : it is advisable, I say, to raise a certain quantity that can be found useful during the winter. The flesh of this species, like all the others, is humectant, pectoral, refreshing, and suitable for tempering the heat of the entrails, when taken as a decoction. There are two kinds of pumpkin: an early one, which is good at the beginning of August, and which is of medium size; and a later one, which is good only at the end of September, and which comes from an extreme size, as I said above: This is what differentiates them, being similar in all respects; the early one can be recognized by another mark, which is that its tail is yellow, while the other is green. This species, both the early and the late, multiplies, like all the others, from its seed, which must be sown in this climate at the beginning of March; because if it is not brought forward a little early, the fruit is prone to ripen only imperfectly, and it is of guard only as much as it is well August. It is placed under a bell, and cared for in the same way as melons and cucumbers; but as the plant is stronger, six seeds are enough under each bell, and when the plant is strong enough, it is replanted in the open ground, and two feet are placed together; this is at the end of April or the beginning of May. We make holes two feet square and a foot deep, which we fill with manure and a few inches of potting soil above; we wet the plant as soon as it is in place, and cover it exactly for s to ó days, unless it rains, as the sun ruins it in this circumstance; when it is picked up again, we lift the covers, and leave it to grow for about six weeks, until the fruit begins to appear: But when the fruit has stopped, which is always 8 or 1o feet from its root, pinch the dragnasse a little above it, and throw a few spades of earth on the node above it, which takes root and gives more nourishment to the fruit: at the same time, rest it on a tile, on the side where it is curved, so that rainwater can run off to the right and left. When the fruit has reached its full size, it should be exposed to the air, i.e. cut off all the leaves that shade it, so that the sun will ripen it and aptly aptly aptly apt it; Once it has reached maturity in August or September, depending on the species, we cut it and leave it exposed to the sun for ten or twelve days before locking it up; we then put it in a dry place on boards where it can breathe and where the frost cannot penetrate. When you find yourself a few piles of sumier or useless compost, no situation suits it better; it grows quickly and prodigiously. It is claimed that there is a male and a female in this plant, and it is at least true that there is a mark that characterizes the two alleged sexes, and it is chance that has produced it, just as single and double seeds come from the wallflower; the female grows two equal leaves, opposite each other, above her two ears, with the stalk coming out of the middle; This is easy to notice, and by experience our market gardeners have recognized that the male bears much more fruit, and that the fruit is bigger and fuller, so they let two second branches grow on these male plants, which give them three and four fruits, while the female is quite busy with one; They are therefore careful, once the seed has sprouted and marked, to uproot all the female plants and replant only the males, which also give better and more abundant seed. I tried it this year, and the fact seemed to me to be true to a greater extent; but as one year does not decide, I establish the certainty of the fact only on the say of the market gardeners who assured me of it. I don't know if the other pumpkin species are in the same situation: as they are not grown in this country, I haven't had the opportunity to notice it: those who grow them should take care. The seed of this fruit, about which I have not yet said anything, is its most valuable part: it is one of the four major cold seeds used so usefully in emulsions; it softens and refreshes the blood; it tempers the ardor of urine, calculus, kidney or bladder ulceration, and even the pain of gout; it also yields an oil that softens the skin, makes it even and erases blemishes, and is commonly used in cosmetic ointments; Everyone knows that it is used in the composition of that refreshing drink we drink in summer, as much for pleasure as for health, which we call orgeat, because barley water used to be its base; but as it is always being perfected, the way it is composed is quite different today; I'll give the recipe for the benefit of those who find themselves remote and isolated in their countryside. Take half a pound of the 4 seeds, which are pumpkin, squash, cucumber and melon seeds; wash and dry them, then add six ounces of sweet almonds and two ounces of bitter almonds, soak them a little in warm water to remove the skin; put the whole in a stone mortar and crush it well, then throw in two pounds of sugar with the skin. of sugar with the skin of a lemon, which you will grind with the seeds, this will make a paste that you will put well pressed in an earthenware or earthenware vase, and that you can keep for a month or more in a dry place. To use it when needed, you will take some from each pint of water, the size of a hen's egg, which you will put in a serge cheesecloth and dilute with a spoon; you will then press the pomace with both hands, and you will throw a few drops of orange blossom on the liqueur; you will then decant it into some jug or bottle which you will cool before drinking it. This seed keeps well for seven to eight years, both for the uses I've just mentioned, and for the seed; it has one more small merit that I don't want to omit, which is to serve as bait to catch rats, mice, field mice, leaches and other insects of this species, which are very fond of it. Before concluding this article, I feel I must say a word about several small species of fruit that are very similar to pumpkins: priest's bonnets, German trumpets, false oranges, coloquintes and so on. All these species have flesh and skin quite similar in small to the pumpkin, but they serve almost only to amuse the eyes, and are of no use to life; their shape and color vary infinitely; some are made into snuffboxes, and this is the surest merit I know of them, some others have properties for certain remedies, but their virtues are not proven enough to make them public, especially since the authors I follow say nothing about them; the first species that I have named, the bonnet-de-prêtre, otherwise known as the Jerusalem artichoke, must nevertheless be distinguished from the others, insofar as it is eaten, and it is not a bad eater: but it is neither fine nor delicate, and its shape is singular, having around its head several horns arranged more or less like those of a priest's cap, from which it takes its name. We have recently acquired a new species, called Giromont, whose leaves are shaped more or less like those of the fig tree, hairy and of medium size, and whose sarmens crawl like all pumpkins, flowering in the same way; but the fruit is different, being very black-green, sometimes striped with yellow, loaded with a few warts, a little elongated in the shape of pears; its flesh is firm and yellow, the great merit of this species is that it bears much fruit and keeps longer than any other, without being subject to rotting; Each plant easily yields 12 to 15 fruits, but the taste is no better than that of the others; on the contrary, I found it bland, and the flesh stringy; perhaps it would appeal better to others, or be better in other climates. It is certain, at least, that there is no species that would be as profitable as this one, if it could become established among country folk. CIVE. CHAPTER XXIX. Description of CIVE, its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. There are three species of Cive, the Cive de Portugal, the grosse Cive d'Angleterre, and the petite, otherwise known as the Civette. They differ only in leaf size, so the same description will apply to all three, noting that the Portuguese species is the strongest. Its flower is also higher and more elongated. The root of this plant is an assembly of small bulbs much like shallots, but which are formed in greater quantity, and which are not enveloped in the same way, being linked together only by roots which are white and loose fibers like those of spring onions; The leaf is long, cylindrical and fistulous, extremely small, with an odor and flavor similar to that of the spring onion; it sometimes sprouts a small stem ending in a spherical bundle of small purplish flowers the size of a filbert; these flowers are followed by a small seed enclosed in the calyx of the flower. In spring, this plant is frequently used in salad dressings, and sometimes in omelettes; I know of no other use or property for it, and medical writers have not mentioned it. Cive can be propagated from seed if necessary; but it is easy to propagate from offshoots, i.e. you separate the old clumps that make up yo, and each tuber you replant forms a clump in the same year: but 2 or 3 are usually left together; it is in March that it is replanted: as soon as it begins to grow, it is placed in beds or borders 8 or 9 inches apart; it requires loose, well-prepared soil, and will support itself in the same place for 4 or 5 years. Weed it as needed, wet it in dry spells and crimp it from time to time, especially in spring. At the end of autumn, cut off all its leaves just above ground level, and cover it with an inch of potting soil to help it grow more vigorously the following spring; the more you cut off the leaf, the more it grows back; and the newer it is, the more tender it becomes. CHAPTER XXX. Description of the CUCUMBER, its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Four species of cucumber are cultivated in this climate for tablé use, apart from the one that is grown for medicinal purposes, or only for the singularity I shall discuss next. These four species are the early and late cucumbers, the bouquet cucumber and the black cucumber. The first two are similar in all respects, except that the early cucumber is smaller and ripens earlier than the late cucumber. The roots of these two species are straight, fibrous, and covered with a lot of hair; the stems are sarmentose, thick, long, branching, and crawl on the ground; the leaves are born alternately borne on a tail six to eight inches long, thick and concave; they are shaped for outline like those of the vine, but larger, much less dissected, without serration at the edges, rough and covered with small prickles, especially below il cort de l'aisselle des vrilles, ou mains de fleurs d'une seule pièce, disposées en cloche, évasées et partagées LCHXPITRE XXX. 26 Prede in five parts, each about half an inch wide, of a pale yellow color, some of which are sterile and others slow; the latter are announced by the fruit which forms an inch long at the same time as the blossom, and even before the blossom opens, this fruit, which gradually expands, grows to a foot long by about three inches diametrically. It is rounded at both ends, sometimes straight, sometimes curved, most often dotted with small warts; white, green or yellow, depending on the species, as there are some of these three colors, its stalk is very thin, its flesh firm, white and transparent, without any odor. detidated, the seed is placed in the middle of the fruit, in three or four compartments lined with a watery pulp. This seed is white and oblong, pointed at both ends, a little larger than that of the melon, and covered with a hard rind under which lies a milky, sweet kernel. The third species, known as the bouquet cucumber or mignon cucumber, differs in several respects from the two preceding species. Its root is quite similar, but its stem, although equally shaped, is much smaller; its stems are shorter and less numerous, rising straight up to the base of the fruit. B rise straight up until the load of the fruit causes them to fall back; it hardly extends beyond eighteen inches, and often the bell is enough. Its fruit comes in bunches along its small stems, three or four of them together; it is green at first, and as it ripens, it takes on a yellow and golden color; its length is usually limited to four or five inches by two inches in diameter; its flesh is similar in all respects to that of the two preceding species, and its seed is the same, but a little smaller: its main merit is that it is very early. The fourth species is quite different from the other three: its root is very short, white and hairy, its leaves are born in crowds one on top of the other, placed alternately, and when they are in their full strength, they extend to fifteen inches and more, very similar in outline to those of the vine, but less deeply cut, rough, blistered and hairy, both above and below, spreading a bad odor; They are borne on a hollow tail the size of a finger, and from fifteen to eighteen inches long.Sometimes there is only one, sometimes there are two or three; it is very large, five-sided and partly hollow; when cut laterally, it represents a star; its length is about three feet. From the armpits of the leaves come the flowers, which are golden-yellow and velvety, bell-shaped, and resemble in every way those of the pumpkin; some are sterile, borne on pedicels three to four inches long; others are already formed before they bloom. At first, the fruit is very small and soft green, but as it grows larger and longer, it takes on a dark, almost black color. Its size and length are very similar to those of the late cucumber, but its skin is much rougher, forming a number of small ribs; its flesh is firm, yellowish in color, and much less watery than the other species. The seed is placed in several chambers separated by a pulp, as in the others, but twice as large, more flared and ruddier. One is called the Barbary cucumber, which is very large and oddly shaped, with a large number of warts; yellow in color, striped with green, the stem and leaf are nothing special, and I don't know of any properties. The other is called the snake cucumber or Luffa; its shape is elongated, but much larger at the head than at the tail; its skin is smooth, pale green, marked at the sides by small protruding fillets, arranged with symmetry; its leaf is cut, quite small, and its arms small; it is used neither in cooking nor in medicine of which the authors have spoken; it seems to me that it is a very new plant for us. A third, much better-known species, and very useful in medicine, is the wild cucumber, which is perennial; its root is long and thick, and it produces several thick stems that rise straight up to a height of fifteen to eighteen inches, and then fall to the ground when loaded with fruit; its leaves are rounded and pointed, quite large, and pillowed at the base; the flowers come from bell-shaped armpits, in one piece, pale yellow in color: its fruits, which come in large numbers. are the shape and size of a large Spanish olive, with a rough, uneven skin; they contain black, flat, almost oval, shiny seeds in three separate chambers. This plant grows naturally in our southern provinces, and is just as easy to find here in any garden where it is sown, both for utility and pleasure; in the latter respect, here is its small merit. When the fruit is ripe, which can be seen by its color, which is yellowing a little, whoever wants to enjoy it gently cuts it with the tail to present it to another, under some imagined pretext, and by presenting it on the side of the tail, and pressing it a little between the fingers opposite the one to whom it is wanted, the tail leaves, and the liquor, as well as the seed that is inside, come out with impetuosity, and rushes to the face up to four paces : we laugh for a moment, and the niece ends there. With regard to its properties, it is a plant of which all the parts are extremely purgative, especially the fruit; it is with its juice that one composes this famous elaterion of the ancients, of which the moderns also recognized the merit; it is employed particularly in old diseases, when there are inveterate obstructions to be removed, of which the ordinary purgatives cannot triumph, or verminous matters to be destroyed; the dose is from twelve to fifteen grains: one finds it at all the apothecaries. Honey in which this fruit has been boiled is given in an ounce or two at most as an enema for B 3 people prone to vapors, and for those who are not regulated. Let me continue with the species suitable for life. The first three do not differ in taste, qualities or properties: they are widely used for life in their season.
