The common man does not, however, pay the same attention to them as to those of a delicate nature, for the reason that they require a somewhat elaborate seasoning, which is not available in all conditions, and that they are perfectly good only with meats, whether fine or common; but, when they have passed through the hands of a good cook, they are well worthy of the attention of people of taste; and moreover, they are healthy and refreshing in themselves. Some modern authors, no doubt working on ancient and false traditions, have accused it of having several vicious, even poisonous qualities: it may well have had them in its origin; but this plant, like many others, having come to naturalize in this climate, which has proved favorable to it, has undoubtedly lost its bad qualities, assuming them to be true; and the fruit is currently recognized as good by everyone, except for cold stomachs, because of its cold quality. It is eaten raw and cooked in twenty different ways, both fatty and lean: We garnish soups with them, and when they're stuffed, the stuffing lifts them up a lot. We put them under chickens or poulardes, and it's a distinguished stew; we put them again under roasted meats, after having cooked and drained them. They are chopped with various meats, as well as with fish, and made into a very delicate stuffing; they are fried in a pan with butter and onion; they are also prepared in a saucepan with cream, parsley and cboule; finally, cooks take particular pleasure in varying the taste and seasoning of this vegetable, which is tasted and desired at the best tables. To eat it raw in a salad, there are two different ways of preparing it: some, after having mixed and sliced it, sprinkle it with coarse salt between two dishes, and stir it from time to time until the watery liquor has run off: they then season it with vinegar, oil and pepper: others cut the fruit into slices, and leave it overnight between two dishes; the next day they press it between their hands to draw out the juice; and, when they want to eat it, they pour oil and vinegar over it, with pepper and salt, and B 4 a few finely chopped herbs. Either way, they taste very good, and some authors claim that they are good for the stomach; but others claim, with more plausibility, that they are very indigestible, when eaten raw as I have just said. The use of cucumber is particularly favorable to hot temperaments whose viscera are overheated: it is its essential property to cool in kidney and bladder diseases, and especially in calculus, where its use is highly recommended; but, in these kinds of cases, it must be cooked. Its pulp, crushed and cooled in ice and applied to a freshly shaved head, is, according to two leading physicians, a specific remedy for frenzy. Its seed is one of the 4 major cold seeds so frequently used in emulsions, and is an ingredient in orgeat. The two early species are the ones that attract the attention of gardeners, and that everyone is eager to have early; their cultivation is difficult: but the other two, which I'll talk about next, are easy and inexpensive to grow. They are both easy to grow, and require great care, as no other plant is so delicate in its birth: they are sown on a bed in November or December; four inches of compost are enough for the seed, which can be mixed on the same bed with the other plants for which this dose is sufficient. Fifteen or twenty seeds can be placed under each bell; some people make holes with their finger and place two seeds in each hole, which they cover very lightly or not at all; others, after arranging their seed at equal distances, push it in with the tip of their finger, and leave the holes open to the air. Either way is arbitrary: I've tried them both, and have found no difference in effect; the only thing to note is that the seedbed must be warm, and the soil fine. As soon as the seed is sown, the bells are lowered, and even bounded if the weather requires it: they are covered overnight, and the same care is given as for melons; I will therefore omit this detail of conduct, which can be found in the melon chapter. Three weeks or a month after sowing, they should be ready to be planted out on a new bed, and only six should be placed under each bell, so that they can get the most out of it: they are strengthened on this second bed, and provided that it is warmed exactly, and that the plant is given as much air as the weather will allow, it is ready a month later to be planted out on a third bed, to remain there. This last layer should be loaded with seven to eight inches of topsoil, and the finest manure should be kept to form the last bed, which will do much to nourish the fruit. We space them two feet apart in a chessboard pattern, like melons, and choose the lightest bells, which helps to bring them forward. Five or six days later, if the feet are strong enough, we make the first pruning, i.e. we cut off the ears, and pinch the stem above the second leaf, or, to put it better, we cut it off: if they are still too weak, we wait to do it until they have strengthened a little. The heat of the layer is maintained by means of stoves, which are loaded as often as needed. We cover and uncover it according to the weather, and let the plant enjoy the sight of the sun as often as it appears; for air is as necessary to it as heat, and when it lacks one or the other, we soon see it melt. Excessive heat is equally pernicious to it, so too much care must be taken to keep it at the right temperature. It is not usual for this plant to need water until the fruit is well established, but this can sometimes happen when the soil or manure used is too dry. In this case, which can easily be seen from the length of the plants, they should be given a light wetting after the water has been warmed in the sun; or, if the sun is not available, a pint or two of boiling water can be thrown over a jug of natural water, to correct its coldness and crudeness. As soon as the stalks begin to make their arms, they should be stopped at two eyes; and when the second branches show fruit, they should be pinched at one eye above, and always re-pruned in the same way, as more grow. You must also avoid confusing the branches, especially as the leaves take up a lot of space, and you must cut off the gourmands exactly; you can also remove some of the leaves, when they cause too much embarrassment and shade the fruit, and consume too much sap, especially those called hard leaves. B 6 As soon as the first fruits appear, begin to give the bells a little air, and gradually accustom them to this; when the arms ask to be extended, let them come out freely; but, if you still fear some frost, be prepared to cover the bed with straw mats by means of a trellis that supports them. Once April arrives, the fruit should begin to strengthen, if it comes from the first seeds of November and December; and, as in this month we begin to have hot days, it is then advisable to wet it copiously as needed; for this plant likes water as much as melons like it little; it also needs to be pruned regularly, and when it is well managed in all respects, it gives fruit for two or three months. The first ones should be good to cut at the beginning of May; I have grown some myself under frames, which were good at the end of April. It's also true that, regardless of the care taken, if the years aren't a little favorable, the fruit is much delayed; by comparing, for example, the winter of 1740, whose rigors were felt until May, with the winter we've just had, it's easy to understand the difference the plants experience. Cucumbers are not like melons, which have a specific point of maturity; they are good at any age, and can be cut as soon as they are two inches in size. In England and Holland, this fruit is harvested much earlier than is common in France, and its duration is extended by three months more; as early as the beginning of April, they begin to enjoy them, and they grow them successively until Christmas. Their method for bringing them in so early, is to sow them in the first days of October in the open ground, and they are careful to cover them during the nights and on bad weather days: the following month they replant them, each plant separately, in a small pot which they place on a warm bed, covered by canopies or frames; they warm it exactly as needed, and give the plant all the care it requires: this plant is strong when the big frosts arrive; and M. Bradley, a famous author, assures us from his own experience that the plant, fortified in this way, is much more resistant to the rigors of winter, flowering in February and bearing fruit at the beginning of April. I haven't tried this method, but I think it's a good one, and there's no doubt that it would be easier to succeed in France than in England, where the climate is much colder, if one wanted to take the trouble. The reason for this is that the artist is not sufficiently rewarded for the fruits of long and assiduous labor; the genius of the nation in general, applied to other objects, is not turned to these small marvels of art, like that of the English, Dutch and Germans, who all surpass us in this genre: in two words, the same emulation is not to be found here; and this is not the only part of agriculture that is neglected. It is to be hoped that we will acquire a greater taste for it, and that the Great, who are the soul of a State and the motive of all the arts, will motivate the worker to make it flourish, since it is true to say (leaving aside other reasons of State policy) that the productions of nature, entrusted by the Creator to the industry of man for his use, are the most precious gift He has given him, and consequently the most worthy of his attachment. This little digression is not superfluous in the context of the subject I am dealing with, and it is better to place it here than elsewhere; for the small number of curious people and amateurs who are to be found in France, moan daily about the indifference of the bulk of the nation to all that is called the study and cultivation of plants; and it is a kind of shame for them that, with a marvellous soil and a favourable sun, we are deprived of a thousand small goods which our neighbors, in an ungrateful position, enjoy rather more abundantly than we do. However, it is not the worker who is guilty of this; if we know him at all, he will never be accused of incapacity or lack of activity; but what use is it to him to lavish his pains and his substance, if no one is willing to put a price on the fruits of his labor? It is up to those at the head of the arts to encourage it, and to inspire a taste for these novelties in the rich people who can consume them. Back to my subject. We have just seen what is done in England to accelerate the ripening of the fruit I am dealing with. All that remains for me to do is to explain how to extend its life until Christmas. Nothing could be simpler: we sow them at the beginning of July on a bed made of dry manure and fresh litter mixed together, which we load with ten inches of soil without any other precaution, because the season requires none. The following November, as the nights become cooler and the white frosts begin, the plant is covered with cloches or frames, and if necessary, straw mats are thrown over it: the plant begins to produce at the end of the same month, and being well cared for, continues to give fruit until the big frosts. I believe, although the English author doesn't mention it, that the bed may need some heating around All Saints' Day, to maintain the action of this plant, which is extremely afraid of the cold; that's what we'll be able to test, if we want to try the effect. I'll now move on to the cultivation of the two other species of cucumber I'd like to talk about. The ordinary cucumber, which we call the late variety, differs from the two early varieties only in size, which is such that we commonly see cucumbers a foot long and three inches across; its flesh is the same, but it fruits later. They can be raised on a bed to be enjoyed earlier, and when they are ready for replanting at the end of April or beginning of May, they are placed in the ground after preparing the site: We usually know how to use muted beds, on which we plant them in a chessboard pattern, like the others, two feet apart; others are content to make one-foot quarried holes, which they fill with consumed manure, with two joints of potting soil on top: they do almost equally well in either way. They are kept covered for a few days, until they are well established; they are then left in the open air. Those who have not taken the precaution of raising them on a bed, sow them in place in mid-April, in holes laid out as I have just said, and they come up in the same way, but later. When you have bells to cover them until the end of May, it is a safety against the frosts of that month, which often kill them; But after this month, they only need to be moistened abundantly, and often pruned, as I explained for the early ones, and in this situation they yield much more than on bedding. It is even claimed that yellow is nothing other than degenerated white: I'm not talking about a third species, green, which is not esteemed, even though it tastes the same. Particular care must be taken to cut the fruit as soon as it is good, as it not only hardens on the vine, but also prevents the young from enjoying it: when cut and closed in a cool place, it keeps even better and lasts longer. When a counterfeit one is spotted, it must be removed; a better-made one benefits from the food. When you want to grow them to make gherkins that can be eaten all winter as a salad, you should only sow them at the end of May in the open ground; they are good for cutting in September, when they are the size of a little finger. This plant is subject to a disease known as miller's disease or white rot, because its leaves flourish and, as they perish, abort the fruit. The only remedy is to cut off all infected leaves; and the best way to prevent the disease, which is better than the remedy, is to cover the beds with straw mats or heavy bedding in cold weather, especially at night. The black cucumber is cultivated like the previous one, but it is not sown in place: it must be raised worm-on-bed, and then replanted in well-smoked soil; its fruit is of a quality quite different from the others; its flesh is neither watery, nor so melting, and its taste approaches that of the chestnut: I find it in my particular bland, pasty, very-inferior to the others; however it has its amateurs. It produces a lot of fruit, and can be stored well into winter, as it is closed off from the air; these two qualities are what make it the most popular: the seed is removed as the fruit is eaten, and can be stored for a long time. The seed is removed as the fruit is consumed; it keeps for a long time. For the first three species, a certain quantity is marked in proportion to need, and left standing until it begins to rot; the seed is then removed, washed in several waters to remove the silt, and left to dry for a few days before being locked up: it keeps well for seven or eight years. Before concluding this article, I will explain how to make gherkins, for the benefit of those who like them and are sure of their digestibility. Choose the smallest or whitest ones; burst and cut off the tail, and put them in a white cloth, rubbing them against each other, to strip them of their down: then blanch them, i.e., throw them into boiling water, for the space of four minutes and immediately put them back into fresh water; remove them, and let them drain on a white cloth: then put them back into the vessel in which you want them to remain, either in a jug or a bottle, arrange them in it as best you can, intermingling a few bay leaves and a few long peppers, and pour white vinegar over them to the surface, after boiling it a little in a pan; then add about an ounce of salt to each pint of vinegar, and cover the vessel with double parchment tied around it. Eight days later they will be good to eat, and will keep from one year to the next; you can still add a handful of percepierre, tarragon or purslane chops, if that's your taste. CHAPTER XXXI. "Description of CORIANDE; its properties, cultivation, etc. Although JUOIQUON makes no use of this plant in food, as it is useful for the pleasures of the senses and the relief of the body in many illnesses, I believe it may deserve a place in a regularly stocked vegetable garden. Its root is small, white and lined with a few fibers; its stem is simple, cylindrical, smooth and soft, rising to eighteen or twenty inches; its lower leaves are rounded and toothed, while the upper ones are more deeply cut and divided into very narrow strips; Its flowers are parasol-shaped at the top of the branches, shaped like roses, with five megaloid, indented, purplish-white petals, and a calyx that changes into two seeds which, when joined together, form a whole sphere, first green, then pale yellow. The odor of the whole plant, but particularly of the fresh seeds, is strong and stenchy; however, it softens as it dries, and the seeds acquire a sweet, pleasant flavor; these seeds are gray, round and pea-sized. They are used for the same purposes as aniseed, with which they are mixed, or substituted when it is lacking; it is stomachic, carminative and antivenomous. What I've said about the virtues of aniseed should also be said about this seed, and I won't repeat it here. I'll just add that its green leaf, cooked with a mound of bread, is good for dissipating inflamed tumors. The seed is also used to make small sugared almonds, which provoke the winds as well as flattering the taste; it is also used as a base for a liqueur, called coriander water for this reason, which is very pleasant to drink and quite beneficial; brewers also add a few kernels to beer, and it gives it a good taste. This plant grows easily in all kinds of prepared soil, and the countryside is covered with it around Paris, near Aubervilliers. The seed is sown in March, and the plant is weeded six weeks later, if weeds take over; but this can usually be dispensed with: there is no other way to care for it, only that there should be no thunderstorms at flowering time, as lightning will ruin it. The seed is best harvested at the end of August: the whole plant is uprooted or cut off; and, as the seed detaches itself at the slightest shake, to avoid losing as much as you would take out, you should have four sheets sewn together in the field, on which it is placed as soon as it is cut, and immediately beaten. A second precaution, equally useful, is to harvest in the morning at dew. The seed remains good to sow for two years. CHAPTER XXXII. Description of CORN-DE-CERF; its properties, cultivation, etc. THIS plant is annual; its root is woody, single, with a few fibers; its leaves emerge from the heart at ground level, eight to ten inches long, narrow, deeply and unevenly cut as they approach their tips, a little hairy, quite dark green; around the heart there are also a few spikes, borne on a round, slender tail, similar to those of the plantain, which bloom imperceptibly : each flower is borne on a small calyx surmounted by a few stamens with no visible petals: these stamens are followed by the seed, which is extremely small, more oval than round, and brown in color. The leaf is used to make salad, and has no other known use or property for life: in fact, it is rarely used today. It is useful in medicine, being astringent through the belly, and aperitive through the urine, vulnerary, and suitable for stopping stomach courses and haemorrhages; it is also good for renal colic, for urine retention, for alleviating stone; for digging up and consolidating wounds. It is sown in March, as sparsely as possible; despite this, there is always too much: two months later, you can start using it, and as you cut its leaves, new ones grow: it should be weeded and watered when young, and placed in loose soil; it requires no further care: its seed ripens in August, and keeps well for two or three years. CHAPTER XXXIII. Description of the gourd, its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. 11 THE gourd is an annual plant of which there are three species: the long gourd, the large gourd and the calabash. The first has a sinewy, white root, divided into several fine fibers; its stems are sarmentose, as big as a finger, two or three toises long, and creeping when not shaken to make them rise; its leaves are round and large, cottony and crenellated at the edges, borne on cylindrical, oblong and concave tails; its flowers emerge from the leaf axils, bell-shaped, white in color, flared and so cut out that they appear to be composed of five distinct petals, hairy on the inside, and trimmed on the outside with a short down; some are sterile, being borne on no embryo; the others are fertile, and supported by embryos that develop into cylindrical fruits up to four feet long; the size of the fruit on the tail side approaches that of the leg, but increases greatly as it grows towards the tip: its bark is thin and whitish-green when young; as it dries, it takes on a yellow color, and hardens like wood. Its flesh is white, bland and a little spongy, usually divided into six quarters filled with compartments, which contain long, flattened seeds, broad at one end and narrowed at the germ end, enclosing a soft, pleasant-tasting white almond under a hard skin. Its flesh is refreshing, but rather insipid; however, in many proTome II. C vinces it is eaten with pleasure, cooked with soup stock; it does not melt like pumpkin, but is nevertheless very tender: it is also made into a highly prized jam: these are its two main properties. Its use is good for hot temperaments, but pernicious for the opposite: it is also used to quench thirst, by drinking the water in which it is infused. Its seed is its essential merit; it is one of the four major cold seeds used in emulsions, for all illnesses resulting from blood acrimony; it also enters into the composition of orgeat, the recipe for which I gave in the Pumpkin article. Its green leaf, applied to the udders of new mothers, causes them to lose milk, according to a great author. Water distilled from the fruit before it ripens is suitable for external inflammations of the eyes, ears and gout; and taken internally, it soothes the body's great heats: its juice, by expression, has the same effect. Its crushed flesh, when raw and applied to burns, heals them and soothes inflammation. Its cultivation is the same as that of pumpkins, with the difference that it must be transplanted to the foot of a south-facing wall, or to the foot of a few strong, high poles, to which it can cling by means of its maidens; for this fruit wants to have air all around it: it comes out longer and more united, and is not subject to spoilage, nor to being pierced by insects, as when it lies on the ground. This species differs from all pumpkins in that it is good to eat only when young, whereas the others need to be well matured and even kept for some time. The second species differs from the first in that its fruit is round and pot-bellied, and grows considerably; it is used for the same purposes. The third species, called calabash or flask, differs from the other two by the shape of its fruit, which is bottle-shaped, with a narrow neck and a large belly; its seed is also browner. This species is particularly used to make flasks for holding wine or water, or whatever else is deemed appropriate; gardeners use them in various places to hold their seeds. The fruit is left to dry well, and then emptied, raking it as well as possible. A small tool like a rake would be very useful for this. I know of a fourth species, whose skin is a coarse green-black, striped with a yellowish-white C 2; but it is considered more of a coloquita than a squash, and I have not heard of any use being made of it. CHAPTER XXXIV. Description of CRAN; its properties, cultivation, etc. THIS plant, also known as horseradish or wild horseradish, is perennial. Its root is long and thick, creeping, white, with a pungent, burning taste; its leaves are fifteen to eighteen inches long, broad in proportion, pointed, a beautiful glossy green, a little blistered, rough and toothed at the edges; sometimes it bears a stem, and often it bears none: This stem rises to a foot and a half or two feet; it is straight, firm, fluted, hollow, and bears small white flowers with four petals, arranged crosswise, followed by small, almost round fruits, which contain the seed. The root, which is the only part of the plant used, stimulates the appetite, and is eaten with meat instead of mustard: when freshly grated, it tastes almost the same, which is why it's called German mustard. It's also eaten with fresh butter, which is made into toast; it's the usual Flemish breakfast. It's a useful resource in remote rural areas, where mustard isn't always on hand; I say useful for those whose taste isn't sufficiently piqued by natural meats. Its medicinal virtues are stomatal, pecteral and anti-scorbutic: it is cut into wheels and infused for twelve hours in a decoction of barley, or boiled to make a herbal tea; the dose is one ounce in a pint of water: scorbutics are greatly relieved by it, and it is one of the greatest remedies for this ailment. Phthisics are also made to drink the milk in which this root has been boiled, and hydropics the white wine in which it has been infused; asthmatics also receive relief from it, and it also has the virtue of stimulating urination. This plant grows naturally along streams, rivers, ponds and damp meadows. It is also cultivated in gardens, and its virtues make it well deserving of a place there. Some claim that there are two species, one larger than the other; but, after 2 giving it enough attention, I attribute the alleged difference only to the quality of the soil, more or less oily, which makes the plant stronger or weaker. It multiplies in three ways: either from seeds sown in spring, or from offshoots separated from old plants, or from the plant itself, which is cut three rows thick and placed back in the ground; but this must be done at the same time as the plant is uprooted, and in a season when the sap is in action: each root forms a root which forms a plant just like the offshoots. Most roots cut in the same way produce the same effect; it's an experiment that's easy to do, and proves that the same plant contains many germs in its substance, as well as in its seed. It must be renewed every year, so as to always have one that follows the other in the degree of goodness it should have; for its root becomes hard and cordate from the third year onwards; so that it is only perfectly good during the second, (I mean for the use of life), needing the first to form. There's nothing special about growing it; just make sure you place it in the freshest soil you can find, and in a slightly shady spot. Description of CRESSON; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Cress is an annual plant used in salad supplies; it has no other use in life, but it has great health benefits. There are three very different species, each with its own foliage, but all tasting more or less the same: common, curly and golden. The common cress, better known as cresson Alenois, has a fairly small leaf, cut deeply like parsley, of a tender green color and a pleasant taste; When it goes to seed, it sprouts a stalk eighteen inches or two feet high, all the branches of which are covered with small white flowers, arranged in a cross, which bloom one after the other, followed by a small, round, flattened capsule enclosing the seed, from which it easily emerges; this seed is dark yellow-orange in color, flat, long, small and hot-tasting. Curly cress differs in its leaf, which C4 is curly and curled like brown cabbage, quite large and dark green; it resembles the previous variety in all other respects. The golden cress has an oblong leaf, about the width of a finger, unevenly cut at the edges, and of a golden yellow, from which it takes its name: its stem is stalked, and its flower white as in the others; but its seed is half as small, and of a lighter color. The leaves and seeds of these three species are used medicinally: both are hot and desiccating, attenuating, aperitive and abstersive; the main use is for swollen spleen, scurvy and mucilaginous tartar of the lungs; the seed brings out measles: it is ground with sain-doux, to rub and heal the head and other scabby parts. The whole plant is specific against worms, especially those of the pericardium. These three species of cress multiply only from seed, which can be sown all year round, either on the bed or on the ground; it is mixed on the bed with all the small seeds, and sprouts after three days: eight days later you begin to cut its leaf, and it gives all the more pleasure, the smaller it is: you must therefore sow a little every two weeks. It requires no special care: four inches of potting soil are enough for this plant. After the months of rigor, it no longer needs the bed, and can be sown in the open ground by the rays; but during hot spells, it should be sown in the shade, and moistened often; it requires loose, slightly loamy soil. If sown in March, it will be ripe in June, and the plants are removed as soon as the first capsules begin to open. It is left to dry for a few days, then threshed and locked up immediately. It keeps well for two years. There is a fourth species of cress that grows naturally in fountains, wherever there is flowing water; I will describe its properties, although it is not one of the cultivated plants: the resemblance it has with the other species authorizes me to do so, all the more so as in large parks, it is quite common to see it around canals and springs. This plant forms several low, creeping stems, which feed in the water and swim on the surface. Its roots are white, numerous and very slender; its stems grow to about a foot; they are curved, fairly large, hollow, twiggy and green, sometimes turning a little red; its leaves are almost round, arranged in rows with several on a rib ending in an odd one, always green, fragrant, with a pleasantly pungent taste; its flowers are born at the ends of the stems and branches, small, white and arranged crosswise. The flower is followed by a silique which divides into two chambers filled with almost round, small, reddish seeds that are pungent to the taste. This species, known as watercress, not only has all the virtues of the others, but also has them in a higher degree, and has been perfectly tested; it is aperitive, diuretic, anti-scorbutic, stomatal and hysteric. A handful of its leaves and stems are added to aperitif broths of crayfish and hepatic herbs, which purify the blood and make it fluid; it also relieves hydropics and hypochondriacs, and diverts soporous affections. Its leaf, boiled in milk, is excellent for ailing breasts (I mean the beverage): taken as a decoction, it is used to purify the blood; at the same time, it is detersive and incisive; it restores menstruation and expectoration; it is the specific remedy for scurvy; it cures grátelle, by rubbing with the leaf: its juice wilts polyps in the nose and makes them fall off, provided they are washed off often; the same juice held in the mouth relieves tongue paralysis, awakens the mind and senses, and makes you sneeze; put in the ear, it soothes tooth pain when it comes from a cold cause. The leaf applied as a poultice, and mixed with sourdough, resolves boils and all kinds of apostumes; it likewise relieves sciatica drops, applied in the same way to the painful part. With so many health-giving properties, this plant also has the advantage of serving as a food: it is eaten with pleasure in salads; it is served under roast poultry, and is no less flattering to the taste: finally, it is well worth the effort of those who have it at home or in the vicinity, to see to its preservation, by ridding it of the weeds that choke it in the places assigned to it by nature, and by preventing cattle from trampling it underfoot when they go out to graze. It should be noted that there is another species of grass around fountains which is quite similar to watercress, and no less so; the leaf, although shaped in much the same way, is pointed and larger. The cress that grows at Cailli in Normandy is particularly prized: the species is smaller, more tender, and has a finer taste than that found near Paris. Those who find themselves in dry, arid countries, far from any stream or fonC6 taine where this plant grows, and who are in need of it at the moment for some illness, can grow a few plants at home, and here's how. Make one or more tubs about two feet in diameter and five to six inches high, with holes drilled in the bottom flush with the bottom on one side; fill them halfway with soil, and plant in them two or three feet of watercress, which you send to be dug up in the nearest place: as soon as it is planted, we flood it with water, so that it exceeds the surface of the earth by a good inch, and leave it in this state: it takes root again and grows as in a fountain, if we observe two things: 1°. always maintain this inch of water on the surface; 2°, change the water from time to time, as it could become corrupted by too long a stay in the heat: simply unplug the hole, and it will run out; and, when it has run out, replace the plug, then pour in new water. When frost approaches, these tubs are locked up, and given as much air as the weather will allow. Description of the ECHALOTE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc... The ECHALOTE is a species of onion; or, to put it another way, it is an assembly of several bulbs joined together, a little larger than a filbert, and carried on a bundle of fibrous roots; these bulbs are aligned, pale red on the outside, and white on the inside, having a taste and odor approaching that of garlic, but less strong and more pleasant. Its leaves are numerous, long, small, cylindrical and fistulous, with the same taste and odor as the bulb: it has neither stems nor flowers, at least I've never seen any; and I think Mr. Lémery was quite mistaken in this respect in the description he gave. There are two species, the common and the large, which resemble each other in all the points I have just mentioned, except for their size. The bulb of the latter is once as large as that of the former, and its leaves are almost as strong as those of the chive: we can see from this that it is of better value than the other; but it is still only in the hands of a few curious people, and I cannot say where it came from; we must be eager to know and multiply it. This plant, by which I mean the bulb, is of great use in all types of cooking; it stimulates the appetite and pleasantly piques the taste; it is mixed into most sauces, both fatty and lean, and goes particularly well with oil and vinegar: it leaves no taste after it like onion and garlic, when it has been eaten; and this is why it appeals better to many people. The leaf is not used. Its bulb is highly aperitive; it is sometimes used medicinally for esquinancies, and its use is good for those with pits and who are subject to urine retention: it is also claimed that when crushed and applied to the bites of rabid dogs, it prevents the unfortunate consequences. It is also good for keeping out bad air, and is used in place of garlic. This plant multiplies from its tubers, which are separated like those of garlic, and are planted at the beginning of March in borders or beds, four inches apart in all directions, taking care not to bury them more than level with the surface of the soil. Four days later, they sprout, and from May onwards, you start using them; but to keep them, you have to wait to pull them up until the tops are completely dry, which is usually at the end of June; they keep perfectly well throughout the winter, provided you let them dry out well before storing them, and keep them in a dry place. Cultivation requires no special care; many gardeners plant them around onion beds, and they do very well in this arrangement, provided the soil is suitable; for I would observe in this respect that it does not succeed in any kind of soil, being very often prone to clouding and rotting in the foot; and I don't know precisely where this depends, or which type of soil is more favorable to it; for I have more than once seen it succeed and fail alternately in light soils, and have the same fate in other, fatter soils. I believe its success depends to a greater or lesser extent on the weather. Everyone will have to find the best place for it in their own soil, and to be on the safe side, you can put it in different places: if it doesn't do well in one, it may do better in another. Moreover, when planting them, care should be taken to choose the most rounded and elongated tubers; the bulb will be more beautiful as a result. CHAPTER XXXVII. Description of the EPINARD; its different species, properties, s4 culture, etc. This plant is an annual; there are two species: the common one, otherwise known as male spinach, and the one known as the large species. Some would like to count a third, which they call female spinach; but they are wrong to consider it a species, since all its flowers are sterile, and it is a degeneration of the other two species, among which this one occurs in all seeds. The root of the common spinach is small, white, simple, with few fibers; its stem is two feet or more high, hollow, cylindrical, fluted, and divided into several branches. Its ferns are almost similar to those of the arroche, borne on long tails; those at the bottom of the stems are sometimes cut on both sides at their base, ending in a point; and those at the top of the stem have only two extensions and are like ears at their base. This plant bears no flowers, but only green fruits, loaded with four whitish filaments; the embryos are born from the leaf axils at the ends of the branches, in clusters piled one on top of the other, which change into a fruit the size of a vetch seed, round, flattened and smooth, ash-colored as it ripens, and filled with a pear-shaped seed; others have it much more flattened, almost triangular and prickly. This difference between the seeds of one species and those of another authorizes some authors to make two different species; but it should be noted that this is the only difference in the plant, and that it is not worth dividing it into two species: moreover, I've found that when I sow prickly seed, I sometimes get plants that make the seed round; and similarly, when I sow round seed, I get plants that make it prickly: so it seems to me that this must be considered simply as a variety and a play of nature. The spinach of the large species differs from the first, in that the plant is much stronger and higher, and the leaves larger, rounder and thicker. Its seed is round like the other, of the same size and color. The first species is more delicate to the taste of some; the second provides more, and according to others, has a more decisive taste; it also withstands winter better, and melts less in the fire: everyone can be satisfied. It can be used for both fatty and lean varieties, but the method of preparation is always the same: first, all the leaves are peeled and washed thoroughly; then they are thrown into boiling water, where they are cushioned, and removed after half an hour to drain. The most common practice is to chop spinach when it is cooked; but good cooks do not do this, and apprehend it as it comes out of the water, having recognized that in this operation it loses most of its juice and taste, so that all that remains is the pomace. The method used by some others is to cook them without water, as they yield enough of their own, and it's true that they taste much better; but you don't want to start with too much fire, which would burn them. In some countries, they are eaten raw in salads, when they are young and tender. Finally, authors unanimously agree that, the way they are used, they are a healthy food, albeit not very nourishing. This dish is used for entremets at the most delicate tables, either with juice or cream, and is always the first dish eaten: simply prepared with butter, and seasoned with onion and spices, it is generally appreciated: others add cream, with a lemon peel and a few drops of orange blossom: under sirloin and leg of lamb, there's no grass that's so delicate, and that takes the juices of meats better; we still make excellent pies with it: it's also used in stuffings, with sorrel, to soften its acidity, as well as in soup. The water in which they are cooked is particularly good for degreasing and cleaning iron, especially roasting spits. Its medicinal properties include softening and loosening the belly, and easing coughs and acridity of the chest. The water distilled from its leaves is also sovereign in soothing the heat of the bowels, and the ardors of a stomach irritated by inflamed bile; its leaves are also used in emollient decocttons and poultices. Asthmatics receive great relief, and are sometimes cured radically, by the frequent use of spinach boiled with veal; and this was the only remedy used by M. Fagon, first physician to Louis XIV, who was greatly troubled by this ailment. Applied externally to the stomach and liver, they dispel inflammation and pain. According to a modern author, too frequent use of this plant makes the blood melancholy; but M. Fagon's experience seems to destroy this opinion. The two species I have mentioned can be cultivated in exactly the same way, and can be sown for a full eight months, from the end of February to October: you need to choose the best, most well-amended soil you have, and top-dress the seed when you can. Those to be sown over winter are broadcast, but those to be eaten in summer are best sown by rays, as they are easier to crimp and cut. The first crop, sown to overwinter, is sown in mid-August, and begins to be used in the first days of October: the second is sown in mid-September, and the spinach is hardly cut before winter: the third is sown in the first days of October; and these, which remain small, are used to succeed the first after winter. We start again at the end of February or in March, and these new seedlings are eaten after the last ones have overwintered. We cut them as soon as they are strong enough; they only need this cut, because afterwards they go to seed, as well as those from the autumn seeds: a fortnight later, we sow a few more which have the same fate: we continue from fortnight to fortnight throughout the summer, when we like this vegetable so much that we can't get enough of it, as is the taste of many people, so that we can eat them all year round, except in times of frost; still, with the precaution of covering them, or cutting some to lock up in the greenhouse when bad weather approaches, where they keep for three weeks, stirring them from time to time, we can have them without interruption. It should be noted that the seed of common spinach is much quicker to set than that of the larger species, which sometimes remains in the ground for two or three weeks. The only cultivation this plant requires after being sown, harrowed and walked on, is to be weeded exactly and wetted if necessary during the summer, otherwise it yellows and rises out of the ground; if it can be put in the shade in very hot weather, the leaf comes out greener and more beautiful. When sowing by rays, you can do as I said for carrots, and even wet the seed as soon as it is sown, and cover the rays the next day; this is the method used by our market gardeners. At the start of spring, those that have spent the winter should be cleaned of all the leaves that winter has spoiled; the heart grows back instead, and the earth, freed of all the garbage that covers it, is more easily put in the right mood; weed them at the same time. In winter and spring, no tools should be used to pick them: they are plucked by hand, flush to the ground with the tail; but in summer this subjection would be unnecessary, since they are only cut once. In some provinces, the whole stalk is cut off: but this method is not a good one, because, in addition to the fact that they cannot grow back, the heart, which is harder than the leaf, is always felt when they are eaten, and is not clean on a well-served table. We keep as many of the first ones sown during the winter as we see fit for seed; they yield more than the last ones, and the seed is rather ripe. As the stem rises very high, by which I mean the larger species, it's a good idea to support it with a few laths, and to defend it as best you can from birds, which are very greedy for it, as well as field mice. The seed of those we sow in spring, although less well nourished, will also serve to make up for the lack of those whose feet have spent the winter, but they are unlikely to provide as much. Finally, the stems are pulled out or cut when they start to turn yellow, without waiting for them to dry out completely; the seed finishes ripening in the sun, spread out on a sheet, and keeps well for three years. Sterile plants, as I said, can be found mixed in with fertile ones; these so-called female plants can be easily distinguished when the plant is raised, in that it is weaker and more yellow, and instead of seeds, it bears groups of small petalless flowers all along its branches, which are, strictly speaking, nothing more than stamens that dissipate and turn to dust as soon as they are touched. Care must be taken to uproot all these false feet as they become known, especially as they are unfruitful and harmful to the good ones. As soon as the seed is dry, it should be threshed and sealed. The common species is of two kinds as regards the seed, as I have said; one makes it round and smooth, the other triangular and prickly; and as the latter is very awkward to handle, both to clean and to sow, the former is rightly preferred. A new species of spinach has recently arrived from America, under the name of basella, which the Americans are making great use of; but it will still be some time before it can be widely grown. I saw it in the King's Garden, and perhaps it is only there: but, as far as I can judge, it will not be very difficult to multiply it with a little effort; and I can say that it is well worth the effort. There are two kinds, differing from each other only in the color of the leaves, one green and the other reddish like beet, with thick purple-red veins, and the stem the same. The stems are heart-shaped, seven to eight inches long at the bottom of the & plant, by four wide, united at the edges, smooth and glossy, very thick: the stem is very thick towards the base, and grows a number of rather loose threads, almost similar to those of beans, which rise up to six feet, and turn around the oars that are placed on them, with a little help: these threads or branches are covered with leaves throughout, and together make a gap of two feet or more in all directions. Flowers appear in great numbers all along the nets, arranged in clusters and borne on short, thick pedicels; but the term "flower" is a misnomer, for they are, strictly speaking, nothing more than small buds which are rose-colored on the surface, without any noticeable petals or stamens, and which change into a soft fruit or berry, the size of a pea, split at the head which is green at first, and which, as it ripens, becomes a black violet. These berries are placed unevenly along the tails where they are born, and each contains a hard seed the size of a peppercorn, which is the seed of the plant. Up to this point, we at the Jardin du Roi had been content to give it the necessary care to preserve it, observing the degree of heat and humidity it could require; we had succeeded perfectly, not only in preserving it, but also in raising it from its own seed: we Tome II. D apparently did not presume that this plant contained so many good qualities, nor that it could multiply in all hands, and we had not pushed our research any further; we had not even had the curiosity to taste it. Knowing it at first sight, I asked for a handful of its leaves, which they were kind enough to give me for testing, and the same day it was done. I had them cooked and prepared in the same way as our ordinary spinach, with the difference that I had the sides of the leaves removed, just as they are removed from perry: I then tasted them, along with three or four other people capable of judging them, and we unanimously agreed that their taste was superior to ours, with none of the pungency we are obliged to correct with sugar or cream; on the contrary, they are sweet on their own, with the advantage of being fleshier and melting much less. All this has given me a strong desire to multiply the species, and I hope to succeed; the difficulty is that it cannot spend the winter in the ground, and that it can only give its seed in the second year, from which it follows that it must be preserved for a winter. Experience has shown that it perishes in an ordinary greenhouse, and that it necessarily needs a warm greenhouse; but I think that, although few people have a warm greenhouse, if a few apply themselves to preserving a certain quantity of seeds, they will easily suffice to supply other curious people: besides, it's quite possible to get some from our American islands; a small quantity will serve for a long time, since a single seed, according to the calculation I made on the small quantity of leaves I picked from a single plant, should provide at different times during the year enough to make two or three good dishes; and provided you manage to get some seed, you'll be able to console yourself with seeing the plant perish at the first frosts, after having enjoyed it for six months or more. This is a particular merit that ours don't have, as they go up in the summer almost as soon as they're up. Moreover, nothing is easier than to preserve it in winter when you have the space; all you have to do is take it with you in May when you leave the bed where you sow it, in the quantity you see fit, and take care to water them as needed: the plants are not nearly as strong there as in the open ground, but they do not fail to give a large quantity of seeds. The one I'm talking about has the advantage of not being difficult to raise, and of growing surprisingly fast. I don't know whether the seed would grow in the ground, it hasn't been tested; but it's D2 certain at least that, replanted in the ground as soon as it comes out of the bed, it grows perfectly there; it's in this situation that I've seen and admired it. Everyone will be able to take advantage of this little discovery as they see fit, and in relation to the explanations I have given. CHAPTER XXXVIII. Description of the ESTRAGON; its qualities and properties, its cultivation, etc. ESTRAGON is a fragrant plant, commonly grown in all gardens, and used in salad dressings with chervil, burnet and others. It is also used in omelettes, chopped finely: a special vinegar is made simply by infusing the leaf in it; mixed with gherkins, it enhances the taste. This plant is cordial, stomatal, incisive, detersive, aperitive and sudorific; it excites urine; it drives away winds; it provokes appetite; it resists venom, and makes you spit when chewed; it is also good for scurvy: infused in boiling water like tea, with a little sugar, it is very good against stomach weakness, indigestion and the desire to vomit; but some people find it difficult to digest, and are prone to have indigestion after eating it. It multiplies equally well from seed, from rooted plants, and from cuttings; but usually a few old clumps are pulled up in spring, separated into several parts, and replanted in well-prepared beds, a foot apart: this planting is done as soon as the spikes begin to emerge from the ground, as the more advanced the spikes, the more difficult it is to regrow. This plant rises to around two feet, and produces several branches where the seed is formed, which is extremely small and preceded by a small, imperceptible flower. At this height, the leaf is too hard, and only those of the young shoots should be used. This leaf is long and narrow, light green, smooth and plain at the edges: we always tend it, taking care to cut off a certain quantity every two weeks, by the stem, which always grows back until the frosts. It should be crimped and weeded if necessary in the heat of the year: it is then cut to D3 level after All Saints' Day, and covered with an inch of compost, if available. Care must be taken not to pull out the root when cutting it, as it holds very little to the soil. It should be renewed every three years. There is no need to take any precautions to preserve it during the winter; it easily withstands bad weather, but its young shoots are often subject to frost at the start of spring. You need mats or dry straw to cover them when you're threatened by frost. If you want to enjoy it during the winter, replant a few feet of it on the bed at All Saints' Day, and give it the same care as the other plants that are replanted at the same time. It can be combined on the same bed with all those that are content with 6 inches of potting soil. CHAPTER XXXIX: "Description of FENNEL; its different species, properties, culling, etc. FENNEL is a species of anise, from which it differs in many ways that make it preferable. Everything about it is useful: the root, the leaf, the seed, both in food and in remedies: advantages that aniseed does not have, and whose merit lies in the seed alone. There are two species, the common and the sweet: I could name a third, of which I have recently received some seed, which I have been assured is superior to the others in fineness; but I have not yet tested it to seed. The threshold is extremely fine and delicate, and the plant is not nearly as strong as the others: I have been given the Italian name fenochio di zuecarro, sweet fennel. Common fennel is perennial, and will last for several years. Its root is straight, white, fairly coarse, with an aromatic flavor mingled with some sweetness; its stem is four to five feet high, straight, cylindrical, fluted, gnarled, smooth, covered with a thin, green bark, filled with a white, fungous pith, divided into several branches towards the top: your leaves are broad, branched, divided into narrow, cylindrical lobes, dark green, sweet-tasting, sweet-smelling; those at the tip are like hairs. These leaves are borne on tails that embrace the stems and branches in a gauntlet-like fashion: at the top of the stems and branches are large, rounded umbrellas, whose D4 FENOUIL. are pink with five fragrant yellow petals, supported by a calyx that turns into a fruit consisting of two oblong seeds, quite large, convex, fluted on one side, flattened on the other, brown in color, with a pungent, slightly strong flavor. This plant grows naturally on rocks and stones in Africa and other countries close to the Line: cultivation softens and changes it a little in more temperate climates, such as ours, and particularly in Italy and Spain, where it is much more widely cultivated than here. Sweet fennel, otherwise known as Florence fennel, has much more perfect qualities than the one I've just mentioned, and also differs in that its stem is lower and its leaves smaller; its seed, on the other hand, is three times larger, whiter and more regularly fluted: The seed, on the other hand, is three times larger, whiter and more regularly fluted; it has a whitened leaf and the stem is also more tender and sweeter; but, for the plant to reach its full perfection, it is claimed that the seed must be taken from Syria or the Azores Islands, and that the seed collected in our climates is very degenerate, which seems to be proven by all the varieties found in this species, which rarely conforms in all respects to the description I have just given: However, in Italy, where it is very successful, only the seed collected there is used, as well as in Languedoc, where it is widely cultivated; but it is true that it is not all equally good, and to get it right, one is rather embarrassed: I have tested it several times; and as a rule, one must observe that it must be of a greenish white, tending towards cinnamon; that which is whiter is degenerated. Both species are cultivated in the same way. The seed is sown in May or June, when the plant is to be blanched and eaten as a salad, and in March when the seed is to be collected. Sowing is done in rows, either in beds or in borders. The soil must be loose and well-prepared: water lightly to encourage emergence, if the weather is dry; when the plant is six weeks or two months old, thin it out and weed it. It requires little water, unless it is intended to be eaten as a stalk, in which case it is transplanted to a bed, like celery, when it is strong enough, and spaced at one foot in all directions. It is cared for in the same way, wetting it frequently and mounding it when it is as D5 FENOUIL. large as it can be; it whitens and forms a stalk much larger than celery, and much superior in quality. Its flavor, delicacy and fragrance appeal to both taste and smell. It is tender at the same time and much less indigestible than celery; in addition to being good for the stomach, it is good for many ailments, as we shall see below in detailing its virtues. The Italians make great use of it, and rightly so: they eat it in salads, or more simply with salt: they also put it in soup. The tips of young leaves are still used in their salad supplies, where they give off a pleasant smell and taste: they even eat the tips of young branches without any seasoning. It's true that, particularly in Rome, it has qualities that you wouldn't believe unless you'd eaten it on the spot. It's a great loss to us that this vegetable is almost unknown here. I agree that the climate not being so favorable to it, it would not have as many good qualities; but from the most to the least, it would always be of great merit: perhaps even that if one studied its culture with care, one would find veins of ground where it would succeed perfectly: I raised some myself which was found to be passably good, in spite of the cold and wet quality of my ground; from which I presume that in a more favorable ground it would be much better. The greatest difficulty I've found is to bleach it without it rusting or rotting, and another is to prevent it from rising. The remedy to these two inconveniences lies, I believe, in the choice of the soil and the amount of water to be given to it.

The seed ripens very well, and is used for many purposes; but I take no comfort in the fact that the merit of this plant for us is limited to the use of the screw; for it has many more beneficial qualities. It is aperitive, diuretic, sudorific, stomatal, pectoral and febrifuge. Its root ranks first among the five great aperitive roots. Its seed is one of the four major hot seeds, and its leaf, though less used in particular, when distilled with the whole plant, produces a water that is sovereign in certain situations. The juice of its roots, taken from three ounces up to six, is an excellent remedy for intermittent fever-quarts, being taken at the beginning of the attack: it excites sweating, and the patient must be careful to cover himself well Dó FENOUIL. after taking it. The decoction of its roots and seeds is specific against smallpox and measles, as well as in malignant and putrid fevers. No other plant, in the opinion of many great physicians, comes close to this one's virtue for opening and resolving. The seed has a particular virtue for dissipating winds and soothing colicky pains: it is boiled with herbs in decoctions to be taken as enemas; and simply chewed or powdered, it produces much the same effect. It is also a sovereign remedy for eye diseases of all kinds, including weakness, obscuration, colyria and humours. This infusion alone, according to a leading physician, radically cured a patient with a well-formed cataract before his very eyes. An essential oil is extracted from its seeds, and is available from all apothecaries. It provides great relief for asthmatics and calms the most obstinate coughs; twelve to fifteen drops are taken in a glass of chopped milk or pectoral tea; six or eight drops are also very useful for colic. Good fennel, a fairly common liqueur, which is nothing other than wine spirit soaked in this oil, has the same effect with one or two spoonfuls, especially in windy colic and indigestion. Thresholds and roots boiled in barley and rice water bring milk to nursing mothers. Some claim that use of this plant makes you slimmer; it is therefore favorable to those with a marked tendency to become overweight. Finally, it has the well-recognized virtue of fortifying the stomach, aiding digestion and dissolving glutens, whether used in food or taken as an infusion. Shouldn't a garden always be stocked with such a useful plant? It's because of its great virtues that the Italian says: Fenochio è pane mi bastua, It's enough for me to have fennel and bread. Description- of the FEVE-DE-MARAIS; its qualities and properties, cultivation, etc. This is one of the hardiest plants, and one of the easiest to raise: it grows in fields as well as gardens, and succeeds in all kinds of climates, provided the soil is a little cool. Its root is partly straight and partly creeping, and furnished with many sibers. Its stem commonly rises to two feet, and more when in good soil: it is quadrangular, fluted and hollow, with leaves along its entire length, placed without symmetry, and divided into three, five or seven parts, separated by a rib to which they are attached: its leaves are oblong, rounded, thick, bluish and smooth: its flowers are born several together from the axils of the ribs on the same pedicel, arranged in order and on the same side; they are leguminous and white, variegated with purplish and purple veins at the base : the lateral leaves are black in the middle and white at the edges; the inner leaf is greenish: the calyx is green, divided into five quarters, from which emerges a pistil which then changes by degree into a long, thick, almost round, fleshy and hairy pod, filled with beans, three, four or five in number; these seeds, being green, are greenish-white, oval in shape, a little quartered, large, flattened, and enveloped in a hard, thick bark called the robe, with a long, black mark where they attach to the pod. As they dry, they turn red, and the inner substance becomes hard and solid. As the seed dries, the pod and plant also dry out, and everything turns black. Each plant produces up to fifteen pods, when the soil and the year are good, especially as the same plant often produces two or three stems. The ways in which it is prepared are fairly well known: it is eaten with butter, bacon or cream; when it's new, it makes an entremets dish, which people who are fond of and delicate are very keen on. For this preparation, we take the marsh bean when it is very small, i.e., the size of a large bean, a little larger: we only remove the tip of the germ with the fingernail to accommodate it. People are more accustomed to bog beans when they are larger: they are then stolen, to use the usual term; they are cooked with a little water, after having been lightly browned in butter; then pepper and salt are added, along with a pinch of savory, whose taste enhances that of the bog bean, which is a little bland by nature. It also has the disadvantage of being heavy and windy, and of tightening up a lot: you mustn't eat too much of it if you don't have a strong stomach. This vegetable has medicinal properties; its flour is one of the four resolvatives commonly used in poultices to soften, resolve and dispose tumors to suppurate: in tummy courses, when it is permissible to stop them, the porridge made with this flour and milk is a good remedy. The ash from the stems and pods of this burnt plant is an aperitif: an ounce is boiled in a pint of water, then filtered and drunk by hydropics. The bark and pod of this grain, infused from evening to morning in a glass of white wine weighing three large, is an almost infallible remedy for urine retention. Water distilled from the flowers is an excellent cosmetic for removing spots and freckles from the face. Five different types of broad bean are grown in this country: the large variety, the julienne, the picarde, and two small varieties called féverolles: the latter two are only suitable for horses, and are only sown in fields. I won't say any more about them. Of the other three species, the large one is the best, and the one you should stick to for your own particular use: the other two are much smaller, and have a wilder taste: they are only used when the first one is lacking, and are only eaten by people who can put up with anything. Few are grown around Paris, although they are consumed as much as the other species: they are brought from outlying countries, in preference to the large species, because being harder, they are more resistant to transport, and the seed is much cheaper for those who traffic in it. The large species is sown in December and February; we risk a little in this first season, when they can be preserved: they are a fortnight earlier than those of the second seed; but they often perish: field mice, magpies and crows eat them, or frosts destroy them, unless they are well sheltered, and carefully covered in times of snow and frost. It is therefore advisable to put off the strongest seed until February. The latter is the best, because it is easier to crimp them; three are enough in each clump, spaced a foot or fifteen inches apart. They are crimped in March or April, depending on their strength, and limed a little at the same time. The flower stops better, the pods come out more beautiful, and the aphid, which is their enemy, attaches itself much less when this part, which is the most tender, is removed. If the aphid has already reached the pods, collect the infected stem ends in baskets and throw them away, or bury them. Before sowing them, many people, slaves to old practices, soak them either in natural water, or in manure water, in the belief that this will make them germinate and sprout; for me, who experimented with this for my rule, the only effect I noticed was that after soaking them in this way, many rotted in the ground and didn't sprout, and the others didn't advance any further: everyone can experience this. You must choose the best soil you have to plant this vegetable, which does not do well in light soils; and the better the soil has been smoked and ploughed, the more it yields. At the end of May, the first seedlings begin to bear their fruit, which is desired by delicate people only as long as it is small: so it should be picked at this time, and the pods, which follow one another, provide three weeks' supply. You can continue to sow them until the end of April, but after this month, the flowers, which come into bloom in the hot weather, are prone to dropping; aphids join in and ruin them. What can be done at no cost and at the risk of the event, is to cut off the first few plants that have borne fruit in May or June, just above ground level. Only as much as you need is set aside for seed, and the stalks are pulled out when the pod and cossate are black and dry; they are then threshed, and the grain is locked up dry, taking care to protect it from the rats and mice that are fond of it. This grain keeps well for two years on land; by the third, it hardly ever rises at all. Some individuals dry it green to eat during Lent, and here's how. They are taken to a good size; their coats are removed; they are threaded into strings, and first placed in the shade for a few days; then they are exposed to the sun until they are quite dry, and they are locked in a dry place; but when they are well appreciated, they are a bad food that turns to mush, and is more disgusting than appetizing. One author has suggested that to fertilize land properly, it should be sown with seeds and ploughed with the whole plant, which should be buried well when it begins to flower, and that this amendment is preferable to all manures: I don't know of anyone who has tried it out, so I can neither approve nor reject it; but I do know, having witnessed it many times, that in the Kingdom of Naples, many private individuals fertilize their land with a similar plant, whose name I haven't remembered, which they let grow very high, and which they bury in the same way: hence I presume that this kind of fertilizer could be good; nr.However, in countries where manure cannot be found, this practice might be good and useful. Description of the GARDEROBE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. ETTE plante n'est d'aucuneut usage dans les alimentations; mais, comme elle sert à la conservation de nos vétemens, qui, dans l'ordre de nos besoins, tiennent le sccond rang, elle mérite bien qu'on lui donne une place dans un Traité de la culture des plantes utiles à l'humanité. There are two types of garderobe, distinguished by male and female. The first, also known as aurone, has a woody root with a few fibers: it grows several sarmentose stems, two or three feet high, hard, brittle, filled with a white, reddish pith, grooved and branched. Its leaves, which are difficult to describe accurately, are endlessly multiplied, cut into lobes slightly wider than those of fennel, and borne on broad tails. They are whitish, with a strong odor and a bitter, acrid taste. The flowers are numerous along the branches, yellowish in color, and similar to those of wormwood; namely, with florets, but composed of a large number of very short, pipe-shaped florets, divided into five parts at their apex, each borne on a seed, and enclosed in a scaly calyx: the flowers are followed by small, oblong, naked seeds, without aigrette, similar to those of wormwood, but smaller. This plant is more or less bitter, depending on the season, climate and terrain. The second species, called by several names, the female aurone, the santoline and the small cypress, has a thick, hard, woody, branching root: it grows stems a cubit or more high, woody, spindly, covered with a whitish down, and divided into several branches, which are surrounded by small, finely serrated leaves, or rather loaded with small tubers that surround it four by four along its entire length: they are whitish, with a bad odor, and a flavor that is at once pungent, bitter and aromatic: each small branch bears a yellow flower with florets, composed of several other pipe-shaped florets, divided into five parts at their apex, separated by gutter-folded leaves, and enclosed in a common, scaly, almost hemispherical calyx; each floret is borne on an embryo that changes into an oblong, striped, brown seed without a tassel. This plant, both male and female, grows naturally in Italy and Provence, in mountains and uncultivated areas, from where it has spread to gardens, where it is very easy to grow: it can be propagated from seed or from rooted plants, and is used to make borders around quarries. The female species has a particular virtue: its pungent odor keeps worms and ringworms away from any place where it is planted, thus preserving clothes and other woollen furniture from the ravages of these insects. Both also have medicinal properties. The first species is very good for killing worms, dissipating winds, and stimulating urination and menstruation, insofar as it removes obstructions of the kidneys and womb: it is substituted for wormwood, its virtues being more or less the same. It is claimed that a decoction of its buds is a specific way of bringing in hair and preventing it from falling out. It forms the basis of a reputed and well-tested ointment for hair, the recipe for which is given below. Take a handful of leaves of male Garderobe, and as much of Capillaire; join to it 1 ounce of honey of Laudanum, 1 large of wild Myrthe; 3 large of seed of Linen, 3 large of Fenugreek, 3 ounces of oil of sweet Almonds, 3 ounces of good white Wine; make infuse the whole together during twenty-four hours, then make it boil until there does not remain any more moisture; pass it by expressing it, and make onctions with this ointment during the new moon. A great physician assures us that the leaves of the second species, dried and reduced to powder, diluted in matricaria water in a dose of one and a half large, taken on an empty stomach for ten days, and then from day to day, stops women's white flowers. Another similarly assures, on the basis of his own experience, that one lump of the same powder is very usefully employed in pleurisy and fluxion of the chest. CHAPTER XLII. Description of the BEAN: its different species, cultivation, etc. The name bean is common to both the plant and the fruit it produces: however, to distinguish the pod, which is eaten green, from the bean when it is separated from its pod, we say green bean and white bean; and when the bean is dry, we say dry bean or bean feve. This plant is universally known, and is widely consumed in all countries: some species spin, i.e. grow upwards; others remain low, hence the name dwarf bean. The leaf is uniform in all species from this country: it is arranged like that of ivy, i.e., divided into three almost equal parts which grow together on the same stem, all three ending in a point, of a beautiful meadow green, smooth, thin and united at the edges; its flowers are odorless, small, irregularly shaped, white or purplish, depending on the species, and emerge from the leaf axils in bunches of four, six, eight or ten, placed two by two in echelon along the branch where they are held: the stem is extremely loose, and only supports itself by clinging to neighboring stems. for lack of any other support. The flower is followed by the pod, which is more or less long, depending on the species, and a finger's breadth wide; it contains five or six seeds, more or less, which detach easily when dry. This vegetable is used so frequently in the kitchen, that it's arguably the most common household staple. It can be eaten in all seasons, in all conditions, and with the most delicate of tastes: it can be eaten fat or lean, and in many different ways. Green with its pod, it can be eaten with juice, butter or cream; but it must be removed exactly from the pod. E it is necessary to remove exactly its fillets and both ends: in tender grains, we give him the same appetizers: under roasted meats it is particularly good. Dry, it can be fried in a variety of ways; it can be eaten in salads and purées. When candied, it holds its place perfectly in entremets, either in juice or in cream; and, although it is very difficult to resist the temptation to eat it, in whatever way it is presented on the table, it is nevertheless advisable to warn that in grain form it is windy and heavy on the stomach, and for this reason, certain temperaments should eat it with moderation. Its medicinal properties are softening, aperitive and resolving: its flour is very commonly used in poultices to soften, resolve and dispose tumors to suppurate. Distilled green bean water, taken in the morning on an empty stomach in a bain-marie, in a quantity of three or four ounces, is good against gravel. Chewed beans applied to horse bites are said to heal the wound. There are an infinite number of bean species. An individual of my acquaintance has collected sixty-three of them out of curiosity, all very distinct in shape and color, but with very little difference in taste and quality: I shall not undertake to detail them, so as not to deviate from my object, which is to make my work less curious than useful, and I shall confine myself to fifteen or sixteen recognized as the best, and very-sufficient for our needs. Those whose climate and terrain are more suited to a few other species will be right to cultivate them; and I have no doubt that some which are only of mediocre quality here, and which, for this reason, are abandoned, could be much better in other countries: I myself remember having eaten with pleasure, in the Levant, several kinds that I have never seen in France. The sixteen species I have chosen are: 1 the jack bean. 2 the grivelé. 3 the early dwarf white bean. 4 the early white flat. the parchmentless. ó the common white. 9 small round white. 10 white Swiss. 11 grey Swiss. 12 red Swiss. 13 de Prague. 14 le gros à confire, de Hollande. 7 Caux kidney. 15 cardinal. 8 from Soissons. 16 from Spain. All these species multiply from seed or grain, which is planted at the end of April in warm, light soils, and in mid-May in later soils. No plant is so delicate, and requires soil so well prepared and smoked at the same time: it must have had a good ploughing before winter, a second one at the end of February, and a hoeing before sowing: these three ways are amply paid by the product, and I have the experience that those who spare the one of February, lose instead of saving. The soil must also be loose by nature, and well amended. If the soil is greasy and damp, the grain is prone to rot, and if it rises, the plant is always languid, turns yellow and produces very little. This plant has one advantage over all the others, which is that it has to be changed every year; but it does better the second year in the same soil, provided it is given a little manure; the grain comes out clearer and more even. This tool is little known in many countries, but is nevertheless the most convenient I know of for most grain seeds, peas, broad beans, Turkey wheat, etc., so I'll explain here how to use it for those who don't know it, and who would like to try it out. I will also explain its shape. The iron is thirteen to fourteen inches long, by eight on the bushing side, and is used at the other end, which is thus square. It should be slightly curved in the middle, and the beans should be sown either in the open field, in beds or in borders. First, two hoes of earth are removed from their intended place, and thrown to one side, one to the right and the other to the left: We then give several blows with this sharp tool to loosen the earth; we pull out another good hoe which we hold in the air with one hand, while with the other we spread the seed at the bottom of the little pit we're making, and we throw this hoe back on top, which we level out a little with a turn of the hand, from two feet to two feet: we continue as long as the ground is long, and according to the species we put in more or less grain. A second row is started when the first is finished, and the clumps are arranged in a chessboard pattern, at the same two-foot distance. Be sure to crush the clumps and remove any stones. After a fortnight, the seed should sprout: but if, in this interval, the tool is placed on the end, which must be of well-beaten steel, one line or one and a half lines thick at most; at the other end is the socket, which must be bent so that the handle returns to the tool and takes the same turn. This handle should be a little curved like the iron, and should only be 5 to 6 inches away from its cutting edge, and three inches away from the socket; its length should be eighteen inches. E 3 times there are stormy rains which beat the earth, the grain which cannot pierce the crust which forms above, especially when there are a few days of heat, needs to be helped; and it is necessary, with some light instrument, to break this crust to give him facility to leave, without which it perishes between two grounds.
