A month later, when the feet have gained a little strength, they are put back on their shoes, i.e., the earth that was thrown to one side when sowing is put back around the clump, and the earth is broken at the same time. If you want to row them, this is also the time to prick the oars, and they produce once more. Three weeks later, if they are rowed, we go through the rows to help the stems, called nets, to hang onto the oars. In some countries, such as around Chartres, we cut the nets as they form, and they never fail to have an abundance of grain: I think this method is very good when they are not rowed, as all the sap remains in the stalk, the first flowers all hold, the grain is better nourished, and it costs less in expenses and trouble: at the very least, when the nets have reached the end of the oars, they must be stopped; for they cause confusion, and uselessly consume much sap from which the bottom would benefit. If there is a lot of weed growth, as happens in rainy years, it must be weeded by hand and with skill, so as not to harm the planters given the last shoe. They are finally picked green in July, if they are needed. Both hands must be used, one to hold the pod's tail, the other to pull it so as not to break the nets; but, for the best, it is advisable to designate a special area for those to be eaten in this way, without touching those to be left to dry; If they are dwarf beans, wait until the plants have been stripped of all their leaves, and the pods have dried thoroughly; make bunches of them, and remove them in dry weather. But if they are bush beans, as the pods only dry one after the other, they must be picked as you go along; otherwise, the bottom pods, which are the first to dry out, may partly open, and the bean may fall out; or it may wilt and rust in its pod, if the weather is rainy; and it's all wasted. If you have room to sow them dry, you'd better not thresh them until you need them, because they keep for two years longer, and the whites keep their whiteness and glaze better too. This vegetable is privileged in that no insect damages it like the others, so there's nothing to fear when they're threshed in the field. They're only good for sowing for two years at most, because by the second year some of them are missing. To advance this fruit and enjoy it from the first days of June, we sow it very thickly on a bed at the beginning of March. It springs up quickly, and great care is taken to cover it in bad weather; it is then transplanted to the foot of the southern walls at the sin of April, where it picks up again easily with a little wetting; but this is only good for early dwarfs. The bed should be filled with six inches of compost. If you want to preserve green beans for the winter, choose the most tender ones and throw them into boiling water for a quarter of an hour; then pass them into fresh water, thread them with string, and put them in the air for two or three days in the shade, and the same number in the sun; or, if there is no sun, let them dry out on racks in the oven, making sure it is only lukewarm: When sufficiently dried, remove and seal in paper boxes or bags. To use them, fry them for twenty-four hours in lukewarm water, into which you have thrown a piece of beurre manié, and cook them in the same water; then season them as you please, and you will find them as tender as in their season; but, to tell the truth, the taste is quite different. Now to the description of the species. The jack bean is one of the first to be sown in early fields, and the first to supply Paris. Its flower is purplish, its pod very long and tender, and its grain of a good size, very elongated and rounded, of a black color, speckled with white. It is usually used only in green, but its grain is one of the softest and best there is. The only drawback is its color, which makes the sauce blackish; however, if you are careful to discard the water when it is half-cooked, and to replace it with boiling water, you can partly remedy this defect. It yields a lot. The kidney bean does not have such a soft grain; it is a similar species in terms of earliness; its flower is purplish, and its pod of mediocre size, rather elongated, tender and striped with red. Its grain is lime-gray speckled with black; it yields a lot when paddled. It is commonly used, like the previous one, only in green, for the same reason that its grain makes the color of the sauce black; it can however be corrected in the same way as we said above. The early dwarf white bean produces its fruit at the same time as the two preceding varieties: it does not spin, as its name suggests, and yet it is extraordinarily profitable, especially if picked often. Its flower is white, and its pod long and plain; its seed is also white, but of a perfect white, smooth and glossy: it is small, elongated and a little rounded. It is eaten both green and dry, and is very tasty either way: of all the species, it is the one that gives the most pleasure and profit in a middle-class garden; except that the dry bean does not lead the way as much as the larger species, which I'll talk about next. E The white flat bean is still in the same class as the previous ones in terms of haste: it spins and loads a lot when rowed. It has white flowers and medium-length pods, with medium-sized, short, flattened and fairly white beans. It is used both green and dry, but when eaten dry, it lacks the perfection of some others. The bean without parchment is the most esteemed to be eaten green, by the reason that its pod does not have inside this small film, called parchment, common to all the other species, and which makes it more tender and more pleasant to eat: it also has the advantage of giving its grain much more than any other; it is notoriously tender and soft, and at the same time as early as the preceding ones; it provides a lot when rowed. Its qualities justly earn it the eagerness of those who know it: it has a white flower, a very long pod, and a short, flat, white, medium-sized grain. It is used for both green and tender beans with the same pleasure: when dry, it has nothing to distinguish it. The common white bean is found everywhere, and is most widely used in provinces where the more distinguished species are not known, and where perhaps they would not be as successful as around Paris. Its flower is white, its pod mediocre, and its grain short, flattened, of a slightly dirty white; it spins and loads a lot when rowed: it is eaten equally green, as a tender grain, and dry. The Caux kidney is so named because its germ is sunken, and its overall shape resembles that of a sheep's kidney; it is a very good and highly esteemed species, and loads a lot when rowed. Its flower is white, and its pod highly elongated, but less full than some others; its grain is a little small, elongated, and quite perfectly white, smooth and glossy. It can be eaten in all ways, but when dried it is one of the most esteemed, being soft and tender; it is the successor to the first species. The Soissons bean ranks first for eating dry or as a tender grain: it is the largest of all, the most tender, and cooks best: it is very heavy when rowed, but is prone to staining in rainy years. Care must be taken to pick the pods as they dry. Its flower is white; its pod very long, but not very full; its grain very flattened, of a white and a glaze superior to all the others: it is the latest species. It is as good in green as the others, when eaten young, but is always reserved for eating as a soft or dry bean. The small, round, white bean is the smallest of all the ordinary species, and the best, to many people's taste, to be eaten dry: it is tender, soft and cooked perfectly, even having something distinguished in the taste. It sails and loads prodigiously when paddled. Its blossom is white, its pod small, but well filled; its grain almost round in all directions, and of a slightly russet white. It is only used dry, and is very good value. The white Swiss bean is a species designed to be eaten green; it carries a lot of weight, even though it is dwarfed. Its flower is white, its pod very tender and long; its bean is medium-sized, rounded, russet-white and of very mediocre quality: it is quite early, so it is hardly used for anything other than green. Grey Swiss differs from the first only in the color of its grain, which is a blackish red with black inlays: it is dwarfed like white, and is intended for green use only. The red bean is of the same class, except that its color is a beautiful red, mottled with several colors that vary according to the terrain. The Prague bean, otherwise known as the Queen's bean, because, it is said, Her Majesty was the first to whom it was presented a few years ago, is a singular species grown only in a few private gardens, and which should be more widespread; its flower is purplish, and its pod extremely small, but very full. Its seeds have no definite shape; some are quartered and round, others pendulous, some smaller, others larger, but all smaller than the smallest peas: its color is isabella, speckled with cinnamon. It is not eaten green, nor as a tender grain, but dry: it has a fine, distinguished taste that makes it invaluable to its fans, especially when served in salads with oil and vinegar. It is sown and cultivated like the other species; it is neither more delicate to raise, nor later to bear fruit: it should only be noted that it must necessarily be rowed, if it is to be truly profitable; and in this arrangement it yields an incredible quantity of pods and grains, which compensates well for its smallness. The large confit bean from Holland, known in German as schewvert, which means saber, because it imitates the shape of a saber, is an extraordinary species for the volume of its pod, which is seven to eight inches long and a good inch wide. Its flower is white and fairly large, and its rounded grain is white and wormy, which is almost the only way it can be used. It is widely consumed in Holland and neighboring countries, but hardly known in France. The cardinal bean is a new species, whose country of origin I do not know. Its flower is white, its pod quite long, but not very full, and its bean flattened and very large; its color is white all around, and purple all around the germ: this is what distinguishes it the most, because it has nothing special about it, either for taste or produce; on the contrary, it has the defect of ripening very late and with great difficulty, which means that it yields little, and sometimes nothing at all. The runner bean is a singular species, cultivated more for its flower than for its fruit; this flower is similar to that of the others, but of a perfect fiery color, and it produces abundantly for three months, provided it is rowed: The flower is followed by the pod, which is very long, coarse green and rough under the finger; the grain it contains is twice the size of all the other species; its color is grayish-delicate, mottled black for the most part. It is not usually eaten; however, people are beginning to develop a taste for it, and having tasted it myself, I found it no different from the others; but it sins by color like the grey and Swiss bean. I mention the four species that follow only to give a few examples of my own. The Chinese bean spins like our own; it has a smaller leaf; its flower is flax-grey in some, and white in others: it emerges from the leaf axils in bunches of ten to twelve, arranged much like a wallflower sprig, and can form as many as twenty-five or thirty on each plant. Most of the flowers bear fruit, and there are usually eight or ten on each cluster, shaped like ordinary pods, but shorter, wider and more inverted, with the added difference that both sides are bristling with small saw-like teeth, and the skin is rough and rough. The mature bean is round and flattened like a lentil, but twice as big, and perfectly black, with a white border around half its circumference. It's because of this resemblance that we call it a Chinese pea; but the leaf, stem and pod are characteristic of the bean. It multiplies extraordinarily; I counted on a single pred that I had raised on a bed, up to two hundred and some pods: in the open ground it would not provide so much; but it always provides a lot, provided that it has been advanced on a bed, and replanted at the foot of some well exposed wall. I cooked a handful to see what it tasted like, and found it peculiar: perhaps it would appeal to connoisseurs; but I must confess that, although there's nothing wrong with it, it didn't flatter me. Perhaps in its natural country it has other qualities that we don't find here, or virtues that we don't know. The first species of Mississippi bean multiplies from seed like the others. It should be sown here early on a bed, and then replanted in a good exposure: The leaves are distributed partly to the right and partly to the left, diametrically opposed, an inch apart, set in a parrot-like echelon, and arranged in three equal parts like those of ordinary beans, but of a completely different shape, only about an inch long, forming a perfect oval, smooth and united at the edges. The fruit-bearing stalks arise from the leaf axils at the bottom of the plant, six or eight in number, and bear twelve to fifteen inches from their birth to the first siliques, which are gathered in the shape of an aigrette at the tip. The flowers are purplish, shaped much like all bean flowers, but so small that their shape is barely noticeable. The flowers are followed by siliques or pods which contain the seed; these siliques are finger-length, rounded and small, like small string: each contains fifteen to eighteen brown seeds, shaped much like the small round white bean, and no bigger than a grain of millet. From this detail, it will be seen that this grain is not suitable for use as food. In fact, only the green silique is used; small as it is, a large quantity is needed to make a dish: from which we must conclude that it apparently has a merit that we do not know. I thought at first that the plant was stronger in Mississippi than it is here; but I was assured that there was very little difference, and that it was an exquisite food for these inhabitants. As far as we are concerned, we can only consider this plant as a curiosity. The second species of Vississipi is completely opposite to the previous one; the stem is weak like that of ordinary beans, and also spins; the leaf is arranged in the same way, but it is larger, and the three parts that make it up are regularly oval, ending in a point: The succeeding pod is extraordinarily long and large, and contains several large, short, almost quartered, russet-white beans with a black germ. I don't know what the pod is; I've only seen it in the Jardin du Roi, where it has been brought recently: I can only assure you that if it were to become naturalized in our climate, it would be of great value; that's what we'll certainly know in a few years' time. The American bean is a spinning species like our own, but with a very slender stem and an extremely small leaf. The flower is proportionate, and the silique that follows it is only about an inch long, and contains only one or two almost round, coffee-colored seeds the size of a grain of hare's lead. From this description, I don't think anyone who grows beans for profit or propagation will be tempted to try this one. There are several other similar species of bean, which I will pass over in silence, as they are of interest only to the curious, as I have already remarked: so I feel I must end this article here. "CHAPTER XLIII. Description of the HYSOPE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. THERE are three species of hyssop; but, as they differ only in the color of the flower, and are perfectly similar in everything else, the description of one dispenses me from describing the others. Its root is thick, woody and hard; it sprouts several stems that rise to a foot or eighteen inches, hard, knotted, twiggy, topped, from the bottom to the top, with long, narrow leaves, a little larger than those of savory : its flowers are spike-shaped, but all turn to one side, and are white, blue or pink, depending on the species; The upper lip is raised, rounded and indented, while the lower is divided into three parts, the middle of which is spoon-shaped, indented and terminated by two points. Each flower is followed by four oblong, brown seeds, enclosed in a capsule that serves as the flower's calyx: these seeds are fragrant, sometimes approaching the smell of musk. This plant is of no use for life, but in gardens it is used to form borders around vegetable patches, where it spreads an aromatic and very pleasant scent, especially before it comes into flower. Its greatest properties are medical: it is incisive, aperitive, digestive, detersive, vulcerative and fortifying: it is mainly used for tartarous diseases of the lung. Its leaves and flowers are used in cephalic decoctions, and in the aromatic wine so frequently used by surgeons to dispel swollen wounds. Distillation yields a water and an essential oil with many properties. Its flowers are used to make a simple syrup, and another compound in which several other bechic and aperitive plants are used, and which is highly esteemed for chest illnesses, especially asthma and obstinate coughs. The minced leaf, mixed with fresh butter and applied externally, is good for bruises. Fresh or dried hyssop buds, soaked in mulled wine and placed in a knot and applied in fomentation to the eyes before going to bed, cure echymosis; and the same fomentation is sovereign for dissolving rumpled blood and resolving it when extravasated. Water or a decoction of the whole plant also cures eye inflammation. It is also used to make an excellent preserve for lung diseases. Finally, it is good for strengthening the brain, making the blood fluid, stimulating the months and urine, and removing obstructions. This plant can be propagated by seed and offspring, but more commonly by the latter, which is safer and easier. It is planted in borders around quarries in March and September, in the same way as lavender. The method for one is the same as for the other. It must be destroyed and renewed every two years, for cleanliness's sake, because when it stays in place longer, it creates a gap that is unpleasant to the eye. It should be placed as far as possible from the sun, in soil that is neither too oily nor too light. It requires no other special care. CHAPTER XLIV. Description of lettuce; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Lettuce is one of the most universal and common of garden plants. It can be found in all four parts of the world, and adapts easily to all climates and soils, provided the soil is well prepared, and the species chosen are suited to the vein of the soil. There are three main species, which vary considerably from one another, and form an infinite number of individual species. The first is that which only produces a large number of large, smooth, elongated leaves, without forming an apple. The second is that with a round leaf, which apples on its own and is called head lettuce. The third is a leaf that is curved and almost smooth, called chicon or romaine. These three species, with the exception of the leaves, which are round or curved, smooth or curly, and of different colors, grow their stems more or less equally; this stem, which rises to two or three feet, is firm, thick, cylindrical and branched: the branches are further divided into smaller ones, loaded with flowers, and spread out like sheaves. These flowers are composed of several yellowish half-florets, borne on embryos, and enclosed in a small, oblong, scaly calyx. These flowers are followed by the seed, which is oblong, flattened and pointed at both ends, white, black or yellow, depending on the species. This plant is so familiar and well-known that it needs no introduction. It is eaten raw in salads with oil, vinegar and salt; and provided it is eaten on its own without any supplies, it is very healthy, and can only upset extremely weak and cold stomachs: digestion, against general prejudice, is easy, and particularly so for those who drink little or no wine. Cooked, it is eaten in soup; it is also mixed with various vegetables, especially peas. It is refreshing and humectant: however, some doctors claim that it is not suitable for asthmatics. It is used almost as much in medicine as in food. A distilled water is extracted from its leaves, and is commonly used as a base for refreshing juleps and sleeping pills. Its leaves are also used internally in refreshing broths and enemas, to combat burning fevers and diseases that threaten internal parts with inflammation. Its seed, which is one of the four small minors, has much the same virtues, and is used in refreshing potions in a dose of two to three large doses. Externally, the leaf is applied to the forehead as a bandage, either alone or fricasseed with vinegar, chervil and purslane, and is very useful and effective against migraine. It is also claimed that frequent use of this plant, which is milky by nature, is very beneficial for nursing mothers to maintain and increase their milk. Its juice is used in all refreshing syrups, and is the main virtue of populeum, so sovereign for inflamed hemorrhoids. In addition to the three species of lettuce distinguished above, there are a few wild species commonly found in hedgerows, which have the same virtues as the cultivated species. Some authors even claim that, being milkier, they are more aperitive and more detersive; but they are not used for life, being hard and bitter; their leaves are usually long, narrow, sinuous, deeply cut on both sides, and armed with fairly rough thorns all along the coast; they flower and bear their seed, which is black, and quite similar to the seed of those grown in gardens. I'll now describe the three species in question. The first is of such little use for the table, and so mediocre, that it should rather be banished from gardens than cultivated: however, if, against my opinion, there are climates and land situations where it succeeds better than the others, as I have sometimes been persuaded, the only way to take advantage of it is to bind it like chicory; when it is in full strength, the heart whitens, but rots easily. The second species, head lettuce, is the most widely cultivated: it seems that nature has amused itself by varying it with perfectly distinct qualities, which have made it all the more varied in its names. The curious and the amateurs should be pleased that I have brought back twenty-five species, with the necessary details, by means of which they can obtain in all kinds of soils, and successively in all seasons, the enjoyment of a present that nature has been so kind as to make us so pleasant and so multiplied: I say in all kinds of soil, because there is no land where it cannot be cultivated; but at the same time, I make the observation that not all subdivisions of lettuce are suitable for all soils, that on the contrary, some are successful only in certain soils, and that it is only after testing one's own soil that one should stick to cultivating those that are the most successful. I therefore subdivide head lettuce into twenty-five varieties: petite Crêpe, grosse Crêpe, Bagnolet, George. l'Aubervilliers, la grosse Blonde, la Dauphine, la Perpignane, la Bapaume, la Batavia, la Laitue brune, la Sanguine, la Coquille, la Passion, la Gènes, la jeune Rouge, la grosse Rouge, l'Italie, la Royale, la Paresseuse, la Versailles, la Cocasse, la grosse Allemande, la Pomme de Berlin, et la longue Vissée. F 2 The third type of lettuce, known as chicon or romaine, is not much less cultivated than the previous one; it is not subject to the bitterness commonly found in head lettuces, which is why it is preferred to be eaten raw. I know twelve to fifteen species; however, only seven are generally known and cultivated, and are more or less equal in quality, the others being degenerate species of little merit, even the one with yellow seeds. These seven species are Romaine hâtive, Chicon vert, Gris, Blond, Rouge, Panaché and Alfange. I now return to head lettuces. I. Petite crêpe, otherwise known as petite noire, because its seed is black, is the smallest of all lettuces: it is yellowish-green, extremely curly and toothed; its head is small in proportion, especially when grown under a bell: it is very tender in this situation; but, to tell the truth, it has little taste, and its main merit is that it succeeds better than any other lettuce on a bed throughout the winter, a season whose harshness makes it find everything good. In the open ground, it is much better, and apples better; but it is only suited to spring: in the other seasons, it rises as soon as it apples; and, in strong soils, it even melts rather than peels: it therefore requires a soft, well-soiled soil, with a southern or eastern exposure, along some wall, or at the foot of some windbreak. It is the first species to give seed, but it gives little, and even that which it does give is very prone to clouding. There is a second, much larger species, whose seed is similarly black, but which does not grow under a bell jar, and which is hardly cultivated today. To grow it in all kinds of weather, intelligent gardeners, and particularly market gardeners, sow it from the end of August on small ados of potting soil with a southern exposure, and then transplant it to small, low beds where it bolts; this first sowing is eaten in December. They sow it on a bed, for the second time, around All Saints' Day; and the plant that comes from there, they replant it in place on another bed, when it is strong enough: it must have been transplanted beforehand: this one is eaten in January. The third seed is sown in December, and they continue to sow it every month until March, so that they always have some in succession; but this third seed requires much more care than the first. For this lettuce, as for all the others that are sown or transplanted, the first thing to do is to fill the bed with only four inches of potting soil: when it is ready to be sown, i.e. when the great fire has passed, the seed is sown under a bell, very clear, and very lightly covered with potting soil: many market gardeners are even content to beat it with their hand against the potting soil without covering it. The seed sprouts a few days later; and, when its two ears are well formed, and the first leaf begins to emerge from the heart, without waiting any longer, it is transplanted two by two, an inch apart, under other cloches. If the layer is still good, we transplant it on top; if not, we put it back on top of another one: sixty or eighty leaves enter under each bell. We leave it to fortify itself in this state until it has four or five leaves, and we take care to maintain its bed in a good warmth: I don't mean heat, because this plant does better with a moderate fire; and it's enough, so to speak, for it to find the bed warm when we sow it, and transplant it, or plant it in place; the two extremes of cold or heat melt it. We are also careful to keep the bells stuffed and covered with bedding, mainly during the nights, and to increase the blankets in proportion to the severity of the weather. When you have straw mats, it's even better to cover the whole layer over the bedding, not only to keep the heat in more securely, but also to more easily shake off any snow that may fall, and which, without this precaution, would mingle with the bedding, which would then have to be changed often, without preventing the cooling of the layer. From time to time, it is important to check that the plant is not overheated. This can be seen when you lift the bells and see hot steam coming out: you should then give them a little air for a few hours. When the weather is mild, or when the sun comes out during frosts, the bells should be lifted during the height of the day, and put back on as soon as the sun goes down. When it has finally reached four or five leaves, it is transplanted again under 4 cloches, on a new layer to remain there and to prune; and this last layer must be loaded with six inches of compost, so that the root does not touch the manure: we put twelve or fifteen, which we then reduce to four or five at most, as soon as they begin to be pressed. Those that are removed are also replanted in fours, under other cloches. Care must be taken not to use new cloches for transplanting at any time; they must have been used for other plants for two weeks, or exposed to the sun for a similar length of time along a wall, to allow them to dry out: experience shows that without this, the plants they cover melt and perish. The same care and heating should then be continued, according to the greater or lesser need, and care should be taken to give the bells a little air from time to time during the best hours of the day, whether the sun is shining or not; because without air, the plant withers and doesn't grow: It's enough to raise the bell by one finger, on the south side, if there's no wind, and you support it in this state with a bit of rolled straw; but if the wind is too strong, whatever it may be, you must always give the air on the opposite side. As they fill the bells, you need to raise them higher with forks, depending on the weather, and then cut them when you've reached the point where you want them. When the apple starts to peel, remove all the low yellowing leaves and press the soil against the base; the apple will be bigger and more beautiful. You must also change the forks every 3 or 4 days, in other words, give air in turn to the four sides of the bell, so that they all benefit equally; otherwise, the one that enjoys the benefit of air to the exclusion of the others, will strengthen itself at their expense, and do them a great deal of harm: try, however, to match this with the wind. II. The large crepe differs from the small one only in size, which is almost twice as large: it also has the same qualities, shape and color. Its main merit is that it is extremely soft and tender; it also requires the same quality of soil and the same exposure. It can be sown and brought forward to be enjoyed in the spring, which is its season: it can even be planted for peeling, but it does not tolerate the bell. It should be left in the open air as soon as it has been replanted, either on a bed or on the ground. Its 5 seeds are white and ripen early: it yields very little. There is another type of crêpe that market gardeners call "la ronde": it is very lightly curled, and comes a little larger than the others; but I don't know if it's the same one I'll talk about below, known more generally as "Bagnolet" or "petite-courte". The seed of both species of crepe is the one taken in preference to any other to make lettuce for cutting, otherwise known as nasturtium, as it is blonder. The way to sow it is to make small rays two inches wide by one inch deep. Others sow it broadcast, or in the field, to use the gardener's term, under cloches, and beat the soil well with the hand without burying it. Twelve to fifteen days after sowing, it can be cut; but to nourish it better, and give it more taste, it should be sown fairly lightly, and left to enjoy until it has two good leaves, in addition to its ears; it takes longer to come, but it gives more profit and pleasure. We sow a little every two weeks from the end of September: this way, we can have them for as long as we want, but we're not so keen on them as soon as the head lettuces start giving. The same care and precautions as I explained above should be observed for those intended for head lettuce. III. The Bagnolet, which others call the petite courte, the printanière, or the dégrebé, grows like the petite crêpe, but beats it in that it is earlier, and the head is larger, yellower and firmer; it also has the advantage of peeling under a bell without needing air, which is a merit. Its leaf is blond and smooth, much less curly than the crêpe, and less prone to melting. Market gardeners don't grow it as much; I don't know why, because it's better in every way; and I'm devoted to it in my own right, for winter and spring, to the exclusion of all others. It succeeds equally well on land and on beds; but it climbs easily as soon as the heat begins. Its seed is white; and for this reason, as much as for its resemblance to the crepe, some call it the white crepe, or the round crepe, as I said in the previous article. Only four should be placed under each bell, and it is 0 a species that everyone should be eager to have: it seeds little, given its smallness, and is very prone to clouding; more should be reserved than less. IV. There are two types of George, one called grosse George, the other white George. The first is grown on a bed, and the apple under a bell like the previous ones, where it succeeds perfectly, provided it is in the air and amply moistened: three are enough under each bell; and if you want to put four, you must space the bells four inches apart. Its leaf is blond and fairly smooth, and its apple tight: it is soft and tender, and can be considered an excellent lettuce, which in its time provides abundantly for all needs. The best time to plant it is at the beginning of April; take care to give it the right amount of air, and cut it as soon as the head is formed, as it rises almost immediately. The seed is white, yields many and ripens from the first. The second type can be sown either on the ground or on the bed; but it only apples on the ground, and particularly at the foot of walls: it comes very large and well-headed, sweet and tender. Its leaves are blond, brittle and not very curly: it requires light, well-soiled soil. It is the first to come on the ground when it has been a little advanced on the bed: it must also be cut as soon as it is heady, having the same defect of rising quickly. Its seed is white, abundant, and mú̂rit of the first. The majority of market gardeners choose it in preference to all the others, to make lettuce for cutting, both because it supplies abundantly, and because its leaf at birth is blonder and wider than the others. V. Aubervilliers is a small spring lettuce that also does well in summer, but its small size has disgraced it from most gardens. Its outer leaves are smooth and coarse green, its head very yellow and very tender: it hardly melts, and can be kept for quite a long time on the head; these advantages would deserve it a happier fate. The seed is white, yields little and ripens early. VI. The grosse blonde is aptly named, being large and very blond: it is tender and sweet, and apples perfectly; but it rises almost as soon as it is plucked, especially in summer: it is in spring and autumn that it is most successful. The seed is white, yields a lot and usually ripens well. VII. The dauphine is a spring lettuce, which is only good in this first season: it is very early and very large, with a flat shape; its head is quite tight: it is sweet and tender, and may be considered one of the best lettuces. It grows well in any kind of soil, provided it is moistened often and generously; it grows a lot of suckers around its first leaves, which must be carefully removed. Its seed is black, yields a lot and ripens early. VIII. Perpignan comes in two varieties: one green, the other speckled, i.e. with yellow spots. The green variety has plain, smooth leaves with a large rib; its apple is very large and very yellow, quite tender; without any bitterness: it holds up well in dry soils, and resists heat: it also climbs only with difficulty; but in damp soils, it rots easily; it must therefore be given its proper soil. Its seed is white: it supplies a lot of seed, but it needs to be sown early for the seed to ripen. The second differs from the other only in its external color, and in its ribs, which are a little smaller; in addition, its qualities are the same, and its seed is also white: it yields a fair amount. IX. Bapaume is a large, very blond lettuce, which stands up very well: it can be grown in all seasons and in all types of soil; this is its main merit. Its head is not tight at the top, but is very full at the bottom, which deceives those who look at it without knowing it. Its seed is black and yields very little. X. Batavia is a species totally different from all the others, both in volume, configuration and size: it is the size of a small cabbage. Its leaves are extremely curly and folded, light green in color, with a hint of red sown around the edges; its head is a little concave, whitening only imperfectly, yet tender and delicate, and at the same time so brittle that it hardly suffers transport. In strong soils, it has a slight bitterness, which is its only defect; but, despite this, it is highly esteemed by people of taste, and preferred to many others, especially as it takes seasoning better than any other. It does not do equally well everywhere: those who find themselves on its own ground can congratulate themselves. It needs to be watered frequently and generously, but only in the morning or evening, as midday watering will cause it to speckle and rot, and it is very sensitive to cool temperatures. After August, therefore, it is no longer to be relied upon, and this must be taken into account when planting it. The seed is white, yields a fair amount and ripens fairly early. XI. Brown lettuce, otherwise known as Dutch lettuce, is a fairly good lettuce that apples very well, and holds up better than many others in droughts; it is of a nice size; its outer leaves are dull green, very smooth, and very plain at the edges; its heart is yellow and full: if it were more tender and delicate, we would have nothing to reproach it with. It's always a good idea to have some in summer, as it doesn't melt and doesn't go up as easily as most of the others: it's at least excellent for cooking, when you find it too hard to eat raw. Its seed is black, and it yields a lot; but it ripens a little late, and in tender years it rots rather than ripens. XII. Sanguine is a medium-sized lettuce, covered with red veins like variegated chicory, and very pleasing to the eye. It apples fairly well in spring, but only in that season; in other seasons, it rises rather than peels. It requires soft soil. Its seed is black: it yields enough, and ripens quickly, XIII. The shell has a leaf that is more green than yellow, round, fairly smooth and fairly large: it is usually hard and bitter, and is good only for soups. Its merit is that it withstands winters better than any other, and is therefore the first on earth to turn pomaceous. When there has been no bedding to raise other species, the seed is sown in mid-August; the plant is strong enough by October to be replanted, and is then planted on the south or east coasts, in two, three or four rows, depending on the width of the beds. During heavy frosts, it is covered with well-shaken bedding, or playon of varying thickness, depending on the severity of the weather: it is carefully removed when the thaws arrive. Cocasse, Italie and chicory, which also survive the winter, can be covered in the same way, provided they are neither too long nor too tough. If you haven't grown crepe and George on a bed during the winter, you can put it on a bed at the end of February, to get it earlier. It is only good on the ground in mid-May, a little earlier or a little later, depending on the year and the soil. The seed is white; but there is another species whose seed is black, and which is valued more highly. However, having examined them both closely, I found little or no difference between them; both grow well and set seed very early. XIV. Passion is a species much like the previous one. Its leaf is green and blistered, of medium size, which also spends the winter; and this is all its merit, being otherwise hard and bitter. In spring, it is used for soups and refreshing broths: it is very useful for those who live in cold, snowy countries; it withstands the rigors of winter better than any other. Its seed is white: it yields a fair amount. XV. Genes come in three varieties, distinguished as blonde, green and red. The first has blond, fairly smooth leaves. Its apple is a little pointed and very white, without bitterness: it is good in spring and autumn; in summer it is cloudy. Its seed is white: it yields a lot, which ripens fairly early. The second has green, curly leaves; its apple is hard and yellow, larger than the first: it does not leaf out. Its season is spring and autumn, and in dry years: it also does well in summer. It should be watered only when badly needed, but needs to be crimped often. Its seed is white: it is very prone to clouding. Reserve more rather than less. The third has curly red leaves and a tender yellow heart. It survives the winter, but should be placed at the foot of the sunset walls, as the sun is against it at this time of year. It should be planted in spring and autumn; it does not do well in summer. Its seed is black and takes a long time to ripen. Medium-sized, it apples very well: soft, tender and very yellow at the core; its outer leaves are soft green, whipped with red, round and almost plain. Its favorite season is spring and autumn; in summer it nuils and melts easily: it requires soft soil. The seed is black, and often fails to ripen, being very late: it must be planted early on the bed, to be sure of harvesting it. XVII. The grosse rouge has all the good qualities of the preceding variety, and surpasses it in size, which is at least twice as large: it also has the advantage of remaining well-appointed for as long and more than any other, and of succeeding in all seasons, when the soil is suitable. It requires a rich soil; in the sands, it comes up thin and hard. It has the added merit of never wilting, at least in fatty soils such as mine: these advantages make me consider it a first-rate lettuce, a must-have in any well-stocked kitchen garden. Its outer leaves are round, almost plain, black-green, shaded with a large, dull red. The head is as yellow as an orange; the seed is black, ripens fairly easily, and yields a lot. XVIII. Italian lettuce has long been the most cultivated of all lettuces, having the advantage of succeeding in all seasons, and of lasting quite a long time on the head: market gardeners have abandoned it in favor of cocasse, which lasts even longer, but is not as good in all other respects. Its leaves are fine and tender green, edged with red; its head is tight and perfectly tasty: its only fault is that it speckles a little in summer; it requires light, lean soil and little water. Its seed is black and ripens well, but it does not yield much. XIX. Royale is one of the best lettuces for summer, provided it is moistened abundantly: it has a good size, apples well, and lasts a long time: it is quite soft and quite tender; its outer leaves are a beautiful green, a little blistered and shiny. It's a pity that it's a little prone to shading and melting; otherwise, it's perfect and of good quality. The seed is white and provides a fair amount of yield, but ripens with difficulty in tender years. It's a good idea to bring forward what you intend to sow. XX. Before the Cocasse and the Versailles were known, the lazy variety was the most cultivated for summer; it really does not climb as much as any other, and is more resistant to drought; but it is always a little hard and bitter. The best way to eat it is cooked. Its apple is very hard and quite large; its outer leaves are a coarse green, very blotchy, and packed one on top of the other. Its seed is white: it yields a lot, but it needs to be brought forward a little for it to ripen more surely. XXI. For the past ten years, cocasse has been the favorite lettuce of all gardeners, and especially of market gardeners, who almost exclusively grow cocasse throughout the summer. This preference is due to its excellent eating qualities, and to the fact that it can be kept on the vine for a very long time, despite heat and drought. Its outer leaves are a large, shiny green, heavily blistered: it is very large. Sown in August and transplanted at All Saints' Day, it survives the winter. These are the advantages that have made it so popular; but it is prone, in many soils, to rot between two hearts, or to spotting, especially in rainy weather. It requires a soil that is neither too light nor too strong; or, if it is light as in some of our marshes, it must be helped with a lot of manure and compost, and watered amply, in which case it succeeds perfectly well. These types of soil are particularly suitable for summer; in strong soils, it only grows leaves and does not close: in this season, it should still be sunk a little when replanting, as the apple forms better. In addition to the above-mentioned defect, it is also hard and a little bitter, and its exterior is not very attractive; In view of these faults, which greatly outweigh its good qualities, I am obliged to say that it deserves the preference it is given, only insofar as the land does not allow others to be raised during the summer, in which case it is better to have it as it is than to have none at all; and market gardeners in particular, who have a great interest in making the most of their plants, are right to be attached to them. To collect the seed, it must be raised on a bed; if the winter seed has perished, replant it on a hillside, and help it to rise by making a cross-shaped incision on the apple, without which the heart often rots because it cannot emerge. Its seed is white, and yields a lot when the season is favorable, but sometimes it doesn't ripen. which many people confuse with the cocasse, and which I had judged at first myself to be one and the same species, under two different names, better examined is certainly a different species. The leaf of the latter is a lighter green, without any freckles, like those of the cocasse; it is also less curly, and has a flatter head; its leaves are less crowded together, and it is less prone to rust. I have often compared them together, so as to be able to argue, against all opposing opinions, that they are two very different species, and that they are similar only in that they are almost equally successful in heat, and that their apples are equally supportive; nevertheless, I place this one above the other, especially as it is not so hard, nor so bitter. It may be, as some claim, that this one was formed from the other; but the origin makes no difference to the present state of this plant. Its seed is white, ripens late and yields more or less, depending on the year: it requires the same precautions as cocasse when harvested. Many market gardeners use this species to make lettuce for cutting, because it is more resistant to frost. XXIII. grosse Allemande, known in Holland and Germany as Impériale, is a lettuce which, although very old, was either lost in France, or never became well established: it is still only known to a small number of people; but its great qualities will soon spread it to all gardens: it can be called the queen of lettuces. There are no good qualities that it does not have, and I know of only slight defects. It is monstrously large, with the same volume as Batavia. Its outer leaves are extraordinarily large and smooth, ending a little pointed when young; its color is a pale, dull green; its apple is very tight, yellow and tender; its taste is sweet when the soil suits it. It can be kept for as long on the head as the cocasse, and does not spit in the same way: it comes in well in all seasons, except for its size, which is not the same in summer as in spring; but I have noticed that in our light soils, such as our marshes in the Faubourg Saint-Germain, it is prone to melting in the warmer months, especially when wet too often; this is one of its faults: another is that in certain areas, it is a little bitter, but this does not prevent it from being eaten with pleasure. It is prone to growing suckers between its lower leaves, which must be carefully removed, as they are harmful to the heart. It must be raised early on the bed so that it can set seed, because, in addition to being difficult to raise, it takes a long time to set apple: it must be planted at a distance of about fifteen inches in all directions. G ron apart in all directions, and whenever it is in good condition, it is tightly packed. This detail will show that it is worthy of preference over all the others; and I have no doubt that, once our market gardeners are familiar with it, they will substitute it for cocasse, if they can prevent it from melting through cultivation. It is advisable not to replant after July, as the apple does not have time to form after this time, being very late, as I have already observed: it has a white seed, and yields a lot when the year is dry. XXIV. The Berlin apple still surpasses the previous one in size, but differs in many respects. I have only had it for a year; the man who gave it to me, a Hanoverian, spoke unfavorably of it, and only announced it to me as a plant remarkable for its size, and in no way superior to the others in quality. But either this foreigner didn't know it, or our climate suits it better than Germany's, I conceived a very different idea of it after the trial: it came to me with all the qualities of a perfect lettuce, sweet, tender, fine, brittle. Its heart whitens very well; its color is a tender green, slightly tinted on the edges with a few red shades. It apples fairly quickly: it succeeds in both spring and autumn seasons, and a single plant is enough to make a reasonable salad. It should be planted eighteen or twenty inches apart in all directions: it apples fairly quickly, but its apple is not perfectly tight, and does not hold together for long. Its seed is black, abundant and ripens early. XXV. La longue vissée is a new lettuce that was sent to me from Italy last year, and which I have not seen anywhere else: it is singular in its shape, which is elongated like a sugar loaf, and ends in a point, with indentations and elevations that turn from bottom to top, and have the same effect as a press screw, which gives it its Italian name that I have francized. The outer leaf is yellowish-green, brittle and curly, much like Batavia: it is soft and tender; all in all, it's a very good species, regardless of its singularity. I wasn't able to test it in all seasons, as I didn't have enough seed. Its seed is black, ripens fairly well, but yields little. Some soils may be suitable for the twenty-five species of G 2 lettuce I have just mentioned; but at least there is no soil that is not suitable for some of them. So everyone, after having tried them all, if he sees fit, will stick to those that will be most successful for him. I don't approve of stubbornly bringing in those for which the stock is not suitable: as the multiplicity of species is only a matter of curiosity, we should be happy when we are provided with a few good ones, which, succeeding one another, can supply our needs throughout the year. I had heard of two new species, one called spinach lettuce, the other long apple. The first is unusual for its leaf, which resembles that of spinach; but it hardly makes an apple, and has no qualities to recommend it. The second makes, like chicory, a very elongated apple: it is always hollow and not very tender. Among the others that I have not mentioned, there may be some that do well in other climates; everyone will do well to keep the species they are happy with. I'll move on to chicory: the first is early romaine, which has the advantage of peeling, or, to put it more accurately, coëffer under a bell; it gives great pleasure in novelty, although it remains a little thin under the bell: its shape is quite similar to blond chicory: its outer color is a little less light, and its leaves more pointed, yet it is hard to tell them apart when they are both raised in the ground, both being cambered and of roughly equal size. They should be sown in beds as early as October, so that they can be enjoyed in April; the method used by some gardeners is to place one foot between four pancakes on their beds. These pancakes, which come much earlier, are removed, leaving the romaine the master of the place; but I find a drawback in this, which is that they occupy the bed for too long: it's better to set it aside, and put only three lettuces, so that they are comfortable, under each bell, which must then be raised on three forks, when the heads of the plants begin to touch the top: its seed is white, abundant, and ripens well. II. The green chicon, of the seven we know, is the most widely cultivated, for the reason that it is the largest and the least delicate in relation to the weather, and that it succeeds well in all seasons. It also has the advantage of being self-sealing; or3 at most, a tie at the end is enough. Its leaf is long, rounded at the tip, rough and a little blistered; its rib is blanshe, and its color a coarse green. The good species must be flattened at the top, which market gardeners call camus; when it ends in a point, it's a sign that it's degenerate: consequently, only those with a flattened shape should be marked for seed. It spends the winter being sown in August and replanted on a coast in October: it is the most profitable crop for those who raise it for sale; but to be eaten raw, it is the least tender and the least delicate of all. When replanting in the open ground, after having overwintered in layers or ados of potting soil, make sure to bury it a little when planting, and butter it: it yields a lot of seed, which is black. III. Gray chicon is not very different from the previous one; its color is a darker green; it has the advantage of being milder and more spring-like, but it also melts easily during the summer, and should only be used for spring. It overwinters well and adapts well to all types of soil: its seed is white and very abundant, but ripens a little late. IV. Blond is much more delicate to eat than the previous varieties: it makes "an equally large, flat and full apple, but melts more easily. It also rises very quickly. Its leaf is yellowish-green, a little pointed at the tip, with a white rib; it is less thick and less blistered than that of the other two varieties. It thrives best in soil that is somewhere between light and heavy, but its success also depends on the season: in tender years, it thrives best in light soil; in dry years, it thrives best in heavy soil. Its seed is white, but it yields less than the green variety, so you need to keep more of it than of other species. V. Red bears this name with justice, its outer leaves being truly red, but its heart is a perfect yellow and tender: its defect is that it is very prone to melting as soon as it is bound, and there are few soils where it succeeds well; strong soil is the one that suits it best, especially in dry years. When absolutely necessary, water should be poured from the mouths of watering cans right up to the ground, so that the plant does not get wet, and it should be cut as soon as its heart is white: this shows that only a very few G.4 should be grown at a time. It has the advantage of being sown very lightly in the months of July and August, along walls facing east and south, and then thinned out to a suitable distance, so that it can be kept until the big frosts, and whitens without needing to be tied. Its seed is black, and it yields a lot. VI. The variegated variety, which others call flagellt or Silesian lettuce, so named because its leaves are whipped with red veins similar to certain yellow tulips, is preferred by connoisseurs over all others, because it is both pleasing to the eye and to the taste: it is sweet and tender, and combines all the good qualities one could wish for. There are two species, one much more prone to melting than the other: the latter, which comes from England, has its outer leaves less variegated than the other; but those in the heart are more so, and it coëffices almost by itself like green chicory. In some soils, both are subject to melting as they whiten. Spring is its season, because in summer it melts and rises, and in autumn it rots. The seed of the first species is black, and that of the second is white: both yield poorly. The variegated variety ripens between the first and last lettuces. VII. Alfangium is a particular species, which is similar to the others in shape only; its leaves are pointed, snake-like, thin and smooth; the color is pale green, with a few red shades at the top. It is very tender and delicate: but it has the double defect of rotting and climbing easily; however, it succeeds very well in some soils, and it is advisable to test it before rejecting it: its seed is white, abundant, and ripens fairly early. All these species need to be bound to whiten. Depending on their strength, one or two straw or rush ties are placed on the bottom of the plant, not too tightly, and a few days later, a third tie is placed on the top, which is tightened even more: Bind them on a fine day, and wait until there is no more dew or humidity, taking care to bind only as much as you need, as they will soon rot after they are white, or go to seed; from eight to eight days, bind as much as you can use. The two types of chicory, red and variegated, which I have just mentioned, do not appear in public markets, nor does alfange: Their natural tendency to melt, as I have shown, is one of the reasons why our market gardeners do not grow them; to which must be added the difficulty they would have in selling them to fruit growers, who would be afraid to take them on, because they cannot endure, like the others, being closed for several days at a time in cellars while waiting for the buyer. The public loses out, because they are incomparably better; and all those who have gardens should endeavor to grow some for themselves in preference to any other, if the land suits them. You won't get much profit out of it, but you'll be compensated by taste. With regard to all chicories, I must point out that when they go to seed, we still make useful use of the stalk, which we call côton; we eat it cooked in white sauce, and it's a pretty good meal; we also pickle it in vinegar, and it's used in winter salads. It now remains for me to tell you what you need to do to grow all the different types of lettuce and chicory I've just mentioned, early in the season. You enjoy them late when you wait to sow them in spring, as is the custom in the provinces, and with most of the middle-class gardeners around here. The practice of our market gardeners is to sow their seeds under a bell as early as September or October, on ados of potting soil exposed to the south. Three weeks later, they transplant them onto other teens, as I explained for pancakes, and give the cloches a little air every day, as weather permits. They leave them to fortify themselves in this state until February, taking care to cover their bells exactly with litter during frosts, and to uncover them at daybreak: they are then strong enough to be replanted in place, if the season is right. For this, a good exposure is chosen; but beforehand, the plant must be accustomed to the open air, by gradually weaning it from the cloches, as the weather permits: for they would melt if they were put in the open ground as soon as they came out of the cloche. Some market gardeners sow them later, and raise them on a bed; but, in addition to saving manure by the above method, it is constant that the plant resists better in the open ground, when it has been raised without so much artifice. In the latter case, care should be taken to wean the plant from the meme des cloches eight or ten days before replanting. In the provinces, where C6́ one hardly knows the compost neither the layers, one can prepare light grounds mixed with horse dung, or manure of rotten sheets, which form a true compost, very good with this use as with several others. Ados can be formed from them, as I have explained; and if you don't have blown bells, you can have assembly pieces, such as those I have described in the chapter on layers. When replanting these lettuces in February or March in the open ground, if it's sunny or sunny, they should be lightly watered the next day at high noon. I have nothing to add to the description I have given of the various lettuces I have chosen and indicated as the best; now we come to the cultivation they require. First, choose the softest, smokiest soil you can find in your garden. When the beds are erected, and earthworked if possible, they are marked out to form five rows in each five-foot-wide bed, seven to eight inches apart; they are marked out very lightly with a chalk line and a pointed stick, so that they can simply be planted in a straight line: for this plant must not be buried; its heart must be flush with the surface of the soil, which must be pressed only slightly against its root with the planter. Water them as soon as they are planted, and continue watering them as the weather requires, observing during the first few days that they should only be watered in the morning, after the cool of the night has straightened out their wilted leaves from the previous day, otherwise the water will mix with the soil, suffocating their heart and delaying their growth. A distinction needs to be made for Batavia, grosse Allemande and Pomme de Berlin; it's to space them at the distance I've set in their article. After they have been well taken up, they are given a little way with the serfouette, and as many times as the soil needs to be weeded, they are serfouised; you must be exact until they are at the point of being eaten. When a lot of rain has fallen, causing them to rust and rot, if the weather is fine afterwards, they should be left to fast on water for several days at a time, so that the sun can revive and restore them. Beetle worms, and another gray worm, often make war on them by cutting their roots; care must be taken, as I said with chicory, to look for them at the foot of those you see wilted. In wet soils, limas, snails and, above all, loaches, destroy them as soon as they are born, to the point where it is sometimes impossible to keep a plant over winter, or to replant it in spring before the end of April. The latter insect devours as many as can be planted: it must then be sought with great patience at the foot of each lettuce that is seen to be gnawed, when the damage is perceptible; for there are some so small that sight can only distinguish them with great difficulty. But, as this operation costs more than it's worth, the shortest way, when you're reduced to this, is to stick to growing lettuce on a bed during these two seasons, and to wait for the onset of heat before replanting in the open ground. Care should be taken to remove as useless those that are beginning to grow; the others have more air and are more profitable. Lettuce that comes up without being replanted is usually more beautiful than that which is replanted, and is more successful as a seed. As it is customary in spring to sow the seed in beds or ribs, from which it is removed to be put back elsewhere, it is only necessary to leave a few for seed, suitably spaced. Don't forget to sow a little seed every two weeks, so you'll always have good seedlings to replant. For plants that are sown or replanted in March and April, and which sometimes need watering because of the fairly ordinary sunshine in these two months, they should only be wet in the morning or at midday. If they are wet in the evening, and there is a slight frost the next morning, they will perish, or if there is no frost, the moisture will attract loaches and limas of all kinds, which will destroy them. There are many soils where the seed, when the great heat begins, heats up in the ground and does not germinate; care must be taken to wet it every day to make it germinate; and when experience shows that this expedient is not sufficient, as is usual in dry and scorching soils, as soon as the seed has been sown and harrowed, the place must be covered with some straw mat, or large straw spread promptly, and wet over it: a few days later, when the seed begins to sprout, remove this cover at sunset, so that the night air hardens it a little. The seed of this plant is harvested in August and September, from plants that have spent the winter, as in spring. Care should be taken to mark the most beautiful apples for seed, and to prick a few sticks at the base to tie up the mounts when they begin to tire of the winds. At the same time

clean plants of all useless leaves which retain sap in the stem, and which then rot, sometimes communicating their rottenness to the stem, especially in rainy seasons: large lettuces are particularly in need of this attention. At flowering time, a small white worm is often formed in the bud as a result of some nuile: an ailment for which there is no remedy; you must therefore keep more than less at different exposures: some sometimes perish, and others escape. But the best precaution is to always have a supply from two previous years; and, if you don't have any, you can resort to another precaution, which is to reserve some for seed from two plantations, i.e., that they be planted a month apart from each other, because since these kinds of nuiles are only ruinous at flowering time, some may not yet have reached or passed this critical moment, if the others are caught. To be picked, when most of the buds are crowned with their aigrettes, and the plant is wilting and yellowing; it is then necessary to cut or uproot the plant, which is exposed upright to the sun for a few days, and as much as possible: it is then beaten, winnowed, and dryly closed by labeling. The German method is better than ours in this respect. After the plants have been exposed to the sun for two days, we take each one separately, and beat them lightly on the side of a broken barrel, at the bottom of which the seed falls as it falls: only the best detaches itself, the other, which is neither dry nor ripe, remains in its pod: we expose it again to the sun to ripen. But this second quality of seed is not nearly as good as the first, so it is only used to make lettuce for cutting: the first makes the plant much stronger and more straightforward. This is a very good practice to follow. This seed keeps well for three years; in the fourth, some of it still comes up, when it has been well-aged; but the safest thing is not to count on it. It is a little prone to bolting when sown in the same year as it is harvested; it is better not to sow it until the second year. When you're in a hurry to get it to rise, put it in a small canvas bag, and soak it in water for twenty-four hours: then tie it to the side of your chimney, or put it in a pile of very hot manure, so that it heats up for two or three days, until you see that it has sprouted; then sow it either on the ground or on the bed: however, this is only a good practice for those you want to sow on the ground; otherwise, on a bed, it always sprouts fairly quickly. It should be noted, moreover, that germs largely perish when handled and sown. CHAPTER XLV. Description of LAVENDER; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. This plant is aromatic. There are eight species: male lavender, female lavender, English lavender, large-leaf lavender, Spanish lavender, Indian lavender, and two species of annual lavender. The male lavender, like the aspic, has a woody root, furnished with several fibers, and grows woody sprays from a foot or eighteen inches to two feet high, furnished with several knotty branches. Its leaves are green, placed in twos, and arranged in saltire, with a strong, pleasant odor and bitter flavor. Its branches all end in spikes, preceded by a long tail, garnished throughout with small bunches of one-piece blue flowers, whose upper lip is upright, rounded, cut into two parts, and the lower divided into three: they are borne on a narrow, oblong calyx, from which a pistil emerges, attached like a nail between four embryos, which change into as many seeds enclosed in a small, oblong, blackish, shiny capsule. The female lavender is similar to the previous one in root, stem and spike arrangement; but its leaf is smaller, narrower and whiter, and its tuft much higher; the odor is also less strong: the flower is of the same shape and color, but larger: the seed is round, small and brown. English lavender is shaped like the preceding varieties, but is not so bushy: its leaves are also thinner and whiter; the flower is white, and its scent sweeter. Large-leaf lavender grows as a shrub and throws out many branches: its leaves are smooth, long and pointed, not very wide, a beautiful green, flowering little or not at all, and with a scent more or less similar to the preceding ones. Spanish lavender, otherwise known as Stæchas by botanists, has extremely fine, dissected leaves of an incipient green, forming a small shrub that grows to twelve or fifteen inches. Its flowers are blue, arranged in spikes like the preceding ones, with a sweeter and slightly different scent. Indian lavender has an oblong, fairly large, thick, dark green leaf, with a scent quite similar to that of the first two species; it grows into a shrub and throws out many branches; its spikes are shorter, its flowers smaller and its color paler. Annual lavender comes in two varieties: one has a dissected, meadow-green leaf, forming a small shrub fifteen to eighteen inches high; its flower is blue, arranged in spikes like the previous two; but it is not nearly as fragrant: its seed is small and rounded, a little elongated, brown in color, tending to cinnamon. The second species grows from meadow to shrub, but its leaves are more regularly cut; it flowers in the same way, and has little odor; its seed is extremely small, longer than round, and its brown color a little reddish. The first three species are used indifferently, and have more or less the same virtues; however, in this climate, only the second is used; the others are more curious than useful. It grows naturally in Provence and part of Languedoc, and in such abundance that it is used to heat ovens, as is the case with rosemary and sage. It has more virtues in its natural climate than it has here, but it has enough everywhere to make it recommendable. Lavender leaf and flower are used interchangeably, although it is agreed that there are more virtues in the flower together with the spike than in the leaf alone. It is even claimed that lavender water, which is nothing other than the flower separated from the spike, and distilled with brandy, or simplemeat infused in a bottle of water exposed to the sun, produces even more sensitive effects: it is sovereign in wounds, in strains, and in all kinds of pain; we rub it repeatedly on the sick part, then leave a cloth or fog paper soaked in it: we mix it in all cephalic and nervous decoctions. But lavender water is not always used in accidents and unpleasant encounters; it is also used to awaken and revive the senses: we rub it on our heads after shaving, and it prevents the freshness from penetrating through the pores: it is used in cleanliness baths for both sexes; and it is as pleasant to the senses as it is useful to the body, from which it removes bad exhalations when we are subject to them. An essential oil is extracted from the whole plant, and is highly prized for diseases of the brain, hysterical vapors and epilepsy; the dose is eight or ten drops taken in a suitable liqueur. It can also be sprinkled on the volatile urine salts so often used by people prone to vapors. Four or five drops of the same oil, taken on an empty stomach, dissipate migraines and fortify the stomach. Mixed with St John's wort and chamomile oil, it makes an excellent liniment for rheumatism, paralysis and other convulsive movements. Lavender oil, also known as aspic oil, is infused into olive oil, and is equally suitable for the arts and medicine. It is used in the composition of the beautiful varnishes used on all precious paintings, and kills worms, bugs and other vermin that attach themselves to the human body. The spikes, loaded with their flowers and dried properly, are excellent, taken as an infusion like tea, for dizziness, trembling hands, convulsive movements, soporous affections, paralysis, asthma, stammering and other diseases of the nerves. Its freshly cut ears are used to make bundles to ward off bad odors; they are put in places where the air is foul, and among linen to give it a good smell. We use the flower in particular, which we detach from the spikes, to make scent sachets; and for this, after we have drawn the quantity of flowers we need, we mix in a handful of cloves and as much fine pepper, more or less, depending on whether we want the scent of lavender or spices to dominate in the sachet: the whole is put in paper bags, the opening of which is closed with glue, to. These bags are then covered with a silk cloth, which envelops them tightly. This scent mixture is far superior, according to the tests we've made of it, to all the perfume jars, which are common in many homes. I don't want to omit an important observation made by several authors on the use of lavender water or oil; it is that as much as it is sovereign when the weakness of the parts comes from cold weather or cold humors, it is just as pernicious when there is heat, because then it increases the illness by affecting the head. The first six species of lavender, which are perennials, can be multiplied by seed, cuttings or rooted plants: the first method is hardly ever used; it is easier to replant them fully formed, especially the second species, which is common in all gardens. I'll speak separately of the others, which require special care: for this one, by which I mean the female, we separate the old plants into several parts, which provide more, and which suddenly form their border. This is usually done in spring or autumn; it grows again easily without any particular care, and any soil is more or less equal to it; it resists all weathers, and stays in the same place for two or three years; but then it must be renewed, otherwise it will spread too far. Its spikes are cut when in full flower, for the use for which they are intended; they are left to dry, if seed is to be obtained, and are harvested in August or September. The first species, by which I mean male lavender, is rarely cultivated in this climate, even though it is no more delicate than the female; the reason, as far as I can judge, is that it supplies less than the other. English lavender is no more so, because it also yields little, and being very delicate, it is prone to perish in winter in the open ground: those who want to keep it safely must put it in pots and lock it up in the greenhouse. Large-leaf lavender is little known; it would, however, seem to have the same virtues, with the same odor and flavor; but, as it necessarily requires to be locked up in the greenhouse, Tome II. H this difficulty, no doubt, will always prevent it from being commonly cultivated. Spanish lavender is in the same class, and serves little purpose other than to satisfy the curiosity of the general public. The two annual species are useless, having far fewer virtues than the others. They are sown in the ground in March, then replanted: the seed ripens in September. They should be watered as needed, as should the other species, which are taken to the greenhouse for storage. With regard to the first species that can be planted from cuttings, I'd like to point out that it's much safer to start them on a warm bed than in the ground. Once they have recovered, they can be transplanted wherever you wish. CHAPTER XLVI. Description of LAUREL; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. There are three main species of laurel; I will not mention others which have no use in cooking, and whose merit is only in the flower, to which some purely medicinal virtues are attributed, such as the two species of Alexandrian laurel, and the two species of laurel: the three species to which I will refer are the frank laurel, the royal laurel, and the cherry laurel. In warm countries, such as Spain, Sicily and the Kingdom of Naples, the bay laurel is more of a tree than a shrub: I've seen some as big as an average oak; but in our climate, which is less favorable to it, it doesn't grow nearly so strong, although it is quite common to find some that grow to ten or twelve feet, and sometimes more. Its roots are large and uneven, with many fibers; its stem is smooth and knotless; its bark is thin and grayish or brown; its wood is porous and fragile; it grows a number of branches that form a beautiful head when the lower part is pruned. Its leaves are oblong, pointed, hard and evergreen, sinewy, smooth, fragrant, with a pungent, aromatic and slightly bitter taste, attached by short tails. Its flowers are one-piece, cut into four or five parts, white or yellowish in color; the flowers are followed by fruits or berries as large as small cherries, oblong, green when born and black when ripe, H 2 under whose skin is a shell containing an oblong seed: these berries are fragrant, aromatic, oily and bitter. The royal laurel differs from the former in the color of its leaves, which are a cheerful green and have neither odor nor aromatic taste; but it resembles it in flower and fruit, with the difference, however, that the flowers of the royal laurel are born in clusters, whereas those of the frank laurel are born from the armpits of the leavesThe cherry laurel is neither a regular tree nor a shrub; It has no stem that forms a true tree body, and its branches are too extensive to be considered a shrub. Its stems are straight and twiggy; its bark is plain brown; its wood is white and very brittle; its leaf is similar to that of the lemon tree, but larger, wider and slightly serrated at the edges: it is very smooth, a beautiful shiny green, with a slightly bitter astringent taste. The flower is small, rose-shaped, with five white, odorless petals, and is followed by a fleshy, almost oval fruit, about the size of a sloe, green when it is born and reddish-black when it ripens, beneath which is a thin shell containing an oblong, bitter seed. This species has no other known cooking qualities than to give boiled milk an almond-like taste: a leaf or 2 is added to soups, and to certain soft cheeses eaten for dessert. The leaf is sometimes used medicinally: it is astringent and fortifies the stomach. This plant keeps its greenery all year round, and in winter is a delight to the eye. In warm countries, it is used to form paths and fences in the same way as we plant bower bushes: pruned in straight lines, it produces a very beautiful effect. Here, where the climate is different, we keep to a few feet, more for pleasure than for real need. We are obliged to place them at the foot of the south-facing walls, to protect them from the severe frosts that often kill them; but the plant usually grows back the following spring. As this plant is very vigorous, it is soon resuscitated: it requires no particular care, other than to be ploughed in the normal seasons, and to be supported by a few trellises or small poles attached to the wall; those who are very curious about it stuff it during the winter, but this care can be dispensed with. It is commonly propagated from offshoots that are detached from old plants, or from cuttings that are left to wither on the ground before being put back in place. 3.
