It can also be propagated from seed, but it will take longer to form. The first two species of laurel are the really useful ones, and are used indifferently; but the first is as common in this country as the second is uncommon. Its dried leaves are used in most stews and short broths, both fatty and lean; they are also used to crown hams; and they are also used, interwoven with fruit, to brighten up winter desserts. Its medicinal properties are far more numerous. Its leaves are astringent, resolving and warm; they fortify the stomach, aid digestion and dispel wind: they are taken in infusions of five to six like tea, or in powder, at a dose of two large ones, to restore the stomach, prevent nausea and dispel the pain of windy colic. Externally, they are used in fomentations with aromatic herbs, to fortify numb parts in cases of paralysis, rheumatism, etc. They are also good externally, for softening tumors caused by wasp stings; taken as a gargle, they soothe toothache. Its berries have even more virtue and warmth than its leaves, especially those brought from hot countries: they are used for diseases of the stomach, liver, rat and bladder; they digest raw humours; they divide and resolve thickened and viscous juices; they awaken appetite, dispel disgust, lift obstructions of the liver and spleen, excite urination, induce menstruation, and push out backwardness. An excellent oil is obtained for nerve diseases, paralysis, convulsions, colic and stomach weakness: this oil is obtained by expresion, by coction in boiling water, or by distillation; and it is given both internally, in small doses of ten to twelve drops, and externally as a liniment. A spirit with the same virtues can also be obtained by fermenting its fruits. For windy colic in particular, and for stomach weakness, one infuses four ounces of good wine with one large berry and two large dried orange peel, and drinks it with a little sugar; I have tried this remedy on myself with perfect success. These berries have virtues that extend to almost everything, and they are used in the composition of many unguens and electuaries, in orvietan, in theriac and in dressings. Laurel grows naturally in all H 4 warm countries, and particularly on sunny sea coasts; it grows straight up to a height of thirty or forty feet, forming a well-stocked, evergreen head that provides pleasant shade. It can be propagated from seed or from marcottes. In the first case, the seed is sown in March in crates or tubs filled with soft earth, mixed with potting soil, at a distance of three inches from one seed to the next, sunk a finger deep, and covered with a little potting soil or chopped dung; beforehand, it's a good idea to soak the seed in manure water for a few days, as it sprouts more quickly and reliably. These boxes are placed in full sun at the foot of a wall, and watered often: sometimes the plant is strong enough to be replanted the following year, either in boxes or in the ground; but the safest thing is to wait until the second year. In the second case, at the end of March, branches from old plants are placed in dummies, where they are held in place with hooks: they take root immediately, and can be weaned the following September; this is the best way to have fairly well-formed plants; but this plant usually grows a lot of offshoots from the foot, which are separated and replanted to form others, with only the care of watering them often in the first year. As for the old plants, they require no cultivation other than to be ploughed during the seasons, and brought closer together from time to time when they grow too far apart: the branches, which are removed and left to dry, are used for the various purposes for which this plant is suited. CHAPTER XLVII. Description of the EPICERIA; its various species, properties, cultivation, etc. THIS plant, although little known to gardeners, is useful for food and health; it is an annual. There are five species, but I will describe only one, as the others have no properties. Botanists call it nigella semine aromatico, to distinguish it from other nielles, a name which is really its own; but the one I give it is the one it bears in Italy. The plant bears a close resemblance to the anemone; its foliage is cut in the same way, but H 5 more delicate, finer and lighter green; its root is yellowish, with many fibers: Its stem is small, fluted and branched; its branches all end in a white, slightly bluish, odorless flower, arranged in a five-petal star shape, with several stamens in the middle, surrounded by a crown of small oblong bodies; the flowers are followed by small, fairly large fruits, ending in five or six horns, and divided into several chambers containing angular, hazelnut-colored seeds with an aromatic odor and a very pungent taste. This seed is sometimes used in foods in place of the four spices; it is true that it has the taste of nutmeg, clove, cinnamon and pepper all at once: however, it is not commonly used in France; but it is used in various parts of Italy. This seed is useful in medicine, because it is incisive, aperitive, vulnerative and resolutive; when chewed, it stimulates salivation, and when taken as a decoction or mixed in food, it increases the milk of nursing mothers; it induces months in women, resists venom and fights quarte fever; it is also good for killing worms and driving away winds. It is prepared according to the type of illness. This plant is sown on a bed in March, and the seedling is good for transplanting in May: it is very delicate, and requires loose, earthy soil. Plants should be spaced six to eight inches apart, and no wider or taller than an ordinary anemone. It thrives best in the hottest climate, which is why it is much stronger in Italy, where its seed is much wittier than here. It should be placed in a good spot, and watered often in dry spells. The seed is harvested in August, and keeps well for several years, both for sowing and for various uses, provided it is kept in well-stoppered bottles. Among the four species I have not mentioned, there is one called nigella cretica, whose seed is even stronger than the previous one, but I do not know its virtues. H6 CHAPTER XLVIII. Description of lamb's lettuce; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Lamb's lettuce is a small winter salad, naturally produced in the countryside in all temperate countries, but which becomes stronger and more abundant when cultivated. It goes by many names, depending on the country where it grows: blanchette, poule grasse, doucette, and salade de chanoine; all these names are its own. It's a small plant, not as wide as your hand; its leaves are long and narrow, and spill to the ground in a smooth, light green. It is cut from the root and eaten whole, with only the bad leaves removed. Some people eat it on its own, while others mix it with celery or chicory, and others with beet and anchovy. It is generally well liked, and much of it is consumed, especially as it is healthy, refreshing, soothing and laxative. It is used in veal and chicken broths to soothe the ardor of fever, and to ease the pain of nephritis. It is also used successfully in rheumatism, gout, scurvy and hypochondriac: lastly, it is very good for correcting the acridity of humors and the excessive saltiness of the blood. The latter differs from the former in that its leaf is much broader, and the plant a little stronger, which makes it more profitable: it is also much later to come up in spring, and consequently serves longer than the other; but it is not so sweet to the mouth, being covered with a kind of down which displeases most people, and which makes it less marketable than the other: our market gardeners grow very little of it. This plant requires very loose, well-amended soil: it can be sown very thickly, because it is always thinned out by pulling out the strongest. The weakest, which is then left to grow, is used to produce seed: it essentially needs to be loosened and moistened often until it has sprouted. The first sowing is done in mid-August, and is eaten at the end of autumn. We continue to sow from fortnight to fortnight until mid-October, to have some without interruption: the one sown in October is the best for Lent, when it has risen well before the frosts. It is weeded when it has emerged, and this is the only way it can be harvested. It can be sown in spring and in the following months, if you have a taste for this plant; it succeeds in all seasons, provided it is well watered, and placed in the shade in the warmer months; but in summer, lettuces are rightly preserved, and all this time lamb's lettuce is forgotten. To collect the seed, at the end of winter a few beds are thinned to three-quarters, and the rest left to grow: each plant, if it is at ease, grows to a spread of a foot in diameter, similar to a flowering talaspicum; and all its little branches are first loaded with small bunches of white flowers, tending to blue, to which the seed follows, which is small, flat, and yellowish in color, I mean common. Italian lamb's lettuce is quite different, being small and long, ashen in color, with a small black dot at one end: its flower is also different, being an obscure white tending to red. As soon as it approaches maturity, it detaches itself at the slightest breath of wind; consequently, you must prevent it from falling, by plucking the stalks in the morning with the dew, as soon as the stems begin to yellow; but far from exposing it to the sun, like other seeds, you must place it in a heap with its cossate in some cool, poorly ventilated place, and let this mass warm up and partially rot; the seed feeds and perfects itself in this humidity. After a fortnight, shake the cossate with a fork, the seed falls out, and is then exposed to the air for a few days; it is then winnowed and enclosed. This seed is good for seven to eight years, I mean the common one; but you mustn't sow it the first year, as it sprouts too late and with too much difficulty. The seed of the other species will only keep for four or five years. Our market gardeners, sometimes lacking clean places or leisure, collect it quite differently; they let it ripen on the ground and fall, then they tear off the cossate, and pick up with a broom all this seed spread on the ground; and as they pick up as much earth as seed, they put the whole in tubs with half-fulls of water, and stir it well: The earth sinks to the bottom, and the seed floats to the top; they remove it cleanly with a skimmer, or in any other way they like, and dry it, after which they lock it up. In light soils with a lot of earth, like theirs, this method is quite practicable; but in fatter and wetter soils, it would be very difficult to follow it, besides the seed would be prone to germinate on the ground, if it stayed there too long, and if it suffered some rain. CHAPTER XLIX. Description of MARIOLAINE; its different species, properties, calture, etc. DA marjoram is an aromatic plant of which there are many species, some perennial, others annual; the main ones cultivated in gardens, both for pleasure and utility, are wild marjoram, common marjoram, shell marjoram, variegated marjoram, small-leaved marjoram and hairy marjoram. Wild marjoram, otherwise known as oregano, has many small, woody, filamentous roots; it grows a number of small, hard, quarrelsome, hairy stems; its leaves are almost heart-shaped, brown-green, hairy, fragrant, and about the size of a child's fingernail. Its flowers are born at the top of its stems in spindly, scaly spikes that form large bunches. These flowers are small, arranged in the shape of a mouth, or a pipe cut into two whitish-red lips at the top: the flowers are followed by very small, almost round seeds, enclosed in an oblong capsule that served as the flower's calyx. Common marjoram is no less abundant in roots, which are also small and fibrous; it grows many small stems, rising to eight or ten inches, which together form a rounded tuft: These stems are woody, twiggy, small, a little hairy and reddish, lined with leaves arranged opposite each other, almost round in shape, soft, whitish, covered with a white down, half the size of oregano, with a strong, penetrating and very pleasant smell, and a slightly acrid and bitter taste. Its flowers are born at the ends of its branches, gathered in the form of a spike or head, rounder and shorter than those of oregano, composed of four rows of leaves laid in scales: these flowers are very small, whitish in color, one-piece in mouth, whose upper lip is upright, rounded, indented, and the lower divided into three parts; the flowers are followed by small, almost round, russet-colored, fragrant and bitter seeds. Shell marjoram, also known as gentile marjoram, differs from this variety in that its leaves are rounder, closer together and hollowed out in the shape of a shell; they are also whiter in color and smell sweeter. The flower is arranged in a spike like its predecessors. variegated marjoram is similar in all respects to the previous variety, except for the color of its leaves, which are mottled pale yellow; some are even completely yellow, making it a pleasing variety to the eye. Small-leaf marjoram differs from the above only in that its leaf is extremely small, similar to that of ordinary thyme, but more rounded: it is also the most fragrant of all. Hairy thyme is a species similar to the previous one, but its leaf is slightly larger and more hairy, which gives it its name: its spikes are also shorter. This plant is not very useful with foodstuffs; however, it is often mixed in, not only to make them more pleasant, but also to correct their flattery and make them easier to digest, especially with peas, beans and fish. It is also very pleasant to the sense of smell and, as much for these reasons as for its particular virtues, there is no garden. where one is not eager to have a few borders of it, or at least a few feet. It is cephalic, pectoral, stomachic, hysteric and sternutatory; all the species have more or less the same virtues. The powder of its leaves and flowers, dried in the shade, is very suitable for making serosities flow through the nose. The infusion of its flowers is also used successfully to suppress urination and menstruation, and is equally effective in making asthmatics and those with stubborn coughs cough up; the former is used in preference to the other species for these illnesses. Its distilled water is a marvellous help in indigestion, sour reports and winds: in these cases, the essential oil of this plant, the syrup or the preserve, can also be used. The oil in particular delights the senses, and soothes tooth pain, by soaking a cotton ball in it and placing it in the hollow of the affected tooth. For head colds and torticollis, oregano is dried over a fire, wrapped warm in a cloth and applied to the head. Marjoram powder, mixed with apricot marmalade or preserved orange blossom, is good for epilepsy, vertigo and trembling. Finally, this plant, however it is used, is recognized as sovereign for all cold diseases of the brain and head, for those of the chest and stomach, and for drawing out all aqueous humors. Marjoram can be propagated from seed, cuttings or offshoots, which are seeded or replanted in the same way as all other aromatic plants. The first two species are usually planted in borders around vegetable garden quarters, and withstand the winter without any particular care; but the others require a greenhouse in this season, and must therefore be raised in pots to enclose them more easily, and give them as much air as possible in their prison, moistening them a little if necessary. It is advisable to renew it from time to time, when you notice that it is being stripped, and that it is growing only weakly. Description of MELISSA: its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. MELISSA, otherwise known as lemon grass, is a perennial, fragrant plant. There are four species: garden lemon balm, wild lemon balm, Roman lemon balm and Pyrenean lemon balm, but the latter three are not cultivated in gardens. Its root is woody, long, round and fibrous; its stems are numerous, rising to a height of about two feet, almost square in shape, firm and stubby; its leaves are oblong and pointed, similar to those of common balsam, covered with short hairs, toothed at the edges, light green, with a pleasant lemon scent and a slightly pungent taste. Its flowers are born in the leaf axils, forming rings that are not complete around the stem, nor completely whorled; they are small, mouth-shaped, reddish or yellowish when born, forming a kind of pipe cut into two lips, supported by a calyx made into a hairy cone: each flower is followed by four slightly oblong seeds, stuck together, enclosed in the calyx where the flower is held. This plant is of little use in food: its young leaves are sometimes used in salad dressings, and some others put them in omelettes, as parsley is used, but this is not common. It delights the sense of smell; that's what's most flattering about it. Its greatest properties are in medicine, where it is often and very usefully employed; it is hysterical, cephalic and stomachic. Its dried or even fresh leaves, infused as a tea in half a pint of water, are sovereign for all diseases of the brain and those of women, for palpitations of the heart, for fainting, for vertigo, even for paralysis and for deciduous disease: a handful can also be lightly boiled in veal stock. A water made from it is sovereign for apoplexy, lethargy and epilepsy, as well as for vapors, colic, menstrual and urinary suppression; a spoonful is taken neat, or mixed in a glass of water, depending on the type of illness, more or less violent. This water, as well known as Eau des Carmes as Eau de Mélisse, is not a special secret, as many people imagine: M. Lémery has given a dispensation of it, which is recognized as the best: any private individual with a still can easily test it; and a pint, which is sold publicly for 20 livres, costs only 6 or 7 livres at most if you make it yourself. Here's how to make it. Take six handfuls of fresh lemon balm leaves, and an ounce of dried lemon peel, as much nutmeg and coriander; add half an ounce of clove and cinnamon; crush these drugs well, crush the leaves, and put the whole into a vessel suitable for distilling them, with two pounds of white wine and half a pound of brandy; Leave this mixture to digest for three days, after covering the vessel with its lid, to which you will add the container, the openings of which you will plug exactly; and then distill this material over a moderate sand fire, or in a bain-marie. A simpler lemon balm water is also made, without mixing the above drugs, to be used in cordial and hysterical potions, in a dose of six or eight ounces, like the others. It is usually only made from rooted plants, although it also comes from seed. We separate the offspring from old plants that produce a lot of it, and plant them in March in good, well-smoked soil, in a slightly shady spot: it does very well around fruit trees. It is sometimes prone to degeneration; when this is noticed, it should be destroyed and new ones planted. If it is not easy to find it in the vicinity, it grows naturally in the woods in certain countries, which must be distinguished from wild lemon balm, which also grows there, and which is very different, having a very unpleasant odor. The one I'm talking about is cut every year in autumn, just above ground level, and grows back in spring: it stays in place for a very long time, and withstands all bad weather without the need for any precautions. Its leaves are used for salad as soon as they begin to form, but are not used for distillation until July and August, when they are more perfected by the sun. CHAPTER CHAPTER LI. Description of the Melon - its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. The melon is a fruit cherished by all nations. The plant that produces it resembles the cucumber in many respects; its roots are extensive, straight, very hairy and yellowish in color; its stems, called arms by all gardeners, are sarmentose, hairy, untied, long, branchy and crawl along the ground. Its leaves alternate in appearance, borne on a three- to four-inch, medium-sized, hollow tail: they are almost round in shape, heart-shaped, light green and a little hairy; from the base and axils of the leaves come clusters of flowers, one-piece, bell-shaped, flared and split into five parts, star-shaped, very pale yellow; some are sterile, others fertile, where the fruit is uncovered even before they bloom: the fruit is smooth, shaped like an olive, green in color, Tome II. I but as it grows it takes on the shape, color and size of its species, which varies greatly, and also ripens sooner or later. its point of ripeness. It is a pleasant, refreshing food, and easy to digest when eaten in moderation; but excess produces wind and colic, sometimes followed by dyssentery and stomach upsets that are difficult to cure: We have also seen very severe quart fevers resulting from the immoderate use of melon, especially among people of a certain age, who should abstain from it, as should those of a pituiteux or melancholic temperament; each person must be his own doctor in this respect, and know how to deprive himself of a food that is harmful to his health. The Italians make an excellent jam from the rib of this fruit, which in their country is very thick, Provence melons; but I don't know if the rib of those we grow here, being much thinner, would be equally suitable for jamming. Here, we only pickle in vinegar, as we do with gherkins, those that are picked and thinned in May, when there is too much knotting, and which are then the size of a Spanish ôlive. Connoisseurs find them very delicate: see the chapter on cucumbers for instructions on how to preserve them. Its seed is one of the four cold seeds; it is used in all emulsions to cool overheated entrails, to temper the ardor of fever, and to provoke urination; it also enters into the composition of orgeat, the recipe for which I have given in the Pumpkin article. The southern countries are the most savory for this fruit; its taste is also much stronger there than elsewhere, and we are not obliged to give it the infinite care that we take here. We sow it in the ground like all vegetables, and let it grow freely without any cultivation other than crimping it once or twice: the sun does the rest, and gives it a quality that ours never have to the same degree; however, there are years when ours come very close to it; I have even seen Italians and Provençals be very pleased with it on more than one occasion. There are an infinite number of melon species, but I'll limit myself to a dozen or so that are the most successful in our climate, without claiming that they should be preferred everywhere to other species; on the contrary, I urge those who live in different climates to stick to species other than those I've adopted, once they've seen them succeed; and I'm happy to repeat I 2 here what I've already said more than once: such and such a soil will not be suitable for such and such a species of plant, which will be perfectly suited to such and such another; el vice versâ; and on this occasion I won't say precisely Tot capita, tot sensus; but rather, more or less and in an equally true sense, Tot littora, tot fructus. The species I want to talk about are: Le Melon Français, De Langeais. otherwise known as- A graine blanche. mé le maraîcher. A graine rouge. Des Carmes, which is Le Morin. of three kinds; the long De Florence, the round, and the white Sucrin de Tours. S. Nicolas à côte. large and medium. In the French melon class, which is the most widely cultivated, there are regularly round ones, flattened ones, and others with an elongated shape; some are more embroidered, others less so; some have more cut foliage, others less so; some are earlier, others later: should we conclude from these differences that the French melon is divided into as many species, or simply believe, as some do!Are we to conclude from these differences that the French melon is divided into so many species, or are we to believe, as some do, that they are simply a game of nature? For my part, without undertaking to treat the matter as a philosopher, I will declare myself in favor of the latter opinion; and I will say that these differences cannot in fact be regarded as characterizing species. In order for a production to claim the dignity of a species, it must be fixed and determined; in order for it to be believed fixed and determined, it must be followed without variation in its productions and multiplications, in much the same way as matter, which, although thrown repeatedly by the caster into the matrix, always renders bodies perfectly equal in form. Now, the productions we are talking about vary in their reproductions: for example, the seed of a round melon sometimes produces elongated ones, sometimes flattened ones; they are therefore without sequence, without determination; they are therefore only a game of nature which has no law for them, and only the effect of a passing meeting of the elements. But whether they are species or accidents, that's what I don't set out to describe; and I'm only concerned with the genus of the simple melon, I mean the market garden melon. Its shape varies, as I have just said, but in general its skin is extremely embroidered around the circumference, with no marked ribs and very full. It differs in these respects from melons from hot countries, which all have marked and very thick ribs, and which are as empty as they are full, with conse3 quently little flesh, albeit delicious. The color is very red, and it has a lot of water; but the taste, an essential ingredient, is not always equally good. In dry and hot years, it is vinous and sweet; but in cold and rainy years, art brings it to the truth, but cannot give it all the quality it could have. The avarice of those who grow them also very often makes this fruit despicable; their main aim is usually to make it large, because they think they can sell it better; and they don't realize that it can only be made large by watering, which takes away all its taste. The long Carmelite melon, like the round one, originally comes from Saumur; it was brought to the King's kitchen garden, from where it passed to the Carmelites, who took particular care in cultivating it. Its flesh is more or less red, full of water, very sweet, with a strong taste; but it is sometimes a little soft and mushy. Don't let it ripen too much: it's good in June if it's been brought forward; the skin yellows a little as it ripens. Some degenerate and ripen a little, and some are even slightly ribbed; but this difference is only external and does not change their quality; they are no less good, very thin-ribbed and very full. The round melon, apart from its shape, which is round and small, has all the same qualities, and ripens at the same time. The white melon has a smooth, whitish skin and a slightly oval shape; it is a good size, and ripens at the same time as the two mentioned above; it is preferred by many connoisseurs: I can assure you that I have eaten some that left nothing to be desired. The Saint Nicolas has an elongated shape, a slightly greenish color, evenly marked ribs, mediocre size, very thin ribs, firm, red flesh, full of water, sweet, vinous, and superior in finesse to those we have mentioned; it ranks first among the species we cultivate: it ripens in July. There is a very similar species, called the Avignon melon: some claim that it is the same under another name; others maintain that it is different: I would rather be of the former opinion than of the latter; for, having compared the two, I have seen only a slight difference in shape, which is a little more pointed in the Avignon melon than in the Saint-Nicolas. The Langeais melon bears the name of the 14 countries where it is best known, if it did not originate there. It has a slightly elongated shape, regularly marked with ribs, is a coarse green at birth, and golden yellow as it ripens; its size varies from year to year, sometimes being very small, and in the past being almost as big as market gardeners. It is also prone to embroidery, more or less, and sometimes not at all. Its flesh is red and firm, its taste sweet and vinous; it has a lot of water and is very full. A considerable quantity used to come from Langeais to Paris every year, but since we've succeeded in raising them well enough here, this little trade no longer exists. However, we must admit that it is better here than it is here, because it grows naturally in its own soil. Now, any fruit that comes without artifice is always superior in quality to that which is forced; it ripens in June and July. The white-seeded melon is a very early species of Carmelite melon; its shape is oval, of medium size; its skin is green and smooth, which changes very little as it ripens; its flesh is full of sweet water, but not sufficiently spicy; it is very delicate to raise: these two defects prevent it from being as widely cultivated as the others: it ripens in June: its seed is white, and gave it its name. CHAPTER LI. 201 The red-seeded melon is round, of medium size; its flesh is firm, red, and has a sweet, vinous taste: it ripens in July: its seed is a golden yellow, almost red. The Morin melon is a market garden variety, round and slightly flattened, with a sort of crown around the eye; its flesh is firm and red, with a sweet, vinous taste. Its flesh is firm and red, its taste sweet and vinous. It is very full, embroiders perfectly, and is usually a fortnight ahead of the maraîcher. It differs from ordinary market gardeners in that the little background that can be seen between the embroidery is a coarse black-green. The Florence melon, whose proper name is cantalupi, comes in four varieties: green, black, orange and white; all four are equally marked, very full and very early; they differ from one another in the following respects. The green one is small, a little elongated, with a few warts; the skin is green, with little embroidery; the flesh is red and sweet: it yellows a little as it ripens on the sunny side: its defect is that it splits. When it ripens perfectly, it's an excellent melon; but in this climate it doesn't always succeed, being good in mid-June. The black melon is a darker L4 green, round and small, with similar warts; it also splits, but does not change color as it ripens; in addition, it has the same qualities as the previous melon. It is the most esteemed of the four, being the sweetest and windiest; in Italy, it is called il melone degli santi, the melon of the saints: it ripens at the same time. The orange melon is elongated without warts, turns yellow as it ripens, embroiders a little and does not split; but its taste is a little less intense than that of the two preceding varieties: it ripens a fortnight later. The white variety is round and ribbed like the others, but larger: its flesh is white, full of water and very sweet; its rib is rather thick, so it has less flesh: it ripens in July. It should be noted that these four species of cantalupi require much more nourishment than the others, as their ribs are thicker and more spongy: the bed should be filled with six to eight inches of potting soil; you can even mix a third of prepared soil with the potting soil, as is done in Holland; the fruit is fatter and better nourished. The gros sucrin de Tours is the size of a market-gardener, extraordinarily embroidered and unevenly round, with imperceptibly marked ribs; its flesh is firm and red, with a sweet, spicy taste, full of water; it turns yellow slightly as it ripens, and is usually good only in August: it is an excellent melon. The small sucrin is at most half the size of the previous one; it is round and flattened; its skin is green: it changes little as it ripens, it is very good and full, with a spicy taste; but its smallness greatly diminishes its merit: it ripens the same way in August. From these details, we can see that the small species surpass the large market melon in all good qualities: water, finesse, sugar, everything is there; they are also earlier, and in the late season they do not lose their good qualities like the large species, which, although it ripens, has no taste after the first days of September. They also have the double advantage of stopping facilemént, and of being generally all good in ordinary years. The previous year (1749), despite all the bad weather that accompanied it, a private individual in Versailles found cantaloupe that were good on the fifteenth of June, and which were sent to the King. However, our market gardeners apply themselves only to the first species, because of its size, and the others are only seen in private homes where they are grown for themselves, which is a great loss to the public. 16 I'm not talking about the little early carmelite, which does very well in what it is, and which ripens first of all; but which, because of its smallness, is not worth the expense of cultivation, being no bigger than a calvil apple, and being a little sweet besides. I've heard a lot of praise for a species from Italy called the crimson melon, because its flesh is crimson red. A foreign lord, curious about this crop, also assured me that it was very successful in Germany, where he grew it himself every year: from which one might conclude that it should be even more successful here; however, it is not known here, and whatever research I have made, I have only been able to obtain imperfect information about it: the curious, within reach of its natural country, will be able to find out more about it. Some people like to grow a particular kind of watermelon, known here as the melon d'eau, and in Provence as the pasteque; it comes round, extraordinarily large, weighing up to thirty pounds and more. The flesh is crimson red, the seed black, and the skin green and smooth; but it is a waste to grow it, as it is not edible here; it is barely edible in its own country for those who have not accustomed their taste to it from youth. Its main merit is that it has a lot of refreshing water; but it's a bland water that neither flatters nor awakens; I testify to this with many people who have often tasted it as I have, both in Italy and Provence. There is another species that is very similar, but smaller, and which differs on the outside only by a string of yellow spots, arranged in the form of ribs that all end at the head of the fruit, whose seed is red, and which is known as the American melon; but it is only used for jam, and is excellent for this purpose. It can be cultivated for this purpose: it succeeds very well, and yields a lot: last year I collected twenty-one on four feet, all well conditioned. Its leaf is extremely indented, similar to that of the watermelon; it stops late, and it's only at the end of its branches that the fruit knots; but it grows visibly as soon as it's stopped: it requires a lot of space and little pruning. I could also name a species that is very excellent in the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily, which is known here as the green Morée melon or the Candie melon, and in Italy as the winter melon. The flesh is white, similar to that of the cucumber, very elongated; the skin smooth, pale green; and it has the advantage of keeping all winter hanging on the floor in a dry, airy place. In Naples, they are tied around the windows of outdoor houses: the temperature of this climate allows this, as it almost never freezes. This melon is full of water and so sweet that its excessive sweetness displeases some people; but this small defect does not prevent it from being a pleasure in the ungrateful season in which it is grown. I've seen it succeed a few times here, when the year has been favorable; but often it has neither taste nor quality. We can always risk the event of a few feet. For those who don't have it, it's time to give them an understanding of melon cultivation, by which I mean cultivation such as nature commonly demands, and not that for which art should be exhausted. It would undoubtedly be pleasant for individuals to be able in some way to have this fruit two months earlier than nature allows; and there is no doubt that by means of layers, it would be possible to serve it at the beginning of May, whereas it is not commonly eaten until July, and only abounds in August and September: I don't even doubt that in Spain, the kingdom of Naples and Sicily, Barbary, America and other regions close to the line, we could, by helping nature in its months of rest, have some throughout the year; we can at least presume this by the example of England, where, although the climate is very different, I mean much less clean, some curious people manage to have some, admittedly devoid of taste, but two months earlier than us: an example that has just been successfully put into practice, by a French Lord * who, with the greatest talents and all the knowledge that makes famous characters, recommendable and dear to the State, has always been a lover of plants, and has never disdained their cultivation. But however rare and satisfying this curiosity must have been here, it could only suit people to whom opulence allows everything; it would not be possible to find many who would devote themselves to it: one needs greenhouses glazed and built at great expense, an understanding man who always watches over them, which one can hardly find; an even and continuous fire, and much care besides, which * M. le Maréchal de Bellisle, having recently found himself in the vicinity of London, noticed this little marvel of nature, and set about imitating it as soon as he got to France. On his return home to Bizy, he actually carried it out, having brought with him an English gardener experienced in this cultivation, who, finding new facilities in our climate, succeeded in the first year, and presented him with some at the beginning of May. The plants are still, to tell the truth, only a fruit for the eyes, and too bad to be eaten. The method which produces melons a little later, but which are good, and which only require costs that everyone can afford, is therefore always to be preferred, and this is the one I'm going to develop. The bed of small melons is prepared at the beginning of January; whatever the quantity of seed you wish to sow, a length of nine feet in the bed is more than sufficient, as each bell can easily contain twenty-five to thirty seeds; on this length you can place twenty or more bells, which would make up five to six hundred feet; this is much more than is necessary for the first seed, even for those who trade in them. Individuals who are not in this situation can fill in as many bells as they see fit, and can occupy the remainder with lai tues or cucumbers. The bed should be no more than 2 and a half feet, or 3 wide, to make it easier to heat up, and three and a half feet high before being filled with compost. The dose of potting soil should not exceed three inches, for the reason I'll explain shortly: of the remainder, it is trained as explained in the chapter on layers. If it is greasy or too coarse, the plants are liable to melt: the same disadvantage results if it has already been used to blanch celery or chicory, as a small amount of hair remains, absorbing the heat and giving off a hint of corruption: if it is too old, it does not have enough virtue to raise the fruit to perfection, and it is often because of this defect that the plant melts halfway through. To do this properly, use only two-year-old compost, which has not produced anything during the second year, and which has been stirred from time to time; in this way, it will have acquired new salts during the resting period: nothing is easier than to set aside a small supply every year for the following year. Market gardeners generally don't start sowing large melons until the end of February, which saves them a month of rigorous care. Their main reason for not hurrying them any further is to save on their manures; for they make two seasons for them, as they put it, i.e., they serve them twice, being first used to raise turnips and lettuces, most of which only come up in March and April, and then for melons; They then turn over the old layers, and mixing the old manure with a third of the new, they make up new ones, on which they replant their melons, which are good in this time to put in place. This shows that it's not the risk of sowing them earlier that holds them back, but only the expense and care involved; for the large species they cultivate is less delicate than the smaller ones: If the weather is set for frost, put an inch of pigeon droppings in the middle of the bed, i.e. the thickness of manure, and cover it with old straw mats or warm manure after it has been sown; this helps it to warm up, and keeps it warmer for longer. When it's ready to sow, the most common practice is to sow the seed under a bell in holes made with a finger, two inches apart. Two or three seeds are placed in each hole, without covering them, or at least very lightly; but when you have sowing frames, which is much more advantageous, as I explained in the chapter on Layers, you sow it in the open .field, and when the soil is covered with it, so that each grain is an inch apart, we press the tip of our finger on each grain to press it in, and then pass our hand over the whole surface of the soil, to cover it lightly; but as there are few people provided with these frames, I must here mainly have in view the practice of bells, which is the most general, and match the principles to this method. It is to be hoped that the day we sow will be a fine one: in which case you can leave the bed uncovered until sunset ; but, as you can't delay, whatever the weather, when it's at its warmest, if you're threatened by snow or ice, or if the frost bites hard, you must cover as soon as you've sown, and bind the bells, i.e. swaddle them with litter or regain, so that they are completely covered, and double the covers during the night, as the weather requires: Fifteen days later, sow a few more bells on another end of the bed, and continue from fifteen to fifteen days until the end of March, to make up for the lack of the first ones when they die, and to have a succession of them until September. It is therefore important to ensure this succession of fruits, to prolong a pleasure that would certainly be too short-lived if we stuck only to the first melons. Your first well-cared-for seedling will sprout six to seven days after it has been placed in the ground, whatever the severity of the weather; for it obeys the warmth of the soil in which it grows; and when the seedling is a few days older, it needs to be put into the ground, i.e. a little bit of soil is brought to the base with the finger, and lightly pressed. The most difficult part of growing melons is preserving the plant: too much or too little heat melts it; too little or too much air has the same effect, and great care must be taken to maintain this degree of heat. To get it to breathe properly, you have to take the moments, so to speak, on the fly. During heavy frosts, the sun usually comes out; you need to take advantage of this, and uncover the bells' bottoms from around ten in the morning, until three or four in the afternoon; but the bottom must always be kept low. Sometimes, too, it's cold and sunless, and that's the worst kind of weather you can have; but you have to choose a few hours during the day to uncover the bells a little, otherwise the plant will turn yellow and melt under the covers. But if the fog is thick, or if it's snowing or raining, leave everything covered for as long as it lasts: the plants are in great danger, but there's no remedy. Manure vapors, as much as the deprivation of air, ruin plants in this situation: they attach themselves to the stems and leaves, and this humidity melts them: they fall again on these young plants in large drops, from the glass where they collect, and rust them. This last disadvantage can be overcome by placing pieces of woollen cloth under each bell, supported by three small sticks between the plants and the glass; the vapour attaches itself to them, and you change them from time to time to make them dry alternately; but I confess that this is a great subjection: when you have frames, the operation is much easier and safer, as I said in the first chapter. When a few fine, mild, quiet days arrive, you need to take advantage of them as much as you can to give the plant a bit of air, since it is stretching out in its shirt and becoming tender; one hour after sunrise, remove all or most of the bedding between the bells; and two hours later, the bell is given a finger's breadth of daylight, on the opposite side to the wind; it is lowered one hour before sunset, and the blankets are put back on, thicker or thinner, according to any change that may have occurred in the weather. The most important thing to keep the plant in vigor is to maintain the warmth of the bed by means of the stoves: every day, you stick your hand into the middle, and as soon as you realize it's cold, you warm it up; a few days later, when the heat of this first stove has considerably diminished, you reshuffle them, and always wet them as you change or reshuffle them, if the manures are dry. Finally, in all respects, follow what I said in the chapter on layers, which I won't repeat here: you should also follow what I've said about blankets; and don't neglect to have straw mats for the ease of shaking off snow when it falls, and to prevent rain from penetrating the layers. They are also very useful to protect them from the sleet of March, which is deadly for plants; nothing cools a bed more: you must be careful to prevent it when the weather seems ready, and remove the mats as soon as the sleet has passed. When the severe cold is over, you should always give the bells a little air during most of the day (a finger's breadth is enough), but when the weather begins to warm up, you should leave the same amount of air night and day. However, it must be said that until the end of April, it is almost always advisable to lower the bells at night. The method I have just described is used by all gardeners and market gardeners in general. I have found myself obliged to place it first, as the most authoritative; but on the example of some very well-meaning individuals, I have tried another which I have recognized as better; you are free to experiment with it. Sow the seed, as I said, on a piece of bedding; don't wait until all the fire has passed, as this seed needs a lot of heat to rise quickly and reliably: as long as you can sustain the heat, albeit with difficulty, by sticking your hand into the soil, that's enough. After four or five days, the seed lifts, and the same care as explained above is applied. A fortnight later, the seedling is strong enough to be transplanted onto another layer, which must be prepared, and it is transplanted much lighter, i.e., one bell should make three; but the layer must not be so hot as for the first seed. We leave it in this state for three weeks; it strengthens, and we transplant it again on another layer, where it should be more at ease: seven to eight feet is enough under each bell. We leave it on this third layer until it is strong enough to be replanted; fifteen days will perfect it, provided the weather is mild. With this new method, I've found that the plant stretches less, roots better, remains stockier, is less prone to melting and makes more progress; The reason for this is that it benefits from the warmth and sap of three new layers, which the one remaining on the same layer does not enjoy equally, even though it has been warmed exactly, so that the seedling you planted at the beginning of January is usually ready to be replanted at the beginning of March. If you follow ordinary practice, you will hardly be able to plant the seedling before the end of March; and it goes without saying that you will have kept the January seedlings, as the February ones are only good in 217. the beginning of April. Finally, in one of these two months you do your planting, and for this purpose you prepare your beds, which must be four and a half feet wide, and which are reduced to four because of the borders; two feet high is enough in this season, (I mean after having been walked on.) The rule is to put only one foot under each bell, and to form two rows in a chessboard: you raise them with a little clod, if you can; and transplanted right away, they tire little. They should not be wetted, as the vapour from the bed throws enough moisture into the soil; but the bells should be kept lowered and covered with a little bedding, until they are well established; and if it is a little hot, they should be covered with straw mats. If the plant is strong, the first pruning should be carried out as soon as it is well established, i.e. seven or eight days later, but not at the same time as planting, as some gardeners do; this often results in a kind of canker forming on the pruning, caused by the vapor from the manure, which spreads to the whole stem, causing it to perish. The best thing to do in this respect, when the plants are too far under the last layer in which they were transplanted, and there are no layers ready for replanting, is to stop them at two Tome II. K eyes, eight days before planting. This will seem surprising to those who have never practiced it, and I myself was not convinced of the good effect it produces until after I had tried it; for it really seems that this small quantity of compost is not capable of nourishing the fruit. One might also suspect that the root would heat up and heal in the manure it is forced to pierce, but experience destroys all arguments against this use. This plaute, as I'll soon say, fears nothing so much as water; and the more the soil abounds, the more moisture it retains, which commuuicates with the foot; the less there is consequently, the less it retains, because the air and the sun have a lot of six, and the water, for the same reason has rather, pierced this mediocre, thickness from where it runs off into the paths: this is the first reason. The second reason is that the plant, having less nourishment, stops growing fruit more quickly, and doesn't grow wood with the vigor that a fatter bottom would give it, which is the usual reason why fruit often sinks as it knots; moreover, we save a lot of work, which the pruning of this quantity of mutilated wood requires: as long as we have the principles of vegetation, we feel the need to make it bear fruit. But, you may ask, between too much humidity, which is admittedly contrary, and too little, is the middle ground sufficiently maintained? In hot weather, can this plant draw enough juice from such a weak substance? My answer is that it can, based on my own experience and that of several market gardeners; and to make the assurance I am giving clearer, it should be borne in mind that a vapor is constantly rising from the manure, which the glass, either cloche or frame, attracts, and which sufficiently moistens the soil; and that, in addition, when there is a great need, this is made up for by light watering done at the right time, in the way I will explain below. I'll add one more reason, which is that the heat of the stoves works much better and more quickly on a small quantity of potting soil, than on a larger one: besides, the root of this plant doesn't prick, and only runs on the surface. The result of this practice is 1° that the plant is less prone to melting due to humidity; 2° that the fruit stops earlier and more reliably; 3° that it ripens more quickly; 4° that it has more taste, because it is molas nourished with water. Experimentation will show the truth of what I'm saying. K 2 It could still be objected that piec, when replanted a little hard, does not find a home in this small quantity of compost. I must say, however, that since the root is so close to the manure, particular care is needed during the first few days, to protect it from the excessive heat of the bed, which sometimes starts a second fire after it has been planted, when the weather warms up: You need to probe it with your finger several times during the day, and especially at high noon; and as soon as you notice that the heat is increasing, you need to lard it, and give the bells a little air: these risks only last a few days, after which you can see the plants benefiting visibly, as the sun makes itself felt. As soon as it has recovered, we perform the first operation, which is to prune its upright at the second leaf, and to cut off its ears, as I said above; but if the stem is not sufficiently formed, we leave it to benefit until it is in a condition to suffer it. A modern author, who has written about this fruit in the context of other subjects, condemns this cutting off of the ears, on the general principle that nature does nothing useless, and that we must not give it laws or do it violence; but, starting from the same principle, it would therefore be wrong to prune trees or vines; it would be wrong to cut the shoots of several roots, in order to profit from them; it would be wrong to pinch peas and beans, melons and cucumbers: how many other operations would be wrong? Practices recognized as good by experience cannot be destroyed by simple reasoning, however specious it may be. Let's return to our subject. When the stems begin to grow arms, they must be pinched at two eyes; and as they grow new branches, they must be cut back again and again with a small, sharp knife. Finally, we must make it a rule to leave only two arms on each stem, and a third, called the false arm, because it grows out of the stump between the good arms: everything that grows more around the stem must be cut off. We always keep one of the false arms, because we know from experience that they often bear fruit more often than the good ones. A small number of gardeners always prune with one eye, and do well, they say: for my part, I neither condemn nor approve this K method, which I have never tried, and which is rarely used. False flowers begin to appear after the second pruning: they should be carefully removed, as should the tendrils that grow on the arms. You should also cut off the gourmands which usually grow straight from the middle of the plant; they ruin the good branches: you can easily distinguish them by their size and liveliness. If the branches are so arranged that they cannot be brought back, then some cut leaf must be used to cover them. There's a bad kind of leaf called hard leaf, which comes out of the arms, and consumes more sap than four good ones; it should be cut close to the stem: you can tell by its darker color than the others, by its thickness, and by its more pointed shape. After the first or second pruning, some hairy branches grow, with pipes five or six inches long without eyes; these must be cut off, as this type of branch rarely or never produces fruit. Genuinely good fruiting wood must be short, by which I mean that it must have its eyes close together; and the closer it is to the foot, the bigger and better the fruit, and the better it holds. Any branch with flat wood is also bad by nature, so it must be removed. During the course of these various operations, the stalks gain strength and the branches multiply; they must be thinned out to avoid confusion, and food must be provided for those most likely to bear fruit: These forks are usually pieces of barrel stave wood, sharpened at one end and enthrited at the other: they are driven into the soil more or less deeply, depending on whether you want to give the plants more or less air, and the edge' of the bell rests on the notch which retains it and even temys conpre the strong winds. But, for greater safety, these forks should always be placed on the opposite side of the wind, and the bells lowered as much as possible during its violence; however, as long as the weather is serene, they should be placed on the side of the rising sun, and all branches should be enclosed under the bell on the K4 1 opposite side, until the fruit is stopped; but some should be allowed to escape at the other edge where the fork is. When pruning, the branches should be distributed so that none stretches out over the paths; they should be thrown back on the sides and in the middle: from time to time, both hands should be pressed a little firmly around the foot, to push it back into the soil. When you start to see some fruit stopping, if it's outside the bell, bend the branch so that it's covered; and if it stops so far from the foot that you can't bring it back without risking forcing the branch, in that case take another bell and cover it; for it is extremely important, for the goodness of the fruit, that neither rainwater nor sprinkling water ever falls on it until it is perfectly ripe; the Provençals themselves observe this, despite the heat of their climate and the dryness of their soil, as I have noticed in the vicinity of Marseille. For this purpose, they raise a small inverted earthen pot, supported on three forks five or six inches above each fruit. They do even more; persuaded by experience that any water is not only contrary to the fruit's goodness, but that it even harms the plant, their method of watering them is quite different from ours: their melons, as I have already said, are in the ground, and are planted in the middle of their boards, which are domed; they put only one row of them, and give only three feet of width to the boards. From this we understand that the two sides are hollow, and form two small ditches into which they let water run when necessary; but this is only at the end, and when the leaves are very wilted; this water filters between two soils, and substains the roots without drowning the foot, as watering cans do, which often causes them to perish. The perfectly curious add to this: when the weather is rainy, or when they foresee a storm, they remove the pots I mentioned from over the forks, and cover the fruit entirely with them, until the fine weather returns: However, they have observed that, despite this precaution, as soon as the year turns rainy, their melons lose a great deal of their good qualities: incontestable proof that authorizes more and more the use of frames, where they never receive more water than they are willing to give. It's also to protect them from sunburn, which is frequent and dangerous in their climate, and at the same time to prevent them from ripening too quickly, which would make them dry and unhealthy; in this way, they prevent the sun from beating down on the melons, as the portion of its rays that revolves around them is enough to ripen them. But in this climate, we hardly need this precautton; for, as much as it is important, when the fruit begins to set, to keep it covered with its leaves so that it benefits better, as much it is necessary, when it approaches its size, to uncover it so that it receives through the bell or the frames the immediate rays of the sun: each one must regulate himself, in this respect, according to his climate. Vegetable growers generally take none of these precautions, even though they know them and are convinced of their good effect: But most do not want to expose their bells to unforeseen hail, and other small daily accrdens; they are much less concerned about the goodness than the beauty of the fruit, which is why they should not be imitated: however, there are only too many individuals who do this; but I have seen them repent more than once. For example, in 1746, there were clouds in May and June, which ruined most of the fruit. Some of my acquaintances promptly used their bells, and put the fruit back under cover; but in an attempt to repair one evil, they created a greater one. The fruit, which had become accustomed to the fullness of the air, found itself deprived of this abundance, so it hung up, hardly professed any more, and ripened badly and later. When you have done so much as remove the eloches, you must never put them back; the most suitable expedient on these occasions is to always keep a small trellis over the beds, ready to receive the doormats, when you have to fear cos kinds of bad weather. As the fruit appears, whether in the first, second or third sap, the branch should always be pruned to one eye above; but if there are several, after a while only one of the first sap should be left, and the strongest chosen; quinno days or three weeks later, you choose a second one from the second sap, and do away with all the rest; it's even much better to leave only the first sap, especially in cold, rainy years. Some market gardeners, greedy for profit, are not so reserved, and sometimes leave R 6 three or four on each plant; but experience shows that the more a plant is loaded, the less quality and size the fruit has: the person who breeds for pleasure must prefer to have one good one to two mediocre ones. However, although I don't want to give a decisive reason for this, we also know from experience that, under stretchers, one plant can produce three, and even four well-conditioned ones: I've seen as many as seven; the reason for this is that heat being evenly distributed throughout the body of the bed, and the temperature of the air being the same throughout the space between the surface of the bed and the glass, the fruit finds greater resources to feed itself; let's add to this that the branches not being violated, as under cloches, where they must be kept tight, nature acts at the same time with greater freedom and prodigality. When this fruit has reached a certain size, many individuals are in the habit of placing it on a piece of tile, with the idea that the humidity communicated by the soil is detrimental to its goodness: this is true in the last season, I mean for all those that have not ripened by the end of August; and this precaution is then very useful, because the soil cools down, as the nights become long and cold : Experience proves that potting soil in some way helps to nourish the fruit and make it swell, because it helps its parts to expand; moreover, it ripens much more as a reflection of the soil's own heat: the proof is clear, since the side of the bed is always riper than the side of the soil. But there is a way to prevent this evil, when it occurs, without falling into other inconveniences: Take small baskets, such as those used for peaches and apricots sold in public markets, which are eight to ten inches long and four to five inches wide, with a one-inch rim; fill them with straw, and place them under the melons; these baskets stop the moth, which cannot pierce them, and the fruit benefits equally from the reflection of the heat that passes through. The timing of all these operations cannot be fixed; they depend on the season and on how far the plants have advanced as a result of the gardener's care; but they are self-evident. Pruning is also determined by need. Nothing is more damaging to the plant and the fruit, as I have already said, than the confusion of branches; they need to be unloaded exactly: in the ordinary course, they need to be worked on at least once a week; and when they are vigorous, every four days? but a lot of trouble is saved when, from birth, you pinch the branches exactly without letting them spread too much, and the fruiting branches show up just as well. When pruning, market gardeners usually cut the wood they are pruning about an inch from the mother branch, to avoid the mess of cankers that often form where the cut is made, and sometimes spread from branch to branch to the perishing plant. This method has its disadvantages, in that it dissipates the spirits by these kinds of slang, which are ugly moreover: the one I follow, and which seems preferable to me, in that the wound covers better, and a canker never forms, is to throw on it a little dry loam, pulverized between the fingers, or to apply a small piece of leaf from the plant, which stops the flow of sap to it, and which dries while the callus is forming; both are equally successful: However, I prefer the use of potting soil, in that the operation is done more quickly, and it remains firmly applied to the wound; instead of the leaf sometimes being disturbed by the shaking of other nearby branches, which are worked on one after the other. Moreover, this precaution is only really important for branches that are cut close to the base; for all the same branches, the risk would be too great, and there is no need. Although the season is advancing, you must not lose sight of the fact that you must always maintain the heat of your layers in a degree of heat that is more or less equal; because it is sometimes appropriate, until the month of May, to reheat them: but in this respect, you must operate in relation to the changes in weather that occur. For example, you may have put in a new stove at the right time, and then a few days of unforeseen chaleturs occur; this stove, as a result of the event, overheats your bed, and threatens the plant; this must be remedied diligently, either by removing it altogether or in part, or by providing plenty of air under the bells, and using suction cups. Finally, the need must determine the remedy, and from time to time the finger must be thrust into the layer to probe its heat, in order to regulate it more reliably. On other, quite opposite occasions, we are sometimes reassured by a few fine days which seem to herald the end of bad weather, and which make us neglect all sorts of precautions; but then cold days and equally cold rains occur: the bed becomes mortified, (in gardening terms) and the plant runs to its doom. You can't be too quick, on these occasions, to revive it with hot sumier stoves, mixed with pigeon droppings; and it's a good idea to make little stoves in them, as I explained in the chapter on Beds; at the same time, keep the plant well covered, until the bed has regained its heat. When the month of May arrives, it is quite usual to see the heat begin; and if it is such that the plants need some light watering, they must be wetted, but with great care and restraint, as I have quite insinuated, and never water during the strong sun, whose bells could suffer as much as the plant. The English are in the habit of only ever wetting the paths, for the same reasons as I said above, and some people also practice this in France: I think everyone would do well to follow this method; but, for the water to be able to communicate itself to the bed, the paths must be at least level with the surface. In addition, the best time to water is from 5 p.m. until dark, or in the morning from daybreak until 7 a.m., if you haven't been able to do it in the evening. It's also very important not to water with water freshly drawn from a well, or from some other reservoir; it must have been left to cool in the sun for a day, more or less, in barrels placed at noon, if you don't have some basin next to the melonnière. The quality of the water also contributes infinitely to the quality of the fruit. Hard, raw water is extremely detrimental to this, and the fruit that is fed on it is never good: The latter are much inferior to the former, and there is only one voice to agree on the cause; to which we can add that the market gardeners of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine wet them much less than those of the other Faubourg, commonly using only one waterway for twelve feet, while the latter use two or three. The layer, which receives neither rain nor dew, and which is uniformly hit by the sun in all its parts through the reflection of the glass, deteriorates much more than an ordinary layer, and consequently needs to be helped. But once the fruit has reached a certain size, it must no longer receive the impressions of water, and neither must the stalk, for the same reasons I have set out above; and to protect them from the damage they would suffer, here is my method. I have a dozen earthen pots, which I cover with preds and fruits, and I wet over them; a jug makes my rule for four feet: these four watered, I lift my pots and put them back on the next four, as for the rest. The operation is neither long nor difficult, and I protect my fruit from the bad effects of water. Some people throw pigeon droppings into the barrels in which they cool the water, and claim that this greatly advances the fruit. I have never wanted to do this test, because apart from the repugnance I have always felt, others have assured me that the effect was not such, and that moreover this droppings could impart a bad quality to the fruit. There are often fruits which become counterfeit by a whim of nature, so that the afflicted part falls as if in paralysis, hardens and hardly profits any more; which makes the fruit not only counterfeit, but also bitter and bad while ripening. If this is noticed early on, it can be remedied by making several cross-shaped scars with the tip of a knife on the curved part, which relaxes it and facilitates its extension: this operation quite often restores them; but if the curve is considerable, the shortest way is to remove these kinds of fruit and wait for better conditioned ones to come along. There are also fruits with a disposition to be bad without resource, they are called hard melons; they can be recognized by their shape which is almost round, and of a large black green. This kind of fruit is never worth anything, even though it is profitable and grows; it must be plucked: the good fruit must be drawn and elongated as it stops, of a light, plain green. If the fruit of the second sap doesn't do well, you have recourse to that of the third, which arrives on Midsummer's Day. If both fail, we fall back on the last, which comes at Magdeleine; but quite often the fruit of this sap does not ripen well. When the first fruits stop ripening, we must take care to cover them completely with a leaf; and if the leaves holding the base are too far apart, we cover them with one of the leaves we cut off when pruning. Violent thunderstorms sometimes occur in May and June, which are dangerous for the fruit and bells that the wind blows away, and which suffer even more when accompanied by hail: it is prudent to always be on guard, and not to move your straw mats too far away, so as to be able to throw them promptly over the bells when the weather threatens.

Here are a few special considerations that I should have placed higher up, but it is better to give them out of place than to keep them quiet. The first is to beware of sunburn, which is quite common in the first days of heat that follow the cold of March and April; its bright rays are a warning: you should then throw some litter on the bottom of the bells, keeping a little air on top: the same precaution should be taken in February, when, after having kept the beds open for a few days due to the harshness of the weather, they are uncovered on a sunny day: the plants, tenderized under the blanket, are soon surprised, if you don't keep a close eye on them. The second is to visit the roots of languishing plants, and when you find them chancie (which is the usual cause), you need to push the plant deeper into the soil: it sprouts roots from the collar, which restore it. The third is to be attentive to the changes in weather that often occur in April and May: during this period, warm rains bring new heat to the layers, however old they may be, and such that all the plants would melt, if care were not taken to give them air in proportion to their needs; you must therefore behave according to their degree of heat, and probe them often so as not to be surprised. Fourth: if you have neglected to sow the last seedlings in March, in order to have fruit in September, and you find yourself pruning your melons in May, you can plant the branches you are pruning to unload them, place them under a bell, not too far forward, and cover them for a few days, as if they were rooted plants: it will perish, but it will survive; that's what I've experienced several times. Fifth: once you've planted as many layers as you intended, if you have any left over, there's little risk of putting it in the ground under any good shelter; the fruit comes later, but is sometimes better than that of the layers, when the summers are hot; I've eaten perfect ones in some years up to the end of September, and last year (1749) I had quite good ones up to All Saints' Day: It's true that the year was very favorable; I also admit that in other years the trouble we took was pure waste, but it doesn't cost much to always try to bring them out. They should be covered with cloches, and cared for in the same way as diapers: when planting them, put in a handful of potting soil, and nothing more; little water, for the same reasons I have already stressed; and in this same position, a pipe covered with straw under the fruit is very necessary, because the soil always returns more freshness than the potting soil. Sixth: in the month of May, as I've already mentioned in passing, clouds often fall, which others call "nielles", and which attach themselves to leaves, stems and fruit, which contract spots in the places where they are trapped by this bad weather, and which ruin them. These clouds are caused by a few dews or cold showers in the morning, interspersed with a few rays of sunshine and a pale sun. As soon as you notice it, if you haven't been able to prevent it by covering your beds with straw mats, you should sprinkle them lightly all over; this water often washes away and corrupts this kind of venom; but if it has bitten so hard that it cannot prevent its bad effect, you must immediately cut off the branches and leaves attacked by it, as well as any fruit that is stained; for however small the stain may appear at first, it makes very rapid progress, and corrupts it completely: or if it stops, it makes the flesh so bitter that it cannot be eaten. Seventh: as the fruit nears maturity, and heavy rains fall, the best part of the fruit often melts and bursts, taking away all its external merit and even its goodness. As soon as the damage begins, and there is reason to fear for the future, the stem should be torn halfway through the wood with the fingernails, two inches from the fruit; this prevents the damage by preventing the sap from entering so abundantly: it is also necessary, as much as possible, to turn the head of the fruit towards the north, because this is the part where it usually cracks; and, as it is the sun which contributes much to making it crack after the rains, it is often preserved by removing the aspect of this star. Eighth: if you want to bring the fruit forward when it's almost at its full size, and has been fully embroidered, remove half the old stoves, and replace what you remove with hot manure; Eight days later, you can cut it, as this new manure has two effects that hasten the fruit's ripening: first, it burns the roots that were filtering through the old stoves, thus weaning it off some of its nourishment; second, it increases the heat of the plant, which helps it ripen earlier. The result of this operation is sometimes that the violence done to it deprives it of some of its quality, especially when very hot weather is pressing on it; but if the weather is a little cool, it is good although premature: besides, it would not be prudent to risk everything, we only risk a layer. Ninth: horseflies and moths, as well as rats and field mice, often wreak havoc in diapers. See Chapter 1 for remedies. When at last, after so much care, one has reached the point of enjoying one's work, that is, of picking the fruit, all that remains is to do it at the right time, and this is another little study: sometimes its maturity is announced by a change in color, that is, it goes from green to yellow; I don't mean a perfect yellow, which is the sign of a bad melon, but a yellowish or russet green: sometimes, too, there is very little change on the outside, especially in the case of the smaller varieties, which need to be picked greener than the larger ones, and which complete their ripening when kept for a few days. The sense of smell, which many people consult, is not always a reliable judge either; for it is more common for a melon to be overripe when it gives off a lot of odour, than for it to be overripe. Some others make up their minds on a few small cracks in the embroidery, similar to fingernail punctures, from which they 'augur well; but all these signs are equivocal, and even vary according to the years and climates: those who are not in the habit of handling them, like our market gardeners, who judge them quite reliably by eye, must try to cone tre the right point by testing. The most certain sign that I couldas, quer, but of which not all melens ger Tome II. is when the tail becomes encircled, that is, when it seems to want to detach from the fruit. The signs by which a melon can be judged are when the stem is large and short, in proportion to the species, when it looks well nourished, when it is heavy in the hand, firm under the finger, and precipitated by the sun; it should also be noted that a freshly cut melon can never have the degree of goodness that it acquires when kept for two or three days. Care must be taken to reserve the seed of the most beautiful fruits, and to take only that of the upper part, that is to say, that which the sun has struck, which is always more August than that below, and to take it only from the fruits of the first or second sap: this seed, which is cleaned as much as possible of its silt, must be placed in the shade to dry and improve, by stirring it from time to time; and when it is quite dry, it is locked in some place where mice cannot get at it: it is good for seven to eight years and more. It is said that the older it is, the better the quality of its fruit; however, many market gardeners sow it in the first year, when they have no other variety. Here's an important observation in this respect. Many people are accustomed to having the fruit they eat cooled in fresh water, or even with ice, and finding it good, they reserve precisely the seed; but it has been observed that this foreign and supernatural freshness alters the seed, and changes the species. I do not undertake to explain the reason for this: in many things of this nature, we must surrender to experience; for the obscurity of the cause does not destroy the effect: it is only a question in this, to go as far as possible, of removing the seed from the fruit as it is collected, which is easy. When you have to send melons a little way, you should take care to pick them a little green, as the road will finish ripening them; and you should cut their tails a little long, leaving even a few leaves. CHAPTER LII. Description of the MELONGEN; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. It is called Meringeane in Provence, Viédase in Languedoc, and Obergine in some other provinces. L 2 It is very common in all hot countries; but in this climate, it is grown only as a curiosity, and this is by default, as it usually succeeds very well: the Provençals nevertheless claim that it tastes better in their region; I leave them with this opinion; but according to my taste, there is little or no difference when summers are a little hot. There are four species; two with red fruit, one elongated and the other round; and two with yellow fruit, one round and the other long. I'll describe these four species separately, starting with the long red one, which is the most common.
