This plant has many long, whitish roots, packed with fibers; its leaf is water-green, covered on the surface with a kind of white powder like flour, elongated, up to seven to eight inches long, three to four wide, wrinkled all around without any serration, attached to long, thick tails; Its stem is thick and branchy, rising to two or three feet, and covered with leaves throughout its branches; its flowers emerge in large numbers from the body of the branches in clusters of 3 or 4, borne on a small pedicel. The flower is purplish, formed in a single piece, but cut in such a way that it represents six petals of equal size, pointed and wrinkled; its base is supported by a calyx, in the center of which rises a pistil, accompanied in its circuit by six species of yellow needles or stamens, which all meet at the tip in the shape of a keel; This pistil is then transformed into a full fruit, roughly shaped like a cucumber, but shorter, the color of a belle-de-nuit, sometimes striped with white and green, rounded at the tip, smooth and glossy, a little curved, with no odor; its flesh is white and soft, quite watery, with seeds arranged in two rows; The fruit's tail and calyx, which expands as it grows and envelops it to about two inches, are bristling with prickly red spines; the seed is small, round and flat, shaped like a small kidney, and whitish or russet in color. The second species is similar in all respects to the first, except for the shape of the fruit, which is round and slightly flattened, and the size of the finger. The third species differs in its fruit, which is round, a little egg-shaped and yellow in color, and in its leaf, which is much more indented; its stem is also less elevated and less dense; in all other respects, it is the same. The fourth species differs greatly from L 3 plus; its stem is very low, though roughly shaped like the others; its leaf is whiter green; it is also more indented, and its veins are lined with rough, prickly spines, both above and below; its flower is smaller, and its fruit of mediocre size, rather elongated. The fruit is greenish at birth, whitens as it matures and turns yellow as it ripens. The taste is more or less the same in all four species, although the yellow ones are more highly esteemed; they are widely consumed in southern countries: this does not, however, determine the excellence of this fruit; each nation has its own tastes, which often do not cross the border. This fruit is of a nature that should be neither overly praised nor overly despised; it is delicate, but tastes a little wild and bland at the same time. The best way to eat it in its natural state is to cut it in half lengthwise, remove the spongy substance where the seed is attached, when it is of a certain strength, and cook it on the grill over a low heat, gradually soaking it in oil or fresh butter, with a little pepper and salt, to which fine herbs are sometimes added: some use an anchovy that melts with the oil. This accompaniment goes a long way to correcting the blandness of the fruit, to which habit completes the taste. Some others cook it in the oven between two dishes, or in a tourtière, prepared in the same way as above; this preparation makes it less likely to smell of smoke. Here, it is more commonly eaten fried in a paste like artichokes, and in my case, it seems much better; but there is one preparation you need to know: as much as possible, the fruit should be chosen a little young; it should be cut lengthwise into thin slices, without removing anything; it should then be placed on a dish proportionate to the quantity, and sprinkled with coarse salt; it should be left in this state for five to six hours; The salt melts, and at the same time carries away the vicious juice of the fruit, from which a black liquor flows; we drain them, and squeeze them again in the hand, to remove the rest of the watery liquor from the pulp; after which we throw them into the batter, and from there into the frying pan. They are still very good and very delicate when cut into pieces, and mixed with meats in stews, and after having soaked for two or three hours in fresh water, and having been peeled beforehand; but they should only be thrown into the stew half an hour before removing it; if they remain there any longer, they will turn to mush. They can also be preserved for winter by drying them, and here's how. You cut them into slices, the thickness L4 of a finger, after removing the skin: you strip them well of their seeds, and throw them for a moment in boiling water; you take them out, and lay them in the sun on racks; after which you put them in a lukewarm oven. They are then placed in a lukewarm oven, where they are repeatedly baked until they are completely dry: they are then dried and, when you want to use them, they are cooked in lukewarm water. The plant and fruit, applied externally, are often used medicinally for inflammations, cancers, burns, hemorrhoids and to soothe pain. Cultivation of this plant is very simple in hot climates; the seed is sown in the open ground in good exposure, and the plant is then transplanted into well-prepared soil, with no care other than frequent watering: but in our climate, it should be sown early on a bed, and then replanted in a checkerboard pattern, eighteen inches apart on a soft bed, or at least in well-smoked and well-exposed soil, with care taken to wet it often in dry spells: moreover, it is not very delicate to raise; but at the first frosts in autumn, it perishes; that's why you need to bring it forward if you want to enjoy it safely. When summers are a little warm, it produces as much here as in southern countries, and the seed itself ripens quite well; but in tender years, neither the fruit nor the seed acquires its perfection, and it is always safer to take the seed from Provence or Languedoc. It should be noted that this fruit is only good when freshly picked; I have sometimes tried to keep it for several days, and I have found that it loses a lot of flavor: I even once brought some from Marseille to Lyon; it no longer had any flavor. CHAPTER LIII. Description of MUSTARD; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. MUSTARD, otherwise known as Senevé, is an annual plant. There are five main species: garden mustard, rabe mustard, arugula mustard, Spanish mustard and Siberian mustard. c Root mustard is woody, brittle, white and full of fibers; its leaves are similar to those of the L5 rabe, but smaller and rougher; its stem grows to a height of four to five feet, round, hairy, divided into several branches with small, yellow, 4-petaled flowers arranged crosswise; When these flowers have fallen, they are followed by rather short, angular and pointed siliques, filled with small, almost round, reddish or blackish seeds, rather like those of turnips, with a pungent, biting taste. Ache mustard has a simple, short, finger-sized, woody, white root, with many very long fibers; its leaves are similar to those of ache, laciniate, especially the lower ones, with rough, pungent hairs; its flowers are similar to those of the preceding species, but attached to longer pedicels, with a pleasant odor; the flowers are followed by hairy, pointed siliques, filled with very pungent, almost round, white seeds. Arugula mustard differs from the two preceding varieties in that the plant is weaker, the leaf cut like that of arugula, and the seed reddish; it is not cultivated in gardens, and grows naturally in stony, damp, maritime places. Spanish mustard is quite similar to the first species, except that its flower is the color of sulfur, and its siliques are smaller. Its seed is relatively so small that its shape is barely distinguishable. In botany, there are three other species of Spanish mustard, which differ in their foliage; but, as they have no interesting qualities, I'll pass over them in silence. Siberian mustard has the advantage over all the others that its leaves, though large and thick, are very good in salads. The first two are used only for the seed, which is also used in food and medicine. When prepared for the first use, this seed awakens the appetite and facilitates digestion: it is used with most meats, fish and vegetables. Pigs in particular require this accompaniment, however they are eaten; black pudding, sausages, andouilles and feet would be unbearable without mustard. It is also eaten with boiled beef; mixed with oil and a few fine herbs, it makes an appetizing seasoning for cold poultry, which we call remoulade: it also pleases in salads with celery. It is also used in salads with celery. L6́ with scorched onion to make a sauce much used under various roasted meats, known as sauce-à-Robert. Finally, although its pungent taste displeases some people, it can be said to please most, and to be useful and almost indispensable, with the health advantage of cooking food and having no harmful qualities. There are several ways of preparing mustard. Some, after crushing the seed, bind it with half-thickened sweet wine, to the required consistency: others dilute it with vinegar, and some add a little flour; it is in this last way that it is most commonly prepared in Paris, and for this reason it is called white mustard. The newer it is made, the better it is: however, it can keep well for quite a long time, if kept in a well-covered vessel. It comes to Paris from various provinces, particularly Dijon and Gien, which are more highly regarded; I don't know if this preference is well-founded. There is another way to prepare it, which extends its life to a year or more: here it is. Take two ounces of powdered mustard, and half an ounce of powdered common cinnamon; make a mass with flour, and a sufficient quantity of vinegar and honey, of which you will make small balls which you will leave to dry in the sun, or in an oven when the bread has been removed; and when you want to use it, you will soak one or more of these small balls with white wine and vinegar : you'll always have a mustard that's pleasant to the taste, good for the stomach, easy to transport, and particularly convenient for people who travel, either by land or sea. This seed is no less useful in medicine: it is a powerful sternutatory and a most effective machicatory: a dragmeg of this seed is enclosed in a cloth, after having been slightly crushed, and is chewed by patients threatened with apoplexy or paralysis; this remedy makes them spit abundantly; it also relieves those whose head is heavy and laden with pituitary. This seed is useful in soporific and lethargic affections; it is also good for people prone to hysterical and hypochondriacal vapors; it is used successfully in pale-colors, scurvy and indigestion; this plant is aperitive, stomachic, antiscorbutic and hysterical. Mustard, as prepared to enhance the taste of meats, is applied to the noses of people of both sexes prone to vapors, relieving them in their attacks; it also awakens the lethargic. The following poultice is a good resolver for sciatic gout, rheumatism and squirrelly tumors. Fry leeks with strong vinegar, after chopping them finely; and when they are cooked, sprinkle them with crushed mustard seed, and apply them to the ailment. Some people make a poultice from pigeon droppings, mustard and turpentine, and apply it to the areas where gout is felt; but wait until the inflammation has subsided. Such a poultice would be very capable of bringing back scabs, the suppuration of which, once removed, would have given rise to a deposit on the chest or some other part. The oil extracted by expression from mustard seed is effective against paralysis, and for resolving cold humors. There's nothing unusual about growing this plant: the seed is sown in March; and, as it's very fine, it must be sown very lightly: if you have beds, it rises earlier and more reliably; if you don't, it's sown at the foot of a well-exposed wall, in loose soil, or in a tub filled with compost: When it is strong enough to be planted, it is transplanted and cared for as usual. The seed is harvested at the end of August or in September, and left to dry out before being stored: it keeps well for sowing for two years. CHAPTER LIV. Description of the turnip; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. The turnip is the root of an annual plant of the same name. This root is of different shape, size and color, depending on the species; it is fleshy and soft, exhaling a pleasant odor; its leaf is a little elongated, deeply cut, rough and hairy, of a coarse green; it lies on the ground: its stem, which rises to two or three feet, is branchy and smooth, more or less large, depending on the species; flowers are born in abundance at the ends of its branches. This flower is yellow, sometimes white, with four leaves arranged crosswise; the calyx grows a pistil which becomes a silique when the flower has passed; this silique is composed of two panels resting on the edges of a partition, which divides this fruit into two chambers, filled with a few round, brown seeds. This fruit is very useful at the table; it is eaten fatty and lean, in many different ways: it is used in soups; it is used with meats of all kinds, but particularly with mutton and duck: it is prepared with white sauce and mustard; it is fried into a paste in certain countries: it is susceptible to all sorts of accommodations; and it is a healthy food, although it is accused of being a little windy. The turnip also has great medicinal properties; its decoction is very useful in broths for the chest: mixed with sugar, it forms a highly-prized syrup for soothing inveterate coughs and asthma. The way to make this syrup is to cut the turnips into wheels, rake them, fill an earthenware pot with them, cover it and seal it with paste: then put it in the oven, after removing the bread; leave it there for twelve or fifteen hours, and separate the juice at the bottom of the pot; on four ounces of this juice, throw an ounce of candy sugar which is left to melt, and take a spoonful on its own, or mixed with a glass of herbal tea: this syrup is sovereign for colds, as well as for softening the acridity of the chest. The seed of this plant is an aperitif: two large pieces are crushed and infused in a glass of white wine. The decoction of turnip also has the virtue of curing chilblains, when the feet or hands are washed often and warmly; others apply the cooked fruit as a poultice to the ailment. There are many species of turnip, of which I will reduce six, which are the best for our climate; I say for our climate, because there are some that are far superior, but which are only suitable for the vein of earth that produces them, such as the turnips of Ferneuse, Saulieu in Burgundy, Saint- Jôme, Gatinois, etc. We bring them in every year from France, France and the United States. Every year, turnips are brought to Paris from all these places; but they cannot be bred there, I mean to have them as good: the species degenerates, and all art cannot prevent it. Of all the plants, it is the one that is least accustomed to changes in terrain, and which grows best against all reason in places where the others only languish. The six species I have chosen are the small Berlin turnip, the Vaugirard turnip, the long white common turnip, the round turnip, the gray turnip, and the Meaux turnip. The Berlin turnip is very small, longer than round, and white; it is the earliest and best; it is not widely known; but those who have tried it prefer it to the others with justice: its taste is very spicy, and it is perfectly tender. The Vaugirard turnip is of mediocre size, a little elongated, dirty white, turning gray at the top, of good taste, and tender: it is very common in Paris, and highly esteemed. - 1. Common turnips, both long and round, are the most commonly grown in Aubervilliers and other neighboring towns, which supply Paris with them: there is little difference in quality between them, but the round variety is larger; the skin is very white, the flesh is soft and tender, and the taste is quite good. The gray turnip has a gray skin, as its name suggests, and a fairly elongated shape: it has its supporters who prefer it to the white variety, because of its slightly spicy taste; but it is not usually so tender, and is more prone to worminess. The Meaux turnip is the most profitable because of its size and length, which is commonly eight to ten inches; its exterior color is yellowish-white, its flesh very white; it is tender and has a very pleasant flavor: it is highly prized, but it has been noted that the one brought from Meaux is better than the one grown near Paris. These six species are cultivated in the same way: they are sown in two stages, in March and August; but in many soils, they do not succeed in spring. The lightest soil is the best for them: in strong, damp soils, this vegetable is almost always worm-eaten and tasteless; it is also important that the soil has been well tilled, and is healthy when sown: too dry or too soaked, the seed does not distribute itself evenly, and does not rise so well; and as this seed is very small, care must be taken not to spread more than is necessary; the best way is to mix it with three times as much ash or sawdust, and to spread it as evenly as possible; It should not be sown too lightly; moreover, when it has emerged and reached a certain point of strength, the plant should be thinned out so that there is a distance of about six inches from one foot to the other; at the same time as this operation is carried out, weeds are weeded out, and this double method is very important: I know that many people dispense with it, especially in the countryside, where whole fields are sown with it; but I also know that it's no better, and our market gardeners around Paris, who know how useful it is, are very exact about it: there's no other precaution to take. This plant is more usually sown on land that has yielded wheat, than in gardens; however, when you have a garden of a certain size, it is pleasant to have it on hand. It has a cruel enemy in the form of the lily; this insect devours both its ears as soon as it is born, and there is no longer any resource: to ward it off, it is suggested that ash be sprinkled on it, or chimney soot in the morning dew; a vain expedient, which I tried out a long time ago, without any success. The shortest way, when the damage has reached a certain point, is to give the soil a new look, to sow another seed which often has the same fate as the first, in which case you have to give up. This inconvenience is common in many soils, especially in dry years, and those who are aware of it must be careful not to waste time and seed. I have observed, however, that by sowing it late, i.e. after mid-August, this insect, which is beginning to retreat, no longer tires it so much. When it succeeds, the turnips are usually good two months later, and should not be left in the ground any longer, as they become ropey, or the worms get into them, or the field mice eat them: they are pulled out by hand, or with a flail if they are too big, and are closed in the greenhouse until needed, after having twisted their tops: those from spring are kept for the summer, and those from August spend the whole winter, being put in the sand. In Aubervilliers, market gardeners sow them in their enclosures, which they leave in the ground all winter, and they don't spoil as they do in many other areas. In countries where they are planted in large quantities, a hole is made in the middle of the room, proportionate to the quantity, and they are placed in it; they are then covered with thatch, and they keep perfectly well, provided that the rainwater has some drainage, and that the weeping of the soil does not flood them. Lovers of this vegetable sow them in beds as early as February, which they enjoy at the beginning of May: in this case, the bed must be filled with eight to nine inches of compost, and its heat must be considerably dampened, because if it is too hot, the turnips fork and become covered with small roots, which is a major defect. In Paris, we don't know another species of turnip, which is very common, and NAVET. Its color is white, both inside and out; its shape is flat, and its circumference is sometimes as large as that of a hat; it has a sweet and pleasant flavor, which outweighs that of all other turnips; but it is perfectly good only in soup; in any other sauce, it is not worth the turnip; however, country people, who are not very delicate, use it in every way. I don't know why it has never found favor in this climate, where it would be perfectly successful, having seen it tested in my own home and in the homes of others. I've heard a lot of praise for another species of turnip found in Germany, whose flesh is yellow like a carrot, and very tender; and I've been told that it's never worm-eaten, because it's attached to the earth only by the tip of its root, and the rest is protruding: those who are curious about it can find out more about it in the vicinity of Darmstad, where I've been told I've seen it. To collect the seed of all turnip species, choose the quantity of the most beautiful fruits you consider appropriate, and put them in the ground in March, a foot apart: they soon sprout their stalk, and the seed is good in August: you pull out the stalks, or cut them in the morning with the dew so that they don't fall off; you leave them to dry for a few more days, after which you beat them and lock them up: they only keep well for two years. CHAPTER LV. Description of the ONION; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Its root, which is the fruit itself, is bulbous, composed of several tunics, fleshy inside and membranous outside, of different colors and shapes, depending on the species, lined at the bottom with white fibers, filled with a subtle and very harsh juice, which grips the eyes and makes them cry; Its leaves are a foot or so long, fistulous, cylindrical and pointed, with a pungent taste like the root. When it goes to seed in its second year, it sprouts a bare, straight stem, three to four feet high, swollen towards the middle, bearing a fist-sized head at the top, composed of lily-like flowers, each with six petals, six stamens, and a pistil which then changes into a rounded fruit, divided into three chambers, filled with rounded, angular seeds, black on the outside and white on the inside. Everyone knows its uses for life; and its properties are such that there is almost no dish where it does not enter at least the juice; and, although there are people who fear it, its taste being softened with meats or vegetables, is bearable to its greatest enemies; and constantly there is little good sauce without the mixture of the onion. It can be used in all meat juices, in soups, to flavour broths, in green salads, and in salads cooked over charcoal, alone or with beet, capers and gherkins. In many countries, it's so popular that it's eaten raw like an apple: there's no other vegetable so widely consumed. Its virtues for health are no less remarkable: it is, by nature, a pectoral and aperitif, and sovereign in many illnesses. During the last plague in Marseille, it cured plague victims. The way to use it is to give the patient the expressed juice of an onion from which the heart has been removed, for which a little theriac has been substituted, and which has then been baked in an oven or under a tureen; as soon as it has been taken, the patient is well covered, and if he is happy enough to sweat, he is surely cured: for double safety, a similar onion that has not been expressed is applied to the bubo. Crushed with honey and salt, it's still a sovereign remedy for rabid dog bites. A famous contemporary physician also asserts that an onion cut into rouelles and infused in half a pint of white wine, taken on the last three days of the moon, is a proven remedy for nephritis. Cooked under embers and eaten with oil and sugar, it also soothes coughs and relieves asthma. Crushed with a little salt and applied to a recent burn, it stops the pain and prevents the formation of bells: the first can be followed by a second, cooked under ashes and kneaded into an ointment; the burned area is then wrapped with a cloth. The heart of a small white onion, cooked under ashes and applied hot to a damaged tooth, often alleviates the pain. For migraines, two onions chopped Tome II. M and soaked in wine spirit, applied to the head, dissipate the pain. Crushed and mixed with fresh butter, it also soothes the pain of hemorrhoids. Its expressed juice, soaked in absorbent cotton and placed in the ear, stops jamming. It also removes stains from the face and, when mixed with chicken fat, dries out the heels of mules. Nephritic colic is surely cured by having the patient take half a pint of white wine, in which an onion cut into pieces has been infused for two hours, and you're lucky when the ailment can give this infusion time. Eaten raw or cooked, it is very good against rheumatic pains in the kidneys. "These are its main virtues, which have often been tried and tested; there are still others that I'm not mentioning, but that's enough to show the merit of this plant: However, according to some doctors, its excessive use in food is harmful, in that it provokes wind and headaches through the fumes it carries, and causes restlessness during sleep: they consider it particularly contrary to bilious temperaments; everyone should be aware of the effect it has on them, and use it accordingly. There are nine very distinct species, and I could count more if I were not convinced that those I have left out are degenerated from the others, or that the difference between them is due to the climate or the quality of the soil. These nine species are the round Red Onion, the Pale; the round White, of which there are two species, the Early and the Late; the Long, which is of two colors, red and white; the Spanish Onion in the same way, and the small one from Florence. The red onion is the most widely grown in Europe, because it is the largest and keeps the longest: Its shape is round, a little flattened; its flesh white, veined with red, and its outer color reddish-purple; it is also the strongest, another reason why its lovers prefer it to the next one; but it does not have the same credit in Paris, where nothing in the foodstuffs is so dominant; so it is used very little: besides its color, which turns purple when it is cooked, displeases the eyes; however it is preferred for the juice. Carpenters prefer to use it to prepare their wares. The pale variety is shaped in the same way, but more flattened: its exterior color varies; some are straw-colored, with a hint of M 2 lemon, while others are a pale red: the first is the most esteemed by those who know it, because it is sweeter; but the other has the advantage of keeping longer: each therefore has its merit and its supporters, and it is the species that is most consumed during the winter. The cultivation of these two species is the same, and they are both sown at the same time; commonly it is only at the end of February, in light soils, and at the end of March, in heavy soils: they can also be sown in August, and transplanted in October; they are more likely to come this way, but they also don't keep that long. The soil must be well amended, and the fatter the soil, the more successful this vegetable will be; in sandy soils, it will not grow: however, care must be taken not to fertilize the soil in the same year as sowing, as this would scald the plant; soils that have been used to grow cabbage the previous year are very suitable for it. The land must be ploughed well on All Saints' Day, and a second ploughing a month before sowing, as the seed does not require such freshly tilled soil. We broadcast it on a fine day, when the soil is healthy, and we spread more or less of it, because a good part of it often perishes in the ground: the ordinary rule is to put two ounces on each plank fifteen toises long by six wide, on which we can settle. We must try to sow it evenly, and in calm weather; the way we bury it must be regulated according to the soil, and according to what we have or don't have to cover it: in soft soil, when the boards are upright, and you have nothing to put on top of the seed, you must first walk on them with your feet together, then spread the seed, and lightly harrow afterwards with the fork, without any other way; but if you have potting soil, you pass the rake after the fork, taking care to pass it very lightly so as not to move the seed, and you spread the potting soil on top as evenly as you can; a finger's breadth is enough. In heavy soils, it's best to sow the seed first on the rough ploughing, as it is: you then walk on it, dragging your feet a little, and harrow afterwards; and, whether or not you're terracing, you mustn't pass the rake over it, as rain and watering beat the soil too much when it's even, and cause it to split. It's a good idea to use potting soil or small amounts of manure in this kind of soil, especially when it's greasy and clayey, as it sometimes screeches and hardens to the point where the onion can't expand and remains almost like a ciboule. Potting soil also has the advantage of keeping the soil fresh, so that one watering has more effect than two when there's nothing on it. Three weeks after sowing, it starts to emerge, and some time later it needs to be weeded: it's a good idea to wet it afterwards, as water reassures the soil; even before weeding, if the soil is a little dry, it needs to be wetted, so that weeds can be pulled out more easily: When it's a little strong, we thin it out so that there are three inches between one and the other; this is what makes it big and well-rounded. When it finally begins to turn, i.e. to round out, you should stop watering it, unless there is an extreme drought, because too much water makes it tender and prevents it from keeping: in some countries, you don't even need to water it at all, but you should consult your own land. When the fruit is fully turned, and about the right size, you have to pull down and twist the stalk with your hands, over the fruit, or press your foot on it: others roll a barrel over the whole board; all this is pretty much equal, provided that the sap is interrupted, and remains in the root, which is more profitable. The people of Aubervilliers don't take this approach, and their onions are no less beautiful for it; but their terrain gives them privileges, as I've said on other occasions. When at last the leaf begins to fall to the side in case it has not been pulled, or begins to yellow, supposing it has been; without waiting, for it preserves better to be pulled a little green, especially the white; and, as it is pulled, the leaf should be cut a good two inches above the fruit, rather more than less : when it is cut closer, the heart grows; and, as it doesn't come to maturity all at once, it must be pulled in two stages, so that it is all set at the point it should be, and left on the ground lying clear for eight to ten days, to finish ripening; But if you fear that it will be stolen during the night, bring it close to the house and lay it out in a courtyard or under a shed, so that it can breathe and dry well. Those who have this convenience of being able to put it under cover, do even better to put it there right away, than to leave it in the open air; because, when the season is rainy, M 4 the humidity does it great harm, and it doesn't keep; this is what I've experienced more than once. Fifteen days later, remove it from there, and take it to the attic, or other place where it is to be kept; and another fifteen days after it is locked up, peel it, i.e., remove any earth that may be on it, and any loose skins, as well as the roots; because this sort of useless garbage sometimes heats it up and spoils it; cleanliness also requires it: It must also be stirred every month, and those that are beginning to sprout or rot removed; this little way, which gives it air, keeps it dry. If you have neglected this precaution, and have been surprised by the frost, you should not think that it has been lost, for it will return to its original state, provided you do not touch it until it has thawed out. There's another way to grow red onions that may seem surprising, but it's no less safe, because I've tried it. In June, when you thin out the planting beds sown in March, you pick up the onion you've pulled up, which most often gets lost; you lay it out very lightly in a well-ventilated place, and forget about it; you can even leave it out in the open in the garden, in some flowerbed, until autumn, when you cover it; The foliage dries out, but the stalk is preserved, and the onion grows to the size of a filbert, even though it receives no nourishment from the earth and is exposed to the sun and the air all summer long. It can be used throughout the summer, but would not be good for winter. To get the same onion in May, there's a second way, which I've also used several times, and which is just as successful; it's to sow a more or less large bed in the usual season, and to sow it so thickly that it touches each other: you let it come up without thinning it or wetting it, however much it seems to need it; you just have to weed it: This onion, which is pressed, remains small to the size of a hazelnut; we pull it out when it is at its peak, and treat it as I explained above; we then replant it in February, and it is good in May; but we must be careful, as it grows its upright, I mean the M 5 pipe that carries the seed, to cut it off at the level of the last leaves. Onions are of such a delicate nature, that in some areas, without taking any of the precautions I've just mentioned, they grow perfectly: our market gardeners in S. Our market gardeners in S. Denis and Aubervilliers, who have perfect soil for vegetables, do no more than plow it and then sow it: their method is to throw into each acre a pound of red onion, two pounds of pale, one pound of white and one pound of leek, all mixed together. They pull out the white onion first, which is the first to ripen, then the red, then the pale: the leek remains until Saint Martin's Day, when they dig small trenches, where they are kept all winter. The fertility of their soil is to be commended; but as there are few like them, we must not model ourselves on them; each must follow what experience has determined to be good in the terrain where he finds himself. There are years when most of the onion seed perishes, and when this happens you have to turn to your neighbors to make sure you're not left out in the cold: so you take what you can pick up from them when they thin out their beds, in May or June, and replant it; but you have to be careful in this respect: quite often this replanted onion succeeds well, and quite often it remains as a spring onion: everyone must know his own terrain; and those whose land, like mine, does not suffer from replanted onions, must not waste costs. There is a kind of capriciousness in soils that would be very difficult to explain; I know of some where this vegetable only does well when replanted, and many others where it can only succeed from seed; we must follow nature's indications, without always wanting to ask her for the reason for her operations. I've said all I can about red and pale onions; now I'll move on to white. There are two types, one of which is earlier than the other; they are distinguished by the leaf, the late variety having a much larger leaf than the other; otherwise, they are perfectly alike. These two species commonly come a little smaller than the red; both are cultivated in the same way, but are not sown at the same time. The early species is sown in July and August, up to mid-September, on light soil like our marshes, and replanted in October, three inches apart. It survives the winter very well, especially if covered with a little bedding or dry leaves during severe frosts and snowy weather, and starts to grow as soon as the fine weather returns: it is replanted in March, if it has lost some during the winter, and is good again in May. If necessary, weed it, and give it plenty of water; as it is not intended to be kept, we should only try to bring it forward and make it grow: this species supplies all summer, but when winter approaches, it is very prone to sprouting or rotting. So as not to lose anything, all those that start to grow should be planted on the coast in November and December: they stand up well to bad weather, and give their seed rather than the one that is replanted after winter; they supply themselves better, i.e., they grow more mounts. The late species can be sown in February and March, and the fruit can be stored over winter; for the rest, it must be cultivated and harvested with the same precautions as the red. These two species are the most prized here, especially as the fruit is sweeter; it is also the only one used from May to autumn, and is still eaten in winter. It is particularly appreciated as a large filbert, for garnishing soups and various kinds of stews: it is easy to obtain by sowing it very thickly; and, although it does not produce so much per bushel, it is not of lesser value, because it always sells for double or triple the price. If you sow it in July or August, make sure you don't water it again as soon as it's emerged; too much moisture causes the worm to grow and die. It should also be noted that the first crop sown in July never turns out as well as the one sown the following month; the only advantage is that, although it is less well formed, it is in a better condition to be used than the other. In addition, depending on the soil, you need to decide whether to sow it earlier or later; in light soils, you need to be in less of a hurry than in heavy soils. I said that the tai dive species would keep better over winter than the hâtive; but I must explain that it is as much as the latter was sown before winter; because, sown in March, it goes almost as far as the tardive. One, for example, is a fortnight or three weeks ahead of the other: this is a species originally grown in Grand Caire; another is harder, and more resistant to winter humidity, snow and frost. Another has the particular merit, when replanted for seed, of yielding extraordinarily well, so that one onion grows up to ten or twelve mounds, forming as many heads, while others grow only one or two. Another has the defect of coming double or twin, which makes it a poor seller. It is only in the long run, I confess, and after a particular study, that one can know these different qualities; each one, according to the idea which I give, and relatively to his views, will try to get the species which will be appropriate to him, by addressing directly the maraïchers, who make a particular traffic of this vegetable, and who are informed by their experiment, of all these differences. The long onion is not well known in the Paris area, but it is well known in Provence; it is almost wrist-sized and up to eight inches long, equal in size at both ends and in the middle. There are red and white varieties, the latter being the mildest and most esteemed; both are essentially good only in salads, or eaten with salt, according to Provençal taste. They are sown in spring, and cultivated like the others; but there are few soils suitable for them: they are kept all winter. The Catalan onion is good only raw, being very sweet: it is extraordinarily large, and spiky, both at the root and at the heart: there are white and red; it does not keep long; it is also cultivated like the others. The Florence onion is a small white onion about the size of a hazelnut, extremely soft and tender, which is eaten green throughout the summer in salads with lettuce: it is split in two with part of its leaf. It is the most weepy of all, and has the advantage of leaving almost no taste in the mouth. It is sown at different times to ensure a constant supply, and is sown very thickly; it requires nothing in particular for cultivation, other than frequent wetting. Onions of all kinds have one major enemy, which is the nightingale worm, and another small white worm common in light soils and dry years. These two insects suck and gnaw at the base of the plant, and sometimes kill entire planks; I know of no remedy. The mole also wreaks havoc in the early stages of the season, and must be kept on sentry duty to destroy it. It is also prone to clouding, an ailment that can neither be preserved nor cured. You must always sow more than less, and in different places; this is the only precaution you can take to avoid running out. Many gardeners are in the bad habit of mixing a little lettuce, turnip or carrot seed into their onion seed; it's easy to see that this does harm to the onion, because these overabundant plants consume the salts in the soil, and by their spread suffocate the plant in its youth; it's therefore a practice that needs to be reformed. Whether or not an onion comes into its own depends to a large extent on the quality of the seeds, which are often poorly ripened and not full, or too old, which is indistinguishable; and this is what you need to be very careful about: the safest way is to collect the seeds yourself. It is collected in August and September, from onions planted before or after winter, as they can be planted in both seasons, as I said above. The best place to plant them is on the south or east coast, six inches apart and about two inches deep in the ground. The custom of many gardeners is to place them flush with the ground; but, either because their method is worthless in itself, or because the difference in situations or soils contributes to it, I have tested both ways in the same row: the one that was flush with the ground was bare, and the other is perfectly fine; I therefore stick to my experience, and I advise everyone to do the same, to know more surely what to stick to. However, it is important to distinguish the season in which it is planted; onions planted before winter need to be buried less than those planted in spring, due to the humidity that causes them to rot when they are too far underground; I would also add, in this respect, that it is very dangerous to plant them before winter in damp soils; it is better to wait until the end of February. The onion planted in this way begins to grow its stem in May! By the end of June, when it is almost at its full height, and its head has formed, it must be supported, either by stilts to which several heads are tied together, or by running battens; for without this support, the hollow, weak stem is easily blown over by the winds: those who cannot find any wood of their own should at least tie five or six heads together with straw or rushes. Care must be taken not to bind them at the top until they have reached their full height, because if this is done earlier, the stem, which is stopped and cannot rise, will burst in the middle and perish. They should be weeded and watered occasionally in very hot weather, especially when planted along a wall: there is no other precaution to take until the seed has reached maturity, which is announced by showing the middle of the head; then it should be cut off, leaving a foot of stem to bind them together in bundles, and hang them on the floor or against a wall, head up, so that the seed does not fall off as it dries. But first, leave them to dry in the sun for a few days, spread out on a sheet; the seed that comes off naturally is the best, and it's a good idea to set it aside: as for the rest, if you're not in a hurry, leave it as it is until you need it; because the seed keeps for up to four years, thus remaining in its stuffing; and winnowed in the field, it hardly makes it through the second year. It's a good idea to always have a year's supply in advance, as it often fails due to the effect of the clouds that attach themselves to the stem, causing it to perish. It's better to sow in the second year than the first; it lifts more easily, and the fruit turns out better: when it's so new, there's a lot left over as chives. Description of the sorrel; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. The sorrel, known in some provinces as Vinette or Surelle, is one of the best-known and most useful vegetable garden plants. Four different species are grown: the large, the long, the round and the perennial yellow. The first, called the grande espèce or virgin sorrel, has an extraordinarily large leaf, up to eighteen inches long and five or six wide. Its color is meadow green, and its root yellow: it is little used in cooking, as it is hard and has little juice, making it more curious than useful; it is, however, agreed that it is sweeter than the others. This species bears no seeds, although it does grow a few mounds: it multiplies from old plants, which are divided into several. Long sorrel, which is the most widely cultivated, comes in two varieties, one with a much larger, blonder leaf than the other, known as Belleville sorrel; otherwise, they are alike in shape, with a long, elongated leaf, preceded by a long, slender, pointed, notched tail, with ears at the base, of meadow green, edged with red when it begins to grow in spring: its root is fibrous, long, yellowish and bitter. When it goes to seed in the second and subsequent years, it sprouts a three-foot-long, fluted, branching stem: it bears a number of petalless flowers, composed of several stamens topped with yellowish peaks, rising from a calyx composed of six leaves; the pistil that emerges from the middle then changes into a triangular, blackish, shiny seed, enclosed in a reddish, leafy, three-sided capsule. There is a third species, similar in shape and size to Belleville, but much blonder, and beginning to spread widely. The round sorrel is shaped quite differently from the preceding ones; its root is small, and runs between two lands; its leaf varies, sometimes being almost round, sometimes pointed and eared, sometimes earless; its color is sea-green, with a sour taste; its stem is low and creeping; but as far as the flower and seed are concerned, it resembles the long sorrel. The yellow perennial has a fairly large leaf, more round than long, and very blond. There is also a wild species that grows in meadows, which could be used in place of the others, although it is drier, harder and more sour. I know of another which is found in the gardens of the curious, and which grows as a shrub; its leaf is quite similar to that of the poplar, smooth, glossy, and plain on the edges, of a light green, which has more or less the taste of the other sorrels; but it is drier, and its most real merit consists in its rarity. The four main species I have described have more or less the same virtues and qualities: however, only the two long sorrels and the perennial yellow one are commonly used for living. They are used in soups, mixed with pear and other herbs: they make a stuffing that can be eaten under œuss, fricandeaux, and various fish: they are also used to color purées, and for many other purposes. Its sour taste awakens the appetite and is generally appreciated, especially as it has no unhealthy qualities. On the contrary, Elie is aperitive and refreshing, and its use is sovereign in bilious temperaments: it quenches thirst and stimulates the appetite: its leaf moderates blood fermentation, and relieves scorbutic patients, mixed in their broths with watercress and spoon grass or cochlearia; this remedy has often cured them radically, and the peoples of the North, who are very prone to scurvy, use it with great success. Stuffed with eggs, it is equally beneficial. Applied as a poultice with sourdough, after cooking under hot ashes in a cabbage leaf, it advances the suppuration of tumors, and suppurates eye humors. Soaked in vinegar and eaten in the morning on an empty stomach, it is a preservative against all kinds of contagious diseases: it also cures fickle fire by applying it to the diseased part after having thoroughly bathed it. Its decoction is excellent against the bite of rabid dogs; it must be drunk several times a day, and the wound wrapped in the leaf washed until healed: the same decoction is effective against jaundice, at a dose of one pint a day. Its root gives the water in which it has been infused a red color, which serves to deceive sick people who want to drink wine: it is also used in most apozemas and refreshing herbal teas: it helps blood circulation when it is thickened or slowed down. The pulverized seed, drunk with water and wine, stops dysentery: it even enters into the composition of many other remedies: and, in all respects, it is a most estimable plant, and one of which a vegetable garden should never be lacking. This leaf also has a number of special virtues: it removes ink stains from linen; it removes rust from copper and iron, and polishes them: used with sand, it perfectly cleans glass, and colors new parquet floors. When your teeth are irritated, chew a few leaves and the irritation passes. There's nothing unusual about growing this plant; it comes in all kinds of soil, and can be sown on the ground from March to August: however, it is very prone to perish from spring frosts, or to be eaten by loaches, when sown too early, especially in heavy soils; the safest thing is to wait until the beginning of May. It can also be sown in beds or in borders around quarries; but it lasts longer in borders, being more at ease and more aerated; it is even better to transplant it eight or ten inches apart than to sow it: it comes out more beautiful. Wherever it is planted, the soil must be well-prepared, loose and healthy; for its seed is so fine that, if there are any clods or stones, it will only rise in places. In the border as well as in the bed, we make small rays, slightly dug, and we spread the seed on them as evenly as we can, and very clear, which we cover with half an inch of earth at the most; we then put back on top a little compost, if we have some, or well broken dung : If the weather is dry, it must be wetted every day until it is well established. Some time later, we thin it out, if we judge it appropriate, and it becomes more beautiful. It is good to cut six weeks after sowing, and the more often it is cut, the more tender the leaf: but care must be taken to cut it close to the ground; it is better to pull it up when you have the time. Finally, it produces without interruption until the frosts: at that time, i.e. in December, it should be cut flush with the ground, and the beds should be completely covered with compost or henhouse dung; it comes out much more beautiful the following spring: for this reason, it is a good idea to have it in beds as well as in borders. When it starts to grow in February, it's a good idea to cover it with burnt grass; and if it is prone to being eaten by partridges, as it is in the capitaineries around Paris, where the game cannot be touched, it is necessary to spread a quantity of vine shoots over it, or to stretch a net, which can be made as long and wide as you like, and which rests on hoops pricked into the ground at both ends, from height to height, and tied together in the middle by a running batten: This is the expedient I resorted to, finding myself so overwhelmed by this game that it was impossible for me to see any sorrel or spinach leaves at home until April. The leaf is finally ready to be picked in February, a little earlier or later, depending on the year, so it must be plucked with its tail, not cut off; it provides until May, when its stem begins to rise; and if you don't care to collect the seed, you cut it off as many times as the plant throws out: it sprouts new leaves, which you use as the first ones: but as it has much more strength in this season than in the first, you need a much smaller quantity for the uses to which it is put. This plant can be kept for ten to twelve years, but care must be taken to cut off its head when it begins to age; it sprouts new suckers which rejuvenate it: care must also be taken to destroy the weeds that intertwine in its roots, particularly couch grass and tern. The seed of this species is harvested in July: it is cut when the calyx has turned from green to reddish-brown, and laid out on a sheet in the sun for a few days, to improve: others pull it by hand all around the stem without cutting it, and in this way it takes longer to collect; but it dries more easily, and takes up less space. It keeps well for two years if winnowed immediately, and for four years if left in its wadding. Birds are very fond of it when it's standing, so you have to defend it as best you can. When you buy this seed, you are often deceived, because it has been picked up in meadows, and this type of sorrel degenerates, for the most part, into patience. There is no mark to distinguish it, so you have to be on your guard. It remains for me to talk about the other two species. The yellow perennial, which is not subject to climbing like the previous one, is not subject to any constraint, and provides a useful supply in this vein of time when the old seedling is climbing, and the new one is not yet in cut; it is moreover less acidic and less green, and therefore pleases many people more; this is why it is advantageous to always have some beds of it. It multiplies by small shoots which are detached from the old plants, and planted a foot apart; the clump grows from year to year, and can be kept for ten years. Our market gardeners don't like it, because it takes longer to regrow than the other variety, once it has been cut; but when you have a certain quantity, you don't notice this defect, which is nothing for people who are not obliged to live as they do on the multiplied produce of their land. Rondo sorrel, which is where I end, can multiply from seed like long sorrel, but it is usually from its offshoots that old plants are detached: it is planted and cultivated in the same way; it also lasts up to ten or twelve years. Some people esteem it more highly than other varieties, but the fact that so little is eaten of it seems to rule it out: I attribute this to the fact that it has little juice, although it is good, N 2 as it is known to provide much less than the long variety. When we want to warm this plant, I mean the long one, to enjoy it during the winter, we have to lay out boards only two feet wide, at the sides of which we dig trenches twelve or fifteen inches wide and two feet deep, which we fill with warm manure, and change every two weeks, from mid-November to the end of January. In times of frost and snow, we keep the beds covered with dry manure, which we remove as soon as the weather softens or the sun comes out. It can also be replanted on beds after All Saints' Day, producing even faster and more abundantly. A bed, more or less, is set aside for this purpose, three feet high and filled with eight to ten inches of potting soil, on which parsley and other plants with strong roots can be transplanted at the same time. Some people are content to cover it with straw mats, supported on a trellis which they load with dry litter, in proportion to the severity of the weather; others put it under a bell; the latter is the safest way, both to advance it and to preserve it: in either case, you need to give it air as much as you can, otherwise the leaf grows white and has no taste. Sorrel is preserved for winter, mixed with other herbs, and is very useful in times of snow and frost. All the necessary herbs are picked at the end of August or September: sorrel, which should make up a third or at most half the quantity; pear, lettuce, spinach, purslane, parsley and chervil, in equal quantities, with a little spring onion, if you don't hate the taste. All these herbs are peeled and washed in several waters: they are left to drain and dry for a while, after which they are chopped coarsely: they are cooked without water in a pot which is filled to the brim, pressing them as hard as possible, taking care to make only a very small sill underneath so that they don't burn: from time to time, we stir them; and when they are sufficiently cooked, we put them in pots which we fill to within an inch, and which we immediately transport to the place where they are to remain; and when they are in place, we pour over them a thickness of about a finger of melted butter, or olive oil; we leave them in this state until they are needed; they keep perfectly well throughout the winter. However, it should be noted that, when they are covered with butter, they fan and toast easily as soon as the jar is opened: they should be eaten immediately; and for this reason, oil should be preferred, as it always comes to the surface, and keeps them in the same state for as long as desired. CHAPTER LVII. Description of the parsnip; its various species, properties, cultivation, etc. Parsnip, otherwise known as Pastenade, is a plant whose entire merit lies in its root. There are three species: the Long, the Round and the Siamese parsnip. The long parsnip has a very long root, almost equal in size throughout its length, white inside and out, uneven and rough on the outside, usually topped with a few filaments or small roots, giving off a strong, sweet smell; its leaves are deeply cut, toothed on the edges, and preceded by a very long tail where they hold; round, slightly fluted, light green and glossy, with no down: the parts of which they are composed are placed two by two, ten to twelve in number, opposite each other, and ending in an odd one; its stem is very thick, deeply grooved and branched, reddening a little on one side: At the end of the branches is a very large parasol, made up of small pink flowers with five equal yellow petals, surmounted by a few stamens, whose calyx turns into an oval, flattened cinnamon-colored fruit that lightens at the edges. The second species, called the round parsnip or panais à la royale, is equally shaped in leaves, stems, flowers and fruit, but the root is larger and shorter, resembling a round turnip. The third species, called Siam parsnip or parsnip bastard, differs from the first only in its root, which holds the middle ground between the other two, being neither as long as the first nor as short as the second, but much more swollen on the head side than in the rest of its length: its flesh is also a little more yellowish. Cultivation of this plant is no different from that of the carrot. It is also sown in two seasons: what I have said for the one will serve for the other, and repetition would not be more instructive. All three species are very good; however, the Siam parsnip is more highly esteemed, as its skin is thinner and its flesh more tender and mellow: in addition, the N4 PANAIS. terrain must play a large part in the choice, as I observed for the carrot. It is also used for soups and juices; but it is not usual to eat it fricasseed or stewed with meats; its sweet taste pleases some, but not most. Beware that there is a sort of nerve in the heart of the root, which must be removed by cutting it, as it is unpleasant for those who eat it. It is of little use in medicine; however, its seed, which is carminative and diuretic, is used in the same dose as aniseed, along with all the other minor hot seeds, which are used to dissipate winds and vapors, to soothe colic and to stop the running of the stomach: but, although it is recognized as good, the seed of the wild parsnip is preferred. This root has no fear of frost, so only as much as can be consumed during the rigors of winter should be kept in the greenhouse. In March, however, the quantity needed to produce seed should be removed, and immediately replanted like carrots, a foot or eighteen inches apart. Then, in July, when the stems have reached about their full height, it's a good idea to support them with stilts, otherwise the wind will blow them over and ruin them. The seed ripens at the end of August, and is only good during the first year, that is, for the two seeds of March and September. CHAPTER LVIII. Description of PATIENCE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. There are eight species of Patience, which I will reduce to three that are the only ones cultivated and the most useful: these are the common Patience, otherwise known as Parelle; the red Patience, also known as Sang-dragon; and the garden Patience, known under the two names of Mountain Rapontic or Monk's Rhubarb. All three are perennial. The first species has a straight, long, thick, yellow, bitter-tasting root; its leaf is roughly similar to that of sorrel, from which it derives its original origin; for we still notice every day that it often degenerates into patience in sandy soils: this leaf is nevertheless longer, firmer, narrower N5 and more pointed, with a bitter and very sour taste; its stem is gnarled, and rises to four or five feet; its flowers are placed along the branches and in rings; They are small, petalless, and composed of six short green stamens with straight white tips, which emerge from a seven-leaf calyx, as in sorrel; the pistil then changes into a triangular seed, enveloped in a membranous capsule composed of three large calyx leaves. This plant is cultivated in gardens, to mix with sorrel and other herbs, but few people use it: it is mainly intended for health purposes. Its root is an aperitif and laxative: it is used for dropsy, pallor, jaundice and other diseases caused by obstruction: it is also used externally for scabs and gravel. Red patience is quite similar to the previous one in some respects; but the leaf is shorter, and crossed by a number of red veins, from which, when broken, a blood-red juice emerges, giving it its name. It is used in food, like the previous one, mixed with other herbs, and is very useful when you need to keep your stomach a little loose. It is also sometimes prescribed in emollient and refreshing broths. Its seed strengthens, tightens and soothes pain: a dram or a dram and a half is taken in any suitable liquor, to stop excessive discharge from the womb, and belly flow accompanied by trenches. A learned author claims to have cured a number of people suffering from the latter disease, by macerating half a drag of this seed in hot wine, which is passed over before drinking. Garden patience, or rapontic, has a long, thick, multi-fibered root, brown on the outside and very yellow on the inside; its stem rises to a man's height; it is fluted, reddish, and divided upwards into many branches; Its leaves are a foot to a foot and a half long, broad, pointed, firm and smooth, dark green, sometimes folded over at the edges, but plain and without crenation, borne on long reddish tails; its flowers are petalless, with stamens similar to those of sorrel, placed all around the branches. The flowers are followed by angular seeds enveloped in membranous follicles. This plant has almost the same principles as bastard rhubarb, whose virtues it also shares. It fortifies the stomach and aids digestion; it slightly purges Nó the bile, is highly astringent, and lifts obstructions of the liver, either by dissolving thick humors or by restoring the tone of slackened fibers; it is also sometimes very usefully employed, in powder or decoction, for flux of the stomach and obstruction of the viscera. The dose is half a dram in powder form, or one and a half drams in infusion. This plant grows naturally on mountains, and is also widely cultivated in gardens. Its cultivation, like that of the preceding plants, requires nothing special. All three are sown in March, with the same care as sorrel. The seed is harvested in August, when the stems are dry and the seed begins to detach. It keeps well for two or three years. CHAPTER LIX. Description of the PERCEPIERRE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. PERCEPIERRE is called by various names: Passepierre, Bacille, Criste marine, Fenouil marin, or Herbe de Saint-Pierre. There are two species, both perennial; the large ex the small. The first has a large, long, woody, whitish root, with a few fibers; its stems are from fifteen to eighteen inches long, paddle-shaped, thick, woody, and usually fall to the ground; its leaves are cut, small, narrow, firm, fleshy, subdivided three by three, watery green, with the odor of ache, and a salty taste; its flowers are born in umbels, made up of a large number of leaves.After the flower has passed, the calyx changes into a fruit filled with seeds that are joined two by two, flat, striped on the back, white, fragrant and pungent-tasting. The second species, which is more commonly cultivated than the larger one, grows to no more than a foot, and is much broader; its root is quite similar to the preceding one; and its leaves are likewise narrow, fleshy, subdivided three by three, but a little wider, green-brown in color, with a salty taste; its flowers are arranged like the other, and yellowish in color: it grows, like the previous one, by the sea in rocks that it seems to pierce, from which it gets its name of percepierre; but with care, it also succeeds in gardens. Its life uses are limited to winter salads, where it is mixed with anchovies, beet, capers, gherkins and so on. Pickled in vinegar, it stimulates the appetite and flatters the taste. It is candied in the same way as gherkins, with which it is usually mixed. Its medicinal properties are scarcely more considerable; however, it is one of the aperitive plants, and is used to cure obstructions of the viscera, for gravel, to alleviate kidney and bladder stones, to stimulate urine and women's months, and for jaundice. In the absence of the candied variety, take a decoction of the leaf, root and seed. It is propagated from seed, which is sown on a bed in March, or in pots filled with potting soil, exposed to full sun; when it has reached a certain strength, it is transplanted to the foot of walls facing south or east. It must be raised with care, as it is very delicate in this climate: the open air and cold are harmful to it; it is therefore a good idea to cover it with some foliage during frosts. Its leaves are cut off at the end of summer, when you want to make use of them. There is no garden, however small, where parsley does not have its place, marked by its continual usefulness in a household. There are six types, namely Common, Big Leaf, Big Root, Macedonian, Curly and Mixed parsley. Common parsley has a long, white root, fairly straight, with a few fibers; the leaves rising from its heart are numerous, extremely indented and toothed, and composed of three or four pairs of small thresholds, arranged on a rib ending in an odd number; The rib is small, rounded on one side and fluted on the other; the stem is thick, fluted and branched; it reaches three or four feet high: the tops of all its branches end in a bouquet of umbrella-shaped flowers with five unequal petals, russet in color, borne on a small calyx that changes PERSIL. into a small, round, gray seed with a very strong odor. Parsley with large leaves is similar in all respects to the preceding variety, except that its leaves are much larger. Parsley with a large root is also similar to the first, except that the rib of its leaves is larger, and its root is also three times as large, as is the seed. There are two species, one with an early green leaf, the other a coarse green. Macedonian parsley has a leaf that is more regularly cut, more hairy and more serrated, and its segments are more rounded and pressed together; its color is also less dark, and the rib is covered with a white down. The tops of all its branches end in bunches of whitish, five-petaled flowers, arranged in a parasol shape, in the same way as common parsley, but larger: its seed is also different, being elongated, swollen at one end and pointed at the other, rounded on one side and convex on the other, ash-colored, and with a strong, odorless flavor. Curly parsley has the same leaf shape as its name suggests, and thus resembles curly cress; moreover, it is shaped like the common variety: same stem, same flower and same seed. The variegated variety imitates the common variety in all respects, except for the color of its leaves, which are mottled with white veins tending to yellow. Of these six species, common parsley is the most commonly cultivated, although they all have more or less the same virtues and properties. It is widely used in cooking to enhance the flavour of meats, fish, eggs and most vegetables: this is its only life-giving property, as it has no inherent appeal as a substitute for food; its root is also used in many stews, and gives a very good flavour to soup. This plant has many health benefits: a decoction of the leaf and root, taken as a drink, provokes vomiting and clears the passages that lead to the heart; the chopped leaf, mixed with breadcrumbs and a little water and placed in a pan over a fire, cures scabs and resolves hardness of the udder; the same remedy causes women in childbirth to lose milk. Its crushed leaf, mixed with a little brandy, is sovereign for cuts and all kinds of wounds, as well as for bruises; it also removes the stench of breath, or at least stops the bad effect for a while. Its root is used in herbal teas and aperitif broths, and its decoction is very useful for smallpox and malignant fevers. Its seed is one of the four major hot seeds, and is also used in the composition of several remedies. This plant is very easy to grow: the seed is sown in March or April, either in borders around quarries, or in beds two inches deep, with five rows in each five-foot bed. Our market gardeners sow it broadcast to get more profit out of it, but it's cleaner to lay it out as I say, and at the same time gives the ease of crimping the plant in its youth, besides being more convenient to cut in this situation. It sprouts after three weeks: weed it, wet it, crimp it until it has taken the upper hand, and then leave it to grow at will, without further care. Any kind of soil is almost equally suited to it, provided it is a little loose, and it requires no expenditure of manure; but if you are abundantly supplied with compost or fine manure, it is not useless to put some on top of the seed, especially in soils prone to cracking. When you want to make use of the root, you need to thin out the plant a lot after it has gained a certain strength, so that it can grow; and you pull up part of it on the eve of frost, which you take to the greenhouse to find it if you need it. Care should be taken in September to cut it flush with the ground, so that it can regrow new leaves in the autumn; they are softer and greener: but in this case you must be prepared to cover it with plenty of litter in times of frost and snow, otherwise it will perish; and if you are not in a position to do this, it is much better not to cut it: its old leaves serve as a shelter for the heart and preserve it. Those who want to heat it on a bed to have it all winter, must take care to pull it out before the ground is sealed by frosts. Replanting is very simple: you put eight to ten feet of it under each bell, after having shortened the root a little, and cut all the foliage down to the heart: it picks up easily and soon sprouts new leaves. Air the plants as much as the weather allows, or at least uncover the bottom of the bells for a few hours. After three weeks, the plant can be cut, and it always grows again as long as you leave it, provided you keep the bed warm; but after February, the plant in the ground starts to produce, and no longer needs to be forced; it only needs eight to ten inches of potting soil. This plant doesn't come up in the first year, and the more you cut off its leaves, the more it grows back; but in the second year it makes its stem: however, when you cut it off in May, the stem grows suckers that last for another year: this means that it doesn't give any seed; but when you leave it free, it starts to come up in May: it flowers in June, and its seed is ripe in August. The stems are cut off at the base, and left for a few days exposed to the sun, spread out on a cloth: this precaution is necessary, otherwise more of the seed will detach and be lost; it is then winnowed and enclosed: it keeps well for four or five years. Parsley leaves are dried in October, to make up for the green ones in winter, and give the same taste to the stews in which they are used. The best way to dry them is to throw them into boiling water for a while, after they have been thoroughly washed and peeled, lay them out in the sun on racks, and then put them in a warm oven; after which they are locked in a dry place, wrapped in paper bags or boxes: others dry them in the shade, tied in bundles and hung from the floor. Now it's time to talk about the other species. Large-leaf parsley has all the virtues and properties of the common variety, and grows in the same way; but it has a defect that has caused it to be abandoned, which is that it aborts in the heart after it has sprouted its first leaves. For this reason, our market gardeners don't grow it. Parsley with a large root is not sufficiently well known in France, and it is inappropriately neglected. The Germans are justly fond of it, and it is the species to which they are most attached: its leaf has no particular merit, but its root, which is about the size of a carrot, and is therefore of great benefit, has the double advantage of being softer and sweeter. It is used in all soups, and gives a perfect taste to the broth: it is also mixed into many stews, where it has a very useful place. There are two species; the dark green leaf is the most cultivated, because it is more resistant to frost than the other, which is prone to yellowing and perishing. Macedonian parsley is not used in green like the others; its taste is different too. It is only used in salads, and even then only after it has been blanched. To make it white, we cut off all the leaves on All Saints' Day, and cover it with a thick layer of dry straw, which we increase in proportion to the weather, so that frosts cannot reach it: it grows new, tender yellow leaves under this covering, which we cut a month or six weeks later. Its taste is not to everyone's liking: we don't even see it in public markets any more. It is sown and raised like any other; it is not very delicate and can be grown in any kind of soil. Curly parsley has the same taste as the others, and can be cultivated just the same; but it has the disadvantage of being very tender in frost, and of perishing easily, which means that it is little cultivated. The variegated variety is more or less the same in taste, but it is very delicate to raise, and yields little: these two reasons prevent it from being grown. There are also two species of parsley that grow naturally, known as Wild Parsley and Marsh Parsley, which are not used for living, but are used for many purposes in pharmacy. As they are not allowed in gardens, and the others are sufficient for our purposes, I will not say more about them. Description of PIMPRENELLE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Pimprenelle is only a salad ingredient, but it is aperitive and refreshing; it purifies the blood. Description of POIREAV; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. THIS plant, which some call leek and others porreau, forms an upright, united and compact body, which is composed of leaves pressed and stuck together, and turned round to the size of a finger; it rises to nearly a foot and a half; and retains the same consistency at 6 or 8 inches from the ground; it then develops, and throws out leaves whose tips fold back against the ground, which are long, narrow and gutter-shaped, bluish-green, smooth and fairly thick, bearing a strong and unpleasant odor: All that is in the ground is white and tender, and this is the best; the rest is green; however, it is used like the foot as long as it has consistency. There are two types of leek, long and short, which differ only in length. The long leek, however, is the most cultivated, because it provides more by its length; but the short one also has the merit of being more resistant to frosts; and for the end of winter, it should always be preferred; it also has the advantage that the worm doesn't attach itself to it so much. The long one should occupy the stage until the frosts. In all likelihood, these two species originate from the wild leek, commonly found in vineyards, and have been perfected through cultivation. In some provinces, it is eaten green in its earliest youth, without having been replanted, and is preferred to the white variety: everyone can be satisfied in this respect, as the taste is the same at all times. As Christmas approaches, we pull up the large species, which is very prone to perish on the vine, and bury it close by in a small trench, which we cover with litter during the frosts; but we leave the short one in place, because it resists bad weather, and keeps well until it goes to seed, i.e. until May: However, we take care to dig up a certain quantity and bury it in the greenhouse, to supply it during the frosts, if we don't have any of the larger species enclosed. After winter, you mark the quantity you want to let go to seed, and destroy the surplus if you have too much. It's good for 2 years; but if you keep it in its shell attached to a floor, as some people do for onions, it keeps for three or four years. Description of PCIRÉE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. THIS plant, called Bette in several provinces, is an annual: two species are grown, the white and the red. The white pear has a cylindrical, woody, white, long, thick root; its thresholds are large, broad, smooth, succulent; sometimes yellowish-green, sometimes true green, nitrous in flavor, odorless, with a thick, broad, white rib; its stem is fluted and branched, rising to 3 or 4 feet: its flowers arise from the leaf axils on long spikes; they are small, composed of several stamens topped with yellowish tops, and emerge from a five-leafed, greenish calyx, which then changes into an unevenly round, gravelly, ashy or russet seed the size of a pea. Red pear differs from the previous variety in that its leaf is smaller, reddish-green and the rib is bright red. It is of no use for life, and is only used medicinally when the former is lacking. The white variety is used in food, where it is mixed with sorrel to soften it, either for soups or stuffings; it is mild and very healthy. Its health properties are much more considerable: its leaf is emollient, soothing, laxative, desiccative and abstersive; it is used in ordinary decoctions and in enemas; its particular juice, well strained and purified, given in a clyster, is singular for emptying fecal matter that resists other laxative clysters; the leaf applied externally to the skin, when it has been removed by bladders or O4 caustics, facilitates the draining of the humor: it can also be applied to a tumor to attract the matter, and is a great help in bringing it to an end: it is also used against inflamed hemorrhoids; and if it doesn't make them suppurate, it at least dissipates the inflammation, and makes them withdraw; it's a good idea to steam them beforehand with the expressed juice. Sucking the juice through the nose, mixed with a little salt-free pot broth, unclogs the ducts and dissolves the pituita that has thickened there. A piece of the rib or root chopped and crushed in the same way, and introduced into the nostrils, has the same effect.
