The juice of the root is a good sternutatory, and when used with its pomace in the nostrils to relieve migraine or headache, it brings great relief by draining the serosities. The root is also used to loosen children's stomachs; to do this, a piece must be introduced into the foundation, after having been sprinkled with salt. This plant is very easy to grow, and any soil is good for it, as long as it is prepared with a good ploughing. It is sown in March in light soils, and in April in heavy soils. It can be sown broadcast, as our market gardeners do, or in rays eight inches apart, as is more common in private gardens: the latter is more convenient for crimping and cutting. Six weeks after it has been sown, you can start using it; and in this season, when the root is still weak, you cut it flush with the ground: it sprouts new leaves, and the more often it is cut, the softer and smoother the leaf becomes; it becomes hard and dry when it is old. It can be sown every month until August, and this last sowing is the one that yields the most and the most abundantly the following spring; but it is also more delicate to overwinter; it must be covered if you don't want to run the risk of losing it. The first plant, sown in March, is stronger and more resilient, but yields later; this one should be cut to the ground in September, so that it can regrow new leaves in autumn. After the frosts, the one that has been covered is uncovered, and given a little shaking to start it growing; when it is ready to be picked, the leaves are blown off at ground level, without the use of any instrument; the heart grows successively for two or three months, and when it begins to curl up to make its amount, it is abandoned; the new seedling then replaces the old one. 5 Pear for chard is a particular species of which there are two types, one extremely blond, the other darker in color, called demi-verte. The first has a wider, softer rib, but it has difficulty surviving the winter; the second is a little less perfect, but it is much more resistant to frost: the blond should therefore only be sown in spring, to be enjoyed in summer and autumn, after which time it is destroyed, with only a few plants left for seed, which is covered as best as possible during the winter: the other should be sown at the end of June, and replanted in mid-August, in borders or beds, eighteen inches apart in all directions, after cutting off half its leaves and the root tip. Both require frequent watering during hot spells, which is what makes the rib tender; during frosts, it must be covered exactly with dry litter, and in spring it is uncovered little by little in the same way as Partichaut: its carding is good by mid-May. Our market gardeners cut off the entire stalk, because custom forces them to do so, and because it would not be saleable in detached leaves: it might also be thought that it is the need they have for space in this circumstance of the weather, which gave rise to this custom; but private individuals who are quite happy to extend its duration, should be content to burst the widest leaves, pulling them to one side; those that remain around the heart strengthen, and are good successively for a month or six weeks. When it finally begins to rise, mark the plants you wish to keep for seed, and destroy the rest. 2 Many people, and our market gardeners in particular, plant these chard plants between their artichokes; I do not approve of this method, for the reasons I gave in the chapter on artichokes. Many people particularly like it with Gruyère or Parma cheese, grated on top: many others don't like it at all; it's true that it's a bit bland, and even in some areas it smells only of earth. This plant, both the simple pear and the two species of chard, multiplies only from seed, which is collected in September from overwintered plants; as they spread out and rise very high, they must be tied to stilts to support them, otherwise the wind will blow them over: they are cut when the seed is partly ripe, i.e. when it turns from green to an ashen or russet colorâO6 POIS. They are then left in the sun for a few days, and immediately locked up. It keeps well for 8 or 10 years. CHAPTER LXIV. Description of the pea; its different species, cultivation, etc. Although peas are widely known and cultivated almost as much as wheat, in order to follow my plan of giving an exact description of all vegetable plants, I will describe this one. The pea in general, of all species, is conformed in more or less the same way; its stem is single, smooth, hollow and weak, rising more or less, according to the species; its leaves are of a small bluish or celadon green, placed from distance to distance along its stem: the leaves are of a small bluish or celadon green, placed at intervals along the stem: they first form two kinds of ears attached to the stem, and from the middle emerges a rib which throws out four or six oval leaves, placed regularly at its sides, and ending in several tendrils which serve to cling to the others to support itself, when it doesn't have the help of oars: from the armpits of these same ears, higher or lower, depending on the species, emerges the flower whose calyx is a toothed cup, which grows the pistil; this flower is composed of four unequal florets, whose color is white or red, depending on the species, marked with a purpurine spot : each floret is usually composed of two equal flowers, sometimes only one, and along the length of the stem there may be as many as six or eight: these flowers are followed by the pod which contains the pea, which is more or less elongated, depending on the species. If this vegetable were as beneficial as it is pleasant to eat, I think most people would want to eat it all year round; but it is rightly criticized for being windy and indigestible: this does not prevent people from being extremely keen on them, especially in the new market, where they are sold in Paris for as much as 100 and 150 pounds a litron, a measure that contains about three half-setiers, or three quarters of a pint. Peas in general are of little use in medicine, apart from chickpeas and lupins, which I'll discuss in more detail; however, their flour is substituted for that of lupins and vetches when necessary; it is equally resolutive and emollient; its decoction is also laxative and soothing. Some claim that peas of all kinds soothe coughs, and one author maintains that they are useful for epileptics. For those who suffer from gravel, they must be avoided at all costs. There are an infinite number of species, of which we know only a few here; but we can make do with the ones we have: besides, nature likes to discover new ones from time to time, or, if you like, to produce new ones, such as the Baron, the Dominé and the Michaux, named after the farmers who discovered them today. These three species are the earliest to ripen, followed by the Lorrain and the Suisse. I will reduce the other most commonly sown peas to the small number of the best that do well in our vicinity, and that can suffice for all seasons; except for those who have other species more suited to their climate and terrain, to cultivate them. I therefore chose the common pea, the Normand, the white and green quarrels, the culpoir, the English green pea, the longuecosse and the pea without parchment. These eight species are all perfectly good, each in its own season. I'll say a word about their cultivation in general, before moving on to their specific cultivation. This grain, though rustic in appearance, must not be planted indiscriminately in all types of soil; it requires a certain combination for sowing; some species require light soil, another wants it to be a little oily, and another is better suited to soil that holds the middle; but all agree in wanting to occupy the same land only from time to time: well-meaning farmers make it a rule to sow their land with this vegetable only once every six years, and this is their method. One year they bring in wheat, and the next year beans; the third they sow in rye or March, and the fourth in vetch or broad beans; the fifth in oats or barley, and the sixth in peas; so that every year, out of six acres, they have one in peas, for which they choose the species appropriate to its vein; And when they have to turn over a meadow, uproot a vineyard or destroy a wood, that place is always reserved for peas, because they don't do any better than in this kind of new land; because manure, which helps other vegetables to bear fruit when the soil is tired, is harmful to them, far from being advantageous; these peas are carried away in wood, and don't bear fruit. This vegetable, more voracious than any other of the earth's natural salts, cannot tolerate any borrowed salts, such as those found in manure. What I have just said should serve as a rule, from the most to the least, for those who grow it in their gardens, to distribute the land they have, so that each year they have a place sufficiently rested to sow this vegetable: If they are careful, they will recognize, as I have often found, that one pole of soil used at the right time will yield more than four used at the wrong time; it even happens sometimes, when you persist in putting it in the same place for several years in a row, that it turns yellow as soon as it sprouts, and yields nothing at all. In small gardens, it is usual to grow a few early peas; but in large plots of land with large houses, it is very common to sow whole quarters of them to supply kitchen needs all year round, and their cultivation is then the same as in the fields; The same species are also used, which is why it's a good idea for me to outline the practice of our farmers with regard to each species in particular, and to begin with everything that relates to their cultivation in general, following the plan I've started with. Peas can be sown in two ways: with a plow or a hoe. The first is not suitable for a garden, so the hoe is the best, because it loosens the soil better. Two people are needed for this operation; one opens the gauge from one end of the square to the other, and the other, who follows, spreads the seed as the square is made; once the gauge is finished, the second is taken up, and the same earth that was lifted is used to cover the first: it is seeded in the same way, and as long as there is land, the same procedure is continued. But, as in a garden we want all the plants to have a certain air of arrangement, which at the same time facilitates the small operations they require, such as crimping them, watering them as needed, picking the fruit, etc., it is advisable to leave an inter valle for the paths, after four rows of seed have been sown. Many gardeners do not know how to handle the hoe; this tool is not known beyond the outskirts of Paris; in this case, four-foot planks must be drawn up, and four rays equally spaced from foot to foot and two or three inches deep, either with the hoe or the corner of the rake; and after spreading the seed and walking it, it is covered with the rake; the soil must have been freshly ploughed beforehand. Eight or ten days later, the seed sprouts, and when the plants are five or six inches high, they should be crimped and shod, making sure that the weather is fine, so that the weeds die right away. If you want to row them, go back two days later, when the weeds are burnt, and plug the oars, making sure to lay them down inside, two by two rows, one on top of the other, so that they don't obstruct the pathways: at the same time, the fruit that follows the oar is picked up more easily on the pathway side. I'll move on to the description of the species, and start with the Michaux pea, which gardeners take great pride in presenting first to their masters, or which is bred mainly by those who make peas an object of their small trade, and who sell them dearly in the primeur, as I've already noted. This pea is white, round, plain, fairly large, very tender, and sweet when eaten green, but of mediocre value, especially as there is usually only one pod in each bunch, and they are stopped at the first blossom, so as to have the fruit instead: it is almost the only one that is grown today for early harvest, although it competes with Baron and Dominé for earliness. Soft soil suits it better than any other, and even the most arid sands will support it, provided the spring is a little tender, or it is helped by watering. In free and black soils, it also grows well, and more reliably, but later. In cold, damp soils, it only languishes, most often rotting during the winter; even when it does escape, it comes so late that it gives no pleasure, and is not worth the care it costs; so the shortest way is to get rid of it when the soil is ungrateful. Here's how to grow it, which requires a great deal of detail. It is sown in mid-November in free soils, and at the beginning of December in light soils, so that it can rise before the frosts; and as it always perishes during the winter, it is a good idea to sow it a little thickly: it should be placed on the south or east coasts, where it is sheltered from bad winds, and within reach of all the sun's rays. Some people sow it in clumps of seven or eight, a foot apart; others sow it in rays two or three inches deep, and form two or three rows in the bed, depending on how wide it is, because you always need to leave two feet free along the walls, to be able to carry out the operations required for espaliers. The latter has always seemed to me the best, because 1. the peas are not piled up on top of each other, so they feed better; 2. the field mice, crows and pigeons, which are very avid eaters, destroy them less in this arrangement, because once they have smelled a clump, they eat every last one. Nor do they pull them so easily from a comb, especially if care has been taken to walk them after sowing them, as should be done; this binds them, so to speak, to the soil; but care must be taken not to sow them, especially in fat soil, until it is healthy; for in damp weather, the operation of walking them would be worthless. After they have been sown and marketed, they are immediately covered, and a little pigeon droppings is thrown on top, if available; this gives the soil a little warmth, which prevents them from melting so easily: after they have risen, they are topped up again with an inch of coarse compost, or horse dung. In the Paris area, there is a type of compost even more favorable than pigeon droppings, either for preserving them or for advancing them: it is commonly called gadoue (sludge); it comes from the roads where the city's sludge and refuse are transported: these materials, matured for a few years, are reduced to compost, and contain wonderful salts for all kinds of plants. It should be removed in the summer, when the weather is dry and it is, so to speak, dusty. Put an inch of it on the bottom of the shelves before sowing peas, and you'll soon realize what a great effect it has. You could make a supply of it anywhere, by collecting the sludge from the streets or nearby roads, and leaving it to ripen in some hole: there is no manure that has as much virtue as this material. Those who have a lot of walls, and who can place a single row of peas at the foot of the walls, without harming the trees, which are often bare at the bottom, enjoy the fruit eight days longer than those who have peas only two feet away, and this eight-day difference certainly makes a big difference to pleasure or profit. Peas sown at the times and in the manner I have just described, are raised, and even having three or four leaves require great care to be defended from the inclemency of the sky: each one, according to his industry and convenience, must preserve them, either with straw mats supported on a kind of trellis that we make at the height of the peas, or with large litter supported in the same way by several poles tied together, so that its weight does not crush these young plants, especially when it is loaded with snow: between the rays, we interweave a little short straw to keep them straight: when the frost becomes stronger, we increase the covers in proportion. Sometimes, for lack of convenience, you don't cover them at all, but they still escape when winters are neither long nor harsh; but it's always risky to leave them to chance. Care must be taken to uncover them a little when there is a fine day of sunshine, provided that the frost has not attacked them under the blankets, in which case the sun would lose them; and as soon as the weather is milder, they must be uncovered completely, always leaving the blankets beside them, so that they can be put back on quickly if necessary: when they remain too long suffocated under the blankets, without air or sun, they turn yellow and melt. Those who have no walls to shelter them, raise slopes of land facing south, and make little straw shelters on the ridge, four feet high: they are no worse off in this situation; but as much as possible, choose light soil, as it warms up much more easily in spring, and the plants are less likely to melt than in greasy, damp bottoms. Once you're past the hard frosts, which usually last until the end of February, at which time the sun begins to gain strength, you remove the blankets, crimp the peas and shoe them; this helps the soil to warm up, and you row them as soon as they are seven to eight inches old: They then begin to show their flower, which is called a loquette; for this kind of pea only grows to eighteen inches or two feet, all the more so as care must be taken to stop them at the third flower; and this operation, which is the last, brings them forward a long way: when only two, or even one, is left, the fruit is still rather ripe. It is often difficult to deprive oneself of half of one's expectations, so everyone can do as he or she sees fit. These pinched tips of the stalk can be used to good effect in soup, giving it a pea-like flavour. After this operation, the pods are visibly fuller, and can be found in April or May, depending on the weather. Care should have been taken to weed them where necessary, and to pull out those that have degenerated; it's easy to identify them, in that the flower has not shown itself as in the others, and the plants are more vigorous. The heat of March sometimes dries out the soil, especially coastal soil, to the point where the plants need to be helped by a little watering; in this case, they should be wetted according to their needs, in the morning with dew, because during the main part of the day, wetting is of no use to them; the fresher they are kept, but without excess, the bigger and more tender they become. It sometimes happens that they perish, despite all the precautions you've taken to preserve them: here's what you can do in such a case to make up for lost time, as far as possible. As soon as you notice them, sow new ones in thick rays on a new layer; they grow quickly and profitably; and when they are four to five inches old, pull them out and replant them in good shelters, reasonably spaced; they regrow very easily, and you gain nearly a month by this advance. Those who have a great eagerness for this vegetable, and who are in a position to make certain expenses, can give themselves the pleasure of enjoying them a month earlier than those who have them in the ground, despite shelter and care, and they can also keep them until Christmas; here's how. Sow them in the first days of November, in baskets 7 to 8 inches high and 10 to 12 inches in diameter, filled with earth and potting soil mixed together, with an inch of manure on top; twenty to twenty-five seeds in each basket are more than enough; We leave them in the open air, sheltered by a wall, until the hard frost; by then they have grown five or six leaves, if autumn is a little fine; we then move them to a greenhouse that is not too hot, and to which we can give air whenever the weather permits: As soon as the weather gets milder, we put them outside, but not too far apart, so as to be quick to bring them in when the frost starts again, and until mid-February we continue to keep them in sight so as not to be surprised: we then change their situation, and put them on warm beds, which we must have prepared for this purpose. These layers must be buried 2 feet deep, and are, strictly speaking, deaf layers; in the middle of the thickness of the manures, we put five to six inches of tan, and two or three inches on the surface, which we then cover with potting soil in such quantity that the baskets are filled all around without exceeding: these baskets are placed on the surface of the manures, and arranged in a chessboard Tome II. I in three rows, so that they are six inches apart from each other: it is important to let the great fire pass through the layers, before putting them in place. They bloom promptly as soon as they have felt this air of warmth; but as they still have to fear the frosts that occur in March, here are the precautions you need to take to guarantee them. Take circles of large barrels; support the two ends, and make them enter the ground on the two edges of the layers which are level with the ground; space them from three to three feet along the whole length, and to maintain them take running laths, with which you will bind them: three rows are enough; and for greater solidity, drive a few stilts into the middle of the layers and tie them to the circles with good wicker; over this trellis, if necessary, throw down straw mats made with string, which envelop the whole circuit, and double them if one is not enough; you will also close the two ends of the layers, so that frost cannot enter. If trained and cared for in this way, they will bear fruit as early as the first days of April, provided the month of March is fine; but whatever the weather, they will always be three weeks ahead of the coastal ones, and once the fruit has been harvested, your layers, which, thanks to the tannin, remain warm for three months, can still be used to grow whatever you see fit. It is understood that you must stop them at the second or third flower, as I said for the others, and that you must empty the baskets when the fruit is picked, dry them, and lock them up, to serve again when you want to use them. As for peas that you want to raise for the late season, sow them at the end of August or in the first days of September, in the same baskets and in the same way as I said. You arrange them along some well-exposed wall, and take care to wet them after they are sown, which you continue to do from two to two days, unless it rains; a few days later they rise, and when they are six to seven inches old you row them; you let them enjoy as long as the weather is fine: they are in full flower a month later, and the pod follows closely. Corn is often subject to frosts in this season, which could ruin it, so bring it close to the house and be ready to lock it up as soon as the weather threatens; and as these kinds of frosts don't last long, put it in the air as soon as it's over, and keep taking it out or bringing it in whenever the weather changes. The fruit starts to taste good at All Saints' Day, and you can pick them from one or the other until Christmas, just as good and just as tender as the spring ones, provided they are always well moistened: I've tried this two or three times. It should be noted that only the Michaux pea succeeds in this season. This quality of pea is not only the best for both spring and autumn, but I find it equally good for all months of the year, and I use it in preference to the others: they are tender and sweet in all seasons, provided they are wetted exactly with morning dew, and eaten as soon as they are shelled, (this circumstance makes a lot:) and you don't languish to enjoy them; in six weeks from the day you sow them, when it's the right season, they give their fruit. The last ones to be sown in the ground are sown in mid-August, and bear fruit in October: if there are no heavy frosts in that month, they can be kept, or, to put it better, they succeed one another until after Saint-Martin's Day, depending on the climate; in any case, sowing can be brought forward or delayed by a few days. In spite of my particular affection for this species of pea, I have no wish to subjugate anyone's taste to my own; each person, according to his or her terrain, will choose the ones that are most successful. It is much better to sow alternately a bed of peas and one of some other plant that is not shaded, such as chervil, parsley, pear and others. When you want to keep a pea bed for seed, you must take care to uproot the plants that degenerate; you can tell by their wood, which is thicker, and their flowers, which are higher; sometimes they don't flower at all. I shouldn't omit to say that whatever the species, they must always be rowed if you want to make a real profit from them, otherwise the field mice and pigeons that prey on them ruin most of them; the free sparrows, which you can't defend them from, already do them enough harm. You don't have to wait until the grain is completely dry to harvest them; as soon as the pods turn yellow, even though the peas are still green, you can pull them out; and they finish ripening exposed to the sun in a courtyard, where birds and other animals don't get in so easily: when they are dry, you beat them and winnow them right away; because rats and mice destroy them in attics, when you lock them up with the cossat. They are good for sowing for two years; in the third year, only part of them come up, and sometimes none at all; but when you are lucky enough to have places free of these insects, and they can stay in their cossat, they keep for four or five years, provided you don't beat them until you want to sow them. To preserve the free species, you need to do what I've said elsewhere, change every year or two with someone a little away from you. With regard to peas that are left to dry to be eaten dry, they should be exposed to the sun for a few days after they have been winnowed, in order to improve their quality and keep them in better condition. One thing should also be kept in mind when cooking them, and that is to use water that is suitable for them, as the more they boil, the harder they become, and the quality of the pea is often blamed for a defect that comes solely from the water. I'll move on to describe the other species. The Dominé pea is the earliest after the Michaux pea, to which it succeeds; and although there is no difference between them other than the fact that one comes eight days earlier than the other, this is always a lot for people who are eager for it, and especially for those who trade in it; However, one does not give way to the other, and for those who are not in a hurry to enjoy it, it is much better value than Michaux, its pods being regularly doubled and fuller; it also rises higher, and requires proportionate oars. It is grown in the same way, and has the advantage of withstanding bad weather better than Michaux, particularly in slightly damp soils: it should be sown light, especially after winter; the grain is white, fairly round and of a good size; it can be sown at any time, but spring is its most favorable season. The Baron pea follows the Dominé very closely, but is very inferior; the pod is extremely small, the grain the same, without sugar or finesse; it was known before the two preceding peas, and its credit was established on its earliness; but since these peas appeared, it has lost a lot, and with 4 justice: however, as it provides a lot, and the flower is not prone to run, it still has some supporters; perhaps also that in other climates it would be better than here. The Lorrain pea is the successor to the previous three, and supplies more abundantly: it is large and fairly sweet, but only succeeds in spring; in the other seasons, the nile attaches itself to it, and the flower perishes: light soil suits it better than any other. It can be eaten dry or green, but is neither as tender nor as soft as many others; its color is white, its shape round and fairly plain. The Swiss pea, otherwise known as the large early pod, is a close successor to the previous varieties, and is more resistant to bad weather. It is grown equally in gardens and in the countryside, and is sown as early as December: Its shape is round and plain, its color a small greenish-yellow and of good size; it fruits a lot, and is not prone to run; its pod is long and full, its grain very tender when green, but when dry it is not used; it is sown until Midsummer, and is very good for the late season, not being prone to nililil like some others: it is one of the most profitable species; it requires good soil. The common pea is about the same in terms of earliness and yield: it is sown like the previous one in December, and bears its fruit within a few days of the other, i.e. at the end of May or the beginning of June, depending on the soil and the year: it is round in circumference, a little flattened on the ridges, which is the effect of the hindrance in which it finds itself in the pod, which is so full that the seeds can barely fit inside: it is of medium size: its color is russet: it must be picked under the flower, i.e., the flower, although dried out, must still hold on to the tail, and it is very tender when picked at this time; but if you wait until the flower has detached, it hardens; it is sown until the end of March, and the last ones sown are good for Midsummer: We don't sow it later, even though it will also come, because the following month the white quarry arrives, and excludes all the others; it requires good soil. The white quarry is the one which, generally speaking, is desired by everyone, and which almost alone occupies the scene as long as it lasts: it is rightly warned in its favor; it is tender and soft, better nourished, fatter, and of a sweeter taste: its color is white as its name announces, its shape uneven and more quarried than round, either green or dry; it is a little late to bring in, rises very high, and does not provide much; these are its faults. We start to sow it at the end of March, and this first sowing is good in July: we continue until the end of May, and we don't go any further; because beyond that it yields almost nothing: it has little taste in the dry, and we must only let it dry for the seed: it requires mediocre soil; in good soil, it only grows wood. This is the species chosen for green drying, and for eating during winter and Lent: it is very delicate and very good, prepared as follows. Select the most tender grains; put them freshly shelled in a boiler with boiling water; after they have made a broth, remove them and put them in fresh water; then lay them out in the air on a white cloth for two or three days, turning them over from time to time; Then put them in a lukewarm oven, clearly laid out on racks, with paper underneath, until they are completely dry. Finally, put them in paper bags and lock them in a dry place. When you want to use them, fry them in lukewarm water, or put a piece of butter married to the flour, and leave them to soak for twenty-four hours; then cook them in the same water, and season them with butter or cream, as you please. Cul noir comes in two varieties, one round and the other quarré, both with a black germ, from which they take their name; the quarré is more highly prized. The former is russet in color; the latter is green, and is used during Lent for purées: it provides a lot, and picked green, it is tender and good. It should not be sown until the end of April, or the beginning of June; sooner or later, the fogs attach themselves to it and make it cloudy: only what is needed for sowing should be kept from the first species, as it is not good to eat dry; it requires good soil. Green quarry differs from white quarry only in its outer color, which is green: it is not so delicate or soft when green, but as a reward it is very useful when dry for purées: it must be very dry before being enclosed, because if it retains any moisture, it will go off and take on a bad taste: it does not provide much, which is its defect like the other. It should be sown at the same time, and placed in slightly worn soil, for the same reason that it grows too much in wood when the soil is too good: some soils make it so hard that it cannot be cooked, particularly in strong soils; care must be taken to place it properly, or to detach it from the soil, if the soil is contrary to it. The Normandy pea is square-shaped, whitish-green and very large: it is tender and soft, eaten green; and dry, it is equally good, and yields more puree than any other species, having an extremely thin skin: it does not fruit much, which is its defect. It is sown from the end of March to Midsummer's Day; later the blossom sinks, and nothing comes of it: the first sown yield much more than the second sown; it requires good soil. The long pod is round, white, plain and clear; its size is mediocre: it fruits a lot and quickly; its pod, which is very long and very full, contains twelve to fourteen grains; it is of all the species that yields the most, and is the most successful for the late season; it does not nuile or curl. It is sown from mid-April to the beginning of July; mediocre soil is more favorable to it than better. For these last seven species, it should be noted that you don't need as much seed for some as for others. The Swiss pea, the common pea, the Norman pea and the cultivated pea want to be sown a little thickly, because they are only one crop; farmers use seven to eight bushels per acre; with regard to the white and green peas, and the long pea pod, they only use five to six bushels, because they fork a lot, and would choke if they were pressed harder. The English green pea was recently brought to us from the country whose name it bears, and is known to only a few people; it is very large, plain, a little oval, of a whitish green, and perfectly good, either green or dry, for purées: it grows quite high, supplies from the stem to the tip, makes its pod large and full, with no flower missing. I sowed it last year for the first time in three or four seasons, and it has always done well: I said elsewhere that my soil was quite strong; I don't know if it would do as well in poorer soil. The pea without parchment, which in some provinces is called the gourmand pea, has very valuable qualities, which make it very popular, except in the vicinity of Paris: I don't know why it is so little appreciated in this capital, where it is hardly to be found in the public markets. It is eaten with the pod like green beans: its taste is sweet and fine, and it is more profitable than any other. There are many species, which I will reduce to 5, as the others seem to me to be degenerated from this one. The most common has a white flower, rises from 5 to 6 feet, and produces a pod of mediocre size: it is the most widely cultivated, the others not being well known: it is quite fertile in grain, provided it is sown light and well branched: the pea is white, uneven, and of mediocre size. The second species has a red flower and grows to seven or eight feet; it therefore requires long, strong oars to withstand the shocks of the wind: it fruits a lot, and gives pods once as big as the previous one, which are very tender and very sweet; the pea is partly reddish and greenish, speckled with purple spots, round, large and smooth. The third has a white flower, rises to the same height and supplies a lot of the same produce as the previous species, but the pod is less wide and more curly; the pea is large and white, fairly smooth and fairly round. The fourth species has a white flower, rises only three or four feet, and produces surprising pods; I have collected some that are eighteen lines wide by four to five inches long, tender and sweet as can be; they do not fruit as much as the previous two; However, their beauty and goodness compensate for this defect, in addition to the fact that they are a fortnight earlier than their predecessors; it should also be taken into account that they are held in a mediocre elevation, which costs neither so many oars, nor so much subjection to defend them from the strong winds: All these advantages make it well worth preferring to any other, when you can get the real thing, which is very hard to find; you have to sow it light like the others; the pea is white, large, smooth and round. The fifth species is the dwarf pea without parchment, which forms a small, rounded, low tuft: its pod is very small, and its taste similar to the others; it is not very heavy, which makes it less useful than curious. These 5 species are cultivated a little differently than the other peas: they are sown in March and April, until the end of May; later on, they are prone to mildew: they are crimped like the others when they are well up, and they are often wet; this is what tenderizes them: They necessarily need to be branched, and when you want to get the most beautiful and earliest fruit, you have to pinch them at the third or fourth flower: three rows in a four-foot plank are enough; the thicker they get, the less they fruit: for the same reason, don't put two planks in a row. This species of pea is extremely sensitive to thunder and lightning, which can ruin it if they occur at flowering time; this is the main reason why it should be sown every two weeks, from the beginning of March to the end of May, because if the first seeds perish, the others, which are more or less advanced, make up for those ruined by the storm. They are eaten fat and lean, with the fillets removed and cooked in boiling water to make them more tender. They are also eaten as green beans, when they are of a reasonable size, and are preferred by connoisseurs over all others: they are tender, soft and have a distinguished taste; they are also very good dry, and cook perfectly; but it is the white kind that should be taken. We reserve as much as we need for seed, and leave them for a long time to dry, because their husk is fat and thick, and only dries out with time and good weather; because if it rains heavily when they are at this point, this husk, which retains water like a sponge, is prone to rot and cause the grain to rot; That's why it's always a good idea to have some from one year to the next, and to tear out any plants that degenerate, which I've found to be particularly the case with the white species. When they come to good, we pull them out, and if we have the time, we seed them right away: I say we shell them, because when they are beaten, half of them remain in the pods, which cannot be detached, the grain being stuck to the pod; this has led me to take the decision in my particular case to tear off the pods as they dry, and I don't even wait until they are completely dry, as I am beset by birds that devour them; they finish drying in the sun, where I expose them for as long as they need. If you can close them safely without shelling them, so that rats can't damage them, they keep much longer. I have experimented this year with drying them green, picked tender, in the same way as beans, the recipe for which can be found in the chapter on this vegetable, and I have found them to be better; it will be very easy to put them to the test. In addition to the fourteen species of peas I have just mentioned, there are a few more of a fancy nature, of which I shall say a word, and a few others about which I feel I must disabuse those who are prejudiced in their favor on the basis of their former reputation; such is, for example, the Charantonneau, of which we were eager before we knew those who now occupy the scene with greater justification: It's a small, hard pea, without sugar or finesse, and much less hasty than the first three species I've named; such is also the small dwarf pea with bouquet, which is not as abandoned as the Charantonneau, but which is hardly better: all its merit is that it takes up little space, and can be stored anywhere; a poor merit, when it is not accompanied by any other quality. The large bouquet pea is of the same order; its singularity is all that recommends it: it rises to six feet, and carries at its summit a group of flowers and pods in a row gathered one on top of the other, which give a very mediocre grain in taste, and it is only by dint of small poles that it can be held upright, a pain it certainly does not deserve. I include in the same class the crown pea, the horn pea, the gray pea, the grosset and others. There is, however, one in the provinces near the Rhône, called Quarantain, which is said to be good and early; I don't know it; it's up to those who grow it to consider whether it wouldn't be even more advantageous for them to sacrifice it to Michaux; for one must always strive for the best. Among the fancy peas (with respect to us), I give first place to the chickpea, which is highly esteemed in Languedoc, as well as in Italy; it is pointed on one side and sunken on the other, resembling the head of a ram: It has a peculiar taste, but one that pleases its enthusiasts; it is very hard and difficult to digest: for this reason, no one pays any attention to it in Paris, where it comes just as well and just as good as in warmer countries; I have tried it several times. I will say, however, for the satisfaction of those who like its taste, but fear its defects even more, that soaking it for twenty-four hours in lukewarm water, with a small bag of ash, before cooking it, makes it lose much of its hardness: you can also, as is the practice in Languedoc, put it in a bowl, pour in a spoonful of olive oil, and rub the grains together; then put it in lukewarm water, with a little salt; leave it there from evening to the next day; then cook it in half-boiling water; this little preparation tenderizes it a lot: We must be careful not to use well water, which is too raw and hardens it; any other water is good. There are two types, one white and large, with a white flower; the other reddish and smaller, with a red flower: the latter is better for pharmacy, being more aperitive; the other is better for life, and is almost exclusively consumed, both in Italy and in our southern provinces: there is a third species which is black; but I don't know its particular qualities. The plant that produces the first two species is quite different from common peas: it only grows to about eighteen inches, and throws out a number of branches that spread out around the base: its leaves are water-green, arranged in twos like those of sain-foin, but shorter, serrated at the edges, and ending in an odd number: From the axils of each leaf, or at least from the largest part, a small flower emerges, with a hairy calyx, divided into six pointed parts, whose pistil turns into a bladder-like, swollen fruit, about an inch long, ending in a small thread that contains one or two seeds. Some people eat them not only when they are dry, but also when they are green, and not only cooked, but raw; however, they are difficult to digest, and in the latter case are only suitable for country people, whose stomachs are accustomed to digesting everything: They are usually only eaten dry in oil, so they are left to dry well and then plucked, beaten and winnowed without further precaution; they keep well for sowing for two or three years, but are best eaten in the first year. In hot countries, it is sometimes used in place of coffee; its taste is somewhat similar, but it is more bitter, and therefore requires more sugar: when it is mixed in equal portions, it is difficult to notice, and in the public cafés of Italy, it is very common to use it. It is sown in March or April in clumps like beans, eighteen inches apart, and five or six seeds are placed together; it is crimped exactly when young, and requires no other method: in Italy it is sown with a plough, but the climate is different. The decoction of this pea is good for suppressing urine, stone and nephritic colic; it is also used for jaundice, to kill worms, to bring milk to nursing mothers, restore menstruation and facilitate childbirth: its flour, used as a poultice, is also suitable for resolving tumors of the udder and testicles; it also cleanses gravel and fickle fire. The pea of every month has a particular merit, which is to flower for four to five months in a row, and to always give fruit successively after the flowers; this is what gives it entry to some gardens: but if you value it rightly, the fruit is worth nothing. The Lupin pea, which is where I end, is generally only cultivated for medicinal purposes, and is only successful in southern countries; however, the Greeks used to eat it in ancient times, as Galen and Pliny assure us with remarkable circumstances, adding that this grain has the virtue of appeasing both hunger and thirst; but they took the precaution of macerating it in hot water, to remove its bitterness and make it pleasant to the taste: This preparation also removes a harmful quality that some other authors have attributed to it, assuming it to be true; but the proof is not well established: even today, in some parts of Italy, the lower classes still eat it, cooked simply in water with salt or vinegar. The root is single, woody, with several fibers; the stem is 12 to 18 inches high, moderately thick, straight, cylindrical, a little hairy, hollow and full of marrow; the leaves are alternate, borne on long tails, composed.s most often of seven oblong, narrow, dark-green segmens, plain at the edges, hairy underneath, and topped with a silvery-white down, fan-shaped by their arrangement; the edges of these segmens approach and narrow at sunset, and incline towards the tail; the flowers are arranged in a spike at the top of the stems; They are leguminous, white, borne on short pedicels; a pistil emerges from the calyx, which turns into a thick, broad, flattened pod, about three inches long, straight, pulpy, yellowish, a little hairy on the outside, containing four or five fairly large, flattened seeds, reddish on the outside and yellow on the inside, and very bitter. The second species, of which I have never been able to see the plant, although I have sown it several times, is, as I have been told, identical in all respects to the previous one, except for the color of the flower and the seed. The flower is a ruddy blue, and the seed a dark purple. This species is almost unknown. The first is very commonly used in medicine; its flour, which is one of the four resolving flours, is used in all emollient poultices; its decoction is aperitive and specific for liver diseases and visceral obstructions; it stimulates months and urine, and kills worms: Its flour produces the same effect, mixed with honey and vinegar; the same decoction is detersive, curing scabies, scabs and ulcers; it also cleanses and decleanses the skin perfectly: boiled with vinegar and applied as a poultice to tumors and scabies, it gradually dissipates them, especially in their birth: the grain is also marvelous for fattening oxen; it is also used in some countries to make powder to powder. Lupin is sown in March in warm countries, where it is easy to raise, and its cultivation is no different from that of other grains; but here, where the climate is too cold, it can only be raised by first sowing it on a bed, from where it is replanted in the warmest possible location: some grow it in pots. CHAPTER LXV. Description of LONG PEPPER; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Three species are cultivated, differing only in the shape of the fruit they produce: one is elongated, slightly curved, and cone-shaped; the other is short and pointed at the tip, and the third is round: their similarities are perfect in all other respects, so I need only describe one of the three. It grows a branching, green, gnarled stem, formed into a shrub that rises to fifteen or eighteen inches; its leaves are oblong, pointed and smooth, of a beautiful glossy green; The flowers emerge in small bunches from the leaf axils, in the form of white stars, borne on a small calyx which changes into a fruit of different shape, depending on the species, which is green at first, and becomes a bright, shiny red, approaching coral as it ripens; it encloses the seed, which is round and flat, of medium size and russet in color. It is used very little in France for living, and is cultivated more for garden decoration and eye candy than for utility; however, it is used for many purposes: it is candied with sugar when green, and eaten at a dose of half an ounce, to fortify the stomach, aid digestion and dissipate the winds: yeast growers also use it to give more strength to vinegar; it is mixed with candied gherkins. Some people use it in their food instead of ordinary pepper, and find it tastier. But in foreign countries, in India, Spain, Italy and even Flanders, it is widely consumed; some eat it preserved in salt and vinegar; others, who have become accustomed to it from youth, eat it raw when it is green: I admit that this may seem surprising to those who are familiar with its pungent taste; but the fact is no less certain, and I have witnessed it a thousand times. This plant grows very easily in this climate, as well as in hot countries, and its cultivation is very simple; it is sown in beds in March, and replanted in May, either in beds a foot apart, or in pots; it requires good soil, a little moist, and a slightly shady situation; too much sun is detrimental to it: it is moistened as needed, and the fruit is cut as desired, green or dry: the seed keeps well for several years. different species, properties, cultivation, etc. THIS plant, although of little use to the table, nevertheless has good enough qualities to be considered one of the best in the garden. Its leaf is small, snowshoe-shaped, thick and fleshy, full of water, odorless, dark green or yellowish, depending on the species, and covered underneath with a snowy white down; its stem is of a very similar consistency, and is used in the same way as the leaf. It grows straight and fairly high, when forced to rise by others; but when placed at ease, it does not rise much, and its branches, which form in fairly large numbers, crawl on the ground. The leaves are arranged two by two, opposite each other, and from their axils come the second branches, which divide into several small twigs, at the end of which form a group of small yellowish flowers, followed by small pointed shells containing the seed. Q2 PURSLANE. When the plant is young and tender, it is used in salads; when stronger, it is used in soups, mixed with other herbs; it is also prepared with cream, and is a familiar dish in many countries, almost unheard of in Paris; but for this to happen, the chops must be the size of two feathers, plain and straight, with no lateral branches: at the same size, they are pickled in vinegar in the same way as gherkins, alone or mixed with pickles, and used in winter salads. Its medicinal properties are much more remarkable: distilled water or the juice of its leaves is used in hot fevers, at a dose of three or four ounces, to calm the impetuosity of the blood and spirits: the water in particular, taken at the same dose, is one of the most effective remedies for haemorrhage and blood loss in women; it is also good for killing worms in children, and in this latter respect the juice of distilled water has the same effect. The plant is also good for scurvy and spitting blood; its chewed leaf cures mouth ulcers and quenches thirst, as well as the pain of irritated teeth: it is also used in many other remedies, but as they are less tried and tested, I will pass over them in silence. Its excessive use in food would, however, be dangerous for those with weak stomachs, who need it more to heal than to refresh: this is what we must take care of. There are three species of purslane, Green, Golden and Wild, which grows in confusion in most gardens, and is a great nuisance to plants of all kinds, without being able to be destroyed: if the other two were lacking, it would be just as useful as a remedy; but for life, it is too dry and hard. There is a fourth, little-known species, formed into a shrub with a hard stem, and which is very delicate to raise and preserve; but as it is only useful for the pleasure of the curious, I will say no more about it. Its root is small and fibrous; it grows several weak, creeping stems, like wild purslane, which do not extend very far; its leaves are narrow and long, thick and fleshy, more or less like percepia, and arranged in a star shape around its leaves, eight or ten in number: the stems are round, smooth and reddish on the sunny side; the tops end in a group of small, petalless flowers, like those of wild purslane, which turn into small, green, elongated shells, wrapped 23 in a thick, white stuffing; they enclose the seed, which is black and even smaller than that of ordinary purslane: its taste is bitter; it would not be suitable, therefore, for the use of life; but it could have other properties that I do not know: it is sown on the bed like the other species, and it comes easily enough; but it must be enclosed during the winter. The first two can be propagated from seed, but are cultivated differently: the golden variety is delicate, and can only tolerate the open air when the heat begins; the green variety, on the contrary, is hard: it is therefore sown on a bed throughout the winter, and is hardly ever sown in the open air. The first seed is sown under a bell in January; however, as the cold can be very harmful, it is common to wait until the hard frosts have passed, i.e., around mid-February: it is buried with small lettuces; the same amount of soil is enough for them: the seed is sown very thickly, without burying it; if you wish, it is enough to beat it a little with the hand, and it rises very well and very quickly. When the plant has risen, care must be taken to keep it well covered, as the slightest hint of freshness will melt it; it does however need to see the sun, and whenever it appears, you must not fail to uncover the bells a little. We cut it as soon as it has two slightly formed leaves, and at this point it is more red than green; but it is such a pleasure, that it is on all new lettuces; we always sow a little from fortnight to fortnight, so as to have a succession until we can risk the other species, which, depending on the year, is sown in the middle or at the end of April, and under cloche as well, because in the open ground you have to wait until mid-May. There are no other precautions to be taken for these first seeds on a bed; but for those sown in the open ground in May, they should be placed along a well-exposed wall, in the loosest soil available; and if they are heavy by nature, they should be loosened with plenty of compost, or sand if there is none: after ploughing, harrow it well with a pitchfork, rake it over, then sow; and as the seed is extremely small, and always escapes more than you want, mix it with sawdust or ash, to control it better. After sowing, lightly beat the soil with the back of a wooden spade, and then spread an inch of loam over it as evenly as you can; lightly wet the spot the next day, and continue every day, until it has risen, unless it rains: if there is no loam, harrow the Q 4 POURPIER. If you don't have potting soil, you have to harrow the soil with a fork after sowing, and then beat it with a spade; but unless you keep it very wet at all times, it can hardly break through the crust; and if you don't have watering cans that sprinkle water in a fine shower, the sprinklings beat the soil so hard that the seed suffocates rather than emerges. In the months of June and July, when new seeds are sown, the coast is no longer so necessary; it can be sown in beds wherever you like, as it does very well everywhere, subject to the same precautions explained above. One important thing to remember is to wet it every day, and only at midday, when it is starting to take shape: watering in the evening or morning takes away its golden color and turns it green. Only a few should be sown at a time, as it is only good in salads when it is young and tender: of course, it must be weeded if necessary. To collect the seed, we replant it from the first seeds we've sown a foot apart: we water it as soon as we've planted it, and continue for two days at a time until the seed has formed; its maturity is revealed by the first hulls, which begin to peel off, revealing the seed; we must then carefully pull out the plants, and have a sheet ready to receive them: You leave them on for a few days to allow the seed to ripen, stirring them from time to time, and then rubbing them with your hands to loosen and enclose them. It's black, round and as fine as grains of sand; it keeps well for eight to ten years. Others put it in a barrel, well pressed with all its stalks, and leave it there until all its stalks are consumed with rot; the seed does not suffer, and is gathered at the bottom of the barrel, from where it is removed; and after washing it, it is dried and locked up. The reason for this practice is that the seed feeds better, and there is none left in the capsules, as it is air-dried: each person will follow whichever of these two methods is more convenient for him or her, because in either case, the seed lifts equally. CHAPTER LXVII. Description of RAIPONCE; its different Species, Properties, Calture, etc. Pumice grows naturally in meadows and hedges. There are four 25 species, all of which have their Latin name, but three of which are known only in botany, and are not used in food: I shall pass over them in silence, and speak only of the one with which we are familiar. Its root is fleshy, long and white, both inside and out, the size of a small turnip, with a mild flavor and no odor; it forms a group of small, oblong, tender-green leaves, similar to lamb's lettuce and arranged in the same way; its stem is branchy and slender, rising from twelve to eighteen inches; its branches are terminated by blue, bell-shaped flowers, in a single piece, cut into a five-rayed star; the calyx, from the middle of which rises a forked thread, becomes a fruit divided into three seed-filled chambers: this seed is one of the finest that can be produced, with a rounded, slightly elongated shape and a yellowish color. In spring, the root and leaf are eaten together, alone or mixed with lamb's lettuce: it is healthy, and many people are eager to eat it; its taste is a little like hazelnut. It is of little use in medicine: however, it is agreed that it is refreshing, and that its decoction is useful in the onset of throat inflammations. This plant comes without any cultivation, as I have said; nevertheless, it is much better nourished and more tender when grown in gardens; but it must be placed in fresh, soft, slightly shaded soil: it is sown in June; and as its seed is extraordinarily small, it must be mixed with sawdust and sown very lightly: one full dice is enough for a large bed; it requires more earth than any other plant, and a little burial. The best way to sow it is to pass the fine rake over the soil, after it has been well tilled, and to spread the seed over it as evenly as possible, without stirring it with a fork; it is then covered with no more than half an inch of potting soil, which is spread lightly with the same rake; it should be moistened often until it is well established, and then weeded: during droughts, it should also be watered regularly. Good raiponces come to us from Meaux en Brie, where the soil is more favorable to this plant than that around Paris; and it's also from there that good seed comes to us. There is no need to take any precautions to preserve it during the winter; it is left in the ground until needed, and we begin to enjoy it from the beginning of Lent until May, after which time it grows its stem, and is no longer good: the seed ripens in the month of July, and what is destined for seed should be left in the ground; for it should be noted that this little root recovers with difficulty when replanted, unless it is pulled out and replanted immediately, without having been washed. CHAPTER LXVIII. Description of RAVE and RADIS; their different species, properties, cultivation, etc. AS turnip and radish are two plants that are quite similar in both taste and form, I will treat them together in this article. Radish, more properly known as Raifort in most provinces, is the root or turnip of a plant that bears the same name; this turnip is more or less long and large, depending on the species, plain, straight, and mostly red on the outside; its flesh is white, firm, brittle, watery and pungent to the taste, with no odor; its leaf is elongated, deeply cut, coarse green, rough and hairy : from the center of its leaves, which are more or less numerous, depending on the species, emerges a stem about the size of a finger, hollow, fluted, reddish and branched, rising to about three feet; the ends of its branches are covered throughout with flowers placed alternately; Its flowers are arranged with four white or reddish petals, supported by an elongated calyx, in the middle of which rises a pistil that changes into a short, swollen, round and pointed silique, which contains five or six round seeds, the size of a grain of hare's lead, which are green at first, and become grooved as they ripen. There are three distinct species of turnip, not to mention several degenerate ones: the smallest is called the hâtive, or four-leaf turnip; the second is called the commune, and the other the grosse. They all resemble each other in foliage, stem, flower and seed, but differ in turnip shape, color and taste, and each has its own season. The early variety is very small, a beautiful red, very tender and sweet, with few leaves. The common variety is twice as big, also red, but a little less tender; it grows a lot of leaves before turning into turnips. The grosse is partly white and partly red, about the size of a thumb, and has a more pungent taste than the preceding varieties. The hâtive is the most esteemed, though the least profitable, because it comes first, and we manage to make it come against all the insults of the bad season. The common variety has the advantage of being large, and of succeeding perfectly in the open ground, either in spring or autumn; it is true, however, that there are areas where it cannot be grown in spring, unless the soil is extremely earthy. The large one has neither the delicacy nor the sweetness of the other two; but in addition to being more profitable, it grows quite well in the warmer months, an advantage that the others do not have. This plant, which can only be eaten raw with salt, has both good and bad qualities, which makes it loved by some and hated by others. Its good qualities are to be pleasant to the taste, to awaken the appetite, and to provide abundantly almost all year round, provided that all due care is taken. Its bad qualities are to be difficult to digest, and contrary to weak stomachs: it also has the defect of giving reports during all the day when one ate some; which is unbearable with many people. However, it is a vegetable which, generally speaking, everyone is eager to eat, especially in spring, and which is consumed immensely, both in Paris and in the provinces; it is also one of the main crops of our market gardeners during winter and spring. It has a number of medicinal virtues, which I must mention: when cooked, it is used for the same purposes as turnips; it is particularly good for kidney and bladder diseases caused by mucus or gravel: its juice is extracted, and three or four ounces are taken in the morning with half an ounce of honey, which is continued for three or four days. Its distilled water is also used up to four ounces in aperitif potions, but should not be given to those suffering from stone, as it carries too much urine salt into the bladder. The root, crushed and applied to the soles of the feet, is good for malignant fevers and dropsy. Some claim that frequent use of this plant is harmful to the eyes; those who perceive this bad effect should refrain from using it. I'll now move on to its cultivation (by which I mean early cultivation). To get it to the degree of perfection required, i.e., to be tender, soft and brittle, even, straight and very red, there is only the layer that can make it so, and this is also where our market gardeners turn all their attention: They prepare their first beds at All Saints' Day, for those which are to start the year in the following January; they give these first beds only two feet in height, and fill them with eight to nine inches of compost; they let them lose almost all their heat before sowing, so that it is only lukewarm; for the turnip comes covered with little filaments when it is hotter than I say, and this is a great defect. For the distribution of the seed, here is their method: some, after having marked the plaoe of their bells on the soil, make holes with their finger all over the place, two inches apart in all directions, and throw three seeds into each hole, where they run a little soil with the doïgt to simply cover them; if more escape, they pull them out after they have risen, and shoe at the same time those that must remain : others, to have it done better, broadcast it, stir up the soil to bury it; and when it's up, they pull out what's left over. The first way is the best; the turnip comes longer and straighter. For the rest, they leave the layers in the air until all the seeds have risen; then they put the bells on only during the nights and bad days, always leaving the plant uncovered as much as the weather allows. If there are frosts, they cover the bells with litter: when you have straw mats, safety is even greater; they are particularly necessary in times of rain, which makes them rust, of course they are placed so that the water runs off into the paths. These first-seeded turnips are usually good in January, provided they have been well cared for and properly warmed, and that the season has not been excessively harsh and contrary. In December, they sow them for the second time, to succeed the first ones; and these are the most difficult to raise all year round, as they only have bad days to go: however, by dint of care they manage to keep them; but they require a stronger layer, and much more covering and warming than the first ones: they also need clean weather, extreme rigor or too much mildness being equally contrary to them. We noted (in 1746) that January and the beginning of February had passed without any cold, so the turnip crop ran out of leaves and did not produce any turnips; most market gardeners were obliged to turn over their beds without having made any profit; but, as these cases do not happen often, this second sowing is always done in December, and the turnip crop is usually good in February or at the beginning of March. What I have just said forms an apparent contrast with what happened in this last winter (1748), when we quite commonly saw raves in the months of January and February, which were as mild as the most beautiful spring, except for two days of frost; But if we had taken a good look at the weather, we would have observed that the sun came out much more frequently in the latter period than in the former, which I mentioned earlier, and there is no doubt that it was the influence of this star that produced this effect, which was the opposite of the other. You can't be too careful, therefore, to take advantage of the slightest ray of sunlight to give this plant the benefit it deserves, and if you can't, you must at least give it as much air as you can; for if it remains suffocated under the covers, it will either wither away without doing any navét, or it will perish, which amounts to the same thing. The third sowing is done in January, and must be covered with bells as soon as it is put in the ground, to conserve heat; the layers must be even stronger than in the previous month, and cared for in the same way. Sow for the fourth time at the beginning of February, and then dispense with the bells, as the season becomes more favorable: we also reduce the volume of the bed, and sow it in full; we space the seed by two or three inches, as I explained above; and, if we want to give an air of cleanliness to the bed, after it is well erected, we stretch a string from end to end that we rub with lime, and this lime, applied to the soil in the distances we judge appropriate, forms straight lines to regulate the holes we make. The holes are made with the finger, as I said, or with a small planter of the same size, cut diametrically, so that the three grains thrown in, as they fall to the bottom, can move apart: we then cover the bed with straw mats, or large litter, until the seed begins to rise; then we remove the cover, and build a small trellis on both edges of the bed, six inches inside and four inches high, on which we place straw mats during the nights and days of bad weather: we load them again with dry litter, if the cold is severe, filling the sides with a good thickness of litter. When, in spite of all these precautions, frost has penetrated and the cowslip is attacked, you must be careful not to uncover it in the sun, which would destroy it: you must let it thaw little by little under the cover, simply removing the bedding that forms the sides, so that the air can pass through: but if the weather is mild without the sun shining through, you must put everything in the air. The rabe from this seed is usually good at the end of March, or the beginning of April, and is the best to eat; for those that have preceded, having suffered much, do not have nearly the same tenderness, nor the same taste; and those that follow begin to become too strong. However, we continue to sow them in March, and they are good in May; but after this month, we no longer sow them on the bed: we mix them with other seeds, when the soil is suitable, and we sow them in this way until the beginning of May, to eat them in June; and we use the common species, which is more beautiful and more profitable. However, those who like them so much that they can't be bored with them can continue to sow them, but as they would be too prickly in full sun, they should be placed in the shade, along a north-facing wall, where a foot of compost will have been added to replace the same amount of soil that has been removed, as the soil makes them hard and cordate in this season. If you don't have a suitably arranged wall, you can make a shelter with straw mats five to six feet high, and sow them behind, watering them exactly every day, and taking care to fill the place with compost. Until September, only people who are determined not to do without them grow these first two species of turnip; but you can sow a little of the larger variety, which doesn't harden so much, provided it is watered daily. Once September arrives, we start sowing them again in the open ground, where they are better than on the bed; and it's always the common species that is to be preferred: we sow them very lightly, they are redder and better; we then mix them into the spinach and lamb's lettuce seeds, into chicory, etc.; wherever we put them, they go well. We continue in October, but these require more attention, as the frosts that start in this month, coming upon them, cause them to perish. They should be sown in a bed under some shelter exposed to the sun, and covered with straw mats or pleyons during bad weather, and especially at night: it is even safer to sow them on old layers, or on ados of potting soil, where they are less likely to rust than in the ground, and are always sweeter to eat; they are also not so exposed to being eaten by insects. If they are well cared for, they provide a succession of crops until Christmas; but they lose much of their taste in the latter season, and if the slightest frost surprises them, they have none at all. The year is over there, and we start again in November, as we said before. To collect the seed, in March or April we replant a sheet, more or less, of the first ones that have been raised on the bed, and we choose the reddest and plainest; we space them a good foot apart, and we water them right away, which must be continued until they are well established: many people leave them free to spare themselves any care; but very often the winds and rainstorms break them and lay them on the ground, where the seed rots for the most part: the more this seed is aired and struck by the sun, the better it is. Birds wage a cruel war on it as it approaches maturity: you have to defend yourself as best you can. When, in August, most of the siliques are yellow, we pull out the stalks and leave them exposed to the sun for a few more days, after which we bind them in bundles and tie them to the floor in some dry place where mice cannot get at them; for this seed needs to remain in its siliques as long as possible: it feeds there and keeps much better. As a rule, I experimented with threshing and winnowing as soon as I had harvested it, and sowing it the following spring on the same bed where I had sown others that I had just threshed: the production was quite different: the new threshing made the turnip bigger, more even and more colorful. This seed keeps well for ten years or more, if left in its siliques. The radish I have yet to discuss is similar in many respects to the turnip, but differs in several others: its leaf is broader, more inverted on the ground, and less cut; its turnip is quite different, and its flesh firmer. not to mention a few others degenerated from these: these eight species are the small white and round radish of every month; the white and long; the gray and long; the long summer black; of the large species, the large winter black; the winter white; of Italy. The small radish of every month is white and round, ending in a slender tail, the size of a small walnut: it is very early, and is sown on the bed, as is the early turnip: it is raised in the same way; so what I have said for the one will serve for the other. It is tender and delicate, sweet and watery; many people prefer it to turnip, which has a more decided taste: it can also be sown on the ground at the end of February, but it doesn't come off as delicate there, unless the soil is top-dressed and always kept very cool. The small, long white radish is quite similar in taste to the previous one, but is less tender and a little more pungent; it is also less early: its size is like that of a finger, and its skin and flesh are a beautiful white: it can be sown on the ground and on the bed, and has the advantage of coming in well all year round, provided it is kept moist in the warmer months. The small gray radish is the same size as the previous one, but has less water, and therefore a stronger taste: its skin is gray, its flesh white, and its shape not very long: it is sown on the ground, like the previous one, throughout the summer, with the same care. The small black summer radish is still of the same size, but its shape is more elongated and its flesh harder and drier: it has a hazelnut taste which outweighs all the others, and which gives it preference over them when it is known: the difficulty is to find the real seed, which is very rare; its skin is completely black. The large radish is very long, about the size of a small egg; its skin is very white, as is its flesh: it is tender and full of water, quite sweet, but not very spicy in taste, and prone to glassiness: it also ropes if not thoroughly wetted, and does not succeed in summer; but in autumn it is very good, and the most profitable for its size: it requires very light soil. The large black radish, otherwise known as the Strasbourg radish, is quite different from the others; its turnip is black, as big as the wrist, and elongated in proportion: it keeps well throughout the winter, if sown in June, and watered frequently: if sown earlier, it rises: its flesh is hard and dry, and its taste extraordinarily pungent; moreover, it has Tome II. R the defect of being very indigestible; however, it has its supporters, and it pleases those who are unable to grow the other species of turnips and radishes during the winter, and find this one in their greenhouse throughout that season; this is the most real merit I know of it: it must be pulled up before the frosts, and buried in sand, or placed close by in a trench, and covered during the frosts. The large white radish differs from the previous one only in its dirty-white outer color and sweeter taste: in all other respects, the resemblance is perfect. The Italian radish, which is the Ravaneli of the Italians, so tasted and so cherished in their country, has truly superior qualities: it does not succeed as perfectly here; however, when you have Italian seed, it comes good enough to erase all the others: its length is commonly from six to eight inches, its size a good inch, and its external color a brilliant white, with some red shading on the side of the head; some are also quite white: its flesh is transparent, extremely soft, tender and brittle, with a lot of water: it requires very loose, well-soiled soil, and lots of watering: we sow it from spring to autumn, with a lot of water.

be sure to place it in the shade in the warmer months; it's a species everyone should be eager to grow. All these species multiply from seed like turnip, and are harvested in the same way: they are redder and smaller; that's the only difference: they can be kept for the same length of time, with the same precautions, which I won't repeat. For the two large winter radishes, the seed is better on the over-wintered fruit, which is replanted in March, than on the seed that could be sown in spring: it feeds better and ripens more surely. With regard to the others, we replant the fruits that come first, as I explained for turnip. It is used medicinally for the same purposes as sage. CHAPTER LXIX. Description of ROSEMARY; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Rosemary is a perennial shrub, fragrant and aromatic, which grows naturally in warm countries and is also cultivated in gardens. There are four species, but I know of only two, and whatever research I've done, I've been unable to find the other two, which M. Tournefort calls rosmarinus spontaneus latiore folio, and rosmarinus almeriensis flore majore purpurascente. The two cultivated species are common and variegated rosemary. The common rosemary grows to about three feet, and produces a large number of branches; its root is woody and covered with many sibers; its leaf is a large, slightly glossy green, white underneath, thick, fluted in the middle, long and very narrow, similar to that of lavender, with a strong, pleasant odor and a bitter, pungent taste: its stem is woody, very branchy, and its young branches are covered with a small white down: the flowers are born in small bunches from the leaf axils. The flower is bluish, shaped like a pipe, cut into two lips at the top, the upper of which is raised, indented and usually inverted: the lower lip is cut into three parts, the middle of which is hollowed out; the stamens are hooked; the calyx is a horn toothed with two or three points, at the bottom of which is a pistil that fits into the hole at the bottom of the flower: this pistil is composed of 4 embryos, which then become as many almost round, brown seeds, enclosed in the capsule that served as the flower's calyx.
