The second species of Rosemary differs from the first in that the stem is taller and fuller, and the leaf is smaller and accidentally yellowish; it also flowers earlier, and this year (1749) was in full bloom as early as January. In all other respects, it bears the same resemblance to the first, and has the same properties: both retain their leaves throughout the winter. This plant is of no use for food, but it has very great properties in medicine, especially in hot countries, where the heat of the sun makes it more spirituous: it is hot, desiccating, incisive, astringent, and essentially cephalic: it is mainly used for apoplexy, epilepsy, vertigo, paralysis and other head ailments: it clears the eyes, strengthens the memory, and revives the heart; it also corrects the stench of breath, and lifts obstructions of the liver and spleen; it is also good for jaundice and for white flowers, taken as an infusion. Simply macerate the leaves and flowers overnight in common water, R, several glasses of which are taken during the day: leaves boiled in wine fortify nerves and joints. Aromatic wine, so commonly used by surgeons as a fomentation to dissipate swelling in wounds, is made from this leaf, mixed with that of Thim and Sage: the leaves, infused like tea over a period of time, are useful in treating écrouelles. It is also claimed that vindind in which the leaves and flowers have been boiled, mixed with a little honey, and taken as a drink before going to bed, is an excellent remedy for asthmatics. Four or five drops of essence of this plant, taken in a suitable liqueur, will often cure third-grade fevers. A leading author also asserts that eau de vie distilled from wine in which rosemary leaves and flowers have been macerated cures scabies, cancers and fistulas that resist other remedies. The well-known eau de la reine de Hongrie is obtained by distilling the flowers of this plant, then digesting them in eau-de-vie, and if the young leaves are added, it is even stronger: it is used daily for fainting, dizziness and vertigo, as well as for hysterical and hypochondriacal vapors: two or three large spoonfuls are taken internally in a glass of water, and rubbed externally on the temples, nose and other nervous and muscular parts, weakened or afflicted by the pains of rheumatism: it is also used successfully for contusions, wounds and cold humours, toothache and even gangrene. Although this plant requires a warm climate, it is easy to grow everywhere, with the difference that in cold countries it must be locked up during the winter, or at least stuffed; but in this one, unless the winters are very harsh, these precautions are unnecessary; it withstands the rigors of bad weather, and needs no special care once rooted. It can be propagated from seed, but usually from cuttings or from rooted plants: in the first case, it must be bedded, or at least moistened often when placed in the ground, and kept covered for some time in the heat of the sun: usually, several cuttings are placed in a pot, kept in the shade until they begin to grow, and then separated for a while: this plant will remain in the same place for a very long time. R 4 AC 2 ===== CHAPTER LXX. Description of the ROQUETTE; its different species, properties, 56 cultivation, etc. There are two species of arugula, the cultivated and the wild, both perennials. The first is grown in gardens: its root is white and slender; its stem rises to eighteen inches or two feet, a little hairy; its leaves are white, long, narrow, deeply cut on both sides, tender, smooth and acrid; Its flowers are born at the top of four-petaled cross-shaped stems, pale yellow with blackish stripes, enclosed in a hairy calyx, from which emerges a pistil that changes into a long silique, borne on a short pedicel, and divided by a partition into two chambers that are filled with yellow, small, round and slightly elongated seeds. The smell and taste of this plant are equally strong; however, it has its enthusiasts, particularly in Italy, where no one expects to eat a good salad without it. This is the only use to which it is put for life, and from which we derive many health benefits; for it stimulates the appetite, aids digestion, and dissolves slimy matter in the stomach. It is good in disgust and indigestion: eaten alone, with oil and vinegar, it excites the urine and slightly irritates the parts destined for the secretion and evacuation of the seed; this is why it is used in compositions intended to awaken love; but as it is very hot by nature, it is not suitable for hot and bilious temperaments, nor for those with a burning stomach. Its seed is used in winter in place of the leaves, and produces the same effects; it ranks first among the anti-scorbutic seeds, and is included in all the medicines suitable for scurvy; it is prescribed in a dose of one large, crushed and infused in a glass of distilled cochlearia water; and in its place, the leaf is also used, which is eaten raw, or the juice extracted from it, which is drunk mixed with wine: the leaf is also boiled in the broths and apozems prescribed for this disease, taking care to boil them only lightly, as they lose their flavor and virtue if left too long in the fire. Its seed is also an excellentR 3 slow preservative against apoplexy, paralysis and soporific affections; chew fifteen to twenty seeds every morning on an empty stomach, alone or mixed with cumin seeds; its use is very favorable, especially for the elderly; and various authors claim to have seen surprising effects. It also has the virtue of making people salivate a lot, and is therefore beneficial to those suffering from pituitary problems. A decoction of its leaves, taken with sugar, is also good for curing children's coughs. Wild arugula has a slightly different shape to the preceding plant; its root is white, thick and long; its stem is very branchy, hollow, fluted and hairy; its leaves are cut like those of the dandelion, dark green, smooth, with a burning taste; its flowers are yellow, arranged like those of the preceding plant; and the flowers are followed by long, angular siliques, filled with seeds similar to those of wild mustard. The whole plant gives off a strong odor, which pleases some and displeases others; its flavor is also pungent, burning and bitter at the end. This plant grows naturally in uncultivated and arid places, and particularly in old walls: it has all the same qualities as the previous one, for medicine, it even surpasses it; but as food, it irritates the taste more because of its pungency; however, country people also eat it in salads, especially in hot countries. It is also eaten finely chopped on buttered toast, like cran. The first species is sown in gardens in March, and requires no special care: any soil is suitable. The seed is harvested in July and August, and keeps well for two years. "========= 1 CHAPTER LXXI. Description of RUE; its different species, properties, cullure, etc. Rue is a species of aromatic plant, which is perennial; there are three species, domestic, wild and small-leaved. The domestic rue has a woody, yellow root with several fibers; it grows like a shrub, and when well cultivated, can reach five to six feet; its stems are as thick as a finger, woody, twiggy, and covered with a whitish bark: its leaves are divided into several parts, small, oblong, fleshy, a little fatty, smooth, sea-green in color, arranged in pairs, on a rib ending in an odd one; its flowers are born at the tops of the branches, R 6 small, composed of four petals, pale yellow in color; The flowers are followed by fruits, usually composed of four capsules, assembled against a stone, and each capsule contains several seeds, most often in the shape of a small rooster's kidney, which are angular and black in color. The whole plant has a very unpleasant odor, and a bitter, acrid taste. The wild rue differs from the previous one in that its stem is lower, and its leaves are divided into longer, narrower parts, with a darker green color, a stronger odor and a more pungent taste: in all other respects, the same resemblance. The rue à feuille menue (small-leaved rue) has a rather large, white, woody root; its leaves turn over on the ground, and are divided very small, pale green in color, with a very strong odor and a pungent taste; between the leaves, two or three stems divided into twigs sometimes arise, which end in bunches of flowers similar to those of the preceding species, but smaller, pale yellow in color; they are followed by fruits, composed, like the others, of four capsules containing small, black, acrid seeds. These last two species grow naturally in Languedoc and Provence, in stony, uncultivated places. We'll confine ourselves here to the plant's nutritional qualities; but in Italy, its young shoots are eaten with pleasure in salads, and even without any seasoning: there, it doesn't have the pungency and bad odor it has here, and this is undoubtedly due to the climate. We'll confine ourselves here to its health-giving properties, the first of which is the most commonly used: it is hysterical, cephalic, stomachic, vermifuge, carminative, anti-scorbutic, cordial and vulnerary. One or two pinches of its fresh leaves, infused in a glass of white hemp, or a dragme of its powder, when dried, is very suitable for restoring the course of the months and soothing hysterical vapors. For the same illnesses, boil a small handful of its leaves with as much hyssop in wine, and drink a hot glass. Preserving the leaves and flowers dissipates indigestion, and the oil extracted from them kills worms. Soak a cotton ball in it and put it in children's navels; if this oil is not available, its expressed juice has the same effect: a few spoonfuls can even be drunk on an empty stomach, mixed with couch grass water. The decoction of its leaves, taken as an enema or applied as a poultice to the stomach, is sovereign for colic: the olive oil in which the leaves and seeds of this plant have been infused is still a powerful remedy for the same ailment; and the essential oil extracted from it is one of the best known for hysterical passion. The leaf is very suitable for treating écrouelles; children afflicted with this disease are made to eat three or four of them on an empty stomach with bread, over a period of time, and this simple remedy has often cured them. If they are too reluctant, they can be made to swallow three ounces of the juice purified from these leaves. Two spoonfuls of the same juice, mixed with the same amount of good wine, are still very good for protecting against bad air, in contagious diseases: the dose can even be increased to a glass, and one is taken in the morning, and another four hours after dinner. In Italy, a vinegar is made from it, which serves as a preservative in these kinds of cases, and especially during the bad weather that reigns every year on the Remne side, from Midsummer to All Saints' Day. It is made by infusing the leaves of this plant in the strongest vinegar, adding a little burnet, betony, a few cloves of garlic, walnuts, juniper berries and a little camphor; the dose is one spoonful in the morning, and as much in the afternoon. The leaf is also very useful for epileptics, being crumpled and introduced into the nostrils at the time of the attack. A decoction of the leaves is also an excellent gargle for the gums of scorbutic patients, and for those with smallpox: this gargle resolves the seeds around the throat; it can also be used to baste around the eyes. Three or four ounces are swallowed, and the pomace is applied to the bite. There is also experience that these leaves, applied to both pulses, prevent drunkenness. Here's another particular virtue of this plant. By boiling a few shirts in a decoction of its leaves and natural water, no pus is ever produced; a useful remedy for those who, by the nature of their flesh, are prone to this vermin. So many virtues indicate that a garden should never be without a few feet of rue, to find it when needed; it is a plant, moreover, that gives no care, and which, once planted, remains abandoned to itself. It has no fear of bad weather, can be kept for many years in the same place, and thrives in any kind of soil, as long as it is slightly exposed to the sun, which enhances its virtues: it can be propagated from seed, cuttings or rooted plants. The third species is sometimes prone to perish in the open ground, when winters are harsh and long: but as the other two suffice us well, and are foolproof, we can dispense with any expense for this one. Description of SALSIFIS from SPAIN; its properties, cultivation, etc. THE merit of Spanish salsify, otherwise known as Scorsonnera, lies in its root, which is one of the best and healthiest. This root is black on the outside, white on the inside, about the size of a little finger, almost equal at both ends, and very straight when the soil is very loose: but in many soils it becomes forked. The leaf is very narrow, up to a third of its length; it then widens precipitously, and ends in a very elongated point; so that its fullness, which is about an inch, is placed at two-thirds of its length, which is eight to nine inches: its edges are trimmed with small, sawtooth-shaped spikes, unevenly placed, and its color is a meadow green; its stem is round and loose, slightly fluted, soft and branchy, trimmed with a few leaves from interval to interval, and about three feet high: its flowers are placed at the end of its small branches, arranged like a daisy, yellow in color: the petals that compose it emerge from a kind of elongated bud, which grows as the flower passes, and which contains the seed, which, coming to ripen, breaks the calyx, and spreads out in the shape of a tassel, the size of a billiard ball, having a clip at the end of each of its seeds, which are long, small and white. Its root is used as a lean food, from All Saints' Day to Easter; but it's mainly used during Lent: it's seasoned with white sauce, or fried with a paste like artichokes. Good cooks accommodate it in many other ways, and give it different shapes; it is also used to make entremets en gras, which are highly esteemed. It has the same health-giving properties. Its main quality is to be cordial and sudorific: it is used in all the teas made for diseases suspected of malignancy, and mainly for smallpox. It is good against the bite of snakes and other venomous beasts; it is also used to provoke women's months: its leaves also have their virtues, and are used in the composition of several distilled waters for chest pains. This plant therefore deserves its place in a vegetable garden. The seed is sown at the end of April in dry soils, and in mid-May in heavy soils. When it is sown earlier, it is prone to rot; the soil must be warmed up a little before it germinates and sprouts: it usually remains for a fortnight or three weeks before coming out. It can also be sown in August. The soil must be perfectly loose and well-prepared, with no clods or stones; because the better it is worked, the more the root shoots forward and comes up straight and even, which is its main merit. In strong soils, it is prone to becoming forked, glassy, and consequently bad, unless you lighten it with a lot of loam, which you mix well with the soil. A very deep ploughing should be done first, in November, and a second one before sowing; and when it can be placed in newly broken ground, it does even better. If this is not possible, the soil should have been smoked the previous year, and occupied by plants that have not crumbled it too much, such as cabbages: furrowing the soil before sowing should be avoided, as all the roots would be counterfeit. The seed is sown in a border or bed, in rays seven to eight inches apart; after the seed is sown, or even before spreading it in the rays, the soil must be left to tan for a few hours; it is then sown, and lightly treaded; it is then covered, and the rake is passed over to unite the soil: the next day, when the soil is a little tanned, wet it well, and continue for two days at a time, if the weather is dry, until it has risen well: Our market gardeners in Aubervilliers, who sow whole fields of it, don't take so many precautions, but they owe the advantage of being able to do without it to the constitution of their soil. This soil, whose parts are supple and loose, almost never seals or cracks; nor does it dry out as quickly as many others, and the roots of all kinds of plants emerge from it with unusual ease: it may also have particular salts and nitrates, which make this root benefit in one year, as much as it does in two in most other soils; this means that it is lifted at the end of the year, and that everywhere else it is left in place for two years, in order to grow to a reasonable size: we must therefore not take them as models in this respect. Six weeks after this root has sprouted, it should be thinned out, leaving a good two inches between each plant: weed it at the same time and wet it afterwards, to reassure the soil and fill in the gaps: after that, we don't water it any more. This plant, different in this respect from all other roots, bears its seed the same year it is sown, without the root receiving any alteration. From the end of June, it begins to rise, and is ripe in July. Care must be taken to remove it as it blooms, as the slightest wind blows it away, and birds, which are very fond of it, shake it off and eat it. When it is completely picked, all the stems must be cut off flush to the ground, and the plant must be thoroughly wetted; it will soon green up again: there is no other way to grow it. If you want to eat it during the winter, you can pull out what you want at the end of November, and bury it in the greenhouse or in a trench, as I've explained for other plants. But if you're saving it for Lent, you only pull it out as and when you eat it; and it's always better fresh from the ground. What I have just said is as much as one would like to eat in the first year; but as this is not usual in private gardens, it is left in place without any care, until one wants to enjoy it, at the end of the second or third year: one is content simply to crimp it at the beginning of spring, when it begins to grow its new leaves which make it recognizable; for during the winter all its foliage perishes. Shortly afterwards, it sprouts its stem, which grows and provides much more than that of the first year; its seed also ripens earlier, and is good to pick at the beginning of July: it should be preferred to that of the first year; and the reason for this is that the stalk, which has more strength, feeds it better. It keeps well for two years. In areas close to woods where birds are common, it is very difficult to save it at this time of year, when neither the seeds nor any other seeds are yet ripe; and we are often obliged to keep it, if the scarecrows are not enough; for, without even waiting for it to ripen, they pierce the husk of the bud, and eat it green. To avoid, at least in part, their damage, when you don't have the convenience of keeping it, you can do what I do: cut off all the buds that are beginning to yellow, without waiting for them to open, and lay them on a sheet in the sun; soon after they develop, and the seed is equally good. This seed is also subject to another scourge, which is nail, which attaches itself to the stems and causes them to perish. There is no remedy for this: you need to reserve more than less, so as not to be deprived. This plant's enemy is the beetle worm, which cuts its roots. As soon as you see a plant with a wilting leaf, look for it quickly, otherwise it will ruin entire rays. The mole also sometimes wreaks havoc: watch out and catch it. CHAPTER LXXIII. Description of common salsify; its properties, cultivation, etc. Common salsify, otherwise known as white salsify, differs from Spanish salsify, which I have just described, in that its root is white both inside and out, and is also larger and less prone to forking. Its leaf is very narrow and smooth, shaped like a gutter, twelve to fifteen inches long, of a whitish water-green: its stem is branched, fairly large, three or four feet high; its flower is a violet-red, sun-shaped: it is placed at the end of its stems, and comes out of an elongated bud in the same way as the Spanish salsify; but the bud and flower are much larger. After the flower has passed, the bud opens, and the seed spreads out in the same way, in the shape of a tassel, each seed being accompanied by its aigrette. The seed is twice as large as that of black salsify, a little longer too, and gray or ashen in color. The root, although less effective than the first species, has the same uses for suspicious diseases. This root, although less spicy in taste than the other, is nevertheless very useful during Lent, and makes a very healthy food; it is eaten prepared in the same way. I won't repeat what I've said about it. It has the advantage over blackcurrants of occupying the land for only one year: it is sown in April or May, depending on the soil, and is ready for harvest as early as All Saints' Day; but it is commonly reserved for Lent. It is grown in the same way as the other variety, and requires the same quality of soil. It is quite resistant to frosts and bad weather, so you don't need to pull it up to use it during Lent: but if you want to use it during the winter, you need to pull up the quantity you think you'll need around Christmas, and put it in a greenhouse in fresh sand, or bury it in a trench dug in the garden, which you take care to cover well during frosts. Leave as much as you want to keep for seed, and if you're worried about frosts damaging it, although there's little risk of that, you can cover the spot with dry sills: manure is too precious to use for this purpose. Its foliage dries out entirely during the winter; but as soon as spring arrives, the leaf grows back, and we immediately give it a little hoeing; soon afterwards it makes its stem, and its seed is ripe in July. The same precautions need to be taken as for the other plant, to be able to preserve it: the birds devour part of it, and the wind carries away the rest, if you are not clever enough to pick it up as it opens out, to make its tassel: there is, however, a way I use to defend against the wind'; it's to cut the flower buds above the seed with scissors, when they start to yellow. It's easy to see how much space the seed occupies in the bud, so as not to damage it. This operation provides a second benefit, which is to pick up the seed clean, because the chisel takes away the burrs that catch the wind, and you don't have to go to the trouble of cleaning it, which is a hassle. After picking it up, leave it exposed to the sun on a sheet for a day or two, winnow it and lock it up: it's only good for sowing in the first year; in the second, some of it still rises, but you don't need to make a sure foundation. Description of the SARRIETTE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. CETTE plante n'est pas d'une grande elle sert quelquefois, et qu'elle a d'autres propriétés, il faut lui donner rang avec les autres: l'on appelle indifféremment Sarriette, Sadrée et Savorée. There are four species, but only one is cultivated usefully; the second is known to us only by relation; and the other two, which are not very widespread, have no merit other than to please the curious. The first species, which we cultivate, forms a rounded, regularly branched tuft, about a foot wide and of the same height; its root is simple, small and woody; its wood is hard, and resembles dry wood; its leaves are narrow and oblong, holding the middle ground between those of thyme and hyssop; its flowers emerge from leaf axils in places; they are mouth-shaped, perfectly similar to those of thyme, white in color, tending to purpurin. When they have passed, they are succeeded by small, almost round, slate-colored seeds enclosed in capsules that served as calyxes for the flowers. Its main cooking advantage is that it enhances the taste of marsh beans, with which it goes very well. To achieve this, sow a little on a bed, then replant it at the foot of a well-exposed wall, so that it comes up at the same time as the first beans: it is also sometimes used in certain sauces that call for strong herbs. The Germans put it in their candied cabbage, which they call Saurkraudt, and claim that it helps to preserve it longer. It is much more useful in medicine, and so good that it is called sauce aux pauvres gens (sauce for the poor); it restores and strengthens the stomach: its decoction, syringed into the ear, is very good in soporous affections, to awaken the sick: it is also useful as a gargle for loosening the uvula, and for inflammation of the tonsils. The powder of its dried leaves, drunk in a glass of wine, relieves chest pains. Some authors extend its virtues much further, but I'll confine myself to those that have proved most effective. S 2 Its cultivation is very simple; it grows easily in any soil, and so easily that it reproduces itself every year, without any care, in places where it has been grown once: it can be used in any degree of strength until it goes to seed; and to collect it, it is left to ripen to the point where it begins to detach from the first capsules; at this point, the whole feet are torn off, and tied into bundles, which are hung on a floor: it does not need to be exposed to the sun; the air is enough to perfect it. It keeps well for four or five years, when left in its capsules. Those who need this plant during the winter should pull out as much as they see fit, before it flowers, and dry it in the shade, attached to a floor that is not extremely exposed to flies. The second species, called Sariette de Candie, is known to us, as I said earlier, only by reputation, and I have never been able to see it. According to M. Chomel, who gives a short description, its scent is much more pleasant than the one I mentioned, and an essential oil with great virtues is extracted from it. He compares its properties to those of thyme, and says no more, but that's enough to make us regret not knowing about it. It seems to me, however, that being common in Candia, whose remoteness is not very considerable, those curious about botany should not remain privẽs of it. The other two, which I saw without having cultivated them, are both perennials, and form a fairly tall shrub: one has an oblong leaf much like that of tarragon, and bears at its apices clusters of bluish-white flowers, borne on a group of small calyxes piled one on top of the other, followed by a small, elongated, russet-colored seed, by which it is produced: it can also be multiplied by its offshoots. It can also be propagated by its offspring, but must be raised in pots and sown in the greenhouse when frost approaches. The other has a small, elongated leaf, and grows small white flowers all along the branches, which bloom imperceptibly; and as it is very delicate, it must be locked up early in a warm greenhouse: it keeps its leaf there all winter. I know of no useful qualities for these two species, and the authors have said nothing about them. - THE SAUGE. CHAPTER LXXV. Description of Sage; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Sage is a perennial and aromatic plant; I know of fourteen different species, and I know that there are a few other less remarkable ones, which I will pass over in silence. These fourteen species are the purplish-flowered grande saugrande, the white-flowered d'Espagne, the lavender-leaved d'Espagne, the variegated yellow, the curly, the berry-bearing, the broad-leaved petite du Levant, the large du Levant, the yellow-flowered d'Afrique, the purple-flowered d'Afrique, and the mountain sage. The large sage, otherwise known as the large species, and in botany as Spacellus Theophrasti, has a woody root with many fibers; Its leaf is oval-shaped, moderately pointed, thick and chagrined, water-green, covered with a small white down, borne on a reddish stalk, with a strong, aromatic odor and flavor; it grows several branching, woody stems, hairy and reddish at the tips, rising to about three feet: Its flowers are born at the end of the stems, and are borne on a kind of spike; they are ash-blue in color, and form a pipe cut into two lips at the top, the upper one arched, and the lower one divided into three parts. From the front of this flower rise the stamens, attached together and arranged in such a way that they do not misrepresent the hioid bone: the calyx is a cone that pushes out from the bottom a pistil composed of four embryos; this pistil fits into a hole at the bottom of the flower, and these embryos subsequently become so many almost round seeds, enclosed in a capsule that served as the flower's calyx. Sage franche, which botanists call Calvia minor aurita and not aurita, is similar in many respects to the preceding variety, but it has more leaves and does not grow so high. Its wood is also redder and more woody, and its leaf more elongated and narrower, sometimes having ears at its base; its grain and color are quite similar, as is its flower. Provence sage, called Salvia folio tenuiore, has the root and wood of its stems equally woody; but its leaves are much smaller, narrower, 4 1 and in greater quantity, being as if piled on top of each other at the end of the branches: its flower is arranged like the others, but bright blue. The large purpurine sage differs from the first only in that its flower is reddish, tending to purple, and its odor is stronger. White-flowered Spanish sage differs from the above in that its leaves are long and narrow, yellowish-green; its stems are also green, sparsely hairy, and its flower white. It grows to about two feet tall, and produces only a few, rather thin branches. Spanish sage, with a lavender leaf, is called by this name because its leaves are long and narrow, a little toothed, whiter than green, and strongly resembling the lavender leaf in all respects. Its stems are also more naked and whitish than the other species. The variegated yellow, otherwise known as omelette, has a leaf mottled with green and yellow, and is a little obtuse; in all other respects, it bears the same resemblance to the others. Frisée has a broad, almost round leaf, toothed and curled at the edges, carried on a long tail, pale water-green, soft on the finger like marshmallow, without any marked grain, and with a less penetrating odor than the others: it only grows to a foot or eighteen inches; its flower is blue, similar to the others. Botanists call it Salvia baccifera for this reason: its leaves are heart-shaped, tender green, yellowish and velvety; its stems are also regularly green, and its scent quite sweet: it forms a very tall shrub, and bears small pea-sized fruits, in which the seed is enclosed. Levant sage, with its broad leaves, is totally different from all the others in that its euilla is winged and arranged like that of the rosebush; but the impaire ending it is considerably larger than the segmens on the sides; it is also very hairy, toothed at the edges and meadow-green; it does not grow upwards, and its stems crawl on the ground; its flower is blue and very large. Levant sage differs from the first species only in its leaf, which is larger. African sage, with its yellow flower, grows like a shrub; its leaf is rounded, smooth at the edges, velvety and sea-green; its wood is ash-colored, and its flower golden yellow. African sage, with violet flowers, also grows as a shrub: its leaves are small, almost round, a little toothed, and whitish water-green; its wood is hazelnut-colored, and its flower violet. Mountain sage, otherwise known as wild sage, has a large, broad, soft leaf, with a garlic-like odor; its flower is yellowish, and grows to three feet or more; but its stems die every year; it must be cut flush with the ground in late autumn, and grows again in spring: it grows naturally in mountainous woods, around bushes and hedges. Some claim that all these species of sage are merely varieties of the first species, which grows naturally in Provence, and that the differences we notice there have gradually arisen from changes in terrain and climate, as well as from cultivation. I cannot accept this opinion; for these species differ too greatly from one another to be regarded as mere varieties: there is an extreme disproportion in size and grain, and even in smell: one grows higher, the other lower; one has a blue flower, the other purple or yellow; the latter bears fruit, etc. All these characteristics must be recognized in the plant. All these characteristics must be recognized as species differences, or they must no longer be admitted in any other plant; for it would then follow that there would only be one species of cabbage, one species of lettuce, etc., because their tastes and other properties are always the same, from the most to the least. I agree that changes of soil and climate diminish or increase a plant's vigor, as well as its virtues; but they don't cut the leaf, if it wasn't cut in the first place; they don't change the color of the flower from white to yellow. Let's take all these species of sage to the rocks of Provence, where they are said to have originated, and I'm convinced that they will always retain the same differences there as they do here. In a word, one came to us from Spain, the other from the Levant, the other from Africa, and so on. Why pretend that these regions, which are so far apart from one another, drew the species they have communicated to us from the same stem, and that these species did not originate naturally in their own bosom? Everyone will conclude as they see fit. The fourteen species I have described all have the same virtues, from the most to the least, and some can be used in the absence of others; however, Spanish sage is reputed by botanists to be the best; little Provence sage comes S6 after it, and frank sage after that; jumping sage has particular qualities, which I will discuss in a separate article. The leaves and flowers of this plant are very useful in aromatic decoctions and fomentations, for strengthening nerves, firming flesh, softening tumors and dissipating the swelling of wounds; It is also good for scurvy, especially if the gums are well bathed with half its juice, and as much cochlearia juice mixed with similar salse and balauste; it makes white flowers pass; but fat women should not be given it, because it promotes menstruation. An infusion of the leaves is taken internally for dizziness, vapors, drowsiness and other affections of the brain, which threaten apoplexy, paralysis and so on. At the same time, it revives the movement of liquors and blood circulation. Eight or ten leaves are infused in half a cup of boiling water, and drunk every morning on an empty stomach with a little sugar, for several days. The same infusion is very useful for suppressing menstruation and urination, indigestion and stomach weakness, wind, colic and spitting blood, killing worms and clearing the lungs of asthmatics; the effect is even more certain when the leaf is smoked like tobacco. The infusion of this leaf in wine is also sovereign for toothache, if two large quantities of good tobacco are added. Water distilled from sage, which is poured over wounds, mundializes them; drawn through the nose, it stops haemorrhaging, fortifies the brain and limbs, and by washing the mouth with it, tightens the gums. Finally, this plant has so many virtues that it is considered by many to be universal and suitable for all ailments; this is why an ancient saying goes: Cur moritur homo cui salvia crescit in horto? and this is why it is called Salvia, from Salvus, healthy. However, although salvia is beneficial in all countries, it is unanimously considered to have more virtues when grown in hot climates, such as Provence. It is said to attract the snakes and toads that intertwine in its branches, and that they spread their venom on the leaves, from which bad effects can ensue, in addition to stinging those who approach them; but the remedy for this inconvenience is to mix in a few feet of rue to keep them away. Wild sage, which, according to M. Tournefort, is a species of Germandrée, has the merit more than the others of removing jaundice and tierce fever, by taking its juice or an insusion in wine; and for dropsy, an infusion of this leaf is given daily in white wine, of which a glass is taken every four hours, with great effect. This plant could be propagated from seed, but as it is easier to propagate from cuttings or rooted plants, and is more enjoyable, we leave it at that for the species that can overwinter in the ground; an old separate plant provides a dozen more or less, which are replanted in spring or autumn, it's all the same; and as the most common use is to form borders around vegetable garden quarters, either outside or inside, a string is stretched out, and a small trench seven to eight inches deep by the same width is opened, and buried close to the end of the stems, i.e. to within four inches, treading the soil with the foot after the trench is filled in. It goes without saying that the roots must be shortened beforehand. No other preparation is required, and there is no lack of it, provided the plants have roots. This plant is by no means delicate; it fears neither frost, nor drought, nor humidity; however, it has more virtue in dry soils than in watery ones; so, as much as possible, it should be placed according to taste. It can be kept in the same place for as long as you like, but as it grows and spreads too much after three years, and makes an ugly effect on the eyes, it should be destroyed at this age, and renewed. When planted from cuttings, a little more care is needed, and it should be planted in spring to give it time to root during the summer. The most important thing is to lay the sprigs down, press them down firmly with your foot after they have been covered with soil, and water often until they are well established; but the safest way is to root them on the bed, and after six weeks, you can remove them with a little clod and place them wherever you like. It should be noted that the two African salges, the curly one and the berry-bearing one, do not overwinter in the open ground; they must be placed in pots, and locked up in the greenhouse when frost approaches; the following spring, they are buried with the pots in a well-exposed spot, as they require a lot of heat. THYM. CHAPTER LXXVI. Description of THYME; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. THYME is an aromatic perennial plant of which there are five main species, not to mention several kinds of wild thyme known as Serpolet. These five species are common garden thyme with small leaves, variegated thyme, Crete thyme, broad-leaved thyme and lemon thyme. Common thyme has a woody root with many fibers; it sprouts a number of small twigs, rising to eight or ten inches, and forming a full, rounded tuft; these twigs are covered throughout with small, oblong, narrow leaves, ash-colored, with a strong, aromatic odor and a pungent taste: The flowers are small, purplish, shaped like a maw and cut into two lips at the top. The flower is followed by a capsule containing four almost round seeds. Thyme panaché differs from the previous variety only in the plume of its leaves, which are partly white and partly ashy; consequently, it is more of a variety than a difference in species. Cretan thyme grows as a shrub to twelve or fifteen inches in height, and produces many large, woody branches with small, opposite, narrow, whitish, pungent-tasting leaves; its flowers are arranged in the same way as the others. Broad-leaved thyme grows lower than its predecessors; its branches fall to the ground in great numbers; its leaves are oblong and much larger, of an obscure green color, with a less penetrating odor. It is very similar to the others, either in root, flower or seed. Lemon thyme differs from the others only in its odor, which is similar to that of lemon, from which it takes its name. These five species have more or less the same virtues; however, Crete thyme would be preferred if it were more common; but as it is very difficult to grow in this climate, we stick to the others, and particularly to the first species, which can be found in every garden. It is used in food with other fine herbs, to enhance the flavor of meat and fish, especially in short broths; it has no other use. In medicine, it is used in many cases; it is resolving, desiccating, attenuating, incisive and discussing; it enters into the aromatic and cephalic decoctions and infusions, so commonly used in fomentation, to basin nervous and muscular parts that are weakened or too swollen. Its powder, mixed with honey and barley flour, relieves sciatic gout when applied to the affected part as a poultice. It fortifies the brain and alleviates pituitary. Its main use is in tartarous affections of the lungs, such as asthma and obstinate coughs: it is also used for windy colic, to stimulate appetite and aid digestion. It is also used externally for cold humors, eye contusions, gout and paralysis. This plant multiplies from seed, cuttings and rooted plants, but more commonly in the latter way than in the other two: it is replanted in autumn or spring, in the same way as I said for sage and lavender. The first, fourth and fifth species are winter-hardy, and require no special care; but the second and third need the greenhouse, and must therefore be raised in pots. The one in gardens is renewed every three years; it forms very clean borders around vegetable garden quarters; and at flowering time, it gives off a very pleasant odor; it is then that we cut what we deem appropriate, for the various uses to which we wish to put it, as the flower greatly increases its virtue; and as it is the sap's forte, all its parts are more spirituous. CHAPTER LXXVII. Description of TOPINAMBOUR; its uses, cultivation, etc. HERE is the worst of all vegetables, in the general opinion; yet the people, who are the most numerous part of humanity, feed on it: I must therefore place this vegetable with the others. Its root is an assembly of a multitude of small roots and fibers, between which bulbs are attached: Its stem is stalked and three to four feet high, about the size of a thumb, fluted, hollow and hairy; its leaves are large, oblong and pointed, a little hairy; each branch ends in a yellow, radiate, sun-shaped flower, all the petals of which are supported by a ball-shaped calyx, which encloses the seed; this seed is small and brown in color. The fruit is egg-sized, sometimes two or three times larger, baroque in shape, with spikes and knots around the circumference, white inside and reddish outside. This fruit, which is the whole point of the plant, is eaten with white sauce, after being cooked in water; others fricassee it in butter with onion: its taste is quite similar to artichoke or salsify, but it is soft and mushy: it keeps all winter until Easter. It is sometimes used medicinally to stop stomach upsets, being by nature detersive, astringent and pectoral: it is eaten cooked, or a decoction is drunk. This plant originated in America, in the land of the Topinambous, from which it takes its name; it is also called Potato. It multiplies from seed, or from its own fruit, which is replanted in March, in the same way as the truffle. Any loose soil is good for it, and it requires no special care: the fruit is pulled up when frost approaches, and placed in a heap in the greenhouse; others run through the winter event, and leave it in the ground until Lent. CHAPTER LXXVIII. Description of TRIQUE-MADAME; its properties, cultivation, etc. LA trique-madame, which others call Trippe-Madame, is a species of small houseleek that grows naturally on old walls, but which cultivation has perfected. Its stem is small, fibrous and blackish; it grows several fat, fleshy, tender, creeping stems, covered with many small, oblong, thick, fat, pointed, bluish-green or reddish leaves, filled with juice: its flowers, which are born at the top of the stems, are small, with several leaves arranged in a pink, and yellow in color; the flowers are followed by a small fruit containing five seeds. The use of this plant is limited to salads, where it is mixed with other supplies; it has its supporters, but not the greatest number. In medicine, it is sometimes substituted for houseleek, as it is humectant and refreshing; good, in particular, for haemorrhoids. It multiplies from seed, cuttings and offshoots; each foot makes many arms, which, when separated and replanted, form as many new feet; it is almost equally successful from cuttings, provided they are watered often and kept out of the sun for a few days. It is planted a foot apart, and watered often; this is what makes it tender. CHAPTER LXXIX. Description of the TRUFFLE; its different species, properties, cultivation, etc. Here is a plant of which no author has spoken, and probably it is out of contempt for it that it has been excluded from the class of vegetable plants; for it is too long known and too widespread for it to have escaped their knowledge; yet there is injustice in omitting a fruit that serves as food for a large proportion of men of all nations. I don't want to elevate it more than it deserves, because I know all its faults, which I'll talk about; but I feel it should have a place with the others, since it serves a useful purpose, and has its enthusiasts. In most of our provinces, it is not only the lower classes and country folk who make a living from it, but even the most affluent people in the cities; and I can also say, from the knowledge I have of it, that many people love it out of passion. Whether this is a well-placed affection, or a depravity of taste, I put aside; it has its supporters, that's enough for me. There are two species of truffle, differing from one another only in external color, one being red, the other white tending to yellow: the latter is preferred, having less pungency than the former. The fruit is born between two earths, and is held to the roots by a kind of pedicel numbering twenty or thirty, some larger, others smaller: this fruit is elongated, rounded at both ends, uneven, with a sort of sunken eyes all around, which are as many sprouts of the plant, three to four inches long, about eighteen lines in diameter: it is covered with a film that lifts easily when cooked: its flesh is white and firm, a little watery, with no odor. The plant grows several branches at a time, which are hard and woody, almost triangular, partly green and partly reddish in color, lined with thresholds and small twigs throughout; these leaves are arranged in the same way as those of the rose, and of similar size, dull green, hairy at the tops of the stems: from the leaf axils emerge a few bunches of flowers borne on a fairly long tail: these flowers are one-piece, star-shaped, flax-gray in color, with a few yellow stamens in the center, whose tips meet and form a sort of keel; they are borne on an embryo at the bottom of the calyx, which turns into a round fruit, the size of a small walnut, which is green at first, turning yellow as it ripens. This fruit is fleshy and contains a number of small seeds, by which the plant can multiply if necessary, but they are not used. This fruit can be seasoned in all sorts of ways: sliced thinly and fried in butter or oil, with a light dusting of flour; cooked in water, with the skin removed, sliced and fried in butter with onion: Others cook it in wine, but the best way is to chop it after cooking, and make a paste with breadcrumbs, a few egg yolks and fine herbs, from which we make dumplings, which are browned in butter in the pan. Common people eat it simply cooked in ashes, with a little salt; and in the mountains, it's made into bread. Finally, it is consumed in considerable quantities, particularly in the provinces near the Rhône; and, in addition to being used as human food, it is also used to fatten animals. I will admit, however, that it is a bland, insipid food, and very hard on the stomach; but it has a certain taste that pleases its lovers: what can one object against it? And when one is accustomed to a thing, how much of its defects does it not lose? One thing is certain: this fruit is nourishing, and by force of habit, it doesn't bother those who have been accustomed to it from youth. What's more, it's very economical for the lower classes: these advantages may well outweigh its faults. It is not unknown in Paris; but it is true that it is abandoned to the common people, and that people of a certain order put it below them to see it appear on their table: I do not want to inspire in them a taste for it, which I do not have myself; but one should not condemn those to whom it pleases and to whom it is profitable. I don't think it has any properties for Tome II. However, a few years ago, it was devised as a powder to be used as a substitute for ordinary powder in times of high grain prices. At first, it met with some success, and the Ministry helped the enterprise with its protection; but when it was put to use, it was found to be too heavy, and not suitable for hair, which caused it to fail, and it is no longer used. This plant is sown in March; it requires loose, fat soil, ploughed deeply: some people make holes with the planter, and throw the seed in: others make rays with the hoe, and spread it in, covering it with three or four inches of soil; this last method is the best. Besides, this seed is nothing other than the fruit itself, which is cut into six, eight or ten pieces, depending on its size; as long as there is an eye in each piece, no more is needed. You can also sow small, hazelnut-sized truffles, which you set aside every year when you dig them up: you space them twelve or fifteen inches apart; when they've risen to a certain height, you crimp them; you don't need any other cultivation. Some, however, cut the tops halfway off when they are at about their height, to make better use of the stalks; others knock them to the ground, and throw a spoonful of earth on top; but most do nothing about it, and I have found that they grow very well without any of these precautions. Around All Saints' Day, we pull out the stalks and detach the fruit, if the soil is not too well sealed; a fork is better for this than any sharp tool: we let the fruit dry out a little and then lock it up, noting that we don't want a greenhouse that's too hot, which would make it sprout, nor a cellar that's too damp, which would make it rot, nor any place where frost could penetrate; once it's in the right place, it keeps until after Easter. I'll say a word in passing about another species of truffle that grows naturally in the ponds of some provinces, particularly in Bourbonnois and Burgundy: it goes by many other names, truffle or water truffle, macer, cornouelle, water chestnut, echarbot, etc. This fruit is produced by an aquatic plant that grows in ponds. This fruit is produced by an aquatic plant; its shape is horny, walnut-sized, its rind brown, and its kernel white; its taste is sweet, approaching that of the chestnut. It is prepared for eating in various ways: some cook it in ash like chestnuts, others in boiling water; it is made into bread and a kind of porridge in Limosin, where children are very fond of it; some eat it raw like hazelnuts; and all the ancient and modern authors who have spoken of it, going back as far as Dioscorides and Theophrastus, have praised it as a refreshing dish and a useful food: It is even said to have properties for certain illnesses: when cooked and applied as a poultice to inflammations, it resolves them; its juice is also very good for eye diseases; and its decoction with honey as a gargle is very suitable for cleaning ulcerated gums. A PARIS Chez DELALAIN fils, Libraire, quai des Augustins, Ne. 38. An XI, 1802. EEI Google IERUET Google A misplaced wisdom is a real follyWanting to bring men back to one's taste, however reasonable it may be, is of all enterprises the least sensible. Each century has its own mores, which must not be contradicted. It would be useless to try to introduce even wiser ones; the shortest way is to follow one's own, without exhausting oneself in reasoning to try to bend others to it. A philosopher by temperament, and perhaps by reflection, will I go and extol to the worldly the charms of retirement, incomprehensible to those whose hearts are not made for it? Gardening is my attraction; for many years I have made it the amusement of my leisure, and the most solid occupation of my life. Is this a reason to flaunt the merits of this exercise? It seems to me that I would do as well as anyone else in painting the golden age, when cultivating the land was the noblest of arts, as it still is the most useful. I could recall men to their natural vocation, and adorn this discourse with touching descriptions, which would hardly make more of an impression on most of my readers, than the sight of a beautiful landscape placed in the cabinet of a rich man, does on these men of the century, accustomed to the pomp and noise of cities; but that is neither my mission, nor my object. I'm not trying to inspire a taste for gardening; I'm writing for those who already have it, and this little work, intended for their instruction, should offer nothing strange to the goal I propose. My birth and the course of affairs in which I was engaged from my youth, should, it seems to me, have left me forever ignorant of all that belongs to Gardening; but who can answer for events? From a hectic and constrained life, I passed almost all of a sudden to a free and quiet life; and the circumstances which detached me from all kinds of business, made me leave the city at the same time. I retired to a country house just outside Paris, which, having belonged to a Minister of State before me, had all the advantages one could imagine. Its happy situation, the good quality of the bottom, its extent and the convenience of the water, attracted me more and more. Finally, I resolved to settle there, and to do so usefully, I made a regular occupation of it. The cultivation of my land was the object to which my taste turned. At first, like many others, I was handed over to an ignorant gardener in bad faith, and I allowed myself to be led by his advice in the first operations I tried, but I soon recognized that they were wrong. Consequently, on other occasions, I wanted to go to the council; but the diversity of feelings and the variety of practices embarrassed me more often than they decided me. I visited all the houses whose gardens seemed to me to be well maintained; I read all the authors who had written most on the subject; in a word, I left no stone unturned in my quest for knowledge: but all this study only served to make me realize that without practice and experience, one acquires only very superficial knowledge. I therefore decided to carry out, by myself, all the operations that were within my reach; and, with the exception of the hard work, I can assure you that I put my hand to everything, i.e., I sowed, planted, pruned, palmed, grafted, etc. I wanted to know everything there was to know. I wanted to know everything inside out, and by doing this myself, I was more likely to notice any defects in the work. My mind worked even harder than my hand; I sought the good and the best; and experience, which I took as my guide, served either to assure me or to disabuse me. It was through this long application that I acquired the knowledge I share with the public. The success of my plantations introduced me to many honored people, who had the same passion, and whom curiosity attracted to me. Finally, a person of the highest esteem asked me one day for some instruction on the cultivation of peach trees, whose fruit she particularly liked, so I made it my duty to oblige her, and wrote down all my views. This little treatise, which pleased her very much, then passed from her hands into those of several curious people, who found it to their taste, and I was urged to publish it. This is the work I am giving today, with no other interest than that of being useful, and of sparing an amateur the mistakes to which inexperience can lead him. If the success of this piece fulfills my intention, I shall successively give some on the cultivation of other fruits, and on all the other parts of gardening. Although several authors have already written on this subject, I think I can say that it has never been more than sketched out, and that none of them has made a sufficient study of it to be able to serve as a guide; however, I rightly exclude M. de la Quintinie, who has given very judicious rules, based on experience and good reasoning: but he has not given his subjects an order that puts the reader at his ease, and he has not said all that the subject requires. I flatter myself that one will find in the manner in which I treat more clearness and exactitude. Perhaps the curious and the true connoisseurs will find it a little too detailed; but they must consider that they form a small number in society, and that the greater number are so little or so poorly instructed, that they need to be led, as it were, by the hand; it is essentially them that I have had in view, and my object will be fulfilled, if I succeed in being useful to them. FROM FISHING. CHAPTER ONE. Fishing in general. PEACH is one of the most excellent fruits of Europe; but in our climate, it is also the one that requires the most care, and consequently the most intelligence, to be cultivated usefully. We owe the abundance we enjoy in Paris and the surrounding area when the years are favorable to the large number of seedlings everyone has made of it; for the way they are usually managed means that we don't get out of a hundred trees what we could get out of twenty if they were managed with a certain art, and that of all the fruit trees that can be planted in a garden, there is none whose yield is so uncertain. It is true, on the other hand, that there is none that so pleasantly lines walls, that offers fruit so bright to the eye and more pleasing to the taste, and that yields so quickly. All these advantages are seductive: so people who are in a position to obtain this satisfaction, should not stop at difficulties or expense. As for those who plant for profit, they must detach themselves from the prejudice that peach tree espaliers are more profitable than other fruits. It is said that M. Girardot, a former King's Musketeer, earned up to thirty thousand pounds in income from a very small area of land he owned in Bagnolet. This example appealed to many, but it's important to distinguish the times. In the past, the cultivation of this fruit was known only to a few people; today, everyone is involved, plantations have multiplied extraordinarily, and this fruit, which has become more common, has decreased in value in proportion to its abundance. Another example is the village of Montreuil, which is said to produce nothing but peaches and a few red fruits, and which, on this simple income, pays the King fifty thousand pounds in taxes every year, to which must be added the rent for the land, which is commonly rented at 200, 250 and up to 300 pounds per acre. The conclusion is that the cultivation of peaches must in itself be very profitable. I don't dispute the Montreuil fact, but there are several things to consider. 1°. The product of these peaches is shared between four thousand inhabitants, who are dedicated to this crop, and who are, as it were, cradled in it. 2°. The location and quality of the soil are highly favorable to this species of tree, which takes five or six years to form and covers its wall from top to bottom, a feature rarely seen elsewhere. 3e. The layout of the espaliers is different from that of ordinary gardens; all the soil is cut by walls, twenty or twenty-five feet apart: these walls, forming shelter after shelter, defend the fruit from bad winds, and preserve it while it perishes elsewhere. 4°. The care that the inhabitants of Montreuil take to make the most of their fruits is inconceivable: they cultivate them with their own hands, and care for them with uncommon intelligence. They watch them night and day; they carry and sell them themselves, in the markets, with a particular art. And what private individual would want to buy them for the same price? I'm talking here about those who plant for their own benefit, and aim only for abundance; It is mainly for the latter that I am writing, and in order to do so with some order, I will begin by examining the different species of peaches, and mark those to be preferred to the others. CHAPTER II. Of the different kinds of Peaches, and the choice to be made. Sentiments vary widely on the different species of peaches. M. de la Quintinie has claimed to know thirty-two, which he has named, without the Brugnons and Pavies; others put the 3 number at forty or fifty. These, or I am very much mistaken, often use the same for two, especially as most have up to two and three names. As far as I'm concerned, I don't have anything specific to say in this regard; I've never even tried very hard to unravel this exact difference. It's a question of knowing the best; and we lose nothing by not knowing all those that are inferior to them. I declare, therefore, that I know of only about fifteen to which we should stop; the others are either very mediocre, or very bad. Others, though good, don't charge, and aren't worth the space they occupy; others are too prone to gum or ant; a few others, finally, are not fashionable, though of fairly good quality, because their elongated or biscornu shape doesn't appeal. But when it doesn't cost more to have the perfect than the defective, we must stick to the former: good exhibitions are too precious not to use them for the best we can get. Provided we have an uninterrupted succession of good peaches, from the sin of July to mid-October, after which time the fruit ripens only imperfectly, we need ask for nothing more. Finally, I would not like to enter into the fantasy of certain people who want to have everything known, good or bad, especially with regard to a fruit that costs so much care, and occupies an expensive place. The fifteen species I have chosen follow each other without interruption; and they are, without question, the most beautiful in color, the best made, the biggest, the best, and the most expensive, as everyone knows them. What I say about them is enough, without stopping to praise each one in particular. If you think it's a good idea to leave it at that, I'd advise you to distribute them as follows. Assuming you have room for 50 trees, you would plant 2. Petite Mignone. 6. Grosse Mignone. 5. Chevreuse. 4. Purple. 2. Madelaine rouge. 5. Persique. 4. Galande. 3. Tetons of Venus. 3. Italian peaches. 3. Early violets. 5. Beurdin. 4. Admirable. 3. Belgarde. 3. Royal. 2. Nivette. 2. Pavie de Pompone. If you have more or less space, you will make a proportionate distribution; and if you only have a very-small garden, where you only have room for 6 feet of trees, I advise you to choose in preference to the others, 1. Grosse Mignone. 1. Pourprée. 1. Early Violet. 1. Admirable. 1. galande. 1. Nivette. I give a place to the violet, which many people esteem only mediocrely, especially since not all soils are suitable for giving it taste and size; but when it comes in its perfection, I put it above all other peaches, and I have many supporters of my taste. V3 O I still put on the range the Pavie de Pompone, which many persoones disregard, and which I don't think much of myself, as far as taste is concerned; but I consider it for three reasons. The first is that its monstrous size and beautiful coloring perfectly decorate a table; the second is that it comes when all the last peaches are finished; and the third is that it is eaten all year long preserved in vinegar like gherkins, and that it surpasses in quality anything that is usually preserved in this way. It has been much sought-after for this reason for some years now, but there is a different way of pickling it from that used for gherkins. We also have a small dwarf peach tree raised in Orléans, which amuses the curious, but is only good for the pleasure of those who want it. It is cultivated in earthenware vases or small crates, where it is sufficiently nourished with the help of watering, and it hardly extends beyond the circumference of a clove plant; the fruit knots there very well, and it sometimes yields up to twenty or twenty-five rather large peaches: The fruit and the stem are served together on a table, and this makes a very pretty effect, especially in the eyes of those who don't know it; but the fruit is insipid, and it is even rare for it to ripen in this climate; perhaps it would be better in southern countries. Those who live in warmer climates than ours may add or subtract from the selection I have made above, whatever their climate may suggest. For example, I make no mention here of all the pavies, which I value highly in Italy and Provence. Nor do I take several kinds of late peaches, which ripen here only halfway, and which have no taste: perhaps they would be very good in these hot countries; it is up to each curious person to examine what is appropriate to his climate: but we must not envy anyone in this respect, because there is no country where this fruit has as many good qualities as it has here. I've eaten them in all the southern countries around us, right down to the depths of Italy and Sicily: our fine peaches don't do well there; the sun hits them too hard. It's a good idea to plant immediately, in the order I've just described, the fifteen species of peach and the pavia I've mentioned. I've never seen anyone do this, and I think it's important, because you don't need to run all your espaliers from one end to the other when you want to pick your fruit. When peaches of the same season are gathered together, you find everything under your hand. What's more, if you need to defend your fruit, either from people or beasts, you only have to watch over one spot. If it's necessary, in times of drought, to give water to trees whose fruit is maturing, you don't have to go so far, and you don't have to beat the ground so much along your espaliers: (I'm assuming, in saying this, that there are contr'espaliers). Finally, as it costs no more to plant them in this order, I strongly urge you to practice it. 4 On the right choice of trees, and how to raise them in nurseries. Iss environs de Paris sont remplis de pépinières; ainsi, on n'est pas embarrassé de trouver des arbres, quand les gelées de l'hiver n'ont pas fait périr les greffages, comme il est arrivé eu eu 1740 et 1742. Vitry, Fontenay-aux-Roses, le Pré-saint- Gervais, are particularly devoted to raising them; but as Vitry has the widest choice, it's the best place to get them. I've sometimes grown them in Orléans, and they've also worked well for me. The essential point is that a tree should not remain exposed to the ravages of time after being uprooted, and that its roots should be kept fresh by the help of moss and good wrapping. They must also be in the condition they should be in: the place where they were born makes no difference, as long as there is no significant difference between the land where they were grown and the land where they are put back, which is something to be careful of. They sell for 5 sous for low stems, 10 sous for half-stems and 15 sous for stems, when the year's grafts have been successful. Those who pay more are always fooled, either by the merchant's vainglorious reputation, or by the person hired to buy them. Nothing could be further from the truth than to imagine that by paying three times as much for them, as some people have the talent to sell them, you'll get better quality, or that you'll be more sure of the cash. With regard to the first point, one has eyes to see them; and with regard to the second, I admit that one can be deceived. In this profession, as in all states of life, there are people of bad faith; but there is this difference from that to the others, which is that they gain little from deceit. I will agree, however, that as there are species whose grafts are very difficult to reproduce, such as the Mignone and the Galande, certain merchants avoid giving as many as they can, and often substitute other, more common species; but this does not mean that they are all unfaithful: in this profession, as in all others, there are people who are jealous of their reputation, and who understand that their own interests depend on it. It's only a question of getting to know them, and to do that you have to get information: the advice I could give in this respect would only be of monientaneous help, since everything changes from one day to the next; so everyone will take the measures they think best. I will only say that it is customary for people of good taste to have a catalog of the plants in their nurseries and grafts, in which they list them as follows: Telle pièce de terre tenant ici, et aboutis sunt là, greffe en pécher, contient tant de rangs d'nne telle espèce, tant de telle autre, etc. You take a look at this catalog, which you have no reason to suspect is false, and by following the rows, you 4 choose what suits you best. If your dealer doesn't have a catalog, don't trust him, and go to another. These precautions are dispensed with for all other pome fruits whose species can be identified by their wood and leaf: but with the exception of four or five species of peaches, namely, grosse and petite Mignones, Madeleines, Violettes and some Pavies, all the others are so similar in wood and leaf that the merchant himself would not recognize them if he did not observe the order I have just described. For all these reasons, it is very important to make your choice yourself, when you are capable of judging it, or to be sure of the person you hire to do it: for, if you rely on your gardener, the bait of a penny per tree, which they have tyrannically subjugated the merchants to give them as a right, makes them docile to whatever they want; and this is the case where you are badly served, because in favor of this bait they pass on everything they have that is defective. With regard to those who live in the provinces, and who, by taste or necessity, are obliged to draw their trees from Paris, Orleans or other places, I wish them a true friend who is willing to make this choice for himself, with the attentions and precautions of which I will speak, and which are exactly in accordance with those I recommend in Chapter XIX, for the transport of trees. 1°. From mid-October onwards, you must go to the nurseries, as the first to arrive always take the best. Peach trees are good to lift at this time, even if the leaf has not yet fallen; and if your land is not ready to plant them, have them buried in a trench, one next to the other, and not in bundles, as those who like their work done quickly do. 2e. Make sure they have not been rebooted: (I'll explain this term for those who don't understand it). Peach trees are not like other trees, which can only be replanted after two, three or four years of grafting; they must be replanted after their first growth, i.e. at the end of the year; and as it often happens that merchants can't sell them all within the year, they cut back at the end of March or in April, what remains to the thickness of half an inch above the graft, from which it immediately grows one or more new shoots; but these kinds of trees usually do not do well, and we mustn't take any: they're easy to spot, and all you have to do is watch out for them. 3e. Make sure your trees are healthy, that the gum has not attacked them, and that they are strong enough. The biggest ones are not the best, because they usually don't have good eyes at the bottom of the stem, below the size they should be pruned; and the thinnest ones, whose thinness is a sign of weakness, don't promise to ever be very vigorous. Avoid some and

the others, and choose the medium-sized ones, in which you'll find well-fed eyes next to the fat, because that's what's important. Everything I've just said applies particularly to low stems. With regard to stems and half-stems, or the same disadvantages that must be avoided, you must take care that the stems are straight, united, clear, without moss, and that they have a good body, i.e., a good inch in diameter, or three inches in circumference at the bottom; for if they are weaker, count on your tree always being puny: it will truly take up like another, and live; but it will not do in four years what a good one will do in two, and will last much less, besides that the fruits will never be well nourished. Take care, moreover, that the graft has grown straight, and that it does not make what is called the trumpet; for the result is sometimes that, despite all your attention to dividing the branches of your tree equally, the side where the graft leans always prevails over the other, which makes your tree defective. When pulling them out, make sure the digging is done at a good distance from the base, so as not to offend the roots, and reject those that are pulled out incorrectly, or whose roots are damaged. "As soon as they are uprooted, have them put in bundles with labels to distinguish the species, and lots of straw around them, which you will take care to have carried to the nursery, so that the bindings and the pack animals that will be transporting them don't skin them: likewise have the roots wrapped in straw, to protect them from the sun and the sun. These precautions, though very important, are often overlooked. In this case, I advise them to find a good merchant, and to give him their commission in good faith, on condition that you receive only what meets all the conditions I have just prescribed. This merchant, who will spare what he is obliged to give to a third party, and who will want to acquire your practice, will have an interest in giving only good, and will find his advantage in doing so by doing yours. Peach trees can be grafted onto three types of subject: the peach pit itself, almond trees and plum trees. Few of the first type are grafted, however, as they are too prone to gum; they are commonly found only on the other two. It's the quality of your soil that should decide whether you choose one or the other. If your soil is light and sandy, you should choose almond trees, because their roots, which prick or pivot, in gardening terms, seek their nourishment further underground than plum trees, and therefore defend themselves better in dry weather. If your soil has body, and if the bottom is tuff or clay, take it from the plum tree, because its root is content with little soil, and only seeks to run on the supersiccia where it is sufficiently nourished. In addition, you should follow what has been practised before you in the place where you will find yourself; for there is scarcely a countryside where this fruit has not been cultivated, and the kind of subject in which it has been kept, after the experiments made, must naturally be the best. I make this observation here, because despite the general rule, which is the one I've just established, it sometimes happens that one of the two produces less gum than the other, especially in soils that hold the middle ground between the two extremes. You can also graft on apricot trees, and the grafting succeeds quite well; but this is only done when you have too many apricot trees, or when you want to graft on a peach of which you are curious, and whose fruit you want to see quickly. You can also, if necessary, graft onto the peach tree itself; and this is a very good practice, when you see a few bad species in a young plant. Grafting is done in escutcheon in September on the young wood of the year, or of two years at most; and to do it with more rule and safety, it is necessary to cut down in March at twelve or fifteen inches of ground the trees which you want to graft; they push back soon after of the young wood, which you take care to disbud, so that you leave only four good branches well spaced, which take all the force, and on which you apply your escutcheons at ease at the end of the summer. They usually do very well, as long as the gum doesn't set in; and that's why you have to make sure there's no sap left in the trees when you graft. CHAPTER IV. The location and exposure required for peach trees, and how to prepare the soil. THE tender peach, generally speaking, does not succeed in full wind in any country. In our climate, the red spring winds, cold rains and white frosts scramble the blossom as well as the leaf, and it is very rare for any fruit to set. In hot countries, the sun's great ardor alters the fruit after it has been tied, and it does not hold on to the tail, so that it falls off in the slightest wind that beats it, and very few are left to ripen; even those that do escape are unwise, and there is neither the water nor the finesse that a more temperate air gives them. The same is not true of certain common species, such as those found near Fontainebleau and in all our southern provinces, which, being harder by nature and of very mediocre coarseness, are quite resistant to the ravages of time, and grow in vineyards and gardens without any cultivation: However, compared to the peaches we grow here, they are almost nothing more than peaches; they are undesirable: consequently, I distinguish from this class the Pavies, which are called Presses, Auberges or Mirlicotons in some provinces: this kind of fruit succeeds perfectly in the open air in all hot countries, and its taste is much stronger there than it is here; but this is its greatest merit, in addition to the hard flesh and little water. However, for want of anything better, we do very well to make do with it, and to grow it abundantly: cultivation is simple and easy, and requires no instruction. Back to our tender peaches. Experience has shown that they can only succeed in espaliers; and in this climate, there are only two suitable exposures: south and east. I know, however, that many private individuals plant them in the sunset position; they do succeed in a few places, but this is rare. I had planted two espaliers of one hundred and fifty toises each at this exposure, which I had the patience to cultivate for 8 years, without getting anything out of them. Tired of such ungrateful cultivation, I cut off their heads a few years ago; I grafted them all into Reine-Claude plums, which, in four years, have almost covered my wall, and give me perfectly beautiful fruit. I would advise anyone in the same situation to do the same, if their trees are suitable for grafting, and others never to plant any at this exposure, at least in this climate, and in cold soils like mine; for, I repeat, there are some situations where this exposure is fairly good for them, especially when the gardens are well sheltered, and I would add that in southern countries, it may even be better for them than the other two. It's up to each individual to know what his or her climate requires. There is one particular care to be taken in this respect, and that is never to plant this species of fruit at the foot of walls that back onto land, and which serve, as it were, as terrace walls; for, although the trees flower, the humidity that these walls communicate almost always ruins the flower, which sinks instead of knotting.
