And it's also quite common for these walls to be full of ants, which destroy the trees, especially as you can't maintain the plaster, which is soon loosened by humidity. Finally, the place of your trees having been decided, in relation to what I've just said, all that remains to be done is to put them in the ground; and this requires no less attention than the rest. I suppose you are making a new espalier: you must have begun by having your land broken up in fine weather, six feet from your wall, and three feet or at least two and a half feet down, if the clay or tuff has not been found closer to the surface, at which caz OF CULTIVATION you must stop where you find it; for the agsured loss of trees is when you want to pierce the tuff. and substitute good soil. Experience has convinced me of this, and the reason is that rainwater, having stayed in this sort of tuff or clay box that you form, rots all the roots after a few years, and the more you plant, the more die, because the soil itself becomes putrescent and has no more virtue; so you must give up putting any more in. However, don't be discouraged when you come across this kind of matter; as long as you have a foot and a half or two feet of good soil, your plum plants will do just fine, especially if it's new soil, or soil that has been occupied by other kinds of fruit; for I would observe that if your land has long been occupied by peach trees, the salts suitable for the production of this fruit are exhausted, and it is very rare for a new plantation to succeed. Here's the remedy. If you have new soil in the vicinity, have some brought in to replace the old; in other words, put in two and a half feet of prosoondeur, five or six feet wide; if you don't have any, or if you have to look for it far away, and the expense of transport is too great, have used manure brought in, and mix it well with a fork with your old soil, as you break it up, so that there is an equal quality from the bottom to the surface. Then, when you plant the trees, take care to keep the manure away from the root zone, where it could heat up and shrivel. I've tried both methods several times, and they worked, at least for a while, because this precaution keeps the trees in good shape for five or six years; but it's not equally certain that they'll continue to do well: often, at the end of this term, the roots, being obliged to work in the neighbouring soil, which they find sealed and worn, make useless efforts, and the tree only languishes. Use the same expedient when you want to replant old espaliers. The best way to get the most out of your land is to change species, i.e. to put stone fruit where there used to be stone fruit, and stone fruit where there used to be stone fruit. But as there are often few good exposures and you want to take advantage of them for fruit that necessarily requires them, stick to what I've just said. CHAPTER V. How to plant trees. Once you have prepared the ground, have your trees dressed, i.e. the roots shortened and cooled, so that the cut is on the ground, and have all the hair cut off; then have a hole made in proportion to their roots, and have loose earth thrown all around, which you will push in between the roots with your fingers; when they are fully covered, you lead the foot, i.e., you press the foot mediocrely all around, to reassure the soil, and take care that the graft is flush with the surface of your land. If you can't avoid either of these extremes, in the first case, you'll always plant them as I've just said, and in the second, you'll dispense with lead; But in both cases, you'll need to build a water channel, to better bind the soil, and thus get your trees working more quickly. Before doing so, be sure to wet the trees, cut them down to six or eight inches above the graft, and turn the cut against the wall. Hold the tree steady with one hand, while you cut it down with the other, so that the effort of the cutter doesn't disturb the foot. I'm assuming here that the soil is greasy and well soaked, because if it's healthy, all you have to do is press your feet down on the root, so that the tip of the shoe rests lightly on the buttress. The same precautions apply to stems and half-stems if they are planted between two plants. But as the graft is at the tip, there's no harm in burying them a little more or a little less. The main thing is to ensure that the heads are all on the same line, or, to put it another way, at the same distance from the coping on your wall. Now it's a question of setting the distances in which they should be planted. If your walls are only six, seven or eight feet high, I advise you to plant only low stems of fifteen in fifteen feet, especially if it's new soil; because in seven or eight years, your well-mannered trees will cover your wall with trellises. If it's old soil, and your walls are nine feet high, you can plant half-stems four feet apart, provided your low stems do well, you prune the underside of your half-stems from year to year, and after about six years, when your low stems have reached the middle of your wall's height, you remove your half-stems altogether, to give the others a chance to grow. In the latter case, to avoid losing anything, you can do what I've done, which is to graft them in March, into plums or apricots, below the old graft, if it's on a plum tree; and the following autumn, you pull them out and give them another place: this makes mid-wind trees, of very good quality, and which defend themselves better from the winds than the others, as they have more body. I have grafted many in this way, all of which have succeeded perfectly; and out of eighty that I replanted in one year, only one failed. Lift them and replant them with the precautions I recommend in Chapter XVI. If you like it better, instead of half-stems, you can plant a marcotte of grapes, either Muscat or Chasselas, which will give you fruit for a few years, and which you will pull up in the same way as the half-stems I have just mentioned, as soon as the lower stems need the space. But make sure that there is always at least a foot and a half between the winter pruning of your low stems and the lowest branches, either of the half-stems, or of the base of your stock; for, in order for the latter to rise easily, they must not be bothered by the shade of the others, and moreover you need space to trellis the new shoots. If your walls are ten to twelve feet or more high, then you must necessarily plant six-foot stems in between your low stems, otherwise you run the risk of not seeing your walls covered for a long time, if ever; there is even enough space for both to survive together without harming each other. For the sake of your trees, I now ask only two things: one, that your walls be in good condition; the other, that they be covered with trellises. For your walls to be in good condition, they must be well plastered on the tree side, and in good lime and sand mortar on the outside, if you want to spare the expense of plaster. In countries where there is none, and where mortar is all that is needed, it must be extremely fatty, i.e. two-fifths good freshly slaked lime on three-fifths water-free sand. If your mortar is thin, frosts will cause it to flake, and rains will soak it and make it run: and insects of all kinds, especially leeches and mice, settle in your walls on all sides, ruining your fruit as it ripens. Happy are those who can build them in brick, as they are in a large part of Italy! Once these walls are built, they can't be touched up again, and insects can't penetrate them; so our plasters and mortars only last a short time, and every ten to twelve years we have to redo the coping and sometimes the plaster. Secondly, your walls need to be lined with trellises. This requires a great deal of detail, because outside the Paris area they are rarely used, and only a small number of people even know how useful they are. Moreover, the expense is a monster, and those who would like to do it often don't know how to go about it in countries far from Paris. To make up for trellises, various expedients are used, all of which are rather poor: some use large iron wires, of which they make five or six runs along their walls, and which they stop from distance to distance with large nails; some even form meshes with this iron wire, as is done with wood. Both methods are equally damaging to the young branches of our peach trees: The wind, which blows them against the iron, causes them to bark, and the gum which soon follows, kills most of them; moreover, these strands of wire are too far apart for the branches to space themselves properly and attach themselves firmly; it is even impossible to secure certain large branches, which sometimes have to be moved from one place to another, and raised or lowered as necessary: I'm omitting other reasons which I could add. The rods that some people use are no more solid: a gust of wind sometimes blows down an entire tree, the branches break on one side, crumple on the other, and the fruit falls off; moreover, arranging all these rods is time-consuming work: You have to drive in pegs or nails to stop them; this spoils the plaster on your wall, and then forms a series of little holes, which are a haven for insects; moreover, you have to renew them often: it's a miserable expedient, all things considered. Some others, when building their walls, insert sheep bones into the masonry, about six inches apart, and protruding three or four times, on which they attach their branches; but, if I am allowed to judge by my eyes, it makes a hideous sight; moreover, one is often obliged to pile several branches on top of each other, and this becomes a very irregular trellis. The nail-pierced loquettes used 24 ** M ul 43 R 4 U 121 D"- 4 R 4 DU PECHER. 25 used by the people of Montreuil and the surrounding area are less dangerous in all respects, and I admit that you can spread out and place your branches as you like, with enough solidity and cleanliness; perhaps they even have some reason to claim that the fruit that is stuck against the wall ripens a little more, because of the reflection of the heat, than when there is a trellis in between. But what work is it not to have to prick three or four hundred nails on the expanse of a tree that is in its strength, and to have as many pieces of cloth to turn around the branches to embrace them? The people who are the most experienced at it, through the observations and comparisons I have made, could not do in less than two and a half hours what is done on trellis in an hour at most. This difference in time is considerable; moreover, the cost of nails and brackets, many of which have to be renewed every year, is a considerable expense. What's more, what is practiced in Montreuil would not be practicable elsewhere. These people have plaster on their doorstep; it costs them only four pounds a muid, while everywhere else it costs eight, ten, twelve, and even fifteen pounds; moreover, their land is full of small stones that they excavate themselves, and which they mix with plaster from the demolition of their old walls. These are the materials they use, and the cost is very low. When these walls are filled with joints and plastered with a good inch of plaster, they are easy to nail wherever they are spiked. X that they are driven in; but in ordinary walls, which are built of hard stone and mortar, often even built of earth, or at the very most re-created in plaster with an open stump, the nails can only encounter the stone, on which they cannot bite, or the mortar, which does not hold them securely. This method of trellising is therefore impractical, and the only good one I know of is trellising, without which I maintain that a tree can never be raised properly. Experience will convince us better than anything I could say: it is by the very operation that we recognize how useful it is, both for giving it the shape we want, and keeping it always full and without confusion, and for dispatching the work in the trellising season, and for preserving the fruit. CHAPTER VI. Description of Trellising, and how to do it. The UTILITY of trellising is not disputed by anyone; but the expense, it is said, is considerable, and one sometimes finds oneself unable to do it. I pity those for whom this expense is an object capable of depriving them of it, and I announce to them that whatever expedient they use to make up for the trellis, they will never see their espaliers regularly furnished, nor their fruit generally well conditioned. Let them restrict themselves to a lesser quantity, twenty toises in good condition will give them 27 more pleasure and more prosit than the ill-understood triple: I have no other advice to give them. But to be useful to everyone, I'm going to give some ways of saving money. It's not by the hands of a garden decorator that we need to pass here: the job of these kinds of people is to make money on the worker; nor by those of certain famous trellis makers who charge a lot for their reputation: for our trellis is not like a cradle where all we're looking for is ornament, and which therefore requires the hand of a skilled man. Trellising is the simplest of all operations: if you're smart enough, you can learn to do it in twenty-four hours, like someone who's been doing it all his life; and around Paris, there are twenty people for every one you can use. A bundle of ready-to-use trellis, which Paris merchants commonly sell for forty cents or more, can be bought for twenty-five or thirty cents at the wood sales where it is made, or from country merchants who have it made: the bundle contains twenty-five mounts, called strands, nine feet long, and when the strands are shorter, the number is proportionately greater; for there must always be two hundred and twenty-five effective feet in the bundle: this is the rule. But, both because of the assemblies that absorb six inches, and for the greater solidity of the work, there is a double advantage in taking all strands of nine feet, X 2 as much as merchants are willing; on which they are not always well treatable. In this respect, care must be taken to ensure that the wood is not greasy, because then it is brittle, and much is lost in dressing. To be of good quality, it must be made from young poles, in which case it is white, straight and knotless, or at least not very. A bundle of trellis is about 2 toises quarrées of work, counting the mesh of eight inches by seven, as it should be; so that half a bundle per toise enters, which, at the price marked below, is worth 15 sous, ci. o l. 15s. There are four hooks per toise, which sell for 5 to 6 sous a dozen, for this... . . . . . . . ........ Iron sil comes in, which costs to s. a pound, for... ... ............ The custom of each toise is commonly paid............... And to paint the trellis with oil, two coats in wood color... 2 2 6 10 Total.....1 1. 14s. Those who wish to have it painted green, must count on triple the expense; but this no longer concerns the utility of the trees, which is our object. It seems to me that this expense should not be so excessive as to be unattainable, since the account I have just given shows that for twenty-five pistols a wall one hundred toises long and nine feet high can be lined. I will now describe these trellises for those who have never seen them, so that they can have them made wherever they are to be found. The wood, as I've just said, should be young chestnut poles, ten to twelve years old; failing that, oak heartwood can be used, which I value no less; but the former is easier to work, and is quite commonly found everywhere. We choose the longest, straightest poles in the coppice, which have not been eaten away by wild cattle, which can damage them badly in some places. Any size is good, as they can be split in two or four if necessary. Each strand, planed and quarried, should be one inch or fourteen lines wide, and nine or ten lines thick; and it is up to the workman who has his wood in front of him, to take care of the thickness of his pole before putting the instrument on it, so that it has the thickness I have just mentioned. He shapes it with the plane, helped by an easel that stops it at one end, while he works on the other. However careful you are in choosing straight poles, it almost always happens that there is still some curved part in the length: but this defect is corrected by a second operaX5 tion. When you're ready to put your wood to work - and this is called dressing the trellis, i.e. straightening it - you hold your wood with your left hand, resting it on a log, and under the curved parts you make a half-wood slanting notch with the sickle; Then, by pressing the hand gently at some distance from the notch, while the strand is held a little above by a sort of iron hinge driven into the end of the trestle, the wood is made to make a little cry which straightens it; and as many curved parts there are, as many notches must be made, until it is straight, and the eye is satisfied. Now that the wood has been prepared, it's time to use it, and here's how. The first thing to do is to calculate how many running laths you'll need to line your wall, according to the mesh you want to make. I assume nine by eight inches, including the wood thicknesses. On this foot, for example, you'll find that a nine-foot wall needs twelve; because nine multiplied by twelve makes one hundred and eight, which is the same height as nine feet reduced to inches. These divisions are marked on the wall, with black chalk or charcoal, approximately from eight toises to eight toises. When all the divisions are marked, two iron pegs are driven into the wall, from one division to the other, on the lines where the hooks are to be set; and a rope is stretched from one peg to the other, to regulate the position of the hooks. To make this clearer, I first assume that three rows of hooks are needed to stop the trellis, the first at the top penultimate stitch, the second at the bottom penultimate dernic̀re, and the third in the middle of these two stitches, i.e., at the sixth or seventh. This arrangement made, we seal the hooks in a chessboard, from three to three feet, with plaster and a few pieces of pipe. Mortar in its present state would be of no value, unless you give it time to dry thoroughly before starting work. When you're in a hurry and don't have any plaster, you can use large hardwood dowels, which you force into the stone joints; and in these dowels you prick the hooks, which in this case should be four to five inches long, instead of the plaster hooks, which should be six to seven inches long, and split at the end into a swallowtail, so that they are better retained in the wall. But both must be angled out by about an inch, to retain the laths. This explanation is only for those who know nothing about it. The hooks must protrude one inch above the wall level, to receive the battens that fit into them, and which are fastened to them with a strand of iron silk, for greater solidity; they must also be flat, and one and a half lines thick by four or five lines wide. As for those intended for wood, they should be round or square, roughly like a large nail, but with the elbow flattened. Once the hooks have been placed along the entire length of X4 your wall, you first lay your three rows of laths on top (I use the terms laths, strands and trellises interchangeably, which are all synonymous here). We must not omit a third operation that the laths require, which is to sharpen them at the ends, i.e., to reduce the thickness of the wood to six inches from the end, so that it comes to nothing (this term is dedicated to what it expresses): we understand that this circumstance is necessary to couple the laths, which by this means are more easily bound together with two meshes of wire. With these three rows of laths in place, the hardest part of the job is done. All that remains to be done is to divide the spaces between the upright strands, which, in the above supposition, should be eight by eight inches, including the thickness of the wood. This division is marked like the first with black chalk, on the lowest and highest of these three rows of laths, taking care to throw a plumb line from distance to distance, so that they are all plumb; and it's especially important to do this at the beginning. To make it easier to pass the superfluous running battens behind the mounts, first lay only one mound, about six feet by six feet; stop the nine running battens on it with lé fil de fer, which remain to be placed of the twelve that should be there, as I said. When they are all in place, the rest of the mounts are put in place, and the whole thing is tied together with the wire. I don't think anyone in any country is unaware of how this is done. I'll just say that you have to tighten the ties as much as you can, with the pliers in your right hand, while with your left you hold the wire, which you always leave in a ball while you use it; then, with a little turn of your hand, you break it between the pliers themselves, when you've made three or four turns back and forth. It should be noted that the finer the wire, the shorter it runs, i.e. the more work it does and the better it does, provided it can withstand the work. To do this, it must be burned, and burned properly, because when it is burned too much or too little, it breaks under the pliers. The time it should remain in the fire is about a quarter of an hour. To return to the trellis, I must not forget that, whether the walls are level or sloping, the mounts must always be plumb, and the running battens placed as I have indicated above. When the wall is on a slope, take care to set the hooks so that the lines of the chalk line are closer together, so that the battens follow the slope of the wall. If it happens that a wall is higher in one part than in another, so that twelve battens are needed at one end, and ten are sufficient at the other, the mesh size must not be changed; and the irregularity of the running battens must fall to the bottom of the wall, and not under the coping. X5 Once the trellis is in place, all that remains is to paint it. Now, as painting is done everywhere, I will only observe in this respect that it is necessary to take a good weather, and not to spare in the color the litarge or the spirit of turpentine, so that it dries promptly; because, when it comes to rain before it is dry, the rain makes it run. If you follow this description exactly, you can, with a little intelligence, obtain the satisfaction of decorating your walls with trellises in any country; otherwise, I repeat, you can never expect real satisfaction from your espaliers, and all the less so, as there are few gardeners in a position to make up by their industry for the lack of conveniences. CHAPTER VII. Pruning. Peach trees are commonly pruned when they are in bloom; some even wait until they have deflowered, and the fruit is knotted, based on the fact that they are more sure of what they leave; but this last usage is subject to many inconveniences. When you start pruning so late, assuming your trees are in full bloom, how many of them don't fall off, no matter how skilful you are? If, on the other hand, they are more advanced, what harm are you doing to them? The sap that would have fed the bottom of your branches, if they had been stopped early, has all gone to the ends; it's only in these ends that the fruit has stopped, and to keep it, you are obliged to leave your branches excessively long, which ruins your trees, or you have to abandon the fruit to keep the tree: a cruel alternative for amateurs. In my first assumption, that the tree is only in full bloom, what constraint is there to trellis it after pruning? What damage would you do to the flowers, and how much more time would you spend on pruning than you would if you had done it sooner? What's more, the eyes that start to grow at the same time as the flowers bloom, partly hide your work, and you can no longer get your pruning close to the eye; so that as many pruned branches produce as many snags to remove for the following year. Your ties, moreover, can be neither so clean nor so well secured, because of the embarrassment caused by the multitude of these flowers. You can no longer see the defects in the wood, if any, nor the old snags that need to be brought together: in short, you work haphazardly. I experienced all these inconveniences the first few years I wanted to work by myself, following the general method. But having subsequently tried the effect of pruning a few trees, the fear I had, according to popular opinion, that they would get too far ahead, and that the spring frosts would ruin the blossom, soon vanished. These trees, which I pruned at the end of January and February X6, were no further advanced than the others I pruned in April: neither the flower nor the wood had suffered. The following year, I continued to prune a greater number with the same success; and in the third year, I pruned them all in the same months, and have continued to do so for many years with complete satisfaction. I therefore advise everyone to do the same: despite the public prejudice that may arise against this novelty, you will soon see that the work is done better, faster and more rapidly. We can see clearly at least in everything we do, and we can distinguish very well in these months between the good flowers and the bad ones; for the dry weather has begun to make the good ones swell, unless the winter has been very long and very hard, in which case, we must postpone it a little later. For it is important, as I have just observed, to be able to distinguish the good buds from the bad ones, and for this purpose, the sap must have acted on the good ones; I mean, they must have swollen to a certain extent. It will be argued that winter has not yet passed in January or February; that such and such a bud may be good then, and perish in the following months; and that we then have no resource left to skirt a few branches in favor of fruit. I agree with this fact: but I would reply that if bad winds blight the blossom in March and April, trees that are not pruned are no more exempt than others. What's more, as four times as many buds are left as could be left if everything went well, I have three quarters to lose through the uncertain accidents I am confronted with before making an actual loss. So I don't run much of a risk: but if it were even more real, the advantages I find in the method I've adopted would make me overlook it. And what's the point of having an abundance of knotting fruit, when you have to sacrifice everything that passes the tree's reach in May or June? Last but not least, my fruit, once tied, is much more profitable than that of trees that are cut in full bloom; and the reason is obvious. The sap has dissipated much less, because it doesn't have to nourish the quantity of branches that are pruned so late, and is carried much more abundantly in the tree's nourishing fibers. I've experienced all of the above, and since I've been following this practice, I've never had any problems. I have always had an abundance of fruit, except in the year 1741, which was generally so fatal to all fruit. Such a complete experience should reassure against all the reasoning of people attached to their prejudices, and warned against all the roads they do not know. I must not omit a circumstance that is more important than you might think: for the sake of the work, and to avoid breaking branches, you should never start pruning a tree until it is completely untrimmed, and well cleaned of all the old rushes and wicker, and the dry leaves that often gather between the wall and the trellis. Apart from the fact that cleanliness is detrimental, it destroys the retreats of many insects that hide there and damage your fruit, especially purple peaches, which limas and limacons are so fond of. This brings me to the description of pruning. The peach trees you have to prune are young or old, vigorous or languid: it's the state of your subject that must regulate your operation; the work it has done tells you what you have to do: in two words, you have to treat it according to its strength and need. I'll start with this year's new plants. If they have only grown weak branches, you will reduce them to two or four well placed on the sides, and equal in strength, which you will prune to five or six inches. If there is a small one with fruit in the middle, you can leave it; but if it is of the same strength as those on the sides, remove it; for, as the middle always fills out enough, you should only be concerned with the sides, etc. It's on the bend you give your tree in the first and second years, that everything depends for the following ones. If your trees have grown two strong, well-placed branches, one on the right and the other on the left, keep them and prune them back to eight or ten inches; at the same time, you can leave a few small twigs here and there for fruit. The method of many gardeners, who regard these kinds of branches as leeches to which they have sworn to do no harm, is to remove them without mercy, and to fall back on the small ones: as for me, experience has taught me not to be always so severe. It has happened to me, when pruning certain stumpy trees, to cut off as many of these branches, which starve the others, as were present, and to be seven or eight years without being able to give them any shape, and without drawing any fruit from them. These same trees then went from one end to the other, and fell into languor. This phenomenon, I confess, has always been incomprehensible to me: but the fact is certain, and the cause is one of the secrets of vegetation, which I do not undertake to investigate. However, it may be conjectured that the roots, which operate and help each other with the branches, being stopped in their action by the repeated violence done to them, tire, so to speak, of acting uselessly, and that the sap, having withdrawn from the branches, is lost in some way in the roots, which likewise remain without action, as soon as the head no longer acts. I have found, on the contrary, that by following the inclination of these kinds of trees, and by pruning the strong branches with a certain amount of care, they soon form a beautiful tree, which after two or three years grows no more. When, in the second and third years, they continued to grow, I pruned not only on the large branches, but also on the small ones, born from those in the same year, to give more diversion to the sap. By doing this, my trees moderated themselves, and from these branches, which were vicious in their origin, a number of good ones sprang up, which quickly covered my wall, and yielded abundantly. The only disadvantage I've sometimes seen resulting from this practice, and which you have to watch out for, is that as the sap is always carried to the ends, the tree doesn't become bare at the bottom: but when you are careful to pinch off the new shoots in May, and to take a lot of pressure off the head of the trellis, you prevent this disadvantage, and the bottom is maintained full. If there is only one of these strong branches on your young trees, this is another case: you must remove it wherever it is; if there are two, one on the right or left, and the other in the middle, you must also cut them off, as the weak side will perish, and your tree will never take shape; you must also then throw your pruning onto the small branches, giving no more load on one side than on the other. I would observe in passing that you would never see these kinds of badly placed branches, if in the month of May you took care to do what I advise in the following chapter; for by unloading the strongest side, the sap would be rejected from the other; but as there are few people who want to take the trouble, it is a question of giving a means of repairing the defect of this operation, when you have missed it. That's how you should behave for the first year. Let's move on to the second through to the sixth. I've explained what to do with trees that get carried away by wood, and that need to be loaded to moderate their fire and force them to set fruit. As for those that grow only moderately, treat them in proportion, and in all things, keep the middle short, and don't load one side more than the other. It very often happens that one side is stronger than the other; you must not let yourself be seduced by the lure of the fruit it promises. Withdraw everything that exceeds the strength of the other, and don't tolerate any branch that is stronger on one side than on the other. As a fundamental rule, the whole economy of your tree should be based on two or four good branches of equal strength, which should be like the mothers of all the others: it's on these that you should take particular care to space them evenly, and allow them as much scope as they can bear. You can give them up to twelve or sixteen inches in height, when they are of reasonable strength. As for the medium-sized buds, leave them in proportion to the vigor of the tree, and prune them from six to eight inches, depending on the place they occupy, and whether the flowering buds are more or less distant from the foot of the branch; for they are often very far from it, especially in certain species; and, as the fruit is our main object, we can sometimes, in its favor, deviate a little from the rules, and prune longer. In this respect, it should be noted that good flowering buds are only those that are double, and have a wood eye between them: those that are single, albeit with a wood eye, flower well, but do not knot, or at least rarely: however, try not to let yourself be tempted too much by the fruit: too much load would first throw confusion into your trees, and then ruin the middle and bottom. With regard to small branches, both those called rags, and the twigs so respected by most gardeners for their fruit, I eliminate them as long as I have better ones, I don't mean big ones, but medium ones, it being unquestionable that a branch with a certain body feeds its fruit better than a weak one, and that it also stops on it, despite the common prejudice that small ones hold it better, as those who want to pay attention will remain convinced. It is therefore only in the absence of the former that I retain the latter: there are, however, exceptions to be made in this respect. 1°. If your tree is extraordinarily vigorous, and needs to be fatigued by the load in order to stop it, you should leave a good portion of these twigs. 2°. If your middle branches don't have flower buds below the right size, and you're curious to have some fruit, you should also leave some of the shortest and most fruit-bearing branches. Besides, I don't understand certain short branches under the name of twigs, which it would be more appropriate to call bunches, since they are usually only one or two inches long. These are precious, and usually yield very fine fruit: I am therefore careful not to detach myself from them. The use I sometimes make of these small branches, which I condemn, is to cut them off at the first eye when they are placed in a spot where I foresee a gap forming. If one of these branches is pruned in this way, it may produce a better one the following year; and if it is still useless to me, even though it is good, I always prune it back to one eye until it is needed: these kinds of branches are resources that it is important to save in order to maintain a tree that is always full, and to make up for branches that have worn out in bearing fruit; this should be done equally on medium-sized branches as on the small ones I am dealing with here. In the case of trees that grow only weakly, it is necessary to examine whether the evil is in the root; in this case, it must be uprooted: but if the root is good, it must be preserved, and smoked in the way I indicate in Chapter XVIII. Manure often restores vigor to these kinds of trees; but as long as they languish, they should be pruned very short and on the best branches. This is my method for managing peach trees during their first few years; to which I'll add, so as not to omit anything, that great care must be taken to trellis them properly after pruning. .1e. As the inclination of trees is always to grow upwards, it is essential to keep the lower part of the tree trimmed, as I have observed, and this is achieved in two ways: firstly, by the effect of good pruning, which I have discussed at some length; secondly, by taking care to bend or constrain the branches on the sides, when training them, and to space them evenly. At the same time, care must be taken to ensure that they don't take on any bad bends; and, if the damage has already been done, this defect must be corrected by removing branches that are piled on top of each other, and those that have been crossed at the wrong time, or that are curved. These are straightened with the help of wickerwork and chopsticks, and skill alone must guide these small operations, which I won't go into here. 2°. Another point to bear in mind when trellising branches is to make sure that the eye at the end of the branch is always turned so that the branch that is to grow from it naturally takes its course over the trellis, and not behind it: this can be seen without a great deal of study; and in this case, with a small rod supported and attached to the trellis if necessary, you can easily make the branches that seek the wall return to the front. To these observations, I would add that wicker should not be tightened too much, because it often happens that being too tight, it cuts the branch when it grows; you should also avoid passing your wicker over the branch's eyes when tying it: a little skill prevents these little faults, which are of no great consequence, but which nevertheless have their disadvantages. As there are often pruned branches that cannot reach the trellis, we use small sticks that are interwoven into the trellis, where we pass a piece of wicker at the end, in the form of a noose, which is attached to the trellis by the other end, and which secures the branch: this is all the more necessary, as when fruit comes to these branches, and they are not supported, it often carries the branch away. These last observations apply to peach trees of all ages. Now back to pruning. I've indicated everything that's appropriate for first-age trees: let's move on to second- and third-age trees. I call second-age peach trees those that are in their full strength; third-age trees are those that are a little on the decline: these cannot be too sparingly cared for; they must be pruned short and only on the best branches: the small ones must not be kept at all, because on old subjects, they give only etic fruit. When, by chance, a vigorous branch emerges from one of these old trees and is capable of renewing the tree, it should be treated with this in mind, and carefully preserved to replace the old branches that are gradually being destroyed; but if it emerges from an old branch, it should be removed. I have nothing more to say about these old trees, except that they should only be cared for when, despite their old age, they are still bearing good fruit; for as soon as this condition is lacking, they must be uprooted. As for the trees of the second age, which are in all their strength, and which load abundantly, as they are those which make our wealth, they deserve the most particular attention. Most gardeners who work without principles, without reasoning, and without concern for the future, manage them in such a way that they are soon ruined. This is why it is generally said that peach trees only have a life span of twelve to fifteen years. I've got a few that are over forty years old, and they're still going strong. They were not under my care for the first twenty years, but they have had the advantage of being well looked after, and since they have been in my hands, I have looked after them so well that they are still bearing good fruit. I have quite a few others that I planted 15 to 18 years ago, which are undoubtedly of great beauty, and which I still only regard as children; so that if I could count on thirty years of life, and if I could always manage them myself, I would be sure that they would still survive all that time. To convince yourself of this, all you have to do is visit the Montreuil plantations: you'll see trees of the age I'm talking about in the homes of certain individuals who have no doubt taken better care of them than is usually the case in this very place, where trees are forced to produce, without bothering about their duration, because the tenants of the land are in a hurry to enjoy it. I have seen trees up to today's toises in length, equally healthy and vigorous throughout, and which I have judged to be fifty years old. So let's get rid of the prejudice that this tree doesn't last: it's bad behavior that makes it perish when it doesn't live about as long as another fruit tree. However, in saying this, I'm assuming that it's in a good soil, and that no accidents happen to it: for, despite good conduct, if the soil is worthless, if it's infested with gum, if the bug or the ant attacks it violently, it must perish. I have the advantage, along with many others, of being free from all these scourges: they should not therefore be considered as inseparably attached to the species, and consequently all care should be given to keep it alive. Pruning is the operation that contributes most to their longevity. This is the art of pruning, which may appear simple, but which is not without its difficulties, given the choice of branches, the work the tree has done, the position of flowering buds, the type of fruit, and many other circumstances on which a few rules can be based. I'm not going to talk about certain cases that can only be decided in relation to the object in question, and which can only be taught by practice. Everyone has his own method, and prunes according to his own ideas. Some prune short on all branches, others lengthen the branches they intend to bear fruit, and leave spurs to give them wood the following year. Mine is quite different, and it's only after much study and experience that I stick to it as the best. I assume that the tree I'm dealing with has been managed in its youth more or less according to my principles, and that it is regularly well stocked; for, if it is defective in any part, it must be treated according to its needs. Starting from my assumption, and finding my tree in good condition, after it has been stripped, I like to make a search for the worn branches, which it is easy to see from their thinness, and the bad sprays they have made, I cut off the worn branch as far as the large branch from which it comes, unless in its extent it has grown some good branch, on which I gully it, if there is nothing in the vicinity to fill the place. I then move on to the current year's branches, and remove any large ones that have grown. By large branches, I mean all those exceeding the average size; I also remove all the small ones, unless one is needed to fill a gap, or to serve as a resource; in which case I trim it to about the thickness of an ecu, as I indicated above. I always exclude the small ones I've mentioned. Once this first retrenchment has been made, I'm left with branches that are equal in strength: I can then see my work clearly, and at last I only have one reform to make in terms of quantity, and here is my rule for that. I leave only one of all those that have grown on the branch I pruned the previous year, and it's the lowest one I leave, because it's always good, thanks to the precautions I took at the time of the pruning. Those who have not done so, will choose the best of the lowest. After this second reform, I move on to the third, which is pruning these branches. I then examine whether my tree was heavily loaded the previous year, and what species it is; depending on these two cases, I shorten or lengthen my pruning. If my tree has loaded a lot, I spare it; and if it's, for example, a Madelaine or a Violet, as these trees are more vigorous than the others, I give them more load: but if my tree is of any other species, and has not been tired of the load, I lengthen my pruning to eight inches, if the place allows, but if I find myself constricted, and if I have nothing below to replace what is exhausted, I keep my pruning short, and give it only three or four inches. It is common to find, by the different arrangement of the places, that half of my branches are lined, and that the other is kept short. In this way, I keep my tree full, and I don't tire it. I said that I never leave more than one branch of all those that came on the branch pruned the previous year. However, there are cases (such as that of a neighboring branch that the gum Tome II. Y will have caused it to perish) where, when I find two good branches equal in strength that have come from the bottom of this pruned branch, and I have a large space to fill, I prune both to five to six inches. If I don't have a definite need, and I'm only afraid that the space will become bare after my branch is exhausted, I give the above pruning to the higher one, and cut back the lower one on its first eye, in order to ensure a good branch for the following year. As far as the tips are concerned, I'm governed by the space I have. If my tree completely covers its wall, I prune so that there is always a good foot's distance between the end of my pruned branch and the edge of the coping, to be able to support the new branches, to which end I cut off everything that has borne fruit during the year, and replace it with new branches, which the underside must provide. M. de la Quintinie, in dealing with this subject, recommends always leaving three feet of distance: I confess that this seems outrageous to me, as walls are too precious to individuals to leave such a large space cu worthless. It may be objected that, by my method of pruning only one fruiting branch, and keeping none for wood, I expose myself to having no good wood left for subsequent years. People will say that these branches, which are exhausted with fruit, only grow thin branches between them, not very capable of bearing fruit; they perish in the end, and consequently your tree is thinning out on all sides. This objection is specious, because in the common order of pruning, most of the fruiting branches are ruined under the load, and are no longer capable of any function, either for wood or for fruit, so that we are obliged to cut off some of them at the end of the same year, and the others at the second or third; but they don't have quite the same fate with me, and don't perish until very late, as I'm going to demonstrate. When you leave two branches, one intended solely for fruit, the other for wood, you naturally feel that the sap is obliged to divide between the two, and that the woody branch, which has no fruit to nourish, benefits much more than the other: Moreover, some of my branches are kept short, as I have just observed, and I spare myself resources wherever I see the slightest danger of emptiness. So I don't run the risks that might frighten people; but above all I have experience, which will convince, as I have, all those who try my method. The method used in Montreuil is similar in some respects to mine, in that they leave few branches, and cut back all the small ones; but it differs in that they load their trees extraordinaiY 2 rement, especially in the first years; they lengthen their main branches up to two and two-and-a-half feet, and at the same time prune a good proportion of the small ones that have grown between their leaves. It's true that the quality of their soil in some way authorizes this practice; and besides, they don't bother about the duration of the tree, nor about its beautiful shape: their whole object is to gather quickly and abundantly; so that the bottom of their wall, after the first four years, is almost always bare: a defect that a curious person must not suffer. But if someone, following their example, wanted to pass over this wall to enjoy a quick harvest, he would certainly fail, unless he came across a vein of earth perfectly similar to theirs. This circumstance may occur, but it is so rare that of all those of my acquaintance who have attempted this practice, not one has succeeded. In a word, I can say, in general, that it is more admirable than imitable. CHAPTER VIII. De l'Ebourgeonnement. In peach tree cultivation, disbudding is the most important operation, and yet the most neglected. When I say most important, I'm excluding pruning, which is a necessity. The usefulness of disbudding lies in the fact that it facilitates all the other operations, and gives the fruit these three advantages: safety, beauty and goodness. M. de la Quintinie has given some very judicious rules on this subject, but he hasn't put his money where his mouth is, and he's even a little vague on the subject at times. I must, however, do him the justice to say that I have benefited greatly from his insights in the remarks I have made based on him, and that his observations have led me to make new ones, which will be of benefit to others after me. Disbudding has a large number of equally interesting objects, and I shall follow them in order. The word "disbudding" carries its meaning with it. Disbudding means removing buds. Nothing could be easier on the face of it; but to remove them properly and with choice requires a perfect understanding of the subject. The best time for disbudding is May, when the buds are sufficiently formed to fix our choice, and are still tender enough to be easily removed by thumb action alone, without the aid of any instrument. Disbudding is usually confused with a second operation, called pinching, and a third, called arresting, since all three are performed together. It's enough to have seen a peach tree once in your life, to know that in spring it's teeming with branches that necessarily need to be thinned out. Now, disbudding means making this retrenchment early on, which should be done at the first Y3 trellising, if it hasn't already been done; but there is an infinite difference in doing it earlier. All peach tree work, as I have already said, can be reduced to two objectives: the tree's beautiful appearance, and an honest yield of good fruit. With this in mind, it must be relieved of everything that is either useless or harmful: I call useless everything that is misplaced, though good; and harmful, everything that is bad in itself. It's these two vices that need to be cut out, and it's particularly on the pruned branches of the year that they are found. Now, as these branches, according to my method, are for the most part seven to eight inches long, and sometimes more, there are as many as eight and ten eyes in this expanse, which are as many branches. This quantity of branches would not feed equally well, and would necessarily form a confusion. I therefore reduce them, according to my place, to two or three, and I choose one or two of the lowest, opposite each other, with the one at the end, in case there is fruit attached, and there is none lower down. If he has tied only at the bottom, or if he has tied all over my brancha, where the number of eyes may be eight or ten; in either case, I cut my branch down to about half, and keep only three or four fruits as far apart as possible, of course I always leave a good branch of the new arrivals at the end; At the same time, I pinch off with my fingernail, to the thickness of two ecus, the surplus branches holding the fruit (which is called stopping), and if there are others without fruit next to them, I cut them off completely, always limiting myself to two or three. If my branch has not retained any fruit, I cut it back to the second of those it has grown, that is, I keep only the two lowest, unless the great vigor of the tree obliges me to leave more to consume and divide the sap. With regard to the branches I have pruned short, I keep only two of the new additions, the highest and the lowest on the opposite side; I remove the others which have no fruit on their side, or I pinch them, if there is fruit; and, when it would not have retained any, I always treat it more or less the same way; sometimes, however, I leave only one of these new branches, and that is the lowest. If a large branch arises, either from my pruned branches of the year, or from the body of my tree itself, I consult its need and vigor. If it is harmful to its neighbors, and useless to me, I cut it off; but if it is useful, either to fill a gap, or to prevent it, or to consume the sap that is too abundant, I pinch it off at four or five leaves; and as from each leaf a new branch comes out, I soon find four or five mediocre ones, Y 4 F from the number of which I choose at the first trellising the one that suits me best. As for the small ones that may emerge from the old wood, I remove them, unless they are needed to fill a gap, or I see them as a resource for the future. But I do keep those little bouquets I mentioned in the previous chapter, wherever they come from. You need to pay close attention to the base of your tree; often branches come out of it that are very useful for replacing others that are beginning to wear out: you need to keep them carefully, and if they grow very strong, pinch them off at five or six eyes. As for the greedy branches, which can be identified, as I said, by their green color, spotted with red spots, and by their size, you must carefully remove them wherever they are, unless they are extremely needed to repair a gap, and you have no other resource; but in this case, they must be pinched back and even re-pinched a second time in June. It often happens that two or three branches grow together from the same eye, especially at the end of your pruning: in this case, leave only one, and choose the one in the best position. When you come across twin peaches, if one is smaller than the other, as is usually the case, you must skillfully detach the smaller one, without shaking the other: but if they are of equal size, remove them, or leave them; it's all one, they'll never work out. These are just about all the attentions that disbudding requires. Now it's time to show how useful it can be. First of all, it's easy to understand that this timely pruning infinitely strengthens what's left, both the fruit and the branches. As they go from mediocre food to good, it's only natural that they should do better. What's more, the branch you cut off, which was poorly placed, and which you would have had to cut off at the first trellising, if you hadn't done so then, was often the one best favored by the sap, and would have made the well-placed branch suffer. You have another advantage in this retrenchment, which is that you detach these branches cleanly, instead of cutting them with the serpette, when you are waiting for the trellising, the confusion in which you are working means that you would not be able to approach your cut, and your branches become covered with snags which are unpleasant to the eye, and which take up a lot of your time when you have to bring them closer for winter pruning, or which make a very ugly effect if you neglect to remove them; In fact, it almost always happens that these snags, left on the trellis, immediately sprout two or three bad shoots that uselessly consume sap, cause confusion and harm the fruit. It also happens that, when cutting off all these superfluous and misplaced branches, the jarring effect of the force of your serpette, and the embarrassment of the worker who cannot see his work, cause part of the fruit to fall off, which must then be greatly regretted, because it has, in a way, passed all the risks. What can I say! these much-desired fruits would be, so to speak, in complete safety, if disbudding had not been neglected. But what happens then? The fruits, hidden, smothered and as if buried in this thick foliage, become tender, as their whiter-than-green color visibly indicates; and suddenly breathing the fresh air, combined with the scorching rays of the sun, which is new to them, they wither for the most part, and fall off: For it should be noted that as the sap is always carried to the extremities, and that moreover it is only these extremities, by which I mean the ends of the branches, that enjoy the benefit of the air and the sun, most of the branches that are suffocated at the bottom are stripped of their leaves, which dry up to a certain distance, and can no longer, therefore, cover the fruit, or cover it only imperfectly. All this does not happen when, on the one hand, these branches have been exposed to the air throughout, and, on the other, you have accustomed your fruit from youth to the small insults of the air and the rays of the sun; they harden in this situation, and once they have reached the size of a walnut, it is very rare for them to fall off, when there are not more of them than the tree can feed. The same operation I'm talking about also has another benefit for the fruit: insects, especially snails, don't try to eat it when it's a little uncovered, as they do when it's smothered under the tenderizing leaves. It's also easy to get some of the fruit off the ground when it's caught between the wicker and the trellis, or between the trellis and the wall. In the first case, all you have to do is let go of the ties, and in the second, pull them out; but if you wait until the trellis is up, the fruit, which has by then reached more than half its size, is counterfeited without remedy. With regard to the branches, it was easy for you to remove those that slipped in at the wrong time from behind the trellis; instead, if you had waited until the trellising, these branches, which are sometimes very important, would have become hard and strong, and broken off when you tried to remove them. This is a good opportunity to talk about Cloaca, but as not everyone understands this term, I'll explain it first. This disease, very common in this climate, is the result of a bad wind, which causes the tree's leaves to curl up. They thicken and become yellow, red and scabby, which is unpleasant to look at, and very harmful to the fruit, in that they uselessly absorb all the sap at the expense of the fruit. When your trees are affected by this blister, Y6 you must not only remove all the bad leaves, but also cut off the branches that are infected with it, which form a sort of hideous tuft. This operation allows the sap to grow new branches underneath, which are also good for the following year. Note, however, that if your tree is completely infected, as sometimes happens, and there are no healthy leaves left to cover the fruit, you must leave some of the bad ones behind, to shelter it until good ones grow again. If you neglect this operation, all these infected leaves consume the sap, and prevent it from seeking other outlets; they then dry out and fall: your fruit, which is then slender, is uncovered; the sun catches it, it withers, and it falls to such an extent that sometimes no watch remains on the tree. The ant and the aphid sometimes cause the same disorder to leaves and branches; in this case, we must use the expedient I have just given; but these insects usually insist on poisoning all the eyes of the branches, and the sap cannot take over: we will see in Chapter XII the remedy that can be applied. If the gum has attacked a branch, you cut it back an inch below the damage, and prevent it from perishing altogether: by cutting it off, it immediately regrows one or two branches below it, and the damage is then of little consequence. The final advantage of disbudding is that the time spent on this operation is amply repaid when it comes to trellising, since there is almost nothing left to cut, and no need to reflect on your work: Each branch that has been left indicates to the worker the place he should give it; it goes there, so to speak, of its own accord, and all he has to do is attach it; which is such a great advance, that I have more than once found that it took no longer to trellis three disbudded trees, than one that had not been disbudded. However, even if this operation has been carried out with the utmost precision, it is still necessary to check the espaliers every eight days, either to remove from under the trellis any branches that slip back in, or to destroy more and more snails and other insects (and it's always after some rain, or after the morning dew, that you find them at work) or to observe the ravages of gum, and remedy them, which is a matter of a few hours, which are very usefully employed. When you have all the time in the world, it's even better to divide everything I've just said about this operation into two stages, and here's how I do it: at the end of April, I start by removing all the misplaced buds, i.e. those on the front and back of my branches, and at the end of May, when the fruit has stopped, I do the rest: everyone can do as much as their leisure allows. The rule I've laid down for doing this disbudding properly does, however, require some distinctions in relation to the different ages of the trees. For those planted this year, I give them a first disbudding at the end of April; in other words, I remove all the buds on the front and back of the stem, leaving only those on the sides; and when one side grows much more than the other, I unload that side to release the sap on the other, and at the end of the following May, I do a second review; and when I find a branch much stronger than the others, I cut it off or pinch it. I do more or less the same thing for the first three or four years, with the difference that if the tree is vigorous, I unload much less at disbudding, the big braches that I left at the first pruning, than the badly placed shoots, keeping everything that comes on the sides, as much as I find room to store it. As for old trees, I remove not only all that is badly placed, but also all that is weak to a certain point, to strengthen the rest. I limit myself to a small number of the best branches, and leave only a small quantity of fruit. I also wait to disbud those after all the others, because their growth is later. I have nothing special to say about trees that are in their full strength: you will find at the beginning of this Chapter, everything that needs to be observed with regard to them. CHAPTER IX. The first trellising. Peach trees are first trellised in June, a little earlier or a little later, depending on how far advanced the year is. Trellising means tying new branches neatly and in order to the trellis. If you have not neglected disbudding, this is the simplest and easiest of all operations: as I have already said, there is almost nothing left to cut. No more reasoning about the choice of branches, no more cutting back on fruit, or very little; no more subjection of any kind: all you have to do is tie up what you find. The whole science consists in spacing the branches well, spreading them out, and making them take the turn they require, to form a pleasing fullness throughout the tree. As for the rest, care must be taken to keep the fruit covered by the leaves as much as possible, so that it can grow bigger and better. You must also be careful never to cross the branches without extreme necessity. The defect of emptiness is the biggest one in the peach tree: this reason alone may excuse it, when it cannot be filled otherwise; for a small evil is to be preferred to a great one. One or two of the small branches born between the leaves of the current year's branches should be kept as far as possible, and it is the lowest ones that should be chosen; for it is often more appropriate the following year to prune on these small branches than on the mother, which its excessive strength, or lack of flower buds, forces to be cut back; and when the tree gets too carried away from the top, the strongest branches should then be cut back on these small ones, to fortify the rest. Small green marsh rush is the best for trellising: Marseille rush, though soaked in hot water, is too hard, and bruises young branches easily; in addition to not being as flexible as the other, it doesn't bind so securely, so you don't get the job done as quickly, and it also spoils the pruning shears badly. The straw or the large horbe that some people use, makes a rather ugly effect, and stops the branches badly. That's all I have to say about this operation, assuming the trees are disbudded: if they weren't, what wouldn't I have to say? With a great deal of time, trouble and precaution, you have to do everything that should have been done a month earlier, with the greatest of ease. It is necessary, in a way, to pierce the chaos, and to make oneself light in the darkness, to arbitrate the retrenchments that must be made, both on the wood and on the fruit. I cannot think of such a work without fear: so I refer the reader to the previous chapter; he will judge what he must do by what has not been done. He must always work on the same principles. The same causes, the same objects, the same disadvantages: it is up to the person who finds himself in the predicament I have described, to come out of it as unscathed as possible. CHAPTER X. The second Palissage. As the sap acts without discontinuity from February to September, we find ourselves obliged, a month or six weeks after the first trellising, to start the same work again; but it is much easier then. If the trees have been disbudded, only a few new branches are formed, because the removed branches have been broken off at birth, and the sap has not been able to penetrate the same places, and has all been carried to the retained branches, or to the fruit. If they have not been disbudded, it is quite common for false shoots to sprout from the feet of branches that have been snipped at the first trellising, and these should be broken off with the thumb, if they are soft enough not to need an instrument. If in any other place some have come up that are useless or misplaced, as they almost always are, in this case, they are removed in the same way: but observe to detach with the thumb, only that which bursts easily; for, if the wood has begun to eudurcate, you would damage the mother branch; and the gum that couldroit̀ occur afterwards, would cause it to perish: use a serpette then, and bring it as close as you can. If one of the branches that was trellised when the first trellis was put up, having found itself next to a greedy branch that has been cut back, has itself become greedy by the abundance of sap that has flowed to it, as often happens with vigorous trees, this branch must be removed, or at least cut back to the lowest of those it has produced. The remainder of this operation consists in giving an extra link to all the branches that have grown up since the first trellising, and cutting back those that exceed it to roughly the level of the coping. Some espaliers are so vigorous that they sometimes need to be trellised a third time in September: if necessary, this should be done in the same way as above. CHAPTER XI. How to uncover the fruit, and when to pick it. As much as it has been necessary to keep fruits covered by their leaves until they are ripe, to protect them from the sun's excessive heat and to give them more nourishment, they also need the sun's view to perfect their taste and give them the beautiful color that is their main ornament. However, it would be dangerous to expose them too soon to the sun's burning rays: they need to be accustomed to it gradually, that is, in three stages. We start to uncover them when the fruit begins to turn, i.e. when it whitens a little; we first remove a few leaves on the west or north side, depending on the exposure of the espalier: three or four days later, we remove a few more on the opposite side; and the same number of days later, we remove those opposite; finally, we put it completely out in the open, so that it doesn't lose any of the sun's rays. Soon after, it takes on color, it ripens; and we pick it when we see that the color is yellowing where the sun hasn't struck, i.e., on the side of the wall: If you're in the habit of picking it, you can tell for sure by looking at it; if you're not, you should observe that it comes off without violence: all you have to do is kiss it whole, pulling it slightly towards you. If the fruit has reached maturity, it remains in the hand, and you must be careful not to press your thumb against it to test it, as some people do, as this bruises the fruit: But if you're picking it to be sold, or to be transported some distance away, you need to pick it firmer, i.e., so that it resists your hand a little when you detach it. An important thing to observe when 1 uncovering the fruit in the manner I have just described, is not to tear off the leaves, but to tear them with the fingernail close to the tail; when they are torn off violently, this evades and spoils the eye of the branch where they are held, and prevents the flower bud from forming for the following year. CHAPTER XII. The various insects that damage the wood and fruit of the peach tree, and the remedies available. First of all, there is a species of green caterpillar which eats the flower bud before it has bloomed: when this damage is noticed, you must look for them; you will surely find them behind some branch, and crush them. Lories, field mice, rats, mice, mezcrines, all these animals with more or less the same coat and face, are the greatest scourges of the peach tree. They sometimes ruin the espalier, so that the master doesn't have the pleasure of tasting a single peach before them. If they stuck to the ones they start, the pain would be more bearable; but they try them all one after the other on the sunny side, as they ripen, and that's as much lost. There are two ways of destroying these kinds of insects: the first is to use dobbies and four ciphers, which should be placed on the walls from distance to distance, and especially around the trees where the fruit is ripening, with the proviso that they should be visited every day, and the bait changed from time to time; but, for the best results, it would be better not to wait until the fruit is ripe, as they are much less eager to use the bait when they have plenty of fruit than when they find nothing to eat. The second means, which does not exclude the first, is to have all the holes in your walls, both inside and out, plugged up to the letter; because when you take away all their retreat, they don't multiply on your premises; they go and find a home elsewhere; and if the species isn't destroyed altogether, it at least thins out considerably: you can still put arsenic kneaded with flour or minced meat along the chaperones; but at the same time you have to beware of the accidents that can result. How easy it would be to find remedies for the ant! This little insect ruins the peach trees it attacks, and we can't guarantee that they won't be affected: we can reduce the quantity; there are various means that we can use: But I don't think it's possible to destroy them completely, and if it's true that they could be made to give up their place by the antipathic virtue of some drug, as some people claim, I maintain, from my own experience, that the evil would only change object; for in that case, they would be thrown back further onto another tree: this is what I've sometimes seen happen quite naturally, without having been able to identify the cause. You must therefore avoid them as much as possible, and be content to clear them up as much as you can to reduce the damage. Of all the methods I've used, the one I've found most successful is to place a freshly killed ox foot at the foot of each afflicted tree, with the skin half removed, and place a half-full tub of water next to it; This foot is then skilfully lifted and thrown into the water, where it drowns all the insects; it is immediately removed and placed back in its original position, where the same effect follows a few hours later; so that the operation can be repeated five or six times a day, destroying many of them; and the foot is changed after a few days, when it is seen to be dried out by the sun and no longer has any virtue. I would observe, however, that this expedient is only effective when the weather is a little warm; for, having tried it in the spring, the ant has not attached itself to it. There is a distinction to be made with regard to what I have just said, which is that it is not possible to guarantee peach trees against this wretched insect: strictly speaking, this should only apply to low stems; as for high and medium stems, it can be avoided, and here's how. First, if the stem is a little flexible, you shake it several times to make the insects fall off, until you can no longer see them. You then need to have the patience to remove all the leaves that are poisoned with their spawn, and the aphid that is inseparable from it: once this is done, you stop it about a foot away from the wall, with a kind of wooden fork, which holds it firm in the position you want; and above this fork, you make a small basin of soft wax all around the stem of the tree, which you then evaporate. By this expedient, the ant, which doesn't like to swim, withdraws at the sight of water, and the tree recovers. There's one more thing to bear in mind in this respect, and that's to pass two or three laths behind your tree, to secure the branches that the wind and the load of the fruit would ruin; it goes without saying that these branches must be tied to the laths as well as possible. Another expedient is used instead of the soft wax basin. Take cotton or oak twine soaked in oil, and tie it around the tree stem: aspic oil is the best; olive oil is good, but neither is always an effective barrier against this insect, although it often keeps it at bay. From time to time, you need to refresh this filasse with oil. The ant is also the scourge of orange trees; and, to defend against it in Italy, where most of the walls are covered with this species of fruit, more suited to the climate than any other, here is the practice observed, and which I noticed in the garden of a curious man in Naples. His trees were planted a good foot from the wall, each with a small stem about a foot and a half long. On this same alignment were buried ten by ten feet, oak poles, four inches square, and the height of the wall, to receive a trellis in the fashion of the country, which, though very different from ours, had the mềme destination. Trees were placed between two of them, and trellised underneath in the same way we erect our contr'espaliers. At the foot of each post and each tree, there was oiled cotton, as I described above. The virtue of the remedy was demonstrated by the beauty of the trees, where the master assured me that the ant had never touched since the espalier was planted; and I saw others a few paces away, set against the wall, which were infected with it. Nothing would be easier than to raise our peach trees in the same way; but by guaranteeing ourselves against one evil, I can't answer that it wouldn't result in another, perhaps even worse. Our climate is very different from that of Italy; the cold winds that slip between the trees and the wall could do them great harm: moreover, fruit deprived of the reflection of the wall could ripen later, and have less taste. If someone finds himself excessively tired of this insect, he can try it out on a few ques toises of espaliers; in any case, the expense and risk are not great. Bugs often attract ants, so during the winter you must take care to rake with a wooden knife all the branches where their brood is found: this attention is absolutely necessary. Slugs and snails also like to eat our peach trees, and especially the violet, of which they are very fond; but if you take care to do a few inspections, either in the morning after the dew, or after some gentle rain, you'll manage to destroy them. Birds are just as curious to taste them, especially when some insect has damaged them; but they can be kept away with scarecrows; and when they don't work, a child can be walked along the espaliers to keep them away. Failing that, here's another method I've seen practised recently by some curious people, but which I haven't tried myself: it's to stretch six inches by six inches over the tree, in all its extent, of red spun wool such as we use for tapestry; we positively assure that this keeps them away, by I don't know what antipathy that it's not easy to understand; and this, it is said, preserves in the same way the grapes of the espaliers: the test is easy, and will cost little to those who will want to do it. It's not as easy to protect against earwigs and wasp flies as it is against other insects. These two enemies sometimes cause Tome II. Z of great damage to this fruit, especially to the small and large cukes, which ripen first. To defend against the former, there is no better remedy than to keep the walls well plastered to prevent them from retreating; and if, despite this, you are still bothered by them, you must put a few sheep's horns or pig's hooves behind the branches, into which this insect retreats: every morning you shake it, and you kill whatever is in it. As far as flies are concerned, we can destroy a few with half-full bottles of water beaten with honey, where they come to drown; but this is a small reduction in the evil, and several other similar expedients are no better. What I've always found really useful is to place a few peaches, already tainted, on the trellis, at a distance from each other, and leave them there, or some other sweet, anti-chewy fruit, such as plum, fig, pear, etc.; they stick to these as long as they can find life in them, and they don't attack the whole fruit. You can even destroy many of them, if you have the courage, several times in the heat of the day, to seize and crush them with your full hand, when you see a certain quantity picked up on these bad fruits, which is very extraordinary; and, to avoid being offended by their sting, you use a bad glove. CHAPTER XIII. Precautions to take during the summer heat. IN good soils, and especially in damp ones, provided your espaliers are well tended with ploughing, unless there is an extraordinary drought, there is nothing to fear, nor any precautions to take; but in arid and scorching sands, drought often causes trees to perish, or at least makes them languid, and the fruit they yield is of neither quality nor size. In this kind of land, I strongly advise all those who have the misfortune to be located there, to throw three lanes of water at the foot of each tree every two weeks, and a few hours later, with a rake, to give it a little polish. At the same time, throw a good load of large litter on top to maintain freshness. As for the stems, I recommend wrapping the body of the trees in long straw, tied with wicker; this will preserve your trees, and you'll see the good effect on your fruit. In southern countries, trees should be covered with straw mats during the hottest part of the day, otherwise the heat of the sun will burn the fruit and cause the tree to perish in a short time. 22 20 Blankets.
