(2) L'Abbé Irminon. 7I DE LA PROPRIÉTÉ TERRIENNE In a previous chapter, it was stated that the Romans, like all conquerors, had largely dispossessed the Gauls of their soil. When the Franks, in their turn, became masters of the country, they spared the first conquerors no more than the latter had spared their predecessors. The Frankish kings, in possession of almost the entire territory, were very generous to their vassals and especially to the fledgling associations. The latter took full advantage of the situation. Land under the Franks was granted in usufruct, i.e. in possession without right of ownership. All goods given to vassals by the king were to return to the domain after the death of the donee. This system enabled Charles Martel, for example, to seize the property of the clergy, as Dagobert had already done and as the men of the 1789 revolution would later do. Charles Martel gave this property to his soldiers as a benefit, so that all of a sudden, laymen found themselves in the place of abbots and bishops. During the tenth, eleventh and twelfth centuries, a large number of country churches were owned by laics. But Charlemagne, seeing that it was in his interest, and perhaps at that time also in the interest of civilization and progress, backed his empire on the power of these great associations, and gave them back a large part of their property, of which the Revolution of 1789 was to dispossess them momentarily for a third time. DIFFERENT KINDS OF POSSESSION (1) There were several types, namely: alleu, domain, colony or cencive, benefice, etc. The alleu is the most common type of property. Alleu appears to be nothing other than a patrimony, and was opposed to acquets. In the course of time, the name "alleu" was applied to everything owned outright, whether by inheritance, purchase or donation. Even the tenures of serfs, especially those of fiscaliers, i.e. royal serfs, were transformed into alleux, in the decadence of the Carlovingian dynasty, but most remained under the obligation to pay cens, and were therefore referred to as cencives. Land owned by monks from abbeys was more or less inalienable, and came to be known as mainmorte. In addition to their tenures, a certain number of tenants themselves owned property in the form of alleux, inheritance, propries or acquets, which they could dispose of as they wished. All landed property of a certain size consisted of two distinct parts: one, occupied by the master, constituted the estate proper; the other, distributed among more or less dependent individuals, formed what were known as tenures. The latter remained perpetually subject to the former, with obligations of various kinds. Tenures were divided into two sections, according to the obligations with which they were charged, and were either liberal or servile. In the first case, tenures were noble and owned (1) B. Guérard (translation by Abbé Irminon) by vassals, and were called benefices. The estate was the main part of the land, reserved by the possessor for direct collection of its fruits. Salic lands were noble lands derived from military benefices distributed by Clovis, and later by Charles Martel, to their principal lieutenants from the imperial domain left vacant by the demise of the Romans. According to Frankish law, daughters were excluded from any sharing with sons in the succession of Salic lands. Inferiority given to women, and from which they have not been able to recover until our century. In the second case, the land was despoiled and placed in the hands of colonists and serfs; it then constituted colonies and cencives. The land was divided into lots and distributed among people of low status. These people, by virtue of the lots of which they had usufruct, were subject to regulated obligations known as the law of the land. Usufruct was granted in several ways: perpetually and hereditarily, for life, for a term or at the master's discretion. Thus, the tenure of the colonist was hereditary and irrevocable; whereas the serf did not legally enjoy this property. From this account of land ownership, we can see that men had a greater or lesser degree of freedom, depending on the donation they possessed. Nothing was definitive, there was no stability, and each person's right was not clearly established. The free man placed himself under the protection of the powerful man, the serf under that of the free man. This practice of recommendation can only exist among barbaric peoples, devoid of the fundamental laws of society. In such cases, private force is most often used to make up for the absence of public force. The advent of Pepin-le-Bref paved the way for Charlemagne's heyday. He knew how to turn the diverse elements of his vast empire into the subjects of a great nation. This prince gave special encouragement to agriculture, and tried to put property and all existing institutions on a firmer footing. He had the officers of the estates give an account of their administration. Bishops, abbots and abbesses were ordered to submit annual statements of their property. Abbot Irminon, superior of the Saint-Germain-des-Prés monastery, was the first to draw up a sort of cadastre of the properties belonging to his monastery. He recorded the names and extent of the estates, the size and nature of the various holdings of which they were composed, and in general, the cultivation, produce, condition and administration of the land. It revealed the fate of the colonists and serfs, how many people made up a family, how they lived, to which class they belonged, and the services they were responsible for. In a word, he established not only the land registry, but a census, as accurate as possible, of the population existing on the abbey's lands. This was administration, order, political and rural economy. With the decadence of the Carlovingian empire, the tributary tenants, following the example of the vassals, appropriated the land of which they were merely the usufructuaries, and feudalism, as it developed, completed the process of fixing ownership in the hands of the possessor. Under Louis the Debonair, confusion became general, new men arose on all sides, petty vassals became great feudatories, and officers of the realm became independent lords. One settler, who had owned only as a farmer, became an owner and passed on his property to his posterity; another, who had lacked the audacity or strength to accomplish this act, fell into servitude. From this state of affairs, feudalism on the one hand, and the frequent uprising of serfs on the other. The difference between these revolts and those of the free citizens of antiquity was that the latter revolted for the love of freedom and the fatherland, while the former revolted out of sheer misery. It has been said that it was under Louis-le-Gros that the communes were officially freed, under what conditions, and what future this act brought to urban populations. These capitularies show that civilization took a major step forward under Charlemagne, as he organized and regulated everything that contributed to the production of the land. The monarch's intentions towards his farmers were good, the only thing was to compel the intendants, sub-intendants and all the rest to carry them out. But these exploiters, instead of supporting the farmers, lived and grew rich at their expense, robbing them as best they could. During the decadence of the Carlovingian empire, the lot of farmers did not improve; for during feudalism, unlike the artisans of the towns who had organized themselves into communities to defend their rights and privileges, the unfortunate farmers had no organization to defend themselves, and remained subject to the goodwill of their lords, who treated them with no other rule than their own pleasure. UNDER THE CARLOVINGIANS It is absolutely essential to know the value of the weights and measures of this period, compared to the units of our metric system, in order to form an idea of the price of land, the value of rents or cens, the price of foodstuffs, and so on. In Merovingian times, weights and measures, like all other institutions, were in a state of disarray. In addition to the measures they brought with them from Germania, the Franks used those of the Gauls, the Romans, the Greeks and even the Jews. MEASURES OF LENGTH (1) The main measure used by the Franks was the foot, more or less the Roman foot, which measured Om 2963. The arpent of the Gauls, like that of the Franks, was equal to a square 120 feet on a side. The league contained 1,500 steps of 5 Roman feet, and was therefore worth 2,222m 25. Today's terrestrial league is given a length of 4444 meters, hence the custom of considering the league as measuring approximately four kilometers. (1) B. Guérard. paré à nos mesures, il y avait de 12 ares 64 centiares, de 13 ares 72 centiares, de 18 ares 26 centiares et de 25 ares. The acre was later enlarged. According to some accounts established on the basis of these data, it has been recognized that the ancients sowed their wheat more lightly than today. The ansange is a measure that remained in use around Paris until the fifteenth century, and was worth around 19 ares. The perch also varied from period to period and from country to country. The aune, used to measure cloth, was worth a foot and a half, or Om 44495. CAPACITY MEASUREMENTS The modius or muid would be worth around 52 liters today. Each country also had its own measures, with different capacities. This measure was used to measure grain, wine, water, milk, pulses and so on. The setier also varied in capacity. The hemin was also a measure of capacity (1). Abbot Irminon's hemin was worth one liter sixty-four centiliters, which was what the rule of Saint-Benoit allowed each monk to drink every day. There was also staupas, which was about half the hemin. WEIGHT The Frankish pound was worth 326 grams until Charlemagne, when it was raised to 406 grams. The ounce was one-twelfth of the pound; until 779, it was worth 27 grams, and later, like the pound, it was increased to 34 grams. The ounce was also a kind of money of account, and was counted in ounces, as well as in pounds of gold and silver. CURRENCIES The Merovingian livre would have a value today of 69 fr. 57 c., the sou, which was the twenty-fifth of the livre, would be worth 2 fr. 782; the denier, which was the twelfth of the sou, would have a value of O fr. 2318. A gold penny worth 40 deniers would sell for 9 fr. 28. The pound of gold, which would produce 87 sous 3/20, would therefore be worth 808 fr. 40. Pepin-le-Bref's penny, being the twenty-second of the pound, would be worth 3 fr. 16 c. and the denarius of the same O fr. 2636. At that time, silver coins were manufactured at one twenty-second of their value. Pepin-le-Bref gave his monies one penny for every twenty-two pennies produced. Charlemagne increased the price of coins quite significantly. The Merovingian pound, as we said, had a value of 69 fr. 57, that of Charlemagne would be worth 86 fr. 97 c.; the sou, which was the twentieth, would now be worth 4 fr. 35 and the denarius of the same period O fr. 3624. This estimate represents the intrinsic value of the coins, but to get a more or less accurate idea of their relative value in our time, we need to quote the table drawn up by B. Guérard, Abbé Irminon's translator. This table required a colossal amount of work on the part of its author, and a great deal of knowledge to draw up. Therefore, we do not change any of the figures, but copy them verbatim. Relative value of coins before 755: one denarius 2 fr. 25; one silver penny 27 francs; one gold penny 90 francs; one silver pound 675 francs; one gold pound 7,841 francs. Relative value of coins from 755 to 778: Un denier 2 fr 56; un sou d'argent 31 francs; une livre d'argent 675 francs. Relative value of coins from 779 to 799: Un denier 3 fr. 52; un sou d'argent 42 francs; une livre d'argent 844 francs. Relative value of coins since 800: Un denier 2 fr. 35; un sou d'argent 28 francs; une livre d'argent 563 francs. After the discovery of America, gold and silver considerably decreased in value, and currencies followed suit. The ancient system of weights and measures certainly lacked the fundamental foundations of our metric system, which is based on our planet itself; but recognized by the competent authorities, it could render useful services to nascent trade and industry. Charlemagne prescribed it throughout his empire, but it was never properly observed, and despite his efforts and those of his successors, the institution went from strength to strength. Each province, each town had its own particular measures, and during feudalism, there were as many systems as there were seigneuries. It was the Revolution of 1789 that brought order to this institution, at least officially, by adopting the metric system. But customs are so difficult to eradicate that, a century after the Revolution, despite people's level of education, we still hear people talking about the old weights and measures, even in Paris. Certainly, in some provinces, the old system is still more widely used than the metric system, which is so simple and within everyone's reach. This institution, like so many others bequeathed by our fathers, is indestructible and imperishable. I say imperishable on purpose. Indeed, it could happen that any cataclysm would destroy all the types, all the standards of our weights and measures; all it would take is a single coin to reconstitute the system as complete and as perfect as it is today. To be edified on this subject, it is necessary to have attended, as a child, even if only for a few years, any of France's elementary school. 984-e8 GO LEUR LOCATION OU CENS SOUS CHARLEMAGNE A settler pays the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés four silver cents (113 francs) for one year's arable land: one acre of vines (12 ares 64 centiares) and half an acre of meadow (6 ares 32 centiares). A courtil (cortilis) 120 feet long by 56 wide, or 5 ares 89 centiares, was sold for 20 sous d'argent, or 563 francs, nearly 1 franc per meter. In 867, 12 bonniers, 15 hectares that had cost five pounds of silver: 2,816 francs, yielded three sous of silver per year: 84 francs. A manse with 13 bonniers, around 17 hectares of arable land; 6 arpents, 76 ares of vines and 6 arpents 76 ares of meadow, yielded a cens of 5 sous 4 deniers, making an average of 8 fr. 57 per hectare. The abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés rents, of course, for the price of 9 deniers: 21 francs per year, nine days of arable land, located in a place called Chaisnes. Compared with today's measurements, a hectare of arable land around Paris used to fetch six to thirteen francs. Land prices have risen considerably since then. At the end of this century, in the suburbs of Paris, a hectare yields an average of three hundred francs in arable land; it's true that it's mainly special crops that are grown here, rather than grasses. In 794, a muid of oats could not be sold for more than one denier: 3 fr. 50; barley, two deniers: 7 francs; rye, 3 deniers: 10 fr. 50; and wheat, 4 deniers: 14 francs. It is estimated that the weight of bread is equal to the weight of grain, the muid being worth 52 liters, this gives us around 40 kilograms. One muid of wheat would have yielded 40 kilograms of bread. Milling and bread-making costs were estimated at a third of the value of the grain. Add 4.50 francs for these costs to the 14 francs for a muid of wheat, for a total of 18.50 francs. These figures bring the price of a kilogram of bread to O fr. 456 during Charlemagne's reign, a relatively high price for the time. As a result, people in the countryside ate only bread made from barley and oat flour, without removing the bran. Wheat bread was considered a luxury item. What can be considered one of the greatest modern advances is the lowering of the power of money over wheat, making wheat bread accessible to everyone. Since Louis XIII, wheat has risen by only 50 0/0, while all other commodities have risen by 300 0/0 (1). In our time, if we pay a high price for bread, relative to the price of wheat, we owe it to agiotage on wheat and flour. Using the calculation we've just made, wheat is worth around twenty francs per (1) Avenel (Richelieu et la Monarchie). But to this price must be added the profits of the miller, the baker and, more often than not, the middlemen who often take the lion's share. Nevertheless, these are the prices established for the two main stakeholders: the producer and the consumer. At the same time, a good horse was worth six sous d'or: 540 francs, and a good steer two sous d'or: 180 francs. These prices were exorbitant for the time, especially when compared to workers' wages. DEIESSS CO The love of society that men bring with them when they are born, and the mutual needs that they are continually obliged to meet, soon led the first men to approach each other and join forces, either to make their existence easier, or to defend themselves more effectively against their enemies. And so, from the earliest civilizations, we see them making attempts at association. Among the Romans, it was the collegium; among the peoples of Germania, it was known as the ghilde, i.e. a banquet at common expense. The purpose of these associations was to defend and help one another. There was mutual insurance for all the major accidents that can occur during a man's life. The qhildes appointed a leader from within their ranks, had a common treasury provided by the followers and the statutes, probably regulations agreed between them, which everyone had to respect at their word. What's more, in keeping with the spirit of the times, each association was under the patronage of a god or hero. The Germans retained the ghilde even after their conversion to Christianity. When the new religion became powerful enough to impose its doctrines, it was only necessary to substitute the invocation of saints for that of gods and heroes; in other words, to change the names, but without changing the principle. Moreover, the fundamental principle of Christianity was the association of the weak against the strong. Its followers knew how to make the most of these associations, and based on this principle, which is so typical of man, they gradually brought them into line with the spirit of the times. Admittedly, these developments were slow, as are all institutions created in a developing society. During the feudal era, ghilds were known as confraternities (confraternities were synonymous with meetings, associations or societies in our time). Today, when we say "confrérie", we mean a religious association. Christianity organized them in such a way that they had a major influence in Paris for several centuries. Especially in the thirteenth century, many had their statutes approved. Their organization was infinitely varied, depending on the trades they represented and the goals they set out to achieve. They followed the trend of the times, and almost all became religious. Despite many abuses, they remained generally moral, through the vigilance they exercised over the morals and conduct of each individual; they were often political, through their intervention in popular movements. These associations almost always worried the authorities, and on several occasions they were abolished by capitularies, and a synod (1) held in Rouen in 1189 reproduced these prohibitions. Despite this, they continued to exist in a spirit of mutual association. After the Wars of Religion, they were overseen by the officers in charge; banquets were attended by sermons, and each table had a pot de l'aumônc. They had dignitaries called provost, dean or alderman. All the emblems of the brotherhood were at home. This office was sought-after, but only the wealthiest could obtain it, as it was very costly for the holder. (1) Le Masson, Calendrier des Confréries de Paris. 908 Each brotherhood had its own banner, coat of arms, attendance tokens and mottos; they also had their chaplains, medals and statutes. Attendance fees were made of lead, sometimes gilded, in the case of the richest brotherhoods. With the invention of printing, these practices fell into disuse, and naive images were substituted to brighten up the craftsman's home. Each member received one as he or she entered, as a sort of diploma. These institutions, like all others, had their abuses. Inevitably, political passions took hold of them, and especially during the Wars of Religion, they became furious; a period to which some people today would like to take us back. The most frequent reproach levelled at them was: drunkenness among confreres (our fathers drank heavily when they were celebrating). There were many different kinds of brotherhoods: many devotional, banter-based, facetious, apocryphal, patriotic, scientific and literary, with a religious element at their core. The devotional brotherhoods included penitents of all colors: white, blue, black, red, gray, green, purple, etc. (1). Among the banter and bachique brotherhoods, one of the best known was the confrérie des fous or innocents; bachique: the drinking horn of the fashionable devotees of the time; satiriques: "les paresseux ou les saoulx d'ouvrer et enragez de rien faire, des baise-c..., des mal mariés, des cornards, dite des Jean". Among the serious ones, the bow and arquebus brotherhoods, the core of the French infantry that saved the monarchy at Bouvines; the first elements of our modern armies, so true is it that whatever has been organized by the public authorities has always been copied from private societies. (1) Le Masson, Calendrier des Confréries de Paris. C Among the scientific brotherhoods, we find the Pontiff brothers, who have facilitated communications and rendered great services to commerce and industry. That of the "master masons", who created and handed down to us the architecture from cathedrals to the humblest village churches - there were few other monuments at the time. The most illustrious of the literary brotherhoods was that of the Passion in 1438, which represented the mysteries of religion, and which Victor Hugo describes in Notre-Dame de Paris. This brotherhood is, in a way, the cradle of our French scènc, and from which the great authors, notably Molière, drew inspiration to create the theater; these entertainments so fashionable since that time. Many of these brotherhoods have now disappeared; the Revolution of 1789 destroyed a large number of them, especially those that were not serious. Of those that have survived to the present day, almost all have a religious character. A scientific brotherhood, that of the "Masonic Masters", has also survived the centuries and is still very powerful today. This brotherhood has taken the name of society and appears to be a mutual aid society, in the fullest sense of the term. One criticism we could level at it is that it has perhaps retained too much of its medieval practices, in its private ceremonies: emblems, rallying signs, etc., which are still very much in evidence today. If we have given all these details on brotherhoods, it's to clearly indicate the spirit of medieval men, who associated themselves for everything, even the most frivolous distractions; not even thieves had their brotherhoods. The oldest gardeners' brotherhoods in existence date back to the thirteenth century, at Saint-Roch, Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, Saint-Yves, Saint-Sulpice and Mont Sainte-Geneviève; they were placed under the invocation of Saint-Jacques and Saint-Christophe. In 1415, under Charles VI, a 908 brotherhood at Saint-Josse was placed under the patronage of Saint-Fiacre. At the same time, another in Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs was given the patronage of Saint-Fiacre and Sainte-Véronique. In 1599, when the gardeners drew up their statutes and officially recognized their community, a chapel was granted to them in Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs. Saint-Médard has also had its own brotherhood since ancient times. The Revolution of 1789 destroyed all these associations, but in our century, as soon as the Bourbols returned, several were reconstituted, although not in the same churches, as the gardeners had retreated. Nevertheless, the Saint-Médard association was reconstituted in the same church; a donation had been made by a certain Durand to celebrate an eternal mass there on Saint-Fiacre's day, in honor of the former brotherhood. Almost forty years ago, we again saw the confrérie des jardiniers de Saint-Médard attend this mass. Its last president (or doyen under the ancien régime) was the honorable M. Charles Debille, descendant of an ancient family of market gardeners, about whom we'll have more to say later. Confraternities can be found in all religions and beliefs, since, as we have said, people are born to live in society and help each other. When they were more scattered and less numerous, they grouped together, forming hamlets, then villages, then towns and states. It was then that they formed guilds, choosing a god, a hero or a saint to patronize their society, according to their religious beliefs. At first, our ancestors placed their brotherhoods under the patronage of St. James and St. Christopher, and celebrated their feast day on July 25. Later, they placed them under the patronage of Saint-Fiacre and Saint-Véronique; of all these saints, only Saint-Fiacre remained. It's likely that this hermit, having devoted himself specifically to the cultivation of vegetables (D00), was closer to the gardener's guild than any other. What's more, he was an Irishman; generally speaking, one is not a prophet in one's own country, and the Irish, in those days, were held in very high esteem by the French; for the blood they had shed for our country. These societies were created mainly to help one another, the mutual aid societies of the time; but often the best institutions degenerate into abuses, especially if these charitable works are transformed into societies giving parties and banquets. What charity establishes, intemperance corrupts. A number of rulings by the Parliament, dating from different periods, forbid the establishment of brotherhoods, or the reunion of members of existing ones. François I, in an edict dated August 1539, abolished all brotherhoods of tradesmen and craftsmen. Only cloth merchants were exempted. Several other trades followed the same route as the clothmakers, and their brotherhoods were re-established. Charles IX, in an edict of 1560, ordered that the money and revenues of these brotherhoods should be used for divine service, and the surplus for the upkeep of schools or almsgiving. This re-establishment of the brotherhoods revived all the disorders that had been abolished. In a general edict issued in January 1563, the same king forbade them to hold any banquet or feast, on pain of a fine of five hundred livres for each person present. Following the example of the masters, the journeymen emancipated themselves by forming brotherhoods among themselves, and were forbidden to do so by an ordinance (1) issued by Charles IX on February 4, 1567, under penalty of a one hundred pound fine for each offender. Henri III confirmed this ordinance on November 21, 1577. (1) Ordinances issued by the kings of France. CONFRERIES D9 By parliamentary decree of December 13, 1660, it was forbidden to establish any assembly, congregation, brotherhood or community without the express permission of the king, and letters patent registered with the court. In compliance with all these regulations, the police magistrate issued an order on November 4, 1670, as follows: "The jurors and masters of the arts and crafts communities of Paris are forbidden to hold any assembly other than before us, and in the presence of the King's Prosecutor, on the pretext of raising money, confraternities or any other business whatsoever, except by virtue of our order and written permission, on pain of a fine of 100 livres against each of the jurors, dismissal from the jury, and a fine of 20 livres against each of the private masters who attend, with the exception however of the assemblies for the election of jurors, which will be continued in the future, on the customary days and places, in the ordinary manner". This was done and given by Messire Gabriel Nicolas de la Reynie, Conseiller d'Etat Ordinaire, Lieutenant General of the City, Provosté and Vicomté of Paris, on the fourth day of November, one thousand six hundred and seventy. Signed: De la Reynie de Ryants; Sagot, Registrar. Los confréries having lost their primordial character of mutual aid, to become simply religious societies, were to be swept away with all the old institutions, by the Revolution of 1789. We'll come back to the brotherhoods of our century in due course. AND STATUTES OF THE FORMER COMMUNAUTÉ DES MAITRES-JARDINIERS When Etienne Boileau urged workers' communities to draw up their statutes, to have them approved, to constitute a kind of workers' legislation, gardeners must already have been numerous under Louis IX, since they fed a population of nearly one hundred and fifty thousand inhabitants. But, either through ignorance or negligence, they never had their trade officially recognized. However, given the large number of guilds in the same situation, we are tempted to believe that all these "retardaires" enjoyed the privileges conferred on them by their respective guilds. This ordinance of the Provost of Paris really only concerns the materials used by gardeners, but we shall see later that the jurors responsible for overseeing the sale of all these products were the jurors of the guild of master gardeners, mareschers and preoliers of Paris and its suburbs. We'll also see that every aspirant to mastery had to produce a masterpiece of his or her own. The masterpiece required of gardeners did not consist of a real horticultural operation, but simply consisted of: "a quarteron of merriens, in good and sufficient work, according to the statement and report of the maistres jurer gardener". The second police ordinance (1) concerning gardeners is dated February 8, 1473; it completes the first, and still has little to do with gardening. This police ordinance supplements the ordinance of the Provost of Paris of 1376. It is a set of statutes, the first part of which, before dealing with trade, is a reproduction of the latter. The second part, the last three articles, deal with the privileges of the guild. It is certain that even before Etienne Boileau, these statutes existed verbally, but probably no abuses occurred, and it was when they did that the community felt the need to react. This ordinance is the first to deal with the work of gardeners, and is considered by some authors to be the oldest in the community. However, it is easy to see that it merely completes the first ordinance, just as the last articles of the last ordinance served as the basis for the statutes of 1599: 1576, August 29 Letters patent from Henri III, confirming purely and simply the regulations given to gardeners by the police ordinance of 1473. Arrêt du Parlement concernant l'ordonnance de police de 1473: 1889, June 27 "La Cour fait inhilition et déffense auxdits jurez jardinsiers, troubler ou empêcher ledit Rigault, vendre ou faire vendre, aux places publiques, ou autres lieux de cette ville, et à tels jours que bon lui semblera, les fruits et herbes creus et recueillis sur les héritages qu'il tient et valoir entre ses mains, lesquels fruits et herbes, pourront être visités par lesdits jurez maîtresjardiniers, tant esdites places que jardins, sous dépens". These lawsuits show that although the old community of gardeners did not yet have definitive statutes, it did enjoy certain privileges, especially the right of inspection, both at market disputes and in the gardens. In those days, even more than today, custom was the rule. It also happened that these representatives of authority wanted to arrogate to themselves rights they didn't have, and that the courts were forced to call them to order so that they would simply return to their privileges. FIRST STATUTES OF THE COMMUNITY OF MASTER GARDENERS 1599, November New statutes presented by the gardeners in seventeen articles, and letters patent from Henri IV confirming them. "The community of master gardeners of our good city, suburb, suburbs, provostry and viscounty of Paris, most humbly point out to Your Majesty that, from time immemorial, they have been numbered among the sworn masters of your city of Paris, and governed by ordinances and statutes particular to their trade, which they have peacefully enjoyed without contradiction until now. Nevertheless, in the shadow that the suppliants would not have obtained letters of confirmation from 0 your Majesty, some private individuals are trying to disturb them, and undertake on their trade, so that the suppliants doubt that this undertaking, if it were tolerated, would harm them and their successors, and hinder the said undertakings, commit several abuses and deceptions which are not to ratify and confirm the articles which follow, and the suppliants will be all the more obliged to pray to God for your noble prosperity and health". 1°. - No one may become a master gardener, in this city, suburbs and suburbs of Paris, unless he has been received as a master in the said trade, and has made a masterpiece by his own hand, as is customary. This masterpiece will be awarded and evaluated by the sworn members of the said trade, in the presence of four former bachelors. 2° item. - Before the masterpiece is given by the swearers to the said journeymen who wish to become master craftsmen, the said swearers are required to inquire into their good life and morals, the master craftsmen they have served, and where they have served their apprenticeship, in order to give or refuse them the said masterpiece, according to the report they find. 3° item. - After the said inquisition has been made, the said journeymen, who aspire to the said maistrise, will be required to make a masterpiece, as will be devised to them by the swearers of iceluy done and perfect, and will make the said swearers their report in the accustomed manner. 4° item. - That no one shall be accepted for master craftsmanship, in order to attain the said maistrise, unless he has been apprenticed under a master of the said trade, in this town and suburbs, for the time and space of four years, and furthermore, served by the masters, after his said apprenticeship time, for the space of two years. 5° item. - The children of the said maistres will be admitted to the maistrise, without any masterpiece or experience, after they have been certified as having been apprenticed, either to their fathers or elsewhere, for the said period of four years. 6° item - That the said maistres jardiniers, after being admitted to the said trade, will give to the confraternity of the said mestier, their right to it, and to maintain the divine service, the sum of thirty-two sols, which they will be obliged to give to the confraternity maistres. 7° item. - That no master may withhold, debauch 08 or give work to any journeymen of the said trade, while they are allotted to another master, unless he first knows from his master whether he is satisfied with him, under penalty of six sous fine applicable as above. 8° item. - That each apprentice of the said trade shall be required, as soon as he is obliged, to pay to the brotherhood of the said trade, for the fees of the said brotherhood, and to maintain the service, the sum of twenty-four sols parisis, and the master with whom the said apprentice will be, shall be required to advance this sum. 9° item. - The widows of maistres, as long as they remain in viduité, will enjoy the same privileges as their deceased husbands, but if they remarry, or fail in their viduité, they will lose the said privilege, and will no longer be able to engage in the said trade. 10° item. -- The said widows may have apprentices who were obligated to their deceased husbands complete their apprenticeship under them, so that they may maintain and practice the said gardener's trade, and so that they do not remarry others of the said trade, otherwise the said widows will be required to place the said apprentices with the mayors of the said juries, who will be required to have them complete their apprenticeship under another sufficient master of the said trade. 11° item. - The said widows may not, as long as they continue to practice the said gardening trade, take on any new apprentices or have them obligated, but will have them trade and merchandise with a journeyman who requires the status. 12° item. - That all persons whatsoever are forbidden to bring or cause to be brought any melons, cucumbers, artichokes, herbs and other things dependent on the said gardening trade, unless they are masters of the said trade, except the burghers of the city and suburbs of Paris, who may have gardens and property, who may bring or cause to be brought on market days, which are Wednesday and Saturday, all kinds of produce growing in their said gardens; which produce. will be inspected by the said swearers, and if they are good, will be exhibited for sale; if they are not, they will be confiscated, and the person who exhibits them for sale will be fined twenty sols, half of which will go to the King, and the other half to the said swearers of the said trade. 008 buy any thing dependent on the state of gardening, in any place other than the said market hall and public markets, so that the swearers have knowledge of it, nor even hold in their houses, or elsewhere, their fruits and herbs at night, insofar as they will be subject to rot and attract the bad air. And to avoid the said abuses that may be committed, the sworn members of the said trade may search the houses of the said sellers for the faults and abuses that they find there, report them in the customary manner, and the said offender may be fined and punished if he so desires. 14° item. - That all persons are forbidden to smoke any garbage or pig droppings in order to plant or sow any goods that depend on their gardening; to avoid the abuses that are committed there, and could be committed hereafter, to avoid contagious and other diseases, on pain of having their goods spilled, and being fined two écus for each offender: 15° item. - That it is forbidden to all masters of the said trade, to purchase from other masters, any trees, or other goods to bring them to sell on the bridge of the said trees, or other public places, on penalty of confiscation of the said trees, and of two écus fine, applicable as above; but may the said masters, sell their trees and flowers there as of any seniority. 16° item. - That all master bachelors and journeymen of the said trade, shall be bound to recognize their former master-jurors, and to show them the respect, honor and reverence due to them. Signed: THOMAS These statutes are the most important act of the ancient community of master jarniniers. From the documents that preceded them, it is easy to see that the community had only incomplete legislation, based on the police ordinance of February 3, 1473. However, as we've already mentioned, around 1260, when Etienne Boileau had a register drawn up and deposited at the Châtelet to record the customs practiced for centuries by the various Parisian trades, our ancestors were already numerous, but they neglected this formality which gave official recognition to their trade. What is certain is that these time-honored practices had the force of law, and successively produced the documents we have just cited. These statutes of 1599 were skilfully drafted for their time, and provided a sufficient guarantee in every respect for the community of master gardeners. They cover the rules of apprenticeship, the rights and duties of journeymen, the masterpieces accomplished 99 to achieve mastery, and the privileges of masters' sons and widows. The election of jurors, their functions and rights, the prohibition against poaching journeymen from one another, the obligation to inquire when hiring someone they didn't know, where he had apprenticed, with which masters he had worked, the reasons why he had left the house: in short, the community policed all its members. As a result, it was not uncommon for journeymen to stay with the same masters for a number of years. Hence the mutual esteem that existed between them, with the pastoral existence so dear to our ancestors. We'll come back to this subject at another time, and try to explain, as far as possible, the reasons why these pastoral customs changed. Masters were not allowed to buy goods from other masters for resale by regrat. They could not smoke their land with pig manure, Paris sludge that was too fresh, or fecal matter, the infection of which, said the Prévost de Paris, could cause contagious diseases. This was a hygiene measure taken by the police against gardeners, given that many of them lived in the city, or even on its outskirts, in fairly densely populated suburbs. Even today, don't we see these police measures taken against the sludge of Paris! The capital's neighboring towns no longer welcome them. The railroad stations where they are shipped create problems for farmers, giving them only a few hours' latitude to unload their wagons and transport the contents to a certain distance from their homes. All these difficulties increase the cost of the city's cleaning service. As a result, the city council has asked the Hygiene Commission to look for a practical way of getting rid of this refuse. The idea is to create large furnaces to incinerate it. This would produce chemical fertilizers that are easy to trans09 port to all parts of the country, but what is indisputable is that the Paris suburbs would suffer a great loss if this system were adopted. Growers and horticulturists within a fifty-kilometer radius have protested against this method, but the idea is still being pursued. However, large-scale cultivation would like nothing better than to receive the slush from Paris, but say the growers we spoke to, that the railway companies should give us the time we need to remove it. Certainly, today, the capital no longer fears famine, as in the old days, thanks to the rapid means of communication, the food we need comes from all sides, according to the season. It is no less true that this great suburb, which supplies the lion's share of the vegetables consumed in Paris, is entitled to some consideration from the big city. It has not even been proven that the price of these products would not rise significantly above current prices. The old police regulations before 1599, concerning gardeners, had to do with trade, the visit of jurors to markets and gardens. Four different people had the right to sell fruits and vegetables from their gardens in the public markets of the city of Paris: master gardeners, journeymen, suburban showmen, and the bourgeois of the city and suburbs who owned gardens they sold. There were regulations for all these different conditions, prescribing what they had to observe, and whose purpose was to provide citizens with an abundance of the simplest and most common healthy foods, often the only ones used to feed the people, and which even the rich would find hard to do without. The maitres alone had the right to display their wares for sale on the mornings of every weekday, ORDONNANCES DE POLICE 908 at the halle aux poirées, from the halle aux blés to the rue Saint-Ionoré. This community was the only one whose journeymen could trade like the masters; in the past, this was only granted to those who owned gardens or marshes that they managed, but since 1627, this right has been extended to those who rent them. Nevertheless, with these old conditions, they were still required to endure the visits of the jurors, to bring their goods to the market hall and other squares only on Wednesdays and Saturdays, which are market days, and to take their place there only after all the masters. These same journeymen also contributed to the community's expenses, even though they were not yet part of it as masters. The burghers of the city, suburbs and suburbs, as well as the showmen of the small surrounding localities, had only the same right as the journeymen gardeners, to exhibit their trees, fruit and vegetables for sale, on both market days, on condition that they also suffered the visits of the jurors. The community left no stone unturned to defend its interests, and it's easy to see that freedom of trade was very limited, and competition virtually impossible: such were the customs of the time. During the nearly two centuries that these statutes remained in force, they underwent no major changes, but simply followed the spirit of the times, one might say the whims of kings. Whereas under Louis XIV, instead of the communauiés appointing their jurors, they were appointed by the king, and the jurors became, so to speak, public servants. This state of affairs could only result in flagrant abuses, which helped to push the ancien régime into the abyss, perhaps even faster than it should have, had it respected the ancient regulations of the workers' communities. A word, in passing, about the signatories of the statutes of 18 1599; of these nine signatories, only one family has kept its name in the guild to this day. The first signatory is a Jean Le Bouteux, which certainly means that he was the principal, and what we today call the president. In our century, we also find a Le Bouteux, as one of the principal founders of the first mutual society created by gardeners. This venerable dean of our corporation was vice-president of this society for almost forty years, and at the end of this century, he is still its honorary vice-president. Another name that has left its mark on the history of gardens is Pierre Lenostre, who must undoubtedly have been one of the ancestors of the great landscape architect who designed the park at Versailles, and thus created a new art of garden design known as the French garden. We've already had occasion to talk about this illustrious gardener. These various lawsuits provide ample evidence of the community's interest in asserting its privileges: they also demonstrate the no less active interest of the companions in reacting against these privileges. It has been said that the organization of workers' communities was part of the feudal system of the Middle Ages. So, when the great reformer Calvin came to preach his doctrines in Paris in the 16th century, they disrupted the existence of the old communities, which set out to maintain the use of courteous arms between industrial competitors; they were violently opposed by the Paris bourgeoisie, who represented them. After the Edict of Nantes, the king obliged tradesmen to accept several religionists, as they called them, into their ranks. The aim of the authorities, in imposing these men on the various organized guilds, was undoubtedly to force them to obey an order from the king, to ensure the supremacy of the Catholic Church. As these religionists were the most literate, this gave them much greater authority over their fellow members. Despite this, many men in the communities, already enlightened and with a certain independence, preferred to go into exile and take their industries to foreign countries, rather than bow to this arbitrary act (1. This unfortunate act cost our country dearly, says Michelet. The act of revocation was signed by the king on October 16, 1685. On October 19, the Paris police brutally told the tradesmen that they had to convert immediately. They were terrified, but raised no objections. The king thought it was all over, and on the 20th authorized Protestants to assemble for a joint declaration of conversion. Those who resisted were looted and robbed, and some were murdered. Women in particular, whose freedom of conscience is even stronger than that of men, had to endure the most odious outrages. Many of them, to force them to give in, were locked up in the convent of the Nouvelies Catholiques, and subjected to all the horrors that an undisciplined soldiery is capable of inflicting on a woman who is handed over to them bound hand and foot. Surely some of our old grandmothers must have suffered these outrages. Whereas before these ridiculous constraints, which had nothing to do with trades, the groups of citizens who made up the ancient communities, constantly in touch with each other through common interests (1) Michelet, Histoire de France. 10, drew up their own little code, and the state intervened only to approve their decisions, taken among peers, and to reap a certain profit from them. Despite the abuses that these societies perpetuated for their own benefit, and which the Revolution did away with by proclaiming individual freedom, it can be said that they had a raison d'être, which argues in favor of the time when they subsisted. The masters upheld the rights and privileges that the ancient nature of their guild gave them, or that they had arrogated to themselves by forming organized and recognized communities. It's true that, from time immemorial, people have had to band together to defend their interests effectively. Unfortunately, the interests we support become abused with time and new men. Even so, it's hard to let go of them when they've been enshrined for centuries. To be fair to the old community of master gardeners, it must be said that they had almost relinquished all their privileges by the time the revolution broke out. This abnegation by our old masters in favor of their privileges is proof of the independence of their character and the generosity of their ideas. If not these men, at least their sons, will be found later on, and we will trace the services they rendered to the corporation, by taking the initiative, at their peril, to introduce new crops. The old community also had to support various lawsuits against the regrattier fruit growers, who were organized as a community long before the gardeners. An article in the statutes of the community of grain growers governed the right of gardeners to sell seeds. It's almost certain that both of these industries originated in gardening. In the early centuries, growers sold their products directly to consumers, as the city was sparsely populated and not very large, 28 but gradually, as the population grew and the city gradually expanded, new needs arose. This led to the creation of the specialties we have just mentioned, which were careful to set themselves up as communities, with their statutes approved by the public authorities. Another specialty more closely related to gardeners was the community of bouquetières, whose first statutes are included in Etienne Boileau's livre des métiers. The fashion of adorning oneself with natural flowers was very much in vogue in the Middle Ages. At joyous gatherings, flower chapels were woven and offered to friends. The art of making chapels was a favorite pastime of the grandes dames, and our Parisian ladies were already distinguished by their good taste and genius for innovating everything to do with grooming. At first, florists copied these grand dames, but in time, they quickly became artists in their art. The community was free, exempt from watch and taxes, authorized to work at night at certain times "establi pour servir les gentuez hommes". At this time, they made wreaths of flowers and herbs, and above all chapels of roses, diadems, crowns or circles, much used in processions; they reserved the right to sell bouquets, hats, wreaths and garlands of flowers in the streets and at church doors; anyone contravening these regulations was fined five hundred pounds. During the season, bouquets of violets, roses and carnations could be sold, but not upright. Gardeners sold their flowers only at the IIalles and Quai de la Mégisserie, until eight o'clock in the morning. Flowers had to be fresh, and sales were supervised by community jurors. Acacia was banned from Corpus Christi processions. All flower chapels had to be set against a background of greenery. Statutes of the Chapelières de fleurs inscribed in Etienne Boileau's guestbook. 1° - Quiconques veut estre chappellières de fleurs à Paris, estre le puet franchement, pour tant ce qu'il sache fère le mestier et il ait de coi. 2° - Quiconques est chappellières de fleurs à Paris, il puet ouvrer et fère ouvrer de jours et de nuiz, de fleurs et d'herbes. 3° - Quiconques est chappellières à Paris, il ne puet ouvrer, ne fère ouvrer au jour de dimenche de nul chapel, se ce n'est de chapiaus de roses, tant sculement, tout comme la seson des roses durent; et se le faisoit, il seroit à 5 sols de tournois d'amende à poier au roy. 4° - Nus chappellières de fleurs ne doit ne peut cueillir, ne fère cueillir au jour de dimenche en ses courtuiz; nules herbes, nules fleurs à chapiaus fère ne à mangier, en celle jornée, qu'il ne soit à 5 sols de tournois à poier au roi. 5° - Quiconques est chappellières de fleurs à Paris, il puet porter et faire porter, vendre ses chapiaus à Paris, en quelque lieu qu'i voudra, et à toz les jours de la semaine, pourtant qu'il trouve place wide. 6° - Nus chappelliers de Paris, ne doit nul coustume, nul paage, ne nule droiture de chose nule qu'i vendent, n'en achaptent apartenanz à leur mestier, soit qu'i envairet de dehors la ville, ou qu'i envoit l'dehors la ville, soit sur cheval ou à col. 7° - Nus chappelliers de fleurs de Paris ne doit point de guet, parce que leur mestier est frans et que il fu establi pour servir les gentuiz hommes. 8° - Si prend oume du mestier se sont ascenti, un preud'oume de leur mestier soit mestre du mestier, li ce que preud'oume doit jurer devant le Prévost de Paris, que il le mestier gardera bien et loiaument, et que toutes les mesproustures qu'il saura qui fétes seront u mestier devant dit, que il au Prévost de Paris ou à son commandement fera scavoir au plus tost que il pourra par reson. Article 4 of the statutes sufficiently indicates that the bouquetières were gardeners, as it forbids Sunday flower-picking in the courtyards. The husband, father, brother or any other worker was responsible for growing the flowers in the garden, and the wife for selling them, according to the customs and fashions of the time, exactly as they are today, with the difference that each one organized himself as he saw fit. These statutes were renewed on August 21, 1677, and make it clear that the community is independent of any other. We note in these statutes certain articles that concern the sale of flowers in the olden days, and which are still in use today, notably: flowers in crates or pots must be sold at the Quai aux fleurs and not at the Ilalles Centrales. 1677, August 21 Statuts des bouquetières, in 21 articles, and letters patent from Louis XIV confirming them (1). ARTICLE 1 No woman or girl may become a master flower-maker in this city and suburbs of Paris, unless she has been a master of the said trade, and has made a masterpiece by her own hand, in the manner accustomed from time immemorial, which masterpiece will be given to aspirants by the jurors of the said trade, in the presence of four former bachelors only, who will be called in turn and by order of the roll. (1) René de Lespinasse. ARTICLE 2 No girl or woman shall be admitted to the master's degree unless she has served her apprenticeship with one of the master craftswomen for four years, and then served the master craftswomen for two years; the apprenticeship certificates shall be notarized in the presence of two jurées and duly registered in the chamber of one of the king's attorneys. And apprentices will be required to pay three pounds to the brotherhood's (boète) at the time of the said patent, which will be advanced by the mistress, who will be reimbursed by her apprentice. ARTICLE 3 Before granting masterpieces to aspirants who present themselves for acceptance, the jurors will be required to ascertain their good life and morals at the home of the mistresses with whom they have served their apprenticeship and as companions, and according to the report made to them, may grant or refuse them masterpieces. ARTICLE 4 The aspirants will make their masterpiece with their own hands, in the presence of the jurées and four former bachelières, who, after it has been made and perfected, will report on it and take the aspirant before one of the king's procurators at the Châtelet, to administer the oath and be received by him in the customary manner, and all the mistresses will be warned to come and see the masterpiece, if they so wish, and attend the administration of the oath, but without charge. ARTICLE 5 The aspirant will be required, at the time of her reception, to put ten livres into the confraternity box, pay sixty sols to each of the jurées and thirty sols to each bachelière, and the ordinary costs of justice, without it being permitted to make her pay any other costs, even when they are voluntarily offered, under penalty of fine and restitution of quadruple against the jurées, bachelières and others who may have received them. ARTICLE 6 Daughters of mistresses may be admitted to the master's program without having completed any masterpieces or experiments, provided they have served as apprentices to their mothers or other mistresses for four years, pay only thirty sols into the brotherhood box, and pay half dues to the jurécs by way of recognition. ARTICLE 7 Those who wish to be received by virtue of letters, without having served an apprenticeship, will pay thirty livres into the confraternity box and will be received by making light experiments, and will pay the said jurée fees. ARTICLE8 The right to display and sell all kinds of bouquets, hats, wreaths and flower garlands shall belong solely to the maitresses bouquetières. Any person who is not of the aforementioned quality is forbidden to make or sell any bouquets, nor to resell or peddle them in the streets or at church gates, under penalty of confiscation of their merchandise and a fine of five hundred pounds, half of which will be for the benefit of the King, and the other half for the benefit of the community of maitresse bouquetières. ARTICLE 9 All kinds of persons may nevertheless sell bouquets of violets, roses and carnations during the seasons, as in the past, with the difference that they may not be mixed with any other flowers, nor may they use canetille to decorate and tie them ARTICLE 10 Masters of the community of gardeners may not display or sell their flowers; whether they are picked, or in pots, crates or mannequins, at church doors, or elsewhere, in front of the stores and squares of the master flower sellers; they must bring their picked flowers to the market every weekday, and their flowers in pots, crates or mannequins to the Quai de la Mégisserie on Wednesdays and Saturdays in the usual manner. ARTICLE 11 In order to preserve the freshness of the flowers, gardeners and other inhabitants of the surrounding suburbs and villages who bring them to the halles, will be required to bring them there very early in the morning and sell them immediately, either to the bourgeois, or to the flower sellers, and will be required, after having completed their sale, to withdraw in summer at eight o'clock, and in winter at nine o'clock, with a prohibition on selling flowers after the said time has passed, on pain of confiscation and fine. ARTICLE 12 Flower sellers will be required to use fresh and new flowers in their bouquets; they are forbidden to use old, wilted flowers, or those that have been salted during the summer, under penalty of confiscation and a fine of ten pounds, applicable, etc. ARTICLE 13 Bouquet-makers are similarly forbidden to use any accacia flowers in their bouquets, nor to make any wreaths or flower hats for Corpus Christi or other holidays, unless they put some green underneath, subject to the same penalties as above. ARTICLE 14 Each bouquetière merchant may not have two apprentices at the same time, and so will be required to be content with having only one; may, nevertheless, with the said apprentice, have one or more companions to help them do their work, and the daughters of maitresses whom they have working for them, will not take the place of an apprentice. ARTICLE 15 No mistress may give work to a girl unless she is a mistress, apprentice or companion. All mistresses are forbidden to take away companions who are rented to another mistress, or to give them work, unless they have first asked permission from the said mistress and know that she is satisfied with the said companion. ARTICLE 16 All mistresses of the said trade are forbidden, under the same penalty of a ten pound fine, to meet gardeners and other persons when they bring their flowers to the market, so that they may be sold and quoted among themselves. 4 ARTICLE 17 For the preservation of the aforementioned trade, there will be in the future, as in the past, four jurées, two of whom will be elected each year before one of the King's procurators at the Châtelet, one a woman and the other a girl, as is customary, These jurors will take care to prevent companies that could be made on the aforementioned trade and will make visits to the maitresses, at least four times a year, and will be paid twenty sols for each visit, may nevertheless make a greater number, but will only be paid the right for four visits, per each year. ARTICLE 18 We forbid all persons who are not maitresses of the said trade, to sell flowers or bouquets at church doors, on street corners, or to carry them into the houses of the bourgeois; nor regratiers and coureuses, to peddle them in the streets, and maitresses bouquetières, to have them sold by the said unqualified persons: all under penalty of confiscation and fine both against the one and the other ARTICLE 19 If any mistress, apprentice or companion of the said trade were convicted of misconduct in her honor, she would lose her privilege, and if she were an apprentice or companion, she would be unworthy of attaining the master's degree. ARTICLE 20 During their first year as jurors, the last two jurors will take care of all matters concerning the brotherhood, which they will continue to maintain in the church of Saint-Leufroy, as they did previously, and will have the customary service said there. ARTICLE 21 The community will be composed of women and girls only, and no boy will be allowed to become a master, or to enter into the said trade, or to make or sell bouquets. We forbid all mistresses to give work to any man, nor to have their bouquets sold by them. To these causes, Louis, by the grace of God, King of France and Navarre, to all present and future; greetings: Nos chères et bien-aimées les jurées et anciennes bachelières de la communauté des maîtresses bouquetières, chapelières en fleurs de notre bonne ville de Paris, nous ont fait remarquer qu'il y a très longtemps que leur art est établi dans ladite ville de Paris, en communauté et corps de métier, qu'elles ont eu des statuts très anciens qui leuront été accordés par les rois nos prédécesseurs, qui contiennent plusieurs beaux droits et privilèges, pour la perfection et la conservation de leur métier; but that through the passage of time, and the negligence of those who preceded them in the office of juror, the originals of the said statutes have been lost, and whatever diligence the aspirants have been able to make, they have been unable to recover them, in such a way that, although the substitutes preserve among themselves the rules of discipline. that they know have always been observed in their community; that they have continued to maintain their confraternity and the divine service that is customary there, that they still have their juries, their apprenticeships, their visits, as they have had from time immemorial, like other communities, they cannot, nevertheless, retain the rights of their trade, nor prevent the undertakings that are daily made by gardeners and other persons, without quality, on their community, if they are not given a name. To this end, they have collected the old memoirs of their statutes and, in accordance with the custom and tradition of their community, have had new ones drawn up, which they have most humbly begged Us to grant them and order them to execute. And having been informed that this community has been established in our good city of Paris for a very long time, that they have their confraternity established in the church of Saint- Leufroy, where they are accustomed to have services said every Sunday for our prosperity; that they have continued to elect jurors every year, to receive maitresses and to take on apprentices, that it would be unjust for the loss of their statutes, which is more excusable, to cause the ruin of the community and state of those who compose it, the just and innocent means of earning their living and supporting their families. Having also considered that the art of flower girls provides a very pleasant and innocent ornament for people of status, and often even serves pious uses of religion, being used to adorn altars and churches, and that it is in the public interest and of our grace, to preserve all the trades formerly established, and give them a means to support themselves in the true rules of justice and their establishment. 909 To these causes. Donné à Versailles le vingt-et-unième jour d'août, l'an de grâce mil-six-cent-solxante-dix-sept, et de notre règne, le trente-cinquième. These new statutes show that the community of bouquetières is completely outside the gardener's guild, since article ten prohibits gardeners from selling their flowers anywhere other than at the Halles and Quai de la Mégisserie. There is no longer any mention, as in the first statutes, of a ban on Sunday flower-picking in the courtyards. Under Louis XIV, this community consisted solely of flower merchants, not gardeners. The communities of master gardeners, bouquetières and regratiers des fruits esgruns (I) were classified as small trades. In the letters patent of Louis XI. containing the distribution of bourgeois, merchants and artisans, under certain banners, for the guard and safety of the city of Paris, tradesmen are divided into fifty-nine banners, according to the Reverend Father Le Masson, in his calendar of the brotherhoods of Paris. The gardeners occupied the fifty-fifth rank and the other two came after. Each banner had a principal and a sub-principal elected every year on the day after Saint John's Day. They were eligible for re-election and were required to swear an oath of loyalty to the king, and to lead the community in arms in defense of the state and the king. The banner was only to be taken out on the king's orders. It was kept by the principal, or failing him, by the sub-principal. To be eligible for these functions, one had to have been a master for at least six years. The communities of the various trades, part of the feudal organization of the Middle Ages, had their own mottos and arms, like the lords and princes of the church. (1) Sour fruits and vegetables. The coat of arms (1) of the community of master gardeners was Sable, with three garden lilies Argent, stems and leaves Vert, two in chief and one in base, and a chief Azure charged with a sun Or. Its motto, inscribed on a token dated 1556 and belonging to the Monnaie collection, depicts an axe-wielding hand amidst a garland of flowers and fruit, with the legend: Manus, fortis, divitias parat (THE STRONG HAND PREPARES RICHES) The axe, in those days, was as much a gardener's tool as the spade. We have seen in their statutes that the masterpiece required to be admitted to the master's program would today represent the work of a trellis-maker rather than a gardener. On another token, which appears to have been made when the community renewed and completed its statutes in 1599, and which became the actual legislation governing the gardener's trade until the Revolution, is written in exergue. Egestatemo, perata est manus remissa (NOVEMBER 1599) In a short work by Mr. Georges Gibault on the former community of master gardeners, published in the Journal de la Société d'Horticulture de France, February 1896, we note the festivals attended by the community in common with the communities of other trades. The pompous procession that preceded the King of France on his solemn entry into Paris was always a great feast for Parisians, and a magnificent sight to behold. The king usually spent the night at the priory of Saint-Ladre (1) Depping, Livre des Métiers. at the top of the faubourg Saint-Denis. At eight o'clock in the morning, placed on a platform, he saw the delegates of his good city parade before him: at the head the mendicant monks, then the clergy of the parishes, then the university followed by its rector, finally the bodies of the city i.e. richly costumed men, chosen from the various trades; some carried with them, either the tools or the insignia of their profession; the others organized militarily in the company of pikemen and harquebusiers, marching seven by seven with fifes and tambourines, all clad in engraved and gilded helmets and cuirasses. The procession then accompanied the king to Notre-Dame (1), through streets adorned with triumphal arches, decorated by the hands of the greatest artists. On June 16, 1549, there were fifty (2) gardeners at the entrance of King Henri II, where the contingent of each of the most powerful guilds reached eighty, while others had only five members in their ranks. The Provost of Paris set the contingent for each trade in the absolutely binding summons he sent to its leaders, and equipping the men was a heavy burden; (3) "and to provide for the fraiz, will be able to compel all those of the said mestier, both in the city and in the suburbs, the strong carrying the weak, etc.". In 1610, when Queen Marie de Médicis was due to enter the town, the gardeners were to provide twenty-six men. Together with the millers, turners, basket makers, etc., they formed a company of one hundred and sixty-four men, commanded by a captain, Sieur Mailly, a lieutenant and an ensign, both shoemakers. The company was therefore made up entirely of small tradesmen, occupying the lowest rank in the classification of trade categories. (1) Entrée de Charles IX dans Paris. The polyptych of Saint-Remy de Reims (information on our ancestors' way of life in this remote era can only be found in these precious documents) sets the price of nine days' work at four deniers: 9 fr. 40, or around 1 fr. 05 per day, after the year 800. This is already a small increase on the previous example. On this subject, I'd like to borrow from my excellent friend, Mr. Georges Gibault, a little pamphlet he published in the Journal de la Société d'Horticulture de France, entitled: La condition et les salaires des anciens jardiniers. This little work is very conscientiously done, and required a great deal of research on the part of its author. It deserves to be quoted in full. If we reserve the name of horticulturist for the cultivator of plants destined for the trade, as correctness demands, all that remains to designate the horticultural professional in general is the vague term gardener; an unfortunate word if ever there was one, since it has created a regrettable confusion between the man of art truly worthy of the name and the laborer who calls himself a gardener. Indeed, the general public, always superficial, is all too unaware of the difference between the various categories of people uniformly referred to as "gardeners". However, some are eminent scholars, artists and authors; others are often distinguished specialists in a most difficult profession; as for the science of simple gardeners' helpers, it's limited to handling the spade and watering can. There can be no doubt that the ill-defined name of gardener, and the resulting disadvantageous comparison for the able practitioner, may have contributed to fixing the latter in a condition inferior to his real merit. Gardening already had against it the old prejudices that discredited work on the land; moreover, the majority of gardeners personally attached to the service of a master, found themselves placed on the fringes of domesticity, less favored than craftsmen and other tradesmen whose nature of their work made them more independent. Are these not the main causes of the current inferiority of the gardening profession? Indeed, while most tradesmen have always followed an upward trend towards a higher social status and better material conditions, gardeners have not been so happy. We must hope that the future will remedy this injustice. A great step will be taken in this direction when the gardener's merit is better known; when we can better appreciate the amount of intelligence and the variety of knowledge required by a profession for which too many people profess only the very relative esteem accorded to purely manual trades. p09 It is probable that the most ancient civilized peoples, such as the Egyptians and Assyrians, already distinguished gardeners from farmers. Tomb paintings prove that Egypt, two or three thousand years before our era, had pushed the luxury of gardens very far, whose cultivation certainly required special workers (1). The Romans used only slave labor to cultivate their gardens. Wealthy Romans owned and employed slaves of all professions, from teachers to shoemakers and gardeners, for their personal service. As a result of advances in gardening, the latter were already specialized: hortulanus seems to indicate, in the texts, the gardener in general, often also the flower gardener; olitor, which took its name from olus, vegetable, took care of the vegetable garden, and topiarius or artist gardener, took care of the decoration of pleasure gardens. In a familiar letter, Cicero wrote: "I have paid a compliment to your gardener decorator (topiarius), who has covered the entire main building with ivy, from the base to the terrace (2)". Topiarii and viridarii were particularly skilled at pruning green trees into the extravagant shapes that were so popular. Under their skilful hands, Yew and Boxwood were transformed into figures of beasts and various objects, while Rosemary and Alexandria Laurel (Ruscus hypoglos- sum) drew in huge letters the name of the gardener or that of the owner. According to Pliny and other authors, these singularities were among the main attractions of beautiful gardens at the time. Because of their highly appreciated talents, topiaries appear to have been treated with some consideration. "... There are certain slaves," says (1) Perrot et Chipiez. Histoire de l'Art dans l'antiquité, t. I, fig. 256, 257, 259, 260. (2) Cicero. Ad. Q. III, 1. Cicero, like the stewards and gardeners (topiarii), who consider themselves far above the rest... (1) ". During the first period of the Middle Ages, the gardener was found only in abbeys. Monasteries were the main centers of civilized life. They preserved the faint remnants of the arts, sciences and letters that had escaped barbarism. As the monastic rule imposed manual labor almost everywhere, gardening was in the limelight. A monk, who was one of the abbey's principal officers, was responsible for overseeing the cultivation of crops; he took the title of hortulanus or gardinarius (2); at the same time, he oversaw the orchards, vineyards and ponds; it was his duty to ensure the decoration of the church with appropriate flowers (3). To carry out the work, he employed religious courtilliers (curticularii) (4); he also had recourse to the corvées owed by the abbey's serfs (5). It's only in the 14th and 15th centuries that the documents preserved in the archives, especially the expense accounts, which are of such great help in understanding private life in the Middle Ages, begin to shed some light on the living conditions of the ancient gardeners. The first forerunners of our modern gardeners to appear in history were, of course, the gardeners of the great lords. The insecurity of feudal times meant that only kings and princes could establish which(1) Cicero, Paradox. v, 2. (2) Gardener; word derived from the Germanic Gartem or Garden meaning garden. As a result, the documents we're talking about come mainly from the royal house of France, the powerful and sumptuous house of Burgundy, the archbishops of Rouen, King René of Anjou and other high-ranking personalities. The already great luxury began to extend to the gardens. Appropriate decoration was needed to harmonize them with the sumptuousness of the homes, furniture and clothing. As a result, from the 13th century onwards, courtyards and vineyard trellises were being built around wealthy residences. The préau, which gave rise to the modern parterre, was a lawn with geometric lines, adorned with shrubs and flowers and surrounded by grass seats. In the following century, this primitive parterre was embellished with carpentry arbors and luxurious pavilions built on artificial mounds. Then came labyrinths, trees pruned in the ancient tradition, grottoes, parquet floors and compartments. The gardening profession thus seems to have originated in the need for special men capable of adorning pleasure gardens with certain accessories which today are more the domain of landscape architects and the horticultural industry. Depending on the taste of the day, the gardener raised the clod (1) to make the courtyards, carpentry work was carried out to build rustic pavilions, trellises and arbors, green trees were sculpted and compartments were designed. Until the 17th century, the gardener seems to have been more a "trellis-maker", a garden decorator than a plant grower. In 1599, the masterpiece required by the old guild of Parisian gardeners for admission to the master's degree program still consisted of simple char(1) Sod removed with a spade. 08 penterie work. The axe was then considered the main emblem of the gardener's trade, quite distinct, it seems, from the vegetable-grower's trade in the Maîtres-Jardiniers-Préoliers-Maraïchers guild (1). If we consider that almost all of our ornamental plants were introduced recently or not very long ago, and that horticulture was in its infancy in those distant days, with neither the pruning of fruit trees nor the art of early produce, we will be less surprised to see the cultivation of many large gardens requiring only the temporary labor of simple field workers. In 1302, in Picardy, Countess Mahaut d'Artois kept "three valleys busy weeding roses" for three days (2). In 1311, she hired laborers to plant "mesliers (Néfliers) pumiers, peskiers, francs-mouriers...". (3). The head gardener's auxiliaries, hired on a yearly basis, were not employed on a permanent basis either, and were also paid a daily wage. This is nothing out of the ordinary; in fact, many women still take part in the hard work in the fields today. In those days, women took on the menial tasks of gardening. Weeding and picking flowers and aromatic herbs, whose importance in the domestic economy was singularly great in the past, were mainly reserved for them. In the 14th century, in the gardens of the Château de Rouvres, belonging to the Dukes of Burgundy, women carried manure, earth and sand in baskets and on their heads. In March, the accounts show that two quarters of strawberry plants are being planted in the "jardin Madame"; young girls are busy with this work, as well as with the "esboicher" of lavender. A quarter of land is "reffouit" to plant Aulx; the men make the rays and the women plant; and the girls are busy weeding "toulz les fraisiers du jardin Madame, hoster l'erbe et ordure, nettoyer et sarcler le lis et l'osilctte"; they then pick the seeds of "pourros, blettes, parsley": they rastellent (rake) the sown beds (4).
