There are two small greenhouses, however, where students can learn about ornamental plants and vine forcing. A small bedding area is used for cuttings of annual plants and for forcing a few vegetables. A few panels of strawberry plants, varieties : Docteur Morère and Marquerite that don't look bad, the rest are insignificant for the season (beginning of May). It's only in autumn that this school is at its best, and its products are noticed every year at the exhibition held by the French Horticultural Society at this time of year. We feel that this is not enough for such a well-designed establishment, given that the students who graduate from it are specially destined to manage bourgeois gardens. As we know, owners who take on a student from a school like to have vegetables in all seasons, especially early ones. Osteed CO AND PUBLIC COURSES The statutes of the community of master gardeners under the old regime contained an article on apprenticeship that provided a valuable advantage for young apprentices and a guarantee for the employer. At the beginning of the century, having retained some of the customs of the past, young people were hired as apprentices and paid as such. Once they had spent some time with the same employer, they became skilled workers, capable of doing their trade well. When, for one reason or another, they left their apprentice boss to work for another, we knew where they'd come from and what they knew how to do. These circumstances helped a great deal in securing contracts, whereas nowadays, a worker comes to work for us declaring that he knows how to do the job, when sometimes he has never set foot in a swamp, or knows very little about the work he has to do. The boss, often believing he's dealing with a good worker, has agreed to pay him as such, but seeing himself deceived, he dismisses him immediately and the worker starts again elsewhere. It also happens that, when the work is urgent, we keep him on for a while, employing him on the big jobs, which are the easiest to do. The worker, for his part, knowing that he does not possess the special aptitudes to fulfill the commitment he has entered into, is convinced in advance that he will be dismissed as soon as the heavy work is finished; he becomes more demanding when he does not leave the job of his own accord. This state of affairs gives rise to unease and discontent on both sides, often extending to the good workers themselves, who then become the victims. Labor is becoming so hard to come by these days, that we have to anticipate the moment when almost everything that is possible will be done on the job. Will this way of working reconcile all interests? Only time will tell. From this brief account, we can see that almost all the evil stems from the lack of training of workers. Without going back to the practices of the Middle Ages, couldn't we require a certificate of apprenticeship from the worker, which would justify the degree of professional instruction of the applicant? This certificate would inform the employer, at the time of hiring, about the work that the worker would be capable of performing. This procedure would make it easier to sign up to new contracts, and would often help them to last longer. In the century of freedom in which we live, it applies to many corporations. In Paris especially, where everything is specialized, there is a huge difference between a worker accustomed to working in one specialty, and another working in another. The method we suggest would not be detrimental to anyone's freedom, and would be of great benefit to both employers and workers. Frequent job changes benefit no one, and on the contrary, often cause a significant loss in the industry where they occur, and always to the workers in their wages. Only one free vocational course exists in the Seine department, given by an experienced practitioner: Mr. Duvillard. This course, paternally given in his beautiful 908 marsh in Arcueil-Cachan, is both theoretical and practical, but it can hardly be applied to apprentices, who above all need to learn manual labor, before knowing when to sow seeds, how to care for plants, how to rotate crops; in a word, all the profit that can be made from the land we cultivate. This course is more useful for those who intend to run private gardens, where horticulture in general is practiced. It is the intellectual and practical side of the profession, not the manual. In the latter case, it is essential that the apprentice knows how to use the tools placed in his hand, before learning how to manage the crop, which he learns by practicing. In spite of everything, we would strongly urge workers to follow this course, which can only strengthen them in their art. It would encourage them to take notes on the various crops they are studying; the results obtained, and so on. Make comparisons with what they see being done elsewhere, and draw their own conclusions. In horticulture in general, and in market gardening in particular, where you have to continually help or fight nature, you never know your job inside out; a fact that vindicates your methods one year vindicates them the next. The horticulturist cannot be compared to the artist; the latter, once he has perfected his art, does so forever. In horticulture, on the other hand, there are always new things to come along that you don't expect, and which you therefore don't know without studying them. It is therefore only through the study of these facts and through experience that the horticulturist can overcome all the difficulties that arise in his cultivation. Until the middle of the 19th century, the trade in horticultural products remained purely local. As a result, gardeners did not feel the need to display their products. But since this trade has become almost international, like that which results from all industries, they have felt the need to make their products known to merchants in all countries. For over thirty years, market gardeners have played a major role in the annual spring exhibitions organized by the French National Horticultural Society. Their products are always much admired by the many visitors to these exhibitions, and win them a large number of prizes for the beauty and, above all, the perfect selection of their plants. Market gardeners don't take part in autumn shows, believing that at this time of year everyone can grow vegetables when there's plenty of water to water them. Despite this, we feel that they could still organize an exhibition at this time of year, where the hand of these skilled practitioners would be recognized, especially in the many varieties of plants they have so artfully selected. These include cauliflowers, tomatoes, celery and other seasonal salads and vegetables. At the 1867 World's Fair, market gardeners wanted to grow crops on the spot, but unless they had a special plot of land suitable for the purpose and considerable resources at their disposal, success was unlikely. In 1878, there were temporary competitions, i.e. the display of products capable of being delivered to the trade for the duration of the Exhibition. In our opinion, this was the only practical way to showcase Parisian market garden production. In 1889, this was the only way to do so, and connoisseurs from all over the world stopped to admire this unique production. This exhibition was the subject of an important report by Mr. Duvillard, secretary and rapporteur of this class. REPORT BY M. DUVILLARD Vegetable plants At the 1889 Universal Exhibition, class 80 centralized all products supplied by market gardening, vegetable growing and related agricultural activities. As with the other classes in Group IX, eleven competitions, representing the various successive periods of cultivation, were organized to enable visitors to follow more easily the different phases and the many advances in market garden production. In this way, everyone was able to get an accurate picture of all the improvements made by our horticulturists, both to increase and to enrich the products delivered for consumption, from the most sought-after early crops to the vegetables that form the staple diet. In the Class 80 competition, for example, we saw a succession of market garden varieties, the most prized of which were strawberries, pineapples, asparagus and melons, grown in the Paris region and available to a privileged few at the start of each season, Thanks to the special care that Parisian growers give to this type of cultivation, without neglecting the products sought after by popular consumers, such as potatoes, cabbages, radishes and salads whose families are so varied. The harvests exhibited in the Class 80 competitions were highly commended for the quality and beauty of their produce, as well as for the diversity of their species. It is indisputable that, for several years now, the horticultural industry has been undergoing the greatest development in Paris and neighbouring regions; workers have never neglected to use all the means at their disposal to facilitate the use and supply of the rich gifts of the earth and nature. The Universal Exhibition showed us that agricultural exhibitors had kept pace with progress, and, through the improvements they had achieved, that they fully understood the importance of the place they occupy in our century of civilization. In the galleries of class 80, all the vegetable products supplied by the Parisian countryside were exhibited in turn, over a relatively short period of time, to supply the Halles and the capital's markets throughout the year. The results obtained by the grain specialists were entirely in line with the very encouraging progress made by the market gardeners; the exhibitors of leguminous species had been able to broaden the scope of this specialty, and not limit it to species grown exclusively in our country; they were thus able to offer visitors specimens of all the varieties harvested throughout the world, which was scarcely possible for vegetables for which freshness and earliness are the primary qualities. From the point of view of education and experience, the exhibition of products grown outside our homeland gave the greatest benefits. We must also point out that all the efforts of our *I workers in the field were not wasted: for the duration of the Exhibition, the products they exhibited continued to be the object of special favor from the public and amateurs, who thus testified to their interest in our agricultural industry. On the other hand, our exhibitors had taken meticulous care to facilitate the study of leguminous plants, presenting them to visitors in a methodical order and layout that enabled them to follow, almost step by step, the progress of vegetable cultivation. The excellent impression made on the public mind was certainly not the result of satisfied curiosity: among our compatriots, as well as foreigners, it was with legitimate pride that we admired the brilliant results due, in large part, to the initiative of the growers who contribute so largely to the life of the capital and the civilized world. This popularity of the public, the great popular jury, did not slow down for a moment: every day we could see a large number of people, belonging to all classes of society, following with keen interest all the work of class 80, and paying great attention to the explanations and information provided by the exhibitors to the visitors; many of them collected important notes, intended as much to fix their memories, as to report to those who were not able, alas! to come and admire the great festival of modern progress, to which France had invited all the peoples of the globe! Farmers in other regions also appreciated the remarkable advantages obtained by Parisian market gardeners and grain growers; they were able to remember a few names or improvements of types, neglected or insufficiently known in their own regions. Thanks to the information they have gathered during their visits to the Exhibition, they will in turn be able to give new impetus to hortiO06 culture and make a powerful contribution to the development of field work, both in the provinces and abroad. From this new point of view, the Class 80 competitions have demonstrated that with intelligent care, sustained hard work and an equitable distribution of agricultural aids, the most advantageous services can be obtained from cultivation in and around Paris, as well as in more clement and hospitable climates. Now that we've talked about agricultural aids, without encroaching on the realm of agronomy, let us briefly mention the most favorable causes that come to the aid of the Parisian or suburban farmer: the main ones in particular are inherent to current progress, and it would perhaps be ingratitude on our part not to pay them the just tribute they deserve. First of all, we find a whole system of perfected agricultural tools and machines. The Universal Exhibition, among all its marvels, showed that science had achieved a great deal, and that it had not yet said its last word: it used to take a great deal of effort and toil to obtain, from rudimentary equipment, results which today would certainly be inadequate for general supply; productive forces were incomplete, cultivation faltered, and land often remained uncultivated, even in our beautiful country of France. Today, we are able to provide for almost all consumer needs. Secondly, we have found powerful collaborators in the fertilizers used in recent years. As the learned agronomist Schwertz said, "Whoever wants to get a lot out of the soil, must also give it a lot". In Paris, more than anywhere else, it was necessary to give a great deal to the fertility of the soil, and if we have just made a quotation from a foreign worker in our country, we 009 also note, to the glory of our national self-esteem, that it is still in France, especially in the vicinity of the City of Light, that the most brilliant results have been obtained in this respect. From all the products exhibited in the Class 80 competitions, it is clear that market gardening, better improved and perhaps better understood, has developed far beyond our expectations. The initiative and dedication of the workers have kept pace with the prodigious activity of consumption, while ensuring the satisfaction of all the requirements of our times. Perhaps the future will bring further improvements, but we are convinced that these will be inspired by the studies that the Exhibition's competitions will have led to. This will be to the credit of our farmers, who will have proved that they have never ceased to keep up with the times and with progress. And it is also with real satisfaction that they will have contributed, within the limits of their attributions, to ensuring the greatness and triumph of the Universal Exhibition which crowned the great centenary of 1789". At the 1900 Exposition, vegetable production will be widely represented in all the competitions taking place, and it is to be hoped that this industry will play a leading role in the great peaceful struggle that will take place on the threshold of the twentieth century. The admission committee for this class (class 44; group VIII) has made every effort to persuade the Exhibition's senior management to include mushroom cultivation. Mushroom cultivation had previously been included in group IX, class 54; harvesting equipment, instruments and products. As we have already said, this cultivation was begun by the gardeners of Paris, at least two centuries ago, and has since been continued by their descendants, a number of whom have become absolute specialists. In the temporary horticultural competitions, visitors and especially enthusiasts will be able to examine this culture as it is grown in the immense quarries surrounding Paris; they will also see the seedling blanks and the products of these blanks. A discovery made by modern scientists. The exhibition will also be retrospective, to show the progress made in each industry. This will not be its least curious aspect, to mark in a clear and well-fixed way the stage humanity has reached in this century of progress. The author, having been asked by his class to prepare this work for our specialty, has produced an abridged version of this history, which has been unanimously accepted both by the board of directors of the Paris region market gardeners' union, and by the committee of the aforementioned class. PLANTES POTAGÈRES gitired by Groupe vin (horticulture), Classe 44 (culture potagère) CULTURE MARAICHÈRE PARISIENNE Fistorique sorrrnaire de l'industrie Market gardening has only really made progress in this century; our ancestors were content to cultivate the plants they had, in the season when nature made them grow. The forced cultivation of the late 19th century, which became the basis of Parisian market garden production, is where most of the science of the modern market gardener resides. It is due in particular to the initiative taken in the 18th century by the illustrious La Quintinie. This art of making plants grow out of season is therefore only two hundred years old, and throughout the last century it has served only to satisfy the culinary tastes of kings and the powerful. At the beginning of the 19th century, a few bold and enterprising market gardeners tried to imitate the great gardener of Louis XIV and his successors, by forcing some plants. These men are the masters of modern gardeners, and we respectfully salute their memory in passing. However, for more than a century (1), market gardeners have been making a few layers in the air to advance the Raves, (1) Delamare, Traité de Police. Radishes, lettuces, etc. The great market gardener mentioned above acknowledged that he had learned a great deal from the Parisian "mareschais" (1). The latter, in turn, as well as their posterity, owe him a tribute of gratitude for the progress in cultivation he made in his royal kitchen garden. At the end of the 18th century, a small number of market gardeners had a few hundred bells and very few frames. Asparagus was first cultivated "à cloches", as indicated by La Quintinie in his Traité de culture potagère; then came other growers who cultivated it "à châssis", a method still used today. Other crops were also tried, by the sons of the former masters of the gardening community. It was not until the Restoration, when tranquility returned and trade took off again in a new and unprecedented way, that these crops became widespread. At the same time, a large number of young men and women left the countryside to set up families in Paris. These less well-off families tried to amass a small nest egg to work for themselves. Establishments were of little value; a spade or two, a rake, a pair of watering cans, a few barrels, a pulley with its rope and buckets, a few hoods, mannes, etc. constituted all the equipment for these arrivals. Consequently, water was drawn by hand, and produce was carried to Les Halles on hoods, as in (1) La Quintinie, Traité de culture potagère. O0 the old days, even though settlements were already moving away from them. At that time, they were located around Louis XVI's enclosure walls (intra and extra-muros), especially for the latter, while the sons of the former masters still lived in the suburbs around Charles V's destroyed enclosure. As the latter had a few frames and a number of bells, they installed cranks (1). This is a very old tool, but it requires the use of a horse to operate, and until then, settlements were not large enough to cover these costs. The arrival of the hand crank was therefore a revolution in market gardening, requiring the use of a horse and carriage, as well as the distribution of water in the marsh; with the bells, frames and accessories that this equipment entailed, this already formed a market gardening establishment, where production could take place all year round. Around 1835, piston and merry-go-round pumps replaced the cranks, thus solving the problem of drawing water from great depths, enabling market gardeners to tackle the plateaux around Paris, since water is the most important issue for market gardeners at all times and in all places. As the population of Paris grew rapidly during the 19th century, and the number of middle-income earners became much greater, early crops were in demand, and market gardeners gradually increased their equipment for these crops. In 1845, Messrs Moreau and Daverne, who wrote the history of their corporation, reveal that in their time it employed three hundred and fifty thousand frames and around two million bells. But since these authors wrote, the greatest economic, industrial and commercial revolution of modern times has taken place. The creation of the railways (1) Malpeyre, Bixio et Bailly, Maison Rustique. 900. Trade has grown steadily since then, and has gone from being local to our corporation to being international, and market gardeners' equipment has increased considerably today. Around 1860, a new advance was made in the guild: the installation of irrigation. This watering system, initially resisted by the older members of the guild, took little more than a decade to become widespread, and helped to increase market-garden production in great proportions, enabling growers to brave the most severe droughts. After 1870, a new crop was added to those already grown by market gardeners: a few young people began to grow the early turnip known as Navet marteau. This crop was a great success, almost doubling the number of market gardeners' frames. The cultivation of other early vegetables followed the same progression, in particular: forced Romaine on bell beds, one of the most marvelous and lucrative crops bequeathed to the guild by the old market gardeners of this century. At the 1889 Universal Exhibition, mechanical engineers presented gas and oil engines; a large number of market gardeners were quick to install these tools to operate the pump, replacing the horse which, given the size of the marshes and their remoteness from the capital, has enough work to do transporting produce to Les Halles and bringing in the manure needed for the farm. These small gas or oil engines worked very well, and young market gardeners quickly learned how to use them. At the end of the century, mechanical power was put to work in market gardening. It's a far cry from the way the first gardeners of the century drew water by hand. A number of gardeners have installed rotating "C" cities in their marshes, with portable rails to enter the squares; this is an innovation that will make its way and replace back-pack transport of vegetables, manure, potting soil, etc., in the century that is about to begin. In the very near future, we can expect to see small motor-driven ploughs replacing the spade. At this point, I realize that I'm encroaching on the future and that I'm leaving the questionnaire that's been imposed on me. MAIN PRODUCTION CENTERS At the end of this century, the main production centers for market gardening proper are on the right bank of the Seine: Maisons-Alfort, Créteil, Champigny Bobigny, Aubervilliers, La Courneuve, Stains, Asnières and Gennevilliers. The localities on the left bank with the largest groups are : Issy-les-Moulineaux, Malakoff, Montrouge, Bagneux, Arcueil-Cachan, Gentilly, Ivry and Vitry. TRADE IN PRODUCTS DURING THE CENTURY (exports and main consumption centers). Our ancestors left no written records to give us an idea of the turnover they were able to achieve, but based on the work so wisely done by Messrs Moreau and Daverne, in 1845, we can, by deduction, establish it approximately. These authors estimated that market gardeners in their day occupied three hundred and fifty thousand frames, about two million bells and that production could amount to thirteen or fourteen million francs annually, including mushroom cultivation, which became a specialty at the end of the century. They also cultivated beautiful1- 61- "1e produit n'appartient plus au domaine "n taking all these facts into account: for forced cultivation in the 208 middle of the century, deducting the cultivation of mushrooms and flowers, which belong to other specialties, we can estimate, without fear of deviating much, market garden production at the beginning of the century, at three or four million francs a year. By the end of the century, market gardeners occupied approximately one million frames and five to six million bells, cultivating around one thousand hectares of land, with an average yield of thirty thousand francs per hectare: in other words, this industry had grown almost tenfold in terms of business and much more in terms of production: the price of early vegetables being lower than at the beginning of the century, and only twenty or twenty-five years ago. So it's consumers in general who are benefiting from this increase in production. It is estimated that more than a third of this produce is exported abroad, notably to England, the largest consumer center for Parisian market garden produce, Belgium, Germany and, to a lesser extent, Russia. Les primeuristes have just presented their products directly at the inter-national horticultural exhibition in Saint Petersburg, where they won almost all the first prizes. This augurs well for opening up new commercial outlets for the market-gardening industry, which fears no competition in terms of product selection and beauty. The national horticultural exhibitions held every year in Paris, and international ones at intervals, are proof of this. The vegetable displays put on by the market gardeners' guild always win top prizes, and are much admired by the many French and foreign visitors. LAND VALUES 2 LEUIS : -- . -. In the mid-19th century, Y tells us that Louis XVI terraces and Louis-Philippe's fortified enclosure were worth between twenty-eight and thirty thousand francs per hectare. Those with no easy access were worth between sixteen and twenty thousand francs, including walls and housing. The sites occupied by market gardeners at the beginning of the century, in the lower suburbs of Charles V's enclosure, were already worth from eighty to one hundred thousand francs per hectare; today they are worth from five hundred to eight hundred francs per meter, and the latter, from fifty to two hundred francs depending on their location. The same authors estimated the rental of well-placed plots at twelve or thirteen hundred francs per hectare, and the second quality at eight to nine hundred francs, all including housing. These prices had roughly doubled since the beginning of the century. Between the time these authors were writing and the end of the century, market gardeners had moved away from Paris, and the same proportion existed for the increase in rents; they had roughly doubled, which meant that they had quadrupled during the course of the century. Today, land suitable for market gardening in the Paris suburbs sells for an average of three to four francs a meter, in field soil of course. To set up a farm: house, outbuildings, fencing, well, etc., you need to spend around twenty thousand francs. Consequently, a hectare of marshland is currently worth between fifty and sixty thousand francs. EXPLOITATION Market gardening, with the enormous equipment it requires, consists in producing rimeurs in autumn, winter and spring, along with 1- C1 11s, the finest commercially available. As for the market gardeners themselves, today they should simply be called "primeuristes": their method of forcing plants has not yet changed much; it is still done by layers of manure, as in La Quintinie's day. But with modern progress in replacing animal traction with mechanical traction, we can expect the price of this raw material to rise, as another industry, that of mushroom growers, employs more and more of it. At some point, therefore, manure production will not keep pace with the needs of this industry. Some market gardeners have already added thermosiphon technology to their crops. When the time comes, they too will be forced to use chemical fertilizers on their other crops. Moreover, the intelligent market gardener who loves his trade is like a traveller climbing a mountain whose sites are unknown to him. With each step he takes forward, new horizons open up before him, increasing the scope of his research and, later, often that of his knowledge. These are the reasons why Class 44 of Group VIII decided to present these questions for discussion at the 1900 Horticultural Congress. It's a sort of preparation for l'Avenir. MARAICH GROWING SOCIETIES AND COURSES The market gardening guild has a mutual aid society, or rather a pension fund. Founded in 1855, the fund has around a thousand members, and has provided, is providing and will continue to provide useful services to its members. In agreement with horticulturists, it has set up a mutual insurance company against damage caused by hail and storms. It also has a professional association, which was set up only a few years ago, and which is also destined to be of great service to the company, both economically and commercially. 900 A free public course in vegetable growing is given once a month in Arcueil-Cachan by Mr. Duvillard, also a teacher with the Chambre syndicale des ouvriers-jardiniers. EXISTENCE IMPROVEMENT (Wages, number of bosses and workers) Although this first question is not included in the questionnaire, it is difficult to talk about workers' wages without saying a word about improving their existence. At the end of this century, market gardeners in Paris are the only ones still feeding their workers; with the spirit of independence that drives the men of our time, the time is not far off when this state of affairs will cease; for, on both sides, people aspire to this moment, which will come with the enlargement and remoteness of establishments, and with other methods of selling produce. The patriarchal mores that existed among the ancients are tending to disappear by the day. There is no longer the mutual esteem that once existed between bosses and workers, and the latter no longer stay with the same boss for many years, as they once did. At the beginning of the century, our ancestors had a Spartan existence, which no worker would be content with today. We might even add that very few workers live as well as market gardeners; they enjoy all the benefits that civilization has given to mankind, they have the fortifying food of city dwellers, and the hygiene and fresh air of country dwellers. A distinguished economist who has established the mortality of men by corporation, estimates that it is one of those where they live the longest. The wages of both male and female workers have quadrupled in the course of the century. Most are paid by the month: from seventy-five to eighty francs in summer, and from fifty-five to sixty in winter. As they are housed and fed by their bosses, they are unaware of the rising cost of living and rents; the women workers who go to Les Halles earn as much as the men. It's quite obvious that the day they're no longer fed and housed, they'll have less profit, or else they'll live worse; however, generosity aspires after that day, which is hardly surprising, as men want to enjoy as much freedom as possible. The market-gardening guild we have just described comprises around one thousand two hundred establishments, making a total of two thousand four hundred male and female bosses, because it's worth saying here that, in this profession, women have, if not more, then as much work and responsibility as men. It's in her department that products are prepared for sale, and until then it's she who goes to sell them at the central Ilalles. These 1,200 establishments employ around 5,000 workers of both sexes, not counting children, who today start work at a younger age than in the past. Since the Third Republic passed a law on primary education, they hardly start work until they are thirteen or fourteen. In a word, and to conclude, market gardening is one of the hardest jobs men can do, but it's also one of the healthiest. In this respect, didn't one of our great classics, Boileau, write the following two superb lines? Work, to men necessary, Makes their felicity rather than their misery. Insects harmful to vegetable plants and their diseases........................................ 287 mencement of the seventeenth century, said that the gardener is "the goldsmith of the earth". He added that the main object of his "mastery" is to know exactly when to sow his various crops, so as to obtain beautiful produce throughout the year. Intensive vegetable cultivation, i.e. that which can be carried out in gardens where fertilizers and water are available, differs from ordinary kitchen garden cultivation in that it must be a successive, uninterrupted cultivation throughout the year, in which several different vegetables are often planted together on the same plot. The first treatise on vegetable gardening written in French that we have been able to find was published in 1393, under the signature "Un bourgeois de Paris"; in fact, it appears to have been written or dictated by a skilled practitioner. The author sets out the various vegetable crops in the chronological order in which they should be grown. Claude Mollet, Louis XIII's famous gardener, did the same in his treatise, which was not published until 1700 by his son André Mollet. The progress made in gardening since the publication of the treatise mentioned above can be seen in this work. In the book we are publishing, we shall be following much the same path as our eminent predecessors. We will deal with the cultivation of all the main vegetables, salads and fruit-vegetables, which require special care, either in forced or ordinary cultivation; the time of sowing, the cultural care to be given to plants during the course of their evolution, the means of conserving them during the winter, etc. Like the authors of the two books we have just quoted, we have adopted a chronological order, which we find has the advantage of sparing the gardener lengthy research, and reminding him, at all times of the year, of the care his crops require, and we have taken as our starting point the month of August, when the seeds are sown that will give rise to the first new vegetables in spring. We have endeavored to maintain a logical link between the work of the various periods, and have summarized it in a Table of Contents, which will enable the reader to easily follow the progress of a given crop. We have devoted a special chapter to X days, a veritable industry in the suburbs of Paris, and to the progress that science promises to make in this crop, which is still only based on routine, especially as regards mycelium selection. Indeed, science is always progressing, and the technical processes themselves are constantly being perfected. Many improvements have been made in the art of vegetable gardening since Claude Mollet, and even since La Quintinie, the great initiator of forced cultivation of fruit and vegetables, up to the present day. The part of this book that deals with forced cultivation is aimed above all at amateur gardeners, who have at their disposal the equipment and elements needed to establish such cultivation, and also at provincial gardeners, who will no doubt be able to practice it on a smaller scale. We hope that the part dealing with the ordinary cultivation of vegetables will be of service to rural populations, for whom such cultivation can provide an appreciable supplement to their resources, almost at no cost. Our goal would be achieved, and our conscience satisfied, if we had been able to contribute to increasing the well-being of our fellow citizens, to the best of our ability, by adding a stone to the edifice on which so many generations have worked before us. J. CURÉ. XI ORDINARY AND FORCED CHAPTER ONE THE LAND Choice of land. - The ancient farmers whose work we have recalled recommended careful selection of suitable soil for vegetable growing, "especially," they said, "in the wettest part of the property". Today, thanks to our ability to obtain water in abundance almost anywhere, vegetable gardens can be set up in any desired location; nevertheless, it is preferable that the land be well exposed, that is, that it receive as little shade as possible, and that it be sufficiently far from buildings and tall trees. The more air the garden has, the better the vegetables will grow, and the less likely they will be to be eaten by all kinds of insects. Soil preparation. - When it comes to soil preparation, all specialists agree. The soil should be ploughed deeply with a spade, loosened up as much as possible, and all clods broken up. Then, the soil should be laid out in planks of varying dimensions, depending on the size of the farm; however, when using frames, the planks should be as wide as the frames themselves, and as long as the number of frames to be placed next to each other. Specialists who have many frames set up their squares for three frames, or a multiple of three, because chests are generally made to support three. However, chests are made for two or even one sash. The paths between the planks or rows of chassis should be no wider than Om, 30 to Om, 35, in order to use as much of the land as possible. When the paths have been laid out, the clods on the surface of the soil are broken up with a fork, and the remaining clods are raked into the path, so that the surface of the board is flat and the path is a little higher than the board, as it will always settle down from being trodden on; when the path is lower than the board, water from watering runs off it, to the detriment of the roots of the plants in the middle of the board. Parisian market-gardeners, who rent their land at a very high price, do away with every other path for open-ground cultivation, and thus combine into a single bed two rows 1.35 m wide, plus the path of Om.30. When frames are not used, the beds are set up in the width and length deemed appropriate. Depending on the layout of the property, the beds should be laid out in the direction that will give the best relief to the vegetable garden, but when chassis are used, we recommend that they be laid out preferably in a north-west to south-east direction, so that the early crops grown under them benefit as much as possible from the sun's rays over the entire surface of the chassis. Fertilizing. - For good vegetable growing, you need to give the soil plenty of fertilizer. The intensive cultivation practiced by market gardeners can only be carried out under this condition, but it should be added that all fertilizers are good. Growers in the Paris suburbs, who supply the capital with a large proportion of the large vegetables consumed there, almost all use gadoues from the big city to fertilize their land, and achieve excellent results with this fertilizer, which costs them very little. As Parisian market gardeners only grow early vegetables and salads, most of them only use compost, of which they have sufficient quantities at their disposal, as a result of the decomposition of the manure that makes up their beds. Before the Revolution, in the days of the master's office, the gardening jurors would visit the gardens to ensure that no slurry, or even pig manure, was being used as fertilizer for vegetables; a police decree prohibited such fertilizers, alleging that they could cause contagious diseases. Today, these prohibitions no longer exist. We believe that all fertilizers are good for growing large vegetables; slurry can only be discussed from the point of view of the unbearable odor it spreads when deposited too close to dwellings, but from a cultural point of view, its effectiveness cannot be disputed. As for the dangers of pig manure, this was a legend from the Middle Ages, which has completely disappeared, like so many others. So we say to people in the countryside who grow vegetables for their own consumption, and especially to women, who are responsible for the household chores of all working people: "Make a compost with sweepings from the house and yard, ashes, poultry droppings and garden detritus; water it with your household water, and you'll get a very good fertilizer. Mud from roads and paths, dry or green leaves and decomposing plants will make another no less excellent fertilizer. Dry matter buried for some time will also be very good. All this can be used in the vegetable garden as fertilizer, and will increase production. Everything is transformed, and nothing should be lost. Don't we see, around big cities, sewage water purifying itself in the soil and producing an admirable crop of vegetables? And it's certainly not these vegetables that cause disease. The agronomists who have dealt with chemical fertilizers have only given us a few fertilizer formulas for the large vegetables that belong to the field of agriculture; however, for some time now, this question has been under study for horticulture in general. Hopefully, scientists will be able to provide us with fertilizer formulas for specific plants, taking into account, as always, the elements contained in the soil in which they are grown. Armed with this information, practitioners will be able, as in agriculture, to give their soil the elements it lacks when they have only manure or composts at their disposal, and, more often than not, in insufficient quantities. The judicious use of chemical fertilizers for vegetable growing would be of immense benefit to people living far from major centers, who have neither sludge nor sewage at their disposal, and who pay too high a price for fertilizers. Crop rotation. - As in agriculture, crop rotation plays a certain role in vegetable growing. Specialists, who can hardly practice it, are astonished to see their crops fail after a certain number of years, despite the amount of fertilizer they give their land. This is precisely where we believe that chemical fertilizers will be of service to growers, by giving the soil the element that the same crop renewed over a certain period of time takes away from it, and which it does not find in sufficient quantity in manure. It has even been claimed that the root residues of plants always grown in the same soil "poison" that soil. This is a scientific question that belongs to the realm of horticultural chemistry, and one that we cannot deal with here; it will be part of the teaching of future generations, but routine has shown us that there is some truth in this saying. All amateur gardeners who grow a certain number of plants should therefore establish a rotation in their crops; where, for example, onions are grown one year, cabbages are planted the next. The same goes for other plants, varying crops as much as possible. If you have trays and are going to grow melons, you'll need to pass them through the entire vegetable garden one after the other; these plants rest the soil and fertilize it with the muted layer created for their cultivation. The following year's harvest from this soil will always be fruitful, whatever the vegetables. Melon is the alfalfa of horticulture. If there are layers in the establishment, the potting soil left over each year will be used to top up spring seedlings. Manure preparation. Layering - For a layer to heat up well and give even heat over its entire surface, it is very important that it is well "mounted". To make good layers, especially in autumn, when gentle heat is needed, and at the start of winter, when stronger, more persistent heat is required, it is useful to have, as far as possible, manure that has been piled up during the summer and has, so to speak, re-dried. To obtain well-dried manure, the heap is made very narrow and fairly high. Market gardeners even finish it off with a roof, just like the stacks of fodder and cereals that farmers put up in the fields. Horse manure in particular, placed in this way, does not rot or lose much of its caloric value, and when used in autumn and winter, once shaken, reworked and mixed with fresh manure from the cowshed, it produces the effect of charcoal mixed with embers, rekindling and giving the layer a slow, persistent warmth. 1. i.e. well made. These piles of manure, set aside during the summer by Parisian practitioners who use a lot of them, require certain precautions. If, for example, "soft" manures are mixed with "straw" manures, it often happens, in August or September, that the pile catches fire as a result of fermentation; the manure thus burns "à l'étouffée". But if combustion reaches a point in contact with the air, the manure ignites immediately. There isn't a year in which such accidents don't occur in the Paris suburbs, and to extinguish the fire, it's absolutely essential to remove all the manure, flooding it with water as you go along, because with each forkful removed, the flames flare up again. This is to demonstrate the amount of caloric energy contained in this dried-up manure. If only fresh manure is used to build layers in autumn or at the start of winter, it gives a shot of fire that tenderizes plants too much at the beginning of their growth, and cools down too quickly afterwards, especially if the winter is rainy or snowy. This is no longer the case for the layers formed at the end of February and in March; at this time of year, the ambient heat gradually replaces the heat in the layer, drying it out, and as the manure decomposes, the heat is renewed by the action of the sun. Even for these layers, particularly those established for early melon cultivation, it is necessary to water the layer copiously when it is set up, so that it does not dry out due to the effect of fermentation combined with the action of the sun. These layers, thus raised, give off a heat that sometimes reaches 70 or 80 degrees; in these conditions, you need to wait a week or so before sowing or planting. Practitioners call this "letting the layer fire". In addition to manure in general, and horse manure in particular, which is used to build up the beds, purely vegetable substances can also be used, with leaves at the top of the list, with the exception, according to some authors, of Plane tree leaves, which undergo little fermentation, are very slow to decompose, and produce only dry, tough compost of no cultivation value. When we want to build up layers with leaves, we need to collect them as soon as they fall, in healthy weather, as much as possible, so that they retain the maximum of their fermentative properties. They are placed in strong, tightly packed, domed millstones, to prevent water from penetrating; in a way, they replace dry manure when none is available. In horticulture, as in agriculture, you have to take advantage of everything. You can also use moss, collected in dry weather, in autumn. However, we always recommend mixing fresh manure with mosses or leaves, as this provides the "embers" to rekindle the other fermentable materials. Laying out the beds - First of all, we need to know where to lay out the beds. To establish early crops, you need good exposure to the sun, and no shade at all if possible. When creating a vegetable garden for this purpose, the rows of frames should be oriented, as far as possible, in a south-east to north-west direction. We prefer this direction to that of I. north to noon, or east to west, to cut off strong winds when giving air and to let the sun shine on the whole surface of the frame for as long as possible. Layers should also be placed in a well-ventilated area, to avoid sunburn when spring arrives. The sheltered locations will be used to establish the first outdoor crops following those in the layers. To avoid labor costs, the beds should be set up in the most suitable location, as close as possible to where the deposits of manure, leaves or moss are to be used to build them up. Layering. - When starting to build up a square of layers, first prepare the place where the first layer will be placed; mark out on the ground, with stakes, the area it will occupy; establish a line or "chain" of dry manure, leaves or moss, depending on what you have available, and, next to or above it, another line of fresh manure. The layer is then built up by superimposing a bed of one and a bed of the other, but never horizontally, so that the layer is well bonded and forms, so to speak, a single block. To do this, create a gauge so that the bottom of the layer is always further forward than the top, so that the manure beds are placed at an angle throughout its thickness. The manure must be stirred well, so that no more or less compact "cakes" remain; the dung must be evenly distributed throughout the surface of the layer, so that the heat rises evenly throughout. Parisian market gardeners make their layers 1m.65 wide, i.e. 1m.35 for the frame or the three rows of bells that will be placed on top, and Om, 30 for the path; but amateurs can give the path up to Om, 60, since it takes a lot of practice to work in narrow paths. The length is calculated according to the number of frames or bells to be placed on it. Practitioners generally make squares of fifteen frames per line. The thickness of the layer will vary according to the season and the crop to be grown. The thickest layers are generally made in December and January. For this thickness, which is difficult to specify, it is necessary to adjust to the quality of the materials used. For example, a layer made only with good horse manure, both dry and fresh, may give more heat, being half as thick, as another layer made with leaves and fresh straw manure. Even so, we can give some approximate indications based on good horse manure, taking into account the different crops we'll be growing and the season we'll be working in. The layers to be made in October for growing lettuces should be no more than om, 20 thick, with at least two-thirds dry manure, especially if the soil is wet. At this time of year, these plants don't need much heat; they need to be dried out, and as these layers are always turned over, the manure continues to decompose when it is turned over again. In November, the thickness of the layer should already be increased, with both dry and fresh manure. From December 1st onwards, the layers used to plant lettuces and sow the first carrots should be the thickest of the year; when good manure is available, they can be as thick as Om,30 or Om,35; a higher proportion of fresh manure is needed, and to prevent them from drying out at this thickness, given the heat they give off, it is useful for the dry manure to be brought in eight or fifteen days in advance, to be loosened, so that it can moisten a little before the layer is put up. The same applies to unturned cloche beds, because in the cultivation of Carrots and Romaines, if the bed dries out again, you won't get good produce. As the sun gets stronger, the thickness of the layers is reduced. When a layer has been built up as described above, it is "stomped" so that it has the same consistency throughout, then levelled by adding manure to the weakest parts to make it absolutely flat. Water if the manure is still too dry. If it's a stretcher bed, we immediately place the boxes on top, lining them up with a chalk line, then load the bed. In autumn, it's best to load with potting soil if available; during winter, especially in February, you can load with soil. Some plants, such as Turnips and Melons, even prefer soil to compost. The thickness of the soil or potting mix also varies with the different crops grown on the bed. Thus, in autumn and even later, when growing Lettuce alone, a thickness of Om, 20 is sufficient; when growing Carrots, Turnips or Romaines, it should be increased to at least Om, 30. Generally speaking, when a layer of lettuce is turned over in autumn or winter, 1. to reconstitute a layer of carrot or a layer of Romaine, soil is brought in and mixed with the compost to give the desired thickness. This is a very good procedure, especially if the soil is not too clayey and crumbles well. When it comes to building up the square of layers, here's how it's done. Beforehand, the soil is lifted in "chains", i.e. by long millstones, across the square. Experience soon shows how much potting soil is needed. For a layer width occupied by three panels, the chain should be 1 metre wide at the base and should be shaped like a roof so that water slides over it without penetrating it, thus allowing the compost to dry out if it gets too wet. In addition, in winter, the entire surface of the soil on which the layers will be placed is covered with dry manure, to prevent frost from penetrating the soil. The soil in place of the second layer is used to load the first, and so on. The pathway between the rows of trunks remains empty, and as the layer cools, it is filled as much as possible with dry manure. As the layer cools down, it is filled as much as possible with dry manure. This manure, thanks to the heat of the layer and the draining of the frames it receives, gradually moistens and heats up, so that it serves as a stove for the layer itself. The first layer of the square should be Om, 30 wider than the others, to form the acot; along the length, om, 30 is also reserved at each end of the square to form the acots. These are built up in manure to the height of the frames, so that the whole square of layers is surrounded by these acots; under these conditions, the frames at the ends of the square heat up as much as those in the middle; this is an important point, especially for practitioners, who remove all the plants at once. To make bell layers, we'll start with the procedure used by the old market gardeners, when they abandoned the folding layers (La Quintinie system). The layer loaded with a good thickness of compost, even mixed with soil, was edged on each side and at the ends with a piece of board, fitted with a handle, called a "bordoir", so that the thickness of the compost was equal everywhere, and then adjusted with a fork. The path, which remained clear exactly as if there had been chests, had to be filled with manure, progressively as in the stretcher beds, and whenever the need arose. Whenever a path had to be reloaded, it had to be done with manure only, so that the intense heat of the layers was not intercepted. We've known market gardeners, the grandsons of the old masters of the 17th century, who proceeded in this way and attached exaggerated importance to ensuring that there was not the slightest trace of soil in the path. It has always seemed to us that this was nothing more than a sense of self-esteem, going back to the traditions of the old masters and handed down to them by their fathers. Today's market gardeners, when they make a square of cloche layers, fill the entire surface with potting soil. Then they adjust the layers, rake the clods into the path, exactly as they would on a square of soil, then sow, if necessary, and cloche afterwards. Provided the layer is sufficient, the plants placed on it do just as well as with the old method, but as the path always deepens a little as you walk on it, it should be kept full of dry manure, for the reasons we'll explain when we talk about growing Romaine in layers in March. Melon beds. - Market gardeners call them "trenches", because only a more or less narrow part of the soil is dug to make them. First-season trenches are as wide as the trunk, and only the pathway is not dug; this is where the melons are most likely to seek their nourishment when they become strong. Practitioners can see when the roots of the plants reach the pathway; the vegetation immediately becomes more luxuriant. As the weather gets warmer, the width of the trenches is reduced, so that the last ones, made around May 20, are barely Om 30 to Om 35 wide by Om 20 to Om 25 thick. At this time of year, some varieties of melon can be grown almost without a bed; but in cold soils, it is always preferable to make a small one, to make it easier for the plants to take root. This is a matter of judgement on the part of the grower, depending on the weather, the climate and the nature of the soil. The amount of soil to be placed on these layers should not exceed Om, 10 to Om, 12 in thickness. The roots of these plants run almost level with the ground in the mulch itself and, as we have already said, seek their nourishment in the surrounding soil; nevertheless, for their growth to be rapid, it is necessary that this soil be kept sufficiently warm, otherwise the plants will yellow and perish. When you have a square of these layers to make, here's how you proceed. Open the first trench, and transport the soil to the other end of the square, i.e. where you will finish. Once the first layer has been established, the second trench is opened to load the first layer with soil, and so on. Layer moisture. - We have said that the thickness of the layer and the amount of potting soil or loam should vary according to the crops to be planted. The same applies to the degree of humidity. For example: the first layers, made in October, are Om, 20 thick, as much as possible in dry manure, since at this time there is always enough natural humidity to wet them, especially given their thinness. As winter progresses, the thickness of the layers is increased. The thickest layers are applied from November to January 15. For layers where Carrots or Turnips are to be sown, as well as for layers with Romaine bells, the manure should always be unctuous and in full decomposition; if it were to dry out again, we wouldn't get a good result from the point of view of the beauty of the produce. The amount of potting soil also varies with the crop. When only Lettuce is to be planted, om, 20 thickness is sufficient. For Carrots, Turnips and Romaine bell layers, at least Om,30 is required. Changing layers. - Some specialists today change their square of layers every two or three years; this is a method we also recommend to amateurs who don't always work at the earliest possible hour. Here's how it's done: about half the amount of potting soil needed for the new layers is transported and mixed with soil taken from the new site, which has been ploughed and raised in a "chain". Another part of the soil remaining from the previous year's layers is used to top up the vegetable garden crops, and the surplus is buried on site. In this way, you have a well-amended and rested soil, on which you can grow any crop under the most advantageous conditions. This soil, impregnated with the manure juice deposited in previous years, is more fertile than any other fertilizer. Manner of turning over the layers. - In professional terms, "turning over a layer" is the work that consists in reworking the entire layer and adding fresh manure to reconstitute it once again, so that new crops can be sown and planted. Among Parisian practitioners, layers are turned, in some cases, up to three times. Here's how it's done: we remove the frames and trunks that are placed on the first layer, we remove the soil that fills it and we transfer it to the other end of the square, as was said for the "trenches" at Melons, so that only the manure that makes up the layer remains. This manure is pulled up with a fork, starting from the side where the fork ended. The manure thus pulled up across the entire width of the layer is placed back in a "chain", and care is taken to mix the manure on the path with that in the middle, since the former is always wetter than the latter. Once the chain of old manure has been built up, a chain of fresh manure is brought in and placed on top of the first, and the layer is reassembled in the same way as the first. The second row of frames is also removed, and its trunks are placed back on the first, which is loaded with the compost from the second, and so on. It's preferable to build the square of layers in full, rather than with masonry tarpaulins, as manure ferments better in contact with the air than when its action is not felt. It's also better to establish it on the surface of the ground than to bury it deeply, as was the practice in the past, especially in clay soils where water runs off with difficulty. In this case, during wet winters, the bed is submerged and this removes a lot of heat, which is detrimental to plant growth. Once the vegetable garden has been set up, as we've just explained, it needs to be seeded. If you sow seeds of degenerate plants, or of varieties that don't like the environment in which they're placed, no matter how well you grow them, you'll never get anything but poor results. This observation applies particularly to the forced cultivation of vegetables, because for this type of cultivation it is not enough to have healthy seeds taken from vigorous plants; it is also necessary to choose certain varieties that lend themselves better than others to forced cultivation. All growers' efforts must therefore be directed towards obtaining well-selected varieties; they must seek out those best suited to the soil they cultivate and the climate in which they find themselves. One variety of plant will grow vigorously in a given soil, while in another it will vegetate with great difficulty. Parisian market gardeners - we say this to their credit, because it's a point recognized by all specialists, and even by seed merchants - achieve perfection in the selection of the plants they grow. To achieve this result, it is first necessary to have a good knowledge of the type of plant being cultivated, in order to choose seed-bearing plants in such a way as to maintain the variety being harvested in its primitive type, or to make it more or less early, to "shrink" or "enlarge" it, to "tenderize" or "harden" it. Onions. - To select Onion seedbeds, a small square of Onions is left to ripen, and when they are fully ripe, they are pulled out and the best chosen as seedbeds. If you want to keep the variety as it is, you'll take as types the smallest Onions, which ripen first, along with medium-sized and larger ones, which ripen last. If you want to make the variety earlier, take only the first to ripen, which are also the smallest. If you want to make the variety fatter, take only the largest and last to ripen, but they will come later. When fully ripe, these onions are placed in a healthy location for winter storage, and replanted in spring. They then go to seed as soon as they grow, and the result is a much purer seed than that which would be harvested from onions that go to seed in the first year. Onion seed retains its germinative capacity for three or four years, but it is preferable to always sow the seed that is harvested the year before sowing. Cabbage. - To maintain or modify varieties, cabbage seedbeds should be chosen according to the same principles as for Onion, except for Cauliflower, whose seed should be harvested from plants that "go up" in the first year, i.e. whose stems elongate, flower and produce seed. Cabbages in general are surprisingly easy to produce, which is why the old-timers used to say: "Sow cabbages, and there will be Raves; sow Raves, and there will be Cabbages". When you've chosen your types, as we've said for the Onion, and the apple is ready to burst, you cut it crosswise as low as possible; you remove the hard leaves that remain around the core, and the eyelets immediately start growing again (the ancients used to say that the plant "rejected"); so that in autumn, for spring-grown varieties, four or five small apples as big as a fist have sometimes grown back. During the summer, we pull up the cabbages to gather them all together in the same spot, so as to better protect them from frost during the winter, and keep them away from other cabbage varieties, cauliflowers, kohlrabi, Brussels sprouts and rutabagas, which, coming into flower at the same time, could, through the influence of their pollen carried by the wind or insects, cause them to degenerate. When seed cabbages flower and the pods begin to form, they must be protected, by syringing with nicotined water, from the white aphid which sometimes comes in such abundance that it destroys everything! Cabbage seeds harvested when fully ripe have a germination period of seven or eight years, but it is always preferable not to wait until this extreme period before harvesting new ones, as the 1. see the chapter on vegetable plant diseases for care instructions. young seed is always more vigorous. For cabbages to be sown in autumn, if the seed harvested the same year is used, sow a few days later, so that the young plants do not go to seed before peeling. Cauliflower. - Cauliflowers are harvested in the same year from the "flower" of the plant itself, which will go to seed if left to grow. The same care is taken when choosing seed-bearing plants as for onions; by choosing the first ones to "take" the apple, we "tenderize" them; by choosing the last ones, we obtain the opposite result. Turnips and carrots should also be harvested from seedbeds that ripened the previous autumn and were replanted in spring, as we said for Onions, and with the same care. Radishes are treated in the same way; only, this plant grows so fast, that when sown at the end of winter, they have time to reach the normal size at which they are eaten, and can then be selected with the same art as the previous plants, and planted in beds. In this way, they produce their seeds in the same year. All these seeds germinate over several years. Sorrel, too, must be carefully selected if it is to remain beautiful and not revert to its primitive state. In autumn, the best clumps in the square are selected, pulled out and replanted together, and the following summer, the seed is harvested from this selection. Celery is also harvested from plants that have reached maturity in autumn, are kept over winter and go to seed the following spring. New varieties are obtained through long and careful selection. It takes perseverance to select from year to year to establish the variety you want. All cultivated plants have a tendency to revert to their primitive state. Celery seeds have a germination period of eight to ten years. Salad seeds require no more care than a good choice of rootstock. The plants remain in place to continue their development, and when the seed is ripe, it is harvested. For Lettuce and Romaine seeds, market gardeners harvest only for their own use, pinching the seed when it's ready to drop. Curly endive and Scarole are left to dry out. Then they are pulled up, placed in a dry place and beaten for harvesting. It's good to know that the longer these seeds remain attached to the plant that produced them, the longer they germinate. As the seeds age to a certain point, they still free the plant, but grow less vigorously than the young ones. For a good crop, therefore, it's best not to use seeds from the same year, but from the previous year. These various salad seeds have a germination period of several years, depending on the care taken in harvesting them; the same applies to all seeds. For leeks, nothing is easier than harvesting good seed, since planting them in May means they can be left until the following May, when they set seed. It can be made shorter or longer by choosing shorter or longer seedbeds. The seed has roughly the same germinative capacity as that of the Onion. Cardoons can be stored over winter, but they must not be allowed to soften with too much covering. Just keep them from freezing. They go to seed in spring. Here's how market gardeners harvest this seed. They cut the cardoon in autumn above ground level; in spring, the heart develops and goes to seed. Treated in this way, the same Cardoon plant can produce seeds for a number of years. Garlic and shallot can also be harvested for seed, but this care is unnecessary. In fact, planting bulbs of these plants in spring produces seeds much more quickly than sowing them. The same applies to Tarragon and Civet. Once you've got one plant, you'll have more the following year, as these plants sucker very easily. The same can be said of Artichoke. This plant suckers very quickly, and all the eyelets that are detached from the mother plant and replanted in spring already yield heads by the end of summer. For all Cucurbitaceae: Melons, Cucumbers, Gherkins, Pumpkins, Squash, etc., it's simply a matter of choosing the most beautiful types of fruit and extracting the seed when they are ripe. As with many other vegetables, the soil in which they are grown has a major influence on the quality of the product. A certain variety of melon, grown in a certain soil, sometimes resembles the same variety grown in another soil only in special respects, known only to practitioners. Tomatoes and eggplants also carry their seeds inside the fruit; you only need to let them ripen properly to extract the seed, which is then dried and put into bags. These plants, especially the first, come in a number of varieties obtained by hybridization and selection. Thus we have the Currant Tomato, the Cherry Tomato, the Apple Tomato, the Pear Tomato and so on. But these varieties are only good for amateurs, more for their originality than for their usefulness. However, these varieties have given rise to new ones. The Cherry Tomato, for example, has grown in size from year to year, thanks to selection. Today, it's a beautiful tomato that has taken its place in everyday trade. We won't mention potatoes. While everyone knows how to reproduce them, only specialists, or a few amateurs, sow seedlings to obtain new varieties. But the number of these varieties is already so great, and the difference between one variety and another often so insignificant, that little attention is paid to them. If chance itself can produce new varieties that are sometimes good, all the more reason to hope for better ones when hybridization is prepared by competent men. By hybridization, or by the selection of seed-bearing plants, specialists have also succeeded in establishing a number of distinct varieties of Beans and Peas. As for the selection of Asparagus plants, we'll have the opportunity to describe this in detail in the January issue. This presentation has made it clear to the reader that 3 specialists do not generally collect their seeds from plants that go to seed in the first year. Exceptions to this rule are the seeds of most lettuces: Lettuce, Romaine, Chicory and Scarolea; those of Cauliflower and Cucurbitaceae: Melons, Cucumbers, Pumpkins, etc. All these seeds are harvested in such a way as to better fix the cultivated varieties. Even so, all these plants can differ enormously depending on the soil in which they are grown. Experience has shown us, through seeds we have harvested ourselves, the great difference there can sometimes be between plants grown in one soil and those grown in another. If we hadn't done the selection and harvesting ourselves, we'd have doubted whether all the seeds came from the same plant. It's true that in cultivation, nothing is absolute or well-defined; as many soils, as many different cases; nevertheless, if the variety grows more or less vigorously, becoming in some soils twice as voluminous as in others, it nonetheless retains its other distinctive characteristics. Glazed frames. - Frames can be of any size; those used by market gardeners in Paris are 1.30 m wide by 1.35 m high; this is a measurement established by tacit agreement between manufacturers, since they have been making this equipment; for private individuals, the size is less important, but a suitable one must be adopted, in order to be able to establish any kind of cultivation. Frames can be made entirely of wood, preferably oak, which is less sensitive to humidity than white wood; however, some manufacturers build them in pitchpin, which isn't bad either, or even in ordinary fir, but these frames don't last as long as their predecessors. Hobbyists can use the cheapest wood they can find, or build their own, if they find it to their advantage. Parisian market gardeners, who use at least a million frames, prefer models with an oak frame, except for the bottom, which must be made of iron, as it is much more prone to deterioration, receiving all the water that runs off the frame. The rods supporting the glass are made of iron, which is more solid and shades the plants underneath less than wooden slats, which are naturally wider. In Paris, horticulture generally uses frames with four rows of glass panes, and glass of the appropriate dimensions is commercially available, known as "frame glass"; but for amateurs this is less important than for specialists. Glazing starts at the top. The second pane crosses the first by a centimetre, and so on with the others. Each 1.35 m row of glass comprises three panes, plus a half-tile at the bottom, called the "base"; this is the one most likely to break, since it has nothing to guarantee it, bearing directly on the wooden or iron frame. Once the panes have been installed, they are puttied in exactly the same way as domestic windows. Before glazing, if the frame is made of wood, it will have been given a coat of paint, or, if it's iron, a coat of minium. Once the putty has been applied, a second coat of paint must be applied, even over the putty, to ensure its preservation and facilitate water drainage. Specialists paint their frames every year, preferably in a grayish-white, as this equipment is used for certain crops, such as melons, until June. If they were painted black, they would over-concentrate the sun's rays, which could harden or burn the plants. As we know, white has the property of reflecting heat. The industry also supplies double frames, forming a two-slope tarpaulin, which can often be very useful; however, they are rarely used by Parisian specialists, because they are more difficult to move and the work that needs to be done underneath them is less practical. This system is perhaps not to be despised by amateurs; it's a question of appreciation. Cof̂fres. - Chests that support vegetable growing frames are usually built to support three frames; they must be portable, CE Fig. 1. - Mobile chest. as they frequently have to be changed places; it is therefore necessary that they are not too heavy. They are most often made: the boards, in fir (those behind are generally Om, 25 wide and those in front Om, 22), and the heads or ends in oak, Om, 18 wide for the end of the squares, and half in the interior, so as not to make holes in the crops. These chests have bars between each frame to support them. These bars come in a variety of designs. The simplest are made of wood, from Om,05 to 0m,06 thick and of the same width, with a dovetail that fits into a notch cut in the boards; this is the old system used by Pari2.° sian market gardeners. Others, also made of wood and of the same size, have iron hooks adapted to the board, either above or below, by means of three screws. The latter are more solid. In this system, the iron fitted underneath must be brought up to the end of the bar at right angles through its entire thickness, to then form the hook. But the best of all, which are widely used now that iron is cheap, are made of T-iron, bent at each end to form the hook, and the T-iron underneath bent close to the board inside the box to form a stop point. Boxes are either nailed or sliding. The former are still the best choice for growers who don't use them very much; those known as "sliding" are preferred by large specialists, because they are easier to store. In slide-in boxes, instead of the boards being nailed in after the feet adjoining the heads (as all systems must have feet nailed in after the heads), they are fixed in place by means of two pegs passing through the boards in a notch made for this purpose. At the end of the pegs, there's a hole through which an iron rod is passed, holding the board tightly against the head, at just the same height as the head, so that there's no gap between the box and the frame. The legs of the trunks should, as far as possible, be made of oak and be about Om,10 to Om, 12 thick and Om, 30 to Om, 35 long; those behind the frames or at the top should always be a little longer than those in front, to facilitate the slope and drain of the frame. Two wooden cleats are nailed into the bottom plank on the outside, extending beyond the trunk by the thickness of the sash, so that when the sash is raised even to its greatest height, it is stopped and does not risk sliding down the path. Today's specialists use iron cleats that hook onto the board, in a small notch of their thickness, so that there is no air between the chassis and the trunk. The best box, from our point of view, is the so-called sliding box: the back and front boards are made of fir, the first being Om,25 wide and the second om,22; the heads are made of oak, those at the ends of the squares being Om,18 wide and those in the middle half as wide, the feet also made of oak, the bars of iron in one piece, and the cleats in the same way. Doormats. - For a very long time, even before they had frames and bells, Parisian market gardeners had been using doormats. In the smallest vegetable garden, it is useful to have a few of these, either to protect plants from spring and autumn frosts, or to make it easier for certain plants to recover during hot spells, and so on. We therefore believe it is useful to indicate how to make them, as all gardeners need to know how to make their own doormats. Parisian market gardeners, having, as we said, uniform equipment, make them all the same size, 1.35 m wide by 2 m long. They have a frame or "loom" of this size, bearing on each of its long sides three pegs or nails, one in the middle and one on each side, at equal distance; a rope is tied to each of these nails by one end, and, by means of a slip knot made at the other end, it is stretched as tightly as possible, leaving a hanging end which will be knotted, as we shall see later. Rye straw is then laid over these ropes, half thick on one side and half thick on the other, so that the straw mat has an even thickness throughout; the quantity needed is about 5 kilogr. of straw per straw mat, but they can be made thicker or thinner, depending on the crops to be secured. If you make them thicker, as their weight requires greater solidity, you'll need to sew four rows instead of three on the dimensions we've indicated. Once the doormat has been stretched, all that's left to do is sew it in place. To do this, wind string around a small piece of wood or spool, Om.15 long, hollowed out in the middle and forming a head at each end; tie the end of this string with the one used to make the slipknot to tighten the mat. With one hand, you hold this spool; with the other hand, you grasp a pinch of straw, and pass the string over and then under the stretched string; at this point, the thumb of the hand holding the straw grasps the string and passes the spool back underneath to form a mesh, or knot, in which the pinch of straw is caught. All that's left to do is pull on the spool to tighten the mesh, while the thumb of the other hand flattens it strongly. Continue in this way to the end of the frame, and tie the last stitch tightly with the stretched string, so that the mat doesn't become unstuck. Stitches should be no more than Om.02 wide, and care should be taken to flatten them with the thumb, if you want a strong, well-built doormat. Always start sewing with the middle row; this way, if the doormat is not evenly stretched, you can even it out as you sew. As the stitches are all the same, the thickness is necessarily the same everywhere. It's the hand that takes the pinch of straw that establishes this regularity; straw is added or removed from one side or the other, as required.
