Once the first row has been sewn, take care to pull the straw underneath so that it is as straight as on top; simply pass your hand through it from place to place to smooth it out. The finished straw mat is unhooked from the side on which the slip knots were made; the other end is then untied and tied firmly with the end of the string used to sew it; finally, the protruding ears are cut off with shears. The result is a clean, solid, even mat. Specialists who use a lot of doormats soak them in a copper sulfate bath to prolong their shelf life. To do this, they set up a wooden or cement basin into which they pour 3 or 4 kilogr. of copper sulfate per hectoliter of water, and soak a certain number of doormats at a time, depending on the size of the basin. Leave them in the bath for a while, so that the straw and twine are well impregnated, then let them dry. Many amateur vegetable gardeners buy their straw mats ready-made and even sulfated, and it's easier when you don't use large quantities. Nevertheless, it is useful for gardeners to know how to make their own doormats, and this is taught at the École nationale d'horticulture de Versailles. Garden bells. - This equipment, so widely used today by Parisian market gardeners, has hardly been known in our country until La Quintinie, who brought together in the King's kitchen garden at Versailles all the improvements made at that time in the art of gardening. However, Olivier de Serres, who lived in Montpellier, spoke of it a century earlier. Glass bells came to us from Italy, where the glass industry had made more rapid progress than in France. Before this material was known, the gardens of the great were equipped with verrines, a kind of tiny greenhouse, mounted in iron with small glass panes, which had the disadvantage of being very expensive. The first bells, as depicted by Olivier de Serres, and even up to the beginning of the 19th century, were made of leaded glass, and were very small in size; this author says they were a foot in diameter and a foot high. We have had occasion to see some dating from the end of the eighteenth century, which were more or less the same. At the beginning of the 19th century, around 1820, Parisian market gardeners began growing Romaine under cloches, and were led to enlarge them in width and height. There was also an improvement in the manufacture of glass; at first, cloches were made of clear glass; they were very hot, as the top cap of the cloche, being quite thick, made the glass magnifying. There were also bells with a handle at the top; this model was good for amateurs, but impractical for specialists. Experience has shown that a further refinement in glass manufacture is required, by giving it a slight blue tint and reducing the thickness of the bonnet. Today, the best garden bells are those made in Lorraine; they must be Om, 41 to Om, 42 in diameter and Om, 35 to om, 36 in height; their weight is two and a half kilograms. These are the first choice for establishing all the crops usually grown under cloche. Bought in bulk, by the hundred, they cost O fr. 85 to 0 fr. 90 each. This material is very fragile, as you might expect, and requires a great deal of care. To transport them, practitioners place them in packs of three; they are first placed on their side, and a finger is passed Fig. 2. - Cloche maraîchère. between the bells, so that they don't squeeze, otherwise they burst immediately. For some time now, we've been making bell-holders: a frame with a small platform on each side, on which we place two packs of bells placed as described above. In this way, the workman can carry four packs, which is just about enough for the strength of one man. Boards fitted with bells for cultivation generally contain three rows of bells; this is the usual width of market-garden frames. They should be placed in a chessboard pattern, not touching each other; to facilitate work and avoid breakage, there should be, on average, a centimetre and a half of space between them in all directions. In the past, gardeners used to put straw between their bells when storing them. This method has been abandoned, however, as it has a serious drawback: if the straw gets wet, it causes the bells to burst. Nowadays, the procedure is as follows: the bells are placed upright on solid ground; if necessary, straw is spread underneath, or dry manure, which is even better, as no grass grows. A small wooden wedge is placed on the bonnet of the bell, so that the second one doesn't squeeze the first, and so on; up to ten are placed per pack. For inexperienced workers, it's a good idea to make sure that the bells turn on the wedges, which indicates that the one just placed is not squeezing the previous one; specialists can tell immediately, just by placing the bell on the wedge, whether there's a danger of breakage. The bundles are arranged in rows, in a checkerboard pattern, exactly as for cultivation, and to protect them from hail, large straw is spread over the top and sides, or old straw mats when available. In winter, when changing crops, avoid leaving cloches in bundles on their sides, because if you're surprised by frost, you can be sure that when the thaw comes, any that touch the ground will come unstuck in that place, especially if there's a little water inside. Despite the fragility of this material, Parisian market gardeners, who use large quantities, handle it with great dexterity. The bells need to be washed inside every year. This operation is generally carried out in November, when there is no longer any fear that the sun's rays will 1. the number of cloches used by these specialists can be estimated at five or six million. cause the young plants underneath to wither. Here's how it's done: take a handful of rye straw, cut to the height of the bells, and bind it down the middle, so that the two ends form a broom: grasp the bell with one hand by the side, dip it in a tub of water, and with the other hand rub it internally with the straw, turning it as you go, guided by the hand holding it. When it's thoroughly cleaned, it's quickly swirled in water to rinse, and when it's removed it's as clean as new. The exterior is always sufficiently washed by the rains and humidity of winter; however, when bells have been bleached to soften the sun's rays, if too much fat has been put on with the Spanish white and it is still partially adhering at the time of washing, it must be removed by hand, since in winter nothing must be left to obstruct the sun's rays. This is another job that market gardeners do with a speed that is astonishing to the layman. In the old days, when labor was cheaper, market gardeners used to mend their bells. It's still done when they're only cracked, but you don't waste much time bringing back the pieces. But here's how it's done. You spread ceruse on the broken part, and glue the detached piece back onto the bell; then you take small pieces of round or square glass, cut for the purpose; you coat them with ceruse on one side, and place them on the Om joint, 05 roughly side by side. Once this operation has been completed, the bell is placed in a dry place, and two or three months later, when the ceruse is completely dry, it becomes as solid as before; more often than not, it's the commodity bells that last the longest, because they're handled more carefully than the others. When you break a bell with your hands, it's rare not to cut yourself; that's reason enough for the worker to take all the necessary precautions. Watering equipment. - To grow vegetables in a small garden, for the personal use of the person who enjoys it, the tools are quite rudimentary: a spade, a rake, an iron fork and watering cans are all you need. If necessary, a wheelbarrow can be used to bring in fertilizer or transport the soil. The most important condition for this type of cultivation is to have water available, either by occupying a marshy spot where the soil is cool enough not to need watering, or by locating near a stream from which water can be drawn. In other circumstances, you need a well to draw the water you need. If you don't have water at your disposal, vegetable growing in the strict sense loses its title and becomes nothing more than field cultivation, the results of which are subject to the fluctuations of the weather. In vegetable gardens that are better constituted and larger than ordinary small gardens, it is necessary to have, from place to place, barrels or basins where the water arrives via underground pipes. In large houses, schools and specialist establishments, the water is raised to a certain height by means of a hydraulic ram or pump of some kind, in order to obtain enough pressure for watering by means of a jet. With this system, taps are placed in the vegetable garden, at equal distances from each other; these taps must be fitted with a screw thread, onto which the rubber hose used for watering fits. This hose has a copper elbow at its end, fitted with a nut to tighten the tap screw, and a nozzle with a jet-breaker, or a watering can head, so that watering can be carried out as required. To avoid damaging the plants with this hose, it is made to follow the paths. To do this, an iron rod is pricked into the ground at the edge of the path. This rod is surrounded by a wooden or metal roller, which greatly assists the operator in guiding the hose. On the trail, between two planks, he must water one on his way to the site, and the other on his way back. The rubber hose must be flexible enough to bend across the width of the path without cutting off the water; moreover, if the pressure is strong enough, it forces the hose to round out. As for the means of raising the water, they are as numerous as they are varied. In the Revue horticole of 1899 and 1900, Mr. Ringelmann reviewed a large number of them. Their use naturally depends on the location and size of the farm. The last type of watering we have just mentioned is used only by specialists and in large houses. However, where the water is not too deep, or around towns where you have water at home, those with a small pleasure garden and vegetable patch can raise it and water using this system, which is rather entertaining than tiring. With a small, lightweight hose, a woman or child can do the job. On larger estates, a horse, a mule or, even easier nowadays, a petroleum engine with the necessary power, move a pump to raise the water to the desired height. The latter device can be used anywhere and operated by anyone, after a few lessons from the fitter. For the pressure watering system, we use a rubber hose that must be very flexible, from Om, 30 to Om, 35 in diameter and of the length required to reach all parts of the vegetable garden. Hobbyists can have much smaller ones, to make them easier to handle. We've already said that to water with this hose, you need to have wooden, or preferably copper, rollers in an iron rod pricked into the ground at the corner of the path where you're watering. Some of these are double, i.e. two iron rods, connected by a third transverse one, which is flush with the ground when the first two are driven in, and also fitted with a roller, like the previous ones. The rubber hose passed through this device, whether pulled from one side or the other, cannot damage plants at the corners of the boards. In the case of small amateur hoses, which are not very heavy to drive, a piece of wood stuck to the corner of the board is enough to prevent the hose from damaging the crop. To keep the rubber hose in good condition when not in use, it must be carefully rolled up so that it does not bend. For this purpose, market gardeners have a sort of small winch, Om.50 in diameter by as long. Spades. - Industry now supplies spades that are much lighter and better made than those used in the past, and a well-made spade is lighter and penetrates the soil better; the worker who uses it Fig. 3. - French flat spade. struggles less and produces more and better work than with those used by our ancestors. American forks and rakes are used everywhere, and everyone recognizes their superiority over the old tools, especially for their lightness. We leave the choice of tools to the specialists, who generally know them well, and amateurs will soon be able to appreciate their qualities or defects by using them. Hoods. - The "hottereau" and the hood are preferable to the wheelbarrow in small vegetable gardens; it's easier to get into the squares and especially where there are layers, since manure constantly has to be carried to fill the paths. Equipped with one of these utensils, the gardener can, with a certain amount of care, deposit the manure in small heaps on the frames or bells, so that all that's left to do is to spread it, by hand rather than with a fork, in this fragile material. Loader. - This is a tripod fitted with two horns, or a piece of curved iron, at the height needed to place the hottereau, without having to stand or stoop. Today's industry supplies well-built, not too heavy and, above all, solid iron ones. In large establishments and schools, Decauville narrow-gauge and portable railroads are increasingly replacing these small accessories. Nevertheless, apart from heavy-duty work, the "hottereau" will still be needed for a long time to come, especially in diaper beds. This is the utensil most often used by Parisian market gardeners to transport their manure, potting soil and vegetables. To collect certain vegetables, such as lettuce, chicory, escarole, radish, spinach, lamb's lettuce, etc., and transport them to Les Halles for sale, they generally use mannes of various sizes; the manne is a round, slightly flared basket; the largest are Om, 80 high, Om, 60 wide at the top and Om, 40 at the bottom. Baskets and baskets. - In other countries, baskets of different shapes are used; those used by gardeners in Dijon, our native France, are called "benatons"; they also come in all sizes. These utensils are also used by winegrowers to collect their harvests; like mannes, they are easy to stack when empty. Square packing baskets would be more convenient than all these utensils for loading and transporting the produce of Parisian market gardeners, but they would have to be splayed to enable them to be stacked like the previous ones, given that once the sale is over, in the morning at the halles, they have to be put away until the next day, and this storage would be very expensive if they were not stacked; the same goes for taking them home. The worker who drives the car usually brings back some manure, to avoid having to make another trip during the day, which is getting longer and longer, given the remoteness of the capital's market-gardening establishments. However, there's no doubt that this is the type of basket that will be used in the future, when the market gardeners are even further away. They will just have to be built in such a way as to fit one inside the other. Various utensils. - Parisian market gardeners also use other utensils: the turnip-planting frame, which we'll describe later, and the bell holder. They also use stretchers to transport the frames, and many have wheelbarrows to bring vegetables in from the marsh to the shed. In the past, there were handles, trays, calais, maniveaux etc.; all these small basketry utensils are disappearing day by day, as the trade changes its habits, awaiting the moment when almost everything will be sold by weight, according to the quality of the products. Rack and pinion wedges. - The rack is used to give air to the frames: it must be well-conditioned for this purpose, as its very shape indicates the progression of the air to be given to the plants under the frames and on the layers. If you don't give enough air, the plant "wilts", remains too tender and produces nothing good; on the contrary, if you give too much all at once, or in too many stages, it wilts, hardens and still produces nothing good. It is therefore in the making of the rack, as we shall describe, that we will find the progression of air that we must give to the plants, taking into account, at all times, the temperature, the state of the plant, etc. The rack is a simple piece of oak, Om,05 thick by Om,10 wide and Om,25 long; at Om,15 a notch is made in the wood, large enough to place the frame on. When you start to give air to very tender plants, you place the rack on the trunk, in its thinnest part; this is what practitioners call "giving air on the flat"; a few days later, when the plant has become accustomed to this new temperature, we place it on the thickest part, which is called "giving air on the side"; later, the rack is placed upright on the trunk and the frame placed in the notch we described above; we say: This is called "giving air on the notch"; finally, on the top of the rack, it's called "giving the big air". It is also necessary to give air sometimes from the top of the frame and sometimes from the bottom, so that the plants on one side or the other can get used to the outside temperature; this is called "changing the air". If you have a square of frames, the same racks are used in each path; so, for example, if the air is at the top of the frame and you want to put it at the bottom, you remove the air from the first row, and the racks in the second row are used for the first, and so on; only those in the first row will be transported to the last, if you don't have any extra for this one. When you start to give air, you must take care 3. that it is not on the windward side, as the plants will immediately wither. If it comes from the end of the square, the air from the first frame is placed at the opposite angle, so that the head of the square is closed; this is called "closing the air". All these little details play a big part in obtaining a regular and profitable crop. Once the plants have been exposed to the fresh air for a week or so, both above and below, you can remove the frames without fear: they can withstand the ambient temperature without risk of deterioration, unless, as often happens in late spring, there is a late frost. It's up to the gardener to decide what to do, if he doesn't want to lose all the fruit of his labor in a single night. There is nothing positive or absolute about this type of cultivation. Forks. - The small pieces of wood used by market gardeners to give air to bells are called forks. These little pieces of wood are pointed at one end so that they can sink into the ground; they should be about Om, 30 long by Om, 05 wide. They are usually made from laths or old barrel staves. A notch is made at Om, 15, then a second Om, 05 higher; as they are sunk into the earth by Om, 10, this makes Om, 05, then Om, 10 and finally Om, 15 of air height, which is given to the bells, and this gradually, as we said for the frames. Practitioners say: "put the air on the first notch", "on the second notch", etc.., In the first two cases, the very shape of this utensil in the ground protects the bells from gales; this is no longer the case when the air is at the top, as happens especially with melons; sometimes hurricanes overturn and break the bells, and what is even more dreadful are the whirlwinds that carry them away, often to great heights, and cause great damage. With the fork firmly planted in the ground, and the bell caught in the notch, it takes a good gust of wind to remove the bell, because the wind has to tear the fork away. The reader will therefore realize that, like the rack for the chassis, the manufacture of the fork also plays a major role in the cultivation of bells. Bell wedges. - These are simply small pieces of wood, 5 centimeters square by Om, 01 thick, used to pack the bells when they are no longer needed, leaving a gap between them, as we said when dealing with this material. CuI TIT AUGUST SOWING AND CULTURAL CARE It's during this month that we start sowing the vegetables that will provide the first harvests of spring. Let's take a look at them in turn. White onions. - There are many varieties of onion, differing greatly in size and color. The best-known and most widespread is the Ognon jaune des Vertus, which is sown on the spot in whole fields; but its cultivation is not sufficiently profitable, given the time it takes to occupy the land, for it to be grown by market gardeners in the suburbs of Paris. Only the Ognon blanc hauif de-Paris (fig. 4) is specially cultivated in the marshes of Paris, and it is this variety that we will focus on here. Ognon blanc hátif de Parïs is sown in nurseries around August 20th; sown before the 15th of that month, it risks going to seed instead of "turning", i.e. forming its bulbs. It's best to choose a marsh that has only been in cultivation for a few years. In old marshes, it is often impossible to obtain Onion seedlings; they "melt" as soon as they are raised, and nothing remains of them. Sow the seeds thickly in a well-tilled bed. If the soil is light, the Fig. 4 - Early white Paris onion. soil is ploughed in after ploughing, and then levelled out. As soon as the seedling has been sown, water it to facilitate emergence, then bury the seed by harrowing with a fork; press the seedling down again with your feet; even out the surface with a rake, and finally top-dress, spreading a 2-centimeter layer of rich loam evenly over the whole surface; the loam from the first melon layers is excellent for this. Finally, give the plant a generous watering. If the weather is very dry, as is often the case at this time of year, water frequently enough to produce a regular emergence; but once the onion is well established, water less, so that it firms up and remains healthy. 1. i.e. compacted with the feet. 2. operation which consists in flattening the surface of the soil by removing the clods. Spinach. - Spinach is also sown around August 20 for winter and early spring consumption; it starts to set seed in May. The most popular variety for this season is Dutch spinach, with round leaves and seeds. Sow in the field, broadcast and clear; one liter of seed should be enough for two acres of land. The soil should not be ploughed deeply, as spinach roots like to "cling" to firm subsoil. The seedbed is harrowed with a fork, plumbed with the feet, levelled with a rake, then covered with a short manure mulch. Under these conditions, emergence takes place after six to seven days. If the weather is dry, the soil should be kept moist by frequent light wetting. Weeding should be done by hand, unless the seed is sown in rays, in which case the hoe can be used. Spinach sown in autumn for winter consumption should not be cut, but picked by hand, leaf by leaf. Choose the largest leaves, those around the edge of each plant, and leave the smallest, those in the heart. In this way, you can pick every fortnight in the same place. Picking under these conditions lasts until the spinach goes to seed, i.e. towards the end of May. Lamb's lettuce. - This plant, commonly known as "doucette" in many countries, is indigenous. It grows wild almost everywhere in our climate, so it can only be grown in the vicinity of large cities. Parisian market gardeners have long been growing a well-selected variety called Mâche ronde; grain merchants even list a number of sub-varieties in their catalogs. Around Paris, hundreds of hectares of this lettuce are grown in autumn. Cultivation is extremely simple. Mâches are sown from August 8; the first plants are ready to eat by October 15. They are usually sown in other crops, such as chicory, scarole, cauliflower and various other cabbages. It is preferable to sow in hard soil rather than in newly tilled ground. Once the seed has been broadcast, the soil is lightly harrowed and compacted. The surface of the soil must then be kept continually fresh so that the seed germinates and rises, otherwise it "cotitates", i.e. the germ formed dries out, and the plant does not rise. To get good Mâches, don't sow too thickly, but it's better to err on the side of too much than too little, given the difficulty of germination at this time of year. As for amateurs, they sow a bed of Lamb's lettuce around August 15, fairly thickly, and as it grows they thin it out, always removing the largest; in this way they have enough to eat throughout the winter until April. Mâches should be watered frequently to protect them from insects, especially spiders, which can destroy them completely. Cabbage. - Cabbage is one of the most diverse types of vegetable in terms of shape and appearance. It is perhaps the oldest cultivated vegetable. Natural variations or selection have given rise to several quite distinct races of the primitive cabbage. In head cabbage, the foliage has developed the most, but without the stem rising, so that the leaves are tightly interlocked, capping each other to form very hard, tight "apples". In cauliflower, on the other hand, the inflorescence has developed considerably, but suddenly aborts, so that it remains shapeless and compact, giving the white, barely grainy "heads" we know. In Brussels sprouts, it's the trunk that's particularly developed, the eyes it bears giving rise to small edible buds. In Kohlrabi, it's the trunk that has developed again, but it bulges considerably at one point. In Turnip cabbage, it's the root; in Forage cabbage, it's both the foliage and the trunk. Head cabbages themselves are divided into two very different races. One has smooth, glaucous-green leaves: Cabbage; the other has more or less blistered, dark-green leaves: Savoy. In general, the cabbage varieties, which are slower to sprout and go to seed, are grown for spring and summer. Savoy cabbages, with their looser heads, are grown in spring, and will bolt very quickly under the influence of heat. The varieties of cabbage that are best grown for spring consumption, because their foliage is hardy, are the head cabbages with more or less long leaves, known as oxheart and York cabbages. Beefheart cabbages (fig. 5) include large and small cabbages. The variety grown by Parisian market gardeners is a large Chou cœur de bœuf that closely resembles those sold in the seed trade as Chou cœur de bœuf Fig. 5 - Chou cœur de bœuf. moyen de la Halle and Chou très hátif d'Étampes (fig. 6). Fig. 6 - Very early cabbage from Étampes. In the Paris climate, cabbage is sown at the end of August and the first days of September. This date is very strict; however, in cold, clayey soils, sowing can start as early as August 25; but Parisian market gardeners, cultivating very fertile soils, often lightened by the quantity of potting soil they use, never sow before August 30. Sown earlier, cabbages set seed before forming their apples. We particularly recommend this crop to anyone with a vegetable garden. Along with white onions, beef cabbage is the first new, fresh vegetable to arrive in spring. We even start to eat the leaves as soon as the apples start to form; we also eat the few cabbages that happen to go to seed at the beginning of April. They are still superior in taste and flavor to those that have spent the winter in gauge. Lettuces and Romaines - A first "season" of Lettuces and Romaines can be sown at the end of summer, and without layers. This first season is sown under cloches, cold, i.e. without layers, at the end of August. To do this, the ground where the seed is to be sown is carefully ploughed, top-dressed to a thickness of 2 to 3 centimetres, and the surface is compacted with the flat of a spade or with a board. You then take a bell and, as you lay it down, imprint its perimeter on the soil. Repeat this procedure as many times as there are bells in the seedbed, and sow into each of the circles thus traced. Cover the seed with a light layer of fine compost. If the sun is too hot, the bells can be covered with straw mats, but as soon as the seeds have sprouted, the bells must be uncovered and blanched. Doormats should be left on the bells only during very hot weather, and the bells should be uncovered as soon as the sun has lost its strength, as plants deprived of light will elongate and wither. We feel we should say a few words, once and for all, about the quantity of seeds that 1. For this type of cultivation, cloches are to be preferred to trays; the plants have more daylight and wither less. If you sow too thickly, you compromise harvest success from the outset. Experienced growers know how to judge the quantity of seeds needed for a bell by feel alone; we'll show those who aren't used to it how to dose this quantity. For seedlings sown at the end of August, each bell should cover no more than four to five hundred seeds; in September, seven to eight hundred; in October, twelve to fourteen hundred, as at this time the plants are less likely to overheat. These figures are calculated on the assumption that transplanting will be done when the plants have only their two cotyledons; if they were to be left longer under the bell, they would have to be sown much less thickly. By this time of year, the plants have developed their cotyledons, and are ready to be transplanted, also under a bell, at a rate of 24 to 30 per bell. To do this properly, start with a row of four, then two rows of five, then four, then three, making a total of 24. If you want to transplant 30 plants per bell, tighten the rows so as to make a row of six plants in the middle. Fig. 7 - Black-seeded Gotte lettuce. The variety of lettuce to be grown cold in autumn is the black-seeded Gotte lettuce (fig. 7). We have never come across another variety so well suited to forced cultivation. The main varieties of Romaine grown commercially are: 1° flat Romaine with cloches, in the first season, under cloches; 2° grey Romaine, also grown under cloches in the first season, and which we recommend to amateurs; it is then used for counterplanting between the cloches and the first plantations in the open ground. Other varieties, which are not suitable for the trade, can satisfy the taste of connoisseurs, such as Ballon Romaines, Royale d'été and Royale d'hiver, Alphange, Brune Anglais, etc. Their cultivation is no different from that of other varieties. Their cultivation is in no way different from that of the preceding varieties. The green Romaine, so widely used in the past for cultivation under cloches or cold frames, has almost disappeared from professional cultivation, as it does not have the same market value as the first mentioned above; however, it is even hardier than them, and in certain cold climates would perhaps be even preferable in forced cultivation. Romaine is grown in the same way as Lettuce; in summer, it requires the same care, and even more water. MISCELLANEOUS OUTDOOR SOWING During August, a number of vegetables continue to be sown outdoors, notably the latest Radishes and Black Radishes, and dwarf varieties of Beans intended to be eaten "in needles". These beans can be sown outdoors in beds facing south; but these late sowings are often surprised by the first frosts of October, and the slightest frost kills the beans; certain precautions must therefore be taken, which we will indicate in due course. Carrots can continue to be sown, preferably in racks. This is more convenient for weeding, as you can destroy the grass between the rays with a small hoe, and all that's left to do is remove the weeds in the carrots by hand. We recommend sowing too thickly rather than too thinly, and then thinning out as necessary. This is the surest way to obtain a good harvest. Turnips can be sown as late as September. At the end of August, and in the first part of September, Chervil is sown for winter and early spring consumption. Chervil is sown as a broadcast crop with lamb's lettuce or spinach, and is thus available throughout the autumn and winter, until May, when it sets seed. The stalks are cut off with a knife, as and when needed, so as not to interfere with the other plants among which it is sown. Leeks are sown by Parisian market gardeners at the same time as white onions and under the same conditions; transplanted at the end of September, they set seed as early as May. This crop can only be grown by gardeners in the vicinity of large cities, where they can sell their produce quickly. MISCELLANEOUS WORK Cabbages sown in the nursery in June are planted out at the beginning of August. They are planted flush with the heart, and bound! immediately1 "Bound" means to press the root of the plant against the soil with the planting tool. diately. A few waterings should be given during the month. Caterpillars and flea beetles should be kept at bay. Broccoli can also be planted in place, about a quarter as thick as cauliflower, and then watered as needed until late summer or even early autumn. At the same time, you can plant Scarole, or sow Lamb's lettuce or spinach. The last Chicory and Scarole sown in the open ground in the month of

July will be planted in August. At this time of year, it's always wise to plant eight days earlier rather than later, as the first frosts often surprise us before the plants have fully emerged. Dandelions can now be planted out in rows, 20 to 25 centimetres apart. In the Paris climate, the first kale plants for spring consumption are sown at the end of September. There are a great many varieties of cauliflower, but they can be divided into three classes: tender, semi-hard and hard. In spring, you can plant anything; the soft ones become thinner and less thick, and are good for eating first; then come the semi-hard ones, and finally the hard ones, which don't flake until July. From this time onwards, we see tender cauliflowers again, which should be grown preferably in summer, as the heat always hardens them sufficiently. However, specialists working for the trade often grow half-hard cauliflowers for the summer, because they are more "full-bodied", but in hot years, such as 1899, market gardeners don't get good plants with these varieties. We advise amateurs to plant tender varieties for the summer. In autumn, demidurs do very well, and can be grown by anyone. Hard-bodied cauliflowers can also be grown in autumn, but should not be planted too late, so that they have time to "grow legs and wood". These cauliflowers take longer to peel, and only the first frosts in November can start them. Cultivation of the "hard" varieties had no other purpose than to provide cauliflowers for consumption at the beginning of winter; it is increasingly abandoned by Parisian market gardeners, because of the competition they face at this time from cauliflowers from Brittany, on the ocean coast, where frost is rare. Throughout the winter, Algeria ships them to France and other countries. We have seen some very fine plantations around Algiers, but they were poorly cared for, especially in terms of covering. Provence sends its produce after Algeria; it immediately precedes the first market garden produce from Paris. All these cauliflowers from different countries are far from being as carefully cultivated as those grown by Parisian market gardeners, and even by growers in the Saint-Germain area, who also grow them as a special crop in autumn. As Olivier de Serres predicted three centuries ago, this cultivation is expanding day by day, covering hundreds of hectares on the plains. There is no doubt that, with a few practical notions, the inhabitants of our countryside could establish it in the autumn, at least for their own consumption, and thus obtain a well-being unknown to them until now. For the first plants to be obtained in spring, and which are planted on a bed, sowing is done at the end of September in the cold, on soil or compost, either under a bell or in a frame. Care should be taken to aerate the seedlings sufficiently to keep them firm and stocky. Then transplant to the nursery. The cauliflowers that follow the first-season cauliflowers are sown at the same time as the first-season cauliflowers, but are planted in cold lettuce or 4 Romaine under chassis. This is exactly the same as for the first season. The last of these seedlings are planted in the open ground in March in Lettuce; if they are planted in Romaine, their place must be left free, so that Romaine does not suffocate them. The same seedling provides three successive cauliflower seasons: the first on a bed in February, the second on a cold frame at the beginning of March, and the third in the ground at the end of March. Romaine. - Romaines can continue to be grown cold under cloches, as we said in August, until the first days of September; the young plants are transplanted and planted out at the beginning of October. This Romaine season follows on from the last outdoor season. During the first days of the month, we continue sowing oxheart cabbage (see August). Lamb's lettuce (see August) can also be sown until September 15. However, when sowing at this time, it sometimes happens that the seeds, not being sufficiently watered, don't germinate immediately; some only germinate at the end of October, when the soil becomes cooler and wetter. In this case, the plants don't have time to develop, but they still go to seed at the same time as the others, so the harvest is very compromised and may no longer be profitable. Around September 15, lettuces are sown for the first layering season. Sowing and transplanting are carried out in the same way as in August. However, it is preferable at this time to transplant a little lighter; no more than 24 lettuces should be planted per bell, if you want to obtain a nice stocky plant. At the end of the month, lettuces will be sown on top of the first layers of carrots planted at the beginning of December. Turnips can be sown until September 15th, but at this late season, as with carrots, extra-early varieties should be sown. As with pink radishes and carrots, these are generally the rounder varieties, which start to turn as soon as the plant has a few leaves, and can be eaten from then on. Radishes can still be sown on the coast, sheltered from the north wind. Finally, chervil can be sown until September 15 for winter and early spring consumption. Do not sow later, as the plant will not be strong enough to withstand heavy frosts. PLANTATIONS AND MISCELLANEOUS WORK The hátif de Paris white onion, sown in August, is being transplanted this month. Amateurs can let it grow in place, thinning it out continuously, but specialists pull it out from September 15 to transplant it in beds. The plant is prepared as follows: the seedling is lifted with a spade, flat, at some depth below the roots; it is then easy to pull it out without damaging it. We take the seedlings one by one, discarding those that are not well formed; we make a handful by arranging them in the hand in such a way that all the bulbs are at the same level, then we cut the roots at about 1 1/2 centimetres from the bulb and shorten the leaves by a few centimetres; the plant should be about 10 centimetres long. Carefully place the handful in a basket, leaving all the bulbs at the same level, so as to pick up the onions in the same way when planting. When you've prepared all you can plant in a day, dip the basket in water long enough for the roots to soak in; this gives them stiffness, and facilitates planting and recovery. This is the procedure used by growers for all the plants they plant in warm weather, even when it's raining. If the onions are not to be planted until the day after they have been dug up, they should be covered with a board on which a heavy weight is placed, so that the plants remain upright; otherwise they will wriggle, which hinders planting and compromises recovery. Let's say once and for all that onions of all varieties should not be sunk more than 2 centimetres into the ground; if they are sunk deeper, they won't turn properly. Very early varieties of Onion are planted very thickly by specialists; they are spaced barely 3 or 4 centimetres apart. If we waited until these onions had reached their maximum size, the soil would be completely covered; but we sell them as soon as they turn. It's in this state that they fetch the highest prices, and you have the advantage of being able to dispose of the land to establish other crops. The next larger varieties are planted a little lighter. But for amateurs whose gardens are not as fertile as the land we're talking about, planting in rows is preferable. Southern France sends white onion to Paris from March onwards. In Algiers, we saw some as early as January. Lettuces and Romaines, sown under cloches at the end of August, are transplanted as soon as they have two leaves, also under cloches, at a rate of thirty per cloche. Beef heart cabbages, sown at the end of August, are transplanted to the nursery towards the end of September. Care should be taken to reject all those whose hearts are not well constituted and those that are degenerate, which can already be distinguished by their "emballement", i.e. the fact that their leaves take on larger dimensions than the others. People with no experience of this type of cultivation would be inclined to believe that these are the most beautiful cabbages; in reality, they are the ones you shouldn't keep, because they only develop leaves and don't form apples. Dandelions sown in July are also transplanted at the beginning of September. Transplanting is done 20 centimetres apart, in freshly tilled soil. It goes without saying that this soil should always be well fertilized. Once the planting is done, it is bounded, then given a few light 1. i.e. those which have a tendency to take on characters different from those which make up the chosen variety. 4. basinages, to facilitate recovery. When transplanted, these plants already have the strength and volume of those harvested in the wild, and when treated in this way, they develop rapidly. For the amateur cultivation we indicate in June, we thin out the seedlings around September 15th, taking the most beautiful plants to be transplanted, for example on the south coast; these will be kept to be blanched at the end of winter and the beginning of spring, while the others will be eaten in autumn and winter, always thinning out and removing the most beautiful as we go along. With this simple procedure, you'll have beautiful Dandelions to eat from the end of September to the end of April, and the crop costs next to nothing, since it occupies the land when you can't put anything else on it. Blond celery, sown at the beginning of May, should be covered with straw a few days before being cut, for blanching. Lovers should cover it only as they eat it. Tomatoes should be leafed out in September, when the sun is weakening, but only part of the leaves should be removed, otherwise the last fruits will not ripen. The leaves should not be completely removed until late September or early October, when all the fruit has fully developed. When tomatoes are plentiful, it's a good idea to preserve them for winter. In a small book by M. Baudry, chef-jardinier at the Aude farm-school, on tomato cultivation in the South of France, we found up to eight recipes for preparing these preserves. In practice, it's mainly tomato sauce that is preserved in middle-class homes; the process is extremely simple and can be found in all cookery manuals. We simply wanted to draw attention here to the services rendered by this preservative, which has so many uses. Strawberry. Forced cultivation. - Forced cultivation of the strawberry plant is now widespread. Like all forced cultivation, it requires special care and attention to ensure that the plants are properly trained. To raise plants for forcing, first proceed in the same way as for nursery cultivation (see April); the flowers are removed from the mother plants, so that the runners can develop in the spring, and by July, if the soil is suitable for the plant, we already have rooted nets. At this time, we pull them out to transplant them in the nursery. By the end of September or the beginning of October, we have some very beautiful plants. Some specialists, as soon as they have marked the nets they want to take, and in particular the first net, place a bucket full of good soil in the ground under the net, before it has taken root. They apply the net firmly to the soil, pressing it in very lightly, then water. When the time comes to plant the strawberry plants in pots for forced cultivation, you'll have ready-made plants that you don't need to transplant. In either of these ways, we've obtained strawberry plants that are already forming attractive clumps. These are placed in 16-centimeter diameter pots, with one clump per pot. These pots are placed in boxes, touch by touch; each box holds 56. The frames are placed on top when the frosts come. In the course of this month, a few more plantings are made, in the ground or on beds. White onions can be planted in the ground until the end of October. After All Saints' Day, however, frosts may prevent them from recovering, so it's best to wait until the end of February. But onions planted at the end of September and beginning of October are always ahead of those planted in spring, especially in dry, light soils. Beef heart cabbage continues to be transplanted in the nursery, as indicated for September. We can start planting them out at the end of October in regions where early frosts are feared. First-season lettuces, sown in cold cloches in August, are planted out at the end of September or in the first days of October, four to a cloche, always in cold conditions. To carry out this work, prepare rows 1.35 m wide, well ploughed and upright; arrange the bells in three rows in a chessboard pattern, but not in ados for this season, as the sun is still sufficiently warm for this procedure not to be necessary. Lettuces can be planted in this way right up to October 15th; however, specialists prefer to plant in small layers at this time of year, as the plants come up more quickly and are often more beautiful. At the beginning of the month, we continue to sow lettuces to be planted on beds. For the transplanting of these seedlings, we recommend the use of ados (see below), as the sun will have lost its strength by this time, and the soil will drain less well. These lettuces can be harvested in late January or early February, depending on the severity of the winter. Finally, from October 10th to 20th, we sow the last lettuces that will be forced, especially on the bell beds, and whose cultivation is combined with that of Romaine. They are planted from the beginning of January to the end of February, and generally eaten from March 15 to April 15. The black-seeded gotte variety is chosen for sowing. Varieties such as white Passion, red Passion, lazy blonde, lazy brown and Palatine lettuces are sown at the end of October and planted outdoors at the end of February and in March. White-seeded gotte lettuces can also be planted in well-sheltered coastal areas; this variety grows even faster than the previous ones, and is especially recommended for sandy soils that are not too cold. The first season of Romaines, sown in cold cloches at the beginning of September and transplanted as we have said, is planted out in the first days of October, at a rate of one plant per cloche, if you want to have good yields. It follows on from the last seasons of Romaines grown in the open air. The first cauliflowers sown under cloche or cold frame at the end of September should be transplanted to the nursery under the same conditions, at a rate of 24 per cloche and 250 to 300 per frame. Care should be taken to give them sufficient air, so that they remain stocky and do not become too tender. The same applies to Lettuces and Romaines, which should be given as much air as the season allows, with the exception of black-seeded Gotte lettuce, which should be given as little air as possible. Forced crops are often damaged by a terrible disease: miller's disease (Peronospora gangliiformis). This disease, similar to downy mildew, can only be effectively combated by preventive treatment. We therefore recommend sulphating the soil, before sowing, transplanting or planting, with a mixture of 4 to 5 kilograms of copper sulphate and the same amount of commercial potash per 100 liters of water. This mixture has given us good results. Lamb's lettuce - Italian or Regency lamb's lettuce is sown outdoors in October. This selected variety, which grows later than round Lamb's lettuce, rises more easily thanks to the humidity of this season; it should be sown a little lighter, to form beautiful, strong clumps in April. Parisian market gardeners used to grow a lot of it to sell at that time, but nowadays a lot of lettuces from the south of France arrive in April; on the other hand, growers in the suburbs have developed their crops of Capuchin Beard, Witloof, White Dandelion, etc., so that the cultivation of Italian Lamb's lettuce, which has become too unremunerative, has been almost totally abandoned by practitioners. Asparagus. - Asparagus shoots destined for forcing into green asparagus should be harvested in autumn before the frosts, or during the winter when it doesn't freeze. For this, choose two- or three-year-old asparagus shoots. For this cultivation, Asparagus claws are placed touch and go on a good layer, with a few centimetres of compost on top, or heated with a thermosiphon; but when these Asparagus claws have developed all their eyelets, they are good to destroy afterwards. Sorrel needs to be terracotta-packed in autumn, so that you can continue to pick it as long as it doesn't freeze. Artichokes can also be grommeted at this time to form new plantations; this procedure is described by M. G. Legros! At the end of September - or better still, in our opinion, in October, since in September there is often still fruit on the vine in the Paris climate - we detach medium-sized eyelets with a good heel, and immediately put them out of the sun. Take pots about 12 centimetres in diameter, and fill with good, clean soil, rather strong than too light. After cleaning and peeling the leaves and crown, plant one eyecup per pot, burying only the heel. Water at the base, avoiding wetting the leaves, then place the pots in a slightly shady spot and continue 1. In the March issue, we describe another carnationing method, which involves watering "drop by drop" until the plant is fully established. At the end of October, we place the pots in stretcher boxes, and if the weather turns bad, snowing or freezing, we put the stretchers on top. These Artichokes are good to put up towards the end of March. This procedure brings the harvest forward considerably, as the plants treated in this way are as advanced, and sometimes more so, than older plantations which have suffered more or less from the rigors of winter. In southern countries, on the Mediterranean coast for example, and in Algeria, notably at Maison-Carrée, where we have seen some very fine artichoke crops, everything is simplified: the eyelets are removed from the mother plants at the end of summer, when vegetation is at rest, planted in September as soon as the first rains fall, and the harvest begins the following January. But this is not the case in our country, where some winters lose almost all artichoke plantations. This is where the method recommended by M. Legros, and also by the late Professor Hardy, comes into its own. Plants placed in frames, secured by acots around the boxes and mats over the frames, easily withstand the rigors of winter. As for mature artichokes, you need to take the necessary measures to protect them as soon as the cold approaches. Once harvested, the flowering stems are cut off flush with the ground, along with the tips of the longest leaves. The remaining leaves are tied together to form the hearts. We plough between the rows and mound the plants, bringing the soil all around to 20 or 25 centimetres above the collar, taking care not to let any soil penetrate into the heart of the plants. 3 heart of the plant. This opening should be reinforced during severe frosts. In some regions, the artichoke is destroyed in winter by a rodent, the vole. You can get rid of them by spreading flour mixed with a third of arsenic, or wheat prâliné in the same mixture; you can also place large terracotta pots in different places, sunk to ground level and half-filled with water; voles that fall into these traps cannot get out and are drowned. Beans. - Dwarf varieties of beans sown in August must be protected from the first frosts, which would destroy them. A lath is prepared above the plants, and when a frost arrives, simply place straw mats on the lath. These first frosts don't usually last more than a few nights, and it's rare that they aren't followed by a period of mild weather, which can last from a month to six weeks. The precaution we've outlined, which costs next to nothing, is therefore sufficient to protect the plant, and ensures that green beans of superior quality to canned beans will be available until late autumn. In the early days of October, Radishes can still be sown in coastal areas, sheltered from the north wind; but these last sowings often only come to fruition with the help of trays, which are only put in place when it freezes. As long as it doesn't freeze, it's best to leave Radishes in the air. BLANCHING OF VARIOUS VEGETABLES Capuchin Beard. - In October, we start to pull up wild Chicory to bleach it and turn it into Capuchin Beard. Once the roots have been removed, they are grown in dark, poorly ventilated cellars. Specialists make a good layer of warm manure and place the bunches of Chicory touch by touch, upright and straight, after stripping them of all their old leaves. After about twenty days, these roots have grown narrow, very white leaves 25 to 30 centimetres long, making an excellent salad. As soon as the roots have developed all their eyelets, they are removed and new ones put in, turning over the layers if they are no longer warm enough. This process continues throughout the winter. This type of cultivation is used on a large scale in the suburbs of Paris. At the École nationale d'horticulture de Versailles, part of the underside of the terraces forming the Potager du Roi has been appropriated to demonstrate this cultivation to students. There is an improved variety of wild chicory. The leaves of this variety are similar in appearance to those of certain green summer lettuces, which are rarely grown. This improved chicory is less bitter than the wild variety, but its yield is not very high. It is grown in large quantities only by a few provincial market gardeners, but can be found in many amateur gardens. Endive or Witloof. - For some time now, we've been blanching a variety of Chicory with a large root or "coffee", of the Brussels race, known as Endive or Witloof 1. It's also known as Chicorée pommée de Bruxelles. Instead of giving long, thin, etiolated and disheveled leaves 1. from the Flemish woit, white, and loof, leaf. like Capuchin Beard, it produces true full apples, relatively tight, elongated, from Om, 10 to Om,15 in length. It is not only an excellent salad, but also a very good cooked vegetable that can be served in a variety of ways, especially in juice. As with ordinary wild chicory, you can force the roots to grow all winter and into spring. Here's the procedure described by Mr. G. Delachevalerie: "From the end of October or in November, we start to pluck part of the roots to force them; we can do this every winter month, so as to have them until spring. To do this, dig a bed Om.50 deep by 1m.30 wide and a length to be determined according to the quantity of roots you want to force out. After draining the subsoil, place a layer of fine soil about twenty centimetres thick, and plant the Chicory roots 3 or 4 centimetres apart, after cutting off the leaves near the collar and shortening the root tips of those that are too long, so as to make them all equal; then add soil between all the roots, with the upper part or collar about 20 centimetres below the edge of the trench, and after consolidating them well, cover them with about 20 centimetres of fine sandy or sifted soil, so as to fill the trench completely. A layer of hot manure, about Om.30 high, is then applied. After a month, these roots will have produced tender, pale-yellow, crisp, slightly bitter apples with a very fine flavor. "The apples are harvested before they reach the height of the manure, while they are still 2 or 3 centimetres from it, because if they were allowed to reach that height, their tips would turn brown and could spoil. "To obtain this vegetable throughout the winter, you successively put hot manure on the part of the layer you want to force. If the weather turns to rain, we cover the manure with obliquely inclined boards, so as to reject the water outside the layer. A month later, we start harvesting chicory apples. When harvesting, care must be taken to detach the apples with a small part of the root collar, so that the lower leaves cannot detach from the apple during transport to market. Endive cultivation has grown enormously in recent years. It's a highly recommended crop for rural dwellers. Cardoon. - Cardoon is also blanched. Start by pulling it all the way up, using a rope attached to a stick planted in the ground, as this plant has sharp prickles. When you've gone all the way round, you tighten the rope, so that the cardoon is upright and its heart enclosed. We then bind it with one or two straw ties, depending on its strength and height. After a while, the heart softens and is ready to eat. If you want to keep it later, you wait until the end of October to raise it as we've just said, and surround it with large straw, which you tie to keep it at the same height as the cardoon. Under these conditions, it can withstand light frosts. There are several varieties of Cardoon. Cardon d'Espagne, which is not very thorny, has the disadvantage of hollow ribs and is not suitable for winter storage. The Cardon de Tours (fig. 8), much more cultivated in our countries, has full ribs and can be overwintered. It is stockier and tastier than the previous variety. In Geneva, we saw a variety called Cardon de Plainpalais, which has a very white heart and bears a strong resemblance to Céleri Chemin or Céleri doré. STRAWBERRY FORCING During the first days of October, we continue to prepare strawberry plants in pots for forcing, as described above. When the time comes to force these plants, from the end of the month onwards, a good layer is established and the pots are buried in soil or potting compost, at a rate of 25 or 26 per panel. If you have a thermosiphon heating system, the pots are placed under the same conditions in the heated tarpaulins. Either way, as long as the necessary heat is available, all that remains is to give the appropriate care to all the plants treated in this way: give them air when Fig. 9. - Fraise Dr Morère. the weather permits, protect them from frost by covering the frames with mats, and by establishing acots around the boxes or tarpaulins. Like all fruit-bearing plants, plants should be kept as close as possible to the glass. The most successful varieties for forcing, or at least those most commonly used for this purpose, are the following: Dr Morère (fig. 9), Marguerite (fig. 10), Général Chanzy, ViesFig. 10. - Strawberry Marguerite. de Thury. These are generally very hardy, large-fruited varieties. We can also force four-season varieties, but their yield is not high enough to make this crop lucrative, given the costs involved. VEGETABLES TO BE INTAKEN Beets need to be brought in before the frosts; they can be stored in cellars or silos to last through the winter and even into spring. Tomatoes - The last tomatoes will also be brought in. Professional growers stop producing flowers after four bunches, but amateurs can let fruit set later, and ripen them under cover. When October arrives, and the first frosts are to be feared, the remaining fruits are picked and placed on straw under a frame, in a greenhouse, or in some other sheltered place where they can receive the sun's rays. Those that have begun to yellow finish ripening under these conditions, and can be harvested until November. Some authors recommend another method, which we think is very practical. When the plants are still full of fruit and have reached their normal size, or at least when there is no longer any hope that they will grow, and the cool nights and continuous rainfall of autumn take away the hope of complete ripening, the tomato plants are pulled up; then the fruit-bearing stems are laid horizontally on a bed of very dry straw, under a frame or in a greenhouse. In this way, the fruit, if not fully ripe, at least acquires a certain finesse and taste similar to those whose ripening has been encouraged by the sun's rays. We think this is a very good method, especially for amateur growers, and will enable them to eat tomatoes very late in the season. CONFECTION DES ADOS Here's how to make ados: A strip of land 2 meters wide is ploughed deeply to establish a line of three rows 5. of bells placed in a chessboard pattern, which will take about. 1m,35 of this width. By ploughing, we lower the part on the south side by about Om,15, and this earth is transferred to the north side, giving a slope of Om,30 (fig. 11); this is the slope that has always 70....... 730 - Fig. 11. - Ados. been judged the most advantageous. The rear part of the ados is consolidated by beating it with a shovel and straightening its edge with a chalk line. Rake it, earth it and bell it, just as if the ground were flat. The bottom row of bells is at ordinary ground level, and the earth excavated from the pathway alone raises the other two rows; it follows that the pathway alone is dug out, and serves as a sewer for the ados. If you have several ados to make next to each other, it is always preferable to increase the distance between them, so that one does not cast a shadow on the other. Transplanting young plants, when they have only two or three leaves, should always be done with the finger; this is the surest way to do a good job. The same applies to spring transplanting; market gardeners do it all by finger pricking. It's not uncommon for them to spend days on their knees doing this work. It's the most practical position for getting the job done quickly. The last lettuces sown in the second half of October are transplanted under cloches. The cloches are lifted to give air when the weather is mild, but they have to be pulled down when frost arrives. If it's a bit frosty, we cover the bells with straw mats; but if we're afraid of very cold weather, this isn't enough, so we have to fill in the gaps between the bells and the edge of the paths with dry manure, chopped straw or any other similar material we have on hand; This is done up to a third of the height of the bell, then progressively more if the frost becomes more severe, but without ever covering the top of the bell, so that the plants always have a little light. The important thing is not to let the frost penetrate the soil, because if it does, the plants will melt at some point in their growth, sooner or later, depending on how deeply they have been affected. Plants affected by frost in this way are said to suffer from "red neck"; the neck of these plants takes on a reddish hue. As soon as the thaw arrives, the stuffing must be removed, and we start airing again when the weather permits. It sometimes happens that, despite all these precautions, the floor of the teenager is frozen. If the frost has penetrated only slightly, the plants may not develop a red collar; they may just wilt, and can be made to "come back" when the thaw comes; only in this case, they must be uncovered carefully and little by little, as the slightest sunburn will damage them. Romaines require much the same care as lettuces, with the only difference being that they are generally given more air. To make their plants even firmer, while avoiding giving them so much air, Parisian market gardeners practice "reinforcement" as follows: after transplanting Romaines at a rate of 30 or 36 per bell, without giving these young plants any air, they prepare new ados in November, before the big frosts, and transplant these plants once again, in the nursery, at a rate of 10, 14 or 19 per bell. This is one way of obtaining very stocky, firm plants. What's more, these Romaines, which are already a few centimetres high, are sunk right down to the first leaves, burying the crown and making the plant more resistant to severe frosts. So, unless winters are very harsh, it's very rare to see red collars on plants treated in this way. They are only given air when they have softened again. Often, even the first season, which is planted on cloches, doesn't need air. Air will only be needed when the plants appear too tender, and especially for the following seasons, which will be used for counter-planting on cloches. From the beginning of November, you can prepare the cloches for Romaines in winter. For this, you need good layers, and, just as for lettuce and Romaine plants, when it gets very cold, you need to fill in with dry manure between the bells and on the paths, and sometimes cover with several straw mats. Under each bell, we simply plant a Romaine, a grey variety for market gardening, and three Lettuces, a gotte variety with black seeds (see fig. 12). Once the harvest has been Fig.12. - Planting a Romaine and three Lettuces under a bell. harvested, the layer is turned over to plant another season's supply of the same plants. There is a variety of Romaine, called Romaine plate à cloches, with which no Lettuces should be planted, as this variety, to become beautiful, must first spread out like a Scarole to meet the edge of the cloche; the leaves then climb up the glass and come to meet on top, pressing against each other - what people in the trade call "coiffer". Cauliflowers grown in cold conditions, under cloches or frames, must be protected by mats against heavy frosts. If very cold weather is forecast, make sure to place mats around the frames or cloches to prevent frost from penetrating deep into the soil. Hard cauliflowers planted in July, when well covered, can easily withstand five or six degrees of cold. Curly Chicory and Winter Scarole should only be tied up in the event of a hard frost. However, towards the beginning of November, frosts often occur which, if left unchecked, can cause serious damage. In this case, if you want to keep Scarole throughout the winter, you need to protect it from these first frosts by covering it, in order to tie it as late as possible, as by this time it is hardly growing at all, and sometimes, after these little frosts have passed, you can keep it in place untied until the end of December and later. Once it's bound, we pull it out and put it in a cellar, but not in a heap; we plant the Scaroles in the sand, one next to the other, or put them in a silo under the same conditions. The latter method is even preferable, because as soon as it freezes, you cover the Scarole with dry manure or dry straw, which you remove after the thaw, and the lettuce continues to whiten as it gradually grows, but in these conditions it is less likely to rot and you can keep a better eye on it. Treated in this way, it can be stored throughout the winter. This crop used to be grown on a large scale in the suburbs of Paris, but shipments of chicory and scarole from the south of France have almost completely abandoned it. Nevertheless, this inexpensive way of preserving lettuces throughout the winter is highly recommended for amateurs and gardeners in small towns where produce from the south of France is not available. And let's not forget that Scarole, blanched in silos, is superior in tenderness and taste to Scarole from the south of France. Leeks for winter consumption will also be harvested before the frosts and stored in cellars, so that they will be available until spring. You can continue to pick sorrel as long as it doesn't freeze. Enthusiasts who want to have it all winter long place a box and cover it with a frame. If you want to keep tarragon fresh through the winter (as it can be stored in dried bunches), you can transport good, stubby, root-ball plants under a frame in a well-exposed spot. In the past, Parisian market gardeners used to force Tarragon under the same conditions as Asparagus, but today this cultivation has been completely abandoned. Hard Celery, grown for winter, can withstand a few degrees of cold; but in November, when heavy frosts are expected, it's a good idea to pull them out and bury them. To do this, we open a trench at the bottom of which we place the Celery plants in rows, spaced 15 centimetres apart; thus preserved, they can withstand fairly severe cold. Finally, when the severe winter frosts arrive, we bury the Celery completely and cover it with dry manure or chaff. This way, you can eat them all winter long, as long as the frost doesn't penetrate the soil. As soon as the frost has thawed, Celery should be uncovered to reduce the risk of rotting. Celeriac. - Celeriac can be stored under the same conditions, but should only be covered to about half the length of the leaves, never all the way to the top. To prevent the heart from freezing, it should be covered with litter or dry manure, but only at the time of severe frosts, and as soon as the thaw occurs, care should be taken to uncover the celeriac and remove dead leaves to prevent rotting. Cardoon. - In the early days of November, you can continue to raise cardoons as described in the previous month; but if the weather turns cold, it's a good idea to wrap them in straw. Finally, when the big frosts arrive, the Cardons should be pulled up and stored in a cellar or silo. In both cases, as far as possible, they should be stored upright. They can be stored this way for most of the winter. Cabbages. - Large varieties of cabbage, such as Milan gros des Vertus, Milan de Pontoise and Milan de Norvège, require special care if they are to be kept over winter. In large-scale cultivation, when heavy frosts are forecast, these cabbages are placed on the ground without being removed; while the stem, held between the two tines of a fork, is inclined towards the ground, this stem and the bottom of the head are covered with soil taken from the sides, taking care that the head always faces north, as the alternating thawing and refreezing is much more damaging to plants than the frost itself. In home cultivation, the procedure is different, especially if less hardy varieties are grown. In a healthy spot, and in front of a north-facing wall, dig a small trench 15 cm deep, parallel to the wall, and transport the cabbages, laying them side by side, with the head always inclined towards the north. The stem and the top of the collar are covered with earth, which is removed at the next gauge and lined in the same way. In very cold weather, this shelter is reinforced by covering the cabbages with straw mats, dry straw, litter, in short, whatever is available. In this way, they can be eaten even during the most severe frosts, without having to be uprooted in advance. Broccoli is pulled up before the big frosts, and replanted very close together, deep enough to bury the whole stem right down to the leaves. During the frosts, they are covered with straw, and in spring the apples develop. In the past, market gardeners devoted all their skill to preserving cauliflowers for most of the winter, but today cauliflowers from various countries are received in large cities, and this crop has been abandoned. Raves should be harvested before the coldest weather, and placed in a silo or in a frost-free place. Lamb's lettuce should be protected from severe frosts with straw or straw mats. Artichokes. - Artichoke plants should also be protected from frost when the thermometer falls below -5°; to do this, dry leaves, litter or manure as dry as possible should be packed around the plants, leaving only the tips of the leaves. These should also be covered if the cold persists. Whenever the frost stops, take care to remove these covers, and put them back on when it starts again. As for eye artichokes, continue to give them the care indicated in the previous month. Cauliflowers. - Chassis and cloches of cauliflowers sown in September should be covered with straw mats during very cold weather; care should also be taken to make acots so that frost does not penetrate deep into the soil. Dandelions should be covered with a large layer of mulch. We continue to give Wild Chicory and Witloof the care we described last month. In October, we described how to force strawberry plants, an operation that can be started or continued in November. Strawberry plants potted for forcing, and placed in boxes, will be covered with frames during frosts, so that there is no interruption in vegetation. Cabbage planting Cabbage planting begins in November, sometimes even at the end of October in regions where early frosts are to be feared. Rays are dug 20 to 25 centimetres apart, and the plants are planted right to the heart. They are spaced 50 to 60 centimetres apart in the row, and arranged in a chessboard pattern. A good precaution to take when planting cabbages is to face south on the right-hand side; this way, the ditch left by the planting cut, which should be filled in as much as possible, is exposed to the south, and any snow or ice that may accumulate there melts more quickly. Cabbages planted at this time can be eaten as early as May in light soils, especially if early varieties are chosen. There are a few selections of cabbage that are very early, notably the one market gardeners call Chou pommé de Paris. Some twenty or thirty years ago, we saw them being brought to Les Halles as early as April 15th or 20th. But since then, as the south of France has been sending increasingly large consignments to Paris, we have gradually had to abandon the cultivation of these small forms of cabbage and adopt larger, later varieties to follow in the footsteps of the Choux du Midi. You have to be with the times, and keep up with the times. However, this only applies to specialists who supply the big city markets. Early varieties are still recommended for hobby growers and certain non-commercial operations. Cabbages can be planted throughout the winter when it doesn't freeze, but when they are caught by heavy frosts before they have recovered, they are thrown to the ground, like onions. It is therefore preferable, for amateurs who have not planted in November, to wait until February 15th before proceeding with this operation. Growing cabbage requires well-smoked soil; before ploughing, it is therefore necessary to bury a good manure; any compost you have at your disposal will be good; gadoues in particular are excellent. Market gardeners often smoke their soil with vegetable detritus, to which they mix manure. This fertilizer is only good for cabbages; if it were used for salads, it would produce "cast iron". Once the fertilizer has been spread on the soil, a good, i.e. deep, ploughing is done to bury it well; then the bed is raked and the rays made. SOWING Carrots are first sown at the end of November, in good beds. 30 or 36 black-seeded gotte lettuces are planted on top of the carrot seedlings in each bed. Some gardeners sow round, very red varieties of radish at the same time. In this case, we'd advise you not to broadcast the seeds, but to wait until the lettuces have been planted, and then pinch the radish seeds into the holes between the lettuces. In this way, each pinch containing twelve to fifteen seeds, the Radishes all form well, they do not harm either the Carrot or the Lettuce, and the harvest is abundant. Other growers plant clumps of spinach seedlings that have been sown in a frame on a bed in a nursery three weeks or a month earlier. These various crops always delay carrots a little, but are highly recommended for provincial gardeners and hobbyists alike. The very short chássis carrot, also known as Carotte grelot, because of its particular shape, is especially suitable for these seedlings; it is the earliest variety, and for this reason, the most widespread in market gardening. It "turns" easily, and can be eaten when it's as big as a marble. If you want to grow new spinach at the end of winter, as we've just said, sow it in a nursery, around November 15, in a small layer under a frame. Sow very thickly. Flanders and English varieties with very green foliage are chosen for this season. They are hardier and more resistant to severe frosts than spinach with broad, blond-green leaves. Peas, like potatoes, are more suited to agriculture than horticulture. Specialists in the greater Paris suburbs, who cultivate for table supply, start sowing as early as November, and continue throughout the winter, weather permitting. They sow not too thickly, in rows spaced 40 to 50 centimeters apart, hoeing as often as necessary, and reseeding the plants. The first peas from these crops are harvested in the first half of June. In the past, Parisian market gardeners used to force this crop, but never on layers, simply under cold frames. Today, as with potatoes, Algeria and the South of France flood the big city markets in winter and spring. On the other hand, the industry is ar4. That is to say, its root bulges and rounds. rived to preserve these vegetables in their green state, and to supply them during the winter and spring almost as good as the new ones, so that forced cultivation has become unnecessary. The Romaine cloche layers, which are no longer to be returned, will be made from December 15 onwards. Their produce will be delivered for consumption at the end of February and the beginning of March, depending on the severity of the winter. A very good system of cultivation consists in sowing Carrots on all these layers, while planting under each bell a gray Romaine and three black-seeded Lettuces gotte, as we said above. Radishes can also be sown, but very lightly (see November). Lettuces sown at the beginning of October can also be planted on these first layers. These lettuces will be harvested at the beginning of February. As we said last month, we continue to sow Peas and Spinach, to protect Celery and Cardoons from frost, to cover Artichokes when it freezes and uncover them when the temperature rises, and to blanch Dandelion, Wild Chicory and Witloof. Cabbages that have not been transplanted in November, and which will be left in place until February, should be protected against severe frosts. To do this, cover them with a little straw or very dry manure, but never with fresh manure. This should be done lightly, so as not to soften the plant too much; only the heart and collar should be protected. Specialists, when they have to plant only in spring (when their land is not free in autumn, for example), "deepen" their plants, i.e. pull them out and press them in at heart level in the nursery; under these conditions, unless you have an extremely harsh winter, which is fortunately quite rare in our climate, you can be fairly sure of obtaining beautiful plants in spring; even if the leaves are all frozen, the heart and crown remain intact. As for late cabbages sown in June, which have their apples half-formed by the end of November, they are much more resistant to heavy frosts than those with well-formed, hard apples. If the cold is not excessive, the heads finish growing and take on a beautiful appearance. During the winter, when the stems are too bare of outer leaves, which frosts cause to fall off, it is useful to butter them up a little by bringing the soil around the stems. This can be done when the soil has dried out a little, after a few fine days. Carrots sown in August and September should be protected from damage.
