Cover them with straw, preferably 10 to 15 centimetres thick. To stock up on carrots during severe frosts, simply move this cover. It is reinforced when the thermometer falls. If winter is mild, and during periods of relaxation, it's best to leave the carrots in the open air. For the other crops of the month, and for the forcing of Strawberry plants, we will continue to proceed as previously indicated. 6 Tomatoes. - In the days when tomatoes were not yet sent to Paris from the Midi, market gardeners grew them as early crops. They sowed them in December or January, in strong layers, transplanted them in the same way, and planted them in layers under a frame; when there was no longer any fear of frost, they were removed and palletized. But this type of cultivation, like that of beans, potatoes, etc., is no longer lucrative enough to be done by Parisian practitioners, and even individuals living near big cities have more advantage in buying early tomatoes on the market than in growing them in their own gardens. The fresh fruit obtained during the winter is obviously superior in quality to preserved fruit, but its cost price is much higher than that of preserved tomatoes or early tomatoes shipped from warmer Fig. 13 - Tomato Chemin. countries, so it can only be an amateur's fantasy. As for cultivation, it differs little from that of spring. If the plants are given the warmth and air necessary for normal vegetation, good fruit will be obtained. In forced cultivation, however, there is a risk of "coulure", caused by excess humidity and lack of sunlight. To promote fertilization, some authors recommend the use of sulfur sprinkled on the leaves, but avoid doing so in full sun. Sulfur is also an excellent preventive remedy against cryptogamic diseases. Experiments carried out by practitioners have shown that certain varieties, such as the Chemin tomato (fig. 13) and the dwarf hâtive de pleine terre (fig. 14), are E ponele. Etresbouro Fig. 14 - Very early field tomato. much less prone to coulure than others, such as Perfection Tomato, Large Smooth Tomato, Ponderosa Tomato and Mikado Tomato. We therefore prefer the former for forced cultivation. The variety used for forced cultivation, which was very lucrative in the first half of the 19th century, was the hátive dwarf tomato. Curly chicory. - In the 18th century, curly chicory was only cultivated in autumn, when it could grow without any artificial means. Parisian market gardeners invented its early cultivation. Around 1791, Stainville, a market gardener established on avenue des Veuves (now avenue de l'Alma), began growing them. The secret of growing chicory before its normal season is to raise the plant properly. The seeds must be sown on a warm bed, so that germination takes place within twenty-four hours. Some growers sow their seeds on this layer without even covering them with potting soil; the heat under the frame, covered with several mats, must be sufficient to germinate the seeds in this short space of time. However, it takes a great deal of experience to achieve this result without the seeds burning. We have seen cases where the seeds were not completely burnt, and germination took place one or two days later; in this case, only the collar is burnt, and the stem becomes unable to elongate; the Chicory would end up rotting on the spot without going to seed. A plant in these conditions grows much more slowly; Chicory has no leaves and grows all heart. It then requires 6. more water than that which grows naturally. This is an old practitioner's remark that we make in passing. The first seedlings are sown around January 15th and planted out towards the end of February or the beginning of March. For cultivation on beds, we choose Chicorée fine parisienne (fig. 15). As soon as the Fig. 15 - Chicorée fine parisienne. seeds have germinated, the mats should be removed to give the young plants some daylight, so that they can turn green, but care must be taken to prevent them from hardening too much under the action of the sun's rays; to achieve this, shade them by spreading mulch over the frame. Eight days after sowing, another layer is prepared, and when it is ready, i.e. after a week or so, the three-leaf seedlings are transplanted, at a rate of 400 to 500 per panel. This crop has always been quite profitable over the last century; it has been particularly well grown by market gardeners in the 15th arrondissement of Paris, where it was a specialty. Cabbage. - If, in January, the cabbages are found to be frozen, a warm layer is immediately prepared and a new seedling is sown on this layer, under a frame. These new seedlings are transplanted onto another layer, and care must be taken to give them air to firm up. In this way, planting can be done towards the end of March or the beginning of April. But this costly way of raising plants should only be used when absolutely necessary, so as not to leave the land unused, as the Cabbages thus obtained are less beautiful and the harvest comes later. Melons. - The first melons grown in and around Paris are sown at the end of January and delivered for consumption in May. To grow this early crop, you need a bed and a hot-water or thermosiphon heating system; however, even today, very few market gardeners use this system. This crop is as difficult to grow out of season as it is easy to grow in the normal season. Melon is sown on a good bed, heated by thermosiphon or steam. When the plant has two leaves, it is replanted, two or three to a frame, on another new layer, also artificially heated. At this time of year, the greatest difficulty is to green the plant and give it the consistency it needs to develop and produce fruit; to do this, it must be given daylight. The earlier you grow melon, the more you need to choose small varieties, which are less likely to ripen "tender", i.e. before they have fully developed. Fruits that ripen tender are of much poorer quality; they can be recognized by their lack of marked slices; the rind is smooth, and the stalk does not tend to detach from the fruit; they also have less weight, for equal volume, than those that have ripened to perfection. Cucumbers. - Cucumbers grow exactly like melons, but are less delicate and require more water. FORCED CULTIVATION OF ASPARAGUS White and green asparagus are available on the market. White asparagus, with its pinkish or purplish tip, is produced first by a kind of forced cultivation, then by ordinary cultivation. Green asparagus is the result of a special system of forced cultivation, then, in full season, it is the product of the simplest cultivation, which consists in letting it grow without buttering it. White asparagus. - Forced cultivation of white asparagus is a time-consuming process, occupying the land for a number of years. During part of our youth, we saw this crop being grown in establishments where it was well established, and later undertook it on our own account. Experience has shown us some improvements that could be made in the rearing of the plant. As for cultivation itself, our fathers, fifty years ago, were already practicing it to perfection. Raising the plant. - Here's how to raise a seedling. When the asparagus emerges from the ground, we select the most beautiful plants, those with the best stems, ending in a beautiful, easily-colored tip; we only collect seeds from plants selected in this way. The seed is sown on January 15th, in a good layer, under a frame, in sufficient quantity for a second selection. When the young asparagus plants are a few centimetres long, they are transplanted to a nursery on another layer, still under a frame, at a rate of 400 plants in each panel, taking care to always select the most beautiful. These plants are treated in the usual way, covered at night to protect them from frosts, aerated as much as the weather allows, and progressively towards the end of winter, to be able to troubleshoot when frosts are no longer a concern. Planting takes place in July (see this month), and forcing can be carried out two years after planting. Forcing. - The procedure for forcing asparagus is much the same as that described by La Quintinie. A space of Om.65 was left between the rows of trunks and in the tips. The paths are dug to almost the same depth, after ploughing. The soil is spread in the trunks all the way to the top, to butter the asparagus, taking care to break up the clods, so that the soil is well loosened, because when an asparagus grows and encounters a clod, it twists and loses its value, no longer being suitable for trimming, even if it is large. With the asparagus mounded, the next step is to grow it in any season, whatever the weather. The paths just dug are filled with good, hot horse manure from the stable, preferably manure from horses well fed on oats, because it contains more nitrogen. Mix it in the same way as if you were building a layer. Once the paths have been filled, place the frames over the asparagus and cover them with one or more mats. After ten days or so, the manure has fermented and settled. New manure is brought in and mixed with the previous one, shuffling everything together. This operation is repeated every 10 or 12 days, depending on the weather and the season, so as to maintain the same temperature throughout the harvest period, which lasts from six weeks to two months. When the heat is allowed to diminish, the asparagus "rusts", as happens at the height of the season when there is cold rain. This accident takes away much of its flavor and beauty, and consequently its value. The cost of manure and labor involved in this type of cultivation, if it is to be successful and remunerative, is obvious. Asparagus is also heated using the thermosiphon, but we haven't had the time to study this process in depth, as we were obliged to give up our profession too early for health reasons. We're inclined to think that when we stop digging the paths, the plants will take more nourishment from them. What's more, with the thermosiphon, we won't have to fear the chill that inevitably occurs when we turn over the trails. But there will be other things to take care of: you'll need to bring in potting soil or soil to butter the asparagus, and take it away after harvesting. As thermosiphon heating produces a drier heat than that released by manure, it will no doubt be necessary to water the plants near the pipes from time to time. All in all, there's a study to be made here, and practice will soon show which system is the most advantageous. We doubt that the forced cultivation of asparagus, which is so costly, will be able to withstand the competition that products from the south of France will increasingly provide. The day specialists go to grow asparagus in Algeria, on the Mediterranean coast, they will be able to ship it for most of the winter. We ate some wild in this country in winter; incidentally, it was much more bitter than that grown in France. We did not see any cultivated asparagus on the Algiers markets, which are nevertheless well stocked with all indigenous products. Picking. - This operation requires a great deal of care, especially at the beginning, when the eyelets are almost all growing together from the claw. You have to dig into the earth with your hand and take great care when picking, so as not to break the ones that are in the ground, and which you uncover while digging. When you reach the claw, you "peel" the asparagus you want to pick by pressing on it with your finger; it's a long, painstaking job. As soon as harvesting is complete, the asparagus is soaked in water and put in the cellar, where it finishes coloring. Bundling. - Bundling early-growing asparagus is an art in itself. First, the plants are sorted; those too small to be put in the bundle are removed and made into separate bundles - because, despite all the care taken in selection, there are always some small ones. Next, we prepare a batch of those that will make up the "ornament" of the boot, another batch of those that will do the rest of the trick, and a batch of medium-sized ones, which will be placed in the middle. Once sorting is complete, a suitable mold is used for bundling (fig. 16). The trimming, G.E Fig. 16. - Oval asparagus bundling mold. or front of the bundle, is placed first in the bottom of the mold. This is followed by the middle bundle, which is gradually filled with medium-sized bundles. As the mold is conditioned so that the round asparagus exceeds the middle one by the thickness of the head, all you have to do is touch it everywhere. Then bind with two tightly tied wicker so that the bundle doesn't deform and remains exactly oval. We'd like to stress the importance of bundling from a commercial point of view. A well-trimmed, well-booted bundle of early asparagus is more valuable to merchants than a poorly-made bundle. As for the gardeners of the big houses who grow this crop, it's better for their personal self-esteem to present a beautiful bunch of Asparagus than a handful or a shapeless heap. It's one of those tricks of the trade for which Élisée Reclus, in his article "Paris agricole" in Géographie universelle, describes Parisian horticulture as unique. Asparagus doesn't last as long when forced as it does in its natural state. When it has been forced four or five times, it is preferable to destroy it and plant another in time to replace it, because as it ages it becomes smaller and yields less and less. In the good soil where we grew it, we managed to pick a large bunch per panel in the first few years, and then the harvest diminished more and more. Amateurs who want to grow this crop should only force a given plant every two years; it will rest in the meantime, and thus be able to supply for longer... Green asparagus. - Forced cultivation of green asparagus is a completely different kind of cultivation. Growers must cultivate hectares of asparagus on the plains, depending on the size of their forcing farm. The plant is pulled up when it is two or three years old, in autumn, before the frosts, or in winter when it doesn't freeze. When you want to force these claws, place them touch by touch in a few centimetres of potting soil, on a thick layer or on a thermosiphon heater set up under frames or in a greenhouse. As these claws are very strongly heated, all the eyelets they carry develop in a short time and grow in the open air; not being buried, Asparagus green in the air, and they are picked when they are Om, 20 to Om, 25 high. They are bundled as we have indicated above. After a short time, the claws are stripped of all their eyes. They are removed and destroyed, as they no longer contain any vegetative principles, and then replaced by others. Understandably, you need to grow a considerable quantity of young asparagus on the plains to maintain a forcing plantation of this kind for almost the whole year. Asparagus is a very expensive crop, requiring a substantial capital outlay. As a result, only a few specialists grow it in the Paris area, notably Compoint, in Saint-Ouen, which has at least 100 hectares of land dedicated to this crop, using a rotation system that is unique in agriculture and horticulture. But, it must be said, this rotation can only be done in the suburbs of Paris, thanks to the diversity of crops and the cheapness of fertilizers, which are nothing other than Parisian sludge. Green asparagus can also be forced on site, by installing thermosiphon pipes under the frames. MISCELLANEOUS WORK Carrots continue to be sown in beds. The main thing to do with these seedlings is to water them copiously as soon as the Radishes or Spinach and Lettuce have been removed. They are, in fact, badly damaged by the successive harvests of all the other plants that grew before they became strong. They need to be reinforced with potting soil, as they are more or less uprooted by the uprooting of these plants, and also by the feet of the trunks in the stretcher beds. These holes are filled by hand with potting soil, and the carrots are relined with a centimetre or two of the same material, so that the neck of the plant is well Fig. 17. - Early short fat carrot. surrounded, otherwise the carrot will turn green, harden at the top, and lose quality and market value. For these last layers of the frame, we use the Early Short Coarse Carrot (fig. 17). Spinach, to follow those sown in November, should be sown by hand in the layers made at the current time, with a few seeds in each hole. This produces beautiful, tender new spinach. We've seen some growers pick the large leaves first, before pulling up the stalks; it's a way of keeping them available until the new spinach arrives in the ground. We continue to plant the last Lettuces and Romaines, which will be consumed in the second half of March and at the beginning of April. We cover the cloches with straw mats in case of frost. The same precautions should be taken for cauliflowers. Romaines can also be planted in cold frames, from the end of December onwards, to take up all the available material. Cabbages sown at the end of August also require some care. We've seen terrible winters where it was very difficult to save cabbage plants, even those planted early in the autumn and perfectly recovered. False thaws" in particular cook the heart, as we say in the trade, and the plant is completely lost. You can protect yourself to a certain extent against these accidents by putting a handful of dry straw or manure on each cabbage when the frost arrives; you remove it when the plant has recovered, i.e. is no longer wilted. It's precisely while the ground is thawing that the sun "cooks" the heart of the plant. In January, we sow leeks on beds and in trays; they are replanted in the first half of April. Peas also continue to be sown. From the end of the month, Radishes can be sown in coastal areas sheltered from the north wind. Finally, we sow Purslane. The seed 1. is called ainst a beginning of thaw, followed by a sudden resumption of frost. being excessively fine, we mix it with ashes so as not to sow too thickly. The greatest difficulty is getting it to rise. The soil has to be constantly wet, otherwise the seed "contitutes", as the market gardeners say, and doesn't germinate. The treatise on vegetable cultivation by Claude Mollet, gardener to Louis XIII, already mentions sowing Purslane on a bed. As in previous months, we continue to pull up wild chicory for blanching, and to protect lamb's lettuce and other vegetables from frost. Artichokes. - In field crops, artichokes can be reproduced by sowing. In this case, the seed is sown in a nursery in February-March, on a good bed and under a frame. When the young seedlings have developed four or five good leaves, they are lifted into a rootball and planted permanently towards the end of April. In this way, a small harvest can be obtained the following autumn. However, this method of reproduction tends to return the plants to the wild type, which is much slower to bear fruit. Cabbages. - In the second half of February, cabbages are sown to follow those sown at the end of Fig. 18. summer. There are a great many varieties; each country has its own, and cultivation is becoming quite elementary; but Parisian market gardeners now grow only one variety, the Paris Flat Cabbage (fig. 18). It is sown in nurseries on beds and in trays. As soon as it has developed cotyledons, it is transplanted to the ground, also in a nursery, at a rate of four hundred per frame or thirty per bell. It is useful to give it plenty of air. Beans. - The forced cultivation of beans has been abandoned by Parisian market gardeners, but it has lasted longer than that of potatoes and peas, and is still practiced by amateurs who present beautiful specimens in January at the Société nationale d'horticulture. We remember seeing it done during the first years we lived in Paris. The method used for this cultivation was the same as that applied by Parisian market gardeners to almost all their forced crops. In the first days of February, they sowed the beans in a nursery, on a good layer and under a frame; eight days later, they prepared a dull layer, which they called "tranchée", to put the seedlings in place, also under a frame. Four rows of beans were planted per frame, in small clumps, four per row. These rows were planted in such a way that the plants, as they lengthened, were fed by laying them down on the rear side of the frame. The aim of this operation was to make them grow more regularly by giving them less air, and to make them bear fruit. We then had to give them as much air as possible, while protecting them from frost by covering the frames with straw mats; we had to peel the beans often, making sure they had no yellow leaves, and finally, we had to pick them on time, because if we delayed by just one day, the "needles" would be too big and lose their value. This crop was extremely labor-intensive, because once picked, it had to be sorted, the larger needles separated from the smaller ones, which cost much more, weighed in half-kilograms and packed in clean paper. Cutting lettuce - In the old days, when market gardeners didn't yet have the extensive equipment they have today, this crop was grown early in the spring, providing an excellent salad as early as April. All varieties of lettuce, if sown thickly, could be used to produce lettuce for cutting; moreover, whenever more than enough seed has been sown for the planting required, the remainder is cut and consumed as young seedlings. However, when a crop was grown specifically for this purpose, a very blond variety of lettuce was used, which only apples with difficulty, and whose seed is white and very long, and is called Cutting Lettuce. Grain manufacturers' catalogs even list several varieties. The first cultivated was sown in beds in February; if you wanted to get some early, you put frames over it, and by March 15, when it had reached 5 or 6 centimetres, you cut it for consumption. The last one was sown in the ground, in a square, at the beginning of March, to be consumed in the first fortnight of April, i.e. before the arrival of the head lettuces planted on the coast, because as soon as these appeared on the market, the lettuce for cutting no longer found buyers. We remember seeing this crop grown in the same way as Radishes and Spinach, i.e. sown between the racks of the last Beef Heart Cabbages, which were delivered for consumption around May 15 or 20. Lettuce didn't bother them much, since it was cut in the first fortnight of April, and then hoeing was carried out to remove the lettuce roots and any weeds in the cabbage. So this crop cost next to nothing. But today, at the time when this Lettuce used to be sold, there are sometimes more Lettuces on the Paris market than in the middle of spring or summer. Practitioners can no longer grow this crop commercially, as it would no longer be profitable; they prefer to sow Radishes, which always find buyers. In countries where early vegetables are not as plentiful as in Paris, lettuce for cutting is not to be disdained; it can even be grown on its own, by sowing in fairly dense rows. Instead of leaving a part of the kitchen garden unused until April 15th for certain crops that cannot be grown earlier, you can harvest a crop that costs only a few waterings if the weather is dry. Enthusiasts who are far from the cities, and who have a few frames and bells at their disposal, can obtain very tender lettuce in this way from the beginning of March until the time when the first head lettuces are ready to eat. Wild chicory. - In the past, Parisian market gardeners used to heat wild chicory, i.e. grow it 7. in beds, and then cold-roast it in frames. These crops have long since been abandoned, as they are no longer lucrative enough for the trade. However, we still saw cold cultivation in our youth, and we heard the old market gardeners tell us how they practiced forced cultivation. We're going to describe it for the information of amateurs who would like to establish it for their own consumption. In the month of February, a small layer of soil is laid on top of a box, or rather a plank; this layer is filled with 10 to 12 centimetres of potting soil, and the frames are placed on top. When the potting soil is warm, a few days after the layer has been set up, the seed is sown very thickly; it is covered with 15 millimeters of potting soil, and the frames are covered with straw mats. When the seed is well established, which takes barely a few days in these conditions, we give it a little light; but as this spring salad must remain very tender and blond-green, we must not give it air to obtain this result. This is more or less the same type of cultivation as for Romaine "reclochage" on cloche beds. Treated in this way, wild chicory is not hard. When it reaches 10 centimetres in length, we cut the leaves 2 centimetres above the ground, to respect the little hearts, which "reject" a second crop twelve or fifteen days later. The same operation could be repeated, but as the plant ages, it is no longer as tender. For cold cultivation, we sow Wild Chicory on well-prepared soil, in beds the length of frames, under the same conditions as for bed-grown chicory. If, for example, you wish to have a continuous supply of tender chicory, you place a frame over it as soon as you have sown it, but without putting the trunk in place. As soon as the plant's leaves come into contact with the glass, the frames are gradually raised, so that the leaves are always close to the glass. When the wild chicory has emerged on the neighbouring bed, where there is no frame, we place a second one, under the same conditions, and this harvest follows the first. This operation can be continued with a third frame, which is placed on the Chicory only when it is half grown. Well watered and shaded under this frame, it soon becomes tender again. In this way, with three frames, you can have very tender wild chicory throughout the spring. Turnips. - After a season or two of lettuces on beds, the first turnips are sown at the beginning of February, on the same beds that have been turned over. To establish this crop properly, market gardeners don't broadcast the seeds; instead, they place them by hand in pre-made holes. Here's how it's done. You have a frame with a surface area just equal to that of the panel, and fitted with as many rods as you want to make rows. Pointed pieces of wood are fixed in each rod, point downwards, spaced out as the Navets are to be. Simply place the frame on the soil and press down to make all the holes at once - usually twelve rows, and twelve Navets per row. - Then, by hand, two or three seeds are placed in each hole, so that if one is missing, the other lifts; more often than not, all the seeds lift. To fill the holes, a lath is passed over the soil, pressing down a little, and the whole thing is smoothed out. When the plants are well established and in good vegetation, we proceed with thinning, leaving only one turnip in each spot. Treated in this way, these early Turnips come on stream very quickly, as selected merchandise, and with almost no waste. The first ones to be grown need to be warmed by a good layer; otherwise they go to seed and therefore no longer have the same flavor or market value. They also need to be watered every day, to keep them tender and prevent them from going worm-eaten. They also need to be given the necessary air, sometimes from the top of the frame, sometimes from the bottom, to keep them in good vegetation, i.e. neither too soft, as they will then "blow away" into leaves, nor too hard, as they will then go to seed before they are fully developed. As you can see, this cultivation, while not delicate, requires a fair amount ofFig. 19. - Navet Marteau. care if you want to obtain a good product. The forced cultivation of turnips, created by Parisian market gardeners twenty-five to thirty years ago, is very prosperous; it produces a vegetable that is highly prized by gourmets, and gives rise to considerable exports to northern countries. Since it has been practiced, it has produced over one hundred million francs, of which more than two-thirds comes from abroad. It should be added that this perfected cultivation of early turnips (in Paris, only Navet Marteau is used for this crop) has completely ruined exports from the south of France. At first, the products of this crop were very expensive, but today prices are affordable for all pockets, and the result, as we noted in general in our book Les Jardiniers de Paris et leur culture à travers les siècles, is that consumption is still increasing. It's a win-win situation for growers, who are expanding their crops, and consumers, who are paying less. Radish. - Practitioners generally only use radish as a catch crop in other crops. They can be sown on carrot beds, and even with lettuce; in these conditions, they must be sown lightly; all radishes turn and do little harm to the other plants with which they are found, given their rapid growth. We have seen some market gardeners plant them in clumps in turnip beds, at the same time as turnips and using the same procedure. Each clump consists of ten to twelve seeds sown in the same hole. You might think that, under these conditions, the plants would get in each other's way, but this is not the case. As they grow, they move away from each other and all take their place in the sun. Radishes can also be grown alone on an air bed; in this case, they are sown very thickly and covered with straw mats when it freezes. From the end of January, they can be sown in coastal areas sheltered from the Fig. 20. - Round pink radish with white tips. north wind, and continue until the first days of October. There is a very large number of varieties of small Fig. 21. - Round scarlet hátif forcing radish. Radishes of all colors, from the purest white to violet, pink, scarlet and dark red. Shapes vary too: round, half-long, long and very long. Enthusiasts are spoilt for choice. Commercial specialists grow only pink, red and white-tipped red radishes. Early varieties are mainly round reds, which turn over more easily in the bad season. After this first season, white-tipped radishes are grown, and later on, all varieties. Spinach. - From February 15th, spinach is sown at any time until the beginning of August, to be harvested when ready for consumption. Cultivation requires no special care, just watering when the weather is dry. Curly chicory. - Also around February 15th, curly chicory is sown for cold cultivation under a frame, following the sowing of bedding plants in January. For Rouen chicory, 24 plants are planted per panel; for Parisian chicory, 30 or 36. Both require the same care, i.e. frequent watering and adequate air supply. Raising the plants requires the same care as for bedded Chicory. Raves. - According to the Vilmorin catalog, the name Rave, given at the same time to certain turnips and long radishes, often leads to confusion when buying seeds. Rave itself is no longer cultivated in vegetable gardens, where it is preferable to grow one or more varieties of Turnip, among which there is such a wide choice, depending on the country and the season. In the 18th and early 19th centuries, Parisian market gardeners used to force-grow turnips on beds and then under cold frames. This forced cultivation was more or less the same as that for turnips, i.e. you had to sow them not too thickly, heat the roots sufficiently through the bed, and water them enough to keep them tender, while giving them the necessary air, so that the leaves were not too soft or "vewy", as we say in the language of the trade. The forced cultivation of Raves was abandoned by market gardeners, and it was not until half a century later that they undertook the forced cultivation of Navets hâtifs race Marteau, which has become so important in the last twenty-five years. Peas. - Peas continue to be sown, as indicated in January. PLANTING AND MISCELLANEOUS WORK From February 15, we will be planting cabbages that could not be planted in November. The first cauliflowers, sown in September, will be planted out in February, on trays with lettuce already half grown. Most often, five cauliflowers are planted per panel; when the Lettuce is removed, care must be taken to give them air whenever the weather permits, so that they remain in good vegetation and are not too tender. It's better for them to be a little hard than too soft. At the end of the month, curly chicory, sown in January, is planted out. To establish this planting, you need to make a good bed, though not as strong as those used for sowing and transplanting. Market gardeners plant thirty-six chicory plants per panel. The same care continues: shading until the plant is fully established, watering accordingly, every day, and aerating according to the weather. In forced cultivation, there are no precise, absolute rules; it's the weather that dictates, and you must carry out its orders without delay. After four or five weeks, every other plant is lifted to bleach it. Chicories that are not lifted take up all the available space and become larger than the others. Under these conditions, the harvest lasts longer. Capuchin beard. - During this month, we continue to pull up wild Chicory for blanching in the cellars (Capuchin Beard), and to take various protective measures, which we have already indicated. Melons. - Melons sown at the end of January should be planted out when they have two leaves. They should be planted on a new bed, with two or three per frame; the bed should be heated with a thermosiphon, as we have already mentioned for sowing. At this time of year, the greatest difficulty is not in obtaining the necessary heat, but in greening the plant and giving it the right consistency to grow vigorously and produce fruit. To do this, you need a heating method that gives it daylight. These first melons are not grown in exactly the same way as those that will be sown later. They are planted at the bottom of the frame, close to the heating pipe. Specialists don't top the plant; they let it grow a single shoot, which they stop when it has five or six eyes. These develop, and are cut off when they have two or three eyes; it's on the latter, when developed, that the flowers begin to appear. Melon produces both male and female flowers; the latter are known as "meshes". When the young fruits reach the size of a pigeon's egg, we choose the most beautiful, the best placed, and we remove all the others as they form, so that they don't take sap from the first, on which all the strength of the vegetation must be concentrated. Once the melon has "stopped", as we say in the trade, pruning becomes secondary. The wood is left to grow, depending on the vigor of the plant, so that it can fill out the panel, since a vigorously growing plant will always produce more beautiful fruit than a weak, painfully vegetating one. Water very little at this time of year, as the soil generally contains enough moisture. Later on, if the weather is warm and the fruit is in full growth, you can water occasionally, but under no circumstances should you water the melon when the fruit is setting, as this would cause it to "sink". Air is given when the weather permits, as far as possible in the opposite direction to that from which the wind blows. It's in this first melon crop that the great advantage of thermosiphon heating comes to the fore, as it allows you to heat and ventilate at the same time; excess humidity is thus expelled from under the frame, and the plants remain healthy. This type of early cultivation requires a great deal of experience, and not all gardeners succeed, even if they have everything they need to combat bad weather. This is why, in the Paris region, it is only grown by a few specialists and by the leading horticultural schools, such as Versailles, Fleury-Meudon, etc. The other melons consumed in Paris in May come from the Midi. True cultivation of these fruit-vegetables, as they used to be called, begins around February 15, when the sun begins to gain strength. When the plant has developed its two cotyledons, it is transplanted to another layer as warm as the first, and when it has three or four well-formed eyes, the first pruning is carried out. This is called topping, and consists in cutting off the head to leave only two eyes growing above the cotyledons; these eyes will provide the arms! Melon is also susceptible to a disease for which no cure has yet been found; it's called nuile disease, and it develops in cold dews, eating away at the plant as it grows, always attacking the young shoots and fruit. Rust, another dangerous disease, generally only attacks older plants, and could be combated more effectively. Aphids, too, attack melons; we combat them with nicotine spread with water. However, we mustn't wait until these insects are too numerous. They multiply very quickly. Cucumbers. - Cucumbers, as we've already 1. The two main branches that make up the plant. are grown in all seasons in the same way as melons. However, when the fruit begins to swell, pruning should be made to one or two eyes, depending on the degree of vegetation. Moreover, to obtain beautiful, well-shaped, upright fruit, they must not touch anything. When there are too many, we remove a few so that they don't harm the others. Early cucumbers are usually grown in greenhouses; the plants are planted close to the glass, so that the fruit hangs in the air, and to ensure they grow straight, they are placed in a glass tube. This is more the culture of an amateur than a practitioner. It is, however, widely practised in England, where coal is much cheaper than in our country. The whole secret of this cultivation consists in keeping the plant always tender; each time you pick, you must take care to remove all the hard leaves, so that everything is green and young, and so that daylight and air can penetrate everywhere. Water often, and when the sun gets hot, shade the frames with Spanish white. When well cared for, cucumbers can be harvested throughout spring and summer, and in autumn in strong soils. Sometimes, after abundant production, the plant becomes tired and there are short intervals between fruiting. This is the time to rejuvenate the plants, by removing all the old wood and allowing young shoots to take their place. This procedure results in plants that

are still growing well. The most important thing to watch out for is aphids; when you see midges fluttering around your plants, there's no time to lose in watering with diluted nicotine. To syringe or spray nicotine on melons and cucumbers, first turn all the stems upside down, placing them carefully on the ground; it's then very easy to spray the underside of the leaves. When the operation is complete, the stems are returned to their original position. These sprays and syringes should be carried out in the evening, so that the sun doesn't burn the moistened foliage. If, in addition to aphids, rust appears on the plants, simply pull them out. Cucumbers fall into two main categories: green (fig. 22) and white. Each of these categories comprises a large number of varieties. For forced cultivation in winter and spring, green varieties are preferred; on the other hand, ribbed varieties are more commercially sought-after than smooth-skinned varieties, at least on the Paris market. It's up to the grower to choose the varieties most in demand on the market where he sells his produce. Lettuces. - The last lettuces sown towards the end of October are removed around February 15th, when heavy frosts are no longer to be feared; if any should occur after removal, care should be taken to cover the plants with straw mats. Romaine. - At the same time, we counter-plant North path South path Fig. 23 - Romaine counter-planting. six rows of other grey Romaines, one between two bells. If we look closely at the figure showing this arrangement (fig. 23), we'll notice that each row of bells is flanked by a row of Romaines in front and behind, making two rows of Romaines for one row of bells. These Romaine feet are placed in the free space between each bell. Artichokes. - From February 15th onwards, we begin to give light watering and increasing amounts of air to artichokes that have been grommeted in the autumn; this gradually hardens them out, so that they can be depanelled at the beginning of March. This month also sees the sowing of a large number of vegetables. Cauliflower. - The first summer cauliflowers are sown in the first fortnight of March, on old soil, i.e. soil with little or no caloric content, and under a frame. Give them plenty of air as soon as the seeds have emerged. If you're not afraid of heavy frosts, you should troubleshoot as soon as the seedlings have firmed up sufficiently. For all summer and autumn cauliflower seedlings, we prefer to sow fairly lightly and not transplant; the plants are more vigorous in these conditions. Carrots. - The last Carrots on a bed are sown in the first days of the month, on a bed with cloches or even on a bed in the open air. Carrots are then sown in the ground throughout spring and summer. After weeding and thinning, it requires no care other than watering when needed. Generally, other vegetables are sown into the carrot, such as radishes and spinach, or lettuces and romaine; however, care must be taken not to sow or plant too close together, so that the carrot also has its place in the sun. Carrot seed is very fine when well winnowed. If you plant Radishes and Lettuce, you need to sow a good centilitre per panel; if you don't plant anything with Carrots, you need a little less seed, because none is wasted. Market gardeners mainly grow the obtuse semi-long carrot for spring and summer, but there are many other varieties. Carrot flesh is divided into two zones: the outer one is more colorful and tender, while the central one is more yellow and more solid. This inner zone, called the "heart", even becomes woody to the point of being inedible, under the influence of certain circumstances, for example when Carrots age, when they go to seed, or when they suffer from thirst. There are two varieties of half-long carrots known as heartless, because their central zone, following a long and skilful selection process, has become as red and as fleshy as the periphery. These are the Nantaise and Chantenay carrots (fig. 24), both of which originate from the market gardens around Nantes. The former has a rounded shape, almost no larger at the neck than at the tip. The second, on the other hand, is very flared at the neck. Both varieties are excellent for growing in small gardens, but their yield is too low for market gardening. To grow them well, it's essential not to let them suffer from alternating drought and humidity, as their hearts would become woody. Large vegetable farms also grow a large carrot, intermediate in length between the early short carrot and the obtuse half-long S carrot, but much more voluminous; Fig. 24 - Chantenay half-long red carrot. this is the Guérande carrot (fig. 25). Very good for Fig. 25. - Carotte rouge demi-longue obtuse de Guérande. cooking, it is high-yielding and drought-resistant; but it is not sought after for market gardening because of its somewhat slow growth. Other red carrots are more widely cultivated; the long ones, along with white carrots, are used as root fodder. Turnips. - Parisian specialists who grow this crop on a large scale (some of them have 500 or 600 panels) plant turnips cold, i.e. in the ground, at the end of March or beginning of April. They set up boxes with 10 to 15-centimeter planks, which they secure in the ground with stakes. They plant the turnips in the same way as explained for growing on beds, and bring the frames from the first crops to the new ones. In the climate of Paris, turnips are planted on beds until March 15th or 20th; it is certain that in colder regions it will be necessary to make beds to establish these crops until April 1st; however, they can be made less strong than those we have indicated for the previous month. At this time, use whatever materials you have on hand. It is essential, however, that the layer does not dry out, otherwise the turnips will become worm-eaten. Cold-grown turnips, like hot-grown ones, need to be watered every day; this is essential if they are to remain tender and not go to seed, which often happens when cultivation is neglected. But the most important thing to watch out for at this time of year is aeration. Almost as soon as the turnips have emerged, you need to give them some air, at first very little, then gradually more, and taking care to change, i.e. to give air sometimes from the top of the frame, sometimes from the bottom. One of the most important points in forced cultivation is knowing how to aerate plants properly. In a special chapter, we have provided the information you need to set up the racks used to regulate aeration. Chicory and Scarolea. - This "cold" cultivation method is also used from the end of March for various other vegetables, such as Chicory, Scarole, etc., for which background heat is no longer essential. As for chicories, the fine Parisian variety and Chicorée Rouennaise are still used for cold cultivation. Leeks. - Along with cabbage and onions, leeks are one of the least delicate vegetables. It can be sown in the open ground in March, fairly early in the season, and grown all year round, taking care to put some in the cellar before the frosts. To obtain beautiful, white leeks, it is necessary to pull them up when they are as big as a schoolboy's pencil, and to replant them by sinking them deeply into the ground, then watering them often, as otherwise they get worm-eaten during severe droughts, and you are obliged to cut them flush with the earth. The most common way to grow leeks, which we could call "everyone's crop", is to sow them at the end of February or the beginning of March, and plant them at the end of May or even in June. This is enough to produce almost all year round. Specialists sell this season's leeks in July and August, and then plant salads in their fields. Leeks can be sown either in nurseries or in the field. In the latter case, you need to sow at least five times lighter than in the nursery. We estimate that you need about 1.5 kilograms of seed per acre in a nursery. Once sown, the seed is harrowed with a pitchfork and then top-dressed; later, weeded and watered as required. In short, to obtain beautiful Leeks, you need to use plenty of fertilizer, plant lightly and deeply, to get white, and water copiously. Treated in this way, especially for amateur growers, Leeks sown in March and transplanted in May will produce all year round. This excellent vegetable, used almost everywhere in soups and stews, can also be eaten in the same way as asparagus. Its taste is hardly inferior to that of Asparagus, and its price is always much lower; it has therefore been nicknamed the poor man's Asparagus. Most of the leeks that arrive at the Halles de Paris are produced by farmers in the outer suburbs, who grow only large vegetables. They sow in March, transplant in May, and sell from late summer to the following spring. There are a number of varieties, almost all of which are good to grow; however, the ones most generally adopted in the Paris area are the Poireau de Rouen and the Poireau long d'hiver de Paris. But, we repeat, it is cultivation that plays the greatest role in obtaining beautiful plants of all varieties. Lettuces and Romaines. - Cold cultivation can be started as early as January, weather permitting and if frames are available. The 8. variety of lettuce most commonly used for this purpose is the white-seeded Gotte lettuce, which grows larger and later than the black-seeded Gotte lettuce. As it needs to be more full-bodied, it can be given a little air, depending on the temperature; this type of cultivation produces very fine products. You can also grow other varieties of lettuce that don't get too carried away. We've grown a small variety of red lettuce ourselves, which did very well. Finally, for this crop, you already have a choice of varieties: either black-seeded gotte lettuce (42 per "market gardener" frame), or white-seeded gotte lettuce (36 per frame), or larger varieties, in which case you'll have to make do with 30, and even then, don't grow the large summer varieties, which would get too carried away and peel with difficulty. You can also plant Romaines for this "cold" culture, at a rate of twenty per panel, or even ten Lettuces and ten Romaines together. The best Romaine variety to choose for this is Romaine grise. All it needs is air and watering. Lettuces and Romaines can also be sown outdoors as early as March. Nothing is easier than growing these plants. The important thing is to water them every day when it's not raining. During the summer, they have a tendency to grow upwards instead of downwards, if they have not been well watered throughout the vegetation period. One month after sowing, they are ready to be planted. From March onwards, they can be sown to produce continuously throughout the summer, until the end of August, when cloche cultivation begins. The state of the moon, to which the ancients attached so much importance, has no appreciable influence. Today, we say to amateurs: Sow when you want, not too thickly, keep your plant tender, plant it young, continue to keep the plants tender by watering, and you'll harvest: that's the secret. When the Romaine is capped, we bind it to soften it even more, and to avoid breaking it when we pull it out. For spring sowing, we especially recommend Romaine blonde, which should be grown as early as possible, but only when there's no longer any need to worry about severe cold, as this variety is particularly tender. This is its great quality. Black radish. - Some Parisian market gardeners grow black radish under cold frames, just like turnips. It is sown towards the end of March or at the beginning of April, in rows under a frame. The best way is the same as for turnips. All you need to do then is water frequently and provide sufficient air so that the leaves don't become too tender; without this care, Black Radishes become worm-eaten or go to seed before they have fully developed. Spinach. - Spinach continues to be sown, generally among other crops such as Lettuce, Romaine, Chicory, Scarole, etc., but with care. Careful, clear sowing yields beautiful crops, which are harvested when ready to eat. In this way, you can have a succession of crops that take up no space and cost almost nothing. However, spinach can also be sown on its own; in this case, it should be sown in rays. It's always preferable to sow spinach in succession during the summer, rather than picking what you've got, because when they grow back they go to seed and are not as beautiful and tender as the young ones. In spring, it's best to sow Holland spinach, Viroflay spinach and lettuce spinach. It's a good idea to water spinach when it's dry, but never when the sun is hot. Water early in the morning, or in the evening, but only when the leaves are no longer hot; otherwise, they become "tavelled", i.e. the cold water literally cooks them. The same phenomenon occurs on lettuces when they are plucked. Sorrel. - Sorrel can be sown throughout spring and summer, but spring is always preferable, so that it can be harvested all year round, since it sets seed as early as May of the following year. Cultivation requires no special care; it is sown in rays, to make weeding easier, and between the rays is planted a row of lettuce, either Lettuce or Romaine, or even both, alternating. Unprotected sorrel remains dormant over winter, but as soon as the ground thaws it starts to grow again. Sorrel needs to be picked with a certain amount of care if it is to look good and be harvested often. In the first treatise on "courtillage" written in French, published in 1393 in the Ménagier de Paris and signed "Un bourgeois de Paris", the author says that it should be picked "à maistrise", i.e. remove all the large leaves around the edge and leave the heart leaves to grow, which, a fortnight later, have in turn become good to pick, and so on. We have nothing to add to what our 11th-century predecessor has to say on this subject. There is a long-established variety of sorrel that doesn't have the disadvantage of climbing; it's called virgin sorrel. It is planted in clumps and kept that way for several years. We believe that this plant comes from ordinary sorrel, which, after having had its flower stalks cut off for a number of seasons, has lost the habit of producing them. Virgin sorrel is mainly grown by private individuals, who need relatively little, whereas ordinary sorrel, which provides a lot, is grown by specialists who supply city markets. Wild chicory. - In March, wild chicory continues to be sown in cold frames, as described last month. As for cultivation in the open ground, in the Paris area this is now done only by growers of large vegetables, and mainly with a view to producing Capuchin Beard. To do this, sow the plants lightly in the open field at the end of March and beginning of April. Care should be taken to avoid tiring these plants too much in summer through repeated harvesting. Cabbage. - The cabbage season, which comes after those sown in beds in February, is very easy to grow. We sow in nurseries, not too thickly, so that the cabbages can grow sufficiently on the spot, without withering, until May, when we replant them. Spring-sown varieties all grow quite large; only three are planted per square metre. All you need to do then is hoe them when necessary and water them according to the water available. If the soil is rich in fat and fertilizer, and you give them plenty of water, you'll get monster cabbages. An example of this is the cabbage that grows on land irrigated by city sewage. This is what can be called large-scale market gardening. Cabbage can be sown in succession until June. Tomato. - In a way, this Solanée is a recent crop in the Paris region; it was only at the beginning of the 19th century that practitioners began to cultivate it. Over the last half-century, its cultivation has expanded considerably. Certainly, it cannot aspire to provide the same services as its sister, the potato, but it nevertheless holds an honourable place among the most useful vegetables. It is more difficult to grow than the Potato, and in the Parisian climate and in much of France, it always needs a few tricks up its sleeve, whereas the Potato requires no special care, except that it must not be allowed to freeze. Country dwellers will do well to grow a few vines for their own consumption, and if necessary to store some for the winter, exactly as is done for Peas and Beans. To grow good tomatoes in the Paris climate, sow the seeds in a nursery on a bed and under a frame around the middle of March. Like all seeds sown under these conditions, they are simply covered with a thin layer of compost. When the seedling is a few centimetres long, it is transplanted to the nursery on another layer; even specialists, after a while, pull it out and transplant it a second time, lighter than the first. Treated in this way, the plant is as big as a finger and can be planted out around May 15, when there is no longer any fear of frost. It is necessary to give it air when it is under the frame, gradually, so that it hardens sufficiently and is not "seized" when planted outside. Its condition tells the grower how much or how little air to give it; nevertheless, it should be kept firm rather than too tender, so that it bears fruit more easily. In our opinion, ordinary tomato cultivation, although requiring some care, should be much more widespread than it is in the countryside. The plant is not delicate in itself, and can grow in all types of soil, like the potato. Instead of using the tricks of the trade, we could sow it in April, along a wall sheltered from the north wind, and let it grow on the spot. A dozen or so plants planted at Om, 50 apart, along a wall, would suffice for a family's consumption, and would provide them with appreciable well-being, as this fruit is very healthy, can be eaten in many ways, and the sauce prepared with its juice pleases just about everyone. Southerners even eat the fruit raw, like an apple. Today, there are a large number of tomato varieties, most of which are amateur varieties. Growers in the suburbs of Paris, who work especially for shipping, cultivate the old ribbed variety (fig. 26), which is the firmest, and therefore crushes less in packing baskets than some of the more modern, rounder, juicier and more tender varieties. Gardeners Fig. 26. - Ribbed Tomato. who grow this crop for the markets of the towns they live in, and amateurs who want to obtain a good Fig. 27. - Path Tomato. production, should preferably grow the Path Tomato (fig. 27). This variety was bred and selected by one of our colleagues, Mr. Chemin, who has been growing it for some twenty years; it has a large, round, juicy, bright-red fruit, like a gigantic cherry. There are also many similar varieties on the market. As for connoisseurs, they can indulge their fantasies, for there are tomato varieties that resemble all kinds of fruit: apple, pear, plum, cherry, red currant, etc. These oddities have their hiding places. These quirks have their own cachet, and give a particular garden a certain originality that is much appreciated by connoisseurs. As tomatoes are prone to cryptogamic diseases, we advise growers to sulphate the stakes used to trellis them. According to the findings of various scientists, notably the late Professor Cornu, sulfating prevents disease from occurring near the stakes, and also helps to preserve them. It's also a good idea to sulfate tomatoes, like grapes, but with weaker solutions, e.g. 1 kilogram of copper sulfate and 1 kilogram of potash per 100 liters of water. This treatment should be applied preventively, and repeated if necessary. Eggplant. - Eggplants, which belong to the same botanical genus as tomatoes, require much the same care in raising seedlings. It is often sown on the same bed, and transplanted in exactly the same way. Once established, however, cultivation is not the same as for tomatoes. The stems of the latter are weak and crawl over the ground if not staked, whereas the Aubergine forms a small shrub at an early age that stands well without needing a stake. Practitioners who prune Aubergines are more concerned with building up this shrub than with obtaining more beautiful fruit. We've been doing this ourselves for a number of years, and we've never noticed that pruned plants produce better fruit than others. The pruning we did was mainly to facilitate access to the patch, as this plant has very hard thorns that prick like needles. We sowed the Aubergine on a bed and under a frame on March 15; we transplanted it on a bed, in a nursery, fifteen or twenty days later, to put it in place in the first fortnight of May. Eggplant cultivation was quite lucrative in the days when the Midi sent little or none to Paris. Today, it has been all but abandoned by Parisian market gardeners. We believe, however, that it could still be profitable. Instead of bringing the crop forward, since the Midi sends its produce early, we could delay it: for example, we could plant Aubergines at the end of June, after the last layers of cloches have been removed, to start harvesting at the end of August, and as soon as the cool September nights arrive, which give the fruit its nil, especially as the plant ages, we could superimpose two boxes one on top of the other and place the frames on them. At this time of year, this would cost nothing, since the frames are stored and not in use; and in this way, by providing plenty of daytime air, we could extend the harvest until well into autumn. Eggplants are not as useful as tomatoes; their fruit is not as widely appreciated. However, southerners, who grow this plant in open fields, are quite fond of it. But the fruit itself doesn't have much flavor, and to make a pleasant dish out of it, you have to prepare it in such a way that the sauce costs more than the fish, as the cooks say. There are several varieties of Aubergine on the market; the long violet (fig. 28), which is black in color, is the preferred variety. The other varieties are more suitable for amateur Fig. 28 - Long violet eggplant. cultivation. One white variety is highly original; its fruit resembles hen's eggs. The shrub is quite pretty, and a few plants in an amateur garden will not disappoint; but its fruit is not edible. Celery. - This old French plant used to be cultivated only in autumn. We say French, because Charlemagne, in his Capitularies, recommended its cultivation to his gardeners. Today, we have a number of varieties, and as early as July we see them on the markets. Among the most recommendable varieties is Céleri Chemin (fig. 29), obtained by the same grower - Fig. 29. - Céleri Chemin. who fixed the tomato variety of the same name. Having noticed some Celery plants in his fields that tended towards blond, he harvested seed from these plants, carried out an ongoing selection process, and finally succeeded in establishing a variety of beautiful golden Celery, which whitens on its own without being covered. This first Celery needs to be sown on a warm enough bed around March 15, and transplanted under the same conditions so that it doesn't go to seed immediately. Market gardeners generally plant it on beds after harvesting early crops such as turnips and carrots. It needs to be planted fairly thickly so that it holds and whitens, or rather gilds better. AHere are now several closely related varieties of collex, called Céleris dorés (golden celery). For mowing, it is preferable to grow Céblos, which should be covered with straw to whiten them. For winter, harder varieties are preferable, in particular green Celery, which has to be buried to blanch, and which keeps longer. At present, some young market gardeners are starting to grow early golden celery on beds and in cold frames, so that their harvest immediately follows that of the last green celery kept over winter. Celery root. - Another very old type of Celery, if not the oldest of all, is Celeriac. It is sown on an old bed in March, transplanted under the same conditions, and the plants put in place in June. There are a number of varieties of Celery root. If you want to keep some over winter, choose the hardiest ones, especially the small-leafed Celerirave, which doesn't have many leaves and stands up well to the cold. Cutting celery. - There's another kind of Celery that's grown for its leaves, called Cutting Celery. It is smaller than the previous ones, and its ribs are hollow. It is mainly used as a condiment in spring and summer, when there are no Golden Celery leaves. Cultivation is straightforward: sow in late March on a well-tilled bed. When the leaves reach 15 or 20 centimetres, cut 2 or 3 centimetres from the ground to spare the little hearts. Clean it up, water it again and, fifteen or twenty days later, cut it again. This process continues until frost. Thus treated, it is very tender and can be eaten as a salad. In the past, market gardeners used to grow a little on beds and under frames, to get some earlier, and then under cold frames. CONDIMENTS A number of condiments are also sown or divided in March. Under this heading, we've grouped vegetable plants that are mainly used for seasoning, either raw, in salads or on certain dishes, or cooked, in sauces. In general, their cultivation takes up little space compared to other crops, and there's no need to aim for large-scale production of condiments. For this reason, we recommend planting them in shady areas, or in areas that are less suitable for other vegetable crops. Chervil can be sown as soon as the ground has thawed, and then throughout the year until September 15. It requires no special care; specialists cut it as soon as it is ripe, and turn over the soil to sow more. Individuals can sow it once and have it for most of the year, because when cut carefully, not too close to the ground, it grows back like sorrel and parsley. The Ciboule is a bulbous plant of the same genus as the Onion, of which it has the same flavor, but the bulbs are less voluminous. It is sown from the end of February to August 15, in rays rather than broadcast, in newly tilled, loose soil. After sowing, specialists generally plant a row of Romaine between the rays of Ciboule. Romaine is ready to eat at the end of May, and doesn't interfere too much with Ciboule, which is still in its infancy. It is only towards midsummer that it begins to grow and is used for consumption; however, amateurs can thin it out before this time. In small vegetable gardens, where Ciboule is left in place for longer, each plant forms cloves the following spring; these are replanted separately, and each forms a new clump, so there's no need to sow them every year. Practitioners, on the other hand, pull up everything in summer or autumn, and sow it again in spring. Naturally, it's only in the vicinity of large cities that you can grow Ciboule over a certain area, as large quantities are never consumed. Garlic and shallot. - Garlic and shallots multiply by separating the cloves formed by the large bulbs. In the case of garlic in particular, it is essential to choose the largest bulbs for propagation, if you do not want to see it degenerate rapidly. Despite this precaution, it has always been observed in Paris that, to obtain large, healthy garlic, you have to buy bulbs from other regions almost every year. Garlic seems to have little difficulty with soil quality. However, without being able to explain exactly why, we sometimes see it "greasy", i.e. affected by a kind of rot that stops its vegetation. In this case, transplanting the garlic onto ridges, to protect it from humidity, excess humus or water stagnation after heavy rains, is often enough to prevent it from greasing. Cresson de fontaine and Cresson alénois. - Watercress is only grown by specialists occupying land that is, if not marshy, at least traversed by watercourses. The water is distributed in ditches, with a gentle current, and sluices are installed to fill or empty the ditches at will. To sow the seed, the ditches are at least partially emptied, and the seed is sown on their reverse side; the ditches are then filled, with a gentle current of water. The plant grows and soon covers the entire surface of these small streams. Then it's just a matter of picking as needed. Enthusiasts who have a stream at their disposal can thus obtain a very good vegetable at low cost. Cresson alénois can be grown in gardens in much the same way as Pourpier, without any further difficulty. Parsnips. - Parsnips are sown in spring, when there is no need to fear heavy frosts. However, they can be sown as early as the end of February, in coastal areas, by planting a few rows of fairly light Romaine among the parsnips. In Paris, this crop is only grown by growers of large vegetables; they sow in April, preferably in rays, and fairly light; in this way, the roots become larger, and the leaves longer. All cultivation consists of hoeing the soil and watering from time to time, if water is available; from midsummer onwards, you can start to consume, and continue through autumn, winter and until the following spring, when the plants go to seed. Parsnips have very limited uses, at least in the Paris region; they are used only to flavour soups. Parsley. - Parsley is sown as soon as the severe frosts have passed, preferably in rays. This plant takes a very long time to grow, so specialists sow Radishes and Spinach at the same time, and plant either Lettuce or Romaine, sometimes both together, alternating them. Once the first crop has been harvested (i.e. spinach or radishes), weeding is carried out and watering is carried out when necessary. But this type of cultivation is only suitable for specialists who sell their produce in the big cities. As for private individuals who only grow for their own needs, they need such a small quantity of parsley that a small corner in a vegetable garden bed is enough to establish it; more often than not, not even all of it is used. In the past, parsley was only used for medicinal purposes; later, it became a condiment plant that took a very important place in the culinary arts. There is no vegetable garden, however small, without a corner reserved for parsley. In fact, it's extremely easy to grow: all you have to do is water it from time to time. The more you water it, the faster it grows and the more it produces. To pick it properly, proceed as we said for Sorrel, always picking the large leaves at the tip and leaving the heart to grow. A variety of parsley is grown for ornamental purposes: dark green curly parsley, which grows vigorously and forms strong, dense clumps. 9. . - m P . . m . W . . W Pimento. - Chillies have never played a major role in market gardening. In the past, however, there were practitioners who devoted a few layers to this crop. Today, there are hardly any. They would sow the seeds on warm soil in March, and in May they would plant them in two rows per bed, spacing the plants 40 to 50 centimetres apart. Chillies can also be planted in the ground, but they grow more slowly than on old beds. Once the fruits are well knotted, you need to give them plenty of water to make them swell. When cultivated as described above, fruits begin to turn red in August, and continue to follow one another until the frosts. Purslane. - In March, start sowing Purslane in the garden (see instructions given in January). Tarragon. - Tarragon, whose name has come to be known as Estragon, can be propagated by splitting. All you need is one foot to reproduce it in profusion. However, as it is used only for its aromatic flavor, only a small quantity is needed if you grow it for your own needs. However, in the vicinity of large cities where there is a significant vinegar and canning industry, this plant can be grown commercially, and some Parisian market gardeners have entire squares of it. It's very easy to grow; all you need to do is water it when it's dry. Of course, it grows better and branches out more when planted in good, clean, deep-tilled soil. Tarragon chips are planted at the end of March and in April, or towards the end of July. Civet. - Civet is also a condiment much used in salads, but requires so little that two plants are perfectly sufficient for a household. It is reproduced, like tarragon, by splitting off pieces. It requires no special cultivation care. Artichokes continue to be sown in March, if you wish to use this method of propagation; but we would point out that the subjects it provides are often inferior to the cultivated type; in general, eyeletting provides a sufficiently rapid means of renewing and increasing the plantation. We are also continuing to sow Radishes, and we are starting to sow Spinach in the ground, which will be harvested at the end of April. PLANTING AND MISCELLANEOUS WORK Artichokes - In small gardens, for example, where frames and boxes are available, artichokes can be oiled in spring, as soon as they can be removed from the mother plants, and transplanted to a warm bed in the nursery. When they are well rooted, they can be removed in clods and planted out, ensuring good vegetation. This method, very practical for those who have the necessary equipment, is market gardening par excellence. It is described by Mr. Ch. Grosdemange. We don't think we can do any better in small-scale cultivation. In the October issue, we also mentioned Mr. Legros' method of preparing carnations in pots in autumn, and placing them in frame boxes over winter. Towards the end of March, these Artichoke carnations grown under frames are ready for planting. They are carefully unstuck and planted in pre-prepared holes. If you don't use this method, and the winter has been very harsh, you won't have many carnations to plant. However, you can replenish your supply of artichoke plants by following the method described by Mr. Grosdemange, which was devised by a horticulturist near Melun after the terrible winter of 1890-91. When he started his artichokes around March 20, he found only 15 or 20 still alive out of 3 or 400. He had the idea of removing these few clods and placing them on a warm layer under a frame; they soon produced numerous eyelets, which enabled the plantation to be reconstituted in May. This is, in fact, an exceptional case. Artichokes usually produce well-constituted eyelets. The amateur who grows a few plants for his own consumption will plant three or four carnations per clump, and with a little watering will ensure a good recovery. The clumps should be spaced 75 centimetres apart, and care should be taken to press the plants in only up to the heel. Many people who are not in the trade think that a plant recovers better when it is well embedded; the opposite is true. Once the artichokes have been planted and taken up, all that's left to do is to hoe them to destroy the weeds and water them copiously, because the more you water them, the more beautiful heads you'll get, especially if the soil has been well smoked. In market gardening, the essential condition for success is to give plenty of fertilizer. At the end of winter, when heavy frosts are no longer to be feared, the artichoke cover is removed and the mounds cut down, then the soil is smoked and ploughed. It's often while this ploughing is being done that we proceed with the "œilletonnage". Two or three well-formed eyelets should be left on vigorous plants, and just one on weaker ones; the best-formed eyelets are used for new plantings, and the smaller ones are discarded if not needed. But in any case, you mustn't leave more than one on each plant, otherwise the plant will become exhausted and produce nothing but small artichokes. Artichoke cultivation generally requires well-developed, rich and fairly moist soil. Near Bray-sur-Seine, we had the opportunity to see one of the most beautiful crops in existence. This crop is grown in peaty soil, on a fine sand base, and Fig. 30. - Large green artichoke from Laon. near the banks of the Seine. It should also be said that this locality is fed by springs that flow under the peat and maintain, by capillary action, a certain constant degree of humidity around the artichoke roots, so that the specialists who grow them do not need to water. There are a number of varieties of artichoke, but the most recommended and cultivated in France is the A. vert de Laon or de Paris (fig. 30). Elsewhere, other varieties are grown, and it could be said that, for artichokes as for cabbages, each country has its own particular variety. The Artichaut Camus de Bretagne, which is earlier than the previous variety, is grown in Brittany and Anjou. An improved sub-variety of Artichaut de Bretagne, called Artichaut de Niort, is grown mainly in the Deux-Sèvres département. These varieties are mainly grown for export. Artichoke vert-gris is grown in south-west France. The green Artichoke of Provence is widespread in the southeast; its heads are prized for eating raw, with pepper. Artichoke violet is grown in Algeria; it's a very delicate variety, but in this country, where there's no fear of frost, it can be grown in complete safety. There are also many sub-varieties derived, by selection, from these various types. Asparagus. - Asparagus is usually grown in the field rather than in the garden. Choose a good one-year-old plant, whose claw has already reached a certain consistency. If you want white asparagus, plant it in wide furrows, 80 cm apart and 60 cm apart in the row. The soil should be well loosened and smoked. Asparagus is not very delicate in terms of soil; however, it prefers sandy soil to clay, but can be grown almost anywhere. Once planted, all you have to do is hoe the soil to keep it clean and loosened. In the third year, you start buttering it for harvesting, but this first year without tiring it too much, i.e. picking for no more than a month; in subsequent years, you can extend picking to six weeks. A well-cultivated asparagus crop, grown in suitable soil and well-smoked, can last ten to twelve years, provided it is fertilized. As for growing green asparagus in the normal season, it's a crop reduced to its simplest form. All you have to do is let the asparagus grow, and pick it before it gets too high, i.e. when it's quite tender, because later its stem becomes woody. Asparagus is grown in vineyards, where certain plants can be grown in vines. Strawberry plants. - The strawberry plant grows spontaneously throughout most of Europe. In the 14th century, under Charles V, it was cultivated more as a decorative plant than for fruit production. Olivier de Serres, in 1600, cultivated it for the product; he says of this plant: "It is so easy to pick up that only small shoots with a few subtle filaments are needed to grow. Suffering as well from cold as from shade, they come naturally, without cultivation, through agrarian forests, among the clump of trees. However, they become engrossed as they are treated. So, to grow large strawberries, transplant them to a sunny spot in the garden, weed them well and, in drought, water them, cut off any running shoots and force them to stay in their lodges. But to get bigger and more plentiful strawberries than common, strawberry plants need special treatment. This is by not allowing them to climb to the ground, thus forcing them to rise to the top, shaping themselves like a small shrub. This is done by cutting off, with the fingernail, the shoots that want to climb to the ground, according to their natural shape. For this reason, the plants are planted a foot apart, in rows. So the land, after cultivation, will yield Strawberries exceeding in size, goodness and abundance the common ones, and in such qualities will make themselves almost admirable if the breed of itself is good. Considering that by such treatment the wildest become free! For ordinary strawberry cultivation, there is little to add to these indications, except that over the last 300 years, successive practitioners have succeeded in establishing a large number of varieties, numbering in the hundreds, many of which produce fruit of colossal dimensions. Now that these varieties are well established, true growers prefer to reproduce them by sowing, which produces more vigorous subjects than the "jettons" mentioned by Olivier de Serres; they are less likely to degenerate, as the great agronomist observed, since he indicated that the vines should be forced to grow taller and all the "jettons" should be cut back, as they always tend to revert to their primitive type. Nevertheless, the majority of strawberry plants grown today come from these "jettons", which we call "nets" or "coulants"; as they take root, they form the plants. Nothing is easier than to 1. olivier de Serres, Théâtre de l'Agriculture. obtain them; all you have to do is let the plant grow freely, but this is to the detriment of production. The best net to take to maintain the purity of the variety and to obtain a good product is the first one to develop. So there are two different ways of growing strawberries. The first is nursery cultivation, the aim of which is to create seedlings using nets. To do this, plant two rows of strawberry plants in a bed, leaving a free space on each side where the runners can take root. To help them do this, cut off all the flowers on the mother plant, so that all the sap flows to the runners.
