These grow very quickly; if possible, water them when the weather is dry, and in autumn you'll have perfectly formed plants which you can plant in place, and which will bear fruit the following spring. The second type of cultivation is that designed to produce fruit. On this point, there's nothing to add to what Olivier de Serres said. This cultivation is the opposite of the previous one: the runners must be carefully removed, so that all the strength of the vegetation is focused on the fruit. We're talking here about four-season strawberries, because most of the varieties grown for the trade are not remontant, they give a season of fruit in spring, and the harvest is over for the year. During the summer, runners develop and take root, but as there is no more fruit, this is not a problem. Thousands of hectares of this crop are grown in the greater Paris suburbs. We say: the greater suburbs, because they extend over a radius of at least 50 kilometers around the capital. Over the past twenty-five years, strawberry growing has developed considerably. In addition to the large quantities of strawberries needed to satisfy the "Paris belly", confectioners use them to make jams, and distillers use them to make a liqueur they call "fraisette". We have said that there are hundreds of varieties of non-remontant strawberries. Today, sowers have succeeded in establishing a few varieties of Quatresaisons, i.e. remontant strawberries, whose fruits have been considerably enlarged by crossing them with large-fruited varieties. These include Jeanne-d'Arc (fig. 31), Belle de Meaux (fig. 32), Saint-Antoine de Padoue, etc., which produce remarkably large fruit right up to the frosts. Until now, these varieties have only been cultivated by Fig. 32 - Strawberry of the Four Seasons Belle de Meaux. amateurs; we don't know whether specialists will adopt them. Ordinary Strawberry cultivation is to be recommended to rural populations, especially that of improved Four-Season Strawberries, which require no special care; for if the nets are allowed to grow, they will bear fruit the following year. The fruit will be a little smaller, but that's of little importance to people who don't grow for profit. A few nets are all you need to quickly expand your crop and enjoy an excellent dessert that costs nothing more than the trouble of picking it. Melons. - When summer̂tés Melons start to develop their two "arms", they are replanted on a third layer! at a rate of two per frame; amateurs can put three, the fruit will simply become a little smaller. You can leave one fruit on each arm. Instead of planting the melons at the bottom of the frame, as we did with those from the previous season, which are heated with the thermosiphon, we now plant them in the middle of the layer, and the arms extend on both sides, towards the top and bottom of the frame. The first pruning these Melons undergo consists in removing the two cotyledons, or first leaves; they are also called ears, and the operation is called the Melon auricle. Subsequent pruning is carried out in the same way as described above. It's the gardener's experience that tells him whether to prune longer or shorter; he must take into account a host of circumstances: the weather, the nature of the soil, the variety he's growing, and so on. The same variety, planted in two different areas, should not be pruned in the same way. However, in principle, the pruning theory can be formulated as follows: prune both 1. For the preparation of this layer, see chapter II. first branches, or arms, with four eyes; those that develop later, with two eyes, and those of the third series with one eye. It is on the latter that the fruits are formed. In short, the important thing is to avoid wood and force the plant to bear fruit; once the fruit is well established, the plant can be left to grow as it pleases. Before market gardeners introduced frames to their equipment, they hardly cultivated anything but the market melon. It was easy to grow, thanks to its hardiness. This melon has a slightly elongated shape, with a green, embroidered rind and slightly pronounced slices, Fig. 33 - Prescott melon, white background. especially on the stem side. Cultivated as a back-season crop until around 1870, it has been more or less abandoned by growers since that time. With the adoption of frames came the cultivation of Cantaloupe melons, already grown in large houses throughout the last century. Today, every market gardener, so to speak, has his own variety, from white (fig. 33) to gray, and of different sizes. For a number of years now, we've been growing the Melon de ChyFig. 34 - Melon Kroumir parisien. pre or varieties that more or less resemble it, including a much-improved one called Melon Kroumir parisien (fig. 34). These melons are very hardy and require less care than Cantaloupes. They can be planted in the open ground, without layers, with cloches simply to facilitate recovery. This is a boon for the working population, as the introduction of the Melon Kroumir makes this fruit accessible to all pockets, and, importantly, everyone can afford an excellent Melon ripe on the vine, in full vegetation, which makes a big difference to the products that come from the Midi, picked eight or fifteen days before ripening, and which ripen on straw or in front of fruit merchants. Finally, market gardeners leave two, three or four fruits on each Kroumir melon plant, so that you can buy a small, top-quality melon for O fr. 50, O fr. 60 or O fr. 75, whereas in the past you had to spend at least 1 fr. 50 to get a good Cantaloup. In fact, when the family is not large, it's much nicer to have a small melon, which can be eaten in a single meal, than to have a large one, part of which you have to save for the next day and which loses much of its flavor. Cucumbers. - Cucumbers are grown in the same way as melons. We'll just add one observation. We have often found, when growing this crop, that it is useful to leave the frames on the plants as late as possible, taking care to shade the squares with Spanish white. This keeps the plants tender and protects them more easily from rust and grayscale, which often attack them as they age, and against which we know of no remedy - a remedy that would be all the more difficult to apply in the case of worn-out plants. White cucumber varieties grown in late season are generally larger and even longer than green cucumbers, and their cultivation is even less delicate, if possible. Onions. - White onions that have not been planted in time before the frosts are planted at the beginning of March. As soon as the severe frosts are no longer to be feared, a number of onion varieties can be sown. The smallest known species, and the earliest, is the very early white Queen's Onion, which measures no more than 3 or 4 centimetres in diameter when fully developed. Sown in March, it starts to form, in other words, it "turns" as early as May. This Onion can be well used for small amateur gardens, but is not grown by market gardeners because of its small volume; it would not provide a sufficient yield for commercial specialists. The largest Onion is the Madeira Onion. It can only be grown in southern countries, and only appears in the trade in large consignments, which are bought for the consumption of troops, penitentiaries, hospices, etc. Soil preparation for cabbage planting Cabbage requires well-smoked soil. So, before ploughing, it is necessary to bury a good manure. Any compost you can get your hands on will do; gadoues, in particular, are excellent. Market gardeners often fertilize with vegetable detritus mixed with manure; this fertilizer is only suitable for cabbages; if it were used for salads, it would produce "cast iron". Once the fertilizer has been spread on the soil, a good, i.e. deep, ploughing is done to bury it. The board is raked and the rays made. If the soil is excessively thin, a supplement of chemical fertilizer can be applied in March. It would be beyond the scope of this article to discuss chemical fertilizers for vegetable growing. We can only advise gardeners to seek advice from competent specialists, or to consult published works on the subject. Let us say, however, that since cabbage is a big "fertilizer eater", there's no need to worry about ploughing 400 kilograms of superphosphate per hectare into the soil beforehand. After planting, or early in the spring, soda nitrate, spread as a cover dressing at a rate of 300 kilograms per hectare, before a good rain, produces a vigorous start to vegetation. At the end of March, a good hoeing will complete the filling of the rays dug for the cabbage plantation, while destroying the grass that is starting to grow, and this hoeing will be repeated. Careful hoeing is particularly useful if you don't have much water at your disposal; hoeing replaces watering to a certain extent. But if you do have water, you need to water copiously as soon as the weather turns hot and dry. Under these conditions, maximum yield is obtained. Cauliflowers. - Full-ground cauliflowers, sown like first- and second-season cauliflowers in September, are planted in March. These are the ones left under the trays after all the best ones for these first two seasons have been removed. Thinned out in this way, they also become very beautiful, all the more so as they will have been depanelled or 10 decloaked as soon as the heavy frosts are over. They shouldn't be given too much water until the plants show their buds, but afterwards they should be given copious watering and a careful covering. These last cauliflowers are delivered for consumption by Parisian market gardeners towards the end of June and the first fortnight of July. Let's say once and for all that in market gardening, cauliflowers are always planted in the spring with other crops such as lettuces, Romaine, radishes and spinach. The same applies to those harvested in summer, which are planted in autumn with chicory and scarolea. In our cauliflower crops at Vaugirard, we have even planted a second season of autumn cauliflowers in summer cauliflowers. But this is a crop that can only be grown in very fertile "marshes", like those of the specialists. Turnips. - When there is no longer any fear of heavy frosts, towards the end of March or the beginning of April, depending on the region, turnips sown in beds at the end of January or the beginning of February can be depanelled. Once this operation has been carried out, they should be covered with straw mats if any more frosts occur, as turnips grown in this way are very tender, and the slightest frost will damage them. Romaine. - When the first season of Romaines, sown at the beginning of October and grown under cloches, has been harvested, the cloches, which have thus become free, are replaced on three of the rows of Romaines that were counter-planted, as we said, in February. We proceed as follows: The paths, on these kinds of layers, are at the same level as the topsoil of the layers. It is therefore conceivable that the rim of a bell can be walked flat on both the path and the loam. We start re-packing from the north side 4 North path South path Fig. 35. - First re-packing of the Romaines. of the layer. If we refer to Fig. 35, we can see that row no. 1 of counter-planted Romaines is located near the edge of the north path. We remove the first row of bells and cover the first row of Romaines with them. A portion of the pathway is thus underneath this first row. To facilitate this operation, the bell at the end where you start is first carried to the other end of the layer. The arrows in figure 35 indicate the direction in which this is done. The second row of bells arrives on the third row of Romaines, and the last row on the fifth. It should be noted that, as a result of the way in which this first reclocking was carried out, the three remaining rows of counter-planted Romaines (nos. 2, 4 and 6 in figure 35) are sheltered from the north winds by the bells covering rows 1, 3 and 5. As soon as this operation has been completed, the top or "bonnet" of the bell and the part facing south are bleached externally, as the sun would harden or even burn the plants. This is usually done with Spanish white diluted in water, to form a slurry that is neither too light nor too thick. A fatty substance, usually milk, is added to prevent the mush from dissolving in the slightest dew. Care must be taken to ensure that the bells always remain white, otherwise, in this season, a single sunburn is enough to burn the plants. Growers can also provide air under the cloches, but in this case the plants grow more slowly and harden off more. When growing for the trade, the first method is preferable, because it produces earlier, and this is what you should be looking for at this time of year. In small crops, and in those where labor is not too expensive and the bells are available for longer periods, the following method can be used to give the Romaines air: each bell is raised above the ground by resting on three wooden wedges. In this way, the Romaines become much larger and remain tender. Let's say once and for all that, in all Romaine cultivations, whether on beds, in cold frames or in the open air, Romaines must be tied as soon as they are capped, i.e. closed. If you tie it earlier, there's a risk that it won't cap easily. Before tying, the rye straw used for the job should be soaked in water for at least twenty minutes, and then thoroughly shredded to make it supple. Green rye straw, dried in the shade, is even preferable to ripe straw. This straw should be cut, to within a few centimetres, to the length required to surround the Romaine, including the tie. To bind a Romaine, take a strand of straw, raise the leaves straight up so that they remain in their natural position, wrap the strand around the Romaine about two-thirds of the way up, and tie as follows: at the point where the two ends of the strand meet, twist them together 10. in two or three spiral turns at most (fig. 36). This twisting gives the ends of the straw strand an extreme stiffness, but by leading them with the finger below the level of the tie and releasing them, they are bowed, and this twisting, which is not even a tie and even less a knot, holds very well right up to the market. Let's hasten to add that, thanks to the skill of the operators (who are almost always women), it takes just five seconds to tie a Romaine. It's much longer and more difficult to describe than to execute. Chou plat de Paris. - Cabbages of this variety, sown on beds in February and transplanted under trays or cloches, should be aerated as much as possible; this is necessary to make them full-bodied and harden them sufficiently to allow them to be depanelled at the beginning of April. COMBINED CROPS Market gardening must be intensive in every sense of the word. To achieve a very close succession of crops on the same plot, you need to know how to combine sowing and planting, so that plants follow one another without getting in each other's way. In spring, for example, you can sow Radishes and Carrots in the same bed, and then plant Lettuce or Romaine, but preferably Romaine. Here are three "seasons" in the same field: Radishes will go first, without disturbing the Carrots too much, then come the Romaine, and then the Carrots will cover the whole surface. You can do the same with other vegetables. The most important thing for these combinations is to know how long the various plants will evolve, so that they help rather than harm each other. When it comes to the varieties of lettuce that lend themselves to this combined cultivation, you're spoilt for choice. The main ones are: Laitues blonde d'été, de Berlin, de Versailles ou de Chavigné, verte grosse, Tennis ball, Natura, blonde et brune de Naples, Chou de Naples, etc. This first season on soil will have been sown, as we have already said, around October 25 and raised under cloche or under frame to overwinter; once planted in place, it only needs watering when the weather is dry, but especially in the last period of its vegetation. Lettuce can be raised on a bed in winter, and is good for planting almost at the same time as the previous variety, but this entails manuring costs, and the plant is often not as stocky or as firm as the first. It is then sown in a cold frame; transplanted in the same way, this season is planted in April. Pumpkins, Giraumons, Gourds, etc. - These plants belong to the Cucurbitaceae family, like Melons, Cucumbers and Gherkins. They fear the cold and are damaged by frost, but they are much hardier than the above plants, especially Melons. Around Paris, their cultivation has almost entirely fallen into the domain of large-scale market gardening; only a few early market gardeners, who have a lot of land, still grow them a little, especially Pumpkins. They sow them on an old bed, under a frame, in April, and plant them out from May 1 to 15. There are several varieties of Pumpkin; the most widely grown around Paris, and therefore the one seen most at the Halles centrales, is the large yellow Paris Pumpkin; there are also bright red Étampes Pumpkins and varieties with more or less embroidered rind. Gourds, Giraumons, Patissons and Pumpkins, of which there are a large number of shapes and varieties, are of more interest to amateurs than to the trade. They are grown like pumpkins. Hobbyists often climb them on cradles, arbors, terraces, etc.; in this case, they are generally sown on the spot, so that the branches can be guided wherever you like, and all you have to do is water to obtain the fruit, which comes in some very bizarre shapes. There are also non-runner varieties, whose fruit is eaten half-ripe, but is often of poor quality. Curly Chicory and Scarolea. - Raising curly chicory and scarole plants for spring cultivation in the open ground requires the same care as for growing them in layers and under cold frames. This is the most important point in growing these plants, and we can't stress it enough. Until May 15th or 20th, it is always preferable to sow seeds on a warm bed, because in some cultures where these precautions have not been taken, we see, until the end of July, plants going to seed before their evolution is complete. Many gardeners attribute this to stormy weather, and it's true that it contributes a little, but a seedling that has been raised in good conditions, i.e. that has had the necessary background heat, has been kept tender by frequent watering, has not received any sun under the frames and has been planted young, will not go to seed, whatever the weather, unless it receives no watering during its growth. It's a general principle that you can't grow vegetables well without water. In this case, market gardening loses its name, and becomes ordinary farming, or almost agri-farming, since it is left defenseless to the influence of all the vagaries of the weather. In the Paris climate, the first Chicory and Scarolea are planted in the open ground from April 15th onwards, in soil that has not been cultivated since winter. Sow Radishes or Spinach, not too thickly, and plant Curly Chicory or Scarole in them, at a rate of eight or ten per square meter, with Scarole a little looser than Curly Chicory. These plants, like Lettuce, should not be sunk into the ground; their collars should be well out, so that they can spread out immediately. We also insist on this point, which is very important for the development of the plants, especially as we have noticed that almost everywhere where these crops are not grown by specialists, this essential condition is not observed. When planting lettuces, chicory or scarole, the neck of the plant must be completely out of the ground. Once the plants have been planted, they should be watered copiously at the base (what growers call "edging" the plants), even if it's raining or the soil is very wet. Water in such a way as to fill the hole or dimple that remains after planting. The watering in this way fixes the roots to the soil, and helps considerably with recovery, which is one of the most important conditions for good cultivation. From the end of March, if the weather is already arid, and until October, we advise all growers, whatever the plant they have to plant, to soak it in a tub of water when digging it out, without letting it stay there, but only so as to moisten all the rootlets; this greatly facilitates recovery. All that's needed then is a few basins of water to help the plants withstand the heat of the sun, and as soon as evening arrives, you'll see them straighten up and grow straight away. All these young plants don't need much water at first, just a few sprinklings if it's very dry. It's only when they're at least halfway through their growth that you need to increase watering, especially towards the end of the plants' development. For seedlings sown from April 20 onwards, you can sow on a warmer, lighter layer, and not transplant until May 20 under these conditions. Chicorée fine parisienne is still grown under cold frames, and you can also start Fig. 37. - Chicorée fine rouennaise. (fig. 37), which can then be grown throughout the summer. In the late season, it is preferable to grow Chicory with large ribs, such as Chicorée de Meaux, Chicorée de Louviers (fig. 38), etc., which are hardier than the above. Scarole varieties are less numerous than Chicory varieties, and also less distinct. This lettuce, which is even more widely grown in autumn than Chicory, thanks to its hardiness, has never been grown in layers by Parisian specialists. The first to be grown, in spring, is under a cold frame. It is then grown throughout the summer, like Chicory, and especially in autumn. Chicory sown in January Fig. 38 - Chicory from Louviers. is planted in late February or early March. After four or five weeks, they can be harvested, and a few days later they can be completely blanched and released for consumption. Thus treated, they become quite round, if not quite large. Chicory sown cold in February requires frequent watering and airing, and can generally be depanning towards the end of April or beginning of May. At this time of year, when vegetation is very active, if you leave the frames on the plants for just a few days too long, they will pack up, and you won't have such good merchandise anymore. As soon as possible, they are lifted and tied up for sale. Cauliflowers. - In April, we continue to sow cauliflowers. They are the most difficult to obtain in every respect, as they are sown at a time when it is already hot, and harvested in August, during the hottest weather. They are sown in the shade, as far as possible, to prevent flea beetles from devouring the plants. They need to be drenched often; drenching keeps these insects away. However, we have seen years when cauliflowers had to be placed in frames bleached with Spanish white for a few days, to protect them from the voracity of this terrible insect. Leeks. - In the first fortnight of April, we plant Leeks which have been sown on beds in January or early February. As they are very costly to raise, they are generally sown very thickly, and we have sometimes seen them planted as big as wires. They are delivered for consumption as early as June, and as they are also planted very thickly, they are often smaller than a little finger when the sale begins. A final sowing is done at the end of April or beginning of May, for planting in June. These leeks are eaten in autumn and winter. Scorzonera, Salsify and Scolymes. - These vegetables, whose roots are the most im1. Small-scale watering. MARKET GARDENING. 11 vegetables require no special care. They are grown especially by large-scale vegetable growers, and in gardens by amateurs; the yield of these plants is too low, given the length of time they occupy the land, for market gardeners to include them in their crops. They are, however, excellent winter vegetables, and their cultivation can be recommended to amateurs with large vegetable gardens, especially Scorsonera, which can be treated as a biennial plant. It is generally sown in April, preferably in rays, at a rate of around 100 grams per are, in deeply dug soil, as the roots prick a lot in the ground. Cool, sandy soils are better suited to these plants than overly compact soils, where the roots are hindered and liable to branch out and become tough and stringy. As soon as the young seedlings have three or four leaves, thin them out by hoeing, leaving about 10 cm between them. If water is available, baste in April to encourage emergence, then water more abundantly when it's dry, to make the roots grow. If you're going to keep these vegetables for more than a year, cut off the stem when it goes to seed, to encourage root growth. Young Scorsonera, Salsify and Scolyma shoots, etiolated in spring, have a very fine flavor and can be eaten in salads. Salsify and Scorsonera crops are subject to a kind of "powdery mildew", which can be combated by alternating sulfur treatments with Bordeaux or Burgundy mixture, or other similar copper sulfate-based solutions. Marsh beans. - These native vegetables, already grown in gardens in Charlemagne's time, are now only cultivated in fields, especially around Paris, where they belong to the domain of large-scale market gardening. Their cultivation, moreover, requires no care other than well-smoked, moist soil, as their name suggests. They are sown towards the end of April, in rows, to facilitate hoeing. In dry soils, provided they are sufficiently watered, Marsh Beans grow faster and are more tender. When the beans are large enough, the pods are harvested for green shelling; if the beans are already a little hard, the first skin is removed for consumption. Fava beans have their place in home gardens, where the aim is to grow as many vegetables as possible to vary the daily diet. It's also a highly nutritious vegetable, judging by the ordinary Fève, which produces excellent flour and grows almost without care. Grain growers' catalogs list a dozen varieties of Fava beans, but for garden use, it is preferable to grow the early dwarf Fava bean, which comes on more quickly, and whose grains are smaller and often more tender. Broad bean crops flourish in the north, as they do in colder climates. But as soon as these crops are grown further south, they are sometimes extraordinarily affected by aphids. To protect the beans, simply apply several syringes of nicotined water, at a rate of one Bordeaux glass of concentrated juice to one liter of water. However, these syringes should not be continued as soon as the pods begin to knot. Beet. - Vegetable beet is a large-capacity crop. It is grown in the same way as fodder beet and sugar beet. Vegetable beets, however, are smaller and can be sown more densely. We've seen them grown in well-established crops by a number of specialists. They are sown at the end of April and beginning of May, in rays spaced 30 centimetres apart, with the same amount of space between rows. Beet requires oily, well-smoked soil and, like sugar beet, the less water it receives in September and October, the more sugar it contains. Watering is all that's needed to get it to emerge, and then to put on weight during the summer. The only care it requires is frequent hoeing to destroy weeds and keep the soil loose. Beet can be eaten as soon as it starts to grow, but it's best used as a winter salad, mixed with Capuchin Beard or Lamb's lettuce; it lifts their blandness by sweetening them a little, and appeals to many people. Grain growers' catalogs contain at least twenty varieties of beet, varying in color from yellow to all shades of red and black. As with many other vegetables, every country has its own favorite varieties. In Paris, it's mainly the long red varieties that are grown commercially. As for amateurs, they are spoilt for choice; but there are some ornamental varieties with brilliant rosewood-red leaves that are a real eye-catcher in the kitchen garden, such as Dell's dwarf red variety. Artichokes. - We have shown how to sow Artichokes on a bed in February-March; they can also be sown on the spot, towards the end of April or the beginning of May, by drawing lines spaced from Om,75 to Om,80, on which holes or small basins are marked at the same distance apart; four or five Artichoke seeds are placed in each hole. This procedure saves on labor, but loses out in terms of production, since the crop is not harvested until the following year. Artichokes sown in beds at the end of winter are also transplanted towards the end of April. Generally speaking, sowing is rarely used; artichokes are mostly propagated by eyeletting (see October and March). Cardoon. - Cardoon is sown at the end of April or beginning of May, on an old bed. Specialists transplant it in a nursery to give it a "foothold", and in June plant it in place, spacing the plants at least 1.30 m apart. Well-watered, they become very large. Cardoon is planted with other vegetables, most often salads of all kinds. It requires only frequent watering as it gains strength. It is blanched in autumn. Potato. - This precious solanaceous plant belongs more to agriculture than horticulture. It is virtually no longer cultivated in gardens, and its cultivation is so easy and so well known that it is almost superfluous to talk about it here. All you have to do is choose the variety you prefer, according to the season in which you grow it, and there are so many varieties that you're spoilt for choice. The potato is so delicate that it can be grown in almost any climate and in almost any soil. All its cultivation consists of good ploughing to plant it, hoeing to destroy weeds, and buttering so that the tubers are not exposed to the air, which turns them green and reduces their quality. From the beginning to the middle of the 19th century, Parisian market gardeners practiced forced potato cultivation, but now that Algeria sends potatoes throughout the winter, and southern France in the spring, this type of cultivation is no longer sufficiently profitable. It is only suitable for wealthy individuals, far from major centers, who want to find everything in their vegetable gardens. It is probably for this reason, and for general professional training, that horticultural schools teach it to their students. Under these conditions, Potatoes are planted at a rate of five or six per frame, on a good layer of manure, loaded with a certain thickness of soil. Care consists above all in giving them air, so that the tops are not too tender, in depanning them at the right moment, and in protecting them from late frosts. Beans. - Beans are as much a part of agriculture as horticulture. Grown in open fields by specialists in dwarf varieties, they are planted in clumps of four to five seeds, spaced 30 to 35 centimetres apart in all directions. Around Paris, we start planting them as early as April 15th, but if there is a late frost, we must take care to butter them with soil to preserve them, as these plants fear frost at least as much as potatoes. The varieties grown in gardens are most often those that can be rowed, and with a little watering when needed, maximum yield is obtained. After cultivation on beds, which we described in another chapter, market gardeners still cultivated beans cold, in April. This cultivation was already less difficult; The seeds could be planted in place, under a frame, and all that was needed was to provide air to keep the plants in good vegetation, i.e. neither too soft nor too hard, and to peel them when necessary, even removing some of the hardest leaves, watering from time to time as the needles begin to form, and depanning when late frosts are no longer to be feared, taking care to harden the plants beforehand in the fresh air. It should also be pointed out that when plants are depanelled, care must be taken over the next few days to ensure that the sun, or simply a little arid wind, does not cause them to wither; if this happens, they must be basked several times a day. But, we repeat, these crops can now only be grown by amateurs, since at the time when these vegetables are produced, the markets are flooded with them at relatively affordable prices. Raves. - As we have already explained, we are dealing here with Raves only as a sort of memorial, since this crop no longer belongs in the realm of horticulture. Let us say, however, that to obtain a yield in the open field, it is preferable to choose fresh soil and not to sow too thickly. Twenty-five Raves per square metre is enough to cover the ground, if you want to obtain good yields. Care is simply a matter of hoeing, carried out as needed. To preserve turnips over the winter, pull them up before the frosts and store them in silos or cellars. Turnips. - Turnips can be sown from spring to September. Among growers in the Paris suburbs, this crop is grown with rare perfection. Growers in and around Croissy, with its warm, light soil on the banks of the Seine, achieve marvelous results. They often start bringing their produce to the Halles de Paris before the market gardeners have finished selling their cold-grown turnips. The secret to growing turnips at the height of the season is not to sow too thickly, but to keep the plant tender at all times, watering it every day when it's not raining. Turnips, like all Cruciferae, fear the ravages of flea beetles; to combat them, as we said about cabbages, you need to water often. Some authors also recommend spraying with tobacco juice at 15°, mixed with 15 liters of water. This can be an excellent method for large crops, but for small crops we prefer to shade young plants for a few days during the hottest hours of the day. In April, more or less early depending on climate and weather, cold-sown turnips are depanning. They should continue to be watered copiously if the weather is dry and hot, especially when we start to pull them up, which is a sort of thinning out, as we remove the largest plants as they grow. As these turnips have been treated in exactly the same way as those grown on beds, there is virtually no waste; however, despite all the precautions taken, the last ones pulled out are more "rooty" than the first ones. Romaines. - In April, the Romaines are reseeded for the second time. After the first recloSentier nord - Sentier sud = Fig. 39 - Second reclochage de la Romaine. chage, as shown in figure 35 (March), all the Romaines remaining in the open air and forming three rows are placed to the south, in relation to the bells. The second re-housing simply consists of placing II. - the bells that have become vacant when the Romaines from the first relocation have left, on the three rows of Romaines in the open air. The movement takes place from north to south, as shown in figure 39; the southern path is thus partly covered in its turn. However, before proceeding with this operation, it is necessary to give the roots a copious watering to soak them thoroughly. It even seems that this heavy watering gives new vigor to the layer, whose manure, however, is already largely decomposed. Romaines left in the open air on the bed have continued to grow, albeit outside, especially at the end of April, when vegetation becomes very vigorous in these conditions; sometimes, all they have to do is "comb their hair" and soften, which generally takes no more than ten to fifteen days. Here again, and more than ever, the bells must be kept well laundered. This last season is delivered for consumption between April 25 and May 15. The cloches are then removed for other crops, such as melons, tomatoes, eggplants, pumpkins, gherkins, etc., or put back if they are no longer needed, and the carrots on the layers are given the necessary care, topdressing and watering. Flat Romaine with bells and blond Romaine for market gardening are not as good as the gray variety for re-housing. In cold climates, we recommend planting the old green Romaine variety, rather than varieties with overly tender foliage; with it, you're more certain of obtaining a product despite bad weather. On the market, Romaines from re-harvesting are distinguished from the others by their more yellowish shade and softer appearance. As for Romaines grown in cold frames, after hardening them by giving them plenty of air, they are depanelled in April, watered copiously every day and then re-panelled. The result is beautiful plants at the end of the month, if they have been well cared for. When we were young, we still remember seeing the old market gardeners do this better than they do today. In the month of April, we depanelled every morning, watered and repanelled in the evening. This type of cultivation, which was very labor-intensive, has long since been abandoned by specialists, but it can be recommended to amateurs, provincial gardeners and establishments where labor costs are low, such as hospices and penitentiaries. It's a convenient way of bringing plants forward and making them very beautiful. Today's specialists are obliged to make their land produce as much as possible. They prefer to depanner their Romaine entirely at the beginning of April, and run a season of cold Chicory with the same frames. Romaine depanelled in this way comes after the last re-cultivations, preceding Romaine grown in the open ground; it still finds a fairly lucrative outlet. Romaine is also grown under cold cloches; three feet are planted under each cloche; air is given when necessary, i.e. when the plants become too tender; the cloches are uncloaked from time to time to water, and when the cloches are full, they are removed for good; then water copiously. Cabbages. - Cabbages sown in February on a bed are de-stemmed at the beginning of April, after having been suitably hardened, and are planted out around the 15th of that month. Parisian market gardeners usually counterplant this cabbage season with lettuces planted in March, and delivered for consumption at the beginning of May. When the lettuces are gone, the cabbages are given a good hoeing, first to destroy the grass, and then to increase the fertilizing power of the soil by loosening it. All that's left to do then is water copiously, and by June 15 you can start eating. Beefheart cabbages grown in the ground should be hoeed at this time of year; hoeing replaces watering to a certain extent. When, in April, the leaves take on a reddish tinge, it's a sign that the soil has not been sufficiently fertilized; when the cabbages have had enough fertilizer, the leaves are green and fat, and in this case, with much less water, a good harvest can be obtained. Cauliflower. - The first cauliflowers, sown at the end of September and planted on beds in February, are harvested from April 1 to 15, depending on the weather and the strength of the plants. It's easy to recognize when the time has come when the plants are too strong to remain under the trays. However, you can delay the operation by holding the frames raised to a certain height above the trunks, using wooden wedges or om, 16 flower pots; this has the advantage of further advancing vegetation. While cauliflowers are growing, they need little watering, right up to the moment when they start to "take the bud", i.e. when the flower appears. The aim of this treatment is to make the stalk grow larger and the leaves sprout. If the plants start to flower before the base is strong enough, the apple will remain small and flake off, without producing a beautiful product. As soon as the bud is set, i.e. when you can see it in the heart of the cauliflower, you need to water it copiously, which will result in a larger head. From this point onwards, the head must be carefully covered. Covering plays an important role in the cultivation of cauliflowers, especially summer cauliflowers. As soon as the apple emerges from the shell, i.e. the core formed by the central leaves, a tender, healthy leaf is broken off and placed on top. This cover is then doubled with hard leaves which are detached from the outer part of the cauliflower. Touching the young leaves in the heart should be avoided if the plant is not to harden excessively. The leaves placed on top of the first one should surround the head, so that it has as little air as possible. Cauliflowers covered in this way remain very white. It is necessary, however, to raise this covering every day, especially in summer, to destroy the caterpillars that come to devour the apples; the same applies in autumn for slugs, especially in wet weather. A single one of these insects considerably deteriorates the apple, depriving it of its freshness, and consequently of much of its commercial value. Care must also be taken to remove caterpillars and slugs that attack the leaves. 1. An apple is said to flake when the buds that make it up pull apart. This description shows the constant care that cauliflowers need, especially in midsummer, if they are to be fresh, beautiful and tasty. These first cauliflowers are generally harvested in the second half of May, when they have been well cultivated and kept under a frame with plenty of air until around April 15th. Let us indicate, once and for all, how to recognize when it's time to uproot cauliflowers, i.e. when they have reached full development. This is very important for commercial gardeners, as cauliflowers make very rapid progress, especially in the last few days; if you wait just a day or two too long, they will flake, spread out and lose their value. So it's at the precise moment when you can see that the cauliflower is beginning to flake slightly at the edges that you should harvest it. As for amateurs, they can eat cauliflowers before they are fully developed, if they have a certain quantity; the quality is the same, only the size differs. Summer cauliflowers, sown in March, are planted in the second half of April. They are usually planted in cold Chicory, but the frames should not be left on these young plantations for more than a fortnight, as they would become overly tender, since Chicory requires a lot of water during its growth. Black radish. - Of all the varieties of large summer and winter Radishes, which in Paris we call Raves, only the Black Radish is cultivated by market gardeners. In fact, it only appears at Les Halles in very small quantities, compared with pink radishes. Growing large radishes is as simple as growing small ones. Sow in rows 20 to 25 centimetres apart, spacing the rows evenly. Care must be taken to keep these radishes very tender through watering. Radishes are sown throughout spring and summer until August 15, or even a little later. In the latter seasons, they are plucked and placed in gauges to be eaten over winter. All other varieties of large Radish can be grown under the same conditions as the Black Radish; but they have more the taste of Raves than the finesse of well-cultivated Pink Radishes. Tarragon. - Tarragon, grown in bursts, is best planted in April, or towards the end of July. Eggplant. - Eggplants sown on layers on March 15th are transplanted fifteen or twenty days later, in nurseries on layers, to be planted in May. Artichokes continue to be eyeballed, and asparagus and strawberry plants are planted. The various varieties of Onion are sown in spring, as soon as the severe frosts have passed. This crop requires no special care, apart from watering in dry weather and weeding. Hobbyists can sow directly on the spot, without transplanting. All these varieties can be eaten after the white onion. They can be stored to last through the winter and into the following spring. Finally, we continue to sow a number of vegetables, such as carrots, lettuces, Romaine, wild chicory, radishes, spinach, sorrel, tomatoes, melons and cucumbers, cabbage, chives, parsnips, parsley, purslane, etc. ES AGR A. dmala dr Cauliflower. - Cauliflowers planted in cold Chicory in April are released when the Chicory is removed for consumption towards the end of May.
