The soil is then mulched with a good layer of old or half-consumed manure, and watered a few times over the mulch. A few days later, you'll see little roots sprouting from the plant's collar. From this point onwards, cauliflowers should not be over-watered until they reach bud stage; once the flowers appear, they should be watered every day, but not too heavily, so that the soil has time to drain as it grows. It's up to the grower to judge how much water to give, according to the nature of the soil. Cauliflowers are carefully covered (see April), and caterpillars are destroyed from the leaves and heart. This season's cauliflower, when well cultivated, is delivered for consumption between July 15 and August 15, sometimes later in some soils, but in this case the plants become larger. In this respect, it's surprising how much the nature of different soils can modify cauliflower varieties. The weather also has a major influence: in rainy summers, cauliflowers tenderize excessively, and come earlier, but smaller. Cauliflowers sown in April are replanted with lettuces when they are half grown. At this time of year, it's particularly important to keep an eye out for caterpillars, especially leaf caterpillars, which often destroy all the foliage. When the lettuces are removed, they are given a crutch, and a good mulch is put on the soil, as for the previous crop. Water sparingly, as already mentioned, until the flowers appear. After summer cauliflowers come autumn cauliflowers. The plants require the same care as the summer ones, since they are sown in May, and the sun is even hotter than in April. Melons. - Melons can be sown up to May 15, always in increasingly thin layers, as the sun makes up for this artificial heat. The last ones planted in the field, from May 1st to June 15th, can be planted under cloches. When they have recovered and begun to elongate, the cloche is vented, and they are left to grow outside. At this time of year, the melon is not delicate, and its cultivation, with the few indications we have given regarding pruning, is within everyone's reach. Gherkins. - In true market gardening, gherkins are sown at the beginning of May, on an old bed that no longer has bottom heat, and under a frame. If sown early enough, they can be left until the end of May, when they are planted out. To facilitate recovery and advance vegetation, we place a bell on each plant, taking care to shade it. Some growers simply place a sheet of white paper over the plant (the same is done for melons), and as the plant picks up, it lifts and throws off the sheet of paper. As soon as the plant picks up again, air is gradually added to the bells until they are released. This procedure brings the harvest forward considerably, because when the cool nights of September arrive, the gherkins are often attacked by nail disease, and also take on rust and gray; the fruit obtained is less beautiful and doesn't keep as well. It's for this reason in particular that specialists are urged to harvest as early as possible. In the past, when Parisian market gardeners grew gherkins, they gave them an intensive first crop, then put them in other plantations planted in March, which had time to be cleared so that they didn't get in the way of the gherkins. But for everyone's cultivation, Gherkins are sown around May 15 or 20, watered if necessary to encourage germination, and hoeed when necessary. It's a good idea to spread mulch over the soil to keep it cool; under these conditions, the plants grow vigorously. At least two meters of space should be left for them to run around. In the provinces, we've seen specialists rowing gherkins; this method of cultivation produces fruit that doesn't have a "layer", i.e. a white spot on the part on the ground; the fruit is all the more beautiful, and should keep better in vinegar. This is the method we recommend to amateurs with a small vegetable garden. Moreover, plants grown in this way take up less space. Pumpkins, Gourds, Giraumons, etc. - These vegetables are planted from May 1 to May 15. To establish the crop properly and produce fruit early, make a square hole om, 50 cm square, and fill it with warm manure; place a layer of Om, 15 soil on top, in which the pumpkins are planted, and cover with a cloche, shading it for the first few days to encourage growth; remove the cloche when frosts are no longer to be feared, after gradually hardening the plants. As a general rule, even the hardest plants grown under chassis or cloches need to be gently acclimatized to the open air, i.e. given a little more air from day to day; otherwise, they are seized when exposed to the open air; they wither, the leaves curl, sometimes even fall; in all cases, the plants become too hard, and the final result is compromised. When you've depanneled or decloaked too early, and the plants are still too tender, there's only one way to avoid the accident we've just mentioned, and that's to baste often, so that there's always a dew on the leaves; after a day or two, the plants are firmed up and the danger is over. Once pumpkins, gourds, etc. have been unstuck, they can be left to grow; as long as their fruits are not large enough, they don't need much water; later, they need to be watered heavily. In the trade, only one or two fruits are left per plant, so that they grow larger; under these conditions, if watered sufficiently, fabulous Pumpkins are obtained, often weighing over 100 kilograms. As for amateurs, they can leave many more fruits on each plant; the fruits are smaller, but just as good. Tomatoes. - Tomatoes sown on beds in March can be planted around May 15, when frost is no longer a concern. Once planted and starting to grow, they need to be pruned. All buds growing in the leaf axils are removed, leaving just one stem per plant. Some growers leave two or three, depending on the type of trellising to be used. When a bunch of flowers appears, we stop the growth of the stem above or below the bunch to facilitate fruit setting, and let the eye grow below or above. The same procedure is followed for all clusters, taking care to visit the plants often and remove any under-eyes that develop, as this plant is surprisingly vigorous in its vegetation. This is when the plant needs to be trellised. Some growers place a stile at each foot, on the north side, and tie the plant to it; others stretch wires, and trellis it in rows. We think both methods are good; what's important is that the stems don't drag on the ground, which would be very detrimental to fruit ripening in cold regions. A number of authors recommend various ways of shaping tomatoes through trellising and pruning. Of course, this is a matter of taste, of interest only to amateurs. When the plant is in place and its branches are developing, it can be given any shape you like, by pruning and then trellising; the essential condition is always to leave enough space between the branches for air and sun to circulate freely, and not to allow the plant to bear more fruit than it can produce in good condition. We believe that four to five well-constituted bunches per plant are quite sufficient; if we want more, it will always be to the detriment of the beauty of the fruit. Practitioners "stop" tomatoes altogether when they have four clusters. All the buds must then be carefully removed, so that all the sap can flow into the fruit. These begin to ripen around August 1st in the Paris climate. Eggplants. - Eggplants are planted in the first fortnight of May, generally after the harvesting of carrots from stretcher beds. The layer is turned over, and a little hot manure is added to give a little warmth to the soil, and two rows of Aubergines are planted per layer, making four plants per panel; as the bells are free at this time, one is placed on each plant, taking care to bleach them if they are no longer sufficiently white. Eggplant planted, bounded, cloched and shaded, soon picks up, especially with the background heat. Air is then gradually added, but the plants are kept under cloches for as long as possible. It's at this stage that they are pinched, which prevents them from rising too quickly and helps the development of the lower eyes. All that's left to do then is water and pick the fruit when it reaches a length of Om, 20 to Om, 25. Chard or Poirnea. - This plant, more than any other, requires rich soil. Parisian market gardeners used to grow it only on their beds, once the early harvest was over. Its cultivation in France goes back a long way, and was recommended by Charlemagne in his Capitularies. Poirée à carde has been more or less abandoned by market gardeners today, as a result of crop specialization. Trade has gone from being local to international, so to speak, which has led to certain crops being grown on a very large scale, with the possibility of finding the flow of produce. Preference is given to vegetables that are planted thickly, for a more remunerative crop. However, the well-cultivated Poirée à Carde still pays for the place it occupies, and is not a crop to be scorned. Its taste is similar to that of Cardoon. Sow it in a nursery, in the first days of May, in the open air, on a piece of old soil that no longer has any heat. All you have to do is water it to make it stand up, and then to keep the plant tender. It is transplanted in June, spacing the plants by Om, 40. There are five or six varieties of Poirée à carde, each quite distinct from the others by the color of the leaves, whose ribs are sometimes yellow, sometimes red, sometimes white. Poirée. - This plant is used more for medicinal purposes than for eating. It had its place in the market gardens of past centuries, where there were many pharmaceutical, aromatic and other plants, of which everyone grew a small quantity, as is still the case in small provincial towns, where the produce is sold on the spot. They were sown in the first days of May, in well-smoked, newly-ploughed and well-trussed soil. Sowing was done in rows and not too thickly, so that the leaves could develop well; all that was then needed was to hoe the soil to destroy the grass, and to water often. When the leaves reach 20 to 25 centimetres, they are cut 2 or 3 centimetres from the ground, so as not to destroy the young hearts that will provide the future cut. For these new harvests, instead of cutting everything with a knife, we pick the largest leaves one after the other, by hand, and we don't stay long without coming back to the same place. Celery. - Blond celery is grown at the beginning of autumn. This is sown in the first days of May; specialists transplant it in a nursery before planting. This procedure, which is applied to almost all plants, produces stockier, more regular specimens, which is a good thing when it comes to vegetables that are to be uprooted all at once and delivered to the trade. Varieties grown for winter must be very green, hard and stocky Celery, with a very full heart. They are sown at the same time as the previous varieties. We continue to sow sorrel. The previous year's sorrel goes to seed in the course of the month; you can cut the stems that go to seed, and the plant then sprouts from the base, but specialists prefer to destroy it and sow new ones every year; it is always more vigorous. It's a good idea to give Peas a few basins in the morning and evening when they are in bloom, as the flowers often burn and part of the harvest is lost when the weather is dry and arid at flowering time. This is particularly the case with the row varieties; by watering them when they need it, maximum yield can be obtained. Towards the end of May, spinach sets seed. At this point, it's best to ruin the planting, i.e. destroy the plants, and sow new ones in March to replace them. Radishes continue to be sown; from May to July and even August, they take eighteen to twenty days to grow in the soil, if well cultivated, and the whole process consists of watering them every day it doesn't rain, from sowing to harvesting. Curly endive and Scarole. - Until May 15 or 20, it's always best to sow these lettuces on a warm bed, to prevent them from setting seed prematurely. From May 20 onwards, seedlings are sown in the open ground, and all that's left to do is water the plants to keep them tender. Care must be taken not to plant too old plants. A young, tender plant recovers better, is more vigorous and grows faster than an old plant which is much stronger. Nature applies the same implacable rule to all living things. Chicory and Scarolea are tied to bleach them. It's best to do this when the lettuces are three-quarters developed, because once they've been tied, the heart continues to grow (albeit white), and the plant "fills out". At this point, watering should not be neglected, as the plant needs to grow fast, and you should try to help it as much as possible. In the provinces, we've seen flowering pots 12 with no holes in the bottom used to blanch these lettuces. They are simply placed on top, and as the heart whitens, it fills the pot. Enthusiasts can start tying when the plants are halfway through, choosing the biggest ones and continuing in this way. This is a practical way of getting the most out of your planting, because if you start eating too late, you can't keep up with the plants as they develop, and they rot. Chicory and Scarolea planted after this first season are counterplanted with Lettuce and Romaine planted at least a fortnight earlier. For Lettuce, however, eight days may suffice, especially in clay soils, which harden very quickly. The care to be given to these salads is the same in all respects; however, here, young plants are often too tenderized by the abundant watering given to Lettuces and Romaines, and when these have gone, it is a good idea to firm up Chicory and Scarole gradually. If the weather is dry and hot, give them a little watering, so they don't harden off too quickly. Witloof chicory. - To obtain large roots of this plant in autumn, sow in May-June, in rows spaced Om, 20 apart, and so that the plants are spaced Om, 20 apart in all directions. If you sow more densely, you'll get smaller roots. We also continue to sow Carrots, Turnips, Lettuce, Cabbage, Cardoons, Artichokes, Beetroot, Purslane, etc., and to plant Strawberries. Leeks. - When a leek plant has been sown in a nursery with a view to transplanting, it is very thick at the time of uprooting. If the soil is hard, the plants are lifted by passing the spade flat under the roots; they are taken one by one, rejecting any that are mediocre, and arranged in handfuls with all the bulbs at exactly the same height, so that one does not overtake the other. When you've got plenty on hand, cut off all the roots 1 cm or 1 1/2 c. from the bulbs, then the tips of the leaves, leaving the plant about 15 cm long. Place the handfuls in a basket, all facing in the same direction and neatly arranged, so that they can be picked up without searching. The basket is immersed in water, but not left to stand, simply to soak the plant, as is done for all vegetables to be planted; if the planting is not done on the same day, a board is placed on the plant and it is loaded, so that it remains flat and upright; otherwise the plants, continuing to grow, twist, making planting much more difficult. With the leek plant thus prepared, here's how Parisian market gardeners proceed. They have planks which are generally 3 meters wide. They draw a radius on the edge of the board, and leave the chalk line there, so as to go straight; then they lay a fir-wood board on the ground, stand on it, and plant by walking backwards, turning the board as they go. In fact, this is the procedure for all open-ground planting. Market gardeners take a handful of seedlings in one hand, and the planter in the other; with each stroke of the planter, which is given deep, to a depth of at least 10 or 12 centimetres, the thumb and forefinger of the other hand prepare the seedling and slide it into this hole, then it is bound with a single stroke of the planter. Some growers do this with surprising dexterity. Once planted, the leek barely emerges from the ground by 1 or 2 centimetres. The holes made by the planter are then watered copiously to fill them with water, and are soon closed again. Leeks planted in this way don't even wilt, and as early as the day after planting, you can already see them growing. All that's left to do is water it if it's dry, and weed it. We've seen a few market gardeners sow Radishes before planting, but this is only possible here, where we always cultivate in fertilizer-rich soil, which is often too rich. Leeks treated in this way come on very quickly. Leeks planted on May 15, for example, are ready for consumption in late July and August, giving the soil a new "season". A little later, this site is used to transplant Lettuce and Romaine plants for forced cultivation. Once the leeks have been harvested, the soil is very healthy and excellent for transplanting. In our opinion, this is the best method for planting leeks. It is practised only by specialists, who plant much more densely than amateurs, and their leeks are sold no larger than an ordinary cork. Planted in this way, the plants are straighter and tighter to take root, and the watering we give goes straight into the dimples left by the planter, i.e. to the roots of the plants themselves. Another method for planting leeks is to use a hoe to open deep gullies spaced 25 to 30 centimetres apart; place the leeks in these lines, spacing them about 12 to 15 centimetres apart, and close the gullies. If you have fertile soil, you'll get beautiful Leeks, but they'll take longer to come up than with the previous method. Once the Leek has been planted, all you have to do is water it copiously, and weed or hoe as required. This plant is easy to grow, and produces enormous numbers when given abundant fertilizer and good humidity. In Achères and Gennevilliers, for example, leeks irrigated with sewage are reaching dimensions unknown before the adoption of this cultivation system. 12. Combined cultivation. - What we said earlier about combined cultivation (see March) also applies to summer. At this time of year, for example, you can sow Radishes or Spinach (all these sowings must not be too thick, as everything will choke and nothing good will come of them) and, after mulching the bed as soon as it is sown, you can plant Lettuce, After mulching the bed as soon as it's seeded, lettuce, romaine, chicory or escarole can be planted at a rate of eight plants per square metre, spaced om.50 apart along the row. This will allow cauliflowers to be planted at a rate of four per metre when the lettuces are half grown. Radishes (or spinach) will go first, then lettuces, and finally cauliflowers. Cauliflower. - We've already mentioned how to care for cauliflowers in terms of covering and watering. Once they have bloomed, they must not be allowed to run out of water, and we must avoid, as far as possible, letting them wilt, which sometimes happens when the weather is stormy. Under these conditions, we give them a drenching in the morning, when the dew has fallen, and a little watering in the afternoon, when the sun loses its strength. When cauliflowers are left to wilt after the flower has begun to develop, they become "mossy", leafy and hard, and lose their beauty and quality. When the head has reached a certain size and a rainstorm occurs, which, as the saying goes, "sets the earth on fire", the cauliflowers must be watered copiously as soon as the rain falls, preferably with well water, to refresh the soil. At this point in their growth, the cauliflowers quickly flake off, and all that remains is to make the best of them by harvesting them all at once; otherwise they would be lost. Market gardeners in Paris can sow cauliflower until June 25th, but amateurs are advised not to sow after the 15th. Melons. - We have nothing to add to what we have said above concerning the cultivation of melons, but it is worth adding a few indications concerning picking. Well-ripe Cantaloupes are very heavy, well-dressed, i.e. the slices are well defined, the rind is firm, and the stalk is beginning to show signs of separation from the body of the fruit. It is by this sign in particular that practitioners working for the trade recognize that a melon is "struck", i.e. ready for picking; often, the rind is not yet ripe, and the peduncle (stem) is already slightly split from the fruit. In mild, rainy weather, this phenomenon can also occur on unripe fruit; in this case, you need to be guided by color and weight, as a ripe melon is fuller and heavier than one that has not fully ripened. It's a good idea to bear these observations in mind, so as not to pick a melon that's too green, when it doesn't yet have any flavor. Nor should it be picked too ripe. Inhabitants of big cities often eat melons that are too advanced, and no longer have any flavour. As soon as these fruits start to turn yellow, during hot spells, they are good to pick, as they ripen inside before the outside turns yellow. Connoisseurs who grow melons for their own consumption pick them as soon as they are ripe, and store them in a cool place until they are ready to eat. It's by observing all these instructions that you can eat a good melon, with all its qualities. It goes without saying that in warm years, melons are tastier and finer, especially at the height of the season, than in rainy years, at least in temperate climates, and even more so in the north. Pumpkins. - Pumpkins are usually not pruned; however, when a fruit is well knotted and about the size of an ordinary melon, it's a good idea to cut the bearing branch an eye or two above the fruit, to force the sap back into the fruit. Poorly ripened fruit is removed in the same way as melon. To give the plant more vegetation, the main branch, i.e. the first branch to develop, is pruned by laying it on the ground and rooting it every 70 or 80 centimetres as it lengthens, and watering copiously. Tomatoes. - Tomatoes require almost no water; however, market gardeners who have water at their disposal water them when the fruit has reached a certain size. Never water before the fruit is well established, as this would prevent the plant from producing any, as it would grow too luxuriantly. Eggplants. - Eggplants are usually ready to be broken up around June 15th; at this time, a good mulch is applied to the soil, mainly to keep it cool, and as the fruit begins to set, we start watering. As the fruit grows, you increase the watering. As with tomatoes, you should never water until the fruit is well established. Picking begins around July 15, and continues until the first autumn frosts, returning to the same spot every three or four days. This was a fairly profitable crop in the days when the Midi did not send large quantities of Aubergines to Paris, as it does now. Chard. - Chard is transplanted in the first fortnight of June; more often than not, it is counterplanted with lettuce, or planted alone, spaced at Om, 50 on the rows, in a checkerboard pattern. All that's left to do is to water it copiously to make it grow; it finds substantial nourishment in this well-wetted layer, its leaves develop quite rapidly, becoming large and thick, and the plant forms a beautiful clump which is tied up on the spot, before being pulled up, to be delivered for consumption. It can also be sown up to June 15, so that it's available until the frosts. In the past, market gardeners used to sow them until July, and the plants from the last sowings were overwintered; as soon as the cold weather arrived, they were covered with straw or leaves; by the end of April or May, they were growing again, and could be eaten. This last type of cultivation has long since been abandoned by specialists. Cardoon. - Cardoon is planted in June, with plants at least 1.30 m apart. Under these conditions, provided they are well watered, they grow very large. Cardoon is planted with other crops, most often salads of all kinds. Cardoon is a delicious vegetable, little known by our rural populations. Its cultivation is highly recommendable, and easy to do, because in strong soils you only have to start it again; then it grows by itself, even if you don't have any water to give it; in that case, it simply grows smaller. Once it has been planted and taken up, all you have to do is bind it to bleach it when it's ready to eat, and take the steps we've indicated so that you can have it all winter long. The difficulty lies in getting it to take up again, as it is a plant with large dry roots that cannot be left with a hair. To avoid this difficulty, amateurs can sow it on the spot, using the following procedure: in a ploughed area 2 meters wide, make two furrows 1 meter apart; mark on a radius, at each meter, the spot for a foot of Cardon; if the soil is soft and good, make a small basin at each spot, in which you place two or three Cardon seeds, which you bury 2 or 3 centimeters apart. In general, the seeds don't need to be buried very much; the closer they are to the surface of the soil, the better they benefit from the sun's rays; but if they are covered very little, care must be taken to keep the soil moist at the surface, since we're doing intensive cultivation here, and the seeds need to germinate quickly. If you want to do better, and have potting soil available, remove a spade of soil from the marked spots and replace it with potting soil. Water the spot copiously enough, and the seed sprouts after a few days. As soon as the plants are well established, they are thinned out, leaving only one plant per clump. Salads can still be planted in this crop, as it's hardly until September that they cover the whole ground. There are several varieties of cardoon: one, Cardon d'Espagne, has the disadvantage of hollow ribs, and can be grown when you don't want to keep any for winter; another, much more widespread in our countries, Cardon de Tours, which is much thornier, has full ribs; it is also much stockier and tastier than the previous one, so it is better for wintering. If you don't water it enough, it will come up like a large green celery plant, making it easy to protect against frost. Celeriac. - Celeriac is planted in June, with plants spaced Om.50 apart along the row, and Om.25 rows apart. It is generally counter-planted in salads of any kind, but the leaves of this Celery spread out a lot, and you mustn't plant it too thickly if you want it to grow large. Once planted, when the salads have gone, give it a good mulch, after hoeing, and all that's left is to water it copiously. Enthusiasts can eat it as soon as it has formed, i.e. the root, because, unlike other varieties, it is the part in the ground that is eaten. It forms a ball that becomes quite large once the soil has been properly smoked and watered. The leaf also makes an excellent condiment for stews, but is generally too tough to be eaten in salads, unless the heart is chosen altogether, especially when it has been buried and overwintered in these conditions. Cabbage. - Cabbages that are to be overwintered are sownFig. 40. - Aubervilliers Savoy cabbage. around June 15th. The hardiest varieties are chosen, in particular Chou de Vaugirard and selected varieties of this breed, followed by the whole category of Choux Milan: des Vertus, d'Aubervilliers (fig. 40), de Pontoise, and so on. Here's how to grow these late varieties: sow them in a nursery, fairly lightly so that they don't wither; give them the necessary care: watering, protection against flea beetles, etc., then plant them in place, using a planter, towards the end of July. These last cabbages will only be eaten at the end of winter and the beginning of spring, while awaiting the harvest of those sown at the end of August. Rapunzel. - Rapunzel has never been widely cultivated; however, Parisian market gardeners used to grow a certain quantity, which has now diminished more and more. We don't even know if any growers still cultivate the plant today. Its roots are used, along with its leaves, which are eaten as a salad in winter, from December to April. Gardeners who would like to have some beautiful Rapunzel should sow it at the end of June, not too thickly, as the leaves of this plant spread out over the ground, a little like a large Lamb's lettuce. The seed is so fine that it's hardly possible, unless you're very experienced, not to sow it too thickly if you sow it on its own; so you mix it with wood ash or fine, dry earth. A thimbleful is enough to sow a 30-metre bed. There's no need to plough the land to sow the seed; a little crutching is all that's needed. Once the seed has been sown, the soil is harrowed with a fork, compacted, lightly mulched with short manure and then watered. Market gardeners usually sow Rapunzel in other crops, for example in the last spring cauliflowers, harvested around July 15. Very fine, shallowly buried seeds are more likely to emerge under these conditions, as cauliflower crops require a lot of water, so the soil is always excessively cool; what's more, the newly sown seed is shaded by cauliflowers. So, as we've already said, one crop helps the other, far from harming it. MARKET GARDENING. 13 Dandelion. - Dandelion grows wild in all temperate countries. Growers near Paris have been cultivating it for at least half a century, and have selected it to a certain extent. It is grown mainly to produce white dandelions, i.e. by sowing in autumn, early enough for the plants to grow in the spring, and half-burying them with fine earth or sludge to whiten the heart, a very tender, fine-tasting salad is obtained. In the last fifteen years or so, Parisian market gardeners have taken over this crop, and have greatly improved the size of the Dandelion, firstly through skilful selection, and also through the cultivation they give it. They produce Dandelions the size of small, black-seeded gotte lettuces. They sow in nurseries, in the second half of June, not too thickly, so that the plants can form from the stalk, and they transplant them in place at the end of August. This simple cultivation, which is highly recommendable from every point of view, can be done by anyone, and with a few precautions in terms of covering during severe frosts, you can have this excellent lettuce throughout the winter and into spring. For amateur growers, here's how to establish a Dandelion crop. Sow towards the end of June, taking care to choose well-selected seed, such as is available from many seed growers, given the importance of this crop. A well-smoked bed is ploughed and levelled, then sown by broadcasting, harrowing with a fork and top-dressing. If you don't have potting soil, you can replace it with a well-consumed mulch. Care must then be taken to keep the soil cool enough to ensure good emergence, and to continue after emergence so that the plants are tender. We continue to sow Turnips (sow not too thickly, and water every day it doesn't rain); we also sow, as we've already said, Lettuces, Curly and Scarole Chicories, Witlooi, Spinach, Radishes, Beans to be consumed in needles, Purslane, Carrots, etc. Last but not least, as we've said many times before, general care consists in hoeing and watering frequently in dry weather. Asparagus grown under forced cultivation, and sown on January 15th, is planted out around July 15th. For this purpose, we choose the most beautiful and best-formed plants, because at this time we can already judge which are the ones whose tips are well formed and color most easily. To do this, however, you need to sow many more seeds and transplant many more plants than you'll need. It's a costly process, it's true, but it produces a plant in one year that's as good as a two-year-old. Asparagus, on the other hand, is better selected than when the seedling is left in place to plant the claws in spring. We have had occasion to note that a claw that gives small stems at the start always continues to give small ones, more numerous, it's true, than the large ones; but in forced cultivation, one large Asparagus is more valuable than five small ones. Finally, when Asparagus is left in place, it is impossible to distinguish between those that color well and those that do not, since they are only planted in claws. To lay out the Asparagus for forcing, prepare one or more planks, the width of which should correspond to that of the trunks to be placed on them later. Between the Asparagus planks, the paths should be about Om, 65. In July, when we were ready to plant, we watered our seedlings copiously before digging, and lifted them with a fork, to preserve all their roots; having been transplanted, the seedlings already had a small, well-constituted heel, and the Asparagus twigs were about fifteen centimetres high. After having undergone the selection process mentioned above, we proceeded with the planting. To do this, we placed a line of chests in the spot where we were to plant, and planted at a rate of four rows per line of chests and sixteen feet per panel, sinking only the heel of the plants into the ground. It's a good idea to put the boxes in place to get a good idea of the position of the plants, so that they are not under the heads or bars of the boxes, but well spaced out under the glass of the frames. This precaution is justified, because in December, January and February, when the sun's heat reaches us much less, we need to keep the surface of the soil as close as possible to the glass, because the glass "pulls" the asparagus and colors it when it emerges from the soil; and if they were placed under a bar or a head of a box, they wouldn't benefit from this powerful auxiliary; already, after a few years, the claws always spread far enough for some of them to find themselves in these poor conditions. Planting was done with a planter, of course. It was then watered copiously, like all summer plantings, and care was taken to keep the soil constantly fresh, especially until the plants were fully established. As soon as they were up and running, the asparagus would "heel" again, and some asparagus as big as a five-year-old's finger would come out. We remember surprising practitioners when we told them it was Asparagus sown the same year. Growing in absolutely fertile marshland, on a sandy base, a soil that Asparagus loves, our crop was helped by the natural state of the soil. Like all market gardeners who grow this crop, we never left our land unoccupied, either in winter or spring. The very first year we planted Asparagus, we sowed Lamb's lettuce at the end of August over the entire surface of the planted area, so that we only lost one crop that first year. The following spring, we gave the Asparagus a good crutch (ploughing with a pitchfork), ploughed the paths with a spade, levelled and put down a good topdressing, then planted a full square of Red Lettuce, and in addition a row of Cauliflower on each path. The Lettuce was gone before it got in the way of the young Asparagus, and the row of Cauliflowers on the path didn't bother them either, since the path was Om, 65 wide. Later on, the Asparagus was no longer put in; besides, it was already strong enough to fill the whole place during the summer. In autumn, when the stalks were ripe, we cut them off. We then sowed another crop of lamb's lettuce, and we sometimes saw asparagus being forced the following February. Harvesting took place in March and April, immediately preceding that in the open ground. However, the plant must not be overworked in the first year. This late-season crop is no longer sufficiently remunerative for specialists working for the trade, due to competition from products from the south of France; but it can still be very good for amateurs, all the more so as it is easy to grow, with the sun already helping a great deal at this time of year. Strawberry plants prepared for forcing already have well-rooted nets in July; these nets are pulled out and transplanted in the nursery, spaced 15 to 20 centimetres apart; they are watered as needed to encourage growth, and very fine plants are obtained at the end of September or beginning of October. Curly Chicory and Scarolea can be sown up to July 20, for planting up to the end of August. It is not wise to continue later. Broccoli is sown in early July, in the open ground, light enough not to require transplanting. There is no need to care for the plant other than watering to keep it tender; it is planted out in the first days of August. To have Poirée in winter, we sow it in July, in rows the width of the frame boxes. When the frosts arrive, we put the boxes in place, surround them with a good acot, and then put in the frames, which we cover with straw mats during the night. In this way, you can have Poirée all winter until May, when it goes to seed. Tarragon. - The end of July is, along with April, the most favorable time to multiply Tarragon by splinters. Sorrel. - It's a good idea to water sorrel frequently during the summer, to avoid the ravages of flea beetles. When sorrel is heavily invaded by flea beetles, it's best to cut it back to ground level, so that it grows back tender. Sorrel can be sown in summer, but spring is always preferable. Finally, carrots, turnips, beans, winter cabbage, radishes, spinach, lettuce, purslane, etc. continue to be sown in July. Mushroom cultivation in France is relatively recent. La Quintinie, in his Traité de culture potagère, speaks of it only vaguely, and seems to rely on chance, on the state of the manure when it is decomposing in the beds, and on the growth of the mycelium that produces the Mushrooms, rather than thinking of organizing an actual culture, where the manure is prepared to perfection and pieces of this mycelium are introduced, spreading rapidly throughout the bed. In the Maison rustique by Malpeyre, Bixio and Bailly, written at the beginning of the century, we find a Traité de culture des Champignons (Mushroom Cultivation Treatise) that shows great progress. However, the authors of this last treatise left out many small details; for, according to the old market gardeners, our ancestors, a century ago, already cultivated Mushrooms well, but in small quantities. Twenty years ago, Lachaume, a renowned specialist, published a work on the cultivation of Cultivated Mushrooms which constitutes the first complete treatise on cultivation as it is practised today; this treatise, which met with great success, is still a classic today. 13. Another skilled specialist, Mr. Duvillard, professor of vegetable cultivation in the Seine department and member of the Chambre syndicale des ouvriers jardiniers, has more recently written another excellent Traité de la culture des Champignons. From the information we obtained from the Syndicat des champignonnistes, much of which we already knew, it appears that mushroom growing has taken on the proportions of an industry. We can estimate the production of this crop, together with the sale of the grindstone, i.e. the manure used, at ten million francs a year. CHOOSING THE LOCATION To grow mushrooms in the best possible conditions, you need a cellar, a basement, or at least a place where the air is not too dry. It's also necessary to be able to ventilate the room properly, with window wells that can be opened or closed according to the needs of the crop. In short, to grow mushrooms successfully, it's not enough to choose the right seed or mycelium, to know how to prepare the manure, set up the layers, or millstones, as practitioners call them, and take the necessary care. You also need a suitable room, where the temperature is regularly maintained between 15° and 20° centigrade, and where the air can be renewed frequently, while remaining fresh without being too humid. Mushrooms can be grown in the greater Paris suburbs, in all the abandoned underground quarries in the Seine, Seine-et-Oise and Seine-et-Marne departments, from which the ashlar, rubble and plaster used to build the city were extracted. Mushrooms can also be grown in the open air, in the vegetable garden; but in this case, a thicker or thinner cover is required, depending on the ambient temperature. We'll explain how to proceed below. PREPARING THE MANURE The ancients claimed, and were probably right, that it was in donkey manure, and later in mule manure, that the mycelium took hold most easily. Horse manure was the next best. As this crop is grown mainly around the capital, horse manure is used almost exclusively. We have never heard of any attempt to grow mushrooms with sheep manure, so we cannot comment on its value. We will confine ourselves here to the cultivation of mushrooms using horse manure; moreover, if the manures of sheep, donkeys, mules or any other animal were good, the work, for the whole cultivation, would be no less the same. As far as possible, fresh manure should be used, i.e. manure that has been out of the stable for no more than a fortnight. If it is older, mix it well with the new manure. In the vegetable garden, or close to where the millstones will be placed, lay out a rectangle 1 m to 1.5 m thick, with a width proportionate to the size of the crop you intend to grow. This operation is called "cutting the manure down to the floor". Care must be taken to place the manure in the same direction and to mix it well, as if you were building up a layer, so as to obtain a homogenous mass and avoid pulling on it to turn it over. As soon as the floor has been knocked down, it is watered copiously to induce uniform fermentation. Once fermentation has lasted eight or ten days, the manure is turned over. This operation consists in taking the last placed manure, turning it over in another direction, making a "gauge" again, and taking care to bring the manure on the edges back into the middle, and vice versa. If, during these operations, the manure were to become too dry in places, it would be necessary to water these places, forming the beds in such a way that the floor heats evenly throughout its surface. It is also necessary to narrow the width of the floor, to keep it at the same thickness. Eight days after this initial turning, the manure, which has continued to ferment as actively as it did at the start, has lost its primitive smell and has already taken on that of Mushrooms. The manure is then turned over again, in the same way as the first time, starting from the side where you finished the previous time. The floor is shrunk again to keep it at the same thickness, and even thicker if the weather is rainy. If, on the other hand, the weather is dry and the manure contains parts that are too dry, water moderately during the operation. By the time it is used for grinding, the manure must be smooth, so that no water comes out when it is pressed by hand. MOUNTING AND BONDING THE MOLLS Once the manure has been prepared, which takes an average of twenty days, the millstones are mounted, i.e. chains of manure in pyramids of Om, 40 at the base, and Om, 45 to Om,50 in height (fig. 41). This work must be done with care. The manure is first brought in and placed in a chain; the operator takes it with his hands to form the wheel, spreading it out well so as not to leave buffers, and treads it with his Fig. 41. - Mushroom wheel. hands and knees. By hand, he removes any manure that protrudes from the sides and does not hold firmly to the mass; this is called "combing" the wheel. After this operation, the wheel has a smooth surface and is as compact at the edges as it is in the middle. A few days later, when the wheel is no longer too hot inside, which you can check by sticking your hand into it, and if the manure no longer stings, i.e. doesn't burn, you can "larder" the wheel, i.e. garnish it with mushroom spawn; we'll explain below how to obtain this spawn or mycelium. To fill the wheel with spawn, we prepare pieces called "mises", 10 centimetres square and Om,01 thick, which we place at Om, 40 from each other, in two rows in a chessboard; the first row is placed as low as possible, a few centimetres from the base, and the second in the middle of the height of the wheel. If the grinding wheel still appears hot, place the bets loosely, to allow the surrounding mass to cool a little. For the same purpose, specialists use a large pointed stake to make holes from distance to distance, which they call suction cups. The millstone is left in this state for twenty to twenty-five days, at least in premises where there is no fear of bad weather; in open-air cultivation, when the weather is rainy, the millstone must not be left to drown, as the manure would rot and the harvest would be null and void. After twenty to twenty-five days, we check to see whether the spawn has begun to vegetate, i.e. whether the stakes have produced filaments that have extended into part of the body of the millstone; if this were not the case, the spawn would be infertile and the operation would fail; but this failure rarely occurs when the manure is well prepared and the spawn is vigorous. When we see that the mycelium has a tendency to develop, and that the little filaments are lengthening on all sides, we proceed with the "gobleting" operation, which consists in covering the mould with uncultivated soil, preferably from the subsoil, to a thickness of one centimetre. Mushrooms will form in this soil and appear two or three weeks later, if all the work has been well done, and if the quarry or cellar has always had more or less the same temperature and a regular draught. When the goblet soil becomes too dry (this depends on where the millstones are set up and on the weather), it should be watered lightly with a fine-headed watering can, so as not to damage the goblet. Before gobbling, pat the sides of the wheel with your hand, placing your knee on the top to support the wheel in all its thickness, and knocking off any protruding bits of manure, so as to make the surface as even as possible. Some time after gobbling, the earth is squeezed onto the wheel with the back of the shovel, so that it adheres well. This operation, which is the last before picking, is called "talochage"; its purpose is to ensure that the soil adheres well to the manure, so that the Mushrooms cannot grow under the layer of soil, but are forced to pierce it. When we pick mushrooms, they generally come out in clumps, called "rocks"; we must take care to "gobble", i.e. remove the stump, after picking, and when there is nothing left after the rock. After ten or fifteen days, a new flock of mushrooms is planted in the same place, and so on until the manure is completely used up. OUTDOOR CULTIVATION If you're going to mount the stacks outside, you'll need to wrap them in a large quantity of dry manure, which will be renewed as often as it becomes too wet. This is called "putting on a shirt", and over it you put a thickness of dry manure that varies according to the weather, to maintain a heat of at least fifteen to twenty degrees. Sometimes, even during severe frosts, the paths have to be filled with manure to prevent the frost from penetrating the earth. Manure must be carefully selected to cover the millstones. First, a light layer of large, dry manure or straw is placed immediately in contact with the grinding wheel, followed by a thicker layer of large, dry manure. Warm manure would give off too much heat, causing the spawn to "spin", i.e. the mycelium would elongate more quickly, be less compact and tend to spread to the edges of the grinding wheel, whereas in good conditions it should form in the interior of the mass, thin, tight and very compact. A millstone that is well covered throughout with this fine, tightly-packed mycelium produces a more abundant, longer-lasting harvest. How long this lasts is hard to say, as it depends on a number of circumstances: firstly, the vigor and hardiness of the mycelium used; secondly, temperature and humidity, as some mycelia require more heat or humidity than others; and thirdly, other influences that have not yet been elucidated in cultivation practice. Generally speaking, however, hot, heavy weather is less favorable to mushroom production than cool, dry weather. DISEASES. - WHITE RENEWAL When the weather is heavy and rainy, quarries lack air and "sulk", say mushroom growers. When this happens, they set up long wooden chimneys over draft holes, and light a strong stove at the bottom of the quarry to expel the stale air it contains and renew it. Despite all these efforts, they often fail to achieve the same results as when the weather is dry and cold. If the millstones sulk, they form "molles", a kind of other cryptogam that penetrates the earth and produces nothing; this represents a leprosy on the surface. If the air is sufficiently renewed, the disease disappears, but always with some benefit to the grower. When the air is vitiated and not sufficiently renewed, crops are often invaded by midges and moths, which are very harmful to them, but which can be eliminated by aerating. Once the manure has been prepared, the most important question, as in all cultivation, is the choice of seed, which we call here blanc de Champignons, and which is to be used to lard the grinding stone, as mentioned above. Virgin spawn, formed by the germination of spores, can be found around piles of manure, in old layers, around piles of sludge from towns and cities, in detritus of any kind, even in meadows where cattle graze. Large-scale mushroom growers sometimes take seed spawn from their own crops, but only if they can't get any better. Here's how they do it. When the wheel is well covered with mycelium, and the mushrooms are beginning to form in the earth covering the wheel, they cut slices of Om,25 from the wheel with a long knife, and remove these slices, which form compact cakes, thanks to the network of mycelium running through them; they then cut them into pieces Om,10 thick, which they place on shelves in a cool, airy place, to dry. Under these conditions, the white can be preserved for a long time. It is used when no other product is available, or when the manure from the millstones is too wet. Some specialist firms supply selected and renewed virgin white in slabs (fig. 42). Virgin whites are always preferable to those that have been cultivated for a number of years, being more vigorous by their very nature, and probably also because they are younger. The purity of the - Fig. 4. - Plate of mushroom spawn. spawn used for larding must also be taken into account, as it is not uncommon for it to be diseased, devoured by another, more voracious cryptogam, which mushroom growers call "verdigris". Care should be taken to peel the white before introducing it into the grinder, removing any parts that appear green, and leaving only what is quite white with very fine, tightly-packed filaments. Chancy" and "plaster" are other inferior fungi that devour cultivated Agaricum, and which must be carefully avoided in cultivation. For some years now, the Institut Pasteur has been working on reproducing mushrooms from seed, by sterilizing the mycelium. The spores are taken from varieties that give and promise a profitable harvest. At the first flush, the most beautiful plants are selected and kept as seedbeds, and sheets of paper are placed underneath to collect the spores, which are then placed in a vase in a dry place. The manure is prepared in exactly the same way as described above, filling glass tubes (fig. 43) and 1 Fig. 43 - Tube of sterilized mushroom spawn. The tube is plugged with a wad of AB absorbent cotton, which overflows into C. The seed is sown in these tubes, which are hermetically sealed and placed in an oven; the spores vegetate vigorously; after a fortnight, the filaments have spread to all parts of the manure and, a few days later, this manure, which we have referred to above as mise, can be used to lard other millstones. To date, specialists have not obtained all the results that might be expected from this innovation. It's a problem that's still under study, and can only be solved by scientific investigation, aided by specialists in practical and commercial aspects. Presumably, this mycelium will have to be renewed once or even twice in the open air, to acquire the necessary rusticity. In short, it will have to be acclimatized to outdoor temperatures, so that it becomes strong enough to produce a profitable harvest. There is every reason to believe that this problem will soon be solved, and that mushroom cultivation, which has so far been based on routine, will one day be able to proceed with certainty. In a word, this great family of Mushrooms, whose species are so difficult to destroy, and whose superior species are no less difficult to cultivate, will have its fundamental basis for cultivation, like all plants, in seed selection, the primordial principle of all good cultivation. Here again, the scientists at the Institut Pasteur will have rendered a signal service to industry, particularly in the Paris suburbs, where this type of cultivation has taken on such great proportions. Of course, we don't pretend to make growers believe that we'll achieve perfection, that cultivated mushrooms will be free of disease; no one is free of disease; but by working on young subjects, there's always more hope of cure than by working on worn-out subjects. Every grower will have to take many facts into account, and it is his or her initiative that will help the scientist and bring out, from his or her theoretical research, the practical results necessary for the prosperity of this industry. POTAGERS AND THEIR DISEASES Among insect pests, one of the most dreaded is the mole cricket. This terrible insect comes as big as a man's thumb, and burrows into the earth exactly like the mole, cutting and gnawing every root it encounters, even Carrots, Turnips, etc. It is especially fearsome in the soil, where it can cause serious damage. It is especially formidable in layers, establishing its lair at the bottom, where it can only be tracked down when the topsoil is removed to reconstitute new layers. The substance that market gardeners use to destroy them is oil or petroleum, which is poured into the holes where they settle, by pouring water over them; a drop of oil that reaches a mole infallibly kills it. But these insects have nests containing hundreds of eggs, so there are always enough to go around, and it's almost impossible to get rid of crickets completely in the terrain where they live. In late spring and summer, they come up for air at night, and cats, who are very fond of them, destroy many of them. White grubs, called horseflies by gardeners, and which are the larvae of cockchafer beetles, are only to be feared in newly-cultivated vegetable gardens, where they cause considerable damage; they are much less pleasant in old vegetable gardens, where the soil is too greasy and too often disturbed. The only way to destroy them is to seek them out without delay at the foot of plants you see withering and kill them; otherwise, when one plant is cut, they move on to another and end up destroying the whole crop. Various aphids also destroy vegetables. One of the most dreaded is a black aphid that attacks Cucurbitaceae. In some years, it multiplies so quickly and abundantly that it is difficult to get rid of. Against all aphids, nicotine cut with water is used in high doses: fifty liters for one liter of nicotine, to the degree to which the Tobacco Administration delivers it, and the plants are watered with this solution, preferably in the evening; but you must not wait until the aphids are too abundant, as you would almost have to destroy the plant to destroy the insect. Caterpillars and larvae of all shapes and colors attack plants in different ways, some through the roots, others, in greater numbers, through the leaves. The only way to get rid of them is to look for them and crush them. However, the caterpillars that eat the leaves of cabbages in general, and cauliflowers in particular, are fairly easy to get rid of; all you need to do is water often; when the leaves are continually wet, the butterflies that produce these caterpillars don't settle on them. Flea beetles, which destroy sorrel and young cabbage plants, can be combated by frequent watering; young cauliflower plants sometimes have to be shaded in late spring to get rid of them. A small white worm, called a guillotine, attaches itself especially to the roots and crown of cabbages of all varieties. It produces a kind of bulge at the root, and the plant perishes. So far, we know of no effective remedy for this plague. Loaches or slugs are very common in certain areas, especially in autumn. To destroy them, powdered lime is sprinkled on the soil, and those affected are burnt. But these insects often hide under the leaves, where they cannot be reached, so care must be taken to find them before destroying them. In some crops, small piles are made of leaves or debris from carrots and other vegetables, where slugs come to take refuge. Unless they are actively hunted down, these insects cause a great deal of damage. Ants can also cause damage to vegetable crops in hot, dry weather, but are quickly eradicated by watering. Grey mould is caused by a tiny Acarus insect that attacks the parenchyma of plants, especially as they age. Cucurbits, beans and celery are particularly susceptible. To combat it, we recommend either diluted nicotine, or the following solution: dissolve 60 grams of white soap in a liter of water, then add 20 grams of naphthol 8, followed by 1 liter of nicotine at 12° and 10 liters of water. You can also add a little quassia amara. Lettuce and Romaine rust, in spring, is due to the action of a microscopic fungus that spreads through sudden changes in temperature, cold sleet, etc. We don't know what causes it either. Nor do we know of any effective way of preventing this disease from occurring, except that young plants sown at the end of winter are less susceptible than those sown in autumn, and even then in certain damp, cold soils. In any case, all affected parts must be cut off and burned to prevent the disease spreading. Asparagus rust can be treated with Bordeaux or Burgundy mixture, as can strawberry rust. Melon blight, which mainly affects early and late-season melons, also appears after cold dews. This disease always attacks young shoots and fruit, when present; it literally cuts them off, and it is very difficult to obtain fruit from diseased plants. Since Cucurbitaceae are inherently cold plants, could it be that a kind of frost is produced on them, when the thermometer is several degrees warmer? Scientists are not yet in agreement on the remedies to be used against this disease; it's a very serious subject of study for anyone involved in horticulture. In the late season, when market gardeners see this cold dew on their plants, they water them to wash it off. Melon canker is cured by cutting away the diseased part and sprinkling the wound with sand or quicklime. Cabbages are sometimes attacked by a disease called hernia or grosfoot, which consists of an enlargement of the roots. Care should be taken to uproot any plants affected and not to leave any debris in the soil. Despite these precautions, however, the disease is still likely to spread if cabbages are grown again in the same soil, unless care is taken to place a good handful of quicklime at the foot of each plant, at the time of transplanting, in a trough six to ten centimetres deep, which is then filled with soil. Dephosphorization slag also prevents the spread of cabbage looper, and is used at a rate of around 1 hectoliter per acre. How many studies remain to be carried out on these various diseases, which often compromise market garden crops! Eggplant cultivation has been abandoned by market gardeners, and tomato cultivation has been seriously compromised, not only because of competition from products from the Midi, but also because of the disease to which these plants are prone when the cool nights of September arrive. However, good results are now being obtained in combating this disease, either with Iysol, spread at a rate of 12 grams per 10 liters of water, or with the following solution: in 1 liter of denatured alcohol, dissolve 250 grams of naphthol g crude powder; the solution is made cold after a few minutes; pour into a tub containing 500 to 600 liters of water, stirring constantly with a stick; this slightly cloudy liquid is sprayed on plants and used to water the soil. A disease of the same type as the previous one, which was not well known, or at least did not cause serious losses before the introduction of early crops, is miller's disease (Peronospora ganglüformis), which attacks lettuces and Romaines under frames and cloches. Plants grown outdoors recover quite easily, when the weather turns dry and warm. As for those grown 14 en primeur, as we have just said, when they are affected, they do not recover; the disease makes more or less progress, depending on the weather, but never disappears completely. The parasite causes the affected leaves to dry out, often seriously damaging the plant. During wet winters, the disease makes much more progress than when the weather is dry and cold. We estimate the losses incurred by market gardeners in the Paris region during these wet winters at several million francs. Forced cultivation of lettuces and Romaines begins in October, and continues throughout the autumn, winter and spring, until the plants are ready for cultivation in the open ground. We estimate the annual production of these early vegetables at one hundred million Lettuces and twenty million Romaines, in the market gardening corporation of the Paris region. About twenty years ago, the miller was already seriously studied by Mr. Maxime Cornu, the late Professor of Culture at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle. This scientist has submitted a memoir to the Académie des Sciences, in which he gives a very precise scientific study of the development of the disease that practitioners know from routine. Science has had many Peronospora to study over the last twenty years; Mr. Cornu once told us that the one that invades Lettuce and Romaine crops bears a close resemblance to the one that attacks Vines and is known as "mildew". As the latter could only be effectively combated with a copper sulfate-based treatment, he felt that the same would be true for market garden crops. PLANT PESTS AND DISEASES. 243 However, in this case, treatment becomes more difficult; as we are dealing with very soft and tender plants, it will be necessary to operate in a different way than for Vines, as the slightest toxicity hardens and retards them, and thereby causes harm to the grower. We therefore believe that, as far as possible, preventive action should be taken to destroy dormant spores. A few growers have already experimented with this approach, guided by routine, and have obtained certain results. With a view to resuming this research in a scientific manner, guided by the scientist who has already attached his name to the study of this disease, we have carried out new experiments, the results of which we are about to publish. Unfortunately - or perhaps fortunately, as our experiments are all the more conclusive - M. Cornu was absent from Paris at the time when preventive treatment should have begun, so we operated on plants already severely invaded by the terrible parasite. On December 20, 1899, we carried out an initial experiment on three panels of lettuces on bedding, half grown, and on ten bells of Romaine plants already showing some strength; these plants were to be planted on bedding with bells at the beginning of January. The treatment used was celestial water, composed of 1 kilogram of copper sulfate and 1,250 grams of commercial ammonia per hundred liters of water. The plants were sprayed. The lettuce being particularly tender, because it was on a bed, the diseased leaves turned red a few days after this operation; the non-diseased parts remained intact; however, the plants as a whole were hardened, but the disease was stopped. A few days after this treatment, the lettuces were peeled of all their diseased leaves, which were then dried; the plants continued to grow, quite healthy, quite clear, i.e. disease-free, and if they had been left for another eight days, they would have produced average, clean produce; but as they were in the first layer of a square that had to be turned over, the grower didn't want to delay his work for such a small quantity of lettuces. The result was still achieved, as there was no longer any disease. The delay caused to these plants, in full growth on the beds, can be estimated at eight or ten days. As the Romaine plants were harder, because they were transplanted cold and on soil, the same phenomenon occurred as for the Lettuces, only a little later. It's also worth noting that this experiment was carried out during a false thaw; as the frost picked up again the following night, it's possible that the plants, after this treatment, weren't sufficiently covered and that this fact contributed to hardening them even more. On January 5, when we made another visit, the miller was back on four of the most seriously affected bells. They were given a new drenching, exactly like the first, even where the disease had not reappeared. Around January 10th, with the thaw having come and the miller seemingly extinct, the plants were peeled of all their diseased leaves, which were also dried, and they continued to vegetate. Only, instead of giving them air as with other, non-diseased plants, they were kept enclosed under the cloches. Despite this, they suffered a delay of at least a fortnight, and instead of being planted around January 10, they were not planted until the end of the same month; a row of cloches had been set up along the entire length of the bed, the better to see the difference with the other plants next to them. Towards the end of February, after a few days of mild weather and a strong westerly wind, the disease invaded the whole square of layers, and the treated row, with a few exceptions here and there, remained unscathed. The plants, which belonged to the flat Romaine de Paris variety, were green and well spread out, while the other diseased plants were already closed, which would make bad merchandise, because, as all practitioners know, this variety, to come into its own, must be spread out at the start of its bed planting, and the leaves must take the edges of the bell to cap (i.e. close) at the bonnet. But with the disease so widespread throughout the square, could these plants remain unharmed until the end? Around March 15, a few traces of the disease could be seen on them. Nevertheless, as they were already strong, they were delivered for consumption at the end of the month, and were still the most beautiful merchandise in the square. Seeing such an appreciable result, we asked Mr. Cornu, accompanied by his assistant Mr. Bois, and former gardeners Mr. Duvillard, Mr. Laurent and Mr. Becquerelle, who had worked with Mr. Cornu on this subject in the past, to verify the results. This experiment was carried out on the premises of Mr. Canard, a market gardener at route de Châtillon, 85, Montrouge, and this practitioner knows only too well the ravages caused by the terrible parasite, in a marsh that is nonetheless exceptionally well tended. We believe, both scholars and practitioners, that this 14. experiment is not complete, having been started too late. Here, then, are the means we recommend, from a practical point of view, to combat this terrible cryptogam. At sowing time, spray celestial water on the soil to be sown and a little on the surrounding area, to destroy the disease spores; at transplanting time, repeat the operation at the place where the plants are to be transplanted; pass the cloches through a solution of sulfated water. For bed planting, M. Cornu felt that watering was no longer sufficient; he recommended the use of fine wood shavings, soaked in the same solution and spread over the bed; we pointed out to him, as an old practitioner, that this was not practical. It was therefore agreed that the wood shavings could be replaced by very dry, fine mulch, such as the body of a grinding wheel. This mulch, placed in a basket of some kind, would be soaked in a solution of celestial water prepared in a barrel; a light layer of this mulch would then be spread over the soil to be planted. As the soil soaked up the solution, the gases would remain active for longer on the surface of the soil, under the bell or frame. The experiment we have just described clearly demonstrates that the disease only reappeared when the gases in the solution were no longer active. In old marshes contaminated by this disease, care should be taken to pass chassis, cloches, etc., through a sulfated water solution. If, between transplanting and planting, the slightest trace of disease should appear, the plant should be bathed with the above solution, but reduced by at least half, so as not to harm vegetation, or preferably with a simple copper sulfate solution, the composition of which is described at the end of this chapter. Perseverance is the only way to eradicate this terrible disease, especially in old contaminated marshes. By publishing these experiments, which were conducted by a professor from the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle, we believe we are providing a useful service to practitioners whose crops are at risk of contracting this disease. It is also up to them to seek other practical means of combating it; we give the one we have used, believing that even better ones can be found. It's in everyone's interest to work towards this goal. Here's a striking example to edify them: Ten or fifteen years ago, when downy mildew was wreaking such havoc in vineyards, and the means of combating it had finally been discovered, some people, resistant to all progress, did not want to sulfate their vines; so in the same vineyard, towards the end of August and September, you would see vines whose leaves were quite green, alongside others whose leaves were yellow or even fallen off; the cause of this difference was that the former had been sulfated and the latter had not. Faced with such a result, even the most reluctant were forced to face the facts, and today all winegrowers sulfate their vines. The difference between the first and the last is that those who agreed to heed the advice of the scientists reaped the rewards, while the others reaped nothing. This example is conclusive enough in itself to encourage the younger generations of gardeners to seek every possible means of combating a plague that devastates their crops during the winter. Today's scientists are well aware of the disease, how it comes about, how it develops, how it spreads, etc.; they tell us the remedies with which we can combat it - not destroy it, that's impossible. It remains for practitioners to find the most effective and convenient ways of applying these remedies. This experiment is all the more conclusive in that we have carried out others with no appreciable results. These experiments were as follows: before planting, we sprayed a few bell beds with Bordeaux mixture, and others with sugar mixture; but the plants were already contaminated, and three weeks or a month after planting, i.e. when the gases produced by these solutions had been extinguished, the sucker reappeared with the same violence as everywhere else. Nevertheless, we invite practitioners to continue trials with the different copper sulfate solutions. To make these studies easier for those unfamiliar with the composition and use of these solutions, we indicate how to prepare and use them. One kilogram of copper sulfate dissolved in three liters of hot water, stirring the crystals; after cooling, add one and a half liters of commercial ammonia at 22° Baumé; pour into one hundred liters of water. BOUILLIE BORDELAISE Two to three kilograms of copper sulfate and two kilograms of slaked lime, all in one hundred INSECTS HAZARDOUS TO PLANTS AND DISEASES. 249, liters of water. First dissolve copper sulfate in ten liters of hot water; slake the lime; after cooling, pour it into the sulfate solution (do not do the reverse); add ninety liters of water. SWEET MUD Dissolve two kilograms of copper sulfate in fifteen or twenty liters of water; add three kilograms of soda crystals dissolved in a few liters of water. When the copper has precipitated, add two kilograms of molasses, leave for twelve hours, then add water to make up one hundred liters. Instead of soda ash (crystals), use two kilograms of crushed lime. SIMPLE SOLUTION Formula: three to five hundred grams of copper sulfate per hectoliter of water. To prepare all these products, use wooden containers. To use them, preferably with a sprayer. The composition of all these solutions has been supplied to us by Mr. Cornu's laboratory at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle. We feel that the simple solution should only be used on plants that have been attacked by the disease despite the preventive treatments we have indicated above.
