Before moving on to the special cultivation of edible plants in our gardens, we believe it will be useful to give a few general indications concerning the quality of soil and fertilizers, and the various methods of operation involved in the science we are about to deal with. SETTING UP A MARKET GARDEN; CHOICE OF LAND. When the gardener has a certain amount of land at his disposal and can choose a site to establish his garden, he will pay less attention to the quality of the soil surface than to the depth of the plant layer. Let him observe, then, that the land is very suitable for market gardening if it is made up of a layer of clean soil, one CULTURE MARAICHÈRE. 2. a meter deep, and if at the same time this layer rests on a subsoil of sand: well-tended soil of this nature promises very fine produce. The same is not true when the topsoil is sandy, not very thick and resting on a loamy subsoil: in this case, if the garden is in a low-lying area and water cannot easily run off through drainage ditches, it is certain that the very spring-like cultivation of vegetables will be impracticable; water stagnates on the subsoil; the topsoil is full of moisture in winter and spring; it is cold and everything is late. The garden also needs to be well ventilated, completely uncovered and sheltered, if possible, from the cold northerly winds by wooden curtains or groves. Low-lying land, if not damp, is more advantageous than arid, mountainous terrain. An essential point not to be lost sight of is the means of water supply to which the crop very often owes its prosperity; for the best soils, those that give easy passage to water, need it during the heat. The proximity of a stream is such an advantage that it can become a determining factor in the choice of land. In the absence of running water, a reservoir set up, if possible, in the middle of the garden, can sometimes make up for it. When building such a reservoir, it's a good idea to find out how deep the water is underground, which can easily be discovered by measuring the water level in the nearest wells. In large gardens, water is distributed by pipes laid under the paths and leading to several reservoirs. If, as is often the case, you are obliged to accept ready-made layouts, gardens already created in advance, all you have to do is divide up the land and adapt it as best you can to the different crops. Division. - When it comes to distribution, whether you're dealing with a previously cultivated site or a brand-new garden, squares and straight, parallel beds should take precedence. The various operations can always be carried out with the greatest ease and promptness. The extent of the large divisions can be arbitrary; however, these squares should be laid out in such a way as to facilitate services as much as possible. Planks should be 1.33 m wide; wider planks make weeding and hoeing inconvenient; a man of average height should be able to reach the middle of the planks without having to walk on them. The narrow paths separating the beds should be level with the beds in dry, sandy soils, whereas they should be dug in wet, clayey soils. Exposure. - The exposure of the garden to the sun must be taken into serious consideration: land facing east or between east and south, with a gentle slope towards one of these sides, is to be preferred to any other for both exposure and slope. Ruts. - Ripping should only be carried out when the topsoil is sandy and shallow, and if it is advantageous to mix it with the underlying clay layer, and vice versa, or when the surface of the land has been depleted by previous cultivation. It's worth noting that plants almost always thrive less in the first and second years after two- to three-foot-deep trenching, but that all plants in general, and root vegetables in particular, benefit considerably thereafter; being able to penetrate deeper into the soil, they produce infinitely better and are more beautiful. One disadvantage of this practice is that it gives rise to a lot of weeds: seeds buried deep in the earth retain their germinative capacity for many years, and soon develop as soon as they come into contact with atmospheric agents. To break up a plot of land, we usually proceed as follows: open a trench of indeterminate length, 1 metre wide and Om,60 to 0m,70 deep or thereabouts; deposit the soil emerging from it at the other end of the plot, where the work is to end; then carry the soil from a second layer to the place of the first, and so on. In order to proceed more rationally when breaking up the soil, an operation which not only entails the cost of difficult and always costly work, but also a loss of produce in the first few years, we recommend breaking up the soil gradually, year by year, by about ten centimetres lower than previously, so that after five or six years the desired depth and movement of soil have been reached. In this way, labor costs are insignificant, and yields, instead of decreasing in the early years, are actually increased. However, the experienced grower knows perfectly well that, in principle, any deeply broken ground requires a lot of fertilizer. This fact can be explained by what happens during plant nutrition. As the plant layer formed by the decomposition of organic animal or vegetable substances is displaced, the land now on the surface is sterile; it must have been subjected for a long time to the influences of the atmospheric air and must have received new fertilizers before plants can find abundant nourishment there. It is for these reasons that we recommend, as stated above, to break up the soil gradually, from year to year. Ploughing. - The ploughing that is commonly carried out in the vegetable garden by "béchage" does not take place all year round, so we first draw attention to autumn ploughing: this is intended to purify the soil, and make it loose and fertile. Any land that is not planted with vegetables in winter should therefore be ploughed or, what we prefer, ridged. Experience shows that ploughing before winter improves the soil, and that frosts have the greatest effect on ploughed land. After prolonged, bitter cold, the soil undergoes a kind of calcination that turns it to dust, as happens to certain metals which, by decomposing part of the atmospheric air, appropriate its oxygen, oxidize and disintegrate. The same ameliorating effects can occur during the summer: subjected to the repeated action of the sun's cha1. leur, a chalky soil calcines and crumbles to dust. Its surface, now soft and loose, offers easy access to the deeper penetration of atmospheric gases essential to the decomposition of fertilizing principles which, having become soluble in water, are now absorbed by the stomata or inhalant mouths found at the ends of plant roots. So, as we can see, ploughing is a means of fertilizing the soil that produces astonishing effects; moreover, it is equally suited to sandy and clayey soils. As for the process of ridging a plot of land, it's the easiest of all: you mark out paths about Om.40 wide with a chalk line, and spade them to the same depth, placing one half on the ridge to the left, and the other half on the ridge to the right. This earth, cut in slices or spaded to a thickness of about one decimeter, will cover the planks everywhere, which are about 1.33 m wide. It will not be broken or harrowed; all the clods will be next to each other or partially superimposed, like tiles on a roof. The greater the surface area of these clods, the more the soil is subjected to the beneficial influences of atmospheric gases charged with the emanations that provide the roots with nourishment and give the soil fertility. Ploughing, or "béchage" as it is known, consists of opening a gauge with the spade, and bringing the soil to the corner of the square where the ploughing is to end; it is then brought back to close the last ray. The first gauge is filled by digging the second, and so on. The gardener must pay close attention to this operation, because the success or failure of the harvest often depends on the good or bad execution of the licking: it is not on the surface of the soil that the clods must be broken, but in the gauge itself; the shovelfuls will not be more than ten centimetres thick, and the gardener, instead of depositing them by turning them over, must break them by shaking them on the spade. Some careless workers walk, for their own convenience, while spading, even in the gauges: it's a vicious routine. The bottom of the shelves sink and settle, and the vegetation suffers. Stubborn, clayey soils can always be ploughed in dry weather; if, on the other hand, you shape them while they are wet, you render them impervious to atmospheric agents and sterile for a long time to come. Levelling and straightening planks. - Since levelling is simply a shaping operation consisting of filling and clearing, according to geometric measurements, we don't think it's worth dwelling on it for long. The same applies to planking, which we explain in Special Crops. So, when the ploughing is finished, and the boards have been given their width by the paths that frame them, all that remains is to level them with the rake to make them suitable for planting or seeding. First and foremost, we feel we must review the various fertilizers used in gardening, which we will divide into two classes: animal fertilizers and plant fertilizers. PQ Sludge. - Among animal fertilizers, we'll start with slurry, the manure that comes from cesspools, also known as Flemish funtier, human manure, which should be appreciated by every good grower and gardener. This manure can be applied to the cultivation of all vegetable plants in general, as we shall see later, and activates vegetation to a very high degree. In sandy soils, as experience has shown, it is very difficult to produce good pea, bean and cabbage crops without the use of this eminently fertilizing substance. Suitably distributed in cultivation, the excremental parts of man can provide a measure of a country's agricultural development. Foreigners like to point to Flanders as a very advanced country in terms of cultivation, and we know what a prodigious quantity of sludge is used there every year. The Chinese are cited as the first people on earth in terms of knowledge of cultivation; and the Chinese value this precious fertilizer so highly that they collect it in vases on public roads and deposit it at the foot of plants. As with all other animal fertilizers, the value of human fertilizer is relative to the nature of the food; it will be all the more energetic the more human consumption consists of high-nitrogen foods, such as meats. It is also on the basis of differences in diet that chemical analyses, in both humans and animals, show such a wide range of results for individuals of the same species, with regard to their excreta. Today, thanks to advances in farming, these substances are used not only in Belgium, but also in Germany, France, Italy, England and Holland. As sludge cannot be used on a daily basis, it must be stored in masonry tanks; if possible, an opening should be left on the north side to allow atmospheric air to enter and accelerate fermentation. These tanks are proportionate to the size of the farm, and can range from 6 to 30 cubic meters. Flemish manure should not be used for cultivation until it has fermented for a few months. It can be used very advantageously in compost and for special crops, as we will often mention in this treatise. Poudrette. - Poudrette is the name given to human fecal matter that has been dried for use. To prepare this fertilizer, the solid matter is mixed with clay after the urine has been drained, then dried in the sun and stored. This method of processing fertilizer is highly unsound: firstly, all the urine, so rich in urate and ammonia phosphate, is lost; as we can see, it's a waste of this excellent fertilizer. This process could therefore be rejected. Although it has lost a large part of its fertilizing properties, poudrette is still a very active fertilizer, but not as long-lasting as sludge. Its action on cereals has been observed to diminish sharply, if not cease, at the time of fruiting. Animalized black. - In order to disinfect human feces, we have found a way to incorporate them intimately with charcoal. The disinfectant properties of charcoal have long been known, but a cheaper alternative had to be found, and this has now been discovered: humus-rich earth, burnt in closed vessels. Humus, like all vegetable substances, becomes carbonaceous and absorbent after combustion. By mixing it with sludge, ammoniacal gases condense in it; the fertilizer remains active for longer, and plants find more lasting nourishment. The richest humus-rich soils are best suited to making animalized black, such as marsh soil, which sometimes contains 50% plant debris. To fix the ammonia hydrosulfate found in cesspools, which produces the foul odor that is so unpleasant, chemistry has provided us with several substances that combine with this gas. Iron sulfate, dissolved in water and mixed with this manure, forms ammonia hydrosulfate, a fixed, odorless salt, while iron oxide precipitates out. Animal black. - Animal black should not be confused with animal black, more properly known as refinery residue black. Sugar refiners purify syrups using blood and animal charcoal, also known as ivory black, obtained by burning bones (lime phosphate) in closed vessels. This residue is a highly active fertilizer, as is easy to understand, since lime phosphate, which is in itself a very good fertilizer, is mixed with blood, a very nitrogenous substance. Sheepfold manure. - This manure is very active and considered a hot fertilizer. This ancient and traditional qualification is nothing if not vague. Since the progress of chemistry, the strength and goodness of fertilizers have been determined according to the more or less nitrogen they contain. Among horned beasts, sheep and goats produce the most nitrogenous manures; it follows that this manure is one of the most fertilizing; furthermore, its physical consistency means that it does not ferment easily, and, in this respect, ammonia losses are less to be feared than in stable manure. Woollen manure is especially suited to cold, clay soils that need a fertilizer that doesn't take too long to work; this is precisely the case with nitrogen-dominant fertilizers, which work quickly and are especially suited to plants that grow quickly: all crucifers benefit considerably from them; hemp grows very strongly from them; tobacco develops extraordinarily well from them. It is also extremely useful in composting. Its action hardly lasts beyond the first year; this characteristic is common to all highly nitrogenous fertilizers. Stable manure. - This is the name given to manure from horses, donkeys and mules. The droppings of these animals, mixed with vegetable substances, undergo various degrees of decomposition through fermentation, making them more or less suitable as plant food. This type of manure is generally used for all crops; it is, so to speak, the only one used for mushroom cultivation, and is eminently suitable for forced cultivation beds. What makes it especially valuable for this type of cultivation is the ease with which its fermentation can be 7 stopped or activated, depending on the need for artificial heat. All you have to do is keep it dry or damp. To keep it in a suitable state of dryness, we keep it in sheds or even in a dry, completely uncovered place: litter or long manure is used for this purpose. It must not be too compressed. You should also avoid rebuilding the piles in order to moderate the heat, which will only reproduce more actively. When it's time to use it, all you have to do is wet it and compress it hard enough: it will ferment and heat up within three days. It's a popular misconception that stable manure is too hot for sandy soils: it's suitable for all soils, but it decomposes more quickly, so its fertilizing power is used up more quickly in such soils. When destined for gardens or fields, it's a good idea to mix it with cow or pig manure, and often wet it with liquid manure; this prevents fermentation and prevents it from burning. Stable manure. - Although it doesn't work as quickly as stable manure, horned-animal manure is more durable for our gardens, and its virtue is felt for a long time. It produces a lot of humus, is a powerful food for plants, and is suitable for all plants and all soils. It makes clay soils soft and loose, and gives consistency to light, sandy soils. Note that it is even better and more durable if it comes from fattening animals; animals fed on straw only produce manure of lesser value. culture liquid fertilizer, which comes from piles of stable manure. It is highly advantageous for vegetable plants, used either pure or mixed with other substances. The horticulturist uses it very advantageously when decomposing a large mass of plant matter: it's an effective way of obtaining an ample supply of potting soil, which market gardening can hardly do without. Pig manure. - Contrary to popular belief, pig manure is more active than horse or cow manure. Pigs are omnivores: they feed not only on vegetable substances such as potatoes and cereals, but also on animal substances such as meat and milk. This being the case, it must necessarily produce a more nitrogenous fertilizer: chemical analysis confirms this. Guano. - Guano is the name given to the droppings of the seabirds that inhabit the coasts of Chile, Peru and Colombia. These birds are found in excessively large flocks in a few small fles, where they have been depositing their droppings for a long series of years. It is this fertilizer that today makes a fairly considerable article of trade; but since guano was found to be mixed with less energetic substances, either by fraud or accident, European trade has become wary of it. Columbine. - Pigeon droppings, one of the most active fertilizers among those derived from poultry, are even more effective than chicken droppings, which already have a great fertilizing power, as we shall see in the cultivation of 2. * onions. Pigeon pellets contain a greater quantity of nitrogen than hen droppings, which in turn contain a greater quantity than the droppings of other animals. Pigeon pellets must be kept dry to be used at the right time. Spread among young leguminous plants, carrots, onions, cauliflower, beans and parsnips, it produces astonishing effects; but its use requires a great deal of caution, and the layer spread must be far from covering the soil. Cucurbits benefit extraordinarily from the use of these fertilizers; diluted in water, they can be used for watering once or twice a year; it's after similar waterings that we've seen ornamental plants, camellias and fuchsias, flourish, so to speak. PLANT FERTILIZERS. As they decompose, plants form fertilizers that differ from animal fertilizers not so much in their constituent principles as in their apparent form. They contain oxygen, hydrogen, carbon and, in some cases, even nitrogen; as with animals, they also contain most mineral substances and salts. It follows that plant manure is a great resource for cultivation. This is why marshes, where the detritus of plant matter has built up layers of humus, are so fertile that the most luxurious crops can be grown there for ten or fifteen years, without the need for further amendment. Crops mowed green and buried always return more fertilizer to the soil than they take away. A soil where grasses grow, die and reproduce, instead of becoming thinner, becomes fatter: if these same grasses were continually removed from this soil, without restoring the extracted principles, it would become poor and sterile. It is on this theory that the various crop rotations are based, and hence all cultivation: giving back to the soil what the harvests have taken away from it. Farmers and agronomists can considerably enrich their land with manure, if they are careful enough to collect the residues of vegetables, flowers, weeds from weeding, leaves from trees, plants that grow on the banks of water, lawns, mosses, ferns, etc., all mixed with animal substances. All this mixed with animal substances makes excellent compost, as we shall see when growing asparagus, pineapples and other plants. Amendments. - Amendments are inorganic or mineral substances such as clay, sand, marl and lime, which change the physical constitution of the soil. Clay makes soil that is too light more consistent; sand loosens clay soil that is too compact; marl, whose use was already known to the ancient Celts, makes soil more porous; it is composed of clay, sand and lime; lime makes sandy soil more consistent, and soil that is too compact less tenacious. However, the action of these bodies is not purely mechanical: they unite with the acids contained in the earth and air, and form salts that are more or less neutral, more or less soluble in water, and which, carried into plant tissues by capillary vessels, can immediately serve to nourish them. Ashes, soot and gypsum are usually included among soil improvers, although in the strictest sense these compound substances are merely fertilizers that simultaneously act mechanically on the nature of the soil. Potting soil. - Potting soil is made up of the remains of plant substances that have passed through the various stages of fermentation. This plant detritus, which necessarily varies according to the plants from which it comes, contributes greatly to loosening the soil, making it permeable to carbonic acid gas, atmospheric air and humidity, all indispensable conditions for beautiful, productive vegetation. Decomposed plant matter becomes humus, which plays a chemical role in plant growth by releasing carbonic acid and nitrogen principles to the roots. SEEDING. Seed selection. - Only the best seeds from the best species will ever be harvested: those from sickly or bastardised individuals, or those collected in soil that is too thin or too smoky, produce stunted, sickly plants. The condition of seeds is usually judged by inspection; the water test is also of some help: bad seeds float to the surface, while good ones sink to the bottom. But the surest way is to count a hundred or so seeds taken at random from those you wish to use: sow them in a small terrine, cover them and maintain the humidity. Placed in a warm apartment, or better still in the greenhouse, or on a bed if it's cold, the terrine gives a measure of the seed's validity; all you have to do is see how many seeds out of a hundred have germinated. Sowing methods. - Although most seeds are placed in the ground around springtime, there are no fixed times for seeding. They are sown according to the phases of life the plants go through, according to the climate to which they belong, and even according to their intended use. Thus, to prolong the use of certain vegetables, they are sown several times during the year. We are no longer in the days when people consulted the course of the moon before sowing, and believed in its influence on vegetation. However, we don't blame the inhabitants of our countryside for their traditional habit of sowing a particular plant on a particular saint's day. This often means that they conform in some way to the appropriate times for sowing, which are favorable to the success of the operation, times that their agricultural occupations would sometimes cause them to forget. It would be difficult to give a general indication of the time required for seeds to germinate, and the time they need to reach full development: we will refer to each crop in particular. In different soils, the same seeds will be sown earlier or later; they will be entrusted to cold, damp clay soil later than to warm, sandy soil. When the soil is too wet, it's best to delay sowing by a few days; it's also wise to consult the barometer, as heavy rain immediately after sowing will 2. compromise the harvest. As for the thickness of the layer to cover the seeds, there's a fairly safe rule of thumb: the finer the seeds, the less they should be covered, so that those the size of a pinhead and below, such as celery, parsley, purslane, lettuce and a host of others, are no more than 9n.02 deep; some very small seeds are content and even better off not being covered: a wetting with the apple watering can fixes them sufficiently. Seedlings require well-prepared, soft, loose and sometimes even terra-cotta soil. They require constant, well-maintained humidity during their young life. It is often necessary to shelter seeds during germination with moss, which is removed as soon as the young plant appears. Sowing is divided into broadcast sowing and sowing in rays or rows. Broadcast sowing involves grasping a handful of seeds between the fingers, and spreading them over the soil as the arm is rotated. Fine seeds are grasped between thumb and forefinger; less fine seeds, such as carrot or onion seeds, are grasped between thumb, forefinger and middle finger: in this way, they are more evenly distributed. For sowing in rows, we draw deep radii, spaced according to what we want to sow. For this purpose, we have had a wooden rake made to the ordinary width of boards, or 1m,35; it has two sets of tines; in one the tines are at Om,10, this is intended for sowing carrots, onions, etc.; in the other, they are at 0m, 13, it is used for sowing parsnips, salsify, scorzonera. The teeth are triangular and pointed; they are 0m,025 thick and Om,09 long. To make it easier to hold the rake along the length of the boards, and to ensure that the rays are straight and parallel, a slat is fixed along the edge of the board with three pegs, against which the first tooth of the rake is pressed as it is drawn. This is how we have successfully sown the plants we have just named, as well as spinach, coffee chicory and others. Seeds are easily covered, taking care to follow the direction of the rows. Sowing in rows is very advantageous, especially in soils where hoeing and weeding must be frequent. Transplanting. - This operation is necessary for all plants that cannot be sown in situ: it consists in lifting the young plants when they have four or six leaves, and planting them in a nursery or in situ. Many plants, such as lettuces, endives and beets, cannot be transplanted in the nursery. Others are very difficult to transplant, such as cabbages, especially red, white and Savoy cabbages. Without transplanting in the nursery, their stems acquire a length that is not only unpleasant to the eye, but also detrimental to their beauty. The root hairs of transplanted plants develop better, and they are more resistant to frost. During transplanting, care must be taken not to trample the roots on themselves, to shorten those that are too long, and to firm the soil by the pressure of the planter without overloading it. It's a good idea to transplant the most delicate and tender plants in the evening, or to cover them until they recover, during bright sunshine; plants that need it are transplanted in the shade. You'll find these details in the special crops section. Counterplants. - To save time, and with the aim of extracting the greatest amount of produce from the soil, the gardener doesn't always wait until the land is empty before dedicating it to another vegetable crop; he often starts cultivating another plant when the first has reached the middle or three quarters of its vegetation; this operation is called counter-planting. This is how market gardeners in Paris counter-plant celeriac or pear-cardea in a chicory bed, chicory in lettuces, tomatoes in romaine, lettuces and romaine in cauliflower, cauliflower in escarole, etc. Interplanting. - Interplanting is the name given to the method of cultivating, between plants specially intended for a plot of land, other plants which, without harming the first, produce a double harvest, so to speak. This is how beets and green cabbage are planted between rows of beans, at the same time as or a few days after the latter; lettuces are planted between cabbages, and cabbages between broad beans, and so on. It's easy to see how these well-made counter-plantings and inter-plantings can considerably increase the year's harvests. We therefore call serious attention to these methods of horticultural cultivation. Topdressing. - Sprinkled on the soil among young plants, potting soil activates their growth and develops their root system; it prevents them from drying out and maintains the porosity of the soil. This operation is known as terreautage. In market gardening, compost or mixtures of decomposed animal and vegetable substances are more commonly referred to as terreau. They can be prepared in a variety of ways, so to speak, for the crops for which they are needed. Cowshed litter with lots of cow dung, stirred several times during the year; leaves packed in a mixture with sludge, stirred several times during the same interval; Jauffret fertilizer or lime mixed with fresh or dried plants, packed and sprinkled with an alkaline solution or with washing water, turned over several times during the year; butcher's blood mixed with lime and soft earth; tannin, blood, lime and sand, treated as above; consumed manure from broken layers used for forced cultivation; colombina, hen droppings and others offer so many composts that can all be very usefully applied to topdressing, as we shall often see in the course of this treatise. Mulching. - This operation, one of the most useful for vegetable growing, is too little practised in Belgium. Easy to carry out, it consists of spreading litter on the surface of the soil, between transplanted or established plants. Its effects on vegetation are the same as those of topdressing; however, mulch cannot be applied to seedlings that have not yet been transplanted. The results of mulching are: to keep the soil fresh, to prevent water from evaporating too quickly during watering, to preserve the porosity of the soil so that water and air can penetrate it more easily; and finally, through the gradual decomposition of litter, mulch provides plants with continuous food that watering and rainfall carry to their roots. It also prevents an unfortunate accident in low plants such as strawberries, cabbage and romaine. Driving rain causes soil particles to splash onto the underside of leaves, clogging their pores and interrupting, if not totally then at least partially, one of the most important physiological functions - the absorption of moisture and gaseous fluids. In addition to these various results, the cleanliness that mulching produces in plants and especially in strawberry fruits, as we shall see later, must also be taken into account. The thickness to be given to the mulch layer is indeterminate; however, we can say that a layer of short manure or litter of Om,08 to 0m,10 is reduced by settling to a thickness of Om, 02 or Om,03. Mulching is carried out after straightening the beds, before or after planting. Tanning. - Here we recommend the use of a material which we have used successfully for a number of years, which would otherwise be improperly called mulching, and which we propose to call tanning. This consists in spreading a layer of tannin, Om,04 or Om,08 thick, over the beds after planting. This material can be used as it comes out of the tanners' vats; and without harming the most delicate plants in the least, it has the precious property of keeping snails away. In contact with air and humidity, tannin decomposes, becomes humus, and is incorporated into the soil by hoeing. Watering. - In all crops, watering is one of the most useful operations. Water carries the salts it dissolves to the roots of plants, and at the same time carries all the nutrients in fertilizers: without water, vegetation is impossible. Apply the most effective fertilizers to plants in a dry state; you won't get any results. Who hasn't seen plants wither and suffer, even on the best soils, on days of scorching heat? Who hasn't seen their corollas and leaves bend sadly? Since their roots can't pump out as much juice as the pores of their leaves have to give up through evaporation, a state of suffering must necessarily permeate their entire organization; and although the beneficial dew in the evening refreshes and revives plants whose existence is threatened, this dew is far from sufficient to continue providing them with the nourishment from which they must constantly draw their strength. This is why watering replaces rainfall, and gives plants strength and health through a generous distribution of water. While we have recently seen some fine results from irrigation in Belgium, France's horticultural industry has for some time now been making remarkable progress with various watering systems. It's easy to believe that a 50-acre marsh in Paris receives up to 100,000 liters of water a day in summer. We don't really know why market gardening in our country has so far been so stingy when it comes to watering, whereas it offers so many resources. In hot weather, evening watering is best: by then, the coolness has already warmed the soil and plants, and water cannot cause the temperature contrast that would occur during the day. In spring and autumn, when the nights are already cool, water only in the morning, and observe the same rule for plants on beds, under frames, in tarpaulins and in greenhouses. No plant, with the exception of strawberries, likes to be watered in bright sunlight. For the same reason, we must avoid watering with icy well water, which, if left cold on the plant, causes a kind of plant catarrh, if I may put it this way: this water tightens the pores of the plant due to its lack of temperature balance, and to the lime sub-carbonate it dissolves. If you don't have a spring or a water source, and you have to use well water, you should pour it into a reservoir to bring it into equilibrium with the air temperature, and at the same time allow the carbonic acid gas to be released, and the lime to precipitate. Untimely watering is often harmful to melons and lettuces, whereas when the time is right, it is very beneficial. It's best to water around the stems and roots. In our gardens, watering is commonly carried out using a watering can with a head pierced with fine holes: the water should always be poured over the plants, very evenly, and fall in small showers; the water should not be allowed to pool or stagnate on the soil; it should be allowed to soak in as it is poured. Weeding. - Weeding consists in removing weeds that live on fertilizer, at the expense of the cultivated plants among which they are found. In vegetable gardens, this operation is usually carried out by hand, by uprooting: if it were very dry, the soil would have to be moistened in the evening, so that work could begin the next day. Weeds can also be removed by hoeing. Hoeing. - Hoeing is an operation that consists in loosening the surface of the soil with the hoe: it's one of the most necessary, and contributes effectively to the beautiful vegetation of all plants. It makes the soil permeable and allows atmospheric gases to exert their influence on roots and fertilizers. Rain easily penetrates the soil, whereas it runs off without penetrating it when the soil is covered with the crusts that form on its surface. The half of the same square that has been hoeed will produce good crops, while the other half, left untouched, will only produce poor vegetation. It's to this often-repeated operation that our Flanders region owes its fine cultivation. Turnips, rapeseed and potatoes are hoeed several times. In other parts of the country, the soil is hardly ever worked in this way. It's also worth noting that hoeing, instead of making the soil drier during hot spells, actually keeps it wetter for longer, making it more resistant to disease. Serfouissage. - This operation, similar to the previous one, has the same aim and the same results: it is performed with the serfouette, an instrument with two or three teeth of varying lengths, depending on the soil to be ploughed. Like hoeing, this operation must be carried out in dry weather. Sealing. - Ploughing consists in treading the 2. ground with jointed feet, or firming it with the back of the spade or shovel. Its purpose is to bring the seeds into immediate contact with the soil, and to give them a slight resistance that makes them sprout faster and more regularly. This operation would be more appropriately called tamping, and is performed in dry weather. Mounding. - This operation consists of piling up earth around the base of the plants; its purpose differs according to the crops and plants to which it is applied. Sometimes it's to protect plants from frost, sometimes to preserve their produce, encourage new roots and give them new growth. Cabbages, for example, are better able to withstand the cold and wind if ridged before winter. This is especially true for potatoes, to protect their produce, give them more vigour and produce a greater number of tubers. When ridged, marsh beans gain new vegetative strength and are better able to withstand winds; the same applies to beans and peas. Buttting is often used to remove the ribbing and leaves from plants: this is how celery, chard, crambe, rhubarb, etc. are bleached. As we shall see later, these different crops are grown not only with soil, but also with manure, leaves and tanning agent. Crop rotation. - To maintain the fertility of the soil, it is essential to alternate crops, i.e. to alternate plants from one family with those from another. For example, plants from the legume family should be followed by plants from the cruciferous, umbelliferous and solanaceous families. Plants with tracing roots, such as strawberries, will be followed by plants with taproots, such as carrots or parsnips. The theory of crop alternation and rotation is of the utmost importance; the herticulturist cannot deviate from it without impoverishing the soil and compromising his harvests. Whether he's renewing his plantings, his beds, his groups; whether he's replacing one vegetable with another, he must never lose sight of the fact that a more or less long period of time is required before plants from the same family can reappear in the same place. Above all, he must never leave his plot empty; by combining and following the right succession of plantings, he will obtain all that the land can produce. If you sow radishes in February, they can be harvested in April, and immediately replaced by lettuce or endive. In May, we counter-plant chicory or romaine, which are in turn counter-planted with cauliflower or savoy cabbage. The last endive or lettuce is harvested in June and replaced by cauliflower. In September, spinach, chervil, lamb's lettuce, etc. are sown on the land that is completely free. The above example shows that six harvests can easily be obtained from the same plot of land in the same year. 4 NATURAL CROPS. VEGETABLES PROPER, LISTED ALPHABETICALLY BY NAME. ARROCH. However, in coarse, sandy, damp soil, this plant does better than in clay soil, which hardens easily with the rains and hailstorms of March. If this happens, the seeds, unable to break through the crusts that cover them, die during germination. If you want to prolong the use of this vegetable, sow it in March and every twenty days thereafter. With the first warm spells, as soon as the plants have reached Om, 15 to 0m, 20, they fruit, continue to grow and reach up to 1m, 50 in height. Seeds germinate in a short space of time and do not keep for more than a year. They are harvested when they turn yellow on the stems, at which point the whole plant is pulled up and hung in a dry place to allow the seeds to ripen. Arrowroot is an annual plant of which there are three varieties, if we consider green as the species: blond, red and very red. In terms of cultivation, the green variety deserves preference. It is a very healthy vegetable, too little cultivated in Belgium. It can easily replace spinach; its taste differs little from that of spinach, and is not even so watery. What's more, the whole plant is edible, with the exception of the root; it can be thinned out as soon as the plant reaches Om.08 to Om.12 in height and used from then on. Arrowroot (artiplex hortensis, Linn.), originally from Asia, was brought to Europe from Tartary at an unknown date. It was highly prized by the ancients: the Greeks called it chrysolachanon or golden vegetable. It belongs to the Chenopoda family; its stems are straight, fluted, stalked and over a meter high; its leaves are alternate, petiolate, pale, soft, smooth, tender, triangular and pointed; the terminal panicle is composed of several single spikes. ARTICHAUT. This vegetable, which is to almost everyone's taste, generally comes to us from foreign markets; our merchant gardeners in particular do not cultivate it enough. Although it requires a great deal of care and expense, this is no reason to neglect its cultivation: vegetables that are expensive to grow are paid for in proportion, especially in winter. In southern countries, cultivation is much easier than under northern skies, where 3. covering is more labor-intensive; not only do you have to cover, but you also have to uncover the plants after every frost, if you expect the thaw to last for some time. Artichokes are best propagated by suckers, which gardeners are accustomed to calling carnations; they are also propagated by sowing: but the first method is preferable, in that it vegetates more quickly and guarantees the preservation of the true species. However, we are often obliged to resort to sowing after harsh winters which, despite the best care, destroy all the old plants. Artichoke soil should be loose and oily; it should be excavated to a depth of Om,50 to Om,60; the roots of this plant, as of almost all those of this family, penetrate very far into the soil. The plants should be spaced 0.80 m apart in all directions: it follows that manure can be saved while promoting plant cultivation. In this way, the points where the eyelets are to be planted are marked out in crossed radii, and the fertilizer is buried on each of the points; in this way, the seedlings are supplied with a greater quantity of nourishing juices, because they are then in immediate contact with all the manure. Cow manure should be preferred for artichoke cultivation; other fertilizers, especially liquid manure and slurry, should not be excluded. Artichokes are prone to rot in cold, wet seasons, and are very sensitive to melting snow. They should be planted on beds that slope slightly towards the south, so that water runs off more easily. The boards should be Om.80 wide, with a line of plants in the middle along the length. The soil is prepared for winter by deep ploughing and fertilizing. At the end of March or the beginning of April, a second ploughing is carried out and the boards are shaped. The points being marked out in a chessboard pattern and at Om,80 apart, we place on each of these points a few handfuls of consumed manure or old tan, and a few handfuls of sand, if the soil is clayey; we mix the manure and sand with a sufficient quantity of the underlying soil, and plant two eyelets 0m,12 apart; or, if a more exact indication is required, on each marked point dig a small circular pit one foot wide and half a foot deep; fill it with consumed manure mixed with sand and soil, as described above. Immediately after planting, you give the plant a thorough wetting, which you repeat for the first few days until the plant has fully recovered. This is easily recognized by the development, cheerful green colour and growth of the young leaves. This is the time to remove one of the plants, especially the weaker one; it's bad practice to leave both plants: what you gain on one, you lose on the other. You can't rationally grow two or more plants on the same spot. This is the theory behind row cropping, which will soon eclipse all other vicious and outmoded methods of cultivation. 8 you will be amply compensated for this trouble in autumn by larger, more beautiful fruit (1). It is also highly advantageous to place consumed manure around the feet of these plants; subsequent watering dissolves the salts contained in the manure, which then serve directly as food for the plants. We have already mentioned that, in northern countries, artichokes need to be covered in winter, otherwise they are inevitably lost. Around November 15th, when the first frosts arrive in Belgium, all dry or rotting leaves are removed, leaving only a length of Om,25 to Om,30 for the rest. Then the plants are mounded with Om,17 to Om,20 of soil: to this end, two lines Om,25 apart are drawn between the rows. Using the spade, and following the line, cut these lines to the depth of the spade, or to Om, 30, and start buttering the feet with the earth that comes out of this trench. When the frost continues, place three or four tree branches or pea oars around the artichokes, and cover the whole plant with leaves or dry litter. Leaves are preferable to litter; they are the best and most natural cover that can be given to outdoor plants in northern climates. (1) Gardeners call the artichoke flower a fruit: this is contrary to the principles of botany. In the artichoke flower, it is the seed that constitutes the fruit; for, according to this science, there is no other fruit than that formed by the pericarp and the seed. (Author's note.) It is very necessary to uncover artichokes when the temperature eases; without this precaution, humidity penetrates to the heart of the plant, and it perishes. In spring, in mid-March or early April, when intense cold is no longer to be feared, mounds and leaves should be removed, but not all at once; the plants, having been deprived of air and light, do badly when suddenly brought into contact with these two agents. They should therefore be uncovered gradually, first on the south side, and only the heart, then the whole stem. In this state, the plants are left to recover for two weeks. After this time, the stems are stripped down to below the eyelets, leaving only two or three of the most beautiful. All the others are cut without leaving any remnants of the heel, which could soon produce other sprays. The best of those cut off are used for propagation by cuttings. At this time, the old stems are also cut off, the plant cleaned, the plants replenished with loose soil, and watered often if the season is dry. Three or four weeks later, the stems come up and form their heads; superfluous branches, or those beyond three or four, must be cut off from the stems; otherwise the plant will have to feed too many branches at once, and the fruit will hardly reach sufficient size. Artichokes are propagated by eyelet in mid-March or early April, as follows: Select the best carnations; keep only the young leaves, and cut off all the outer leaves at 0m.09 or Om.12; remove the woody part by which the carnation was attached to the base of the stem; leave only the tender part, as this is the most likely to produce new roots. When planting these eyelets, care must be taken not to cover the heart of the cutting; this must also be observed for cuttings of all plants in general; without this precaution, they are sure to be lost. If eyelets are planted in dry weather, it's a good idea to cover them for ten or fifteen days with upside-down, bottomless pots; take care to lift these pots every evening and put them back every morning; even when the weather is gloomy, you mustn't neglect to do this. It's very wise to take this little trouble, because very often cuttings from a large number of plants are lost because this care is neglected. This measure is also very useful, as it guarantees the success of rootless carnations planted in the nursery, to be put into place the following August. If you take good care of the carnations you plant in spring, especially if you water the growing plant from time to time with manure water (purin), you can expect to have fruit at the beginning of autumn. Two or three sprinklings of liquid manure, given a month apart, are enough for the whole summer: this practice ensures very good yields. Artichokes produce a second harvest in late autumn, when the stems and superfluous eyelets have been cut off after the first harvest, and the plant has been replanted with new, fat soil. To obtain large fruit, it is necessary to plough the soil deeply before winter, make gullies and use good manure, preferably half-consumed cow manure. Furrows are particularly recommended in wet, clayey soils, where capillary roots penetrate better, which has a major influence on the development and perfection of the heads. Damp soils are not suitable for artichokes, and even less so those that are subject to submergence. Keeping artichokes in winter in Belgium's climate is perhaps the greatest obstacle to extending their cultivation; however, with care, this difficulty can be overcome: experience has shown that they are lost in winter in both dry and damp soils, especially when winter is preceded by a rainy autumn. Here's how to avoid these mishaps: as soon as the autumn frost threatens to set in, cut off the plant's leaves at 0.10 m above the ground: once this has been done, remove the stumps from the soil without damaging the roots, and transport them to a cellar where sufficient daylight penetrates. Bring them together without touching, and place them in dry rather than wet sand, at the same depth as they occupied in the open ground, or even a little deeper. As soon as the weather permits, air is added. In this way, the plants keep extremely well. Another advantage of overwintering artichokes in cellars, orangeries or other places where frost cannot penetrate, is that artichoke fruit can be had throughout the winter; to this end, the most developed head of the plant is removed in autumn; the secondary fruit thus acquires greater strength and continues to vegetate in sheltered places until spring. Another advantage of overwintering artichokes is that the young shoots used for propagation detach much more easily from the stumps than when they are kept in the ground. Artichokes grown in cellars should not be replanted too early: from April 15th to 30th, depending on the weather. At the end of the third year, or in the spring of the fourth, planting should be renewed: it's not that the artichoke is a three-year plant, as gardeners say; but then the plants decline considerably; so, although they are fertilized again, they no longer like the same place; they need to be given new ground. Multiplication by eyelets, as we have already said, is preferable for perpetuating good varieties, which degenerate easily through sowing; in this case, gardeners say that the artichoke has turned into a thistle; indeed, through degeneration the leaves have become thorny. If you want to propagate artichokes from seed, sow them in late April or early May. Seedlings can be sown in nurseries or in the field, and those sown in the field are the best; three or four seeds should be sown in triangles or squares Om, 8 apart. Sowing in rows or broadcasting is only successful in substantial, soft soil; cover the seeds with Om,5 of soil; water them if it's dry; they take twenty to thirty days to sprout. As soon as the leaves are 0.08 to 0.miO long, we pull out the young plants that turn into thistles, i.e. the varieties with thorny leaves. We remove the most beautiful heads by eliminating the others; we tilt the seed-bearing heads towards the ground, so that water cannot stagnate on the receptacle, which would rot the seeds, and also to preserve them from goldfinches, which are greedy for them. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS: The common artichoke (cmara scolymus, Linn.) is a member of the Compositae family. It has a thick, cottony stem, 0.60 to 0.90 m high; the leaves are alternate, large, soft, indented, slightly winged, pinnate and toothed; the calyx scales are oval, thick and fleshy. The artichoke seems to have originated in Africa. The learned Belgian botanist Charles de l'Escluse (Clusius), born in Arras in 1526, says it grows abundantly in the wild in Portugal and Spain, along the Guadiana River, which rises in New Castile. It fills entire fields in the provinces of Alentejo and Estramadure, where it is a nuisance, as is the common thistle (serratula arvensis, Linn.) in some Belgian fields. Artichokes come in several varieties: the gros vert, or Laon artichoke, with large green heads; the violet, less font, with violet heads; the blanc, with very small whitish heads; the rouge, with very small purple-red heads. The large green one is the best and most esteemed. The artichoke differs little from another market-garden plant, which is very close to it; this is the Spanish cardoon, whose petioles and tenderized ribs are edible. 2. are edible, while the artichoke's calyx receptacles and leaflets are commonly used for culinary purposes. Pliny says that artichokes used to be preserved in honey and vinegar, to which a few aromas were added. Pierre-André Mathiolus, physician and botanographer, tells us that the Walloons used them throughout the winter. To this end, they covered the plants with sand in summer, leaving them white, tender and soft: they ate all the grass with salt and pepper. Is it not the Spanish carden that this author is referring to? Even today in France, the young heads of artichokes are eaten with salt and pepper; it's called eating artichokes "à la poivrade". The seeds keep well for five or six years. ASPARAGUS. Growing asparagus doesn't require the diligent care and attention to detail that old-time gardeners used to enjoy. Anyone with a garden of good, loose, free-flowing soil, sandy rather than clayey, can easily grow this precious vegetable, which lends itself so well to supplying our major markets and even exporting to foreign markets. What still stands in the way of popularizing the cultivation of this plant today is the fear of having to spend an immense quantity of manure. This is a mistake. You can very easily start growing this crop without using large quantities of fertilizer. It goes without saying that the land on which you want to establish asparagus beds must be loose and previously used for vegetables or cereals, or that the soil is suitable and in the right conditions; such could be a forested wood. Half a foot of manure piled up in the pits is enough, whether the beds are formed by two-year-old seedlings or by in-place sowing. It is generally believed that asparagus cannot be grown without cow manure. Of course, when cow manure is freely available, it deserves preference; but not having cow manure is no obstacle to growing asparagus. The careful and intelligent gardener can create a compost or mixture that is an excellent substitute for manure that has to be bought at too high a price, or that is needed in the fields. This compost can be made from leaves, decomposing wood and turf, which have been stratified, i.e. arranged alternately in beds, and stirred every three or four months. In the absence of these substances, you can obtain tannée, which is valued at almost nothing in some Belgian towns, at a very low price, or even free of charge. In Liége, among other places, tanners abandon hundreds of carts of it each year to the waters of the Meuse. After eighteen months, the heaped tannin, mixed with butcher's blood and lime, makes an excellent fertilizer, substantial enough to grow camellia; that's what experience has shown me. Liquid manure is also used very favorably to water the substances we have just listed from time to time; and, above all else, it should be added to one of the mixtures indicated, human excrement, commonly known as sludge. From time to time, piles of leaves, grass, tan or litter are sprinkled with this fecal matter, which must be diluted with a sufficient quantity of water if it is not sufficiently diluted by urine. This manure par excellence, which is used copiously and daily for large-scale cultivation in the province of Antwerp, is almost entirely lost in other parts of the country: on the banks of the Meuse, in Limbourg, it is too rarely used. FIRST CULTIVATION METHOD. First, the soil is broken to a depth of 0m.70. This first operation is best carried out in autumn, when the soil is drier than in spring, allowing it to divide better. You should avoid sifting the soil, as some authors suggest; it's a mistake you'll almost always regret: the soil settles too tightly afterwards, and instead of being looser, it becomes more compact, impenetrable to the beneficial influence of the atmosphere, making the soil unsuitable for cultivation. If the soil is stony, stones are removed by hand during drying. The soil from the ripping is piled up and stored, if possible close to the beds being formed, but always in such a way that it cannot shade the young plants, which need light and air. Once this has been done, level out the bottom of the beds perfectly, and arrange a layer of shards, tiles, broken flower pots or gravel, interlaced with short tree branches for ease of arrangement. On top of this first layer of shards and branches, place a bed of half-consumed stable manure, or one of the consumed mixes we mentioned earlier. This well-packed bed of manure should be at least Om 15 thick. If you have plenty of manure at your disposal, let this first bed be 0.20 to Om.30 thick, and you'll lose nothing. But the circumstance of not having fertilizer in abundance should not put off anyone who wants to start this crop; for, as we have said, the retail gardener or amateur can undertake it very well by simply packing the pits with suitable manure 0œ,15 thick. This is easy to understand. Asparagus beds should be worthwhile for fifteen to twenty years, so it's not the fertilizer applied once to the bottom of the beds that can give or keep asparagus beautiful vegetation for that length of time; every farmer with a little intelligence or practice should know that such manure, even if much more, cannot nourish the plants for that length of time. It's the manure we give them every year that must feed these plants, which are quite voracious, by the way. To this end, we add fertilizer, and a lot of it towards the end of each autumn, for which we are amply rewarded. We'll tell you in a moment which fertilizer deserves preference in this respect. Once the manure layer is firmed up and evened out, a bed of loose soil is placed on top, and if possible, 4. substantial soil, i.e. mixed with loam. This bed should be between Om.18 and 0m.20 thick, as the fibrous roots of the asparagus that terminate at the bottom of the claws penetrate quite far into the soil. It is through these roots that the plant draws the juices necessary for its nutrition, and not through the large, almost horizontal roots that lie between the fibrous roots and the collar or crown. These large roots are called fingers or legs, because of their resemblance to these organs. The asparagus plants or seeds are then placed in three parallel rows on 1.30 m wide boards, over an indeterminate length. The plants or seeds should be placed in a checkerboard pattern, spaced 0.50 m apart in all directions. If two-year-old plants are used to form the beds, mark the points where the plants should be alternately, then place a small mound of potting soil on each marked point, on which the roots are placed at an angle. Without this precaution, the roots would break under the load of the soil; they are very fragile, and must be handled with great care. After this, the claws are covered with Om,09 soil. This planting is done in March, at the beginning of the month if possible, or as soon as the weather permits. During the summer, asparagus needs no care other than weeding, hoeing and watering in dry spells. Needless to say, watering should be done in the evening. In November of the same year, cut the stalks to ground level, and fertilize with one of the fertilizers we have mentioned. If this fertilization is done with stable manure, cover the beds with a thick layer of Om,05 or thereabouts; if powdery or slush is used, this layer should be Om,02 or thereabouts; if sheep manure is used, it should be Om,02 to Om,03; if liquid manure is used, it should be sprinkled on the beds in the proportion of about 5 hectoliters on a bed 15 meters long and 1m,30 wide. Street mud can also be used, but the layer should be 0*.07 to 0m.08 thick. These quantities are given here for the first year; in November of the second year, these quantities should be doubled and remain the same for subsequent years. Next spring, plough the beds and cover the plant with Om, 10 of soil. Then give the crop the same care as after planting. In November, provide twice as much fertilizer as in the first year and cover the beds with Om, 10 of soil; the plants will then be covered with Om, 30 of soil. After that, you won't need to give this crop any special care; all you need to do is maintain it as well as possible. In November of each year, cut the stems to ground level and fertilize them with the same amount of fertilizer as in the second year. In summer, the beds should be cleared of weeds as they appear; the asparagus should be hoeed and weeded whenever the soil has crusted as a result of heavy rain. To protect the soil against this accident, which is always fatal to vegetation, it's a good idea to apply a light layer of consumed manure, or, failing that, a layer of old tan. These substances, which prevent the accident, also provide good nourishment for the plant. SECOND PROCESS. The formation of beds by seed is preferable and will, in time, become more widespread. Arrange the pits, the first layer of fertilizer and the soil as described above. In February, the seeds are placed on this soil three by three at the same distance as the claws, and covered with Om,02 of soil. When the plants are a little developed, we leave only the strongest at each point, and carefully remove the others. For the rest, observe what we said in the first procedure. In November, it's time to apply fertilizer; quantities should be as we have established for claw planting. If you use liquid manure, mix it with half the water and water the beds every eight days for four weeks. Poudrette or cesspit manure mixed with water, and even, when the plant has become stronger, without the addition of this liquid, is still preferable; poudrette manuring is only done once, and in November each year. In summer, it's a good idea to water asparagus with washing water; it's very beneficial. THIRD PROCESS. There's still one more method to mention, and it's one that really helps to populate20 this precious plant. Here's what we recommend: plant either seeds or two-year-old seedlings in healthy, well-kept soil, i.e. in a vegetable garden or a field that has been well fertilized and spaded for several years. Don't dig any pits; just smoke the planks as you would cabbages or potatoes; these planks will have the width we have indicated for those of the first method; plant them at ground level, observing the same distances as we have given above. Through annual loading, the boards acquire a domed shape. In November of each year, we give a good manuring; we continue in summer the other cares, such as weeding and hoeing, and we are sure to obtain excellent asparagus. If the beds are more exposed to the cold, cover the edges with leaves or litter. This method is also ideal for large-scale cultivation. Around large cities such as London or Paris, a single gardener sometimes devotes a large number of hectares to the cultivation of this plant: how would he go about buying manure? Considerable advances would be needed to cultivate several hectares using the old method, which would also require immense labor costs. Once the beds have been formed in this way, especially if Fon were to establish them with seedlings in situ, cultivation would cost less than a third of what it would if we dug pits and buried a thick layer of manure. We're not saying that you should be parsimonious with manure; no, we've never heard of a farmer being impoverished by using a lot of manure; but we're not saying that you should be parsimonious with manure, and for the labor savings and fertilizer application all at once. FOURTH PROCESS. We have another method of arranging beds and plantations in Belgium's terres fortes (I). The deeply loosened soil is placed in large 1-meter-wide ridges, with dividing furrows Om,40 to 0m,45 deep, Om,40 wide at the top and Om,30 wide at the bottom. These furrows are traced and made with a chalk line and a spade. Frosts and thaws loosen the soil and prepare it for the pits to be established in February or March. These pits should be Om, 50 deep and 1m, 30 wide; a light layer of small branches, with no stones or shards added, is put in, followed by a layer of consumed cow or sheep manure, 0m, 25 to 0m, 30 thick. The pits are filled to ground level. The claws are planted in a checkerboard pattern on three equidistant lines, the two outermost of which will be at Om, 25 from the edge of the board. The plant is placed in the rows at Om, 50 apart. In October, a layer of manure is added, and gutters are dug between the planks, at a distance of (1) Strong, compact and damp soils can be improved: 1° under the influence of severe drought, they calcine, fall into dust and become fertile; 2° by the action of frosts, they become loose; 3° by the addition of sand and manure, with lime and liquid manure in the first line, they improve considerably. The earth from the trench is used to cover the manure on the boards. These trenches also serve as service paths. When things are set up in this way, it's a good idea to throw leaves into the trenches, so that they half-burn in winter, protect the plants from heavy frosts, and cover the beds when harvesting ceases. Asparagus grown in strong soil is beautiful and lasts about ten years. Some growers use three-year-old asparagus plants to form beds, and start harvesting as early as the second year. This method of cultivation differs above all from the previous ones in that gullies are made here, which at the same time serve as service paths, whereas in the previous processes, in addition to the paths, spaces as wide as the beds must be reserved, where the soil used as pits is placed, and which is to be used to successively cover the young plant. These beds of earth are called "ados", and can be used to grow low plants such as bush beans, lettuces, radishes, broad beans, etc., which cannot shade young asparagus. In Belgium, asparagus can be planted in autumn or spring; there are no fixed rules to be established in this respect: we adjust according to the rather variable temperature and weather in our climate. Sowing asparagus in nurseries is best done in March, at the end rather than the beginning. Avoid sowing them too close together when you intend to sell the claws. The roots of this plant are so intertwined that it is difficult to separate them without breaking off many of them. The seeds are sown in rows 0.25 m apart, making it easy to weed and hoe the young plants. Seeds should only be covered from 0m,006 to 0m,010. Asparagus cultivation is based on a property inherent in its nature. No matter how deep the claws are buried, they always tend to grow closer to the soil surface. If we examine this feature closely, we soon discover its source: it depends on the renewal of the claw fingers. These fingers partially perish every year, becoming empty and leaving only a thin film, similar to the membrane of an intestine, a kind of sac that soon destroys itself. The empty fingers are replaced each year by young fingers growing from the bottom of the stems, immediately above those that have just died. This fact explains why the asparagus plant must be replenished with soil and manure every year; without this care, the claws would soon grow out of the soil. An important point to remember is that during the asparagus harvest, which starts in April, great care must be taken not to damage the crowns of the plants. The shoots are cut with a special knife, shown opposite. It is essential to stop harvesting completely at 10 Saint-Jean, June 24, otherwise the layers will weaken and the following harvest will be considerably reduced. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Asparagus (asparagus officinalis, Linn.) is indigenous to Belgium, where it grows in maritime sands; it is also found on the sea coasts of southern France. In Italy and Sicily, it thrives on the banks of streams and ravines. In the wild, asparagus shoots are no bigger than a goose feather tip, but their taste is stronger and finer. The stem rises to a height of 1 or 2 meters, and is herbaceous, straight and very wiry. Leaves are long, linear, soft, setaceous, gathered in clusters; flowers are solitary, berries bright red when ripe. There are several varieties of asparagus named after their place of origin, such as: asparagus from Holland, Marchiennes, Strasbourg, Sarrelouis, Gravelines, Besançon, Vendôme, Erfurt, Ghent, etc. In the last two cities, asparagus is available from a wide variety of sources. In the last two cities, you can buy very good seeds or plants from the leading horticulturalists. Cut shoots are best and most easily preserved in a water-filled vat, covered to block out the light and kept in the cellar. Fresh water is added daily. In this way, asparagus keeps for at least eight days. 4. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Beet (beta cycla, Linn.) belongs to the Chenopoda family; it has a hard, cylindrical root; its lower leaves are oval, the others similar to those of beet, of which it appears to be the type. Several varieties are grown, known as blond, green, white and red, according to the shade of their leaves and especially their veins. To produce cardoons at the end of summer, sow in April or May, in good, deeply-tilled soil. Mark out squares Om,90 apart in all directions; make small pits, Om,25 to Om,30 wide and deep; fill them with consumed manure covered with 0m,06 to 0m 09 of compost. Three or four seeds are placed in each pit, Om, 06 apart and 0m, 03 deep. When the young plant has reached its sixth leaf, leave only the most beautiful and uproot all the others. The gaps left between the young cardoons should be used to grow small vegetables such as 1 radish, lettuce, chervil, etc. These small plants can't do any harm, because they're too small. These small plants can't do any harm, because they've already been harvested when the cardoons start to develop. Until October, cardoons need to be crimped from time to time. Their growth is accelerated by watering them more abundantly as the summer gets hotter. In September or October, the cardoons can be put to their intended use. Their long leaves, from 1.50 to 2 meters long, provide the edible part of the plant: these are the petioles and midribs, commonly known as leaf tails and ribs. As each plant acquires the necessary strength and size, it is bound in dry weather with three or four ties of straw or matting; then it is wrapped up to the tip of the leaves with long straw, placed in its natural direction, with the spikes facing upwards: several straw ties maintain this covering. The soil is also mounded around the stalk, covering the lower end of the straw by a few centimetres and preventing it from being blown by the wind. Three weeks after this operation, the cardoon is white and ready to eat; the thicker the straw cover, the faster it whitens. The cardoons should therefore only be tied successively, by giving their straw jackets different thicknesses. This practice is necessary so that they don't all blanch at once, because as soon as they are blanched they need to be consumed, as they don't keep long in a shrivelled state and are bound to rot. 5. If you want to have them in summer, in June or July, sow earlier; but then it becomes necessary to raise the young plant under glass frames, either in pots or in a layer of soil, and put it in the ground when it has four to six leaves. In this case, sow in February, preferably in pots, as the plant, which retains all its root ball when planted in the ground, remains in full vegetation and requires no care other than watering. This planting should be done in a cool, northerly location; otherwise, most of the plants will go to seed. When the frosts start, the cardoons are tied without being stuffed; they are mounded from Om, 20 to Om, 25 high. In the event of more severe frosts, they should be moved to an orangery or frost-free location, where they should be lifted into a root ball and placed in sand, and given air when the temperature eases. The cardoons will blanch and keep until spring. They can also be kept in the open ground: to this end, make a trench 1m,00 deep, 1m,30 wide and as long as you like: cover one of the outer ends of this trench with straw placed upright; against this straw, place three or four feet of cardoon raised in a clod, against these more straw, leaving all the leaves in contact with the air; then a second row of cardoons, and so on. When the cold weather makes shelter necessary, we cover them with sloping straw mats to prevent snow and rain from penetrating. To harvest cardoon seeds, we leave a few plants in the ground, which need to be cared for more meticulously than artichokes. Cardoons are much more sensitive to cold than artichokes, so they need to be covered with a good layer of leaves at the onset of frost, and this layer increased in proportion to the cold. The seeds, which are very similar to those of artichokes, keep for eight to ten years. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Cardoon (cynara cardunculus, Linn.), a member of the Compositae family, was imported to Europe from Candia in 1658. Its variety is the artichoke. We grow Tours cardoon, which is very thorny; Spanish cardoon, solid cardoon without thorns and artichoke-leaf cardoon. The last two have thick, full, thornless ribs; the last is preferable for quality, and is the best of all. The former is the least good, not only because it is more difficult to manage and the gardener is often injured by its thorns, but also because it is more prone to climbing and its ribs are much thinner. Another remarkable variety is the Puvis cardoon. Worthy of perpetuating the memory of the French agronomist whose name it bears, this cardoon is truly a variety worthy of cultivation in more ways than one. Its leaves, of considerable breadth, with half-full ribs, are thornless, and the plant has such a majestic habit that it is at the same time a true ornamental plant. 18 CULTIVATION. Celery, being a marsh plant, likes moist, oily soil, and lots of watering during droughts, until it is fully grown. To have them all year round, you need to sow them in several seasons, the first time in January, under a glass frame, in loose soil mixed with compost. When the seedlings have three or four leaves, transplant them to another layer Om, 04 or 0m, 05 apart; this operation is useless if the seedlings are not too tightly packed in the first layer. Give the seedlings air whenever the temperature is mild, and protect them from frost by closing the frames and covering them with straw mats or other covers, depending on the intensity of the cold. At the beginning of April, when the seedling is strong enough, prepare a well-smoked and well-amended plot of land, so that it is damp rather than dry. Alternately form a plank and an ados, each 0.80 m wide and of any length; here's how: mark the oblique edges of the planks with a chalk line, to the depth and using an ordinary spade, without disturbing the soil other than by the notch made by the spade along the chalk line. Then, according to the length of the edges just traced, a trench is opened to the depth and width of the spade; the earth that emerges is used to form the ados. As the boards are roughly the width of four times the 14 spade, it follows that after opening the two trenches, a sort of ridge remains; the soil from this ridge should be spread over the board and mixed with consumed manure. Plant four rows of celery about om 22 apart in all directions, so that the outer rows are only Om,06 from the edges; this distance is sufficient. Needless to say, the plants are placed in a chessboard pattern. All that remains is to hoe, weed and water in due course. Celery sown in January should be fully developed by June; then, while the weather is dry, each plant should be tied by one of its outer leaves, without detaching it from the root. This small operation consists in twisting this leaf around the others; while these are held tight with the left hand, a half-knot is made by the top of the leaf itself. Needless to say, rush, straw or matting can also be used. Some people make three ligatures one above the other; we consider a single ligature to be sufficient. As soon as it is tied, the celery is mounded with about Om, 05, om, 06, Om, 07 or 0m, 08 of earth taken from the ados. Eight days later, it's mounded again, and then mounded for the third time, right up to the tips of the leaves. In a month, the celery will be sufficiently blanched. In February, a second sowing is done on a bed or in the ground, with a good southern exposure and sheltered from the north wind. It is of the utmost importance that celery seed be lightly covered and kept constantly fresh; without this precaution, it will not germinate. The young plant is planted as soon as it has acquired the necessary strength. Treat it as described above, bind it and bleach it, so that it succeeds the first seedling in August. In April, a third seedling is planted in the open ground; trained and cultivated as above, it succeeds the second seedling in October. From this third planting, some can be reserved for winter supply. In the autumn months, celery benefits greatly from good soil; it can also be buttered harder than the first crop, even up to four or five times. In our climate, it can overwinter in the ground, but you mustn't neglect to cover it with leaves, increasing the number of covers according to the intensity of the cold; it must also be uncovered during thaws, otherwise the leaves above ground will rot and spread rot to the whole plant. It can also be stored in a cellar or other frost-free place: placed in fresh sand up to the tips of the leaves, and, for greater ease, laid with the roots against the side of the wall in rows alternating with the layers of sand. Air should be provided whenever possible; celery fears humidity and lack of air. It is understood that this refers to the cultivation of common celery. The cultivation of celeriac is the same, except that it does not need to be ridged, and also that it should be given a little more space in all directions. The edible part is the root, which is tender and voluminous. In common celery, the root, tails and blanched ribs are edible. Celery seed-bearing plants require no special care, but celery root should not be planted close to common celery; they could degenerate through reciprocal hybridization. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Celery, or ache (Apium graveolens, Linn.), a member of the Umbelliferae family, is mainly found in the marshes along the Mediterranean coast. Its beneficial qualities are so well appreciated that country folk call it the good herb. However, some botanographers consider a variety found in the wild to be suspect or poisonous. Cultivated celery is an excellent vegetable; it is digestive, that is, it helps the stomach to digest food.
