The celery stalk reaches a height of Om, 40 to Om, 60; it is ridged, thick and stalky; the leaves are twice or thrice winged, the leaflets broad, smooth, incised and lobed; umbels axillary and sessile. Among the cultivated varieties we distinguish the following: ache or small cutting celery, hollow celery; solid white, red, pink, adobe, Turkish, celeriac and celery root. Celery root has produced a variety with red veins; it is very good, with a voluminous root. The large violet celery from Tours is one of the largest of the varieties; its ribs are tinted a purplish red. Very large Erfurt celery and large Leipsick glabrous celery are also very good varieties. Celery goes to seed in spring; the seed is harvested in September: it keeps for three or four years, but the new one is always the best; and you should never sow another, of any variety, if you want to obtain good products. CERFEUIL. CULTIVATION. From the beginning of spring to October, we sow the

common chervil, every two weeks, in beds or borders. It can be broadcast, but preferably in rays. Seeds should be lightly covered; they germinate in a few days. The first sowings are done in February, at the foot of a wall or hedge, and in the south; in June and during the summer, sow in the north, in the shade; and at any exposure at other times. The seed ripens within the year and keeps for two years; the first year's is best. Curly chervil, which is very pretty, requires the same cultivation. The seeds of musk chervil are sown in spring, and germinate in twenty or thirty days. Few people like the aromatic, musky taste of this last species. Although chervil and its varieties can be grown in any soil, they grow best in fat, well-soiled soil. Chervil beds should be well weeded at all times, to guard against the poisonous plants that sometimes get mixed in. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS This plant, which holds a kind of middle ground between what we call a vegetable and a seasoning, is 2. very healthy; it also seems to have been cultivated since time immemorial. This herb is widely used in our kitchens to add flavor to dishes. Although the common species is an annual, it can be grown all year round if sown frequently. Common chervil (scandix serfolium, Linn.), a member of the Umbelliferae family, is indigenous to Europe. Musk chervil (scandix odorata, Linn.) is perennial and native to Spain. The first species has a stem a foot or more high; leaves are light green, tender, winged and pinnatifid; leaflets incised; umbels sessile; seeds smooth, black, Om,012 to Om,015 long. It is not necessary to go into great detail about the poisonous plants mentioned above, but it is important to be able to distinguish between them: we will therefore indicate the characteristics of these plants in such a way that they can be understood by everyone. Hemlock (conium maculatum, Linn.), whose poison is very subtle, has a mottled stem; the leaves are dark green, and the whole plant, when crumpled, exhales a wormy odor. Little hemlock (œthusa cynapium, Linn.) has fluted stems. Evil chervil (chœrophyllum temulum, Linn.) has stems that are swollen at the joints and rough to the touch; the leaves are hairy on both sides. P9 CULTURE. Under this name we shall include three varieties of chicory, and in a separate article we shall deal with the cultivation of the other varieties, referring to them by the name of endives, under which they are generally known in Belgium. The wild chicory varieties are: 1° common chicory, found in the wild in fields and meadows; 2° variegated chicory, whose green leaves bear red veins that become very bright when blanched; 3° coffee chicory or native coffee, whose dried, roasted and powdered roots are used as an adjuvant or auxiliary to coffee, either for taste or economy. This powder is commercially known as chicory or coffee-chicory. The variety that produces chicory powder is cultivated in some Belgian provinces, notably Antwerp, and supplies a fairly considerable trade item. A second use for wild chicory is to convert it into what is commonly known as "capucin beard": the blanched or etiolated leaves make an excellent winter salad. This salad goes perfectly with lamb's lettuce, baked beet or finely chopped red cabbage. Various processes are used to reduce the amount of wilted chicory. In spring, sow wild chicory in beds 1.30 m wide, in good soil that has been thoroughly spaded and smoked before winter. During the summer, it requires no care other than weeding, thinning and hoeing. From the beginning to the end of November, depending on the state of the weather, we remove the long, straight, conical chicory roots. Then each plant, one by one, passes through the hands to have its leaves cut off, with the exception of the nascent central leaf, which retains a length of around 10 to 15 millimeters. As the leaves are removed, they are placed in a heap, with the roots on the same side; once this is done, they can be etiolated by one of the following processes. First procedure. - In November, trenches 1m,00 wide and Om,30 deep are dug in the open air. The roots are laid in horizontal layers, all on the same side, leaving only the root collar uncovered. These trenches are covered with poles or branches resting on both edges; straw is spread over them, and it's a good idea to cover it with sufficient leaves to intercept light and protect against frost. The new shoots soon develop, and can be used throughout the winter to make salads or stews, which are very tasty and healthy. Second process. - Layers of hot manure are prepared in cellars or basements, sheltered from light and outside air, and bunches of chicory, about 0.20 m thick, are placed upright and close together. After a few days, the chicory sprouts white, tender, long and thin leaves; as soon as they reach a length of 0m,15 to 0m, 20, they are cut off above the collar for use or sale; they soon grow back, can be cut off again, and so on until a third time. This leaves the roots, which are also edible and prepared with a vinegar sauce; they are bitter and healthy, but not to everyone's taste. If they are not used in cooking, they can be sold to manufacturers of café-chicorée. Third process. - Chicory can also be blanched in uncovered crates, lying on their sides in dark cellars; the roots are arranged in superimposed layers, leaving only the collars exposed. The roots alternate with layers of potting soil Om,05 to 0m,06 thick. Alternatively, in the cellar, barrel circles are placed on beds of soil Om.05 to Om.08 thick, followed by a horizontal layer of roots whose collars rest on the circle; these roots are covered with a new layer of soil, on which a hoop is placed, leaving the lower collars free; a second layer of roots is then placed, and so on, until the stacks are 1m.00 to 1m.50 high. Here's another way of blanching wild chicory: in November, arrange the roots in a barrel with a hole in one end and a few small holes in the other. At about O ,09 to 0m, 10 above the bottom, we make a line of holes all around the barrel, as close together as possible. These openings can be the same size as the bunghole, so that a bunch of chicory can pass through each one. At the bottom, a bed of potting soil is laid up to the level of the lower part of the openings; the bunches of roots are placed there, with the heads or collars in the openings; they are covered with Om,09 or Om, 10 of potting soil: there is a second row of holes, above this one a third, and so on, up to the top of the barrel, which is placed upright. When the barrel is lined, a dampening is given, which is sometimes sufficient for the whole winter; however, if the leaves wilt, a second dampening must be given. Fourth process. - A final, very simple method, which remains to be discussed, consists in spreading a layer of Om,05 to Om,07 soil in the cellar; on top of this, a layer of chicory roots, collar out; then a bed of soil or compost of the same thickness; on top of this bed, a new layer of roots, and so on. D DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Wild chicory (cichorium intybus, Linn.), a member of the Compositae family, is indigenous and perennial. The stem, 5 to 6 decimeters high, rises much higher when cultivated; it is cylindrical, firm, branched and hairy below; its leaves are lanceolate, sinuate and toothed like those of the dandelion, a little hairy on their sides. Flowers are blue, almost axillary. Seeds keep for up to ten years. CHICORÉE SAUVAGE, see Lion's tooth. CHOUX. CULTIVATION. This genus contains a few species and many varieties, some of which make healthy, pleasant foods; most are easy to grow. First, we'll look at the most popular varieties, in particular white and red cabbage; then we'll review the other varieties, some of which require special cultivation. White cabbage. - All soils are suitable for cabbages: sandy as well as clay soils. In sandy soils, with good, half-consumed cow manure, you can still obtain mediocre cabbages; these same soils, amended with clay and the aforementioned manure, can give a very fine product; in strong or clayey soils, you can even gain very fine cabbages, without adding sand, provided that the soil has been spaded in good time, and that you have given a good manuring of cowshed or stable manure, half-consumed. Here, it should be noted that cow manure is preferable, even if the soil is damp and compact by nature. A fertilizer that is extraordinarily suitable for cabbages is pond mud, in sufficient quantity. This mud must have been exposed to the open air for one or two years, and stirred three or 99 four times a year. This fertilizer is highly recommended, and can be made even more active by adding cesspit manure. The last fertilizer is added in the following way: a square, wide trench is opened in the upper part of the heap, which itself is square; the above-mentioned stercoral matter is poured into it; one or two days later, when the liquid matter of the fertilizer has penetrated the heap, the trench is closed again with the earth or mud that has come out of it, and the heap is turned and mixed well to form a homogeneous mass. With this kind of fertilizer, you're almost certain to get good cabbage products. Cabbage is a great soil leavener. As a general rule, any plant that greatly depletes the soil needs a lot of food, which means a lot of fertilizer. A famous agronomist has said that cabbage is a plant that impoverishes the farm garden, if it is not consumed on the farm itself by men and cattle. In the latter case, we return to the soil what has been taken from it. We've said that mediocre cabbages can be obtained from the least fertile soil: sand. It follows that excellent products can be obtained from good free soil, i.e. a mixture of clay and sand. We remind you here that the land to be planted should be deeply ploughed, and fertilized with half-consumed cow manure, pure pond sludge, or better still, mixed with sludge or pudding. It is not necessary to spade the soil for a long time before planting: eight or ten days are enough, by which time the soil has already settled down suitably. Cabbage prefers moist soil, provided there is no stagnation of water, to dry soil: drought and hot weather are not good for it. Watering is always to its advantage, and cabbage thrives in warm rains. Cabbage beds can be ploughed flat; this is the most suitable method: watering is easier, as are hoeing, ridging, etc. For wet soils, we recommend planting on slopes inclined to the south; this method has a number of disadvantages: 1° by reflecting the heat back to the plant, these inclined slopes give it extra heat, which it doesn't need in summer; 2° the beneficial rainwater runs off at the bottom of the slopes, and the cabbages don't get enough of it; 3° if it's to prevent water from stagnating on the roots in winter, we believe that this accident cannot be prevented in damp soils, by planting cabbages on slopes; for, these eminences are hardly raised above Om, 50 from the base to the top: this elevation is insufficient to prevent water from remaining on the roots of cabbages planted in the middle of the slope. In some of our provinces, Limbourg in particular, we have seen cabbages grown in the same way as in the south of France: they are planted on flat ground, in furrows Om.10 wide and as deep. This is detrimental to the plant in winter: water stagnates in these gullies; snow and ice accumulate there and do great harm. In Belgium, this method is only suitable for summer planting. All in all, we recommend planting on flat ground. As cabbage cultivation requires constant care, hoeing, ridging and watering are much easier on even soil. If you can't raise seedbeds, and harvest perfectly free seed yourself, which is very-difficult in some provinces, you can get top-quality seed from good trading houses or reliable gardeners who live where the species or varieties you want to grow grow best. That's how we get the seeds for large white and red cabbages from Maestricht. Nowhere in Belgium do they come better; they thrive there without bastardizing, better than in other parts of the country. Good cabbage seed, grown to perfection, is black, shiny and uniform, without a mixture of red or wrinkled grain; it retains its reproductive capacity for six or seven years. Cabbage seedlings are sown from August 15th to the beginning of September; varieties such as York sprouts and other small early varieties are not sown before the end of August. These seedlings are planted out in October or November, as are large white or red cabbages; or they are transplanted from nurseries and planted out in February and March. These should be spaced Om, 60 to Om, 90 apart, and staggered. If the soil is good and oily, and if you have the large species, the distance of 0m, 90 in all directions is preferable to any other. Hoeing should be carried out whenever the soil is more or less beaten by rain or watering. Young plants should be hoeed as soon as they are big enough to undergo this operation, which should not be delayed too long: the leaves, having become large and broad, no longer allow you to approach them for hoeing without breaking them, which is always very harmful to the plant. If you have neglected to hoe them, and they have become a little too large, you should wait until the most favorable moment of the day, i.e. when the leaves are flaccid from the heat and bend without breaking. Mounding is done with a hoe or spade; the plant is well surrounded by soil, but care should be taken not to cover the heart. The cabbages we've just mentioned are also sown on the bed in February; the plants from these seedlings are put in place at the end of March and during April; their produce follows that of autumn. Sow again in early March, in a well-soiled bed, at the foot of a wall and facing south. Later, until the end of the month, we continue to sow in well-soiled soil and a little shade: flea beetles, the bitter enemy of the entire crucifer family, don't attack them as quickly in shade as in full sun. These last seedlings are planted out permanently in May. To help the growth of cabbages that are already in the best conditions to thrive, and that have good, clean soil, rather strong and moist than light and dry, well fertilized with the manure we have indicated; to help, shall we say, their growth, we can still smoke the plants with liquid manure or sludge. There's no need to worry about giving them too much fertilizer; on the contrary, by administering large doses, you can make them grow, so to speak, at will. The main varieties of white cabbage are as follows: large German cabbage, Alsatian cabbage or quintal cabbage; it has a short, very thick stem, and the apples become enormous in rich, cool soil; this variety is mainly used to make sauerkraut; - large Dutch cabbage, stubby Brunswick cabbage; the latter has an extremely short stem, and the apples are tightly packed, flattened and resting on the ground without showing their stems; a good variety, but the apples do not become as large as in common cabbage. Other very good varieties include: England's super-fine hâtif; Battersel's hâtif; imperial hope; hâtif non pareil; and the Germans' gros centner, known as 100 pounds. Lesoinne cabbage enriches the genus with two excellent varieties belonging to the white cabbage series. One apples well; the second, like our green cabbages, does not. According to Professor Morren, who describes this plant in the Annales de Gand, these two precious varieties were discovered by Mr. Adolphe Lesoinne, in the vicinity of the small town of Avilès, in Asturias. One advantage worth noting for the cultivation of this cabbage is that it seems to keep well and without degenerating, under Belgian skies; we know that some species or varieties, as we would like to call them, are excessively sensitive to expatriation; example: the cabbage-sprout. The Avilès cabbage can be recognized by its unique characteristics: its white ribs open out into equally white veins in the pale-green parenchyma of the leaves. Understandably, these nuances give this new cruciferous plant, introduced to Belgium in 1842, a very pleasing appearance. It is grown in the same way as our white cabbages. York cabbage. - The sub-varieties are: York cabbage, small, oval, elongated head; very early and highly prized; it has in turn sub-varieties: choucabbage or superfin, smaller, very early; - early dwarf cabbage, shorter stem and head; - groschoud'York, the head is stronger; it is a little later:- sugarloaf cabbage, early, a little greenish-blond, conical apple, tender and of very good quality; - Winnigstadt cabbage, a precious variety recently imported from England: it has the advantage over other cabbages of peeling, not only in spring like these, but also in the late season; consequently it can be planted before or after winter, whereas the other cabbages in this series must be planted before winter; - the Pomeranian conical cabbage, an excellent variety, but prone to degeneration. These York cabbages and their sub-varieties are all excellent vegetables; it's surprising that they aren't widely grown in Belgium. If you go anywhere in the province of Antwerp, you'll hardly find a single plant. Not so in the province of Liége, where this cabbage is appreciated to the full; around the city of Liége, this plant occupies extensive land and offers the consumer and vendor considerable produce. The only difference between York cabbage and its varieties is that it requires spacing of only 0.45 to 0.50, 0.55 to 0.60 meters in all directions, depending on the strength of the variety and the fertility of the soil. Red cabbage. - This is just one variety of MARAICULTURE. 2. white cabbage; it has several sub-varieties, and is grown like white cabbage. Among the red cabbages, we'd like to mention the following: very large Ghent cabbage, large, early Dutch blood cabbage; - the same late variety; - Erfort blood cabbage; - Erfort blue cabbage; - and the small, super-fine Utrecht black cabbage; all good varieties. Savoy cabbage. - Milan or pommé-frisé cabbage, as the French call it, is generally known in Belgium as Savoy cabbage, and not without reason, since it spread from Savoy to Italy, France, Germany and Belgium. Two varieties are cultivated in particular: the early Savoy cabbage and the late Savoy cabbage. The early Savoy cabbage is sown at the same time as the white cabbage, from April 15 to September, in loose, rich soil. Then, in October or November, it is planted in staggered rows, 0.45 m apart in all directions, or planted in nurseries for permanent replanting in early spring, as soon as the soil is in a suitable condition. It should be noted here that early Savoy cabbage should never be planted in spring, when it can be done in autumn; it's a big delay to do it then; it should always be planted before winter, behind a wall, building, hedge or wood that protects it from the north winds and frosts; in this case, it's sure to be available long before those grown in the middle of the garden and without shelter. A final remark to make is that it is of the utmost importance to hoe the soil in spring as soon as the weather permits. The same cabbage can be sown at different times of the year; a large garden should never be deprived of this good vegetable. For example, in addition to autumn sowing, spring sowing is done in March, April and May; sowing in these three months successively provides edible plants for the whole summer. For autumn and winter, we have the other variety, late Savoy cabbage; cultivation is absolutely the same, except that it is only sown once, in March, for planting in May. This variety differs from the other in that its leaves are more finely curled, less blistered; its apples are harder, tighter, and most often have a sort of hollow at the heart. Savoy cabbages also have several sub-varieties, all called Milan cabbages by the French: Milan très-hâtif d'Ulm, medium-sized, very easy to pick, excellent; - Milan à tête lonque, small, pointed, excellent; - Milan des vertus, large, hardy, resistant to cold; - Milan d'automne, very large, hardy, good; - Milan d'Allemagne, dark green, tender and very good; - Pancalier de Touraine, dark green, very good, frost-resistant; - Pancalier blond, similar to the above, less frost-resistant; - Würzinger green; - Drumhead, delicious; - Ulm late, large; - Bloemendael yellow; - Utrecht yellow, early; and Vienna cabbage, early, low, suitable for forcing. These and other varieties, not all of which can be mentioned here, are vegetables that deserve the attention of growers in every respect. Brussels sprout, rosette or spray cabbage. - This cabbage is a product of our soil. Other countries are obliged to bring in their seeds from Belgium, in order to obtain this excellent vegetable. It provides gardeners with great advantages: the sale of this product is always assured; grown in large quantities, this cabbage finds an easy placement. Although the plant is found in Belgium on its native soil, there are nevertheless places where it has a special liking; this is how we see it grow with exceptional vegetation in the vicinity of Brussels, Louvain, Antwerp, Mechelen, Lierre and so on. The seeds of this cabbage are sown from the end of March to the beginning of May; sown later, the little apples along the stem, called rosettes, no longer have time to form properly. It is planted in staggered rows, 0.45 m apart. In terms of fertilization and soil preparation, cultivation is the same as for cabbage. Some gardeners still follow a routine that is detrimental to the production of beautiful rosettes; it consists in stripping the stem of the large leaves that cover it from base to tip. Without needing to be torn off, these leaves fall spontaneously, after having given the rosettes vigor, by giving up part of their descending sap before withering. Bastard broccoli, known as boeren-spruit, is a later variety than Brussels sprouts, producing longer and setting seed more slowly. Its flavor, which is derived from the type from which it is derived, is milder and more pleasant than that of ordinary cabbage. Brussels sprouts are more frost-resistant than Savoy cabbages, withstanding 5° R. and colder; they only freeze when there's a continuous northerly breeze, at which point the plant really dries out; this happens especially when there's no snow and the sun destroys anything green or tender. So, despite the hardiness of this cabbage, you can lose the most precious winter supply. There are ways of avoiding this unfortunate accident: Before the frosts, remove all the plants by lifting them with a spade and grasping them close to the roots so as not to injure the rosettes. They are then transported to a square, where they are placed in tight rows in furrows dug in the same way as for ordinary drying; when the second furrow is dug, the first is filled in, where the cabbages, which have retained their entire root ball, lie obliquely, with their heads facing south. When placing the cabbages in the furrows, care should be taken not to lay the plants so flat that the rosettes rest on the soil, as this would cause them to yellow and even rot. Once this has been done, straw and leaves 7. can be thrown on top during intense cold, and the plants will be guaranteed. This method is very practical for large-scale cultivation. If another method of preservation is desired, a trench can be dug in proportion to the quantity of cabbages to be protected; this trench will be Om 30 deep, and the soil coming out of it will be placed on the edges. The cabbages are planted upright, one beside the other, without the rosettes touching. At the onset of frost, straw stakes are formed, resting on poles in the shape of a double roof; an entrance is made in the stakes, and the rosettes are harvested there throughout the winter. Another method used in our country is to cover the base of the cabbage stem, while at the same time ridging the soil. To this end, the cabbages are removed from every fifth row; a trench is dug along the entire length of this row, Om 30 wide by the same depth; the soil is thrown to the right and left, covering the entire bed; the cabbage stalks are ridged, making the soil healthier; any weeds that may be found on the beds are covered and serve to amend the soil. This is a good and rational practice. For seedbeds for this cabbage, choose the most beautiful plants with tight, closely-spaced rosettes; the plant should be stocky, large and medium-sized. Care should be taken not to plant it near any other cabbage; the breed is highly susceptible to cross-breeding. This rule applies to all species and varieties of the genus. Green cabbages. - These cabbages, some of which are of excellent quality, are not grown in all parts of Belgium. However, they grow everywhere without any marked preference for certain soils or exposures, which is a real advantage. Green cabbages are the fastest-growing; they never spike; the leaves and petioles are taut and delicate, enough to be eaten without spiking. They deserve to be cultivated in every respect: good produce, excellent flavor, healthy food, they come in a season when other vegetables are lacking. They are sown from early April to May 15. They are grown in the same way as Brussels sprouts, except that they need more space in the rows (Om.60). They are even hardier than Brussels sprouts; they need neither to be covered nor tucked away under straw mats or other shelters. All you have to do is lay them down with their heads tilted towards the south; frosts not only do them no harm, but they must be frozen before they are fit to eat; frost makes them tender without wilting them. We count the following varieties among the green cabbages: pancalier or green kale, curly kale, variegated kale, tricolored kale and fuzzy kale. This section also includes the cavalier or tree cabbage, which reaches a height of five to six feet; the mille tétes cabbage, which is less tall, but produces a large number of lateral sprays; the grand frisé du Nord cabbage, which is very tall, has dissected leaves and resists the cold well; and the palm cabbage, whose leaves are gathered at the top in a rosette. Other varieties of superior quality are beginning to appear in our gardens: green kale, low-stemmed and very tender; blue or violet kale, low-stemmed; there is a sub-variety with higher stems and broader leaves; both are very good and very hardy against frost. Kohlrabi. - Kohlrabi stems are highly-developed and swollen to form a ball above the ground, called a tuber or apple by some; this apple is as delicate as cauliflower; however, kohlrabi is not grown in such large quantities. They like good, open, fertile soil and lots of watering: then the apples or kohlrabi develop more quickly and are more tender. They are sown from the beginning of April to the beginning of June, and planted at a distance of Om, 50 in all directions. In addition to watering, all they require is timely hoeing. There are three varieties of kohlrabi: Kohlrabi or Siam kohlrabi, forming balls above the ground with bulges from Om,10 to 0m,15 in diameter; purple kohlrabi, more voluminous than the first; yellow kohlrabi. These three varieties have further sub-varieties: late white, dwarf hátif, Vienna white, small-leafed, early; Vienna blue, small-leafed; early English white and blue, artichoke-leafed, etc. Kohlrabi raves or apples are formed in August, September and October, depending on when they are planted. The latest-forming kohlrabi are the best for winter storage, and have no woody streaks in the interior, which is sometimes the case with those that have matured too long. Kohlrabi are harvested in October and stored in a cellar, roots in sand, to keep them well into winter. To harvest the seeds, we set aside the most beautiful, large, round plants, with leaves that are small and few in number rather than strong and numerous. These seedbeds are planted in the open ground, away from other seed cabbages, around mid-March or early April, depending on temperature. Turnip cabbage, turneps, or Lapland cabbage. - Savoy cabbages are closely related to kohlrabi, and are perhaps only varieties of the latter. Their cultivation is the same, and differs only in that the kohlrabi can remain on the spot where they were sown. In this case, sow lightly, weed and hoe as for those planted in rows. Kohlrabi or turneps produce a fleshy root, oblong like a large turnip; this is where they get their name from; they have the flavor of kohlrabi, and like kohlrabi, are healthy and easily digested. Several varieties are known today: ordinary kohlrabi; early, tender kohlrabi; red-necked kohlrabi, with red-tinted ribs and veins; white or large late English turneps; early white English turneps; large purple English turneps; yellow English turneps; etc. Some of these varieties are no different from the others. Some of these varieties differ only in shape or color. Rutabaga cabbage or Swedish turnip. - Rutabaga deserves preference as a vegetable among the turnip cabbage varieties; it resembles turneps, but vegetates more quickly. Its root is yellowish. It is grown like kohlrabi or beet. Still in the ground, it withstands frosts much better than turnips; in heaps, it doesn't keep much better than turnips; it is also grown for cattle, feeding them well; all livestock seek it out. CAULIFLOWERS. Growing cauliflower requires a little more care than other cabbages. The same fertilizers we have indicated for cabbages are suitable for cauliflowers. The same does not apply to the type of soil: while cabbages thrive in strong, moist soil, cauliflowers prefer lighter, loose, well-soiled soil. Three main varieties are grown: the tender-headed cauliflower, which is earlier than the others; it is less fussy about the quality of the soil, but as its head, which is less voluminous and not very tight, is prone to opening, gardeners usually prefer the other two varieties, known as semi-hard-headed and hard-headed cauliflowers. Tender cauliflower differs from the latter two varieties in having narrower leaves and less volume in all parts of the plant. Semi-hard-headed cauliflower deserves to be grown in preference to all the others; it is the best of all; the apples acquire a large volume. It is a little slower to form than the previous variety, but by compensation it lasts longer. The plant is strong, the leaves broad and long. The hard-headed cauliflower is the slowest-growing; the market gardener doesn't like to grow it, because it waits too long. We recommend it to the amateur with large gardens; while cultivating the others for their earliness, he can give this one a bed; it gives bigger, firmer and whiter apples; it succeeds all the others and resists a little frost. We especially recommend the following two varieties: Petit Salomon, early, tender-flavored, excellent; good shape, tight; fine and never becoming very large. Gros Salomon belongs to the demidur class, giving very large apples; a little later than the previous one. These two varieties are the most widely grown by Paris market gardeners. Autumn sowing for spring. - From August 15 to September 15, sow in the open ground on old potting soil or on consumed cow manure, spread and compared in the proportion of three barrows on a bed 4 meters long and Om, 50 wide; for this same space, 16 grams of seed are more than enough. The bed should face south. As soon as the seedlings are Om.06 to Om.09 in height, they are transplanted under a glass frame onto good free soil, covered or mixed with a few centimetres of compost. As long as frosts are not to be feared, the frames should not be used; otherwise, the plants will grow too quickly and wither due to lack of air, an accident to which cauliflower is very prone. If the plant is found to be overgrown, it should be removed and immediately replanted in the same place. The space given to the plant when transplanting is Om, 10 in all directions and in rows. When planting cauliflowers under glass frames, take care to place them as close to the glass as possible; this is another way of preventing them from shrivelling. For those who don't have a frame, and this is often the case with commercial gardeners, the best way to overwinter cauliflower plants is to plant them in the economic tarpaulin: this is a casing made up of four planks Om,30 wide; the two longest are 2 meters, the other two 1m,30 long. These four planks are inserted into a trench of the same dimensions, held in place by a few stakes driven down to ground level and the edges of the planks. A wooden cover is placed over the trench, loaded with leaves, litter, straw mats, etc., according to the intensity of the cold, never neglecting to provide air whenever the weather permits. Overwintered seedlings are planted in February, March or early April; no fixed time can be determined, as planting must be regulated according to the weather. They are planted staggered at a distance of Om,60 in all directions. Whether sown on a bed or in the ground, seedlings should be carefully uprooted to preserve as much soil as possible for the roots. Replant quickly, without giving the plants time to become flaccid; the success of the crop depends in part on the speed of replanting. When the weather is hot, we recommend planting in the evening and watering; evening should be preferred for planting all cabbages in general. After this initial watering, no more should be given for two weeks; experience has shown that, after 21 8 leaving the cauliflower in this way, it produces apples of better quality and more quickly, and is less prone to borgner (which is abortion of the apple) than if it were watered every day after being planted. Winter and spring sowing for summer. - In the early days of February, sow on a warm bed or under a frame. Three weeks later, or when the seedling has four or six leaves, it is transplanted to another bed. At the end of March or in April, the seedling can be planted in the ground. To protect it from night frosts, cover it every evening when frost threatens, either with flower pots or conical baskets made for the purpose. This cauliflower yields its product in June-July. Sow from March 1 to 15 in a sheltered bed under a frame or straw mat. Three or four weeks later, the seedling can be planted without prior transplanting. It produces in July. From April 15th to May 15th, seedlings continue to be sown in the open ground several times, so that there are seedlings to follow the first ones; they are planted without prior transplanting. These plantings bear fruit from July to September. During the months of June, July, August and September, if the summer is dry and hot, cauliflowers require copious watering, especially when their buds are closing. Summer sowing for autumn. - From May 15 to June 15, the last cauliflower seedlings are sown. These flower in the last months of autumn, and keep well into winter. They are sown in earthen beds in the shade, and put in place without being transplanted. In our Flemish provinces, a few good growers take special care in preparing the land to be used for cauliflowers. In October, they cover the squares intended for spring planting with 10 to 13 centimeters of half-consumed cow manure; they then cover this fertilizer with a layer of soil of the same thickness, making line-drawn trenches 0.25 to 0.30 meters wide and of equal depth. In this way, the soil is ridged, which keeps it healthy over the winter. Not content with this amount of fertilizer, some growers still water the cauliflowers with liquid manure from time to time, during the course of their vegetation. It's easy to see that this is a good, rational way of growing cauliflower, and one worth following. When planting young cauliflower plants, both for transplanting and for setting, it is important never to bury the stem beyond the root collar. Cauliflower wants to be shaken by the wind, so never butter it. When fully developed, cauliflower apples should be covered by the upper part of the leaves, which should be flexed by breaking the ribs from the outside in. This small operation protects the apples from too much sun and rain, and helps them keep longer. As for cauliflower seed, although it can be obtained in Belgium, we recommend bringing it from Holland, which supplies very good quality. If, however, you want to obtain the seed yourself, you choose and keep the best cauliflower plants to put in the open air after the spring frosts. The apples must be large, firm and hard, with white seeds and short stems. Seeds ripen in August-September. Don't wait to harvest until the last siliques have ripened. As soon as about half of them have ripened or turned yellow, carefully pull up the plants and place them with their clods in sand or damp earth in a shed or other place accessible to air and wind. The seeds ripen there, protected from the avid birds and the strong winds which, shaking the siliques, cause most of them to be lost. Conservation - Before the first frosts, cut the stems as close to the root collar as possible; remove the leaves, leaving Om,08 or Om,10 of the rib that supports them, then place them on boards in a dry place. Ripe cauliflowers can be stored in this way for one to two months. When you want to use them, dip the stalks in water up to the head, for one or two days; they come back and are as fresh as when harvested. However, they should be used early enough, otherwise they will melt when cooked, leaving only a fibrous mass. Some cauliflowers from recent plantings may not have sprouted at the start of the frosts; in this case, we remove them, cut off some of the outer leaves, and plant them very close together with their root ball in a trench 0.60 m deep and the width of a frame trunk; we then place the trunk and frames, which we surround with new manure, on the outside. Treated in this way, cauliflowers are not very large, but can be enjoyed well into the season, sometimes as late as March. Broccoli seeds are sown very lightly and for the first time from April 12 to 18; the second, from May 18 to 24; the third, from August 19 to 25. When the young plant has six to eight leaves, it is planted two feet apart, in loose, greasy soil watered with liquid manure. After planting the strongest plants from the second sowing or from May, those that were left in the bed because of their weakness are potted in loose, oily soil. Place them in the shade for some time, but never let them suffer from drought. In July or August, we bury these pots so that the edges are two or three inches below the surface of the soil; then we dig a furrow around and near the edges of the pots so that watering is easy. In autumn, the plants are ridged to resist the wind. Cultivated according to this procedure, which is followed by English gardeners, broccoli produces its apples in October, before the first frosts. In November or December, depending on whether cold weather threatens to set in, all pots are removed and placed under a frame, or only frost-free; a well-lit, well-ventilated cellar at a mild temperature may suffice in a pinch. The apples, which were only in their infancy when the plants were brought in, continue to form and complete 8. their development. Treated in this way, this vegetable provides an ample supply throughout the winter. The plants are potted in October, and their apples are used in spring. The method we have just described was devised by Mr. Maher and described in Belgium Horticulture. Broccoli is most similar to cauliflower; its general characteristics are absolutely the same; it differs only in a few secondary properties, such as the color of the apple. Its flavor is at least as good as that of cauliflower, and many people prefer it to cauliflower. Its value as a vegetable crop is not sufficiently appreciated in our country. In England, where several varieties are grown, it is generally preferred; however, our overseas neighbors, though sometimes a little odd, are not without good taste. In any case, the plant is well worth the gardener's care and should be popularized. This excellent vegetable produces apples that are often larger than those of cauliflower; they come in a variety of colors: green, yellow, green mixed with purple, purple, etc. . Since broccoli can be grown very well in the same way as cauliflower, sown at the same time, in May-June, so as not to confuse ourselves, we'll just say that it requires a little more space than cauliflower, and we'll mention the main varieties: Dwarf purple hátif broccoli. - English white broccoli. - Green apple broccoli. - Autumn purple broccoli; green apple mixed with purple. - Early purple broccoli; purple apple mixed with light green; its stems sometimes reach 1 meter in height and, in addition to its main apple, it produces small lateral heads in the leaf axils. - Dwarf purple broccoli; conical-shaped purple apple with a delicate taste. It is very late and forms its head very slowly. The plant remains very low. - Green broccoli with tight head; the head is green. Small and very late. This year's plants often bear their apples in January and February of the following year. Sulfur-yellow broccoli is one of the best, but also very slow to produce apples; sown in April, it produces apples in April of the following year. - Large-apple broccoli; this larger, more developed plant requires more space, Om, 90 in all directions. Sow in March to obtain heads at the same time the following year. - Portsmouth broccoli; gives the largest apples of all known varieties; requires the same spacing as the previous variety. - Broccoli with bracts; this variety differs from the others in that the bracts or leaves that grow between the branches of the apple reflect inwards and cover it. - Broccoli from Denmark or Siberia; this is the best variety for our climate and for the open ground; more robust than the others, it resists frost and temperature variations. Its pale-green stems are just as large and high quality as other broccolis. The earliest varieties are ready for harvest in autumn; the others continue to develop, even in winter, if the rigors of our climate don't get in the way, as is usually the case. If the winter is mild, they can still be harvested; to this end, they are laid down with their stems facing south, and before the onset of frost, they are covered with leaves that must be removed whenever the weather permits. They can also be removed as rootballs and overwintered under glass frames; their development then continues, and their use is assured until February and March. Needless to say, you'll need to cover the frames with straw mats during frosts, and uncover and ventilate them whenever the weather warms up. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS We won't go into the botanical characteristics of cabbage, but we will say in passing that rapeseed (brassica campestris, L.) appears to be its primitive strain; at least that's what botanists think. All other cabbages are merely varieties that are highly susceptible to cross-fertilization and hybridization, such as: cabbage (brassica oleracea capitata); cauliflower (brassica oleracea botrytis); kale (brassica oleracea viridis); kohlrabi (brassica oleracea gongyloides). Cabbage was highly esteemed by the ancients. If certain authors are to be believed, the Romans did without doctors for four centuries, using cabbage as a universal remedy. Cabbage's enemy is the flea beetle. However, if we can't destroy them all in a short space of time, we can at least paralyze their unfortunate effects and save time for the young plant, which becomes stronger and too hard to be penetrated by the mandibles of these insects. First of all, hoe the soil where the young cabbage is planted; the flea beetle escapes in part from these movements of the soil surface. Every morning, while the dew is still wetting the leaves, we sprinkle the plant with a mixture of wood ash and chimney soot until they disappear. A strong infusion of wormwood (1) has also been recommended for watering the plant. It's worth noting that the earth flea is never found on some plants that are in some way unsympathetic to it. We recommend trying to water young cabbage plants with cooled decoctions of these plants; among others, conifer leaves could be used for this purpose; they have never been seen on parsley and many other plants. We have already talked about the preservation of the cabbage species grown in our gardens; it remains for us to say a word about the preservation of head cabbages, such as cabbages and Savoy cabbages. Savoy cabbages keep quite well in shallow trenches, lying close together and in rows, roots covered with soil, heads inclined to the south and covered first with straw and then with a sufficient quantity of leaves, depending on the severity of the winter. To prevent rotting, it's a good idea to place the heads on a layer of straw about Om.04 to Om.08 thick. When the thaw comes, the overwintered cabbages are uncovered. Bring the cabbages into a dry, well-ventilated cellar; place them in beds one on top of the other, with the roots facing the wall on slightly fresh sand or earth; place a light layer of straw on top of each row of apples. A draught should be provided. White and red cabbages can also be kept hanging upside down in attics or other places sheltered from rain and frost. (1) See this plant at the beginning of chapter nine. Recommended by the French missionaries Voisin and Tesson as a highly productive food plant, providing China with apples of considerable weight, Pe-tsai, or Chinese cabbage, has not yet produced satisfactory results in Belgium in terms of cultivation: Firstly, the young plants are of such a soft, tender consistency that great care is needed when handling them for transplanting; they are more fragile than our Roman lettuces, with which, incidentally, they bear a striking resemblance; secondly, we have experienced serious difficulties in getting them to peel. Nevertheless, the plant is worthy of further trials. Pe-tsai has long been known in our European botanical gardens, where it was included under the name brassica sinensis. Its roots are small, filamentous and do not swivel like the cabbages of our countries, so it is content with a very thin layer of vegetation and does very well in light soil. Another obstacle to growing this excellent vegetable is its tendency to go to seed quickly; it has been found that the best way to overcome this disadvantage is to use two-year-old seeds. Easy to digest, Pe-tsai is a very healthy foodstuff, and its cultivation is undoubtedly worth extending, as it is in every respect the same as that of Roman lettuce. Another species of Chinese cabbage is the pak-choï; 6 like the previous one, it is a very good vegetable, but also has the same inherent properties of going to seed. Its glabrous, shiny-green, sharply-ribbed leaves make it resemble cardoon. It is grown in the same way as pe-tsai. MARITIME CABBAGE, SEA CABBAGE, SEA CABBAGE. Cultivated as a vegetable, this perennial plant grows spontaneously in the sand along the coast. Chance has led to its discovery. The waves of the sea having buried some of these plants under the sand, it was found that they had turned yellow and had become tender: their usually hard stems and leaves were then succulent and good for eating. Since then, it has been introduced into vegetable gardens. In spring, it appears abundantly on the markets of the main cities of England especially, and always finds buyers. It is an excellent vegetable. Crambe or sea cabbage belongs to the cruciferous family; it has long roots and naturally likes sandy soil. It is difficult to grow in strong, clay soil. The cultivated plant requires soil spaded deeply in autumn and smoked with cow manure. In spring, in March or April, sow five or six seeds in holes 3 to 4 cm deep and 0.60 m apart; the plants grow strong. The seeds sprout after three to four weeks. Remove superfluous seedlings and leave just one plant in each spot. We do not recommend transplanting, as this is uncertain. During the summer, crambe requires no care other than weeding and hoeing; it's a good idea to cover the bed with a layer of half-consumed manure; like all other cabbages, crambe loves fertilizer. By the third year, the plants will be strong enough to undergo pruning. In December, January or February, mix half-consumed dead leaves with soil, and cover the plants entirely with a layer proportionate to their strength. Depending on the severity of the cold or the severity of the winter, manure is added around this mixture of leaves and soil. After six weeks, if the cold hasn't been too severe, you'll be able to harvest whitened leaves and petioles. Or you can do it as follows: cover the plants with pots proportionate to their size, and surround and cover these pots with fresh stable manure to help the plants vegetate and protect them from the cold. After cutting off the blanched sprays, the pots are placed back on the plants and again surrounded with manure; each plant yields up to three harvests in a year. In this case, wait until March to give a first ridging of 0m,06 to Om,10; then give a second and a third; the leaves acquire Om, 30 to 0m, 40 in length. Maritime cabbage multiplies very easily from cuttings; it resists the most intense frosts in sandy soils; it often melts or rots in loamy or heavy soils. In Moravia, Wallachia, Hungary and Tartary, another species of crambe grows, bearing the epithet tartarica. The root, which has a circumference of Om, 25 to Om, 35 and a length of Om, 40, is soft, fleshy and succulent. It is used in the same way we use celery. The gardeners of Bath, England, who grow a lot of crambe, are quick and easy. Each plant, not staggered but facing each other, is spaced two and a half feet apart, and one foot apart in the rows. Gutters are cut in the widest spacing, and the void can be filled with ashes and leaves, which when consumed provide excellent fertilizer and loosen the soil. In the second year, after sowing or planting, the plants are not yet strong enough to be eroded by means of hot manure; but with this method, not only are the second-year shoots already used, but also the plants undergo a kind of pruning that strengthens them and encourages the emission of lateral shoots. Towards the end of February, if the soil is dry enough, 12-inch-wide gullies are dug along the length of the largest spacing, and the young plants are covered with 8-9 inches of soil. In spring, the shoots are examined by stripping them by hand, and when they begin to emerge from the surface of the soil, when they are 7 or 8 inches long, they are cut off below the lower leaf. Towards the end of April, the gullies are filled in by removing the mounds. When the soil is level, any buds that may have been left behind are cut off, otherwise they will go to seed, weakening the plants for years to come. Sea cabbages destined to wither are never allowed to go to seed. The following winter, we start forcing for consumption. In November, we cover the teenagers with long manure to prevent frost from penetrating the soil. Around mid-December, remove the litter, cover the teas with soil from the gutters, then level the entire surface with fermenting manure. Four weeks after this operation, the manure is removed with a fork or by hand, and the bare heads are ready for consumption. The roots must be covered again with soil and manure to protect them from frost. By the third year, the plants are very stunted; only a sufficient number of shoots are kept; the excess, which would weaken the plants, and any that are too close to the gutters, are removed. Cultivation continues as long as the plants remain strong and healthy, and they live a long life. The etiolated sprays of crambé consist of the stems and nascent leaves united in a kind of elongated apple, perfectly tender. CLAYTONIA PERFOLIATA. A member of the Portulaceae family, native to North America, this plant was introduced in 1794. Its thick, rhomboidal leaves are tristender and slightly acidic in flavor. This easy-to-cultivate annual deserves its place in the market garden in every respect. It thrives in virtually any type of soil and at any exposure; it grows from 12 to 15 inches tall. It can be sown all year round, either broadcast or in rows. 92 It can be cut several times and used in the same way as purslane and spinach. Raw, it can be mixed with lettuces, endives and lamb's lettuce. Under cover, it produces abundantly throughout the winter. WATERCRESS. So far, watercress cultivation has not become established in Belgium; we are content to gather it from the banks of streams or fountains. It would undoubtedly be worthwhile to create watercress nurseries along the lines of those that have existed for many years in Germany and France. Near a city such as Brussels, this type of cultivation could, it seems to us, be successful. This plant is very healthy; it is antiscorbutic and purifies the blood. In the spring, street vendors in Paris offer it to passers-by, advertising it as a health-giving plant. We recommend that anyone with a small source of running water in their garden, or a pond or stream running through it, cultivate this plant, which is so easy to grow that it can be called spontaneous. As the plant is native to Belgium and grows in almost all streams, it's easy to get hold of a few plants and plant them at the water's edge in your garden. If you don't have a small trickle of water, you can dig a sort of channel, levelling the bottom and covering it with a layer of Om,05 to Om,06 potting soil. The watercress is planted in the channel and then submerged in a few inches of water. It will soon appear on the surface, and can be harvested in winter and spring. Cress is a member of the cruciferous family; it should not be confused with the axillary umbel (sium nodiflorum, L.), which is usually found in its vicinity. The latter plant is poisonous; it can be distinguished from cress by its umbellate flowers and saw-toothed leaves. LIONS TOOTH. So far, as far as we know, the dandelion or dentde-lion has not been cultivated; however, this plant, which is sought in spring in the wild for use as a salad, could with care become a good vegetable crop. On river banks, dandelion makes a very healthy salad every spring, similar in every way to blanched chicory. On the banks of the Meuse and Scheldt rivers, in meadows that have been flooded and covered with a few centimetres of sand, dandelion is harvested when the tops of its leaves are showing. It can also be found in the molehills of our pastures. These tenderized leaves are slightly less bitter than chicory. In stews, they are difficult to distinguish from our best endives; in soups, they give absolutely the flavor of scorsonera. To grow dandelion, sow it in spring in strong or sandy soil, taking care to harvest the seeds from the hardiest varieties found in meadows. Then, butter or cover the plants with sand; this is essential. If covered with heavy soil, the leaves will turn white less quickly and be more bitter. The varieties whose cultivation we describe here are known to the French as chicorée; indeed, they belong to this genus; but, as the Belgians know them more particularly as endives, we gladly give them this name, which moreover lends itself to differentiating them from wild chicory, whose cultivation we have described. However, it should be pointed out that, although the famous Linnaeus considered chicory to be a distinct and specific species under the name endive chicory (cichorium endivia), it seems no less likely that it derives from wild chicory and is merely a variety of it. Endive grown in our gardens includes the following varieties: endive de Meaux, with cut, crenulated leaves: when sown early, or when new seed is used, it is prone to bolting; sown in May and June, it does well;- endive fine d'Italie, early and with delicate leaves, is less prone to bolting, and is preferable for spring sowing:- endive scarole, which can be used like the previous varieties; it has the following souvariety: grande scarole dite de Hollande; ronde, with short leaves, likely to peel; blonde, with yellowish leaves. The latter varieties are all broad-leafed. They can be sown from February to July, first indoors, then outdoors. Endive seeds should be lightly covered; they won't sprout if they're over-covered. Sow lightly in a flowerbed, against a wall, in the rising sun. The first sowings in spring 9. should only be of Italian endive, which is not prone to going to seed. The latest endive sowings are the most advantageous; they come in a season when fresh vegetables are in short supply. Those sown in July and August can be tied in September and October, and keep well into winter. When the endive is fully developed and you want to bleach it, then, in dry weather, lift all the leaves and, without compressing them, bind them down with a single tie of rush, straw or matting. Leave them in this state for a week, so that the central leaves can still benefit; then place a second tie towards the end of the plant, and, if it is very strong, tie the middle of the apple again, lest the central leaves escape. About a month after the endive has sprouted, it is strong enough to be transplanted; it is planted in staggered rows at Om, 35 to 0m 40 apart in all directions. The plant requires a lot of water during its growth and until it is ready to be bound. This operation should always be carried out in dry weather: if the endive is bound while wet inside, it will rot. It takes a fortnight to three weeks to blanch. If the weather is hot and very dry, and if watering is deemed necessary, it should be done with the nozzle of a watering can without a spray, wetting the base of the plants without running water into the apples. Sometimes, even rainfall followed by hot weather can cause them to rot. If, at the first frosts, all the endives have not yet been bound, they should be removed from the ground and placed upright in a dry cellar, with the roots in sand, where they will finish blanching. never sow new seed; there is always a risk that the seedlings from these young seeds will sprout. Endive seed retains the ability to germinate for five or seven years and beyond; always sow the oldest. There's no need to talk about the kind of soil this plant requires; any loose soil, whether sandy or well-smoked clay, is good. However, good, free-flowing soil, without excess clay, is preferable. SPINACH. Spinach likes oily, loose soil that's more humid than dry. In addition to the less leafy, spiny-seeded species from which spinach takes its name (spica, thorn, and nardus, back), there is a broad-leaved variety known as Flanders spinach. This is the variety that should be preferred for cultivation; it is more productive because of the breadth of its leaves; as a vegetable, it is even more beautiful because of its vegetation. Spinach is sown from early spring to autumn. In large-scale cultivation, where the grower needs to supply the market with spinach throughout the year, it must be sown every month. The amateur finds it more advantageous to sow at the end of summer, in August. These seedlings, which provide a winter and spring supply when other fresh vegetables are in short supply, are the most pleasant. As soon as the young plants are strong enough to be harvested, they are cut off a few centimetres above the ground, leaving the small emerging leaves in the heart intact. These are intended for a second harvest. When the plants have become more robust, they are no longer cut, but the outer leaves are picked one by one; in this way, a third or even fourth harvest is guaranteed, as everyone knows. Spinach sown in August and September leaves the ground empty in May and June for other vegetables, such as savoy cabbages, beans, potatoes, lettuces, endives, etc. If you sow them in summer, you need to choose a cool spot with some shade. Spinach, which is very prone to set seed in hot weather, hardly bears fruit in cool, shady conditions, or when it does, it has already been harvested. The plant requires no care during its growth other than to be weeded, hoeed and thinned out if it is too tightly packed: the distance between plants, from Om,10 to Om,20, is the most suitable for the broad-leaved variety from Flanders or Holland, also known as round-seeded spinach. This variety has a sub-variety called Esquermes. Its leaves are rounder and it appears a little more robust. In the coldest weather, it should be given a light covering of leaves or litter, which should be removed in February or March, depending on whether heavy frosts are no longer to be feared. Spinach leaves acquire a sort of semi-transparency during frost, which makes them appear frozen and lost: they are in no way frozen and easily regain their natural greenness if soaked for an hour or two in cold water and left to dry on straw for a while. Treated in this way, spinach is more valuable for the market and for cooking. Spinach (spinacca, oleracea, L.), a member of the Chenopoda family, is a dioecious plant, that is, it produces female flowers on one foot and male flowers on the other. Plants sown in autumn come into fruit in May. Once fruiting has taken place, the male plants are pulled out and the females supported by stakes. The seeds can be stored for two to three years. Originally from northern Asia, its introduction into Europe is not well known; it probably dates back to the Crusades; some authors say that the plant was imported into Spain by the Saracens in 1568. BEANS. Marsh beans require well-tilled, amended and smoked soil, and are strong rather than light. They are sown in December and January at the foot of walls, facing south. These initial seedlings are then transplanted into beds towards the end of February or in the course of March, depending on the weather and the strength of the plants. The beans placed against the walls occupy a very small space; one square meter can accommodate three liters; they are sown pell-mell, one against the other; they are covered with. Om,05 to Om,06 of soil. As soon as they are five centimetres above the ground, they can be placed, two or three together, at Om,30 in one direction and Om,50 in the other. The same distance should be observed for seedlings planted without transplanting. 4 As soon as they are 0m,10 to Om,15 in height, they should be deadheaded. This operation considerably increases the strength of the plants, as they form new roots in the new soil around them. At the same time, they are crimped; this is all the care that broad beans require from the moment they are planted to the end of their vegetation. However, crimping must be repeated when the soil is more or less beaten. Never shy away from this light work, especially during droughts; it has been found that one hoeing in very dry soil is worth several waterings. After ridging, Savoy or Brussels sprouts can be planted between the rows; horseradish, lettuce or carrots can also be sown. Early seedlings planted against walls or other shelters should be protected from frost with straw mats or, better still, leaves. From time to time, we uncover a corner of the cover to see if the field mice don't damage it; this happens quite frequently. We now have a quick and effective way of getting rid of these animals: just mix a little phosphorus with wheat flour paste in the proportion of 1/16 ounce of phosphorus to two ounces of flour. Place small balls of the paste in the burrows. When making this paste, avoid touching it with your fingers. These marsh bean seedlings can also be sown in cellars or other frost-free locations, in crates or pots. Here are the main varieties grown in our vegetable gardens: Mazagan or Portuguese beans, which are always small. This variety is best suited to being forced; it is the earliest; it comes to us from Africa, from a place formerly in the possession of the Portuguese. - Fêve verte de Gênes, a little less early and a little larger than the previous variety; it does not produce much; the pods do not contain more than two or three beans -Fève verte de la Chine; much more tender than the previous variety, it has the advantage of always remaining a beautiful green color, even when ripe. Suitable for candying, it will appear as fresh on the table in winter. Productive. - A red-flowered bean, it is early, but has a harsh flavor; it is not highly prized. - Windsor bean, also known as long-podded bean; this is one of the best, very productive; the large, beautiful beans have a frank taste and are not herbaceous, as is sometimes the case with smaller species. - Fêve en éventail; this is the smallest, hardly exceeding Om,10 to Om,15; it is not productive enough for the merchant gardener; but it is perfectly suited to being forced under frame as an early plant. At flowering time, the tops of the plants should be pinched back to prevent the flower from sinking and to protect them from aphids, which then spread all over the plant and spoil it completely. In this respect, the earliest seedlings are the best; aphids prefer to attack seedlings planted after April. It's not easy to get them in autumn; sometimes you can get them very well by cutting the plants when they have given their first green harvest; they then sprout a large number of shoots which bear fruit and produce as they did the first time. For autumn beans, you can also - and this practice should be preferred - cut the flowering plant at ground level. As the plant is still in full vegetative strength, it grows back better than if you cut it only when its fruits are already half-developed. Seed beans are harvested when the pods are black; they are not removed from their shells. They are dried in the attic and kept in this state until the time of sowing, taking care to leave those not needed in their pods. In a dry place and in their husks, they can be kept for three or four years, whereas it is difficult to keep them for more than a year without them. If you need to go to the merchant to buy seeds, you can boldly entrust white ones to the plantation; you'll reject any that are yellow-brown or blackish; they're old and won't sprout. The broad bean (vicia faba, Linn.), an annual plant, belongs to the legume family; it is native to Persia. BEANS. To distinguish beans, we'll divide them into two series: in the first we'll place those with climbing stems; they need to cling to stakes and are called pole beans. This first series is subdivided into long-stemmed beans and medium-stemmed beans. In the second major series are dwarf beans or beans without oars. 2C should be given a good ploughing before winter; however, if the soil has been well tended, i.e. if it has been deeply spaded and well smoked for a previous crop, such as potatoes, cabbage, onions, etc., it is sufficient to spade it well in spring, preferably amend it with cow manure, and plant in due course. Beans thrive in light, sandy rather than hard, compact soil. In hard or clay soils, they should be planted eight or ten days later than in light, soft, warm soils. They can be planted in rows or in clumps; the latter method is preferable, especially for long-stemmed beans; they should be driven and tied around the poles as they begin to cling to them. In row plantations, it would be difficult to carry out this very necessary operation. Although we are strongly in favor of row planting for large farms, we see neither the need nor the usefulness of this modification; on the contrary, planted in clumps, dwarf or pole beans are easier to maintain. Seedlings are planted in staggered rows in hand-made pits 0.03 m deep, spaced Om 70 apart in all directions for beans in the first series, and Om 50 apart in all directions for bush beans. While making these pits, loosen the small clods of earth between the fingers and place 7 to 10 beans in them, spaced Om,02 to 0m, 03 apart. Preferably planted in dry weather. If the surface of the soil becomes too dry, and the beans are planted in the MARAICH GROWING. 2. 10 dust, the seeds would not germinate and would wait for rain to come up, which would not only cause a detrimental delay, but would also make the plants sickly and languid, as in this case they would have gone through a state of demigrination. To avoid this inconvenience, turn the soil to a depth of half a spade at the points where the clumps should be, while covering the beans immediately with this fresh soil. It doesn't matter whether you plant in hot or cold weather: if it's rainy and hot, you can leave the beans in the ground; if it's rainy and cold, you won't plant; the seeds usually rot, so it's better to wait a few days. Beans grow very well under a light layer of wood ash; this fertilizer has a strong influence on their vegetation; it is used for this purpose in some of our country's provinces, especially Antwerp and Flanders. We have never seen it used for this purpose in the province of Limburg. After planting, this layer of ash, Om,006 to 0m,010 thick, is placed on the soil covering the beans. We disapprove of this method; it's better to sow a few days later and in place than to use this unfortunate practice. Because of its delicate roots in its early youth, the bean doesn't like transplanting. For this vegetable, as for the others, we won't be afraid to give it a lot of fertilizer. So, even if the soil is good on its own because of winter cultivation, it can still be improved and strengthened, if I may say so, by using poudrette or liquid manure as an auxiliary. Here's how to use it: a fortnight before sowing the beans, use the hoe or spade to open holes at the points where you're going to plant; in each hole, put a quarter-liter of slurry or half a liter of liquid manure (cow and ox urine). When it's time to sow, i.e. a fortnight after applying this fertilizer (1), the soil is levelled by putting the soil that has come out back into the holes, taking care to break it up and loosen it properly. Then, on top of this manure, without making the slightest excavation, we sow the beans and immediately cover them, making slight mounds or eminences in the shape of an inverted plate. This method, based on experience, is highly recommended; all things being equal, i.e., if the season is favorable, if the beans are of a good type, and cared for in good time, the yield will be considerable with this change in cultivation. In light soils, beans are first sown at the beginning of May; in heavy soils, they are planted only after the middle of the same month. If the beans are hit by a white frost, they are lost; at zero, the temperature is already fatal to them. Planting is done in squares, beds or borders. After heavy rains, if the beans have not yet emerged, and if the soil is (1) Poudrette, pigeon or chicken droppings, etc., should only be used with caution, especially for delicate plants; it is necessary to release the ammonia gas, which cauterizes the plants and destroys their tissues. (Autcur's note.) beaten and hardened, the crust covering them must be carefully cut and divided, so that they cannot make their way through. Beans are not only sown from the beginning and middle of May, but continue to be sown until July, so that they can be enjoyed until the first frosts. As for those sown at the end of April or the very beginning of May, we never put the oars or poles in place before they are out of the ground; since in this season there are still cold rains, the water would run down the poles and stop at the hole of the seeds, which would rot due to this excess of cold humidity. This is not the case for June sowing; a warm rain does no harm; if you want to place the oars before sowing, you can sow around them soon afterwards. Beans require at least three hoeing operations; the first is carried out as soon as they have four leaves, the second after setting the oars, which is done a few days later; at the same time, they are lightly ridged, and the third when they are Om.30 high; they are then ridged again, and quite heavily. If, as is almost always the case, weeds appear during their vegetation, we crimp them again. In Belgium, where we're exposed to fairly strong winds, we're in the habit of fixing the oars with wicker two by two or four by four; or, after tying them two by two, we attach them to other poles or oars, which we lay horizontally between the crossed tops. Fir poles are the best; their tough, rough bark gives the climbing bean stems plenty of grip; then, being straight, they can be neatly placed in the rows. For medium-sized beans, branching oaks or beeches are preferable. Without harming pole beans, either kale or beet can be planted very advantageously between the rows. In all aspects of cultivation, dwarf beans or beans without oars require absolutely the same care, with the only difference that instead of forming clumps of 7 or 10 seeds, only two or three beans are planted at Om, 50 apart; needless to say, they are never given oars. 10. The bean's flower is weakly attached to its stem; this is an unequivocal sign that the plant belongs to a climate where strong winds prevail less than in the northern regions of our globe; for this reason, they should always be planted sheltered from westerly winds, if possible; And for the same reason, the first harvests should be entrusted to hands skilled enough not to shake too much the stems, which are still full of flowers at the top, while the pods are already being picked at the bottom. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Beans (phaséolus, Lin.) belong to the legume family; the fruits of this natural family are called pods, or legumes, which should not be confused with the word "vegetable", commonly used to designate all edible vegetable plants. Native to warmer climates, it could not be cultivated in Belgium if all the phases of its vegetation were not rapid; it hardly lasts more than three to five months. Beans originated in South America and India, and were introduced to Belgium at the end of the 16th century. For a long time, the species or varieties were limited to the dwarf bean, the pole bean and the princess bean. Today, there are many known varieties, numbering up to three hundred. We don't need to list them all here, as our book is too short. We shall only mention the most widely cultivated varieties: 13 I.-A. The long-stemmed beans are as follows: Soissons bean: this is the common white bean; the young pods are eaten with the husks; the bean is used in winter, either dried or mashed. - Gigantic bean, flattened, larger than the Soissons. White and purple runner bean; more sensitive to cold than the others; very productive; its bean is delicious. Saber bean: owes its name to the shape of its pods, which are wide and long; it is an hon product. In Belgium, Holland and Prussia, the pods are cut into thin strips before the bean is fully developed; they are eaten fresh or candied for winter, or dried slowly in the oven after being lightly cooked. German runner bean or "cossé"; very high stem; medium-sized, flat seeds; large pods: very good in green. Butter beans, early, excellent. Other large-shafted beans include: prudhomme, with very tender pods and small, round seeds. Princess bean, a variety of the previous one; it has sub-varieties, with more or less round grain, all excellent and very tender; the pods, eaten green, remain tender until they are fully developed and even until they turn yellow. Dried in the oven after a light cooking, these beans are excellent for winter provision, and keep for two or three years. Lafayette bean, excellent all-rounder; pods are two fingers wide and Om, 20 long, very tender and stringless; paddles very high; grain yield not considerable. The introduction of this bean is quite recent; so far it is not very widespread. Translucent bean, a singular variety in terms of the color of its pods, which are a beautiful fresh buttery yellow when fully developed. Only then are they eaten, and they are most tender and productive; the grain is good and dry. We highly recommend growing this excellent variety. B.
