Runner bean: this is the most dwarf of all beans; it is distinguished by the absence of the inner membrane, commonly called parchment, which is found on most varieties when the bean begins to form. White American bean, slightly elongated, small, very productive, good eaten dry. Another rather arbitrary division, based on the use of beans in cooking, divides these vegetables into three series: shelling beans, those best eaten dry; green beans, those best eaten green; snap beans, those used with pod and bean. All beans, with a few exceptions, can be eaten green, just as the grain of most of them can be eaten dry. Some varieties are prized for the delicacy of their pods alone. We advise both the amateur and the horticulturist to try every variety they can get their hands on; it's a very easy thing to do; by planting a single clump of either the dwarf or the pole variety, you can explore its qualities. In years of famine, they have been a great resource for populations reduced to poverty; moreover, they are a very nutritious and healthy food. LETTUCE. Lettuces are grown in good free-range garden soil. Spring lettuces are sown in February or March, to be transplanted in April; summer lettuces are sown from April 15 to July, to be transplanted successively every two weeks and supplied throughout the season. Winter lettuces are sown from August 15th to September 15th, and at different times, to be transplanted in November and spend the winter in place under a blanket of leaves, which are removed during the thaws. Cutting lettuce is sown on a warm or cold bed under a frame in December and January; it is never transplanted. In February and March, the same variety is sown on walls facing east or south, either on a bed or in the ground; this lettuce is sown very thickly and harvested as soon as it has four leaves. Lettuce is transplanted using a planter, without pressing the soil too hard against the root or covering the heart of the plant, which should only be level with the surface of the soil. They are planted in staggered rows, the larger ones at Om, 40, the medium ones at Om, 30, and the smaller ones at Om, 20 apart. Lettuces grow quickly and with difficulty in warm, light, dry soil; in cold, clayey soils, they grow too slowly; consequently, good, free-flowing, soft soil, as we have already said, is best and most suitable. For all plantings made in the first heat of spring and summer, choose the evening and water immediately after transplanting. For spring planting, as long as the nights are still cold and the soil is not sufficiently moist, water in the morning or around mid-day. As for the choice of varieties, which are very numerous and rather poorly described or determined, it will be made according to what the gardener finds most advantageous, giving preference to those that leave the ground free as soon as possible for other crops. There are three types of lettuce, each containing a large number of varieties: A. Spring lettuces with round heads: Dolphin lettuce, one of the best spring lettuces; flattened, large, full, tender head; black seed. Cordon rouge lettuce; small; blond-green leaves; red-tinted top; white seed. Lettuce small, blond, early; rises quickly. B. Summer lettuces. Lettuce blonde de Versailles, tender, difficult to set seed; likes light soil and frequent watering; white seed. Turkish lettuce, large, white-green leaves; very large head; one of the best summer lettuces; black seed. The following summer lettuces are also grown: blond stock lettuce, Berni lettuce, royal lettuce, Maltese lettuce, Batavia lettuce, Batavia cabbage lettuce, etc. The last two are very favorable to watering. The last two are very favorable for farmers' gardens, and can even be grown in fields, because they are not difficult on the quality of the soil, while at the same time they make excellent food for pigs, who are very eager to eat them. Lazy blond lettuce: produces large heads; very slow to bolt. Beautiful and good lettuce, old but excellent variety; sometimes huge heads; brittle and very tender. The new varieties on the market as Victoria lettuce and Bath brown lettuce are worth spreading. C. Winter lettuces. Crepe or small crepe lettuce, small; it apples little, and comes well under cloche in winter. Small black lettuce, a sub-variety of the previous one; comes under frames or cloches. Morine lettuce, greener than the next; lasts longer; white seed. Passion lettuce, apples around Holy Week: hence its name; copper-colored, dotted with reddish spots. Gotte lettuce, of which two varieties are grown, one with a black seed and the other with a white seed, larger than the small black one and less pale green. Suitable for bedding. D. Roman lettuces. These lettuces are distinguished from head lettuces by their shape; their leaves are elongated, narrow at the base, broad and almost always rounded at the tips; they are not curled or blistered and do not lie flat on the ground, but stand upright and do not nod. Almost all varieties need to be tied like endives in order to tenderize and etiolate. The main ones are : Early spring and summer green romaine, very large; not very difficult on the quality of the soil; the seed is black. Romaine maraichère d'été, long, dark-green leaves; the least delicate in terms of soil; successful in all seasons, it is the most widely cultivated. Romaine blonde de Brunoy, green-yellow, more tender than the next, but more prone to bolting; white seed. Romaine grise du printemps, not successful in summer or autumn. Red romaine, red-tinted outer leaves; best in autumn; black seed. Romaine lettuces, also known simply as romaine, chicory or elongated lettuce, are all worthy of cultivation. The English and Germans also grow other varieties, such as bourg, etc. The cultivation of head lettuces is applicable in all respects to romaine lettuces, except that they need to be tied like endives, and some varieties are particularly suitable for forced cultivation. - See this cultivation. Winter romaine lettuces are followed by winter lettuces, such as passion lettuce, morine, petite crêpe, etc.; after these come lettuces for cutting. Small, early varieties are generally preferred for this purpose. Chicory lettuce, with its kinky leaves, and spinach lettuce, with its lobed, incised leaves, are particularly recommended for the same purpose. Spring and summer salads follow. Lettuce (lactuca sativa, L.) is a member of the semi-flowering family; its native soil is unknown to us. It has been grown in Belgium for over two centuries. It is widely consumed throughout Europe every year. It is a healthy vegetable, slightly sleep-inducing. Today, a medicine known as thridace is prepared from its milky juice; it shares the soporific properties of opium. MACHE. Mâche, doucette, blanchette, poule-grasse, salade de chanoine, salade de blé, oreille-de-lièvre, are all synonyms for a small salad native to Belgium. A small, low-growing annual, it is common in fields and can be cultivated in 21 11 vegetable gardens, where it becomes a little stronger and is easier to collect when grouped in a small space. Two varieties of this plant are known: Italian lamb's lettuce, which is stronger in all its proportions and has slightly hairy leaves; it is less prized than the common variety. The latter is more tender, with smaller, narrower leaves. Lamb's lettuce can be sown from August 15 to October 15, in well-tilled, well-amended soil. In poor soil, the plant is less tender and sometimes tough. As the seed is very fine, it is covered very little, if at all. All it requires for cultivation is weeding. Sowings in August, September and October successively produce lamb's lettuce that can be harvested throughout the winter and spring. Corn wouldn't fit in here, if it hadn't long since acquired the right of ownership in many country gardens, where it doesn't look too bad. In fact, this is how a plant sometimes becomes a field crop. We know that the potato, before becoming generally cultivated, was first used in many gardens as an ornamental plant, and then, long afterwards, as a field crop. Corn doesn't always do well in our climate: sown late, it fails to ripen its seeds; sown too early, it sometimes freezes. If its yield were as certain as that of wheat, corn would be the equivalent of this precious cereal; it would compensate most fully for the cost of cultivation. It likes light, sandy, warm and very fertile soil; it needs a lot of fertilizer. Sow as soon as frosts are no longer a threat, in April, or even at the beginning of the month, to ensure ripe seeds. Corn withstands a slight degree of cold and grows again in good soil, if the first leaf has been destroyed. It is sown in rows spaced from Om, 75 to Om, 90. In the rows, seeds placed in twos or threes 0m, 30 apart should be lightly covered. During its vegetation, it requires no care other than weeding and hoeing, then to be strongly ridged when it is 0°, 50 high. All overabundant plants, superfluous shoots and later overabundant ears are removed, leaving only two or three of the strongest. Corn is harvested when the husk is dry and the kernel hard; the cobs are removed and dried in the granary or in a dry, well-ventilated place. Ordinary corn or corn with large yellow kernels yields a lot of produce; quarantine corn is smaller, yields less, but vegetates more quickly and comes into Belgium better than large corn. As a forage plant, corn deserves to be widespread in every respect. Horned cattle are very fond of it. To this end, it is sown from April 15 to June, either broadcast or in rows closer together than usual. It is cut above the roots as soon as it begins to flower, or before. It is cut with a chopper and fed with chopped straw to cows, etc. It is a good successor to clover, potatoes, rapeseed and beet. It originates from Peru and is widely cultivated in America; the Mexicans trade in it extensively; it seems to have come to us from Turkey. It seems to have come to us from Turkey, so everyone knows that it still bears the name of Turkish wheat. There are several varieties, differing only in the color of the grain, which is yellow, red, purple, white, variegated and variously marbled. At the time of writing, seeds of a corn from Upper Peru are being imported into Belgium, which the introducer calls Cusco corn. The seeds are a beautiful white, flattened and large: at first glance, they could be mistaken for bog beans. They appear to belong to a variety, or rather a species, that is very robust in every respect. In Bolivia, the plant is cultivated on the slopes of high mountains, where the climate is perhaps harsher than in Belgium. According to the introducer, who himself brought the seeds to our country, Cusco maize is of immense value in field cultivation. Let us mention here the introducer, Mr. Mariano de Rivero, ambassador of the Peruvian Republic to the Belgian government. Perhaps our grateful country will one day name this corn zea mariano de Rivero. 18 CULTIVATION. The onion requires light, loose soil, especially containing a mixture of consumed manure left over from previous crops. So, when we say light soil, we don't mean sandy soil that is often thin, but soil that is either clayey or sandy, improved by successive fertilizations, from which nourishing juices remain and which have made it loose. If you have land in the conditions we have just described, the success of a good onion crop depends on good soil preparation. Before winter, the land is ploughed with a spade, and half-consumed cow manure is ploughed in at the same time. We recommend half-consumed manure, because onions, like all bulbous plants, fear new and still fermenting manure. Fifteen or eight days before sowing, to allow the soil to settle properly, we give the second and final ploughing. Onions are sown at the end of February in light soils, and in March in heavy soils. If the soil to be sown is light, once it has been suitably levelled, it should be plumbed a little with the back of the spade, the seed sown abundantly, the rake passed lightly in the direction of the length of the planks and only once, as one passes the harrow over a sown field, so that the rake does not return to the same spot and the seeds sown are not piled up, as happens when the rake makes these movements11. movements that spoil the proper distribution of seeds on the ground. After lightly harrowing with the rake, cover the beds with a layer of potting soil about 0m, 007 thick. This layer of loam could be given a thickness of Om,03 or Om,07, but then it would have to be scattered over the beds beforehand, and sown on. In strong soils, you won't behave quite the same way. It is bad practice to combine these soils in minute detail, since the rains then pound and harden them, and the hailstorms complete the process of rendering them almost sterile, by forming a crust that splits and cracks; on these soils, distributing a layer of loam is infinitely favorable; consequently, if you had no loam, you would sow on rough ploughing in heavy soils and harrow lightly with the rake. The above principles should be clearly understood with regard to light and compact soils. When the seed has risen and the young plant is fairly firm, weed and thin, then water to firm the soil around the roots. The most suitable distance to leave for onions, in all directions, is Om,07 to 0m,09. Breaking the leaves on onions is a pretty useless operation: when done while they are still growing, it is harmful; when they are nearing maturity, the leaves lie down on their own; the only time this operation might be appropriate is when winter is approaching and, consequently, ripening needs to be accelerated. As soon as the leaves have dried, the bulbs are harvested; they are laid out for about ten days in a garden alley, or under a shed where the wind circulates, then taken to the attic; a fortnight later, they are cleaned of roots and leaves; they are laid out next to each other in a place sheltered from the cold, or covered with dry leaves. As for the seedbeds, choose the largest and most beautiful onions. Plant them in the ground in February, 0.25 m apart in all directions and at such a depth that the top of the bulb emerges slightly from the soil. As soon as the fistulous stems go to seed, surround them with stakes, otherwise they will fall over under their own weight, or be broken by strong winds. Don't wait to harvest the seeds until the triangular capsules enclosing them have dried out. As soon as the seed is black, it is ripe, or at least ripe enough to be harvested and fully ripen in a dry, airy place; if you wait any longer, much of it will be lost. The seed heads should be cut with Om, 30 of stem. Once dried out, the seeds are beaten and stored in a dry place. Their germination period is two years. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS The onion (allium cœpa, L.), a member of the Liliaceae family, has several varieties. As far as we know, not all of them have yet been tried in Belgium. The best-known varieties here are dark red, pale red and yellow; the latter is valued because it keeps better in winter than the others, although all are fairly easy to store. Next come white onions, Spanish onions, Portuguese onions, Deptfort onions, Strasbourg onions and so on. Under the name of potato onion, we grow a variety that reproduces from cloves growing around the main bulb. These cloves are separated in winter and planted in early spring. Another variety, the Egyptian onion, which has been cultivated in our country for a long time, produces bulblets on its stalk and also multiplies through these. The latter two belong to warmer climates and do not produce as perfect a product here as in their native soil; we do not recommend their cultivation. The white or spring onion is an excellent variety; it has a milder flavor and is more frost-resistant than the others. Sow from August 1st to around the 15th of the same month, covering the seeds only with a 1 or 2 cm layer of compost. This onion should be sown very close together, to be planted out at the end of October or in November, leaving a distance of Om.07 to Om.09 between plants on well-ploughed, leaded and terra-cotta-coated soil. When this transplanting is done, the young plants are about the height of Om, 15. The ends of the leaves should not be cut off, only the tips of their roots pinched a little, then transplanted with the planter at the same depth they occupied before transplanting. The seedling can also be planted out in spring, but sow in the second half of August. For our climate, it's always wise to cover these young onions with leaves during severe cold and uncover them during thaws. White onions planted in October, November or March will be large enough to be used in May or June, leaving the ground free for other crops such as potatoes, Savoy cabbage, green cabbage, endives, carrots, yellow and red onions; Madeira onions, which grow to a considerable size; Nocera onions, brought in from Italy, are white, small and of very good quality. We draw special attention to the quality of fertilizer used in England, where horticulturalists are very keen on growing onions. After ploughing the land with great care, they spread potting soil over the beds, sow the seeds and then cover them by hand with soil taken from the paths between the beds. For many years they grow onions in the same place, with no significant difference in yield. This is hardly surprising; the plants find ever-new nourishment in this way, and their cultivation in the same place could, without differing much, continue in perpetuity. Moreover, we consider this method to be very good. This consists of a mixture of butcher's blood, quicklime and a small quantity of free earth. This well-mixed compost is piled up a year in advance; it is used as a dry powder and spread on the soil at the same time as the seed. We also recommend, and we know from experience that this fertilizer is excellent, the use of clay rubble from thatched cottages, etc. This clay, mixed with water, can be used as a fertilizer. This clay, mixed with liquid manure and sheep dung, and piled up for three to six months, spreads over the beds and gives the onions a beautiful vegetation. What we did ourselves, many years ago, was to spread chicken droppings to a thickness of about 1 centimeter between young onions the size of a goose feather pipe; we have never seen bigger onions than after using this fertilizer. Pigeon droppings would undoubtedly produce the same effect, but as their strength is proportionately greater, the quantity to be used should be a little less. SORREL. Sorrel is a perennial, indigenous plant of the polygon family. It produces pleasantly acidic leaves from the root collar all year round. It enhances the bland taste of some other vegetables, such as spinach, and at the same time corrects the greasiness of certain dishes, such as eels. Sorrel is very easy to grow: the commercial horticulturist, as well as the amateur, almost never plants or sows it other than in borders, next to beds or squares. Once planted, which is done by splitting off the plants, it can remain for twelve to fifteen years; however, we don't recommend leaving it beyond five or six years without renewing it. During the summer, sorrel needs no care other than to be weeded, and to have the stems cut back when they show a disposition to climb. In winter, the soil and plants are fertilized with horse manure or compost. Leaves do not freeze quickly; however, this sometimes happens. To get some in winter, just cover them with litter and uncover them when the thaw comes. We grow: Belleville sorrel, broad-leafed, not very acidic; - petite eccille, the most acidic; - Holland sorrel, broad-leafed, the best. All species and varieties of sorrel can be grown in any kind of soil and in any kind of exposure; in the north and in the shade, their acidity is less pronounced than in the south and in bright sunshine. PERSIL. CULTIVATION. Parsley, a seasoning plant, thrives in loose, oily soil, and although it thrives in any kind of exposure, as a southern European plant it prefers a southern exposure. It can be sown from March to August and throughout the summer, in beds, borders or rays. Seeds should be covered with only 0m,002 of soil; they are quite fine, and we know that any fine seed, if it is too well covered, will not germinate. They must be kept wet from the very first days of sowing, until they have acquired a certain strength: seeds take thirty to forty days to germinate. The first sowings in spring and the last ones in autumn should be at the foot of a wall and facing south. By the second year, the plant has gone to seed; however, it can be kept for at least three years, if the stems are cut off as soon as they come up. Parsley is rare on Belgian markets in winter. Some people dry the leaves in summer, then store them in closed vases or jars. Leaves preserved in this way are inert and almost tasteless. All aromatic plants, more or less 1, owe their aroma and virtue to a volatile oil, of which almost nothing remains after the plant has dried. The plant itself is not very delicate; it doesn't freeze; its roots brave the cold; but the part you need, the leaf, freezes. Parsley can be stored very easily under a layer of leaves, the thickness of which is increased according to the intensity of the cold. Under this layer, you'll always find healthy leaves suitable for culinary use. All the more reason to keep it well under glass. We also recommend, especially for small households, to sow it in a terrine or flowerpot filled with potting soil and to keep this terrine or pot in the house. It goes without saying that parsley is discovered covered in leaves during the thaw. Parsley stems go to seed in May; the seeds ripen in August. When half the seeds appear ripe, the whole plant is cut and dried in the sun, so that the seeds cannot be lost: they fall out as they ripen. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Common parsley (apium petroselinum, Linn.) belongs to the Umbelliferae family. The stem, two to three feet high, is glabrous, ridged and stalked; its leaves are twice winged; the upper leaflets linear; the lower cuneate; terminal umbels. Parsley is even easier to confuse with some native poisonous plants than chervil, since hemlock and little hemlock resemble parsley more than chervil in habit. - See this last plant on page 23. Parsley is native to Sardinia. There are several varieties and sub-varieties, such as: curly parsley, the very curly dwarf parsley, the broad-leafed parsley, whose fleshy root is used in cooking in Belgium and Holland; Naples parsley, with large ribs, or parsley-celeriac, which is more robust in all its parts and whose ribs have turned white and are eaten like celery; its cultivation is also the same as that of celery. Parsley grown by gardeners around large cities can provide an excellent market-gardening trade item in winter. For this purpose, it should be grown under glass frames, and sown lightly, in the first fortnight of July, in light soil. The seeds should be properly watered every day; although this watering should be repeated daily, it may not be enough in the middle of the scorching summer heat: in this case, the seedling should be covered with a layer of moss one to two fingers thick, which should be wetted once or twice a day, until the seeds emerge; the moss should then be removed, so don't neglect to look after it from the twenty-fifth day of sowing. PHYTOLACCA. The American grape, ten-stamens phytolacca, phytolacca decandra, L., is a large perennial plant from North America. Its stems rise to 2, 3 and 4 meters in height; they are reddish, as are 2. 12 the leaves, which are broad, oval, lanceolate and pointed. This plant is cultivated in some gardens to protect young seedlings from the sun. Creoles eat its leaves, just as Europeans eat spinach, and it is a very valuable food for negroes. The same cannot be said of phytolacca esculenta. This new vegetable, with the slightly peppery flavor of its leaves, is considered excellent by some and not very pleasant by others. What is certain is that it is less bland than spinach. Sow in a bed in February or March; transplant in April, about Om.50 apart and staggered. The plant likes oily soil. CULTIVATED PICRIDIE. Picridie cultivée, terre crépie, terra crepola, picridium vulgare, Desf. of the Compositae family, grows spontaneously in France, along roadsides, particularly near Montpellier; it was cultivated in Italy long ago. M. Vilmorin, a French horticulturist, spread it to the gardens of northern France, where it is now quite common. This easy-to-cultivate annual likes sandy soil. From the end of March to April, it is sown as a broadcast crop or in fairly tight rows. Young plants, used like endives, can be cut several times and grow back abundantly. 28 Soil preparation for leeks is the same as for onions. The soil must be fertile, loose and smoky from the previous year. Fertilizers suitable for onions are also suitable for leeks. Some gardeners who deal with the cultivation of this plant speak of fertilizers with a sort of aversion, as if this exceptional vegetable didn't need them; they're wrong! As a general rule, no plant can grow well without fertilizer; every organized being needs nourishment. Leek seeds can be sown quite thickly, within reach of the land on which they are to be planted. Sow in February or March, in rows or broadcast. The young plant needs only to be weeded, hoeed and watered in good time. Around mid-June, it is planted at Om, 18 apart in all directions and at a depth of Om, 10 to Om, 15, depending on the size of the plant, which must be at least the size of a goose feather pipe. As far as possible, choose rainy, overcast weather for transplanting. Once the plant has been pulled out, the lower parts of the fibrous roots are removed and the tops of the leaves cut off. A seedling is placed in each hole made with the planter, and without plunging the soil with this instrument, a generous watering is given to draw the soil into the holes and close them up without the need for further firming. During the summer, water frequently, and in September, interrupt the circulation of the sap in the leaves so that it moves towards the roots or, to put it better, towards the tuberous bulge above the roots themselves, which is the leek or edible part. To achieve this, the leaves of each plant are tied together with a simple knot. Others cut them off once or twice during the autumn; we don't like the latter procedure: strong mutilations are rarely beneficial to the plants. To preserve leeks, we lay the plants down to the leaves, one beside the other, in shallow trenches that we cover with litter or leaves during the frosts. This is done in November, when the weather is dry, and the leek will keep until May. In the same month, each plant sprouts a single stem rising from Om.60 to 1m.20 in height, ending in an onion-like head. As soon as the capsules open and show their black seeds, the stems are cut, leaving them Om,20 to Om,30 long; they are tied in bundles and dried on a cloth in the sun, or hung in a shed, with the precaution of putting paper, cloth or something else underneath, to catch any seeds that fall out. Those that remain in the capsules are left there until it's time to use them; they keep better there, and their germinative capacity lasts for two years. Leeks can be left to grow upwards, reserving a corner of the plantation, or, better still, they can be planted in March, choosing the best and biggest plants; they are placed at a slightly shorter distance than that indicated for onion seedbeds, since, as we have said, each leek plant produces only one stem, whereas onions produce from one to five stems per individual. Animal fertilizers, especially chicken or pigeon droppings, etc., sown on the soil in leek plantations, are suitable. We've also found it very easy to make furrows with the hoe, dragging it between the rows as we walk backwards; we fill these furrows or little trenches with dry or liquid slurry; we leave everything in this state for two weeks, then, by hoeing, we combine the soil as before. Leeks (allium porrum, L.) belong to the Liliaceae family. It grows spontaneously in Switzerland and France. Its cultivation is not very fortunate and, if well cared for, the product is quite profitable for the gardener-merchant. It is widely consumed in large cities, while country folk use up a small supply every year. There are two known varieties of leek: the short, fat leek from Rouen, known as the monster leek, and the long leek, which yields more. PEAS. CULTIVATION. Peas, which have long been grown in Belgium and other European countries, have yet to be subjected to a specific cultivation system. Even renowned growers say that peas should not be grown on recently-smoked soil or fields. - This is true, and we agree wholeheartedly with their 12. -4 their opinion, as regards fresh, unfermented, urine-soaked manure. But on the other hand, let's not forget to say: Peas want substantial soil, where they can find abundant humus or nourishing juices to make them vegetate perfectly. Consequently, loose, fertile soil that has been well smoked in previous years is ideal for peas. They also thrive in slightly calcareous soil; if the fertilizers previously applied to the land contained lime or calcareous salts, such as sulfate, subcarbonate or lime phosphate, they will find excellent nourishment. Wood ash is another suitable fertilizer for this type of plant. In humus- or loam-rich soil, peas can withstand the intense heat that almost always kills them in walled city gardens, where the sun's rays shine directly on them through reverberation. There, they are often yellowed from the stem and in a state of complete decay at or shortly after flowering. It should be noted that in suitable soil, as we have just mentioned, they should not be sown or planted as thickly as in poor or barren soil, where the plant acquires little volume. Peas should not be grown two years in a row on the same plot; there must be an interval of several years before they can be planted again in the same place. Peas are first planted in November on south-facing slopes, using early species in rays or pockets. November 25 is the day usually taken in our various provinces for these first sowings: without attaching great importance to this date, we are far from blaming the habit of ancient gardeners with regard to the fixing of days for sowing or planting; it may have its disadvantages, but it results in some order in the work, and then country people find it a certain ease; their agricultural work often coincides with those of gardening and sometimes makes them neglect the latter. The other sowings take place consecutively, weather permitting, in December, January, February and so on. As soon as the first seedlings emerge from the ground, they are sown again, and in the same way throughout the spring and summer, providing an uninterrupted succession of pods to be picked from spring to autumn. The last sowings are of late varieties, such as Clamart peas, Marly peas, broad bean peas, giant peas, Norman peas, and especially wrinkled or Knight peas. Seedlings for autumn peas should never be of early varieties; these are only suitable for spring and summer; by autumn these varieties no longer knot, and give flowers without fruit. The rows are spaced Om, 25 apart; the tufts within the rows are planted at the same distance, or at 0m, 30 for the strongest and tallest species. The holes are opened with a hoe, small spade or hoe, and 6 to 10 seeds are sown in each hole, covered with Om.05 to 0m.08 of soil. Until harvest, the peas are cared for by breaking up any crust that may have formed on the surface of the planting beds, hoeing the plants when they are about Om,10 in height, and weeding and raking them. For the first seedlings, which are sown in late autumn and overwinter in the ground, Dutch peas and Michaux peas are the preferred varieties. Overwintering peas in the ground is not recommended for the commercial horticulturist in our country. If they are a few days earlier, they are not as productive as those sown in February, March and April. The late peas we mentioned above can only be sown in June, so that they can be harvested in the late season, towards winter. If you want larger yields from these peas and want to have them earlier, you should sow them in April, so that their ripening grain can be eaten dry in winter. Pea seeds should always be selected so that the pods closest to the ground are harvested. It's a good idea to let the seed ripen in one or more beds, depending on the size of the crop, so as to have a separate supply of seeds. Peas can be preserved in their pods or shelled; we prefer to shell them as soon as they are ripe and dry. It seems to us, although we're not quite sure, that bruchids attack them more strongly in the pods than without them. However, this insect particularly attacks the lobes or cotyledons, sparing the sprouts in most cases, so that worm-eaten peas sprout just as well as those that have remained intact. They retain their germination capacity for two years. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Cultivated peas (pisum sativum, Linn.) belong to the natural legume family. Their fruit is called a legume or pod. Peas are therefore divided into three sections, according to their use in the domestic economy. Shelling peas are those whose valves are hard and lined with a membrane called parchment; these valves can only be used for cattle feed. - Snow peas are those that are eaten with or without pods; they are particularly useful for the staff of large farms; they produce a lot and don't need time to be shelled. - Dry shelled peas are particularly suitable for eating dry. They can also be shelled green, but it's a good idea to keep them for winter supplies, as they produce a lot and their very flaky grains soften perfectly when cooked, making excellent purées. The large green Norman pea is the best for this purpose, producing the most to be used dry. The most noteworthy varieties are: Pois Michaux, early, tender and sweet green; mediocre yield, white grain; Pois Michaux de Hollande, preferable to the previous variety, high yield, earlier. - Prince Albert pea: dwarf, eight days earlier than all the others, introduced from England in 1842. The English have strongly recommended it. - Pois crochu; not the earliest, but excellent, very sweet and very productive. - Pois de Marly, late, excellent, very productive. - Clamart pea, very good, best suited to very late harvests. - Knight's wrinkled pea has two varieties, one with a green grain, the other with a white grain. Both are very productive and of very good quality. - Turkish pea, very high, tender and sweet. - Sickle pea, very large and curved pod. - Waite's queen of the dwarf peace, very dwarf, reaches no more than six inches (0m, 18). marrow peace, dwarf, very full pods. - Princess Olga pea, early, high yielding. - Flacks duarf peas, productive, two to three feet tall. Chickpea (cicer arietinum, Linn.). The shape of the seed resembles that of a ram's head; hence the epithet or specific name of the plant. Chickpea seeds are also known as cicerelles, pesettes, garvances, from their Spanish name garbanzillo. This vegetable was highly esteemed by the Romans, and is still used today by the Spaniards. It has a pleasant taste both green and mashed. It is a healthy food, but not suitable for weak stomachs. PURSLANE. Purslane (portulaca oleracea, Linn.) is an annual plant of the Portulaceae family, brought to us from India. From the end of April to the end of summer, purslane is sown on potting soil mixed with the surface of the previously spaded ground. The very fine seeds are broadcast and do not need to be covered with soil. After sowing, the seeds are wetted to attach them to the soil. During the growing season, purslane is frequently wetted, making the leaves all the more tender. They are used in soups or steamed. A variety known as golden purslane, with 16 yellowish leaves, is more highly esteemed and more widely cultivated than the common green-leaved variety. The seeds are harvested as soon as the first capsules open; the plants are pulled out and dried on a sheet in the sun. Seeds kept in a dry place can be stored for nine or ten years. The germinative capacity of this plant's seeds is such that, once cultivated in a garden, the plant will return for a long series of years. To harvest its leaves in January and February, purslane is sown on a bed under a frame - see forced cultivation. WHITE QUINOA. White quinoa, anserine quinoa, chenopodium quinoa, Wildenow, is an annual plant of the Chenopoda family, excellent, very healthy and easy to digest. From April to July, it is sown in substantial soil that is damp rather than dry. Care should be taken to thin out the young plant, which spreads out and grows to a height of one or two meters. Growing in rows is preferable, as it makes it easier to keep the young plants at a suitable distance from one another, 0.30 to 0.40 m apart in all directions. Quinoa seeds keep for two years. Its leaves, unctuous and as wide as the hand, acquire greater width by means of topping, which should be carried out when the plant is about Om,40 in height; it is these leaves that are used; they exude vesicular globules and have this property in common with a species indigenous to our country: chenopodium bonus Ilenricus, Linn. Europe in 1779. Its cultivation was abandoned, and the plant lost to our gardens reappeared in England in 1822. Widely cultivated in lower Peru and on the high plateaus, its floury seeds constitute, alongside potatoes, the main food of the people; but cultivation has declined considerably since fine cereals were introduced from Europe. Quinoa is often confused with other species of anserine, notably with Schroder's chenopodium rubricaule. Kunth, based on specimens found in the herbarium of the famous travelers de Humboldt and Bonpland, speaks of two chenopods, one with a red stem and the other with a green stem: these plants, of Peruvian or Chilean origin, have also been mistaken, though perhaps wrongly, for white quinoa. RHUBARBS. Rhubarb, rheum, has been used as an edible plant in England for many years, and among the most widely cultivated are: currant rhubarb, early Elford rhubarb, late Ayton rhubarb, Nepaul rhubarb, wavy rhubarb and a hybrid that resembles Myatt rhubarb. The petioles and young etiolated leaves (1) are offered, even in winter, on the markets of the cities of Great Britain; in spring, gardeners continue to provide for consumption an immense quantity of bunches of white petioles (tails) which (1) We point out that the herbaceous parts of rhubarb are in no way purgative; the root alone enjoys this property. (Author's note.) They also make excellent pies. Hybrid rhubarb and Elford rhubarb are used in particular for this purpose. Also, under the name of rhufleurs and as a substitute for cauliflower, unhatched pompons with their stalks still tender are served on the best tables (1). These perennial plants of the polygon family, mostly native to the colder regions of our hemisphere, require no cultivation care: planted 1.40 m apart because of the size of their leaves, all that's needed is to hoe them in spring and bleach their petioles by buttage. Propagation takes place in the spring by root bursts or seeds, which should be sown immediately when mature, although they keep for two years. TETRAGON. Tetragonia (Tetragonia expansa), annual plant from New Zealand. It is already widespread in our gardens. It contributes to the taste and color of spinach. Its stem, as the specific name implies, is spread out over the ground and occupies a large space, so plants should be at least Om.50 apart. Sow in April or May, on potting soil. As soon as the plants are sufficiently developed, the ends of the stems are cut off along with the leaves; they are sure to grow back. These leaves and twigs are prepared in the same way as spinach. (1) The method of rhubarb stripping is not absolute; however, we recommend it because it tenderizes the plant while removing some of its acidity. MARKET GARDENING. 2. 13 NATURAL CROPS. ROOT VEGETABLES. BETTERAVE. CULTIVATION. We are talking here only about varieties grown in gardens; the others are part of field cultivation and are described in agricultural treatises. Beet thrives best in clean, loose, fertile, deeply tilled soil. It also thrives in sandy and clayey soil; however, it should be noted that, in good free soil, the roots grow larger than in light or sandy soil. They are either sown in situ or transplanted: in gardens, transplanting is generally used. For sowing, choose a well-tilled bed with good exposure, and sow from April 15 to May 15. If sown too early, beet rises and the roots are lost. Transplanting is done in May or June, with plants the size of a little finger, at a distance of Om.50 for the largest species and Om.35 for the smallest, in all directions. If the weather is dry, the soil is lightly tilled, or the roots are soaked in cow dung mixed with manure water, and planted immediately. When planting, take particular care not to turn the tip of the young root over in the hole. Once the beet has recovered, it requires no care other than weeding and hoeing; it is very resistant to drought and almost never needs watering. It serves well as an in-between plant for pole beans. Beet should not be thinned out: this is a bad practice, and instead of increasing the yield, it only reduces it. Harvesting takes place in October, when the leaves are removed without cutting anything from the crown, and fed to livestock. The roots are placed in a frost-free place, where they can be stored until June. In March or April, plant healthy, well-formed beet seedlings 0.90 m apart. As soon as the seeds are ripe, cut off the branches with the ripest seeds and dry them in the sun or under a shed. Seeds keep for two to three years. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Beetroot (Beta vulgaris, Linn.) is a biennial, native to southern Europe. It has been known in Belgium since 1600. In France, beet cultivation now covers 55,000 hectares or so. Beet cultivation has expanded considerably in Belgium since sugar refiners learned how to cultivate it better and extract more product from it. Four varieties of beet are grown in gardens for food use: the common large red, the Castelnaudary small red, the common yellow and the Castelnaudary yellow. The petite rouge is the best for culinary use, being more delicate than the others. When grown for livestock, as is often the case in farmers' gardens, it is better to use the variety known as disette or pink beet, or the white beet from Silesia, which is the sugar beet. The former is the largest and produces a lot; sugar beet is the most nourishing. The plant is too well known to be described in detail here. CARROTS. GROWING. Carrots thrive in clean, soft, sandy soil. The soil must be deeply ploughed. New fertilizer is harmful to this root; fertilizer applied the previous year, or at the latest the previous autumn, is preferable to recent fertilizer. In the case of recent manure, the roots are often forked, affected by rust spots, and their flavor is less sweet. The first sowings begin in February, and continue over the following months until June. For the first sowings, the species known as toupie de Hollande should be preferred, as it is earlier and has a good 16 taste as long as it is yellow. It is also suitable for seedlings sown in September, which produce in spring and early summer. Earlier in the summer, towards autumn and winter, the pale yellow or white Flanders variety should be preferred; it is mild and sweet, whereas the Dutch toupie, which is always very good in spring, becomes pungent and therefore unappetizing. Seedlings are quite dense; it's easy to thin and place young carrots at a suitable distance, starting with Om.06 for market garden varieties. Continue thinning as needed, so that by the end they are spaced Om, 15 or Om 20 apart. In sandy soils, after sowing, lightly harrow with a rake and press the soil with the back of the spade. In heavy soils, after sowing, and without using the rake, cover the seeds with a light layer of potting soil of about Om, 01. This cover has the double advantage of providing nourishment for the young seedling and preventing the formation of crusts on the soil, always so pernicious to the success of crops. Seedlings need to be weeded first, then thinned and watered if necessary. When growing this plant in rows, hoe often. This operation considerably benefits the roots. Sowing in rows is rarely done except on large farms, and the crop has flourished since this change. Carrots are very prone to shrivelling. This is the name given to a disease that affects them as soon as they emerge from the ground: they turn yellow and dis13. appear, without any definite cause. We are inclined to believe that it is the cold that affects them in this way in their early youth, producing a kind of stasis in the circulatory vessels. What is even more detrimental is a species of spider that attacks and devours them when they are very young. To get rid of this enemy, we recommend drenching the plants with an infusion of soot. Carrot seeds are only really good for two years; they still germinate after three or four years, but many are missing. To obtain good seed, we advise the grower to provide for it himself, to take care to choose the most beautiful roots as seed-bearers, to entrust them to the open ground as early as February, and to harvest the strongest umbels, whose seeds are ripe in August-September. Carrots harvested in November or December can be stored in a cellar, vegetable greenhouse or other frost-free location. After cutting off the leaves near the collar, the roots are pulled in and bedded in sand. They should be given air when the temperature permits. Although carrots are quite resistant to frosts, even slightly severe ones, those that are to be kept in the ground should be covered with litter or, better still, dry leaves. Under this last cover, seedlings can be overwintered and planted before winter at the desired distance (Om, 90). In this case, the seedlings are stronger and healthier than those kept in the cellar. If carrots were to be sown in large numbers, they would require a lot of covers and a lot of labor; it would therefore be easier and more economical to overwinter them in close rows, taking care to remove the cover whenever the temperature is mild. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS Carrots (Daucus carota, Linn.), members of the Umbelliferae family, are indigenous to Europe. It is derived from the wild carrot, which grows abundantly in fields and meadows. The varieties produced by cultivation today are quite numerous; we will mention only the most cultivated: the early Dutch spinach; short, reddish-yellow root, obtuse cone shape; it is the best for early spring sowing, as well as for being forced. Also known as rouge courte. - Red long, a variety of the previous one, with the same taste and color; more productive, but perhaps a little less early. - Spanish violet, very sweet; sown early in spring, it rises quickly; it does not keep well in winter. - The very pale yellow carrots, known as blanches in some places and which are none other than the yellow Flanders carrot or varieties thereof, are also very good, productive and sweet; they keep very late. For field cultivation, the following varieties are preferred: - Alteringham carrot, sweet, very large; - Brunswick carrot, long, red; - Breteuil white carrot, green-necked carrot and Vosges carrot. They are used as livestock feed. We have already mentioned the advantages of growing this root vegetable in rows. However, in gardens, the space between rows should not be Om,55 to Om,60, as for carrots in large-scale cultivation, but only Om,15 to Om,20. This distance would allow ploughing with great ease, using the small hoe or the serfouette. In all cases, the width of the beds should be such that the middle can be easily reached for weeding, hoeing, etc. To thin carrots, we never wait until they are edible; we start this operation as soon as they have four leaves, in addition to the cotyledons or seminal leaves. CHERVIS. Chervis, also known as cherul, chirouis, giroles, berle chervis, is Sium sisarum, Linn. of the Umbelliferae family. Chervis seed is sown in March, in rays or broadcast, in good, loose, deeply spaded soil. This plant likes damp rather than dry, sandy rather than clayey soil, because in heavy soil that has not been loosened with compost, as well as in dry or stony soil, the roots remain small, forked and woody. Frequent watering is highly profitable for this plant, which must also be weeded, hoeed and thinned. The roots, which are fleshy and sweet, are used in the same way as scorzonera and are preserved in winter in exactly the same way. They are white, covered with a russet film, from Om,18 to 0m,25 long, and from Om,020 to Om,025 in diameter. In the same year as sowing, the plant produces a stem that rises from Om, 60 to Om 90; but care must be taken to cut it off before it reaches this height, and therefore before flowering time, as the great development of the stem would prevent the root from acquiring a suitable volume. Chervis is a perennial plant and appears to have originated in China; it was introduced into Europe very long ago, and Pliny reports that the Emperor Tiberius was so fond of the plant that he demanded it as an annual tribute from the Germans. The seeds keep for three years. - Intelligent horticulturists recommend sowing chervis seeds as soon as they reach maturity. In this case, they should be planted out in September and the young plants transplanted in spring. NAVETS. The soil has such a strong influence on the quality of turnips that it is often enough to change the variety. Turnips grow best in light, sandy soils. Rarely is this plant grown in gardens. Markets are supplied with roots from the surrounding countryside. So it would be very difficult to obtain even passable turnips in walled or tree-planted gardens. As a market-garden plant, we would hardly need to mention the turnip if we didn't intend to make known the usefulness of using the ribs of its leaves in the domestic economy. Turnip seeds are sown fairly thickly, in spring or autumn. In autumn, peas, Savoy cabbage, potatoes, etc. can be sown afterwards. The young plants on these previously smoked soils develop rapidly; they can't spread out wide, being too close together; they spin and give almost dreite leaves. When these leaves are Om,30 to 0m,45 long, they can be used to great advantage as a vegetable. To this end, the plants are pulled up by the bootful, the undeveloped roots are cut off and fed to livestock, then the leafy parts are removed by sliding them between the fingers, and the ribs are cut together into pieces of Om,005 to Om,010. They are then prepared in the same way as green cabbage, with or without potatoes. This process of using turnip leaf petioles is not new to some parts of our country, while in others it is not practiced at all, and is even completely unknown. These same ribs, arranged as we have just said, can be candied like sauerkraut, and come in very handy as winter provisions for farms and large establishments. For the latter use, sow in August and September. The varieties that provide the best roots for cooking are: Freneuse turnip, saulieu, petit berlin; their roots are rounded; the plants are known as dry turnips. In strong soils, they completely lose their good qualities. We'd also like to mention the Schaerbeek turnip, the Tilsond turnip and the red May turnip, an early variety; these are sown from the first fine days of spring to harvest the roots in May: they are yellowish inside, of medium size and without pungency. Yellow turnips, which are beginning to spread in Belgium, are very useful. Other varieties with large roots, such as gros long d'Alsace, blanc plat, blanc long, etc., are absolutely part of mainstream cultivation and cannot be dealt with here. Turnip seedlings should be sown, if possible, in overcast or rainy weather. If the weather is dry, it should be watered; in this case, the seeds germinate more quickly and are less in danger of being eaten by flea beetles, the same insect that so disastrously attacks cabbage seedlings. To reduce its ravages, sprinkle the young plants every morning with wood ash and soot, until it is destroyed or disappears. Turnip (brassica napus, Linn.) is a biennial plant of the cruciferous family. Turnips should not be left in flower next to cabbages intended for seed harvesting. The turnip, belonging to the cabbage genus, fertilizes the cabbage and is fertilized in turn, producing hybridization. OLLUCO. Olluco (ullucus tuberosus, Caldas) is a tuberous, almost creeping plant. Its flat-lying stems take root at every point where they touch the ground; this would provide an excellent means of propagation, were it not for the fact that the tubers make multiplication extremely easy. The leaves are large, thick and fleshy. Flowers are small, greenish-yellow and appear in spikes in the axils of the leaves. Tubers are yellow and resemble the potato known as goat's horn. The plant is widely cultivated in Upper Peru, where it is known as oca quina. The name oca is also given to two species of oxalis, notably oxalis tuberosa. In Peru, the plant is grown in the same way as potatoes, i.e. in furrows, into which the tuber is thrown with fertilizer. It is planted from July 25 to August 10 and harvested at the end of April. Indians use tubers too small for consumption as seed. Recently imported to Europe from Quito, olluco is still only available to a handful of enthusiasts. The first plants were received in Paris in January 1848. They were distributed by the Minister of Agriculture to the main horticulturists. Messrs Vilmorin and Masson tried their hand at growing it, with success that was not very reassuring for the former, but quite satisfactory for the latter. In Brussels, M. de Jonghe cultivated olluco in the same year. Open, loose, fat soil is ideal for olluco. At the beginning of May, it should be planted in rays spaced Om, 50 apart, with the plants at the same distance apart in the rays. The exposure should not be too hot; the plant does not do well in the highest summer temperatures. Remember that the climate of the region from which it comes is not excessively hot. From August to April, the nights are very cold in high Peru, tempering the heat of the day. In the central plains, where spring reigns eternally, the plant is sheltered from the cold that renders sterile the high mountains of the Nevadas, whose elevation exceeds 7,000 4 and at whose foot it is mostly cultivated. It seems to grow best there during the rainy season, when the temperature is more even. For our part, we advise all agronomists to take up the cultivation of this plant; it could one day be of great service, if it can be acclimatized in our country. CRENELLATED OXALIS. Crenellated oxalis (oxalis crenata) is a bulbous plant of the geraniaceae family; first cultivated in Germany, then in England, it moved on to Belgium and France, where it was introduced in 1829. It originates from Peru. It has been alternately promoted and abandoned, so that its value as a market garden or field crop is still at least doubtful for Belgium's climate. This plant likes sandy, substantial soil; it is propagated from its bulbs, which multiply excessively; 500 to 600 and more have been counted, produced from a single tuber planted in spring. These bulbs are yellowish and have eyes. They are planted in spring, as soon as frosts are no longer a threat, at a distance of 1.30 m in all directions and at a depth of Om.05. Some growers prefer to plant in furrows, the sides of which can be used to butter the plants at different times. Ridging begins when the stems have reached Om, 10 in height. Then they are spread out on the ground, laying them down from inside to outside, and covered, leaving only the tips sticking out. The bulbs form in September and October; they are harvested 2. 14 the size of a pigeon's egg; most are smaller, rarely larger. They are stored in sand, in the cellar, vegetable greenhouse or orangery. The plant's leaves and stems, which regrow with great activity, can be cut several times during the course of their vegetation and used as cattle feed; however, they should not be given to dairy cows: the oxalic acid they contain, either free or combined with alkalis, could reduce milk production in these animals. We also believe that not cutting the leaves and stems is better for development. As we can see, the bulbs of crenellated oxalis form a little slowly; if we succeeded in obtaining an earlier variety from seed, with larger roots, then such a plant would be of immense service to agriculture and horticulture. - This root vegetable has a taste similar to that of the potato; its particular flavour is different, but pleasant (1). Deppe's oxalis. - We won't mention Deppe's oxalis (oxalis Deppei), a bulbous plant like the previous one; it is less productive, in that its bulbs don't multiply so copiously. (1) The inhabitants of Chile and Peru refer to potatoes as papas, the oxalis we're talking about as papitas, and various tuberous plants as papaliza. Parsnips are sown from November and December through to March, in rich, well-deep soil with absolutely no recent fertilization. Germinated seeds or seedlings can withstand the coldest weather and never perish. The first sowings are therefore the most lucrative for the commercial gardener and the most enjoyable for the amateur. The seeds should be spread thickly over the bed or beds, to thin out the plants later on. Don't wait until the young parsnips can be used; thin out as soon as the plant has four or six leaves. It's quite difficult to cover seeds with a rake; some return to the surface of the soil, while others bury themselves too deeply. To obviate this inconvenience, we cover them with soil taken from the paths of the beds; we also scatter it with a spade or by hand. For thinning, plants should be spaced Om, 10 to Om, 15 apart, and hoeed and weeded in good time. Like carrots, parsnips are salubrious and easy to digest; they are widely grown in Belgium, Holland and England, but not in France, where they are only cultivated on the northern borders and in Brittany. The plant belongs to the Umbelliferae family, and appears to derive from the wild parsnip. Because of its hardiness, mentioned above, this root vegetable needs no shelter in winter. Its seeds do not keep long; after a year they no longer sprout; they are harvested like carrots. DANDELION. See Dent-de-lion. POTATOES. The cultivation of the potato as a vegetable is very important; it is thanks to it that we see the first tubers of the early varieties appearing on our markets; it is also thanks to it that the disease, which attacked late potatoes for several years, was mitigated. Only early varieties should be planted in gardens. The time of planting is not exactly specified, but you can start in February and continue until June. Potatoes grow in all types of soil, but loose, sandy, loose and healthy soil is better suited to them than strong, clayey, compact soil. The quality of the soil has such an influence on the quality of the tubers that a very good variety of potato becomes unrecognizable in damp, peaty or purely clay soil. This has led some people to think that the potato degenerates, but this is not the case: it becomes good again in suitable soils. We know that our country's best potatoes grow in the sandy soils of the Kempen. True, the yield is not as high; the tubers are not as voluminous 20 as in greasy, clayey soils, but their taste is infinitely better; they are drier, more floury; they contain, all other things being equal, more starch and are therefore more salubrious. The same result would be obtained in dry, sandy gardens: anyone with such a garden can therefore count on good quality produce. It should also be noted that, in order to obtain potatoes with a good flavor, the soil must not be recently smoked, unless it is with potting soil; it must have been fertilized before winter, and even this type of soil can be grown very well in good garden soil after another harvest, such as that of cabbages, onions, etc., for which good fertilization has been given. We repeat: if you lose a little in terms of quantity, you gain in terms of quality. We mention these facts, which are also positive, to explain the nature of this plant. We are well aware that the merchant horticulturist, who sometimes rents his land at a high price, and the agronomist farmer, need to extract the greatest amount of product from the soil, and cannot follow our advice in this respect; but people who are not in these conditions will always find it easy to comply with the precepts we have just set out, concerning the garden cultivation of this plant. The varieties we recommend for cultivation are as follows: long red or goat's horn; this was grown exclusively in the lower part of the province of Limbourg; it has declined considerably over the last few years, having either been affected by disease like its congeners, or given over to con14. sumption without any sparing even for planting. This variety deserves to be widely propagated in every respect; it is productive and excellent. Early yellow lonque or yellow goat's horn; productive, very good. This is the earliest known variety: as soon as its tubers are the size of a good oak acorn, they are already edible, which is not the case with any other variety; the tubers are long, the skin smooth and the eyes not very pronounced, which is another good quality. The asparagus potato is long and early; it has the particularity of growing part of its tubers on the surface of the soil; it necessarily requires ridging, otherwise the tubers, which are in contact with light, turn green and become pungent. It is an excellent variety. - The Circassian, early, round, flattened, very productive and mealy: it belongs to the blue potato breed; its eyes are tinted bluish purple. - The Saint-Jean de Malines, earlier than the Circassian, is an excellent variety, especially for forced cultivation. - The nine-week-old variety, early, round and blue-eyed, is productive. - The August truffle, pale red, round, a little later than the preceding varieties, is mealy and very good. -The shaw, yellow, round, earlier than the August truffle. - The early dwarf, yellow, round, very early. We also recommend the flat yellow, known as langue de bœuf, which is long, flattened, light and mealy; it is widely grown around Liège, Tongres and Maestricht. It has a sub-variety of the same shape and characteristics, only pink in color. - Finally, the vitelotte de Paris is a very good variety. These are not the only early potato varieties grown in various parts of the country. In any case, we advise the horticulturist to limit his choice to three or four good varieties; a greater number leads to confusion, without any advantage. The same number is sufficient for the farmer. But what should never be lost sight of is the need to continue sowing the seeds of good varieties, to improve them still further. In these laudable trials, we must not neglect to grow young potatoes in sandy soil, in order to have definite data on their value or non-value. For we must not forget that this solana is a plant of the high mountains of South America; therefore, although this plant does not refuse to grow in our fields or valleys, it is no less true that it prefers a soil that more or less resembles its native soil, i.e., a soft, sandy, light, substantial and healthy soil. In gardens, plants are usually planted with a spade or hoe, in deeply loosened soil, loosened by ploughing and amended with fresh manure ploughed in immediately before or during planting. The spacing to be given to them varies slightly according to the varieties with stronger or weaker and higher stems: the smallest are given Om, 30 in the rows and 0m, 45 in the rows between them; the largest, from Om, 45 in all directions to Om, 50 and Om, 60. In our Flanders region, in the provinces of Antwerp and Brabant, we commonly plant at lesser distances than the one we have just indicated. It's a very bad routine and a very bad economy. If it's true that a plant can be too far away, it can also be too close: both extremes should be avoided. The Malinese method. - There's a highly recommended method for growing potatoes: it consists in planting the tubers with their sprouts. But this excellent practice requires special precautions. First of all, the shoots must be medium-sized or have Om,04 to Om,07; too long and planting is difficult; etiolated, they rot in part and the potatoes come out irregularly, which would hinder the much-needed work of hoeing and ridging. Here's how we've practised it ourselves, with the greatest success: at the beginning of February, in a frost-free spot, we spread a layer of oat bales or old tan bales, to the thickness of Om,04 or Om,08. On this layer we place the tubers close together, top up. (We call the top the part where the eyes that will form the stems or shoots are joined together.) They project their roots into these bales of oats or tannin, and, when they are removed for planting, carry away between their fibers what served as a layer, so that the roots are preserved intact and the plants continue their vegetation very-actively; we know that the jets form at the same time as the roots. We need hardly remind you that these potatoes must be handled with care before and during planting; they must be gently removed one by one from their roots and placed in baskets. By following this procedure, you can bring forward by at least a fortnight, and that's a long time, all the vegetative phases of the same variety of potato, planted at the same time, in the same soil, but which has not been treated according to this method. The Berlin method differs from the Malines method in that Berlin market gardeners plant shoots without tubers. As for winter cultivation, which consists of burying the tubers more or less deeply and protecting them against frost with layers of litter, we are not strong supporters. While there have been some somewhat satisfactory successes in England, we don't think we have much to commend about the trials tried in Belgium. The greatest difficulty lies in the fact that the potato doesn't germinate until spring, so it has to be forced to do so before its natural season, and this is how it's done. Instead of bringing the tubers in, they are left to green up and dry for a few weeks in the sun in the field, then placed in the attic. At the end of October, they're planted on a south-facing hillside, and soon start to grow: then, during the winter, they're covered with cloches on which litter or leaves are placed, depending on frost. In January or February, the plants can produce quite beautiful tubers. For planting, large or medium-sized tubers are best, and should be preferred to small ones, peels and chopped roots. Everyone will have noticed that large tubers produce large stems; well, it's these large stems that in turn produce the largest tubers. We cover them with Om,08 to Om, 10 of soil, and, for early plantings in February, with Om, 15. As soon as the first leaves appear, we give a first crimping, and, when the stems are Om, 15 to Om, 20 high, we hoe them a first time; a few days later, a second time. Weed and hoe again. The potato soil must be loosened and stirred up; this is one of the principles on which the cultivation of this plant is based. Potatoes are stored in cellars. Tubers of early varieties are of little use in winter; they are only kept for planting purposes: late varieties are much preferable for winter consumption. In spring, as soon as you notice that the sprouts are developing, pull them out. This operation should be repeated every fifteen or twenty days. When frosts are no longer to be feared, they are best stored in an attic or other dry place. DETAILS AND DISTINCTIVE CHARACTERISTICS The potato (solanum tuberosum, Linn.) belongs to the solanaceae family. The plant is too widely known for us to give any description. We have already mentioned that it originates from South America. It was introduced into Belgium in 1588. Charles de l'Escluse, a Belgian botanist, was the first person in our country to describe and spread it. From Belgium it passed to England, but in those days it traveled more as an ornamental plant than as an edible one. It took a long time to make this precious plant popular. It was only at the beginning of the 17th century that it began to be cultivated more widely, in Germany, France and Belgium. Today, we see potato cultivation occupying a very large proportion of our country's arable land. Radishes, of which we now have a large number of varieties, are sown from February to July. Properly cultivated, they can be eaten in twenty-five days. The first seedlings are sown in the south, under cover. Cover them during the cold nights of February and March with straw mats or other covers. They need rich soil, covered with Om, 05 to Om, 06 of compost. The well-trodden and loosened soil is gently harrowed with a rake. The seed is only lightly covered, and the soil is compacted with the back of the spade. Radishes are usually grown among lettuces. The main varieties are: round pink, early; white, early; salmon, violet, small gray, black, yellow, summer gray, peppery, firm and full-fleshed; China pink or winter, cylindroid or conical, peppery and tender. On top of these good qualities, it has the merit of being autumnal: sown in September, it is ready for harvest in October or November; sown in October or November and kept in a greenhouse, it continues to grow and can be served in winter. We owe its introduction to a French missionary, Abbé Voisin, to whom we are also indebted for another excellent radish, the Chinese violet, which only grows well in autumn. Manure and watering must be spared if you want radishes that grow quickly and are therefore tender. Summer seedlings should be planted out of the sun for three-quarters of the day, so that they are exposed to the sun's rays until nine or ten o'clock in the morning. Exposed to heat all day long, they become hard, split and are no longer edible. The cultivated radish (raphanus sativus, Linn.) is an annual plant in the cruciferous family. It originated in China and was imported to Europe in the late Middle Ages. Radishes are shaped like little round turnips. RAVE. These radishes differ from those described above only in the shape of the root. It has the same shades of color, white, pink, gray, etc., only longer. This radish is less esteemed than the small radish or the one with small rounded roots. CULTIVATED HORSERADISH. Horseradish differs from radish in that it is never sown before June; earlier sowing risks it going to seed, in which case its root is of no value. Horseradish prefers clay rather than sandy soil, so if the soil is light, the plant should be trampled or firmed before sowing. Horseradish is rarely planted in specific beds; it is usually sown in paths between beds of onions, carrots, etc., and at the edges of flowerbeds. Horseradish roots are larger than radish roots, firmer in consistency, always black or gray on the outside, and shaped like round or elongated turnips. Horseradish keeps well in sand and under cover 23 from frost, all winter long. According to botanists, it is simply a variety of the small radish, and is therefore called raphanus sativus by Linnaeus. But, for the gardener and as a vegetable plant, it differs in many respects, as we have just seen, from WILD RAIFORT. This plant should not be confused with the one above. It is perennial, whereas cultivated horseradish is annual. Wild horseradish, also a member of the cruciferous family, belongs to a completely different genus: it's Linnaeus' cochlearia armoracia. Its real French name is cranson. It is also known by the following trivial names: cranson rustique, cran de Bretagne, meeredik, mérédic, capuchin mustard, German mustard, English cram. The plant thrives in damp places and on the banks of streams. Its radical leaves are very large, straight, petiolate, oval-oblong; the flowers are small, white; the stems are 1.00 m high. The plant's roots, which are yellow on the outside and white on the inside, are large and long. They are grated, and vinegar and salt are added to season meats and stimulate the appetite. This root is not unhealthy; it is an exciter and antiscorbutic. This plant is rarely found in the wild in Belgium, and all too rarely in gardens. However, it's easy to give it a little corner where nothing else will grow: the plant is content with this and will live for half a century without the slightest care. When you want to use it up, detach one or more roots, re2 18 close the soil, and the plant continues to vegetate as before. RAIPONCE. Rapunzel (campanula rapunculus, Linn.), of the campanulaceae family, biennial and indigenous plant. Found in meadows, hedgerows and woodland edges. It is used as a vegetable for its soft, sweet roots, which are rabe-shaped and the size of a finger peel. It is used in salads: the roots are cut into pieces and mixed with other salads, such as lamb's lettuce. It is grown in the garden, where the root becomes larger and more delicate, to provide a winter or spring salad. Riponce is sown in July; sown earlier, it will sometimes set seed in autumn, and will always perish afterwards. The seeds of this campanella are very fine; they should not be covered with soil at all. Just give them a moistening to attach them to the soil after sowing. The roots and small emerging leaves are used mainly in spring. SALSIFY AND SCORZONERA. These two plants require absolutely the same cultivation. The best soil for them is open, slightly damp, loose and, above all, deeply tilled and smoked the previous year. You can hardly expect to get a good yield from these root vegetables in strong, compact, clayey soil, unless you amend it with a lot of manure and loosen it by repeated ploughing. The taproots, unable to go far enough into the soil, seek other directions, becoming forked and misshapen. Sow salsify and scorzonera seeds from mid-March to September, in rows spaced 0.15 m apart. If it is dry, germination should be stimulated by evening and morning watering. You need to sow thickly; a quarter or a fifth of the seed is almost always sterile; then, the birds are very greedy, and even if it is well covered, they still destroy it when it has already sprouted. This is because the cotyledons or seminal leaves remain enclosed in the episperm (seed coat) for some time. To prevent this, black woollen or linen threads should be crossed over the boards in different directions. Experience shows that birds are more afraid of the black than the white color of this scarecrow. The seeds of these two plants are very difficult to cover, so it's best here, as we've advised elsewhere, to cover them with soil taken from the paths of the boards, and to spread this soil over the seeds, dispersing it evenly with a spade or by hand, until no more seeds are visible. Once in vegetation, salsify and scorzonera require no more care than a few weedings and hoeings during the summer. Salsify, also known as sersify, is harvested in the first winter after sowing. The roots are white, longer than those of scorsonera; the flowers are a beautiful violet; the leaves, narrower, smoother and tender, are used as a salad throughout the summer. This is Linnaeus' tragopogon porrifolium. It grows spontaneously in the southern provinces of France. The root of this plant is very dirty, as is that of scorsonera. The latter is black, with yellow flowers and downy, broader leaves. It is native to Spain and southern France. It is Linnaeus' scorsonera hispanica. Its roots can be harvested in the first or second year; to harvest in the first year, sow in March; if left to grow until the second winter, it can be sown from March to August. Its seed is only good for one year; it must be harvested every morning as soon as the dew has disappeared; it falls daily. Salsify and scorzonera do not freeze; they can be left in the ground uncovered, with the precaution only of removing part of them before heavy frosts, for winter consumption. Roots are fully developed by the second year. Plants go to seed in the first and second years of vegetation; the stems are cut off, which, instead of hindering growth, gives the roots more volume. SCOLYMA. Spanish bark beetle thrives in deep, cool soil, such as that recommended for salsify and scorzonera. It is sown in May and June, in rows or broadcast; sown earlier, it sets seed and its root is no longer edible. When the young plant has four leaves, it should be thinned out and spaced about 0*, 20 apart in all directions. Plants should not be allowed to grow to full size; as soon as the root has the volume of a scorsonera, it should be given up for consumption; as it is still young, it is tender. The plant needs to be covered in winter. The scolymus root must be stripped of its woody center; the part surrounding this tough pivot is the only edible part; it shares the taste of scorsonera without surpassing it; we therefore doubt that the plant will ever be very successful in Belgium. The scolymus (scolymus hispanicus, Linn.) inhabits southern France and Spain, and is a member of the Compositae family. It has a thistle-like habit, with very prickly leaves and yellow flowers. It is also known as cardouille, yellow thorn or cardoussés. SOUCHET. A perennial plant whose habit resembles that of grasses. Souchet, also known as ground almond, edible souchet, cyperus esculentus, Linn. of the Cyperaceae family, grows spontaneously in damp meadows in several provinces of France. In the market garden, it is cultivated for the use of its floury, tender tubers, which are found at the ends of its root composed of fine fibers. These tubers are about the size of a hazelnut and are eaten cooked or roasted. In early April, they are planted to a depth of one inch, in pockets of 4 or 5 tubers, at a distance of 0.40 m. During the summer, the plant requires only weeding, hoeing and watering. Tubers are 15. removed in October and stored in sand to protect them from frost. They are very pleasant to the taste. The Spaniards and Italians express the juice and, with the addition of water and sugar, make a very pleasant kind of orgeat. TARNOTES. Native to Belgium and France, this perennial plant has long been known: our ancestors called it aerdnooten, and the names marcusson, anette, marron de terre, souris à queue, gland de terre are all synonyms; it is the tuberous chaste, Lathyrus tuberosus de Linn. of the legume family. It grows on weak, angular stems, Om,3 or Om,4 high; its pink flowers are borne five or six together on long axillary peduncles. The tarnote belongs among the edible plants as a tuber; in fact, its long, blackish-grey roots, white on the inside, attached to deep, creeping nets, and not unlike those of some of our peonies, can provide an undoubtedly pleasant dish; they have a mild flavour, very similar to that of our chestnuts. But let us say in passing, so as not to mislead, that while we recommend introducing a few plants of this species into the garden, we are far from recommending it to any great extent.
