Note that if de l'Escluse says that chamabalanos (tarnotes) were once eaten like turnips and parsnips, then we were not yet in possession of our excellent and productive potatoes, 18 As for cultivation, the plant requires no special care. When the stalks begin to grow, they are reamed like peas; to harvest tubers, the soil is dug up around the plant, without removing it. TOPINAMBOUR. The plant requires neither special cultivation nor meticulous care. It is for this very reason that this root vegetable should attract the grower's full attention, mainly from an agricultural point of view. So far, the Jerusalem artichoke has not been very successful in the vegetable garden, for two reasons: firstly, it is very difficult to get rid of once the plant has taken root in the garden. The smallest tubers are enough to keep the plant multiplying, and all the more so as they can withstand the most rigorous cold; the second reason is that, in good soil, you can grow a more valuable plant, such as the potato. As a result, we are not very inclined to recommend this plant for small-scale market gardening. However, we would like to express our opinion on the cultivation of Jerusalem artichokes to make use of lost or uncultivated land, such as we see a lot of in the Campine: we recommend trying it out in sandy soils that are currently uncultivated or almost sterile. There, even if the plant yields only half a crop, it will still be very profitable for the grower. The tubers, stems and leaves are eaten avidly by livestock. The broad leaves and 3 stems, which reach up to 2*,00 in height, provide copious fodder, which is precisely what is lacking in the Kempen and so powerfully counteracts land clearance. Jerusalem artichoke (helianthus tuberosus, Linn.), also known as Canada artichoke, Jerusalem artichoke, earth pear, is a member of the Compositae family, originally from Brazil. Its roots are planted and used like potatoes; they are starchy, sweet and come in a wide variety of shapes. They contribute to the artichoke's taste. Digized "( NATURAL CROPS. VEGETABLE PLANTS WITH EDIBLE FRUIT. PUMPKIN. Pumpkins and all cucurbits, or plants of the same family, are native to warm countries; all are fast-growing and beautiful, but very sensitive to cold. They like warmth, humidity and the most earthy soil possible. These plants, by virtue of a property inherent in their constitution, are not afraid of fermenting manure; on the contrary, they grow and develop there with luxuriant strength, an indication of their well-being and the abundant nourishment they find there. Some horticulturists, taking advantage of this circumstance, grow pumpkins on a pile of manure that must not be used during the year or while the pumpkins are growing; they become monstrous there. In May, pits 1m,00 wide and 0m,50 deep are made in the ground, filled with tightly packed manure and covered with Om, 08 to Om, 10 of potting soil; then three pumpkin seeds are placed in them, covered with Om, 02 of this potting soil, and only the strongest stalk is left. The pumpkin is not pruned, but the superfluous lateral shoots on the main stem are removed. As soon as this stem has reached a length of 2m,00 to 3m,00, a dimple 0m,08 or Om, 09 deep is dug; the stem is attached by means of a hook to a joint or knot which is covered with compost. Layering should be repeated in the same way, three times, 1m,00 or 2m,00 apart: the plant takes root at the joints and draws a stronger dose of nourishing juices from the soil. As soon as a fruit is knotted, the upper part of each stem is removed at Om, 40 or Om, 50 above each fruit, leaving at least two leaves. When you want to produce pumpkins of immense size, sometimes weighing 100 kilograms, you leave only one stem and one fruit; you remove everything else, except the leaves. In ordinary cultivation, each plant bears two stems and two fruits. If you have tarpaulins or greenhouses, it's best to first force the young pumpkin plant onto a warm bed. To do this, sow the seeds as early as March in small pots filled with potting soil; bury the pots right up to the edges. Air is added whenever the temperature permits, to get the plants used to it. By treating them in this way, you gain a lot in terms of vegetation. Plant them as described above, leaving the entire root ball. In the early days of planting, they are protected from strong sunlight; towards evening, they are uncovered, unless a cold night or strong wind can be foreseen: in this case, the plants are kept in their shelters. Similarly, when they are young, they should not be left covered if the weather is mild and rainy. Pumpkins require frequent and copious watering, which is partly responsible for their vigorous growth and the size of their fruit, which ripen in September. They are not cut when perfectly ripe, but a little earlier; if this precaution is taken, they keep better in winter. Their seeds retain their productive capacity for five or six years. These plants and a few species of this type are not sufficiently cultivated in our country; their usefulness in the domestic economy is not well known. In France, they are frequently used in soups and for frying. If they were not used as human food, they should at least be cultivated for livestock. The pig breed is not only very avid, but also feeds very well on them. The pumpkin, more properly known as squash (cucurbita pepo, Linn.), is the type of the Cucurbitaceae family. This plant and many other species of this genus are found in the East Indies and seem to have come to us from there. The following are also cultivated as food plants: Siam ball gourd; flattened fruit, less voluminous than the previous species; firmer flesh, longer shelf life. Messinèze squash, with plain whitish skin and red flesh. Nutmeg squash, pear-shaped, reddish skin with blood-colored pulp. Brazilian sugar squash, sweet, juicy flesh. These squashes still have numerous sub-varieties, many of which are grown as ornamental plants or as curiosities. Giraumont. - This breed is distinguished by the oblong shape of its fruit. It has a large number of sub-varieties in terms of green, yellow or white color, and fruit size. The largest, with the smoothest skin, are the best. Their fine, delicate flesh, less watery than that of cucumbers, is suitable for the same uses; it does not have the strong and sometimes unpleasant taste. They keep well into winter. Pastisson, commonly known as bonnet d'électeur, bonnet de prêtre, etc., offers great diversity in shape, size and fruit color, which varies from pale to dark yellow, often mottled or striped with green. The stalks, which hang from stakes, are 1.00 to 1.50 m long. The flesh is firm and brittle; sliced and fried, it imitates the taste of artichokes. Watermelon (cucurbita anguria, Duch.). This species, also known as laciniated squash, is distinguished from the others by its deeply cut leaves, its smooth, orbicular fruit speckled with star-shaped spots, its often reddish flesh, and its black or red, not whitish, seeds. There are several varieties. The name watermelon is reserved for those whose firm fruit is only eaten candied or fried. The name watermelon is given more particularly to varieties with melting, watery flesh. In common usage, the name pumpkin is not given to this species. They have trailing stems like those of pumpkins, and are grown in the same way as pumpkins. Marrow or vegetable marrow. - We're inclined to call this cucurbit squash cauliflower, because the fruit, while green, imitates the taste of cauliflower to a fault. In 1849, we cultivated the vegetable marrow, and we tet hace - V we are assured of the fact that we are making progress. It can be grown like pumpkins. We give it a warm southern exposure on a bed, close to a wall or hedge. Do not entrust seeds or young plants to the open ground before May 15, unless they are sheltered from cold nights in the garden. 2. 16 200gl0 cloches. In this case, they can be planted as early as mid-April, which is preferable; even better is to advance the seedlings on a warm bed and under a frame; they can then be placed on potting soil, as described for pumpkins, and covered with cloches during cold nights. They can be harvested for most of the summer; six to twelve plants are more than enough for a household. The squash is not pruned, but left to grow freely. The fruit is used before it turns yellow. We would like to draw the grower's attention to the cultivation of marrow squash; it can be seasoned in a variety of ways and makes an excellent dish. Treated in large-scale cultivation, marrow squash is a considerable source of high-quality livestock feed. Its fruit can be kept until February, and even longer. Simply store them in a dry, frost-free place, like pumpkins. CUCUMBERS AND GHERKINS. Cucumbers should be sown from May 15 onwards; sowing earlier risks losing them: the slightest white frost will destroy them. If the land to be planted is not very rich, pits of Om, 25 cubes are made, 0.60 m apart. These are filled with manure or compost, and three seeds are planted in each; when the plant is secure, only one plant is left in each pit. The rest of the cultivation consists of weeding, and removing a few branches that intertwine and cause confusion. In September, we start to cut the small fruits, called gherkins, which are preserved in vinegar for seasoning. Several varieties are known: the snake cucumber (cucumis flexuosus), which is grown for the uniqueness of its long, flexuous fruit. Only a few centimetres long, it is also candied in vinegar. - The hátif white cucumber, elongated and round at both ends. - Bonneuil white, larger than the previous one. - Black, with brown rind and yellow stripes. - Bouquet or mignon de Russic, almost round, very hasty. - Hâtif de Hollande, turning yellow as it ripens. - The green gherkin; this is the most important because of the benefits it provides, although the small, green fruit of all varieties can also be candied. The following varieties are new; seeds are available from leading growers: Conqueror; - Walken's Long; - Manchester Prize; - Hero of Surrey; - Victory of Bath; - Man of Kent. The cucumber (cucumis sativus, Linn.) originates from the Orient. STRAWBERRY. This excellent fruit, the improvement of which has made immense progress in recent years, has not yet said its last word. The ease with which new varieties can be obtained from seed should encourage the horticulturist to constantly sow the best known fruits, and thus tend to produce better and better. The strawberry plant thrives in good, loose, earthy soil, sandy rather than clayey, and not in the shade, although the type, or primary species, is native to the woods. It needs to be ploughed, tilled and hoeed, and watered if it is to thrive. And, singularly, not only does it tolerate being watered in bright sunshine, but it must even be watered during the hottest periods, when the sun is shining on the plants. Observation and experience have shown that it prefers watering to rain, so careful growers always give it a generous sprinkling before thunderstorms; only then, when the plant has received a good soaking from the watering can, is rain very beneficial. The soil should be prepared by ploughing to a depth of at least Om 40. It is fertilized with half-consumed cow manure, or compost made from liquid manure, lime and consumed grass. This compost should have been in a heap for at least a year, and stirred from time to time. Strawberry plants are planted in beds, beds or borders in September, March or April. Use runners, rooted cuttings or seedlings. For Belgium's climate, it's best to plant from

September 1st to 15th. Although this fortnightly interval is not essential, we recommend it because, planted earlier, strawberry plants sometimes suffer from the heat, and, planted later, they root only imperfectly; as a result, they are lifted in winter by frost, so that their roots are out of the ground, and the plants freeze. The most suitable distance between plants is Om,40 to Om,45 for varieties with small leaves, and 0m,50 to 0m,60 in all directions for those with robust leaves and fruit. The space left between strawberry plants is not a loss of land; on the contrary, it's a gain; the fruit yield will be greater; harvesting, hoeing and maintenance work will be easier and more convenient. Strawberries do not require this distance when planted around the edges of squares; a space of Om.30 to Om.40 is sufficient. It is entirely optional to give the beds a width according to taste or desire; however, observe that only three rows per bed, or four at most, should be planted, otherwise care and harvesting will become difficult. In August, young plants that have taken root and are produced from nets or runners are placed in the nursery; this prepares them for better root formation and fortification. In the first fortnight of September, we put them in place, as we said above, taking care to cut off the root tips and leaving them only Om 08 to 0m, 09 long. Soon after this pruning, new and multiplied roots will form; withered or yellowed leaves and superfluous ones will also be cut off, leaving only a few young leaves. After planting, water immediately if the weather is dry. Then we mulch: this involves spreading a light layer of fresh stable manure or litter between the rows of strawberry plants. Some gardeners mulch before planting, which is more convenient. In the following spring, this fertilizer will be sufficiently consumed to be ploughed in when the first hoeing is done; it should then be mulched again. Every year around this time, 16. between the rows, gutters are made and a good liquid fertilizer, such as slurry, is poured in. Two or three days later, these trenches are closed. Mulch should be left on the beds throughout the summer; it maintains a gentle humidity, provides food for the plants through its gradual putrefaction, and keeps the fruit clean, as otherwise it is constantly laden with sand or earth, which diminishes its beauty and good quality. Runners should be cut off, not pulled out, as some people do, as they form on the mother plants, exhausting them and reducing the yield. Cutting begins when the strawberry plants begin to flower, and continues for as long as the runners reproduce; however, some should be kept if new plantings are to be made. Strawberry beds should be renewed after three years. Every year, the strawberry plants should be replanted with a sufficient quantity of potting soil; without this precaution, the plantations will have to be renewed at the end of the second year. As you know, strawberry plants absorb all the nutritive juices they can get their hands on, and as soon as they run out of them, they languish, producing insignificant yields. As a result, they heal, their roots bare, and, by the admirable organization that the Creator has given to living beings, the plants that are born with stolons or runners go further, away from their mother, and seek their nourishment in a new soil, as it were. So, we repeat, this plant needs to be fertilized at least every year, and after the third year, a new plot of land should be designated for its cultivation. It will only return to the land it has occupied after five to eight years, once it has been given other crops. Some people cut the plants at the end of the summer and say they like it; others condemn the practice. For our part, we've never tried it, and are suspending our judgment in this regard. Strawberries are sown in June, immediately after the fruit has ripened, from which the most beautiful and the best varieties should be chosen. In the past, strawberry plants were sown on beds in the ground. We recommend sowing in terrines or small wooden crates, 10 to 12 mm deep, 50 to 0.60 mm long and 25 to 30 mm wide. These crates are filled with light, earthy soil, with one-sixth sand mixed in. Sow the seeds in them, covering them very lightly, by 2 to 3 millimeters only. The seeds are then lightly moistened, and repeated carefully so as not to dry out the surface of the soil. The terrines or crates should be placed in the shade, so that they only receive the first rays of the rising sun. It would be very wise to keep seeds sown under a frame; heavy rain can cause seeds and labor to be lost forever in a matter of moments. Treated in this way, the seeds germinate in a fortnight, and the young plants can still be transplanted into nurseries in August or September. The following varieties are well worth cultivating, and will soon make outdated species and varieties of lesser value disappear from our gardens: Deptford pine, very large fruit, fine, vinous flavor, excellent;-Black Prince, early; - Royal-pine, dark red fruit with excellent flavor; - Hooper's seedling, very large fruit, veryabundant; - la Liégeoise (Haquin), very-early, calabash-shaped fruit, excellent, vinous flavor; - British Queen, obtuse, scarlet-red fruit; excellent flavor; good yield; - Imperial (Bath), excellent, large fruit; - Bicton white, rounded white fruit, the size of a pigeon's egg; strong flavor; - Keen's seedling, early; - Mammouth, very large fruit. We would also like to point out the following varieties, which can be chosen by both the amateur and the commercial gardener: Comte de Paris; - Forest; - Myatt's fertilized Hautbois; - Myatt's carly prolific; - Princesse Royale (Pelvelain); - Pineapple of Deptford; - Prince Albert; - Queen of the British Isles; - Princess Alice Maud; - Patrick seedling; - Elton pine. The name remontant is given to strawberry plants which, after a first harvest, form new stems and flowers and continue to bear fruit until autumn. This is a valuable quality in strawberries: unfortunately, it is only found in the smallest number of varieties, notably in the Alpine strawberry, known as the four-season strawberry, and in a few of its very limited varieties. Good things are said of a new remontant strawberry, named perpetuelle de Saint-Gilles by M. de Jonghe of Brussels. Non-remontant strawberry plants have only one season to flower and bear fruit. So anyone who doesn't have a remontant or perpetual variety in his collection can only expect to pick strawberries for five or six weeks, whereas remontant varieties provide a continuation of fruit for four or five months. The tomato or love apple (solanum lycopersicon, Linn.), an annuclle plant of the solanaceae family, is native to Mexico. It is very easy to grow: simply sow it at the beginning of May in good, loose, oily soil, in a warm spot, at the foot of a wall; in this case, its fruit ripens in September. If you want them in August, sow them in a bed in February, and put the young plants with rootballs in the ground around May 15th. The plant, which comes from a warm region, is very sensitive to cold; a cool night, without the thermometer even going down to 0°, will kill it. Tomatoes are planted Om, 40 apart. To speed up fruit ripening, when they start to turn red, pinch the ends of the branches and remove a few leaves. If the tomatoes are surprised by the first cold spells of autumn, they should be stored in an orangery or in a dry place exposed to the sun. There, the fruit, which is more or less formed but not yet colored, will finish ripening. We grow two types of tomato: the red and the large-fruited yellow. The latter, being hardier, is preferred for our country's climate. In the south of France and in Italy, love apples are grown in open fields; fried in oil with onions, they are a dish that is part of the daily diet of the people. In France, the fruit is used to make a much-appreciated sweet and sour sauce. It is used to season meats and soups. The fruit can be stored well into winter, on boards or dressers, in a dry place away from frost. FORCED CULTIVATION. GENERAL CONCEPTS. The purpose of forced cultivation is to grow and ripen plants or fruit using shelters, greenhouses, tarpaulins, layers, etc., either before or after the time set by nature. This is how we pick the most delicious fruits in warm countries in the middle of winter, and how the industrial gardener procures pineapples, strawberries, peas, etc. in the middle of the harsh season. The most lucrative and important branch of horticulture is forced cultivation. Its extension leaves much to be desired in our country; however, its future looks brighter here than with our French neighbors: there, it is severely hampered by easy communication with the south of France, either by steamboat or by rail, which brings back in a few hours melons, early peas and other fruits, grown in the open ground, without layers, without frames, without artificial fire, and consequently without cost. Horticulturalists in the north of France are therefore unable to fight off this fatal competition. We don't think the same thing is to be feared for Belgium: the distance to be covered and the transport costs will save our gardeners from this inconvenience. This branch of cultivation therefore deserves the care and attention of our intelligent gardeners. Before going into details concerning the cultivation of the various vegetables and edible plants that we are accustomed to forcing, we must necessarily preface this with a brief explanation of the means we employ to help nature in its productions; these means are: accots, rechauds, côtières, ados, cloches, layers, chassis, tarpaulins and greenhouses. PHYSICAL CHANGES IN THE SOIL. Soil color has a significant influence on the physical properties of the soil. Black soils absorb caloric energy, while yellow or whitish clays reflect it. As a result, the soil can be made to absorb a greater dose of caloric energy by changing its color. If you spread black loam, soot or burnt tan on the soil, you increase the heat of the earth, in that the caloric penetrates it more easily. The same caloric that escapes from the earth during the night, because all bodies naturally tend to come into equilibrium, places plants in a warm ambient atmosphere, and, as we can see, acts favorably on their growth. Hard, white soil, on the other hand, repels heat during the day and is cold at night. To obtain inexpensive black soil that achieves the above-mentioned aim, we recommend watering a heap of tannin with a solution of iron sulfate two or three times a year. This mixture will then take on a pronounced black hue. Oak bark is known to contain high levels of gallic acid. This acid, when combined with iron oxide, forms iron gallate, a salt that strongly colors black. Here's how it's done: on ten carts of tanned or oak bark from the tanners' vats, ten kilograms of iron sulfate dissolved in enough water to wet the whole mass is poured, stirred with forks and then, six months later and as the bark decomposes, subjected to the same operation. After eighteen months to two years, you can use it to your advantage. (Iron sulfate, couperose or green vitriol, is a cheap salt and can be found at all color merchants). SHELTERS. Walls. - Facing east to west, walls provide excellent shelter for spring vegetables, protecting them from the north winds; they hasten the development of vegetables and fruit; at the same time they offer the most favorable exposure for vines, peach trees and other fruit trees, and on the north side shelter for vegetables too delicate to withstand the sun's scorching rays in midsummer. It's against these walls that the coastal plantations so favorable to early crops are established. Hedges. - Hedges from east to west also provide shelter for forcing vegetables. Forming narrow four0 rees of branching vegetation that break the cold winds, they should be composed of trees or shrubs with taproot or little tracery that have the property of growing in tight, rigid lines, of being susceptible to mowing, of retaining all or part of their leaves in winter; of keeping themselves bushy from the root collar to the end of the intertwining twigs. Beech, which retains its dry leaves for a long time, Western red cedar, which can withstand shearing very well, and yew, which is a little slow-growing, all lend themselves well to hedge formation. The same is true of many other plants, such as dogwood, privet, various thorns (cratœgus and mespilus), and even plum, apple and other fruit trees and shrubs. Windbreaks. - Windbreaks are used to protect plants grown on teas. By means of these shelters, plants that would not have been able to withstand being in the ground are placed in a different position and, so to speak, in a different climate. Windbreaks are very useful for many delicate plants; they can be used to form ados and counter-ados in flat terrain. These are plantations of closely-spaced trees, which are given a height according to the plants they are intended to grow. Cedars, cypresses, poplars and robinias can all be used. Dead hedges are also used as windbreaks. They consist of a close alignment of fir or other wood poles, the ends of which are charred to make them last longer. Doormats. - If you don't have any hedges or walls 2. 17 to place in a suitable direction, you can make up for this by using doormats held upright by stakes to which they are attached vertically. Some plants need to be sheltered not only from gales, hail or rain, but also from the sun's fierce rays. These shelters, which can easily be given a height for cultivation, are placed for early plants from east to west, so that not a single ray of sunlight is lost. In this way, the plants are forced to produce several days before those grown in open fields, whether the land is ploughed flat or sloping to the south. The market gardeners of Paris have a large number of these straw mats in their vegetable gardens; they are made of dry reeds or rye straw; their height varies from one to two meters. On the north-facing side, delicate plants are protected from the heat; lettuces, purslane, claytonia, spinach, chervil and parsley are grown here; cruciferous plants such as cauliflower and Savoy cabbage are sown here; flea beetles are less likely to attack these plants in the shade. - These shelters simply consist of a thin layer of straw held between two wooden rods which are attached to stakes placed at intervals. Doormats are also essential for covering greenhouses, tarpaulins, layers and bells during cold winter nights and days, and even hot summer days. TEENS. Ados, which are found in some growers' gardens, should be established in every vegetable garden without exception; they cost only a little trouble, which the gardener is wrong to be stingy about. Ados are formed in the most sheltered parts of the garden, and best in south-east-facing locations. They are trained as follows: By giving the soil a deep drying, soil is removed from the front and carried to the back, so as to form an inclined plane, the elevation of which exceeds by Om 20 to Om, 30 the most sloping or front part. Early crops such as radishes, lettuces, carrots and cauliflower thrive best here. If you fill the 0.10 to 0.15 m ados with good potting soil, vegetation is accelerated, especially if it's black potting soil, which absorbs the sun's rays and increases heat considerably. Even better results are obtained when plants are covered with cloches or frames. COTIERS. The only difference between cotiere plants and ados is that they can be set up in the middle of the garden, forming slopes inclined to the south; they are still called borders. These various methods considerably advance vegetation. CLOCHES. Cloches are glass vases used temporarily to shelter certain delicate plants in their youth, which have difficulty withstanding 8 the temperature variations of our climate, and especially white frosts. They vary in size according to the size of the plants and the purpose for which they are to be used; most often they are in one piece, with a diameter of Om,40 to Om,45 at the base and Om,20 to Om,25 at the top; the height is equal to the diameter of the base. White glass is generally preferred. Their price varies from 70 c. to 1 fr. They are available from the main glassworks in Belgium, and can be ordered according to shape and size. Bells are also built with fir, oak or other types of wood. The five spokes are fitted at the top to a kind of wooden pentagon which crowns them, leaving an opening so that air can be blown in at will. These bells range from half a meter to a meter in diameter. Lead bells are also oval and vary in size. Each layer consists of two distinct parts: the manure bed and the soil bed. The manure bed, regularly arranged and compacted, consists of animal or vegetable substances likely to enter into fermentation and thereby give off gentle heat, at the same time as exhaling beneficial moisture. These two qualities - warmth and humidity - are the prerequisites for producing beautiful, long-lasting vegetation in the happiest climates. The more or less thick, more or less substantial bed of earth with which the manure is covered is intended to support and nourish the plants. The thickness of this bed, whose soil must always be loose and of good quality, varies from Om.16 to Om.30. The thickness of the manure bed also varies according to the amount of heat required. Depending on the thickness and quality of the manure bed, the layers can be distinguished as warm, tepid or dull. Warm layer. - The warm layer is made up of horse manure recently removed from the stable. This manure has the added advantage of being usable at all times, provided it is kept dry and in the form of a millstone: to use it, it must be sufficiently moistened; the manure soon begins to ferment and produce heat. The layers are built up by laying the manure in successive, even beds. The manure should be firmed up and trodden on, at the same time as any pits or unevennesses are filled in, and watered with a watering can if it is not damp enough on its own. The bed should be of equal thickness everywhere; this is what determines 17. the uniformity of heat in the soil. The thickness of warm layers varies from Om, 60 to 1m, 00 and beyond; the width also varies: it can be from Om, 80 to 1m,32; the length is indeterminate, but rarely is it less than. 2*,60. The narrowest layers, or those with a width of Om.80, are used for the earliest forced cultivation, because they are easier to keep warm with stoves. The name "stoves" is given to the manure that surrounds the layer when its heat begins to drop. This manure must be trodden down like the manure in the bed itself, as we have said. Accot. - Manure, leaves or tanning cloth are raised around the layers to keep out the cold. Accot is given a thickness of Om, 40 to Om, 60, depending on the material used and the intensity of the cold. Their height should reach the full height of the layer. Stoves. - From November to April, you need to keep the layers warm, without having to repeat them. To this end, new manure is compacted in the surrounding paths; every two weeks, this manure is stirred and compacted again, adding new manure if necessary. For stoves, dry manure is used if the weather is rainy, and wet manure if it's dry. In the harsher season, the beds and stoves are covered at the same time. On top of the layer, a casing called a trunk is placed.... A. This box is inclined to the south and higher at the back than at the front, so that water doesn't drip into the interior and the frame receives the sun's rays better. An ordinary box is from Om,15 to Om,28 high at the front and from Om,28 to 0m,32 at the back. It is also optional to give the trunks a greater or lesser inclination, depending on the size of E A and the nature of the plants to be grown. The box is designed to support the frame or panel.... B. This consists of a wooden or, better still, laminated iron frame with grooves, which supports the glass. The panes must be wider than they are long, overlap by only Om.005 and have a slightly rounded cut. These conditions apply to both diaper and tarpaulin frames, and to greenhouse and orangery frames. Glass should only be covered with 0m,005, because a larger covered surface accommodates a greater quantity of water, which stagnates, freezes and cracks the panes; moreover, the dirt that would inevitably collect there would intercept the light, and the view would be unpleasantly affected. All those who are not dominated by the old and vicious routine will be careful not to give the glass any other arrangement than the one we have just indicated. The rounded cut serves to channel rainwater through the middle of the tiles, preventing it from penetrating the grooves and producing a drip that is always fatal to plants. Those who are more careful - and when it comes to horticulture, you can never be too careful - have the glass fitted in two putties, i.e., the putty is first placed in the iron or wooden grooves, then the panes are fitted and receive the ordinary layer of putty on the outside. They also apply a gray or white oil color to the part of the glass where the panes overlap. This makes it impossible for frozen water to break the panes, and prevents dirt from getting in. For each sash, there must be a zigzag-notched piece of wood, used to open the sash by degrees..... This is called a rack and is sometimes made of iron. Warm layers. - The arrangement of warm layers is the same in all respects as that of hot layers; they differ only in the nature of the fermentable materials used. While stable manure is used for the construction of warm layers, a mixture of litter or manure from other livestock, or leaves either dry or harvested as they fall, or tanning with leaves or litter, all with or without stable manure, is used for these. The same chests and frames are used. Tepid layers, although made of less hot manure, sometimes develop considerable heat; this happens when the manure used contains a fairly large quantity of animal matter and is very damp: in this case, before placing young plants or seeds in it, the heat of the layer should be explored by dipping the hand in it, or, which is better, the degrees of heat are measured by means of a thermometer, which is placed for a few minutes in the soil of the layer. It's not uncommon to see the thermometer mark 80° centigrade in the horse manure of warm layers, imparting 45 to 50° of heat to the soil in the layer. It's easy to see that this heat is far too great, and that you need to wait before sowing or planting until, as gardeners say, the fire has gone out and the thermometer, immersed in the potting soil, registers between 30 and 40 degrees at most. In the same way as for hot layers, we explore the degrees of heat of tepid layers before using them. Heat develops three to four days after the manure has been compacted. Deaf layers. - For the formation of muted layers, half-consumed manure is used, which is no longer likely to heat up much. It only produces a muted heat that is slightly higher than that of the earth surrounding the layer. What further distinguishes deaf-beds is that they are made in spring, cannot be heated with stoves, and instead of frames, cloches are used to cover them at the points where melons or other plants raised on hot beds are planted. Deaf-beds are always built in trenches or in a pit Om,50 to Om,60 deep. Their usual dimensions are Om,70 thick, 1m,30 wide and of indeterminate length. Their topsoil-covered surface will be slightly domed. In spring and late autumn, we are often obliged to shelter the plants from frost under cloches, with litter, leaves or straw mats attached to half-barrel poles and held in place by three transverse rods. Being in more immediate contact with atmospheric air and water, manure decomposes more rapidly and produces more active heat. Layers in which the soil is excavated to place the manure are called "boxed". They are preferable to bordered layers: they look better, are better suited to the arrangement of the manure, and, if they are a little less hot at the beginning, on the other hand their heat is more durable. The use of boiling water, by means of the thermosiphon, combined with manure, produces the safest and easiest heat to direct. Once the initial set-up costs have been met, these layers are more economical in that the quantity of manure can be reduced and, by extending the heat pipes, a large number of layers can be heated at the same time. - All layers are covered with straw mats and other shelter, such as leaves, straw, litter, etc., depending on the intensity of the cold. RACHES. Tarpaulins differ from layers in several respects: in addition to the beds of more or less hot manure they contain in brick boxes, they enable pipes to be laid to conduct heat, either by means of hot air, according to the old system, or by hot water or steam. They are of such dimensions that a standing man can easily walk through them in a corridor known as the service path. Under this pathway are the pipes; it is covered by a ladder-like trellis, the rungs of which, spaced at Om,05 or Om,06, A are Om,07 thick, and which allows the heat released by the pipes to escape freely into the tarpaulin. This mesh should be mobile, so that it can be lifted in the evening, during the most severe frosts, to allow the heat, which is always more or less intercepted by it, to spread completely and unhindered through the tarpaulin. Finally, we can say that tarpaulins are greenhouses in a lesser sense; they often take the place of greenhouses for growing flowers. Since they are almost always not very high, it's easy to cover and uncover them with A straw mats, which protect them from the cold and shelter them from the scorching summer sun. Usually, to provide more humidity for the plants and keep the temperature more even, the ground of the tarpaulin is made Om,50 to 0m,60 lower than the ground outside. In dry or mountainous terrain, this depth can be as much as 1.80 m. In this case, the frames are placed on the front at ground level. The English often grow camellias in these types of covers. They are not well suited to growing vegetables or fruit plants. Vegetables are grown either in the open ground, or in buried pots. They are sown or planted according to the time of year when the vegetables or fruit are to be harvested; cultivation begins at the onset of winter, and continues through spring and summer. Trees grown here include vines, cherries, peaches, apricots and figs. Edible fruit plants include strawberries, melons and pineapples; vegetables include peas, beans, lettuce, radishes and more. Depending on the length of the walls, boards or dressers can be placed on which strawberry plants or flowers can be placed. We can see how much pleasure this kind of small garden can provide, in the middle of winter and the frosty season, where we encounter both the sweet perfumes of spring flowers and the tasty fruits of summer. In the course of this work, we also mention how useful and profitable tarpaulins can be to the horticulturist. FORCED CULTIVATION. VEGETABLES PROPER. ASPARAGUS. Winter asparagus or early asparagus is grown on beds and under glass frames. From the outset, the beds must be laid out in such a way as to be able to accept wooden frames or boxes on which the frames or panels rest. The boards, 1.30 m wide, will be spaced by 0.60 m paths to accommodate the stoves. These boards are lined with three rows of two- to three-year-old asparagus; the plants are spaced 0m,30 apart in all directions, so that on each side of the board there is a free, fairly wide edge. For three years, the asparagus is cared for as in ordinary cultivation. In the fourth year, from November to March, we heat the asparagus: after removing the soil from the paths to a depth of Om.50 to Om.60, we replace it with warm, well-trampled and well-packed manure: we spread this loosened and divided soil over a good 2. 18 layer of potting soil on the beds; we level it off quickly. All that remains to be done is to spread a 0.16 m layer of manure, neither too dry nor too damp, over the entire surface of the bed, and place the boxes and frames on top. If the temperature is cold, we cover the frames with straw mats and never give them air. If the cold becomes very intense, doormats will not suffice; you will have to cover the frames with a thick layer of leaves or long manure and place the doormats on top; similarly, you will have to surround the chests with a similar covering. Twelve or fifteen days after placing the trays, check whether the asparagus are growing, removing a little of the manure. Then remove the manure and renew the stoves, if necessary. After three weeks, the asparagus is ready to be cut. After four or six weeks, you can stop harvesting if you want to preserve the plant. Carefully managed in this way, a forced asparagus plant can last a very long time, and can be heated every two years. The plants recover during a year of rest, and their vigor returns completely. The following year, they can be forced again. The asparagus obtained in this way is called white asparagus; the variety known as Dutch asparagus is the most suitable. In April, we remove the frames, boxes and manure, and return the beds to their previous condition. Green asparagus, also known as pea asparagus, is grown using a different method. In December or March, layers of manure are trampled and tamped down to maintain an elevation of 1.60 m to Om.80 m, and a width of Om.30 m. The boxes are placed on these layers, and the asparagus is then placed on the boards. The trunks are placed on top, followed by a layer of Om,09 to 0m,12 of compost; the frames are placed on top, covered with straw mats and left to catch fire. The roots are shaped, leaving a length of Om, 25 to Om, 30. They are placed upright next to each other, filling in the empty spaces between them with potting soil as the work progresses. Care should be taken to ensure that the crowns of the plants are at the same level; the collars should be lightly covered. After these operations, close the frames and maintain the heat. The asparagus will soon come into vegetation: a layer hardly lasts more than three weeks. Plants that have been used for this type of cultivation are destined for removal. Those involved in large-scale forced cultivation successively plant three or four times during the winter, and make very considerable profits from these plantings. MUSHROOMS. The cultivation of mushrooms offers great benefits to the merchant horticulturist, especially if he lives near large cities: the sale of this plant is always assured. As a foodstuff, mushrooms form a kind of middle ground between plant and animal substances, and their chemical characteristics make them a good match for both; indeed, as with animals, they contain fairly high levels of nitrogen. Like other plants, mushrooms undoubtedly reproduce by a kind of fertilization and fructification, which takes place in a truly mysterious way, and which botanists have tried in vain to understand. The edible mushroom or agaric, which is harvested in late summer in the meadows of Belgium, is also free from poisonous qualities, provided it is harvested and eaten before it begins to putrefy. We know that in this same state, in this beginning of decomposition, animal substances are dangerous and give rise to serious illnesses. As for edible agaric, all danger disappears if it is used before the end of its complete vegetation, and if it is not mixed with other deleterious and dangerous species of mushroom. Healthy, semi-dark cellars, underground passages and quarries free of humidity are the ideal places to grow mushrooms. Mushroom beds need measured levels of humidity and a constant temperature not exceeding 15° R. and not falling below 10° R. of heat. Autumn is a particularly good time to grow mushrooms. And, although success can be achieved at any time, it should be remembered that the most favorable time for cultivating any plant is always that which is closest to the time of its natural vegetation, or, in other words, to the time when the plant begins to develop in the climate it inhabits. Manure preparation. - Urine-impregnated horse manure is generally preferred. In this respect, manure that has been in the stable for a few days is the best. As it comes out, it should be piled up until there is a sufficient quantity. As soon as it has fermented long enough, after five or six weeks, the heap is broken up into a uniform mass, while the cakes formed by humidity and heat are broken up with a fork, and all foreign bodies, such as straw not impregnated with urine, wood and stones, are discarded. Arranged in this way, the manure is transported to the place where the layers are to be formed. Here, squares of Om 75 in height are laid out. Water the parts that are not slightly moist, level them out and beat them firmly with the back of the spade. After an interval of ten to fifteen days, the pile is broken up again; the mass is made as homogeneous as possible, and the grinding stone is erected. This is the name given to the layer of manure destined to produce mushrooms. Millstones. - Grindstones are formed in the shape of a humpback or roof, with a base width of Om, 80 and a height of Om, 60 over any length; they must be neatly arranged and beaten with the back of the shovel. It would be difficult to give an exact description of the degree of consistency of the manure; the gardener's tact and habit should make up for this. However, the manure should be thoroughly mixed, with what was on the outside brought to the center; it should be fat, unctuous and homogeneous. If, by compressing it with force in the hand, liquid were to come out, this would be a very bad sign; there would be reason to doubt the success of the cultivation; therefore, water only during the heat of summer or when the manure is too dry. After four or five days, millstones prepared in this way produce a gentle, long-lasting heat. Now it's time to "larder" them; this operation consists of introducing mushroom spawn onto the surface of the layers. These are whitish, filamentous patches 18. formed from the residues of depleted layers that have supplied many mushrooms. Pieces of this mushroom spawn are inserted into the sides of the layer by making chessboard-shaped openings with the hand, at Om, 16 from one another. These openings must be such that they are closed by the fragments of spawn, 0m,08 to Om, 09 wide and long, which are deposited in them. The manure is pressed lightly all around, and the surface of the grinding wheel is levelled by gently tapping it with the back of the shovel. Make sure that the upper part of each fragment is level with this same surface. As soon as the white has set, which can be recognized by the networks of white filaments crawling over the manure, it is covered with a layer of light earth, about Om, 03 thick. This soil must be neither too dry nor too wet, but in a moist state that will hold it to the walls of the layer, after being carefully levelled with the shovel. If it were too dry, it would have to be moistened with the fine-headed watering can while still being mixed; if it were too damp, dry earth would have to be added. As for the soil used to cover the millstones, a mixture of leaf compost and sand is perfectly suitable. Three to six weeks after the operations just described, the mushrooms start to produce; harvesting takes about two months. Mushroom spawn can be purchased from the mushroom merchants of our major cities; it can also be obtained by first growing it in the layers of manure being prepared, preferably in donkey manure, which is the easiest to spawn, followed by mule and horse manure, the latter being the most widely used because it is readily available. The simplest way to obtain mushroom spawn, if you want to make it yourself, is to place in the cellar, at any time of the year, a quantity of horse manure which has remained in the stable for two weeks and which, as a result, is impregnated with a lot of urine and mixed with a lot of dung. This manure will spontaneously turn white after a certain length of time, but usually after three or four months; it is then all white and musty. In this state, simply spread it to a thickness of Om,07 to 0m,10 over trodden or trampled horse manure; then cover with Om,16 of compost. The surface is levelled and firmed with the back of a shovel. Or, to make it even simpler, we make millstones Om, 80 wide and Om,60 high, which we erect at an angle against the cellar wall; we use manure of the same quality. As soon as the plant has formed, it is covered with potting soil as above, and shaped in the same way. Mushrooms grow there. If the same layer is sprinkled with water in which fresh mushrooms, crushed or cut into pieces, have been washed, the operation is safer. As for harvesting the mushrooms, it's best to pick them every other day, and to take the precaution of rotating them on their pedicel while detaching them, so as not to disturb the tray which is to supply them. After picking, if the soil dries out, lightly baste it, because, as we must repeat, mushrooms like uniform temperature and humidity. Their cultivation in the open ground is fortunate, so they are not widely used; rainfall from storms, or rain that lasts too long, are obstacles to success. It differs little from the cultivation we have just described; only, in the open ground, the layers are wrapped in a straw covering called a chemise, which serves to give them the darkness they naturally find in cellars. Cultivated underground, they are not as white as those grown in the open ground, but their flavor does not differ. For mushroom cultivation, the English take advantage of the walls of the greenhouses they use to force fruits and vegetables, or to shelter flowers. Against these walls, on northern exposures, they erect a tile or slate roof that rests at the bottom on a supporting wall high enough not to interfere with service. Along the entire length of this kind of greenhouse, on both sides of the pathway that runs through the middle, there are shelved dressers on which the layers or grindstones are placed, prepared as mentioned above, although it should be noted that they prefer pure manure to stable manure. It should also be noted that the heat-conducting pipes must continue their course in these constructions, and that there is usually a ceiling under the roof to better conserve heat. Mushrooms can also be grown in temperate greenhouses, and even in hot ones. Wooden crates Om, 25 to Om, 30 high, of indeterminate width and length, with a very wide-mesh wire bottom, are placed on legs, so that the heated air surrounds them on all sides; straw or small branches are placed at the bottom of these crates, followed by manure, which is suitably compacted. When the first heat has passed, lay the spawn in large slabs and cover the whole with a layer of 0.03 m thick turf with light, loose soil. Water in due course, and note that mushrooms need not be protected from air circulation. Parisians cultivate their mushrooms almost exclusively in the immense quarries from which building stone is extracted, and which have been considerably enlarged since Paris was surrounded by its walls: the consumption of this plant is prodigious; it is estimated that three million baskets of mushrooms are sold annually in this metropolis, not counting what passes through the départements. In these underground tunnels, the Parisians place their millstones in two rows, with a service path in the middle. They prepare the horse manure in the open air, forming large piles which they wet and rework several times, until it has acquired the necessary moisture and smoothness. It is then layered in the underground, larded with the spawn and gobbled (covered) with light earth, as described above. If a mushroom layer doesn't work, don't blame the gardener. For, in spite of the best care, in absolutely identical circumstances and conditions, we have seen mushroom beds of the best cultivation fail, without anyone being able to notice this accident. Fertilizer from green-fed animals should never be used; it is the use of this fertilizer that is attributed as one of the causes of failure. Cellars should also be kept draught-free. Vulgar gardeners, or those infatuated with a routine they don't want to deviate from, sometimes attribute their disappointments to rainbows or thunderstorms. We won't discuss these prejudices here. The edible mushroom (agaricus edulis, Bull.) is medium-sized, white on top, pinkish underneath, fleshy, brittle, peelable, with a pleasant smell and taste. Belgian horticulturists such as Van Sterbeck, Necker, Van den Spiegel and d'Hoogvorst have successfully cultivated mushrooms. CAULIFLOWER. Cauliflower seedlings sown between August 25 and September 25, and to be harvested in April or early May, are grown on a bed in November as follows: a mixture of half horse manure and half cow manure is used, so that the bed does not heat up too much and lose heat too quickly. Eight days before the layer is to be smoked, it is placed in a heap so that it heats up properly and settles evenly; in frosty weather, it is covered with straw. Then, after arranging it in layers, we trample it. As soon as it reaches a thickness of Om.60, we lay the boxes and frames on top. Leave the layer in this state for eight days, opening up the frames a little; then cover it with Om, 30 to Om, 35 of good compost that is not too light. For a few days afterwards, the pile is turned so that it heats up completely, and the cauliflowers are planted from December 1st to December 10th, in a checkerboard pattern, at a distance of Om,40 to Om, 50 in all directions. This space can be filled with radish and lettuce seedlings. The cauliflowers should be given air every day, unless the temperature does not allow it. As soon as the plants touch the windows, we raise the boxes by placing them on manure, taking care to fill the void. At the end of March or beginning of April, you can remove the frames and, a little later, the boxes, which are then used to grow melons. Water the cauliflowers generously, but always in the morning. When the apples begin to develop, they are covered by bending the lower leaves inwards; they form more quickly and better than if left exposed to the light. The second planting of cauliflowers is done in December, and the third in January, still in the same way as above. In February, cauliflowers are still planted on beds, but they have already taken over from other early crops, such as radishes, lettuces, etc., and the beds on which they are grown have given off their heat. ENDIVES. In February, Italian endive seed is sown on a very warm bed. The seed must be old; those six years old and older set perfectly well and set seed with difficulty, which is necessary for spring cultivation of this plant. The seed is broadcast and must be very lightly covered; it sprouts in a short time under the frame covered with a mat or matting. Air is only given once the plant has emerged, and if the weather is fine during the day, the mats are only put back at night. Fifteen days later, the seedling is strong enough to be transplanted to another bed, where it is planted out at a distance of about Om.05 cm. It is watered and covered with straw mats for one or two days to ensure a good start. About a month after transplanting, it can be placed at a distance of Om 25 in all directions, in a new layer on which Om, 15 to Om, 20 of compost has been spread. All the rest of the cultivation is limited to watering in the morning, if necessary; providing air when the temperature permits, and putting up the frames on cold nights. GREEN BEANS. Properly managed, forced cultivation of beans is unlikely to be unsuccessful. It can be started in the first days of February; a temperature of 16° Réaumur, successively raised to 18 and 20 0 degrees, is the most suitable. A layer is formed and covered with Om, 15 of potting soil; boxes, frames and, if it's freezing, straw mats are placed. Four or five days later, sow dwarf French beans and flageolet, the best varieties for forcing. Runner beans are earlier than flageolet beans, but the latter are hardier. The distance between clumps should be Om, 25 in all directions; each clump is made up of two or three plants spaced Om, 04 apart. They should be covered with Om, 02 potting soil only. The frames and straw mats are placed immediately. As soon as the beans have sprouted, they are given air every day, weather permitting. The weather can be fine and very cold at the same time, so it must be implied here that, depending on the temperature, the frames will be opened more or less, gradually from Om,01 to Om,10 in February, and from Om,10 to Om,60 in March. But this graduation is not absolute, and the gardener will have to adjust according to the degree of cold. Beans are also sown in rays, and when they have formed their first two leaves, they are transplanted to another layer at the same depth as before transplanting. The trays are immediately closed, and the mats put back in place to ensure the young plant's recovery. Beans should be transplanted very young, as their success becomes doubtful as soon as they are transplanted, when they have their fourth leaf. Beans sown in February already bear in March or early April, and for two months provide their pods under the name of green beans. Care should be taken to water moderately, without wetting the flowers or leaves. During flowering, hariCULTURE MARAICHÈRE. 2. 1e cots under frame conditions require air and light; in this respect, their cultivation benefits greatly when heated by thermosiphon or hot water: the heat, produced here uniformly and without any interruption, enables the temperature to be raised from 20 to 25 degrees, and to give, so to speak, daylight at will; whereas ordinary beds must be covered with their straw mats, night and day, if the cold is more or less intense. In March, in Belgium's climate, beans are still grown on beds, as described above. At the beginning of April, they are also forced into the ground at a very young age, and covered with cloches during cold nights and days. In this way, we bring forward their natural growth, which doesn't take place in the open ground until the first fortnight of May. In the big cities, forced beans find an easy and secure placement. In Paris, as in London, it is not uncommon to see them selling for 5 to 30 francs a kilogram in winter. LETTUCE. Passion, morine, crêpe and petite noire lettuces are the most suitable for forcing. Crêpe and petite noire, so called because of the color of their seeds, are better suited to this type of cultivation than the other two: they can withstand air deprivation during cold weather. In August, September and up to October, they are sown in well-tilled soil, the surface of which is covered with Om.05 to Om.10 of compost. Lightly cover the seed, press down with the back of the spade and, four or five days after sowing, water if the weather is dry. As soon as the lettuces have two leaves, in addition to their cotyledons, they are transplanted in place on layers that need not be very thick. Om,30 to Om, 35 of well-packed manure covered with Om, 25 to Om, 30 of good garden soil mixed with potting compost, are enough. Chassis windows should not be far from the lettuces, but as close to them as possible. Any plant that vegetates quickly and goes through the phases of its life without resting, loves daylight. Lettuces that have been bedded in October and properly cared for will be ready for harvesting in December, under a frame or cloche. At the end of October or beginning of November, lettuces are again sown on beds, unless there are still good plants available from previous sowings; in this case, the best ones are selected; they are then transplanted onto new beds, where they will flower in January. In December, January and February, we continue sowing in the same way, to transplant the seedlings onto a slightly warmer bed: the manure will be packed to a thickness of Om.45 to Om.60, and covered with soil and compost, as we said earlier. The seed should be sown lighter than for autumn sowing. As soon as the seedlings are placed under a bell or under a frame, you need to pay close attention to the care you need to give them. Covering the frames with straw mats during cold spells, increasing these covers when the cold increases, covering them with litter or leaves as the cold becomes more intense, providing air whenever the temperature permits - these are the continuous care requirements for almost all forced cultivation. The heat of the manure layers can vary for lettuces from 10 to 15° Réaumur. Plant spacing should be approximately Om, 20 to Om, 25 staggered. From autumn to the time of the new head lettuces, we sow the seed of lettuces to be cut every two weeks. For this purpose, we use the lettuces listed above. They are sown very thickly to cut small lettuces at the root collar as soon as they have their fourth leaf. All lettuces without distinction can be used for this purpose; two varieties in particular are particularly well-suited to this purpose: chicory lettuce and spinach lettuce. Spinach can be cut several times at intervals of a few days. PEAS. Tarpaulins are undoubtedly the best place to establish layers for forcing peas. Unfortunately, tarpaulins, which are nothing more than small greenhouses heated with manure or by thermosiphon, are not available to everyone. Usually, peas are simply forced onto ordinary warm layers, which are thinned out so that they don't generate too much heat. The first seedlings are sown at the beginning of November, and can be continued fortnightly until the end of January. The soil in which the peas are transplanted or planted should be lukewarm. Om, 38 to Om, 45 of packed manure covered with Om, 35 of good loose soil, a little earthy if you like, but not too oily, are perfectly suitable. If the layer of soil covering the manure is thinner, the roots may penetrate into the manure itself; in this case, vegetation is exuberant; the peas are carried away and produce beautiful foliage without fruit. On a bed as described above, which is 1°, 30 wide by an indeterminate length, you can space the rows Om, 20 apart and sow 3 to 5 pea seeds per pocket spaced Om, 15 apart. When the peas are about 20 cm high, you can bed them by tilting them to the higher side of the frame and placing light slats over the feet of the plants. The purpose of this operation is to hasten flowering and encourage the emergence of lateral stems, which increase the yield. After four or five days, the inclined stems straighten out, at which point the laths should be removed. If the temperature is mild, the frames should be opened every day. Normally, only four flowers are left on each stem, and the others are removed by cutting off the tips of the terminal shoots. Peas can be grown in the same way in a tarpaulin, except that they can be given oars, and they grow more quickly because they don't have to block the light by covering the windows with mats to prevent the cold from penetrating, especially if you use thermosiphon heating. In greenhouses where vines or cherry trees are grown, they are best planted along the walls, on the beds where the trees are located. In this case, all you need to do is provide them with stakes at the right time, and water them if the soil is too dry. 19. Another inexpensive method, often used, is to sow the plants thickly against a south-facing wall in late October or early November. As soon as the peas have reached a height of om, 06 to 0m, 08, they are planted in a trench about Om, 15 deep and appropriate in width and length to the frames intended to cover them. They are planted in good garden soil, without a layer of manure, at the distance we have indicated above, and conforming in all other respects to the other rules prescribed for growing early peas. PURSLANE. Purslane is sown on a bed from January to March; the manure is loaded with Om, 10 to Om, 15 of loam only. Then sow without covering the seed or with very little coverage. If the compost is damp enough, do not water; if the surface dries out, lightly baste with a watering can with a fine-holed head. We prefer to grow the variety known as golden purslane (Portulaca sativa E). Forced cultivation of this vegetable is rarely practised, but it deserves it in every respect. Purslane is a very healthy and refreshing plant. If you treat it as we have just described, you can use it up almost two months sooner than if you grow it in the open ground without a frame. As we know, it can't be sown in the open ground before the end of April or the beginning of May. You can harvest purslane five or six weeks after sowing it in a bed. FORCED CULTIVATION. ROOT VEGETABLES. -- BATATE. Convolvulus batatas, a member of the convolvulaceae family, is native to South America. Batate is the name given by the natives to this precious plant which, in their country, grows without care or cultivation, like bindweed in our hedgerows. It is to be regretted that in Belgium we have to abandon the cultivation of a plant of such eminent value: in our country, it requires a warm greenhouse; it can be grown as a simple curiosity in a pineapple greenhouse. Obviously, it can never be grown in the open ground with any hope of covering the cultivation costs, unless a robust variety is obtained. Nature rarely gives plants qualities in their natural soil that they would need in other climates. Batatas were introduced to Europe at the end of the 16th century. Several well-educated horticulturists made attempts to cultivate or acclimatize it; among them the illustrious André Thouin was one of the most zealous, but their efforts were not crowned with success. If you wanted to try growing this plant in the open ground, you'd have to put the tubers on a bed and under a frame as early as March or April, at a distance of Om, 80, and cover them with cloches like melons. A few days after planting, numerous shoots appear, which can be cut into small pots under cloches and on a warm bed, buried right up to the edges. These cuttings are used for planting, which is always done on a bed, or in the greenhouse or against a wall facing south. They are harvested in October. Tubers are not easy to store: they must be placed alternately in beds of dry sand, in a crate in a dry place where the heat does not fall below 10° Réaumur. The varieties of batate or potato are: yam, yellow batate, violet, red and white. TUBEROUS NASTURTIUM. We mention in passing this food plant, whose tubers can be kept from one year to the next without wilting or sprouting, in a dry, frost-free place. It has this advantage over all other root vegetables. But what hinders its cultivation is that the plant does not go through its vegetative phases quickly enough, in the open ground, in Belgium's climate. From May to October, it doesn't fully ripen, as beans and potatoes do. Cultivation begins on a warm bed towards the end of January, and is completed in the open ground. Here's how: Tubers are planted at Om, 10 apart, covered with Om, 03 earth only. They soon produce numerous shoots, from which cuttings are made under cloches in very small pots. As soon as the roots have formed, which takes from fifteen to twenty days, the cloches are removed. In the first days of April, we plant them in the open ground, under cloches, in substantial, loose, sandy soil; we mound the stems several times, as they grow: by this operation, we obtain a greater number of tubers. Tubers can also be planted in the open ground around April 15th, but they must always be protected by cloches to prevent light frosts from destroying the young stems. The strong, peppery flavor of tuberous nasturtium (mayna or tropœolum tuberosum) is not to everyone's taste. Entire populations of South America make this plant their usual food. The raw, sliced tubers are used to season our salads. CARROT. The Dutch carrot is the earliest and most suitable of all for forced cultivation. In December, warm beds are planted with equal parts of soil and compost. Heat is kept to a minimum in the early stages, gradually rising from 10 to 20 degrees. Air is breathed in from time to time, and the soil is lightly basked if the surface dries out, which is quite rare, since the humid exhalation of hot manure successively penetrates the soil on which the carrots are sown and maintains a suitable, moderate moisture level. If watering is necessary, however, it should be done with distilled water, which is a general rule for all watering of bedded plants. The compacted layer of manure should be about Om, 60 thick; the mixture of soil and compost should be Om, 35 thick. Carrot seedlings continue in January and February; those sown in December yield at the end of March and in April. Thinning is done as soon as the young plants are the size of a little finger. At the end of February, and throughout March and April, we take great care to open the frames to prevent sunburn or excessively high temperatures, which are so harmful to bedding plants. Half an hour in which the sun beams down on the glass can sometimes mean the loss of all hope of harvesting, and all the trouble you've gone to. In May, if there are still carrots on the bed from seedlings sown in December and January, the frames are lifted: the plants, already strong, stand up well to the open air and even acquire a more delicate flavour. For seedlings sown in March and early April, we don't remove the trays in May, but we smear them inside with chalk crushed in whey; or, better still, we cover them with a lath that sufficiently intercepts the sun's rays while leaving the plants enough light. During this month, the frames should be open during the day and closed only at night. Parsnips and radishes. - Parsnips and round and half-round pink radishes are grown in exactly the same way; except that for radishes, forced cultivation is not repeated until March, because by then they have already been sown in the open ground under cover and with good exposure. POTATOES. The forced cultivation of potatoes can, in some cases, be lucrative for the merchant gardener: we know that the early products of this plant easily find buyers who give rather high prices for them, especially if the gardener can offer them in March or April; because he has to conform to the taste, even to the oddity of his world. There are those who always prefer new potatoes, whatever the season, regardless of the precious qualities of these perfectly ripe tubers, which are abundant in starch and constitute a most wholesome food. The English have such a predilection for new potatoes that they prefer them to the best late-season potatoes. To obtain potatoes very early, in March or April, we plant whole tubers of the earliest varieties in January and February, on a warm bed and under a frame, such as: early dwarf, marjolin (kidney early), yellow goat's horn. These varieties produce short stems and can be quite close together, at Om, 20 or Om, 25 in all directions. The soil covering the manure layer should be good, rich garden soil with no recent fertilization. Plant to such a depth that the tubers 14 are covered with Om, 03 to 0m, 04 of this soil. As soon as their stems are Om, 10 high, they are ridged; a few days later, they are ridged again. The remaining care consists in covering them with straw mats at night, uncovering them in the morning, and giving them air when the temperature permits. DISLESd=COC FORCED CROPS. VEGETABLE PLANTS WITH EDIBLE FRUIT. ANANAS. For a long time, pineapple cultivation remained restricted; it was shrouded in mystery and charlatanism, and because of this its delicious fruit was only accessible to the wealthy, and appeared only on the table of kings. Thanks to gardeners of good faith, to lovers of the truth, the day was made; and it is to them that we owe all the progress made by horticultural science. Preferring a just reputation and the esteem of their fellow citizens to monopoly and lucre, they made themselves worthy of their country, and made it share in their discoveries and the good processes of their cultivation. The English have taken a special interest in the cultivation of this plant. Their methods, followed exactly or modified, have been adopted by other nations: in Belgium, Holland, France, Germany, Russia, and so on. A child of the tropics, this plant absolutely 2. 20 wants the temperature of its native country, at least for the time needed to ripen its fruit. In warm regions, where it grows spontaneously, the fruit is infinitely better and much more fragrant than here. The degree of artificial heat required to grow this plant has led to an error that has put off many enthusiasts. It was generally believed that a hot greenhouse or purpose-built tarpaulin, heated almost continuously, was required. This theory, or rather this error, has disappeared. Today, we know that it's not difficult to grow this precious fruit without a fire or hearth. A warm layer of good tannin is all it takes: stable manure covered with a layer of tannin, or the same manure mixed in layers with leaves, are all ways of producing sufficient and healthy artificial heat. The pineapple is no more difficult to grow than the early cucumber, but the fruit always fetches a very high price; rarely does it sell for less than 5 francs; more often it goes for 10, 15 and even 20 francs. It's true that you have to wait for the fruit, and the manure, time and labor costs lavished on it by the grower have to be taken into account; but the fact remains that the product yields, after deduction of all costs, an interest rate of 25 percent. Those starting out in this field should be circumspect in their choice of carnations, taking only the best known varieties or species. Those growing for sale will do well to choose Antigoa violet; it combines to an eminent degree the two conditions that make it so popular for this purpose, i.e. volume and quality. The English call it black Jamaica. The following species are also very good and widely cultivated: the queen, the Muscovite queen, the thornless Cayenne pineapple; they are early-ripening; their fruits, less voluminous, are exquisitely tasty. The following two species, one of which we have already mentioned, are preferable for the sales gardener who is keen to produce large fruit: Trinidad pineapple and Antigoa violet. Pineapples require good, substantial, light, soft soil. The Germans recommend the following compost, and say it's one of the best known: "Cut some peaty loam sod in a meadow, and pile it up without dividing or stirring it. As soon as this peaty loam is to be used, it is broken up by hand, and, to make it more nourishing, a quarter of one of the following ingredients is added to it: butcher's blood, bones, intestines and butcher's debris, or cow dung without straw or other residues. Any of these substances must be fermented, dried and pulverized. Finally, a small amount of lime can be added for better binding. Other compost: - Mix two parts normal earth, one part heather earth, one part potting soil and one part fatty manure. This mixture should be prepared at least six months in advance. The English recommend the following mixture, which dispenses with the need for heather soil, which is difficult to obtain in some localities: In the first spring, sods of Om, 06 to 0m, 10 thick are raised on a lawn, the soil of which must be a fat, substantial earth. The best are those found in a meadow whose soil consists of a frank, soft, yellowish earth. They are laid out in a pasture where sheep are frequently driven, so that they are well polluted with urine and excrement. At the end of summer, these lawns are well divided by the spade, and piled to form a homogeneous mass. Once a month, the pile is turned over, and after six months the mixture can be used. If you can leave it longer before using it, it will be all the better. Don't put it through a sieve; it will become too compact. This soil should not be used pure; especially for young plants, leaf compost and sand should be added in the following proportion: three parts of the above-mentioned soil, one part leaf compost and two parts coarse sand. For plants ready to bear fruit, three parts of compost are mixed with two parts of potting soil and a little chimney soot. Either of these composts can make pineapples thrive, under the guidance of a vigilant gardener. We'd like to point out a fourth compost which requires little care and which we consider to be very good: In a meadow whose soil is soft, light and yellowish (i.e. composed of good free soil; - almost all meadows in Belgium contain it; the provinces of Antwerp, Brabant, East and West Flanders especially provide this excellent free soil; It is not compact and contains sufficient sand), we cut sods from Om,06 to 0m, 10 thick; we place two or three layers of these sods on top of each other, and then a layer of leaves from Om, 20 to Om, 30 thick. Continue in this way until the pile has the right volume for the use and quantity of pineapples you intend to grow. Every month or every six weeks, this compost is turned over and a few buckets of liquid manure are poured into it, or a dozen buckets, assuming that the heap is 3a.50 wide in all directions and 1m.50 high. This soil can be used after a year's time; if you can leave it for two years, so much the better; but then you just have to turn it over every three months. When you start using it, add enough sand if the turf you're using isn't sandy enough on its own. Alternatively, when the first layer of turf and leaves has been laid, a layer of sand two inches (Om.06) thick can be added. In this case, the sand becomes impregnated with the liquid manure and the whole is more homogeneous. This mixture can be used indiscriminately for plants of any age. However, the quantity of sand can be increased for the multiplication of crowns and eyelets. The following compost can also be used: One third normal earth or free earth - this is known to be composed of clay and sand, in a suitable proportion; - one third heather earth and one third good compost, consisting of well-consumed cow manure with a lot of dung. These substances must have been mixed and stirred several times during the year. It is bad practice, as some authors advise, to store pineapple soils and composts in sheds or otherwise, sheltered from the rain: by drying out, fertilizers lose their virtues; it is preferable to leave them 20. freely in contact with atmospheric agents. If the soil is too wet when you need to use it, it's easy to bring a quantity indoors; it dries out properly in a few days. We advise those who have not yet grown pineapples to start in June. We repeat: anyone who has a garden and can set up a bed under a frame can grow pineapples. This is no longer in doubt today, whereas in the past it was impossible to grow pineapples unless you had a warm greenhouse or tarpaulins built specifically for the purpose. Large growers in particular can cultivate pineapples at almost no cost. They can set up the tarpaulins on the south side of the barns or stables, and have little to pay for them other than the glass frames and small walls on the front and sides of the tarpaulin. None of the stable manure they use goes to waste; it is consumed in the tarpaulin and converted into excellent potting soil for all root crops. As for the laborers, they sometimes have sons who would find it a happy occupation, or a servant intelligent enough to be trained in a short time. To create a pineapple bed, we look for a way to supply ourselves with crowns or carnations in June, and we keep them ready for planting at the end of the month.
