You can buy them from restaurateurs in our big cities or from castle gardeners. - In Europe, pineapples don't multiply by seed, but here, as with all plants that don't produce seeds in abundance, nature provides in another way: pineapples produce sufficient young shoots on the stem and at the root collar. These young shoots are called "eyelets": they are true cuttings. The fruit also ends in a bundle of leaves called a crown; this is another cutting, and is even preferred to eyelets, because they are generally considered to develop more rapidly. As for eyelets, those at the top of the stem are preferred to those at the root collar or at the base of the stem. Sometimes the crowns are not very sharp, so they should be rejected. Crowns that do not have at least Om.20 circumference at the heel should also be rejected. - The base of the crown and eyelets is called the heel. - Once the crowns or eyelets are detached, the heel is levelled with a sharp knife, and the cuttings are left to rest for eight days to three weeks. All parts of the pineapple are very succulent; a lot of moisture transpires from the freshly cut heel; if planted in this state and without the wound having healed, the young plant would be prone to rot. As soon as a sufficient number of seedlings are available to fill a bed, this is made up of new stable manure mixed with leaves. This mixture, or alternating beds of manure and leaves, produces strong, long-lasting heat. We're not saying it's stronger than unmixed stable manure, but it's longer-lasting. As pineapples tolerate high temperatures well, it would never be appropriate for horse manure to be too thin, i.e. it must contain a large quantity of excrement, and straw must not be overabundant. Once the layer of manure has been compacted and levelled, it is covered with 0.32 m of new tannin. The pineapple is a plant that bears fruit before the third year is up. Sometimes it produces after eighteen months. This is mainly the case with the early species. Pineapple cultivation is divided into three periods, each lasting about a year. As a consequence of this division, the greenhouse must have three compartments, or three separate tarpaulins, available for when they are needed. Heat must also be graduated according to these three periods. In the first year, we form what we call the nursery, i.e. the planting and management of young plants. In pots with a diameter of Om,10 to Om,15 and a depth of Om,18 to 0m,20, and with three slits in the bottom to allow water to run off, place coarse sand or gravel at Om,03 or 0m,04 high; then fill them with compost, preferably one made up of one-third free-range soil, one-third heather soil and one-third potting compost, made from cow manure and left to stand in the open air for a year. By mixing these three ingredients instantly, you can use them for cuttings just as well as if they had been mixed for a year. At the time of use, the soil must be in a suitable state of moisture, but not so wet that it can be kneaded between the fingers. Do not pack it into the pots, but fill them so that it forms a rounded mound, the top of which rises 0.07 to 0.08 m above the rim of the pot. Push the heel of the cutting into the middle of this light soil, to the depth of Om, 05 to 0m, 06, without making an opening other than by the pressure of the heel; then compress the soil all around the base of the eyecup, using both hands. If, while compressing, you find that the cutting and the soil are sinking too much, add a little soil; if, after firming, there is still too much soil in the pot, remove some until the rim of the pot is free of about Om, 010 to Om, 015. This method is the best of all, not only for pineapples, but for all cuttings without exception. Then bury all the pots in rows of the same height in the tan layer, taking care to ensure that the windows of the frames on the roof are very close to the plants, without touching them. If planted in spring, cover the frames with straw mats during the night, if it's cold, and with clear canvas during the day, if it's hot. Three to four weeks later, the cuttings are rooted, as can be seen from the young shoots and new roots. At this point, we start to water them properly, without wetting the heart of the plant, as this could rot the cuttings that have not yet taken root. As the weather warms up and the plants grow, we increase the watering, and above all we wet the young plant with the fine rain given by means of the fine-headed syringe. It's essential that the water used for watering has been kept in a greenhouse or tarpaulin, so that it doesn't reach a temperature much lower than that of the pineapples. Assuming that planting has been carried out from spring to June or July, we commonly wait until October before placing the plants on a new warm layer, made as before of new manure mixed with leaves. On this layer, either in a tarpaulin or in the warm greenhouse, the pineapple overwinters. Care is taken to cover them carefully with good mulch during the cold months. Six months after planting, the pineapples are changed into new pots, so that those planted in spring are transferred before winter, and those planted in autumn are repotted after winter. The new pots should be around Om, 17 to 0m, 20 in diameter; the soil should also be renewed; it can be made from the same mix as for the cuttings. Examine the roots, cleaning them of any rot, but without injuring the healthy roots: injuries to living pineapple roots are fatal. O2 loosens some of the old soil, thus increasing the dose of new soil and giving the plant stronger vegetation. However, it's worth pointing out that, when repotting, the pots must not be too large: the plant would then grow too vigorously and fruiting would be considerably delayed. In the first year, pineapples can be forced to bear fruit by heat. This process is flawed; it's better to wait until the second and even better the third year before making them bear fruit. The English usually wait until the third year, when they have bigger and better fruit. In the third year, the pineapples need to be re-potted; by this time, the plants are fully developed; they are also given soil as before: the potting soil used could be in greater quantities, or, leaving the ingredients in the proportions indicated above, they can be watered from time to time in spring with an excellent and powerful liquid fertilizer, which consists of a mixture of columbine, sheep dung and water. For this last repotting, the pots are about Om, 25 to 0m, 30 in diameter. The three periods of pineapple cultivation are determined by the age of the plants. Suitable soil and well-graduated heat are the main elements of this crop. In the first year, the temperature of the tarpaulins should vary from 8° to 20° R., depending on the season. Too much heat is dangerous: it causes pineapples to bear fruit. In the second year, if you don't want the young plants to fructify, the temperature should be graduated between 12° and 25° R. During the third year, the true fructification period, the most intense heat is the most suitable: it cannot be below 30° R. and can rise to 45° R. without any inconvenience. When the sun is shining, the frames are rarely opened, but shade is provided by loosely-fitting gray linen. During the day, water the slabs or paths several times, using tarpaulins or greenhouses. As soon as vegetation becomes stationary, stop watering; this is done in winter. There are no fixed rules for watering in summer: plants are watered when they are thirsty. Some authors, however, recommend watering once a week in spring and autumn, and twice a week in summer. These precepts are flawed; watering should be adjusted according to circumstances. The same is true of giving air; pineapples are often given air, but it may be appropriate, even on the hottest days, not to give air; this is done, for example, when there is a hot, dry wind, which carries away dust and dirties the plants. In this case, it's best to cover the frames with canvas, as we've said. These small operations, which together contribute greatly to good cultivation, must be carried out at the right time and as the gardener sees fit. The cloths can be placed inside or outside the tarpaulins; it is preferable to apply them inside, because in the latter case they are not exposed to the rain and wind that wear them out more quickly. These tarpaulins are held in place by cylinders, so that they can be raised or lowered at will by means of two ropes. In very cold weather, the frames are covered with straw mats, mats or plank shelves that fit into the grooves. This last covering, since it completely intercepts the light, should only be used during the coldest weather, and only at night. When pineapples are treated in tarpaulins with no heat other than that of the manure, a tarpaulin must be available for when the exhausted layer needs to be renewed. The same applies to tanning; it hardly keeps sufficient heat for more than three months. The gentle heat of tanning is usually combined with that of steam or boiling water. When this artificial heat is used instead of the heat produced by manure, the tannage can be passed through the pipes conducting the steam or boiling water, or the tarpaulins or greenhouse can be passed through these same pipes, either around the perimeter of the layers, or under the paths, if paths are provided all around them. As for water heat, it undoubtedly provides excellent warmth; but this means of heating is not within everyone's reach, and it would be especially difficult to apply to small-scale cultivation; whereas we have seen, and see every day, this water vapor being lost in large factories: what a precious and easy means of establishing warm greenhouses for pineapples or other tropical plants! The only costs here would be those of the initial set-up, i.e. the side and front walls, and the glass frames. We estimate that pineapple crops grown in this way could produce 50 p. c. of interest. The pineapple (bromelia ananas, Linn.) was dedicated by Linnaeus to his friend Bromel, a Swedish botanist. This plant belongs to the Bromeliaceae family, with firm, gutter-shaped leaves extending from the root collar, with saw-like spines along the edges. In the middle, a strong stem supports a spike of bluish flowers ending in a crown of small leaves. These flowers are followed by three-lobed berries crowned with calyx lobes; together, these berries form a pulpy, pyramidal mass resembling a pine cone, growing from Om, 10 to 0m, 30 in height. A large number of varieties of pineapple are known; here are the main ones: yellow pineapple, a pyramid-shaped, golden-yellow fruit; sugar loaf pineapple, more elongated, larger; Montserrat pineapple (one of the West Indies), a little greenish, one of the best; kidney apple pineapple, oval, small, greenish, 2. 21 pineapple; the white pineapple, oval, orange-yellow, with white, acidic flesh; the thornless pineapple or pitte, with small fruit and non-spiny leaves; the latter appears to be a distinct species; it grows in the woods of Cayenne; Its narrow leaves are 1.00 m long and longer, and are used in this country, where it is hardly cultivated, to make ropes, as is done in the West Indies with agave americana and agave fœtida. The Mahipouri pineapple is grown in Cayenne; its purple, conical fruit is of good quality, with a height of Om, 25 to Om, 30. It is thought to be the same as the Providence pineapple. - The following are still grown: red pineapple, oval fruit, very elongated, pleasant yellow when ripe; pineapple with large purple fruit, round, not very fragrant; new pineapple, with large fruit, weighing up to 9 or 10 kilograms; giant pineapple, lemon-yellow fruit, sweet, melting, height from Om, 25 to Om.30; negro pineapple, with large fruit, weighing up to 9 or 10 kilograms.The pyramidal pineapple with variegated leaves, long, yellow fruit, excellent, leaves striped with red, green and yellow. - There are still other species or varieties; sometimes the same variety has several names, as is the case with almost all plants that pass through the hands of different gardeners. The name pineapple was given to this plant by the Portuguese, from nana, the name given to it by the natives of Brazil. It is very widespread in both Indies, where it grows spontaneously in savannahs and damp, sandy places. According to some naturalists, it originated in the equatorial parts of America, from where it was brought to Indostan by missionaries during the reign of Emperor Akbar. It was also brought from the West Indies by a horticulturist from Leiden, Holland. According to the learned Professor Ch. Morren, to whom Belgian horticulture owes eminent progress, the pineapple was introduced and cultivated in Belgium by the Abbots of Afflighem, long before 1633. Pineapple buds usually appear in October; the fruit ripens at various times, which is more of an advantage than a disadvantage, both for the gardener and the amateur. If such an excellent fruit only had a very short season, the gardener would have to get rid of it at all costs, and the amateur would have too much for consumption. We have already mentioned that the cultivation of this plant is divided into three periods, and that three covers under glass frames are therefore necessary for repotting, which takes place in the spring of each year. If pineapples are grown in a greenhouse heated by the combined heat of manure and thermosiphon, the same greenhouse can have three compartments separated by glass partitions. It is not strictly necessary to grow pineapples in pots; they can be planted in a layer of greasy compost, in the tarpaulin or in the greenhouse; they benefit extraordinarily from this method. However, this method of cultivation has one drawback: it is impossible to put the plant back into pots without removing all its roots, and it has to be reduced once again to the state of cuttings; but, singularly enough, the plant can withstand being martyred in this way without any noticeable delay in vegetation. So, taking them out of the ground, we cut off all the roots, without sparing any; we plant it again and treat it like cuttings, i.e., after putting it in pots, we keep it under a frame, deprived of air and shaded for a few days. This type of pineapple planting is commonly called "bare-bottomed". It is based on the fact that pineapples, whose roots renew themselves every year, do not tolerate injury to their roots: the rotting and pruning that would be harmful to pineapples, in order to put them in pots after having removed them from the ground, means that the roots have to be completely removed, leaving nature to give them new ones. In some countries, there is so little fear of subjecting the pineapple to this operation, that we don't even bother to preserve the roots during decanting, when there would be no disadvantage in keeping them; it's true, as we've already said, that experience has shown that the delays caused to vegetation by this manipulation are not very noticeable; However, for our part, we prefer repotting with preservation of the plant's main nutritional organs whenever possible, i.e. whenever transplanting can be done without significantly damaging the roots. This latter method is followed by the English: in transplanting, they keep all the roots healthy, and cut out all those that are altered or aged. The French, on the other hand, generally follow the method of cutting out all roots, or bare potting. Pineapples are called triennial by gardeners; considered from the point of view of botanical principles, the plant is perennial. It doesn't die after bearing fruit; it produces sprays that continue to grow and develop; by cutting off all but one of the eyelets, it will produce a plant that, in turn, will bear fruit. There's no need to use this method, given the ease of reproduction by eyelets and crowns. Only a few growers keep these old plants to propagate rare species. Pineapples are often infested, as are cacti and aloes, with a species of whitish scale insect. This enemy of the plant is commonly known as the louse, and is destroyed by means of a concentrated infusion of tobacco, as follows: the leaves of the plant are bound together without injury; the soil of the pot is covered with moss, which is tied tightly with a ligature. Once this is done, plunge the whole plant, stem inverted, into the infusion in a suitably large tub. The plant can remain in the infusion at a temperature of 25° to 30° R., for 8 to 10 minutes, without the slightest inconvenience. The plant is then hung upside down to drain. After this operation, most insects are destroyed. Some authors advise repotting plants for this purpose: we consider this work, if not harmful, at least useless; the roots are not attacked by the insect, only the leaves; then, unnecessary repotting is always an unpleasant task. We have already said that it is not difficult to grow pineapples without the use of a fireplace; we have said how the farmer can, at little cost, give himself great profit and pleasure at the same time by this cultivation; we have said how the industrialist who employs steam engines can use the one that is lost; we have one piece of advice left to give to the rich owner who freely disposes of his capital. We advise him to grow pineapples, at least those of the third year, in the open ground, 21. in tarpaulins or greenhouses; the vegetation is then magnificent, and the plants, more robust in all their parts, give bigger and tastier fruit. We're not saying that this process is absolutely new, no; but it's not practiced enough. AUBERGINE. In January or February, eggplants are sown on a bed.

and under a frame covered with straw mats. The layer should be made up of Om, 60 of compacted manure, covered with about Om, 25 of good garden soil. The seed, which should be sown light, should only be covered with Om, 005 to Om, 010 of potting soil. As soon as the young plants have reached sufficient consistency, they are transplanted separately into pots and placed on a warm bed, the pots buried up to the edges, the plants covered with cloches. Around May, the plants can be de-potted and placed in the ground at the foot of a wall. They bear fruit in September. If you prefer to grow eggplants on a bed without transplanting them into the ground, you can grow them as follows: As soon as the young plant has four to six leaves, it is transplanted in a nursery onto another bed; about a fortnight later, it is transplanted again onto another bed, giving the plants Om, 60 apart. Air is given when the temperature is mild, and the frames are removed around May 15, by which time the plants can do without them. Subsequent care of eggplants consists in removing shoots from the base of the plants, removing leaves that are drying out and watering. Let the plant grow up a single stem, cutting off the lateral shoots. In this way, the fruit acquires greater volume and is of better quality. Eggplant is an annual plant native to Africa. It is the solanum melongena of Linnaeus, to which we have given the trivial names mérangène, mayenne, eggplant, mélongène. Several varieties are known, the most widely cultivated of which is the long-fruited purple eggplant. Its stems are 0",60 to 0m,90 high, thick, purplish; its leaves are petiolate, hairy, long from Om,15 to Om, 25 and wide from Om, 08 to Om, 10. Its fruit, quite large, is oblong, dirty purple in color; its flesh is white. It has one variety with round, red fruit; another with round, yellowish fruit; yet another with long, yellow fruit. The last three varieties differ in habit and fruit size, and are less widely cultivated. Eggplant fruit is quite delicate and pleasant-tasting, and can be fried, grilled or stewed. These plants, whose fruit is edible, should not be confused with another eggplant grown as an ornamental. It's known as the egg-laying hen or egg plant (solanum melongena ovifera). Its shiny white fruit is absolutely egg-like and poisonous. CUCUMBERS. Cucumbers are sown from December to the beginning of March. They are grown in the same way as melons. The seeds are sown singly in small pots, sunk to the rim in the bed. When the young plant has two leaves, in addition to the seminal leaves or cotyledons, it is transplanted to another warm layer, leaving all the soil in the pot as a clod. Cucumbers are fairly slow to bear fruit; although they are treated on warm beds, they take no less than two months to produce their first crop, which is harvested two weeks after the fruit has set. In order to have them successively from spring to autumn, they need to be sown several times. Chassis plants require a moderate temperature, which can vary from 14° to 25° R. They need to be slowly acclimatized to the air, which they will never be denied when the weather is mild or hot; then, as with other forced plants, open the chassis gradually, according to the degree of heat of the outside temperature. In March, April and May, it is also necessary to break the sun's rays, by means of leafy branches or other shelters, which do not totally prevent daylight from reaching the plants. In fact, this type of care is used in most forced cultivation. If, in winter, the temperature in the beds falls below 10°, we must hurry to set up heaters for this purpose next to the bed. Cucumbers should be spaced Om, 50 to Om, 60 apart, and when the stem is about Om, 15 to 0m, 20 long, it should be bent back by cutting it with a knife above the second leaf; this is called pruning. The bent stem will grow two branches: these must be cut back to their second leaf. As soon as more branches sprout, and their fruit is knotted, pinch them at two eyes above the fruit. Sterile branches, or those that could cause confusion in the future, should also be pruned. It's up to the horticulturist to direct and space the sprays of this plant appropriately on the bed: this is very easy if the gardener does it in time and before the branches have become an inextricable network. Watering should always be done with lukewarm or sun-warmed water, or even better, with water drawn from a reservoir inside the greenhouse. STRAWBERRIES. The excellent strawberry fruit is one of the most pleasant and healthiest products in the vegetable kingdom. Refreshing, sweet, fragrant - these are the qualities of this generally esteemed fruit. As a result, horticultural merchants and amateurs are always well compensated for their efforts when they cultivate this plant properly. In the open air, the first strawberries are usually harvested in June, and the last in October. The gardener's aim should therefore be to grow strawberries during this period, i.e. from November to May. Forced cultivation provides us with this means in several ways: In March, we lay out beds 1.33 m wide, leaving paths of Om.60 between them. Each bed will contain four rows of strawberry plants, spaced Om.30 apart in a checkerboard pattern, if we use those known as Alpine or Four Seasons. If some of these strawberry plants bloom in spring or summer, the flowering stems should be removed; the runners should be carefully removed as they are born. The rest of the summer care consists of mulching with short manure, weeding, hoeing and watering. As soon as the cold weather arrives, we place the trunks, whose ordinary size is such that they enclose the planks right up to the edges of the paths. These paths are then filled with warm manure, which is well compacted and raised to the height of the frames placed on the boxes. Every evening, the mats are unrolled over the frames, and removed in the morning; air is also provided if the temperature is mild. The gardener's particular attention should be paid to destroying the snails which, throughout the winter under the frames, do immense damage to the strawberry plants, gnawing away at the most tender parts, and in particular the buds of new flowers. One person holds the frame open, while another, light in hand, hunts them down with tweezers. Another way of forcing strawberry plants is to put them in pots well in advance. In spring, in pots Om.16 to Om.20 deep, with the same diameter at the top and inner walls, plant seedlings from the previous year's nets in good, loose, terra-cotta soil. These pots will be exposed to the rising sun, so that the plants receive the sun's beneficial rays from morning until eleven o'clock throughout the summer. The pots should be buried up to their edges in the soil of the bed or flowerbed. The space left between them should be such that, once they have reached full growth, the plants do not touch each other. Great care should be taken with watering, especially during droughts when the roots cannot draw any moisture from the soil other than that in the pots. Flowers and netting are removed during the summer. From November onwards, these potted plants are placed under glass frames, without a layer of manure, just to protect them from frost damage. In December, January or February, depending on when they are to be forced, they are placed in the greenhouse or under canvas, where the heat is raised to 10° up to and during flowering, and to 15° during fruit formation. The time that elapses from the moment the strawberry plants are brought into the greenhouse until the first fruits are harvested is about 60 to 70 days. If you want an uninterrupted succession of fruits, you need to replenish the greenhouse every twenty days, until March 15th, with pots that are ready under the frame. Cultivation is rarely successful when begun before January, but it is always successful when begun in February and March, and fruit is more tasty and abundant the closer it is to spring. This is mainly because there is often no sun in winter, and strawberries, like pineapples and so many other fruits, want to be invigorated by its rays. A few pots of strawberry plants can be placed in the pineapple greenhouse; but, as the temperature of the greenhouse intended for these plants is usually quite high, it follows that the strawberry plants vegetate too quickly and give only an unsatisfactory product. Strawberry plants can be brought in when their fruit is half-ripe, where they finish ripening. Forced strawberry plants require frequent watering around the root collar; watering over the flowers aborts some of them and significantly reduces the harvest. Potted plants thrive best when the surface of the soil is covered with earth. To do this, remove the Om, 03 deep layer and replace it with consumed cow dung. The strawberry plant is very fond of loam and substantial soil; it is an enemy of fresh manure, languishing in it, and its leaves turn yellow. If heat can be supplied by means of a thermosiphon in the greenhouse, cultivation is considerably facilitated and accelerated. For large strawberries, we recommend Keen's seedling and rose-berry for forced cultivation. In fact, we have yet to discover an excellent large-fruited variety that is also suitable for forced cultivation. We still recommend Myatt's surprise and Swainston's seedling for this purpose. MELON. The melon (cucumis melo, Linn.), a member of the gourd or cucurbit family, is native to Armenia; consequently, in northern climates, it can only be grown under cloche or chassis, in a tarpaulin or greenhouse, if ripe fruit is to be obtained before mid- or late summer. If it is possible to grow it outdoors, as we'll explain later, the plant requires some preliminary care that plants grown outdoors in our climate can do without. This is not to say 14 that cultivation is difficult, it's far from it; on the contrary, we consider it very easy. For early melons, or those due to ripen before summer, a bed is prepared in January under a frame. When the temperature of the potting soil covering the manure has dropped to -25 or 30° centigrade, the seed is sown in potting soil mixed with one-sixth sand and covered with Om,010 to 0m,015 of the same potting soil. After five to six days, the seed sprouts. Seedlings can be sown in small pots, which are buried up to their edges in the soil; one seed is placed in each pot. The frames are then placed and covered with mulch or litter. After the seed has sprouted, when the sun is shining brightly and the outside temperature is above zero, air should be supplied from 11 a.m. to 2 a.m., by lifting the panels from behind from Om, 03 to 0m, 06. At the same time, the doormats must be removed, an operation that should never be neglected, even when the temperature is 5° or 6° Réaumur, provided the sun is shining on the frames. Heat must be maintained by means of stoves, which must be changed from time to time. If, despite the stoves, the heat of the bed were to fall below -10° centigrade, a new bed would have to be made on which to transport the pots. Layers made of stable manure, mixed with leaves or tannin, retain heat for a very long time, and can sometimes be sufficient until it's time to put the plant up permanently. By growing the plant in pots until it's ready for transplanting, it's easier to put it in place, and the rootball stays intact if you know how to remove it with a little dexterity. These pots for CULTURE MARAICHERE. 2. 22) melon pots are from Om,07 to 0m,10 in diameter; they are arranged side by side to avoid wasting space in the bed. We would point out that the plants must not be kept in these small pots for too long, as they will then become stunted, and their roots, which completely cover the walls of the pots, cannot all be preserved. As soon as the first leaves appear above the cotyledons, you need to check whether the plant has sufficient roots. This is done by placing the left hand on the pot, passing the plant by its base between the middle and ring fingers; at the same time, with the right hand, the pot is tilted so that the clod of earth rests entirely on the left hand, while the empty pot is in the right hand. If the lump of earth is difficult to remove, we give it a few jolts by lightly tapping the rim of the pot on the wood of the chest. These little operations are familiar to all gardeners, so we'll only mention them for the inexperienced. As soon as the melons have two leaves, not including the cotyledons, the head Om, 006 to Om, 007 is cut off above these second leaves, and a little dust is put on the wound of the young stem, which then heals more quickly. After this initial pruning, two branches will soon grow from the leaf axils, spreading away from each other. These, in turn, should be stopped when they have developed sufficiently to be cut off above their fourth leaf. Each leaf gives rise to a new stem, eight for the two initial branches. These eight branches are cut off above their third leaf. All these branches are distributed evenly, so that they form rays that diverge from the base of the plant. Female flowers soon appear on these third branches, distinguished by the development of their ovary, which forms the nascent fruit. Pruning is then carried out for the fourth time, with the aim of better knotting the fruit, which would not benefit from the sap that would be carried uselessly in the superfluous branches or leaves; at least, this is the generally accepted opinion. As soon as the fruit is about the size of a hen's egg, all the runts or malformed fruits are removed from the same plant, leaving a few of the larger ones, which are then cut off as soon as it is seen that two fruits are continuing to develop on two different branches. Only two fruits are left on each plant; some gardeners even keep just one. At the second pruning, the soil should be covered with a light layer of litter; if you wait any longer, the multiple branches will interfere with this operation, which is carried out to prevent the plants and their fruit from resting on the soil, whose humidity can sometimes lead to cankers or rot. Young fruit should be protected from the hot summer sun, either by covering the frames with tree branches or straw mats, or by covering the fruit itself, by tilting a surrounding leaf over it without breaking it. It's essential to use water sparingly, and never water the flowers while the fruit is setting; wetting them can cause many to abort. If necessary, water around the base of the melon. Once the fruit has set, it is no longer harmful to give the whole plant a light wetting from time to time, either with water that has been kept in a greenhouse, or with rainwater that has recently fallen while the temperature is mild; but cold well water should never be used. You can tell when a melon has reached the right stage of ripeness when there is a slight tear at the stem, indicating that the fruit is about to detach itself, when the flesh gives way a little at this point under the pressure of your finger, when it changes color and becomes fragrant. Instead of taking care of melon seedlings in pots until they are in place, you can sow them in the same layer from the start, transplant them in due course to a new layer by removing them in clods, and treat them otherwise as described above. Under each panel, plant only two melon plants at Om, 25 one from the other, regardless of how they were previously treated. As we have said, first-season melons are sown in January, second-season melons in February, and third-season melons in March. For all these periods, cultivation does not vary much; however, melons sown in March or late February can be grown under cloches on muted or less warm beds. Melons sown in January ripen, if properly managed, in May; those sown in mid-February can produce ripe fruit towards the end of June. We'd now like to talk about growing melons in the ground, and this is not the least interesting. In good soil and with a good exposure, they fruit constantly when the year is favorable, i.e. if the summer is hot and dry. On the contrary, the year is unfavorable if the summer is cold and rainy. It follows from this that cultivation in the open ground is somewhat fortunate, but also that fruit grown in the open ground is tastier, and cultivation is much less costly. In March or April, open a trench Om,35 deep and Om,60 to Om,80 wide, and fill it to Om,35 above the outside soil with well-packed horse manure or other manure likely to heat up; cover this manure to Om 25 with good garden soil containing plenty of decomposing fertilizer. Seeds or young plants are planted 2m,00 apart and immediately covered with cloches. Pruning is the same. To grow melons in their simplest form, square or round holes of Om,50 in diameter, Om,25 deep and 2m,00 apart are opened. These holes are filled with half-consumed manure, Om, 25 high above ground level. The soil used to cover these well-packed manure cones should be good garden soil mixed with potting soil. As soon as pruning is complete and the branches are touching the sides of the bells, remove the bells and place them back on three pieces of wood, so that the melons can enjoy the air without the rain reaching them. Melons are often attacked by the grise, a microscopic insect that lodges itself by the billions on the 22. surface of the leaves, giving them a floury, powdery hue. This insect does not attack healthy melons; everything leads us to believe that it only attacks melons that have been left to languish from thirst, and which have been kept under closed frames due to excessive heat, while the sun is scorching. The parenchyma and epidermis of the leaves undergo an alteration, after which the insect appears to emerge. This insect can be destroyed by spraying with water in which a small quantity of potassium sub-carbonate is dissolved, or by burning soot under the frames. Melons vary constantly from seed to seed, so you can never be sure of reproducing a variety identical to the one from which the seed was taken. Melon brodé or maraicher is the best and only melon that lends itself well to cultivation in the open ground: it has the following varieties: melon maraicher, round; melon langeais, oval; melon brodé à chair verte, very-brodé; melon sucrin à chair blanche, oval, small, melting; melon d'Honfleur, large; melon de Coulommiers, large, green fruit. Among the best varieties grown indoors, we'd like to mention first and foremost the white-fleshed Prescott melon. Next come: cantaloupe melon, sometimes warty; early fine cantaloupe melon, depressed, small; orange cantaloupe melon, very early; large black Dutch cantaloupe melon, oval, very large; large Portuguese cantaloupe melon, with high, scabby ribs; South Carolina melon, a deserving variety; small, embroidered, oval fruit, no ribs; very sweet, spicy flesh; very thin rind. Among the melons with smooth rind, which keep longer in the fruit store than the others and are known as water melons, winter melons, the following deserve the grower's attention: Maltese melon, white flesh, elongated fruit; Morée melon, elongated fruit; Maltese melon with red flesh; Peruvian melon; Odessa melon. These melons are called water melons because their flesh is very watery, very melting and more or less sweet. Outwardly, they are distinguished by their smooth rind, whipped light and dark green; their red or greenish-white flesh, odorless fruit. No watermelon is as good as the cantaloupe or the brodé melon; but their long shelf-life until the end of February, in the fruit store, is certainly worth something; then we must take into consideration that this fruit is one of the healthiest and much less indigestible than other melons. CHILI. Pepper (capsicum annuum, Linn.) is a plant of the solanaceae family, native to South America. It is known as pepper, pimentcorail, Guinea pepper, long pepper and Spanish pepper. There are several varieties, differing in the shape of the fruit and the degree of pepperiness. In India, it is widely used as a seasoning that stimulates the appetite in the same way as mustard and other spices, which act on the salivary glands. Orientals cut the fruit into small pieces and eat it with every mouthful of meat. In Belgium, chillies are also cultivated for their fruits, which are usually preserved in vinegar like gherkins. The milder fruits of some varieties are eaten raw in salads: the sweet chili pepper, the chile pepper, the yellow pimenttomate with small, rounded, yellow, sweet fruits; the large, sweet purple chili pepper, with long, paunchy, purple fruit. Sow in February or March on warm soil, under a frame. As soon as the plant is strong enough, it is removed as a clod and planted on another layer; or in May, it is planted in rows along a warm wall. Fruit ripens during the summer. Dietsed G CULTIVATION OF SEASONING PLANTS. ABSINTHE. Wormwood can be propagated from seed or broken plants. This plant thrives in all types of soil and exposure. It is not mentioned here either as a seasoning or as a vegetable, but since time immemorial it has been given a small corner in humble country gardens, and rightly so. Wormwood has well-characterized medicinal virtues; its use is not dangerous. Shepherds and farmers know how to use it on many occasions. In some provinces of Belgium, absinthe is also used according to a traditional religious custom: it is blessed with a few other aromatic plants such as tansy, chamomile, etc. These plants are kept in the hearth of the fireplace, where they are used to make the most of the sun's rays. These plants are kept in the domestic hearth, and when a storm breaks out, a portion of these aromatics is burned, and the smoke of this poor man's incense rises to ward off the storm! These simple customs, which only impiety would dare call superstitions, are all too often lost! - Do they not come from our fathers, whom we respect in them? In recent times, wormwood has been recommended as a sure way of driving fleas or flea beetles away from cauliflowers and other plants of the crucifer family. For this purpose, boil or digest a few pounds of this herb in water; decant the liquid carefully and sprinkle over the plants. Aphids flee and cannot tolerate the bitterness of the plant. Petite wormwood (artemisia pontica, Linn.) can be grown in the same way and is used as a seasoning for pigeons. GARLIC. Garlic grows well in all types of soil, but prefers light, sandy, substantial and warm. It does not usually reproduce from seed, even in countries where it is widely cultivated, such as southern France, Italy and Spain, and where it is an indispensable part of people's diet. It is propagated in cloves, which must not be planted upside down. In Belgium's climate, these onions are planted at the end of March or beginning of April, in beds or borders at a distance of Om, 12 to Om, 15 and at a depth of Om, 03 or Om, 04. When the leaves are dry, which takes place in July and August, the onions are lifted and left for a dozen days on the ground, in the air and sun; then they are made into bundles and hung in a dry place. In Belgium, where garlic cultivation is not as important, it is used only as a seasoning, and always in small quantities2 . There are, however, dishes where its presence is pleasing and, in a way, indispensable. Garlic bulbs are composed of juxtaposed scales, called cloves; they are wrapped in a common membrane or pellicle, from which they must be removed only when they are to be used. ANETH. Dill (anethum graveolens, Linn.) is an annual plant of the Umbelliferae family. In most horticultural literature, it is confused with fennel, which belongs to the same family and genus, but is a different species. The two plants are essentially different. The plant we are concerned with here has lower stems than fennel. In dill, they are only Om, 50 to 1m, 00; then the leaves are shorter, as are the leaflets; the seeds are compressed, concave on one side, convex on the other. They have an aromatic scent of their own, and are used to season pickled onions. Dill is sown in April by dropping a few seeds among the onions or at the edge of flowerbeds. A few plants are more than enough for a household. The seeds retain their aroma for many years. ANISE. Anise is sown in spring, in beds or borders, in light soil kept moist until the seed has emerged. Thinning the plant when it is strong, weeding it and watering it in dry spells are the only care it requires. The stems are cut in August and exposed to the sun for a few days. The dry seeds are beaten and stored in a dry place. The seeds are used. Anise (pimpinella anisum, Linn.) is native to the Levant. The plant is an annual. ARMOISE. Sagebrush (artemisia abrotanum, Linn.), a member of the Compositae family, is a shrub from Om, 60 to Om, 90 in height; its leaves are petiolate, with setaceous divisions, and give off a lemon and camphor scent. A warm exposure and light, substantial soil are all it needs. In spring, it can be propagated by bursting the stems. This plant, native to southern Europe, is scarcely used in Belgium as a condiment or seasoning: it is cultivated rather for its aromatic scent. BASIL. Common basil (ocymum basilicum, Linn.), a member of the Labiatae family, is native to India. This small aromatic plant is sown in March on a bed and planted in May, Om, 25 apart, in a shady spot on soil mixed with compost. This species has the following varieties: green, fine green, violet, fine violet, lettuce-leaf and nettle-leaf. 11 Basil seeds are very fine, so when sowing them, they must be covered with very little soil. Also, when transplanting, care must be taken to lift the young plants into clods. To obtain mature seeds in our climate, we recommend potting a few plants that can be brought into the greenhouse in autumn. These little plants like to be watered frequently. To preserve dry basil, as it is used in many foods, we pull it out before flowering, dry it on a shaded floor, then put it in boxes or jars. Seeds keep for three years. BORAGE. Borage (borrago officinalis, Linn.) is a plant native to Belgium, giving its name to the borraginae family. It is sometimes found on the high edges of meadows. Its blue, pink or white flowers make a beautiful ornament to salads. It is for this purpose that some amateurs cultivate it in the garden. The plant is sown in October or spring; the seed should be spread very lightly and without covering it. It sprouts spontaneously. However, if you wish to harvest the seeds, it would be wise to remove the plants as soon as they begin to yellow and fade: later, the seeds have already emerged from their capsules. CAPUCIN. Nasturtium (tropœolum majus, Linn.) is an annual plant in our region, belonging to the geraniaceae family. 2. 23 16 In its native Peru, it is a perennial. Both large and small nasturtiums are grown in gardens. The flowers of both are pretty, serve as salad supplies and make a very pleasant seasoning. The flower buds and half-developed or pea-sized seeds are good for pickling in vinegar. - They are sown in April, either in the open ground, with good exposure against a wall or tree for support, or in small pots to place the young plants in the open ground, where you see fit. The flowers represent a sort of helmet and the leaves a shield; they have been thought to represent a kind of trophy: hence the name tropæolum, from a Greek word meaning trophy. CHENILLETTE. A small plant of the legume family, of little use; at most, it can only satisfy lovers of the unusual, who like to put it in salads to surprise people who don't know the fruit of this plant. Its French name, chenille, and its Latinized Greek name, meaning scorpion's tail, indicate the similarities that have been seen in the pods of the plants that make up this genus. The seeds of this species, like those of the others, should be sown in April, in substantial soil with a southern exposure. They soon sprout a stem that spreads to a maximum of Om,30; it is lined with oblong leaves, from whose axils small yellow butterfly-like flowers are born in July: these are followed by bristly, hair-covered pods resembling rolled caterpillars. The chenillette, vermiculated caterpillar (scorpiurus vermiculata, Linn.), inhabits the southern provinces of France. CIBOULE. Chives (allium fissile) are sown in March in substantial, light soil, so that the young plants can be transplanted in May, two by two, at a distance of Om, 15 in all directions. The bulbs soon grow and multiply, forming an assembly of small, elongated bulbs that adhere to one another; they are called "tufts of chives". The leaves of this small species of garlic are 0a, 20 to Om, 25 long, spindly, cylindrical and fistulous; they are used, along with the bulbs, as a salad dressing. Garlic is still sown in July, and yields the following spring in April and May. Varieties are known as white, red and early. These small plants are annuals and grow very quickly. If sown in autumn, they should be covered with leaves or litter, depending on how cold it is. Perennial chives can be grown in rows or borders; for all care, clumps should be divided when they become too strong. CHIVEL. The chive (allium schœnoprasum) is smaller than the above; it is perennial and is grown in borders. Its leaves are used as a salad dressing. The plant requires no special care, but Jes tufts should be divided when they have grown too large. Like the common onion, these small plants are particularly fond of poultry droppings. LEMONWOOD. Lemongrass (melissa offic., Linn.), a member of the Labiatae family, is a plant cultivated in our gardens for its pleasant lemon-like scent. It is perennial; its leaves are petiolate, oval and slightly heart-shaped; the flowers are small, white or incarnate in color. It can be propagated from seed or by splitting stumps; the latter is easier. Citronella is native to France and common in the southern departments. Large-flowered lemon balm (melissa grandifl., L.) is worth mentioning; its larger flowers, arranged in one-sided clusters, are purple-pink. We have a variety with variegated leaves. CRESS ALÉNOIS. Watercress is used as a salad dressing, and is considered the best of all plants used for this purpose. With its pronounced, slightly piquant taste, it is a pleasant seasoning for the first salads of spring. It is a powerful aid to digestion and, like 08 watercress, is antiscorbutic and depurative. Sow it from the first days of March and consecutively every eight days, if you want to have it all summer long. The seed lifts very quickly, and the plant is no less quick to set seed, sometimes ten or twelve days after sowing. Cress should therefore be cut very young; once it has set fruit, it can no longer be used. In summer, it needs shade and watering; the more it is watered, the more tender it remains; drought makes it hard and tough. Cultivated passerage (lepidium sativum, Linn.) is an annual plant of the cruciferous family, native to Persia. In addition to the ordinary species, five varieties are known: curly, broad-leaved, golden, Normandy passerage and another curly-leaved variety. PERENNIAL CRESS. Perennial cress (erysinum prœcox, Smith) is a plant that can replace watercress, with the same taste and properties. It is sown in spring, in rays, in a damp spot, on light, open soil. The seeds are small and should be covered with very little soil. SHALLOT. The shallot (allium ascalonicum, Linn.) is a small bulb that encloses four to twelve cloves under a common com23. 14 mum envelope. A variety is grown under the name of grosse échalote, which appears to differ from the former only in the volume of its bulb. Cultivation of this plant is much the same as that of garlic. However, with shallots, one precaution is essential: they must be planted flush with the ground; if buried too deeply, they will rot. Planted in February or March, the bulbs can be used as early as May. ESTRAGON. Tarragon (artemisia dracuneulus, Linn.), a member of the floscose family, is a Siberian perennial. In our gardens, we usually grow a clump of it at the edge of a square, to be used as a seasoning. Its young stems and tender leaves give candied gherkins and salads a pleasant taste that is at once pungent, sweet and aromatic. The plant needs to be cut from time to time during the summer to rejuvenate itself. It multiplies from splinters and requires no care. FENNEL. A perennial plant of the Umbelliferae family, native to Africa. It is found in stony places in some provinces of southern France. It is Linné's anethum fœniculum. It has a variety known as sweet fennel; its seeds are used by confectioners and in veterinary medicine. The root of this plant is 10 straight and tapering; its stems are cylindrical, 1 to 2 meters high, smooth and twiggy; leaves long, three times winged; hairy leaflets, terminal umbels; flowers yellow, small; seeds oblong, flattened on one side, convex and grooved on the other. Fennel seeds are sown in May, in beds or borders, in tilled soil. As soon as the plants are strong enough, plant them in a checkerboard pattern, 0.35 m apart. Water often. They are ridged a first time when they are Om, 15 to 0m, 20 high, and so on up to three or four times as the plant develops. It is used in the same way as celery, to which it is said to be superior. HYSOPE. Hyssop (hyssopus off., Linn.), a sub-shrub from Om,40 to Om,60, of the Labiatae family, is native to France. Its tapering stems have linear-lanceolate leaves, ending in spikes of flowers that vary from white to blue or red. In the market garden, we reserve a small place for it because it is used as a seasoning like thyme. Seeds are sown in March, and it can also be propagated by splinters and cuttings. LAVENDER. Lavender (lavandula spica, Linn.) is a perennial plant of the Labiatae family, with woody, gregarious, quadrangular stems and blue flowers in a terminal, whorled spike. The whole plant gives off a very pleasant, aromatic 16-odour. It multiplies by seed or, more usually, by bursting, in March, April or September. It is planted in clumps or in borders on light, warm soil: it comes to us from the south of France. MARJOLAINE. Marjoram (origanum majoranoïdes, Wild.), a small plant of the Labiatae family, a little woody at the base, has petiolate, obtuse, elliptical, entire, whitish leaves; the spikes are tetragonal, rounded at the top, and the corollas are white. This perennial plant is native to Barbary. Cultivated in France as a condiment, marjoram is an aromatic and fortifying herb used in stews. One or two plants are sufficient in the garden. MINT. One or two clumps of spearmint (mentha crispa, piperita, Linn.), a member of the Labiatae family, are grown in gardens. These and many other species are native, perennial and very hardy. They are easily propagated by separating clumps. ORIGAN. Common oregano (origanum vulgare, Linn.), a member of the Labiatae family, grows on the edges of woods and along hedges. Its aroma is less fine and delicate than that of marjoram, but it has the same uses and requires no care in cultivation. PERCE-PIERRE. Stonewort (crithmum maritimum), a member of the umbelliferous family, is a natural inhabitant of seashores and rocks. This salad plant has almost fallen into disuse. The plant is rarely found in the vegetable garden, but its aromatic flavor and health-giving qualities merit it a square foot of space in the garden. The stone borer absolutely requires sandy soil, or even better, the foot of an old wall, where it establishes its roots and draws nourishment from the calcareous salts. Sow in spring; the plant requires no care; it is perennial and likes sunny exposures. PIMPRENELLE. Burnet (poterium sanguisorba) is a native perennial, frequently used as a salad dressing. Its slightly astringent properties have earned it a place among medicinal plants. For salad supplies, burnet must be kept tender by frequent watering and cut back from time to time. It can be propagated by splitting plants in autumn, or by sowing as soon as the seeds are ripe. It thrives in any soil, and is so easy to grow that it can be cultivated in the most inhospitable soils, where it always provides much sought-after food for woollen animals. ROCAMBOLE. Rocambole (allium scorodoprasum, Linn.), improperly called Spanish garlic, is native to Denmark. It has the characteristic of producing bulbils on its stem, in the axils of its leaves. These bulblets, like the cloves, are used for reproduction. Rocambole is very similar to ordinary garlic; it has the same uses, and is cultivated in the same way. It never bears seed; a few small flowers appear among the saboli, but they abort. ROSEMARY. Rosemary (rosmarinus off., Linn.), a member of the Labiatae family, is an aromatic evergreen shrub 1 to 2 meters tall. It is native to southern France. It is easy to propagate from cuttings in the open ground and in the shade. For all care, the plant needs to be stuffed or sheltered during intense cold. SAVORY. Savory (saturica hortensis, Linn.), a member of the Labiatae family, is a small annual plant that reproduces by itself in gardens once its seeds have ripened. It is used as a seasoning for marsh beans, giving them a slightly peppery, aromatic taste. PERENNIAL SAVORY. Savory virace, mountain savory (saturica montana, Linn.), a member of the Labiatae family, is a plant with hard, woody stems rising to 0.03 m. In spring, it can be propagated from seed or by bursting clumps and planting them in a warm spot, in the corner of a flowerbed or in a border. Its seeds keep well for four years. Like garden savory, it is used to season baked beans and hams. This plant grows spontaneously in barren, mountainous areas of France's southern provinces. SAUGE. Sage (salvia off., Linn.) is a perennial of the Labiatae family. If some plants are favored in the garden for their health-giving qualities, it's sage that claims this right. As a seasoning plant, many people enjoy it with fried or stewed fish, etc. The plant requires no special preparation. The plant requires no care whatsoever on the part of the gardener. Thyme (thymus vulgaris, Linn.), a perennial of the Labiatae family, grows wild in the southern provinces of France and in Spain. Although native to a warmer soil than that of Belgium, this plant is highly resistant to our cold winters. There are several varieties, including narrow-leaved thyme, broad-leaved thyme and variegated thyme. Thyme needs only warm exposure and light soil. In spring, it can be propagated by splintering. Another small aromatic plant, thyme-serpollet, is frequently found on our hillsides, and you could very easily introduce a plant into your garden. Like common thyme, it likes a warm exposure and can be used as a border. Both can be used to season meat and fish sauces. These little plants are tonic, hearty and stomachic. Serpollet varieties include lemon-scented, hairless and white-flowered. LEÉGUMISTE OR MARANCHEE GARDENER'S CALENDAR. The gardener who is observant dominates his colleagues in the direction of cultivation and by the abundance of produce his garden provides. He has many signs on which he bases the timeliness of his work. These signs are drawn from the instincts of animals and the phenomena of plant life. For example, the departure of travelling birds warns him of the approach of winter, which will be all the harsher the more these animals leave in greater numbers. Beetle larvae and ants, which live at varying depths in the soil, are further signs of a more or less severe winter. The gardener can therefore use these and an infinite number of other forecasts, such as the abundance of hawthorn fruit, leaf fall, etc., to direct his work and provide himself in good time with everything he needs to preserve his plants and protect his early and delicate plants from the cold. The same applies to the prognoses that the farmer can draw from the early signs that herald a more or less early season: the return of birds, such as plu2. 24 viers, lapwings, snipe, woodcock, thrushes, and finally the swallows tell him of the cessation of frosts and the return of spring. When the passerines gather in flocks at dawn, calling and twittering, it's a clear sign of good weather. The beautiful song of the blackbird announces the same thing when heard in our woods. The calls of the short-eared owl are a sure sign of cold weather, rain and snow. The late mating of magpies augurs a late spring. In one year, these birds were already mated and nesting in January, followed by a very early and beautiful spring. This year (1850), these birds are not yet mating, and we are on March 24th. Some plants also tell us, even in winter, that fine days are more or less at hand. In December or January, hemerocallis fulva is already showing its first leaves above ground, if winter is not to be very harsh. The blossoming of cuckoo, alder, elborium, spring scilla and snow-pearl galanthus are further signs that spring is on its way. Finally, we advise growers who pride themselves on their horticultural knowledge to pay close attention to all the signs which, taken together, can provide a prognosis of the coming weather. - The ancients have already bequeathed us some of these signs, which are invaluable to us today. Shepherds and shepherds were sometimes very expert in this science. We once knew an old shepherd who was never wrong about the weather for the following day, or even for several consecutive days. When asked for information, he would immediately look around, his head raised, and the oracle would speak. We tried in vain to fathom his secret; simple and honest as he was, he wouldn't hide it from anyone, but he didn't know how to communicate it. All the signs that the horticulturist can come to know, combined with those of the barometer, thermometer and hygrometer, lead him to a kind of certainty that rarely makes him fail in his work. - A whole harvest is at risk if he sows a little before the storm; however, if he consults the barometer, that indispensable instrument for every farmer, he will be safe from such accidents. After all, let's avoid a vicious routine and not be afraid to rely on the lessons of our great masters and our own experience. JANUARY. Work in January includes ploughing, preparing and transporting compost, soil and manure, and trimming hedges. Carrots, celery, cardoons, artichokes, cabbages, etc. are placed in sand in the vegetable greenhouse. Sow marsh beans, early peas and parsnips in warm soil. The sprinkler system is covered with litter or leaves to stimulate vegetation in the passes. Layers are set out under frames and fitted with straw mats; melons, tomatoes, eggplants, lettuces, radishes, supplies and purslane are sown. If you have tarpaulins or greenhouses, you can force all kinds of vegetables into them, such as peas, beans, lettuce of all kinds, asparagus, mushrooms, etc.; all kinds of fruit: strawberries, pineapples, etc. You can also heat third-grade pineapples. We heat third-year pineapples, white and green asparagus. Frames are placed over strawberry plants that are to be forced into the ground. Dutch beans are transplanted on beds and under frames. Reheating is carried out; air is given when the sun is shining, and artichokes in the open ground are uncovered, weather permitting. The gardener uses the rainy or snowy weather to clean seeds and make doormats. FEBRUARY. Red and white cabbages, Savoy cabbages, early potatoes and romaine lettuces are planted. Cabbage, carrots, parsnips, onions, celery, leeks, etc. are planted, and covered when it freezes. Plant small bulbs of garlic, shallots and spring onions. Sow peas, broad beans, onions, spinach, carrots, parsnips, cabbage, asparagus, lettuce, parsley, chervil, celery, radish, watercress and chicory. We transplant beans and peas sown in November and December. New beds are built; worn-out ones are demolished; cantaloupes and market gardeners are sown; those that are sufficiently advanced in vegetation are transplanted onto other beds. Beds on which lettuces, radishes, etc. have been harvested can be ploughed to be sown with other vegetables, or to receive cauliflower, lettuce, etc. seedlings. Beans can be sown on a bed and transplanted to the ground in March, covered with cloches on cold nights. Artichokes are uncovered when the weather is mild. Rhubarb is hoeed; sea cabbage is ridged; York sprouts, sown in early September, are planted. Green romaine sown at the beginning of October is planted on the coast; cauliflower sown in September is counter-planted, and early carrots and leeks are sown among them. Spinach is sown as a starter to early cabbage. - The first melons and cucumbers are sown on beds and in trays; pink radishes are planted with early carrots; celeriac and common celery, red and Savoy cabbage, and eggplant. We continue to heat white asparagus, sow endives and Dutch beans. MARCH. In March, the previous month's sowing and planting continues, either in the ground or on beds. Cabbages, early potatoes, peas, broad beans, etc. are planted in the open ground. Sow onions, carrots, parsnips, turnips, chervil, salsify, scorzonera, turnips, radishes, chicory, chervil, spinach, arrowroot, sorrel, pear, cauliflower. Beet and turnip seedlings are planted. - With few exceptions, all seedlings are sown in the open ground. Peas sown in November are rowed, as the rowing guarantees wind protection and the peas benefit more. We remove covers from plants in the open ground; we clean artichokes; we mulch strawberry plants; we earth up; we crimp and hoe cabbages. Plants in trays are given plenty of air, and watered in the morning. New beds are prepared for melons and cucumbers already transplanted or grown on the first bed. All last month's seedlings continue to be sown. As24. perges are sown, and new plantings are made. Seedlings that could not be planted the previous month are also planted. Tarragon, lavender, lemongrass, hyssop, mint and oregano are multiplied by splinters. Chervil and leaf lettuces are sown as onion interplant. Tomatoes, eggplants and melons are planted on the bed, and pumpkins are sown. The last chicory shoots are etiolated. APRIL. All March sowings are renewed; in addition, white and red cabbage, York sprouts, Savoy cabbage, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower seeds are sown. Peas continue to be planted in uninterrupted succession. It's time to sow cardoons, lentils, chicory, endives, escarole, arrochia, tetragonia, baselle, perry, etc. At the end of the month, beans, pumpkins, giraumonts, tomatoes and peppers are sown in the open ground in good exposure. Artichokes are grilled and planted. During this month, all plants that are to produce later, such as cabbages, cauliflowers, peas, broad beans, carrots and onions, should be crimped and hoeed thoroughly. Plants that require these operations are mulched and earthworked. Melons are trained and pruned; the mushroom bed is cared for. The beds are dismantled and prepared for further cultivation. - It's time to plant nutsedge. Chard, picridie, burnet, watercress and, until July, white quinoa are sown. 16 Squares are planted with Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, Savoy cabbage, cabbage, York sprouts and so on. Spinach is crimped and weeded. Part of the previous month's work continues, with planting of all kinds of cucurbits, melons, gherkins, squash, etc., in the open ground. It's time for the main bean sowing; time to weed, hoe, transplant, water many plants, thin out onions and carrots. Pink and white radishes, pink and violet turnips, which came on beds, are exhausted in this month; the beds have been given another destination. The care of melons, strawberry plants and other early crops in trays continues apace. Strawberry seedlings are being transplanted onto old beds. Pineapples continue to be cared for. Melons and batatas are planted under cloches. Purslane is sown. Doormats need to be brought in as weather permits. SUIN. As at the end of May, planting of cabbage species and varieties continues. We plant leeks and the last melons; we sow the last pea seedlings; we sow more arrowroot, radishes, lettuce supplies, purslane, raiponium, spinach, cauliflower, carrots, broad beans, beans to have their produce in autumn. After the first harvest, artichokes are grommeted and flayed, for a second harvest in autumn. Early potatoes, small carrots and onions are already being harvested. With this harvesting, the caD0 rotte and onion seedlings are thinned out. This is the time to spread manure between the young onions, if this operation has not already been carried out. As we said in the article on the cultivation of this plant, it thrives extraordinarily well. Seed harvesting begins with lamb's lettuce and chervil, and is soon followed by several other plants. The bells are pulled in, and the panels and trunks removed. Watering must be given every evening to the plants that need it; it's one of the great occupations of summer. JULY. Large Savoy cabbages are transplanted. Leek planting continues. We can still sow all the seeds of plants that can be harvested before winter. The last cauliflowers are planted, whose apples can be used before or during the winter. A host of seeds are harvested: spinach, raab, lettuce, cabbage, carrots, beans and peas. Celery, crenellated oxalis and olluco are harvested. In this month, early melons produce their excellent fruit; they are soon followed by second-harvest melons, which are usually the first to be cultivated by amateurs. If they are later, their quality is almost always superior. Scorers are sown to harvest their roots the following year. At this time of year, strawberry plants require abundant watering. Transplanted strawberry seedlings are planted in May. 28 Celery is ridged; cardoons and endives are tied and stuffed to blanch them. Strawberry plants are planted in the ground. Strawberry beds are well cared for, either in pots or in the ground, to force them into winter. Pick seeds from chives, radishes, turnips, celery, parsley, carrots, beet, onions, leeks, chervil, lettuces, etc. Artichoke heads are tilted to harvest the seeds and protect them from humidity. Watering continues, as do weeding, hoeing and ridging. Early potatoes are removed and put in a dry place for next year's planting. Start sowing cauliflower, spinach, chervil, etc. Manure is prepared for the first mushroom wheels. Spinach and lamb's lettuce are sown for autumn, and gotte lettuce is transplanted on a worn layer; - at the beginning of the month, white onions are sown for autumn transplanting, and towards the end for spring transplanting. Rhubarb is also sown. SEPTEMBER. In this month, spinach, cabbage, cauliflower and York sprouts continue to be sown; leeks are planted. Marsh beans and crambe seeds are harvested. We plough up layers that have ceased to yield to sow cauliflower or to plant. The time has come to make mushroom wheels; in this season more than any other, their success is assured. We are busy with pineapples; we are multiplying watercress; we are sowing carrots, peas and beans 18 from Holland to bouquet, lettuces to be cultivated under chassis to have the products in winter. The last melons ripen; cucumbers, giraumonts, pastissons, pumpkins, winter melons and other edible cucurbits are harvested to be preserved for varying lengths of time in winter. Eggplants and tomatoes are also harvested. Tomatoes are first sown in trays. - Cabbages and Savoy cabbages are transplanted in nurseries. Asparagus, cardoon, celery, endives, escarole, chicory, arrowroot, salad burnet, pear and beet seeds must also be harvested. OCTOBER. During this month, spinach, radishes, chervil, lamb's lettuce, cauliflower, early peas, etc. are sown in warm conditions. We arrange the greenhouse for the vegetables. Sand is stocked to preserve vegetables; cardoons are stuffed and placed in sand in the cellar as frost approaches. Asparagus stalks are cut and the beds cleaned. Break up all the old layers; pile up all the manure and compost from them to cover the manure in the new layers. We stock up on leaves, and place them near the artichokes to cover them even in the event of light frosts. We transplant little black lettuce to provide the first early salad. We transplant red and white cabbage, Savoy cabbage and cauliflower; we thin out spinach and hoe it. We clean vegetable beds intended for forced cultivation, such as those for strawberries, asparagus, cauliflower, etc. Pineapples and mushroom beds are treated. Yellow nutsedge is harvested in this month. NOVEMBER. Forced cultivation begins, requiring a great deal of attention. Asparagus is grown on hot beds surrounded by stoves. Cauliflowers and lettuces are planted on the same bed; root crops continue to be harvested and placed in sand in the cellar or vegetable greenhouse. Cauliflower, kohlrabi, broccoli, cabbage, Savoy cabbage, salsisis and scorsonera, endives, artichokes, cardoons, beet, potatoes, celery, etc. are brought in. A number of these vegetables and roots are planted in gauges in the open ground. We plant St. Catherine's peas, fertilize asparagus and collect leaves to cover many plants. Brussels sprouts and green cabbages are put in gauges. We also take care of hedge planting, mowing, soil movement and so on. Chicory is arranged to prepare it for shrivelling. Broccoli clods are removed and placed in trenches to be covered with frames or straw mats during the frosts. Artichokes should be buttered, and stuffed if the weather warrants. - Similarly, depending on the degree of cold, cloches and layer frames should be covered. DECEMBER. The work of the previous month continues. Melons are sown on beds and under frames. Early crops such as carrots, radishes, lettuces, beans and peas are also sown. Strawberries are forced; p8 pineapples are tended. Cauliflowers are planted; stoves are set up if the layers lose heat. Increase blankets if the cold becomes more intense. Care is taken to ensure that the blankets around the artichokes are not too light; they are increased as the frosts continue. Finally, we visit the vegetable cellars and greenhouses, and take care of the mushroom beds. During this month, the focus is on arranging composts and working the manure and compost heaps. END. Van Hulle, which we are publishing, a work which we feel it would be useful to reproduce. This work is entitled Tableau d'assolement d'un jardin potager, and contains very precise details on the way in which the succession of harvests should be carried out. As can be seen from the table, the land devoted to growing vegetables is divided into four main zones, corresponding to the number of years making up the rotation period. These zones are in turn subdivided into more or less extensive areas, a sort of park where edible plants are arranged according to the species or class to which they belong. In spite of the numerous remarks it contains, the model crop rotation at the end of this volume would perhaps have been only imperfectly understood if a few explanatory details had been neglected. The author seems to us to have fully grasped the disadvantages of too much obscurity in this circumstance; by prefacing his work with preliminary observations, he wished to avoid a gap which would often have had the CULTURE MARAICHÈRE. 2. 26 often distorted his thinking. - With the same aim in mind, we have translated the lines that we felt related to the attached table, and we have inserted them verbatim so as not to destroy the overall concept. Market garden produce generally falls into four distinct categories: 1° Root crops. - Chicory, carrots, radishes, parsnips, scorzonera. 2° Mealy products. - Lentils, peas, broad beans, etc. 3° Stem plants. - All varieties of cabbage, cabbage shoots, cauliflower, etc. 4° Herbs. - Chervil, purslane, sa- lads and other plants not included in any of the preceding classes. When starting a vegetable garden, whatever its nature or exposure, it is divided into four more or less equal parts, depending on the qualities of the soil and whether it is more or less capable of producing one or other of the aforementioned crops. The market gardener's year begins in February or March, except in the case of forced cultivation and a few other exceptions. The most fertile part is set aside for herbs such as chervil, spinach, etc., which, being partly removed in May or June, are followed by other herbs of the same species, such as celery, leeks or endives, which do perfectly well after fertilizing, but even better 99 without fertilizer. All of these are removed, or have already been removed, in winter; then layers of manure are spread on the field as soon as possible, and wheat lettuce can be sown in it, if (as often happens) the season is not too far advanced. The year is thus over; two harvests have been made, and the land is prepared, or begins to prepare itself again, to receive the next year's crops. The second part, immediately after the first in terms of fertility, is ready to receive root crops. The early carrots are removed in June or July, when salad endives, celery, horseradish or purslane are grown, choosing from among these plants those that are more or less exhausting, depending on the amount of manure expected to be available the following year. Carrots, parsnips, chicory and scorzonera, which are sown later, are removed in November; it is then difficult to harvest any more from this field; the best thing to do is to spread layers of manure as soon as possible. The year is thus also over for root crops. The third part receives beans and peas. When the early peas are removed, they are replaced by leeks, purslane, endives or celery; often dwarf beans are planted in the purslane as a third product. After the leek, etc., manure is usually spread. Spinach can also be sown after early peas, producing well into winter. After late peas, plants that can be harvested later in the season can be brought in, or the field can be used to grow strawberries; in the latter case, the soil needs to be heavily fertilized. Princesses and beans are most prized at the end of the year. For abundant harvests, they should be sown after early peas; they are then perfectly successful, and are also much sought-after by consumers at this time of year. However, spinach or small radishes can still be sown, as they are formed before the frosts and can be enjoyed for some time. In all other cases, the soil is heavily fertilized, then wheat salad is sown. In this way, the third zone, like the previous two, completes its laborious career. The fourth area is used for cabbages of all kinds. Red cabbages are sometimes planted before winter. Sprouts and green cabbages are planted in land that had previously been used for other crops, such as spinach and early lettuce. Green cabbages are transplanted too late to leave the field unproductive until planting time. Cauliflowers, although belonging to the fourth section, are planted in the best soils, because they never succeed in poor soil. Moreover, cauliflowers can be planted in the same place all year round, as they follow on from each other without any problems. They can also be planted as a second crop after onions and shallots. After the various cabbage species, it's impossible to sow anything else. We therefore spread manure on this field as soon as possible, and sow rye, which we cut and bury green; but in this case, it's a good idea to scatter the manure between the plants as early as October; cover with soil taken from the furrows or gutters, and sow between red and green cabbages, and sprouts, which are left to grow, until they begin to freeze hard; the year also ends there for the fourth section. These details suffice to explain how the garden will be planted during the first year. What will be grown during the following season, and what crops will follow the plants we have just described? To avoid any confusion, here's how it's done: The vegetable plot is given over to stem plants, which thrive there almost without fertilizing. As most of these vegetable plants are removed early in the season, we can plant certain stem plants, such as red cabbage, even before winter. This year, we reserve the root-plant area for vegetable plants, taking care to ensure that the least difficult vegetable plants follow the most exhausting root plants: for example, leeks after chicory. The space occupied in the first year by floury crops will be occupied in the second by root crops. The vegetables that are sown first, as the rear crop after the mealy crops, are heavily fertilized; in this way, root crops can be obtained the following year without further fertilization. Finally, the fourth part, which was used for stem plants, will be occupied in the second year by mealy products. The same applies to the third and fourth years: by the fifth year, all the products have, so to speak, returned to their original position. In our opinion, this is the easiest, most regular and most rational crop rotation.
