We have assumed that we are speaking to men who are already well versed in the practice of gardening, and for this reason we have not returned to the first principles of the art, such as, for example, the making up of beds and the construction of frames, greenhouses, etc. These sorts of things are, moreover, easy to understand. Besides, these sorts of things can be found in all gardening books. The art of forcing plants to give their produce in all seasons of the year is still far from attaining the persection of which we think it is capable; may our work excite the emulation of growers, and the goal we have set ourselves, that of being useful, will seem very close to being achieved. 2 Coogle --- - T4 PRIME GARDENER. A ABRICOTIER (Prunus armeniaca by Linnaeus; armeniaca vulgaris by modern botanists); a third-growth tree, native to Armenia, from where, we are told, it was transported to Rome and from there to the rest of Europe. The apricot tree, too well known to be described here, offers a fairly large number of varieties. We shall mention the best and most widespread. 1. ABRICOTIX, or Early Apricot. In espaliers, it ripens at the end of June, and in July if grown in the open air. Small, rounded, yellow or reddish on the sunny side. Its flesh is musky and of rather mediocre quality, tending towards yellowish. Its kernel is bitter. This variety reproduces very well from stones, so it doesn't need to be grafted, and in this case the tree lasts a very long time. As its greatest merit lies in its earliness, it is customary to raise it in espaliers with warm exposure. 2. WHITE ABRICOT. It ripens a little later than the previous variety, i.e. at the beginning of July; it is about the same size, with whiter skin and flesh; the latter has a slight peach flavor, which makes it a little more pleasant. Its kernel is bitter. It does well in the open air, but prefers a warm espalier position. 3. ARRicor ANGOUMOIS. Ripens around July 15. It is smaller and usually more elongated than the previous variety. Its color is amber-yellow, more or less reddish and speckled with brown, depending on whether it has been more or less exposed to the sun during its development. The flesh is yellow to reddish, very aromatic, melting and pleasant, but a little acidic. Its kernel is very good and often double. 4. ABRiCOr COMMUR. Ripens at the same time as the previous variety. It is fairly large, reddish-yellow in color, and may be scabby on the light side, or even cracked if the year has been rainy. Its flesh is melting and quite good when grown in the open air, but becomes mushy if ripening is too advanced. Amaude amere. A vigorously vegetating tree, but rapidly thinning out. It is never espaliered, and as it reproduces identically from stones, it is often not grafted; in this case, it is much less robust, which is common in apricot trees. 5. HOLLAND ABRICOT, or filbert almond. Ripens at the end of July. Its fruit is small, reddish, yellowish, with a reddish-brown spot on the light side; its flesh is juicy, vinous, melting, quite pleasant, and its sweet almond has the taste of filbert, from which comes one of the names it bears in the trade. It does better in espaliers than in the open air. 6. ABRICOT DE PROVENCE. Ripens at the end of July. It is small, slightly compressed on the sides, yellowish, reddish on the light side; its flesh is juicy, quite full-bodied, but still a little dry in certain warm years, sweet, vinous. The stone is rough and the tart sweet. 7. ABRICOT DE PORTUGAL, or male apricot. Ripens around August 15. The flesh is yellow, melting, fragrant, with a very pleasant flavor. The tree is delicate and, in our climate, requires a warm espalier. 8. ABRICOT ALBERGE. Ripens around August 15. Its flesh is firm, fragrant, good and excellent for jam. Sweet almond. The tree grows quite tall, is very vigorous, and bears a large quantity of fruit, which sometimes degenerates. It reproduces its variety identically by sowing. There are three sub-varieties: Abricot de Montgamet, ripening a little later, larger, less round, with more melting flesh and the same perfume. Sweet almond. Abricot de Tours, ripening at the same time, larger, more fragrant, better quality. Amande douce. Apricot aveline, differing only slightly from Montgamet, from which it has the same quality. Sweet almond. 9. ABRICOT PÊCHE, or Nancy apricot. Ripens around August 15th; very large, compressed, more or less brownish-reddish-yellow, especially in high winds, and often becomes scabby on the light side if the season is rainy. The flesh is reddish, very melting, with a distinctive and very pleasant fragrance. A distinctive feature of this fruit is the hole in the stone through which a pin can easily be inserted. The tree is of average vigor, and its foliage is usually wilted. It has given rise to a large number of sub-varieties, because it always reproduces more or less well by sowing. 10. ABRICOT ROTAL. Ripens around mid-August. Slightly smaller than the previous variety, more rounded, yellowish, lightly colored, with melted, yellow, fragrant flesh, better than that of the peach apricot. The tree is very vigorous; it is remarkable for the size of its leaves and the length of their petiole. 11. AbRicor MUSCn. ripens at the end of July. It is almost round, with very thin, yellow skin, revealing the stone through the flesh, which is very delicate, fragrant and excellent. This variety requires a very warm espalier. 12. ApRIcor caos MUSCH. It ripens at the end of July. Its flesh, which does not adhere to the stone, is melting and fragrant; its kernel is sweet; the tree is more vigorous than the previous one. 13. ABRICOT NOIR Ou DU rAPX. (Prunus dasicarpa, by Willdenow.) Round, small, dark wine-red; flesh red and clinging to the pit; bland, very poor quality, except in extremely hot years. I have seen other new varieties obtained by Mr. Noiseite, such as the Apricot Vinux, the Apricot de Paris, etc., etc., but they are not as widespread as they should be. PRIMEUR. Apricot trees are only very rarely forced to grow in Paris, either because their fruit is not valued as highly here as it is in the north, since we have an abundance of them in season; or because we suspect difficulties in this operation which do not exist; or, finally, because this carelessness too often results in France in an uncertain sale which sometimes cannot compensate for the cost of cultivation. The apricot tree, so well naturalized in France, has not yet become so in northern Europe above the fiftieth degree of latitude, and particularly in Russia. It's no more than sixty years since the apricots eaten in St. Petersburg were brought there from Paris, and although care was taken to pack them a little before they were ripe and with meticulous care, it's easy to judge their condition after such a long journey. tried growing apricots in greenhouses. He succeeded perfectly, made his fortune, and only then stopped making a secret of his process. Until then, he convinced those who came to buy them from him at an exorbitant price that he was bringing them from Paris. Since then, Russia has harvested enough of these fruits to satisfy the consumption of wealthy people. When it comes to forcing an apricot tree, the variety is not indifferent; those that lend themselves most easily to this kind of cultivation are: the apricotin, the petit musch, the common apricot and its varieties named blanc-groszeespèce, commun hatif and blanc de Provence; the angoumois hatif, and some sub-varieties of the apricot-pêche. Nevertheless, the others could succeed in certain climates, given proper care (1). The tree must be young, vigorous, absolutely gum-free, well furnished with wood so as not to occupy too much space unnecessarily, and provided with a quantity of good fruiting eyes. Without this condition, the flower appears, the fruit sets, but often deteriorates and falls for lack of sap, as the leaves alone have the ability to attract it and concentrate it on the young fruit. A tree destined to be forced must be prepared for this as early as spring, i.e. at the time of the first disbudding. All branches should be left to grow, so that the fruit can ripen in the following order: 1. apricotin, 2. angoumois hatif, 3. petit musch, 4. commun bitif, 5. blanc-grosse-espèce, 6. apricot de Provence, q. apricot-pêche and its varieties. In very cold climates, the latter and its sub-varieties are preferable to the others, although they are less likely to produce fruit, and we extract those that are only likely to bear fruit. We act in the same way and according to the same principles during the second disbudding. As soon as the sap is suspended, spread a layer of three to four fingers of compost over the entire surface of the soil to be covered by the greenhouse, mixing it with the soil by ploughing with a fork, the depth of which will always be proportionate to the more or less superficial arrangement of the roots. It is essential that the fertilizer is fully consumed, because it will immediately provide abundant nourishment for the vegetation, and because if it were still susceptible to fermentation, it would attract and fix moisture to the roots, causing them to mildew or give rise to the deadly disease known as powdery mildew. In autumn, shortly after the leaves have fallen, if you want very early fruit, or more usually in January, you prune short to obtain more beautiful fruit, especially if you want to preserve the trees; in the opposite case, you prune long, and the fruit is more numerous, but of lesser quality. If, as a result of this operation, gummy ooze forms, either on the large limbs or on the cut branches, this inconvenience is remedied by removing the gum or ulcerated part with a scraper, and by applying a little grafting wax to cover the wounds when necessary. The apricot tree flowers and ripens fruit in four months, when its vegetation follows its normal course. Forcing could hasten the process, but to avoid heat stroke, it's much better to delay vegetation a little, and allow four and a half months from the time you start forcing to the time you obtain results. To obtain certain results, it takes about a month to bring a tree into flower. This means that if you want apricots in April, you have to start heating in January. But an intelligent gardener can try to force it on much earlier, and success will crown his care in mild winters, especially in those where the sun often appears. An early season gardener can therefore, by employing the method generally in use, provide fruit from the beginning of April right through to the plein-terre season. He can extend the latter season until the end of September, by planting espaliers in the north, in cool soil and exposure, and by choosing late varieties, such as Portuguese apricots, peaches, royal, alberge and others. There are several ways of forcing apricots. We'll describe them all in detail, because we'll be giving here the general notions that can be applied to all other stone trees, and we'll often refer the reader to them. 1. forcing in crates and greenhouses. This method is scarcely used in regions where the cold does not fall below eighteen degrees, a temperature below which apricot trees cannot survive in the open ground; but it is widely used in Sweden and Russia. The trees are grown in pots or crates, just as oraugers are grown here, given the same care, and wintered in greenhouses. To fortify them, we place them in heated tarpaulins, and treat them in the same way as those we force into flying greenhouses. It would therefore be pointless to give a breakdown of the details that follow. 2. Forcing in a flying greenhouse and in an espalier against a wall. After selecting the tree to be heated and preparing it for this operation by pruning and disbudding, place the flying greenhouse as follows. This greenhouse (fig. 11.) consists of a light framework, which can be dismantled at will, and is made up of cross-members to support glass panels of varying lengths, depending on the height of the trees to be forced, but usually not exceeding eight or nine feet. If the panels are long enough to exceed the height of the trees by only a few inches, they can be placed on the ground with their tops against the wall, but more commonly they are supported on a small plank balustrade, eighteen inches to two feet high. In this case, manure stoves are set up along this support during frosts. Sometimes, to make greater use of the flying greenhouse, it is placed on a bed for early fruit and vegetables, as we're about to say, but it should be noted that this method has the disadvantage of making the trees much harder to defend against humidity. Here's how it's done. At two feet from the wall, a warm layer is raised and given a width of four feet; it must be given just the right height so that it can ferment and emit heat. When established according to ordinary principles, solid stakes are driven one foot from the outer edge, through the entire thickness of the layer and into the ground. These piles should be spaced so that each has a purlin to support, and their tops should be flush with the bed. A long cross-beam is nailed solidly to these stakes, to support the panels and hold them in place, so that they don't sink with the layer as it sinks due to the consumption of manure. Usually, this crosspiece consists of a piece of oak two or three inches wide and twelve to eighteen lines thick, but it would be better to make it from a solid plank one foot wide, covering the outside of the bed and sloping slightly to keep rainwater away from the panels. At other times, the layer is only three feet thick, and the stakes supporting the crosspieces are planted against them and on the outside. This is even the most common method, although it doesn't have the same advantages as the previous one. Here's why: when it comes to heating the layer, the stoves have to be placed outside, and can only be covered with litter, which is not enough to prevent the water from the panels from getting in between them and the layer, and cooling them both. In all cases, i.e. whether there is a bed or not, when the crosspieces are mounted, the glazed panels are placed on top, and their length must be proportionate to the height of the espalier. However, the most convenient are never more than eight feet long. They are secured at the bottom with small iron pegs set into the crosspiece, and at the top with a false coping made of plaster, wood or lime mortar. It's essential that air and cold can't penetrate through any of the joints, so we seal them with moss. On the sides of the greenhouse, which are sealed with perfectly joined planks, there is a door on the east side, and a window on the west side. I assume that the espalier faces south, because if it faced either east or west, the door would have to face south. The door would have to be glazed to make it easier to see what's going on inside, which is more difficult than through the glass of the panels. However, this is not the case. Between the door and the bed, if there is one, we build a brick furnace, or place a stove, but with the extreme precaution of isolating it from the bed, for fear of accident. We must light from outside, and the pipe, which can be made of sheet metal or cast iron, will be much better in the ground. It should cross the entire length of the greenhouse, on the surface of the ground; then, when it reaches the end, it bends upwards, runs along one side of the window, and exits at the top near the last panel. To avoid obstructing the passageway, which has only two feet, if there's a layer, we let him run along it, but never less so than by isolating him sufficiently so that we don't have to worry about him setting fire to it. To avoid this accident, and for other reasons, here's how to arrange the layer inside. Five-foot stakes will be driven against the edge, and these stakes will be used to hold planks lying against each other and encasing the layer; they can be held in place by means of a few nails. In this way, the inside of the greenhouse can be kept clean, there's no danger of fire, and when the layer sags, it can't widen. Finally, it can be loaded with tan, or even potting soil, to force flowers, strawberries, small vegetables, etc. We assume that all these preparations are complete. Now it's time to place thermometers at intervals, to check the temperature. We immediately start building a fire to warm up the greenhouse. It is essential not to let any smoke into the greenhouse, as it is fatal not only for the apricot tree, but for all the plants exposed to it. The temperature must not be raised very high all at once, as too sudden a transition will cause the tree to sprout flowing, etiolated buds, incapable of producing anything, or even preserving themselves; it may also result in fruit buds aborting and developing into wood. For the first eight days, simply set the Réaumur thermometer at between eight and ten degrees, then gradually raise the temperature each day, until it reaches between ten and twelve; maintain this temperature until the bud is very swollen and ready to bloom. In the meantime, there are a number of essential treatments we should mention. At least twice a day, the greenhouse should be visited and entered carefully, i.e. with the door open as little as possible, so as not to let the cold in. If an icy wind is blowing in the direction of the door, sew a heavy canvas curtain or mat over it, and let it fall behind you before opening and entering. If the greenhouse were considerable, and the produce capable of compensating for expenses, it would be even better to build a sort of vestibule out of planks, with a first door, which you would close behind you before opening the door. The pathway is swept and cleaned to remove any matter that might retain humidity. The espalier is carefully peeled of any dead leaves that may have remained, and which would certainly lead to contagious mould; the insects, kermes and aphids, that have hatched as a result of the heat, are carefully destroyed; and lastly, any means that circumstances may require are employed to chase away the humidity. The surest way to do this is to provide air, but this requires great precautions, even if the outside temperature is only a few degrees below that inside. If we were to open without further care, the plant's insensitive transpiration would be completely suppressed, leading to sudden death or defoliation. If the damage did not go that far, the tree would remain languid, and some or all of the fruit would abort. If the outside temperature in the shade is below five degrees Celsius, don't let any air in; if it's between five and eight degrees Celsius, let some in, but don't open the door for as long as necessary; finally, if the temperature is between eight and fifteen degrees Celsius, you can let some air in by opening the door and window, but before doing so, prepare the plants so they won't be inconvenienced. This preparation consists in turning off the furnace until the inside thermometers show that the inside and outside temperatures are more or less in equilibrium, 2 although the greenhouse temperature is still a few degrees higher. Let's return to our espalier, which we left when the flower buds were ready to develop, with the greenhouse atmozphere heated to between ten and fifteen degrees. If the gems are seen to swell much more rapidly than they usually do, it is likely that the tree has been pushed too fast. In this case, the organs of fertilization have not had time to develop fully, so they remain languid, the anthers contain little pollen and, still imperfect, the non-irritable stigma cannot be stimulated by the prolific liquor, resulting in fruit abortion. To overcome this major drawback, the thermometer is lowered by a few degrees, air is given and the sap is suspended for a few days; during this time, the fruiting bodies perfect themselves and acquire all the energy necessary for the act of fertilization. This brings us to the critical moment of flowering. If my advice has been followed to date, and the greenhouse has been heated evenly throughout, almost all the flowers will appear at once, and flowering will only last a few days. But it's during this interval that you need to redouble your care and precautions. Keep the temperature strictly between ten and twelve degrees, no more and no less. If the heat is allowed to drop, abortion will occur through weakness; if it is increased, there will be what is known as erosion and brülure, i.e. the drying out of the authenticae and stigmata. These two pitfalls are easily avoided by monitoring day and night for some time, but a third, humidity, is even more fatal. To avoid this, air is given several times a day, from eleven o'clock in the morning until three o'clock in the afternoon, and more or less loug-time each time, depending on the outside temperature. Old 3 1 13 2 ABR 13 rags are used to wipe off any drops of water that stick to the glass panels. Finally, we provide the necessary watering for the strawberry plants or other plants we grow in the greenhouse, either on the bed if there is one, or in pots placed on the shelves we have arranged for this purpose, and we give them only what is strictly essential. Smoke is particularly dangerous during the flowering period, so great care must be taken to avoid letting it get inside the greenhouse, otherwise all the flowers will abort. As soon as they have reached a third of their size, we increase the heat, but gradually, so that it takes at least eight days to raise the thermometer to twelve or fifteen degrees and keep it there. During the course of this education, the tree should be given the care that circumstances dictate. For example, unnecessary branches should be cut back, branches should be trellised as they lengthen; branches should be disbudded and removed if they are crumpled, etiolated or mouldy. When the tree reaches maturity, remove any leaves that may be hiding the fruit, to let it enjoy the sun's rays. When it's very cold, place good mats over the panels at night, and remove them whenever necessary. Finally, we'll take the most scrupulous care to maintain the interior temperature constantly at the same thermometer reading. If there's a layer, we'll probe it from time to time, and when we see that it's starting to cool, we'll place thick stoves of hot manure all along the outside. You can even pull a good portion of the old manure from the outside, and replace it with new manure from the stable. 3. Forcing into espalier frames. In the north of France, or even around Paris, when you don't have a large expanse of wall for espaliers, you can use M. Noisette's espalier à chassis. Here's how it works: in a direction from east to west, plant two rows of apricot trees, ten or twelve feet apart in each row, with the rows five feet apart. Between the two lines, behind each tree, is a wooden trellis against which each espalier is trellised. These trellis frames are six feet high, plus or minus, and iucliated dedaus between the two planting lines, so that the upper end of those in the right-hand line bears on the top of those in the left-hand league, thus A. When the trees trellised on the frames or trellises represented by the sides of this reversed A, have reached the top, their highest branches touch each other, and their growth is directed in such a way as to force them to die out to the right and left without going any higher. In addition, they are bent for pruning like ordinary espaliers. They can be trained as espaliers à la Moutreuil, à la Française, or en palmette, and this last form is the most advantageous in this case, because the tree occupies half the surface area. For heating purposes, trees are prepared and pruned as described above. The glazed paunches are installed, or a furnace is set up, with an earthen pipe running the length of the espalier, passing through the middle of the canopy formed by the coppice of the two lines of trees. Heat it up, taking care to keep it absolutely warm, as we've said, and take the same care as we've taught you. A warm layer can also be used. To do this, dig a pit two and a half feet wide and ten inches deep under the vault, and fill it with hot manure. On top of this manure, we build a hot bed three and a half feet wide at the nozzle, two and a half feet wide at the top, and we raise it three feet; to preserve its heat, we redo it every two weeks. A furnace is set up as above, but the pipe is passed over the bed, or along one of the sides. This method has been used in the past, but offers no advantage; often, in spite of every precaution, the dampness of the manure attaches itself to the twigs and leaves of the trees, causing them to mildew. In addition to this, only a very small part of the bed can be harvested, because with the exception of mushrooms, asparagus, white chicory and a few other vegetables that can only be eaten blanched, the other vegetables cannot be grown there. In northern climates, where the espalier is used only to obtain fruit in the regular season, and where it would not ripen without this precaution, it is sufficient to place nine- to ten-foot panels in the autumn, leaning them against each other in a vault (the glass must be at least six inches from the surface of the foliage). The joints of the panels are hermetically sealed with moss, so that air and cold cannot penetrate inside; along the panels, at their foot, a bed of hot manure two feet high and two or three wide is placed, and everything stops there. Air is supplied whenever the temperature permits, and the panels are removed entirely when the season is warm enough to allow the fruit to grow and ripen. In this way, apricot trees blossom and set fruit long before the outside trees begin to vegetate, and they have time to improve over the course of the summer. This method can also be used for espaliers against a wall. 4°. Forcing in greenhouses and in the open. For this type of cultivation, you need a warm greenhouse that is entirely glazed, or at least glazed on three sides and above, as described in the article on vines. Apricot trees are grown in crates, and when they are strong enough to produce fruit soon, they are removed with the root ball and transplanted into the greenhouse, in the open ground. If you wish, you can grow them as bushes, but the best way is to espalier them. The care required is absolutely the same as for the flying greenhouse. However, it should be remembered that the more light the trees receive, the easier it is for the fruit to set. So place them as close as possible to the glass. We won't go into detail here on how to build and heat the greenhouse, how to raise the layers, etc. For all these articles, we refer you to the "Greenhouse" section. For all these articles, we refer the reader to general works on horticulture. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. The apricot tree does well in all soils, provided they are not too wet; however, it prefers light, sandy and deep soils, especially when it is free-standing or grafted onto an almond tree, as in this case its roots are taprooted. It can be propagated from seed or by grafting. If you want to sow it - and this is the best thing to do in areas where it doesn't seem to do very well - choose varieties that reproduce identically from the kernel, such as early apricot, common apricot, alberge, peach, etc. Preference is given to the kernels that are the most resistant to disease. Preference is given to the largest kernels, coming from the most beautiful fruits; they are immediately stratified, i.e. placed in a crate, alternating a bed of kernels and a bed of damp sand, and then placed in a frost-free cellar over winter. In October, or better still in spring, we take them out of the sand, and, after having well loosened and ploughed the soil, we plant them two inches deep, in place, or in a nursery eighteen inches or two feet apart; and, if we have planted in autumn, we cover the seedlings with a good thickness of litter or dry leaves, in order to protect their delicate sprouts, already developed to a certain extent, from the effects of frosts. If you want a very vigorous tree, you must sow it in place; if you don't, you must replant it in its second year, and if the soil is deep, you must be careful to follow the authors' advice and cut the pivot. The good gardener falls into this error by recommending that the pivot be cut from trees that are to be trained in espaliers. He gives the pretext that the less vigorous growth is easier to manage. Far from sharing this opinion, I believe that a tree can never be vigorous enough, when it is managed by an intelligent gardener who knows his trade. In fact, a tree grown from noyan behaves and grows in exactly the same way as one that has been grafted. Its fruit is usually a little smaller, but just as good, and the tree is more difficult to gum. Apricot trees are never grafted onto themselves, as this method produces trees that are languid and much more prone to gum than others. All varieties do very well on damanoir, cerisette and Saint-Julien plums, but not on almonds; the crests of peach, angoumois and alberge apricots are prone to peeling off when placed on this species. Grafting is usually done with a dormant-eye escutcheon. I would point out that the plants on which it is placed must always come from seed and never from offshoots. In hot, dry soils, apricot trees are best planted facing east; in cold, damp soils, they are best planted facing south. Open-air varieties produce smaller fruit, but in greater quantities and with a more fragrant taste. Three years after planting, this tree starts to bear fruit, and it lasts because of the quality of the soil. Its flowers appear from the first days of spring, but are liable to be destroyed by late frosts, unless care is taken to shelter them from the slightest danger with mats or canvas. When exposed to the full force of the wind, apricot trees will rapidly thin out towards the base of the branches if they are not pruned, at least during the first four or five years. Pruning consists of hollowing out the inside of the tree's head to allow easy access to air and light, cutting off all misplaced or useless branches, and draining the sap towards the lower part of the branches. As for espaliers, they can be trained in palmette, French or Montreuil style, like peach trees; it's true that the wood is irregular and less suited to symmetrical shapes, but as this tree has the quality of growing back on old wood, with intelligence it can always be trained. Fruit-bearing branches should be pruned short, and even, when trellising, it is sometimes necessary to remove part of the shelters, otherwise the tree will be exhausted and remain sterile the following year; those that remain become much bigger and better. The small lambourdes are left intact. When ripe, if you carelessly uncover the fruits by suddenly pulling back the leaves under which they are hidden, the sun will catch them, burn them and make them fall. This operation must therefore be carried out carefully and gradually. When an apricot tree is bald, either because of age or because you've neglected to prune it, you pull it back close to the trunk, and it soon forms a new head. But it soon wears out and perishes after producing a few harvests. For further details on ordinary cultivation, not only of the apricot tree, but of all the plants mentioned in this book, please refer to the excellent Manual by our collaborator Mr. Noisette. 14 1 ABSINTHE (GRANDE), ALUINX, ARSINTEE ROMAINE, ADSINTES COMMUNE, ARMOISE AMÈRE (artemisia Absinthium); perennial, indigenous plant, aromatic in all its parts, which is taken as an infusion and used to make liqueurs. Absinth retains all its cultivation qualities when dried out, and has never been subjected to forced cultivation; we need only mention its ordinary cultivation here. It thrives in all types of soil, but prefers those that are substantial, light and slightly damp, albeit warm. In the south, it lasts fourteen or fifteen years, and acquires much more energetic virtues. It could be propagated from seed, but it's much easier and quicker to spread it from clumps or suckers, which you separate and plant in autumn or spring. What's more, it is very often self-sowing, and all that's needed to multiply it abundantly is to care for the young plants that grow naturally around the mother plant, and transplant them in spring. In Issv, near Paris, some inhabitants grow this plant extensively, to supply it to the capital's distillers (1). GARLIC (Allium sativum); this plant, which is little used in Paris but much used in the south of France, has no need to be grown as a primeur, since its bulbs keep very well all year round, if placed in a dry, frost-free place. PRIMEUR. Nevertheless, as some people are in the habit of using, as a seasoning, what they call garlic tails, i.e. the green top of the leaf, it is worth saying how one can (1) Absinthe "energetic properties; it is tonic, stomachic, vermifuge, etc. obtain it all year round. All you need to do is choose large, very healthy, well-fed bulbs, plant them in potting soil in a tied layer, among other vegetables grown under cloches or trays, and repeat this planting every fortnight during the bad season, so that the leaves can be cut off until you can get some in the ground. The holes in which the plants are planted are made with a planter; the bottom is filled with a little sand to reduce humidity, and the bulb is sunk to an inch and a half. As the stem must be a beautiful green, care is taken to place the garlics in the brightest part of the bed. ROcAmRolr (Allium scorodoprasum) is preferable for this type of cultivation. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Garlic should be planted in the open ground towards the end of February or the beginning of March; however, it still has time to succeed if planting is delayed until the beginning of May, or even later, in light, warm and substantial soils. In southern France, it is sometimes planted in November, but more often in February. It is planted in borders or beds, three inches deep and six bulbs apart. The plant is hardy, and requires only a few weedings to rid it of weeds. When the leaves dry out, maturity is recognized; the plants should then be pulled up and left to lie on the ground for a few days, to allow the air to absorb their excess moisture. When the garlics are quite dry, they are cleaned of any earth that may be attached to them, bundled together and hung in the place where they are to be kept. I've seen a few people use a particular cultivation method, with the sole aim of obtaining extraordinarily large garlics. Here's how they do it: in August, they plant preserved garlic bulbs from the previous year in substantial soil; they leave them in the ground until the heads have grown to the size of walnuts; then they pull them out, dry them in the shade, exposed to a draught, and keep them until spring, to replant them whole in February and March. This method produces monstrously large heads of garlic, but is this advantage enough to offset the doubled cost of cultivation? Garlic, like rocambola, is a very rare seed-bearer, so we only propagate them by their bulblets. Both like warm, light, sandy soil, but they do well everywhere. As with all bulbous plants, they need much-consumed fertilizers, as fresh manure causes them to rot. REGULAR CULTIVATION. Oxalis, which some people eat in the same way as sorrel, although it is more acidic, can be grown in light, sandy, slightly damp soil in the vegetable garden, with a northern exposure. The best fertilizer for it is threshold compost or heather soil. In the spring, propagate from seeds, barely covering them with soil, to allow the roots to sprout. If you want a seedling to succeed, mulch it with chopped moss. Mice are extremely fond of its root tubers, so every care must be taken to keep them away. If you are forced to grow it in open, warm areas, it needs a lot of watering. AMANDIER (Amygdalus communis); Medium-sized tree, native to Asia, whose fruit and various uses are well known. As the amaudier does not succeed above the 48th degree of latitude, where spring frosts constantly destroy its flowers, in northern France we are obliged to subject it to artificial cultivation. It is planted at the foot of a wall in the south, in an espalier, and depending on how cold the climate is, it is sheltered during flowering by canvas, straw mats or glass panels. In Europe's most northerly countries, it is treated in the same way as the apricot. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Almond trees thrive in light, warm, deep soil. They are propagated by sowing or grafting onto themselves, or, more rarely, onto plum trees, and only in shallow, strong, damp soil. Almonds are stratified in January and planted in nurseries or, better still, in the spring. Ordinary weeding, hoeing, etc. is carried out, and the young trees are usually ready for grafting the following year. Grafting is done in buds, with a growing eye in spring, or with a dormant eye in September. All other care is the same as for peach trees. AMBROISIE, CHÉNOPODE AMBROISIE, TEÉ DU MEXIQUE, ANSÉRINE (Chenopodium ambrozoides); annual plant, native to Mexico, which is only cultivated for use in tea infusions, because of the sweet smell it gives off. As it retains its sequential qualities after drying, we don't usually force it into the soil. It grows well in any soil, provided it is warm, but it prefers light, sandy and substantial soils. It is propagated from seed, sown in spring, and when the plant is strong enough, transplanted into the soil. It requires no special care, and does well in all seasons if sown under a bell or frame, on a warm bed with supplies (1). ANGELICA, ANGELICA OFFICIMALE, RACINZ DU SAINT-ESPAIT (Angelica archangelica); biennial plant, growing naturally in the Alps. The ribs of its leaves and young stems are preserved in sugar, its leaves are used to make liqueurs, and its seeds are used to make dragées, from which it follows that, since it can be preserved by these various preparations, it would be absolutely useless to subject this plant to aruficial cultivation (a). (4) This plant can be usefully employed in medicine for pulmonary catharsis, humid asthma, and all diseases of the chest which are not yet declared phthisis; in a word, it can be placed among the bechic stimulans, whose properties are best proven. (a) Angelica is considered stomachic, carminative and diaphoretic. It is a mildly stimulating tonic. Angelica is hardy and fairly easy to grow. It likes open, substantial, slightly damp soil with a sunny exposure; nevertheless, it does well everywhere, provided it is given some watering during summer droughts. It should be sown as soon as the seeds ripen, or in September, because if you wait until spring, the seeds often fail to set. It is undoubtedly on this particularity that a widespread prejudice has been established in the south of France: it is believed that its seeds lose their germinative capacity when harvested with the bare hand. They need little covering and frequent soaking, and usually sprout after a month and a half or two months, sometimes only the following spring. If you leave the young plants in place, they require little care, but if you transplant them, you need to take a few precautions to ensure they take root again. Transplant them into a well-trodden, loosened soil, amended with reconstituted potting compost, and give them a few weedings and waterings. In winter, when the stems have disappeared, the plants are covered with a little compost, and in May and June of the second year, the stems can be cut. Although this plant is biennial, it often grows back in the third and even fourth years. ANISE, ROUCAGE, ARIS VEAT (Fimpinella anisum); a biennial plant, native to the Orient, the seeds of which are used to make small sugared almonds and liqueurs. There would be no point in forcing you to plant it, so we'll just talk here about its ordinary cultivation (1). (1) Anise has the same green characteristics as angelica. The seeds: are tonic, stimulating, carminative, etc. warm, perfectly loosened, amended with old compost. Sow it in spring, in March or April, and give it frequent basins to help germination. Weed the young plant, or water it during droughts, and it sets seed in August. To collect them, the stems are cut close to the ground, left to dry in the sun, then beaten. The plants usually regrow in spring and provide a second crop of seeds, but the roots often perish in winter, so it's wise to sow them every spring. This is also the practice of the inhabitants of southern France and Touraine, where anise is grown extensively. Anise seeds retain their germinative properties for three years. ARACHIDE, PISTACHE-DE TERRE, AMANDE-DE-TEREE (Arachys hypogœa); annual plant, native to Mexico where it is highly cultivated, has many similarities with the bean, and can be grown in much the same way. Its seed, roughly the shape of a large bean, is eaten cooked in water or under ashes; an oil is extracted that is good to eat and suitable for a variety of uses. After flowering, as soon as the pod has formed, the stalk inclines towards the s.I., the pod sinks into the earth, and the seed is found two or three inches below the surface when ripe. Peanuts were brought to France around thirty years ago. Agronomists, struck by the benefits it could bring, strongly recommended it to farmers in the south of France (as it can only succeed in large-scale cultivation in provinces where melons produce good yields in the open ground). In the Landes department, its cultivation succeeded perfectly, but it was soon abandoned because growers could not afford to dispose of its products, which were unavailable on the market. We have never tried to force peanuts, but it could be done with the greatest of ease. All you have to do, in any season, is sow three or four seedlings in a pot six to seven inches in diameter, which you then press into the tan of a warm layer, either in a pineapple greenhouse or under a frame. Leave the plant in this way until it is strong enough to be germinated in the pot, and then place it with the rootball in the potting soil of a warm melon bed under a frame. The same care should be given as to early beans. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Peanuts like warm, substantial, light or sandy soil, so that they can easily sink their pods into the soil, amended with well-consumed potting soil or, better still, leaf compost. In spring, when the soil is sufficiently warmed up, sow in rays or clumps, covering the seeds with two inches of soil. We hoe, weed, and finally give it the same care as beans. M. Noisette recommends soaking the seeds in water forty-eight hours before sowing, to hasten germination. If sown in rays, plants should be spaced fifteen inches apart; two feet apart if sown in clumps. ARROCHE DES JARDINS, BONNE-DAME, BELLÉDAME, IRIBLE, FOLETTE, CHOU D'AMOUR Ou D'ARMOU (Atriplex hortensis); annual plant that comes to us from Tartary. We use it to mix with sorrel to soften its acidity; despite its insipidity, in the south of France we use a lot of it in herb broth. Three varieties are grown: blond, with yellowish-green leaves; red, with pale-red foliage; and very red, with dark-red leaves. PRIMEUR. This plant rises very easily, grows rapidly and is not at all delicate; these reasons make it very easy to grow as a primeur. From October onwards, it is sown thickly in the compost of early bedding, along with supplies, radishes, etc.; fifteen or twenty days later, leaves have to be cut, and it must be sown again in a warmer bed. Sowing continues fortnightly until February, when the seeds can be planted in the open ground. As it is quite water-loving, it should be placed on beds where plants requiring watering are grown. ORDINARY GROWING. It can be sown in March, and as it grows very quickly, sowing should be repeated every twenty days, so that the plant is available all year round. The seed must be harvested a little before maturity, otherwise it is easily scattered by the winds. The stalks are cut, dried in the shade, then shaken on a cloth; the seeds detach and are collected with the greatest of ease. ARTICHAUT (cynara Scolymus); perennial plant, native to Barbary.
