There are several ways of obtaining early artichokes, which we will describe in detail below. To obtain artichokes in April, we force them into place. Carnations are planted in the middle of May, and cared for in the same way as full-grown plants, until the cold sets in. You don't want to plant earlier, nor choose carnations that are too big, so that they don't set fruit in autumn, but only form strong, vigorous plants. You get wicker cages, with bars spaced a good inch apart, cylindrical, about like a barrel split at both ends, eighteen inches wide and two feet high. (fig. 3.) As soon as the first frosts threaten, each artichoke plant is mounded with a little soil taken from a nearby square, the leaves are bundled together, after cutting off those at the bottom that threaten to dry out or rot, and a cage is placed over each plant. Arrange the foliage in the cage in such a way as to give the leaves, especially those in the heart of the plant, as much air and light as possible. Once all the cages are in place, spread a well-trampled bed of manure, at least six to eight inches thick, over the entire surface between each cage. When frost arrives, we surround the cages up to the top with a bed of dry litter, against which we raise a good bed of manure. Close the top of the cage with a good plug of broken straw, and cover the whole with a cap of long straw, to keep out rainwater. Whenever the thermometer indicates that the outside temperature is above freezing, remove the plug to let in air and light. You can even leave the plants uncovered during rain, as long as it doesn't last several days in a row, as artichokes are more afraid of shrivelling than humidity when they have air. Every three or four days, as soon as the plants are uncovered, we visit them to remove any rotten leaves, and to replace in a more favorable position those which the deprivation of air and light would threaten to shrivel. Care is taken to avoid being caught out by the frost, and when the thermometer falls, the straw pads are replaced exactly on the cages every evening. When spring arrives and frosts are no longer to be feared, the cages and surrounding fumter are removed, but left on the square until the soil has warmed up enough to allow the first hoeing to take place without any inconvenience. This easy method produces artichokes from Easter to May. It is essential, I repeat, that the plant be young if you want to obtain them at the times indicated. Older plants treated in this way are more likely to be preserved and produce fruit earlier, but only fifteen to twenty days earlier than the others. Artichokes can also be forced in situ, to produce fruit in February and March. Here's how it's done. You dig three pits one foot wide and as deep, parallel to each other and eighteen inches apart; their length is indeterminate; you fill these pits with old manure and potting soil, on which you can make small spring and summer seedlings. In May, strong artichoke eyelets are planted in the beds between the pits. They can be cultivated early in the summer, just like those from an ordinary plantation. When the cold weather is about to arrive, we remove the old manure and compost from the three pits, and replace it with warm manure; or enclose the two rows of artichoke plants in wicker cages similar to those we've already mentioned, but only eighteen inches high. Around the cages and over the pits, a warm layer is established, which is consequently six feet wide by an indeterminate length, and in the middle of which the artichoke vines are placed in voids held by the cages. The layer is raised eighteen inches, and when it is level with the cages, a two-foot-wide, fourteen- to fifteen-inch-high verrine is placed on each plant (fig. 5)." The whole is left in this state until the frosts become intense, at which point the layer is replenished with six or seven inches of warm manure, and, during the night, the verrines are covered with straw mats and large bedding. Needless to say, the bed must be welded often, to see if it loses heat, and whenever this happens, it must be reshaped, new manure added, lined with good stoves, and every means employed to keep it at a constantly high temperature. Whenever the thermometer is between five and eight degrees, or higher, we take advantage of moments of sunshine to give the air by lifting the verrines a few inches. We wipe off the moisture and water droplets that cling to the glass, peel the plants and clean them of aphids, rid them of rotten or moldy leaves, etc., etc.. The third way of forcing artichokes is the one to be preferred, because produce can be obtained from December to April. In spring, baskets or manes are purchased, fourteen to fifteen inches wide and eighteen inches deep. These are filled with a mixture of good, free-flowing soil and well-consumed loam, and in April, one or two artichoke carnations are planted in each basket. These baskets are buried in one of the garden's flowerbeds, and the plant is cared for as if it were in the ground. A gardener with a little experience will easily see if the plant is in danger of remaining too weak to produce in December and January; if so, he'll push it a little with water to get it going. If, on the other hand, the vigor of its vegetation makes him fear that it will bear fruit in the ordinary autumn season, he will remove the basket of soil, and give the rootball only the humidity strictly necessary to prevent the plant from perishing. At the end of October or the beginning of November, depending on whether the plant is more or less advanced, the baskets are removed and carried to a tarpaulin where they are placed in a warm layer. The plants are peeled, aphids are destroyed, air is given, ponds are made where necessary, and all the general care necessary for the plants is taken. In this way, you'll soon obtain prôduits that succeed one another throughout the winter, if the plants are not all of equal strength. Some people don't take such precautions. In October or December, they simply remove old artichoke plants with the root ball, and replant them in a hole made for them in the warm layer of a tarpaulin, and in which they have placed a certain quantity of the soil whose composition we have indicated. This method has the advantage of being more economical, but the results are neither as rapid nor as certain, because whatever precautions are taken to lift the plant, the roots are always damaged to a greater or lesser extent, and transplanting is an operation that tires and delays the plant. If you have a tarpaulin and you don't want to speculate on the product, you can make use of the lost space by forcing a few artichoke plants into it. To do this, all you need is a few eighteen-inch-diameter, deep boxes. Fill them with the soil mentioned above, and in September, plant a strong artichoke plant in each one, and let it recover in the open air. When the first white frosts make themselves felt, we cut off some of the leaves at the base to save space, and transport the crates to the tarpaulin, where all we have to do is give the plants the usual care. We would nevertheless point out that, treated in this way, they require more frequent watering. Finally, we'll end this article on early plants, by teaching you a very simple procedure which can be used to keep arlichauts for part of the winter at low cost. When the cold weather arrives, we cut the fruiting artichoke stems on the ground and, in the vegetable greenhouse or simply in a good cellar, we plant them in damp sand; the heads are thus preserved for a very long time with almost all their qualities. A preferable way of destroying an artichoke patch is to pull up the whole plant and plant it as we have just said, taking care to remove most of the leaves. The teles continue to grow and can supply part of the winter, and this resource is all the more precious as it requires no expense. Sometimes artichokes may run out in a jar din between the two harvests, i.e. in August and early September. This inconvenience, caused by summer drought, is easily avoided by daytime trussing of plants that failed to produce in spring. This method brings fruiting forward by one and a half to two months. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. The artichoke thrives in free soil, rich in nutrient juices, but especially deep, because its roots are pivotal. It can be propagated by graiues, which often produce the same product in the same year, but as they do not reproduce their summer variety, it is customary to propagate only by crilletons. In spring, when the leaves of the mother plants have reached about a foot in length, i.e. in April, the crown is removed, taking care not to damage the roots, and the eyelets growing around the stump are detached by hand. Only three of the most vigorous are left. Of these, the strongest are chosen, with a few roots in the nut, i.e. the crown that forms the collar. However, a carnation will grow well without them, and if you didn't have many, the lack of roots would not be a reason to discourage them. Horticultural experts recommend cutting the leaves to six inches long before replanting the carnations, but three years of comparative experiments at my place have shown me that they are mistaken; the artichoke plants to which I have subjected this operation have always been less vigorous, and above all much less eager than those to which I have left their leaves in their full length. Moreover, this is easy to understand: we know that leaves, as much as roots, contribute to plant nutrition, and if you remove these organs from a plant that already lacks roots, it will no longer be able to draw anything from the air, nutrition will be almost nil, and consequently, recovery will be much longer and more difficult. This is a general rule that applies to all plants. Whatever the case, after having perfectly cleared and loosened the ground intended for planting, and after having suitably amended it with a consummate fertilizer, the eyelets are planted in staggered rows, two and a half feet apart in mediocre soils, and three apart in good soils. Two of them are placed four inches apart, so that there is no gap in the plantation if any are missing. They should not be planted too deeply, to avoid heart rot. From time to time, you give the plants a little water to help them get back on their feet; you hoe and weed to destroy weeds, and that's all you do until winter approaches. If a few plants are missing, they can still be successfully replaced in May, either by detaching new eyelets from the mother plants, or by removing one where both plants have recovered. When a plantation has been well cared for and planted at the right time, two-thirds of the plants start producing the following autumn. As soon as the first frosts appear, all the stems are cut as close as possible to the stump, the base leaves are removed and the others are bundled together. This operation consists in bringing the soil around the stem to protect it from frost. A very pernicious and, unfortunately, all-too-common practice is to take the soil from the bed itself, between the feet, thus uncovering the roots and exposing them to the rigors of the frosts. When this first operation is complete, dry leaves, fern or barley bales are heaped around the plants, and the whole thing is covered with a large bedding. In wet soils, "it is necessary," says M. Noisette, "to open gullies between each row of artichokes, and to use the earth removed to butter the feet. The entire square, except for the gutters, is covered with a layer of dry sumier, which is made thicker around each plant, taking care not to bring the manure into contact with the plants, which are placed at the bottom of a funnel. This funnel is covered with dry litter during the frosts, and the straw is combed to keep rainwater away from the plants. "Whenever the weather gets milder and the sun appears, we remove the litter and replace it during the night. In my opinion, the best way to protect artichokes from the cold, to which they are less sensitive than one might think, and from humidity, shrivelling and the resulting rot, which are the ordinary causes of their loss, is to house them in the cages I mentioned in the article on early vegetables, and to manage them absolutely as I said on page 31. For the last three winters, I have used no other method in my garden, and since then I have always obtained very satisfactory results. The artichoke cover can be removed entirely at the end of March, or earlier if frosts are no longer to be feared. A good ploughing is done, burying the manure from the cover and scattering the soil used to butter the artichoke. The artichoke is then oiled as we said, and other care is limited to a few hoeings to open the pores of the soil and destroy parasitic weeds. Artichokes, though perennial, are only profitable for three years; after the fourth, their yields diminish considerably in quantity and size. For this reason, planting should be renewed every three years. When an old square is destroyed, the leaves can be blanched like cardoons, and used in cooking in the same way. Some authors have printed that they are more delicate; I've experienced this myself, and I can't agree with them. Sowing artichokes can only be useful if you want to obtain new varieties, or if you are short of eyelets. The seed is collected from the best terminal heads, and kept on the artichoke's receptacle until sowing. From flowering to maturity, the stem must be bent to prevent rainwater penetrating through the scales into the heart of the fruit, which would cause the seeds to abort and rot. In February and March, sow in pots sunk into the warm layer of a frame, or wait until the end of April to sow in situ. In the former case, transplant the young plant as soon as it is strong enough; in the latter, thin out, hoe and give it the usual care. Artichokes sown on a bed almost all bear fruit the following autumn, but the others hardly produce their first heads until spring. Seed artichokes are not equally good; many are very thorny, hardly bigger than a thistle head, and must be pulled up; but if you have sown Laon seed, you will get many that are large and excellent. ASPERGE (Asparagus officinalis); native perennial, growing naturally on the sandy beaches of almost all the rivers of France and Germany. Its uses are generally well known. There are several breeds, for example: white asparagus, or Dutch asparagus, green asparagus, violet asparagus, etc.; but the slight differences between them are purely local, and we must not hope to fix them when we change country and culture (1). (1) Asparagus is a very good vegetable, but it has the singular disadvantage of imparting a foul odor to the urine of those who eat it. This odor is easily destroyed by putting muriatic acid or vinegar in the chamberpot; if, after eating asparagus, you swallow a small pill of turpentine, the urine, far from smelling bad, absolutely exalts the odor of violets. PAIMEUR. Market gardeners in Paris produce a lot of early asparagus, using two processes that we'll describe in detail below. In one case, they heat on the spot; in the other, they force the asparagus into a frame. On-site heating. In dry, light, warm soils, the soil is laid out in planks or beds four feet wide; in cold, strong, low-porosity soils, only three feet wide. A two-foot-wide path is left between each bed. The beds are perfectly loosened, and the soil is lightened as much as possible with old topsoil that has been completely used up. In spring, in March in the south of France and in April in the Paris climate, asparagus claws are planted in the beds in the usual way. The difference, however, is that the plant is spaced less widely; ten inches between each plant is sufficient. The main thing is to leave six to eight inches of empty space along both sides of each bed. The plantation is raised and cultivated without any special care until its third year, that is, until the plants are strong enough to be heated. Then, from December to April, depending on whether you want to produce earlier or later, you dig the two-foot-wide paths you've left around the planks to eighteen or twenty inches, and remove the soil after loading the two- or three-inch-thick strips. The pits are filled with well-packed hot manure, and these stoves are raised a foot above the board, and the board itself is covered a foot thick with the same manure. A bed of long litter is placed on top to keep rainwater away from the bed. If the planting is to be done on soil with some consistency, transverse vaults can be dug from distance to distance, under each bed, and filled to measure with hot manure. 8If you have frames, you can save a lot of manure; after raising the stoves as we've just said, cover the board with only six inches of manure, and place the frames with their panels over them at night, especially when it's freezing; cover the whole thing with straw mats, and it's best not to remove them until it's sunny. Fifteen or twenty days later, the asparagus should have emerged from the soil. Remove the manure from the top of the bed, cut off those that are long enough, and replace the manure. If it has lost its heat, mix it with new manure, or even replace it entirely, as well as the manure from the stoves. This is de rigueur whether or not there are frames. However, some market gardeners do things differently: when the asparagus start to grow, they remove the manure from under the frames, and never put it back in. They simply renew the stoves more often. Here's why they do it this way: asparagus growing in manure is deprived of light, and remains white along its entire length, whereas asparagus growing in light under the glass panels turns green or red along its entire length outside the soil. As the heat of the soil is greatly reduced by not replacing the manure, vegetation is delayed, and only by covering with dry leaves and straw mats is it possible to avoid suspending vegetation entirely during very cold weather, this method seems to us to be vicious. All the more so as nothing is as easy as giving asparagus its color. To do this, we gather the asparagus into small bunches of ten to twelve, prick the bunches up to half their length into the soil of a warm vegetable layer, and cover them with a transparent glass cloche. Twenty-four or forty-eight hours later, the asparagus is perfectly colored. So, far from recommending this method used by some market gardeners, who may be unaware of the very simple practice I've just taught, I'd advise you, on the contrary, to load the boards under the frame with a foot of manure when the cold becomes more intense. It's enough for the glass of the boards to be six inches away from the surface of the layer. However, care must be taken not to generate enough heat to burn the asparagus. If you take care to keep rainwater away from the layers, which would cool them down, and if you maintain their heat by reheating the stoves every fortnight, you can cut asparagus every other day for a month and a half or two months. When they stop producing, the soil is thrown back into the paths, and if there are still frosts to be feared, a certain thickness of manure is left on the beds, which is not removed until April, to preserve the roots. In spring, the asparagus grows only a few skinny, flabby stalks, which you must be careful not to cut off; but the following year they have regained enough vigor, if you don't cut them off in spring to be able to be heated again. A plantation in good soil, well managed, can last ten years, and, by alternately heating it two years at a time, provide five harvests of early crops. We should point out that forcing beds can also be encouraged by sowing; only, instead of heating in the third year, you'll have to wait until the fourth, but the yield will never be as good. As we have said, market gardeners hardly start forcing asparagus until the beginning of December, and they continue until February, or March at the latest, because it is during this part of the year that asparagus is most valuable. But the same success can be obtained by heating as soon as the stalks begin to turn yellow, and even as soon as the seed has acquired that red color which heralds its maturity. Heating on a bed. In November, we raise a warm layer eighteen to twenty inches high and three feet wide; if we want to heat later, when winter is in full force, we make the layer three feet thick and four feet wide: the manure, being in a larger mass, heats up more easily and retains its heat better. The layer is filled with three to four inches of very light earth, or old potting soil mixed with half garden soil. Place glass frames over it, and leave it there until the heat has passed. When there's no longer a risk of burning the asparagus roots, we get at least four-year-old claws, shorten the roots so that they are only eight or nine inches long, and lay them upright, very close together, so that they support each other, and take care that all the collars are roughly level. Once this has been done, use your hand to slide potting soil between the roots until all the interstices are well filled, and then spread half a finger's worth of potting soil over the whole plant. A fortnight later, the asparagus begins to grow, and you can start cutting. They are very green, but very thin, so we usually eat them as peas. After fifteen or twenty days, the claws are exhausted and no longer produce; all that's left to do is undo and throw the claws away, because they're burnt. Old squares of asparagus that are destroyed provide excellent roots to be heated in this way. This is the ordinary method used by most of the market gardeners in Paris. Mr. Noisette has made a few modifications, the results of which have been bigger produce, in greater quantities, and lasting longer. Let co tavant agriculteur speak for himself. "At the same times as for the other on-site cultivation (from November to March), layers of hot manure are prepared, eighteen to twenty inches high and four or five inches wide. - When they're at their hottest, we "cover them with ten inches of compost, to which we've mixed" a third of light earth. We place on top, six inches apart, claws aged four years or more, and on top of which we spread a two-inch bed of the same potting soil, and on top a little hot fu mier. Leave the bed in this state for a few days, and when you think the asparagus "are about to start growing, remove the manure and replace it with three inches of new compost," after which the frames are placed. The "chi" of the layer is renewed by means of heaters, which are changed every - time they are needed. After "twelve to fifteen days, the asparagus begin to produce, and we cut for as long as they "give, which is about a month, more or less. - Gardeners who have tarpaulins sometimes make use of places lost in the dark, such as the underside of tiers, back corners, etc., by forcing asparagus into baskets. Nothing is as simple as the means they employ. They procure mannes or baskets, ten inches deep by an indeterminate width; at the bottom they place a bed of straw or litter, over which they spread a layer of sand one inch thick. They finish filling the basket with consumed potting soil mixed with a fifth of light garden loam. In each basket they plant four old claws at the rate of each square foot, and, instead of cutting the roots, they intertwine them with each other. They give a light basking and place these baskets in lost places. The asparagus develops rapidly, and when the claws are exhausted, they replace them with new ones. Some growers place similar baskets in the 2 21 * * Y 2 2 i63 L 16 13 empty places of the warm layers they have in baches, and even in the open air under a frame. ORDINAIRX CULTIVATION. Asparagus like light, sandy, substantial soil; they become superb in fertile sands. They can be propagated from seed, which can be dried in situ or in a nursery. In the latter case, the roots, known as pates or claws, are planted in situ. Sowing takes place in November or October in southern France, in March in the Paris climate, and in April in more northerly regions. To sow in a nursery, prepare the soil with good ploughing and suitable amendments; when the soil is perfectly loosened, sow by broadcasting or in very light rays, and cover the seeds with a fingerful of reconstituted compost. Oh gives a few light basins, if the season is dry, and the seeds usually rise in forty days. We hoe lightly, pull out weeds carefully so as not to uproot the young plant, and give a few sprinklings if necessary. As winter approaches, all stems are cut off, and the plant is covered with three inches of potting soil, which is mixed, if desired, with half light or sandy soil. The following year, if sowing has been perfectly successful, you can remove the claws and put them in place. If not, wait until the second year, but never later. When pulling out the roots, great care must be taken to avoid breaking the large fibers that extend laterally around the collar. If the plant is to be sown in place, a few modifications are made to what has just been said; after preparing the ground as for planting, a hole one inch deep is made in each place where the plant is to be, into which five or six seeds are sown, covered with potting soil, and when they have risen, the most vigorous plant is left and all the others pulled out, or better still, cored below the collar, so as not to undermine the roots of the one that remains. During the first year, watering, hoeing and weeding are carried out in the same way as for the nursery, and in subsequent years the seedling is managed in the same way as the plantation. An asparagus plant established by this method produces its crop a year later, but the plants are more vigorous and last longer. Asparagus plants are planted in different ways. It is done at the same time as sowing, in beds or squares. For both, it's best to prepare the ground the previous autumn. To plant in beds, you open pits two feet deep in dry soils, three feet deep in wet soils, four feet wide and of any length. Between each plank, a sufficient interval is left to receive the soil from the excavation, without forming too high an ados. In wet soils, a foot-thick bed of plaster, gravel, pebbles or anything else capable of allowing water to pass through is placed in each pit. Once this is done, a foot-thick layer of good fertilizer is placed at the bottom, consisting of manure, turf, street mud, etc., which is trampled down as much as possible to prevent it from settling. This is the method used by all growers; but I must confess that I don't quite understand its usefulness, as the asparagus claw only produces a very short, very short hair, always extending laterally; each claw lasts only three years, after which it perishes, and a new one forms above it to replace it. What influence, then, can this fertilizer have on a root that never reaches it, that moves away from it every year, and that can receive no nutritive juices from it since it is placed above it? In any case, we spread three inches of well loosened soil from the excavation on top of this fertilizer, and mix it with enough compost to make it very light. Using a chalk line, draw three equally spaced lines, and fifteen or eighteen inches apart on each line, mark the places where the claws are to be placed, by raising a very small mound of compost. Choose good claws, with long, white, healthy roots; if any are fractured, cut them very cleanly with a serpette; then spread one on each mound, taking care to incline the roots a little. Cover the whole with three fingers of soil similar to that on which you planted. During the course of the year, ordinary care is given, consisting of weeding, watering and so on. In November, the beds are replenished with three fingers of soil taken from the ados which, until then, have been used to sow lettuces, supplies and other plants whose cultivation requires no more than six months' time, and which are not tall enough to provide shade. The following year, the same care is taken, and in autumn, after cutting the dried stems, three new fingers of soil are covered, on which a certain thickness of consumed manure is spread. In the third spring, while hoeing, we bury this fertilizer, and already we can start cutting the biggest asparagus. Every year, you continue with the same cultivation, loading the bed with three fingers of new soil and giving it new fertilizers. In this way, an asparagus plantation is in full production by the fifth year, and can last fourteen or fifteen years. Never cut later than July. If you plant in squares, the costs are a little higher, but the produce is more beautiful, and asparagus usually lasts from fifteen to twenty years. The soil is prepared in August of the previous year, and fertilizers are mixed in to lighten it; if the soil is strong, sand, heather and leached ashes are best. The following spring, in March or early April, the soil is divided into five-foot planks, the first of which is dug with a good spade-shot, and the soil is dumped onto the next one; then it is dug to a depth of eighteen inches in dry soils, and two feet in wet ones, and the soil is placed in a storage area. If two feet have been dug, a six-inch bed of rubble or gravel is placed at the bottom of the pit to facilitate drainage. On top of this, a second bed a foot thick is laid with consumed manure or other fertilizer. The pit is then completely filled with the soil first removed during excavation. In this way, it is in the middle of the rest of the soil. Once this has been done, the second bed is prepared in the same way, then the third, and so on, until the end of the square, which is now at the same level as before the operation. We sow or plant as we have said, giving the same care throughout the year, and by autumn, the soil has settled enough to allow us to top up with three fingers of compost. Every year, in autumn, new fertilizer is brought into the square, which is buried in the spring when the first ploughing is done, and so that in the long run the square does not become too raised, an inch or two of soil is removed from the surface, to be replaced by better soil. The asparagus seed is harvested from the most vigorous stalks, which should not be cut in the spring for this purpose. The stalks are cut off, the berries removed and left to dry in the air for two weeks; they are then crushed in the hands and washed in a vase filled with water. The husks float to the surface, and the seeds sink to the bottom. B BASELLE ROUGE, ÉTINARD DU MALARAR ( Basella rubra); biennial, climbing plant, native to the Indies, cultivated

like Rancux BAselle (Basella alba), and used for the same purposes. These two plants are ideal for replacing spinach, which has the same taste and qualities. They produce much more, and all summer long. PRIMEUR. I don't think that baselle has ever been grown as an early crop, probably because, as it is not well known on the Paris markets, market gardeners would not be able to sell it. It would, however, be very easy to grow for those who use tarpaulins, flying greenhouses or hothouses. In May, plant it in baskets in a bed against a wall facing south. In September, it would be tucked into the tarpaulin, planted with its basket in a bed against a wall, which it would line by trellising against it, and, by this means, it would make use of wasted space. If it had enough light, it would produce very good leaves, which could be harvested until spring. A single plant of boselle can provide, in four or five months, enough leaves for three or four dishes. CULTURX ORDINAIRX. Baselles are sown in March, on a warm bed under a frame, in substantial, loose soil. When frosts, to which they are very sensitive, are no longer to be feared, they are lifted with the rootball, and transplanted into the ground, at the foot of a wall facing south. Weed, hoe and, in hot weather, water frequently, as these plants love water. They should be planted against a trellis, to give their climbing stems (red or green, depending on the species) an easy grip. One of the most vigorous plants is left untouched to obtain seeds, which usually ripen very well. BASILIC (Ocymum basilicum); small annual plant, very aromatic in all its parts, native to Persia. It has several varieties: large-leafed, purple-leafed, lettuce-leafed, aniseed-flavored, etc. They are used as an assortment, and sometimes as a salad ingredient. Basil can be sown in any season, on a warm layer of tarpaulin, under a frame or under a bell. It germinates very easily and grows quite rapidly. If you want to use it for seasoning, wait until its stems have grown to at least five or six inches; for salad, cut it very young, otherwise its strong, aromatic flavor may displease some people. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Basil is sown in the soil in March. In May, it is transplanted to a warm spot in light, well-dressed soil. It requires copious and frequent watering throughout its life. The seed is harvested in autumn. BÉNINCASE GLAUQUE (Benincasa cerifera), and BÉNINCASE CYLINDRIQUE (Benincasa cylindrica); in this article, I bring together these two species or varieties of cucurbits, which I believe belong to the cucumber genus. Believed to have originated in Senegal, they have only been cultivated in Paris since 1826. They are still not very widespread. Their fruits are about the size of a cucumber, elongated, dark green and covered, especially the first, with a thick, viscous, glaucous dust. The flesh is white, firm and quite similar to that of cucumbers, but with a preferable taste; moreover, it can be eaten in the same way. PRIMEUR. These plants are still too little known in France for us to have tried to grow them early, but it is almost certain that, to obtain them in the off-season, we would have to force them in the same way as melons, and manage and prune them in the same way. We therefore refer the reader to this article. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Benincases can be grown in two ways: on a bed or in the ground. In both cases, they are sown in pots at the beginning of April, on a warm bed and under cloches, or under a frame. Seeds germinate with difficulty if they are not given sufficient warmth and humidity. When the plant has risen to a certain strength, it is removed from the soil and placed on an old bed, or at least in an earthen bed, at the foot of a south-facing wall. The stem is pruned over two eyes, and the branches over three or four nodes; moderate watering is given, as they fear too much humidity, and they are steered like melons. I believe that, sown in the open ground around April 15th, they could also succeed in ordinary years, i.e. those that are not too cold or rainy. But to do this, you'd have to sow in bunches, and here's how. Holes eighteen inches deep and two feet wide should be dug in good soil and exposure, and filled with warm, well-packed, trampled manure. In the middle of this manure, we'd make a new funnel-shaped hole, eight inches deep in the middle and a foot wide, which we'd fill with a mixture of three-quarters old topsoil and one-quarter light earth. Sow in this compost, and cover with a cloche or verrine, around which place a hot manure stove, seven to eight inches wide. The seeds would certainly sprout, and all that remained was to remove the stoves and verrines, around the fifteenth of May, perhaps earlier, if the season was favorable. A valuable quality of benincase fruits is that they keep perfectly well throughout the winter, if stored in a very dry place and protected from light frost. In 1828, I saw some at my colloborateur's, Mr. Noisette, on the first of March, and they seemed healthy enough to give him hope that they would keep for some time yet. BETTERAVE (Betta vulgaris); biennial plant, growing spontaneously in southern Europe. It is too well known to list all the uses to which it is put. Its main varieties are: grosse rouge, fairly long and the most widely cultivated of all. Petite rouge, more precocious, with a milder flavor. The round red, also early, of the same quality, but rounded. Yellow, large, elongated and the sweetest of all. Large and small white, very tender, delicate, but a little bland in flavor. Yellow with white flesh, the best for providing sugar. Detterave champétre, or starvation root, is grown only in large quantities, and for sourrage. We don't usually force beet, because the root, the only part we use, keeps perfectly well in a vegetable greenhouse, or simply in a dry cellar, until March and April. If at this time you choose the healthiest roots, place them in fine, very dry sand, in a box and put them in a dry, poorly ventilated place, you can still have them in May and June, and longer if you take the precaution of visiting them often and cutting off the buds as they grow. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Beets do more or less well in all soils that have been suitably loosened and amended, but they take on enormous dimensions in warm, deep, free and light soils, well broken up, and heavily amended from the previous year, or with fertilizers consumed from the beginning of March until May; after two good ploughings, they are sown broadcast or in rays. When the plant has risen, which happens after a fortnight, it is thinned out so that the plants are fifteen inches apart in mediocre soils, and eighteen or twenty in good soils. We hoe, weed, destroy parasitic weeds and, if the season is dry, water deeply. November is harvest time. We pull out the roots and leave them to dry out, then we twist or cut the leaves, and put them in the vegetable greenhouse to pull them out as we use them. Beet has a slight fear of transplanting, so when thinning out the seedling, if you want to transplant where there is a shortage, you must do so immediately and before the air has dried the surface of the roots. Sometimes, when the rácine is as big as a finger, you sow it in a nursery before transplanting it into the field. Transplanting should be carried out with the same care, and care should be taken to avoid injuring or breaking the root, which should never be cut back. If you have to wait before transplanting, soak them in a mixture of soil, water, manure and cow dung, to protect them from contact with the air. At harvest time, some of the best beets are left in the ground to provide seed. During hard frosts, we cover them with straw or dry litter. Sometimes, however, they cannot be preserved, in which case the best and healthiest beets in the vegetable garden are planted in the spring. Let grains retain their germinative virtues for only two or three years. C CAPUCIN. Two species are grown: the CrArD* CAPUCINE (Tropœolum majus), whose stems are very long and climbing, and the reTire CArUCINE (Tropœolum minus,) whose short stems need no support. The flowers of both are used to garnish salads; the buds are candied in vinegar before they open, and the flowers before they ripen. For this purpose, the smaller variety is preferable, as it flowers more abundantly than the larger. It would be of little importance to force the nasturtium if its use were limited to decorating salads, but its double-flowered variety is a very pretty ornamental plant, and can be used in the same way. This is the only one we're going to talk about. Nasturtiums, native to Peru, are perennials in their own country; but as they ripen their seeds in the space of a summer, we are accustomed to growing them as annuals. The double-flowered variety, which does not set seed, is propagated by taking cuttings under a bell or under a frame, in pots sunk in a warm layer. They can be taken from March to August. From September onwards, especially if there are cold rains, the pots are transported to a warm greenhouse, and if you want to enjoy the flowers all winter long, they are placed in a warm layer of tannin, in as much light as possible. The care they require is limited to removing dead leaves, directing the branches so that each enjoys the same amount of light and air, and moderating watering, as this plant is very sensitive to rot. I think that by sowing the little nasturtium in autumn and transporting it to the warm greenhouse before the weather turns sour, it will also flower in winter, and keep for several years. It's a good idea to take cuttings from double nasturtiums every year or two at the most, as experience has shown that young plants are the most resistant in the greenhouse. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Large and small nasturtiums grow well everywhere, but they do best in open, light soil with warm exposure. They are sown in April, and watered frequently during the heat of summer. They sometimes resow themselves. CARDON or Carde (Cynara cardunculus); perennial plant, native to Barbary. Everyone knows that it is grown for its leaf ribs. It has produced several varieties, including Cardou d'Espagne, which has no thorns, but grows very quickly, and has thin ribs. Cardon de Tours, preferred to the first, although very thorny, because it holds well and its ribs are wider and softer. Cardon plein sans épines (full cardoon without thorns), which has the same qualities as the previous one, but with the added advantage of being thornless. Artichoke-leaf cardoon, with very full, reddish, excellent ribs that are also thornless. PRIMEUR. In ordinary cultivation, cardoons supply from October to at least February. We will now describe the procedures to be used to obtain cardoons from March to September. At the beginning of November, prepare a warm bed under a frame. Sow two seeds of Tours cardoon or full cardoon without thorns, in small pots four inches in diameter, filled with a mixture of half light soil and old potting soil fully consumed. This first sowing can be done on a warm layer in the open air, using cloches or verrines. A similar sowing is repeated in December, and a third in January, but these last two should be done under a frame or tarpaulin. In any case, all three can be carried out as described below. When the plant has emerged, one of the two is cut off below the collar, if both seeds have germinated, and only the most vigorous is kept. When it begins to show its third leaf, remove it from its pot with the rootball, and place it in a larger vase with the same soil. A new warm layer of soil is then placed under the frame, and the pot is pushed into it. When the plant is strong enough, we establish a three-foot-thick muted layer at the foot of a south-facing wall, in very dry soil, covered with a foot of good compost mixed with a quarter of light earth. The cardoons are unstuck and planted in the potting soil, two feet apart, in all directions; the frame is placed on top, and surrounded by good stoves that are changed every time they are needed. If you notice that the bed is getting cold, you open a trench two feet wide and four deep around the frame against the bed; you lard it with new manure from underneath, and fill the pit with it to serve as stoves. If the cultivation is carried out in such a way as never to allow the heat to drop in the bed, nor the cold to penetrate into the frame, cardoons can be blanched for kitchen use as early as the month of murs; in April, from the second sowing, and in May, from the third. In March, choose the most vigorous plants from the second and third sowings and plant them out in a bed at the foot of a south-facing wall. Each will be covered with a bell to shelter them from the cool nights and gradually accustom them to the open air. If, during this month, the sun is strong and prickly, they should be sheltered from its rays for part of the day, using light-colored cloths. Otherwise, they should be cared for in the same way as full-earth seedlings, and will start to bind well in June and July, but many will fail; nevertheless, with careful watering and cultivation, they will produce until the time when full-earth cardoons start to yield. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Cardoons like substantial, light, deep soil, as well as abundant watering. You can easily get trained ones as early as August, with the precaution of sowing them in small pots, under a frame, in March, and transplanting them in April, when they require only ordinary care. For late-season and winter plants, sow them in the ground in April and May, and proceed as follows: loosen and fine the soil, which should be perfectly loosened and warm. Three feet apart in all directions, dig holes one pled wide and as deep, fill them with well-consumed manure mixed with a small amount of soil to give it body, then sow two or three seeds in each and cover with two fingers of the same soil. Water frequently, weed and hoe, and keep insects, especially aphids, away from the young plant. When the plant has two or three leaves, we thin it out so as to leave only one leaf in each hole. If watering is not spared, the cardoons will grow with great vigor, and their leaves can reach up to six feet in length. When they are sufficiently formed to be ridged, the soil from the holes is brought together around the plants, and piled as high as possible with a wooden fork. The leaves are brought together to form a sort of bundle, and held in this position with wicker, straw or string ties. They are then covered with a thick shirt of long straw, which is held in place in the same way. The plant is left hidden for three weeks, and this time is always sufficient to soften and whiten the rib. If you were to wait any longer before releasing it for consumption, it would inevitably rot from lack of air and light; as a result, cardoons should only be buttered and tied as necessary. When white frost begins to set in, remove the cardoons and place them in the vegetable greenhouse to protect them from the cold, as they are very sensitive to it. Place them with their root ball in damp sand, after lifting their leaves to make them take up less space, but without squeezing them too tightly, so that air can still circulate between them, which is essential to prevent them from rotting. Some gardeners, lacking sufficient space, are content to place them upright, against a wall and leaning against each other; they often visit them to remove rotten leaves, and to deliver for consumption those whose rot threatens to spread to the heart. If you have a frame at your disposal, it's easy to preserve cardoons without a greenhouse. Choose the hottest, driest spot, open a trench the width of the trunk and three feet deep. Place the box on top, and throw the soil from the trench against its outer walls. A good bed of long, dry straw is placed upright against one side of the trench, and leaned against a row of cardoons; against these a second bed of straw is laid, then a second row of cardoons, and so on until the chassis trunk is filled. Care should be taken to leave the upper third of the length of the leaves exposed to light and air. Once this is done, the glass panels are placed to prevent cold and damp from penetrating to the plants. Whenever the air is dry and it's not freezing, the panels are removed, but they must be rigorously replaced every evening. Some people are content to place their cardoons in an uncovered trench, as described above. They protect them from frost and rain by spreading a thick blanket of dry litter over them, which they take care to remove whenever air can be supplied. Cardoon seeds are harvested in the same way as artichokes. In autumn, a few plants are sheltered as we said for artichokes (see page 31); in spring, they are uncovered and cultivated in the same way as artichokes. The seed retains its germinative properties for five or six years. CARROT (Daucus carota); biennial plant that "sprouts spontaneously in southern Europe, and of which several varieties are grown, namely: The RED ones, often preferred to the others for cooking, because they are generally found to have a spicier taste. The sub-varieties are Short red hative or Dutch, excellent and very early, preferable for autumn and early spring sowing. Its smaller, slightly fatter sub-variety is used almost exclusively by market gardeners in Paris. Rouge-longue, very good, but grown more in Germany than in France. Red pale, from Flanders, good, with the same qualities as yellow. JaUnes, sweet, very good. The sub-varieties are : Long yellow, one of the oldest cultivated varieties, and still considered by many to be one of the best. Young short or round yellow, as good as the previous variety. BLaNCuis, quite good, but especially esteemed for its long, easy shelf-life. Ordinary white, of mediocre quality and not widely grown. Blanche de Breteuil, half-short, often a slightly yellowish color, better than the previous variety. Blanche ronde, very mediocre. Blanche hors de terre, very large, very long, with green collar, quite good. Violet, very sweet and very large, but has the disadvantage of staining broths and stews. Spanish violet, of the same quality and size as the previous one, but usually yellow on the inside, which means it does not stain broth. It is easy to store. PRIMEUR. In order to obtain fresh carrots in winter, spring and early summer, we have subjected these plants to a special cultivation method. Spring-sown carrots keep well through the winter, but they never taste as delicate, nor are they as tender, and it is for these reasons that fresh carrots are preferred as soon as they have reached the size of a little finger or close to it. For the early season, the short rouga from Hollende is the preferred variety, because it is the earliest, the one that rises the least, and one of those that, on the bed, is content with the least thickness of soil. The choice of seeds is not indifferent either, as experience has shown that new varieties produce individuals that grow very quickly. The best seeds are therefore those that are two years old, and older ones should not be sown. It is customary to sow it from September to February on the warm beds prepared for celery, cabbage, lettuce, radishes and supplies; however, as the roots grow quite deep, the bed is reloaded in the area intended for carrots, so that there is eight inches of potting soil; it is advisable, when reloading the bed, to mix two thirds of light earth with the potting soil, which must be thoroughly used up. Carrots sown in potting soil that is too grainy and not sufficiently consumed are prone to staining and bad taste. When the layer is fully warm, sow thickly, cover the seeds with a finger of fine compost, hoe lightly and cover with the frame. In layers where only cloches are used, seeds are sometimes sown in clumps, but in other layers, seeds are broadcast, often between other plants in the empty spaces. Air is given whenever the temperature permits, watering is carried out as needed, and the hard crust that may form on the surface of the soil is carefully broken. As soon as the carrots have emerged, the plant is thinned out by cutting with the nails below the cotiledons the overabundant plants that are to be destroyed; by this means, which should always be used for delicate seedlings, you are never exposed to shaking the roots of the individuals that are to remain. Some time later, when the carrots have gained strength and are showing three leaves, they are thinned out a second time, so that the seedlings are spaced two inches apart. All that's left for the seedlings is the usual care, consisting of new stoves when the warmth of the soil decreases, watering, hoeing, etc. When the carrots have reached their full size, they are ready for planting. When the carrots have reached the right size for the intended use, we pull them out, always choosing those closest together, so that those remaining have more room to develop. Doing as we've just said, you'll have roots of varying size, very tender and very good, until the autumn seedlings in the open ground begin to produce. To grow carrots in spring and early summer, there is no need for beds or frames. Sow the indicated variety in September, with the same care as described in the article on ordinary cultivation, but in light soil with warm exposure. Carrots do not fear the cold, but they are sensitive to it, especially when young. So, when frost sets in, cover them with a good layer of bedding or dry leaves, and give them air whenever the weather permits. In hard winters, such seedlings produce very early. REGULAR CULTIVATION. The quality of carrots depends much more on the type of soil in which they are grown than on the variety to which they belong. In sandy, fertile, deep soils, it is excellent, as well as in those that are free-flowing, soft and substantial. It doesn't like fresh fertilizer, so you need to fertilize the land where you want to plant it at least six months in advance, or at least only with consumed manure; in any other case, it forks, i.e. its root splits into two or more branches. Once the soil has been well loosened and loosened, sowing can begin in February, but with warm exposure, and continue until June, with any exposure. Sow broadcast or in rays spaced six to eight inches apart, covering lightly with a rake or harrowing with a fork. In heavy soils, prone to pounding from rain or watering, spread a fingerful of three-quarter-used potting soil, or a light mulch. If the season is dry, frequent watering helps germination. When carrots begin to sprout, and until they have reached a certain strength, they require a great deal of care, as they are subject to slugs, spiders and other insects that are very avid eaters. As for slugs, there's only one way to get rid of them, and that's to hunt them assiduously in the evenings, mornings and after mild spring rains. Spiders are easily kept at bay by frequent drenching with water infused with a little soot. We hoe from time to time, and keep the seedling free of weeds. When the seedling has no more than three leaves, never later, we start to thin out the thickest areas, so that we can transplant where there is a shortage. This operation requires great care to prevent the transplanted cavottes from forking. We choose a moment when the soil is soaked by a gentle rain; with a florist's hoe, or simply a small wooden palette, we pull out the young plant, taking great care not to break the end of its root; in the place where it is to be transplanted, we make a large hole with the planter, we place the root in it, taking extreme care to place it very vertically and not to bend its end, then we pour soil all around with the tip of the planter. Water immediately and continue to do so until recovery is perfect, but take care not to over-wet. As the carrots grow, you continue to thin them out, and when they are finger-sized, which usually happens around midsummer, you start using the thinned ones for cooking. These can be removed successively for use, until the plants are five or six inches apart, at which point they are no longer touched. In November or December, depending on the severity of the season, the carrots are harvested and stored in the greenhouse. We pull them out with a flat-tined fork, so as to cut less; we clean them of any earth that may be attached to them, cut or twist the leaves above the collar, then, in the greenhouse, we place them in sand, taking care to leave the collar outside and level with the surface of the sand. If you don't have a greenhouse, you can also place them in a cellar or other place sheltered from the rigors of the cold. Air the greenhouse whenever it's safe to do so. When you realize that they have grown a lot of leaves, which can exhaust them or at least rob them of a large part of their qualities, you undo the layer of sand, cut off the collar below the new shoots, and replace them again in the sand, as they were before. With these simple precautions, they can be stored easily and for a very long time. Carrots also keep very well in an open trench in dry soil, but this method is rarely used unless they are grown in large quantities for cattle feed; nevertheless, we'll teach you how. We dig a pit at least four feet deep, four or five wide, and of a length determined by the quantity of carrots to be placed in it. A good bed of rubble or gravel is placed at the bottom, over which a layer of dry sand is spread. This is followed by a bed of carrots, with the snares turned towards the middle of the pit; a bed of sand is then added, followed by a bed of carrots, and so on, alternately, until the trench is full. A good thickness of long straw is spread over the whole, and the earth from the excavation is thrown on top, forming a steep ados to divert rainwater. Some people don't go to such lengths, especially when cultivating dry, light soil. They don't pull the carrots out of the bed where they were grown, but simply defend them against the extreme cold with a good cover of litter, dry leaves or fern. This is certainly the most convenient and economical method, but by no means the safest. It sometimes happens, when heavy frosts follow long rains, that most of the roots perish despite this shelter. Carrot seed retains its germinative capacity for two years. To obtain them, we keep the biggest and best roots in the greenhouse, taking care not to cut their collars, as they would otherwise fail to grow. Sometimes we leave them in the ground, and to protect them from frost, we cover them with a thick layer of litter, which we remove whenever the weather is mild. Those that have been uprooted are replanted in March, in very loose, well-amended soil. They bolt in May, and the seed is harvested in August. The stems are cut or hung in a dry place, and the seeds are not removed from the umbels until it's time to sow them. To rid them of the hairs that cause them to cling and curl up together, they are rubbed in the hands with fine sand or ash. CARUBEAN (ceratonia siliqua); second-growth tree, native to southern France. Its fruit, a foot long, consists of a flat, fleshy silique enclosing a reddish, sweet pulp with its seeds, good for eating when dry, but slightly purgative. PRIIXUR. The carob tree fears frost and hardly ripens its fruit in Paris without special care. It is planted at the foot of a wall in a warm, south-facing position, and trellised. For the first few years, that is, until it is strong enough to blossom, we content ourselveŝte, to protect it from the cold, with stuffing it in the manner of fig trees, but with much more care. When it has developed enough to give hope of obtaining fruit, we stuff it as we said; but in the first days of February, we remove these covers, perfectly net the branches of any garbage that may be heaped on them, and palisate those that need it. Eighteen inches from the base of the tree, a warm layer is erected parallel to the wall, on which glass panels are placed, with their tops resting against the wall above the tree. The sides of this flying greenhouse are closed with planks, the joints of which are sealed with moss to prevent the frost from penetrating. Air is supplied for one or two hours a day, and only when the sun is shining. The bed can be used to sow small vegetables. That's all it takes to advance vegetation and give the tree time to ripen its fruit. The glass panels can only be completely removed at the beginning of June. REGULAR CULTIVATION. Carob trees thrive in free, warm, amended soils with a southern exposure, where they are protected from frost as mentioned above. In the Paris climate, it is wise to have a few plants in orangeries. They can sometimes be propagated by strangling marcottes, but they grow back with great difficulty, and this method of propagation is very time-consuming. It is therefore preferable to use the seedling method. In spring, fill pots with clean, substantial or orange-tree soil, sow a few seeds in each one, and bury them in a warm layer of compost. When the young carob trees have risen, leave just one in each vase, and give them the care ordinary to orangery plants. When the plant is two or three years old, and judged capable of withstanding full soil, it is removed from the vase and 1 44 3 placed with the root ball. The roots should not be touched, and frequent watering should be given to ensure recovery; once it begins to vegetate, watering should be stopped, unless the soil becomes absolutely dry in very hot weather. Carob wood is extremely hard, and is considered incorruptible. CELERY (apium graveolens); biennial plant, growing spontaneously in the marshes of southern France. Cultivation has caused it to lose its pungency, and it is used in cooking, raw or cooked. There are several varieties. Hollow celery, small celery, chopping celery. Leaves are small and spread out, and can hardly be used for anything other than supplies. Dwarf curly celery, very tender, very crisp, used, like the previous one, as a garnish. Full white celery, very large, very fleshy, one of the most widely grown. It has two sub-varieties: Turkish or Prussian celery, which has the same qualities but is larger; and pink celery, which differs only in the pinkish tint of its ribs. Céleri gros violet de Tours. Its ribs are a more pronounced purplish-pink than the previous variety; it is the largest of all the varieties. It is remarkable for the thickness of its ribs and the size of its stalk. Celery root. There are three sub-varieties: long white celeriac, whose root is very large and elongated; round white celeriac, whose root is large and rounded; and red celeriac, whose root is veined with red and purple. The roots of the last three are eaten cooked. PRIMEUR. Early celery is grown for ordinary use, as well as for salads and other purposes. For the latter, hollow celery and curly dwarf celery are grown as follows: on a bed intended for small vegetables, laid out in November and filled with only four inches of compost, sow lightly, cover the seed lightly, baste well and cover with cloches or frames. It is not necessary to provide air until the plants have emerged; simply maintain the humidity of the compost by frequent but moderate watering. Once the celery has risen, start lifting the bells or panels, weather permitting. Thin out so as to leave two or three inches between each plant. As soon as they have three leaves, air becomes much more necessary, and you must give them air whenever you can without inconvenience. We start cutting as soon as the leaves have reached four or five inches in length, and we do this with the care of cutting one plant between two, so as to give the other remaining plants more space until the first ones to be cut have grown back leaves; then we cut the others, and so on alternately. In this way, plants can be grown much closer together without harming each other, and this is all the more advantageous as the great art of early cultivation is to obtain a lot in a little space. We continue to sow on a bed for supply, until the season allows sowing or transplanting in the open ground. Celery grown for other purposes is treated differently. With the precautions described in the article on ordinary cultivation, celery keeps very well until the end of April. Early crops should therefore be cultivated in such a way as to produce celery from May through to August, since seedlings sown in the open ground begin to yield at this time. In December, to obtain produce in May; in January, to obtain it in June; in February, to obtain it in July; in March, to obtain it in August; we sow on beds and under cloches or frames as we shall see. December sowing is done on a warm bed, with three to four inches of compost. Sow lightly, water lightly and cover with cloches or frames. When the plant has risen, air is given and the plants are governed as we have said. When they have three leaves, we transplant them onto a new warm layer filled with six inches of potting soil, two or three inches apart so they don't wilt, and continue the same care until March. At the beginning of this month, in warm, dry soil, establish a muted layer filled with eight inches of potting soil mixed with a small amount of light garden soil, and transplant the celery, staggered, in rays seven to eight inches apart; water, and cover with bells or panels to facilitate recovery. When growth is assured, simply protect the plant from cool nights and cold rains with straw mats or dry litter. Bleaching can begin as early as the end of April. Sowing in January, February and March is done and managed in exactly the same way, but the young plants, instead of being permanently transplanted on a warm bed, are transplanted into the ground as they become strong enough, but not before the beginning of April. In light soil, well amended and loosened, they are transplanted in rays spaced eight to nine inches apart, watered immediately to facilitate recovery, and as this plant is very water-loving, care is taken to keep the soil constantly moist. Needless to say, hoe from time to time, and keep the bed free of weeds. When the celery is strong enough, we blanch it. To do this, you can choose the most advantageous of the methods described below. For example, if you want to enjoy a large quantity at a time, you can butter it; otherwise, you can bind it and cover it several times. REGULAR CULTIVATION. Celery seedlings sown in April, May and June provide good yields from September until the frosts, and until the following spring when the plant is sheltered. The April sowing is usually done in a nursery for transplanting, but the May and June sowings should be done in the field, so that the celery is not delayed by transplanting, and has time to grow to full size before winter. For the nursery, choose a bed in the south, break it up, loosen the soil and mix it with as much compost as you can. Sow very lightly and water frequently. When the seedling is large enough, it is transplanted permanently into beds prepared in the same way as for in-place sowing. Let's take a look at the latter. In clean, substantial soil that is both warm and slightly moist, or in ordinary soil amended with good consumable fertilizers, we prepare beds four feet wide by an indeterminate length. If you want to bind the soil for blanching, leave a path one foot wide between the boards, but if you want to butter the soil, leave a strip three feet wide, so that when the time comes, you can pull out the soil for ridging; you use it to sow lettuces and other plants that will have produced their produce before the first frost. The soil is loosened, a rake is passed over it, and parallel rays are drawn with a string, nine inches apart. Sow the seeds in each ray thickly enough to fill the bed even if half the seeds fail to germinate. Water daily, prick out and thin out the seedlings once they have three leaves. Transplant in places where leaves are lacking, and give the usual care to seedlings. A few days later, when the plant is strong enough to be sure it won't melt any more, we thin out for the last time, so as to leave an eight-inch gap between each plant, and transplant again in the empty places if there are any. The same care is continued until it's time to blanch. To do this, choose dry weather, and bind each plant with three straw or rush ties, after bringing the leaves together in a bundle. The space between the plants is filled with litter, so that only the tips of the leaves are exposed to light and air. Sometimes, after tying, the soil from the flowerbed left next to the plant is thrown back onto the bed and heaped around the plants to a quarter of their height the first time, half that eight days later, and three-quarters another eight days later; the fourth quarter is left uncovered. Some gardeners, to avoid these embarrassments, are content to carefully uproot the celery they want to bleach, and bury it in potting soil, leaving only the tips of the leaves showing. In all cases, it usually turns white within three weeks, and can be used for consumption after that time. Winter celery can be kept in place during the bad season, by means of good earthing-up, but this method has its drawbacks; it is very difficult to dig it up for use when the ground is heavily frozen or covered with snow; then, if prolonged cold rains follow severe cold, most of it rots. It is therefore best to transport it to the vegetable greenhouse, where it is buried in sand up to a third of its length; it is given air whenever you are not afraid of the cold or damp, and is visited often to remove rotten leaves that would spoil the others if left. Celery seedlings are much less successful in very dry soils than in others, unless a method widely used in the south of France is adopted. The soil is thrown in on both sides; once this has been done, the bottom of this kind of pit is chiselled, loosened and perfectly smoked, and the celery is sown and raised as we have said. It finds there a sustained humidity which is very favorable to its vegetation. To butter it, the soil removed before sowing is thrown back onto the boards. To obtain seed, leave a few of the most beautiful plants in place, chosen from among those whose varieties have remained perfectly straightforward. To protect them from the cold, they are mounded up to half their height, and covered with dry litter or, better still, bales of barley or wheat, if you are not afraid of mice, which are often attracted by this kind of covering. Air is provided whenever the temperature permits. In March, the plants are uncovered and dethatched, the rotten leaves are removed, the plant is peeled and soon shows its stems. The seed ripens and is harvested in September; it retains its germinative powers for three or four years, but the newer it is, the better it is. Celery root can be grown in the same way as above, with the difference that it cannot be mounded. To preserve it over winter, simply transport it to the vegetable greenhouse, where it is buried in sand up to the collar. Seed-bearing plants are covered with litter or dry leaves to protect them from frost. CERFEUIL (scandix cerefolium); annual, native, aromatic plant, used in cooking as a garnish and seasoning. A curly-leaved variety is available for the same uses and can be grown in the same way. PRIMEUR. Chervil is only sensitive to very hard frosts, so it produces throughout the winter if sown at the end of September and in October. In countries where the cold is very harsh and snow abundant, it can be sown from December to February, on a warm bed, mixed with other supplies. It rises and supplies promptly, but also passes very quickly, making it necessary to sow at least three or four times during the winter, if you don't want to run the risk of running out. The seedbed is filled with four inches of loam, sown fairly lightly, lightly covered and covered with cloches or frames. The rest is taken care of in the usual way. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Chervil is not at all difficult to grow; it adapts to any soil and any exposure, but as it goes to seed very quickly, we are obliged to sow it every two weeks, in order to always have tender chervil. From March to May, it is sown in warm, loosened and amended soil; from June to the end of August, it is sown in cool or even damp soil, in the shade and with a northern exposure. Autumn sowing takes place at the foot of a wall facing south. During the heat of summer, the only care chervil requires is frequent watering and removal of parasitic weeds. The best seeds are those that ripen in June and July; they keep well for three years, but are safest when new. CERFEUIL MUSQUÉ ou D'ESPAGNE (scandiz odorata); perennial plant, native to Spain, larger than the preceding one, used for the same purposes, but with a stronger, distinctive flavor that is not to everyone's taste. Its fleshy, rather large root is used in soup like carrots and parsnips, and gives it a very pleasant taste; cooked 2 in broth, many people eat it with pleasure. PRIMEUR. Musk chervil is so widely used that it is rarely grown on the ground. Moreover, if we were to do so, it would only be to obtain supplies, as the plant is perennial and grows in the open ground, and we can pull up its roots throughout the winter for consumption. To obtain tender leaves during the frosts, all you have to do is prepare a spot on a warm bed with large vegetables, so that the soil is thick enough, remove a few plants of musk chervil sown the previous year with the root ball, plant them there, and cover them with cloches or frames. With a little watering, the plants will recover easily, and as they develop leaves, they can be cut for use. "ORDINARY CULTIVATION: This species thrives in free-light soils with very warm exposure. As it is rather averse to transplanting, it should be sown in the field as soon as the seeds are mature, otherwise they will only germinate very slowly, and several months after sowing; when the seeds are more than a year old, they no longer germinate. As the plant is quite large, we thin it out and leave at least a foot between each one. If you want to make use of the roots, water them abundantly, so that they are both tender and large.
