Small, acidic, red fruit, ripening successively from June to the first white frosts. M. Noisette has obtained a sub-variety with larger fruit. 4 Griottier. Griottier ordinaire. Medium-sized fruit, black, good, ripening in September and October, and often kept on the tree until November 15th, espaliered to the north. German sour cherry. Medium-sized fruit with red pulp, very poor quality, ripening around mid-July. Griottier de Portu gal. Fruit less acid than the preceding ones, ripening in August. PRIMEUR. Using the various varieties we have just listed, cherries can be obtained naturally from the end of April to the fifteenth of November. To get cherries in winter, you need to heat them, and there are several ways of doing this. The most common is the flying greenhouse, the construction and use of which are described in the article on Apricots. Cherry trees are treated in the same way as other trees, and require similar care, so we won't come back to this point. It is also heated when planted in the greenhouse, and for details of this process, we refer the reader to the article on Vines. It is best grown as an A-grown apricot. We'll now deal with the question of how to heat them in a greenhouse vase. Several varieties can be grown in this way, but those with the best chances of success are: the early dwarf cherry, the English hätive, Dutch broad-leaved, Prussian, cherry-gin, royal hätive and late English cherry. Three or four years in advance, we prepare the trees to be forced by grafting them onto mahalèb, four or six inches from the ground. They are pruned into bushes or cattails, letting them spread out their wood only to the extent of the space they will require in the greenhouse. When the plant is the right size, in autumn, it is lifted with the rootball, and planted in a crate or basket, in good free soil, half mixed with potting compost. Leave it for a year, to allow it to recover, and during this time give it all the care it needs, such as burying the vase, watering, hoeing, etc. Persoons who are not afraid to make the necessary expenditure to raise these subjects in vases (boxes or pots), from their youth, will always achieve more satisfactory success. In any case, from October onwards, a warm layer of half horse manure and half dry leaves is prepared in a greenhouse or a tarpaulin. When the heat is at its peak, holes deep enough to accommodate the vases or baskets are made in the layer, at distances calculated according to the width of the cherry trees. A sufficient thickness of compost is then spread over the entire layer, to ensure that the trees have a well-filled collar, and that the edges of the vases do not show. The trees must be spaced far enough apart, so that air and light can circulate perfectly between all their branches, even when they are leafed out: it is also essential that they are as close as possible to the glasses. We start heating, and it doesn't take long for the gems to swell and develop into leaves and flower buds. Calculate the time of flowering, and don't be afraid to bring it forward or delay it a little, by lowering or raising the heat, so as to take advantage of a few days of sunshine, which is always found in ordinary winters, so that the flowering and fertilization are protected by the light of its rays. If you're lucky enough to seize this favorable moment, almost all the fruit will set, which doesn't always happen when the sky is dark and cloudy. This is a general rule that should be applied to all species of fruit trees, without exception. In any case, the ordinary scins are given in the article on apricot trees. When a currant tree has borne fruit, M you want to keep 1 for another year, don't hurry to put it back in the ground, especially if frosts are still to be feared. Leave it in the greenhouse until March, or move it to an orangery. In spring, we place it in the open ground with good exposure, but nevertheless leaving it in its vase, or, which is much better, placing it with its root ball in a new basket. It is pruned very short to develop wood in the first year. In the second spring, we give it the usual pruning, and the following autumn, if we think it has recovered well enough, we can heat it again. Some trees can only withstand this kind of cultivation for a few years, and perish after being heated twice; others, on the contrary, last a very long time. We need hardly say that to ensure a succession of fruit harvests in the greenhouse, you must not place all the trees in the greenhouse at the same time, but rather from month to month or fortnight to fortnight. ORDINARY CULTIVATION. Cherry trees grow well in all types of soil; however, they only develop their full beauty and longevity in deep, light soils, which are dry for bigarreautier and merisier, and a little cool for cherry and griottier, but not wet. All of them also fear clay soils and stagnant humidity. In the granitic mountains of the Rhône department, I have seen wild or grafted cherry trees grow with astonishing speed and vigor, reaching a height of sixty to eighty feet, in soils where rye can only provide a small harvest every eight or ten years. Cherry trees can be propagated by seed or offspring, but the latter are never as robust as the former, and are almost always attacked by pomom disease. In many countries, we don't bother to sow seedlings, because there are plenty of young trees in the woods suitable for transplanting to the nursery. Varieties are propagated by grafting, on wildings or subjects from wild cherry seeds, if you want to grow large trees; on griottier for medium-sized trees; and on mahaleb, when you want to grow them in cattails or espaliers. We would point out that when grafting onto cherry trees, preference should be given to those with red or white fruit, as the graft is stronger and the trees less prone to gum. In marly or chalky soils, mahaleb provides the best subjects. In addition, it can be grafted with a dormant or growing eye, and even with a split when the stems are a little strong. Cherry trees are not pruned, but they should be pruned for the first two or three years, to give them a nice head. Pruning of espaliers and cattails is carried out according to the same principles as for other stone trees; only, for espaliers, the small fruit-bearing branches that have grown in front are retained. When a cherry tree begins to age, thin out and produce little fruit, it is pruned back to the large branches or even to the trunk, and vigorous scions grow which produce a lot for a few years. CHESTNUT (fagus Castanea); a large, indigenous tree, producing a generally well-known fruit. Several varieties are grown, the main ones being: Chataigne égalade, or exalade, slightly flattened, very large and excellent. The tree produces a lot, but quickly wears out. Pourtalonne, very productive, large and good. La verte du limousin, which is large, good and keeps very well. Maron, known by the names of the country where it is grown, for example: maron de Lyon, de Luc, d'Agen, d'Aubray, etc. This is the biggest, best and most sought-after variety. PRIMEUR. It's impossible to force chestnuts into cultivation, but they can be kept all year round. By leaving them in their husks and placing them in dry sand, wheat or bran, in a dry but cool place, you can easily get green ones until April. If you want to enjoy them for longer, as soon as they are picked, they must be dried first in the sun, then in an oven after being baked. Thus treated, they can be stored for two years without difficulty, provided they are kept in a dry place. ORDINAIRX CULTIVATION. Chestnut thrives in deep, granite soils, and does poorly in damp, clayey soils. It is propagated from seed, and to preserve varieties, it is grafted into flutes or growing eyes. Chestnuts are stratified in January; in spring, they are planted or nursed, producing vigorous trees that are pruned every year until their stems have reached a suitable height. If planted in a nursery, holes are dug at least a year in advance. Plant them in autumn, and when they are well established, i.e. one year after planting, graft them and leave them to nature's care. However, care must be taken to protect them from the teeth of cattle, by wrapping thorn bundles around their trunks. We should point out that the chestnut tree fears shade very much, and usually becomes sterile when deprived of the influences of sun and light. When several are planted, they should therefore be spaced appropriately. When a tree becomes old, its large branches are cut back to within three or four feet of the trunk, more or less, depending on their size; a new head is formed, which produces little fruit, to be sure, but very large and of excellent quality. CHENILLETTE (Scorpiurus vermiculata); annual plant, from the south of France, remarkable for its spiral-rolled, bristly, caterpillar-like pods. They are sometimes used as salad greens, with the intention of surprising people who don't know them, and making them mistake them for disgusting insects. In the past, they were preserved in vinegar and used in the same way as capers. It would be pointless to produce early versions of this plant, so it can only be grown in ordinary conditions. It thrives in light, sandy, warm soils, but does well in all, provided it has good exposure. Sow in April, and the seeds ripen perfectly during the summer. If you want to preserve them in vinegar, pick them before they are fully developed, otherwise they will be too hard to eat. We can also cultivate other species, all curious for their pods: for example, the SCORPIURUS RUDX, (Scorpiurus muricata,) whose pod is slender, slightly striated, with small, scattered, short and inconspicuous tubercles on the back, straight in its lower part and curving towards the top, so as to resemble the larva of certain insects. SCORPIURX VELU, (Scorpiurus subvillosa,) and SCORPIURUS SILLONNÉ, (Scorpiurus sulcata,) whose pods are spiral-shaped like snails. CHERVIS, GIROLLE (Sium sitarum); native perennial plant with fleshy, sweet, slightly aromatic roots, eaten like the scorsonera, mainly fried. 42 Since chervis does not fear frost and is perennial, it is not necessary to cultivate it early, since its roots are available all year round. It's true that those that haven't gone to seed are always the most delicate and therefore the best, so it's a good idea to adopt a cultivation method that can provide young ones all year round. To this end, we sow in spring those that are to be eaten over winter, and in autumn those destined to be eaten the following summer. This plant likes soft, fresh, deep soil, amended a few months in advance or at least with used compost, and perfectly loosened. Sow in April and September, and roots from the first sowing can be harvested as early as November. Seeds are sown in rays, or broadcast, and covered with a rake. Once they have emerged, hoe and weed them, and above all water them very frequently if you want to obtain large, tender tubers, as this plant is very water-loving. Chervis can also be propagated by separating its tubers, with the precaution of leaving a piece of the old stem neck with each one; but it has been noted that the roots obtained by this process never have the delicacy of those resulting from sowing. Chervis produces stems in the same year as sowing, but the seeds they produce are usually sterile. They should therefore only be collected from two-year-old plants. They ripen in September, and retain their germinative qualities for three years; nevertheless, the youngest are the best. WILD CHICORIUM (Cichorium intrbus); native perennial, eaten as a salad when very young, or after blanching. Three varieties are grown: The common variety, found wild on paths, and the most common in gardens. variegated, with red-veined leaves. Coffee chicory, whose long, fleshy, parsnip-like roots are used to replace and, more often, adulterate coffee when, after drying, they have been roasted and ground into powder. Its leaves are eaten in salads like those of the previous two varieties. PRIMEUR. Chicory can be grown in the ground all winter long, but it is hard and almost unbearably bitter, so if you want good winter chicory, grow it on a bed. If you don't grow a large quantity, you can grow it on a bed with small vegetables, because, as it is cut very young and when the leaves have reached two to three inches in length, four inches of soil are enough for it. The first sowing, under cloches or trays, can be done in November, and we continue to sow every twenty days so as not to run out during the winter. Sow fairly thickly, covering the seeds sparingly, and basking frequently. Don't stop sowing on the bed until you can safely entrust the seeds to the soil. This young chicory cannot be blanched. A very white, etiolated chicory known as Barbe-de-capucin is sold on the markets, and is considered an excellent winter salad. We'll explain how it's obtained. Depending on the quantity required, there are different procedures. If you only want it for home use, you grow it in barrels, but if you want it for speculation, you blanch it in layers. Here's how it's done. In autumn (rarely in any other season, although this process can be used every month of the year), take an old barrel, split on one side, and drill round holes seven or eight lines in diameter, in the following order. Assuming the barrel is standing on its bottom, make a row of holes all the way around, four inches from the ground, and spaced an inch or two apart. Make a second row four inches above, a third at the same distance, and so on, all the way to the top of the barrel, which should be placed in a warm, dark cellar. Once the barrel has been laid out in this way, obtain wild chicory roots from a year's sowing, and take care not to break them when pulling them out. After spreading a layer of sand in the bottom of the barrel, up to the level of the first row of holes, lay the roots on top, so that the collars pass through the holes, but do not overflow them by more than a line or two. Add a second bed of sand up to the height of the second row of holes, and put in a new row of roots; and so on, until the barrel is full. Water each bed of sand as you go, or use damp sand, so that you don't need to water when the barrel is full, which would cause the planting to sag and the root collars to pull out of the holes through which they are to grow. If you only had coarse sand that was too raw or washed out, you could mix in a little potting soil. If planted in October or November, it produces very good lettuce all winter long, and a row can be cut every two or three days. If you intend to sell the capuchin beard in tins, use a different method. Using sand, potting soil or even light earth, a first bed two inches thick, two to three feet wide and of indeterminate length is laid in a cellar or other dark, warm place. The chicory roots are laid on top, horizontally and with their heads outwards; then a second bed of soil and roots is made in the same way, a third, and so on, up to a suitable height. The beds should be placed slightly back, one on top of the other, to form a sloping layer and avoid 8 landslides. Water well, and soon the long, etiolated, colorless leaves appear, as in the previous crop. The roots are pulled out of the bed, bundled and delivered to the trade. Market gardeners often blanch chicory in a simpler way. They either pull it into bunches and bury the bunches in hot manure, or leave them on the ground and cover them with dry manure. This method is expeditious, but no better, because no new leaves grow, and it's the old ones that turn white and always remain hard and bitter. ORDIKARY CULTIVATION. Wild chicory does well in any soil deep enough for it to spread its long tap roots, but it thrives best in substantial free soil. To obtain young leaves all year round, it must be sown every two weeks. Sowing starts at the end of April, in light, loamy soil; later sowing continues in heavier soil. Sow thickly, water frequently and weed if necessary. Those intended for blanching or graining are sown light, in rays, in spring. The leaves it produces in the course of the year are used only to feed cattle and rabbits. The seed-bearing plants, which are left in the ground without any care, overwinter very well. The following spring, they rise, and their seeds, which keep for ten years or more, ripen in September, WHITE CHICORICE OR ERDIVE (Cichorium endivia); annual plant, native to India. Blonde or lettuce-leaved, yellowish at birth, very good, but delicate and very sensitive to humidity. La courte or Célestine, very small, but very tender, with little height, and the earliest of all. It has become quite rare in Paris. PRIEUR. Preferred varieties for this type of cultivation are: Itafie chicory, white chicory, white escarole and Célestine. In November, we sow chicory that is always white, on a warm bed and under cloches or frames to cut the young leaves, or the other three varieties to be delivered for consumption only when they have formed. The first is sown fairly thickly, on three or four inches of compost, and sowing should take place every fortnight, if you want to have a constant supply. The most important thing is to give only as much water as is necessary for vegetation, otherwise the humidity, which these plants fear greatly, will melt them before they have produced their products. It is also essential that the beds are constantly maintained at a good level of heat, either by means of reheating or reshuffling, or by renewing them as needed; otherwise, the seeds will rot and grow poorly. Air is given when it is safe to do so, and to let them enjoy the light they need, doormats are removed during the day, whenever it is not freezing, or when there is no fear of frost penetrating under the glass. Seeds of all varieties refuse to germinate if buried, so after throwing them into the soil, simply press them down with the flat of your hand or a small plank palette. Chicory, which is always white, is cut as soon as its leaves have reached three or four inches in length. As for the varieties to be left to form, you can start sowing at the same time, and continue until March. The beds should be kept very warm and covered with six inches of compost. Sow lighter, do not cover the seeds, water moderately, and give air and light as much as possible. Summer chicory, or Italian chicory, is the most successful in this type of cultivation. When the plant is strong enough, it is transplanted onto a new layer, always under a bell and under a frame; it is protected as much as possible from humidity, which is very harmful, and if no care is neglected, chicory can be ready for consumption as early as February. Sometimes, when the season is warm, March seedlings can be transplanted in the open ground, but in warm conditions, in well-soiled beds under cloches. If you want to get very beautiful and good results from January and February seedlings, prepare a muted bed in dry, south-facing soil, plant the seedlings in it, and cover with glass panels. Cloches can also be used, filling the gaps between them with dry manure and bedding. In case of rain, cover with straw mats. There are two ways to grow chicory in December and January: 1° to keep plants grown in the open ground in the vegetable greenhouse; 2° to prick out on bedding. It's the latter that we're going to deal with here. From the beginning of September to October, we sow Meaux chicory in an earthen bed at the foot of a south-facing wall, and leave it there until the approach of the white frosts. Then raise a warm layer filled with six inches of potting soil, remove the plant with the rootball, and plant it in the layer, taking care to water it immediately to help it take root. Cover with cloches or trays, and grow as usual. ORDINARY CULTIVATION: All chicory varieties degenerate rapidly if not properly cared for. In March and April, sow on a south-facing terrace, and later in a bed of light, loose earth, suitably top-dressed. Blond cabbage is preferred to the previous variety by many people, because its leaves are softer and have a milder flavor. It is also hardy. Cabbage with large collars and fringed leaves differs from the previous varieties only in its green leaves with fringed edges. It can be grown in the same way, and is no more sensitive to cold. As all these cabbages produce in winter as well as in summer, they do not need to be forced, so we will only consider them from the point of view of their ordinary cultivation. It is customary to sow them in nurseries in March and April, in well-soiled and perfectly loosened beds with good exposure. In April and May, i.e. when the plant is strong enough, it is permanently repotted, spacing each variety as we have said. Ordinary care is given, and it produces in winter and spring. In July and August, sow in beds with northern exposure, water frequently and transplant permanently in September and November. The plants from these seedlings produce during the following summer. Nevertheless, these times are not so rigorous that you can't advantageously sow every month from spring to autumn. All green cabbages, with the exceptions we have mentioned in each article where necessary, are grown in the same way. They do very well broadcast and in open fields, provided the soil is prepared with good fertilizers and ploughing. In this case, they are very profitable as green fodder for the cowshed during the bad season. II. MILAN cabbage, or Poutis-raisis. Cabbages of this breed are easy to recognize by their short stalks, loosely packed heads, and more or less embossed and braided leaves. They are usually softer and more delicate than cabbages, and taste much less like musk. Apple as large as that of a large cabbage, which it resembles a little in the way it is made, and in its leaves, which are less blistered than in the preceding varieties and sometimes of a glaucous green. Vilmorin from Boston, has leaves cut to the rib, in narrow, irregular and stiff strips; its stem is a foot high, its apple round, of medium size, very tender and excellent. Savoy cabbages can be stored well until spring, so there's no need to grow them as early as possible. They are sown in two seasons: 1. from the end of February to May; 2. in August and September. The earliest are sown in June, and they follow one another without interruption until the frosts. When the young plant has been sown in a well-drained and loosened bed, watered, weeded and carefully thinned out, it can be planted out after a month or five weeks. Transplant in rows or staggered rows, spacing the larger species three feet apart and the smaller ones eighteen inches apart. They require only the usual care, i.e. watering during the heat, and hoeing from time to time. When the frosts come, you can leave outside those whose head is not yet fully formed, and particularly the Tourraine pancalier and the ordinary milan, as they finish peeling very well, either in the interval between the frosts, or when they are over. Varieties that fear the cold more, such as the blond pancalier, the long-headed kite, etc., are lifted from the ground with the root ball, and after having detached part of their large leaves, they are taken to the vegetable greenhouse, where they are buried in dry sand up to the bottom of the apple. They keep perfectly well until March or even April. Savoy cabbages can also be stored without a vegetable greenhouse. Before the cold weather sets in, a little soil is removed from the base of each cabbage in the first row, and on the north side, the cabbages are tilted into these sort of trenches, but with as little uprooting as possible. The holes in the second row are started, and the soil is thrown over the roots and stems of those in the first, continuing in this way until all the rows have been laid down. In this way, rainwater slides over the leaves and prevents it from penetrating the heart of the plant, which would inevitably cause it to rot. During hard frosts, we throw a little straw or bedding over the cabbages to protect them from the excess cold. To save space, by making them occupy a much smaller area, you can also dig a pit one foot deep by a width and length determined by the number of cabbages you want to shelter. We pull them out, or carry them into the pit, and place them there, one against the other, in an inclined position, and throw a little earth on their roots. During frosts, they are covered with straw mats, long litter or dry leaves. Finally, some people are content to store them in a cellar, where they keep quite well if it's neither too hot nor too dry. 9 this breed are numerous and widely cultivated; their heads are very tight and very hard, but they often have a musky odor that many people dislike.
