FRUIT GARDEN. - This month's work is limited to little else. Nevertheless, we are keeping an eye on Peach tree vegetation, in order to maintain the balance of the sap. Trees that had grown too vigorously during the previous month are grafted, and the fruit is protected from the voracity of birds and insects. We give the last hoeing. 1. ORNAMENTAL GARDEN. - Same care and maintenance as in previous months. This is the best time to sow lawns with grass, as there is still enough time for it to cover the ground before winter, and in spring it is in a position to resist drought, which is very contrary to it. This is also the time to mow boxwood borders, sow Clarkias, Collinsias, Coréopsis, Crépis, Énothères, Alyssum maritimum, Gilias, Mufliers, Némophiles, Œillets de Chine, Silènes, Saponaire de Calabre. Thlaspis, etc., and prick out the plants in the nursery before winter, before planting them in the spring. Sow Anagallis, Brachycomes, Centranthus, Eucharidium, Leptosiphon, Nemesia, Nycterinia, Malopes, Phlox Drummondi, Schizanthus, Trachymene and Viscaria in pots and winter them under a frame. Also plant Iris Germanica, sow Giroflées quarantaines to transplant on teens, or in pots, which we bring in as soon as the cold sets in. Sow Ranunculus and Anemone in pots or in the ground. Separate and replant herbaceous Peonies, but in such a way that the buds are only covered by about Om, 5 or Om, 3 of soil. Plant Pancratiums Illyricum, bulbous Fumeterres and Alstræmerias, which can withstand full soil; also plant Daffodils Om, 5 or Om, 6 deep, as well as Muscaris, Hyacinths, Crocuses, early Tulips and Narcissus, which you want to heat through the winter. You can also take cuttings of Calceolaria, Ageratum Mexicanum, white-flowered Chrysanthemums and Verbena. GREENHOUSES. - Around the 15th, we bring in the warm greenhouse plants, which will suffer from the drop in temperature. Temperate greenhouse and orangery plants are repotted, so that they can be taken up before they are brought in, and panels are put back on greenhouses and tarpaulins. OCTOBER. Average barometer height, 754 mill. 465. Mean temperature, maximum - 14°.73. minimum - 90.46. Rainfall, 48 mill. 10, Hygrometer reading, 82°,5. GENERAL WORKS. - Start winter ploughing, planting work and changes to garden layout; make tree holes, plant even if in a hurry. Separate borders and clumps of perennials, prune hardy trees, start mowing hedges, cover delicate plants; harvest seeds, fruit and vegetables. If you have land to move for certain garden layouts, you can get started. In the evening, we make mats, so as to be able to cover the frames and greenhouses in the course of the following month. VEGETABLE GARDEN. Layers. - Green asparagus is first heated, and pineapple eyelets are planted in pots proportionate to the strength of each; immediately after planting, the pots are placed on a layer, and from this time until spring, the heaters must be reshuffled every month. Plants planted at the same time the previous year should be removed from the soil and placed in the greenhouse. In the first fortnight, we sow small black lettuces under cloches and on ados; we raise these lettuces without ever giving them air. At the same time, we sow Romaine verte maraîchère, and in the second fortnight Laitue rouge, Laitue gotte and Romaine blonde ou grise maraîchère. When the plant begins to have a few leaves, place three rows of bells along the length of the bed, and transplant around thirty plants under each row. For the first week after planting, give the plant some air by raising the bells by about Om, 3, then after this time, gradually increase to Om, 8, and only lower the bells when it freezes at 2 or 3 degrees. When properly cared for, this plant will be used for all plantings from December to the end of February. Early cauliflowers and cabbages are transplanted in the nursery. N. 6 Towards the end of the month or at the beginning of November, fine Chicory sown in the first fortnight of September and two rows of Cauliflower sown in the first days of September are planted on the ground, but under a frame. If, towards the end of the month, we fear frost, we should put the panels on the Lettuces planted n. 3. Open ground, n. 19 - Spinach is sown for spring. In the second half of the year, white onions sown in the second half of August are transplanted to n. 18, and chervil or lamb's lettuce are sown in between. The last sowings of bulbous Chervil are made. Towards the end of the month, or at the beginning of November, cut off the old Asparagus stems, and give each bed a light hoeing with a fork, then spread a good mulch of manure. Celery and cardoons continue to be blanched. FRUIT GARDEN. - There's nothing left to do to the trees until it's time to prune them; however, we can mark those we intend to remove, so that they can be lifted the following month. This is the time to pick the fruit and place it in the fruit garden, which should only be done when the weather is dry and as the trees stop vegetating. ORNAMENTAL GARDEN. - Cut the stems of perennials that have stopped flowering. Clean, smoke and plough flowerbeds before planting plants that will flower in the spring. Collect leaves that have fallen into the pathways and give them a final facelift. Sow in place Cynoglosses, Larkspur, Poppies, Mahon's Clover, Adonides, etc. Redo borders of Mignardise, Boxwood, Marjoram, Thyme and Hyssop; wean Carnation marcots, and plant them in pots or in the ground. Plant Hyacinths at Om, 10 deep, and pot those intended for heating. Plant Spanish and English irises at Om, 3 deep; Crocus in pots, borders or lawns, where they will produce a charming effect in spring and will be deflowered before it is necessary to cut the lawn. Tulips should be planted about Om.6 deep. You should also plant Golden Garlic and Italian Scillium, and raise Gladioli planted in spring. As soon as the first frosts set in, remove Dahlias, Erythrins and Balisiers from the soil, and place them in the orangery or in a dry cellar to overwinter. Do the same with all greenhouse plants planted in the spring to line beds and flowerbeds. They should be pruned and potted; then, to restore them, put them under a panel for some time. GREENHOUSES. - Pelargoniums are brought in during the first fortnight, and orange, pomegranate and laurel trees during the second, unless there is premature cold. The most delicate plants, those that need air and light, are placed close to daylight, and the hardiest are placed behind. When all the plants have been brought in, we hoe the soil in the pots or crates, and give them a light watering. NOVEMBER. Average barometer height, 755 mill. 614. Average temperature, maximum - 10°,15. minimum - 4°,74. Quantity of rain, 55 mill. 87. Hygrometer status, 820.2. GENERAL WORKS. - We begin planting and plowing, as well as clearing the land for new planting. Care is taken to preserve plants that fear frost, and leaves are collected to make layers and cover frames. When you have a choice, Oak and Chestnut leaves are the ones to be preferred. VEGETABLE GARDEN. Layers. - We continue to heat green asparagus and start heating white asparagus. In the first few days of the month, we sow Peas under chassis, but in the ground, for replanting under chassis. We sow Georges Lettuce under cloches and on ados, and treat the plant as we have indicated for red Lettuce and gottes. Green Romaines are lifted and immediately replanted under cloches, but this time only twelve or fifteen are planted per cloche. If the Romaine blonde or gris plant advances too much, it must be transplanted a second time, as with the Romaines vertes. In the event of severe frosts, the bells covering the Lettuce and Romaine plants should be lined with dry old manure or leaves, and a stove raised to the surface of the bells should be used to line the back of the bed. The cover should be increased according to the intensity of the cold, and the bells uncovered when the sun is shining; but it is necessary to check first whether the plant is not affected by frost, because then, instead of uncovering, the cover should be increased and the plant should be allowed to thaw gradually. Open ground. - We pull out the Celery planted in n. 37, to replant it in rows in a trench; when heavy frosts come, we cover it with litter or leaves, which we remove when the weather becomes milder. N. 31. Towards the end of the month, we sow Michaux Peas, and, in the intervals, Lettuce for cutting. Artichoke stalks and the longest leaves are cut off, then mounded, an operation which consists in raising the soil around each clump, so that it is buried almost to the top. When there's a hard frost, we cover them with litter or leaves, which are removed when the weather is mild. To make sure you don't run out of supplies during frosts, all vegetables that could be damaged by frost or prevented from being pulled out, such as carrots, beets, turnips, chicory, scarole, celery and cardoons, should be pulled out and placed in a gauge, either in the vegetable greenhouse or in the vegetable garden. You'll need to cover with straw or leaves any plants you've straddled in the garden, such as leeks, salsify, scorzonera and turnips, and uncover them whenever the weather permits. Also, during the month, pull out the cabbages from which the apples are made, and put them in gauges, so as to be able to use them during the frosts. Later in the month, but as late as possible, cut cauliflower heads, which should only be done when the weather is dry, and put them in the vegetable greenhouse, where they can be stored until April. FRUIT GARDEN. - Prune old or debilitated trees, to prevent the sap from rising in the buds that need to be removed, and the tree from becoming exhausted. Grub out trees that you intend to remove. Start planting fruit trees in chalky, light or sandy soils, where it is always preferable to plant in autumn, except for Mulberry and Fig trees, which should only be planted in spring. Fruit trees intended for heating the following year should also be planted in pots. If a few panels are available in the first fortnight, they should be placed in front of the vine espalier; in this way, grapes can be preserved in all their beauty until January. Towards the end of the month, Fig trees can be stuffed, or, if the branches are flexible enough to be lowered to the ground, they can be secured with wooden hooks, then covered with soil. ORNAMENTAL GARDEN. - Spade lawn edges. Pull up defoliated annuals. Plough flowerbeds and beds. Divide and replant perennials whose clumps have become too large. Put yellow Giroflées in place, as well as Hollyhocks, Poetic Carnations, Golden Corbels and Thlaspis. Finish planting tulips, hyacinths and daffodils. Sow the first Sweet Peas. Weed out Dahlias in the second half of the month, if the weather has been favorable enough to leave them in the ground until then. Butter the free-standing roses, which usually suffer in our winters. Start planting ornamental trees and shrubs, except for resinous trees, Catalpas, Magnolias grandiflora and Tulip trees, which should not be planted until spring. When it starts to freeze, pot carnations, large-flowered wallflowers and Cocardeau should be covered or placed in the greenhouse. GREENHOUSE. - All greenhouse plant care consists in renewing the air as often as possible, keeping them clean and only wetting them with the utmost reserve. We start covering the warm greenhouse at night, and continue until April. When, in the evening, the weather is clear, the wind is easterly, and the thermometer registers no more than 3 or 4 degrees above zero, cover all the frames and greenhouses with straw mats. DECEMBER. GENERAL WORKS. - Work in the open ground is very limited; fertilizers can be transported and spread on the soil in which they are to be buried. Plowing continues, frost permitting. Towards the end of the month or at the beginning of January, the trenches are emptied of the old melon beds, so that the site can be laid out. VEGETABLE GARDEN. Layers. - The cessation of work in the open ground gives gardeners time to take care of their beds, which require all their care. As soon as the beds indicated for this month are made, they should be covered with panels, so that the manure will ferment more quickly; and, unless there is weather to the contrary, those on which you have sown or planted can be uncovered every day, taking care to cover before nightfall. Continue heating white and green asparagus. In the first fortnight, sow early Raves, and in the second fortnight Leeks. N. 3. around the 15th of this month, sow early short carrots on beds and under frames, and plant small black lettuce sown in the first fortnight of October. N. 4 Plant clumps of sorrel on beds and under frames. N. 5. in the first fortnight, transplant Peas sown in the first days of November to the ground, but under a frame. Open ground. - At the onset of frost, Broccoli are lifted into clods and planted close together, deep enough for the stem to be buried up to the first leaves. Cardoons are tied, lifted into clods and moved into the vegetable greenhouse. Parsley is covered with straw or leaves, and when the weather is mild, artichokes are uncovered a little; but it's wise to cover them in the evening; and, if the frost increases, they should be covered with a greater quantity of leaves or litter. We continue to sow Michaux Peas, and in the first fortnight we plant at n. 12 York Cabbages sown in the first days of September. FRUIT GARDEN. - Planting continues, and in heavy, clayey or damp soils, holes are made only for planting in February or March. The soil is ripped, smoked and ploughed, and towards the end of the month the mobile greenhouses are placed on the Vines and espaliered fruit trees to be heated. ORNAMENTAL GARDEN. - Continue with layout changes, prune trees, break up old lawns for reseeding, repair damaged paths and continue planting. Renonculas can be planted in the second fortnight. GREENHOUSE. - Maintain the temperature of the pineapple greenhouse, fill the strawberry shelves, renew the air in the temperate greenhouse and orangery when it's not freezing, and close them before the sun disappears. Cover Camellias, Rhododendrons, Magnolias and other hardy shrubs. Although they can remain three months without light and without any care, it is nevertheless a good idea to visit them occasionally to remove the mildew that the absence of air can produce. JANUARY. Mean barometer height, 757 mill. 759. Mean temperature, maximum - 7°,10. minimum - 4°,41. Rainfall, 36 mill. 27. Hygrometer reading, 86°,5. GENERAL WORK. - This month is usually cold and wet; but, weather permitting, we continue the ripping and plowing that could not take place during the previous month; and we open the asparagus pits for spring; we also bring to the field manure destined to be buried; we pile up that which will be used to make layers, stoves, etc.. When the weather is severe enough to prevent outdoor work, the necessary repairs are made to the gardening tools, the seeds are cleaned and everything necessary for subsequent operations is prepared. The gardener who has greenhouses and beds has a constant occupation, and at this time of year they require all his care. If the weather is wet, you must remove the bedding covering the artichokes and cover them as soon as you fear the return of the cold. VEGETABLE GARDEN. Layers. - Layers must be cared for, stoves must be refilled, and those that don't need refilling must be filled so that they are always as high as the surface area of the panels. Unless the weather is unfavorable, uncover the panels every day, and give the plants some air when the sun is shining by lifting the panels on the side opposite the wind; it's a good idea to cover them before frost forms on the glass. We start heating pineapples that are ready to bear fruit, continue heating white and green asparagus, and plant Marjolin potatoes. The first fine Chicory is sown on very hot beds, for planting under frames. Parsley is also sown in trays, or new plants are planted. Continue planting sorrel clumps. Early Peas are sown in cloches or under frames, to be transplanted into the ground, and towards the end of the month, frames are put over the Strawberry plants that we want to force into the ground. N. 4 In the second half of the month, transplant Dutch Beans sown in the first half of the month, on a bed and under a frame. N. 7. we make a layer on which we place three rows of bells. Under each bell, plant four small black lettuces (sown in the first fortnight of October), and in the middle a green Romaine, chosen from those sown in the first days of October. Open ground. - There is little work to be done in the open ground; however, if it doesn't freeze towards the end of the month, you can plant York and Oxheart cabbages, sown in the first few days of September, and Romaine verte, sown in the first fortnight of October, in light soil with good exposure; then sow early carrots and leeks among them. FRUIT GARDEN. - Continue planting and, weather permitting, start pruning espalier and cattail apple and pear trees when it's not freezing, continuing until March, always starting with the least vigorous; remove dead wood and destroy caterpillar nests. Cut branches for grafting, or take cuttings and bury them in sand to the north, away from frost and atmospheric influences. When cold weather or other circumstances prevent trees intended for planting from being put in place immediately, they should be laid out in gauges and their roots covered to protect them from frost. Dull the trees and treat them with lime milk, to destroy lichens and insects that attach themselves to the bark. For the same purpose, whiten the walls of espaliered trees, which can be done with a garden syringe similar to the one used to wash greenhouse plants. Start heating Vines, Cherry, Peach, Plum and Fig trees. ORNAMENTAL GARDEN. - There is little work to be done in the harsh season; however, we take advantage of the favorable weather to do the groundwork, plow the beds and bury the leaves. Planting can also continue. In the second half of this month, we can start sowing Madagascar Periwinkle on a hot bed. GREENHOUSE. - Put potted Hyacinths, Narcissus, early Tulips, Bengal Roses, Lilacs, Rhododendrons, etc., whose flowering is to be brought forward, under chassis or in the greenhouse. Uncover the greenhouses every day, unless the weather is adverse, and, when the sun is shining, give the orangery and the temperate greenhouse a little air; lastly, carefully visit the plants placed in the greenhouses, and make sure they are not affected by rot. ORNAMENTAL GARDEN. - Plough copses and beds, as well as lawns to be sown at the end of the month. Planting can continue until March. Sow larkspur, poppies, Mahon wallflowers, Thlaspis, reseda, if not sown in autumn. Plant Ranunculus, Om, 05 deep. Sow in the bed: Giroflées quarantaines, Amarantes, Pervenches, Petunias, Mimulus, Lobélias; almost all annual plants, except autumn ones; then, when the seedling is strong enough, transplant it in the nursery, to be planted out only in April and May. GENERAL WORKS. - This month's work is the first of the year to require the full activity of gardeners. We must hurry to finish ploughing, bury manures and fertilizers and redo the borders everywhere. Plants that have been ridged and covered to protect them from frost are uncovered; seedlings and plantations must still be covered with a small layer of compost or light mulch, to protect them from spring frosts and sunst, and seedlings that have been stored in a gauge or in the vegetable greenhouse are planted. FRUIT GARDEN - In addition to general work, the gardener must take care to maintain the balance between the different parts of his trees and to encourage their development. Those that remain in the greenhouse should be given fresh air, sheltered from the sun's rays and watered as needed. CHAPTER III. Gardening tools. All the instruments listed in this chapter are indispensable for cultivating a garden; and, although we have no intention of charging those who draw information from our book, we advise them to obtain most of them, in order to simplify operations. § I. - Tools for ploughing and planting. BÈCHE DE SOISSONS. - The blade is a little hollowed out in the middle; it is Om, 27 long by 0.20 wide at the top, and Om, 16 at the bottom. Instead of having a socket, the blade is fixed to the handle with two riveted pins. BÈCHE DE SENLIS. - The handle is 1 meter long, not including the part inserted in the socket; the iron is Om, 30 high, Om, 22 wide at the top and Om, 18 at the bottom. BINETTE. - The hoe is a small hoe whose blade is just Om, 16 long by Om, 12 wide. It is used to stir up the soil between plants whose rows are a little apart, and to make holes for planting beans and potatoes. FANG HOE. - This hoe has a double blade, with a cutting edge on one side and two long teeth on the other. HOYAU. - A tool for making trenches, uprooting trees and preparing compact soils for ploughing with a spade. The handle has Om, 76, and the blade, which forms a right angle with the handle, Om, 32. HOULETTE. - The houlette is a small spade whose blade, about Om, 15 long, Om, 10 wide, is folded cylindrically on its sides: it is intended for lifting cloddy plants. PICKAXE OR TURNER. - This instrument is particularly used for earthworks; it is also useful for making holes and removing large trees. PLANTOIR. - To make a planter, select a tree branch bent at the end, then taper the part to be driven into the ground, and to make it more durable and penetrable, have it lined with iron or copper. TRIDENT TRACEOIR - The advantage of this instrument is that you don't have to move the chalk line as many times as you need rays in a board. To trace six rays, you need only stretch the string twice, and for five rays only once, placing it in the middle of the board. The spokes can be made more or less widely spaced, as the two side branches are fixed at the bottom by means of a hinge, and on the crosspiece by a small movable pin, which enables them to be moved further apart or closer together as required. SHEARING SCISSORS. - These are large scissors, Om 40 in length, whose handles form a very open angle with the blade; they are used for mowing hedges, lawns, borders, etc. The blades should have some play and not be too sharp. The blades must have some play and not be tightened by a nut. To use them, the blades must be pressed together with opposing forces. SIMPLE IRON-TOOTHED RAKE. - Used to clean paths, smooth the surface of newly-ploughed ground, then lightly cover seedlings. You need at least two of them, one about Om, 30, and the other about Om, 45. RATISSOIRE A POUSSER. - Handle, 1m, 40 long; blade, Om, 20. SHOOTING SHOVEL. - Used in areas where the earth is hardest. The blade, which is Om, 20 wide, is made from a piece of old scythe. The handle is 1m, 15 long. ROLLER. - The roller is a large cast-iron or stone cylinder, fitted at each end with a rounded auricle, turning like an axle in an iron loop; it is used with advantage for rolling earth and turf. SARCLOIR. - This instrument is used to weed between plants that are not sown too thickly. Its total length is Om, 25. SII. - Transport tools. WHEELBARROW WITH TRUNK. - The proportions of a wheelbarrow are: length, 1m,50 to 1m,60; width of the trunk, Om, 50 to Om, 55; spacing of the arms at their ends, Om, 65; outside diameter of the wheel, Ou, 48. HOOK FOR CARRYING BOXES. - These hooks are made of iron, and one end forms a loop through which a 2-meter-long stretcher is passed; with the help of these hooks, two men can easily transport very heavy crates. DIABLE. - This device is indispensable for entering and removing crates that cannot be transported using the hooks. To remove them, approach the device in such a way as to engage the chins under the crate; chock the wheels, and press down on the jib so that the crate is positioned obliquely; you can then easily direct it wherever you wish. FOURCHE ORDINAIRE (ORDINARY FORK) - This instrument is used to make beds, transport manure and harrow vegetable garden beds. HOTTEREAU (pronounced HOTTRIAU). - Used to transport manure and potting soil. In market gardens, it replaces the wheelbarrow. WOODEN SHOVEL. - As this instrument is more or less the same everywhere, we think it unnecessary to give its proportions; it is used to remove earth and potting soil, to pile them up, and so on. SIII. - Watering instruments. WATERING CAN. - This instrument, which must be made of copper to last longer, holds about ten liters of water. SPRINKLER for wetting greenhouses. It should be at least a third smaller than the apple watering can. To water seedlings and cuttings, use the apple instead of the extension spout. POMPE A MAIN ET A JET CONTINUUU, by M. Petit. - This instrument, which sprays water from a height of 5 or 6 meters, is used to water trees that are too high to use a syringe. SERINGUE for washing tree heads and orangery and greenhouse plants. Its total length is Om, E0. § IV. - Instruments for pruning and trimming trees. GROWING. - This instrument, whose blade is placed at the end of a more or less long handle, is used for pruning trees and weeding; but for the latter purpose, it is advantageously substituted for the weeder, whose operation is much less tiring. BUD CUTTER. - A type of secateur with curved blades, used for disbudding and facilitating this operation. ECHENILLOIR. - In certain circumstances, this instrument can be replaced by the crescent, but the latter is always less convenient. SEWER. - The choice of this instrument is of the utmost importance, for if it is badly made, it will skin the branches and harm the tree's vegetation. Its advantage over the pruning knife is that it makes pruning easier, but it cannot compete in all circumstances with the latter, which always makes sharper wounds. HAND SAW, designed to remove branches that cannot be cut with pruning shears. Its overall length is Om, 25. EGOHINE, used to cut branches in places where the hand saw cannot reach. SERPET. - Various sizes are made, but the most commonly used have a handle about Om, 12, long, and a blade from Om, 08 to Om, 09. SERPE. - Used for felling large branches, making the points of stakes and stakes, etc. CHAPTER IV. Ripping and Lahours. When establishing a new garden, the first thing to do is to assess the condition and depth of the soil, which is essential, especially if trees are to be planted. If the top layer of soil is poor, or has been under cultivation for a very long time, and the fertility has been exhausted, it must be broken up. If, as is often the case, the land is covered with tall grasses, they should be pulled up, piled together and burned when dry enough. The ashes should be spread over the site after breaking, which should be done in autumn or winter as follows: At one end of the site, open a trench 1.60 to 2 meters wide (called a gauge). Usually, all you need to do is remove two spade-heads, and dig the bottom of the trench before filling it. However, in some areas, the trench must be dug much deeper. The site is divided into two, three or four parts, depending on the number of workers. The earth from the first trench is deposited at the end where the work is to be completed, to fill the void in the last trench. Each trench is successively replaced by another of the same length, taking care to bring the soil from the bottom to the surface. Remove all the bad earth and stones, and place them in the large alleys, from which all the good earth will be removed. Once the earth has been broken up, give it a good blow with a fork to break up the clods and even out the surface; then rake out the stones, which will be used to fill in the alleys. 1. Ploughing - In light soils, deep ploughing should be carried out annually on fine winter days; in compact, damp soils, chains of ploughing should be carried out in autumn, i.e. the soil should be removed from the surface of the ground, and brought together in mounds or, better still, in parallel lines. Frosts will dry them out, and in spring they will be much easier to cultivate. In gardens, work is done with a spade. Before starting, remove soil to form a gauge a good spade-shank deep (Om 25 to Om, 30 approx.), Om, 30 to Om, 35 wide, and the length of a single man's plank. If two planks are to be ploughed side by side, the soil from the gauge is placed on the next plank and on the same end. If you only have one, place it at the end where you want to finish, so as to have enough to fill the last gauge. As it is also at this time of year that manure is buried, it should be spread evenly over the whole plot, which often makes it possible to plough during frosts; without this precaution, the cold would harden the surface of the soil and prevent any work. We plough backwards, taking the soil by spadeful, which we replace on the other edge of the gauge, turning it over each time so that the bottom one is on top, then we push manure into each gauge, taking care not to bury it too deeply, so that it is within reach of the roots. The clods of earth should be picked up with a spade, and any stones thrown aside. When ploughing, be especially careful to put the 3. soil from the paths into the bed, as it will have had a year's rest. For winter ploughing, the surface of the land should not be too even; only when planting or sowing is required, it should be levelled with a fork. Proceed as described for the entire garden, always maintaining the same gauge width. When ploughing at the foot of trees, care must be taken not to damage their roots. Whenever you want to follow one crop with another, you should plough the land, but not as deeply as in winter, and take care to remove weeds beforehand, whose seeds will germinate quickly once buried. In extremely thin soils, where some fertilizer is always necessary, it should only be used very sparingly. 2. Weeding. - Weeding consists in removing foreign plants and weeds from the soil. This operation is carried out by hand, and requires a certain amount of practice to distinguish at a glance which plants need to be removed and which need to be kept. It is easy to understand that this work must be very difficult when the soil is dry: that's why, in this case, you must take care to baste, at least one hour before starting this operation, the beds that need to be weeded. 3. Hoeing. - Hoeing is an operation no less necessary for vegetable plants than weeding; it is carried out with the hoe, and, as required, with the blade or teeth. The purpose of hoeing is to divide the soil surface, making it permeable to atmospheric influences and watering. In some circumstances (e.g. for transplanted plants), hoeing can replace weeding, and sometimes a rake can be used instead of a hoe. CHAPTER V. Manure and fertilizers. We will only discuss the most common fertilizers; the others, such as horn shavings, animal black, dried blood, bone powder, guano and perazote fertilizer, are used only in large-scale cultivation. The ones we recommend, and which are easiest to obtain, are decomposing plant debris. You can also use pond sludge and street sweepings, which are also good fertilizers, but only after they have been left in piles for a long time, stirred several times during the winter and matured by the influences of the atmosphere. The pomace of grapes and cider pears is also very good, when it has been left in the heap long enough to prevent the seeds from germinating once in the ground. Pigeon and hen droppings should only be used very dry and reduced to dust, and, like poudrette, lightly broadcast, and only in strong soils. This type of manure can only be used in very limited circumstances, whereas manure made from litter mixed with the urine and excrement of domestic animals can be found in abundance everywhere. The hottest manures are horse, mule, donkey and sheep; the most compact and coldest are beef, cow and pig. Whatever manure is used, we believe it should be buried only after fermentation, without waiting until it has been fully consumed; fresh manure does not act as fertilizer, but as an amendment; therefore, in strong, damp and cold soils, which need to be divided, only unconsumed manures should ever be used. Another disadvantage of these manures is that they still contain seeds whose fermentation has not been able to destroy the germinative principle, and which quickly cover the soil with weeds. For light, hot soils that need to be bound, use cow manure; if this is not available, use another type, but it should only be used when half consumed. Manure should be spread in all areas where it is to be buried, in winter and during the first frosts. Whatever fertilizer you use, you should apply as much as possible every year, especially to vegetable beds that are always under cultivation. Manures and leaves almost consumed from old beds should be reserved for spreading each year as mulch on flowerbeds and all growing areas, which is still a good fertilizer; but garden weeds should not be mixed with these manures until they have been completely reduced to potting soil. Fertilizers should be buried early enough so that they have had time to consume themselves before plant roots can reach them, especially fleshy roots. Some vegetable plants, such as Leeks and Onions, do better in smoked soil from the previous year. Watering. 49 As water is one of the main agents of vegetation, it is indispensable in a garden. When you don't have a watercourse to dispose of as you please, it is necessary to obtain water by every possible means. Rainwater, which is more beneficial to vegetation than any water flowing on the surface of the ground, must be collected with care; to this end, all roofs must be fitted with gutters, so as not to let any rainwater escape. The water should be collected in a reservoir placed at a certain height, to facilitate the distribution of water through pipes to all parts of the garden. In the absence of running or gushing water, you will have to resort to well water. In this circumstance, you will need to consider the best way of drawing it; for it is deplorable that in many localities we are still reduced to the necessity of using rope and buckets, an exercise that is as long as it is tiring; whereas with a triple-acting pump, we can easily obtain 12 to 1,500 liters of water per hour. It's true that you need a horse to do this, and that many people are so unconcerned about their gardener that they'd rather leave their horses in the stable than put one at his disposal for a few hours each day during the summer months; however, this would be highly advantageous, as well water almost always contains carbonate and often sulfate of lime; In some places, these substances are so abundant that the water deposits a layer of calcareous salts on the soil and plant leaves, preventing the roots from benefiting from atmospheric influences and the leaves from fulfilling their physiological functions, which sometimes leads to the loss of crops, or more often to a state of languor no less detrimental. In such cases, it is essential to have a reservoir so that the water can be used only a few hours after it has been drawn off, allowing the harmful substances it contains to settle. It's also a good idea to let the water warm up in the sun; for the watering of delicate plants or those grown on beds, the water should never be less than 8 to 10 degrees hot. The same is not true for large vegetables; on the contrary, the water should be used as soon as it is drawn from the well, otherwise it would activate their vegetation too much, and they would not be able to develop to their full potential. Soil fertility can be enhanced by watering with manure, cow dung, sheep dung or other animal matter. Pellets, poudrette and guano, used in small doses of around 3 or 4 kilograms per hectoliter of water, also make a good liquid fertilizer, and can be used to water potted or outdoor plants once a week during the summer. The quantity and frequency of watering cannot be determined in advance; we can only say that it should be more or less abundant, depending on the temperature and nature of the soil. To ensure that plants benefit as much as possible from watering during the hot days of June, July and August, water only in the afternoon; in spring and autumn, when nights are usually cool, water in the morning. The most frequently used watering cans, especially for wetting seedlings and recently transplanted plants, are those with knobs; spouted watering cans are used for wetting potted plants. Apple watering cans are used to wet delicate, newly transplanted plants. CHAPTER VII. Diapers. In northern climates, where vegetation is suspended by the cold for varying lengths of time, gardeners resort to artificial means to compensate for the sun's heat and produce premature crops. Even in the humblest garden, it is impossible to do without a bed, even if only to sow certain flower or vegetable seeds that cannot succeed in the open ground or only produce late. I. LAYERS FOR EARLY PLANTS. - Layers should always face south, and the site on which they are planted should be dug out by about Om 20. Their thickness depends on several circumstances: 1° Those made in December, January and February should be thicker than at any other time of the year; 2° On cold, damp soil, they should be thicker than on sandy soil; 3° The narrower they are, the thicker they should be. We usually make them Im, 30 wide, plus a path of Om, 40 which we leave between each one and which we fill with manure; to maintain and revive the heat, we surround the layers with stoves of new manure, which we renew from time to time. New horse manure, i.e. that which comes out of the stable, is preferred for the layers: the more it is soaked with urine, the better it is. We mix it with half tree leaves, grape marc or a third of manure from old layers. The heat is not as strong as with manure alone, but it lasts much longer, is more regular, and you have less to fear from excessive heat development, which can sometimes lead to the loss of young plants. In the absence of manure, you could even make do with leaves or grape marc. New manure alone should be used only for warmers and some seedlings, such as melons. Before starting to build up a layer, to mix the manures evenly, place them as close as possible to the place they are to occupy. Always work backwards, taking care to mix the dry parts with those most impregnated with urine, and to distribute the manure evenly. The edges of the layer should be raised vertically; and as soon as a bed of manure has been formed, it is wetted more or less, as required, with the apple watering can, so that everything is damp enough to produce prolonged fermentation and prevent the manure from drying out in the center, which could compromise the result of the operation. To give the layer an even density at all points, it is tamped down with the feet and the back of the fork; then manure is added in the hollow places, so that the thickness is even. The same is done with each bed, until the layer has reached the desired height, after which the paths are filled in and the troughs are placed. Once the coffers have been placed, the layer is loaded with potting soil; then the panels are laid, which must be kept covered for a few days to facilitate fermentation. Before sowing or planting on a new layer, it is advisable to wait until the initial heat has moderated. If, in spite of this precaution, the heat develops too much, the stoves should be quickly removed from the trunk; and if this is not enough, a few watering cans should be poured around the bed to cool it down. Thermosiphon. - In some circumstances, manure layers can be replaced by thermosiphon heating. This is usually done by laying a very thin layer (1) to protect the plants from the dampness of the soil, and then running the pipes over the layer. Alternatively, a wooden floor can be laid underneath (1) Figure 2 shows a double-walled copper boiler filled with water; the A feed pipe is also used to introduce the water into the boiler; it communicates with the B circulation pipes by means of an elbow of the same diameter. As soon as it is exchanged, the water in the boiler expands, pushing the water in the pipes up to point C, where it is circulated by the thermosiphon pipes; but plants grown on this floor require too frequent watering; This is why we think it would be better (for crops where it would be necessary to heat the soil) to run the pipes in the paths, i.e. between the chests; and in this case we would cover them with boards and straw, or any other poor conductor of caloric. What leads us to believe that this method would be applicable to the cultivation of vegetables forced under panels is that, for certain crops, it is only by means of stoves that the heat required by the plants can be obtained. II. MUTED LAYERS. - It's hardly until April that we start using these kinds of beds. To establish them, we make a trench Om, 75 to I mêtre wide and about Om, 35 deep. The same materials are used to make them, as are used to heat the boiler and circulate it back through the pipes when it is sufficiently hot. As for the pipes, when the course is of a certain extent, they are given a flat shape, in order to heat a larger surface area than in cylindrical pipes, and to contain a smaller quantity of water that can reach boiling point more quickly than in the latter. These pipes are generally given a thickness of Om,02 to Om, 03 over a variable height of Om, 10 to Om, 15, depending on the cube of air and the need to raise the temperature. Pipes measuring Om, 21 by Om, 2 are quite commonly used. In fact, cylindrical pipes with an external surface corresponding to that of the Om, 21 high on Om, 2 pipe contain 4 liters 20 of water, and the same length of pipe with a similar external surface, i.e. with a diameter of Om, 15, would contain 15 liters 17. It's true that the hot water contained in the cylindrical pipe will cool less vitc than in the other; but also it will have been necessary to burn more fuel to bring it to the boil without having obtained more heating surface, and consequently more heat, the previous ones; they are given Om, 60 to Om, 80 in thickness; they must be slightly domed in the middle. They are filled with potting soil or good earth, depending on the type of crop to be grown; then covered with a long bed of manure to concentrate the heat. 1. stove. - Throughout the cold season, i.e. from the end of November to mid-April, it is necessary to maintain or revive the warmth of the layers, without having to repeat them. This is achieved by means of reheaters, which consist, as we said earlier, of filling the paths around the layers with new or annealed manure, and reshuffling them every fortnight or every week; then, as required, adding a portion of new manure each time. In doing so, the state of the atmosphere must be taken into account, i.e. if the weather is dry, wet manure should be used, and if it's damp, dry manure; then care should be taken to cover them with straw mats during bad weather, in order to concentrate the heat. 2. Teens. - Ados are a safe and economical way to encourage the cultivation of early crops: plants do better there than on horizontal ground. They consist of a slope of Im, 33, facing the sun. To set up an ados, proceed as follows: after choosing a favorable site, the soil is ploughed well, taking care to remove the soil necessary to recharge the backside by about Om, 20; after which the soil is united; then about Om 10 of earth mixed with loam is spread over the whole. These ados are first used to sow Radishes, and then three rows of bells are placed to sow lettuce and transplant young plants. CHAPTER VIII. Plant propagation. Under this heading, we cover the series of operations involved in multiplying plants, but we have only given each of them a scope proportionate to the actual difficulty they present. We invite our readers to read this chapter carefully, so as to become fully acquainted with the principles it sets out; and, by faithfully following our instructions, they will acquire the manual skill necessary to count on certain success. S I. - Sowing. Whatever the method of sowing, preparation of the soil is a preliminary operation of the utmost importance. The soil must be carefully ploughed, so that the clods are well divided, and after ploughing, the stones and clods on the surface are removed with a fork and a rake. Most vegetable seeds can be sown in spring, then successively, at intervals calculated according to the length of vegetation of each plant. With the exception of some lettuces, vegetables that are to be eaten in the same year should not be sown later than July. Before sowing, therefore, it is necessary to know not only how long the seeds will germinate, but also how long it will take for the plants to reach full development. The time of sowing should then be brought forward or back according to the nature of the soil; for the colder and wetter the soil, the later the sowing and the less the seeds need to be covered; and the finer the seeds, the less they need to be buried; for some, it is even sufficient to spread a little potting soil over them after harrowing and treading; others need not be covered, but only shaded with a little litter. There are two main methods of sowing: overplanting and sowing in the ground. I. SOWING ON A BED. - As it is often necessary to sow at a time when the temperature does not allow the seeds to be delivered to the soil, it is necessary to sow on a bed. Although the heat of the bed must vary according to the different species of seed, we can say that 12 to 15 degrees seems to be the most favorable temperature (except for Melons, Eggplants and Chicory, which require more heat); for all the vegetable seeds we have subjected to this temperature have succeeded perfectly. Sowing on a bed does not differ in any way from sowing in the ground, i.e. the seeds must always be covered in proportion to their fineness. These seedlings are often much more successful than those sown in the ground, because the temperature, light and humidity conditions required for perfect seed development can be altered at will. II. SOWING IN THE GROUND. - These seedlings are broadcast, in rows or rays, and in pockets. 1. Broadcast sowing. - The soil is prepared as described above, and a small amount of fine soil is raked to the edge of the bed. A handful of seeds is then taken and spread over the soil, passing between the fingers with a brisk, regular back-and-forth movement. In order to sow more evenly and avoid spilling seeds into the pathways, sow the width of the bed in two passes, starting at the edges. When the seeds are good, they should not be sown too thickly, in order to produce vigorous plants; and if, despite this precaution, they are too thick, they should be thinned out by hand.

mix with dry sand or fine tere. After sowing, the soil should be harrowed lightly with a fork, then trodden a little, although this should not be done if the soil is damp. To cover the seeds, use the back of the rake to spread the soil around the edges of the bed, leaving a little to retain water from watering. You can also spread a little well-consumed manure over the seedlings. If the weather is dry, germination should be encouraged by watering the seeds with an apple watering can. 2. Sowing in rows or rays. - Using either a hoe or a tracing knife, draw rays about Om, 3, or Om 5 deep, and more or less distant from each other, depending on what you want to sow; after scattering the seed, cover it lightly, raking up some of the soil from the sides with the back of the rake. When the seedling is out of the ground, we finish filling the rays by passing the rake or hoe between each row. This method of sowing is highly advantageous, especially in areas where frequent hoeing is required. 3. Sowing in pockets. - This consists in making holes with the hoe, arranged in a chessboard pattern, the distance and depth of which will be calculated according to the development that each clump should take; then, after placing a few seeds in each hole, we cover them by folding back the soil a little, and, when the plants are high enough, we finish filling the holes by passing a stroke of rake between each clump. SII. - Transplanting. Transplanting is necessary for all plants which cannot be sown in situ; and, to be sure of the success of the operation, you must not wait until the plant is too old, because not only is recovery more difficult, but the products are less beautiful; for plants which take root slowly, you must, before putting them in situ, transplant them in a nursery, i.e. put them in a good position and very close to each other. Successive transplanting has the advantage of producing a large quantity of shoots, which will ensure that the plants take root again when they are finally planted. Transplanting should only take place in well-prepared soil, on which a short mulch of manure has been spread, to ensure that the plant benefits as long as possible from watering, and that watering does not cause the plant to stick to the soil, which often leads to leaf rot. Transplanting in summer should, as far as possible, be carried out when the weather is overcast; and, if the weather is not favorable, the operation should be carried out towards the end of the day, and the recovery facilitated by watering. When you have a lot of plants to transplant and the weather is very dry, don't wait until you've finished before starting to water. SIII. - Onions. The only care to be taken to obtain success with bulbous plants you wish to propagate is to choose them in good health and plant them in circumstances most favorable to their growth. § IV. - Bulbs. This is the name given to the small bulbs or onions which form around the crown of bulbous plants such as Tulips, Hyacinths, etc., and which serve to multiply them. Caiuses should only be removed when they are ripe, which is when the leaves are completely dry. Cloves should always be planted in soft soil, at least one month before flowering onions, as they dry out more quickly due to their small volume. These onions usually wither after three or four years. § V. - Bulbils. Several bulbous plants produce on their stems, often in place of seeds, small onions called bulbils, which serve to multiply them; they should be removed when ripe, and treated like bulblets. §VI. - Tubers. Tubers are fleshy masses of underground stems, from which small fibrous roots usually grow. Some plants, such as Potatoes, Potatoes, etc., have eyes capable of providing new stems; and, to multiply them, they can be cut into as many pieces as there are eyes: each section will produce a new plant. Others have eyes on only part of the plant: these are Dahlias, Iris Germanica, herbaceous Peonies, and in such cases, when dividing them, care must be taken to leave each part of the collar of the plant; otherwise they would not grow. § VIF. - Claws or Paws. These are the names given to the roots of Ranunculus, Anemones, etc.; they are separated by splinters, but in such a way that there is always an eye for each. SVIII. - Eyelets. This is the name given to the offshoots that grow around certain plants (artichokes, etc.); they are separated from the old plants, taking care to remove them as far as possible with a heel; they should not be left to wither, so that they will grow again more quickly. S IX. - Root separation. Some perennial plants, such as Peonies, have roots that start from a common collar, and have one or more eyes that develop the following year. To multiply them, they can be split into as many parts as there are eyes. Other plants, such as Chrysanthemums, have their roots almost at the surface of the soil, and form thick clumps which can be divided into small parts; they must then be lifted from the ground, and, after separating them, only the circumference is replanted, which will produce much more beautiful clumps than if the center were replanted, which, being the oldest part of the plant, is naturally the least vigorous. SX. - Stolons or Flowers. Some plants, such as Strawberries, have runners, which produce offshoots at each node, rooting into the soil. Separated and transplanted in a favorable season, they produce as many new plants. SXI. - Marcottes. Marcottes are branches that are laid down in spring, either in the ground or in pots, and only separated from the mother branch when they have produced roots. When the branches you wish to propagate are placed in such a way that they cannot be lowered to the ground, you need pots or cups with slits in the sides, which you hold on a small board nailed to a support, the end of which you push into the ground. There are several ways of marcotting: we will only mention the most commonly used; but, whatever the method used, the soil in which the marcottes are placed must be constantly moist, to encourage the roots to emerge; and, to preserve the moisture of the watering, it is a good idea to cover the soil with consumed manure or moss. 1. simple Marcottes. - These are used to propagate plants that root easily, such as Vines, etc. The whole operation consists in laying a branch down in a trench of varying depth, depending on its size. After removing any leaves or buds on the part to be planted, the end is carefully bent to avoid breaking it. If you don't need to bury them deeply, you can secure them in the ground with a wooden hook. 2. Marcottes by strangulation. - These differ from the previous ones in that the bark is tightened, without cutting it, with a wire on the part which is in the ground; the result is a bead from which new roots sprout. 3. Marcottes by incision. - We'll describe this poeration as it's used to propagate carnations. In July, stop watering for a while before layering, to make the branches more flexible, and choose stems long enough to be laid down. Cut off the lower leaves, so that the part in the ground is free of them; then lower each stem into a small trench made with a finger, and straighten the end of the branch above the bend. Using the blade of the grafting machine, make an incision about Om, 02 in length, so that the notched part forms a tongue, the end of which is cut cleanly below a node, taking care not to cut into the other half of the stem. Each marcotte is held in place by a hook or a piece of wicker passed underneath, the two ends of which are pressed into the earth; then the whole is covered with earth fine enough to penetrate everywhere, taking care to let a little of it penetrate between the separate parts, which usually remain apart due to the effect of the curvature. Once the operation is complete, we usually cut off the tips of the leaves to prevent them from withering; then we spread a light mulch of half-consumed manure and wet with a watering can with very fine holes, so as not to shake the marcottes, which usually take root after a short time. 4. Sprouting by cutting. - This method involves cutting a tree or shrub at ground level in spring and covering the stump with soil. It soon produces suckers, which are removed once they have taken root. This is how the coignassier is propagated, to provide subjects for grafting. 5. Root marcottes. - To make this type of marcotte, cut the end of a root and leave the wound open to the air; the sap forms a bead from which buds soon develop; from among these, choose the most vigorous, and remove the others; then, in autumn, weed it by cutting the root close to the stump. S XII. - Cuttings, Almost all serous plants can be propagated by cuttings. This operation, which is extremely simple, consists in cutting off any part of a plant, even a leaf for some species, and making it produce roots. Some plants are very easy to propagate, but others require a great deal of care, and can only be propagated by horticultural merchants, who have special tarpaulins for this operation. We will therefore limit ourselves to indicating which cuttings can be taken in the open air, and which need to be smothered, but which are very successful if you only have cloches and a frame. 1. Open air cuttings. - This is the way to propagate many ornamental trees and shrubs. In January, cut the year's twigs into trunks of Om, 10 to Om, 20 in length, depending on the species; cut the lower part cleanly below one eye; group them by species and bury them at half their length in sand or fine earth, but in a place sheltered from sun and frost; from the end of February to the beginning of April, they are planted in well-prepared soil and, as far as possible, in a shady spot; they are planted in such a way as to leave two or three eyes above ground; after planting, the soil is mulched, and when dryness begins to make itself felt, the humidity of the soil is maintained by watering. 2. Cuttings under cloches and frames. - Many orangery and temperate greenhouse plants can be propagated from cuttings in spring on a warm bed; this is done in February and March. For this purpose, prepare a thin layer, so as to obtain only gentle heat; surround it with a stove, and cover it with a bed of fine potting soil, to which a little heather may be added; then place cloches over it, or cover it with a frame; but in this case, the height of the layer should be calculated so that the cuttings are not far from the glass. When the layer has warmed up, cut the cuttings with or without heel on the most vigorous branches; top them by giving them Om, 08 to Om, 10 in length, always taking care to cut the lower part cleanly below one eye; then transplant them immediately onto the layer using a small planter, pushing them in from Om, 02 to Om, 03. These cuttings can also be transplanted into pots which are then pressed into the bed: this is how Heliotropes, Petunias, Verbena, etc. can be propagated. After covering the borders with clochies or frames, shade them when the sun is shining, and cover them at night with straw mats. They should be watered from time to time with a small watering can, as the cuttings can only take root if the soil is kept constantly fresh; when they start to grow, and you're sure they have roots, give them a little air during the day, by lifting the cloches or frames, and after a while pinch off the longest ends, then lift the cuttings, trying to keep each one a small root ball. They are then planted in pots, which can be replaced on the same layer after watering, and, if deemed necessary, the warmth of the layer is rekindled by making new warmers; other 4. care is limited to gradually airing them and watering them as needed. All plants treated in this way will be strong and hardy enough to be put in the ground at the same time as they are planted in beds and flowerbeds. The same operation can be carried out in summer, in a shady spot; only, at this time, there is no need for a bed: this is how Pelargoniums, etc., are propagated. The best time to take these cuttings is from the end of July to the end of August. After preparing them as described above, transplant them at Om, 03 or Om, 04 apart into pots filled with soil and heather mixed with a little potting compost, and after transplanting, water them lightly; then place the pots under a bell or under a frame, but away from the sun. In autumn, the cuttings will have taken root, and can be separated, which is done by dividing the pot into as many parts as there are cuttings; then they are potted separately; having been treated in this way, you are sure to have plants with the strength to flower the following spring. The following procedure can also be used for plants that are difficult to root: take an ordinary pot, then another pot, narrower, but as high as possible; invert it into this one, fill the space with soil appropriate to the needs of the cuttings you intend to make, put a small pinch of soil on the hole, then transplant the cuttings; finally, bury the whole on a layer, and place a bell on top, 3. Cuttings by root sections. - Some plants can be propagated by cutting a root into sections, which are planted either in the ground or on a bed, but leaving the end exposed to the air, from which buds soon emerge. CHAPTER IX. Grafting. We will not describe grafting at length, as this operation is too widely known for that; we will only say that its purpose is to multiply, conserve and perfect useful and pleasant varieties, and to make a wild trunk bear brilliant flowers or tasty fruits destined to embellish our gardens and increase the no less appreciable products of our orchards. This operation, which has been written about so many times and at such length, simply requires a little observation and a certain manual skill. It is based on three fundamental points: 1° an appreciation of the circumstances in which the grafting is to be carried out, i.e. the moment when the plants, watered by sap, are ready to vegetate; 2° the choice of the subject, which must be in a suitable state of vigour and health, and above all suitable for grafting, which can only be carried out on species united by close affinities, 3° the manual operation, which requires only a short apprenticeship and can be considered the least difficult of the three, since by observing the two preceding conditions, success can be achieved which cannot be attained, no matter how careful the grafter, if the circumstances in which he operates are unfavorable. There are various types of grafting, but most are purely for pleasure. We shall therefore limit ourselves to describing the main ones, which can be considered as the type of all the others that can be performed once you are familiar with those we have indicated. 1. escutcheon graft. This is the most commonly used graft, and can be carried out at several times of the year: firstly, from May to July, which is known as budding grafting; this name comes from the fact that these grafts start to grow as soon as the escutcheon is taken up; there are even some, on Roses for example, which in autumn of the same year already form a beautiful head. The second period is from August to September, when the sap begins to slow down, and is known as "dormant eye" grafting, because at this time the escutcheon only becomes attached to the subject, and doesn't grow until the following year. Fruit trees are best grafted at this time of year. Some time before the operation, you need to prepare the tree to receive the graft, i.e. select the branches on which you want to graft, and remove the others, especially those below the grafts. If the trees you want to graft start to lose their sap, you need to water them to revive their vegetation. When the time is right, select the best eyes of the species you wish to propagate, cut off the leaf above the eye without damaging the petiole, and remove any prickles from the bud. Then, using the blade of the grafting machine, surround the eye so that you can remove it with part of the surrounding bark, which will be shaped roughly like the bud (see A, fig. 3). To detach it, lift it slightly with the tip of the grafting tool, then with the spatula, taking care to remove all the woody parts adhering to the escutcheon, which would prevent it coming into contact with the wood of the subject, unless the branch is tender enough for this operation not to be necessary; And if the root of the eye were to be removed, as is easy to see from the resulting gap, the crest would have to be reformed, and its recovery would be doubtful. Another method can also be used to lift the escutcheon, and is particularly advantageous when the grafts are small. Fig. 3. - Escutcheon graft. consists in detaching the escutcheon with a silk thread or horsehair (see B, fig. 3), after lifting the upper part. 3), lift the edges of the wound by sliding the spatula under the bark, so as to easily place the escutcheon, which is inserted by holding it by the petiole and pressing lightly on the upper part; If it is not possible to insert the entire length of the escutcheon, its end must be cut off to ensure that it coincides with the subject; the edges of the notch are then brought together on the escutcheon, and the whole is wrapped with a wool ligature, taking particular care not to engage the eye (see D, fig. 3). The ligature is shown further apart than it should be, so that the position of the escutcheon can be seen. Early petiole fall is a sign of graft recovery, which usually takes place ten or fifteen days after the operation; the tree should then be cut back to a few centimetres above the graft. Be sure to remove any shoots that appear on the subject, and pinch the terminal bud of the grafts so as to encourage the development of the lower eyes. 2. Ring grafting. - The months of April and August are the best times for this type of grafting. Fig. 4 - Ring grafting. Suitable for hardwood trees, particularly walnut. A branch of the same size as the tree to be grafted is selected from the tree to be propagated; the bark is encircled circularly below and above an eye, so as to form a ring which is detached by splitting it perpendicularly on the part adjacent to the eye (see C. fig. 4); it is then removed using the spatula of the grafting machine. A ring of the same width is then removed from the subject (see B, fig. 4), and the section of bark removed is returned to its place on the tree to be propagated. To be sure of success, the bark must be joined at the top and bottom; then the grafts are secured with a wool ligature, taking particular care not to engage the eye. Do not cut back the branches or the head of the tree until the graft's recovery is assured. This grafting technique has the advantage of never mutilating the tree, because if the graft does not vegetate, the ring of bark remains and takes the place of the one that was removed. 3. Split grafting. - This graft can be done in spring or autumn; and, to be sure of success, there must be enough sap to make the graft grow, but still enough to weld it to the subject, so that it doesn't dry out in the winter. To graft in the spring, you need to take the precaution of cutting off the previous year's shoots from each species of tree you wish to propagate, and then bury them in sand in a northern exposure, so as to delay vegetation as long as possible. To be sure of the success of these grafts, the sap must have begun to rise in the subject, but not yet have swollen the buds of the shoot you wish to graft. The first fortnight of April is usually the most favourable time for this operation: we then cut the head of the tree horizontally, and split it in the middle of its diameter, so as to make a notch of Om,03 to Om,06, depending on the strength of the tree, and taking care that this notch is always a little deeper and wider than the graft to be inserted would appear to require. When the subject is large and vigorous, several notches can be made (see A, B, fig. 5); but they must be opposite each other, so that they do not meet. Once the tree is ready to be grafted, select a branch with good eyes, from Om, 06 to Om, 10 in length, so that after insertion in the notch, there are at least two or three eyes on the outside. The lower part of this branch is then pruned to form two bevels of Om, 03 to Om, 06 in length (see C, fig. 5), whatever the thickness of the outer part, care is taken to preserve its bark; then open the slit with the spatula of the grafting machine or with a wedge, and insert the graft so that its bark coincides exactly with that of the subject; then wrap the whole with a 14 M Fig. 5. - Grafting in slit. ligature, and cover the end of the subject with grafting wax (1). Finally, take care to remove any shoots that develop on the subject, as they will live at the expense of the graft. 4 - Slit graft on tuber. - This graft is particularly useful for multiplying tree peonies. In August, take a tuber of herbaceous Peony, cut the top transversely, make a slit on one side and insert a branch with the lower part bevelled, then plant the tuber in a pot, but in such a way that the whole graft is buried. The pots (1) The grafting wax is composed of two parts of pitch-resin, two parts of yellow wax and one part of tallow, melted together. are placed on a warm layer, and the grafts are covered with a bell which must be shaded for fifteen or twenty days. The following spring, each of these grafts can be planted in the ground. 5. Veneer grafting. - The branch to be grafted is pruned into an elongated flute-beak shape (see A, fig. 6), then a portion of bark is removed (see B, fig. 6) Fig. 6. - Veneer graft. exactly the same size as the pruned part of the graft; the two parts are joined together, and a ligature made. These grafts grow back easily, but for this to happen, they must be smothered under a bell. 6. Vine grafting. - In March, cut the subject at the root collar, at about Om, 08 to Om, 10 in the ground, and leave the wound to dry for a few days; if you grafted immediately, the sap would rise so abundantly that it could drown the graft. The branches are prepared as for other split grafts, then one or more notches are made, depending on the strength of the subject, and the grafts are placed, leaving two or three eyes above ground. The graft and the tip are then covered with grafting wax; some people even compress the soil around the graft, taking great care not to disturb the branches. In the south of France, modified split grafting is used in the following way: after removing the heel of the stock used as a subject, it is cut a little above the ground, split right through, and a knife-edge graft is inserted laterally about halfway along its length, with the lower end plunging into the ground at Om, 15 to Om, 20; this serves to feed the graft until it is perfectly fused with the subject. Herbaceous graft. - This graft differs from the split graft only in the time at which it is performed. It can be used to propagate almost all plants still in the herbaceous state, particularly resinous trees and some ornamental shrubs. The time for grafting varies according to the state of the season; usually, the best time is May. The tip of the bud is cut off above one or more leaves, which must be carefully spared to attract the sap to the graft. The tree is then split from about Om, 03 to Om, 06 in length, and the shoot is prepared as for split grafting, taking care not to thin it too much. For this operation, a sharp, well-sharpened instrument must be used, in order to make a clean cut. Once the graft has been prepared, it is inserted into the subject's cleft, and secured with a wool ligature. To avoid cutting the head of the tree, we can proceed in another way: we make an incision, as if to place a crest; then, after having cut the branch into a bevel elongated on one side, like a flute's beak, we introduce it between the wood and the bark, and as always, we maintain the graft with a ligature, which must be removed about a month after the operation. To ensure that the grafts take root again, they must be protected from the sun and the sun's rays; so, if you're working on potted plants, you'll need to put them under a frame, which you'll need to shade; and if you're working on plants in the ground, you'll need to protect them by wrapping them in a paper cone, a vine leaf, or some other shelter, which you can remove ten or fifteen days after the operation. Grafting can also be used to propagate tuberous plants: in spring, young shoots of the best Dahlia varieties are grafted onto tubers of inferior varieties. To do this, take a tuber, cut off the top horizontally and split it on one side, then choose a branch that is not yet hollow, which happens when they are already strong, and cut the lower part with a slightly sharp bevel, taking care to remove only the epidermis; then insert it into the slit in the tuber, which is planted in a pot, so that the whole graft is buried. The pots are placed on a warm surface and covered with a cloche, which must be shaded for several days. Herbaceous grafting is also performed on grapevines. This operation should be carried out in May or June, on buds of Om, 20 or Om, 25 in length. It differs in no way from ordinary slit grafting; the only difference is that, after wrapping the graft in wool or wax, it is placed in a wide-necked bottle (canning jar), attached to a stake or other support, and corked with fresh moss. After twelve or fifteen days, when recovery is certain, the bottle is uncorked to fortify the graft, and soon afterwards left to air. These grafts sometimes bear fruit in the very first year, which means that this process can be used with advantage, not only as a means of propagation, but also to judge the merit of new varieties. Crown grafting, known as Pliny grafting. - This graft is used when the subject is too strong to be split grafted; it must be done at the same time as the latter graft, and care must also be taken to cut off, during the winter, some of the raE Fig. 7. - Crown graft. meaux of the subject to be propagated, to prevent them from coming into vegetation too early. The head of the tree to be grafted should be cut horizontally (see fig. 7), and the tip should be wrapped with a ligature to hold the bark in place, lest it split when the cuts are made; a small wedge of iron or hardwood is then driven to a depth of about Om, 05 between the bark and the wood, then the shoot is bevelled, and after removing the wedge, the graft is driven in so that the entire bevel is hidden (see fig. 7). The number of grafts placed on the same subject should be proportionate to its size. They should be placed about Om, 05 apart; and, as soon as the operation is complete, the tip of the subject and the edges of the bark should be covered with grafting wax. 7. Ordinary approach grafting. - This operation consists in applying a branch of the variety to be grafted against a branch or stem of a tree of the same species; it can be performed while the trees are in vegetation. The procedure should be as follows: after bringing the two branches together in parallel (see fig. 8), remove part of the bark on each one, so as to form a longitudinal wound, the length of which should always be proportionate to the strength of the individuals; then apply them one Fig. 8 - Grafting by approach. It is often necessary to loosen the ligature as soon as the grafts have been taken up, so that the force of the vegetation does not cause strangulation, which not only forms bulges, but also hinders the taking up of the grafts. The grafts should not be detached until it is certain that they are solidly welded; in fact, it is often more prudent to start by cutting off the head of the subject, only half-cutting the part that is to be cut off, and not weaning it completely until some time later, when it should be cut as close as possible to the graft, so that the sap covers the wound more easily. This operation requires great care, so as not to cut the subject with the grafting blade. 8. Grafting by complicated approach. - This graft differs little from the previous one: it is specially used to give solidity to hedges. The branches are crossed so as to form a rhombus; at the point where they meet, a longitudinal wound is made on each branch, taking care to ensure that the bark coincides; the two parts are held together by means of a ligature, and the operation is repeated as the branches grow. CHAPTER X.. Plant Conservation. In this chapter, we will limit ourselves to saying that the northern situation of our country, the irregularity of the seasons, and the humidity of our springs and autumns would make the cultivation of certain exotic plants impracticable, if we did not have recourse to artificial means of conservation and multiplication. These means are of several kinds: starting with the simplest, they include the most complex: I. cloches; 2. frames; 3. the orangery or cold greenhouse; 4. the temperate greenhouse; 5. the hot greenhouse. 1. cloches. - Glass cloches are the simplest of all shelters; they serve to protect delicate plants and cuttings from cold and humidity, and to concentrate heat on those that need a higher temperature than that of the atmosphere. Choose cloches with the whitest glass, as they are prone to tarnishing after a few years. Take the precaution of washing them from time to time, and when they are no longer in use, place them one inside the other, taking care to separate them with a bit of straw to avoid breakage. 2. Chassis. - The purpose of frames is to activate the germination of certain seeds, to increase the heat of the layers, to enable the cultivation of vegetable plants that do not succeed in the open air, and to protect delicate plants from the insults of the air. They [consist of two parts: the trunk a, a (fig. 9), and the panels c. Each trunk is usually 4 meters long and Im, 33 wide; it is made of four boards nailed to four feet placed internally at the four corners. The back of the trunk should always be higher than the front, so that the panels are inclined to the south. The spacing is maintained by two bars b. b, dovetailed at the top and bottom, which support the panels. The glazed panels should be made of thick oak. They consist of a frame 1.33 m wide and of arbitrary length, divided by three small bars of equal thickness, which can be advantageously replaced by iron uprights, fixed to the crosspieces from top to bottom. A handle is placed at each end, so that they can be removed, and before glazing, they are painted with oil, an operation that should be repeated every year in autumn. Doormats. - Doormats are used to cover diapers, bells, frames, greenhouses and so on. With the gardeners' doormat loom, you can easily make your own doormats. This loom consists of a wooden frame 2 meters long by Im, 33 wide, with as many headless pegs at either end as you want to stretch strings through it, depending on the length you give the doormat. It is customary to make only three rows; however, it would be better to make four, for greater solidity. The strings are tied to the bottom pegs with a fixed loop, and to the top with a slipknot, allowing them to be stretched as much as necessary. Once each string has been tightened, it is left twice the length of the frame; this excess length is used to sew the mat, after which two layers of rye straw are laid across it, as evenly as possible, and laid head to tail; and, after rolling the middle row of string onto a kind of shuttle made from a piece of wood Om, 08 in length and hollowed out on the sides, we take a pinch of straw, and pass the shuttle from right to left under the straw and over the string, then return to the top to engage it in the loop formed by the string, and tighten by pulling straight ahead, taking care to press the straw between the thumb and forefinger of the left hand, so as to obtain a flat rather than round mesh; then continue with the same shuttle along the length of the mat, and when you've reached the end, tie a knot to stop the string. You then move on to the other rows, which you sew in the same way, guiding the edge stitches onto the middle ones; and, once the doormat is finished, you cut off the overhanging ears on either side. Although these doormats are intended to cover panels Im, 33 wide, they should be given a length of 2 meters, because when damp they shorten by about Om, 50, leaving them only as long as required. 3. Orangery. - The orangery, or cold greenhouse, is designed to keep out the cold for certain plants that require only a small amount of heat. Its shape is a long square, and its dimensions, both in height and width, must be in proportion to the number of plants it is designed to contain.
