The walls must be thick enough to prevent frost from easily penetrating them. The front will be fitted with windows as large as possible, and the entrance door, placed in the center, will be glazed and open in two parts. A stove will be built, with pipes running around the interior walls, but fire will only be needed in the event of extraordinary feoids. To preserve the health of the plants, it is sufficient to prevent frost from penetrating into the greenhouse; to this end, a thermometer should be placed in the greenhouse, to be consulted often, in order to maintain the necessary temperature for each plant. Water intended for watering orangery plants, and even those in adjoining greenhouses, should enter the building through underground pipes, and be collected in a basin or barrel to warm up a little. 5. §I. - On the entry of orangery plants and their treatment in winter. Plants should be brought into the orangery in the second half of October, rarely later. They should only be brought in when the weather is dry, and care should be taken to place the highest plants at the back, so that they form a tier, and all get as much light as possible. In addition to orange trees, laurel, pomegranate and many other hardy plants can spend the winter in the orangery; they can even be placed behind or between the orange trees, without any inconvenience; but this is not the case for myrtles, which can also be placed in the orangery; they must receive direct light, otherwise they will lose their leaves. Large Pelargoniums zonale (Red Geraniums) can be placed on the shelves: their hardiness is such that they are perfectly happy in the orangery; they should be watered very little (but not allowed to dry out), to prevent them from vegetating during their stay in the greenhouse, when the shoots are so tender that they have to be cut back as they come out. During the frosts, you can still place potted carnations and large wallflowers in the orangery, but you need to put them outside as soon as the temperature permits. At first, leave the orangery fully open day and night. When it starts to get cold, close it at night; then, when it's freezing, close it during the day. Then all the windows must be hermetically sealed and fitted with mats on the outside. Whenever the thermometer outside registers 3 or 4 degrees above zero, air is given in, unless the atmosphere is too humid or the wind too violent. Plants in the orangery should be watered only when they need it, and only as much water as is absolutely necessary for their maintenance. As winter is a time of rest for plants, it is important to avoid reviving vegetation at this time, which would exhaust them. §1I. - The plants can only be brought out in the first fortnight of May, and we always start with the hardiest; but to accustom them to atmospheric influences, we must give them as much air as possible a long time in advance, and wait for overcast or rainy weather before bringing them out. All plants should be placed (as is almost always the case) close to the house, but always with a good exposure and sheltered from the wind; double-flowered oleanders and pomegranates should be placed in the extreme south, if you want them to flower every year. As soon as they have been removed, any plants needing to be re-boxed, either because they require more space or because the boxes need replacing, should be re-boxed only after they have been placed in their proper positions, to prevent them from being shaken in transit. In all circumstances, we advise you to give larger crates only gradually, and with a great deal of reserve; because if they are too large, Laurel and Pomegranate trees grow a lot, but do not flower, and Orange trees languish. Up to the age of eight or ten, Orange trees should be pruned about every two or three years, and then every five or six years; but Laurel and Pomegranate trees should be pruned more frequently, as the development of branches and twigs is always related to that of the roots, and as these shrubs vegetate much more vigorously than Orange trees, they should be pruned more often. If, while waiting for the time for re-embedding, the leaves of the shrubs turn yellow, without this being due to excessive humidity, they should be given a half-embedding, which consists in cutting away Om, 05 to Om, 10 of the soil around the box and replacing it with new soil suited to the plant's needs. At the end of this chapter, we will indicate which soil is suitable for each plant. Since potting differs little from repotting, except in the way it is carried out, which must be modified, we refer you to this article for the details. After the operation, we cover the surface of the soil with a mulch of consumed manure, and give each plant a good watering. As with winter watering, the water used should be left in a barrel for some time; it would even be a good idea to water from time to time with water in which animal or vegetable substances have been left to decompose. Watering should take place at least once a day in summer. Finally, they should be more or less abundant, depending on the temperature; then gradually decrease as the temperature cools. Towards the end of August or the beginning of September, orange trees need to be pruned, which involves removing dead wood and all unnecessary or misplaced branches, such as those on the inside, which make the head too compact and hinder the circulation of sap. Finally, whether you're growing Orange trees in a rounded or cylindrical shape, you need to cut off the tips of all slender branches, so as to give each tree a regular shape; it's also at this time that you can reduce the head of those that are growing too much, or which, no longer growing, need to be rejuvenated, which is done by cutting back all branches more or less close to the trunk, depending on the tree's strength. Laurel trees can be subjected to the same treatment when they overgrow; but they must not be pruned annually, as this would deprive them of flowers. As soon as they are out of bloom, cut off the ends of the branches that used to bear the flowers, so as to obtain trees with well rounded heads. Myrtles need to be sheared regularly, as soon as they are defoliated; Grenadiers also need to be sheared every year, to keep their shape as graceful as possible; but this pruning should only take place at the time of re-entry. To complete our information on orangery plants as much as possible, we'd like to point out that Pelargoniums zonale should also be trimmed before being placed in the greenhouse. §111 - Soil composition for the following plants. ORANGERS. - One quarter free soil, one quarter good vegetable garden soil, one quarter heather soil, one quarter fat compost. MYRTS. - Pure heather soil. GRENADIERS and ROSE LAUREL. - Good vegetable garden soil mixed with fatty loam. 4. Temperate greenhouse. - This greenhouse differs from the orangery in that it is much brighter, an indispensable condition for the preservation of the plants we recommend placing there; it will be adjoining the orangery, and will communicate from one to the other: it will be 8 meters long by 3 wide, and, starting from the interior floor, it will be 2m, 45 high at the back; the front will be Om, 80 high and will be glazed. The small sashes that will close it will be hinged at the top, and will open horizontally from bottom to top; they will bear from below on a small support wall covered with a slab, and they will beat on the uprights that support the lower part of the rafters, which must be, like the rest, made of oak and placed at Im, 33 one from the other, so as to receive the glazed panels with which the greenhouse is to be covered. The first row of panels will be 2 m long by Im, 33 wide; they will bear from the bottom on a gutter board designed to discharge rainwater, and from the top on a crosspiece called a spacer, which must run from one rafter to the other. The panels of the second row will be only Im, 36 in length, and so that they can bear on the rafters, it is necessary to apply a sole on each of them, so as to form the thickness of the bottom panels, on which those of the second row will have to bear about Om, 03, and from the top on a crosspiece which, like that of the bottom, must go from one rafter to the other. The panels will be fixed at the top by hooks placed inside, and to give air, the bottom will be raised and held open by small iron racks. At the top of the greenhouse, a small roof will be placed over which you can walk to service the doormats. To prevent you from slipping on the panels, place a handrail along the entire length of the greenhouse. Inside, a pathway Om, 75 wide, supported by a supporting wall, will be provided at orangery floor level, as the rest of the greenhouse must be Om, 50 lower. The middle will be occupied by a tier Im, 25 wide, made up of six shelves; the height of the tier must be calculated so that the plants are no more than Om, 60 or Om, 80 from the glass; in front of the tier we'll make a path Om, 50 wide, so that we can circulate all around it, then we'll, establish a shelf against the back wall, and another path Om, 50 wide on the front of the greenhouse and under which will circulate the pipes of the stove, whose mouth must always be outside. An opening will be made in the gable of this greenhouse, and it will be fitted with a double door, which will serve as an entrance during frosts, thus avoiding having to open that of the orangery. §IV. - Temperate greenhouse plants and their winter treatment. The plants must be brought in during October, but it is impossible for us to determine the exact time; we will only say that it is important to avoid as much as possible that they remain exposed to the autumn humidity, and especially that they are not affected by the first frosts. By the beginning of the month, the panels should be ready to be placed on the greenhouse; the interior should be cleaned and any repairs made; finally, by this time, it should be ready to receive the plants, which should be placed in the following order, although this should only be done after cleaning the pots and lightly scraping the surface of the soil, so as not to leave any grass or moss. Pelargoniums, Calceolaria, Cinerea and Verbena are placed on the tier, while Hydrangea, Erythrina, Balisier or Dahlia tubers can be placed underneath. Succulents or plants requiring little care during winter are placed on the shelf against the back wall, but the front shelf is reserved for Camellias, which should always be placed in the brightest part of the greenhouse. All these plants should be placed on the shelves, in rows of the same size, spaced so that their heads do not touch each other; and during their stay in the greenhouse, they should be turned over from time to time, so that all their parts are successively exposed to the light; for without this precaution, they would all be inclined to the same side, leaving them with an unsightly shape. From the moment the plants are placed in the greenhouse until spring, watering should be moderate and only be carried out as and when the plants really need it. Watering should be done with a small watering can, to which an extension spout should be added to reach distant plants, and the water used should have been kept at greenhouse temperature for some time. Other care consists in keeping the house clean and renewing the air as often as possible, while avoiding opening the frames on overcast or rainy days, so as not to introduce humidity into the greenhouse; Then, as soon as the cold approaches, all openings should be hermetically sealed with moss, and when the weather clears in the evening and the outside thermometer registers only 3 or 4 degrees of heat, the greenhouse should be covered with mats, as it is likely to freeze overnight. In December, the small frames at the front of the greenhouse should be fitted with a stove made of dry manure; and, whatever the temperature, it is advisable to cover the greenhouse every night, taking care to remove the mats during the day, unless the weather is overcast and the cold is severe. Moreover, you can uncover the greenhouse without any inconvenience whenever the thermometer shows no more than 4 or 5 degrees of cold; however, you must be careful to replace the doormats before frost has formed on the windows; and if at that time you have to let in some air, you must always close the door before the sun disappears, in order to concentrate the heat in the greenhouse, which can often save you the trouble of making a fire at night; finally, either by doubling the mats, or by making a small fire (which should only be done with great reserve), care should be taken to ensure that the temperature of the greenhouse does not fall below 5 degrees of heat, and if it is necessary to make a fire, it should not be raised to more than 6 to 8 degrees, as the essential point is to maintain the plants in a state of rest from which they should only emerge towards the end of winter. As almost all the plants we have mentioned are prone to aphid attack, tobacco fumigation should be used as often as necessary, after closing everything (1). Once March arrives, there's no longer any need to light a fire in the greenhouse, as the sun usually heats the atmosphere sufficiently. Often, when the sun shines directly on the greenhouse, it's even necessary to spread a light-colored cloth over the panels, to prevent (1) This operation must be carried out using a cylindrical copper device called a fumigator. It consists of two parts: the upper part rubs against the lower part; a plate with fine holes is fixed internally to receive the tobacco and prevent it from passing through the pipes. To operate the unit, the end of a bellows is inserted into the pipe at the bottom of the unit, and as it blows, the smoke escapes through the tube attached to one side of the upper part. This prevents the foliage of the plants from being burnt. From this point onwards, watering should gradually become more frequent and more abundant; it is even necessary to syringe the plants from time to time, an operation which at this time should take place in the morning. But however beneficial these waterings may be, they should be suspended as soon as the first Pelargonium flowers bloom, as they will quickly dull their radiance. In the first days of April, gradually introduce more air into the greenhouse, depending on the temperature, to fortify the plants, which will soon be exposed to the open air. If you want Pelargoniums to bloom brilliantly, take them out of the greenhouse as soon as the temperature permits, and place them in a good position, taking care to arrange them so that they can be easily covered at night, should the temperature so require; then leave them there until the first flowers begin to bloom, at which point they can be returned to the greenhouse: In this way, the plants will be less slender, more robust, and the flowers more vividly colored. If some circumstance prevents the Pelargoniums from being put out as soon as indicated, air should be supplied through all the openings in the greenhouse to remedy the situation as far as possible. § V. - Removal of temperate greenhouse plants and their treatment in summer. In the first fortnight of May, and as much as possible on an overcast day, take the plants out of the greenhouse, except for Pelargoniums and Calceolaria, which should be taken out only after they have deflowered, in order to enjoy all the beauty of their flowering; and then treat them as we shall indicate when talking about the plants to be taken out. Place them in a shady spot for a few days, to strengthen them; and before putting them in place, repot those that need it, which must be done every year for those that grow a lot. But not all plants can be repotted at the same time; for this operation to be carried out properly, it must always take place some time before the plants come into vegetation, and it is wrong that many gardeners still indiscriminately repot all plants in autumn. It's easy to understand why we find this practice so reprehensible: repotting can hardly take place without damaging the roots; it often happens that, once the hair has completely covered the root ball, it becomes necessary to cut it back; it's certain then that this operation can be useless, if not harmful, when it takes place at a time when the plants are due to rest for several months. It is therefore preferable to repot plants in spring. However, plants like Pelargoniums, which vegetate towards the end of winter, should be repotted towards the end of August or the beginning of September, in a word, in time for them to put down new roots before winter. Now that we've come to the subject of Pelargoniums, we'd like to point out that they should always be pruned a fortnight before repotting; this operation consists in removing any thin or badly placed branches, and cutting back the current year's branches two or three eyes below their insertion, depending on their position and the vigour of the plants, but always so as to form a well-rounded head. Immediately after potting, details of which will be given in the next chapter, water the plants with the apple watering can, then place them in pruning rows in a well-ventilated spot, but in part-shade as far as possible; and, if there is no natural shelter, form palisades from small reeds attached at the top and bottom to gaulettes held in place by stakes; keep watering as required; you can even continue syringing, which, during the hot days of June, July and August, should only take place towards the end of the day. If heavy rainfall occurs shortly after potting, the pots should be temporarily laid to one side, to prevent excessive humidity from rotting the roots. Although we have given a general description of the care to be given to temperate greenhouse plants, it can be applied to all pot-grown plants, unless the plants are planted in the ground with their pots, which can only be done for Verbenas, Petunias, Hydrangeas, Pelargoniums and some varieties of Calceolaria, all plants with which you can form very graceful groups. There's no need to protect them from the sun's rays; they just need to be cut back and repotted in time for them to have recovered by the time they return to the greenhouse. SVI. - Repotting. Before repotting, the soil should have been prepared for each plant, as described at the end of this chapter. When everything is ready, take advantage of overcast weather as much as possible, or, failing that, move to a shady spot. We then take each plant in turn, carefully unstacking it by placing the left hand on the surface of the soil, so that the stem passes between the fingers, then we turn the plant upside down, and, supporting the pot with the right hand, we lightly tap its rim on a point of support, and once the rootball is out of the pot, we visit it. If, as is often the case, the lining of the rootball is made up of a tissue of dried-out roots, it is cut away cleanly, then, by scraping lightly, a greater or lesser part of the old soil is removed, depending on the degree of decomposition; broken or rotten roots are then removed. After preparing the clod in this way, if it happens to be very dry, we plunge it into water until it is well soaked. After draining, place it in the pot intended for it, which should always be proportionate to the volume of the roots and the vigor of the plant. However, this should only be done after placing a shard or a bed of gravel at the bottom of the pot, to facilitate drainage of the water used for watering. Next, a bed of soil is placed, the thickness of which should be calculated so that the surface of the rootball is 0.04m to 0.05m below the rim of the pot; then soil is poured between the rootball and the sides of the pot, taking care to keep the plant stem right in the middle, and, to ensure there are no voids, it is tamped down with a spatula; The bottom of the pot is lightly tapped, then filled with soil, this time compacted with the thumbs, leaving the surface of the soil about Om, Ol lower than the sides of the pot, to receive water for watering. This is all the care that temperate greenhouse plants require. Although given in a very succinct manner, this advice will always suffice for the cultivation of all plants that do not deviate from ordinary cultivation. §VII. - Composition of the soil to be used for the following plants. PELARGONIUMS. - One third heather soil, one third free-range soil, one third leaf compost, or, in the absence of manure, a little well-sieved poudrette (1). CALCÉOLAIRES. - Heather soil, free earth and leaf compost. VERVEINES. - Heather soil mixed with a portion of good vegetable garden soil. CINEMA. - Heather soil and compost. CAMELIAS. - Pure heather soil. HORTENSIAS. - Pure heather soil. SUCCULENTS. - Heather soil mixed with a little well-sieved powdered earth. 5. Warm greenhouse. - Like the temperate greenhouse, this greenhouse communicates with the orangery. As its structure is exactly the same as that of the temperate greenhouse, we refer to the latter for its construction, and will only discuss the interior layout. The inside path will be Om, 75 wide, and the bed 2m,25, including a small supporting wall Om, 45 high to support it; and another on the front of the (1) As in all circumstances the soil for potting must be very loose and well mixed, it must always be screened. The claie consists of a wooden frame, lined vertically with iron rods spaced about 0m,015 apart. These rods are supported by a crosspiece placed in the middle of the frame. To use it, you lean it (taking care to tilt it slightly) on a good stake. The sieve is a basket whose bottom is lined with wicker or wire mesh of varying widths, depending on the degree of loosening required. ANUEL DE JARDINAGE. greenhouse, where the pipes of the stove run, the mouth of which will always be on the outside. The shelf placed against the back wall is designed to hold potted strawberry plants. The manure layer can be replaced by a thermosiphon, with pipes running under a floor covered with a bed of tannin thick enough to bury the pots, and the inside temperature can be produced by the same device using pipes running above the layer. As the cultivation of greenhouse plants is very limited, we will limit ourselves to saying that during the winter, the temperature of the greenhouse should be maintained between 15 and 18 degrees centigrade. In April, we start to crimp the plants and give them a little air around mid-day. In the second half of May, we take out the hardiest plants, and bring them back in during September; finally, we can say that the general care to be given to hot-house plants is the same as that indicated for temperate greenhouse plants. CHAPTER XI. Vegetable garden. GARLIC (Allium sativum). - Multiplies from cloves planted in beds and borders towards the end of February and beginning of March. All soils are suitable, but it prefers those that are light and substantial. At the beginning of June, we tie a knot with the leaves and stem, in order to stop the sap flowing to the bulbs, which we pull off as soon as the leaves begin to dry out. Before putting them into bunches, we leave them on the ground for some time, where they finish ripening; then we hang them in a dry place to keep them until spring. Spanish garlic or Rocambole. - This species, less widespread than the previous one, differs in that it produces bulblets instead of seeds, which can be used for reproduction. Cultivation is the same. ANANAS (Ananassa sativa). - To raise pineapples and prepare them for fruiting, you need frames 1.65 m long by 1.33 m wide, and a well-exposed greenhouse with one or two gentle slopes, so that the plants are not too far from the glass. The first half of October is the best time to plant crowns and eyelets, because the young plants won't need any more care to overwinter in the ground than the old ones, and by spring the plants will already be strong and well rooted. Towards the end of September, prepare a good layer about Ou. 60 thick, made up of half new manure, half mixed leaves, or, failing that, part manure from old layers. The height of the layer should be calculated in such a way that, after being reloaded with Om, 20 or Om, 30. of tannin, or, failing that, moss, the plants are as close to the glass as possible. Eyelets for planting should preferably be taken from the leaf axils, where they are always strongest. After removing the eyelets, keep the old plants only if you are short of plants, and then only until they have produced the number of eyelets you need. Before planting the carnations, remove the leaves from the part to be planted (about Om, 05 to Om, 06); then cleanly cool the wound, and plant them immediately in pots Om, 10 to Om, 12 in diameter, depending on their strength. What we recommend for eyelets is, in all circumstances, applicable to crowns. If need be, crowns can be stored for at least a month in a shady, dry place. For planting, use pure heather soil or, failing that, a soil composed of one-fifth free earth, half heather soil and one-sixth compost, all prepared at least six months previously, stirred several times and put through a sieve. At the time of potting, this soil must not be damp, but must not be parched, although it is better to use it dry than damp. Immediately after planting, the pots are placed in the bed, starting with the top row and always choosing the highest plants. This must be observed each time they are replaced, because of the slope that must always be given to the frames. Take care to space them according to their strength. At night, cover the frames with straw mats; during the day, reduce the intensity of the sun's rays with canvas or mulch, which is spread over the frames; finally, for a month, the time needed for them to take root, care for them like cuttings. When they begin to vegetate, we give them a little air by lifting the frames when the sun is shining; then we water them at the base, but only as and when necessary. Around the beginning of November, i.e. when it's cold and wet, we surround the trunk with a good manure warmer, which should go down to the same depth as the bed, and from then until spring, it should be stirred at least every month, adding a portion of new manure each time. When the cold is severe, double the mats at night, spread a good layer of bedding over them, and keep the stoves at frame height; then uncover the panels every day, unless the thermometer falls below 4 or 5 degrees Celsius. In spring, watering should be more frequent and abundant, and more and more water is given as the sun gains strength. In the first days of May, a bed is laid, which must be much longer than the autumn bed, due to the development of the plants; but, as the temperature is milder, it need not be as warm as in autumn. The same applies to the stoves, which we don't make as deep and only remodel from time to time. This time, we replace the tan with a 32-centimeter-thick layer of soil, similar to that used for potting carnations; then we unstuff the pineapples, inspect the roots, and if any are rotten, we remove them; if not, we spare them all; After this, they are planted on the bed, taking care to press them in so that the old root ball is covered by a few centimetres of soil, to encourage new roots to emerge from the collar. Some time after planting, you begin to give the plants a little air; then you gradually increase the amount, depending on the temperature. At this point, it's preferable not to accustom pineapples to being shaded; in this way, you'll have much hardier plants, but you'll understand that you need to give them more air. During hot spells, they can be watered with a watering can, especially if planted on a good bed, as humidity is only really harmful in winter. Treated in this way, the pineapples will have developed by autumn to a degree that would scarcely be found in those grown constantly in pots for two years. Towards the end of September or the beginning of October, the Pineapples are lifted from the ground; all the eyelets are removed, followed by a few lower leaves; and as the Pineapple is one of the plants whose roots perish each year and are replaced by new ones, all the old ones are removed by cutting them close to the plant; after which the Pineapples are tied with a straw tie, so as to make them easier to repot, which should be done in pots of Om, 24 in diameter only. This operation is called bare-bottom potting. After potting, we place them on a new layer, and until they have new roots, we give them the same care as we would for first-age carnations. Around January, we place them in a greenhouse, where we've prepared a layer about 6.65 m thick and the full width of the recess, which must not be less than 2 meters wide. This layer should be filled with a good bed of tannin or moss, so that the pots can be easily buried in it, and placed about Om, 50 apart in all directions; finally, depending on the strength of the plants, they are left in this way until they set fruit, i.e. from April to July, when they are planted in the open ground on the same layer, after reshuffling it and replacing the tannin with a bed of soil. For as long as the pineapples remain in the greenhouse, the layer mentioned above can be replaced by thermosiphon heating; in this case, the tanning bed, and consequently the soil, is placed on a floor under which the heating pipes run. The heating is adjusted so as to maintain a temperature of around 25 to 30 degrees Celsius in the layer, which is quite sufficient for the needs of these plants. In spring, we start heating less, and stop completely in May, because from then until September, the sun's heat is sufficient. The greenhouse in which pineapples are placed is usually divided in two by a glass partition, so that there are two seasons. The strongest plants are placed in the first compartment, and we usually start heating them towards the end of January. From then on, the temperature of the greenhouse should be maintained at a constant 25 to 30 degrees; at night, until the end of April, the greenhouse is covered with mulch, which must be removed every day. For watering at the foot of the plants, use water in which animal or vegetable substances have been decomposed. In winter, watering should be subordinated to the warmth of the bed, and care should be taken to ensure that the water is at the temperature of the greenhouse; in summer, however, watering should be abundant, with occasional ponding. As we have already indicated, it is necessary to provide plenty of air, to avoid shading. First-season fruit usually ripens from July to September. Care should be taken not to raise the temperature on the side of the greenhouse where the second-season plants are placed to more than 12 degrees; but in March, when we usually start heating them, we should observe all that has been indicated for the first season. Second-season fruit usually ripens from September to December. As we can see, treating pineapples as we have just described will produce fruit that can be harvested twenty or twenty-six months after the eyelets have been planted, conclusively demonstrating the superiority of this method of cultivation over that used in the past. Varieties. - From Martinique. - Cayenne. - From Jamaica. - From Providence - From Mont-Serrat. - Duchesse-d'Orléans. - Comte-de-Paris. - Enville. - Poli blanc. - Charlotte Rothschild. ARROCHE DES JARDINS. Belle-Dame, Bonne-Dame (Atriplex horensis). - This plant is grown only to soften the acidity of sorrel. It is sown in spring and requires no care; it usually reseeds itself and, when you have a few plants, it is rarely necessary to sow them. Arroche seeds keep well for only one year. Varieties. - Arroche blonde. - Arroche rouge. artichoke (cynara scolymus). - To grow artichokes successfully, you need soft, substantial soil; they like warmth, and fear cold humidity. They can be propagated from seed sown on a bed in February and March, or immediately placed in April and May; but, as they rarely reproduce their varieties, it is preferable to propagate them by eyelet. This is done as follows: In April, the shoots born at the collar of old plants are broken off, taking care to remove them with the heel or portion of the root collar; then the strongest are selected, the leaf tips are shortened, and, after preparing the soil well, they are planted in a chessboard pattern, at about Om, 75 in slightly poor soils, and at I meter in those where vigorous vegetation is hoped for. If well hoeed and watered, a good proportion of these carnations will bear fruit in autumn, and all will bear abundant fruit the following spring. Each year, in the autumn, the old stems and the tips of the longest leaves must be cut off; then, in November, in a word, before the frosts, they must be "buttered", an operation which consists in raising the soil around each plant; and when the frosts begin to make themselves felt, they are completely covered with leaves or litter, which is removed every time the weather gets milder. In March, when frosts are no longer to be feared, we destroy the artichoke mounds and give them a good ploughing; then, in April, we grommet them, as previously indicated, so as to leave only the two or three most beautiful grommets on each plant. Artichoke plantations only produce abundantly after four years, so replant every three years to avoid any interruption in harvesting. As artichoke roots do not grow very deep, they do not exhaust the surrounding soil, and young artichokes can be counter-planted in advance between those to be destroyed, so that when the old artichokes are uprooted, the soil is covered with young plants in full ratio. It's easy to bring forward the artichoke production period. Whether you force them into place, or raise them in clods in November to plant them in a trunk, care consists in surrounding the trunk with a manure stove during frosts, covering the panels at night and providing air during the day. Artichokes treated in this way produce in April. Alternatively, and much more simply, Artichokes can be forced as follows: In the first fortnight of February, remove the soil from the paths around the bed to a depth of about Om.50, and replace it with a stove of new manure; then place hoops far and wide across the bed, to support the mats used to cover the artichokes at night and in bad weather; The soil is then covered with hot manure, to activate vegetation, and the stoves are changed every ten or fifteen days, each time adding more or less new manure, depending on the temperature. Artichoke seeds keep well for up to five years. Varieties. - Vert de Provence. - Vert de Laon. - Camus de Bretagne. - Violet. ASPARAGUS (Asparagus officinalis). - Two varieties are grown: the common or green asparagus, and the large purple or Dutch asparagus. Asparagus from Marchiennes, Ulm, Besançon and Vendôme are only varieties of the latter, the result of local influences. Asparagus is propagated from seed, which is sown in March, either in the field or in a nursery, in the ground or on a bed, for subsequent planting. Planting methods vary from country to country, but the one described here has produced excellent results in all the localities where it has been used, so we feel we should give it preference. After selecting a favorable site, in autumn Om, 25 to Om, 30 of soil is removed from the entire surface of the land to be planted. If, at this depth, the soil is not of good quality, we remove an extra spade shoe, which we replace with an equal quantity of good soil taken from the surface of the ground or from any other part of the garden. You could even mix in some old, consumed turf or the remains of old layers, if the soil is too damp or too compact and able to retain water; but, in either case, you spread a good bed of cow manure or other good fertilizer at the bottom of the trench; for Asparagus to do well, it needs soil that is not only light and sandy, but also well amended; Then, on top of all this, a bed of good soil is brought in, the thickness of which must be calculated so that the Asparagus claws are planted at Om, 15 deep, instead of Om, 35 which used to be indicated as a result of an error that experience has shown to be necessary to modify. In the course of March, a good ploughing is given, and a rake is passed over the whole area to remove clods and stones; the land is divided into plots Im, 33 wide, between each of which a path of about Om,50 is left; after which four rows are marked out, which must be equally spaced from each other, and in such a way that the two outer rows are Om, 16 from the edges of the plank. Then take one- or two-year-old seedlings, carefully pulled out with a fork, so that the roots are not broken; place the claws about Om, 40 apart on the line, and, after spreading the roots well, cover them with loose soil; it would even have to be put through the rake, if it were mixed with stones from clods or badly broken soil. Once the beds are evenly covered, we spread a good mulch of half-consumed fnmier over each one. Each year, in autumn, old stems are cut off, lightly hoeed and then mulched with half-consumed manure. If you proceed in this way, the asparagus will be in full ratio by the third shoot, and the larger ones will be cut off with an asparagus knife. This can be done at this point without affecting the following year's harvest. Sowing can also be done in situ, after preparing the beds as described above. You sow in rows in February or March, and when the plant is strong enough, you thin it out, leaving only the most beautiful plants at a distance equal to the one we have indicated; after which the other care to be given is the same as for planted Asparagus. We would like to add another procedure, communicated to the Cercle Général d'Horticulture by Mr. Lenormand, who has been practicing it successfully for many years. We'll leave it to this skilled horticulturist to explain how he establishes his asparagus plantations: "In April 1834, I made trenches Im, 30 wide by Om, 33 deep, in which I made layers, which, trodden and wetted, were from Om, 38 to Om, 40 thick; after covering them with well-levelled earth, I placed the boxes intended to receive the frames, and in each frame I planted twelve claws of Asparagus of one year's sowing. After planting, I covered the soil with a good mulch and planted two vines of Melons, which came up perfectly without harming the Asparagus. When the melon plants were three-quarters strong, I added four cauliflowers per frame, and after the melon harvest, in September, I sowed lamb's lettuce for the winter; the whole thing was a complete success. "The following February, the layer having settled, I reseeded my claws with soil from the paths, then planted Lettuces and Romaines on top, with two rows of Cauliflowers per bed, which made all traces of the layer disappear. The whole thing grew with amazing speed and strength, as I got Asparagus of Om, 07 in circumference. By improving the soil in this way, we can obtain two harvests a year, independently of the Asparagus, which we can force from the second year, and continue in this way, leaving them one year of rest out of three. This plant, established in 1834, still exists today, which proves that the claws lose none of their vigor, even though they are brought into relationship three years earlier than they could have been by the old process." Argenteuil growers, whose market garden produce enjoys a justly-deserved reputation, cultivate asparagus in rows, usually between vines, of which there are large tracts in this locality. Planted shallowly, I meters apart in all directions, Argenteuil asparagus is regularly smoked every two years. They are hoeed as often as necessary, and dethatched every year in November, which involves removing a few centimetres of the soil surface; they are then ridged in February or March. If practised intelligently, this method of cultivation gives such remarkable results that it can be adopted with confidence by all those who wish to harvest very large quantities of asparagus. If you want to have early Asparagus, you can start forcing a bed in the first days of November, and continue successively until February, which is done in the following way: after placing the trunks on the beds you wish to force, spread a bed of potting soil over the Asparagus, then remove the soil from the paths to a depth of Om, 50, and place it on the beds in such a way as to reload them with Om, 33 approximately, in order to obtain much longer Asparagus; then replace the soil in the paths with a new manure stove, which should be raised to the height of the panels with which you cover the boxes; but before placing the panels, spread a bed of manure on the boards, to activate vegetation; take care, however, to remove this fu nier as soon as the Asparagus begin to emerge from the ground. Whatever the state of the weather, don't give the asparagus any air. During the night and in bad weather, we cover the panels with good straw mats, to concentrate the heat. The stoves are changed every ten or fifteen days or so, adding more or less new manure each time, depending on the temperature, so as to obtain a heat under the panels of not less than 15 degrees, and no more than 25. These Asparagus are usually good to cut twenty or twenty-five days (depending on the temperature) after you start forcing them. Old asparagus or asparagus to be destroyed can be planted on a bed, where they will produce, once only, thin, green asparagus to be eaten as peas. To do this, prepare a layer of Om, 60 to Om, 80 thick, with a heat of 20 to 25 degrees; lay down boxes, fill the layer with a few centimetres of potting soil, then fill the paths, but only halfway. When the layer has caught its first fire, we take the asparagus claws and, without subtracting anything from the length of the roots, we place them on the layer one beside the other; we leave them in this state for a few days, after which we pour a little potting soil between the claws, so as to cover them slightly, then we finish filling the paths, and reshape them if necessary. At night, we cover the panels with straw mats, and as soon as the asparagus start to grow, we give them air during the day, unless the temperature is too unfavorable. After twelve or fifteen days, the Asparagus starts to produce, and we cut for as long as it lasts, which is about three months. Asparagus seeds ripen towards the end of October, and are good for four years. AUBERGINE or MÉLONGÈNE (Solanum Melongena). - In the Paris climate, Aubergine is sown towards the end of December or at the beginning of January, on a bed with a temperature of 20 to 25 degrees. Two or three weeks after sowing, the seedling is transplanted into the nursery, but on a layer less warm than the first; after a while, it is lifted and transplanted a second time before being put in place. When the plant has recovered and the temperature permits, we start to give it some air. In the course of March, a final layer is prepared, the length of which should be proportionate to the number of plants to be grown; the boxes are placed, the layer is filled with potting soil, and when the layer is warm enough (15 to 20 degrees), four eggplants are planted under each 1m, 33. panel; After that, we start to give a little air, either from the top or from the bottom of the panels; then we gradually increase the amount as the season progresses, so as to remove the panels and trunks in the course of May. Other care consists of watering as needed, and cleaning leaves attacked by kermes. Eggplant seeds are good for seven years, Varieties. - Violet, - white, - variegated, - giant. BASELLE (Basella). - Climbing plant whose leaves replace spinach. Sow in March on a bed, and when there are no more frosts to worry about, plant out in the open ground, at the foot of a wall, with good exposure. Baselle seeds germinate for three years. Varieties. - Red Baselle, - White Baselle. COMMON BASILICO (Ocimum Basilicum). - An annual plant used, along with its varieties, as a seasoning. All are sown in March, in the soil, to be replanted in May in a shady spot. Basilie seeds can be stored for six years. BETTERAVE (Beta vulgaris). - It is sown at the end of April or beginning of May, in rows or broadcast, in deeply ploughed and smoked soil from the previous year; then, when the plants have five or six leaves, they are lit so that they are about Om, 35 apart, and replanted in places where they are lacking, an operation that should only be carried out in rainy weather. During the summer, they are hoeed several times, and towards the end of October or the beginning of November, the roots are harvested after the leaves have been cut off. Put them in the greenhouse or in a healthy cellar, where they can be stored until May. Beet seeds ripen in September and keep well for five or six years. Varieties. - Rouge, - rouge de Castelnaudary, - rouge foncé de Whyte, - Turnep, - jaune, - jaune de Castelnaudary. BOURRACHE (Borrago officinalis). - A plant whose flowers are used to decorate salads; it grows in all types of soil, and is planted in spring and autumn. Borage seeds germinate in three years. LARGE CAPUCIN (Tropœolum majus). - Sow in April at the foot of a wall, in a well-exposed spot. It can also be sown on its own, but must be raked. The flowers are used to dress salads; the seeds, picked while still green, can be preserved in vinegar and used in place of capers. Nasturtium seeds last five years. CARDON (Cynara Cardunculus). - Cardoons need soft, deep soil and frequent watering in summer. They propagate from seed sown in April on a bed, or better still in May, immediately in the field. Holes are made about a meter apart, filled with potting soil, and two or three seeds are sown in each. When the seeds have sprouted, the most vigorous plant is chosen and the others removed. If you have to fear the ravages of grubs or crickets, you should sow them in pots at the same time, so that you can replenish the empty spaces. Around September, when they are strong enough to be blanched, they are stuffed by attaching a tie made of litter to the plant's collar, then rolling it up and down so that only the tips of the leaves are visible. After a fortnight or three weeks, the ribs are white and must be eaten immediately, otherwise they will rot; they must therefore be stuffed one after the other. Before heavy frosts, we pull up the Cardoon clods to replant them close together in the vegetable greenhouse, where they will blanch without covering; but we must visit them often and remove all rotten leaves. In this way, they can be kept until March. Cardoon seeds ripen in the first half of September, and are good for seven years. Varieties. - Cardon de Tours, - d'Espagne, - Puvis, - plein inerme, - à côtés rouges. CARROT (Daucus carota). - The first seedlings are sown on a bed in December. A layer of Om, 35 to Om, 40 thick, with a heat of 15 to 20 degrees, is prepared; the boxes are placed, the Om, 15 layer is filled with potting soil, and, unless it's very cold, the paths are only half-filled. When the layer is warm enough, sow the variety known as Early Short Carrot or Dutch Carrot. Among the carrots, you can transplant a few small black lettuces, or sow a few pink radishes. During the night, we cover the panels with straw mats; when the sowing is well under way, we rework the warmers, which we then make the full height of the trunks. These carrots are usually ready for harvesting in April. If, in the second half of March, the weather is mild and the panels covering the carrots are needed, they can be removed, along with the trunks, but harvesting then takes longer. In the open ground, the first sowings can be made as early as February, and continued until July. However, this can only be done for the Early Short Carrot; for the other varieties, sowing should not go beyond April, so that they can reach full development before winter. Whatever the time of sowing, the soil must be well prepared, after which it must be broadcast. The soil is lightly harrowed with a fork, tilled and a layer of compost is spread over each bed. Rake lightly over the whole area, and water whenever necessary. When the carrots have emerged, we thin out the plant, which is almost always thick if the sowing has been successful. In November, we cut off the collar of each carrot; we put them in gauge, then we cover them with large manure during the frosts, or we deposit them in the vegetable greenhouse, in order to have some during the winter. In light, healthy soils, there's no need to uproot them; simply cover the carrot plants during the frosts. Carrot seeds are harvested in August; their germination period is four years. Varieties. - Rouge courte de Hollande, - demi-longue, - longue, - d'Altringham, - jaune longue, - rouge pâle de Flandre, - blanche, - violette d'Espagne. CULTIVATED CELERY. - A variety of Apium graveolens, it is sown on a bed in the open air as early as February; the seed should be very lightly covered. In April, plant in the open ground at a distance of about Om, 33 cm. From April to June, sow in the ground in a shady spot and plant out immediately. We encourage seed germination by frequent watering, and if the plant is too thick, it should be thinned out to prevent it withering away. In June and July, the seedlings are transplanted into place. Four rows of Om, 33 wide are drawn per bed, then planted at Om, 33 apart along the line. Immediately after planting, water to facilitate recovery, and continue until the Celery is strong enough to be blanched: a trench 1 m wide is opened, with the soil thrown in to the right and left, after which the Celery is lifted in clods and planted in the trench; eight clods are placed in each row, then potting soil is poured in between each row, so that it is completely buried, except for the tips of the leaves. After a fortnight, it's usually white enough to be harvested; but as it doesn't keep for long after that, you should only bleach it successively, so as to prolong the harvest as long as possible. During frosts, it is covered with litter, which is removed whenever the temperature permits. With care, it can be kept until the end of February. Varieties. - Plein blanc, - Turc, - Cole's superb red, - Plein rose, - violet, - for cutting. Celeriac. - Sowing can take place in April, in the open ground, in a shady spot; but it's better to sow in February on a bed, transplant the seedling on a bed; then put it in the open ground, after cutting off the large leaves and all the lateral roots. Water abundantly during the summer; then remove all unnecessary leaves, taking care to spare those in the heart, an operation which should be repeated as often as necessary to encourage the development of the tuber. Celeriac is pulled out at the beginning of winter to put it in gauge, and covered during the frosts; or it is put into the vegetable greenhouse after the leaves have been cut off. Treated in this way, it can easily be stored until March. CERFEUIL (Scandix cerefolium). - Sow almost year-round; in spring and autumn, at the foot of a wall and with good exposure, and in hot weather, in a northern exposure. Curly chervil. - This variety requires nothing more than ordinary Chervil; it is used for the same purposes, and has the advantage over the latter of not being confused with Hemlock. Chervil seeds ripen in June, and keep for two years. Bulbous chervil (hœrophyllum bulbosum). - Bulbous chervil is an edible plant whose roots do not extend beyond the base of the plant.

proportions of a small Dutch Carrot. It is very starchy and has a pleasant flavor. Bulbous Chervil is sown in September, i.e. as soon as the seeds have been harvested; otherwise, they won't germinate until the second year, unless you take the precaution of storing them in sand until sowing time, which may not be until spring. After sowing, the seed is covered with a good layer of potting soil; once this is done, bulbous chervil requires no special care other than the weeding and watering that all garden produce requires. Regardless of when it is sown, bulbous chervil is good for harvesting in July. Bulbous Chervil seed is harvested in July. It is only good for one year. COMESTIBLE MUSHROOM (Agaricus edulis). - The success of mushroom beds depends on the choice and preparation of the manure and the care given to the beds. To set up a Mushroom wheel, you need to use manure from horses that do hard work; as it is renewed less often, it is softer, i.e. more impregnated with urine, and contains more dung than that of luxury horses. The manure is first deposited in a heap, to allow it to ferment; then, about a month later, it is taken up with a fork to form a layer (called a planchée) about Om, 65 thick by Im, 33 wide. We spread a first bed, taking care to remove the longest straws, ties and hay, then mix the dry parts well with those most impregnated with urine; and to form the edges of the layer we turn the manure on its sides, so that the ends are inside. Once a bed of manure has been formed, it is wetted with the watering can, then trodden down with the feet. We then make a second bed, which we treat in the same way, and so on until we have reached the height indicated. Eight or ten days later, the bed is reshuffled, starting at one end, then turned over in the same way as the first time, but taking care to return what was on the edges and on top to the center. After leaving it to ferment for a further eight or ten days, the manure should finally be ready for grinding, i.e. it should be fat but not too wet, and should have only the right amount of heat for the operation. As summer thunderstorms often abort the spawn, we don't start cultivating mushrooms in the open air until September, and then continue successively until December. After ensuring that the manure is in good condition, we start erecting the millstones, which should be Om.50 wide at the base and the same height. The manure is tamped down as the wheel is raised, to ensure that it is compacted as little as possible. It is mounted in the shape of a humpback, so that it is only Om, 10 wide at the top. During the operation, the sides of the grinding wheel are carefully firmed by lightly tapping with the back of the shovel, then the long straws protruding from each side are removed with the rake. If, after the millstones have been set up, heavy rain should fall, they should be wrapped in a shirt (a large litter blanket), which, in favorable weather, should only take place after the millstones have been gobbled up, an operation we'll talk about later. After eight to ten days, check the degree of heat with a diaper thermometer, and if it doesn't mark more than 15 to 18 degrees, you can larder the millstone, i.e. cut a row of small openings on both sides, at Om, 10 or Om, 15 from the ground, depending on whether it's dry or damp, a row of small openings to be made by hand, at Om, 33 from each other, in which to place the spawn (1) flush with the side of the wheel, then ap(1) Mushroom spawn is the name given to small white filaments, rather like mold, that form in manure. They can be found either in manure that has been in piles for a long time, where very good ones are often formed, or in old melon beds; failing that, they can be taken from a millstone that is already in use, but where only one harvest has yet been made. Mushroom spawn can be kept in a dry place for up to two years. lightly stink to bring the spawn into perfect contact with the manure; but if you fear that there is still too much heat, bring the manure closer only after a few days. If, eight or ten days after larding the millstone, small whitish filaments begin to spread over the whole surface, take light, lean earth, salped as much as possible, pass it over the claie and spread it out to a thickness of about Om, 03, which you press down lightly with the back of the shovel, which is called gobetering. If you don't notice the traces we've mentioned, you'll have to repeat the operation, putting new white into openings next to the old ones. If the weather is mild and dry, the grinding stone can be cooled by lightly dabbing it with water, but care must be taken not to give it too much water at once, as excess humidity will destroy the nascent mushrooms. After gobbling, cover the wheel with a liner of Om, 05 to Om, 06 of large bedding (a thicker liner could cause the manure to ferment again, which would destroy all hope of harvesting), increasing it during frosts and according to the severity of the cold. About six weeks later, we'll start picking the first mushrooms. To find them, carefully lift the bedding, and after picking them, fill the holes they occupied with soil of the same type as that used to gobet the millstone. If you find a few small places where the young Mushrooms have perished, remove all the destroyed part and replace with new soil. At all times, even after one side of the wheel has been used up, it should be carefully covered with bedding. A millstone can produce for three to five months at any time, but 7. best in summer. You can set up your millstones in a dimly-lit cellar, and then, given the equality of temperature that prevails in these localities, it becomes unnecessary to cover the millstones with litter. CHENILLETTE (Scorpiurus vermiculata), VeRS (Astragalus hamosus). LIMAÇON (Medicago turbinata). - Native annual plants of the Papilionaceae family, whose fruits imitate caterpillars, worms or limacons, and which should be sown in place, in April and May, about Om, 30 apart. CHERVIS or CHIROUIS (Sium sisarum). - A plant whose fleshy, very sweet roots can be eaten like Scorsonera. Sow in spring or September, in loose open soil, then hoe and water frequently. Chervis seeds germinate in two years. CHICORICE. Wild chicory (Cichorium intubus). - The emerging leaves of this species are used to make a highly prized salad, which can be obtained almost all year round by sowing in beds from March onwards, then in the open ground from April until autumn. If the roots are to be used to make the salad known as Barbe-de-capucin, they must be sown in rays in April, with hoeing and watering being all that's required; then, as frost approaches, the roots are pulled out, lifted with a fork to avoid breaking them. In October, when this work is usually started, a layer about Om40 thick is prepared, at a temperature of 15 to 20 degrees Celsius. The best place for this operation is a low cellar with no air or light. Once the bed has caught its first fire, the roots are put together in bunches, but only after careful removal of old leaves and any parts likely to cause mildew; they are then placed upright on the bed, and watered frequently with the apple watering can; but, as always, watering must be in proportion to the heat of the bed; as soon as the Chicory starts to grow, watering must be done very sparingly to avoid rotting the inside of the bunches. Chicory is usually long enough to be harvested after fifteen to eighteen days. Chicory can be successively blanched from October or November to April. Chicory can also be blanched by burying roots on a bed covered with solid-framed panels, to intercept light, or with ordinary panels, which are kept constantly covered with straw mats. Wild chicory seeds ripen in September, and keep well for eight to ten years. Curly chicory (Cichorium endivia). - The first seedlings can be sown in September under cloches, but cold. From then until June, curly or Italian chicory is sown. In the first days of October, the seedling is transplanted, also under cloches, and towards the end of October or the beginning of November, Chicory is planted on the ground, but under panels; air is given as often as possible, and during frosts, the panels are covered at night. In January or February, sow on a warm bed under panels. The bed must not be less than 20 to 25 degrees hot, because to obtain a plant that doesn't bolt, the seeds must germinate within twenty-four hours, regardless of the time of year; it's better to start sowing again 'than to transplant a plant that has languished. Twelve or fifteen days after sowing, the seedling is transplanted into the nursery, to be planted a fortnight or three weeks later, still under panels, but on a softer layer. In the second half of March, you can start transplanting Chicory in the open ground, but under cloches or panels, which you remove as soon as the weather is favorable. In April, May and June, Chicory is still sown on beds, but then the plant can be transplanted immediately into the ground. Draw four rows per bed, Im, 33 wide, and plant Om, 40 apart along the line. In June and July, Chicorée de Meaux is sown in the ground in a shady spot. However, in many areas, it would be better to continue sowing in the soil, but in the open air. When the plant is strong enough to be transplanted, spread a good mulch on each bed, then plant at the distance indicated above, and give it a good watering to help it take root; other care consists of pulling out weeds and wetting if necessary. When the Chicory is sufficiently covered, take advantage of dry weather to lift the leaves, which are then tied with rushes or straw to whiten the inside; but as they whiten in a short time, they should only be tied in proportion to consumption. As soon as they are bound, they should be watered only at the neck, to avoid wetting them, which could cause them to rot, and, as soon as the first frosts set in, they should be covered with straw mats or bedding, which should be removed whenever the weather permits; then, as the frosts increase, they should be uprooted and returned to the vegetable greenhouse, where they should be half-buried in sand: in this way, they can be kept until January. Chicorée frisée de la Passion. - This interesting variety, which we owe to the kindness of M. Charvet, owner at La Cellette, near Blois, is just as hardy as the Lettuce whose name it bears. Sown in August, transplanted in September and planted out in October, Passion Chicory is good for harvesting in March and April, a time of year when garden produce is generally scarce. As such, Curly Passion Chicory can be considered a good buy. Ever-white chicory. - This variety is not as widely grown as it deserves, as it can be a good substitute for spinach, especially in summer, when spinach is often hard to come by. It can be sown in the field or in the ground, from February to August. Scarole. - Scarole is a variety of Chicory whose cultivation is very similar to that of Chicorée de Meaux. The seeds are good for harvesting at the end of September, and keep for five or six years. Varieties. - Frisée de Meaux, - fine d'été or d'Italie, - de Rouen, or corne-de-cerf, - de la Passion, - always white, - sauvage, - panachée, - améliorée, - Scarole ordinaire, - blonde or à feuilles de laitue. CABBAGE (Brassica). - Cabbages need cool, well-smoked soil, because the more fertilizer they receive, the fatter they become. They come in many varieties, but all can be divided into five main races: 1° cabbages, 2° savoy cabbages, 3° green cabbages, 4° kohlrabi, and 5° cauliflowers and broccoli. N. 1. head cabbage. - Towards the end of August or in the first days of September, early cabbages are sown. In October, transplant the seedlings in a nursery along a wall with good exposure, for planting in late November or early December, and in February or March in cold or damp soils. If winter is harsh, it will be necessary to secure the plant, either with bedding or with mats laid on top of gaulettes. If you run out of plants in spring, you can sow them in February on a bed and in March on a well-soiled bed. Second-season and late-season cabbages are usually only sown in February or March; however, they can also be sown in August. Whatever the time of sowing, these cabbages should be transplanted immediately into place, 50, 60 or 80 centimetres apart, depending on the proportions of the varieties to be grown. The soil should be well fertilized, as it should not be forgotten that it is only by dint of manure and water that we can obtain all that this plant should produce. Varieties. - Cabus hâtifs, d'York, - cœur-de-bœuf. - Pain-desucre. Cabus 2nd season, Pomerania, - Winigstadt, - Joannet, - Schweinfurt. Cabus tardifs, from Saint-Denis, - from Holland, - vert de Vaugirard, - from Germany dit Quintal, - dark red. Cabbage preservation. - As heavy frosts are very detrimental to cabbages, in November, all cabbages with apples should be uprooted and placed on a plank, close to each other and with their heads slightly inclined. When there is a heavy frost, cover them with litter or leaves, and remove them as soon as the weather is mild. In light soils, you can bury the head instead of the roots: in this way, cabbages can be kept until May without covering; it is a good idea, however, to cover part of them, so as to be able to pull them out during frosts. N. 2 Savoy cabbage. - They are sown from the end of February to June, and transplanted immediately into the ground like Savoy cabbages. More hardy than the latter, Savoy cabbages usually withstand winter without shelter. Varieties. - Hâtif d'Ulm, - pied-court, - Victoria, - ordinaire, - doré, - pancalier, - des Vertus, - de Bruxelles. N. 3 Green cabbages. - We divide them into the only ones grown in the kitchen garden; the others are grown extensively as fodder, and some as plants are even more pleasant to eat when frost has softened them. Varieties. - Big-ribbed cabbage, - Fringed big-ribbed cabbage, - Strawberry cabbage. Cabbages of the second category are sown in July and August, or better still in March and April, and the seedling is transplanted immediately; but they can also be sown in place, either in rows or broadcast. These cabbages produce leaves throughout the winter and into their second year. Varieties. - Cavalier or Tree cabbage. - Caulet de Flandre. - branchu de Poitou. - de grand Jouan. N. 4 Kohlrabi. - The first sowings take place towards the end of February, and can continue until June; they are sown on a composted bed, and later put in place. These cabbages differ from the others by their neck, which is swollen and fleshy, and which is used in cooking like turnips; but, to keep them tender, they must be watered frequently in summer. Varieties - White or Siam, - early white. - violet. - early purple. Chou-navet, quite similar to the preceding variety, produces a fleshy tuber with the same flavor as kohlrabi. It is sown in the field in May and June, either in rows or as a broadcast crop. The next step is to thin out the plant so that the cabbages are about Om.40 apart. They have little fear of frost, and, barring a severe winter, can be pulled up only as and when needed. Cabbage seeds ripen in July; they keep well for five or six years. Varieties. - White turnip cabbage, - Rutabaga or Swedish turnip. N. 5 Cauliflower. - These are much more delicate than the other cabbage varieties, and like light, well-smoked soil, with plenty of watering in summer. Several varieties are grown, but it is impossible to recommend one over another, as results depend solely on local causes. The first seedlings are sown in September, in a well-soiled bed or on an old layer, to be transplanted in October, in a nursery, on a bed; and when it freezes, cloches or panels are placed over the plant. Care must be taken to provide air every day, as long as the temperature permits. If, in spite of this precaution, the plant should advance too far, it should be uprooted and replanted to delay vegetation; then, when the cold becomes severe, surround the bells with litter, and cover the whole with straw mats; uncover whenever the weather permits, and provide air. In December, you can plant some of your cauliflowers on beds and under panels, with a few lettuces in between. During the night, cover the panels with straw mats, water as needed, and provide air whenever the temperature permits; then, when the cauliflowers reach the stained-glass windows, take care to raise the boxes; if the weather is favorable in the second half of March, remove the panels. These cauliflowers will produce in April and May; in March, we plant the other part in the ground, and they will give from the end of May to July. They can also be sown on a bed in February and March, and shortly afterwards transplanted on a bed and planted out in late March or early April, producing in June and July. The last cauliflowers are sown in June: this is the time when most cauliflowers are sown, and when cultivation is easiest: it's the same as for ordinary cabbages, and all success depends on abundant watering, which must be very frequent, especially during the first few months. Sow in a shady spot in a well-soiled bed; when the plant is strong enough, transplant immediately. These cauliflowers produce from the end of August to November; they can even be kept until February, and sometimes until April. To do this, cut them as late as possible, and especially when the weather is dry, so as not to bring them in until they are well dried out, as this will determine how long they can be kept. Preserving cauliflowers. - After removing all the leaves from cauliflowers, place them on the shelves of the vegetable greenhouse, or, which is even better, hang them upside down. As they shrink a lot as they dry out, the day before you want to eat them, refresh the tips of the cores and soak them in fresh water for a few hours, taking care not to get the heads wet; they soon regain their original shape, without losing any of their quality. Cauliflower seed is harvested in September. They germinate for five years. Varieties. - Tender or petit Salomon, - demi-dur or gros Salomon, - Lenormand, - dur de Paris, - d'Angleterre, - de Hollande. Broccoli. - Broccoli is sown in March, April and May, starting with the earliest varieties. When the plant is strong enough, it is transplanted to the nursery, and later planted in rows like cauliflower. Early varieties sown in March are good for harvesting in September. Others produce successively during winter and spring. More hardy than cauliflower, Broccoli can withstand a few degrees of cold without suffering. However, it's a good idea to remove the clods as frost approaches, and replant them in a trench over which frames or straw mats have been placed. Broccoli seeds germinate for five years. Varieties. - Early white, - Late white, - Early violet. - Sprouting (this last variety produces small apples like Brussels sprouts). CHOU MARIN (Crambe maritima). - Crambe is a very good vegetable, whose emerging leaves are eaten and blanched by ridding the stalk; it is hardy and easy to grow. Under favorable conditions (i.e. sandy, well-smoked soil), it produces for a very long time. We have seen a plantation of Crambés in full report, which for fifteen years has given several harvests each year. It can be propagated from seed sown in the field or in the nursery soon after harvest, as autumn sowings are generally more successful than spring ones. Crambes can also be propagated by root cuttings, but sowing always produces, as is easy to understand, more vigorous plants. Crambes are planted in autumn or spring. Two rows are drawn in an Im, 33-wide bed, and planted at Om, 50 apart along the line. Each year, in autumn, the dead leaves are removed, the plants are hoeed, and a good bed of half-consumed manure is spread over the beds. You could start cutting the leaves off the Crambes as early as the second flush, but it's better to wait until the third, by which time they'll be in full vegetative growth, and you'll be able to keep them much longer. We usually start buttering Crambes towards the end of January or the beginning of February; but, so that they don't all give together, we only butter part of them, and the rest a fortnight later, which is done in the following way: we place on each plant a heap of compost (or light earth) of about Om, 20, and cover the whole with a good bed of manure or leaves, in order to activate vegetation; about a month later, when the tips of the leaves begin to appear, we cut them back to the ground, but taking care to spare the eyes at the neck of the plant, as without this precaution it would no longer grow. After harvesting, they are ridged again, and produce a second crop that is often as abundant as the first. After the second cut, destroy the mounds, spread some of the compost on the beds, and remove the rest. You can also force Crambé under panels, like Asparagus: this simply involves placing boxes and panels over the Crambés in January or February, after having ridged them; if you don't have solid-frame panels, you can use ordinary panels, provided you keep them constantly covered with straw mats. To stimulate Crambé vegetation, you can surround the boxes with a manure stove, as heat does nothing to harm this plant. You can even, as is done in England, place large clumps of Crambes in the greenhouse to be forced during the winter, so as to have good ones to harvest ahead of time, or give the forced ones away on the spot. Crambé seeds are harvested in August; they keep well for three years. CIBOULE COMMUNE (Allium fistulosum). - The first seedlings are sown in February, in the field and broadcast; from then on, sowing can continue successively until July. After sowing, the seeds are covered with a light layer of compost, and watered whenever necessary. If you don't want to run out of Ciboule in winter, pull it out in November, put it in gauges, then cover it with dry litter during the frosts. The seeds ripen in August, and keep for two years. Perennial Ciboule - Multiplies by splinters in spring or autumn. CIBOULETTE. Civet (Allium Schœnoprasum). - This plant multiplies by its cloves, which are separated in February and March for planting in borders. The more often it is cut, the more tender it becomes and the better it grows. To overwinter, cut at ground level and cover with compost. CUCUMBER (Cucumis sativus). - Cucumbers are sown in January, February and March, on a warm bed and under panels. When the cotyledons and first leaves are well-developed, they are transplanted into small pots, sown on a warm bed and planted some time later, also on a bed and under panels. Later, when frosts are no longer a threat, cucumbers can be planted in the ground. In light soils that are easy to warm up, cucumbers can even be sown in place, in small pits filled with potting soil. Like melons, cucumbers need to be pruned to produce good fruit, as described in the Melon article. Small green gherkin cucumber. - Sow in early May on beds and under panels. Shortly afterwards, the seedling is transplanted to the nursery, also on beds and under panels. As soon as it has taken root, we start to give it a little air, to strengthen it, and towards the end of May or the beginning of June, we raise it in clods to put it in the ground in good exposure, Om, 60 apart. Gherkins can also be sown in the ground; they are even hardier than other cucumbers, and don't need pruning. In naturally damp soils, Cucumbers and Gherkins should be rowed like Peas and Beans, so that they do not lie on the ground, in order to harvest good fruit. Cucumber seeds germinate for five years. Varieties. - Early white, - large white, - long yellow, - English long green, - Russian, - snake. PUMPKIN (Cucurbita maxima). - Pumpkins are sown in March, on a warm bed and under panels; in April, they are transplanted in the nursery, also on a bed and under panels. A few days after transplanting, we start to give them a little air, in order to strengthen the plant; and, in May, we prepare holes which we arrange so that the Pumpkins are at least 1m, 65 from each other. The holes are filled with manure and covered with about Om, 15 of compost. If, after planting, there are small white frosts during the night, cover the Pumpkins with cloches, or, failing that, with litter. While they are growing, they should be watered abundantly, and other care consists in pinching the first stem above the second eye, to encourage the development of one or two branches on each. When they are about Im,50 in length, we marcotte them, which consists in laying the branches in the ground, so that they produce roots; in this way, we obtain much more vigorous vegetation. As soon as a fruit is knotted and deemed worthy of preservation, the branch bearing it should be pinched off two or three eyes above the fruit; and if you want to obtain large fruits, you should leave only one or two on each plant, except for the Dutch variety, whose fruits are smaller but of excellent quality; In fact, this is the variety best reserved for winter provisions: picked before the frosts and placed on the shelves of the fruit tree or orangery, it often keeps well into March and April. Marrow squash, full squash from Naples, Ohio, Valparaiso, Barbary, Madeira, Patagonia, Giraumont turban and Patisson, are grown in exactly the same way as Pumpkins. The germination period of pumpkin seeds is five years. Varieties: - large yellow, - Spanish, - Dutch, - white, - Corfu. FONTAINE CRESSON (Nasturtium officinale). - This plant, hitherto used in cooking only as a salad and supply, can also be prepared in the manner of spinach, and in this form has a very pleasant flavor. The consumption of watercress has become so considerable that, in a radius very close to Paris, large areas of land are devoted to this crop. These cressonnières are fed by natural or artificial springs, and arranged so as to be submerged at will. The land is divided into pits, each about 3 meters wide by Om, 40 or so deep, separated by raised beds for various types of crops, such as artichokes, cabbage and so on. Cress can be propagated from seeds sown in spring, or even better from cuttings taken in August. Before planting, the soil should be well consolidated, and if it is not sufficiently moist, a little water should be left to run off. Once the soil is well prepared, watercress is taken and placed at the bottom of the pits in small pinches, about Om, 12 to Om, 15 apart. After a short time, it has taken root and completely covers the soil; then a light layer of well-consumed cow manure is spread over the whole surface; by means of a board with an obliquely placed handle, the whole is slightly compressed; after which, Om, 10 to Om, 12 of water is introduced, a quantity quite sufficient for this crop. In summer, watercress is picked every two or three weeks. To make harvesting easier, a plank is laid across the pit. As soon as a pit has been harvested, we dry it out and spread a little cow manure over it, pressing it down with the above-mentioned instrument, an operation that must be repeated immediately after each cut. When a pit has been in production for a year, it is destroyed and replanted as described above, but only after removing the old roots and manure debris, which form a fairly considerable thickness at the bottom. It can also be sown or planted on the banks of watercourses, as is often the case in pleasure gardens. The stems spread quickly, and can be cut back every year until the frosts, provided this is done often enough to prevent them from going to seed. Watercress seeds germinate in four years. Cresson de terre, Cresson vivace (Erysimum prœcox). - It can be used in place of watercress, and has all the flavor of watercress. Sow in spring, in rays, in clean, light, moist soil. The germination period of watercress seeds is three years. Watercress (Lepidium sativum). - As this plant goes to seed very quickly, it is necessary to sow it very often; sowing is done in rays, in spring on a bed, and in summer in a shady spot.
