Cresson alénois seeds ripen in June, and keep for five years. Varieties. - Cressou alénois frisé. - Golden cress. ECHALOTE (Allium Ascalonicum). - Successfully grown only in light, substantial soil smoked from the previous year. It multiplies from cloves planted in February and March, at Om, 08 or Om, 10 apart, and almost flush with the ground, to avoid humidity, which is very harmful. For replanting, choose the thinnest and most elongated shallots, as they produce the most beautiful bulbs. Pull them up in July or August, when the leaves are dry, and leave them for two or three days in the sun, then store them in a dry place. SPINACH (Spinacia oleracea). - They are sown in rows or broadcast from March to the end of October, and as they remain in the ground for only a short time, they are often sown among newly transplanted plants or to line beds to be used for another crop a month or so later. Summer seedlings should be sown in a shady spot, and watered frequently to prevent them from bolting. Spinach seeds ripen in July, and keep for five years. Varieties. - Spinach from Holland, - England, - Flanders, - Esquermes, with lettuce leaves. ESTRAGON (Artemisia dracunculus). - It is propagated from seed, but more frequently by splintering plants and replanting them in spring in good exposure. Cut the stems at the onset of winter, and cover the clumps with a few centimetres of compost. FENOUH, (Anethum feniculum). - Several varieties are grown, but as a vegetable, sweet fennel is the most highly regarded. It is propagated from seeds taken from Italy every year; those harvested in our gardens degenerate quickly. Sow from March to June, either in the field or in a nursery, and transplant to Om, 40 cm apart; then hoe and water frequently during drought. When Fennel is strong enough, it is blanched in the same way as Celery. The roots and young shoots are eaten. Fennel seeds germinate for five years. BEANS (Faba vulgaris). - The first broad beans are sown in January, under panels (to sow at this time, early dwarf broad beans are preferred); in February, they are transplanted in slightly deep rays, which are traced at Om, 35 from each other; During bad weather, they are covered with litter, and when they are a few centimeters high, they are hoeed, then the rays are filled in, which increases the vigor of the plants and the produce; when they are deflowered, all the ends are pinched off, to force the sap to 135 bear towards the fruit. In February, we sow in the open ground, in clumps or in rays; from this time onwards, sowing can be continued successively until the end of May; finally, whatever the time of sowing, care consists in giving a few hoeings and pinching the ends of the stems, as previously indicated. Bean seeds germinate for six years. Varieties. - Early dwarf, - Julienne, - Marsh. - de Windsor, - evergreen, - violet, - purple flower, - long pod. STRAWBERRY (Fragaria vesca). - We propagate Strawberry plants from seed or from nets, which should only be taken from one-year-old plants; those from old clumps produce much less, and the fruit is less beautiful and of poorer quality. Sow in March, in a shady spot; cover the seeds with a light layer of fine soil mixed with compost, and keep the soil cool by watering. As soon as the plant has four or five leaves, it is transplanted, two by two, onto an old bed. Immediately after transplanting, we baste with an apple watering can, and continue to do so as needed. For a few days, we protect the young plants from the sun with a little litter, which we spread lightly. At the beginning of July, the clods are lifted and planted out in the ground, about Om, 15 apart, and, as after the first transplanting, the new growth is protected by frequent watering. The result of these transplantings is to encourage the development of a large number of young roots; and the more the Strawberry plants are furnished with them, the more productive they become. From this time onwards, until they are ready to be planted, we take care to remove all the flowers and netting that develop on the young plant, and to pull out those that appear to be degenerating, which can be easily recognized by their vigor and the absence of flowers. Towards the end of September, the beds in which the Strawberry plants are to be planted are given a good ploughing; and if the soil is not of good quality, only well-consumed fertilizers should be used to improve it: for when the Strawberry roots reach the unconsumed manure, the leaves dry up successively, and often the clumps perish. After preparing the soil well, draw five rows per bed, Om, 33 wide; then plant your Strawberry plants at Om, 35 apart on the line, which however should only be done for Four Seasons Strawberries, as for those with very large fruits, such as Keen's seedling Strawberry, draw four rows only, and plant at Om, 50 apart on the line; after which, we continue to cut the flowers and netting from each clump before they are rooted, in order to concentrate the reproductive power they are endowed with on each plant. In spring, we hoe each bed; as soon as the flowers begin to appear, we cover the soil with a slightly long mulch, which on the one hand has the advantage of conserving soil moisture, and on the other prevents the fruit from bearing on the soil. Watering should be done with apple watering cans, in the morning in spring and in the evening in summer. The following year, the same care is continued; but, as the produce degenerates after a few years, Strawberry plants should not be kept for more than two years. However, in good soil, they can be kept for three or four years, taking care to replant them each spring with new soil. Strawberry plants propagated from nets should be planted in July, and as what we have just said about Strawberry plants from seed is entirely applicable to the latter, we believe it unnecessary to deal with this subject at greater length. Forced strawberry plants. - Strawberries grown for forcing are: Fraisier des Quatre-Saisons, Keen's seedling, Princesse Royale, Marguerite Lebreton, Victoria Trolopp, Elton. In January or the first few days of February, boxes, then panels, are placed on the boards of the strawberry plants to be forced; the soil is removed from the paths surrounding the boxes to a depth of about Om.45, after which the paths are filled with manure, but only up to ground level, and in the first fortnight of February the filling is completed. From then on, care must be taken to maintain them to the height of the panels: for this, manure is brought in as and when it is needed. We cover the panels at night with straw mats, and give them air when the sun is shining. Towards the end of April, we start giving a few basins, if the temperature requires it, which we continue to do as needed. Strawberry plants treated in this way will begin to ripen in April. After harvesting, we remove the panels (which can still be used to cover the melons), which will not prevent the strawberry plants, especially those from Quatre-Saisons, from bearing fruit until the frosts. However, Keen's seedling and other large-fruited varieties can also be harvested a second time. To do this, they must be deprived of water for 8. some time, in order to stop their vegetation; and when the clumps are almost wilted, remove most of the leaves, hoe them lightly, then encourage their vegetation with good watering. In the first days of August, a second fruiting will take place, just as abundant as the first. Instead of destroying potted strawberry plants after harvest, as is usually done, you can remove the old roots and renew the soil in the pots in autumn. After this operation, treated like the young plants that are renewed each year, these strawberry plants produce fruit just as beautiful and abundant as the young plants. In Tours, at the home of Mr. Bellanger, a friend of ours, we have seen strawberry plants that have been subjected to this treatment for fifteen years, and whose vigor leaves nothing to be desired. Since the adoption of thermosiphon heating, the forced cultivation of strawberry plants has been modified. Thus, after having treated the strawberry plants as we have indicated, towards the end of September or the beginning of October, they are lifted in clods and planted in Om, 15 pots. For potting, we use good, soft soil, which has been raked, and immediately after planting, we place the pots next to each other in a trunk, so as to protect them from heavy rain and frosts, by placing frames or straw mats over them; then we water them to make it easier for them to recover, and, as for plants grown in the open ground, we remove the netting and flowers as they appear. In January, we prepare the boxes to receive the strawberry plants; then we place them on the ground, all next to each other, or on a tier under which we run the thermosiphon pipes. Once everything is in place, we hoe the soil in the pots, remove any dead leaves, and lay the panels, which we cover with straw matting overnight. At this point, we start heating them, which should be done only moderately and in such a way as to maintain a temperature of 12 to 15 degrees under the panels, and, as we indicated for Strawberry plants forced into the ground, we baste and give air whenever the temperature is favorable. In this way, you can have ripe fruit as early as the first days of March. Like those grown in the open ground, Strawberry plants forced into pots are likely to produce a second crop; all you need to do is remove the soil, plant them in the open ground and give them the care indicated above. Strawberry plants are divided into several sections, each containing a large number of varieties. We will only mention those most commonly grown. Strawberry seeds germinate for three years. Varieties: - Des Quatre-Saisons, - Ambroisia, - Amiral Dundas. - British Queen, - Eleonor Myatt, - Elton. - Jacunda, - Keen's sedling, - Lucas, - Marguerite Lebreton, - Napoléon III, - Princesse royale, - Sir Harry, - Victoria Trolopp, - Vicomtesse Héricart de Thury. BEANS (Phaseolus vulgaris). - The first Beans are sown in December, on beds and under panels; but, as at this time there is often a complete absence of sun, which is very unfavorable to this type of cultivation, it is preferable not to start this work until January, and from then on you can continue until the end of March. Sow on beds and under panels, and as soon as the cotyledons have developed, transplant the beans in the nursery, always preparing a layer about Om, 50 thick with a heat of 20 to 25 degrees; lay the boxes, load the layer with Om, 12 to Om, 15 of light soil, and plant the beans. Four rows are marked out per box, and the beans are planted at about Om, 15 on the line; after which, the care to be given consists in re-stoking from time to time, in order to maintain the necessary heat in the layer; covering the panels during the night; giving air whenever the temperature allows it; When the beans are about Om.25 in height, they are placed on top of the trunk, and held in this position by means of small wooden rods placed on the stems. A few days later, the ends of the stems are raised (the rods can then be removed), but the lower part remains lying on the ground. Treated in this way, the first beans are usually picked six weeks after sowing. It is often a mistake to destroy beans as soon as they have been harvested, because if you clean them carefully, removing dead leaves and any fruit found too small to be picked, after a while they will produce a second harvest as abundant as the first. Thermosiphon heating can also be used to grow beans under panels. All that's needed is to prepare a very thin layer, with the sole aim of protecting the beans from the dampness of the soil; then the pipes of the appliance are wired above the layer; the heat is maintained at 15 to 20 degrees under the panels; and as the heating can be regulated at will, the beans are uncovered every day, regardless of the state of the temperature, and air is given as often as necessary, which contributes greatly to the success of the operation. In April, we still sow on beds, but we transplant in the open ground and under cloches. Three beans are transplanted under each cloche; after a few days, air begins to circulate, and the cloches are removed when frosts are no longer to be feared and the temperature is favorable. It goes without saying that either cloches or panels can be used. Sow in the open ground in May; in light soil, sow in the first fortnight of the month; in heavy soil, only in the second fortnight, in clumps, or better still, in rays, as this produces much more vigorous vegetation, and consequently more abundant produce. Rays are traced about Om, 05 deep, Om, 40 apart, after which the beans are sown one by one, Om, 15 or Om, 20 apart on the line, then covered with about Om, 02 of soil. To sow in clumps, holes are made Om, 05 to Om, 06 deep, arranged in a checkerboard pattern, Om, 40 apart; five or six Beans are sown in each, then covered with the same amount of soil as those sown in rays. Some time later, we hoe to facilitate seed emergence; but it's only when the beans are well up that we finish filling the holes or combs. From the time indicated above, beans can be sown in the open ground until mid-August, to be eaten green (the beans grown particularly for this purpose are: Nain de Hollande, Flageolet and Bagnolet); but if you want to harvest dry, don't sow after May, except for a few early dwarf varieties, which can still be sown in the first fortnight of June. We still grow a large number of bean varieties, which can be divided into two categories. Bean seeds have a germination period of three years, and can be eaten green or shelled. Om, 30, - Belgian black, h. Om, 35, - Soissons dwarf, h. Om, 50 - Chinese, h. Om, 35, - Flageolet, h. Om,35, - Fl. yellow, h. Om, 40,- Swiss white, Om,45, - S. gray, h. Om45, - de Chartres, h. Im,40,- de Soissons, h. 2m, - Sabre, h. 2m, - Rice, h. Om,60. Beans without parchment or Mange-tout. - White dwarf, h. Om, 50, - Sabre dwarf, h. Om, 50, - marbled Prague dwarf, h. Om,45. - Princess dwarf, h. Om, 40, - Canadian yellow, h. Om, 40, - Butter dwarf, h. Om, 35, - Predomme, h. 1m,50, - Princess, h. 2m. - Butter 2m,50, - White butter, h. 2m. - Prague red, h. 2m,50, - marbled P., h. 2m, - P. bicolor, h. 2m,50, - Villetaneuse, h. 2m. CHINESE IGNAMUS (Dioscorea Batatas). - Introduced to France in 1848, this plant has stood the test of time, under which many new plants have succumbed. It increasingly justifies the hopes founded on the services it renders in its native country, and we can now say that it is worthy in every respect of first place on the list of our vegetable plants. The taste of the tuberous roots of the Chinese Yam differs little from that of the Potato; they are also rich in starch, and can, like the Potato, be used for all kinds of seasonings. The roots of the Chinese Yam grow every year, but only after having given birth to new roots, which grow from the collar of the plant. The Chinese Yam is propagated by planting, in March or April, with no more care than is required for the well understood cultivation of the Potato, either the bulbils which are born in the leaf axils, or the young roots produced by the bulbils, or finally the collar of the roots destined for consumption. Chinese yams are planted in rows, Om, 20 or O,, 25 apart, in all directions. In siliceous soils, which are better suited than all others to the cultivation of this plant, Chinese yams can be harvested the same year they are planted. Harvesting costs are not significantly higher than those for long carrots, for example. Nevertheless, to get the most out of this plant, the roots must be left in the ground for two years. From what we have been able to observe in our own cultivations, the root yield of Chinese Yam always far exceeds in the second year what the same area of land could have produced of Potatoes. The result is that, despite two years of cultivation and the cost of uprooting, this operation still offers definite advantages. Although the stems of Chinese yam are climbing, they don't need to be raked, and can be left to crawl along the ground. If they grow too much in the second year, they can be fed to cattle, which are happy to eat them as fresh fodder. Chinese yam is not very sensitive to the cold; in the climate of Paris, it survives ordinary winters very well in the open ground. However, it is advisable to uproot Chinese yams as soon as the stems are completely dry. Placed in the same conditions as potatoes, 3 Chinese yams can easily be kept for five or six months out of the ground. LATTUE (Lactuca sativa). - Two main breeds are grown: head lettuces (Lactuca capitata) and romaine lettuces (Lactuca romana). Lettuces. - These are divided into head, spring, summer, winter and cutting lettuces. Spring lettuces. - In the first fortnight of October, we sow the variety known as petite noire, on a south-facing bed; when the cotyledons are well developed and the first small leaves begin to appear, we place three rows of bells on the bed, and transplant around thirty plants under each one; then we raise these Lettuces without ever giving them air. But this is not the case for the other varieties, which are sown in the second half of the month: when the plant is well established, as can be seen when it begins to vegetate, we give it a little air by lifting the bells by about Om, 03 on the opposite side to the wind. After a few days, the amount of air is gradually increased, depending on the temperature and to strengthen the plant. The bells should only be lowered when it freezes at 2 or 3 degrees. When the frost becomes more severe, the bells are lined with dry manure, which is increased according to the intensity of the cold. The bells are uncovered as soon as the sun comes out, but first check that the plant is not suffering from frost, because then, instead of uncovering, you'd have to increase the cover and let it thaw gradually. In the first fortnight of November, we plant on beds (under panels or cloches), and from then on, we continue successively until the end of February. In March, we plant in the open ground, in good exposure, always with plants taken from the same bed. Towards the end of February or at the beginning of March, we sow on beds and under panels; and when the plant is strong enough, we transplant it into beds that we have carefully mulched before planting. Varieties. - Crepe or little black. - Gotte. - Georges. - Red-edged. - Bigotte. These varieties are also sown in August and September; they are planted on old beds, topped up with compost, so that they are close to the glass; but only when it freezes are they covered with panels, taking care to give them as much air as possible. They are often kept until December. Summer lettuces. - They are sown from the first days of April through to July, successively every two weeks, so as to have a succession of lettuces throughout the season. Care is the same as above, but because of the time of year, watering must be much more frequent. Varieties. - Blonde de Versailles. - Blonde d'été. - Berlin blond. - Batavia blonde. - Bl. brown. - Maltese. - Turkish. - Imperial. - Green of Genoa. - Big lazy brown - Palatine. - Chartreuse red. - Red with yellow seeds. - Bloody or flagellated. Winter lettuces. - Start sowing in August, and continue until mid-September. In October, they are planted in a bed with good exposure, and are protected from heavy frost and snow by covering with litter, which is removed whenever the weather permits. Varieties. - Passion. - Morine. - Winter brown. Cutting lettuces. - You can easily have them almost all year round, starting with bedding in January and February, then in the open ground from March successively until November. Varieties. - Pinch. - Chicory. - Spinach. Romaine lettuces. - Several varieties are grown which, like head lettuces, can be classified as spring, summer and winter Romaine. Spring Romaine. - In the first fortnight of October, we sow the early green Romaine, and in the second, the blond and grey Romaines maraîchère; we treat the plant like that of the head lettuces grown at that time; only, in the course of November, we raise the plant of the green Romaines to replant it immediately; but then we only place twelve or fifteen per bell. Towards the end of December or the beginning of January, we start planting under panels or cloches, and from then on we continue successively until the end of February; in March, we plant in the open ground, with good exposure. Summer Romaine. - They are grown in exactly the same way as summer lettuces, with the only difference being that varieties that do not cover themselves are tied with one or two straw ties to make them blanch. This operation should only be carried out when the weather is dry, and the leaves should not be allowed to get wet when watering. Varieties. - Alphange, - blonde de Brunoy, - Monstrueuse. - Panachée. - Golden. - Oak-leaved. Winter Romaine. - They are treated like winter Lettuces, and when sowing at this time of year, preference is generally given to the red winter Romaine, a very hardy variety that withstands frost the best. Lettuce and Romaine seeds ripen in August, and keep well for five years. LENTILLES (Ervum lens). - This plant is grown more in open fields than in gardens; it is weeded into rays in March and April. In dry, sandy soil, it produces much more than in greasy, damp soil, because it vegetates a lot, but produces very few seeds. The Gallardon variety is generally preferred. Lentil seeds germinate in three years. HOLLAND MACHE (Valerianella olitoria). - It likes soft, well-smoked soil. Sowing begins in August and continues until the end of October. It is sown broadcast, and after harrowing with a fork, lightly covered with a rake, and watered if the weather is dry. If sown in October, it will do well in spring. There is a new variety of Lamb's lettuce with variegated leaves, which can be grown in exactly the same way. Italian or Regency Lamb's lettuce. - This is a broader-leafed but later variety, often sown among the Dutch variety to extend the sowing period. Lamb's lettuce seeds are good for harvesting in June, and keep for four or five years. Corn (Zea maïs). - In the garden, Corn is particularly cultivated for its young ears, which can be pickled in vinegar like gherkins, or eaten boiled like potatoes. We sow it in May in the open ground, or in April on a bed, and then transplant it Om, 60 cm apart. As the plants gain strength, they are ridged, and the buds at the base are cut off. Corn seeds germinate in two years. Varieties. - Early white. - Quarantain, - for chickens. - Sweet. MELONS (Cucumis Melo). - The cultivation of melons, on which many treatises have already appeared, rarely written by practitioners, could not be easier; however, in our countries it requires assiduous and intelligent care, especially for those in the first season: Good cultivation has such an influence on the quality of the fruit that, despite being grown in far less favorable conditions, our Cantaloupe melons are usually superior in quality to those grown in southern regions, where they are sown in open fields and left to their own devices. They can be grown in three ways: under panels, under cloches or in the open ground. Panel-grown melons. - Only Cantaloup Prescott fond blanc and its varieties are grown under panels. The first melons are sown in the early days of January, but in ordinary cultivation, they are only sown in the early days of February. A layer about Om, 75 thick is prepared, made up of half new manure, half annealed manure. This is filled with Om, 10 of potting soil, so that the seedling is not far from the glass. Surround the trunk with a good manure stove, and when the heat of the layer is favorable (25 to 30 degrees), trace out rays, sow seeds, which are lightly covered; keep the panels covered with straw mats for two or three days, until the seeds have risen; then uncover every day, taking care to cover before dark. A few days after the seeds have emerged, we start to give a little air through the top of the panels whenever the weather permits, in order to strengthen the plant. When the cotyledons are well developed, we prepare another layer, of the same thickness as the previous one, but whose length should be proportional to the number of plants we want to transplant; then we load it with potting soil. The boxes are placed, the potting soil spread evenly, and when the layer is warm enough, the most vigorous seedling is chosen and transplanted with the finger, as you would with a planter. We usually make ten rows per trunk, and transplant our Melons at Om, 12 apart on the line, taking care to press them down to the cotyledons; or we press Om, 08 diameter pots onto the bed; These are filled with good soft soil mixed with loam, lightly treaded, and when the heat is favorable, a melon plant is transplanted into each pot (1); in this case as in the other, the panels are kept covered with straw mats for three or four days, to make it easier for the plant to grow. (1) These two transplanting methods are still used in market gardening. However, many market gardeners have abandoned pot transplanting, as experience has shown that a melon whose roots are twisted (which necessarily happens to pot-transplanted plants if planting is delayed by a few days) should vegetate less vigorously than one transplanted on a bed, and whose roots have not been hindered in their development. the plant's recovery, after which it is uncovered every day and given a little air when the sun comes out. First pruning. - When the primitive stem has three or four leaves, it is cut above the second leaf (fig. Il); then the cotyledons are removed, lest the humidity rot these organs and spoil the stem. In the second half of February, layers of Om, 60 thick and Im, 33 wide, made up of new manure, tree leaves and grape marc; or new manure and a third of manure from old layers, are prepared. We load them with about Om, 15 of good vegetable garden soil mixed with loam; we place the trunks, and after spreading the soil well in the trunks, we place the panels, fill the paths halfway, and, when the layer has thrown its first fire, we plant two feet of Melon under each panel. Before planting, we make a row of holes in the middle of the bed; then, if we've transplanted onto the bed, we lift the plants with a good clod, and plant a melon plant in each hole, taking care to press it in up to the first leaves. If you've transplanted into a pot, carefully remove the plant from the pot. To do this, take the pot with your right hand, place your left hand on the surface of the soil, so that the stem is between two fingers. Turn the pot upside down, tap lightly on the edge of the trunk, and when the rootball is out of the pot, plant the melon as described. Immediately after planting, water the root ball a little; when the sun is shining, shade the panels with a little bedding, and for a few days refrain from letting in air. A few days after planting, we surround the trunks with a good manure stove, and finish filling in the paths. During the night and in bad weather, we cover the panels with mats, then give air whenever the temperature permits. Second pruning. - The first pruning, i.e. the pinching of the primitive stem, having determined the development of two lateral branches, we direct one towards the top of the trunk and the other towards the bottom; and when they Fig. 12. - Melon, second pruning. are about Om, 33 in length, we prune them above the third or fourth leaf (fig. 12), depending on the vigor of the plants. At this point, and before any new branches develop, spread a good mulch of half-consumed manure over the entire layer. Third pruning. - The second pruning determines the development of three or four branches on each side branch. While they are growing, they are directed so that they do not cross each other; and when they are about Om, 33 in length, they are pruned above the third leaf (fig. 13), without taking into account the flowers, which are removed, because the first flowers of the melon are usually male flowers, called false flowers; if by chance there are some female flowers called meshes, we also remove the branches where they are, because then the plants are not yet strong enough, and the fruits would be much inferior to those obtained later. After the third pruning, we carefully monitor the development of the new branches; and when we have young knotted fruits, we choose the best one; we pinch the branch that bears it two eyes above the fruit, which we secure with the surrounding leaves, so as to& E Fig. 13. - Melon, third pruning, so that it is not affected by the direct rays of the sun, which would harden it; then immediately remove all the other fruit on each plant, to encourage the development of the one left, and pinch off all the other branches above the second leaf (fig. 13). As it sometimes happens that the young fruit does not have a regular shape, or that it elongates too much, in this case it is removed, and another mesh is chosen. Finally, when the fruit has just about reached its full size, if the plants are vigorous, a second fruit is selected from among the newly-knotted ones on each plant, but always under the same conditions as for the first, after which all the others are removed, making one or two melons on each plant. Other care is limited to cutting off all new branches above their first leaves, and removing the tips of any branches that may have grown out of the trunk. For all operations requiring removal of the panels, choose the time of day when the temperature is mildest, so that the cold does not seize the Melons, which are excessively tender. When watering becomes necessary, use the apple watering can; but at this time, the water used must be at the same temperature as the atmosphere in which it is poured, so as not to delay vegetation. If melons are growing very vigorously, it's a good idea not to water them, or to give them very little water, until they have knotted fruit, because the more vigorous they are, the less likely they are to bear fruit. Every day, when the sun is shining, give the panels some air, taking care to lift them away from the wind. As far as possible, you shouldn't get them used to being shaded; it's better to give them more air as the sun gets stronger. Indeed, once you've started, you need to keep going, and with great precision, because often it only takes a ray of sunlight to burn the leaves. We continue to cover the panels every night; and from the time of planting, we must maintain the stoves at the height of the panels and reshape them every month or so, adding at least half as much new manure each time, in order to maintain the warmth of the layer; but we must not reshape the stoves to their full depth once the Melons are growing vigorously, as they have roots that crawl almost to the surface of the soil; and as they develop rapidly9. This is why it's important to refrain from any operation that might stop their development. With this treatment, first-season fruits begin to ripen in the first fortnight of April, and those sown in February produce in May (1). Early melons are among the plants that benefit from thermosiphon heating, as one of the most unfavorable conditions for this crop is the absence of sunshine, which often occurs in January and February; and since, despite the rigorous temperature, it is necessary to baste the melons, because of the heat of the layer, it often happens that the atmosphere of the frame is loaded with moisture and that numerous droplets of water form on all the interior surface of the panels; now, if the temperature does not make it possible to give air, this excess of moisture causes the flowers to drop. This is where the beneficial effect of the thermosiphon can be appreciated. As you can adjust this heating at will, you (1) A fact that's quite important to know is the precise point at which melons ripen. On this subject, we'd like to say that it's not always essential to wait for a melon to reach full ripeness before harvesting it; it's enough for it to be struck, i.e. to begin to change color or hue; when it has reached this point, it can be picked and placed in a cool place, where it will finish ripening without losing any of its quality; in this way, the harvest can easily be prolonged. Although it's not always easy to tell when a melon is ripe, we'd say that it's ready to be eaten when it takes on a yellow color, which becomes quite intense in light-colored varieties; when the tail becomes encircled at its point of insertion, as if it were about to detach; and finally when the fruit gives off a pleasant odor, and when, by gently squeezing the umbilicus (the point opposite the tail), you feel it flex under your finger. Thin-peeled varieties are the easiest to distinguish, while Cantaloupes are more uncertain. can give air whenever it's needed. In this way, care is exactly the same as above, except that the layer is much thinner, and the pipes of the machine are run underneath. A second season of melons is sown in the second half of February. At the time when these melons are ready to be planted, the temperature starts to become more favorable, so the layers are not as thick, and the reheaters do not need to be repeated as often. A fortnight after transplanting, we choose a site with good exposure to the south, but where we haven't grown melons the previous year; for this crop to be a complete success, we mustn't plant two years in a row on the same plot. A first trench is made, one metre wide and Om, 33 deep; the soil is deposited at the end of the square, i.e. where the last trench is to be made; then a good layer is prepared, about Om, 66 thick, made up, as for first-season Melons, of manure, leaves or grape marc. Then open a trench Om, 66 from the first, and with soil, if it's not too compact, load the Om, 15 layer; make a layer in the second, and so on to the end of the square, where you'll find the soil from the first trench to load the last layer. After that, we plow the paths, place the chests, spread the soil inside the chests, lay the panels, then surround the chests with a good manure stove, and fill the paths. When the layer is warm enough, plant two melon plants under each panel and give them the same care as first-season melons. Melon under cloches. - For planting under cloches, you can still sow Prescott cantaloupe melons, but many gardeners prefer embroidered melons, which fruit much better. Towards the end of March or the beginning of April, sow in beds and under panels, taking care to observe all that has been indicated for the education of the first-season plant. Some time before planting, we make a trench Om, 65 wide by Om, 40 deep, then prepare a layer about Om, 75 thick. This is lightly crowned in the middle, and covered with a bed of good soil mixed with loam. When the layer is warm enough, plant the melons in a row, Om, 66 apart. Immediately after planting, each Melon is covered with a bell, which is wrapped in litter for two or three days, to encourage the young plant to take root; during the night, the bells are covered with straw mats. As soon as the melons start to vegetate, the cloches are lifted during the day to give them a little air, then gradually increased until the time comes to remove them, which takes place when they can no longer hold the branches, but which should only be done in fine weather, as it would be better to delay this operation than to remove them in wet weather. From the above-mentioned time to Midsummer's Day (June 20-25), you can successively plant several seasons of Melons sous cloches. Plant training, pruning and other care are all the same as for melons grown under panels. Melons grown on mounds. - We will now describe a simple and inexpensive method recently indicated by M. Loisel. In May, cone-shaped mounds of half-consumed manure, leaves or moss are raised on the ground. They should be about Om 50 or Om 60 in diameter at the base, Om 60 in height, and set about I meter apart. The manures should be prepared in the same way as for the other layers, i.e. they should be mixed well, and wetted if too dry; then, as they are used, they should be trodden down so that the mounds are compacted as little as possible; and, whatever the nature of the substances used to build these mounds, they should be covered with about Om, 15 of good soil, prepared as previously indicated. At the top of each mound, make a small hole of about Om, 10 and sow three or four seeds in each one, leaving only the two most vigorous plants, or, even better, plant them high up. In both cases, they should be immediately covered with a bell, which should be removed when it can no longer contain the branches. For the care to be given and the first pruning, we refer you to what was said about Melons under frame. Before removing the bells, lightly hoe the mounds, taking care to preserve their rounded shape, as well as the surrounding soil, then cover them completely with a mulch of manure, which can be spread about 1 m around. This cover has the advantage of keeping the watering fresh. Visit the mounds from time to time. The care to be given consists in pulling down any branches that are going in the wrong direction, pulling out weeds as they appear, and when the branches have reached about the middle of the mound, pinching off the ends. This operation will give rise to new branches, which will soon be loaded with flowers and fruit; and as they quickly reach the bottom of the mound, all the ends should be cut off one last time, when they begin to crawl along the ground. Once you've reached this point, all you need to do is water them as needed, and place a tile or a piece of plank under each fruit when it's about half its size. In addition to saving money, these mounds offer the advantage of being more easily penetrated by the sun's rays, which is an important point in crops of this kind. On the other hand, the inclination of the branches is so favorable to fruiting, that each mound can easily produce 10 or 12 good Melons in the course of the summer; the first ones usually begin to ripen in the second half of July, and continue to give fruit until September. Melons are divided into three breeds, whose best varieties we will describe below: Melons brodés. - Maraîcher. - Sucrin de Tour. - S. with white flesh. - Ananas d'Amérique, - d'Arkangel, - de Grammont. - de Honfleur, - de Cavaillon. Cantaloupe melons. - Orange. - Noir des Carmes, - de VingtHuit Jours. - Prescott white background, - Pr. grey background. - Galeux green background, - de Portugal. - Holland black. Smooth-peel melons. - Maltese, - M. red-fleshed. - Winter, - Persian (1). Watermelons (Cucurbita Citrullus). - They are grown in the same way as bell melons, with the difference that (1) These melons, stored in a dry place, can be kept unaltered until January, and sometimes longer. The germination period of melon seeds is five years. NAVET (Brassio Napus). - Turnips do well in all types of soil, but prefer soft, sandy soil; only in this type of soil do they acquire good quality. They are broadcast sown from May to the beginning of September, whenever possible in wet weather. When the plant is strong enough, it is lighted more or less, depending on the size of the variety. Those intended for winter consumption should be sown in July and August. As cold weather approaches, we pull them up and cut off the tops, so that they don't grow back; then we gauge them and cover them with straw during the frosts; in this way, we can keep them until April. A large number of varieties are grown, divided into tender, semi-tender and dry turnips; for the first and last sowings, it's the tender ones that should be chosen, as they are the earliest. Turnip seeds ripen in June, and keep well for five years. Tender turnips. - Des Vertus. - Early flat white. - Early flat red. - Snowball. Semi-tender turnips. - Holland yellow. - Scottish yellow. - Malta yellow. - J. of Finland. - Rose du Palatinat. - Rond de Croissy. - Gris de Morigny. Turnip sces. - De Freneuse, - de Meaux, - de Berlin petit. - Long yellow. ONION (Allium cepa). - Onions like soft, substantial soil, smoked from the previous year; they are broadcast in the second half of January, if the weather is favorable, or even better in February and March in strong soils. After sowing, the ground is harrowed and trodden; in light soils, the soil should even be firmed up before sowing; then the seeds are raked and covered with a light layer of compost. If the weather is dry, water from time to time, to encourage germination; then, when the seeds have sprouted, thin out where the plant is too thick, and transplant in places where it is lacking. During their growth, onions require no care other than hoeing and watering, which should be stopped as soon as they begin to turn. Quite often, when they have reached their full size, the tops are cut off with the back of a rake, to stop the flow of sap to the onion. Onions are harvested towards the end of August or the beginning of September; after being pulled, they are left on the ground for two weeks to ripen, after which they are placed in an attic. If you take care to spread them out and remove anything that could cause rot, you can keep them until the end of May. Varieties. - Dark red. - Pale red. - Vertus yellow. - Spanish soufflé. - Pyriform, - Madeira. They can also be sown in August: in this way, onions are even produced two months earlier, but many often go to seed in spring. White onion. - Sow in nurseries and broadcast in the first fortnight of August, for transplanting in October, and towards the end of the same month for transplanting in March. In October in light soils, and in March in heavy soils, we prepare the ground for planting the white onion. Mark out 10 or 12 rows per bed, Im, 33 wide, and transplant the onions Om, 10 apart along the line. In harsh winters, it's a good idea to cover the plant with bedding. White onions can be harvested towards the end of April or the beginning of May. If, due to unforeseen circumstances, there is a shortage of plants or the quantity is insufficient, they can be sown in January or February on beds and under panels; they can also be sown in the open ground in February and March; these onions will produce much earlier than other varieties sown at the same time. Varieties. - Early white onion. - Large white onion, Egyptian onion or Rocambole. - It differs from the others in that it bears bulblets on its stem, which serve to multiply it. They are planted in March, at Om, 12 from each other, and each of these bulblets produces a good, large onion, which is pulled off when the leaves turn yellow; they are placed in a very dry place to be used for consumption, taking care to reserve the necessary number for planting, which must take place in the following March. Each of these onions grows up the stem, producing bulblets which are kept for replanting at the time indicated above. Onion Potato. - It is planted in February or earlier, weather permitting, at Om, 30 or Om, 40 apart; during its vegetation, it is ridged several times, to encourage the development of the bulbs which grow around the mother Onion. Onion seeds are harvested in August, and keep for two years. GARLIC (Rumex acetosa). - This plant is propagated in the spring by splitting plants or sowing seeds, which are sown in rays from March to July. After sowing, cover the seeds with a light layer of potting soil, and water frequently: it's usually used as a border plant, but to make sure you don't run out of it in summer, it should also be grown in beds, with copious watering during drought. The last crop is harvested towards the end of October, after which it is hoeed and a good mulch of half-consumed manure is spread over each bed, or, at the same time, the sorrel clumps are lifted to make them more manageable for winter heating. For this purpose, prepare a layer of Om, 35 to Om, 40 thick, with a heat of 10 to 12 degrees; place the boxes, and load the layer of Om, 15 to Om, 20 with potting soil; then plant 10 to 12 rows of sorrel per box. During frosts, we cover the panels with straw mats; we give air as often as possible. You can also force sorrel into place. To do this, place boxes on the boards, then panels. The paths around the chests are dug out, and a dung stove is raised and remodeled from time to time. We start heating sorrel towards the end of November or the beginning of December, and can continue successively until the end of February. Sorrel seeds ripen in July, and keep for two years. Varieties. - Vierge, - de Belleville, - de Frévent. Sorrel Spinach. - Garden Patience, Rumex Patientia, is grown under this name. This plant has large, elongated leaves; its flavor is milder than that of sorrel, and it multiplies easily, either from seeds sown in spring, in the field or in a nursery, to be transplanted, or by sprouting. Place them about 1 m apart. Patience seeds germinate for three years. OXALIS CRENELÉE (Oxalis crenata). - This plant is very easy to propagate and grow; it produces a large number of small tubers, but the flavor is generally not very appealing. The leaves and tops of the shoots can be eaten like spinach. It is propagated by tubers or cuttings, which are planted in April and May, 1 metre apart; as soon as they have grown about Om, 12, we begin to: butter them in the center, to force each shoot to take a horizontal direction; then, as they lengthen, we successively load them with soil until September, when the tubers begin to form. As frost approaches, a layer of manure or leaves is spread on the ground, so that harvesting doesn't take place until as late as possible, as the tubers grow until quite late in the season. PANAIS (Pastinaca sativa). - They need deep, substantial soil. They can be grown in the same way as carrots, but they need to be thinned out more, as the tops are much wider. They can be left in the ground over winter, as they have no fear of frost. Parsnips ripen towards the end of August and are good for only one year. Varieties. - Long parsnip. - Round parsnip. SWEET PATATO (Convolvulus Batatas). - Sweet potatoes are grown on beds and under frames, or on bare beds and in the open ground. They are propagated from seed, which is sown in March on a bed and under a frame; but as they are rarely harvested, they are most often propagated in the following way: in the early days of January, a few of the best-preserved tubers are selected; they are placed on a warm bed and covered with a frame, over which straw mats are spread overnight; shortly afterwards, they begin to grow. They are then covered with Om, 05 or Om, 06 light soil, and at planting time, the seedling is detached from the mother tuber and planted immediately in place; or, if you want to have seedlings that are easier to take up, the young shoots are removed as they reach Om, 06 or Om, 08 in length, and transplanted into pots of around Om, 06 which are buried on a bed; When the cuttings have taken root, which happens fairly quickly, we start to lift the bell a little, and gradually increase the pressure to remove it completely when they can stand the air without wilting. 1. Potatoes on beds and under frames. - In the first fortnight of February, prepare a layer of Om, 60 to Om, 70 thick, half manure and half leaves. The height of the layer should be calculated so that after it has been loaded with about Om, 25 of good soil mixed with loam, the whole is no more than Om, 10 from the glass. After placing the boxes, the panels are laid, and when the warmth of the layer is favorable, the Potatoes are planted in two rows and Om,60 apart on the line. When planting them, care must be taken to spread the roots well; for if they were contorted, this would essentially harm tuber production. During the night, the panels are covered with straw mats, then the stoves are rearranged from time to time, to maintain the heat of the layer; the soil is basked if necessary, and air is given whenever the weather permits. As the tubers grow, they often emerge from the ground, and care must be taken to cover them with a few centimetres of earth. Potatoes treated in this way can be harvested in May or June at the latest; the larger ones are removed, and if the roots are carefully covered, they will continue to vegetate until autumn. Watering should be suspended in September, so as not to prolong vegetation, which would be essentially detrimental to tuber maturity. 2. Potatoes on a deaf layer. - In the course of April, prepare a deaf layer about 1 m wide and Om, 50 thick; cover with Om, 20 to Om, 25 of good, light, substantial soil, and towards the end of April or beginning of May, plant the potatoes in a row and Om, 65 apart; After a few days, you begin to give them air, lifting the bells during the day, and removing them when they can no longer hold the branches. During vegetation, care is limited to watering whenever necessary. Towards the end of August or the beginning of September, tubers are ready to be eaten, but it's only in October that the harvest is complete. This must be done with great care, as potatoes that are broken or crumpled rot quickly. 3. Potatoes in the ground. - In May, make holes from Om,60 to Om, 60, Om, 50 wide and Om, 35 to Om, 40 deep; fill the bottom with manure, cover with about Om, 20 of light, substantial soil, and plant three Potatoes in each hole, arranging them so that they are about Om, 8 apart. Water, cover with a bell, and shade as needed. In light, healthy soils, in the Paris climate, potatoes can be grown simply in the ground, on mounds 0.80 m high, or on planks about 1 m wide, with a ridge in the middle, on the crest of which a row of potatoes is planted. After planting, they are protected from the sun's scorching rays until they recover perfectly, after which all care consists of watering them as needed. 4. Preserving potatoes. - The simplest way to preserve potatoes is to store them in a dry place where the temperature, being as even as possible, does not fall below 12 degrees. In this way, potatoes can easily be kept unaltered until February and March. Potatoes can also be preserved in situ, as M. Souchet, gardener at the Château de Fontainebleau, does, by covering them with glass panels and doormats, so as to prevent the cold from penetrating under the panels. Varieties. - White - Yellow - Yellow - Malaga pink - Violet. PERCE-PIERRE. Sea fennel (Crithmum maritimum). - We sow it as soon as the seeds are ripe or in March, on a bed, to transplant it at the foot of a wall, facing south or east; we cover it with litter during the winter, because it is delicate and sensitive to frosts. Perce-pierre seed retains its germinative quality for only one year. PARSLEY (Petroselinum sativum). - It is sown in rays from February to May and June, and to avoid running out in winter, it should be covered with leaves or litter as soon as the frosts approach. Finally, in January or February, you can sow on the ground, but under panels; in this way, you'll have young Parsley in the second half of March. Parsley seeds ripen in August, and keep for three years. Varieties. - Curly. - Very curly dwarf with large root. PEPPER (Capsicum annuum). - Sow in a bed in February or March, in April in an earthen bed, and plant out at the end of April or beginning of May in the open ground, in good exposure. Pimento seeds germinate for four years. Varieties: -Long,-round,-Chile,-Spanish sweet,-Tomato. PRIPRENELLE (PETITE) (Poterium Sanquisora). - Sown in spring or autumn, it is usually used for borders, which are extremely hardy. Pimprenelle seeds ripen in September, and keep for two years. DANDELION. Lion's tooth (Taraxacum dens leonis). - This plant is not widely cultivated, as it is found in abundance in meadows; however, when dandelions are sown in spring, they are more beautiful and of better quality, especially if the seeds are harvested from the individuals with the broadest leaves. In addition to the salad they produce towards the end of winter, they can be blanched in autumn. Simply cover them with Om, 12 to Om, 15 of well-consumed compost, and as soon as they begin to break through the layer of compost, cut them off at the root collar. Dandelion seeds germinate for two years. PEAR (Allium Porrum). - Leeks are sown at the end of December or beginning of January, on beds and under panels; at the end of February or beginning of March, the plant is transplanted into the ground and broadcast; at the end of April, i.e. when the plant is strong enough, eight or ten rows are laid out in beds 1m, 33 wide, and the leek is transplanted at Om, 15 apart on the line. We pull out the plant needed for planting by thinning out the seedling, and we start to eat the plants left in place, which gives the new ones time to form. It can also be sown in July and transplanted at the beginning of September; then, in the second half of September, a final sowing is carried out, and, as always, the seed is broadcast, but very lightly, as it is not then transplanted. This leek is good for harvesting in June. Leek seeds are good for harvesting in August, and keep for only two years. Varieties. - Short, - long, - monstrous from Rouen, - yellow from Poitou. BLONDE PEAR (Beta vulgaris). - It is dried in rays, from May to August; and to keep the leaves 169 tender, they must be cut often and watered frequently during the drought. To make sure you don't run out of leaves in winter, as soon as the frosts are approaching, you can lift the roots and plant them on a bed; or you can place boxes and panels on boards laid out for this purpose. Lift the soil from the paths, then surround the boxes with a stove made of old manure, and give them air as often as possible. Poirée blonde can be eaten as spinach if required. Poirée à cardes. - Sow in nurseries in May and June. When the plant is strong enough, it is transplanted immediately. Three rows per bed, 1m 33 wide, are planted out at Om, 50 apart along the line. During drought, water abundantly to ensure large, tender chard. During frosts, we cover them with litter, and only in spring do we start to harvest them. Poirée seeds ripen in September, and keep well for five or six years. Varieties. - White chard. - Red chard. - Yellow chard. - From Chile. The most remarkable of all chard pears for the development and rich coloration of its ribs. PEAS (Pisum sativum). - At the beginning of November, we sow the first Peas on the ground, but under panels, to transplant the plant also under panels. In the course of December, the boxes for planting are placed, and a good spade-head is removed from each one, so as to have Om, 45 to Om, 50 deep under the panels; the soil is deposited in the paths, which serve to support the boxes; after which the ground is levelled, the rake passed, and four rays about Om,08 deep are traced in 10 each trunk, taking care to space them equally, but in such a way as to leave more space towards the bottom of the trunk, which is naturally the wettest part. Once the site has been prepared, and as soon as the plant is Om, 08 or Om, 10 high, it is lifted, so as not to break the roots by pulling it out, then it is transplanted by 3 or 4 together and about Om 20 apart on the line. When the Peas are Om, 20 to Om25 high, all the stems are laid down towards the top of the trunk; and to keep them in this position, they are covered with a little earth. A few days later, the ends of the stems rise and continue to grow; they soon flower; then we pinch all the stems above the third or fourth flower, to make them bear fruit more quickly. During the night, we cover the panels with straw mats; we give air whenever the temperature allows it, and we make some basins, which must take place with a lot of care, in order not to determine a too vigorous vegetation, which would essentially harm the harvest. When you have a good coastline and are short of panels, you can sow peas under cloches towards the end of January and during February; then, depending on the temperature, you transplant them into slightly deep rays; then you cover them with litter during bad weather. These peas bear fruit after those grown under panels, but much earlier than Peas.

Rays are planted slightly deep and at Om, 25 from each other. After sowing, cover the peas with a few centimeters of compost, and when they are Om, 15 or Om, 20 high, hoe them and fill in the rays.
