California ZAUSCHNÈRIA (Zauschneria Californica). - A charming little plant with scarlet-red flowers, propagated from cuttings or seeds sown in July in a nursery. The young plant is overwintered in a greenhouse, and in spring planted out in groups like Verbena and Petunia. SECTION IV - Greenhouse plants that can be grown in the open ground during the summer. For general care of summer-grown greenhouse plants, see page 91. ALTERNANTHERA SPATULATA - Herbaceous, bushy plant; height Om, 10 to Om, 15, spatula-shaped leaves, light green irregularly variegated with pink, salmon and yellow. Treated like Coleus, this charming plant can be used for exactly the same purposes. BEGONIA. - Grown outdoors in summer, Begonias produce a charming effect, with their beautiful leaves and abundant, long-lasting flowers. They can be planted in the second half of May, in heather soil, in rows or in beds. They can be propagated by taking cuttings and overwintering them in a warm greenhouse. Varieties - Fuchsioides, - Ingrami, - Lucida, - Prestoniensis. CALADIUM ESCULENTUM. - Although this is a hot-greenhouse plant, it can be grown outdoors during the summer. In fact, judging by the way Caladium esculentum develops when grown in the ground, this is the most suitable growing method. Like all vigorous plants, Caladium esculentum require good fertilization and copious watering during hot spells. They can be planted in the second half of May, singly or in clumps, then lifted as frost approaches to overwinter in a warm greenhouse. woody calceolaria. - Much hardier than herbaceous Calceolaria, woody Calceolaria can be grown in the open ground throughout the summer. The beautiful yellow flowers of these plants produce a charming effect in the center of a bed of red Geranium or blue-flowered Lobelia erinus. Woody Calceolaria can be propagated from cuttings taken under cloches in August and September, and overwintered in a greenhouse. These cuttings are good for planting out in May (1). CANNA INDICA. - This plant, most remarkable for its .(1) Herbaceous calceolaria. - Herbaceous Calceolaria are sown in August and September in light soil, made up of heather soil, loam and potting compost, under a frame in a shady spot. When the plant has three or four leaves, it is transplanted into small pots, which are then placed under a frame to overwinter. In February or March, Calceolaria seedlings are given larger pots, after which they can be placed in the temperate greenhouse to enjoy the beauty of their flowers. Calceolaria, with its leaves as well as its flowers, can be grown in the open ground during the summer. With warmth, water and fertilizer, Canna's vigor surpasses anything our climate allows us to hope for. To obtain Canna similar to those seen every year in the squares of Paris, they need to be bedded out in the second half of March. When the suckers are about Om, 10 in length, we detach them with a portion of tuber, then plant them in pots which we keep on bedding until May, when we can put the Canna in the ground. After enjoying the beauty of this plant throughout the summer, it is lifted as frost approaches, to be stored in a dry cellar, or on the tier of a temperate greenhouse, just like the Dahlias. Varieties that don't produce tubers should be pulled out and placed in pots to overwinter in a warm greenhouse. Canna can be propagated from suckers, as described above, or from seed, which is sown on a bed in spring. Varieties. - Annei, - Discolor, Edulis, - Gigantea, - Indica, - Indica superba, - Leptophylla, - Liliiflora, - Lutea, - Peruviana, - Zebrina, - Warscewezii. CASSIA - Cassia are beautiful shrubs with yellow flowers in corymbs, which can be placed on lawns in summer. When young, they produce little effect, but as they vegetate vigorously when grown in the ground, medium-sized specimens can be planted if strong specimens are lacking. They are planted in May, then lifted as frost approaches, to be stored in the orangery until the following spring. Varieties. - Floribunda, - Corymbosa, - Tomentosa. CHAMÆROPS HUMILIS (Dwarf Palm). - Despite this plant's well-known hardiness, in the Paris climate it must be grown in pots. Arranged in groups on lawns, Chamærops humilis produce an entirely new effect in summer, with leaves so different from those of other plants. Chamærops humilis is easy to keep in the orangery in winter. CHEIRANTHUS DELILIANUS - A charming little wallflower with purplish-red, long-lasting flowers that can be grown in the open ground in summer. It can be propagated from cuttings and overwintered in a greenhouse. CHEIRANTHUS MARSHALLI. - Equally recommendable, this plant differs from Cheiranthus Delilianus in the color of its flowers, which are a beautiful yellow; it can be grown in exactly the same way. CHRYSANTHÈME frutescent (Chrysanthemum with white flowers). - This plant, whose flowers bear a slight resemblance to meadow daisies, is particularly well-suited to bedding because of its hardiness and long-lasting blooms. It is propagated from cuttings taken under glass in August and September. Overwintered under glass, frutescent Chrysanthemums can be delivered to the garden in May (1). COLEUS VERSCHAFFELTI. - All Coleus are remar(1) Hybrid Cineraria. - To grow beautiful Cineraria, you need a richly colored leaf, but they are delicate. Only the species named Verschaffelti can be grown in the open ground during the summer, like Lantana, Heliotrope and Salvia. Nothing can give an idea of the beauty of this plant, when it has been properly cared for. Coleus Verschaffelti are propagated by taking cuttings and overwintering them in a warm greenhouse. CUPREA. - Cuphea should, in keeping with their small size, be placed at the edge of beds. Grown in the open ground during the summer, these charming little plants produce flowers until the frosts; they can be propagated from seed or cuttings and overwintered in a greenhouse. Varieties. - Platycentra, - Ignea, - Strigulosa. ERYTHRINA. - Like all plants that vegetate vigorously, Erythrina needs a lot of food to produce beautiful flowers. So, unless the soil is cold and damp, it's better to grow them in the open ground during the summer than to keep them in pots. This shrub is worthy of a place in any garden, thanks to the beauty of its large red flowers. It can be planted singly or in clumps. During winter, it is stored in the orangery, where it remains until spring. Varieties. - Crista galli, - Bellengerii, - Floribunda, - Madame Bellengé. - Marie Bellengé, - Ruberrima. give them a light soil, made up of heather soil, loam and potting soil. Sow in August and September, in a shady frame. Transplanted and repotted at the appropriate time, Cineraria seedlings can be used to decorate greenhouses and apartments in spring. EUCALYPTUS GLOBULUS. - Eucalyptus globulus is a large, beautiful Australian tree that can be grown in the open ground during the summer. Endowed with uncommon vigor, it can reach 5 meters in height in a single year; its leaves, covered with a whitish dust when young, are essentially different from those of our garden trees. Multiplication by seed, sown towards the end of summer, to produce plants suitable for planting the following year. DATURA ARBOREA. - Datura arborea is, if not the first greenhouse plant to be cultivated in the open ground during the summer, at least one of the first; its flowers, often as long as Om, 32, are pendulous, white and very fragrant. In large gardens, beds of Datura arborea can be formed; but everywhere else, it is preferable to grow this beautiful plant on its own. Datura arborea is propagated from cuttings, which are overwintered in the orangery, like the old plants. FUCHSIA. - Grown in the open ground during the summer, Fuchsias produce flowers until the frosts, requiring no care other than watering in proportion to the temperature. They can be propagated from seed or from cuttings, which are grown in greenhouses or under frames. Varieties. - Flowers more or less dark red, or white with red corolla. HELIOTROPES. - For beautiful Heliotropes, grow them in the open ground during the summer. They can be propagated by sowing or, better still, by taking cuttings in layers in January and February. Planted in May, Heliotrope cuttings grow rapidly and produce flowers until the frosts. A few Heliotrope plants overwintered in the greenhouse are enough each year to produce as many cuttings as are needed to fill a garden. Varieties. - From Peru. - Triomphe de Liége, - Gloire des massifs. - Anna Thurell. LANTANA. - Lantana are charming little plants with corymb flowers, first yellow, then red or lilac, which can be used to create delightful beds. Lantana can be propagated from seed or from cuttings taken from the bed in January and February. By giving these cuttings the warmth they need, they can be delivered to the field in the second half of May. Lantana needs light soil, with plenty of fertilizer. Varieties. - Aurantiaca, - Delicatissima. - Mutabilis. LOBELIA RAMOSA. - A border plant with beautiful blue flowers. Grown in the garden in summer, Lobelia ramosa produces flowers until the frosts. It can be propagated from seed or cuttings in August and September. Overwintered in a greenhouse, Lobelia ramosa cuttings can be delivered to the garden in May. MMULUS - The difficulty of preserving Mimulus over winter means that we have to make do with growing them as annuals. Sown in beds in February and March, Mimulus can be delivered to the garden in the second half of May. Grown in light soil mixed with potting mix, 19 Mimulus form large clumps when the ends of the stems are suitably pinched. Varieties. - Variegatus, - Cardinalis. Musk Mimulus is a creeping species with small yellow flowers, which can be grown in the shade, in heathland. NICOTIANA WIGANDIOIDES. - A perennial orangery plant that can be grown in the open ground during the summer, just like Datura. Placed in favorable conditions, Nicotiana wigandioides makes a beautiful ornamental leafy plant that can be propagated from seed or cuttings, NIEREMBERGIA GRACILIS. - Nierembergia gracilis is particularly suitable for making borders, by laying the branches on the ground. Grown in the ground in summer, it produces flowers until the frosts. It can be propagated by sowing or, better still, by taking cuttings and overwintering them in a greenhouse. Much more vigorous, Nierembergia frutescent deserves preference in every respect. PELARGONIUM ZONALE. - Much better known under the name of Geranium than Pelargonium, this plant is now one of the most beautiful additions to our gardens. Just as commendable for its hardiness as for the brilliance, abundance and long life of its flowers, Geranium zonale is particularly suitable for vases and beds. It can be propagated from seed or, better still, from cuttings taken under cloches in August and September. Geranium zonale are winter-harvested in greenhouses or under frames, and can be delivered to the garden in May. As they develop rapidly, it is much simpler to plant young Geraniums each year than to keep the old plants. Varieties. - Red, pink or white flowers, or red with white variegated leaves. The species known as Ivy-leaved Geranium can be grown as a summer border plant. PETUNIA. - Having long since recognized that it is much simpler to grow Petunia as annuals than to keep the old plants, they are now sown in March on beds, then transplanted as soon as the planting is sufficiently advanced, or sown in April, immediately in place. For double-flowered varieties that you want to keep, take cuttings in August and September, and overwinter them under glass. Grown in the open ground during the summer, Petunias produce flowers right up to the frosts. Of all the plants used to decorate gardens, none are better suited than Petunias for lining vases and beds, or making borders by laying branches on the ground (1), SALVIA SPLENDENS. - Although the flowers of this beautiful plant appear a little late, its cultivation should not be neglected, for when delivered to the open ground in June, it produces long spikes throughout the autumn (1) PRIMULA Sinensis. - Primula Sinensis is one of the most suitable plants for decorating greenhouses and apartments during the winter. Sow in March and April in a greenhouse, then transplant into pots. It requires heather soil mixed with a quarter of potting compost. red flowers, of such brilliance that it is impossible to fix them for long. Salvia splendens can be propagated by sowing or, better still, by taking cuttings on a bed in March and April. A few plants of Salvia splendens, overwintered in a warm greenhouse, are enough each year to produce as many cuttings as are needed to fill a garden. SOLANUM. - From an ornamental point of view, Solanum plants are of immense interest. Grown in the open ground during the summer, certain species produce a remarkable effect with their beautiful leaves. They can be used to form clumps; however, it is preferable to place them singly on lawns. Solanum can be propagated from seed or cuttings, and overwintered in a warm greenhouse. Varieties. - Atropurpureum, - Betaceum, - Callicarqum, - Marginatum, - Purpureum, - Pyracanthum, - Robustum. SENECIO CINÉRARIA (Cineraria maritima). - Rough plant with pinnate leaves covered, like the stems, with a tamentous down. Arranged in rows around beds of Coleus or any other brightly-colored plant, Cineraria maritima produces a charming effect; it can overwinter outdoors if necessary, but it's best to take cuttings every year to replace old plants that grow too large. Centaurea candidissima can be used in the same circumstances; it is even whiter than Cineraria maritime, only less hardy. STATICE LATIFOLIA. - This perennial, with radical leaves and branching stems, forms a paniculate corymb; blue flowers from July to September. Propagates from seed in June and July. Although hardy, Statice latifolia should be grown in pots and overwintered in a greenhouse. TAGETES LUCIDA. - The flowers of this plant are a beautiful yellow. They are small, but very numerous and long-lasting. If required, Tagetes lucida can replace woody Calceolaria in the composition of beds where yellow flowers are desired. It can be propagated from seed or cuttings and overwintered in a greenhouse. TRADESCANTIA zebrina. - Creeping plant, suitable for lining the surface of beds dedicated to the cultivation of greenhouse plants during the summer. The exceptional conditions in which Tradescantia zebrina thrives add to the interest of this charming plant, already remarkable for the beauty of its leaves. Tradescantia zebrina is propagated from cuttings and overwintered in a warm greenhouse. hybrid Verbena. - The seeds from these charming little plants produce a considerable number of varieties of all shades every year. Sown in February and March, hybrid Verbena plants can be transplanted into pots, or planted out immediately, like all annuals sown in spring. Despite the simplicity of this method of cultivation, Verbena cuttings are most often propagated in August and September; overwintered in frames, Verbena cuttings are good for putting in the ground in April and May. The brilliance, freshness and long life of Verbena flowers make these plants particularly recommended for making up beds or borders by laying the branches on the ground. woody veronicas. - Woody Veronica is not to be confused with perennial Veronica, whose stems die back each year. Arranged in long clusters of red, pink or lilac, the flowers of woody Veronica turn successively white. They can be propagated from seed or from cuttings taken under cloches in August and September. Overwintered under glass, woody Veronica cuttings can be delivered to the garden in May. Varieties. - Andersoni, - Lindleyana, - Splendida. WIGANDIA Caracasana. - Of all the greenhouse plants cultivated for the beauty of their leaves, none is more ornamental than Wigandia Caracasana. It is propagated from seed or root cuttings in September and October; overwintered in the greenhouse or under glass, Wigandia Caracasana cuttings can be delivered to the field towards the end of May. To obtain the full effect that this beautiful plant can produce, reserve a place for it on lawns and give it a light soil amply supplied with consumed fertilizers. ROSE TREES. - This beautiful genus is very numerous in species, and thanks to remontant varieties, we can now enjoy the beauty of its charming flowers for a good part of the year. Roses like a clean, slightly cool soil, amended from time to time with fertilizer; they can be propagated by seed, offspring, marcots, cuttings and grafts. 1. Sowing. - This method of propagation is only used when new varieties are desired. Seeds are sown as soon as they reach maturity, either in terrines, which are brought in during the winter, or in a bed at sunrise, taking care to cover the seedlings during the frosts. 20. 2 Cuttings. - We remove them in autumn, and put them in gauge to replant them in February or March; they are easy to take up; they don't even need to have many roots; a good heel is often enough. 3. Marcottes. - Softwood species are pruned by incision, in May and June, either in the ground or in pruning pots, and woody species are pruned by vine. (See Marcottes article.) 4. Cuttings. - Almost all species can be propagated with cuttings, but on a bed and smothered. Only the Bengals and the Bourbon Islands can do without this care. Species that are to be raised on stems are propagated mainly by scape grafting, using the long-fruited Rose Hip as the subject, followed by the Four Seasons Rose or the ordinary Bengal for species that have some affinity with the latter, and in cases where only low stems are required. Roses are grafted in July and August, taking care, as indicated in the article on Grafting, to take advantage of the time when the plants are most healthy. As for the choice of species, each person must choose according to his or her taste, and the only recommendation we have to make to people who have roses to graft is that they should always prefer species that can withstand the rigors of our winters without suffering. In addition to grafted Roses, we also grow a large number of free-standing varieties, with which we create charming beds. But as many of them suffer from our winters, to preserve them, you need to butter them as the cold approaches, then cover them with leaves or litter if there are heavy frosts. Finally, in February, when frosts are no longer to be feared, the roses are uncovered and the mounds destroyed. In this way, all the varieties that are usually grown in pots can be brought out into the open. You can easily bring forward the flowering of species such as Quatre-Saisons, du Roi, Bengale ordinaire and some of its varieties. To do this, you need to have roses planted in pots from the previous year; you prune them in autumn, and as early as January you can start to force some of them, either by placing them in a heated greenhouse, always as close as possible to the stained-glass windows, or under a frame; but then you need to dig a good trench around the trunk; then you raise a stove of new manure, 'which you reshuffle more or less often, depending on the season. Cover the frames at night, and give them some air when the sun comes out. All roses grown in the open ground flower in June; later on, those of remontant species flower a second time, but there is necessarily an interruption between the first and second flowerings. To remedy this, simply remove the flower buds from a number of remontant Roses. Stopped for a moment in their development, these Roses soon produce new branches, whose flowers succeed the first Roses. Then comes the second natural flowering, so that by this means you have Roses all through the summer. There's nothing special about growing Roses; all you have to do is prune them in March, more or less short, depending on their vigor, and while they're growing, pinch off the ends of any branches that are growing too vigorously; then carefully remove all the branches that grow from the base or from the stem. White and violet Petunias, or Gladiolus, which also produce a beautiful effect, can be planted at the base of slightly high grafted Roses to garnish the stem. For the same purpose, sow a little dwarf larkspur seed in spring between those grown in beds. Byzantina). - Similar to the above, but a little lower. American black walnut (Juglans nigra). - Very tall, vigorous tree; catkin-shaped flowers in April and May; small, round, very hard-shelled fruit. Varieties. - Ashy. - White. - Ash-leaved. - Heterophyllous. Common elm (Ulmus campestris). - Very tall tree, remarkable for its hardiness; whitish flowers, in scaly clusters, in April. Narrow-leaved elm (U. stricta). - A variety of the preceding; it is used to form very rustic palisades. Varieties. - Broad-leaved, - Variegated, - Weeping, - Pyramidal. American elm (U. Americana). - Taller than the common elm; reddish branches, curving towards the tip. PAULOWNIA IMPERIALIS. - Japanese tree, introduced in 1834; Catalpa-like habit; remarkable vegetation; very large leaves, especially on young specimens; blue flowers in April. To enjoy the full beauty of its foliage, it should be cut back every year, so as to have young branches on which the leaves are always much wider. DOUBLE-FLOWERED PEACH (Amygdalus Persica flore pleno). - An admirable tree during its flowering period, which takes place in March and April; it is grown as a stem or bush. Varieties. - Alba plena, - Rubra plena. - Versicolor, - Flore pleno, - Camelliæflora, - Dianthiflora. POPLAR (Populus). - All Poplars are tall, fast-growing trees; they thrive in damp soils and are suitable for landscaped gardens; the most remarkable are: Varieties. - Nivea. - Angulata, - Balsamifera, - Canadensis, - Pyramidalis, - Grandidentata, - Heterophylla, - Ontariensis,- Tremula, - Molinifera. PLANERA CRENATA, Siberian elm. - Just as hardy as the common elm, with which it is closely related, the Planera crenata has the advantage of never being attacked by insects. LOTUS or Italian PLAQUEMIN (Diospyros lotus). - Height, 8m, 33 to 10 meters; lanceolate, green leaves; greenish, inconspicuous flowers in June and July; yellowish, edible fruit. PLAQUEMINIER de Virginie (D. Virginiana). - Higher than the preceding; good eating fruit. Oriental PLATAN (Platanus orientalis). - Very tall tree with a beautiful habit; palmate leaves; flowers in globular catkins in April and May. PLATANE d'Occident (P. occidentalis). - Same habit as above, only with broader leaves. Varieties. - Maple-leaved. - With laciniate leaves. - Wavy, - Starry. DOUBLE-FLOWERED PEAR (Pyrus communis flore pleno). - Variety of the common pear tree; height, 4 meters; double white flowers in April. Cottony PEAR (P. Polveria). - Height, 5 meters; leaves and twigs covered with white down; white flowers in May. DOUBLE-FLOWERED APPLE (Malus communis flore pleno). - Variety of the common apple tree; 4 meters high, pinkish-white flowers in May. Bacciferous or Siberian APPLE (M. Baccata). - Height, 2.65 m; large, pinkish-white flowers in April; red, berry-shaped fruit. Chinese apple (M. spectabilis). - Height, 4 meters; beautiful carmine flowers before blossoming, then white washed with pink, in May; very small fruit. Evergreen APPLE (Malus sempervirens). - Leaves are almost evergreen; flowers are pink before blooming, then almost white in May. fragrant apple (M. coronaria). - Large, fragrant white flowers in May. DOUBLE BLOSSOM PLUM (Prunus flore pleno). - Variety of the common plum, cultivated for the beauty of its flowers. Varieties. - Sinensis alba plena, - Sinensis rosea plena, - Trilobata, - Blanc. Mirobolan plum (P, mirobolana). - Two varieties are grown, one with red fruit, the other with yellow. ROBINIER blanc, White Acacia (Robinia pseudo-acacia). - Tall tree with elegant foliage; thorny branches; very fragrant white flowers in May and June. Varieties: - Pyramidalis, - Pendula, - Flore luteo, - Amœna, Decaisneana. - The thornless varieties grown under the names Spectabilis, Inermis, Crispa are also derived from white Robinia. ROBINIER visqueux (R. viscosa). - White Acacia habit; thorny when young; slimy branches; pale pink flowers in June and July. ROBINIER rose (R. hispida). - Height, 4 meters; very broken branches, covered with reddish hairs; beautiful pink flowers from June to August. Grafted on the ground, it forms a charming shrub. weeping sapling (Salix Babylonica). - Very picturesque tree; long, flexible branches, hanging to the ground; lanceolate leaves; catkin-shaped flowers in April and May. Varieties. - Laurel-leaved, - Rosemary-leaved, - Silvery, - Ring-shaped. All willows can be used to advantage in landscaped gardens: they are particularly suited to damp soils. Japanese SOPHORA (Sophora Japonica). - Large, beautiful tree; dark green leaves; slightly pendulous branches; whitish flowers in July. Variety with hanging branches. BIRDSORB (Sorbus aucuparia). - Height, 5 to 6 meters; long, often pendulous branches; white flowers in May; attractive red fruit. Domestic sorb (S. domestica). - Much taller than the preceding; white flowers in May; pyriform, reddish fruit. Varieties. - Hybrid, - American, - Elder-leaved. European lime (Tilia Europgea). - A tall, hardy tree with a pyramidal habit. This tree is covered with leaves from the first days of spring, but loses them much earlier than all the others. It is used to form avenues. It is easy to manage and can be mowed regularly. Fragrant, whitish flowers from March to June. Varieties. - Coral, - Weeping, - With laciniate leaves. - variegated leaves. SILVER LINDEN (T. argentea). - European lime habit, only slightly lower; leaves dark green above, white and cottony below. American lime (T. Americana). - Very tall tree; very large, toothed leaves. TULIPIER de Virginie (Liriodendron tulipifera). - An attractive tree, remarkable for the shape of its leaves and for its flowers, of a greenish-yellow mingled with red, similar to a Tulip in shape and size; flowers in June and July. Tulip trees should only be planted in spring, and cutting off any branches should be avoided as far as possible, as amputations are very harmful to them, especially when young. Varieties. - With whole leaves, - With yellow flowers. VIRGILIER à bois jaune (Virgilia lutea). - Height, about 10 meters; very beautiful white flowers in June. SECTION XII. - Resinous trees. Resinous trees, commonly called green trees, should be planted young, preferably in April and May, when they begin to vegetate. If you are forced to plant in autumn, you should do so from the end of September, otherwise you risk losing a large number of trees. Yews, Thuias and Sequoia sempervirens can be pruned; as for the others, they should not be cut; and if ever it becomes necessary to remove a few branches, they should be cut a few centimetres from the stem, to avoid a loss of sap, which is always detrimental. Green trees are propagated from seed, sown in April, or by herbaceous grafting, using the most common varieties as subjects. ARAUCARIA IMBRICATA. - Pyramidal tree, very graceful; branches covered with lanceolate leaves, prickly at the top. Cedar of Lebanon (Cedrus Libhani). - Very tall, pyramidal tree; horizontal branches; oblong, oval cones, without asperities. It should always be planted singly, to enjoy its majestic effect. DEODORA CEDAR (Cedrus deodora). - This tree, so remarkable for its pendulous branches and the beautiful glaucous green of its leaves, is fast-growing and capable of great elevation. CRYPTOMERIA JAPONICA. - This tree differs essentially from other green trees in its leaves and the arrangement of its branches. To enjoy the full beauty of Cryptomeria, they should be planted in isolation. CYPRESS (Cupressus). - These shade-green trees are all suitable for the pleasure garden; they can be planted in rows or singly, depending on their shape. Cupressus disticha alone requires cool soil to thrive. Varieties. - Sempervirens (pyramidal), - Funebris, - Lawso niana, - Lambertiana, - Disticha (bald). common juniper (Juniperus communis). - Shrub 4 to 5 meters high; diffuse branches, prickly leaves; spherical, blackish-blue berries. Varieties. - Virginia, - Oriental. Common Ir. (Taxus baccata). - Hardy, very common tree; red berries. Can be made to take different shapes by annual mowing. Varieties. - With variegated leaves, - Pyramidal. EUROPEAN LARCH (Larix Europœa). - Very tall, pyramidal tree; horizontal branches; deciduous leaves; very small cones. Varieties. - With hanging branches, - American black. PINES (Pinus). - Very tall, hardy, evergreen trees, invaluable for landscaped gardens; placed singly or in groups, their dark shade contrasts pleasantly with the foliage of other trees. Varieties. - Sylvestris (from Scotland), - Laricio (from Corsica). - Austriaca. - Benthamiana. - Lambertiana. - Pinaster, - Ponderosa, - Pyrenaica, - Strobus, - Sabiniana. FIR TREES (Abies). - Firs are generally tall trees; they differ from pines in their pyramidal shape. All can be grown in large gardens. Varieties. - Alba (White Fir). - Excelsa (Spruce). - Canadensis (Hemlock), - Cephalonica, - Cilicica, - Balsamea (Balsam). - Douglasii, - Morinda. - Nobilis, - Nordmanniana, Pectinata (S. argenté), - Pinsapo. SEQUOIA SEMPERVIRENS (Taxodium sempervirens). - A large, beautiful, fast-growing, hardy California tree. Sequoia can be left to grow naturally, or pruned like Yew trees, essential qualities that should make it eagerly sought after. SEQUOIA GIGANTEA (Wellingtonia gigantea). - Also native to California, this tree can grow to gigantic proportions. To produce its full effect, it must be grown in isolation. CANADA THUIA (Thuia orientalis). - Height, 8m, 33; pyramidal crown; vertical branches; flat, imbricate, green leaves. THUIA de la Chine (T. occidentalis) -Higher than the preceding; flexible branches; russet-green foliage. Varieties. - Aurca, - Pendula. - Gigantea, - Lobbii CHAPTER XVI Destruction of pests. The vegetable garden, orchard and pleasure garden are, all too frequently for the horticulturist, exposed to the ravages of birds, small mammals and insects, which, at every stage of their lives, from the moment they emerge from the egg to their metamorphosis, live at the expense of the plants we raise for our use or enjoyment. Traps and poisoned pellets are used to destroy small rodents, such as mice, rats, dormice and ferrets. Traps, scarecrows and a few rifle shots keep birds away; but the grower must know how to distinguish between his friends and his enemies, and exclude from this proscription warblers and other fine beaks, swallows and insectivorous birds, which at all times of the year live on insects, and in winter on seeds or a few small berries left on bushes. Sparrows and other granivores destroy a prodigious quantity of insects when their young are being raised, and should be spared during this season; it's around July that you should start to hunt them mercilessly. As for insects, which are so numerous, and which by their multiplicity and smallness escape our means of destruction, their numbers are well reduced, it's true, by the active hunting that birds do for them; but their multiplication is so rapid, that they brave these bad odds and seem only to become more inconvenient. A large number of means have been proposed to eradicate them, but few of them are successful; and of all those that have been employed, careful and persevering research is without doubt the most time-consuming, but the most certain. Hedgehogs, tortoiseshells and small night birds, such as the owl, are bred in gardens. They devour a large number of insects, and are the most destructive of all; their usefulness is all the greater as they only hunt at night, and it is at this time of day that many insects wreak their havoc. We therefore advise horticulturalists to keep one of these animals in their garden, as they cost nothing and provide great service. You should also be careful not to destroy bats, which feed only on moths and butterflies. Some insects, such as ladybugs, hoverflies, calosomes, ichneumons and sphexes, destroy large numbers of insects and caterpillars; ladybugs and hoverflies eat aphids, and can be left to multiply without fear; but it often happens that certain carnivorous insects become pests in their turn when they have nothing left to eat. Ichneumons, sphexes and hoverflies should be excluded: they are always useful and never harmful. Spiders (garden spiders) can also be counted among the animals that render great service. BEES, GUESTS - Ripe fruit is often attacked by these insects, which cause considerable damage to espaliers. They are destroyed by hanging small vials filled with honey water from the branches, in which they drown; wasp nests are sought out, and their inhabitants asphyxiated with sulfur smoke or boiling water. ACARUS, commonly known as the gray one. - One of the most dangerous causes of the destruction of trees in our orchards are the stings of the acarus, which attacks peach trees and kills them. It attaches itself under the leaves, sucking the parenchyma, and, despite its small size, is so numerous that it kills the most vigorous tree. Powdered sulfur, applied after basking, is the most effective remedy that can be used to destroy peach blight. Melons, cucumbers, beans and cabbages attacked by this arachnid can also be treated by the same method. SPIDERS. - If the large spider is harmless, the same cannot be said of the small ones, which run quickly over the soil: they attack young seedlings, particularly carrots, prick the stem, suck the sap and kill them. They are kept at bay by sprinkling powdered soot on the soil, and, when the weather permits, they are bathed in water. COURTILIÈRES. - These insects, which are very large and therefore easy to detect, wreak great havoc on vegetable plants, and particularly on diapers. The various means of destroying them are to sprinkle the soil with water laden with black soap or oil, and to plant pots half-full of water in the direction of the cricket's galleries, in order to drown them. Gardeners simply crush them as they find them by turning over the beds, and deliver small piles of manure in which they come to nest. caterpillars and larvae. - In orchards, careful weeding is one of the most foolproof methods, as it destroys both the eggs and the following generations; and if a few nests escape, it is necessary, as advised by Mr. Samuel Curtis, a skilled English amateur, to sprinkle the trees with quicklime just as the leaves begin to develop, and before the flowers bloom. M. le docteur Bailly also says that caterpillars can easily be destroyed when they are gathered together, by sprinkling them with water mixed with black soap, using a broom: it seems that as soon as they are touched, they are instantly struck dead; he even says that prussic acid does not act with greater promptitude. The larvae of insects of the Tenthrède genus are a source of despair for Rose lovers: together with the other enemies of this shrub, they attack the young shoots, causing the flowers to abort. The best time to destroy them is in spring, in April. The best time of day is in the morning, before they have begun to disperse; look for them in the tips of twigs, which are swollen by their presence, and crush them by pressure, or even split the branch with the tip of a penknife and extract the larva. When the disease is too far advanced, cut off the diseased branches. Hylotoma rosce larvae gnaw on the leaves of roses, and can easily be destroyed by crushing them. As for the caterpillars that devour vegetable plants and hide under plant leaves or in the soil, after other natural means of destruction, try decoctions of soot and walnut stain to kill them, but rely even more on research. Careful horticulturists should destroy all butterflies without mercy, as they are the propagators of the enemies of their crops. FORMS. - The inconvenience of these small insects is well known: they harm roots by lifting the soil in which they make their homes; they attack leaves and fruit, and escape many means of destruction because of their smallness and agility. To keep them from climbing trees, wrap a cord of well-carded wool around their feet; keep them away from pots and crates by surrounding them with water, either by a support or by small vases that are kept constantly full. Bottles of honeyed water hung from trees attract ants, which die in considerable numbers. Finally, you can destroy them, like mites, with water mixed with black soap or oil. KERMES, MEALYBUGS, GALLINSECTS. - Kermes insects cause considerable damage to peach trees and fruit trees in general. In spring, they cling so tightly to the branches that a rough brush is needed to remove them. The best time to look for them is in April, before they have laid their eggs, and before they have left the branches where they have spent the winter, to disperse on the leaves of the trees. There are several species of kermes, all generally applied to branches like small warts. LIMAÇONS (Garden propellers). - To get rid of them22 , the best thing to do is to pick them up as you come across them, especially in the morning or after rain; you should also carefully destroy them whenever you come across eggs. LILACES (or Buhottes). - They are very damaging to plants, which they devour with incredible voracity. The best way to destroy them is undoubtedly to use powdered hydrated lime. To spread it, stand downwind and throw it by hand, shaving the ground as hard and evenly as possible. EARTHWORMS. - Earthworms do no harm to plants other than lifting the soil to dig their galleries, and it is only in beds where young seedlings have been planted that they should be destroyed. They are brought out by beating the soil, or by poking a stick into it and shaking it in all directions: they then emerge from the earth; they are placed in a pot and drowned, crushed or, better still, fed to poultry. EAR DRILLS or FORFICLES - Like all insects that come out particularly at night, earwigs attack plant leaves, flowers and fruit, piercing them to make their homes. Carnations, dahlias and hollyhocks are all prey to their voracity. To destroy them, the simplest method is to place small upside-down flower pots on sticks, with a bit of moss at the bottom; the traps are visited every morning, and any earwigs that have taken refuge in them are destroyed by immersing them in a tub full of water. APHIDS. - Aphids, of which there are a large number of species, attack all plants in general. Whether they are grey, like woolly aphids, or green, like rose aphids, they cause the same devastation and cause plants to perish through the repeated sucking they exert on their leaves; the ants they attract add to the damage they cause. They can be destroyed by cleaning branches or leaves one by one, removing those that have been too deeply altered, or by smoking them with slightly damp tobacco, using the device known as a fumigator, or by washing the plants with a little black soap water; pyrethrum powder, recommended for destroying aphids, can be advantageously replaced by powdered tobacco. TAUPES. - This small insectivorous quadruped is still actively hunted, although it causes little harm except through its galleries, as it lives only on insects and worms; but it stirs up all the soil, upsetting it and cutting roots in the direction of its corridors. The mole works three times a day: in the morning, at midday, and in the evening at sunset; you must take advantage of this time to remove it with a spade, while it re-establishes its gallery, which you first pushed in with your foot. A trap baited with walnuts boiled in lye, which the mole is very fond of, is also placed in the gallery, which is then unblocked. Earthworms cut into pieces and sprinkled with walnuts are also placed in the water. TICKS (BLUE FLEA BEETLE). - These small, extremely agile insects, which leap away from any hand that tries to grab them, wreak considerable havoc on cabbage, radish and turnip seedlings. There are few ways of destroying them, but they can be kept at bay by spraying the plants with a decoction of tobacco or pungent plants. WHITE WOLVES - These insects, harmful to fruit trees, vines, ornamental shrubs and vegetable plants, are difficult to destroy, not because of their agility, since in their larval stage they crawl slowly under the soil, but because they wreak their havoc hidden in the bosom of the earth, and their presence is only noticed when the damage is irreparable. As soon as you see the leaves of a plant wilting, you have to dig at the base, and you're sure to find one or two white grubs. If you want to protect valuable plants, such as fruit trees or young plantations, from grubs, plant strawberries, lettuces, etc. near them, as grubs are very fond of them. Another precaution to take is to pursue chafer beetles with the greatest care, and destroy them as soon as they appear. This must be done in the morning: the beetles, numbed by the cool of the night, are then weakly attached to the branches and easily fall to the ground. M. Duval, who seems to have studied the habits of the cockchafer with great care, claims that simple hoeing is enough to destroy the larvae of this insect. However, hoeing must be carried out at the right time. According to him, it's after egg-laying that the land usually ravaged by the white grub should be hoeed, in order to bring the eggs in the soil to the surface. At this time, the action of light is sufficient, according to his observations, to destroy all the eggs that can be reached. CHAPTER XVII Vocabulary of the main gardening terms. Accor. Manure raised around layers to prevent the cold from penetrating. Apos. Sloping ground facing the sun. Ados are used for sowing and transplanting young plants. AMEND. To improve a soil by fertilizing. ANNUAL. This name is given to plants that germinate, flower, bear seeds and die during the year. AUGUST. Said of young branches that have reached the necessary consistency to withstand winter. ARROSER. Synonymous with wet. BASSINER. To water lightly with a watering can, so that the water falls as rain. BIFURQUÉ. To divide into two branches. BINER. To divide the surface of the soil with the hoe, so that it does not harden. BISANNUAL. Plants that last two years. BOURGEONS. Leaves and stems that are beginning to develop. BUTTERFLY. Eyes placed in the axils of leaves and at the tips of twigs. ADVENTIONAL BUTTERFLIES: those born elsewhere than in the leaf axils and at the ends of twigs. 22. BRINDLE. Thin, short, fringed branch. BULB. Onion plant. BUTTER. To raise the soil around the base of plants to protect them from frost, to whiten them or to promote tuber development. CADUQUES (leaves). Falling every year. CAÏEU. A bud that forms on the side of large onions. CHARGE UNE COUCHE. Placing on it the soil or potting compost required by the plants to be grown. COLLET. A kind of knot placed between the root and the stem. COUNTER-ESPALIER. Trees planted parallel to the espalier and whose branches are attached to a low trellis. COUNTER-PLANTING. This operation consists of planting between the rows of a bed lined with plants that are half or three-quarters grown, the plants that will follow them. CÔTIÈRE. A more or less wide bed, sheltered by a wall or windbreak, where vegetables are grown that come earlier than in the garden. COTYLEDON. Seminal lobes or leaves. COURSON. Branches cut short. DRAGEONS. Young shoots growing from roots. ÉCLAIRCIR. To pull up a plant when it has been sown too thickly, so that the remaining plant will benefit more. ECLATER. To separate the roots of a plant that grows several stems. ESPALIER. A tree whose branches are spread out against a wall. SPLIT. To cut with the nails the main stem of a plant, so as to facilitate the development of the lower branches. FORCE. To force a plant or tree to produce earlier than it would naturally. FRAPPÉ. Said of a melon that, having reached its full size, begins to change color and hue. GERM. Part of the seed from which a plant is formed. GOBTER. To cover mushroom wheels with light earth. HALE. Dry, drying wind. HERBACEOUS. Green, soft, succulent stems. HERSER. This operation consists in breaking up clods of earth with a fork after plowing. GAUGE. The ditch formed by the earth that must be removed before ploughing. LARDER. To introduce the white into mushroom wheels. LINEAR. From the nature of wood. FURNITURE. Said of land well divided by ploughing. WET. Synonymous with watering. EYE. A small point which appears in the axils of leaves and at the end of twigs. In the following spring, this small point becomes a woody or fruit bud. EYE. Offshoots produced by certain plants and used to propagate the species. OMBRACE. To spread canvas or mulch over the frames, to attenuate the intensity of the sun's rays. PAILLER. To spread short manure on the ground, to prevent the rapid evaporation of water from watering. PALISSER. This operation consists in fixing only the branches and buds of espaliered trees. PERSISTENT. Leaves that remain on the tree for several years are called evergreen. PINCH. To cut the tips of young branches with the nails, to encourage the development of lower branches. RAMEAU. A small branch that is a division of the larger ones. RATISSER. To cut the grass between two plots of land with a rake, in alleys and plantations. RECHAUD. New manure raised around layers to warm or maintain heat. REMONTANTS. Roses and other plants that bloom twice in the same year. REPIQUERING. Transplanting consists in planting young plants from seedlings with a planter. RUSTIC. Easy to grow, winter hardy plant. SARCLER. To pull out weeds that grow in cultivated beds. SENTIER. A narrow path left between each bed. TERREAUTER. Spreading a layer of compost over a seedling. TRACER. To make lines along the length of the boards, for sowing or planting. TUBERCULES. Fleshy, rounded parts from which small fibrous roots usually sprout. TURION. Eye or bud arising immediately on roots. VIVACE. Perennials are all plants that survive for more than three years, whether or not they lose their leaves or stems each year. 2 4 S 63 6 55 N 5 1E I 4 61 S E 7 60 60 2 27 28 ? Pages, Alphabetical catalog of subjects... 17 Catalogue in methodical order of subjects or series. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 25 General catalog of works published by the Lacroix bookshop, other than those forming part of the library . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 71 OAO PROFESSIONS INDUSTRIELLES ET AGRICOLES Publiée par Eugène LACROIX 2 AVERTISSEMENT Since 1816, i.e. in the sixty years since our company was founded (1), our predecessors have published, and we continue to publish, works on the sciences applied to industry, arts and crafts, and agriculture. Taken together, these publications form a very varied collection: we had therefore created a Bibliothèque des professions industrielles et agricoles. But the scope of some of these works, the more or less scientific or more particularly practical teaching they contain, the typographical form, different for most, and finally the high price (1) Merger (in 1856) of the former houses Malher et Ce (founded in 1816), Aug. Mathias (founded in 1827), Comptoir des Imprimeursunis (founded in 1842), G. Comon (founded in 1848). Some of them could not be understood serially in an encyclopedia accessible, by form, content and price, to people who most often need practical indications on the profession they are learning, or in which they want to become more intelligently skilled. For these people, of whom there are many, there is a need for accurate practical guides, in a convenient format, at a moderate price, written with clarity and method, in the same way that direct teaching from teacher to pupil or master to apprentice is clear and methodical. Such was our thinking when we began, in 1863, the publication of the Bibliothèque des professions industrielles et agricoles. We are confident that we will achieve the goal we have set ourselves, thanks to the sustained sales of the series already published, to the number and merit, both as scholars and as practitioners, of the contributors to the work, and to the subscriptions we receive from all sides and in all forms. Our publication is aimed at the engineer, the industrialist, the mechanic in each of the special professions, the craftsman in all trades, the schoolteacher, the farmer; some series are suitable for the man of the world who wishes to satisfy his curiosity, or who wishes to augment the notions already acquired, with specific knowledge of the professions which provide society as a whole with the elements of material well-being, the indispensable basis of moral progress. It is therefore to a very large number of readers, or rather workers, that we offer effective assistance in the study and application of questions of private or public utility. We appeal directly to them, reminding them that the only way to lower the selling price of a book is to print it in a very large number of copies, in anticipation of a large number of buyers: indeed, the initial expenses, i.e. engraving the wood and plates, typographical composition of the text and the author's work, are the same for one copy as for a thousand, ten thousand, etc. We hope that the number of copies will increase in the future. In the hope that the number of subscribers to our work will not cease to increase, - that editors and subscribers will lend us their increasingly effective support, - we shall continue to publish the volumes announced, as quickly as possible. The selling price of each volume will be determined by the cost of producing it. This Library is composed of nine Series, subdivided as follows: SERIES A. - Exact sciences... ... ... . 9 vols. B. - Observational sciences... . 24 " C. - Civil engineering... ... ... ... ... ... ... D. - Mining and metallurgy . . . . . " E. - Power machinery... " F. - Military and maritime professions. G. - Industrial occupations... ..." H. - Agriculture, gardening, etc. ..." I. - Home economics, accounting29 57 lity, legislation, mixtures... 29 1 X 1 Total. ... 250 vols. The volumes in this series are published in the large in-18 format, most of them illustrated with engravings to enhance understanding of the text; atlases contain drawings that need to be represented on a larger scale and in greater detail. Price of 2 volumes. 15 fr." Since heat has been used as a motive force by means of steam engines, and we have thus been practically led to regard a certain quantity of work as equivalent to the heat necessary to produce it, it has been natural to seek theoretically for a definite relationship between a quantity of heat and the work it is possible to make it produce, and to use this relationship to deduce conclusions about the essence and laws of heat itself." So says Mr. Clausius at the beginning of his first Memoir. These lines suffice to illustrate the importance of a question whose study is essential today for scientists and practical men who want to derive from the steam engine all the useful effect it can give. 4. Regarding the Livre de poche du Charpentier, we repeat what was said about another book by M. Merly. Both works deserve the same praise. Mr. Merly is not a scholar who must strive to forget the technology of the School in order to speak the ordinary language of most of his listeners; Mr. Merly is, on the contrary, a worker, a practical man, who has sought to make himself understood by the fellow workers to whom he addressed himself, and who has arrived at demonstrations so clear, at explanations so natural, that theorists themselves have soon had to draw inspiration from his work. Nothing is sharper than his drawings, nothing simpler than his precepts: in a way, it is by playing with himself that he arrives at the most complicated designs. The education, multiplication and improvement of farmyard animals have made considerable progress in the last fifteen years. Special chapters are devoted to diseases, gallinaceous pharmacy, statistics on hens and eggs in France, etc. 19. 2° Éducation lucrative des Oies et des Canards, by the same author, i vol. 180 p. with numerous figures in the text. 2 fr. Both monographs are useful, instructive and entertaining. The author describes the particular habits of each species, and indicates the type of food that is favorable to their multiplication and profitable for breeders. All these notions, interspersed with historical data, anecdotes and philosophical reflections, make for very attractive reading. 20. Guide pratique du Pisoiculteur, by M. BAILLIÈRE ET FILS 19, RUE HAUTEFEUILLE, PRÈS DU BOULEVARD SAINT-GERMAIN 1893 All rights reserved ANCIEN LIRECTEUR DES ASILES PUBLICS DE CADILLAC ET DE BORDEAUX TÉMOIGNAGE D'ESTIME ET DE RECONNAISSANCE ERNEST BERGER. There aren't many books on practical market gardening; at least those that can be consulted with advantage, those written by men in the trade, who have put their hands to the grindstone, as the saying goes. The good ones are expensive; the others are incomplete, too old or written especially for certain regions. It was to fill this gap, and to offer a book that could be consulted with profit just about everywhere in France, that we wrote Vegetable Plants and Market Gardening. This work, conceived on a new plan, can be consulted by the amateur as well as the gardener: each will find information of interest. We have emphasized only the practical side of cultivation, what it is necessary to know in order to do well. After giving some general ideas on how to create and set up a low-cost market garden, we go on to describe each plant: 1° Origin; 2° Cultivation in the open ground and early crops on beds and under frames, appropriate to different climates; 3° Description of the best varieties to grow; 4° Seeds, practical means of harvesting and preserving them, and their germination period; 5° Diseases and pests, and the best ways of destroying them; 6° Uses and economic and nutritional properties of plants. The last part includes a calendar of sowing and planting for the twelve months of the year. The book is illustrated with 64 figures, thanks in large part to the kindness of Messrs Vilmorin et Cie, which show the appearance of the species described and make it easier to recognize them. All the plants, even almost all the varieties we mention, have been cultivated, tested and studied by us with the greatest care. We can therefore affirm that by following exactly our cultivation instructions, which are the fruit of serious and reliable observations, good results will be obtained. October 1892. E. BERGER THE MARKET GARDEN PART ONE ESTABLISHING A MARKET GARDEN CHAPTER ONE THE SOIL I. CHOICE OF SOIL. - When you want to create a market garden, you need to choose good soil, of such a type that its composition lends itself to the cultivation of the various vegetable plants and activates their vegetation. Three main types of soil, taken separately or in combination, meet these conditions. 1° Free soils. - These are composed of: one-tenth carbonate of lime, one-tenth humus, three-fifths alumina or clay. This is the most fertile type of soil, and is generally suitable for growing all vegetable plants. It is easy to work with, and can do without soil improvers; it accepts all fertilizers, which it keeps decomposing for a long time, and from which it gradually benefits; it is also used as a base for composts intended for temperate greenhouse plants: BERGER, Plantes potagères. finally, it is used in mixtures with potting soil intended for seedlings or early plantings. In general, this type of soil is found at low altitudes. 2° Marsh soils - Composed of small quantities of sand, peat and humus, and very similar in fertility to free soil, these soils become much more fertile when amended with limestone or lean sand, which gives them porosity and makes them lighter and therefore easier to work. In their natural state, these types of soil are poorly vegetated and water remains stagnant for part of the year. In this case, when the subsoil is not too bad, the earth removed from the ditches is thrown back onto the other parts of the soil to raise it up; this work should preferably be done during drought, so as not to be hindered by water. This type of soil is particularly suitable for summer: because of the moisture in which the plant roots are located, they grow vigorously and magnificent results are obtained. In winter, it becomes too cold, and some plants suffer. 3° Siliceous-clay soils. - Their base is sand mixed with clay and limestone. They are easy to work, and most vegetable plants thrive in them; however, in hot weather, they can be a little scorching. There are many other intermediate soils. They are generally referred to by names that recall the two dominant parts. For example: Clay-limestone - composed mainly of clay and lime. Silico-calcareous. - Composed mainly of sand and lime. Many of these soils become excellent after a few years of cultivation, provided they have not been starved of fertilizer. In general, all soils that are not too compact are good for market gardening; sand, which is absolutely pure and very thin, can, with hard work and manuring, improve remarkably and become a first-rate soil for this type of cultivation. As the subsoil influences the quality of the top layer, its nature and depth must be taken into account. If the subsoil is compact and tenacious, and retains water, the plant layer will be constantly damp during heavy rains, and the plants planted there will suffer from this overabundance of water. If, on the other hand, the subsoil is porous and absorbent, the top layer will always be healthy. It is possible (though rare) for the top layer to be thick enough for the subsoil to exert no influence on it. It is therefore important to carefully study and choose your soil as upper and lower layers; those that are light, soft and deep are the best. II. exposure, orientation. - The choice of exposure is no less important, because of the major role it plays in plant growth. The best exposures are gentle slopes facing south, east or west, but always sheltered from the north as much as possible. In slightly steeply sloping soils, we prefer those dominated by clay. These soils retain a fair amount of moisture, as we have said, when they are on the plains, but here, because of their sloping surface, they quickly lose this excess of moisture through drainage and almost always remain healthy and warm, with the sun's rays acting more intensely than on the plains, whereas light soils, placed in the same conditions at the time of great heat, become scorching and even sterile; these same soils, placed on the plains or on gentle slopes, are excellent and completely fertile. To sum up, strong soils should be chosen as far as possible on slopes, and light soils on plains; however, these various conditions are often difficult to achieve because of the layout of the location or the means at our disposal, but we will get as close as possible. As important as it is not to have a soil that is too wet, it is equally important to choose a site that is supplied with the water essential for watering during hot spells, because without water in summer in dry soil, market gardening is impossible. CHAPTER II SOIL PREPARATION I. RUNNING. - Raking is an operation which consists in stirring up all or part of the plant layer, depending on its depth, so that the top soil takes the place of the soil below. This work should be carried out in autumn and during part of winter, in dry or cold weather. Avoid doing it in rainy weather, as compacted soil dries with great difficulty and has a poor effect on plant roots. Not all soils require deep ripping: in some low, damp soils, a good spade is all that's needed; a natural meadow, which has been worked for a long time, usually provides excellent soil that is very suitable for vegetable plants, and here deep ripping would be of no use. The spade is used for this purpose. Start by removing the turf in thin slabs, arranging them in square piles and placing them in beds, with the surface underneath; if the soil in which you are working lacks limestone, powdered quicklime or, failing that, well-crushed marl, or even plaster, is added; fermentation soon takes place, and after a year spent in this state, the whole thing forms a kind of potting soil that is spread in equal parts over cultivated squares. Such is the method used by certain growers in central France, which is worth noting and imitating. Once the turf has been removed, we start breaking up the soil, taking care to turn the top parts underneath. When deep trenching is required, the ground is divided into squares, so as to proceed in an orderly fashion, and to cut only those parts where the work can be completed. After this layout, a trench or gauge is opened, varying from 70 to 80 centimetres and even 1 metre in width. The soil from this first trench is transported to the site where the work is to be completed. The depth varies according to the nature of the soil and the thickness of the plant layer, at Om, 50 or Om, 60 at the most; this is quite sufficient for growing vegetables. Once the first trench has been opened, a second of the same width is dug, and the soil from this one is used to fill in the first. This process continues until the work is completed, and the last trench is filled in with the soil from the first one, which was transported there at the beginning. The tools most commonly used to carry out these major jobs are the German shovel, the Piedmont or Correze pickaxe, and the beche. Sometimes, a forked hoe is also used. If the land is very large, it may not be possible to break it all in the first year. In this case, the broken part will be reserved for tap-rooted plants such as salsify, carrots, etc., and the other part, which will only receive a good ploughing with a spade, will be reserved for tracing-rooted plants such as peas, beans, etc..... As the soil is broken up, a layer of half-consumed manure is spread over the broken-up area. This is spread regularly, and successive rains and frosts soak up the salts, which infiltrate the new soil and fertilize it. When this layer of manure is more or less stripped of its principles, a month or six weeks later, a new layer is spread and buried. In this way, the soil can be used for all kinds of crops from the very first year. As you break up the soil, you remove any stones, tuffs or pebbles likely to hinder plant growth; all these materials are buried in the alleys in place of the good soil, which is then transported to the squares. By this exchange, we put everything in its place, taking advantage of everything; the pebbles or stones will strengthen the soil in the alleys, and the good soil removed will benefit the jar- din by increasing the vegetation layer. II. TRACÉ. - Once the ground has been levelled and its composition evened out, we finish levelling it and lay out the paths. As for the width and number of these, we must keep in mind the principle that, since cultivation is the goal, we must divert as little land as possible, taking rigorous account of the necessities or conveniences of farming; from this point of view, we will lay out the necessary paths. The layout and direction of the paths will take into account the nature of the site, the position of the water supply, the ease with which it can be distributed, the location of watering wells, manure pits, obstacles, ditches or watering holes, etc.When the layout of the land allows a regular layout to be made, we begin by dividing it up by laying out the main path, which should be a good 1.50 m wide, in the direction of the slope of the land; we then lay out another transverse path of roughly the same width; after which, we divide the remaining land into squares, varying from 10, 15 or 20 m long by the same width, separated by 1 m paths. These alleys are lined with useful plants such as sorrel, thyme, strawberry and savory. On the other hand, manure pits should be placed at a distance from the house, because of the unhealthy fumes they give off, and the unpleasant sight of them should be concealed by planting green trees such as thuya, ligustrum, laurel-tin, etc. around the pits. Although the proximity of fruit trees is generally harmful to vegetable crops, if the trench is deep enough, two rows of apple or pear trees can be planted along the main paths. These trees, which should be raised to a certain height above ground level to reduce their impact on crops, should be trained and pruned every year, choosing varieties of average vigor that set fruit quickly. HI. AMENDMENTS. - Amending a plot of land means providing it with the elements it lacks, and introducing the improving substances needed to correct its nature and enable it to produce the plants you intend to grow there. It's important to carry out such work only after careful study of the soil, because it means recomposing the soil; giving it what it lacks, and in such a proportion that the result of the amendment is an improvement rather than the sterility that could occur if it were done badly; and finally, it means giving consistency to soil that is too light, and porosity to strong soil. Compact, clayey soils can be successfully amended by adding a reasonable proportion of lean sand. However, in some soils that are too clayey, the sand is unable to combine with the other elements, and tends constantly to penetrate the plant layer, arriving in the subsoil without having acted. In this case, crushed terracotta debris, broken oyster shells, coal ash, etc. are used to advantage. It has also been suggested that the surface crust of the topsoil should be calcined: under the effect of the heat of the fire, clay cracks, hardens and, as a result, produces the same effect as gravel. This is a good and practical procedure in certain regions where other types of soil improver are unavailable and would become very expensive. Light soils, which generally become very hot in summer, should be amended with compact materials, but 1 See D. Bois, Le petit Jardin, Paris, 1889 (Bibliothèque des connaissances utiles). Clay that is too compact will only produce a mediocre amendment, and clayey marls are preferable. Marsh soil, excavated or cleared soil, river mud and cistern sludge produce excellent effects on these soils, as they not only serve as an amendment, but also as fertilizer. The various types of marl that can be used on almost any type of soil "except limestone" produce good soil improvers if you know how to make the most of them, but you mustn't overuse them, as their role is not that of fertilizer, and too much of them would be harmful. Marl is usually applied to the soil in autumn. It is deposited in heaps; the frosts and rains of winter begin to disintegrate it, and in spring it is spread out and mixed with the soil. In market gardening, this type of amendment is rarely used, as it is time-consuming and sometimes costly. IV. CHAULAGE. - In certain limestone-free soils, liming is an excellent operation that considerably increases the value and fertility of the soil. Not only is lime a good soil improver, but it also destroys insects and weeds, and promotes the decomposition of plant and animal debris in the soil. All soils, regardless of their composition, adapt more or less well to lime amendments, which is why we advise you to carry out a few partial tests before working on large areas. We use stone lime just out of the kiln, which is laid out in small heaps, 5 to 7 meters apart, covered with a layer of earth about 25 centimeters thick. They remain in this state for two weeks 1. and, when melting is complete, we take advantage of a fine day to spread it and then bury it immediately, mixing it well with the soil; liming must be renewed every five years. V. DRAINAGE. - Soils that are too wet are unsuitable for all crops, and it is essential to rid them of this excess moisture. This is achieved by drainage, which consists in draining water through underground conduits. To this end, ditches are dug about 80 centimetres or 1 metre deep, 60 or 80 centimetres wide, and spaced 5 to 15 metres apart or more, depending on the degree of moisture in the soil. In these ditches, a series of clay, concrete or cement pipes are laid end-to-end, carefully covering the joints with shards of brick or tile, coarse gravel or broken stone, to prevent soil from penetrating; the pipes should be secured as they are laid. In certain localities where stone is readily available, the pipes can be replaced by gutter-shaped conduits, built by laying out the rubble, or by placing rough stone in the bottom of the ditches. As many cavities as possible are left, then covered with gravel, clinker, pebbles, crushed stone and so on. Pine wood is preferable to any other species, as it rots very slowly in the ground. This latter method is widely used in the south-west, mainly in the Landes region. VI. SANITATION. - Sanitation or external drainage consists of draining water into the open air, through wide ditches that are dug more or less deeply, depending on the humidity of the soil; these ditches are directed in the direction of the slope of the land. When water is plentiful, the first ditches are cut with cross ditches to speed up drainage. In all cases, a collecting ditch will receive the whole, discharging the water into the lowest parts and, preferably, into a stream. CHAPTER III LABOURING LAND Ploughing means stirring up and turning over the topsoil, loosening it by dividing its parts, in order to make it suitable for growing new crops. By turning over the soil, we bring to the surface the lower parts impregnated with the salts that have precipitated there as a result of the infiltration of water through fertilizers. Ploughing is generally carried out with a spade or fork, and in some regions, with a hoe. Today, spade ploughing is the only method used by market gardeners in major centers (Paris, Lyon, Marseille, etc.). In strong soils, the fork is sometimes of great use, even indispensable for getting the work done, as it digs in more easily. For this purpose, very strong forks, specially manufactured for this purpose, are used. When ploughing land for immediate planting or sowing, the clods are broken up and crushed as much as possible, so that the roots of the plants can easily penetrate and adapt. Ploughing should be more or less deep, depending on the plants to be cultivated. Plants with taproots, which penetrate perpendicularly into the soil to achieve normal development, require slightly deeper ploughing. Plants with tracer roots, on the other hand, require shallow ploughing. As a general rule, however, wherever possible, good ploughing should be carried out with a full spade. Clay-limestone soils are difficult to work in summer, because of their extreme hardness, and because they then form a compact, tenacious mass. In such soils, when irrigation is possible, this hardness is remedied by running water through the soil, leaving it to stand for a few hours; two days later, when the soil is dry again, ploughing begins; but if irrigation is not possible, and the spade is unable to divide the parts, the soil is first broken up with a hoe; then ploughed with a spade, breaking up the clods. In winter, strong soils require little ploughing; once the harvest has been removed, rough spading is carried out, retaining as many clods as possible. In summer, these soils need to be ploughed frequently, so that the heat can penetrate them more easily and remove the moisture they contain. This procedure is hardly applicable to vegetable growing, as you would never choose a strong soil for commercial cultivation. Light, sandy soils that are dry by nature retain their looseness for a long time, and require less ploughing than heavy soils. It is mainly in winter that deep ploughing will be beneficial, as rain and frost will correct the lack of moisture by impregnating the soil. In summer, it's best to choose a rainy or dark day to carry out the frequent plowing, hoeing and weeding required by this type of soil. In excessively wet soils, where water remains in winter, it is customary, as soon as heavy rains approach, to spade the free soil into large furrows or ados, and let it spend the winter in this state, until it is possible to penetrate it and bury the fertilizers. When a plot of land of a certain size needs to be spaded, the most expeditious means of reducing labor costs should be sought. First, divide the land into as many planks as you deem necessary, and then, at even number, open a trench with a good spade iron, and place the earth with the wheelbarrow on the end of the plank where you will finish. The surface of the soil is then turned over and levelled. Fertilizers are buried more or less deeply, depending on the type of plant you intend to put in them. Before reaching the end of this first plank, we move to the opposite side of the second, in order to break it in while keeping the surface uniform and the gauge equal; this means is the most appreciated and the most expeditious. In a market garden, cultivation is so intensive that it is impossible to determine the time of ploughing, which is carried out at all times, as a bed is emptied: ploughing, smoking and planting are carried out immediately. In a well-managed vegetable garden, you should never see any free squares. This advice applies above all to middle-class and public-establishment cultivation. CHAPTER IV SECONDARY WORK I. STRAIGHTENING, LAYOUT OF BEDS. - After ploughing, if the edges of the squares are not marked by a border, they are drawn with a chalk line, then the soil is divided into planks 1m, 25 to 1m, 40 and more wide, depending on the type of plants to be sown. The division paths are marked out by stretching the chalk line out straight, holding it between the two feet as you walk, and spacing them out more or less according to the width you wish to give the paths. When planting vegetables, which require a certain amount of space between plants, first draw the two outer lines, using the iron tracer or a simple piece of tapered wood, which serve as a guide for drawing the central line, without having to replace the string. With a little practice, it's easy to draw straight lines: for example, on a board where you want to draw seven lines, you'll only need to draw the cord for the middle line and the one on each side, i.e. for three lines only. This is the same way for ray sowing, except that the lines are drawn with the narrow end of the hoe, so that they are a little deeper. For transplanting certain plants in summer, and even seedlings, it is customary in dry soils to form beds with large edges; to do this, the soil is raked back into the paths and along the edges; in this way, the water used for watering is of greater benefit to the plants, as it does not spill onto the paths. II. HEDGING. - Whatever the method of sowing or the type of planting, soil preparation is of paramount importance, firstly for success and secondly for the eye. After the beds have been laid, if the surface of the ground is not suitable for sowing, it is raked or harrowed. This is done by walking a fork back and forth across the ground, breaking up clods, loosening the surface and bringing up stones. After sowing, the soil is harrowed again, this time to distribute the seeds and bring them into contact with the soil, covering them as it were; in light soil, this operation is sufficient to cover the seeds by a small volume. Around Paris, and in the neighbouring départements, this system is widely used, and is very rapid. III. WEEDING. - Weeding consists in pulling out weeds from young seedlings or plantations, and making them disappear: for seedlings, this work should be done when they are still young, so as not to shake them too much and lift them up. At the same time, if necessary, they should be thinned out. To be done properly, thinning requires a certain amount of practice, to be able to distinguish without trial and error which plants need to be removed. Women are generally better at this work than men; they operate with greater dexterity. In summer, when the soil is dry, water at least one hour before starting to weed, to give the plants and the soil surface time to dry out. Weeding should not be carried out during the hottest periods, as young seedlings will suffer and have difficulty recovering. As far as possible, choose dark or not too hot days, and if you can only work in the evening, especially if the area to be weeded is not very large, this will be preferable, as the night firms up the plants, and the coolness makes them stand upright. Whatever the time of year, unless it is raining, before leaving the work, give the weeded areas a good watering. IV. HOEING. - Hoeing is a superficial ploughing operation whose aim is to loosen the surface of the soil around the plants, making it more permeable to atmospheric influences and at the same time preventing weeds from growing. This work is carried out with a tool known as a hoe, and can be done in any season. The soil is disturbed to a depth of between 8 and 12 centimetres, depending on the type of plant being hoeed. Avoid hoeing when the soil is too wet, and wait until the morning dew has fallen; experience has shown that hoeing is most profitable when the plants are completely dry. As soon as the soil begins to harden, hoe again, as the more the soil is loosened around the plants, the better they will thrive. V. PLUMBING. - Leading is designed to bring the seeds into contact with the soil: it is done after harrowing with a fork and after raking, as far as possible, in dry weather and mainly in light soils; in strong soils, it would produce poor results. This work consists of treading the soil, either with the feet and walking at a slow pace, or with a stick, the back of a digging shovel, or even, in certain regions, with a small hand roller. This operation becomes necessary in soils that are too light, and ensures success by encouraging germination. CHAPTER VE FERTILIZERS AND FUNURES S4 Fertilized soil would be rapidly exhausted if it were not given back the fertilizing principles and salts it has lost through successive cultivation. This is the only way to maintain and perpetuate soil fertility. I. CHEMICAL FERTILIZERS. - There are a large number of chemically compounded fertilizers available today, but they have never given very good results and are therefore rarely used in market gardening. II. MANURES AND NATURAL FERTILIZERS. - The fertilizers best known and appreciated by gardeners are rotten or consumed manures; horse, donkey or mule manure is the most popular, and consequently the most widely used. In their fresh state, these manures give off a gentle warmth that lasts quite a long time, and are used in winter to make layers for planting and sowing early crops. When decomposition is complete, the resulting potting soil forms the base for crops or beds. In a vegetable garden, nothing should be wasted; all plant detritus from vegetable dressing, grasses, sweepings, in short anything likely to decompose through fermentation, should be piled up; on its own, this detritus would only form a fertilizer, not of zero effect, but of too slow efficiency; that's why it's preferable to combine it with other animal manures which, while improving it, also activate its fermentation. Not all soils are suited to the same fertilizers, so they should be distributed with discretion, according to the nature and needs of the soil.
