Horned cattle manure, which is greasy and unctuous, is suited to light, warm soils; by fertilizing them, it gives them the tenacity that binds their parts together and preserves a certain moisture. Pig manure, which is very cold, is also suitable for these same soils. Half-rotted manure from horses, mules and donkeys is suitable for cold, damp soils, lightening them by dividing the parts. This type of fertilizer is the most widely used, and is generally suitable for all soils, provided that decomposition is allowed to take place according to the nature of the soil for which it is intended. Rabbit and sheep manure are very hot and activate vegetation enormously. Pigeon and hen droppings, otherwise known as colombine, are the most powerful fertilizers known; they should only be used with caution, as they are so hot that they burn plant roots; soaking them in water for twelve to fifteen hours produces a liquid manure that is excellent for activating the vegetation of vegetable plants, especially cucurbits. Fecal matter is a very energetic fertilizer that always gives good results, but must be used with care. Used alone, they would burn the plants; mixed with manures, they produce very rapid fermentation, and consequently a highly stimulating fertilizer that all plants, especially cabbages, can handle. Whatever type of manure you use, we advise you not to use it straight from the stable; you need to pile it up for a few days, to allow fermentation and even decomposition to begin. Winter, autumn and the beginning of spring are the most favorable seasons for fertilizing land; however, when cultivating intensively, we fertilize in all seasons when the soil is ready, and with each new crop, so as not to exhaust the soil. There are exceptions to this rule, however, as root vegetables such as carrots and salifis do not adapt, or adapt poorly, to recent fertilization. During our excursions across France, we noticed that in certain regions, notably Vienne, Charentes and part of Gironde, farmers did not know how to collect and dispose of their fertilizers: as the manure leaves the stable, it is piled unevenly in a corner, outside or in the open air, exposed to sun, rain and anything else that dries it out and destroys its soluble and volatile principles. In this way, fermentation takes place only very unevenly, and the result is a poor fertilizer that lacks any stimulant, and fertilizes the soil only imperfectly; growers who treat their fertilizers in this way never get good results, and there's no reason to be surprised. To get good fertilizer, you have to do things differently. You dig pits of varying depths, depending on the needs of the farm, from 50 centimetres to 1 metre and more, 2 to 3 metres wide and 4 or 5 metres long; the bottom of the pits is sloped; in the lowest part, a hole of a certain width is reserved to receive the liquid manure, which is removed as the hole fills up, to be distributed over the various squares under cultivation. During hot spells, fertilizers in fermentation are often watered with this liquid manure, to speed up decomposition. When you can build masonry manure pits, coated with cement on the inside, you should not neglect to do so, as you will gain by preventing liquid fertilizers from escaping through infiltration. Alternatively, and less expensively, you can coat the bottom of the pits and even the walls with clay, into which you add a little hydraulic lime. Leached wood ashes, soot and plaster, although not considered proper fertilizers, can be used as good stimulants, influencing vegetation by stimulating plant organs to draw more nourishment from the earth and the atmosphere. They can be spread on plants as they begin to develop, in dry, warm weather; plaster is particularly good for crucifers, turnips, cabbage, etc. Poultry feather is a very powerful fertilizer that is not as widespread as it should be. Market gardeners in the south-west of France, particularly around Bordeaux, use it extensively. It gives very good results on all vegetable plants. Its effect is immediate, so to speak, but short-lived: about two months, or seventy days, are enough for this fertilizer to give all it can. It can be used at any time of year, and the results are always excellent, though preferably when vegetation is active in spring and summer. Leafy vegetables, i.e. those whose aerial parts can be eaten, such as lettuce, cabbage, spinach, sorrel, etc., seem to do better with it than root vegetables. Gardeners use this fertilizer in several ways. In the case of seedlings, the soil is hoeed, the manure placed in the gauge and a layer of feathers spread over it, so that it is about 5 centimetres above the soil. For transplants, cabbages, tomatoes, etc., they put a handful of manure on each plant, opening a hole with a hoe or by hand. In regions where planting is done with a hoe, the feather should be put in while forming the rays. As far as possible, use this fertilizer only when it is fresh, i.e. before it has undergone any kind of fermentation. III. LIQUID FERTILIZERS. - All manure juices make excellent fertilizers; they activate vegetation and should be used in the morning or evening, especially in hot weather. Care should be taken to ensure that the leaves of the plants to be watered are not too saturated. Fresh fecal matter, diluted ten times its volume, is excellent for activating the vegetation of all vegetable plants; if you have only this fertilizer at your disposal, you're sure to get magnificent results. Never use it unless the plants have fully recovered. IV. MULCH. - Mulch is short manure, rather dry than fatty, which is used to cover cultivated beds throughout the summer, to intercept the sun's drying rays and prevent the soil from being beaten up by watering. Seedlings benefit from being covered with a light mulch: as well as conserving moisture, it prevents the seeds from being disturbed by watering as they germinate; it is spread as evenly as possible, dividing the molecules well. It is particularly suitable for dry, hot soils. V. POT. - Potting soil is the result of the complete decomposition of manure, grasses, leaves, etc., reduced to a friable state. Potting soil made from layers of horse manure is considered the best. It is used to cover fine-seeded seedlings in the open ground, to protect them and ensure their emergence; it is also used to fill new layers for early crops, and to cover seedlings grown in pots. It is always a good idea to have a sufficient quantity of this type of potting soil at hand. CHAPTER VI WAYS OF ACTIVATING PLANT VEGETATION I. LAYING. - Layers are a powerful and indispensable means of activating the vegetation of certain vegetable plants. Since a large proportion of them cannot be sown in the open ground, which is not yet sufficiently heated to cause the seeds to germinate quickly, it is through layers that many of our cultivated plants begin their first development in winter and then complete their vegetation in the open ground, when the heat is sufficient. Any organic material that can generate heat when fermented can be used to make layers. Horse manure is the best choice for long-lasting warmth; working horse manure is preferable, as the straw is better broken down and impregnated than in luxury horse manure. These manures give very strong heat, but their action can be moderated by mixing them with annealed manures, hornbeam, oak or lime leaves, grass or moss. The heat of the layers depends on the materials used in their construction, and also on the thickness they are given; the thicker the layer, the stronger and longer-lasting the heat. It is therefore important to know the degree of heat required by the plants you want to grow, in order to place them in the conditions that will best promote their development. In market gardening, three types of layers are used. 1° Warm layers. - Hot beds are erected from December to March; their dimensions vary according to the length and width of the boxes to be placed on them; their thickness is proportionate to the heat required by the plants: it varies between 40 and 70 centimetres. Before starting to build the layer, the manure is mixed, if necessary, then the four sides are marked out with ropes and stakes. The manure is then taken in bunches and laid flat, going backwards; the impregnated parts are mixed with the dried parts. The impregnated parts are mixed with the dried parts and spread evenly over all the points to form a first even bed; each forkful is pressed down firmly with the back of the tool; any overhanging straw is brought in to form a straight, solid edge. Once this first bed has been spread out, it is trodden on, watered if the manure is too dry, then a second bed is placed, then a third, until the desired height is reached. The surface should be as flat as possible, with a few forks of manure in the hollows. If the bed is to be used for bells, it is edged; if, on the other hand, it is to be used for chests, these are placed as soon as the last bed is in place, and a small layer of manure is spread inside, tamped down and loaded with potting soil. The frames are then put in place, and covered with straw mats to help the bed get its first light, which takes six or eight days. Many growers around Paris and in the north of France build their beds all at once, which is quicker, but it takes a great deal of practice to ensure uniformity, and the results are no better than those obtained using the method just described. 2° Warm coats. - Warm layers are made in the same way as the previous ones; they are made from annealed or previously used manure, with a little fresh manure to give a stimulating effect; leaves, herbs, etc. are also added. All these ingredients must be well mixed and sufficiently moistened. These beds are very useful in January, February and March, for sowing or transplanting celery, tomatoes, chillies, etc. When a warm layer has been used up and has produced just about all the effect expected, it can still be used, as the manure has not yet been used up, so it can be reworked by mixing it with the same care as the first time; a little new manure can be added and an excellent warm layer can be formed. 3° Muted layers. - They are made in the same way as the others, and are very useful for transplanting seedlings made on warm layers, and for planting certain types of plants. Pits or holes for melons, which are made in the spring in the open ground, are merely deaf layers. Based on our experience, we believe that when you have good soil at your disposal, you should not neglect to mix it with the composts intended for cultivation in layers, after having sieved it thoroughly; this mixture gives consistency, prevents the soil from drying out too quickly, and plants develop much better in it than in pure potting soils. Layers are generally placed in a healthy location with good exposure, facing south, but in such a way that they can be reached as much as possible in winter by the sun's rays from east to west. II. ReCHaups. - In winter, when a layer begins to cool, it needs to be revived; this is done with the help of rechaups, i.e. by piling up good fresh manure or leaves in the paths and around the trunks, which are firmly tamped; they are often reshuffled, each time adding to them to fill the voids produced by settling. III. AccoT. - The accot differs from the rechaud in that, instead of using new manure, we use leaves, old manure, straw or fern. The aim is to prevent the cold from penetrating the inside of the trunk, so it's not necessary to build them up very thickly; 15 to 20 centimetres is enough. Pile them up around the trunks to their full height, keep the outer edge straight, and place E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 2 a frame of slats held in place by good stakes firmly driven into the ground. An accot lasts a whole winter, if you take care to reload as the soil settles. IV. EDGE. - Layers that are not to receive coffers should be edged, to prevent the soil placed on them from collapsing. There are several ways of edging a layer, either with strong straw pads, or with long, slightly twisted manures, which are secured with long wooden or wire pegs. Some growers border with a large board that they place sideways on the edge of the bed; the soil is then brought down to the foot and firmly packed, the board is supported by strong wire or wooden pegs; this is a good, inexpensive way. V. Apos. - Ados are flowerbeds, sloping to the south, that are successively established in a square or along a wall. Once the site has been chosen, the procedure is as follows: once the soil has been well tilled, lines are drawn at varying distances according to the width to be given to the ados, from 1.50 to 2 meters, then with the spade, the earth is removed from the front to reload the back. The back of the spade is used to beat the top of the glacis to hold the soil in place, or even better, to hold it in place with planks, which is preferable. The slope to be given to the teens is 15 centimetres per metre, then the rake is passed over the whole, and a certain thickness of compost is spread. This kind of work is excellent, as it produces vegetation earlier than flat cultivation, and always guarantees good results; it's especially during winter and spring that ados are needed. Only in the vicinity of Paris, in the north and east of France, are teas successfully used; in the Midi, they would only give good results in winter, at the time of the coldest weather. CHAPTER VII POTTING PLANT MULTIPLICATION Propagation by seed is the most natural method of reproduction, and also the one that gives the best results. Almost all plants can be propagated by sowing, except for a few genera which do not produce fertile seeds, such as tarragon and chives. As the choice of good seeds is one of the main conditions for success, the grower should harvest most of the seeds needed for his operation himself, and carefully select and raise all his seedbeds so that they are kept clean. All similar varieties should be kept away from each other, to prevent the mixing of fertilizing dust. Seeds should be harvested only when they are fully ripe and not completely dry; those of some genera, such as lamb's lettuce and sorrel, should be picked before they are fully ripe. Drying is completed by spreading them out on canvas. Certain types, such as spinach and salsify, which only ripen their seeds successively, should be visited every day; as soon as they start to turn yellow, they should be picked to complete their drying in semi-shade. Plants such as carrots, celery, parsley and cabbage, whose seeds, though ripe and even dry, are difficult to detach from their receptacle, should be tied up in bundles and hung in a well-ventilated attic, where the seeds will mature and dry out. Many seeds, such as sorrel and parsnips, only retain their germinative qualities for a short time, and only sprout in the first year. To avoid disappointment, you should choose seeds from the last harvest. Other seeds, on the other hand - beans, broad beans, peas, etc., all papilionaceous plants in general - retain their germinative power for a long time; their longevity is even considerably increased when stored in their silique or pod. In short, all seeds retain their ability to germinate to a greater or lesser extent, depending on the degree of permeability of their envelope, their consistency and their chemical composition. All these considerations must be taken into account by the grower, who must be familiar with the different types of seeds, know how long they germinate, and know how long it takes each plant to reach full development. This knowledge can be acquired quickly, with a little attention and, above all, practice. I. SOWING IN THE GROUND. - Not all seeds can be sown under the same conditions, and sowing must be modified according to the nature of the soil, the climate, and the size or tenacity of the seeds. The finer the seeds, the less they should be buried in the ground; some types even germinate without needing to be covered: raiponce, purslane, etc. All you need to do is lightly plumb the soil, spread a good mulch and water often if the weather is hot. Medium-sized seeds such as spinach, carrots and radishes should be sufficiently covered, while beans, peas and broad beans should be covered more thoroughly. Any seed should be covered with twice its volume. Light, loose soils are generally suitable for all kinds of seeds at almost any time, because their porosity makes them more suitable than others for germination and subsequent emergence. In strong soils, many seeds would not germinate, or would only germinate with difficulty, if they were not covered with loose soil or light loam. For certain seedlings sown in hot weather, if the soil in which they are to be planted is dry, it is a good idea to soak the seed in water for a few hours, to hasten germination. Beans and radishes lend themselves well to this system. We would point out, however, that many procedures have been advocated, none of which has produced good results. Let nature take care of itself, and we'll be better off. It is preferable to sow a little thickly, as it is easy to thin out afterwards, whereas if we do the opposite, it is not always easy to resow or transplant. II. broadcast sowing. - Broadcast sowing is the most commonly used method; most of our vegetable plants are perfectly suited to it. When this type of sowing is done in a plot of land divided into beds, only half is sown at a time. You take a handful of seeds with your right hand, and, with a rapid series of wrist movements in a semicircle, you give the seed free passage by squeezing or spreading your fingers more or less. You follow it with your eyes as it falls, to distribute it evenly. 2. Do the same on the other half of the board, avoiding spreading the seed over the part already sown, and in the path. On large plots, broadcast sowing is done differently. You take a handful of seeds and, by moving your arm back and forth in a slight semicircle, spread them over the soil; in large-scale cultivation, this is how it's done. When broadcasting fine seed, many gardeners mix it with fine sand, wood ash or potting soil to distribute it more evenly. A good sower does not need to resort to this expedient (except for raiponce), and we can affirm that we have always sown our seeds as they were presented. III. SOWING IN RAYS OR ROWS. - Once the soil has been loosened and evened out, trace out the necessary number of parallel rows, spaced out according to the development required by the plants you wish to sow. The depth of these rows varies between 4 and 6 centimetres. The seed is placed at the bottom of the comb, with the hand raised 15 centimetres above it; the wrist is moved back and forth slightly in the direction of the combs. The seed is then covered by folding back the edges with the rake. When sowing in rows and beds, it is customary not to fold over the seed, but to leave the outer edges of the two end spokes to form a bead, so that this bead, serving as a frame for the bed, arrests its shape and retains water for watering. In strong soils, it is sometimes difficult to cover ray seedlings well, so potting soils or sifted earth are used, which are distributed as evenly as possible in the ray; straw, if necessary, and water. To draw the lines for the seedlings, use the narrow end of the hoe, a pointed piece of wood, a tracing tool, etc. Some growers in the North, when sowing fine seeds in rows, use their feet to draw two rays at a time, spacing them more or less according to the distance between each ray. This procedure is very quick, but can only be used on light, recently ploughed land. IV. SOWING IN CLUMPS OR BUNCHES. - To sow in clumps, deep rays can be traced as for row sowing, and sown at the desired distance and in a chessboard pattern; they are covered by folding back one of the edges of the ray; the hoe, planter or hand can also be used if the soil is light. The most common method, however, is to dig holes with the hoe at equal intervals, more or less deep, depending on what you want to sow; you cover by rejecting some of the soil, and at the first hoeing, when the plants are a little larger, you finish levelling the soil. This method is particularly suitable for planting potatoes or any other large seed. In some central and western regions, beans are sown in this way, as a counter-plant to other crops. V. DIFFERENT WAYS OF COVERING SEEDLINGS. - There are several ways to cover field seedlings. In many fields, well-applied harrowing with a fork is sufficient for most small-volume seeds. A rake is also used, with the tines pressed lightly and quickly into the soil, then passed over the surface to smooth it out. This is the system that predominates in France and gives good results in light soils. After sowing, lightly harrow the soil with a fork, and plow if necessary; then, using a full or forked hoe, remove a certain amount of soil from the paths, throwing it right and left onto each half of the bed; distribute it as evenly as possible, pass the rake over it, then mulch if necessary. When sowing fine seeds in compacted soils, fine potting soils or sieved soils are used to cover them, bearing in mind that the seeds need to be buried to a greater or lesser extent depending on their volume. It will be objected that this procedure is not practical over large areas; this is true, but we are addressing amateurs, who often have vegetable gardens in poor soil. A market gardener, who makes a living of it, will not choose a clay soil to cultivate it. Gardeners in the north of France use a lot of potting soil, and most of their crops are grown in terra-cotta; this is a good method that can be applied to all soils. In the Midi, terreautage is not widely practiced; it is hardly used at all: gardeners say they are wasting their time; this is a big mistake, because in the opposite case, they would obtain better results, despite the fact that the mild climate favors cultivation. VI. SOWING ON BEDS. - Many of our vegetable plants, which provide us with their produce and ripen their seeds in a relatively short time, would yield little or nothing if we waited until the soil was sufficiently warm to sow them. By means of early sowing on warm beds, we are able to raise plants of a certain strength; we plant them when the soil is sufficiently warmed, a time which coincides with that when, without the help of beds, we would only be able to sow. Layer sowing differs little from full-earth sowing; it is done in rays or broadcast; lightly press down with the hand or bat, cover with light loam and water with a fine apple. Above all, it's important not to sow before the seedbed has had its first light. Despite all precautions, seedlings often wither; to avoid this, give them as much air as possible, in proportion to the strength of the young plants; keep the soil moderately moist, and shade delicate plants to avoid sunburn. CHAPTER VIII PLANTING - TRANSPLANTING I. TRANSPLANTING FROM THE GROUND TO THE NURSERY. - Transplanting into a nursery is very advantageous for many vegetable plants that cannot be sown in situ, such as cabbages, celery, etc.; it favors root emission and the plant's outward development; by transplanting, we obtain well-branched, perfectly formed individuals, whose recovery is assured when set in place. The plants to be transplanted should be chosen in their infancy, when the first two leaves are beginning to develop; if they are too old, they will not cope well with successive transplanting and will become less attractive. The soil in which transplanting is to take place must be recently ploughed and loosened. If transplanting takes place during hot weather, mulch lightly and only operate in the evening; if the heat is very intense, shade during the three or four days following transplanting. This work, while not difficult, does require care and attention. First of all, it must be carried out promptly, ensuring that the young plant is in perfect contact with the soil, without too much settling, and that the hole is properly filled underneath. Care must also be taken to ensure that the roots are not in any way turned back, as this would have a detrimental effect on recovery. II. PERMANENT PLANTING. - When a plant is sufficiently developed, whether it has been transplanted in the nursery or left on the bed, it must be planted permanently; this operation is carried out in the same way as above, with the difference that the distance between plants is calculated according to their own development. Plants are generally planted in a staggered pattern, and watered immediately after planting. In some dry, hard summer soils, a superficial wetting is done before transplanting, which prevents the soil from clogging the holes, and helps to speed up the work. When planting peppers, eggplants and melons in layers, keep the roots as clod-free as possible; dig the holes beforehand with a spade or hoe, and use a hoe to do the planting. Subjects planted in this way suffer little from this change. Planting with the hoe is preferable to any other method, but as it is less expeditious than with the planter, it is more commonly used. For summer planting, a dark or rainy day should be chosen; otherwise, planting should be done in the evening; never during the day, as the sun's rays would damage the plants and delay their recovery. III. DEPLANTATION. - Instead of pulling them out with force, at the risk of breaking almost all the rootlets, which slows down recovery, if the soil is a little hard, use a trowel, spade, hoe or fork; plunge the tool deep into the soil, lifting it up in large clods, then remove the young plants without breaking the roots. If the soil is too dry, water a few hours before uprooting. As far as possible, only pull a few plants at a time, to prevent them from wilting. IV. PLANT PREPARATION. - Many young plants, such as strawberries, leeks, chicory, celery, etc., need to be prepared before being put out to pasture, by cutting off about half the leaves and some of the roots. Chicory and escarole seem to grow more slowly in spring, if you take the precaution of sufficiently cutting the pivot. This preparation is useful, as it promotes balance between the above-ground and below-ground parts, i.e. between the stem and the root. As a general rule, all plants to be transplanted should have their pivots cut to improve their future performance. Parsley, for example, which has hitherto been regarded as a plant to be sown in situ, produces magnificent results when transplanted with the poppy cut off first. V. LAYERED TRANSPLANTING. - Transplanting in layers differs significantly from transplanting in the ground. Tomatoes, peppers and eggplants, which are sown early and very thickly over a relatively small area, must be transplanted when the first leaves begin to appear; the bed must be suitably prepared and filled with good potting soil; once transplanting is complete, the plants are watered and covered with frames, which are kept closed for a few days to facilitate straightening. Air is then given, ensuring that the young plants do not wither, and that there is no overabundance of humidity; shade is applied if necessary. CHAPTER IX WATERING I. WATERING SYSTEM. - Watering being the active agent of market gardening, having water nearby and in abundance is an important advantage, especially in soils prone to drought, especially as it is during hot weather that vegetables are most valuable; the most advantageous means of obtaining water should therefore be studied. In certain soils where water is found at average depths, it is customary to dig wells, as far as possible in the highest part; a pump is installed, and then, at each corner of the square, iron-rimmed barrels are buried, 25 or 30 centimeters above ground level; oil or petroleum barrels are generally used. In the south-west and south of France, cement sump pits are used, either made on site or ready-made by certain manufacturers. Water is channeled through underground pipes or cement, wood, cast-iron or zinc slabs, passing from one barrel to the next, all the way to the far end of the garden. Although this method is not very costly, it does require continuous and arduous work for the worker in charge of operating the pump. It is preferable to set up a merry-go-round that can be driven by a horse for the duration of the watering operation. Today, there are few market gardens that are not equipped with a merry-go-round and even larger or smaller collecting basins, depending on the surface area to be watered. With these, watering is quick and easy. If they are high enough, you can use a lance, a watering can and even drip irrigation. II. DIFFERENT QUALITIES OF WATER. - All water does not have the same qualities; it is more or less suitable for watering, depending on the substances it contains, and the substances that make up the soil it passes through. Well water, if dug in limestone soils, contains carbonate of lime; it is considered the least good for watering, due to the salts it holds in solution, which form a crust on the surface that prevents plants from enjoying atmospheric influences, and hinders vegetation. To be beneficial, all well water must be exposed to the air for a few hours before use. Water that is brought to the surface by pumps, or any other means that stirs it sufficiently, can be used immediately, because its passage through the various pipes warms it up to some extent. Running water from streams, rivers, channels, etc., is the best for watering; it is all the better if its point of origin is further away, and especially if it is beaten by the waterwheels of factories. These waters, which are aerated and warm, are generally suitable for watering all vegetable plants. Rainwater is recognized as the best and purest, and can be used for a variety of watering purposes, provided it has not been left to stagnate for too long. The stagnant waters of ponds, cisterns, fish ponds, etc., with little or no renewal, become, because of the innumerable substances that putrefy in them, veritable liquid fertilizers that must be used with circumspection, otherwise the plants watered will perish: because of the fatty matter they contain, they prevent the oxygen in the air from penetrating the roots of the plants. III. EpOquE OF WATERING. - It is hardly possible to determine the right time and circumstances for watering each type of plant. The nature of the soil, altitude, exposure, atmospheric disturbances, etc., are all causes which make it impossible to specify the right time. Watering in the open ground begins in April and does not end until September. Watering from April to the end of May and in autumn should be carried out mainly in the morning, or even during the day. At this time of year, when the nights are still cool, evening watering would keep the plants at a temperature that is too cold in relation to the heat of the day, and would slow down their growth. On the contrary, from the end of May until September, watering should preferably be done in the evening or early morning, never during the day, because of the high heat. If it's morning, the plants will benefit from watering all day long. If you water in the evening, evaporation or absorption will no longer take place as it does under the drying rays of the sun, and the roots will be able to draw assimilable principles from the water they have been given; the opposite happens if you water during very hot weather: evaporation takes place so quickly that it cannot benefit the plants. IV. DIFFERENT WAYS OF WATERING. - Not all plants need to be watered in the same way. Some should only be watered with great care, especially young seedlings or newly planted transplants. They are watered with the apple, the holes in which are more or less fine, depending on the strength of the plants. Often, too much watering will bed them down and mix them together, making it difficult for them to stand up again. Seedlings planted in beds or terra-cotta flowerbeds should be watered with apples with fine holes, as over-watering scatters the soil, burying some seeds too deeply and uncovering others, so that emergence is uneven and defective. When watering carrot, salsify and turnip seedlings in the open ground, the surface of the soil can sometimes become so hard during hot spells that one watering is not enough to moisten it all the way down to the roots. In this case, a light drenching is used to moisten the surface of the soil and prepare it for a second watering. If, despite this, the soil is not sufficiently soaked, water a third, even a fourth time, if necessary. In dry summer soils, water the surface before planting, then water each plant immediately and give it a good general soaking. For plants that are far away and already strong, water them with the spout, taking care not to uproot them, pour the water gently and close to the base, and to prevent it spreading too much, make a small funnel-shaped basin around each subject. Watering with a hose is a good idea, as it provides plenty of water. However, in certain calcareous soils, the soil compacts and hardens quickly, and frequent hoeing is needed to loosen the surface. V. IRRIGATION. - Irrigation or imbibition is an excellent way of stimulating vegetation during the hot summer months, but it is not applicable to all soils. Most gardens in southern France, Spain and Portugal are irrigated. The land is divided into narrow plots, or furrows, separated by a gutter, and water is successively brought to each of them. When one plot seems sufficiently watered, it is diverted to the second, and so on. This is an excellent method that always gives excellent results, so we must not neglect to apply it whenever possible. In a market garden, the various waterings must be carried out with discernment and proportioned in the same way, so that each plant is watered at the right time. Watering should be more or less frequent, depending on the intensity of the heat, the soil and the size of the plant. CHAPTER X CROP ROTATION AND COUNTER-PLANTING I. ASSOLEMENTS. - In market gardening, rotation is one of the first keys to success; it always produces beautiful, magnificent produce. Assolating a plot of land means alternating crops and fertilizers, so that the same type of plant only comes back every three or four years in the same soil, because a plant placed several years in a row in the same square, even if the land is well tilled and smoked, cannot produce a good harvest if the type is exhausting. In this case, what happens is this: the first year, the harvest is perfect; the second, there will be a decrease in the product; the third, the subjects will be puny, stunted, woody, degenerate and bastardized. So it's important to alternate crops, with exhausting plants following non-exhausting ones. The crop rotation that seems to give the best results, and which we have always practiced, is the three-year rotation, with a layer in the first year. The squares in part 1 are given copious manuring: vegetables requiring good manuring are planted there; the other part is also fertilized with decomposed compost; the third part, which was copiously fertilized the previous year, receives only liquid fertilizers, liquid manure, sewage, etc. The second part is fertilized with a mixture of fertilizers and compost. Fertilization distributed in this way is not very expensive, and gives just as good results as fertilizing with large quantities of fertilizers that are poorly distributed. Proper crop rotation reduces the use of fertilizers without reducing the soil's fertility; on the contrary, it improves it. Not all plants require the same amount of fertilizer, and each kind of plant draws its own principles from the soil, so that what is not beneficial to one kind of plant is beneficial to another. Taprooted plants do not do well with recent fertilization, but if they are planted after crops that received copious fertilization the previous year (leeks), they do well and grow vigorously; despite this, mulching and topdressing must not be neglected. We will exclude from this category all poor soils recently under cultivation, as they do not yet have the fertility required to be sown, and it is only after a certain number of years of cultivation, with annual manuring and good fertilizers, that we can begin crop rotation. II. CROP INTENSITY, COUNTER-PLANTATION. - Crop intensity depends on crop rotation; it's thanks to this principle and to well-understood counter-planting that some market gardeners harvest an enormous quantity of produce from a relatively small area of land. Here are a few examples of intensive cultivation, or rather counter-planting. Let's assume a well-exposed bed. In the second half of January, you prepare the soil well, then sow white-tipped radishes, or others, and cover them carefully; you then plant lettuces, raised under a frame: you can even plant green romaine; you interplant a few early marjolin or early rose potatoes; you harvest first the radishes, then the lettuces, then the potatoes. - Towards the end of February, cauliflowers are counter-planted in the potatoes. Once the potatoes have been harvested, the cabbages are worked well and sown with radishes, chicory, spinach, sorrel, etc., harrowed with a fork. Under no circumstances should you counter-plant a plant that could harm the one you are growing. In a square of cauliflower or other summer species, sown very early on a good exposure or on a bed, and usually planted around March 20th, alternate with romaine or spring lettuces; before planting cabbages and romaine, radishes can be sown; radishes are harvested first, then romaine, then cabbages. As the cabbage harvest begins, we plough the open ground well, then sow spinach or chervil, even purslane. When the cabbage harvest is completely finished, chicory, escarole or leeks are planted in its place. You can also remove every third row of romaine or chicory from a first-season plot, plow it under and plant tomatoes. Once the romaine has been harvested, draw two rows on either side of the tomatoes, sow them with spinach or radishes, or plant summer lettuces, reserving a small path for watering. As the tomato harvest draws to a close, we spade the intervals, then plant long leeks, after sowing radishes. At the end of winter, before the leeks are fully developed, as they are always needed for blanching or for sale, we first pull up every third or fourth row and transplant bacalan cabbage. It's easy to vary crops and make the most of them, depending on the gardener's intelligence. But as good and advantageous as this process is when it is well directed, it becomes onerous if it is not well understood, as counter-planting varies greatly and undergoes numerous modifications, depending on the nature of the land and its altitudes; it is especially in light, fertile soils that counter-planting can be varied ad infinitum. We have noted some good fertile soils, notably in the Charente and Gironde regions, where cultivation is still routine. Most of these soils are in the hands of winegrowers or bad growers, who due to their lack of method, their bias to work only according to their own ideas, and their disregard for all good practices, are making a hard living where, with less routine, more intelligent and more scientifically sound cultivation, they could find relative ease. But what is certain is that, in this trade as in any other, you can't know if you haven't learned, and you only become skilled through years of persevering, sustained work, preceded by well-understood teaching. The best apprenticeship is practice under the watchful eye of capable parents or teachers. Brought up in gardens, in the midst of cultivation, you acquire a taste for it, you inherit intelligent traditions, and, broken in early to current practice, you find yourself in a position to advance it later, for market gardening is an art, a science that can only be acquired through persevering effort, intelligent study and consummate experience. III. PREJUDICE, ROUTINE. - Many farmers are unfortunately too prone to prejudice and routine, a tradition that in some regions is handed down from generation to generation, and always faithfully observed. For example, many market gardeners claim that, for certain seedlings to be successful, they must be sown on the day of or the day after a certain festival, follow the course of the moon, soak the seeds in rainwater or old wine, sow on an old moon so that the plants don't bolt, etc. All this is a mistake, an error, a mistake! Mistake, mistake, all these are prejudices, above which any sensible man must know how to rise. The lunar star has no influence whatsoever on success; what is required is that the soil be suitably prepared, then sow in good conditions, and you will always succeed. 8 The description we are about to give of each type of plant is the fruit of serious and reliable observations; almost all the varieties we mention have been cultivated, experimented and studied by us. We have adopted an alphabetical description, which is better than botanical classification by family, which can only be understood by those already familiar with the science. In addition to the origin of the plants, we describe their cultivation in the open ground, in its various forms and adapted to different climates; the early cultivation of the most common plants; how to harvest the seeds, their germination period; the diseases and animals harmful to each plant, and the means of destroying them; the uses and economic and nutritional properties of the plants. ASSINTHE Artemisia Absinthium L. Compositae. Native, perennial; multiplies from seed in spring or from splinters or clumps. Used as a seasoning and vermifuge. CULTIVATED GARLIC OR ORDINARY GARLIC (fig. 1). Allium sativum L. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - Linnaeus first gave Sicily as the homeland of Allium sativum, but later gave no origin. Several authors agree in denying Linné's assertions, but none of them gives a definite homeland for garlic. De Candollo claims that garlic was found spontaneously in the Kirghi desert of Soongarie in temperate western Asia. It has been cultivated for over 2,000 years. The English call it garlic, the Germans Knoblauch, the Basques baratchouria, the Bretons quinen, the Arabs thoum, the Chinese suan, the Spanish aïo, the Italian aglio, etc. CULTIVATION. - Cultivated garlic is one of the hardiest vegetable plants. FIG. 1: Common garlic. It can be grown in all types of soil and climate, with generally satisfactory success. The soils that seem best suited to its cultivation are lightly sandy open and marsh soils. Recent manuring with fresh manure seems to be contrary to its good cultivation, and arranges the bulbs to be greased in parts, i.e. instead of forming a rounded head at the top, the upper part of the cloves spreads out, bursting the film that covers them and no longer presenting any regularity in shape. Garlic of this nature, although losing none of its qualities, is depreciated by consumers. Garlic grown for a long time in the same soil gradually diminishes in volume, producing only walnut-sized bulbs with a dozen or so cloves. From time to time, garlic needs to be planted in different types of soil, and the seed renewed. The best time to plant garlic is from October 20 to November 20; you can continue until March, but the last plantings only produce round bulbs, sometimes quite large, which are highly appreciated on the markets, but not very profitable for the gardener. To get an early crop of green garlic, called aillet, you can start planting the cloves in September, and very thickly, 8 centimeters along the row and 15 centimeters between the rows; plant deep to get plenty of white. For good garlic planting, the soil must first be well ploughed with a spade. Smoke the soil with a well-consumed fertilizer, then mark out 1.10-metre-wide planks, dividing them into five rays; make a path 40 centimetres wide, then plant, taking the clove between thumb and forefinger and pushing it 3 or 4 centimetres perpendicularly into the soil, then raking it over to finish covering it. In some regions, notably in the West, garlic is planted with a flat or forked hoe, known in the country as a pic. The cloves are placed a few centimetres above the bottom of the ray; they are pushed in slightly to hold them in place; as the second ray is formed, the first is covered, and so on. In the seventh, no pods are used to form the pathway, but York sprouts, escarole, lettuce, etc. are planted. Before planting, all the small pods are set aside and planted separately, either for household use or for green sales; they are then placed at a short distance from each other and planted a little deeper to ensure plenty of white; they can even be buttered. When the plants have reached a height of 10 or 12 centimetres, the first light hoeing is carried out; a month later, a second, slightly deeper hoeing is carried out; then, around mid-April or in the first days of May, a third hoeing is carried out, but deep enough to plant lettuces, romaine and cabbages between each row of garlic. You can also sow beans, radishes, turnips, etc., or any other plants whose roots don't go deep into the soil. When the tops begin to change color, it is customary in some parts of the south-west to tie them in knots, as this is said to make the heads grow larger. This operation, which is nothing more than an old routine, produces no effect, and in no way increases the size of the bulbs. In our western and south-western regions, this is usually done in the second half of June and the first few days of July. Choose a nice, warm day. In light soils, weeding can be carried out fairly easily by hand, by pulling on the tops; but in strong, compact soils, we use the hoe or a small hoe. The bulbs are spread out as evenly as possible in the alleys or along the edges of the squares; they are arranged in equal rows; they are left like this for a few days, then turned over in the opposite direction. After this reshuffling, one day is enough to finish ripening the bulbs, at which point they need to be brought in. This work should be done in the morning, as the cool of the night has moistened the leaves and there is less risk of breaking them. Garlic is spread out in an attic or under a shed; you can even make uneven bunches, tying them two by two and hanging them in this state. As they ripen and dry, they are cleaned, counted and woven into bunches for sale on bad weather days. VARIETIES. - There are two perfectly distinct varieties of ordinary garlic. Early pink or black garlic. - The cloves are broad, thick, slightly elongated, obtuse and well arched; the skin enveloping the flesh is pale pink, sometimes grayish; this variety is more resistant to humidity than the following one, and is suitable for marshes where it reaches large dimensions. It is the most widely planted, productive and highly appreciated variety. Late white garlic. - A very valuable variety because of its slow growth rate.

can be stored for twelve to thirteen months. The pods are elongated, pointed, slightly curved and rarely very large; the tops are more elongated and spindly than in the previous variety, and the leaves more numerous; this is an excellent species. SEEDS. - Ordinary garlic has never produced seeds in our climate. DISEASES, PESTS. - Few diseases attack garlic. Sometimes, however, due to fertilizers and the nature of the soil, some heads rot and are affected by Rhizoctonia alluï. There's nothing you can do about this disease, which is due to the development of a parasitic fungus that starts at the base of the cloves, between the skins, in the form of numerous small white filaments, which then decompose them, giving off a putrid odor. Sometimes the leaves are affected by uredo or rust, but this disease is harmless. No animal attacks garlic, apart from slugs and snails which, when very young, will devour a few plants, but rarely. USES. - In cooking, garlic is used to enhance the flavor of dishes, making it an energetic condiment. In the south of France, people eat it raw with bread, drizzling it with oil, and consume a great deal of it. In the North, on the other hand, they use it sparingly. It is preserved in vinegar, like gherkins. Crushed and mixed with oil, egg yolk, salt and pepper, it makes up the aïoli of the Marseillais and is used to mask cold meats. Daily use of raw garlic, because of its pungent, acrid flavor, can cause stomach illness. Its highly viscous juice is used as a lut to glue pieces of broken porcelain. SPANISH GARLIC, ROCAMBOLE Allium Scorodoprasum Lin. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - It is not known exactly where the plant grows spontaneously: it is found around Paris, according to Cosson and Germain; in eastern France, according to Grenier and Godron; in the Alpes-Maritimes, according to Messrs Burnat and Ledebourt. It also grows in Russia, from Finland to the Crimea. It is not spontaneous in Spain, as its name might suggest. CULTURE. - Rocambole is a perennial plant, which differs from common garlic in that its bulbs become larger and its stems rise each year, bearing at their tips a number of small bulblets in place of seeds; for propagation, the use of cloves is preferable and quicker. Cultivation of this variety is the same as that of common garlic, with the difference that it is preferable to plant in January or the first fortnight of February, either for bulbils or cloves. If you don't want to harvest bulblets, pinch off the stems as soon as they appear. SEEDS. - Purplish flowers change into bulblets, which take the place of seeds. When the stems supporting them start to yellow, it's time to collect them. They are spread out in a well-ventilated, dry place, and when they appear sufficiently ripe, they are collected in boxes; they keep for a year. DISEASES, PESTS. - This variety suffers from the same diseases as ordinary garlic; insects have little or no effect. USES. - Although less pungent than common garlic, its uses are the same. ORIENTAL GARLIC Allium Ampeloprasum L. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - Oriental garlic is considered a variety of wild leek. In fact, this plant bears many similarities to the wild leek: same growth habit, fuller in all its parts, same more pronounced flavor with a slight garlic taste. This flavor is somewhat repugnant, which is probably why it is rarely cultivated. CULTIVATION. - Oriental garlic can be propagated either by sowing its seeds in January and February in good exposure: when the young plants have reached a suitable size, they are planted and treated like leeks; or by planting its cloves in autumn, in November, and treating them like common garlic. To keep the heads looking good, it's best to pull them out only every two years. SEEDS. - This variety goes to seed every year, and good seed is obtained from two-year-old plants. It keeps well for three years, but we recommend sowing current-year seed if possible. DISEASES, PESTS. - Like leeks, Oriental garlic is sometimes affected by a worm that gnaws at the heart. There is only one remedy for this: cut off the stems below the insect's ravages, and bury the cut parts far away. Rust or uredo sometimes affects it, but this disease is not dangerous. USES. - The cloves can be used like common garlic; the green tops or stems, like leeks. ALKEKENGE, COMESTIBLE PEQUER Physalis philadelphica Lamk; Physalis chenopodiifolia Lam; Physalis atriplicifolia Jacq; Physalis violacea Carr; Phy- salis edulis Sims. Solanaceae. ORIGIN. - According to M. Bois, it was reintroduced in 1873 or 1874 by M. Balarce, then Minister Plenipotentiary of the Argentine Confederation in Paris, who sent seeds to the Société d'Acclimatation under the name of petite tomate du Mexique. This plant was studied by M. Bossin, who gave it the name Physalis edulis, already applied to another species. In 1882, M. Carrière found it, without any indication of origin, in the garden of the Société d'Horticulture d'Étampes, and named it Physalis violacea. GROWING. - Sow in March, under a warm frame, in layers. The seed is lightly covered and sprouts in a few days. Once the seedlings have developed their first leaves, transplant them to a warm bed, to help them branch out and grow hair. In May, we pull them up with their rootballs and set them at 0.60 in all directions, preferably in recently ploughed and copiously smoked soil. When the plants have grown sufficiently, a stake is placed at each foot, in order to attach and support the numerous branches, which can reach a height of 1 metre or more. A heavy mulch is laid around the plants, and they are watered copiously throughout the summer, hoeing deeply and often, especially at the beginning. When the stems have reached the desired development, they are pinched off. large quantity of small, smooth, round fruits (fig. 2), greenish at first, then light yellow when ripe. These fruits, covered by the calyx, which is purplish next to the stalk, must be picked as soon4. as they come into contact with it, otherwise the calyx will burst at the top and, due to the weakness of the stalk, the fruit will become heavy when it reaches this size, detach easily and fall at the slightest shock. It is therefore important to look after them every day, so that they can be picked fresh and in good condition. SEEDS. - To harvest the seeds, select a few beautiful, ripe fruits, place them in a warm place and, when they begin to rot, take out the seeds, wash them and dry them in the shade. They keep for eight years. We know from experience that, when this plant has been cultivated in a garden, it is rare to lose the species; there are always a few fruits that fall and whose seeds rise the following year. DISEASES, PESTS. - We know of no particular diseases that attack this plant. Slugs and snails devour it when it is young. USES. - In France, the various varieties of cockerel are not much appreciated; only in the Midi region are they eaten raw. In Spain, Germany and Switzerland, however, they can be found on the best tables. Pickled in vinegar, like gherkins, they can replace them; in fact, this is the main use we had for them in the public establishment where we ran the cultivation for a few years; the patients were very fond of these fruits, and most of them preferred them to other fruits pickled in vinegar. You can also make a very good jam by choosing absolutely ripe fruit and adding sugar of equal weight, lemon, orange peel, vanilla, etc.; reduce to three-quarters. ALKEKENGE OFFICINAL, COQUERET OFFICINAL Physalis officinalis Mœnch. Native perennial plant, found spontaneously in most of France. We found it in abundance, especially in the vineyards around Cognac (Charente); in some places, the soil was covered with it. The farmers of Charente do not like this plant and destroy it without mercy; they call it coqurou. USES. - We have known several connoisseurs who cultivate the officinal cockle for the beauty of its fruits, which are cherry-red when ripe; these fruits, which are eaten in certain regions, are generally known by the names of "cerise de Juif", "cerise de Mahon", "cerise d'hiver", "mirabelle de Corse", "coccigrolle", "baguenaude", "herbe à cloque", "physalide", etc., etc... But this species is most useful as a medicinal plant. The leaves, flowers and roots are aperitive; the fruits are diuretic. In some parts of France, the fruit is used to color butter red. ANETH A nethum graveolens L. Umbelliferae. Annual plant of southern Europe. Sow outdoors in spring. Seeds are used to flavor pickles and other preserves; leaves are used like fennel. ANGELICA OFFICINALE (fig. 3). Angelica Archangelica Lin. Archangelica officinalis Hoffmann. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - Native to the Alps, where it grows at low altitudes, particularly in damp locations. FIG. 3 - Angelica officinalis. CULTIVATION - A perennial, or rather a triennial in our cultivation, angelica thrives best in deep, cool soil, fertilized with good, strong fertilizers. Sow from the second half of March to July, in nurseries, in racks. Cover the seed sufficiently with loose soil or compost. Water copiously when necessary, thin out, hoe and weed. In autumn or the following spring, plant them in rows 10 cm apart in all directions. The tips of the leaves are trimmed back slightly, without damaging the roots. Water immediately after planting; a few days later, hoe deeply, as much as possible after a good rain. You can start harvesting leaves as early as the second year. In the third year, the plant goes to seed, and continues to do so every year. For this reason, it is customary to destroy plantations that have reached this age; it is claimed, with good reason, that the leaves develop much less when the plant goes to seed. A plantation of angelica can last ten years or more, and we know of some that have outlived this age, and which nevertheless, with care, produce very fine products. Angelica is grown mainly around Niort (Deux-Sèvres) and near Clermont-Ferrand, in Auvergne, as a large export crop; it is also grown extensively in Bohemia. In Auvergne, growers usually plant 15,000 plants per hectare, and harvest 11 to 12,000 kilos of fresh stems, plus the roots, which can be dried, and even the leaves, which keep well once dried. It's a very profitable product, provided you have good, deep, moist soil that can be submerged if necessary. VARIETY. - Angelica has not produced any sub-varieties as such. The following varieties form distinct races that are grown in Europe only in botanical gardens. Angelica atro-purpurea Lin. - From America, where it replaces our Angelica officinalis, especially in the United States, where it is highly esteemed. Angelica lucida Lin. - Also from America, where it is much sought-after, especially in Canada. Same properties as Angelica officinalis. SEEDS. - The plant does not go to seed until the third year. As they detach easily from their receptacle, it's a good idea to collect the umbels as they turn yellow, and lay them out on cloths in the shade to dry. They keep for one to two years. DISEASES, PESTS. - There are few diseases that attack angelica; sometimes uredo or rust claims a few victims. Snails and slugs attack plants when they are young, but they don't seem to be too fond of them. Aphids, on the other hand, are more terrible, attacking the flowering stems as they are born and leaving them only when they die, i.e. when they are completely dry. The only way to combat them is to spray them often with nicotine reduced to 3 or 4 degrees. USES. - The highly aromatic angelica seed is used by confectioners to make highly prized liqueurs. Stalks and stems preserved in sugar make highly sought-after preserves. We even make a spirituous liqueur known as angelica ratafia. Here's how it's made: fresh angelica stems and bitter almonds are macerated in brandy, mixed with sugar syrup and filtered after a few hours' rest. It is said that Lapps eat the leaves, root and seeds. The stems are used to make an excellent cream, which is prepared as follows: 250 grams of fresh stems are cut into small pieces and infused for six weeks in 3 liters of brandy with 4 grams of cinnamon, 2 cloves, 6 grams of nutmeg and 1 kilogram of sugar melted in three-quarters of a liter of water. This liqueur is excellent for the stomach, and stimulates digestion. Stems also make very good jam: cut to length, throw into almost boiling water, remove from heat and leave to infuse for an hour, then remove the epidermis, i.e. the first skin. Then boil them until they are white and tender, let them drain, and throw them into a boiling sugar syrup two or three times. Leave to cool, then boil the syrup again the next day, add the stems and leave for twelve hours, remove and dry. We obtain 1 kilogram of candied stems with 185,500 of fresh stems. These candied stems are used extensively in pastry-making, and especially in making gingerbread. As for real angelica liqueur, here's the formula: Angelica seeds... ... ... ... . 30 grams Fresh angelica stems ... ... ... . 30 - Bitter almonds, blanched and crushed ... . 50 - White sugar ... ... ... . Alcohol 600... . Water ... ... ... ... . 1kg,500 ... . 6 liters ... . 1 liter. The root, which is the most active part, is used in many pharmaceutical preparations, notably in angelica wine. ANISE Pimpinella Anisum L. Umbelliferae. Oriental annual. Sow in spring in a well-placed spot. Seeds are used as a vermifuge and as a condiment in making liqueurs, sweets, etc. ARMOISE Artemisia vulgaris L. Compositae. Native perennial. Sows in spring in nurseries. It can also be propagated by separating clumps. Leaves are sometimes used as a condiment or decoction. GARDEN ARROW Atriplex hortensis L. Chenopodea. ORIGIN. - Annual, native to northern Europe and Siberia. Cultivated for less than two thousand years, it has become naturalized in Europe and in some parts of France. It grows abundantly in gardens and fields, mainly in topsoil, rubble and embankments, where it sometimes reaches considerable growth. In France, it is known by several names, the best known being: arrode, arronse, belle-dame, bonne-dame, érode, follette, irible, prude-femme, glorieuse, rouble, armol, etc. E. BERGER, Vegetable plants. CULTURE. - Garden arroche is not difficult to grow in the right soil, and succeeds everywhere, provided fertilizer is plentiful and the soil is sufficiently loosened. It is best sown in place, from March to August, in shallow rays 30 to 40 centimetres apart; sow lightly and cover lightly; and, if sowing during the heat of summer, mulch and water abundantly. When the young plant has developed its first three or four leaves, thin out and transplant if necessary, then give the first light hoeing; this operation should be repeated often, as should weeding. As arrowroot sets seed quickly, it's a good idea to sow often, at least every twenty days, so as not to run out. This plant freezes easily, and the first frosts destroy it; green arrowroot is the most resistant. VARIETIES. - There are four main varieties of edible arrowroot: Green arrowroot (Atriplex hortensis). - Typical species with dark-green, thick, fat, rounded foliage and strong, angular stems; very vigorous plant, not widely cultivated; the blond variety is preferable. Arroche blonde (Atriplex hortensis lutea). - The best and most commonly cultivated, and generally much appreciated; it's just a variety of the previous one; yellow-green leaves, very fleshy and fat. Red arrowroot (Atriplex rubra). - Stem and leaves are a beautiful carmine red. This color disappears with cooking; however, to remove it, it is a good idea to boil it in a first water. Less prized than the blond variety. Dark red arrowroot (Atriplex ruberrima). - Stems and leaves are a beautiful bright carmine red. This variety is rarely grown in the kitchen garden. It's best thought of as an ornamental plant, producing a very attractive effect when grouped in clumps. When cultivated for seed, these varieties should be kept far apart, as cross-fertilization is rapid and colors fade. SEEDS. - First-season seedlings ripen their seeds within the year. These seeds detach from the plant with extreme ease, and the slightest wind blows them away. To avoid this inconvenience, the uprights should be collected before the seeds are fully ripe. Once dry, the seeds are detached by beating them with a small flexible stick, or better still, by passing the stems between the two hands. They keep well for five or six years. Each gram contains around 250 seeds. DISEASES. ANIMAL PESTS. - Green and sometimes blond arrowroot sometimes suffer from a disease similar to powdery mildew, which develops on rose leaves. Affected leaves are stopped in their growth, curled, curled up, twisted, and the plant becomes stunted and no longer grows. This disease seems to develop on suffering plants, but is fortunately quite rare. Affected plants should be uprooted as soon as possible, and disposed of or buried. There is perhaps no vegetable plant, especially when young, that slugs and snails are more fond of, even devouring the root. There are even soils where it is hardly possible to grow it. These animals must be destroyed by all known means. USES. - Arrowroot is used in cooking to make herb soups. It is used in the same way as spinach, and many people prefer it to spinach. It is mixed with sorrel to correct its acidity. ARTICHAUT Cynara Scolymus Lin. Compounds. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant. According to De Candolle, it comes from the Cardoon (Cynara Cardunculus) found in southern Europe, northern Africa, the Canary Islands and Madeira. Moreover, he says, the artichoke has not been found outside gardens, and as the Mediterranean region, home of all Cynaras, has been thoroughly explored, it can be asserted that it exists nowhere spontaneously. CULTIVATION. - Artichokes thrive best in deep, well-smoked, slightly damp soil, and liquid fertilizers are ideal. The latter is less common and less practical than the former, as the plants that emerge from it rarely possess the qualities of the varieties from which they came: degeneration occurs easily; however, in a sowing of a certain size, there are plants equivalent to the seed-bearing type. This means of propagation is only useful for obtaining new varieties, or for countries where eyelets cannot be transported. Sow in February and March in pots, under frames, on a warm bed; or in April or May, in the field. Small holes 20 to 30 centimetres wide are prepared, filled with half-rotted manure and packed well. Cover with good loose soil, then sow five or six seeds per hole. Water immediately to facilitate germination, and when the young plants are strong enough, thin out, leaving three in each hole, hoe FIG.74. - Artichoke. and water. Seedlings, sown in pots, are planted under the same conditions. Whether sown in the field, in pots or in nurseries, many plants begin to bear fruit in August or September; you can then make a judicious choice of the best varieties by pulling out all the inferior ones; it is only in the second year, however, that it is easier to judge the varieties you have obtained; those you keep will then be multiplied by eyeletting. 4. Carnation is usually carried out towards the end of March, April or May, depending on the climate, after the old plants have been dethatched, i.e. cleared of the clods of earth or straw that surrounded them to protect them from frost. All the smallest carnations are removed, leaving only three or four of the finest for production. The best carnations that are removed and destined for new plantings must be carefully detached from the stump. Before planting, the cut is cooled a little with a knife, and the tips of the leaves are trimmed. The carnation is planted immediately, and a certain number of plants are set aside in the nursery to replace the missing ones in July and August. An old routine practiced by many market gardeners is to replant in September the base of stems that have ceased to produce, in other words, the old cores. They are planted in situ, or better still in a nursery, to be replanted the following spring. In this way, you can obtain vigorous plants that are sure to grow again, but care must be taken when detaching the stems to retain a good portion of the stump. This is a good procedure to imitate. Whatever the propagation method, the land to be planted must be recently ploughed deeply, and smoked copiously. Plant with a chalk line or forked hoe at 90 centimetres or 1 metre in all directions, and set two or three eyelets together at 10 centimetres in the shape of a triangle. Firmly pack the soil around the roots and water throughout the summer, weeding and hoeing frequently. In a market garden, artichokes are rarely planted alone; cabbages, romaine and even white onions are intercropped. When the old plants have yielded their first crop in the second half of July, cut off the stems and remove the dry leaves. Then water copiously, or irrigate if possible. This way, you'll still have a half-harvest in autumn. After this last harvest, the stems that have produced are also removed and, in November, they are worked into a strong cone of earth around each tuft, compacted well with the back of the spade. Some authors recommend surrounding them with straw or manure, an excellent system but impractical for large quantities. This method is only practical for the north, west, east and part of central France; the south-west from Bor- deaux and the south don't need this precaution, artichokes rarely freeze in these regions, although the winter of 1890-91 destroyed some plantations. In the last few days of March or the beginning of April, if the weather looks like it's going to be fine, we start, smoke and plow with a spade to bury the manure well. We then proceed with carnationing as described above. For an artichoke plantation to produce good yields, it must be renewed every four years, or five at the most. This operation must be carried out partially, so that production is staggered. This method, so well understood, is practiced by gardeners in the north of France, but not in the south-west, where, in some regions, artichoke plantations are kept for ten, twelve or even more years. So what happens? the produce becomes increasingly inferior in volume and, as a result, depreciated and less sold on our markets. To increase fruit size, we recommend splitting the stem in four immediately below the receptacle and inserting two pieces of wood or reed crosswise. This system is used by some growers in Perpignan, who obtain enormous artichokes in this way. VARIETIES. - At least forty varieties of artichoke are known, taking their names from the localities where they are most commonly grown. Among the best are: Artichaut gros vert de Laon. - Very large, fleshy, fertile, half-aged, scales spread at the top. This is the species most commonly grown around Paris. *Artichoke from Brittany. - Very large, excessively fleshy, white, very broad scales, very vigorous and productive plant, worthy of recommendation. Artichoke from Niort. - Very vigorous, very productive, seemingly derived from the previous variety, of which it has all the characteristics, widely grown in Deux-Sèvres, Poitou and part of Anjou. Artichaut vert de Provence. - Very early, medium-sized, very tender, not very fleshy, excellent for eating with pepper. The plant is more sensitive to cold than the preceding varieties; grown extensively in the Midi and Bordeaux regions, among the vines. Long purple artichoke or gray artichoke. - A fairly vigorous plant producing elongated, loose apples with loosely packed scales. Very early, this is the variety that is grown in large quantities in the Pyrénées-Orientales region and is shipped almost year-round to Paris. Purple artichoke. - Very early, small-headed, widespread in Charentes and Spain, very productive, excellent for eating raw. Artichoke from Macau (Gironde). - In our opinion, this is just a variety of the Camus de Bretagne, highly esteemed on the Bordeaux markets. Fairly large green, very tender, with tight, wide scales. The plant is vigorous and fairly cold-resistant. In the Médoc, at Macau, it is grown mainly among the vines. Saint Laud oblong artichoke. - Very large apples. Artichoke from Brittany. - Round heads, purple at first, then taking on a coppery hue, dwarf plant, fairly large, pointed scales. Roscoff artichoke. - Sweet Genoa artichoke. - Purple artichoke from Tuscany. - Widely cultivated around Florence and in Sicily. SEEDS. - To harvest the seed, let the first fruit rise, i.e. the one in the center, which is always more beautiful and better nourished than the others that follow. It should not be picked until it is ripe and almost dry. Seeds keep for six years. USES. - By blanching the base of the petioles in the same way as cardoons, they can be eaten in the same way as cardoons, as the flavor is much the same. When the friuts have reached half their size, they can be covered with a thick canvas, straw or moss bag, to keep them in the dark. After a few days, the fruit turns a bleached white and can be used for a variety of culinary purposes, with an exquisite taste. The receptacle is eaten either cooked or raw. The dried flowers, commonly known as hay or thistle, are used to curdle milk. As the plant is rich in tannin, it is used by buttermakers, who prefer to use the flower heads. Dyers sometimes use the leaves in a decoction. The leaves dye bismuth-treated wool golden yellow. Burnt stems yield a lot of potash. ASPARAGUS Asparagus officinalis Lin. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant, native to southern Europe. Grows spontaneously in many parts of France, notably on the Rhône and Loire islands. Asparagus has been cultivated since time immemorial, and the Greeks considered it a delicacy. The Romans sought it out with a kind of passion, especially the Ravenna variety, three of which, according to Pliny, were enough to weigh a pound. It was La Quintinie, head gardener of the Versailles kitchen garden under Louis XIV, who devised a way of growing asparagus. CULTIVATION - Asparagus thrives best in sandy soils with a significant clay content, on a healthy, permeable subsoil free of stagnant moisture. Asparagus is propagated by sowing the seed from February 15 to April, either broadcast, in beds, or better still in rays, spaced Om,40 apart. The seeds are covered with Om,04 or Om,05 of loose earth or light loam, and usually emerge within fifteen to twenty days; a few weeks later, the young plants are thinned out. Hoe and weed several times a year, and water during hot spells. Young asparagus should be used for planting after a year's sowing, as it is at this age that they will suffer the least from transplanting, and will therefore be the most successful (fig. 5). Two-year-old claws are still very good. After this period, I would not recommend planting, as older asparagus claws do not recover well, and you have to come back several times to get a complete plantation. Care must be taken when pulling out the claws, so as not to damage the roots too much; to do this, use a fork or a forked hoe, but don't be afraid to open up a good trench. In many regions, growers have the bad habit of planting too deep, with the result that the produce obtained is always inferior in size and quantity. This is because this plant, like any other, thrives and succeeds best in soil that is sufficiently smoky and, above all, warmed by the sun; and it's not by digging pits 50 or 60 centimetres deep that these conditions are met. So what happens? The soil in which the claws are to grow, being new and never disturbed or amended, receives the sun's rays only indirectly or, to put it another way, never at all; the result is poor vegetation. Here's M. Vilmorin's opinion on the subject! Generally speaking, we can say that the most important point, and the one on which success mainly depends, is not to remove the asparagus claw from the influence of heat, and to place it at the same time in an environment where it can find the food it needs in abundance. The claw must therefore be planted at a shallow depth, and covered with a fairly thick layer of soil only during the bedding season, when it is absolutely necessary to obtain asparagus of sufficient length". There are no special rules for planting asparagus; it is done according to the layout of the land, either in isolated rows between the vine rows, as is often done in the Gironde region; in rows along the walls, or in squares, or in beds. As this last method is recognized as the most practical, and the most widely adopted, we will describe it below. In autumn or early winter, the land to be planted is deeply ploughed. 1 Vilmorin, Les Plantes potagères. When it's time to plant, i.e. in February and March, and not in November as we've sometimes seen, we start by marking the spot where each bed is to be planted. The 1-meter planks, intended to receive the claws, are dug 15 to 20 centimeters deep, no more; the soil is thrown back into the 1.50-meter space left free for the path. After working the bottom of the pits, spread a 5-centimeter layer of well-consumed manure or potting soil, dried river mud or any other fertilizer; tamp it down by walking on it, cover with 5 centimeters of loose soil and level it off. Then draw two lines 25 centimetres from the edges, or 50 centimetres apart, and plant the claws 90 centimetres along the line, in a chessboard pattern. It's important, when placing them, to form a small pyramid of soil under each one, to give the roots a chance to sink in and seat the claw. The young roots are compacted with the hand to make them adhere to the soil, then covered with 4 or 5 centimetres of loose soil; the top is levelled, as are the intervals of the beds used for planting romaine, cabbage, radishes, turnips, etc., but the time needed for them to develop must be calculated, so that the intervals are free at the time when the beds need to be loaded or unloaded, fertilizers distributed and so on. Other care for the claws in this first year consists of frequent weeding and hoeing. In November or December, the stems are cut to 13 or 15 centimetres above ground level, then the soil is removed to a few centimetres above the level of the claw; a small layer of manure is spread on E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 3 each bed with a small layer of fat manure or good potting soil, and leave to overwinter in this state. In March of the following year, a good ploughing is carefully carried out, so as not to damage the roots; a little fertilizer is added, and the whole is buried in the soil; a small thickness of earth is added. The plantation spends the summer in this state, receiving the same care as the first year: weeding, hoeing, mulching, if useful; during hot spells, we water any plants that appear to be suffering. However, the heat hardly tires them at all in the first year. In the third year, the same operations are carried out, and in the spring, the plants are mounded more firmly; about 25 centimetres of soil is spread over the whole bed; the surface is levelled, as well as the bottom of the gaps. You can then start to produce a good small harvest. But it's not until the fourth year that a general harvest can be made. Thereafter, the same care is taken with cultivation; each year, more ridging is done to obtain longer asparagus. As for fertilizing, once the soil has been sufficiently amended, fertilizing should only be carried out every two years; in this case, in the year when fertilizing is not carried out, watering should be done with liquid manure; this is a very good operation which activates vegetation enormously. Planting between vines, as is often done in the South-West, particularly in the Gironde region around Bazas, is done in the same way, with the only difference being that there is only one row of claws per joualle; other care is exactly the same. A well-managed asparagus plantation can last from fourteen to sixteen years, producing magnificent products. However, when we pull up old plantations, despite the best we can do, we must be careful not to plant them again; this would be a bad operation. It's when the shoots start to appear above ground that it's time to pick them. This operation must be carried out with care, so as not to damage the new shoots. A special tool in the shape of a gouge is used, which is slid as perpendicularly as possible alongside the asparagus to be cut; once it has reached a certain depth, it is cut off. Many growers claim that it's better to remove the asparagus by hand or with a wooden spatula, and to split it at the base. This is how many good growers in Argenteuil operate.
