FORCED CULTIVATION. - Asparagus can be forced from October to February, in the open ground or on warm beds. In the open ground, forcing can only give good results if the planting has been done with this intention. The claws should be much closer together, so that no ground is lost; 30 or 40 centimetres in all is sufficient. Two or three rows are planted per board, depending on the width of the trunks to be placed on them. You don't start forcing until the fourth year; to do this, you dig 50-centimeter-wide, 40-centimeter-deep ditches on each side of the board, which you fill with good, well-packed horse manure from the stable; as you dig, you throw some of the earth back onto the board, place the chests with their panels, and form a good stove around them, which you often have to reshuffle and add new manure each time. Planks that have been forced the first year cannot be forced the second; this would compromise the harvest and ruin the claws. The same bed should therefore only be forced every two years. Forced cultivation on a warm bed is easier, gives better results, and is quicker and less expensive. But you need to have plenty of claws at your disposal, which is easy if you sow a few rows every year. Three- to five-year-old seedlings are the best for this type of cultivation. Old clumps that you want to destroy still give a good harvest. At the same time as we have indicated, we prepare good layers 40 to 60 centimetres thick. Place the boxes on top, add a little manure on the inside, tamping it down with your feet, then cover with 5 or 7 centimetres of a good mixture, half vegetable garden soil, half potting soil. Cover with a frame, and leave in this state until the layer has burned down; one week is enough. The claws are then placed upright, leaning against each other, with the collar at the same height. The ends of roots that are too long are trimmed back a little, and the soil is slid in with a small wooden palette; then water lightly, and cover with 5 or 6 centimetres of compost or more, depending on whether you want long, white asparagus. Some growers cover with moss, wood bran, even sand, etc. Eight to twelve days after these operations, the shoots begin to appear; they are cut as they develop. Care should be taken with the layers, putting heaters on them when they cool, and covering them with mats during the day, depending on whether you want green or white asparagus. VARIETIES. - Several varieties are grown, taking their names from the localities where they are widely cultivated, but in reality there are only two main breeds: green asparagus and violet asparagus. All those known as Ulm, Besançon, Polish, Marchienne, Ghent, Vendôme, Dutch, Bazas, Argenteuil, etc. asparagus are descended from these two races; all these varieties are improved by cultivation, and certainly have a special and distinctive merit. But it's the same with this plant as with many others: one variety produces magnificent products in certain localities, and very poor ones in others; moreover, all plants from seed are subject to sometimes singular variations. The growers of Argenteuil, who have been cultivating this plant for a long time, have succeeded by successive selections in improving the purple asparagus in a remarkable way. The resulting varieties have long been recognized as the best. SEEDS. - To harvest asparagus seeds, we choose the best shoots, when fertilization has taken place and the ovaries containing the seeds are beginning to appear; we put a stake on them, so that the wind doesn't break them; then, when autumn comes, after the first frosts, we pick up the ovaries, which have taken on a beautiful minium red color; we crush them in water, the seeds precipitate to the bottom, and the skins swim to the surface; it's therefore easy to get rid of them. The seeds are then spread out on cloths or boards, and exposed to the sun for a while, or better still in a well-ventilated place, in a draught where they dry out completely. They are then packed in small canvas or paper bags. They keep well for two years, but it's always best to sow the previous year's seed. DISEASES, NUISSIBLE ANIMALS. - We know of no disease that attacks asparagus. Sometimes, however, asparagus claws rot in autumn; this is due to the plant's poor constitution or to overly damp soil. In damp autumn soils, we recommend not covering with manure at this time, to avoid this disease. Slugs and snails are very fond of young asparagus shoots, gnawing at them and sometimes digging holes in them. These animals must therefore be destroyed by all known means. Geoffroy's Crioceris rubra is the most terrible enemy of asparagus. It's a small red insect, speckled with small gray and white spots, known as the asparagus tiger. The beetle lays two eggs, one in spring and the other in June and July. After the female has been fertilized, she wanders around the stems, looking for a place to lay her eggs. Each egg emerges from the body, coated with a material that sticks to it. After a fortnight, these eggs hatch into a multitude of greenish, dirty larvae, which devour the softer parts of the asparagus. It is in the larval stage that the locust does most of its damage, mainly because of the large numbers involved. When you notice that a patch of asparagus has been invaded by this insect, you must try to destroy it. To do this, take an airtight container into which a little oil has been poured; place the container under the plant, shake the stalks lightly, and all the insects fall in; the oil prevents them from escaping, so they are crushed. White grubs are also a terrible enemy of asparagus in certain soils. Destroying it is difficult, as there is only one way to do it, and that is to crush it. All the means that have been advocated, such as lime ash, tobacco juice, sulfur or other ingredients, have never given good results. Moles do not destroy asparagus, but they do wreak havoc, digging underground galleries that often expose their claws. They can be easily destroyed by placing wooden traps in freshly dug galleries. USES. - In France, white asparagus is eaten just as it appears. In Portugal and Italy, asparagus is eaten only after it has been left to green up, i.e. when it is a dozen centimetres above the ground. Asparagus root is one of the five aperitive roots, often used as a diuretic. The root's active ingredient is asparagine. Young asparagus shoots, known as tips, provide two medicines: syrup and extract. In Provence, the stalks are used to filter wine coming out of the vat. By fermentation and distillation, asparagus berries yield a very pure alcohol that makes excellent table liqueur. AUBERGINE or MÉLONGÈNE Solanum Melongena Lin. Solanum esculentum Lun. Solanaceae. ORIGIN. - Annual plant, native to India, known locally as Bringèle, Marignan, Mayenne, Béringène, Bréhème, Mélanzanne, Œuf végétal, Pon- deuse and in Gascon dialect as Biédaze or Viédaze, etc. CULTIVATION. - The eggplant is propagated from seed, which is sown on a bed from January to the end of March. Cover the seed with about a centimeter of light, well-sieved potting soil; water and cover with panels; you can even leave them in the dark while germination takes place, by placing straw mats over the panels. Germination usually takes eighty or ninety hours. From this point onwards, the mats are removed, the plants are shaded in case of sunburn, and air is gradually added to prevent the plant from over-extending itself. Around four weeks after sowing, the seedlings will have sufficiently developed their second leaf. They are transplanted onto a warm bed prepared in advance and filled with 10 centimetres of a good mix of potting soil and loam. Place them 4 or 5 centimetres apart. As soon as they've been transplanted, water them and keep them smothered for two or three days to help them take root. Air is then given whenever the temperature permits, and around April 20 the panels can be removed, at least in the South-West; in colder regions, it's better to wait until May, but plenty of air must be given. Eggplants do very well, preferably in warm locations. In the vegetable garden, choose the best exposed squares for planting. In a well-sheltered bed, along a wall, it succeeds perfectly, but needs copious watering in summer, otherwise only small fruits are obtained. Eggplants can only be planted in the first half of May. Before then, as the soil is not sufficiently warmed, the young plants suffer and remain without any vegetation. There are several ways to set up the plants. Some market gardeners prepare the ground in advance, sowing radishes, lettuces or other vegetables, and when it's time to plant the eggplants, they plant among the other crops. These plants are harvested before they can harm the eggplants. The best way to plant eggplants is to spade and smoke the soil, which is then divided into plots 1.10 m wide. Mark out three radii on each one, observing a path 40 to 50 centimetres wide, then plant in a chessboard pattern 40 to 45 centimetres along the line, with a hoe, keeping a good clod at each foot, or with a strong planter. Water immediately and, a few days later, spread a good mulch over all the beds. Other care consists of weeding, hoeing and, above all, copious watering during the summer; liquid fertilizers are particularly suitable for this plant. We cut back the lowest branches, leaving three or four of the best placed, which should be pinched back when they have two or three flowers each. This is the best way to prune them, as experience has shown. VARIETIES. - We know several varieties: Early dwarf purple eggplant. - Low-growing plant, rarely exceeding 30 to 35 centimetres in height, well-branched from the base; medium-sized fruit of a beautiful purple-black color, very early and of excellent quality. Very early purple eggplant. - A new variety, derived from the previous one, of which it has more or5. less the same characteristics; fruits are smaller and more plentiful; particularly suitable for early cultivation. Long purple eggplant (fig. 6). - Excellent variety FIG. 6 - Long violet eggplant. fairly early, producing beautiful, superb fruit, very productive, the most popular on the market. Round purple eggplant - Very old variety producing large, elongated fruit; late, but very productive. Péhin black eggplant. - Round, dark purple, almost black, as well as part of the stem; semi-early, very productive and of good quality. Eggplant monstrueuse de New-York. - Improved variety of the old round one, producing enormous fruit; late and of mediocre quality. There are several other varieties of eggplant, but these should be considered more as collector's items than as varieties to be cultivated for profit. Among the best are Eggplant panachée de la Guadeloupe. - Esteemed by Creoles; White Aubergine (Solanum ovigerum), or egg plant. - More of an ornamental plant, it is said to be very unhealthy. Yellow eggplant; green eggplant, etc. SEEDS. - Sometimes, when the year is rainy in autumn, eggplant has difficulty ripening its fruit. So, when you want to harvest the seed, choose the best fruit early and let it ripen until the first frost. Then pick it, and when it starts to rot, take out the seed, wash it and dry it in the shade. It keeps well for four years. According to Vilmorin, one gram contains around 250 seeds. pests, harmful animals. - Sometimes, a few plants wither and desiccate almost suddenly: this is blanc or meunier, a cryptogamic disease, well known to market gardeners, which attacks the roots and destroys the plant; no effective remedy has been found. Sometimes, uredo attacks the leaves and fruit and, without destroying the plantation, does great harm to the plant by stopping its development. Well-dosed Bordeaux mixture is an excellent remedy. Slugs and snails are very fond of young fruit, which they partly devour by forming bizarre arabesques on the skin, which they seem to prefer to the flesh. They must be hunted down regularly to destroy them. USES. - Eggplant is a laxative and not very nourishing food. It should only be used when the fruit is perfectly ripe, otherwise it may cause discomfort through its pungency, due to the large amount of solanine it contains. In southern countries, eggplants are cooked on the grill over a low heat, after being cut into slices. They are then gradually soaked in oil or fresh butter, with a little salt and pepper, garlic and a few fine herbs. It can also be baked in the oven between two courses, making it an excellent dish. In our part of the world, it's eaten pan-fried like porcini mushrooms, with the same aftertaste, as a stew, in a white sauce, and so on. A few hours before cooking, we recommend sprinkling it with salt and pepper to draw out its water. It can also be dried: cut into thin slices, remove the skin and the spongy part. Throw it into boiling water for a few minutes, then remove it and lay it out on racks or linen. Dry in the sun or in an oven, and when the pieces are completely dry, store them in a healthy place. To use, fry in lukewarm water. Young fruit can be pickled in vinegar, like gherkins. AURONE Artemisia Abrotanum L. Compositae. Perennial, frutescent. Reproduces from seeds sown in April-May or from cuttings, which grow well in spring; for this, care must be taken to bring in old plants in autumn; the plant is not resistant to northern winters. Used like wormwood. BASELLE Basella. Chenopodea. ORIGIN. - East Indies. In America, where it is widely cultivated, it is known as Brèdes d'Angole. In France, it is known by several names: Epinard du Malabar, Epinard d'Amérique, Epinard de Chine, Epinard des Indes. CULTIVATION. - Baselle is not widely cultivated; this is a mistake, as it is easy to grow and can be very useful in summer, when the spinach it so advantageously replaces so easily goes to seed. In its native country, baselle is a biennial; but in our region, it's as an annual that it should be treated; perhaps in the Midi, on the shores of the Mediterranean, it could be considered as in its country of origin, i.e. biennial. Very easy to grow, Baselle thrives in any good, warm, well-smoked soil. Sow in a bed in March and transplant in May, always choosing the best exposure. It can also be sown after May 15 in rows 40 cm apart. Watering should be copious and regular. As the stems of this plant are somewhat voluble, for best production, they should be twigged with branches that are well branched at the base. For seedlings planted in rows, if they are too thick, thin them out to leave a space of at least Om, 10 between each plant. VARIETIES. - There are several varieties, almost all edible; the best are : Red Baselle and White Baselle, the most popular. Very broad-leaved Chinese Baselle (Basella cordifolia Lamk.), not widely cultivated. SEEDS. - Placed in a well-exposed spot, Baselle produces an abundance of good seeds. As they ripen only successively, they should be picked as they appear to be good; as soon as they are picked, they should be laid out in the sun for a few hours, then dried and ripened in the shade. They keep well for five years; 30 grams contain 1010 seeds; a liter weighs 460 grams. pests and animals. - Snails and slugs are very fond of young leaves; when seedlings start to emerge, sprinkle them with soot, ashes or powdered lime to prevent them from being eaten. Flea beetles sometimes attack baselle, especially in dry years. USES. - The leaves, which are thick and fleshy, are used in the same way as spinach; they have a finer, less bland taste, and are even said to be easily digestible and healthier than spinach leaves. In India, the fruits of the red baselle are used to dye Indian cloth, as in Senegal, but this dye is not very strong. BASILIC Ocimum Basilicum Labiatae. ORIGIN. - India, in dry, arid places. CULTIVATION. - Basil is not an essential plant, but it should have a place in the vegetable garden. Sow in February or March on warm or hot beds, or in April or May, in the open ground. You can also sow in well-drained pots or crates, which can be moved at will; emergence generally takes place in a short time, from forty to sixty hours, depending on the warmth of the bed or atmosphere. When the young plants have two leaves, they are transplanted onto another layer, watered and covered with panels to facilitate recovery. Once this has taken place, air is gradually added, and after a few days, the panels are removed. In May, we plant them in the open ground in a good warm exposure, in beds or, better still, in borders at Om,15 or Om,20 in all directions. During hot spells, water sufficiently and, to keep stems fresh and tender, cut them often, especially to prevent them from flowering. VARIETIES. - There are several varieties of basil; the best for the vegetable garden are : Lettuce-leaf basil. - Very good plant, with broad, thick leaves; very fragrant. Basilie grand violet. - A highly recommendable variety; dark purple leaves and stem, less broad than the previous one; very fragrant. Basilie grand vert. - Typical species, with dark green leaves and stems; fragrant, very hardy. In the second category, we'd like to mention: Basilie frisé. - Aniseed basil. - Fine purple basil. - Stocky varieties, forming tight, compact clumps, suitable for pot cultivation. In the south-west, gardeners grow few others. Basil tree (Ocimum Basilicum). - A plant with a very pleasant fragrance, growing to a height of 50 or 60 centimeters, a very good variety for growing in pots. SEEDS. - A few plants are left to grow, and when the ears are ripe and turning from green to red, they are cut and spread out on a cloth which is exposed to the sun for a few hours. The ripe seeds detach easily and fall onto the cloth. They are collected and dried in the shade; 30 grams contain at least 24,000 seeds; a liter weighs 530 grams; germination lasts eight years. DISEASES, PESTS. - We know of no disease as such that attacks basil. Snails and slugs are very fond of it, especially when the plants are newborn. To prevent them from being eaten, sprinkle with soot, ash, quicklime or sulfur. USES. - Basil is used as a condiment and to flavor sauces, all kinds of dishes and especially peas. It is also used to smoke hams and perfume hot baths. In medicine, it is used in infusions like tea. It is also used in vulnerary alcohol. BETTERAVE Beta vulgaris Lin. Beta rapa Moq.-Tan. Chenopodea. ORIGIN. - Biennial plant believed to be derived from chard or pear. (See Poirée.) Moquin-Tandon has divided this genus into three main varieties: 1° Beta maritima, the type species, which grows in the Canary Islands, on the Mediterranean and Ocean shores; 2° Beta cycla, the cultivated chard pear. 3° Beta rapa, the fleshy-rooted beet varieties. CULTIVATION. - Strong, free soils, well fertilized with good consumable fertilizers, are particularly suitable for growing this plant; adding a notable proportion of faecal matter or liquid manure to these fertilizers will produce magnificent vegetation. Beet is sown from March to May, in rows, nurseries or in the field. Nursery sowing is generally the most common in gardens. The narrow end of the hoe is used to trace small rays, 5 to 6 centimetres deep, 40 centimetres apart, 4 per bed. After sowing, the rake is passed over the whole area to cover the seeds. If the soil is too strong, cover with sifted earth or potting soil to encourage emergence. For in-place sowing, draw rays at the same depth, but 60 centimetres apart. The seed is covered with the rake, and when the seedlings have four or five leaves, they are thinned out, hoeed and even watered if possible during hot spells. Some growers use ploughs or hoes to make large furrows and sow or transplant beet on top. This method, which is generally used in agriculture, seems to give good results; we have seen some remarkable crops grown in this way. The best way to grow beets in gardens is to sow them in nurseries and then transplant them in place, in beds of four rows, 40 centimetres apart; a 60-centimetre pathway is left. On the line, we plant at 30 or 35 centimetres, depending on the variety. For transplanting, take advantage of a dark, rainy day and water each plant immediately after planting. When removing nursery-raised plants for transplanting elsewhere, give them a good wetting beforehand, so that they pull well. Before planting, trim the tips of the leaves and the pivot, if it is too long, and plant with a planter, taking care to pack the soil well around each plant. About a month after planting, give the first hoeing, which should be repeated two or three times during the course of vegetation. Water a lot if you want to obtain good yields. As soon as the beets start to grow, gardeners who grow for sale will start taking them to market, just as the amateur will start eating them. To make the best use of the land, sow radishes or lettuce among the beets. Beet to be kept over winter should be harvested in the second half of October. Choose dry weather and put them under cover in a cellar or other place where frost cannot penetrate. In regions where beet is grown for cattle, most growers don't have the space to house them indoors, so they choose a good, sheltered spot outside. They drive a good stake into the ground, then place the beets around it in a pyramid shape, the higher the pile, the wider the base. Once set up, the whole is covered with straw, heather, hay, etc., which is held in place by slats or straw braids attached to the top of the stake, and at the base to small stakes driven into the ground. Beets keep very well in this state until spring. VARIETIES. - Red beet, round. - Early, small, with rounded, half-flattened root, very dark, very good flesh. Red, black, flat Egyptian beet. - Very early, round root, irregularly flattened, entirely out of the ground, medium size, excellent quality. We have grown it extensively for a long time, and have always been satisfied with it. Bassano flat red beet. - A little rounder than the previous one, and more regular in all its parts, very dark and good flesh, medium earliness, fairly large. Dark red Whythe beet. - Elongated, medium size, very good quality, very sweet flesh; keeps very well. Red toad beet. - Very old variety, easy to distinguish from other species by its rough, thick, toad-like skin; very good, sweet, tender, keeps well, excellent baked. Dwarf red beet from Del. - New variety, round, pointed, fairly sweet, small, not very productive. Beet jaune de Castelnaudary. - Very old long variety, small, very sweet, excellent, but of average yield; highly esteemed in the South-West where it is widely grown. Long red or large red beet. - Late bloomer, the most voluminous of the varieties, with red flesh, but of mediocre quality, very well suited to large-scale cultivation. Eclipse" beet. - New variety with very sweet dark-red flesh, early but small. Reine des Noires" beet. - New variety, ovoid shape, dark red, sweet flesh, excellent quality; dark red foliage, very ornamental, medium size. Covent-Garden red beet. - Smooth root, slightly elongated, dark red, sweet flesh, very dark foliage, medium size. Strasbourg piriform beet. - Red salad beet from Treviso. - Early red beet from Dewcing. - These are new varieties. The last is very early, but small. We also grow a few yellow-fleshed varieties, but they don't have the same flavor as the red-fleshed varieties, so are superior in every way. In any case, yellow beets are not very popular. Big long yellow beet (fig. 7). - Very sweet, but tough, becoming quite large. Round yellow beet. - Very sweet, better than the previous one, more tender, more productive. SEEDS. - To harvest beet seed, in autumn, we pull up the most beautiful plants that characterize the species, store them separately in sand, and in spring, when frosts are no longer a threat, we plant them at a short distance from each other; we water immediately to settle the soil around them. When the uprights start to grow a little taller, they should be supported by stakes, or horizontally-laid laths, to which each stem should be attached. Care should be taken during vegetation to remove any shoots that develop late. In July and August, when the stems start to turn yellow, cut them back as the seeds ripen. Ripe seeds can even be collected from the stalk without cutting it off. Dry in the shade, attic or shed. They keep well for four or five years. Each gram contains 50 capsules or seeds, some of which have several embryos. The seed harvested in the North is superior to that harvested in a climate where the temperature is irregular and too high. DISEASES, PESTS. - Only slugs and snails destroy beet as it begins to grow; they can be preserved by sprinkling with ash or quicklime. USES FIG. 7 - Long beet. USES. - Beet is very healthy and refreshing. It is eaten in salads, after being boiled or baked. The leaf can be used in the same way as the Poirée. With sweet wine, it makes good jams. The young shoots that the roots throw into the cellar in winter are eaten as salad. BOURRACHE Borrago officinalis Lin. Borraginaceae. ORIGIN. - Annual plant, native to Mediterranean regions, more medicinal than vegetable; borage should nevertheless have a place in the vegetable garden. CULTIVATION. - It is not very difficult to grow in the right soil, and succeeds everywhere. Its hardiness is even legendary, as it is sometimes found growing vigorously on walls. Sow in August-September or February-March. Autumn sowings are preferable, in that the plants, already strong in spring, acquire greater vigor and flower more. When the young seedlings have two or three leaves, transplant them at a distance of 40 cm, as you would a lettuce or chicory. Water immediately after planting, and weed and hoe when necessary. For this plant, choose the worst spots in the garden. However, if planted in good, well-smoked soil with sufficient exposure, it will produce better results. VARIETY. - There are three varieties of this breed: the first, with blue flowers, is the most common; the second, with pink flowers, and the third, with white flowers. SEEDS. - The seeds, which are very fine, fall as soon as they are ripe; so, to collect them, we must seize the moment when the ovaries appear ripe. They are picked and spread out on a cloth to dry out the seed. It is rare, once borage has been cultivated in a field, for it not to reseed itself in the second year. We once saw a borage bed that had been turned into a temporary walkway after the soil had been turned over. Three years later, the land was put back into cultivation, the whole area was spaded, and an innumerable number of borage plants sprouted shortly afterwards. The seeds keep well for eight years. USES. - Borage flowers, mixed with nasturtium flowers, are used to garnish salads. The chopped leaves, seasoned with vinegar, are eaten as an appetizer. In England and Italy, the flowers and leaves are cooked or fried. The flowers give a green color suitable for painting. BUNIAS D'ORIENT Bunias orientalis Lin. Cruciferous. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant, native to western Asia (Russia) and naturalized in northern France. CULTIVATION. - This little-known plant is grown like wild chicory. It resembles wild horseradish and belongs to the same family. It needs good, deep, well-smoked, humus-rich soil, which will produce well-branched stems over a metre high. Once the soil has been ploughed, sow the seed in the autumn or, better still, in spring, either in rows or in rows, covering the seed lightly. Thin out if the seed is too thick, then weed, hoe and water during the hottest periods. It's a good idea to renew plantings every four years, if you want to have good vegetation. Young plants that have been thinned out can be transplanted, but you need to choose dark, rainy weather, as they suffer from transplanting during hot spells. Transplanted plants become much more beautiful than those left in place. SEEDS. - After a year's care, bunias go to seed the following spring. When the uprights start to turn yellow, pick them up and lay them out on cloths in a shady, well-ventilated spot. Seeds keep well for three years. DISEASES, PESTS. - Snails and slugs devour them when the plants are still young. The most damaging insect is the flea beetle, the terrible enemy of crucifers, which perforates the leaves with a host of tiny holes, stopping the sap flow. USES. - In field crops, it is used as green fodder. In vegetable growing, however, the young, tender shoots are eaten in white sauce, or boiled in water and eaten in vinegar; these young shoots, blanched like a capuchin beard, are delicious. CAPRIER Capparis spincsa L., Capparis sativa Pers. Capparidae. ORIGIN. - A thorny shrub from southern France, growing in Provence and throughout the orange-growing region. GROWING. - In northern France, caper cultivation becomes difficult and unprofitable, as the shrub freezes easily and needs to be carefully covered to survive the winter. Capers thrive best in dry places, on rubble, demolitions and old walls. If you have a retaining wall, or an embankment to the south, plant it in it, with the roots in the wall or embankment. The stems are brought out through a hole dug for the purpose. Every year, at the onset of winter, cut off the stems and fill the hole with straw or litter, moss, etc., to prevent frost from penetrating to the roots. It can also be grown in back-to-back greenhouses, tarpaulins, frames, and in pots or crates buried in summer at the foot of a well-exposed wall, where the pots or crates are sunk in tannin; in winter, they are moved into a greenhouse or orangery. Capers can be propagated by seed, marcottes or cuttings. For our variety, layering is preferable in that it produces a fast-growing plant. Propagation by seed is slower, as seedlings do not always clearly characterize the type, and many only flower after a few years. The thornless variety, Capparis inermis, propagates readily from seed. Sow in March on a warm bed, in pots or cups filled with a mixture of light, sandy loam: at least two years of greenhouse cultivation are needed before it can be grown as described above. SPECIES, VARIETIES. - The genus Capparis comprises several species; the main ones are : Egyptian caper (Capparis Ægyptia Lamk.). - A species highly esteemed by the Egyptians, who use it as a seasoning. The flower buds, preserved in vinegar, have the same properties as those of Capparis spinosa; they are antiscorbutic and stimulating. E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 6 and the young shoots. Mount Sinai Caper (Capparis Sinaica). - The flower buds of this variety are very large. They are candied in vinegar; same property. Câprier des Antilles (Capparis Breynia Lin ), long-fruited caper or devil's bean. - This variety is little cultivated in Europe. Capparis ferruginea Lin, Capparis amygdalina Lamk, Capparis octandra Jacq, bois caca, partly because of the color of its wood. - West Indian variety. We still grow: 1° Capparis mithridatica Forsk, from Egypt; 2° Capparis Dahi Forsk, from Egypt; 3° Capparis ovata, M. v. B. from Barbary. SEEDS. - Caper seeds do not ripen in northern France, unless the plants are kept in greenhouses. But in Provence, where the plant is widely cultivated for industry, they are easy to obtain. They keep well for three years. DISEASES AND PESTS. - We know of no disease or insect that attacks this plant. USES. - What is commercially available under the name of capers are flower buds picked before they bloom; they are all the more appreciated for their smaller size, and are used as a stimulating appetizer. The aqueous or alcoholic infusion of the stems serves as an excellent chemical reagent, for discovering acids and alkalis. With acids, it gives a fiery red color; with alkalis, it gives a very beautiful green color. Tropœolum majus L. Tropéolées. ORIGIN. - From Peru, where it was brought in 1684. Perennial in its native country and in our greenhouses, but annual in our outdoor cultivations. GROWING. - Nasturtium thrives in good, cool, well-fertilized soil; during hot spells, it needs copious watering to develop vigorously. It can be propagated from seed, sown in pots on beds in March, or from cuttings smothered in cloches, taken in August and overwintered. You can also sow in place, in April or May. As this plant is an obvious climber, to ensure sufficient growth, it is best to place it near a trellis, where it can be twined up with numerous branches, so that the tendrils can cling to it. Watering should be copious and regular throughout the summer, as the more water it receives, the better it will grow. VARIETIES. - Several dwarf varieties, some with dark flowers, are derived from the tall nasturtium; same cultivation and same uses. SEEDS. - A few of the most vigorous plants should be staked, so that the first flowers to appear are preserved, as it is these flowers that give the best seeds. They should be collected as they ripen, otherwise they fall off easily. Then dry them in the shade. They keep well for five years; one gram contains 7 or 8. DISEASES, PESTS. - In some iron-deficient soils, nasturtiums become chlorotic and grow poorly; in this case, simply add a little good layered compost mixed with silica sand to each plant, and they will soon regain their normal vigor. Slugs and snails are very fond of them when the plants are young; to keep them away, simply sprinkle them with the ingredients indicated above. USES. - The flower buds before they bloom, and the still-green seeds, can be prepared in vinegar for the same uses as capers. Place in vinegar, salt, pepper and bay leaves; boil, skim and throw in the well-cleaned seeds; remove three or four minutes later, drain and cool, and seal in jars with new vinegar; in this way, they keep for a long time and are very good. The flowers are used to decorate salads and roasts. The plant's juice dyes wool a solid yellow, but the color is not pleasant. LITTLE CAPUCIN Tropœolum minus. Tro péolées. ORIGIN. - Peru; also known as India cress. CULTIVATION. - Same as above. VARIETIES. - This variety should not be confused with the other dwarf species derived from Tropœolum majus. It forms a separate race which has produced its own varieties; it is frankly dwarf. SEEDS. - Same care as above. Many seeds fall to the ground before they are ripe; despite this, they are very good and should be collected. DISEASES, PESTS. - Same as nasturtium grande. USES. - Same as above. Tropœolum tuberosum. Tropoeolae. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant, native to South America; little cultivated and therefore little known. CULTIVATION. - Tubers, which are the size of a hen's egg, are planted in April in the open ground, in as loose, light, well-exposed soil as possible, 40 to 60 centimetres apart in all directions, in rows, in a chessboard pattern. Several deep hoeings are given during vegetation, until the numerous stems have completely invaded the soil. Once the first frosts have destroyed these stems, in November, we can start digging. Tubers, as long as they are buried in the ground, are not affected by frosts, so you can only pull them as and when you need to. USES. - M. Vilmorin says: "Cooked in water like carrots and potatoes, tuberous nasturtium roots are watery and have a rather unpleasant, albeit fragrant, taste. In Bolivia, where the plant is widely cultivated, the tubers are frozen after cooking. In this state, they are considered a delicacy and highly sought-after. Elsewhere, they are exposed to the open air in canvas bags and eaten half-dried. So it's hardly surprising that fresh tubers don't seem very good to us, since even in the country of origin, they are only eaten prepared. For our part, we have tried this tuber, cooking it in 6. several ways; we have never found it to be excellent. CARDON Cynara Cardunculus Lin. Cynara sylvestris Lamk. Composites. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant, native to southern Europe. De Candolle says that cardoon is indigenous to Madeira, the Canaries, the mountains of Morocco near Moga- dor, the south and east of the Iberian peninsula, the south of France, Italy and Greece, and the islands of the Mediterranean Sea as far as Cyprus. A few years ago, it was moved to Montevideo, where it has multiplied to such an extent that it occupies immense plains and invades the Uruguay and Plata countryside, as well as part of the Buenos Aires region, to the point of hindering communications. It is also becoming a nuisance in Chile. CULTIVATION. - Cardoon can be propagated from seed, sown from April 15 to June, in warm beds under a frame, or in the open air in May. You could sow earlier on warm beds, but most of the plants will bolt, making them unsuitable for cultivation. Sow in pots or nurseries. If you have sown in a nursery under a frame, you can plant them when the third leaf begins to develop in pits prepared as described below. For in-place sowing, each pit is planted with three plants arranged in a triangle. Water immediately after planting. Potted seedlings are planted in the same way, leaving only three of the best plants. For seedlings planted in situ, dig 40-centimetre-square pits, 1.20 m apart. These are filled with good, well-decomposed manure, which is well trodden down. This manure is then covered with a few centimetres of loose soil, then four or six seeds are sown per hole, and pressed in with the finger. Sprinkle lightly with the apple, and all that's left to do is monitor emergence. When the plants are strong enough, we thin them out, leaving only three feet per hole. After this, lightly hoe and water. Experience has shown that it is preferable to raise young plants in nurseries, and then transplant them into the field; success is just as good, and sometimes better; but care must be taken when planting to cut the pivot at each plant. As these plants don't invade the entire space reserved for them within a few months, lettuces are counter-planted, and radishes, spinach, pumice, etc. are seeded. During the summer, the plants are hoeed several times and watered copiously, especially during the first hot spells. In October, we start to bleach them, and successively throughout the winter. First, select the strongest plants, tie the leaves together without compressing them too much, then surround them with straw and tie them in place. About twenty days after this operation, the cardoons are sufficiently white (fig. 8), and can be eaten; left longer, they would rot. Cardoons are sensitive to hard frosts; as winter approaches, they should be surrounded by earth, new manure or fern, which should be stirred from time to time to prevent rotting. In this way, they keep perfectly well. They can also be uprooted and placed in a gauge along a well-exposed wall; they are covered every evening with mulch- FIG. 8. Bleached cardoon. sounds, but care must be taken to clean them often, otherwise they will rot quickly. Alternatively, after trimming the tips of the leaves, place them upright in chests, a short distance apart; dry sand is slipped into the gaps. In this way, they whiten in a short time, with the advantage that they do not rot. The sand could be replaced by dry leaf, in which case they would blanch more quickly. VARIETIES. - Several varieties are grown: Cardons de Tours. - This is the most esteemed variety, with thick, full ribs that blanch well without deteriorating too much; but it has many thorns. In spite of this, it is cultivated and much appreciated. Spanish cardoon. - A very vigorous variety, with broad, half-full, thornless ribs, widely grown in southern France and Spain. Cardon plein inerme. - Another very vigorous variety, and despite its name, the ribs are less full than those of the preceding varieties; very ample in all its parts, whitens well and quickly. Cardon Puvis. - Another very vigorous variety with no spines, very broad, half-full ribs, ample leaves, good quality. Red-ribbed cardoon. - Not very old and widely cultivated variety, differs from Spanish cardoon only in its red-tinted, half-full ribs. SEEDS. - Cardoon only goes to seed in the second year after sowing; if it goes to seed before then, it has been sown too early, and the seeds it produces are worthless. To harvest good seed, you need to select a few of the best plants as seedbeds. It can last fifteen years or more; on the contrary, the older it is, the better the seeds will be. These seedbeds should be treated in the same way as artichokes, i.e. they should be deadheaded each winter, and eyeballed in spring; only one fruit should be left on each stem, the middle one. In August, when they are ripe, they are cut, gathered in bundles, hung in a dry place away from rodents, and, during the winter evenings, the seed is cleaned, which keeps well for seven years. One gram contains 25 to 30 grams; the weight per liter is 630 grams. DISEASES, PESTS. - Cardoon is subject to the same diseases as artichokes (see p. 69). USES. - The blanched ribs are eaten after boiling in water to remove their bitterness; they are then prepared with a white sauce, or with roasts of any kind, which is always a delicious dish. The flower, generally known as Cardonnette or Chardonnette, is frequently used in the countryside to curdle milk, and is said to be an excellent substitute for rennet. Cardoon is appetizing and nourishing, but also very warming. The Romans ate the receptacle that bears the flowers, and the Italians also eat it under the name of Girello. Modern farmers cultivate cardoon for the fleshy part of the leaves. (De Candolle.) CARROT Daucus Carota Lin. Daucus vulgaris Neck. Caucalis Carota Roth. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - Native biennial plant also found in temperate western Asia, cultivated for over two thousand years. The typical species is found throughout France, particularly in Poitou, Périgord and Angoumois, in uncultivated fields, in high, dry meadows and along rural roadsides. The carrot is second only to the potato as a cultivated vegetable. Its continual use in cooking means that considerable quantities are consumed. EARLY CROPS. - Although carrots can be grown in all types of soil, they prefer light, moist, soft, healthy soil, and above all, soil that has been sufficiently improved with good fertilizers. Carrots are sown in warm layers from December to February, in layers about 40 to 50 centimetres thick, built up with new manure and leaves. Fill them with 12 to 15 centimetres of a good mixture of potting soil and well-sieved vegetable garden soil. When the layer has set fire to, pack the potting soil well, then sow the seed, covering it with a centimetre or so of the same mixture. Water immediately, and put up the panels. Leave in this state, without letting in air, until emergence, which takes place in eight or ten days. From then on, you need to make sure you give the plants some air when the sun comes out, to prevent the young plants from withering away. Stoves are maintained to keep the heat more or less even. We thin out the plants as the need arises; however, we can leave them a little thick, because as soon as the carrots are big enough to be eaten, we start to remove them, always thinning out. In January, during the hottest hours of the day, we give them plenty of air when they start to get strong. In light, sandy soils, you can sow in the open ground in October or November among radishes, and cover with litter or straw mats, to produce new carrots in the early spring, which sell very well. But it's hardly possible to do this in strong, compact soils saturated with moisture. When you have a large number of frames and boxes at your disposal, you can place them on the beds, and then care for them like other seedlings. You can also sow on layers prepared as described above, at a good exposure, along a wall; but in the open air, without boxes or frames, these layers must be well bordered, sufficiently packed and covered with wind-breaking mats or litter. Produce grown in this way can be harvested early and well before that grown in the ground. This process and the previous one are what can be called hasty cultivation. FULL-GROUND CULTIVATION. - Carrots can be sown in the ground from February to September, all year round in the warm, light soils of the Midi and part of the South-West. But the best time to sow, which offers almost certain success, is spring, from March 20 to May 15. April is the month when growers generally sow carrots. Summer sowing is generally very successful from July 15 to September; in strong soils, sowing at this time often gives better results than spring sowing. For success to be good, the soil must at all times be suitably prepared and fertilized with good, well-consumed fertilizers, as fresh fertilizers, because of the ammonia and nitrogen principles they release, force vegetation too much and cause the produce to fork, i.e. instead of having beautiful, well-shaped, round and conical carrots, most divide into several roots of equal size, produce of this nature is little esteemed. There are several ways to sow carrots, either in rows or in beds. The latter is the best and most common method adopted by gardeners. When the soil is ready, lay out beds 1.20 to 1.30 meters wide. Proceed as described in the article on training (p. 14). Sow in fine weather. The soil is taken from the paths, thrown to the right and left, then raked to level and break up the clods, which are brought back to the paths. Mulch if necessary. The subsoil is sufficiently moist for capillary action to bring moisture to the surface. In certain soils where the soil is difficult to divide, we would do a poor job if we operated in this way; we simply pass the fork back and forth and across (we harrow, in other words), which partly covers the seeds, we pass the rake to bring the stones to the sides, to form a rim, and divide the paths. We've been doing this for a long time, and it's always worked out well for us. For sowing in rows, we draw four rays per 1.20 m bed, 4 or 5 centimetres deep; we cover the seed lightly with the rake, taking care to make the loosest soil fall into it; if the soil is too strong, we cover with soil or potting mix passed through the rake. In general, spring seedlings can do without mulch; but the same cannot be said of summer seedlings, which must be mulched without exception, unless you are working in damp soil, or better still in land where you will be watering often in the morning and evening. At this time of year, water evaporates so quickly that it is of no benefit to the plants if you don't water them thoroughly. Carrots need to develop quickly, so they need constant humidity, especially when young. Seeds usually germinate in twelve or eighteen days, depending on the time of sowing and the warmth of the soil. When they are 7 to 10 centimetres high, they are thinned out and weeded, a task that requires great care and attention. It's generally left to the women, who do it very well. If the soil is dry, the seedling is wetted a few hours before the operation, so that the weeding can be done easily; after the weeding, the seedling is watered again to facilitate the raising of the plants that have been shaken by the operation. As a general rule, carrots should not be thick if they are to produce good results. Three months after sowing, you can start harvesting, especially if you have sown early varieties. E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. Although carrots do not fear the cold, they can be damaged by frost, so they need to be covered. In November, cut off the tops and fill each bed with 10 centimetres of soil taken from the paths, levelling the surface. You can also cover with heather mats and leaves. Soil is preferable, however, in that you don't have to worry about it afterwards. We pull them out as and when we need them for the household or for sale. In the latter case, when they are destined for the market, as the tops are lacking, they are replaced by a heather stem, so that they can be tied and bundled. VARIETIES. - For early seedlings, early varieties are preferred: Early short carrot from Holland. - Introduced to our crops in 1800, it is one of the best varieties to grow. Very short carrot with frame (fig. 9). - Variety of the preceding one, very early, but yields little, suitable only for early crops. Half-length carrot, Nantaise or heartless. - A very good variety, becoming very large and of excellent quality. Carotte demi-longue d'Eysines, known in Bordeaux as the carrot à jus. - An excellent variety, derived from the old demi-longue, improved by the market gardeners of Eysines near Bordeaux. Becomes very large. Carotte demi-longue du Luc. - Very good variety, fairly early, productive and good storage life. Carotte demi-longue pointue. - An old variety, grown almost everywhere, very good for marshland cultivation; becomes very large. Carotte demi-courte obtuse de Guérande. - Very good species for cultivation in rich soils, becomes very large, very good quality. Danvers half-long carrot. - Very good variety, productive and fairly early, new. We also grow yellow- and white-fleshed varieties, but only in large-scale cultivation. They are good for animals, but not popular. Among the best are: Long yellow carrot. - Short yellow carrot. - White carrot with green collar. - White carrot with green collar from Orthe. - Vosges white carrot. - Carotte blanche de Breteuil. This variety is becoming huge. SEEDS. - To harvest carrot seed, most growers select the best plants in autumn and transplant them separately. In June-July, the umbels begin to ripen. The most advanced are picked first, and so on as they mature. Grain merchants don't operate this way: they leave the carrots in place, and remove only the degenerate or bastardized subjects. Seeds harvested in this way are just as good as those harvested in the previous way, but they also yield many more seeds. They keep well for four years; 30 grams contain 24,300 seeds, and a liter weighs 360 grams. DISEASES, PESTS. - Few diseases attack carrots; only uredo, in rainy years, partially destroys the leaves. On the other hand, loaches, slugs and snails are very fond of them. When the plants are young, they devour them. They must therefore be destroyed by any means necessary. USES. - Carrots are a good, healthy food; they are used in stews, casseroles, sauces, fried, etc. All doctors recommend them. All doctors recommend it. The old seeds are used to make liqueurs. Applied to animal feed, the carrot is one of the most useful plants; it is eagerly sought after by all kinds of livestock, and is particularly suitable for horses. Sliced and mixed with chopped straw, it makes an excellent feed for sheep. Carrots are also an excellent feed for cows, but they should be given sparingly and mixed with other substances: eaten alone and in excessive quantities, they would be rather harmful. Carrots contain 9 to 10% of a sugar that has been reported to crystallize. It also contains phosphates, alkaline salts and a volatile oil that gives it its exciting properties and odor. In northern France and Belgium, carrots are used to make a syrup known as poiré. The flower is the basis of the liqueur known as Venus oil. Root juice is also used to artificially color butter. The flowers dye paper dark red; the dirty red decoction dyes wool, silk, cotton and linen lilac after boiling for a few minutes; blue red with the addition of sulfuric acid, and blue gray with alum. CELERY Apium graveolens Lin. Sium Apium Roth. Seseli graveolens Led. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - Native biennial plant. The typical species is found in many parts of France, notably Boulogne, growing in damp places. Wild celery has an extensive habitat. It can be found from Sweden to Algeria, Egypt and Abyssinia, and in Asia from the Caucasus to Baluchistan and the mountains of English India. It has been cultivated for over two thousand years (De Candolle). The typical species is known by several synonyms: ache, ache d'eau, ache des marais, épraux, etc. CULTIVATION. - Cultivated celery thrives best in cool, well-amended soils with good, energetic fertilizers; marshy soils are generally very good for growing this plant. The first celery plants are sown on warm beds in January and February. When the young plants are strong enough to withstand transplanting, they are transplanted to another bed or even to another earthen bed with a good southern exposure. These plants, especially those raised under panels, are good for setting out towards the end of May. Three months later, you can start harvesting them. In April or the first fortnight of May, depending on the region, seedlings are sown in the ground, but care must always be taken to choose a good, well-exposed spot. Once the soil has been well ploughed, the necessary beds are laid out, carefully raked to ensure a perfectly flat surface, sown and lightly covered with compost, then spread a little long manure evenly over the entire sown area. This manure is used to soften the impact of watering on the seeds, and to protect the young plants from excessive heat. Most of the time, these kinds of open-ground seedlings don't do well, either because the soil is stony or compact, or because slugs and snails devour them. It's much better to sow in thick layers, and when the plants are strong enough, transplant them into the open ground in a nursery. Shade them for a few days, until they are ready to take root; these young plants, if well cared for, soon develop rapidly, and in this way, you always have beautiful, well-fed plants to put in place. It's towards the end of May and in the course of June that we put them into final position. There are several ways of doing this, depending on the region: in some countries, plants are planted flat, while in others they are planted in pits. Pit planting is the most widely adopted. When the soil is well ploughed with a spade, pits are dug 45 centimetres deep if two rows are to be planted, or 30 centimetres deep if only one row is to be planted, 25 to 30 centimetres deep and 1.30 to 1.50 centimetres apart. The bottom of the pits is worked a little, then 10 centimetres of well-consumed manure is spread in the bottom, which is compacted by trampling on it several times. This manure is covered with 12 centimetres of soil taken from the edges and raked down; the bottom is levelled, then one or two lines are drawn and the celery is planted with a planter, after cutting off the tips of the leaves and trimming the roots. In between, plant rows of lettuces, radishes and spinach. For flat cultivation, which in some soils gives just as good results as pit cultivation, there are two ways to proceed: The first is to spade the soil, spread the necessary manure over it, then cultivate with a flat or forked hoe. Then plant one or two rows of celery and four rows of romaine or chicory, etc. The second method consists in digging up the soil and burying the manure, then drawing the necessary lines and transplanting with a planter. This method is quicker and gives just as good results as the first. Whether you do it one way or the other, remember that celery needs a lot of water to grow quickly, as well as good fertilizers. Hoe and mulch during hot weather. STUFFING. - Butting is an operation designed to whiten the base of the petioles, making them tender and edible. For this operation to be successful, butting must be done at least three times. The first ridging should be light, followed by a second one about three weeks later, and a third and final one a few days later. The soil must be well levelled out between each plant, so that there are no gaps, and care must be taken to ensure that not too much soil gets into the eye: to avoid this, celery plants are tied up, or held by a worker. Ridging should only be carried out when the plants are well dried out and the weather is dry. In some localities, market gardeners plant celery in beds like chicory, and bed them with annealed manure, leaf or litter; others pull up the stalks and place them in a trench side by side, and bed them with soil; still others place them in sand. Any method works, as long as you succeed. Celery is not particularly sensitive to frost, but high humidity is detrimental. VARIETY. - The best varieties of full-grown celery are: 7. Large celery. - Very vigorous plant, keeps well, very full ribs, good quality. Céteri gros violet de Tours. - Very vigorous variety, full ribs, good quality, excessively productive. Céteri plein blanc court à grosses côtes. - Very good variety, very wide full ribs, upright foliage, less ample in all its parts than the previous one, very pro- ductive, due to the width of its ribs. Full white celery. - A good, vigorous, full-ribbed variety, reaching 40 to 50 cm in height. Early short white celery. - Early variety, good for early cultivation. Céleri plein blanc frisé. - As above, good for early crops, but not very productive. Céleri plein blanc chemin or golden celery. - Excellent variety, highly recommended, the ribs are very full and of a golden yellow that makes them always appear blanched, and, because of this, this celery can do without ridging, provided the top and bottom are attached. We particularly recommend its cultivation. Céteri Pascal, full white (fig. 11). - New variety, semi-short, with wide, fleshy, tender ribs, good winter storage life. Light yellow ribs, very good, good storage life. SEEDS. - There are two ways of harvesting celery seed: the first is to plant the plants separately, with the same care as for ordinary cultivation, during the summer, but without ridging. Care must be taken to remove any plants that are not typical of the species. You can also, at the time of uprooting, select the most beautiful plants and transplant them immediately, at 30 or 40 centimetres; if you are too afraid of frost, you can cover them with straw mats or leaves; in spring, you can smoke them well, or water them with liquid manure. Towards the end of July, in August or September, depending on the region, the umbels ripen successively. They are picked as they ripen, FIG. 11 - Céleri Pascal, full white. and dried by laying them out on cloths in the shade; to detach them from their receptacle, they are struck with a small stick, or rubbed between the hands. They keep well for eight years. One gram contains 2,500 seeds. MAlaDiEs, NUISiBlE ANIMALS. - Celery is often attacked by uredo or rust. So, in the Charentes region of France, celeriac growers call it "brumé". The best way to destroy this disease, which only attacks the leaves, is to treat celery with Bordeaux mixture, two or three times, in the same proportions as for vines. This procedure has given us good results. Centipedes and white grubs are very fond of celery, and in areas where these animals thrive, it is not uncommon to find several plants completely lost, and fortunately the damage is only noticed once it has been done. To keep them at bay, we recommend placing a handful of crushed oyster shells at the foot of each celery plant. USES. - Celery plays an important role in the culinary arts, and is used in stews, casseroles, pâtés and other dishes. It is eaten cooked under meat, or on its own, fried or with white sauce. In many places, it is eaten raw as a salad, but in this state it is very indigestible. The root and leaves contain significant quantities of mannite. The offshoots and residues are eaten by cattle. CELERI-RAVE Apium Rapa L. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - A biennial plant in our cultivations, derived from full celery, improved by cultivation which has developed the root instead of the leaves. Celery root is nowhere found spontaneously. CULTIVATION. - Celery root is sown in March or April in beds in the open air, or better still, covered with panels. When the young plants are strong enough, transplant them to the nursery in the same way as for full-grown celery. In light, well-fertilized soils, seedlings can be sown in well-exposed beds; taking care not to sow too thickly, transplanting can be avoided. However, this operation should not be neglected whenever possible, as it promotes the plant's development. In June, set them out in good, well-ploughed soil, thoroughly fertilized with good, widely-used fertilizers. They are laid out in beds 1.25 m wide, divided into five rows at equal distances. Leave a path 40 to 50 cm wide between each bed, and plant 30 cm into the row, preferably in a checkerboard pattern; water immediately after planting, and continue throughout the summer. FIO. 12 - Celeriac. Before planting, the root tips and leaf tops are lightly trimmed, hoeing is carried out several times during the summer, and the lower leaves, which are yellowing and spreading on the ground, are often removed. Towards the end of August, each plant is lightly dethatched, even removing the few roots that may be in the way, and left in this state; about a month later, the soil is put back in place, with more soil added; this operation, which is practiced in Alsace, is designed to encourage root development, as it is mainly in August and September that roots form. Harvesting can begin in October and continue until March. In southern regions, they survive the winter without suffering, but in departments with harsh winters, it's a good idea to butter them up, cover them with straw mats and even tuck them in and bury them in sand. VEGETABLES. - Erfurth celeriac. - Very old variety, widely cultivated, early, the root is fleshy, becomes very large, and is of good quality. Céleri-rave gros lisse de Paris. - A very good variety to grow, probably derived from the ordinary celeriac, with very large roots, the largest of its kind, good quality. Ordinary celeriac. - A very old variety, quite productive, but no longer cultivated today in favor of earlier varieties. Small-leaf celeriac. - Very early variety, derived from the Erfurth celeriac, few roots, small rootstock. Giant Prague celeriac. - Very good new variety, with very large, clean root, short foliage and relatively few roots. Céleri-rave de Paris amélioré. - A new, improved variety, producing enormous turnips. Celeriac with variegated leaves. - New yellow variegated breed, round, fairly regular celeriac (curious variety to grow). SEEDS. - To harvest celeriac seed, proceed in much the same way as for full celery. Seeds keep well for five or six years. DISEASES, PESTS. - Same diseases as full-grown celery, although it seems to us that uredo rages less vigorously on this breed. Insects are the same. USES. - Celery root can be served with white sauce or fat; it also goes well with roasts, and is sometimes used in stews to replace parsnips. CERFEUIL Scandix Cerefolium Lin. Anthriscus Cerefolium Hoff. Cerefolium sativum Haller. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - Annual plant, long considered spontaneous in France. De Candolle says: "... In western and southern Europe, it appears to be adventive, more or less naturalized; but in southeastern Russia and temperate western Asia, it appears to be spontaneous. Greek authors did not mention it; the first ancient mention is in Columella and Pliny, who call it Cerefolium. The species had probably been introduced into the Greco-Roman world since Theophrastus. CULTIVATION. - Chervil is very hardy, adapting well to any soil; when well smoked, it succeeds in certain shady exposures, where it would be impossible to grow anything else. Sow in shallow rows 25 cm apart, from February to October. Seedlings sown from February to July go to seed immediately and produce few leaves; to avoid running out, sow every two weeks. During hot spells, water copiously and choose a shady spot. Seedlings sown from August to October don't come up until April the following year, after having produced abundantly over winter and part of spring. At this time, they can be sown among spinach, carrots, salsify, cabbage, lamb's lettuce and so on. Weed them as and when needed, before they harm other plants. VARIETIES. - Common chervil. - Most commonly grown for markets, with deeply cut, serrated leaves, winged in two or three rows, borne on a long stalk; semi-cylindrical, canaliculated on top and covered with very fine hairs. Curly chervil or double chervil with curly leaflets. - A variety that reproduces fairly well from seed; a few plants always revert to the type species, but a selection of rootstocks produces good results. This is an elegant variety, preferable to common chervil for decorating dishes; it has the same flavor and fragrance: cultivation is the same, but it seems a little less hardy. SEEDS. - Spring sowings grow quickly, but the seed is not very good; it is better to harvest it from autumn sowings, which provide a greater quantity; ripening takes place in June and July. The stems should be picked before the seeds are fully ripe; they dry out in the shade. These seeds keep well for two years. DISEASES, PESTS. - In silica-deficient soils, chervil does not grow well, if not well smoked, and takes on a yellow, stunted hue, which leads us to believe that this plant likes soils where iron is found in large quantities. It is rarely attacked by uredo. In most areas, young seedlings, especially those sown in spring, fall prey to slugs and snails, which are very greedy: the damage is greater in wet weather. This can be remedied by throwing soot or powdered quicklime on them early in the morning, or even better, by sprinkling them with milk of lime. White grubs and mites sometimes eat away at the roots, destroying part of the plant. USES. - Chervil is used as a seasoning in stews and sauces, and as a salad garnish; it is also used to dress cold meats. Doctors have often observed poisoning caused by hemlock, a wild plant that resembles the common chervil in every way, but is much taller, less green and has a fetid odor when crumpled, which distinguishes it from chervil. To avoid these mistakes, M. Vilmorin recommends growing curly chervil, which cannot be confused with chervil. TUBEROUS CHERFEUIL Chœrophyllum bulbosum L. Umbelliferae ORIGIN. - A biennial plant, originating in the same regions as common chervil; it is a very old species that is still little cultivated. This is a mistake, as it is only through cultivation that we will succeed in improving it, and if today the products are not very profitable, they could be very profitable. CULTIVATION. - After stratifying the seed in fine sand kept fresh since November, sow very thickly in February and March, covering sparingly. Choose a good sunny exposure, which is absolutely essential for this plant to ripen its bulbs. You can sow in autumn, but as germination only occurs in spring, it's best to stratify. Some time after seed emergence, and when the young seedlings are sufficiently developed, we give a first light hoeing, which must be repeated often, to keep the plants in a perfect state of cleanliness; we water copiously during hot spells. It's time to harvest the tubers when the foliage begins to yellow and dry out. Pull them out and put them under cover in a healthy place. They are best eaten fresh. SEEDS. - Tubers intended for seed production should be planted in March, 10 cm apart in all directions. When the stems begin to rise, they are staked to prevent them from being uprooted by the wind. Harvesting of the umbels begins in July; the seeds that ripen first are the best, and keep well for a year. DISEASES, PESTS. - This variety is subject to the same diseases as common chervil, and is eaten by the same insects. USES. - The flavor of this tuber is very similar to that of chestnuts. It is prepared like potatoes, and used in sauces like salsify; the flesh is very starchy and sweet, with a very pronounced, pleasant aromatic taste. It's a very delicate food, much sought-after in Asia. After soaking for a few hours in water, this tuber is very refreshing and aids digestion. Myrrhis odorata Scop. Chærophyllum aromaticum L. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - Native perennial; grows in mountainous regions of southern Europe, mainly in the Alps, forming clumps 80 to 90 centimeters high; very hardy. CULTIVATION. - This plant is not very difficult to grow in the right soil, and succeeds just about anywhere. The seed is sown as soon as it matures in a nursery, or stratified in fresh sand, like tuberous chervil, for sowing in March. Sow very thickly, as this plant needs to be transplanted to succeed. Once the young plants have developed their first five or six leaves, transplant them into place, spacing them 50 to 60 centimetres apart, weeding and hoeing several times; they can be kept this way for several years. SEEDS. - In the second year of planting, the plants go to seed. We select the most beautiful stems and remove all the others. These umbels ripen in July. As the seed does not retain its germinative capacity for even one year, it should be sown as soon as it matures. DISEASES, PESTS. - Few diseases attack this plant, and, because of its rather strong odor, snails are not very fond of it. USES. - Its foliage is used like common chervil. In Spain, where it is generally grown, it is preferred. In France, it is little known and little cultivated. The plant turns yellow. COMESTIBLE MUSHROOM Agaricus campestris Lin. Agaricus alutarius Pers. Amanita edulis Lamk. ORIGIN. - Absolutely unknown. CULTIVATION. - In recent years, the mushroom has been widely cultivated. Not so long ago, the mushroom was grown only in and around Paris. The catacombs of Paris are particularly well-suited to this type of cultivation; in France, there are other quarries where success is just as certain: Chancelade, near Périgueux, Langoiran, in the Gironde, Mouthiers, Saint-Même, Bompart, Giget, near Angoulême, in the Charente. The latter have not yet been used for mushroom cultivation. It's astonishing that no industrialist or market-gardener has tried. For our part, we have no doubts about success. Although the mushroom is best cultivated in quarries where the temperature is more or less regular, it can nevertheless be grown successfully in cellars, caves, caverns or any dark place, and can also be grown in the shade outdoors from March to October. Wherever you choose to establish a mushroom bed, the key to success is to choose good horse or mule manure, well impregnated with urine, from strong, vigorous, well-fed animals that work hard and receive little bedding. Luxury horses, or those fed on green fodder or bran, produce poor manure, unsuitable for this crop. When leaving the stable, place the manure in a heap 70 to 80 centimetres wide and 50 centimetres high, close to where you intend to place the millstones; when heaping the manure, divide it well and discard any large straw. Tamp it down and water lightly, preferably on the inside, to prevent it from heating up. Eight or ten days after this second operation, the manure should be ready for grinding, brown in color, soft to the touch and creamy. The millstones are given a width of 60 to 70 centimeters, and a height of about the same at the top. They are then mounted in the shape of a humpback or slope, decreasing steadily until the desired height is reached. Once set up, the sides are combed with the spread-tine rake or fork, and the sides and top are beaten with the back of the shovel or the beater. If you're working in the open air, cover with a layer of litter or straw to prevent the surface from drying out too quickly; indoors, this precaution is unnecessary. Grindstones can be mounted in a variety of ways, either on square or half-square planks that can be leaned against each other and moved at will, or in tubs, half-barrels, wooden crates, etc., all of which make little difference to production. However, the two-slope grindstone generally gives the best results. You can see that the millstones have acquired the necessary degree of heat, i.e. 18 to 20 degrees centigrade, by inserting an ordinary thermometer, or even a stake thermometer. Most growers of this type use round pieces of wood, which they push into the millstone: a few hours later, they remove them and, taking them by the handful, check the heat; it takes a great deal of skill to get it right. Then the grindstones are larded, i.e. the white is introduced into them and divided into pebbles the width and thickness of the hand. With the right hand, the patties are introduced into the grinding wheel, while the manure is lifted with the left. The lardons are laid out in rows, 20 centimetres apart. The first row is placed 15 to 20 centimetres from the ground. Once the lardons are in place, the manure is put back in as before, pressing lightly with the hand. After seven or eight days, you come back to check on the operation. If the operation has been successful, you can tell by the small white filaments that are beginning to invade the manure; if any are missing, replace them, then cover the wheel with a small layer of about 3 centimetres of potting soil or kitchen garden soil, mixed in equal parts with demolition soil containing platras. The mixture is spread over all parts of the grinding stone, then tapped with the back of a hollow shovel to hold it in place; a fine apple is used to water very lightly and cover with bedding, if the grinding stone is placed outside, to prevent heavy rains from disturbing the soil; care is taken to ensure that the surface does not dry out. Fifteen or twenty days after the operation, depending on the temperature, the mushrooms begin to appear; as they are picked, the hole left by the mushroom must be filled in; a little earth is poured in. Every two days at least, you have to come and pick them. If you know how to maintain it, it can last for two or three months. Part of this maintenance consists in watering it from time to time with liquid manure, with plenty of water and a little saltpetre or guano added. If this solution can be heated to 25 or 30 degrees, success will be better, but in this case you need to water sparingly and little at a time. There are several other ways to grow. Although we haven't tried them, we feel we should reproduce them here. Dr. Labordette's method consists in replacing manure with lime sulfate or plaster stone, which is well compacted and to which is added a sufficient quantity of potassium nitrate; mushrooms weighing 600 grams obtained by this method are quoted. The ancients cultivated the mushroom, but by certain procedures that seem dubious and bizarre to us. A fig tree stump covered with manure was often sprinkled with a mixture of wine and water, or a black poplar stump, or the soil was frequently sprinkled with water in which laurel berries had been boiled. The Chinese, in order to obtain several species that are good to eat, place pieces of rotten bark and wood from poplar, elm, chestnut, mulberry and other species in good soil and in a suitable exposure; after a few weeks spent in this state, the mushrooms appear. Coffee grounds, when rotted and placed in a damp place under suitable conditions, give rise to an agaric that is highly prized in Naples. In Italy, blocks of a stone called Pietra fungaja are sold. It consists of hardened earth, mixed with black ramifications, and has been recognized as the mycelium of a species of boletus, Boletus tuberaster, which is much sought-after in Naples and other countries. These stones, placed in a cellar and watered, produce a harvest of mushrooms overnight. These blocks sell at a high price and are exported as far north as France, but they degenerate and, in most of France, a greenhouse would be indispensable for this type of cultivation. Here's another method: You need: 1° a wheelbarrow of cow dung without straw; 2° a jar of mushroom spawn, saltpetre or nitre; 3° a wooden box without a lid, one metre long and 50 centimetres wide. The dung is left to dry in the shade for two weeks, then piled into the box in a heap less wide and less long than the box, leaving about 15 centimetres all around. The dung is spread in layers by hand, mixed with good fine earth and sprinkled with a little water in which the saltpetre has been sprayed. The finished wheel will be about 10 or 12 centimeters high, and will contain all the saltpetre; it should be firmly packed. The white is then spread out, without breaking it up too much, and covered with dung, followed by 3 centimetres of earth. Tamp it all down, place it in the dark in a cellar, under a staircase, anywhere, cover it with a straw liner and you're done. Six weeks later, the layer is covered with mushrooms, which continue to grow for about a year, after which it's demolished and a new one is made with the white that has invaded the dung. When the layer is too dry, water lightly, but excess moisture is very bad. USES. - Every year, several families perish as victims of carelessness or good faith. Age, temperament, the degree of development of the mushrooms, the environment in which they have grown (the method of preparation, the length of time they have been eaten, the quantity ingested, etc.), all influence their properties. Cases have been reported of people experiencing symptoms of poisoning after eating small quantities of mushrooms that others had eaten in abundance without experiencing anything. In most cases, fear caused all the harm. Some species, eaten even in considerable quantities, cause only discomfort, heaviness and swelling; others produce weakness, stupor and temporary delirium; but unfortunately, too many are subtle poisons. Nausea, vomiting, collapse, stupor, convulsions and death are the symptoms of mushroom poisoning. As soon as these symptoms appear, a doctor should be called, but until he or she arrives, a vomiting agent or, better still, a vomit-purgative should be administered as a matter of urgency; if the appropriate help has not been given in time, or if the accidents only manifest themselves a few hours after ingestion, a purgative should be used, for example a potion made with castor oil and nerprum or peach blossom syrup, enemas made with cassia, senna and magnesia sulphate, or failing that, a strong decoction of tobacco. Vinegar, ether or salt water should be avoided, as they would spread the poison throughout the economy! 1 See Gautier, Les Champignons considérés dans leurs rapports avec la médecine, l'hygiène publique et privée, l'agriculture et l'industrie, 1884, 1 vol. gr. in-8 with color plates. E. BERGER, Vegetable plants. Mushrooms can be prepared in a number of ways: the best and most widespread is Bordeaux-style, at least for ceps. After the mushrooms have been washed and cleaned in various waters, they are drained and wiped dry with a white cloth, browned on the grill to dry out their water, then plunged into a frying pan full of boiling olive oil, butter or fat (oil is preferable). Then add the necessary condiments: garlic, pepper, salt, parsley, etc. This is a highly sought-after dish, and all mushrooms can be prepared in this way. Mushrooms are preserved by laying them out for a few hours in an oven, or in the sun to dry. Dried, these mushrooms are used to flavour sauces, salmis and stews; they can also be preserved in salted water, in vinegar for flavouring, or in olive oil. Cultivated mushrooms are widely used as food in London, Vienna, St. Petersburg and especially Paris. CHENIL Pulses. ORIGIN. - Indigenous and annual, it grows in uncultivated fields, old abandoned artificial meadows and, preferably, in stony, arid soils. CULTIVATION. - Cultivation is extremely simple. Sow in place from the end of March to May, preferably in a border, in a sunny spot. Weed and hoe several times during the summer, and water slightly during hot spells. VARIETIES. - Four different types: Large caterpillar (Scor piurus vermiculata L.). - Small caterpillar (Scorpiurus muricata L.). - Striped caterpillar (Scorpiurus sulcata L.). - Hairy caterpillar (Scorpiurus subvillosa L.). USES. - The fruits, which resemble certain caterpillars, are put in salads to provide surprises for people who don't know them. CHERVIS or GIROLLES Sium Sisarum Lin. Umbelliferes.
