ORIGIN. - A perennial plant native to Upper Asia, De Candolle says it grows spontaneously in Altaic Siberia and Northern Persia. It is doubtful, he says, that it was discovered in China or the Himalayas, and it is also doubtful that the ancient Greeks or Romans knew this plant. Littré derives chervis from the Spanish chirivia, but it is more likely that the latter derives from the French. One of its varieties has been cultivated in China since time immemorial, under the name Ninzy. It enjoys a great reputation there, and is said to revive the vital forces. Introduced to our shores around 1548, chervis soon spread to gardens and fields. Its roots were served as a delicacy. Linnaeus reports that in his day, chervis was grown in most gardens; later, it was dethroned by the potato, and since 1869, it has been rehabilitated. CULTIVATION. - Chervis is propagated by sowing seeds in March and April, or in August, September and October, either in the field or in a nursery. When the seedlings are strong enough, they can be planted in well-tilled, cool soil, with copious watering and frequent hoeing throughout the summer. You can also propagate chervis by splitting off the stem and keeping part of the crown, treating them like plants from seed. The resulting plants are less attractive than those grown from seed. The roots are not affected by frost. They should therefore be pulled out only as needed. SEEDS. - Chervis goes to seed in the first year, but the seed is worthless, and is only good in the second year. It is ripe in August-September. Cut the stems, or simply the umbels, lay them in the sun for two days, beat them and winnow them. They keep well for three years. DISEASES, PESTS. - Slugs and snails are quite fond of young chervis plants. Keep a close eye on them and destroy them. USES. - The root is eaten in the same way as salsify, fried or cooked in hot water; it can also be used to make very good purées. It is said to be very healthy. The flesh is white, firm yet tender, sweet, very floury, but sometimes a little fibrous. The flavor is mild, very sweet, fragrant, with a hint of celery. According to Mr. Sacc, it is the richest in nutrients of all food roots, and is so easy to digest that it was once recommended as one of the most powerful analeptics. It can provide starch, sugar and alcohol. The leaves are highly prized by cattle. CURLED CHICORICE or ENDIVE Cichorium endivia crispa L. Compositae. ORIGIN. - Annual and biennial. This spontaneous plant grows throughout the region centered on the Mediterranean, from Madeira, Morocco and Algeria to Palestine, the Caucasus and Turkestan. It is especially common on the Mediterranean islands and in Greece. On the western side, in Spain and Madeira for example, it is likely to have become naturalized through cultivation, as it grows in fields and along roadsides. There is no positive evidence in ancient texts of the use of this plant by the Greeks and Romans, but it is probable that they used it as they did several other chicories. The vulgar names give no indication, as they may have been applied to both species of Cichorium. They are not very varied, and lead us to presume a culture that has emerged from the Greco-Roman environment; one Hindu name is cited, Kasni and Tamul Koschi, but no Sanskrit name, which indicates a late extension of the culture to the East (De Candolle). EARLY CROPS. - The first curly chico. rees are sown from mid-December to March, on warm beds. The seed should emerge in twenty-four or thirty-six hours at most, so that the plant grows more slowly. If the seed germinates slowly, the chicory will rise immediately before developing. Once emerged, if sunburn occurs, give the panels some air to prevent the young plants from withering. When they have seven or eight leaves, transplant them permanently onto another 40-centimeter-thick layer, previously filled with 12 to 15 centimeters of a mixture of half potting soil, half sifted 3. garden soil. Plant at 15 to 20 centimetres in all directions, lightly water each plant and cover with a frame. Once the chicories have recovered, which takes two days, you can start to give them a little air, weather permitting, because in addition to the loss of growth caused by lack of air, chicories grown under frames are subject to a fungal disease, Peronospora gan- gliformis, whose development is favored by the concentration of air. Chicory can also be grown under cloches. Once a bed has been established, it is edged and loaded with the same mixture as described above. Place the cloches in position and plant five chicory plants under each one. Cover with straw mats in cold weather and keep warm. Radishes can be sown in the spaces left between each bell. OUTDOOR CULTIVATION. - Curly endive can be grown in any soil, but does best in slightly damp, well-fertilized soils. In dry soils, it requires a lot of watering. Sow outdoors from April to July. For the first sowings, choose a good exposure, and for summer sowings, a half-shaded exposure, if possible. Once the plants have developed, and are strong rather than weak, trim off half the leaves and the root tips, mainly the pivot, and place them in ploughed, smoked soil. If you use a hoe, the distance to be observed between each plant is 25 centimetres in all directions; cover the plants up to about half their total length, and water. Each bed usually consists of five or ten rays. In many parts of France, chicory is transplanted in 1.20-meter beds, divided into five or six rows. They are then planted with a planter, at 20 or 25 centimeters depending on the variety. For us, here's the way we've always done it: after the soil has been well ploughed and fertilized, we mark out with our feet the divisions of the beds, which should be 1.25 m wide; we sow radishes or lettuce to be cut, we harrow this sowing well, then we mark out six lines and plant the chicory. Radishes or lettuce are best harvested and removed before harming the chicory; after complete removal of these plants, a good hoeing is given, repeated at intervals of a few days, and copious watering is given if the soil is dry. Some authors recommend mulching the beds before planting; this is an excellent method that gives very good results and should not be neglected, especially in dry soils. However, no matter how practical, this method can only be applied to small areas of land: if large-scale growers were to mulch, the operation would become costly; we recommend keeping the soil surface constantly moist and sufficiently loosened. When chicories have reached the right stage of development, they are blanched. There are several ways of blanching chicory: gardeners in Bordeaux tie them with straw or rushes several times, always starting at the base; a few days later, the top is tied; chicory tied in this way whitens better than if it were tied all at once. In the Charente region, as in many other places, chicory is tied in a single operation; once all the leaves have been brought back vertically, a tie is passed over them and attached a few centimetres above about half the length of the leaves. This procedure is more expeditious than the previous one, in the sense that you don't have to come back to it. Other growers bleach them in the ground; they open a slanting trench, in the direction of the chessboard planting, bring all the lettuce leaves in, as if to bind them, and lay them in the trench more or less horizontally; they uproot a little, but never entirely; they are held in this state with the left hand, and the tool, held with the right hand, brings the earth over them: The soil from the second trench fills in the first, and so on; by this means, they blanch very well in eight or ten days, and are very tender. You can pull them out entirely and place them elsewhere in a trench, but they rot more easily. They can also be covered with mats, leaves, litter, etc., just as they can be uprooted and, after being thoroughly cleaned, placed side by side in the sand in a cellar or storeroom. Whichever method is chosen, the lettuces must be well wiped dry, otherwise the concen- tration of moisture in the heart will lead to fermentation and rotting of the outer leaves. Chicory can also be preserved well into winter, either by covering it during the frosts with heather, fern, straw, etc., which is removed during the day and put back in place in the evening, or with windbreaks, straw mats, wooden panels, or chests, so as to cover a few planks; this method of preservation only applies to northern regions where the temperature drops very low. In the Midi, this precaution becomes unnecessary, as plants do not freeze. VARIETIES. - Summer or Italian fine chicory. - Early variety, medium size, very old, leaves in tight rosettes, cut in the upper half. Suitable for first-season and early-season seedlings, it doesn't keep well in the late season and rots quickly. It is preferred over fine summer chicory (race d'Anjou), with tighter, more finely cut leaves and a larger, more rounded rosette. Chicorée frisée de Rouen (fig. 13). - An excellent variety, forming large, very full rosettes that blanch easily almost by themselves, provided they are planted close to FIO. 13 - Curly chicory from Rouen is grown in large quantities around Paris, as well as in the North and South of France; in Bordeaux, it is much appreciated at markets. Well suited to late crops, it is highly recommended. Chicorée frisée béglaise. - Excellent variety, derived from Rouen curly chicory and improved by market gardeners in Bègles, near Bordeaux; very full rosette, reaching 35 to 40 centimeters, whitens very well, not very sensitive to frost, highly recommendable in all respects. Chicorée de Louviers. - Another variety apparently derived from the fine Rouen chicory; very full, tight, rounded rosette, not very large, whitens well and keeps well into the late season. Chicorée mousse. - Variety forming a small rosette, leaves finely cut, curled, frizzy, tight, crisp, narrow white ribs; produces little, and must be planted fairly close together; particularly suitable for cultivation under panels or cloches. Chicorée frisée de Ruffec. - A variety highly esteemed in the West, with very ample rosettes, thick, tender, fleshy ribs, and a full heart that whitens well and in a short time; perfectly suited to summer and fall cultivation; we know of no other variety that is more resistant to cold, says M. Vilmorin; highly recommendable. Chicorée frisée de Meaux. - Very hardy variety, voluminous, 50 to 60 centimeters in diameter, very large ribs, tinted pink in their lower parts, long, erect leaves, loosely packed heart; gives a considerable yield, suitable for institutions for the insane or hospitals, does well in autumn. Picpus curly chicory. - Another very good variety for outdoor cultivation, somewhat similar in appearance to Chicorée de Meaux, from which it probably originated; tight rosette, very full heart, very curly, finely shredded leaves; does very well in dry soils. Chicorée frisée impériale. - White variety, wide rosettes, tall and full, finely-cut, evenly-curled leaves, upright, broad ribs; almost self-blanching, good for summer; in autumn, it is the first to suffer from uredo. Curly chicory always white. - Low yield, sparsely packed rosette, narrow ribs, well-cut, lacy, pink-washed leaves, pale yellow in color, giving it an etiolated appearance. Chicorée bâtarde de Bordeaux. - Intermediate breed between escarole and chicory, highly esteemed in the Southwest, very vigorous; rosette 50 to 60 cm in diameter or more, long, broad, erect, lobed leaves, loosely packed heart, whitens well when tied several times, good for growing in large establishments. Performs well in autumn, fears disease. Curly chicory, large pancalier. - A very good, new variety with a fairly full heart and broad, upright curly leaves that turn white without being tied. Chicorée frisée fine de Guillande. - New variety sent to us in 1886 by MM. Dupanloup et Cie, grain merchants in Paris; like the previous one, it is good for winter cultivation. Winter chicory queen. - A new variety with broad, curly, shredded leaves, it does well in winter in the Southwest. Winter curly chicory. - Breed very similar to fine Guillande chicory; stores well in winter; does not grow very large, but has a full heart. SEEDS. - To harvest chicory seed, sow in February or March, in warm soil, or even in the open ground in good exposure. When the plant is strong enough, it is transplanted in June. Select the most beautiful, well-stocked plants from the heart, and uproot the others. By August-September, the seeds are ripe. The stems are pulled out when they begin to yellow and dry out. They are laid out in the sun for a few days, shaded if possible, after which they are threshed. As the seed is difficult to detach from its receptacle, they should be soaked several hours before threshing, or even the day before. They keep well for nine or ten years. One gram contains around 600 grams. DISEASES, PESTS. - Every year, we have had to fight uredo, the same disease found on full-grown celery, generally known as rust. This parasite usually appears towards the end of August or the first fortnight of September, and almost always after alternating periods of rain and very hot sun. A few days later, all the leaves are invaded by powdery red spots, followed by rot, and chicory is done for. All that remains of the leaves is the toughest part of the midrib. This fungus spreads very quickly, so as soon as a few plants are found to be affected, they are uprooted and bleached underground. We tried several remedies: the one that gave us the best results was the following: 2 kilograms of fat lime diluted in 10 liters of water, add 500 grams of well-pulverized soot, mix everything together and brush each diseased foot. Repeating this treatment several times will eliminate the disease. The same mixture works well on celery. Peronos pora glangliformis or meunier rarely attacks open-ground plantations. Only under-frame crops are sometimes affected, but this parasite acts less intensely on chicory than on lettuce, which it destroys entirely. In soils where there are many white grubs or Turkish worms, it is not uncommon to see several chicories whose roots have been devoured by this insect. Unfortunately, we don't notice its ravages until the damage is done; but it seems that we've just discovered the remedy for this scourge; this remedy, called Botrytis tenella, is a cryptogam that attacks the worm and destroys it completely in a few days. All you have to do is put a few contaminated worms in the soil, and all those present will quickly be affected. The fungus is said to grow very well in boiled potato mashed potato. We even sell tubes in various doses, ready-made for a certain area of land. According to the authors, the remedy is infallible and always effective. When they are numerous in a plot of land, mites or fumaroles, known as bars in the Bordeaux region, wreak havoc by cutting the root between two plots of land and digging numerous galleries. They must therefore be destroyed. The roots of some chicories, particularly escarole, are also sometimes host to innumerable greyish aphids, which suck the root and halt the plant's development. Several remedies have been tried, but they were more damaging to the plant than the plague itself. Water the base of the plant with soot water, mixed with a little fat lime; this is the only harmless remedy for the plant that has given us good results. Phenic acid strongly mixed with water has been mentioned, but this remedy imparts a bad odor to plants. USES. - After being blanched, chicory is mainly used as a salad. It also goes very well with all kinds of meat, especially mutton and pork, in white sauces made with milk or butter; it is also an excellent seasoning for roast chicken. E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 8 Leaves are aperitif, tonic and refreshing. SCAROLE CHICORY Cichorium endivia latifolia Lin. Compositae. ORIGIN. - Same origin as curly endive, of which it is only a broad-leafed variety. CULTIVATION. - Scarole is grown in much the same way as chicory. It is sown from June to September, to be eaten in autumn and part of winter. It makes an excellent salad, tender and tasty; it is less sensitive to frost than chicory: some varieties survive the winter very well without suffering too much. Blanched underground, it is excellent and very tender. VARIETIES. - Autumn green round chicory. - Excellent early variety, well-filled, tightly packed heart, almost headless, wide rosettes, thick whole leaves, toothed, wavy at the edges, wide, thick, white, crunchy and very tender ribs. It is fairly hardy, withstanding cold temperatures of 4 or 6 degrees. It is one of our best varieties, albeit an old one. Chicory from Limay. - More voluminous than the previous variety, with ample, waffled leaves, broad, thick ribs and a fairly full, but not very tight, heart. Well-bleached, it flatters the eye, but is tougher than the previous variety. In good, moist soil, it produces a lot, becoming very large. Not yet widespread. Blonde chicory with lettuce leaves. - Rosette slightly wider than round escarole, very sensitive to humidity in the late season, broad, upright leaves, slightly wavy and waffled, a little leathery, heart not very tight. This variety needs to be planted close together, so that it can bleach on its own. Less hardy than the previous two, very sensitive to uredo. Turkish endive. - This variety, improperly known as béglaise escarole, is widespread throughout the West and South-West. It's one of our main winter salads, as it doesn't freeze easily in these regions. The leaves are almost as broad as they are long, with numerous long teeth along the edges. The inner leaves, folded inwards, form a kind of apple, sometimes very hard; blanched, they are tender. Sowing in September provides good planting in October-November. You can even plant later, harvesting in March-April, at the same time as winter lettuces. SEEDS. - As escarole can survive the winter without suffering too much, in the south-western departments and part of western France, it is planted very late in November with a view to harvesting the seed; these plants come up in the spring and the harvest is very abundant. In other regions, where the cold is more rigorous, we sow very early on the bed, as for chicory. MAlADIES, PEST ANIMALS. - Uredo invades round green escarole and blond leaf lettuce very easily, especially if cold rains persist for a few days. Same treatment as for chicory. USES. - Same uses as curly endive. WILD CHICORY Cichorium Intybus Lin. Compositae. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant, native to France and Europe, as well as northern Africa and western Asia, cultivated for nearly two thousand years, known as peasant's hair, écoubette. GROWING. - Wild chicory is very hardy, thriving in almost any well-amended soil. However, it thrives best in deep soils, where its long roots are at ease. It can be sown from March to July; April and May sowings are the best, and are the ones to choose especially, as the plants do not bolt. In gardens, it can be planted in borders and flowerbeds, sown in nurseries or in the field in shallow rays, about 3 centimetres wide and 20 to 25 centimetres apart. When the young plants have four or five well-developed leaves, they are thinned out if sown in place, and transplanted if sown in nurseries. Transplanted plants are always more beautiful than those sown in situ. The first light hoeing is carried out as soon as the soil hardens on the surface. Repeat the operation several times during the year, watering whenever necessary. Nursery plants are transplanted at 10 or 12 centimetres from the line, and if the soil is good, you'll get remarkably beautiful plants that produce a lot of leaves. Despite its bitter taste and roughness, wild chicory is much sought-after as a salad; it should be picked young to make it more tender and less bitter. There are several ways to grow capuchin beard in winter, a highly prized salad in Paris, northern France and even abroad. Here are a few of the most practical. We start blanching in the second half of November. To this end, a small layer of good horse or donkey manure is prepared in a dark cellar or storeroom. We pull up the chicories, and bundle them into bundles of about twenty feet each, holding the collars at exactly the same FIG. 14. - Bleached Capuchin beard. height. Securely tied with wicker, they are placed upright on the bed, side by side, the edges are formed with manure, and as the bundles are placed, the gaps are filled with the same manure or with potting soil. When you've finished placing the bunches, spread a few shovelfuls of potting soil over them, then water. After fifteen or twenty days, the chicory is ready for harvesting, and if you take care to cut the leaves flush with the collar without damaging it, it grows a second time; in Paris, it is usually sold with the root (fig. 14). When vegetation is exhausted, the bed can be reshuffled, a little new manure added, and other chicory planted again. If you don't have a cellar (which is more practical for gardeners), you can work under a frame. Once a good layer has been made, the boxes are placed, and the chicory planted as we have indicated. The panels are then placed and covered with straw mats and leaves, to provide the maximum shade necessary for wilting. Here's a method we think is worth quoting1. In the second half of June, sow wild chicory in rays 30 centimetres apart, with enough light in each ray for the plants to gain sufficient strength; during vegetation, water and hoe as much as necessary. For blanching in the cellar, I use either of the following two systems: either a frame made of four planks, 1 meter long and 1.50 or 2 meters high, which you lean upright against the wall in a dark place in the cellar, or one or more barrels (even barrels that have contained cement) which you drill with several rows of holes 2 to 3 centimeters in diameter and 7 or 8 centimeters apart. In November, a quantity of roots proportionate to consumption needs is pulled up. The root tips and leaves are cut off 2 or 3 centimetres1 Manuel pratique des jardins et des champs, by M. Daurel (Moniteur d'horticulture de Paris). from the collar. If using a frame, close the front of the frame, starting at the bottom, with a ceiling batten. Fill with soil up to the top of this lath, then place the roots horizontally on this layer of soil, with the collar in front and 4 or 5 centimetres apart; place a second lath on top of the first, leaving a sufficient gap between them to allow the shoots to pass through, cover with a second layer of soil on which roots are placed; continue in this way up to the top of the frame. If barrels are used, a layer of soil is also placed at the bottom, up to the level of the first row of holes, which are then filled with roots, with the collar slightly protruding, so that the settling of the soil doesn't drag them inside; soil and roots continue to be placed right up to the top of the barrel, which is, of course, ripped open. The barrels, like the frames, should be placed in the darkest corner of the cellar. In January, new frames or barrels can be set up, providing abundant salad over the winter. Although this procedure is said to give good results, we believe that success can be achieved by operating in the following way. Start by placing a thin layer of new manure mixed with annealed manure in a dark cellar, arrange it in a circle and trample it down hard, then place bunches of chicory in a pyramid shape: as you place the bunches, fill in the gaps with manure, which you must pound well with your hand. The layers are placed one on top of the other, with a slight gap between them. Once the pyramid is set up, you finish by throwing in a few shovelfuls of earth, then watering the whole thing. In this way, you can make heaps of any height and size; it's a good process that we recommend to amateurs. In some regions, notably around Paris, growers don't pull up chicory. In winter, they cover with heather, straw, manure or soil taken from paths, to a depth of 4 or 6 centimeters. When the chicory has grown sufficiently, we cut it between two plots of land, as we would an asparagus. VARIETIES. - Wild bitter chicory from Paris. - Variety closest to the type and probably the source of all other varieties: long, hairy, strongly toothed leaves, with acute lobes, sail- lant ribs, green or red. Placed in suitable soil, it produces many leaves, which can be cut several times during the summer, and are eaten either green or dry by cattle. It is the most esteemed and the best for making capuchin beard. Improved wild chicory. - Differs greatly from ordinary wild chicory in its broad leaves, much like a cone-shaped escarole; it is dulled and blistered, forming a small apple that is sometimes compact, fairly hard and tender; it is hardy and produces a lot. This variety was bred by M. Jacquin aîné; until now, it was thought to be a cross with escarole chicory. M. Vilmorin? claims the opposite, and we share his opinion. It's a highly recommendable variety which, in certain cases, can be blanched like chicory, and from which you can obtain ex-cellent nasturtium beard. 1 Vilmorin, Les, Plantes potagères. Improved variegated wild chicory. - Derived from the previous variety, it has the same characteristics, with the only difference being that the leaves are flagellated and spotted with reddish-brown. This color is brighter due to the plant's darker development, making it a very pretty salad when blanched. Improved curly wild chicory. - A variety that appears to be a cross between improved wild chicory and curly chicory; the leaves are lacy, cut, almost hairless. Do not sow these varieties before May, as they bolt. Among the large-rooted varieties, we'd like to mention: Chicorée à grosse racine de Brunsvick. - A variety with cut, almost spreading, long leaves and a large, long root. It is grown extensively in Germany and Belgium to make chicory coffee. Magdeburg large-root chicory. - A variety with whole, erect leaves, with few or no teeth, and very large, long, smooth roots. It is widely grown in northern France for the preparation of chicory coffee. Brussels or Withloof chicory. - A variety derived from Magdeburg chicory, widely grown in Belgium, where it is one of the main winter salads. We've grown it for a long time, and it has always given us magnificent results, so we have no hesitation in recommending its cultivation. It is grown in the same way as Paris bitter chicory: at the start of winter, it is uprooted and cleaned, with any inferior or undersized plants set aside. The leaves are cut off 3 or 4 millimeters above the collar; any shoots that have grown up around the9. collar are removed, and the root tips are cut off, reducing them to roughly equal length. Place them in a trench 40 or 50 centimetres deep, into which 20 centimetres of loose soil or compost has already been placed. They are planted in this potting soil 8 centimetres apart, with the collar at exactly the same height, and 15 or 20 centimetres below the top level of the trench, which must be filled with the mixture mentioned above. If you want them to start growing, spread 40 centimetres or more of good horse manure on the surface, depending on the temperature; three weeks later, you can start harvesting: to do this, remove the manure, dig up the root, and cut off the blanched apple, keeping a small portion of the neck. Roots replanted after this operation, and treated like capuchin beard, still grow and develop several excellent stems. Withloof makes an excellent, tender and appetizing salad. The regularity of its growth, which forms a small, tightly-packed head, makes it more appreciated than capuchin beard. In the public establishment where we ran the market garden for nearly a decade, we operated in a very simple way for blanching our withloof, and here's how: The chicory plants were pulled out of the ground as needed, prepared and placed side by side on a warm, fairly thick layer of fresh manure, mixed with a few leaves. The plants were buried up to the collar, either in sand, light loam, tannin, wood bran, etc... Once placed, they were watered, then covered with 10 or 15 centimetres of dry leaves or moss. The panels were placed on the trunk, and covered with double or triple mats to prevent daylight penetration; eight days later, harvesting began. It's a very quick process, and suitable for all crops. Here's how Mr. Poiret Délan! proceeds. In August, I cut the leaves 3 or 4 centimetres above the crown: these leaves can be eaten in salads, or fed to rabbits. When the time comes to take advantage of them, which is from November to March, I pull up my chicory, clean the roots, leaving them only 20 centimetres long; I cut the leaves about 5 centimetres from the collar, then place these roots upright under a bell, one against the other, in potting soil, on a pile of leaves. Even better is a mixture of manure and leaves which, through light fermentation, produces a temperature of 10 to 15 degrees centigrade, which activates the work. To make it easier for the plants to wither, the cloches are covered with manure or leaves. Under these conditions, this particular state of etiolation is achieved in twelve or fifteen days. Care must be taken during hard frosts, so as not to run out of plants suitable for consumption. The work should be repeated every eight or fifteen days. We think this method is excellent, and particularly suitable for amateurs who don't eat much of it, because if you work as Mr. Délan indicates, you'll always have good fresh produce at your disposal. SEEDS. - Although perennial, wild chicory goes to seed in its second year. This seed is ripe in August 1 Rerue horticole. September; the stalks are cut off and exposed to the sun; when they are dry enough to detach the seed from the receptacle, they are left outside overnight, to be threshed the next day, or they are wetted, and two or three hours later, they are beaten with a stick, and rubbed well between the two hands. The seed is then easily detached; it is winnowed and cleaned. One gram contains 700 seeds; it keeps well for eight years. DISEASES, PESTS. - This plant suffers from the same diseases as curly endive, and is eaten by the same insects. USES. - The large-rooted varieties are used to make chicory coffee. This type of production seems to have originated in Holland, and was introduced into Belgium towards the beginning of this century. The roots, after being boiled in various waters, can be eaten like salsify. In Sweden, the poor make bread from the root. Wild chicory is said to be excellent as animal fodder. Rabbits in particular are very fond of it, and it is a very good food for them. It can be cut several times a year, and last for eight or ten years. The whole plant turns a faint yellow. CULTIVATED CABBAGE Brassica oleracea L. Cruciferae. ORIGIN. - The typical species, with a tall, twiggy stem and glaucous, lobed, fleshy leaves, grows spontaneously on the seashore in southern England and Ireland, on the islands of Jersey and Guernsey, on the island of Laland in Denmark, on the island of Heligoland; in France, on the coasts of Normandy and Charente-Inférieure, on the northern Mediterranean coast near Nice, in Genoa and Lucca. Cultivated from time immemorial, the ancients applied it to all kinds of ailments and used it as an exclusive remedy. CULTIVATION. - Cabbage is very hardy, thriving in all types of heavily fertilized soil, and can be found just about anywhere, at a wide range of altitudes. However, it seems to do best in slightly strong, damp, slightly chalky soils. The best fertilizers for cabbage are manures mixed with fecal matter, sludge and city refuse, which should be used before decomposition. Watering each plant several times with liquid manure will produce magnificent results, even in poor-quality soils, but care must be taken when using this fertilizer, otherwise the results will not be what you expect. As a general rule, and with the right choice of varieties, cabbages can be sown almost all year round, in the open ground, with the exception of December and January, when it would be better to sow on a bed and then transplant to a good exposure. But the best seedlings, those which give the best results, and which are the most widely used in the South-West, are spring seedlings for the curly kite breed, and autumn seedlings for the cabbage breed - a rule adopted throughout France. Cabbage seedlings are usually planted in beds 1.20 m wide. They are broadcast a little thickly if you intend to transplant them, and less thickly if you intend to leave them on the bed. Lightly cover them with a fork and then with a rake, or spread 1/2 centimeter of soil taken from paths or from the ground over the beds. If sowing in hot weather, spread a light mulch over the beds and water often. When the plants are strong enough, and the first two or three leaves begin to appear, they are transplanted into beds, in rows 8 centimetres apart in all directions. Water as you go along. As far as possible, this transplanting work should be done when the weather is dark or in the evening, when the sun is less bright. It's a very good operation, which is almost essential for this type of plant, at least if you want to obtain beautiful, well-branched, strong plants with lots of hair. When the operation is carried out in very hot weather, it is urgent to shade the plants with windbreaks to facilitate recovery. The ground where the transplanting is to take place should be well ploughed and smoked beforehand, and the surface loosened with a rake. In many parts of France, such as Angoumois, Saintonge, Lot, Vienne, etc., market gardeners plant cabbages permanently with a forked or flat hoe; they form large rays and plant in alternate rays, so that the cabbages are 60 or 70 centimetres apart in all directions and in a chessboard pattern. Scarole, romaine, lettuce or any other vegetable is counter-planted in the false rays and between each cabbage, and removed before harming the cabbages. Smoke when planting, after first spreading the manure on the soil, and when making the comb, slide it into the bottom with one side of the tool. Consumed fertilizers should be used whenever possible. Old market gardeners claim that by doing this, the cabbages become much more beautiful. It's usually the women who place the cabbages. Those who are used to this kind of work are very quick. As soon as the cabbage is in place, they quickly pull a handful of loose soil over the roots, which they take from the bottom of the shelf, to hold the plant in place. A good racker can, without too much fatigue, give work to three people. As soon as the cabbages are covered, they are watered with the spout. Sometimes, in summer, when it's hot, we water a little on the soil, once it's been placed on the roots, but this doesn't prevent us from watering a lot once the cabbage has been buried. Planting with a planter is much quicker, and gives equally good results. The soil is well fertilized and ploughed, then radii are traced at 60 centimetres or more, depending on the species, then planted and watered, taking care not to pound the soil too much when doing the work. This is the way we've always done it, and we've never complained. Four or five weeks after planting, when the plants are well established, we give them a first deep hoeing, which must be repeated often. In areas where irrigation is possible, they should not be spared water, as they will grow all the better for the warmth and humidity they receive. DISEASES, PESTS. - Most cabbage seedlings, whatever the variety, and we could even say crucifers in general, have to suffer, especially in summer, from the bites of a small insect called the ground flea, because of its resemblance to the flea, but whose name is altise or tiquet (Altica oleracea). This little creature, which seems to prefer the young cotyledons and early leaves, pierces them through with an infinite number of tiny holes, stopping vegetation in its tracks; most affected plants succumb. There is no effective way of destroying them. We have tried several remedies, but have only succeeded in keeping them away for a while; the one that has given us the best results is this: Macerate soot in water, in which soda crystals have been dissolved; add a little plaster or lime to fix the product on the leaves, and brush with this mixture. You can also boil aromatic plants such as thyme, lavender, hyssop, wormwood, laurel, etc., mix this decoction with tobacco juice, or better still, boil the whole together, and sprinkle with this product. Another method: Throw soot, wood ash or lime on the young plants. When a cabbage seedling has suffered from drought, and vegetation has been slowed down, it is attacked at the base of the plant by a small white worm, which produces a nodule in which it is enclosed; there are sometimes quite a few on the same plant. We recommend popping them off with a fingernail or pruning-hook, and removing the insect. However, there's not much to fear from this worm, as almost all large cabbages, and kites in particular, have greater or lesser quantities, depending on the type of soil in which they are planted. Another insect that causes a lot of damage in certain years is the caterpillar. The best way to destroy them is to hunt for their eggs before they hatch; at the end of winter and summer, small butterflies of the piéride genus, with yellow wings spotted with black, flutter over the plantation and deposit their eggs, in hundreds, on the underside of the leaves; the eggs must be crushed immediately after they have been laid. USES. - Cabbage is a popular vegetable and is frequently used, especially by country dwellers. In northern Europe, it is the staple of the diet. It appears on the table of the rich and the poor alike. It is eaten cooked either lean or fatty; the classic cabbage soup is accompanied by the petit-salé of the Auvergnats; it goes very well with pigeon, goose or turkey quarters, or even partridge; it is delicious with sausages. Boiled cauliflower can be eaten au gratin, seasoned with butter, just as Brussels sprouts are delicious fried in butter. Young heads of any variety, boiled in salted water, can be eaten in vinaigrette like asparagus. Cabbage is a very healthy and restorative food, especially when prepared with meat. Robust, strong stomachs digest it easily and it does them a lot of good; but as healthy as it is for them, it is not very suitable for delicate people; it can produce serious indigestion and cause serious stomach illness. It is also forbidden to convalescents and the elderly. It is claimed that cabbage has laxative properties, and that people who use it frequently rarely need a purgative. It has been wrongly claimed, I believe, that cabbage imparts an unpleasant flavor to the milk and butter of cows fed on it. VARIETIES. - Now that we've covered the basics of general cultivation, let's move on to a description of the best varieties, highlighting the type of cultivation specific to each one. Botanists have divided cabbages into five classes: 1° Head cabbage; 2° Savoy cabbage; 3° Green cabbage; 4° Kohlrabi; 5° Cauliflower. HEAD cabbages Brassica capitata Hort. Cabbages in this class generally have a very large stalk, swollen in the middle; the leaves are fairly broad and smooth; the veins are prominent and numerous, with the median vein always well-developed and extending to the top of the leaf blade; glaucous in color, with a metallic sheen in some varieties (York oxheart). CULTIVATION. - Can be sown all year round, but the best time is July, August and September. They are planted as soon as the seedling is good. In ordinary winters, when the temperature doesn't drop above 8 degrees centigrade, they resist perfectly, and when the sun comes out, they develop rapidly. They can even be left in the nursery and not planted until spring; they do just as well, but are less early. Varieties such as Schweinfurt, Quintal, Bonneuil, Joanet, etc., have been very successful for us, sown in spring, and have produced magnificent products in autumn. For summer sowings, the varieties known as Bacalan gros, Bacalan hâtif and Bonneuil are those preferred by market gardeners. VARIETIES. - Varieties in this class are, in order of earliness: Chou d'Yorh petit and gros. - Two distinct varieties, rather small than large. Sugarloaf cabbage. - Slightly larger than the previous one. Beef heart cabbage small (fig. 15). - Medium-sized, very good and tender. Heart of beef cabbage large. - Similar to sugarloaf cabbage. Chou Bacalan gros. - The best and most esteemed of this class, very large, tightly packed, white and rustic. Bacalan hátif is a smaller sub-variety, a few days harsher. Chou de TourFIG. 15 - Heart of beef cabbage. laville - Very similar in shape to the above, but dwarfed and with blistered folded leaves. Lingreville cabbage. - Short-stalked, with large, wavy, blistered leaves and a pointed, very white head; not very productive. Joanet or Nantais cabbage. - Very good short-stalked variety; very hard, flattened, very white head; successful, sown in autumn. Brunswick or Tabouret cabbage. - Highly esteemed variety in Angoumois and Saintonge, where it is widely grown; very short stem; large, broad apples, very flattened at the top; highly recommended variety; does very well in fall and spring. Schweinfurth cabbage. - A very good variety, highly esteemed everywhere; very large, loosely packed apples, best sown in spring; the highest-yielding variety. Particularly suitable for large establishments, hospitals, asylums, etc. It is grown in large quantities in the departments of Vienne, Haute-Vienne and Loire-Inférieure, which ship them in batches to the Paris markets. Chou quintal. - Variety closely resembling Schweinfurth cabbage, but flatter; very large, firm head; a little late, but very high yielding; most widely grown in Germany for making sauerkraut, Pomeranian conical cabbage. - Late, high stem, cone-shaped, very tight and fairly large head, very productive, does well sown in spring; widely grown in Germany. Winigstadt pointed cabbage. - Similar in shape to oxheart cabbage; tight-knit, medium-sized head, late; does well in southwestern France, sown in autumn like Bacalan cabbage. Vaugirard cabbage. - Very hardy, withstands winter well without suffering too much; highly esteemed at Paris markets. Growers around Paris sow it late, in June, so that it does not begin to peel until after the frosts. Dax cabbage. - A highly esteemed variety grown extensively in the Landes and Pyrenees regions; similar in habit to the Milan cabbage of virtues; round, loosely packed, medium-sized head. Semi-tardy. Habas cabbage. - An excellent variety, widely grown in the Agenais region. It resembles the previous variety in shape; the head is larger, tighter and forms more quickly. Several other varieties of cabbage are also grown, which appear excellent and produce magnificent products in their country of origin, but which give very poor results elsewhere. We mention the following varieties as having been cultivated: Chou de Fumel or female cabbage. - Produces very fine products in Hérault and Haute-Garonne. Chou rouge gros, chou rouge petit, chou vert glacé d'Amérique, chou marbré de Bourgogne, chou rouge petit d'Utrecht, chou rouge conique, chou rouge foncé hâtif d'Erfurth, chou très hâtif d'Étampes. Among the new varieties introduced to the market in recent years, we should mention: Express cabbage, non-pareil cabbage, early Rennes cabbage, Christmas cabbage, Amager cabbage. MILAN CROW Brassica oleracea bullata. Race with more or less blistered, wrinkled or curled, intense green leaves (fig. 16); prominent midrib, acuminate in the upper part, rarely obtuse; the secondary veins are strongly apparent in some varieties and extend to the upper part of the leaf blade. The apples generally have less consistency than cabbages and are smaller, better tasting and more tender, especially when the first frosts have taken away the green taste. This breed of cabbage is more highly esteemed than cabbages, as they are less musky. CULTIVATION. - April and May are the best months to sow savoy cabbages. They are broadcast in beds. Mulch and water lightly to maintain constant soil moisture. When the plant is strong enough, it is thinned out and transplanted into a nursery. These cabbages are good for planting from June to August. 16 - Savoy cabbage. Early varieties can be sown as early as March for final planting in May and June. In summer, however, these varieties need plenty of water or cool soil to reach full growth. VARIETIES. - We will list them in order of earliness: Very early Savoy cabbage. - Very good, early variety, still little known, medium-sized head. Highly recommended. Small, early Ulm Savoy cabbage. - Variety with a small head, fairly high stem, strongly blistered leaves; very early, but not very productive; suitable for first-season planting. Very early Savoy cabbage from Paris. - Early variety, widely grown around Paris; medium-sized, firm head; glossy, dark-green leaves; very good for the first winter season (fig. 16). Early short savoy cabbage. - One of our best winter varieties. Short stalk, broad, finely blistered, dark-green leaves, firm, depressed head. This cabbage is very hardy and has good flavor. It is highly regarded at the market. Ordinary Milan cabbage. - An old variety that still has its merit; tall stalk, glaucous-green, slightly broad, blistered leaves, medium-sized, fairly firm head; highly esteemed in southwestern and western France, not very fussy about soil quality; excellent taste. Chou de Milan gros des vertus, also known as chou de Milan gros frisé d'Allemagne or chou de Paris - Very old variety, grown all over France; considerable consumption; tall stalk, large leaves, blistered at the top, dark glaucous green; fairly tight, flattened head. A very good winter breed. Milan cabbage, Pontoise late winter. - A tall variety with broadly blistered, glaucous, dark-green leaves and a large, very hard, late-ripening head. Generally formed in winter, it is the successor to Milan cabbage. This variety is said to be the type of the old Milan cabbage that Parisian market gardeners have improved. It's an excellent cabbage that we have no hesitation in recommending. Norwegian savoy cabbage. - Very late variety, fairly tall stem, erect, slightly blistered leaves, purplish in color, medium-sized, loosely packed head, forming very late. In winter, it withstands the most intense cold. Several other varieties are still grown, but are of little value outside their country of origin: Long-headed Savoy cabbage. - The elongated shape of the head is reminiscent of sugarloaf cabbage; it does very well in the late season. Early Savoy cabbage from Limay. - Very early and firm, very small head. Cabbage pancalier, small Joulin hâtif. - Very small head; very early. Pancalier cabbage from Tours. - Very early, but not very productive. Victoria Savoy cabbage. - Quite a good species, doing well in good, moist soil. Cape Savoy. - Very high stalk, tight head, degenerates easily, so that in a seedling there are only a few plants that pump well; fears frosts. Golden Savoy cabbage. - Short-stalked variety, medium-sized head, elongated, not very tight, yellow in color; prominent veins, very tender after the frosts have passed over it. New varieties include: Early Savoy cabbage from Aubervillers. - Early Agen cabbage. CROUX DE BRUXELLES - CHOUX ROSETTES Brussels sprouts are thought to have originated from Savoy cabbage. Its leaves, especially in the dwarf Brussels sprout, are very similar to those of the curly Savoy; they are blistered, dark green and form a small apple at the end of the stem. CULTIVATION. - Sow from March to June, in nursery beds, broadcast. The first seedlings, planted in June, will begin to produce towards the end of summer and throughout the winter. May sowings produce a little later, but the difference is so great that it is preferable to sow only once in the first half of April, and plant as soon as the seedling is good. E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 10 Cultivation is the same as for Savoy cabbage, except that the plants need to be spaced further apart so that they can pass easily between the rows and pick up the small apples; 50 to 60 centimeters is enough for the ordinary variety, and 40 to 50 centimeters for the dwarf variety. This cabbage thrives in good, moist soil, but should not be fertilized with strong fertilizers that force vegetation and cause the apples to grease, or to put it another way, prevent them from peeling. In order to encourage apple development, some growers have advised pinching the Brussels sprout once it has reached a certain height. We experimented with this procedure several times, pinching back every other row. The pinched row did not sprout earlier than the other, so we conclude that pinching reduces the yield without advancing development, so it's better not to pinch at all. Brussels sprouts are fairly cold-hardy, making them an excellent winter vegetable, very delicate and very fine, provided the apples are picked when they are firm; the smaller they are, the better they are appreciated. Brussels sprouts are not cultivated enough in France; this is a mistake, because a plot of land planted with this vegetable yields a lot. We have made comparisons, and have always found an advantage in its favor. In the establishment where we ran the cultivation for several years, we grew it in large quantities, and certainly, the production was good, and not only did we use the shoots as a dish, but the leaves were given to rabbits: in spring, when the plant was about to come up, all the heads that were a little plump, made tender by the frosts, were used for soup or certain dishes; they were very good. VARIETIES. - Ordinary Brussels sprouts (fig. 17). - The best variety, very productive, excellent quality; stems 70 cm to 1 m high, slender; spoon-shaped leaves, strongly petiolate and slightly blistered, slightly purplish. Numerous, widely spaced, very firm, small shoots, much appreciated in the markets. Dwarf Brussels sprouts. - Tall variety, 50 to 60 cm, with thick stem, broader, more blistered leaves than the previous one, larger shoots, closer together, less firm; perhaps a little earlier, but less productive. Sellier half-dwarf Brussels sprout. - This variety was sent to us in 1885 by MM. Dupanloup et Cie. We tried it, and the results were not as satisfactory as they had promised. It is a rather dwarf variety, but very vigorous, with fairly large, loosely packed shoots; needs to be improved. Brussels sprouts no longer ultra. - We have received this variety from Bordeaux, and it has given us very good results, but we don't think it can be made into a separate variety; it resembles the ordinary Brussels sprout in every way, but is perhaps not as tall. Half-dwarf Brussels sprout from La Halle. - A new variety not exceeding 65 centimeters, hardy and very productive. CHOU A GROSSES COTES ORDINAIRE This breed of cabbage, which botanists have classified as a Milan cabbage, is of little interest. It is grown very little in France, but a lot in England; it has the advantage of not being affected by even the coldest weather, which, on the contrary, is necessary for its qualities. CULTIVATION. - It is sown at the same time as Savoy cabbage, and cultivation is the same. It is mainly in autumn, under the influence of rain, that this variety develops most vigorously. The stem is short, the leaves are close together, very thick-veined and prominent, whitish yellow or greenish, with a thick, well-developed midrib. The head is small and usually absent. Cabbage with large fringed ribs. - A sub-variety of the previous one, but preferable for quality and production. Market gardeners near Paris grow a variety of green cabbage they call Bricoli; it appears to be descended from the cabbage with large fringed ribs, of which it is undoubtedly a bastard. It doesn't apple, but produces a large quantity of thick, extremely curly, lobed, petiolate leaves. It is very hardy and can withstand the coldest weather. GREEN CABBAGE. - FORAGE KOLS. - NON-POMMED CABBAGE Brassica virens. This class comes under the heading of agriculture, since the main use of its various varieties is as animal feed. However, once the leaves have been softened by frost, they can be used for a variety of culinary purposes. When the plant goes to seed, which happens every two years, the young, tender shoots are picked and eaten like asparagus or broccoli. Farmers in Charentes, Poitou, Haute-Vienne, Dordogne, Vendée, etc., take them to market. In general, all varieties of green cabbage have fleshy, fairly broad, almost smooth leaves, except for a few blisters (and those that are laciniated), the midrib is very well developed, the petiole is

long and very large, especially at the base. CULTIVATION. - Sow from March and April to July in good, freshly-turned soil; spring sowings are generally preferred. These cabbages are so hardy that the seedlings, though large, can be transplanted: we have replanted some very strong ones, which have recovered perfectly and developed vigorously. VARIETIES. - The same varieties to grow are : Cavalier or cow cabbage. - The most widely grown, very productive, develops very quickly, very hardy. Chou vert branchu du Poitou. - Very productive, hardy variety, highly esteemed in Poitou and Limousin. Chou moellier blanc. - Excellent variety, very productive and fast-growing; the stalk becomes very thick and strongly swollen in the middle; cut into thin slices, it is very tender and, like beet, is used as animal feed in winter. It can be used cooked or raw. Less hardy than beets, it fears the cold. In northern France, it is harvested before the frosts. - It differs from white moellier by the purplish tint of its stem; it is hardier and seems to withstand the cold better. Animals prefer white cabbage; its color, which probably has a particular odor and flavor, seems to repel them. Flanders cabbage. - Red, very hardy and productive. Chou mille têtes. - Native to the Vendée region, where it is widely grown, very productive, but sensitive to cold. 40. Chou de Lannilis blond. - Highly esteemed variety in Brittany, fairly productive. Daubenton's perennial cabbage. - Particular variety with long, hanging branches, fairly productive. Mowing cabbage. - Stems are almost nonexistent, giving rise to a number of lobed, green leaves with grayish-white petioles, forming a strong clump that can be mowed several times. This variety gives good results only if planted in good, cool soil. i ne" Sarthe forage cabbage. - Very good variety, ample foliage, widely blistered, fleshy petiole, very hardy. Also worth mentioning: Palmetto. - Very attractive, but not very productive. Naples kale. - More ornamental than vegetable, it produces swellings like kohlrabi, which suggests that it is intermediate between cauliflower and kohlrabi. 0192 Large green kale. - More ornamental than vegetable, this variety is very hardy. Short-stalked green kale. - Short-stalked red kale. - Red variegated kale. - White variegated kale. - Variegated laciniated kale. - Variegated poliferous kale. - Large red kale. All these varieties are particularly ornamental. CABBAGE Brassica oleraeca gongiloides L. ORIGIN. - According to De Candolle, it originated in the ancient world. Here's what he says: 1° Brassicas with fleshy roots are native to temperate Europe. 2° Their cultivation spread to Europe and India before and after the invasion of the Aryas. Cultivation of the various brassica species has spread to south-west Asia since the time of the ancient Hebrews, bringing the origin of its cultivation to over 4,000 years ago. - Kohlrabi is sown from March to June, in sufficiently loosened, fresh soil, in beds, in nurseries. Water and mulch according to the time of sowing. When the young plants begin to grow a little strong, they are FIG. 18 - Kohlrabi. thinned out to prevent the root from shrivelling, which would then become an obstacle to the growth of the fleshy part, which needs very rapid development to be succulent and tender. They are planted when they are a little strong, in the same way as other cabbage varieties. They are generally planted in rows of six, 35 cm apart. Water as you plant, and keep watering throughout the growing season. For, if they lack water, they become woody and cordate, and therefore unsuitable for consumption; nor should we neglect hoeing and weeding, which must be repeated often. Remove the yellow leaves from the base. These cabbages survive the winter fairly well without suffering. VARIETY. - Early white Vienne kohlrabi. - Very early variety, small size, short leaves, few in number; can be eaten three months after sowing. White kohlrabi (fig. 18). - A very good hardy variety, reaching a high volume. Early violet Vienne kohlrabi. - An early variety with more or less the same characteristics as early white kohlrabi, but with the difference that the kohlrabi is surrounded by a purple skin that extends to the leaf petioles and veins. Ordinary purple kohlrabi. - A variety derived from white kohlrabi, but distinguished by its violet color; it is hardy and grows very large. Goliath violet kohlrabi. - A new variety, remarkable for its size; we've had balls weighing 7 and 8 kilograms; it's likely that in very good, moist soil, you can get better; tender and tasty. CHOU-NAVET. - RUTABAGA. - TURNEPS Cabbage Brassica oleracea Napus. Another breed quite different from kohlrabi in that the tuber it produces is almost entirely in the ground, forming an ovoid mass almost as long as it is wide (fig. 19). This tuber becomes quite voluminous, especially in good, fresh, well-smoked soils. In dry, chalky soils, it has given poor results. CULTIVATION. - Like kohlrabi, it is sown from March to June, either in the field or in nurseries. We tried both types of cultivation to compare results. Plants raised in the nursery and transplanted developed as vigorously as those sown in the field; we therefore conclude that it is better to sow in the nursery and then transplant in the field. Cultivation care is the same as for kohlrabi. However, in England, Ireland and much of Brittany, this vegetable is grown on a large scale, just as beet is in the North. In these regions, cattle are very fond of this turnip, which is an excellent winter feed and seems to fatten them up quickly. In general, this plant keeps very well and can spend the winter outdoors without suffering too much from the cold. However, they should be eaten during the winter, as they quickly go to seed and become tough in spring. VARIETY. - White turnip cabbage - FIG. 19. Turnip cabbage. An excellent variety that keeps well, forming a very large, tender turnip with good flavor. Highly esteemed in the Angoumois region, where it is grown in large quantities, it is one of the best varieties. White turnip with red collar. - It differs from the previous variety by the reddish tint of the collar; the flesh is very white and tender. White smooth cabbage with short leaves. - Flattened variety, similar in appearance or shape to the flat Egyptian beet, very early, medium size, very firm white flesh, excellent as a vegetable variety. Yellow turnip or green-necked rutabaga. - Rutabagas are all yellow-fleshed, and therefore form a breed of their own. The above-mentioned variety produces a large, spherical, slightly rounded turnip with a greenish-purple collar. Red-necked rutabaga. - A variety with more or less the same characteristics as the previous one, except for the purplish-red collar; the flesh is very good. Yellow, flat, early Rutabaga. - Very early variety, medium size; highly recommended for the vegetable garden. Champion rutabaga. - Excellent variety, very productive, good for large-scale cultivation, highly esteemed in northern and eastern France. Drummond rutabaga, red-necked. - Skirving rutabaga (red collar). - West-Nor folk rutabaga (red collar). - Laing rutabaga (whole leaf). - Oval rutabaga. - These last varieties, like almost all others, are of English origin. Cauliflower Brassica oleracea Botrytis. Cauliflower is a breed apart and quite distinct from other cabbage varieties. Leaves are generally upright, whole, elongated, smooth, with smooth edges, rarely divided, bluish-green, more or less dark. Petioles are very large and prominent, both above and below, and yellowish-white with strong veins at the base. The apple, which is in a way nothing more than an assembly of the flower's supports, should be very tightly grained and white, with the middle more developed than the edges; these are the main characteristics of a good variety. CULTIVATION. - The best production centers in France are near Paris, Châlons, Saint-Brieuc, Arras, and a large part of Brittany; these products are shipped in complete vagons to the Paris market. Many growers specialize in this area, and are sure to make a good living from it. Many of our products are shipped to London. Cauliflower is also grown in Germany, England and Switzerland. As you can see, cauliflower is mainly grown in northern countries; it does well there, because there is always some humidity, it rains often, and cabbage only grows vigorously when the atmosphere is damp. This explains why cabbages planted in dry soils do not develop in summer, and when autumn comes, with its frequent rains, they grow vigorously. When you have land with a moist bottom, you're always sure of the result. Growing cauliflower is not difficult, but it does require a certain amount of know-how if it is to be a success; without this, a lot of trouble is taken, only to end in cruel disappointment, as we have seen time and again. Cauliflower needs rapid development. Otherwise, the apples don't form well, they are small, not very tight, they look like fruit that has suffered, and are therefore little appreciated. To obtain this rapid growth, especially in summer, when cauliflowers are most widely planted, they need to be placed in moist soil, sufficiently fertilized with good, energetic fertilizers, and given abundant watering or irrigation. However, there are certain dry soils where summer cultivation, despite copious watering, always gives poor results. To prove the point, let's take a look at our comparative experiments. At the same time, we planted demidur Paris cauliflowers in three squares of different soil types: the first square was marsh soil, a little peaty, and consequently very wet. The second square was alluvial, with a high clay content. The third square was a silico-calcareous soil, very dry in summer. The plantations in the first two squares were not watered, while those in the third square were watered copiously throughout the hot season. At harvest, the apples in square number 1 were magnificent, with very tight, white berries; those in number 2 were quite pretty, but much smaller; those in number 3 were small, poorly formed and hard. It is therefore easy to conclude that cauliflower thrives best in strong, deep or moist soils, or in soils that are difficult to dry out. Cauliflower is sown at three different times: 1° in winter, for spring and summer; 2° in summer, for autumn; 3° finally, in autumn, for spring. The first seedlings are usually sown in a greenhouse or under a cloche, in January or February, on a warm bed. When the plant is strong enough to withstand transplanting, it is placed on another warm layer. During cold spells, they are covered with straw mats and gradually given air to get them used to the outside temperature. Towards the end of March or the beginning of April, they are transplanted into place, and produce in June-July. From the end of March to May 15th, we sow in the open ground, with good exposure; we transplant in place, as and when the plants are good, and we have products which follow one another from July to September. For these kinds of seedlings, it's best to choose tender or Salomon cauliflower, or even better, semi-hard Paris. The latter variety always does well, sown at any time of year, and is used almost exclusively by Parisian market gardeners. Summer seedlings can be sown from June 1st to 15th; they are planted in July or August, on a dark or rainy day. Properly treated, these plants bear fruit in October and November. This cultivation, which seems simple, becomes difficult if you don't have a lot of water. The last seedlings are sown in the ground in August-September, in well-exposed beds. The seedlings are planted out in good exposure and, when the cold arrives, covered with windbreak mulch. In the south of France, they overwinter fairly well without suffering, or keep very well under the slightest shelter. They are planted in March, and produce in May or June. Hard cauliflower is well suited to this season. When planted out, they are arranged as described for head cabbage. Lettuce or chicory can be counter-planted. Tender cauliflower can be planted much more tightly than other varieties. When the young plants are taken up, if possible, they should be watered well with liquid manure, and this operation should be repeated often while they are young. Hoe several times, and deeply. Often, as frost approaches, the apples on many plants are barely formed and too small to be eaten straight away. So, although they grow little, E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 11 during cold spells, we recommend the following method, which has worked well for us. Bring all the leaves over the apple in the shape of a cap, tie them loosely with a raffia or a rush; then leave them in this state for a few days; it takes cold temperatures of 8 or 10 degrees to reach the apples thus swaddled. When you want to keep some apples in winter, you can still try this method. When you realize that the temperature is going to drop, you choose a fine day, when the cabbages will be well wiped. Tear them off and put them in a cellar or storeroom. After removing the outer leaves, plant them upright in sand, which should be dry rather than damp. They should be visited frequently to remove any rotting leaves. Aerate them whenever the temperature permits. They can also be stored for some time, by hanging them upside down and keeping some of the leaves. This method requires a great deal of care to succeed, as the leaves quickly become moldy, so they need to be visited often. They can also be stored as follows: Start by forming a circular layer with good horse manure, which should be well compacted; when it is 15 centimetres high, place the first row of cauliflowers, previously stripped of most of their leaves and with their roots; arrange them in a circle, side by side, without squeezing them too much, with the apple outside the manure. Once the first row has been planted, the roots are covered with manure, which is carefully placed between each plant. Place a second bed of manure high enough so that the second row of cauliflowers doesn't touch the first, and continue in this way until the wheel is completely finished, which can be raised as high as you like. It's essential that the middle is always below the edges, to form a conical wheel. If they are placed in a healthy, warm environment, they will keep for a long time without deteriorating. In general, heads of cauliflower, placed in the various conditions we have just described, almost always wilt. The best way to restore them to their original freshness is to leave them with a fairly long stalk, which can be lightly pressed into damp sand, or even better, into wet moss; in this way, cauliflowers are as fresh as when they were growing. VARIETIES. - The cauliflower genus, thought to derive from green cabbage, has been classified into three main varieties: tender, semi-hard and hard. There is no particular characteristic that distinguishes them at first sight: the difference exists only in earliness, in the more or less tight grain, and in quality. Tender cauliflower - Generally small, very early, producing a small, tight head and dividing quickly. Semi-hard cauliflower. - It produces a fairly strong, upright plant, with a much larger, tighter-grained, whiter head than soft cauliflower. Hard cauliflower. - This is a strong plant, producing a large globular head, excessively tightly packed, very fine-grained and of excellent quality. Tender Paris or Salomon cauliflower. - Very early, forming a medium-sized, loosely packed head that does not keep long, suitable for winter and summer sowing. Early Erfurth dwarf cauliflower. - Very early variety, very short stalk, good head, grain a little tighter than Salomon, very white, does not keep well pure; its seeds must be obtained from Germany if you want to have very good products. Semi-hard Paris cauliflower. - Excellent variety, can be grown in any season, and produces fine products; large, firm, tight-grained apples; stores well; very hardy, highly esteemed on the markets. Chou-fieur Lenormand. - A very hardy, productive variety, which gave birth to the following variety and, it is claimed, has been advantageously replaced by it. Lenormand short-stalked cauliflower. - Very valuable variety in all respects, rustic; very short stem, leaves a little spread out, short, very thick, large, very firm head; long-lasting, extremely productive. Chou-fleur demi-dur de Saint-Brieuc. - A variety widely grown in Brittany, very hardy, producing globular apples with an excessively tight, very firm texture and a slightly musky, bland taste; ideal for export. Paris hard cauliflower. - A very common variety around Paris, where it is grown in large quantities, very late, hardy, forming large, regular apples with very tight, firm seeds. Dutch hard cabbage. - A semi-late variety grown on a large scale in Germany, where it is highly esteemed; we have tried growing it several times, but find that in slightly warm climates, the apples are relatively small compared with the development of the plant, which is excessively vigorous. Stadthold cauliflower. - A late variety, with a good, tight head and about the same growth habit as the hard Dutch variety, not widely grown in France. Walheren hard cauliflower. - A very late variety, to be sown in late March, first half of April, for autumn production. Sown in May or June, like broccoli, it spends the winter very well and apples very early in the spring. Excellent, tight-grained and firm. Giant Naples cauliflower. - About as hardy as Walkeren's, very large, very tall, very large head, firm, tight grain. English hard cauliflower. - Very late and resistant to cold. Alger cauliflower. - Very vigorous, with a large, high stem, a little late. Sicilian black cauliflower. - Vigorous and hardy; sown in autumn, it overwinters and apples in spring. New or little-known varieties include: Fournier's improved all-season hard cauliflower. - Similar to the old hard cauliflower, but a few days earlier; large, globular head with tight, white seeds; suitable for autumn cultivation. Châlons improved cauliflower. - Magnificent species with very large head, fine, tight grain, very firm, does well in autumn, its main season. The Dupanloup house in Paris, from which we obtained these two varieties, won first prize for this variety in 1885. Early dwarf Alleaume cauliflower. - Short stalk, large head with tight, white seeds; suitable for early crops. Lemaître short-stalked cauliflower. - Very good variety, early white, fairly large. Giant Naples cauliflower, half-early. - High-yielding variety, should be planted quite far apart. SEEDS. - Cauliflower seed is extremely difficult to obtain pure, which explains why it is always so expensive, costing from 70 to 120 francs per kilogram. When a variety is localized, it reproduces freely; the same variety sown elsewhere will produce bastardized plants. To harvest good cauliflower seeds, sow in September. In February or March, or even April, depending on the region, when they are ready for harvest, you choose the best-formed, stocky, vigorous plants, with a firm, tight head, free from small leaves mixed with grain. We cover the formed apple with a leaf to prevent it from hardening off; when it starts to open, it will rise, so it must be uncovered; we often water around the stem with the neck of the watering can. When the seedlings start to bloom, pinch off the tips of the most vigorous ones to feed the branches below. Watch out for aphids, and destroy them by spraying with salt water or nicotine, or sprinkling with powdered quicklime. As the siliques ripen, cut them off and lay them out on a cloth to dry in the sun; all that's left to do is winnow and clean them; it's said that the seed that's ripe first is the best. Seeds are good for five years; 30 grams contain 9880 seeds. BROCOLI Brassica Botrytis cymosa Broccoli (fig. 20) is an excessively late variety of cauliflower. It is assumed that all our early varieties are descended from this race, which itself comes from kale. The leaves are longer, narrower, more numerous, less darkly colored, with stronger, whiter veins than in cauliflower. The stalk becomes much FIG. 20. - Broccoli cauliflower. more voluminous, the apples in the whites are generally very large, fairly firm and very fine-grained. CULTIVATION. - Cultivation differs little from that of cauliflower, but is much easier. Sow from April to June in nurseries. Transplant if possible, and plant out when strong enough, at least 60 cm apart in all directions for large varieties such as Mammoth, and 50 cm apart for others. Hoe often and water copiously during the summer. Between each cabbage and in the false row, lettuces, romaine, chicory, etc. are counter-planted, or purslane, radishes, etc. are sown. In the south, south-west and part of western France, broccoli winters quite well without any shelter, but in the north it must be protected from frost. The most practical way to do this is to lay it down, face north, and cover as much of the stalk as possible with soil up to the first leaves. It must therefore be planted deep, and the best way is to adopt furrow cultivation; plant at the bottom, and when winter comes all you have to do is lay the plant on one side and bring the soil over it. VARIETY. - Early white broccoli. - Very early, easy to grow, very hardy, apples well and tightly, fine-grained, firm, keeps for quite a long time. Easter broccoli. - Small, very early variety, many grayish leaves, very regular, medium-sized head, firm, tight-grained; very good quality. Ordinary white broccoli. - Very hardy, semi-late variety, reaching a high volume; fairly large, very white, tight head; keeps for a long time without spreading. Roscoff white broccoli. - Fairly early variety, resembling early white broccoli, of which it is probably only a sub-variety; fairly large, regular, tight, rounded, hard-grained head; keeps well, widely grown in Brittany, mainly around Quimper, highly esteemed in England. Mammoth white broccoli. - Very late variety, very hardy; large, white head, tight, fine-grained, rounded and firm; highly recommended. Angers early white broccoli. - Very good, hardy variety with good production. Late white broccoli from Angers. - Good hardy variety with very large, very white heads. Purple broccoli. - Breed improved by t4 FIG. 21 - Broccoli violet branchu. market gardeners from Bordeaux, very hardy; fairly large, purplish apple, highly esteemed in the South-West. Branchy purple broccoli (fig. 21). - Widely cultivated throughout the Midi. Leaves are very dark purple, broad and somewhat wavy or curled. The shoots are also purple, long and form small apples at the ends. These broccolis are much sought-after11. by the working class, who eat them like green asparagus; they are tender and very tasty. Extra-early white broccoli. - New variety, highly praised. Very white, fine-grained, medium-sized head; fairly hardy. SEEDS. - Broccoli seed is easier to harvest than cauliflower seed, and less expensive. It requires the same care in cultivation and the same precautions in harvesting. When the stalks are strong and loaded with a quantity of sometimes very heavy capsules, to prevent them from being broken by the wind, they are tied to stakes or slats. When the fruit begins to ripen, care must be taken to keep out the birds, which are quite fond of it and must be chased away with scarecrows. It keeps well for five years. COMMON CIBBAGE Allium fistulosum L. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant from Siberia (from the Kirghiz country to Baïcal); according to Donn, it was introduced in 1629. GROWING. - Chives are propagated from seed, sown in March or April and again in August, either in the field or in a nursery in good, well-smoked, recently tilled soil; the seed is lightly covered and lightly treaded. If sown in a nursery, when the young plants are strong enough, they are transplanted in place, either in beds or in borders, after trimming the roots, as is done for onions. Water lightly to facilitate recovery; other care consists of weeding and hoeing, and good watering in summer. This plant can also be propagated by dividing the stems, which are kept over winter under a leaf shelter, to be planted in spring. However, as it goes to seed every year, and provides many seeds, it is preferable to sow it, as it is more vigorous. In harsh winters, it should be covered with dry leaves or earth, and if you don't want to run out, place the clumps under a frame. VAriérés. - Ciboule commune. - Most commonly grown, hardy, elongated bulges, copper-red, very productive, fast-growing. Ciboule blanche hâtive. - Smaller than the previous variety in all its parts, with shorter, pinkish-white bulges; stiff, short, dark green, glaucous leaves. Less strong, with a finer flavor than common chives; more sensitive to cold. SEEDS. - The plant goes to seed in the second year, and is harvested in August; it is collected and processed like onions. It keeps well for three years; 30 grams contain around 2000 seeds. MAlaDIES. - When it develops rapidly, chives are sometimes subject to scald like shallots; this disease is due to the development of an underground fungus (Rhizoctonia) which attacks the roots and causes the plants to die. There are few remedies for this disease; just pull out the diseased clumps as soon as you notice them. USES. - Chives are frequently used in cooking, and the leaves are used as condiments in salads and omelettes. In the south of France, country people eat them raw with bread. CIBOULE VIVACE or CIBOULE DE SAINT-JACQUES Allium lusitanicum Lam. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant, native to the same regions as the above. CULTIVATION. - This breed is distinguished from the others by its numerous, elongated, reddish-brown bulbs and large, stiff, glaucous-green leaves. It does not produce fertile seeds. A few flower stalks develop in spring, but the ovaries remain sterile. It can be propagated by dividing clumps and separating them in March or April. Same cultivation care and uses as for the previous species. It is sometimes confused with the chive: however, it is easy to avoid confusion, as the chive is much less voluminous in all its parts. CIBOULET Allium Schœnoprasum L. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - Perennial, found growing wild in southern France, temperate and northern Europe, Siberia, Kamchatka, northern America (Lake Huron). Cultivated for over two thousand years. CULTIVATION. - This plant, generally known as civet, reproduces by bursting its clumps in March or April; it is planted in borders at 20 cm in all directions, or in flowerbeds. Hoe often, water during the summer and spread a good mulch over the beds or around the plants.
