As these plants only need to be renewed every three or four years, every winter they are "terreauteed", i.e., after a good hoeing, about 4 or 5 centimetres of compost is spread over the bed or borders. Chives can withstand the coldest weather, but even so, it's a good idea, especially in northern climates, to cover them with leaves or manure. As they don't grow at this time of year, if you want leaves, pull up a few clumps and put them under a frame, on a warm layer as close as possible to the glass. You can even put them in pots and place them on the benches of a greenhouse. SEEDS. - Although chives produce a number of flower stalks topped by a bunch of purplish-red flowers, they do not produce fertile seeds. We have tried several times to get them to produce seeds by artificial fertilization, but have never succeeded. DISEASES. - According to our observations, this plant appears to be disease-free. USES. - More or less the same as the common spring onion; however, it is more frequently used in salads, herb omelettes and ham; it also goes well with snails. CUCUMBER Cucumis sativus L. Cucurbitaceae. ORIGIN. - An annual plant native to India, where it has been cultivated for over three thousand years; introduced into China two centuries before the Christian era. The cucumber is a creeping plant, with angular stems, rough to the touch and flexible; the alternate leaves are right-angled or shallowly cut; the flowers are yellow, single-petaled, cut into five roughly equal divisions, solitary, or more often in bunches of seven, eight or more, depending on the variety; it is mainly the male flowers that are grouped in this way and in greater numbers; but there is always a female flower, which can be recognized by the ovary already formed before the flower blooms. The flower is composed of a style with three stigmas, and three or four stamens without anthers. Female flowers are usually solitary, sometimes geminate. The fruit is cylindrical, oblong, smooth or lined with protuberances ending in a thorn, sometimes quite prickly. The rind is yellow, green or yellowish; the flesh is firm, transparent and watery. Cucumber cultivation is much the same as that of the melon, which it resembles in its botanical characteristics. It thrives in a variety of well-prepared, fertilizer-rich soils, but seems to do best in soft, slightly damp soils. The first cucumbers are sown in well-prepared soil from late March to June. This soil can be prepared in several ways. Some growers make holes 30 to 40 centimetres square, as deep, and 1m 20 apart. These holes are filled with good warm manure, which is firmly tamped down, covered with a few centimetres of soil and then sown. This is not a new process, but it gives fairly good results, especially in strong soils, as only a little soil is disturbed at a time. The most commonly used method consists in opening trenches, 25 to 40 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres deep. These are filled with fresh or half-consumed manure, compacted well and then covered with the looser soil removed from the trench; this is then stirred and crushed again with the spade. Rake over the whole to form a kind of ridge, and sow on the top of this ridge, after having formed a small trough where the seeds are to be placed; better still, trace a small radius with the hoe, sow along the whole line and cover with sifted loam mixed with half the soil; this precaution is essential for strong soils if you want good results. You can also sow in 10-centimeter pots placed on warm beds and without a frame; when the plants have developed their first two leaves, place them in well-prepared soil. This method works well: plants raised in this way produce earlier than seedlings planted in situ, but produce less: we have carried out comparative trials. When you have good soil at your disposal, i.e. sufficiently fertilized and fresh, you can operate in a different way. Once the soil has been well ploughed and fertilized, hoe it into rays 8 to 10 centimetres deep and 1.5 metres apart, and bring the soil from the edge of the rays to the middle, where the path should be, so that it is high; 50 centimetres from each side of the main ray, draw a small line for planting Romaines, which will be removed before harming the cucumbers; sow the seeds 10 centimetres apart on the line, cover with the mixture indicated above, or soil if fine enough, and water. Towards the end of April, this method can be tried with success. Once the young shoots have developed their fourth leaf, we recommend pinching them back, as this first pinch will soon give rise to four new branches, which will lengthen appreciably with their own particular vigor. The buds themselves will be pinched off at their third leaf, giving rise to a new series of branches which will be left to their own devices, but the tips of any that overgrow will be trimmed. Other care consists of watering during the hot season, hoeing, weeding and spreading a good mulch over the surface of the beds or at least around the plants. When cucumbers are grown for canning, they should be picked small and green. Picking should be done every two days, and the fruit should never be allowed to swell if you intend to pick small ones, as the crop would soon be exhausted; it's better to mark a few plants and let all the fruit swell. With a little care and time, con- combers can be rowed in the same way as peas, but with numerous branches. The first ascent of the stems is facilitated by tying them with rushes, after which they cling to themselves with their tendrils. They can also be trained in espaliers, as practiced in England and Russia, and directed as desired, as they lend themselves well to all sorts of shapes, provided you have the time to visit them often. Indeed, all these methods are better suited to an amateur than to a market gardener, who at this time of year is overwhelmed with work. In England, where cucumbers are grown extensively, special greenhouses are devoted to them, with the stalks attached to trellises a few centimetres from the glass, and when the whole greenhouse is furnished, the effect produced by the fruit hanging from all sides is quite original. VARIETIES. - Green cucumber, Petit de Paris. - A vigorous, high-yielding plant, much appreciated by confectioners, with small, attractive green fruits. Excellent variety for green harvesting. Generally grown everywhere. Large yellow cucumber. - Hardy, productive variety, producing beautiful fruit, good for green harvesting, generally grown everywhere. Very long green cucumber from China. - Little-known, new variety, fairly productive. Picked young, the fruit is long, green, with a few spines. Particularly suitable for candying. Ordinary long green cucumber. - A very good variety for outdoor use, giving fairly good yields, with long, green, good-quality fruit. Very large white Bonneuil cucumber. - An old variety with very large fruit, very productive, perhaps the hardiest, grown extensively around Paris for the perfume industry. Unsuitable for green harvesting, due to the yellow color of the fruit. Russian embroidered cucumber. - An early variety, producing small, dull yellow fruits dotted with small grayish lines, giving them a dirty appearance; can be grown for green harvesting. Long green Athens cucumber. - Vigorous, stocky, long, large fruit, keeps well, very hardy and fairly productive. Rollison's telegraph cucumber. - Variety bred by an English gardener, Mr. Walkelm, head gardener at the Manorhouse in Tooting, highly esteemed in England, where it is most commonly grown; long, early, crisp fruit; suitable for forced cultivation. Fournier cucumber, long green, early finish. - A new variety, very vigorous and fairly early; long, not very thorny, green fruit, very good for cultivation in the garden and for pickling. Fine Meaux gherkin cucumber. - New variety, not yet widespread, very productive, early, very good for preserving. Bourbonne improved gherkin cucumber - New variety, very productive, long, firm, green fruit, very good for preserving. Large, green, early gherkin. - New variety, high production, green, oblong, slightly elongated fruit, very good for confectioners. The following varieties are also grown: Early yellow cucumber from Holland. - Early white cucumber. - Parisian long white cucumber (fig. 22). Almost all these varieties do not perform well in northern France when grown outdoors. SEEDS. - To obtain good seeds, choose FIG. 22 - Parisian long white cucumber. a few plants. When the fruit is characteristic of the variety, we mark it with stakes and add labels. We leave the fruit on the stalks until it begins to rot, then take out the seed, put it in a cloth and wash it with plenty of water. Dry in the shade. It keeps well for eight years. 30 grams contain around 1,500 seeds, and a liter weighs 500 grams. slugs and pests. - In addition to the slugs and snails that eat cucumbers, especially when they start to grow, cucumbers are also affected by a parasitic disease known as sucker disease. This is a small microscopic fungus that develops on the underside of the leaves, covering them with white or yellowish dust. Plants affected by this disease should be watered for a few days with a solution of lime and copper sulfate; if the disease persists, the sickest leaves should be removed and burned. This disease prefers etiolated, sickly plants, especially those lacking water. USES. - Cucumbers have long been used as food: their flesh is white, unpalatable, not very nutritious, and only suitable for strong stomachs. It is widely consumed in hot countries, due to its refreshing but somewhat laxative properties. It is eaten raw, in salads, with a strong seasoning, or cooked with lean or fat, and drizzled with the juices of roasted meats: raw, it is indigestible; cooked, it refreshes. The first fruits, picked before they are ripe and preserved in vinegar with various herbs, are known as gherkins, and frequently served on tables to stimulate the appetite. Cucumber pulp is used to make cucumber ointment, a cosmetic that is said to soften the skin. They are combined with sweet almonds to make calming and refreshing emulsions. SNAKE CUCUMBER Cucumis fiexuosus. Cucurbitaceae. ORIGIN. - India. CULTIVATION. - This plant is cultivated like melons, of which it is only a form; so it is wrong to call it a cucumber: it is called a snake because of the peculiarity of its fruits, which resemble a large contoured snake. We've had some plants whose fruits have become quite large and were not contoured: they were club-shaped; they ripened; they tasted more like melons than cucumbers. This plant is easy to grow. It is very hardy and more resistant to heat than gherkin cucumbers. SEEDS. - When the fruit is ripe, the seed is removed and cared for in the same way as for melons. MAlabiEs. - Virtually disease-free. USES. - When young, the fruit is used in the same way as gherkins, i.e. pickled in vinegar. This is the only use we know of. Cucumis Anguria L. Cucumis echinatus Mœnch. ORIGIN. - Annual plant from Jamaica; highly prized variety in Brazil, in Montevideo and Rio-Janeiro. GROWING. - Fruits are small, green and lined with fleshy, pointed, slightly curved protuberances, some of which form spines. The plant should be sown a little late, in May, to ensure sufficient warmth for rapid development. Same cultivation care as gherkin cucumber. USES. - Fruits can be preserved in vinegar or boiled and cooked in butter. GROSSED CUCUMBER Cucumis myriocarpus. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant of doubtful origin. Fruits are very small, quite good to eat, but bristling with long greenish hairs. Same cultivation and uses as above. ANE CUCUMBER Ecbalium agreste. ORIGIN. - Plant with perennial root, which becomes very large; small fruits, supported by a long, straight stalk, have the property of throwing their seeds forcefully and quite far, which is a great surprise to people unfamiliar with them. USES. - The fruits have been advocated as edible, but their pungent, bitter taste has caused them to be rejected. Cucurbits Cucurbita L. Cucurbitaceae. The squash genus includes all the varieties of Cucurbitaceae included under the names pumpkin, giraumon, gourd. In spite of the large number of varieties that exist, there are only three main races that cannot cross-fertilize each other; it is on these principles that M. Naudin's classification is based, to which we conform. CULTIVATION. - The cultivation of these different races is more or less the same. Squash are sown in the open ground, at the same time as cucumbers, in the second half of April, or in the first days of May. Pits are dug 45 to 60 centimetres wide and 15 or 20 centimetres deep. Fill them with good horse manure, mixed with other fermentable detritus. The manure is heavily compacted by walking on it. Cover the manure with loose soil, or potting compost mixed with vegetable garden soil. Sow three or four seeds per hole, cover with 4 cm and water. Instead of sowing in the field, you can sow in pots on warm layers and, when the cotyledons have developed, place them in the holes. Make a small basin around each plant and water. The distance between each hole varies according to the vigour of the variety you intend to grow. Generally speaking, 2 meters are required for small varieties, and 3 meters for others. When the squash start to grow, select the first two stems, then cut immediately above them; these stems soon grow vigorously. When they have reached 1.50 m, they are "marcotte", i.e. placed in a small gutter. They are held in this state by a small hook, and covered with soil. The buried part soon takes root, resulting in better vegetation. This operation can be performed two or three times on the same stem. On each of these stems, only one fruit is left; then the end of the branch two leaves above is pinched off; this must wait until the fruit is well knotted. A few days later, pinch back any fruit that has grown back into the leaf axils. Because of their very rapid growth and their herbaceous, watery constitution, these plants need copious watering in summer, especially if you want huge fruits, such as we have sometimes obtained weighing 80 to 100 kilograms, which is not uncommon, especially with large yellow pumpkins. Light hoeing is done at the base, and good, fat manure is used to mulch the crop. In general, farmers sow squash on piles of compost, or decomposing rubbish, and leave them to their own devices. The fruit develops quite well, but never becomes large, and this is just a fancy crop; these plants give better results grown in open fields. A few years ago, we planted them among our tomatoes, and as they were tied fairly high, the squash developed perfectly without harming the tomatoes. We encourage you to try this system, as you won't lose any ground. BREEDS AND VARIETIES. - Here is the list of cultivated races and varieties, according to M. Naudin's classification. Potir ons. SEEDS. - To harvest the seeds of the different varieties of squash, giraumons, coloquintes, etc., we choose the best shaped, best characterized specimens, take out the seed, spread it on a cloth and leave it to dry in the shade; once it is dry, we enclose it in canvas or paper bags. It keeps well for five years. DISEASES, PESTS. - Squash is sometimes affected by a disease similar to celery uredo, a yellowish dust that clings to the underside of the leaves and acts on them like mildew on vines. Milk of lime and copper sulfate in the same proportions as for vines are excellent remedies. Sometimes, after vegetating for some time, the plant turns yellow and becomes chlorotic; the only remedy is to uproot it. In many cases, this chlorosis is only artificial, and is due to the ravages of the white worm that gnaws at the roots; before uprooting, it is therefore important to ascertain the cause of the disease. Sometimes subterranean fungi develop on the main roots, at the root collar, and in a short time the plant is lost. When young, plants are liable to be eaten by snails and loaches, which are fond of them. USES. - Gourds are frequently used, especially by the poorer classes. They are eaten in a variety of ways, usually cooked to make excellent lean soups or purées. Mixing them with milk, to which they go very well, makes excellent soups, but they are not suitable for weak stomachs. They are also used to make jams, marmalades and preserves similar to sauerkraut. Given to cows, they increase milk secretion. Fruits picked very young and small can be preserved in vinegar like gherkins. They are also used to make CRAMBÉ MARITIME orgeat. - CHOU MARIN Crambe maritima. Cruciferous. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant, native to the coasts of Western Europe. Native to our coasts. CULTIVATION. - In France, it is grown very little, but in England, considerable crops are grown; at certain times of the year, London markets abound with this sea cale, which the English hold in high esteem. Crambé is propagated from seed, which must be sown as soon as it matures, in rows, leaving the desired distance between each plant, or better still, in nurseries. To do this, open small gullies 15 or 20 centimetres apart, 4 or 5 centimetres deep, and cover slightly with loose soil or compost. As soon as the seedlings have four or six leaves, place them in moist soil, as far as possible, well prepared and smoked to 60 centimetres in all directions. Seedlings are sown in the same way as cardoons, in bunches of three or four plants per clump. Put in more seeds than you need plants, thin out and water thoroughly. Instead of sowing the seeds as soon as they ripen, you can wait until spring, and sow early on warm beds, in small cups, at a rate of seven or eight seeds each. You can even sow on the bed very thickly, as some of the seeds have lost their ability to germinate and many do not germinate at all. Once the seedlings are strong enough, they can be planted. There is still a way of multiplying them, and it's the safest and the FIC. 26. - Crambe maritima, faster, but for this you need to have old plants at your disposal: we mean by sections or root cuttings. This is done in January and February. You divide old clumps of crambe, as you would an old sorrel plant. Put them in place, then water immediately. No matter how you plant it, you need to give it copious summer watering, frequent hoeing and weeding, and it's only after two or three years of good cultivation that you can begin to harvest; this harvest can last from eight to ten years. Before being released for consumption, crambé must be blanched (fig. 26) like cardoons; otherwise, the taste would be unbearably pungent and unpalatable; it is blanched from August to December. There are several ways to do this, either by imprisoning the stems in flowerpots or hollow tiles, placed side by side, covering the top and surrounding the base with earth so that no light can penetrate, or by using straw bedding, upturned wooden tubs, etc. Crambe can also be forced in the same way as for sorrel. As the roots always tend to emerge from the ground, cut the shoots fairly deeply, and as far as possible, don't let them go to seed, otherwise the plants will soon be exhausted. This plant grows spontaneously in seaside sands, i.e. in salty soils, and it is claimed that by spreading sea salt or ingredients containing brine, such as oyster shells, mussels and other shellfish, around the roots, we have a powerful fertilizer that contributes enormously to vegetation. SEEDS. - To harvest the seed, choose very vigorous clumps. They are left to grow, and when the seeds, which are very large, start to turn yellow, we pick up the stems where they have finished ripening in the shade. They keep for a year, rarely longer. DISEASES, PESTS. - Like all crucifers, crambe maritime is prone, especially when young, to flea beetle, which perforates the young cotyledons and first leaves. We recommend watering with salt water dissolved in limestone, as for cabbages. Slugs and snails are very fond of it, so it should be hunted down. USES. - Petioles are eaten blanched, like asparagus or cardoons, in a white sauce like celery root; cooked with sausage, they are delicious. They have a nutty flavor that's quite appealing. WALNUT CRESS Lepidium sativum. Cruciferous. ORIGIN. - An annual plant of doubtful origin, according to De Candolle. I am inclined to believe that it originated in Persia, from where it may have spread to the gardens of India, Syria, Greece, Egypt and as far as Abyssinia: it was introduced into our crops in 1562. The plant is grown in Europe, northern Africa, western Asia and India. CULTIVATION. - Alen cress is an excellent plant, too little cultivated and too little known. Extremely hardy and easy to grow, it thrives almost carefree in any location and on any soil. Watercress is propagated from seed, which is sown almost all year round, except during the coldest months. Seedlings are sown in rays and very thickly. Cover little. During hot spells, sow in the shade, and since it is so easy to set seed, sow at least once a fortnight to avoid running out, and water abundantly if the soil is dry to ensure tender products. VARIETIES. - Cresson alénois frisé. - Deep-cut, almost laciniate, contoured leaves. Cresson alénois à larges feuilles. - Very good species, with broad, slightly serrated leaves, more abundant than in curly cress, less pungent. Cresson alénois doré. - A sub-variety of the previous one, differing in its pale green to yellow foliage, very vigorous and hardy, much appreciated. A few years ago, it was announced as a new variety; this was a mistake, as we found it mentioned in 1789. Dwarf, very curly watercress. - A new variety, producing a small tuft of attractive decorative effect. SEEDS. - Perhaps no other plant reproduces so easily. The seed germinates very quickly. At a temperature of 13 to 15 degrees, it sprouts in eighteen or twenty-two hours. When the stems begin to change color, they are collected and laid out on cloths in the sun. When they begin to dry, they are beaten; the seeds detach very easily. They keep for five years. DISEASES, PESTS. - Slugs and snails are not very fond of them and don't touch them. Only the flea beetle occasionally perforates the first leaves, but this does not cause much damage. We know of no disease that attacks it. USES. - The leaves are used as a salad garnish, or to garnish roasts. In winter, the seeds, because they germinate easily, are used to provide greenery indoors. It can be sown in planters or pots filled with moss or damp sand, in sponges, around a bottle or in clay, which can be given the most original shapes. EARTH CRESS Erysimum præcox. Cruciferous. ORIGIN. - Native biennial plant, found in a spontaneous state, growing mainly in damp, shady places and in demolition soil. CULTIVATION. - Sow from March to August, omE. BERGER, Vegetables. 13 bre as much as possible, especially during the summer, in rays, or better, broadcast in beds; use a fork or rake to cover. Emergence is easy. When the plant is strong enough, as it only goes to seed in the second year, it is eaten by picking the largest leaves in succession. In the second year, when the plant goes to seed, one or two more harvests of leaves can be made, then the whole plant is harvested. This is usually done even in the first year. This plant is very hardy and not very fussy about the choice of soil; it does well everywhere; a few weedings and waterings in summer are enough; seedlings must be renewed every year, so that there is always a harvest to be had. SEEDS. - To harvest seeds, let the previous year's seedlings rise. The stems are collected, as with Alen cress, and stored in the same way. It remains good for three years. USES. - The leaves are eaten in salads, mixed with romaine or chicory. They are also used with steak. The English are very fond of this plant. CRESSON DE FONTAINE Sisymbrium Nasturtium L. Cardamine Nasturtium Mœnch. Nasturtium officinale Scop. Cardamine fontana Lamk. Crucifers. ORIGIN. - Perennial, native and spontaneous throughout Europe and northern Asia. Called cailli, watercress, fountain cress, body health, etc. (fig. 27), this plant is known and appreciated just about everywhere. CULTIVATION. - Cultivation is not difficult, but a good source of clear water is required. Attempts have been made to grow it in tubs or basins filled with soil, with the water changed frequently, but this method is rarely used except by amateurs. Besides, plants grown in this way are never very beautiful. Once you have a suitable plot of land, you can try growing them, as they are very productive. FIG. 27: Watercress. Most often, we dig pits 40 to 45 centimetres deep, 2, 3 or even 4 metres wide, divided by beds at least 5 or 6 metres wide, which we use for cultivation. These pits should be laid out in such a way that they can be submerged if necessary, and have a slight slope to allow the water to drain off slowly. If, on the other hand, the land is on a slope, and the source is in the upper part, ditches are dug across it, and the water from one will pass into the other successively. But to do this, the water must be well regulated, so that all the pits have water at the same time and none dries out. The size of the pits has no influence whatsoever on good cultivation: we've seen magnificent results obtained with very small spaces. Once the pits have been dug, the bottom is smoked and ploughed, and levelled as best as possible. Once this operation has been completed, cress stems are transplanted 10 or 12 centimetres apart, chosen from among the most vigorous and beautiful. Water is added gradually, and harvesting doesn't begin until the stems are well developed and cover the bottom of the pits. This operation should be carried out in spring and during August. If, on the other hand, you want to propagate cress by sowing, in spring, once the pits have been prepared, you make shallow furrows 20 centimetres apart and sow the seed. Then rake over the whole area, and beat in with a beater. At first, only a thin trickle of water is left to lightly sprinkle the surface; too much will wash the seed away. When the seedling has grown sufficiently, submerge it completely and continue. Propagation by seed is much more time-consuming, and so is rarely practised by true cress growers; the first method we have indicated is the most expeditious and practical, but there are not always enough cress fields to supply the seedlings. Watercress is harvested using large planks or boards, which are placed across the pits. Cutting is done with a serpette, taking care not to disturb the roots, which would be detrimental to future production. After cutting, the roots are pushed up with a long-handled bat. You can even spread a light layer of well-consumed cow manure over the entire surface, which is then pressed down at the same time. Watercress likes shade, and too much heat is harmful. They should therefore be secured with lath or heather trays, placed on prepared frames with strong stakes driven into the soil of the watercress bed. These stakes must be high enough to allow you to work under them easily. In the heat of summer and spring, the same pit can be cut every twenty days. But in winter, reproduction is slower. When extreme cold is expected, watercress should be submerged to keep it from freezing, and the water drained off when the temperature eases. A well-maintained watercress bed can last for several years. When it needs renewing, proceed as described above. SEEDS. - When you want to harvest cress seed, you let some of it rise in spring and, when the stems start to turn yellow, you cut them and dry them by laying them out for a few hours a day in the sun, then you beat them and put them in bags. A liter of seeds weighs 600 grams; 30 grams contain 121,600 seeds. Germination lasts five years. DISEASES, PESTS. - Watercress has few enemies. Flea beetles sometimes pierce the leaves, but this only happens in watercress beds where there has been a lack of water and the plant has suffered. On the other hand, it is prone to being invaded and suffocated by other plants which, although not parasitic, take over the water so quickly that it becomes impossible to grow. These harmful plants are: duckweed, beccabunga speedwell and bergamot. The latter is less harmful than the former, which multiply very quickly. So, when renewing a watercress bed, make sure you don't add any. USES. - Watercress is eaten in salads or raw under roasted meats: the legendary watercress steak is far from out of fashion. Chopped with spinach or sorrel, it makes a delicate dish. JAPANESE CROSN Stachys affinis. Labiatae. ORIGIN. - Japan-China. - Introduced in 1882, propagated by M. Pailleux, who named them after Crosnes, the village in Seine-et-Oise where he lives. M. Naudin has proposed naming this vegetable Stachys tuberifera. GROWING. - Propagates by rhizomes and cuttings taken in spring. Rhizome propagation is preferable; they are planted in April, at a good exposure, in light soil, well amended to 40 or 50 centimetres. Towards the end of May, when the stems have reached 15 or 20 centimetres, they are weeded and ridged. After that, only light weeding is needed to avoid disturbing the rootlets; water during hot spells. Towards the end of October, you can start eating the rhizomes successively throughout the winter; they are all the better for having been freshly plucked. There's no need to fear frost, as they can withstand temperatures of 20 degrees below zero. VARIETY. - Choro-Gi. - New variety announced by M. de Vilmorin. USES. - In this plant, the food part is provided by the rhizome-shaped roots in a pearly white string, the size of an Oxalis crenata. They can be eaten like fresh flageolet beans, or as a garnish around roast meats, fried in boiling fat after having been previously cooked in fatty broth; au gratin with truffles or mushrooms, in simple or mixed salads, in macedoine, in butter with chopped parsley à la maître d'hôtel. They are preserved in vinegar like gherkins and capers, and taste like artichokes. They are a top-quality foodstuff, containing all the substances you need to eat. The yield is sufficiently high for this plant to occupy a place in every home garden. CUMIN OF MALTA Cuminum Cyminum L. Umbelliferae. Native to Upper Egypt. An annual, this plant is sown in the open ground in May. The seeds are used in pastries and liqueurs. COMMON ECHALOTE Allium ascalonicum L. Liliaceae. ORIGIN. - Ancient authors have, to this day, given Palestine as the homeland of the shallot. It was brought back during the Crusades. It was found in the vicinity of the town of Ascalon; hence the scientific name Allium ascalonicum, corrupted into escaloigne, echalogne and finally échalote. But De Candolle destroys this assertion and says of this plant: "Despite the progress of botanical investigations in the East and India, this form of allium has not been found in the wild with any certainty. It therefore seems to me to be more than ever a modification of cepa, which occurred around the beginning of the Christian era, a modification less considerable than many of those observed in other cultivated plants. CULTIVATION. - The shallot is one of the easiest perennials to grow. It is very hardy and adapts well to any soil. It thrives in new demolition soils and platras, and seems to prefer soils with a certain amount of limestone. Most authors who have written about this plant claim that it does not adapt to recent fertilization; this is a mistake. By using only well-rotted manures, you can smoke the soil immediately before planting, and the shallot will succeed perfectly. Shallots are propagated by their bulbs, which are planted from November to February; autumn plantings are preferable in the south and south-west. Medium-sized bulbs are chosen, and buried so that the top part is level with the soil being worked. In some parts of the Midi and the West, bulbs are planted with a hoe, and the soil is raked as described above for garlic. But in general, and especially in the North, planting is done with a non-tapered planter, or simply with the thumb and forefinger, which is quicker; but the soil must be freshly worked. It is divided into plots of five or six rays, spaced 20 or 25 centimetres apart. The line is set at 20 centimetres. During the course of vegetation, we hoe and weed several times. When the tops begin to yellow, in June or the first two weeks of July, we pull them off and lay them flat on the ground. Leave them like this for three days, turn them over several times, then bring them into a well-aerated attic or shed, early in the morning when the tops are still moist and not brittle, to keep them intact. VARIETIES. - Common shallot. - This variety, which is the most commonly grown, is undoubtedly the best and most esteemed; very hardy, it produces abundantly. There are several other varieties, all derived from this one: Échalote hâtive de Niort. - Bulbs slightly larger than the common shallot; produces less. Échalote grosse de Noisy. - A variety highly esteemed in Paris; grows very large and keeps well. Echalote petite hâtive de Bagnolet. - Bulbs as small as a small spring onion, produces a lot and early. SEEDS. - The common shallot rarely flowers and produces few or no seeds. We have tried every possible means to obtain seeds, but have been unsuccessful. MAlAPiES, NUiSiBlE ANImALS. - In certain areas, shallots are subject to a disease that gardeners call scald, but which is produced by Rhizoctonia allii, a parasitic fungus with whitish or grayish filaments; this parasite attacks the base of bulbs and causes them to rot. We noticed that it always developed on buried clumps. To prevent this disease, which we have seen destroy whole fields of shallots, you need to dig up the diseased plants, and this operation will not only stop the disease, but also make the bulbs grow. 13. Uredo or rust sometimes invades the tops, but this disease only develops in the late season, i.e. when the shallot is ready to be pulled. USES. - Shallots are frequently used in cooking to enhance the flavour of dishes, such as the traditional shallot steak. It is also preserved in vinegar, like and in the company of gherkins. In some places, it's cooked under an open fire, and eaten with pepper or seasoned with oil. It's a delicacy that, it's said, was highly prized by the ancients. Picked young and still tender, the leaves are used as a salad ingredient, and can replace chives. Echalotte is an aperitif, but frequent use is harmful to health. JERSEV SHALLOT Quite a different breed from the common shallot, resembling an onion and tasting a little like one. Leaves are glaucous, long and quite bulbous in the middle. Bulbs are small, averaging six to ten per clump. CULTIVATION. - Same cultivation as the common shallot. SEEDS. - This breed goes to seed every year and produces fertile seed. If sown in July-August, a fairly good crop of bulbs can be obtained the following year. In some parts of the Charentes region, this breed is known as the onion of plenty, and is often confused with the potato onion. USES. - The Jersey shallot is highly esteemed in England and Ireland. It can be used for a host of culinary purposes, such as stews, sauces, or candied in vinegar; it keeps quite well, especially if care has been taken to let it ripen properly. OROINARY SPINACH Spinacia oleracea L. Miller. Chenopodea. ORIGIN. - The origin of this plant is doubtful. Olivier claims to have found it in the wild in Persia; according to FIG. 28 - Common spinach. Cassini, it comes from Asia Minor and was cultivated by the Arabs, to whom we owe its introduction into Europe. It does not appear to have been known to the Greeks or the Romans, although several scholars believe they recognized it in the Greek Crysalachanon. Pierre de Crescence claims that the spiny-fruited species was the first to be cultivated, which would explain the name spinach given to the genus. Spinach has been cultivated in Europe for around two centuries. De Candolle gives Persia as the home of the common spinach, where it has been cultivated for 2,000 years. It is also highly esteemed in China and Manchuria. CULTIVATION. - This is one of the easiest vegetables to grow. It is sown from February to November, in rows spaced 30 to 35 centimetres apart, or broadcast in beds. Cover the seed with the loosest soil possible. Spinach does well in a variety of growing soils, but preferably in low-moisture, well-smoked soil, with good, energetic fertilizers; feces and feather are suitable. When young, watering with liquid manure gives good results. Seedlings sown from February to July go to seed within the year; so, to ensure that you always have some to pick, it's essential to renew seedlings at least every fifteen or twenty days. Water copiously and often. On the other hand, seedlings sown from August to November only come up the following year, in April, after having given an abundant harvest throughout the winter, and round-seeded varieties are preferred. Viroflay spinach has always given us good results. For spring and summer, choose the prickly-seeded varieties, which give a better harvest and rise more slowly than the round-seeded variety; to hasten germination, market gardeners usually soak the seeds in water for twelve or fifteen hours. Once the seeds have sprouted, they need to be watered copiously and often, to prevent them from rising so quickly, and as soon as the plants are sufficiently developed, they can be pulled out for consumption. For winter plants, on the other hand, we start by picking the lower leaves, and only pull them out in spring, when the plant is rising. The most developed leaves are picked one by one, respecting the youngest. This apparently time-consuming operation can be carried out quickly, especially by people who are used to it; women are good at it. In general, market gardeners don't sow spinach on its own; it's always combined with lettuces, lamb's lettuce, chervil, etc. When it's ready to sell, we pull it out, always thinning it out; the roots are used to tie it up in small bunches. VARIETIES. - Spinach has been divided into two classes: prickly-seeded and round-seeded. Spinach with prickly seed (Spinacia spinosa Mœnch). - Common spinach. - A variety closely resembling the wild plant cultivated in some areas. Leaves are long, narrow, sharp, very sagittate and of mediocre quality. English or winter spinach. - A recommendable variety, producing very broad, long, thick leaves; it is very hardy and stands up fairly well to our winters; it is very good and well suited to spring and summer sowing. Epinard camus de Bordeaux. - Probably derived from the previous variety and improved by market gardeners in the Bordeaux area. Produces a rosette of rounded, well-developed, thick leaves; highly esteemed on markets in the South-West region. Round-seeded spinach (Spinacia glabra Miller). - This breed differs from the previous one in its seeds and vegetation. The leaves are broader and fuller, forming a compact, tight tuft; the leaves are fuller in all their parts than the other breed; they are said to taste better. Spinach monstrueux de Viroflay - A highly recommendable variety, producing very broad, sometimes 20 to 25 cm-long, thick leaves; very hardy, suitable for autumn sowing. Flanders spinach. - A widespread variety grown extensively in northern France; broad, hardy leaves; can be sown all year round. Lettuce leaf spinach. - Variety with broad, dark-green, very blistered leaves, spreading, compact clump, medium size, hardy, medium yield. Slow-rising spinach. - A little-known variety, which goes to seed less quickly than its predecessors. Green, blistered leaves; tight, compact clump; good yield, does well sown in autumn. Catillon's lazy spinach. - New variety, broad, thick, slightly blistered leaves, very heat-resistant. SEEDS. - Some authors recommend harvesting seed from spring-sown varieties, as this produces more and faster, but the seed is less nourished and not as good as that taken from autumn-sown plants. It's best to choose autumn-sown plants that have produced several leaf harvests. They start to come up in April, and the seed is ready for harvesting towards the end of June or July, depending on the soil. Generally, the seeds don't ripen all at once, and when you notice that a few plants are turning yellow and that the seeds clustered around the stem are changing color, pull them out and lay them on sheets or blankets in part-shade. From then on, you'll need to spend most of your time with them, until you've finished pulling them out. When they are completely dry, remove them from the stem by passing them between your fingers, clean them and bag them. They keep well for up to four years. 30 grams contain 2360 seeds, a liter weighs 530 grams. DISEASES, PESTS. - Spinach is sometimes affected by a fungus of the miller genus, which attacks the roots and kills the plant in a few days. This disease seems to thrive particularly in chalky, heavily smoked soils, as we have observed several times in our crops. There is no cure for this disease. Cutworms sometimes cause serious damage, cutting the root a few centimeters below soil level, causing the plant to turn yellow and die; the damage is only noticed when the roots are cut out; the best remedy is to destroy these worms by digging up the soil. Cutworms and white grubs are most common in light soils. If Botrytis tenella gives good results in destroying white grubs, as announced, let's hope it will be possible to wipe them out. USES. - Spinach is frequently used in cooking. Deprived of its primary water, it is a light, healthy food. It is used in lean soups. It can be prepared in a variety of ways, with butter or fat, or mixed with sorrel to soften its acidity. Alexandre Dumas was very fond of spinach, and prepared it in his own way: after boiling it, he seasoned it with goose fat. The leaves dye the wool prepared with bismuth nitrate a bright, solid, greenish lemon-yellow. Dried leaves produce a green alcoholic dye used to color table liqueurs. ESTRAGON Artemisia dracunculus L. Oligosporus condimentarius H. Cass. Composites. ORIGIN. - Herbaceous perennial, native to northern Asia, introduced into our cultures in 1596, known as serpentine, dragon herb, dragone, etc. FIG. 29: Tarragon (Artemisia dracunculus). "CULTURE. - Tarragon does not produce fertile seeds, so it is propagated by separating clumps in spring or July. It is generally planted in well-ploughed, well-smoked beds with good exposure. Lines are drawn and planted at 30 to 35 centimetres in all directions, watering as soon as planting is done and copiously during hot spells. In May, spread a good mulch over the beds, and loosen the soil surface with good hoeing. Although native to Siberian regions, tarragon fears the extreme cold of our winters, and to preserve it as frost approaches, cover the clumps with a few centimetres of compost, manure, straw or, better still, dry leaves; planting should be renewed every three years. To make sure you don't run out of tarragon in winter, place trunks on the boards; surround the trunks with thick stoves, rearranging and renewing them often. You can also prepare good layers, place the chests and panels on them, then pull out the clumps of tarragon and place them as tightly as possible, covering them with 6 centimetres of potting soil. When the stems start to appear, air them frequently. Cover with straw mats overnight to keep the stems fresh all winter long. Seeds of a plant called Russian tarragon (Artemisia Redwskii), which has the habit and appearance of tarragon but nowhere near the flavour, are commercially available; unscrupulous seed merchants sell the seeds of this plant as those of true tarragon, which produces none. The annual Tagetes lucida has also been recommended as a possible replacement for tarragon, its leaves having much the same odour and flavour. We doubt that cultivation of this plant will become widespread. SEEDS. - We have already said that tarragon does not produce seeds. The flower, however, is well formed. All the organs are perfect, so why this infertility? Could it be that too much heat at flowering time over-excites certain generative organs to the detriment of others? We can't say for sure, but there's something abnormal going on to keep this plant sterile. In the past, it must have produced a few seeds, because all the old authors who wrote about horticulture before 1800 mention it as multiplying from seed. Perhaps this is a mistake. DISEASES AND PESTS. - We know of no disease or insect that attacks this plant, probably because of its strong odor. USES. - Tarragon is widely used as an excellent condiment and salad dressing. It is also used to make omelettes and in pickles, which are preserved in vinegar. By macerating it for a few hours in vinegar, it flavors it. In Persia, people eat it mixed with bread. FLORENCE FENNEL Fœniculum dulce L. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - Annual plant native to Italy. CULTIVATION. - Florence fennel is sown in March-April, in shallow rays 45 to 50 centimeters apart. The seed is lightly covered, and sprouts within a few days. When the plants are sufficiently developed, they are thinned out so that the remaining ones are 10 to 15 centimetres apart. During hot spells, water copiously and hoe several times. Young plants that have been thinned out can be transplanted into a bed prepared for this purpose; they recover quite well and produce a crop that succeeds those left in place. In July-August, a new seedling is sown for winter harvesting. When the base of the petioles is sufficiently developed and the whole forms a fairly voluminous whole, the soil is mounded and brought in around it. A fortnight later, you can start harvesting, continuing successively with the most advanced and the first ridged plants. SEEDS. - Fennel seeds are harvested from the first seedlings sown in spring. Choose the most beautiful plants that come up in summer; the seed is best harvested in August-September. It degenerates easily; it keeps well for four years. 30 grams contain 3450 seeds, a liter weighs 240 grams. DISEASES, PESTS. - Young fennel plants are sometimes eaten by large yellow slugs that gnaw at the base of the stalks; they can be destroyed by skewering them with a wire rod; or they can be kept away by putting unleached ash or quicklime around the stalks. USES. - The petiole base is eaten after blanching, like celery. The leaves are used to garnish cold meats. They can be boiled and eaten as a salad, or used to flavour certain dishes. A few leaves boiled with chestnuts give them an excellent taste. In France, fennel is little used. A knob of fennel is added to the court bouillon in which fish is cooked; but in Italy, it is the leading vegetable, and this is probably the origin of the popular Italian saying: Finocchio e pane mi bastan (I only need fennel and bread). In Italy and Provence, young shoots are eaten in soup or salad; on the Cape of Good Hope, they are cooked or roasted. Seeds are preserved with gherkins. Seeds are used to make liqueurs. The whole plant turns dark yellow. The essential oil is widely used in perfumery. BITTER FENNEL Fœniculum vulgare Gært. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - A perennial that grows naturally in France, preferably in rubble, roadsides and dry, arid places. Some authors give this plant as originating in Africa, where it grows abundantly in wasteland, to such an extent that it is considered a weed. CULTIVATION. - Same as Florence fennel. USES. - This variety is little cultivated; as a vegetable, it is preferred to the superior Florence fennel; in some regions, it is grown for its seeds, which are used to make liqueurs. SWEET FENNEL Fœniculum officinale. Umbelliferae. ORIGIN. - Same origin as the previous variety. Perennial, biennial, distinguished from the preceding race by its less slender, thicker stems, more glaucous in color, by its sheathing petioles, swollen at the bottom, by its seed, which is much larger and twice as long, and finally by its less elevated, stockier habit. CULTIVATION. - Same care in cultivation. USES. - Same uses. Orobus faba Brot. Faba vulgaris Mill. Faba vicia L. Faba major Rivinus. Potamogeton bifolium Lapeyr. Leguminosae, Papilionaceae. ORIGIN. - According to De Candolle, the cultivation of fava beans dates back to prehistoric times in Europe, Egypt and Arabia. It was introduced into Europe, probably by the Western Aryans, during their first migrations (Pelasges, Celts, Slavs). It was later brought to China, a century before the Christian era, and even later to Japan, and more recently to India. As for the spontaneous habitat, it's possible that it was doubled a few thousand years ago, one center being south of the Caspian Sea, the other in northern Africa. The bean would therefore originate from the south of the Caspian Sea and has been cultivated for over 4,000 years. CULTIVATION. - Fava beans thrive in all types of well-smoked soils, but they do best in strong, free soils. The first beans are sown in October, and then fortnight by fortnight until March, so as not to run out. After all, they're only eaten green and half-formed, and successive sowings mean you can enjoy them for a long time, and make good use of them. Depending on the soil, they can be planted in rows of 40 or 50 centimetres, or in beds of four rows of 35 or 40 centimetres. Follow a 60-centimeter path. We sow at 50 centimetres, on the line, further apart if necessary when the soil is good, because with these kinds of plants we must avoid confusion,

which causes them to wither and delays early production. 237 In most cases, the lines are traced with a tracing tool, or simply stretched out with a string, then the beans are sown by pushing them in with the thumb at a distance of around 5 centimetres, or with a lightly eulogized planter. In either case, a little soil is brought in to cover them. In the south-west of France, farmers sow beans in furrows, at least 70 or 80 centimetres apart, putting four or five rows in each. This system is not bad in that the plants, although a little tightly packed, still receive air and don't wither. Production is generally very good. When the beans have reached a height of 7 to 8 centimetres, the first light hoeing is carried out when all traces of dew have disappeared. This operation is repeated every few weeks. Beans should never be watered, as the high humidity causes them to turn yellow. When the plant has reached a height of 35 to 40 centimetres, we pinch off the tip, which usually coincides with the tenth or twelfth leaf, and pinch off the top. The purpose of this operation is to stop the upward movement of the plant and to force the sap into the lower parts of the plant, which greatly advances fruit formation. In Angoumois, Saintonge and Quercy, beans are sown in small furrows with a forked or flat hoe; this is not a bad way of working, but it cannot be applied to all soils. VAriéTés. - Aguadulce bean with long pods (fig. 30). - One of the best varieties to grow in gardens, the pods are very long, from 35 to 40 cen- FIG. 30. - Aguadulce bean with long pods. 239 centimeters by 4 centimeters thick, they are particularly suitable for green sales. Seville bean. - An early variety with very long pods, highly recommended for green sales. Fêve de Windsor. - Hardy variety with numerous short pods, containing only two seeds. Fêve Julienne. - Variety with numerous pods containing only three beans, they are upright and grouped in threes and fours; very hardy, very good for green manure. Fève Julienne verte. - Distinguished from the previous variety by the green color of the bean, it is a later variety. Early dwarf broad bean. - A completely dwarf variety, it does not exceed 35 or 40 centimeters in height, with small, upright, very numerous pods, grouped in twos or threes, containing two or three square, thick, swollen beans. Suitable for early and forced cultivation. Fève de Mazagran. - A very good variety for large-scale cultivation, with numerous pods and small seeds. Fève naine verte de Beck. - Bean with white flowers. - Beans with long pods. - Violet bean, etc. SEEDS. - To harvest good seed, you must sow with this intention, i.e. treat the plants with the cultivation care we have indicated, but leave all the fruit, not picking any, as the first to form are the best and earliest. The plants are left to dry on the spot, then brought in, and when the weather is bad, they are shucked. The seed keeps well for five or six years. However, we recommend choosing seed from the previous year. 500 grams contain around 250 to 300 beans; a liter weighs 620 grams. MAlADIES, PEST ANIMALS. - Sometimes in poor soils, beans are affected by rust or uredo. It is difficult to destroy this disease, which rapidly invades plants, and the remedy we have indicated for chicory is the only one that has given us good results. The bean's cruelest enemy is the black aphid (Aphis nigra), which develops more especially on the upper part of the stem, but if you take the precaution of pinching early enough, its progress is impeded; several remedies have been tried, none of which produced any effect; nicotine alone seems to have given some results. USES. - Broad beans are an invaluable source of nourishment, and it is to be regretted that their use is not more widespread, as they could be of great help to the less well-off classes. Like beans and lentils, broad beans are very nourishing, and contain a considerable proportion of a nitrogenous substance, legumin, which is very similar to animal casein and contributes greatly to their nutritional qualities. According to Payen, 100 parts of beans contain: 24.40 legumin; 1.50 fat; 51.50 dextrin and sugar starch; 3 cellulose; 3.60 mineral salts; 16 water. Picked before they are fully ripe, when they are still green and dried, the product is less abundant but even more nourishing. Young shoots are eaten in salads and used in lean soups. E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 14 Fava beans are frequently used to fatten animals, and can be used as a good substitute for oats for horses. In some countries, it is mixed with wheat flour. The sweet scent of fava bean flowers has led to their use in perfumery in the form of distilled water; this water is used as a cosmetic, as is fava bean flour, which has been attributed with the property of removing freckles. In England, broad beans are cooked with honey and used as fish bait. Dry stalks yield a lot of potash when incinerated. GLACIAL FICOID Mesembryanthemum crystallinum L. Ficoidae. ORIGIN. - Native to the Cape of Good Hope. Perennial in greenhouses, but grown as an annual in our gardens. CULTIVATION. - Sow in the same way as spinach, in March, April or, better still, February on warm beds, transplant into small pots and plant out in May. Other care consists of weeding and hoeing, and above all good watering throughout the summer. This plant is resistant to the hottest weather, but the leaves are small and not very succulent. It's best to keep it well watered, as the yield will be quintupled. SEEDS. - To harvest the seed, select a few good plants and let them flower. When the capsules are ripe, they are collected, left to dry and the seeds extracted. One gram contains 5700 seeds, a liter weighs 760 grams and lasts five years. USES. - The leaves are chopped and cooked like spinach. Used in herb broths. It is said to be very healthy and nourishing. In Bourbon, the leaves are often eaten as a vegetable. In the Canaries, the seeds are pulverized and cooked; in the same islands, soda ash is extracted from this plant. FRAISIER COMMUN, FRAISIER DES BOIS Fragaria vesca L. Fragaria vulgaris Ehr. Rosaceae. ORIGIN. - The common strawberry is native to Europe, from the Shetland Islands and Lapland to the mountainous regions of the Midi, Madeira, Spain, Sicily and Greece. It is also found in Asia, from northern Syria and Armenia to Daourie. The strawberry plants of the Himalayas and Japan, which various authors have attributed to this species, are perhaps not, and this makes me doubt the habitat in China given by a missionary. It occurs spontaneously in Iceland, in the northeastern United States, around Fort Cumberland and on the northwest coast, perhaps even in the Sierra Nevada of California; the habitat therefore extends around the Arctic pole, with the exception of eastern Siberia and the Amur River region. The strawberry plant has been known since antiquity, but was little cultivated. Virgil and Pliny only mention it in passing. Cultivation was introduced to France in the 15th or 16th century. Champier, in the 16th century, spoke of it as a novelty in northern France, but it already existed in the Midi and in England (De Candolle). In France, the common strawberry is found in a spontaneous state just about everywhere, usually growing at the edges of hedges bordering forests, in high forest woods, where it seems to prefer damp clearings. Today, Fragaria vesca is rarely cultivated, preferring the Alpine strawberry, which has the advantage of producing fruit for part of the summer. CULTIVATION. - Same cultivation as the four-season strawberry. VARIETIES. - This breed has produced two distinct varieties in terms of fruit shape: Fraise des bois petite hâtive de Chatenay. - Early, small, round, dark-red fruit, very fragrant, does not come up. Strawberry from Montreuil. - Vigorous, very fertile plant with elongated, dark-red fruit, very late and productive, does not come up. USES. - Same uses as the four-season strawberry. ALPES OR FOUR SEASONS STRAWBERRY Fragaria alpina Pers. Fragaria semperftorens Hayne. ORIGIN. - This breed originates from the Alps, where it grows at fairly high altitudes. It was brought to France in 1754 by Fougeroux de Bondaroy, who had picked it on Mont Cenis. - Strawberry plants in general, and the small-fruited breeds in particular, are not very fussy about choice of soil; however, light, moist, healthy soil is preferable. In dry soils, watering is essential in summer if good production is to be achieved. Strawberry plants are propagated by runners, which are planted at two different times: in March or April, or at the end of summer, in August, September or even November. Planting in August and September is best, as the young plants have time to recover before the cold sets in, making them more resistant to the low temperatures of winter. In the early summer, they grow vigorously and, depending on the soil, form good clumps that produce abundantly. Those planted in April-May, on the other hand, don't bear fruit until the following year, apart from a few rare flowers here and there. Common and Alpine strawberries reproduce readily by sowing; sow as soon as the seeds are ripe, in June or July, in a slightly shaded bed with light, loose soil. Sow in small rays, lightly covered with good potting soil, and in ten or twenty days the seeds will sprout. As soon as the seedlings can withstand transplanting, they are thinned out and planted out in a nursery, and when it's time to set out in September, they are put in place as you would another runner. In spring, they produce as abundantly as those propagated in any other way. You can also sow in March-April, on a warm bed; the seedling is transplanted, on another cold bed, or in the open ground, and put in place towards the end of May or June. This procedure is somewhat safer, but also takes longer. Whichever propagation method you choose, the soil must first be ploughed deeply and fertilized with good, well-decomposed fertilizers. Horned cattle manure seems to be a good choice. Strawberries are planted in beds 1.20 m wide, with four 30-centimetre radii divided by 50-centimetre paths. Plant at 30 cm 14. along the line and in a checkerboard pattern. If the plant is small, put two together and, as soon as planting is complete, lightly water each plant to pack the soil around the roots. Before planting, trim off as much as possible of the root tips and leaves, and choose plants with white roots. Avoid planting FIO plants. 31. - Strawberry plants with black roots are a sure sign that they are too old. In the first days of March, as the new leaves begin to develop, hoe them deeply, taking care not to uproot them. We hoe again in April, then spread a good mulch over each bed. Other care consists of weeding, and above all, frequent watering, if you want to obtain good production. In seasonally dry soils, irrigation produces excellent results. In October, remove all runners and dead or yellowed leaves. The following year, the same cultivation care is required, as in the third year. After this period, most clumps die back and rot in winter, making planting irregular and requiring renewal. What's more, the fruit on vicious plants is smaller and less fragrant. FORCED CULTIVATION. - This breed of strawberry can hardly be forced. For this cultivation, see pineapple strawberry. VARIETIES. - La Meudonnaise, once highly esteemed around Paris; slightly blistered, blond-green leaves; large, dark-red, conical fruit, ripens late, very fragrant. Janus strawberry. - Good improved variety of the Alpine strawberry, very fertile, elongated fruit, bright red when ripe and remontant. Belle de Meaux (fig. 31). - New variety; large, conical, dark carmine-red fruit, very fragrant. It is said to be far superior to other varieties in terms of production and taste finesse. Fraisier des Alpes sans filets or Gaillon strawberry with red fruit. - This variety is very different from the others; it does not produce nets and multiplies by dividing clumps. Particularly suitable for borders, it is very hardy and produces abundantly throughout the summer. Netless Alpine strawberry with white fruit. - Same cultivation and hardiness as the previous variety, but the fruit is not very fragrant and not much appreciated on the markets. ANANAS STRAWBERRIES Fragaria grandiflora Ehrh. Fragaria ananassa Duch. ORIGIN. - Very obscure origin; it has never been known where it came from. It is from this breed, crossed with the Chilean strawberry, that the innumerable varieties of large hybrid strawberries, commonly known as English strawberries, originate. OUTDOOR CULTIVATION. - Cultivation is much the same as for the four-season strawberry. Preference should be given to runners that develop in the late season, and care should be taken to ensure that the plants from which they come are productive, as often the most beautiful runners are chosen from poor plants that are vigorous but not very productive, leading to degeneration. Multiplication by sowing is only done to obtain new varieties: in a sowing, there are always few subjects that characterize the species well. FORCED THERMOSIPHON CULTIVATION. - Forced cultivation is certainly not difficult, but it does require a certain amount of practice to succeed. There are several ways of doing this. In this type of cultivation, the most important point is how to prepare the plants for fruiting, since success depends on this and on the aeration of the plants at flowering time. In June or July, select the best runners and plant them 10 cm apart in a well-prepared bed, with plenty of smoke and, if possible, in part-shade. Water often. In October, pull out the runners and put them in six- to seven-inch pots filled with a mixture of 1/4 bedding mix, 1/2 garden mix and 1/4 leaf mix. Put three or four runners per pot, close to the sides rather than in the middle, and the plants develop much better. Once repotted, the pots are half-embedded in sand, tan, potting soil, etc., and shaded for a few days to facilitate growth. Shade them for a few days to help them recover, and leave them in this state until it's time to put them under tarpaulins or in greenhouses to force them out. Cover them if the cold is too severe. When the time comes to force them, i.e. around December 15, we clean them well, remove the yellow and dead leaves and put a certain quantity in place to be heated. We stagger the plants so as to have some to force until those in the open ground begin to produce. Push the pots about halfway into the tan or escarbill and space them 5 to 6 centimetres apart in all directions, then start heating. At first, a gentle heat of 12 to 15 degrees centigrade is maintained, day and night, until the fruit begins to knot, at which point the heat is increased to 20 to 25 degrees. From the moment we start heating, we take care to water the plants, which must be done regularly so that none dries out and wilts, which is their downfall. Water often and lightly, until the flowers appear; from then on, water no more. Once the fruit has set its knots, continue the operation until maturity. Whenever it's possible to give the fruit some air, this should be done, especially when sunburn occurs, rapidly raising the temperature under the windows. The fruit must not touch the ground. You can keep them elevated with rush ties supported by small sticks placed around the pots, or even better, you can make your own little wire rings that last for several years. Another very good way of preparing plants for forcing is to select the best runners in June and July and, without disturbing their attachment to the mother plant, repot them in small cups which you bury in the ground. They are held in place by wooden hooks. These young plants, under the influence of copious watering, develop rapidly and by the end of the summer are beautiful subjects perfectly prepared for forced cultivation. When the plants are weaned in October, they are potted into larger pots, of which there can be three in each 6-inch pot. Of course, this process is time-consuming and costly, but the plants grow vigorously and always produce excellent results. It's an excellent process, highly recommended for amateurs. The varieties that lend themselves best to forced cultivation are : Docteur Morère. - Docteur Nicaise. - Lucie Flament. - Gloire de Zuidwick. - Duc de Malakoff. - La Chalonnaise. - Marguerite. - Jacunda, etc.- Young plantations from the previous year, which have produced a first crop in the open ground, can also give good results if potted early and treated as described above. As for heating, the best systems are small, very low gabled greenhouses, 3 meters wide inside, with benches 1.10 meters wide on each side, and a passageway 80 centimeters wide in the middle. The benches are secured by T-irons resting on dice driven into the ground. The floors of these benches are made of terracotta tiles, also supported by T-irons and angle irons; one or two hot-water pipes run 25 or 30 centimeters along the underside of the bench. The tops of the benches are filled with tan, wood bran or sand to accommodate the pots, which are half-buried. Tarpaulins 1, 60 or 2 meters wide can also be used, with a tiled floor as described for the greenhouse, and a hot water pipe running underneath, 25 centimetres from the wall. As all the heat is concentrated underneath, you need to create openings that can be closed off at will, to let a little warm air into the part above where the plants are located. This tarpaulin system is very good, and gives very good results, but we prefer the small greenhouse where it's easier to keep an eye on the plants. HATÉE CULTIVATION UNDER CHASSIS. - In the early days of January, prepare good layers at least 50 or 60 centimetres thick, with 10 or 15 centimetres of charcoal or tannin residue, let the first fires start and place the strawberry pots in them, burying them about halfway. Cover with a frame. Other care consists of aeration as often as possible, to avoid mildew, as the damp heat of the layer often kills the strawberry plant. Water very sparingly, just to prevent the plant from wilting; you don't need to dunk the plants in water, the mist that comes off is enough; it's only when the fruit has set that you need to water seriously. Water is poured at the base of the plant, without wetting the leaves. Keep warm around the trunks and cover with mats at night to concentrate as much heat as possible. When the fruit has set, we give it plenty of air, and if the sun shines too hot, we shade it. When the heat of the layer diminishes, we prepare another and place them on top. Plants put into forcing in the first days of January won't bear fruit until the end of March, or the first fortnight of April. Another way of bringing forward the ripening of strawberries by a few days in spring is to place boxes and their panels on the beds in March; the paths are dug 20 centimetres deep, and filled with good warm manure up to the height of the boxes. From time to time, these stoves are reshuffled to maintain fermentation; air is given frequently, the plants are watered and cleaned often; in this way, ripe strawberries are produced a few days before those grown in the open ground. VARIETIES. - Here is a list of good varieties. Hybrid strawberries. - Carolina superba. - Vigorous, hairy plant, glossy green leaves, large, slightly flattened, short vermilion fruit; semi-late. Docteur Morère. - Very vigorous, hairy plant, large, broad, dark-green foliage, very large, slightly short, enlarged fruit; very productive. This variety is grown almost everywhere; it is one of the most recommended. Docteur Nicaise. - Plant of average vigor, relative fertility, very large fruit, weighing 40 to 50 grams; semi-hasty. Duc de Malahoff. - Very vigorous plant with large, dark-green leaves; large, enlarged, short fruit; very juicy yellow flesh; excellent, highly recommended variety. Marguerite. - Very vigorous, dark green foliage, very large, elongated, vermilion-red fruit, very sweet, fragrant white flesh; ripens late. Gloire de Zuidvick. - Excessively vigorous, attractive grayish-green leaves, large, conical, semi-early fruit, bright scarlet color, melting flesh. Strawberry Lucas. - Vigorous plant, bright green leaves, oblong, fairly large, dark red fruit, pale pink flesh, juicy, fragrant.
