Fournier. FRAISIER CAPRON Fragaria elatior Ehrh. Fragaria moschata Duch. ORIGIN. - Perennial, indigenous plant. In the past, this breed was honored and cultivated everywhere; today, it is grown only in botanical gardens, where hybrid strawberries are preferred. CULTIVATION. - This type of strawberry is very hardy, multiplying easily through its numerous runners, but as there are both male and female individuals, it is essential to plant both for fertilization to take place, and when you intend to plant, you will need to label both at the time of production. Like the wild strawberry, this breed produces only one crop in spring, and does not come up again. VARIETIES. - Raspberry Capron. - The best-known and most widely cultivated in the past. The plant is very tall, with blond-green foliage and numerous, spherical, purplish or wine-colored fruits. The flesh is white, slightly yellowish, with a raspberry flavor. Belle Bordelaise. - Plant stockier than above, blond-green foliage, slightly grayish, large fruit, E. BERGER, Plantes potagères. 15 254 FRAISIER ÉCARLATE DE VIRGINIE - FRAISIER DU CHILI elongated sometimes, very fragrant, raspberry-like, sometimes rises. It is still grown near Bordeaux. VIRGINIA STRAWBERRY Fragaria virginiana Ehrh. ORIGIN. - Perennial, from South America. CULTIVATION. - A little-known breed that is little cultivated today, due to its fruits, which are small and few in number, and do not come up. It is very hardy, and can remain in the same soil for longer than other breeds. An attempt has been made to fertilize this breed with the pineapple strawberry, and the resulting plants are very beautiful and hardy; same cultivation as the "four seasons" variety. CHILE STRAWBERRY Fragaria chilensis Ehrb. ORIGIN. - Perennial plant from Chile, brought back in 1714 by Frézier. Very common in the Andes, it is found everywhere. It is said to be so invasive in some parts of Chile that it has to be destroyed. CULTIVATION. - Plants belonging to this race are vigorous, stocky, with dark green foliage and very large, irregularly-shaped, bright orange fruits. It is from this breed, fertilized with the pineapple strawberry, that we have obtained the so-called hybrid or English varieties, some of whose fruits weigh up to 70 grams, and we certainly won't stop there: sowings and fertilizations continue, and there is no doubt that before long we'll be able to achieve something better. The Chilean strawberry is a little delicate; it fears the cold and especially winter humidity. In Brittany, it is grown extensively, but in healthy, sandy soils. Same cultivation as hybrid varieties. SEEDS. - To extract the strawberry seed, select the ripest, prettiest fruit; place on a shaded board; when decomposition begins, crush in a container full of water; the seeds will sink to the bottom and be scooped up for immediate sowing or drying. There's no need to wait until the fruit has decomposed. Once picked, if the fruit is ripe enough, the seeds can be removed. They keep well for up to three years. One gram contains between 800 and 2,500 seeds, depending on the species. pests, pests, pests. - The only pest that attacks this plant is white mould, which seems to develop mainly in plantations planted on top soil and where strawberries have been grown for a long time; the best remedy is to water the affected plants with a very clear milk of lime. We have tried iron sulfate, dissolved in plenty of water, but the results have not been satisfactory. Although few diseases attack strawberry plants, pests are very numerous. The white grub or chafer larva is very fond of its roots; in soils where they swarm, it is not uncommon to see entire beds destroyed in a short space of time; until now, the only means of destruction has been to kill it. Cutworms are still a terrible enemy, and there are some soils where you can't grow them because of this worm. If Botrytis tenella can destroy white and cutworms, growers will be delighted. Ants sometimes attack strawberries, but more often than not, they take up residence at the base of strawberry plants and dig galleries, or almost cover the plant with earth; to destroy them, place plates coated with honey on the ground; they go in and can't get out; then dip the plate in boiling water. Slugs are very fond of strawberries, which they gnaw off completely. Only those that touch the ground are damaged. Destroying these beasts is difficult, in the sense that they are always to be found. You hunt them morning and night, skewer them with a sharp wire, and throw them in a bit of slaked lime. You can also place cabbage leaves or pieces of carrot or turnip at some distance from the snail's body; the snail will take refuge under them to devour them, and then they're easy to catch. Snails rarely attack strawberries. The green and grey caterpillar sometimes devours the leaves in spring, so we look for it and crush it, which is the only way to get rid of it. The mole causes considerable damage to plantations, knocking them over and uprooting them by forming underground galleries. You must try to destroy them, either by setting traps or by lying in wait to kill them. We use wooden traps, which are better and safer than iron ones. The millipede is a very long, extraordinarily flexible little worm, which walks both forwards and backwards. It gets into strawberries that touch the ground, in very large numbers, and the inside of the fruit is completely devoured. There's no known way of destroying it. The molewort wreaks havoc in young plantations; it is especially in sandy soils, where they are abundant, that care should be taken. USES. - Strawberries can be served in a variety of ways, with wine, cognac, kirsch, rum, Madeira or even better, champagne. They can be eaten on their own, with sugar or mixed with raspberries. It is said that strawberries lose their fragrance when washed, but this is wrong. If you take the time to wash them half an hour before eating them, they recover their smell, and are cleaner and more appetizing. Strawberries are very digestive. Dissolved in water, they make a pleasant, soothing drink. They are preserved in jams and jellies. They even make an excellent liqueur when mixed with raspberries. Strawberries are used to make a syrup that is used to flavor creams and jellies. Strawberries quickly undergo vinous, alcoholic and acetic fermentation, and can be used to make wine, brandy and vinegar. Strawberries are balsamic and refreshing, and can only be criticized for their slightly laxative properties, which can be corrected with sugar and a little wine. However, as they are generally quite cold, it might be unwise to overindulge in them, especially after a big dinner; but on an empty stomach in the morning, or when the work of digestion has been completed, they are a most salutary dish. Perfumers use distillation to obtain strawberry scents that are very pleasant, and to which they attribute the property of making freckles disappear. In some countries, strawberry leaves are used instead of tea. Today, strawberries are the subject of a sizeable trade. We've managed to package them and ship them over fairly long distances, without them suffering too much. They still fetch a high price on the market, which proves that cultivation is lucrative. CULTIVATED RASPBERRY - -- Rubus idœus L. Rubus frambœsianus Lamk. Rosaceae dryadae. ORIGIN. - A shrub native to Mount Ida; at least, that's where it was first observed, but it is found spontaneously in mountainous regions throughout most of Europe, especially in woods and stony places. Rarer in wooded plains. GROWING. - The raspberry is a perennial shrub that is extremely easy to grow. It thrives in all soils, provided they are not too dry or chalky. It does best, however, in moist soils and semi-shaded exposures. We have seen it planted in northern exposures with very good results. It is propagated by rooting offshoots, which spring up in large numbers around old plants. Preferably choose those with the best roots and medium size; prune them a little if they are too long, refresh the roots a little and plant. The ground on which you intend to plant, whether in a bed or in a square, must first be ploughed well and deeply, and thoroughly fertilized with good, energetic fertilizers. Raspberries are usually planted from November to March. They are planted in rows 90 cm to 1 m apart, sometimes further apart, depending on the fertility of the soil. Raspberries are widely grown in the Charente region, particularly around Angoulême. Market gardeners counter-plant garlic or shallots, as these are radiated with the forked or flat hoe, so they only put in raspberry plants every three or four rays, which gives about the distance indicated; it's an excellent planting system that we recommend. In general, once the land has been well prepared and laid out, market gardeners dig small square holes 15 or 20 centimetres apart, and plant, putting loose soil over the roots. Once the raspberry planting is complete, onions, romaine, lettuce, Bacalan cabbage, etc. are intercropped. Other cultivation care for this first year consists of frequent spading or raking of the soil. In autumn, after pruning, we give the plants a good drying, taking care not to uproot the plants that are to bear fruit. Smoke again, and every year again, as the raspberry bush is an exhausting plant: we remove the new shoots, which would thrive at the expense of the fruit-bearing stems. Watering is useless, because if you have to water with a watering can, it's better not to plant raspberries (unless you can irrigate abundantly). Raspberries will only perform well if the soil is naturally moist. Raspberries should not be left to grow freely, as some growers have found. It is preferable to train or trellis the plant, which is more regular and more tasteful, and the growing costs are never higher. The best method is counter-trellising, which consists of planting a few 1.50 m high stakes at each end of the row and in the middle, which are driven in 30 cm. Three rows of wire are stretched, the first 40 centimetres from the ground, the second 40 centimetres from the first, and the third at the top of the stake. The fruit-bearing branches are attached by bending them at 45 degrees, and the new suckers that develop and are well placed as fruit-bearing branches for the following year are attached vertically to the wire as they grow. A well-tended raspberry plantation can last ten years or more. The Dutch plant in 25-centimeter-deep troughs, with a little ridging each year so that the roots, which always tend to rise to the surface of the soil, are at a suitable depth. PRUNING. - In certain favorable soils, the raspberry bush acquires great vigor; the stems become very strong. These stems are biennial, meaning they grow the first year, bear fruit the second and then die. Pruning should be carried out during winter, from November to February. Choose four of the most beautiful and best-placed stems, fewer if the plant is not very vigorous, and cut them off above one eye, at about a third of their total length, sometimes more, depending on their vigor. All old wood from the previous year is removed, cut flush with the ground, and all unnecessary suckers are removed. VARIETIES. - Some sixty years ago, we only had a few varieties of little merit and completely primitive. Today, we have some excellent ones. Among the best are A fruit rouge. - Merveille des quatre saisons red - with large conical red fruit, reaching up to the frosts. Perpetual red. - Remontant, very fructiferous and fragrant. Belle de Fontenay. - Large, dark-red fruit. Catawissa d'Amérique. - Very remontant, with red fruit and good taste, very fragrant. Falstaff. - Excessively fertile, very good quality, medium red fruit. Superb from England. - Fertile, large conical red fruit; highly recommended variety. Double bearing. - Very beautiful red fruit, remontant, one of the best varieties to grow for the market. Belle de Palluau. - Very large, conical fruit; fairly productive. Hornet. - Very large red fruit, fragrant; productive, good quality. Framboise de Brabant. - Red conical fruit; fairly productive. Yellow or orange fruit. - Merveille des quatre saisons yellow. - Very large, very fragrant fruit; productive. Chile yellow. - Very fertile variety, large yellow fruit, very good quality. Jaune d'Anvers. - Large, conical, yellow fruit; very productive. Brinhles'Orange. - Vigorous, fertile plant with large, bright orange fruit. SEEDS. - To harvest seeds, do as for strawberries: wash the fruit and the seeds will preci15. pent at the bottom of the water, collect them and dry them in the shade. Seeds should only be sown with the aim of obtaining new varieties: it is rare for a seed to faithfully reproduce its species; as far as possible, only fresh seeds should be sown, as they only keep for a year or two at most. USES. - Raspberries are widely used as a healthy, refreshing and soothing food. It is eaten in the same way as strawberries, with which it is often associated. Raspberries, sugar and water are used to make a pleasant drink. It can be used to make wine, alcohol or mead. To make wine, blend 15 kilograms of red raspberries and 3 kilograms of freshly picked redcurrants. The stems and bunches are removed and crushed in the same mortar. After resting for twenty-four hours, the juice is squeezed and the following is added per liter: half a pound of sugar; half a liter of brandy. Mix well and leave to stand until blackberry season. Then take 5 pounds of these fruits, crush them with a liter of water, throw in a broth and let stand thirty-six hours; press and add: Half a pound of sugar; 3 decanters of brandy per liter of liqueur obtained, and mix the two liqueurs which are shaken vigorously. This wine is good to drink only after one year. Raspberry ratafia is obtained by mixing : 600 grams raspberry juice; 1 kilogram sugar; 2 liters brandy. The liqueur is left to settle and bottled. The syrup is made with two-thirds raspberries and one-third redcurrants. Infused in wine, raspberries give it a delicious taste and aroma; with white vinegar, they give raspberry vinegar, which is used to make syrup. In industry, raspberries are frequently used to make carbonated lemonades. It is also used to make jams, jellies, preserves, compotes, etc. Confectioners and pharmacists use it daily, making cakes, tarts, ice creams and more. In some French vineyards, raspberries are added to the vat to give the wine its aroma. Lathyrus sativus L. Cicercula alata Mœnch. Leguminous plants. ORIGIN. - Annual plant of doubtful origin. I consider it probable," says De Candolle, "that the species existed before being cultivated, from the southern Caucasus or the Caspian Sea to northern India, and that it spread to Europe as a result of ancient cultivation, perhaps mixed with cereals. It is therefore a mistake to believe that the plant is indigenous. The Greeks called it Lathyros and the Latins Cicercula. It has several synonyms: Dent de brebis - Jarra. - Domestic chickweed. - Swiss lentil. - Spanish lentil. - Breton pea. - Lentillin. - Square pea. - Pois gras, etc. 263 CULTURE. - Chickling is not widely cultivated in gardens; it is mainly used in field crops. It is sown in March-April, in rows 50 centimeters apart, preferably in sandy soil, with plenty of smoke, so that the grain is cooked, since there is perhaps no other plant on which the nature of the soil has as much influence as on this one. Indeed, chaff harvested in strong soils succeeds perfectly and even produces a lot, but the grain is not cooked, and therefore becomes inedible; at most, it is good for animals. Other cultivation requirements are the same as for peas. - Chickweed is virtually disease-free; only snails and loaches are very keen on it when the plant starts to grow. Mice and voles devour it as soon as it is sown, but fortunately this is rare. USES. - The seeds are eaten like beans; they are very nutritious and have highly appreciated lactiferous properties. Flour is made from them to fatten poultry and pigs; properly cooked, the seeds make an excellent and very healthy food, and the opposite occurs when they are not perfectly cooked. GOMEO Hibiscus esculentus L. Hibiscus ficifolius Mill. A belmoschus esculentus Mœnch. Malvaceae ORIGIN. - Annual plant, native to South America, little cultivated and little appreciated in France. GROWING. - Okra is propagated from seed, which is sown on warm beds from February to April; when the young plants have grown their second leaf, they are transplanted to another warm bed 10 or 15 centimetres apart. In May, when frosts are no longer a threat, they are planted out at 65 centimetres. It's best to choose FIG. 32 - Long-fruited okra. a good exposure and sufficiently amended soil, as this plant needs a lot of heat to ripen its seeds. When first transplanted, they can also be placed in pots and cared for in the same way as other plants. This way, they won't have to suffer from transplanting. Other cultivation care consists of frequent hoeing around the plants and copious watering in summer. VARIETY. - Long-fruited okra (fig. 32). - Low stem not exceeding 55 centimeters, leaf cut like that of mallow, upright fruit 15 to 20 centimeters long, pointed, thin, 2 to 3 centimeters in diameter. A sub-variety with larger, hanging fruit is grown. Round-fruited okra. - Stem 49 to 50 centimeters long, fruit 16 to 17 centimeters long by 40 centimeters wide, obtuse; earlier than the previous variety. SEEDS. - In Paris and northern France, seeds rarely ripen in the open ground, they need the greenhouse; from the Charentes, and moving up to the southwest and south of France, they ripen perfectly in good exposure. When the fruits containing the seeds have changed color, they are ripe: they are picked and laid out to dry in the sun. The seed then detaches quite well; it keeps well for five years, 30 grams contain 450 grams, a liter weighs 620 grams. USES. - When not yet fully developed, sliced and boiled in soups, sauces or even flavored water, okra fruits make these liquids thick and viscous, giving them a tangy flavor that the Creoles of Martinique and Guadeloupe find very pleasant, as they eat a lot of them. The seeds have been advocated as a substitute for coffee, and we have tried them; we doubt their use will spread. In Brazil, the fruit is eaten cooked with poultry. ORDINARY CURRANT Ribes rubrum L. ORIGIN. - The red currant is native to northern and temperate Europe, as well as to Siberia as far as Kamtschatka, and in America from Canada and Vermont to the mouth of the Mackensie River. Unknown to the Greeks and Romans, cultivation of this plant was only introduced in the Middle Ages. The cultivated plant differs little from the wild plant". (De Candolle). CULTIVATION. - The currant generally adapts well to all kinds of soil, and even exposure, as it can be found at many different altitudes. We know of some that have been planted under large trees, and mixed with other shrubs. Despite this, they grow well and produce a lot. However, this plant prefers cool, deep soil and a well exposed position. The currant can be propagated from seed, but this is a time-consuming and expensive method. It is rarely sown except to obtain larger-fruited varieties. The best way to propagate is by cuttings, which take very well. We choose young shoots of the year for this purpose, and put them in place or in a nursery, but they take so well that it's preferable to put them directly in place; this avoids transplanting, which is always detrimental to the plant. Cuttings are taken from October to February. Cuttings taken in autumn will always give better results than those taken later. Redcurrants can also be propagated by splintering rooted plants, which can be found in fairly large quantities in old clumps. Other cultivation techniques include removing dead wood and cutting back large stems to rejuvenate them. We spade around the plants at least twice a year, and give them several rakes or hoeings to prevent weeds from getting into the clump. PRUNING. - You can give the currant any shape you like. By pruning, you can form counter-trees on wire, in a ball, in a cone, in cords, etc. Pruning consists in removing dead wood and clearing the interior to avoid confusion, and all the current year's shoots are cut at five or six eyes above the previous year's size, i.e. above the impasto. VARIETIES. - Red currants. - Dutch red currant. - Long, tight bunches, very large, light-red fruit; late and very vigorous. Queen Victoria currant. - Loose, very long clusters; fairly productive. Versailles redcurrant. - Numerous, very large, light-red fruits in long, tightly-packed bunches. Hátive de Bertin. - Tight clusters, dark red fruit; very early. Cherry currant, large fruit. - Short, sparsely-packed bunches; large, light-red fruit; vigorous, stocky plant. Chenonceau currant. - Beautiful, loosely packed clusters. Glory currant from Sablons. - Fertile de Palluau - Fertile d'Angers, etc. White-fruited currants. - White currant from Holland. - Quite large fruit of very good quality, firm, transparent flesh. Transparent currant. - Very long clusters with large berries. Boulogne currant. - Imperial cherry. - Versaillaise. - Whites grapes - Verrières blanches, etc. GROSEILLER A FRUIT NOIR, CASSIS Ribes nigrum L. Ribes olidum Mœnch. ORIGIN. - The origin of the word blackcurrant is not well known. It is thought to derive from the highly esteemed liqueurs once made in Cassis, Provence, exclusively from the fruit of this plant. According to De Candolle, "blackcurrants exist in a spontaneous state in northern Europe, from Scotland and Lapland to northern France and Italy, Bosnia, Armenia, all Siberia and the region of the Amur River and the western Himalayas, often naturalizing, for example, in central France." CULTIVATION. - The blackcurrant differs from the redcurrant only in its slightly larger size, its lighter green leaves and the scent of its wood. The fruit, which is a beautiful jet-black color, must be picked as soon as it ripens, otherwise it will fall off. Cultivation is the same as for the redcurrant. As blackcurrants regrow less than redcurrants, you should not cut off too much old wood, which would reduce production. Same pruning. THORNY CURRANT. MACKEREL CURRANT Ribes Uva crispa L. Ribes spinosum Lamk. ORIGIN. - De Candolle says: "This currant grows spontaneously throughout temperate Europe, from southern Sweden to the mountainous parts of central Spain, Italy and Greece. It is also found in northern Africa, in the Aures mountains. Mr. Ball has found a fairly distinct variety in the Atlas mountains of Morocco, it exists in the Caucasus, and in more or less different forms, in the western Himalayas". This shrub grows in arid, stony areas. CULTIVATION. - The thorny currant is propagated from seed, marcottes, cuttings taken from two-year-old wood and rooted splinters. Cuttings take root with greater difficulty than other varieties. Because of its numerous, tight thorns, it is very suitable for forming impenetrable hedges, and is so hardy that it can be planted in all exposures and soils, VARIETY. - There are several varieties. Some come from England or America, where they are highly prized; green, red, purple or yellow fruit. Among the best are: Britannica, downy yellow. - Justicia, fluffy white. - Creeping Jane, smooth yellow - Favorite rouge, smooth red. - Whinhams Industry, large, dark red-brown fruit. - Washington, spiky pink. - Peace-Maher, smooth red - Roaring Lion, smooth red. - White-Smith, smooth green. French varieties include Ovoid green, transparent spiky, dull red, yellow, etc. SEEDS. - To harvest seeds, we select the most beautiful fruits and spread them out on planks. When they are fully ripe, they are crushed in water; the seeds sink to the bottom, are collected and dried in the shade; they keep well for a year. For best success when sowing in spring, they should be stratified in sand immediately after harvesting. DISEASES, PESTS. - The currant is sometimes affected by a disease that rapidly destroys it. This is a species of white fungus that develops on the roots and causes them to rot. It is frequently found in soils that are too damp. It has been suggested that diseased plants be watered with a very clear milk of lime. Small green caterpillars that devour leaves are also sometimes found, depending on the year, especially on red currants. We have seen young plantations completely stripped of leaves. The remedy is very difficult: you have to look for the eggs, which are laid in the shape of rings on two- or three-year-old wood, and destroy them. USES. - The currant is widely used. The fruit is eaten, and jellies are made from it. The fruit is used to make soothing and refreshing drinks, syrup and a pleasant wine that is drunk in the North, and even brandy. In medicine, redcurrants are refreshing and astringent, and stimulate the appetite. The acidity of redcurrants, more intense in the red varieties, results from the abundance of malic and citric acids. The currant is a medicated food that nourishes and refreshes. The leaves are used to dye yellow, the branches to dye black. The gooseberry breed is so named because the fruit is used green in a sauce for mackerel. In France, the fruits are used for little other than eating them raw, but in England they are used to spice up certain sauces before they are ripe. They can be eaten on their own, or as an accessory to meats. They are also used to make delicious cakes. When ripe, they are used to make a highly prized wine. Blackcurrants produce an excellent tonic liqueur, good for the stomach. It also makes a very good ratafia. As well as the seeds, unscrupulous confectioners use the wood and leaves to give perfume to a syrup they call blackcurrant. The fruit juice is dyed blue by alkali, purple by tin salt. A lacquer is obtained. The leaves give a yellow dye used to color brandy. COMMON BEANS Phaseolus vulgaris. L. Leguminosae, Papilionaceae. ORIGIN. - An annual plant of uncertain origin. It is said to have originated in South America, and to have been imported in the 14th century; it has not been found growing spontaneously anywhere, which proves that it has been cultivated for a very long time. The bean has several synonyms: Faverolle, faviole, fayau, faséole, fayon, fève à visage, fève de mer, mongette, banette, etc. OUTDOOR CULTIVATION. - In general, beans thrive in all sufficiently fertilized soils; however, they do better in light, moist soils. The first beans are sown in the open ground in the first half of April, and successively until June. In the south of France, you can start sowing in March. Early varieties are preferred. There are several ways to arrange bean sowing, with each region following its own traditions. In the Charentes, Dordogne, Vienne, Vendée and Deux-Sèvres regions, for example, beans are combed with a forked or flat hoe, as is done for garlic. This is an excellent method. In the South-West and part of the Midi, it is sown in beds, and here's how it's done for dwarf breeds. Once the soil has been well prepared and smoked, use the narrow end of the hoe to make small gullies Om, 10 and 50 centimetres deep. Sow in clumps at 25 or 30 centimetres along the line, or grain by grain at 8 centimetres. Cover lightly by about 3 or 4 centimetres, depending on the size of the seed. If the soil is too compact, cover with fine earth or compost. Rowing varieties destined to succeed dwarf breeds are laid out in rows of three rays at 40 centimetres. A fourth line is traced with the tracer to plant romaine, which is removed before it harms the beans. These are divided by a 50-centimetre path, which, once the lettuces have been removed, gives a 90-centimetre passage between each bed. This distance is necessary, firstly to form a bead of earth on each side, to retain water for watering and for the worker to pass through with his watering cans. You can also sow in clumps, using a hoe or a thin planter to make holes 40 centimetres apart in a chessboard pattern, in which you place five or six beans and cover. As beans in general, and row beans in particular, need a lot of air to grow well and produce a lot, this last method is the best and can be adopted everywhere. In some regions, notably the Charente, market gardeners have laid out their rowing bean beds in five rays at 30 centimeters. This distance is much too close, because once the beans are a little high, the middle three rows receive very little air and light, and consequently produce little. We've made this observation to a few growers, who have continued as before anyway - it's a routine that's hard to change. Whatever the sowing method used and whatever the variety, when the beans have reached a height of a dozen centimetres, they are hoeed, and then repeated at intervals of a few days. Chestnut, oak, plane and hazelnut are suitable for this purpose; in the Landes and part of the south-west, where there are many pine woods, they are used almost exclusively. A lath is placed on each bean, or tuft, and the appearance of these branches, generally very straight, produces a pretty eye-catching effect. The two rows around the edges are planted with the tallest branches slightly inclined towards each other, while the shorter middle branches are planted vertically. When the bush beans have reached a certain level of development, they are ridged; this operation is necessary in summer to maintain constant humidity and prevent the roots from being affected by heat, which would be detrimental to the plants. During hot spells, if the soil in which you have sown is dry, you must not spare watering, which must be very copious, and we even recommend irrigation if possible, as production will depend on watering if the soil is not naturally damp; without water, plants dry out, flower badly and often die before they have produced a quarter of their yield. Sometimes, in strong soils, as soon as the beans are sown, a heavy rainstorm settles and hardens the soil surface. In this case, the seeds would not stand up well if left as they are, so this crust needs to be broken by light hoeing. EARLY CROPS. - Beans in their green state are generally preferred by consumers, and when they can be harvested early, they represent a good source of income. Early beans can be grown in a variety of ways, using thermosiphon-heated tarpaulins, hot-layer frames or cloches. Thermosiphon cultivation is quick and successful. Sowing can start after December 15, and harvesting can begin in the second half of February. Thermosiphon will always give the best results, as the heat is even and the beans develop very well and produce a lot, but its use becomes expensive. As growing beans in hot frames is more difficult, and is the most widely used method, we will describe it below: In the second half of January, prepare a good layer 60 centimetres thick. Load it with 15 centimeters of good potting soil mixed with equal parts of vegetable garden soil. After this, the beans are sown in small clumps of three together, 35 or 40 centimetres apart. Four rows are planted per 1.33 m. After sowing, cover and pack well, water very lightly, and put up the panels. You can also sow one by one at 15 centimetres along the row. Under the influence of the background heat, the beans are quick to sprout; from this point onwards, you need to watch out for mildew, which is the main enemy of this crop; you need to go over it often to remove the affected parts, and give it air as much as the temperature allows, and gradually. Cover with straw mats during the night, surround the trunks with good stoves and reshape them often, adding manure each time. When the beans have reached a height of 25 centimetres, they are tilted towards the top of the trunk, secured with small wooden hooks. The ends of the stalks soon rise after forming a circuit, but the lower part remains flat. Despite this operation, which is only intended to prevent the beans from touching the glass, the trunks can be raised if necessary. When the flowers start to appear, give them plenty of air and frequent watering. Instead of sowing beans in place on the bed, as we have just indicated, some growers transplant them, i.e. they sow on a very small area, and when the plants have grown their first leaves, they transplant them on a bed prepared in advance. This method gives just as good results as sowing in place. So you can choose either system. The first beans are usually harvested six weeks after sowing. Cultivation under cloches starts in the second half of March, and is carried out in much the same way. Once the bed has been prepared, it is edged, the soil is put in, the cloches are placed in a chessboard pattern, and three or four beans are sown under each one, or transplanted, which is preferable. As soon as the crop has recovered, air is added. Keep the bells above them for as long as possible, raising them on three stakes or flowerpots, and remove them when all danger has passed. When it's cold, especially at night, cover with bedding or straw mats. The varieties that lend themselves best to these various growing systems are: 1° Belgian dwarf black bean; 2° White and yellow flageolet bean; 3° Early Dutch dwarf bean; 4° White bean with waffle leaves; 5° Russian Emperor bean; 6° Early Lyon glory bean; 7° Dwarf flageolet bean, the triumph of the châs- sis; an excellent novelty for this crop. SEEDS. - To harvest bean seeds, keep a piece of planking without picking them, and leave them to ripen on the ground. They are then picked and laid out in the shade in a well-ventilated, rodent-proof place. They are husked and put into small bags until the time comes to sow them. For varieties with oars, we recommend preventing them from climbing by pinching them. This will produce a very good crop of beans. Although beans retain their germinative powers for a long time, three years and sometimes more depending on the variety, it is preferable to choose seed from the previous year if you want to be successful. Red Soissons bean. - Harlequin bean, etc. MALaDlEs, NUISIBLE ANIMALS. - Sometimes, especially in silica-poor soils, beans are affected by chlorosis, turn yellow and stop growing; the best remedy is to water them from time to time with liquid manure in which a little iron sulfate has been dissolved, about 100 grams per 10 liters of water, and water at the foot as much as possible. Sometimes, as a result of sudden changes in temperature and too much prolonged humidity, the beans are affected by rot and rust or uredo; the pods are strewn with circular red spots which perforate the parchment and reach the beans, which are completely deteriorated. There's nothing to be done about it; fortunately, these diseases are fairly rare, and only show up in autumn, when the bean harvest is well advanced. White grubs, slugs, snails and crickets, when they swarm in a field, cause real damage to young bean seedlings. So we have to wage a fierce war against them. To protect the crop, surround the plant with powdered quicklime, soot and unleached ash, mixed in equal parts. USES. - Beans are widely used in the diet: along with potatoes, they are the staple of the poor man's diet. On the rich man's table, they are almost always served with a variety of meats, mainly mutton; everyone knows the ancient and traditional gigot aux flageolets, the delight of Parisians, or to put it better, of the majority of French people. Beans are popular simply because they're cheap. The ancients knew beans; Galen says that the Romans began their meals with beans preserved in vinegar and garum, to whet their appetites. Green beans are eaten half-formed. In Auvergne and Poitou, and even in Limousin, it is widely cultivated to be eaten dry, and in these regions is the main food of the peasants. It is very nourishing, but should not be eaten by weak stomachs or those with poor digestion. The pods can be pickled in vinegar like gherkins. Green beans can be preserved in several ways. Usually, they are blanched by throwing them into boiling, slightly salted water and leaving them for a few minutes after removing them from the heat; they are then drained, dried on cloths and placed several times in an oven, like prunes, on racks. Before using them, soak them first thing in the morning in lukewarm water. Alternatively, to preserve the beans, pour boiling water over them and leave them in for a few minutes, then cook them in boiling salted water, so that they are a little crunchy, drain them, sauté them in butter with parsley, and bottle them with their sauce when they are cold; in the bottles, they are given a five-minute boil. Flageolet beans can be preserved in the same way, but need to boil for three hours. They make excellent flour for fattening domestic animals. Burnt stalks yield a lot of potash. SPANISH BEANS Phaseolus multiflorus Wild. Phaseolus coccineus I.. ORIGIN. - South American plant. Perennial in its native country, but annual in our cultivations, called Haricot bouquet, Haricot à fleurs, etc. CULTIVATION. - Runner beans are excessively vigorous and hardy plants, at least in the Midi; they become more delicate in the North, due to the lack of heat. The varied colors of their flowers make them highly appreciated as ornamental plants. Runner beans are grown in the same way as Phascolus vulgaris, but as they are very vigorous, they need to be rowed with high branches. VARIETIES. - Runner bean. - Large, vigorous, productive variety; broad, short pods, light wine-red beans with black spots, red flowers. White runner bean. - Very vigorous variety, the best to grow for eating, reaching 3 meters or more in height; white flowers in numerous clusters; broad, flattened pods; very large, thick, white beans. Bicolor runner bean. - A vigorous variety, highly original for the oddity of its flowers, which are half red and half white; highly esteemed in the North, where it is grown as an ornamental. Black runner bean. - Very vigorous, fairly hardy; short, broad pods; completely black bean. Hybrid runner bean. - Very vigorous variety; flowers with the same variegation as the bi-colored bean; broad pods; grayish-yellow grain, spotted with brown. DISEASES, PESTS. - This breed is much hardier than Phaseolus vulgaris, resists disease and is rarely attacked by insects: slugs and snails will devour a few young plants. USES. - The runner bean is a very popular plant in the South of France. It can be eaten as a half-formed bean or green, when it is edible; but when dry, it is not as good as an ordinary bean, is not very floury and has an unpleasant pungent taste. In southern Spain and part of Portugal, this breed is grown to the exclusion of all others. The liter weighs between 730 and 735 grams, and 100 grams contain around 75 beans. LIMA BEANS, Phaseolus lunatus L. Phaseolus inamœnus L. Phaseolus lunatus macrocarpus Bentham. ORIGIN. - Perennial in its native country, annual in our cultivations. This breed is mainly cultivated by E. BERGER, Vegetables. 17 in the Argentine Republic, the United States, the West Indies, Havana, almost all the French colonies in America and throughout Africa. CULTIVATION. - Cultivation of this breed is much the same as that of the above-mentioned varieties, with the difference that in the North and in Paris the pods almost never, or rarely, all reach maturity. In cold years with rainy autumns, they don't ripen at all. Throughout the Midi, and particularly in Provence, it does fairly well; it's only from Toulouse onwards that we can begin to grow it successfully. The Lima bean should be sown early, towards the end of April or first fortnight of May, at the best possible exposure. In temperate climates, we recommend sowing in pots, under a frame, and then planting in the open ground, when the soil is sufficiently warm. It requires the same cultivation care as row varieties. As it grows very tall, it should be given sufficiently high stalks. VARIETIES. - Lima bean. - Very late; broad, short pods, joined by several together; white, yellowish, flattened bean, very elongated and broad, a little kidney-shaped. 90 seeds weigh 100 grams. American growers' catalogs mention several other sub-varieties of this bean, with green, yellow and white seeds. Marbled Cape bean. - Very characteristic variety; dark red beans around the umbilicus and at one end; the rest are white with red dots. Each bean weighs 1 gram. Stéva bean. - A variety of Phaseolus lunatus, known in Havana as the fève plate or fève créole, this bean is highly prized by rich and poor alike. Very early: the first pods ripen quite well in the northern climate and in Paris. In the Midi, it is a perfect success. Yellowish-white grain, similar to Lima, but smaller. COWPEA BEAN. DOLIQUE MONGETTE. Dolichos unguiculatus L. ORIGIN. - Annual plant, native to South America, highly esteemed in tropical countries, and in Europe. in warm countries such as Portugal, Spain, Italy, etc., and in France in the southern zone. CULTURE. - This breed, which grows to no more than 60 centimeters in height, does quite well in Paris and the North, provided it is given very good exposure. Cultivation is the same as for dwarf common beans; straight or curved pods, almost cylindrical, 20 to 25 centimeters long; dirty white grain, with a small black spot around the umbilicus. Grain merchants in Italy and Portugal mention several varieties, differing from this one only in grain size. USES. - This breed is eaten green and half-formed; dry, the quality is far inferior to the others. Dolichos sesquipedalis L. ORIGIN. - Annual. From South America. Highly valued in Buenos-Ayres, Montevideo, Chile. CULTIVATION. - In some parts of Provence, this species is widely cultivated and does very well. We have grown it in Bordeaux and have been very satisfied. Cultivation is the same as for Soissons string beans. As this plant is very heat-loving, it needs a good, sunny exposure and lots of watering in summer. This is the only way to ensure success. VARIETIES. - Cuban cowpea bean. - An extremely curious variety of the asparagus cowpea bean, introduced from Havana some ten years ago: it is far superior to the previous variety. We have grown it for a very long time and have always been satisfied with the results it has given us. This variety is vigorous and relatively hardy: it grows very tall, up to 3.50 m, or more, depending on the soil. Very numerous pods, grouped in threes and fours, 50 to 60 centimetres long. SEEDS. - Pale, wine-yellow color, white umbilicus encircled by a small black line; small seeds. 100 grams contain 630 seeds. USES. - The pods are eaten green, very tender and tasty, especially when they are about half as long. Dried, the asparagus bean has no flavor and is rather bad than good. DOLIC BEAN LABLAB Lablab vulgaris Savi. Dolichos Lablab L. ORIGIN. - This species is widely cultivated in India and tropical Africa, says De Candolle. Cultivation is at least three thousand years old: "The lablab is unquestionably spontaneous in India, and even, it is said, in Java. It has become naturalized in the Seychelles Islands as a result of cultivation. The authors' indications do not allow us to say that it is spontaneous in Africa. CULTURE. - The lablab bean is grown very little in France, a lot in Egypt, and a little in Spain and Italy. This breed is very vigorous: it can reach 4 to 5 meters in height; very productive in hot countries. Same cultivation as paddle varieties. Should be considered more as an ornamental plant than as a vegetable variety. Not very productive in the North. The seeds, three or four per pod, are white or black, as there are two varieties, one with white flowers, the other with purple. USES. - In America, the lablab is cultivated for its grain, which is eaten like soissons in France. HVSOPE Hyssopus officinalis L. Hyssopus decussatus Persoon. Hyssopus myrtifolius Desf. Hyssopus ruber Mich. Labiatae. ORIGIN. - Perennial, evergreen plant, or rather sub-shrub, native to Spain, according to some authors, and Italy, according to others. GROWING. - Hyssop is easy to grow. It is usually planted in borders and pruned, like thyme, twice a year, in March and September. It is propagated by sowing seeds in rows in spring. Cover sparingly, as the seed is very fine. When the young plants have reached 7 or 8 centimetres in height, they are transplanted to the edges of driveways. Weed and hoe frequently to rid them of weeds. It can also be propagated with rooted cuttings and cold cuttings. It thrives best in strong, chalky soils, and is hardy enough to withstand the ordinary winters of northern France. Plantations should be renewed at least every four years. SEEDS. - In spring, we keep a few plants, which we don't prune as they rise, and in July, when the ears are ripe and before they are completely dry, we pick them with care, as the seed detaches very easily. They are spread out on a cloth and exposed to the sun for one or two days. The seeds are collected and winnowed. They keep well for three years. According to Vilmorin, 1 gram contains 850 seeds. DISEASES, PESTS. - In very rich, heavily fertilized soils, every year many plants succumb to the attacks of powdery mildew, which attacks the roots and especially the crown. Affected plants first wilt, then turn yellow. We know of no effective remedy to destroy this parasite. As soon as it is noticed, the plants must be pulled up without mercy and thrown away or burned. The site should be spaded as closely as possible to other plants, in order to destroy all the germs of the disease. As for insects, they are not very fond of this plant, and hardly touch it, probably because of the strongly aromatic smell of all its parts. Sometimes, however, flea beetles pierce the leaves, but we have never observed any significant damage. USES. - Hyssop is used in cooking to enhance the flavor of dishes, especially sauces. It is frequently used, especially in northern France, with thyme in green pea stews. The buds of the young, still-tender branches are used in particular. It is also used in Russian salads. The Jews used hyssop to make purification brushes. CHINESE IGNAMUS Dioscorea Batatas Decaisne. Dioscorea Japonica Hort. 295 ORIGIN. - The Chinese call it Sain-in. According to Dr. Bretschneider, this plant is indigenous to China, as it is mentioned in the oldest work on medical matters, that of Emperor Schen nung. According to M. de Vilmorin, the yam was introduced to France in 1848 by M. de Montigny, French consul in Shanghai. There are several races of yam, all cultivated and highly esteemed in warm countries, particularly India, Japan and China. CULTIVATION. - Chinese yam is not widely cultivated in France, at least not as a standard crop, due to the great difficulty involved in digging up the tubers, which are usually found between 60 cm and 1 m deep. This plant can be propagated from bulblets born in the leaf axils, but this method does not give as good results as propagation from medium-sized tubers about the size of an index finger, which are planted whole. These tubers can be put into vegetation as early as March, in 10-centimeter pots placed on beds. In May, the tubers are removed from the pot and planted in the ground; this will produce earlier and more abundant crops. Otherwise, the best time to plant tubers is the first half of May in temperate regions, and April in the south. The soil in which you intend to plant must be well-developed and of good natural composition: you can't expect to get good results from poor-quality soil. Water, too, must not be lacking, and if possible, irrigation should not be neglected, as the plant stops growing when it lacks moisture; however, this moisture must not be stagnant. Once the soil has been prepared, plant with a chalk line or draw lines spaced Om, 40 apart. Plant at 25 centimetres on the line, tighter if you want smaller tubers. Twenty days after planting, we ream them up with branches at least 1 metre long, which is enough for the stems to wrap around them, and at the same time, hoeing is much easier than if the plants were lying on the ground. During the summer, the plants are hoeed several times, and then pulled out in November. The tubers, which are sometimes very long and large, weighing up to 1 kilogram, keep very well, much like potatoes. VARIETIES. - There are several varieties of yam, all imported from Japan or China. SEEDS. - In our regions, the bulblets that sprout from the leaf axils take the place of seeds. They are harvested in autumn, before the plant is grubbed up. DISEASES, PESTS. - The yam's natural enemies are snails and slugs, which devour the young stalks as they begin to grow. Cutworms can also eat tubers. The plant sometimes turns yellow towards midsummer, but this is due to excessive humidity or the soil's lack of siliceous matter. USES. - The rhizomes are eaten like potatoes; the flesh is white, light, floury and very pleasant to the taste. CULTIVATED LETTUCE Lactuca sativa L. Composites. ORIGIN. - An annual plant of ancient origin. It is said that the first seeds were sent from Rome to France in 1540 by Rabelais, who sent them to Cardinal d'Estrée. The typical species grows in southern Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. The Lactuca genus has been divided by botanists into two distinct races: head lettuces and romaine lettuces; the habit of each of these genera is so different that it is easy to recognize them. HATÉE AND EARLY LETTUCES. - The cultivation of early lettuces is extremely easy: all you need is the right tools, and sufficient equipment consisting of bells and panels. Twenty years ago, Parisian market gardeners used to grow this type of lettuce extensively, and found it a profitable winter crop. Today, early lettuce is still grown, but less so than in the past. The capital's markets are invaded by fresh produce from the Midi, Spain, Algeria, etc., which contributes to a decline in all similar products. What's more, for some years now, lettuces grown under glass have been subject to a terrible disease, Perono- spora gangliformis. The first early lettuces are sown towards the end of September and October, under frames or cloches on the ground, with good exposure. However, if sowing without panels, make sure the seedlings are as close as possible 17. to the glass. If sowing under cloches, first prepare the soil with a spade, then spread a small layer of potting soil over the surface. The cloches are placed before sowing, to fix the exact location, then the seed is sown, treaded and covered with potting soil; under a frame, the same procedure is followed, with watering. Don't let the air in; once the plant has risen, if it's too thick, thin it out a little, and if it's sunburned, shade it. When the plant is strong enough to be transplanted permanently, prepare an ados, place three or four rows of bells in a chessboard pattern, lift the plant as much as possible with the root ball, and plant five to eight lettuces under each one, depending on the species, water and press lightly on the top of each bell to fix them firmly to the ground, so that no air penetrates. Shade or smear the inside with loosened soil. Panel planting is preferable, as there is no wasted ground; generally, six or seven rows are planted in 1.33 panels. When the sun's rays are hot, if the glass is not smeared, it must be shaded; similarly, when frosts occur, it must be covered with straw mats. If the weather is too cold, the cloches should be lined with bedding or dry manure, with the straw mats on top. In this case, it's preferable to use cone-shaped straw mats, which fit over the bell, thus saving a lot of labor. The plantations are visited from time to time, dead or rotten leaves removed, weeded and lightly watered if necessary. About a month or forty-five days after sowing, the lettuces should be ready to harvest. Sowing should be staggered from fortnight to fortnight until February, so as not to run out. From November onwards, sow on warm beds. The cultivation methods described above apply to the north of France, as well as to temperate regions. In the south of France, a good sheltered exposure is sufficient in winter. All the varieties known as spring lettuces lend themselves very well to early cultivation. These are the only varieties that can give good results. CULTIVATION IN THE OPEN GROUND. - Head lettuces generally thrive in all soils that are sufficiently fertilized, and preferably in those that have been under cultivation for a long time. Lettuces should be planted in recently tilled soil: they are planted in rows of four at 25 centimetres apart, 20 or 25 centimetres apart on the row, sometimes more, depending on the species. Smaller varieties, such as gotte or crepe lettuces, can be planted closer together. Each plant is watered with the spout as soon as it is transplanted. A few weeks later, when the lettuces have started to grow, we give them a first hoeing, which we repeat a few days later. The surface of the soil must be constantly loose to encourage growth. VARIETIES. - Gardeners divide lettuces into four groups: 1° Spring lettuces; 2° Summer and autumn lettuces; 3° Winter lettuces; 4° Cutting lettuces. 1° Spring lettuces. - These varieties are all small or medium-sized. They are sown from February to the end of April. The first sowings should be made on warm beds, or in a well-exposed bed, or at least sheltered by windbreakers. In northern France, the first plantings in March are made on costières or ados. But in parts of the West, South-West and South of France, this precaution is not necessary. Laitue gotte (white seed). - A very old species, small in size and well suited to forced cultivation. Laitue gotte (black seed). - Little different from the previous one, very early. Slow-growing gotte lettuce. - Excellent variety, almost all apple.

Pancake lettuce (with white and black seeds). - Two small varieties, very good for forced cultivation. Tennisball lettuce (black seed). - A very old variety in cultivation, a little bulkier than crepe, apples well. Red-edged or red cord lettuce. - Excellent variety, larger than gotte, very good and highly regarded on the markets. Tom-Pouce lettuce. - A new, highly recommendable species, small in size and good for forced cultivation. 2° Summer and autumn lettuces. - There are a great many lettuces in this class, and some are very large. They are sown in nurseries from March to July. Transplant when the plant is strong enough, and water copiously during hot spells. A good mulch is necessary in dry soils. Blonde summer lettuce or non pareille lettuce, royal lettuce. - This variety is universally known. It is grown almost everywhere; medium size; round, tight head; white seed. Laitue blonde de Versailles. - A very fine variety with a large, elongated, firm head; white seed. Berlin blond lettuce. - Black-seeded variety, fairly tight head, tender and tasty. Chavigné blond lettuce. - Quite large head, very full and tight, forming quickly, very slow to set, highly recommended. Lettuce Bossin. - Large, not very tight, very wide, up to 40 cm in diameter. The midrib, very accentuated at the bottom, makes it depreciate, very tender, black seed. Maltese lettuce. - Quite large, not very tight, very tender, resists heat well; white seed; suitable for the Midi. Brown Batavia lettuce. - Tall, elongated head, not very tight, tender, rises quickly, very good for hot climates. Naples cabbage lettuce. - Very large variety, like apple, which is tight and firm; keeps well; white seed. Batavia blond lettuce. - Tender, loose-headed variety; white seed. Big brown lazy lettuce. - Excellent variety, known as meterelle lettuce in the Southwest; very hardy; black seed. Big lazy blond lettuce. - A very good summer variety, good head and tight; white seed. Lettuce merveille des quatre saisons or red Besson lettuce. - Very good hardy variety, can be sown in any season; black seed. Palatine or red lettuce. - Very good variety for summer, good head, black seed. Other varieties include Simpson's early lettuce. - Small, white seed. Red Dutch lettuce. - Black seed. Blood lettuce, improved. - White seed. Greasy green lettuce. - Small, peeling well, black seed. Lorthois or Trocadero lettuce. - Small, white seed. Big Normandy lettuce. - Medium, yellow-seeded. New or recent varieties include: Giant blond lettuce. - Very fine variety, apple FIG. 35 - Giant blond lettuce. large, firm, hardy, good heat resistance, white seed (fig. 35). Large, stubborn brown lettuce. - Firm and tight. Ohio lettuce. - Firm head, good size, very good for summer, white seed. Triumph lettuce. - Rounded head, very large, very hardy, difficult to set seed. 3° Winter lettuces. - These varieties are very hardy, and survive our ordinary winters quite well with some shelter. They are sown from August to October. Young plants, when strong enough, should be transplanted to a good exposure, to speed up production. The first seedlings produce lettuces that are good for harvesting before or during the winter, but the last plantings in October, or the first two weeks of November, overwinter, and vegetation starts up again in February. They bolt towards the end of April and are followed by spring seedlings. Passion or babiana lettuce. - Excellent variety, good head, medium size, very hardy, successful only at this time of year, white seed. Red winter lettuce. - Very fine variety, hardy, good head, good size, very good for the South-West, white seed. Brown winter lettuce. - Medium-sized variety, small, tight head, very hardy; white seed. Large blond winter lettuce. - Very fine variety, hardy and of good quality; white seed. New varieties include Trémont winter lettuce. - Excellent variety, hardy, fairly strong head, tight; white seed. White Passion lettuce. - Hardy and of good quality; black seed. 4° Cutting lettuces. - This breed includes varieties that do not head, that are sown very thickly, in all seasons on beds, on ados or in the open ground; in general, they are always mixed with other crops. Some of these varieties form a small apple, but not very tightly packed. Among the best are Beauregard leaf lettuce. - A very fine, tender variety, much appreciated in the markets. American leaf lettuce. - Leaves tinted bronze-red, very tender. California leaf lettuce. - Very vigorous variety, high yielding, very tender and tasty. Ordinary cutting lettuce - Blonde cutting lettuce. Generally speaking, all varieties of head lettuce can be grown as cutting lettuces; they just need to be picked young, although certain breeds are always hardy. In Bordeaux, these are called baby lettuces. SEEDS. - Seeds are easy to harvest. Spring and summer lettuces bolt the first year, only winter lettuces bolt the following year. Varieties sown after June do not ripen their seeds in the North. When the height of the plants is sufficiently high, and the seeds begin to form, you need to keep an eye on the birds, which are very fond of them. They keep well for four years. DISEASES, PESTS - Early lettuces, grown under cloches or panels where they need as little air as possible to succeed, have for some years been invaded by a cryptogam that rapidly destroys them, the Peronospora gangliformis, called miller by Parisian market gardeners. This parasite develops with extraordinary rapidity under the influence of concentrated humid heat, and generally begins with small, barely visible yellowish or white spots on the underside of the leaves, usually near the veins, especially the midrib. When the spots come together, a multitude of small, vertical, mold-like fibers become visible, each fiber or arbuscule surmounted by a reproductive sporule. After a few hours of rejoining, the oldest affected part becomes mortified and decomposes, leaving the leaf as a rotten mass. On the advice of Mr. Millardet, Professor of Botany at the Bordeaux Faculty of Science, we have carried out several trials to curb this disease. Bordeaux mixture, as used today for vines, would give good results, but the toxic principles of copper are an obstacle to its use; however, by washing the lettuces in clear water with a little sulfuric acid, there is nothing to fear. A very simple and above all harmless treatment, which has given us the best results, is as follows. Dissolve one kilogram of white plaster in 10 liters of water, add a little well-sieved soot, mix everything together, and use it to drench lettuces affected by the disease; ensure that the liquid is distributed over the leaves in the form of rain, a syringe for drenching greenhouses works well; to remove the plaster adhering to the leaves, drench them with fresh water a few hours before cutting them, and then wash them with plenty of water. Nicotine, reduced to a tenth and mixed with fat lime, has not given satisfactory results. Brown lettuces seem to be more resistant to this disease than blondes. This disease seems to develop especially on plants grown on beds. Let's hope it doesn't become more hardy, and that our outdoor plantings don't suffer from it! Slugs and snails are very fond of young lettuce plants, as are white grubs and cutworms, which cut the roots. Destroy them by any means necessary. USES. - Lettuce is an excellent vegetable, much appreciated on all tables. It is used either cooked in fat or raw in salads. ROMAINE LETTUCE CULTIVATION. - Romaine lettuces, which have a different shape to ordinary lettuces, can be grown in the same way. VARIETIES. - They are classified into winter, spring and summer varieties. 1° Winter romaine lettuces. - Sow not too thickly, in August-September, in a well-smoked bed. When strong enough, they are planted in good, recently ploughed, smoked soil and watered immediately. The last plantings should be done in the first fortnight of November, no later. Green winter romaine lettuce. - Very old variety, good head, not very sensitive to cold, black seed. Winter green Romaine. - Fairly hardy variety; medium-sized head, fairly tight, black seed. Winter red Romaine. - Very hardy, high, fairly large, tight head, very slow to bolt, black seed. 2° Spring romaine lettuces. - Balloon romaine lettuce. - Very bulky variety, strong, tight, white head, black seed. Blonde romaine lettuce. - A very old variety, grown just about everywhere, hardy, adaptable to all temperate climates, as long as it has plenty of water in summer. Early, it can be grown under frames or cloches, white seed. Lettuce verte maraîchère. - A very old variety, excellent, not very tight and white, hardy, white seed. Romaine grise maraichère. - Highly esteemed by growers around Paris for early vegetables, medium size, apples well. Slow-growing blond lettuce. - A new, little-known variety, it bolts very late, with black seeds. Trianon early blond romaine lettuce. - New variety, large, very full head, white seed. Early flat romaine lettuce. - New, very good for cultivation under cloches, white seed. Potato lettuce. - Very small, black seed. 3° Summer romaine lettuces. - These varieties are more resistant to summer heat, but can be sown in spring, just as spring varieties can be sown at this time. They can be sown from the second half of May to July. Among the best varieties are Alphange romaine lettuce. - Black and white seeds, two varieties with little distinction. English brown romaine lettuce. - White and black seeds. Perfected variegated or blood lettuce. - Flagellated with reddish spots; very tender. SEEDS. - Seeds are harvested in the same way as head lettuces. USES. - Same uses. LAVENDER Lavandula Spica D. C. Labiatae. Indigenous, perennial, this plant reproduces by separating clumps and taking cuttings in autumn and spring; can be propagated by sowing. Used as a condiment in sauces. LENTILLE Ervum Lens L. Lens esculenta Mœnch. Leguminosae. ORIGIN. - Native annual. COOKING. - The lentil (fig. 36) is a plant of great FIO. 86. - Lentil. cultivation, it is rarely grown in gardens. It prefers a soft, light soil, which is where it produces the most and at the same time where the grains are the hottest. This legume is very easy to grow. It is sown in March, in rows or bunches. Weed when necessary. It requires no further care until harvesting, which takes place towards the end of August, beginning of September. SEEDS. - To preserve lentils well for sowing, it's best to leave them in their pods until it's time to sow them. They keep well for four years. VARIETIES. - Lentille large blonde or lentille de Lorraine. - Green Puy lentil. - March lentil. - Winter lentil. Common lentil, a variety grown extensively in Eastern Europe and Germany. lentils, pests. - Lentils are sometimes affected by bruchids, a small beetle whose larvae develop in the grain, partially gnawing it, and then dying. Lentils, ravaged by this insect, are unpalatable and harmful to health. Many remedies have been tried to prevent the bruchid from depositing its eggs, but none has worked. As a result, lentil cultivation has been abandoned in many parts of northern France, where the insect is rampant. USES. - Same uses as beans. Valerianella olitoria Mœnch. Valeriana Locusta L. Valerianae. ORIGIN. - Indigenous annual herbaceous plant, known locally as Boursette, Blanquette, Clairette, Poule grasse, Barbe de chanoine, Coquille, Pommette, Laitue de brebis, Orillette, etc. CULTIVATION. - Lamb's lettuce is not very difficult to grow in any type of soil. However, it seems to do best in light, well-smoked soils. They are sown from August to October, broadcast, in beds, alone or among other crops such as turnips or radishes. Sow fairly thickly, covering sparingly; the most important thing is to tread the soil sufficiently after sowing. Other cultivation care consists of weeding, in order to remove the weeds that invade. FIG. 37. - Round-leaf lamb's lettuce. VAbieTes. - Round-leaf lamb's lettuce (fig. 37). - A very good, hardy, tender variety, highly esteemed on the markets, especially in Paris, where market gardeners grow it almost exclusively. Mâche verte d'Etampes. - Very good variety, forming a rosette of tight leaves, tender, withstands cold well. Mâche verte à cœur plein. - Tight, firm rosette, short, intense green leaves, very good variety, less hardy than the preceding ones. Large-seeded Dutch lamb's lettuce. - Hardy, productive variety, comes very large and very good for northern countries. Italian or Regency Lamb's lettuce (Valerianella eriocarpa Desv.). - Distinct from common lamb's lettuce in that it is blonder in all its parts, and in the length of its foliage. Rosette, fairly full, tender and tasty, it is especially suited to the Midi. Italian lamb's lettuce. - A variety derived from the previous one, with broader, rosette-shaped leaves, very strong and full. Mâche de Lyon. - A good new variety, highly regarded at Lyon markets, with broad, spoon-shaped leaves. Mâche à feuilles panachées. - Variety with variegated or marbled yellow or white leaves; not very productive, it seems destined to disappear from cultivation. SEEDS. - Seeds are harvested from seedlings sown in October. They generally ripen in June. As soon as they are ripe, the seeds detach easily; it is therefore necessary to pick the uprights before they are fully ripe, and lay them out on cloths in the shade, where they will complete their drying, then simply beat them with a stick to detach the seeds. Some seeds always fall to the ground. In this case, once the seed carriers have been removed, we recommend sweeping the surface of the soil, removing the largest clumps of earth and immersing the whole lot in a tub of water. The seeds float to the surface, where they are collected and dried in the shade. They keep well for four years. For seedlings, it's best to choose seeds that are two or three years old; they germinate better and faster than those from the previous year. DISEASES, PESTS. - In naturally damp winter soils, lamb's lettuce sometimes suffers from uredo or rust; excess humidity can also cause yellowing, but there's no need to worry too much about these diseases, which are rare. Slugs are very keen on young seedlings, which they would devour completely if we weren't careful. Ashes, soot, quicklime or hydraulic lime thrown on the seedlings will keep them away or kill them. USES. - Lamb's lettuce is used especially in salads. SWEET CORN Zea Mays L. Grasses. ORIGIN. - Corn was imported from America to Europe around the middle of the sixteenth century. An annual plant, it is known locally as Turkish wheat, Spanish wheat, Barbary wheat, Garouille (in the Charentes region), Indian wheat, etc. CULTIVATION. - Corn is sown in place, in April-May, in well-smoked soil. It is laid out in rows 50 centimeters apart, and at the same distance along the row; during the summer, it is hoeed and weeded several times, and it is customary to bring back the soil a little around each plant, in the form of a mound, to prevent the roots from being affected by excessive drought. Many growers, in order not to lose ground and at the same time to guarantee it, sow a tuft of dwarf beans between each corn plant. This is an excellent method. VARIETIES. - Early dwarf sweet corn. - Very good dwarf species, not exceeding 70 centimeters, white grain, very sweet. Sweet corn, wrinkled, evergreen. - Late and fairly tall. Vigorous, very tender ears. There are still a dozen varieties of sweet corn, highly esteemed in the United States, where this vegetable is in honor. In France, they are rarely grown. Varieties cultivated in large-scale farming, although less sweet than the above-mentioned breed, can nevertheless be used for the same purposes. SEEDS. - To obtain good sweet corn seeds, select a few vigorous plants, and keep their first fruits. When they are ripe, in September, or even earlier depending on the region, they are harvested, then their husks are removed by turning them towards the base of the cob. In this state, they are exposed to the air and sun, where they ripen completely. The seed keeps for two years. DISEASES. - The only disease we know of is ergot, which develops on the ears of corn. There is no remedy, but affected ears must be removed, as it is a poison. USES. - Sweet corn is widely used in the United States, where it is served on every table. The young cob is used, when the kernels are still in their milky state, just as beans are used in France. The whole ear is also used when it is just formed. In France, the main use is to pick the ears very young and pickle them in vinegar like gherkins. In this state, they make an excellent condiment. MARJOLAINE VIVACE Origanum vulgare L. Labiatae. A native perennial that can be propagated in the same way as thyme. It has the same uses. WHITE MARRUB Marrubium vulgare L. Labiatae. Indigenous, perennial, sown in the spring. It can also be propagated by dividing clumps. The leaves are used as a condiment. MARTYNIA Martynia lutea Lindl. Sesame. From Brazil, annual, this plant requires a lot of E. BERGER, Vegetable plants. 18 heat to develop. Sow on a bed in March; plant in the open ground along a wall facing south in May. The oddly shaped fruit can be pickled in vinegar like gherkins. CURWOOD Malva crispa L. Malvaceae. Annual, from the East. Sow in a nursery in April, preferably on a bed; transplant when plants are about 8 cm high. The leaves are used to garnish desserts. Melissa officinalis L. Labiatae Perennial plant of southern Europe. Reproduces by dividing clumps in spring. During winter, it must be covered with litter or long manure, especially in northern regions. The leaves are used as a condiment and in the preparation of liqueurs. MELON Cucumis Melo L. Cucurbitaceae. ORIGIN. - Annual plant, native to tropical Asia, cultivated since time immemorial. The cantaloupe melon (cantalupo) was imported from Italy to France by Charles VIII in 1405. EARLY CROPS. - Growing early melons is much easier than you might think. Here's the one that has always worked for us, and which is the most practical. In January, prepare a good thick layer of horse manure and oak leaves; place the trunk and fill with 12 or 15 centimeters of soil mixed with free-range earth. The fires are allowed to burn through the layer, which takes three or four days, then the seed is sown in rows 95 centimetres apart, the seed is covered, and the straw mats are spread over the panels and maintained until emergence, which takes thirty-six or forty hours. During the day, we remove the mats, weather permitting, wipe off any mist, give the plants some air if the sun appears, and shade them. When the young plants are strong enough, i.e. when the first two leaves begin to appear, they are transplanted into 10-centimeter pots, planted up to the cotyledons, and at a rate of two plants per pot, face to face close to the sides; once this is done, the pots are watered and buried in a new layer, where good warmers have been set up to the height of the trunk. When the young melons have grown sufficiently, they are topped above the first two leaves. This pinching, which constitutes the first pruning, encourages the two branches to emerge from the axils of each leaf. Once they have reached this stage of development, the melons must be placed in their final position. In a layer prepared as described above, and this time filled with 14 or 15 centimetres of potting soil, two or four plants are planted in the middle of the trunk, depending on the species. Water lightly, then cover with panels, keeping a close eye on the mould that is bound to grow inside the trunks. Also, when the sun comes out, air is gradually supplied and warmers are set up, often needing to be reworked to maintain their warmth; pruning must not be neglected either, and must be carried out in good time. Towards the end of April, give the plants plenty of air and lightly baste them. Cover with mats every evening until this time, to prevent chilling. In May, the melons begin to ripen, and successively until mid-June or even later, if sown a few days apart. The best varieties for this type of cultivation, and at the same time those whose fruit is best appreciated, are: the cantaloup Prescott petit hâtif; the cantaloup noir des Carmes; the cantaloup de Bellegarde, etc. There is no need to grow other varieties. HATÉE OR SEASONAL CULTIVATION. - Parisian market gardeners, who excel in melon cultivation, have adopted a system they call culture de saison (seasonal cultivation), but which in reality is nothing more than hasty cultivation. Towards the end of March, beginning of April, a good bed is prepared for sowing, in the same way as indicated above. Once the seedlings are sufficiently developed, they are transplanted into 9-centimetre pots, which are then buried on the bed, or transplanted directly onto the bed at a distance of 10 centimetres in all directions. In May, prepare a series of layers, one in front of the other, in a vegetable patch where the previous year's fertilization had been imperfect; place the trunks in them and fill them with 15 centimetres of the best soil in the patch, levelling it as best you can. Three days after this operation, the melons are planted, either in clods, if they have been transplanted onto the bed, or in pots. When the plants are well established, and even when they have grown sufficiently, temperature permitting, the panels are removed and cultivation takes place in the open air. CULTIVATION UNDER CLOCHES. - Melons are sown at the same time as above. Around May 15, in the North, or earlier if the region is temperate, trenches 50 or 60 centimetres wide and 35 centimetres deep are prepared, filled with warm manure at least 50 centimetres thick and then loaded with the best loose soil, producing a sufficiently rounded bed. Rake well to even out the top and plant 1 metre apart along the line. Immediately after planting, cover the melons with cloches and wrap them in litter or heather for a few days to help the plant take root. As soon as the melons have picked up and are beginning to vegetate, the cloches are lifted to give them a little air, gradually increasing until they are removed, i.e. when the branches can no longer fit under the cloches. In many cases, growers keep the cloches up for a few days, supporting them with three racks placed in a triangle. In this way, it is said, the plants benefit from a greater amount of heat than in the open air. However, around June 10, they can be removed. Other cultivation care is the same as for plants grown without panels. Water sufficiently, but not excessively. These cultivation methods apply to temperate regions and the north of France. In the Midi, Centre and South-West, they are not applied in the same way. GROWING ON TEENS. - Growing on teens is the most common method, and the best for full soil. Once the soil has been ploughed with a spade, lines are drawn with a chalk line, 1.40 m apart. The ends are marked with stakes; once this is done, a 40-centimeter trench is opened with the spade, i.e. 20 centimeters are taken from each side of the line, to a depth of 35 to 40 centimeters. The soil from the trenches is discarded to the right and left. The trenches are then filled with good horse manure, well moistened with urine, 18. tamped down by trampling on it several times, then covered with soil, preferably the best. A rake is passed over the whole, which should form a bulging part in the middle, the axis of which should be the line originally traced, which is re-established by placing the string in the holes of the stakes left for this purpose at the start of the operation. Once the melons have been sown or transplanted into pots, towards the end of April or May, they are planted in pairs, 1 or 1.20 m apart on the line. When planting, form a good basin around them for watering, and cover with cloches or small glazed wooden squares specially designed for this purpose, much used in the South-West. Other care consists of watering, pinching and light hoeing around the plants. CULTIVATION IN THE GROUND. - Open-ground cultivation is very easy, and is the practice in the South of France: Toulouse, Avignon, Arles, Mont- pellier, Perpignan, Narbonne, etc. In Tours, Angers and Nantes, this type of cultivation is practiced, but only on limited areas. Farmers in Gironde and Lot-et-Garonne grow it among vines and in open fields. In the first few days of May, the ground where the melons are to be planted is thoroughly hoeed, then round holes 40 to 50 centimetres in diameter are dug, 40 centimetres deep at 1.50 or 2 metres apart. Fill them with still-warm horse manure, tamp it down and mound the soil, forming a kind of funnel at the top, then sow. Place four or five seeds per hole and water lightly with an apple. When the melons have sprouted, select three of the most beautiful and uproot the others; then spread a light mulch around them; all that remains is to prune them. In general, growers only topped the plants and then left them to grow wild; despite this, we have seen some really beautiful products, but they need the sun of the Midi. The best varieties for this type of cultivation are the maraicher melon, the Cavaillon melon, the sucrin de Tours melon and the green melon, etc. PRUNING MELONS. - There are two main pruning systems advocated by melon growers, and they apply to all varieties and all crops. First system. First pruning. - When the stem is sufficiently developed, it is pinched above the first two leaves, giving rise to two lateral branches in the axils of each leaf. While performing this first pinch, remove the two buds that begin to appear under the cotyledons. Second pruning. - As the two lateral branches mentioned above have sufficiently developed their third leaf, they are pruned above the second, giving rise to four new branches.
