As for yield, this varies enormously from year to year, and can be estimated at between 18 and 30 hectolitres per hectare. When you want to produce seed, it's a good idea to make prior arrangements with the company that is to buy it, which will supply the seed needed to make the plant and will usually reserve the right to inspect the plantation and reform any plants that don't seem to correspond to the variety grown. BRUSSELS KALE Two slightly different types of this cabbage breed are grown: the ordinary Brussels sprout and the dwarf Brussels sprout. The first of these two types (fig. 39), which is by far the most widespread in cultivation, is a vigorous plant bearing long-stalked leaves on a stem up to a meter high, with a spoon-shaped blade. These leaves come together at the top of the stem to form a kind of poorly formed apple. In the axils of all stem petioles, buds form small apples the size of walnuts. In this variety, these apples are tightly packed and very well formed. In the dwarf variety, instead of being smooth, the leaves are slightly blistered and very close together on the stem, which acquires smaller proportions than in the previous variety. As a result of the close-knit leaves, the small apples are tightly packed together; they are, moreover, less well formed than in ordinary Brussels sprouts and therefore less prized for sale. Uses. - We eat the lateral buds or small apples, which must be firm and have the average volume of a small walnut. Cultivation. - This cabbage is sown at two different times. The first in February or March, and the second in March or April, to prolong the harvest. Sowing is done in the nursery by broadcasting, taking the same care as indicated above; then, after four to six weeks, transplanting is done directly in situ. For this type of cultivation, in contrast to the other types, it is advisable to choose relatively thin soil, otherwise there is a high risk that the small apples will not form, but that the cabbage will grow all leafy, without producing the expected product. For this reason, this crop is much more successful in open fields than in gardens, where the soil is usually too rich. Brussel sprouts are planted at Om,60, in all directions, Fig. 39 - Ordinary brussel sprouts. and bound tightly. When the stem has reached about Om,50, the terminal bud is pinched off, to encourage the development of the lateral buds. We also hasten the development of the latter by cutting off the base leaves. This cabbage does not fear frost, so harvesting, which can start as early as October for the first sowings, lasts until March for second-season sowings. Yields vary greatly according to the soil in which the crop is grown, but are usually around 350 liters per acre. Seed crops. - As seed-bearing plants, we choose those with well-shaped, hard apples close together on the stem; we mark the plants early and do not harvest small apples from them. In April, we plant them at Om, 75, giving them a stake; we cut off the head of the cabbage if this operation has not been done previously and remove the small apples at the bottom, which are poorly made, as well as those at the top whose development is incomplete, leaving only those in the middle to flower. Harvesting care is the same as above. CHIOUX VERTS Varieties. - Non-pollinating cabbages have given rise to a considerable number of cultivated varieties, most of which we won't go into, since they are part of agricultural crops and are most often grown as fodder. We will only mention those varieties that are suitable for human consumption. CABBAGE WITH LARGE RIBS. - This cabbage is just starting to apple, and could be considered as the transition from cabbage to green cabbage. It is characterized by curly leaves with well-developed veins. It is grown in vegetable gardens because of its resistance to cold. MOEILLIER CABBAGE. - This variety, which reaches a height of 1.50 m when fully developed, has ample leaves which, like those of all its congeners, are sometimes used; but we mention it mainly for the reason that its stem bulges towards the middle, as a result of the development of its cellular tissue. In this way, it is the gateway to the cabbages whose stems we eat. Cultivation. - There is nothing special to say about the cultivation of these cabbages, which are grown in the same way as the previous ones. CHIOUX-RAVES Varieties. - Choux-Raves are characterized by the often very voluminous swelling of their stems above ground level. The varieties most commonly grown in vegetable gardens are the following two: WHITE HATIF KOHLRABI. - This variety has a small number of sparsely-developed leaves. The bulge forms quickly (fig. 40). HATIF VIOLET KOHLRABI. - This kohlrabi differs from the previous one in that its stem and leaf petioles are colored light purple. Uses. - The swollen stem is eaten cooked. The cellular tissue contained within has a pleasant taste; it is widely used throughout eastern France, particularly in Alsace. Cultivation. - Kohlrabi is sown in spring, from March to June, in good soil. When the plant has three or four leaves, it is transplanted in place, spaced Om, 25 apart in all directions. Water several times during vegetation, and two months or so after planting, these cabbages can be delivered for consumption. They can be kept for a long time, provided they are pulled up and taken down to the cellar. CHOUX-NAVETS Varieties. - Turnip cabbages, or Rutabagas, whose edible part is formed by the lower part of the stem, and by the root which has gorged itself with cellular tissue, vary from one another in the coloring of the leaves and stems. The most common variety grown in vegetable gardens is the following: WHITE, SMOOTH KOHLRABI. - The fleshy part is shorter than it is wide. The flesh is white (fig. 41). Uses. - Kohlrabi is eaten cooked and prepared in a variety of ways. Cultivation. - Kohlrabi can be sown either in rows Fig. 41 - White, smooth Kohlrabi, or broadcast in spring; after emergence, thin out to leave a space of Om, 40 between plants in all directions. During the summer, we water and hoe. Harvesting takes place in autumn and early winter. CAULIFLOWER Varieties. - Cauliflowers, in which the inflorescence has developed into a globular mass while still young, are classified as tender, semi-hard and hard cauliflowers, according to their greater or lesser hardiness and the time they require to reach full development. LNI9 A Fig. 42. - Lenormand short-stalked cauliflower. CAULIFLOWER SMALL, SALOMON. - This variety, which is still known as Chou-Fleur tendre de Paris, is early and is used particularly in forced cultivation; its head is not very large, but it is quite white and takes little time to form. LARGE CAULIFLOWER, SALOMON. - This demidure variety is more developed than the previous one, without however acquiring a very large volume; its head is tight and of good quality, CHOU-FLEUR LENORMAND A PIED COURT. - This is certainly the most widely grown variety. It is very well suited to growing in pleme terre, and its head develops well (fig. 42). PARIS HARD CAULIFLOWER. - This variety is characterized by the fact that its head, which is slow to form, remains hard and tight for a long time. This variety is mainly used for autumn produce grown in the open ground. Uses. - The inflorescence is cooked and eaten in a variety of ways. Field-grown. - Cauliflower production has become very widespread throughout France, but mainly in the vicinity of large cities. Near Paris, as we'll show later, this large-scale crop is generally very profitable. Cauliflowers like a permeable soil, but one that is not free from a certain coolness, especially when the crop is grown in summer. Soils in which silica is a dominant element are particularly suitable. They require abundant fertilization, using, if possible, fertilizers that have already decomposed and are in a state that allows them to be intimately mixed with the soil. City sludge and manure from the soil, either from early crops or from mushroom quarries, are the preferred fertilizers, which, as we can see, correspond to rapidly assimilable nitrogenous matter. Water is necessary for this crop, but in very variable proportions, depending on the environment in theDYRONSRI. - Vegetable growing. 13 in which it is grown. For example, while irrigation is necessary in the South of France and Algeria, in the climate of Paris this plant can do without watering. However, when watering is possible, it can only produce good results. In the Gennevilliers plain, for example, which is irrigated with sewage water, good results are obtained. In our Parisian climate, we generally grow three crops in the open air during the course of the year, so as to obtain, if not an absolutely consistent product throughout the summer, at least harvests that are very close together. It is therefore necessary to study these three different methods of cultivation, which we classify as spring, summer and autumn crops. Spring cultivation. - To grow cauliflowers in spring, they need to be sown in the autumn of the previous year. Market gardeners usually sow their seeds between September 15 and 20, in the open air on old potting soil, or simply in well loosened soil covered with compost. As soon as the seeds have been sown and covered with a little soil, they are lightly basked and watered repeatedly to keep the soil constantly moist. Seed emergence takes about ten days. If the year is cold, it's a good idea to follow the example of market gardeners, who cover their seedlings with cloches; but this precaution isn't essential and, as we've just said, you can simply sow in the open air. In any case, when the seedlings have grown two leaves in addition to their two cotyledons, it's time to transplant them. There are two ways to do this

One is to use cloches, the other is to transplant under frames; both give satisfactory results, so the choice will depend on the equipment available. To transplant under cloches, the soil is laid out in ados, i.e. in a sort of sloping plank on the south side, so that, starting from ground level, the highest side facing north is about Om, 20. The width of these ados is such that three rows of cloches can be laid out in staggered rows. In this way, a series of ados can be laid out, one behind the other. The soil used to build them must be of very good quality, and must be topped up and covered with potting soil. Once the "ados" have been built, a bell is placed on each of them to indicate where each one should be planted. Nineteen feet are planted per bell. When frames are used instead of bells, they are placed at a slight angle and the inside is lined with potting soil up to Om, 12 of the glass. Transplant at Om, 08 in all directions, equivalent to planting 200 per frame. After transplanting, water. Throughout the winter, care will consist of providing air whenever it doesn't freeze. If, on the other hand, the cold should become intense, not only should doormats be placed over the bells and frames, but the trunks of the latter should also be covered with a bundle of old manure or leaves, so as to prevent frost from penetrating through the boards. If it freezes during the day, the mats should remain on the windows for the duration of the cold, and when the thaw comes, the plants should not be made to pass through sudden transitions, i.e. air should only be uncovered and given gradually. Towards the end of March, we'll uproot the plants kept in trays and plant them out. Care should be taken to reform any plants that are blind, i.e. whose heart has been destroyed. If you want to plant early, choose a bed of earth sheltered by a wall; but you can also plant in a square, provided you get later-ripening plants. As we have said, the soil should be abundantly fertilized and well prepared by ploughing, if the land is free, as transplanting is often carried out in half-planted crops such as carrots or lettuce. Plant at about Om. 70 in all directions and in staggered rows; increase this distance if you have intercrops to manage. If the weather is dry, water again the following day. Watering should be continued throughout the vegetation period, as this crop is mainly grown in the vegetable garden, not in the fields. As soon as the intercrops have risen, we hoe them, cover the soil with mulch and water. Apples start to appear towards the end of April. As soon as they begin to free themselves from the surrounding leaves, they must be protected from the action of air and light, which would make them yellow, hard and unmarketable. They are protected by breaking off the lower leaves and placing them on this apple. Every two or three days, we go back between the rows and cover the apples with new leaves, always taken from the bottom of the plant. The fresh leaves are placed on top of the apple, and the wilted ones on top of these; this constitutes an absolute covering that will leave the apple white and tightly grained. Before the inflorescence branches begin to drop off, i.e. when the cauliflower is at its most valuable, it is harvested by cutting off the head and some of the central leaves that protect it. Harvesting begins towards the end of May for plants planted on a ridge, and continues through June for those grown in a square. Summer cultivation. - For this crop, which is the most difficult to grow, you need to sow seeds of semi-hard cauliflower on a bed under glass at the beginning of April. This sowing must be done fairly lightly, as the young plant will not be transplanted in the nursery. This would cause the apples to appear too early, and result in insufficient volume of produce. Once the seedling has emerged, the frame is lifted and the plant is gradually acclimatized to the outside air. About five weeks after sowing, the plant has taken on four or five leaves, and it's time to put it in place. A fresh, rich soil is absolutely essential; this planting will require frequent watering to give good results, so it should only be done in vegetable gardens where a large quantity of water is available. Transplant at Om, 80 in all directions, taking care to press the plant down to the first leaves. After sowing radishes, the soil is firmly bound and mulched. We can't stress enough that throughout the summer you must water heavily and often: market gardeners water every day; this is the only way to get good apples, which otherwise fall apart and don't produce anything. Care must be taken to ensure that the cauliflowers are well covered when the flower begins to show; the slightest ray of sunlight hitting them for just a few hours will damage them completely. Harvesting begins at the end of July and throughout August. As soon as the apples are good, they must be cut, otherwise they would deteriorate in a few days. In insufficiently watered crops, we have to put up with the ravages of flea beetles, which cause great damage and often destroy the entire crop. Autumn cultivation. - Autumn cultivation of cauliflower is one of the most widespread, for the dual reason that it requires relatively little care and yet gives assured results. Although it is grown by market gardeners and in vegetable gardens, it is mainly a large-scale crop. This type of production is recommended wherever the soil is rich and fresh, and where the expense of abundant manuring is not an obstacle. It is grown extensively in the Paris area, and to give an accurate idea, we can do no better than to describe the details of this cultivation as it is practiced in Chambourcy. The cultivation of this plant, to which other vegetables have gradually been added, has been the source of this locality's wealth. Chambourcy cultivation. - In this locality, where cauliflower production is one of the dominant crops, the soil admirably meets the requirements of the vegetable we are dealing with. Rich, moderately compact and cool even in summer, the soil slopes gently to the north. The plant we use comes from seedlings sown in May. The seeds are sown along a wall to protect them from the midday sun. Sowing is done in the open, as the plant will not be transplanted in the nursery, and care is taken to cover it with mulch so that it can be watered repeatedly without gullying or beating the soil. This daily watering is the best way to prevent flea beetles, which would otherwise wreak havoc. Sowing begins in May and continues until mid-June, to stagger the harvest. This result can be accentuated by using half-hard cauliflowers, then hard cauliflowers at the end of the season. Many growers don't grow the plants themselves, but buy them from market gardeners in Paris at 10 francs a thousand. The land to be planted must be abundantly smoked, as we said. At Chambourcy, slurry is used at a rate of 1 cubic meter per are; the price of this fertilizer delivered to the field is 6 francs per meter. The fertilizer is ploughed in well, followed by two harrows to make the soil perfectly loose. Following ploughing, planting takes place from June 15 to July 25. It is carried out with a planter, spacing the plants by Om, 80 in all directions. The recovery of this plant would be very poor if it were not watered, so growers do not fail to take this precaution. They carry the water on foot, using barrels placed on carts, and watering is done with a watering can without apples. Watering is done very sparingly; one lane of water is enough to water a hundred plants. If the weather's fine, the next day we repeat the operation, and that's all the water these plants will receive for the duration of their vegetation. This watering can be done fairly quickly, at no great expense, whatever the size of the crop. There are growers who plant no less than 60 or 80,000 cauliflowers, sometimes more, and who still do it, and it is estimated that two men, with a horse-drawn cart at their service, can wet a hectare's plantation in a single day. During vegetation, the soil needs to be hoeed twice, to loosen it and prevent it from drying out, while at the same time ridding it of weeds. In the past, these hoeings were done by hand, and were very expensive; today, they are done with a cheyal hoe, and it's easy to get them done for 12 to 15 francs. The hoe is passed between the rows, then a man completes the work using a hand hoe, in the immediate vicinity of the cauliflowers. When the apple appears, it is covered; a woman is employed for this work, who can easily oversee a hectare of cultivation. Harvesting begins in October, for semi-hard cauliflowers sown early, and lasts until late November. The timing and quality of this harvest varies enormously. In general, cauliflowers produce rather poor quality products if the summer is rainy, as they develop as soon as they are planted and without the plant having had time to develop an abundant root system. On the contrary, if dry weather prevails for a month or so after planting and after the seedling has taken root, the seedlings, far from suffering, take advantage of it, as the natural humidity of the soil is more than sufficient to multiply the foliage. If, after this drought, rainfall favors the development of the leaves, and a few days of mild weather in October help the apples to form, the harvest will take place in the best possible conditions, and the produce will fetch a very high price on the markets. As a result of this inevitable subordination of the value of this vegetable to the climatic conditions that govern its development, if its cultivation is remunerative even in average years, it can, in exceptionally favorable conditions, become very profitable. As we are fully aware of all cultivation costs, we can calculate the total as follows, for an area of one hectare: Soil rent............................ Manuring; 100 cubic meters at 6 fr........ When the season has been totally unsatisfactory, cauliflowers are sold for 15 francs per 100, but rarely less; if, on the other hand, everything has gone well, the price rises to 50 francs. Assuming a price of 30 francs, which is more or less the average, the gross revenue from 15,600 plants per hectare is 4,680 francs. Lowering the price to 25 francs would still yield 3900 francs, giving a net profit of 3460 francs in the first case, and 2680 francs in the second. As you can see, this is still a very respectable figure, which should encourage the grower to further extend this production, all work on which can be carried out using the tools at his disposal. Forced cultivation of cauliflower. - Only the earliest, most tender varieties of cauliflower are usually used for early crops. In this case, we use seedlings obtained by exactly the same procedure as that described above for spring cauliflowers, i.e. the seedling sown in September is transplanted into a nursery under a bell, or in a frame, where it is left until the time comes to plant it on a bed. Around New Year's Eve, we start building the beds that will receive the first cauliflower season. This layer is built with a mixture of annealed manure and new manure, to which leaves can also be added in varying proportions. This layer should be about Om, 50 high, to obtain 20 degrees of heat. Once the layer is built up, place the chests in which you will load Om 18 with compost. When the shot is fired, the cauliflower plant is carefully removed and planted by hand in the potting soil of the bed. Plant in two rows, two or three to a frame, depending on whether you're dealing with a variety with stronger or weaker development. As cauliflowers develop quite slowly in the early stages, the space left between the plants is usually used to grow either radishes or lettuce, or sometimes both at the same time. This is not a great disadvantage, as they will be harvested before the cauliflowers are fully developed. Cauliflower requires some watering as it grows. This crop should be given air whenever the weather permits. When the leaves have developed sufficiently to touch the glass, the boxes should be lifted with screw jacks, and the base secured with manure. Apples begin to form in April, and as soon as they appear, the same care as that described above for outdoor cultivation should be applied. Harvesting takes place towards the end of the same month. This harvest, provided by cultivation under a frame, can be prolonged by renewing the plantations, spacing them fortnightly, until they can be planted in the open air; in this way, sustained produce can be obtained throughout the spring. Market gardeners use the beds they build in November and December for growing lettuces, reworking them at the end of January or in February, and mixing a certain proportion of new manure with the old manure to bring back fermentation and produce renewed heat. In April, the carrots are harvested, and as the cauliflowers begin to touch the glass, the frames are removed, vegetation is completed in the open air, and the harvest takes place in May or June, depending on the variety and the time of planting. Growing for seed. - Producing cauliflower seed is not always a successful operation, which explains why it fetches such a high price on the market. Whatever the variety, cauliflowers for seed should always come from seedlings sown in September and kept in a greenhouse. When the apples appear in spring, choose the plants that will give the best results, i.e. those with a firm, tight texture. Avoid choosing apples that are mossy or have insufficient development. Once the selection has been made, only one leaf should be left on each apple to prevent it from hardening under the action of the sun; this leaf should be removed once the inflorescence has developed. Once flowering has taken place, it's a good idea to pinch off the tips of flowering shoots, to ensure the formation of the siliques placed at the base of the inflorescence. As soon as the fruits turn yellow, harvest them and leave them to mature under cover. Insects and parasites affecting cauliflowers are the same as those affecting cabbages and broccoli. BROCOLLI cabbages Broccolis are very similar to cauliflowers, but differ in a number of vegetative characteristics that make them easy to distinguish. They are grown as biennial plants, meaning that, sown in the course of one year, they only produce in the spring of the following Fig. 43 - Early white broccoli. year. Broccoli leaves are narrower and more numerous than those of Cauliflower; the petioles bearing them are usually bare for a long length. The stems are long, so that the apple is often more than 50 centimetres above the ground. The apples are fine-grained, white and of very good quality in the advanced varieties. Uses. - Same as for cauliflower. Varieties. - Broccoli varieties are relatively few in number; a few with colored apples are known, but the most sought-after are those with fine grain and which are as close as possible to our cauliflowers proper, whose ancestors, according to some authors, they are. WHITE BROCCOLI HATIF. - This variety vegetates quickly, with abundant leaves and very wavy edges. The apples are white and of good quality (fig. 43). ROSCOFF BROCCOLI. - Not very distinctive variety, grown mainly throughout Brittany, where it performs well in winter, supplying markets throughout the season. MAMMOTH BROCCOLI. - A late variety producing very good quality apples. Introduced to the market by English growers, it quickly spread to crops around Paris. Cultivation. - Broccoli cultivation has expanded considerably in recent years. Indeed, it has the great advantage of being able to supply produce when cauliflower is in short supply; it supplies the big city markets throughout the winter and part of the spring. Considerable quantities are sold at the Paris market halls; Aveyron, Poitou and a large part of Brittany supply this consumption in the big cities. Produce from the Paris region only arrives later, succeeding that from the regions just mentioned. Cultivation in the Bay of Mont Saint-Michel. - The following information, which we owe to Mr. Lelasseux, a farmer in Saint-Broladre, relates to procedures followed throughout the temperate region of France, which provides winter supplies. Starting in April, an area of variable size is prepared by deep ploughing and harrowing with a rake, depending on the size of the crop, and on the basis that one hectare needs to be sown in order to plant one hectare. Once the soil has been prepared, the seed is broadcast at a rate of 5 kilograms per are. Immediately afterwards, the seed is raked in and, if possible, covered with a light mulch. Watering is usually unnecessary, as germination is easy thanks to the natural humidity of the soil at this time of year. By May, plants with three to four leaves are ready for planting. The soil for this crop must be rich and loose, but it is useful if the richness does not come from fresh fertilizers, but from manuring done the previous year. Fresh fertilizers, especially those coming from cowsheds, would have the serious disadvantage of making Broccoli grow in leaves, while the apple would only take on a small volume. The soil is made loose by double ploughing followed by harrowing. Broccoli is planted in rows, using a planter, with a strong border. It is advisable to leave one meter between the rows on which the Broccolis are planted at Om, 60, thus obtaining a plantation of about 15,000 plants per hectare. During the vegetation period, two or three hoeing operations are necessary; these can be carried out using a horse hoe, which simplifies the operation and reduces its cost. In autumn, it's a good idea to use the spade to bring the soil down to the base of the Broccoli, to protect it from frost. In November, the apples start to appear. To keep them very white, we cover them with leaves taken from the base, as we said when talking about Cauliflower; but here this operation is less essential, for the reason that Broccoli, being amply covered with leaves, and the sun rarely appearing at the time when the apples are forming, they run little risk of yellowing. However, by covering them, we obtain more beautiful and therefore more saleable products. Harvesting begins as early as December, in any case before the seeds have spread. The apples are snipped, leaving a sufficient number of leaves to wrap them, which facilitates packing; this is done by placing the Broccolis in a sort of large open-worked cages, about Im, 20 square, which are covered with straw held in place by strings. Selling prices vary according to the beauty of the produce, and also according to the year; they range from 10 to 25 francs per hundred. Growing around Paris. - In this region, seedlings are sown in the second half of April. To hasten vegetation, it's a good idea to sow the seeds either on an old bed, or in a northern exposure, in garden soil, which is covered with compost. The seeds are buried with a rake, and the soil mulched after being lightly trodden. As soon as the plant has produced three leaves, not including cotyledons, it is transplanted into the nursery, in troughs spaced Om, 15 cm apart. Care must be taken to press the plant down to the first leaves, and to water after transplanting. Planting out, which usually takes place in June, is done by removing the rootball plant with a spade and replanting it in a square at a distance of Om, 80 in all directions. The soil should be rich in decomposed fertilizers such as old topsoil. During the autumn, the soil is hoeed several times, taking care to bring the soil back onto the plant, to make a light ridge. Broccoli plantings are often intercropped. To protect the plants, not from the cold, to which they are not very sensitive, when these do not exceed about 8 degrees below zero, but rather to avoid the sudden alternations of freezing and thawing, it is customary in November to spade a hole next to each plant, on the north side. Pressing down on the plant, we then incline it in this sort of small pit, and if very heavy frosts occur, we throw a layer of long litter over the plant, enough to shelter it from the frosts. This is how growers in the Oise region do it. We have grown Broccoli in the Paris climate, in DYBOWSRI. - Vegetable growing. 14 by planting them in troughs to a depth of about Om, 15. A little leaf sprinkling in the troughs goes a long way towards protecting the plants from frost. The buds appear in March and April. It is a good idea to cover them and harvest them as soon as they have reached full development, otherwise they will quickly lose their value. Insect pests and parasites. - All cabbages have numerous enemies, which attack the various organs of the plant. From a young age, and often as soon as the two cotyledons appear, cabbages and cauliflowers are often attacked, especially in dry, south-facing soils, by a beetle called Altica brassicer, known in gardens as the tiquet or earth flea. This insect often wreaks such havoc that part or even all of the young plant may perish. Preventive treatment consists in sowing in summer, especially with a northern exposure, and keeping the soil moist by frequent watering, which benefits the cabbage. Curative treatment, on the other hand, involves spreading fresh horse manure, or soot, wood ash or sawdust, soaked in heavy oil. Later, the cutworm or larye of the harvest moth (Agrostis segetum) gnaws at the roots of young cabbages; there's no other way to get rid of it than to look for it and crush it. The Cabbage White (Pieris brassteæ) and the Cabbage Moth (Hadina brassicæ) lay eggs on cabbages, giving rise to larvae whose ravages are very fearsome. In some years, the entire leaf parenchyma is completely devoured by these caterpillars, which also attack cauliflower apples, sometimes so badly damaged that they cannot be eaten. If the number of caterpillars is small, the best thing to do is to collect them by hand; this is what the market gardeners and growers of Chambourcy do. If, on the other hand, their numbers are very large, a good method is to syringe them with water, in which carbon sulfide is emulsified at a rate of around 10%. Cabbages, particularly cauliflower and broccoli, are attacked by a parasitic fungus that manifests itself as a sort of white efflorescence, which practitioners call white, mennter or plaster. This fungus, which goes by the name of Cystopus candidus, is unfortunately impossible to combat, because it lives inside the plant's tissues. It manifests itself externally when cabbages and cauliflowers are going to seed; it also wreaks havoc on seedbeds, often absolutely destroying inflorescences. Plants affected by this disease must be burned to destroy the germs. This plant, to which Linnaeus gave the Latin name Cucumis sativus, seems, as de Candolle predicted and as herbal botanists have confirmed, to have originated in north-west India. It grows abundantly and spontaneously at the foot of the Himalayas. It does not appear there with all the vegetative characteristics we know, but the age of its cultivation, which was already known to the Greeks and Romans, may well have modified them. There's every reason to believe that the cucumbers found in the Himalayas, although referred to by some botanists under different names, are closely related to our own Cucumis satieus, whose ancestors they are. The Cucumber is an annual plant whose recumbent stems bear alternate, large, palmate leaves, cordate at the base and forming five rounded lobes, sometimes toothed. These stems bear tendrils, which are the terminations of aborted axes. The inflorescence is monoecious. Male flowers appear first. After fertilization, the ovary develops into a fruit of variable length, size and color. These fruits are sometimes smooth, sometimes covered with a kind of small protuberance ending in prickles, which are found on all plant organs. The seeds are inside the fruit, embedded in a kind of pulp that is the result of the disintegrated placentas. These seeds look a little like a pear seed; they are white. They retain their germinative capacity for seven to eight years. Uses. - Cucumbers are used in a wide variety of culinary preparations. They are eaten cooked and stuffed, or raw in salads when fully developed. They are often eaten when only half-developed. They can be marinated either in vinegar, which is what gherkins are made of, or in water with aromatic herbs, as is common practice in northern Europe. Varieties. - Cucumbers have been cultivated for a very long time, so their fruit shapes and sizes have varied greatly. In practice, they are divided into two classes, some with white fruit, others that remain green. BONNEUIL WHITE CUCUMBER. - Large fruit, swollen in the middle. The plant that bears them is hardy and very well suited to outdoor cultivation (fig. 44). HATIF WHITE CUCUMBER. - Differs from the preceding cucumber only in that its fruit is long and cylindrical rather than bulging. Green when young, turning white as it develops. GREEN GHERKIN CUCUMBER. - Fruit covered with warts, green, becoming yellowish when ripe. This highly fertile variety is specially cultivated for harvesting as soon as the fruit reaches finger size and length. ROLLINSON GREEN CUCUMBER. - Very long, stalkless green fruit with longitudinal grooves. Clearly distinguishable from previous varieties in that it is strangled near the stalk into a 6 Fig. 44. - White cucumber Fig. 45. - Green cucumber. de Bonneuil. Rollinson. sort of narrow neck (fig. 45). It is particularly suited to forced cultivation, for which it is almost exclusively used. Open-ground cultivation. - Cucumbers multiply by means of the seed, which always germinates with the greatest ease. The varieties most commonly used for outdoor cultivation are the green gherkin cucumber and the early white cucumber. Although hardy, cucumbers are very sensitive to frost, and a drop in temperature to zero is enough to kill them. For this reason, seedlings can only be sown late, or shelters must be used to protect them until the time when white frosts are no longer feared, which in our climate is the second half of May. Given the need to avoid a drop in temperature, there are two possible methods: one involves sowing in situ and sheltering the young plant under cloches, the other involves sowing in a frame and replanting in situ. On-site sowing is done by opening trenches in the soil, Om, 10 deep and Om, 50 wide, which Ton fills either with manure from old layers, or with leaves, and then covers with the soil removed from the trench. The length of these trenches varies according to the size of the crop. Between each trench, leave about 1.20 m. Once the soil has been prepared, sow cucumber seedpots in the middle of the trench, Om.60 apart, place five or six seeds and cover them with a bell. When emergence has occurred, leave two or three plants under each bell, and pull out the others, which can be used to make a new plantation. As soon as the seedling takes its first leaves, it should be given some air to gradually get used to its action, so that the cloches can be removed at the beginning of June. If sowing under a frame, this should be done in the first few days of May on a warm bed. When the plant has two cotyledons, it is transplanted one by one into cups of Om, 10, and placed in a terrau prepared as above, towards the end of May. In the Midi region, seed is simply sown in a square, without the use of trenches or bells. Whichever method is used, once the plant has two leaves, it is pruned to encourage rapid branching. After this initial pruning, the plant is usually left to its own devices. Fruits appear at the end of June; we leave whatever the plant is willing to produce if these fruits are destined for making gherkins, in which case they are harvested as soon as they are the size of a finger. Harvesting should take place every two days. If, on the other hand, you want large cucumbers, you should leave only about ten per plant. In dry soils, cucumbers should be watered frequently; in cool soils, on the other hand, water should only be given if the drought becomes persistent. Gherkins, which are produced in large quantities around Massy, Palaiseau and Verrières, are sold by weight at the Halles. The price is usually O fr. 30 to O fr. 50 per kilogram. As for cucumbers, they are sold by the dozen, and their price varies greatly according to the season and the development they have acquired. In Paris, white cucumbers are sold by the dozen for between 2 fr. 50 and 3 francs during the summer. For seed, we choose the best-formed fruit and let it mature on the vine. When the fruit is judged to be completely ripe, which can be recognized by its lighter color, we open it and remove the seeds inside. Wash with plenty of water, then dry in the shade. Cucumber cultivation is very successful throughout the intertropical zone, making it a valuable resource for vegetable growing in our colonies in this region. Here, seedlings are sown in situ, without the use of soil or compost. Cultivation on a bed. - Paris market gardeners frequently grow cucumbers as early crops. They have succeeded in perfecting their cultivation methods to such an extent that their produce appears at the halles in the early months of the year. We owe the following information to M. Curé, one of the most expert market gardeners in this type of cultivation. Sowing begins in the first fortnight of December. The seeds are sown on a very hot bed equipped with heaters; one by one, they are pushed into the soil with the tip of the finger. Emergence takes place after a few days, and as soon as the two cotyledons are fully developed and the first leaf begins to appear, the plant is transplanted. For this purpose, Om10 diameter cups are placed on a new bed, at a rate of 100 per frame. In the middle of each of these cups, placed on the layer and filled with potting soil, we transplant a cucumber seedling using a finger or a planter, taking care to press it in up to the cotyledons. Water lightly, then close the trays and cover with straw mats overnight. If it freezes very hard, it's often necessary to leave the mats on for part or all of the day. But it's important to remember that this occlusion is detrimental to young plants, which quickly wither, so avoid prolonging it. As soon as the young plant has two well-developed leaves, the stem above them is cut. As a result, the buds in the axils of the two leaves develop into two shoots, and the plant is ready for planting. Before this happens, if winter is severe, it is often useful during the vegetation period either to reshuffle the layer's warmers, or even to build a new layer on which the seedlings or cups are transported. A month and a half after sowing, the seedling is ready for planting. A new, warm layer is prepared and filled with potting soil, half-mixed with garden soil. As the layer warms up, a longitudinal line is drawn across the potting soil, dividing its height in two. The young cucumber plants are planted along this line. Two or three are placed per panel; this is done by removing the cups and pushing the seedlings down to the cotyledons. When recovery is assured and the two branches - the result of pruning - begin to elongate, cover the soil with a light mulch and maintain adequate humidity with watering. As the two branches lengthen rapidly, they are directed so that one moves towards the top of the frame, the other towards the bottom. These two branches are not allowed to elongate indefinitely, and are pruned above the fourth or fifth leaf. The result of this operation is the production of as many new branches as leaves have been left. Each of these new productions will bear, in the axil of each leaf, flowers, some of which will be male, others female, and it is not uncommon for there to be several female flowers in the axil of each leaf, giving rise to as many young cucumbers. From then on, pruning consists of pinching off each extension as soon as it has a single leaf. Pruning in this early crop can therefore be summarized as follows: first pruning to two leaves, then pruning to four leaves, and finally repeated pruning to one leaf. As soon as the fruits appear, they are, as we've just said, often grouped in pairs in the leaf axils. Immediately after flowering, the best one is chosen to cut off the second. This leaves three or four, then a few more, so that each plant produces a total of eight or ten fruits throughout its life. Fertilization of the female flowers is not usually a concern, as it takes care of itself; however, in early cultivation, it is sometimes useful to transport the pollen with a brush. When the fruits begin to grow, we help them to develop by placing each one in a lamp glass, which has the advantage of making them grow straight and giving them uniform coloring. The 1 green varieties are the only ones used for this early crop. For very early production, the Rollinson variety is generally used, but the market gardeners of Paris prefer to use it in their bedding crops for a breed they have bred themselves, which is similar to the Green Gherkin Cucumber. Each time the fruit is harvested, which takes place a fortnight or so after the flower that produced it has bloomed, all the leaves that are beginning to turn a little yellow are removed, to make room for the new leaves, which are carefully not crumpled or foxed. The old leaves are set aside and used for packaging. These cucumbers are sold by the dozen: they are wrapped six at a time, first in a few leaves, then in white paper, so that only the ends are visible. At the beginning of the season, these fruits sell for up to 20 and 25 francs a dozen, but the price drops rapidly to just 3 to 6 francs in May. There is a large export trade in the first fruits to the capitals of northern Europe, particularly St. Petersburg. Enemies. - Cucumbers are often attacked by aphids. This can be seen when the plants stop growing and the leaves wrinkle irregularly. This parasite can be eliminated with a few syringes of water in which dried tobacco leaves have been cooked. Cucumbers are also attacked by a parasite to which practitioners give the name "gray" because of its color, and which invades the leaves and stems with such intensity that the plant quickly perishes. No effective remedy is yet known, so in certain regions where this disease occurs abundantly, it is impossible to grow cucumbers in the open air, while those grown in frames are usually spared. Squashes, which for many years have been plunged into deep chaos, have now been neatly and precisely classified by M. Naudin. According to this author's remarkable work, all the diverse forms of squash found in gardens can be related to three main species: Cueurbita maxima Michaux, Cucurbita pepo Linné and Cucurbita moschata Michaux. It follows that all the countless so-called species that have been created over and over again should be considered as nothing more than varieties of the types we have just listed. Uses. - Despite being of different types, all gourds are used for the same purposes, which consist in their use in the preparation of either special dishes or various soups. However, their qualities differ greatly from one variety to another. The fleshy part of the pericarp is very poor in fibrous tissue, so the flesh disintegrates completely when cooked. These fruits contain mucilage, starch and sugar in their tissues, in highly variable proportions; the predominance of one or other of these substances results in different properties and uses. The sweetest of these fruits can be used to make a variety of jams. They are also used to make resins. Some of them, reduced to marmalades and flavored, make excellent jams whose color is reminiscent of that of apricots. Squash fruit is frequently used to adulterate commercial apricot pastes. In general, all gourds are not very delicate plants; they are grown in the same way, whatever their species. It is worth indicating the distinctive characteristics of each of the three species that have provided the varieties for our crops. I. - Cucurbita maxima. This species includes all varieties with very large fruits, and in particular all those commonly known as pumpkins. The vegetative characteristics of this species consist in the shape of the leaves, which are always large, kidney-shaped and with shallow margins; in the numerous hairs that cover all the organs of the plant; these hairs are not very hard and never take on the consistency of prickles. Fruit stalks are smooth and often swollen. The shape of the fruit varies markedly from one race to another, but in general the fruit is raised with more or less pronounced ribs, and more often than not its diameter exceeds its length. According to research carried out, M. de Candolle considers this species to have originated in the warmer parts of the Old World, from where Europeans brought it to America. In support of this opinion, we should mention the fact that the species was discovered in a spontaneous state in Guinea, on the banks of the Niger. Varieties. - There are a considerable number of varieties of this species, differing in color, shape and size. The most widely cultivated are POTIRON GRIS DE BOULOGNE. - A vigorous variety whose very large fruit often reaches almost a meter in size ( Fig. 46. - Bright red pumpkin from Étampes. diameter. Its name comes from the fact that the rind is covered with embroidery, giving it a gray appearance. The flesh is mealy, yellow and very thick. It keeps well. POTIRON ROUGE VIF D'ÉTAMPES. - Fruit with large ribs and smooth, bright orange-red skin. Average size, usually not reaching that of the previous variety (fig. 46).
