This variety is highly prized at the market. GIRAUMON SQUASH. - This variety, whose fruit is relatively small, has a very distinctive shape due to Fig. 47 - Giraumon squash. the hypertrphia of the fruit's eye. The flesh is of good quality (fig. 47). II. - Cucurbita Pepo. This species, which seems to have originated in America, is distinguished from the previous one by a number of characteristics derived from the organs of vegetation, which are found in the innumerable varieties found in cultivation. The leaves are lobed, sometimes even fidate, and bear numerous indentations; they are covered with epidermal productions that often become hard and form true prickles found on petioles and stems. DYBOWSKI. - Culture, 2nd ed. 15 Fruits are usually longer than they are wide, with the exception of a few irregular-fruited varieties in which the diameter exceeds the height of the fruit in length. Fruit rind is generally hard, which increases shelf life. Varieties. - These are very numerous, but only a small number are commonly grown; among the main ones, we should mention: COURGE DES PATAGONS. - A vigorous, hardy variety, producing cylindrical fruit up to Om.50 long by Om.20 in diameter, with five longitudinal ribs, forming rounded, protruding cords on the surface. Very dark green in color. The yellow flesh is of average quality and keeps for a long timeFig. 48. - Pa- temps squash (fig. 48). tagons. TOURAINE PUMPKIN SQUASH. - A variety with very large fruit, generally considered to be a forage crop. ITALIAN LONG SQUASH. - Non-running plant, whose very short stem forms a large tuft of leaves on the spot. Fruits long Om, 60 by Om, 10 in diameter. Flesh not very abundant. This variety is mainly cultivated to harvest the young fruit, the size of a small cucumber, which is eaten stuffed like eggplant. MARROW GOURD. - Cultivated for the same uses as the previous variety, particularly in England. The fruit is similar in shape to the Patagonian squash, but much smaller in size. Two sub-varieties are widely cultivated in England, one with a white rind, the other with green mottling. III. - Cucurbita moschata. Although not absolutely certain, this species is thought to originate in the Far East. The reason for this is that, of the many varieties of squash whose seeds we received from Japan, all those representing races formerly cultivated in the country were related to this species. The stems of this species are usually elongated. The rounded-lobed leaves have white spots in many varieties. The fruits, with very good-quality flesh, have a thin rind and poor keeping qualities. MELON-SHAPED SQUASH. - This variety, whose seeds first came to us from Japan in 1877, has fruits that absolutely resemble a strong, dark-green cantaloupe melon. The flesh is of excellent quality and is ideal for jams and pastes. COURGE PLEINE DE NAPLES. - A vigorous variety with vigorously developing stems. Fruits about 50 cm long, with the distinctive feature that the entire upper part, narrower than the tip, is completely full; the seed-bearing placentas are found only in the swollen part. This is a good variety, which unfortunately has the disadvantage of not always ripening well in the Paris climate, due to its late flowering. CARABACETTE SQUASH. - A new variety of excellent quality. Characterized by very long fruits with a diameter of Om.10 to Om.15. The fruits are full for most of their length. Flesh is orange-red, sweet and suitable for dishes and jams. Cultivation. - Squashes multiply exelusively by means of the seed, and, although these plants easily produce adventitious roots, this property is not used in practice to propagate by marcotting or cutting. Seed germination is always very easy, and we sometimes take advantage of this to sow seeds on the spot, but this is a defective procedure which has the double disadvantage of occupying the soil for too long and producing products which often mature only imperfectly. For these reasons, preference should be given to seedlings sown on a bed or under a frame. Until recently, squash was part of market garden production, but since pumpkins have fallen significantly in price as a result of the expansion of this crop, these plants have been abandoned by market gardeners, and today can only be found on the plains around large cities. Despite having passed through different hands, cultivation has remained as it was in the past. Seedlings must, as we have said, be sown under a frame; for this purpose, a warm layer is built up at the beginning of April, or an old layer that has already been used to grow other vegetables is used. Finger-sow the seeds in the bed, i.e. make a hole with your finger and place a single seed in it. These seeds are pricked out at about Om, 07 in all directions, sowing around 300 seeds per frame. Lightly basked, then covered with a frame, these seeds germinate rapidly. As soon as the young plants, in addition to two cotyledons, have shown a leaf, they should be transplanted. Transplanting must be done by hand, and the squash plant is replanted again under a frame, at a rate of one hundred plants per panel. Care must be taken when planting to press the young plants down to the level of the two cotyledons, which has the advantage of producing adventitious roots in the entire buried part, thus increasing the vigor of the plant. In garden cultivation, seedlings are usually planted in Om-10 diameter pots, which makes them easier to transplant. Sometimes, we even go so far as to sow the seeds directly into the cups and leave them there until they are ready for planting. This is a faulty procedure, as squash tolerate transplanting very well, which has the undeniable advantage of producing stocky, vigorous plants by pressing the seedlings down to the cotyledons, which is not the case with direct sowing. For the reasons given above, direct sowing is not to be recommended. However, if you do wish to sow in the field, it would be useful to arrange the soil in a sort of trough, into which the seeds are sown; this procedure provides a sort of ridging, while leaving a small basin around the plant for watering. With plants prepared under a frame, planting usually takes place in the second half of May. If you plant earlier, you will need to use cloches to protect the plant from spring frosts, to which it is very sensitive. Before planting, the soil must be prepared. This preparation consists in drawing lines on the field to be used for this crop, leaving a distance between them which varies according to the breed being grown, but which in general should not be less than 2 meters and, in the case of pumpkins, should be as much as 3 meters. On the rows thus laid out, small pits of Om, 40 on a side and of roughly equal depth are made every Im, 50. These pits are filled with decomposed manure, leaves or any other material capable of providing the nitrogen fertilizer needed for the rapid development of squash, along with a little heat from fermentation. Once these materials have been deposited in the pits, they are trodden down and watered, then covered with soil from the excavation to form a conical mound in the shape of a vast molehill, ending at the top in a sort of small basin in which to plant a squash plant. When setting up, use flat baskets or trays to transport the plants to the site, whether they have been grown in a full frame and raised into a clod, or with the cups into which they have been transplanted and from which they will be extracted. When planting, care should be taken to spread out the roots of the young plant, which should be buried up to the cotyledons. Immediately after planting, give the seedlings copious watering; it is useful to shelter them for the first few days, by covering them with a bell, an upturned pot or simply a cabbage leaf, which is removed as soon as, after a few days, recovery is judged to have taken place. Young plants are quick to grow; it is useful, though not always done, to cut the stem above the first two leaves, not including the cotyledons. This pruning results in the development of two branches, which can be stopped when they have produced five or six leaves. Flowers appear on the third-generation branches, the first of which are male; later, female flowers are produced, recognizable by the round, inferior ovary beneath the flower. We must be careful not to remove the male flowers, as we have sometimes seen done, on the pretext that they never bear fruit, and not to forget that their presence is essential for fertilization, as the female flowers usually bear no trace of fertile stamens. As soon as the young fruits are about the size of an apple, it's time to decide which ones to leave. In large-fruited varieties, such as Pumpkins, only one fruit is left per plant, and all the others are removed as they appear; this is the only way to obtain a well-developed Pumpkin. In small-fruited varieties, the number of fruits left can vary from three to five. Finally, for varieties where these fruits are eaten young, leave as many as the plant is willing to produce, removing them only when their volume is deemed sufficient. To increase fruit size, growers take care to bury the stems at certain points along their course; in this way, as adventitious roots develop in the buried areas, fruit nutrition is increased accordingly, and there is a noticeable increase in volume. Once you've decided which fruits to keep, you prune the branches carrying them, two or three leaves above their point of attachment. At the same time, cut off the tips of all branches not bearing fruit. Squashes are greedy for water and fertilizer; so, although watering can be dispensed with, their development can be significantly exaggerated by giving them a few sprinklings of water, either simple or with a solution of some kind of fertilizer, while they are growing. We sometimes use piles of manure or compost, which must remain unused during the summer, by planting a few squash vines on them, whose fruits then develop considerably. Fruit should be harvested at the latest as soon as the white frosts begin to set in. Cut the fruit off, removing with it a fragment of the branch that bore it. They should be stored in a shed to protect them from rain, which could cause them to rot, and from frost, which could damage them. The sale takes place in autumn. The Pottrons are then taken to the market, where they are sold by the piece; the price varies according to size. Prices vary according to size, from 1.50 francs for small fruits to 5 francs for large ones. Given that they are planted 3 meters apart in one direction and Im, 50 in the other, and that only one is left per plant for the large-fruited varieties, one hectare can produce around 2, 200 fruits. Seeds should always be harvested from the largest, best-formed fruits that correspond as closely as possible to the type of variety, as these plants are very prone to degeneration as a result of hybridization between varieties grown in close proximity to one another. These seeds retain their germination capacity for five to six years. 2 . 4 Crambe or Sea cabbage (Crambe maritima Linné) is native to temperate western Europe. The plant is characterized by broad, thick leaves with variously cut margins, glaucous on both sides; the thick, fleshy petioles are purplish-brown at their base; this color is evenly distributed on the leaf blades of young leaves. The inflorescence is a compound cluster, bearing white cruciform flowers followed by siliques containing a single seed. Fertilization does not always occur, and the flowers are very often sterile. The seeds retain their germinative powers for only a short time. Uses. - Crambé is widely eaten in England. In France, it has been little cultivated to date, so we are dependent on England, which sends us fairly large quantities every year. We eat the petioles, which have been blanched by the deprivation of light. They are eaten in the same way as asparagus or cardoons, and make a very fine, highly sought-after vegetable. Sowing. - Crambé is difficult to propagate by sowing, due to the short germination period of the seeds. To give it some chance of success, it's best to obtain seed as soon as it ripens, in the course of the summer, and place it in stratification in fine sand. For best results, the best procedure is to sow the stratified seeds on a bed in spring, and then transplant them into the ground. Sowing in the open air has little chance of success, unless done in May, sheltered by a north-facing wall. Flea beetles are fond of young plants, and must be removed by spraying in the morning, before the dew disappears. Multiplication by cuttings. - If you already have Crambé plants, it's a good idea to use a cutting procedure described by Mr. Berthaut in the Bulletin de la Société centrale d'horticulture de France. Here's how it should be done: Towards the end of April, the old plants are pulled out, and all the roots cut into sections of Om, 10 to Om, 12 in length. These sections are divided into two categories, one consisting of all roots at least Om, 008 in diameter, the other of all the smaller rootlets. The small roots of the second batch are nursed at Om, 10 in all directions, to be used only the following year. The larger roots, on the other hand, are used directly. Whether you have at your disposal seedlings raised by sowing, sections of large roots or small roots that have spent a year in the nursery, you will use them indiscriminately, when it's time to put them in place; however, sections of roots are infinitely better than seedlings raised by sowing; the product they will provide will be more abundant than that of plants raised from seed. It is important to know that only roots are suitable for making cuttings; underground stem fragments, which we are often tempted to use, do not give any good results. This is because roots easily produce adventitious buds, whereas stems only produce roots with difficulty. Planting. - To grow Crambé, you need well-smoked, loose soil. It is prepared by deep ploughing; then the soil is divided into 1.20 m planks, leaving paths of Om.50 between each one. On each plank, five rays are traced with the hoe, giving them a depth of about Om.10, and the Crambés are transplanted into the rays at Om.20 intervals. Watering is necessary to help the cuttings take root. Their recovery is assured, and by June, the square is covered with thick greenery. The water from the sprinklers washes away the soil, filling in the furrows and burying the Crambés plants a few centimetres deep. Shrinking. - Things are left in this state until March, when the plants are hoeed, the soil is brought back to the Crambés rows, and each plant is covered with a large upside-down pot. The leaves soon start to grow, forming one to three rosettes on each plant, which are removed with a knife when the petioles have reached a length of about Om, 12 (fig. 49). Forced cultivation. - Instead of thinning at the time of natural growth, it is usually done by forced cultivation, using two different methods: either forcing the Crambés on the spot, or putting them on a bed. In the second of these two methods, we start by building a layer in December or January with horse manure, giving it a thickness of Om, 60, with well-established stoves. The Om, 20 layer is filled with potting soil inside the trunks, and 50 plants per frame are planted. Panels, either glazed or simply planked, are placed over the whole; these panels are covered with a double layer of doormats or simply a thick layer of leaves. Harvesting can be done about three weeks after forcing begins. Forcing on site produces more beautiful products, but the operation takes a little longer. It consists of placing boxes fitted with plank panels over the Crambés crops. Then, digging out the paths, a layer of hot manure is laid on top of Fig. 49 - Crambé maritime. the boards, which is then reworked if the temperature drops below the frames. The panels are covered with mats or manure, and forcing is similar in every way to that used for Asparagus (fig. 13). After a month of forcing, the crop can be harvested. Yield. - Treated as described above, Crambé yields around 2,500 kilos per frame. This English vegetable sells in Paris for around 4 francs a kilogram in December and January, and for 1.50 in March. Although these prices will undoubtedly fall rapidly, Crambé cultivation will nonetheless remain worthwhile, either for sale or for direct consumption. There's a long way to go from the methods used in the past to the one recommended by Mr. Berthaut; we've tried it out and obtained the best results. In general, therefore, we should abandon the seedling system, which is not very advantageous, in that it is very uncertain, especially as it is easy to obtain as many root cuttings as you want, since all the plants that have been forced once are now cut after heating in April, to make new cuttings, which in turn will produce the following year. This system therefore requires only one year, whereas previous planting methods required two or three. Watercress (Nasturtium officinale, R. Bronn) grows wild in all streams and ponds in temperate Europe and Asia. For a long time, it was simply harvested where it grew spontaneously, but the ever-increasing need for it soon led to its regulated cultivation, which is now as widespread as it is lucrative. Cress (fig. 50) is characterized by succulent, fleshy twigs bearing alternate pinnate leaves with rounded segments, the terminal one always larger than those on the sides. These branches terminate in a bractless, clustered inflorescence. The white, cruciform flowers are small and give rise to long fruits (siliques) containing small, flattened, orange-yellow seeds. Uses. - In addition to the medicinal uses of watercress, due to the high proportion of iodine (1) in its tissue, watercress makes very tasty and widely used salads and seasonings. Its reputation as a powerful depurative has earned it the nickname Santé du corps (1) Chatin, le Cresson. Varieties. - Strictly speaking, these don't exist, and it's more or less the wild watercress that's grown on every farm. However, a few skilled growers have, through well-managed selection, formed breeds for cultivation that are more advantageous than the standard plant, in that the leaves become wider and form more compact rosettes with -c-f..-...-.AA... Fig. 50. - Watercress. the tips of the branches, give a higher yield. At the same time, the dark green to reddish-brown color of its leaves and stems gives it a vigorous appearance that makes it highly sought-after. On the other hand, there are types degenerated by poor cultivation, in which the leaves become narrow and frizzy, giving low yields. Cultivation. - As we have said, watercress grows spontaneously on the banks of small streams of running water, and sometimes also on the edges of ponds. But there is a considerable difference in the products obtained in either case, and watercress from flowing water is infinitely preferable to that which grows in stagnant water, for the reason that the latter usually takes on a muddy taste which robs it of much of its quality. Choice of water. - When growing cress, it's important to choose the best conditions. A watercress bed can therefore only be established if a certain quality of running water is available. But it doesn't matter what kind of water you use. Water from a small river or open stream, while sufficient for watercress cultivation, would be totally unsuitable for industrial production. As we shall see, for a watercress farm to become truly lucrative, it is first and foremost necessary to be able to harvest watercress during the winter. Water from a stream would have the disadvantage of being at an inconsistent temperature and subject to variations in ambient air temperature. For these reasons, the only water that can be used is that supplied by springs and reaching the watercress bed in a covered canal. It is also necessary for this water to come from deep strata, which, by regulating its temperature and making it constant, will have the added advantage of providing a flow rate that will not be influenced by external conditions, so that it will remain uniform during the hiyer as well as during the summer. DVBONSKI. - Culture, 2nd ed. 16 The composition of the water is also important. Water loaded with gypsum or carbonate of lime has the disadvantage of forming deposits on the leaves, making them dirty and reducing their value. Water from peaty soils, which is laden with organic matter, gives watercress a very unpleasant muddy odor. The best waters, therefore, are those that can be used for human consumption, in other words, those that are drinkable. Watercress pits. - When you have access to water that meets the conditions we have just described, you can think about setting up watercress pits, but you mustn't lose sight of the fact that under different conditions, it would be risky to engage in this type of production, at least for commercial purposes. In order to regulate the water supply and the quantity of water to be supplied to the plants, pits are dug in the ground of varying dimensions, depending on the importance of the crop and the quantity of water available. In industrial cultivation, the most common dimensions are 60 to 80 meters in length. It would be a disadvantage to exceed this length, as the end of the pit receiving water that has been in contact with the air for a long time would behave badly, for the reasons we have already set out. It is important not to give these pits too great a width, as we must not lose sight of the fact that the water supplied by the inlet canals will lose all the more of its speed the greater the surface area, so that by exaggerating this width the current could become almost nil, or in any case insufluously sensitive; the water would then become croupy, and the Cress would take on a bad taste. The most suitable width is around three meters. However, this width will vary according to the strength of the water flowing into the pit. A water flow of 25 liters per minute is required for a width of one metre, i.e. 75 liters for the same time and a pit three metres wide. This is the only way to obtain sufficient current. A single pit is not sufficient for continuous watering. You need to set up several so that the produce from one alternates with that from the other. There are watercress cultivations in the départements around Paris, with no less than a hundred pits, and sometimes more. It doesn't matter how these pits are arranged in the field. Understandably, it would be unwise to use the water from one pit to feed a second, as the water would then be in temperature equilibrium with the outside air, and would freeze during the winter. Pits should be placed parallel to each other, with a 1-meter-wide bank between them. In the past, the banks or embankments were given over to vegetable cultivation, and for this purpose they were given a greater width, but this practice is more or less abandoned nowadays. It follows from the layout of the pits that the water must flow in the direction of their length, then divide into a transverse channel with as many arms as there are pits to be served (fig. 51). Each arm is controlled by a valve that regulates the water flow to each pit. It doesn't matter if the pits are set up in any type of soil. Siliceous soils would have the disadvantage of producing insufficiently watertight pits8 N 3 -3 4 2 21 4 F. 8 18 E 4 al 2 ~~~ ~ a CS 6 6~ 3. R * 4 2 E Mna Fig. 51 - Plan of a three-pit cressonnière. ches. Clay or clay-limestone soils are best suited to their construction. The depth of the pits is not in itself very important, but they must be at least Om, 40 in this sense, although it is understandable that this height should be increased at one end of the pit if it is built on sloping ground. In fact, the bottom of the pit should only have a very slight slope equal to about 2 millimeters per meter, i.e. Om, 16 for a pit 80 meters long. The bottom of the ditch can be ploughed and smoked if it is of very poor quality, but more often than not it is simply flooded a few days before planting. As the bottom is softened by the water, it is left to drain before planting. Multiplying watercress. - Cress produces seeds that germinate easily, but this method of propagation is rarely used. The reason for this is that we grow plants whose leaves are as broad as possible; by using the seed we would often be exposing ourselves to degeneration, or at the very least we wouldn't obtain as uniform a product as by planting, which is done using twigs that, as soon as they come into contact with the soil, rapidly emit adventitious roots. If, however, it is necessary to sow seeds, as may be the case when establishing new watercress beds, the water should be removed from the pits by closing the sluice valves in spring or summer, and the seeds sown on the mud. Once the seedlings have grown well, the water is gradually released. Planting, which, as we've just said, is the most common method of propagation, is usually done in August. To do this, we take branches of watercress from a pit in full development, simply by pulling on them. The planting starts at the head of the pit, i.e. on the side from which the water comes, and usually the watercress is deposited in small clumps on the mud of the pit. Keep Om, 10 between the feet on and between the rows, and lay the watercress in such a way that the leafy end of its branches faces the head of the pit. It would be advantageous not just to throw the watercress on the ground in this way, but to transplant it, so that it picks up better and the harvest is a few days earlier. Four to five days after planting, the watercress has taken possession of the soil and the ends of its branches have straightened out. At this point, let enough water run off to cover the soil with 3 to 4 centimetres of water. It's now time to give the watercress its first fertilizer application. This consists of half-decomposed stable manure, which is thrown in handfuls over the watercress to cover it partially. To prevent the manure from being carried away by the water, it is applied to the soil with a light bat consisting of a board attached to a long handle. A few days after applying the manure, the watercress reappears vigorously above the layer of fertilizer. From then on, the pit is given all the water it needs, and a few days later the harvest can begin. Replanting should be done every year; after the pit has been cleaned and the silt removed, replant as described above. Harvesting watercress. - As we have just seen, harvesting begins soon after planting and can last all year, provided the necessary precautions are taken. In regions too far from Paris, watercress is only harvested during the winter, when the produce reaches its maximum value. In the Oise region, for example, harvesting only takes place from November to May, as the summer produce is too low in value to bear the cost of transport. For a watercress farm to produce abundant and remunerative products, it is therefore very important, as we have said, that the water does not get cold in winter, and that it does not freeze in the pits. It is also essential, in order to obtain good harvests, to smoke after each cut, following the procedure indicated above. To make the cut, a board is placed across the pits, on which the cutter stands. He kneels down and bends forward; with his left hand he grasps the watercress, lifts it up and cuts it with a serpette held in his right hand. As soon as enough cress has been harvested to make a handful, he binds it with wicker, a small bundle of which he wears on his belt. The lower end of the bundle is smoothed with a serpette, then the handle is thrown into the water on the shady side. When the worker is skilled, he cuts a hundred handles an hour. Each one weighs around 300 grams. In the evening, the bunches are packed into large conical baskets, in which they are placed so that the leaves are in the center, with the other end resting against the wall of the basket. As a result, a central cavity remains unoccupied in the pamer. The bundles are consolidated by covering them with a little straw and tying them with string. Each basket contains around 18 to 20 dozen bundles. The whole lot is then shipped by high-speed train or transported by car to the market. Winter prices generally range from 1 franc to 1.50 francs per dozen. In summer, the price is reduced by three-quarters. The yield from a watercress farm varies greatly according to the situation, the quantity of water used and the care taken. In any case, growers admit that the benefits are often considerable. Although watercress does not produce products similar to those we harvest in France, it does provide good harvests in our equatorial colonies, where we recommend its cultivation. Cress is attacked by a number of insects, notably the flea beetle (Altica sisymbrii), which can be removed by temporarily submerging the pits. It is also important to prevent the pits from being invaded by aquatic plants, which would hinder the watercress's development. CESSON ALÉNOIS Cress alénois (Lepidium sativum, Linné) is a small cruciferous plant that seems to have originated in Persia. This annual plant produces a rosette of deeply dissected leaves, from the center of which a branched stem rises after a few months of vegetation, giving rise to clusters of small, white, cruciform flowers followed by fruits (siliques) containing a small number of oblong, orange seeds. They remain germinative for five years. Uses. - The leaves are used as a condiment or to make salads. Varieties. - In addition to the primitive type, which is by far the most widespread, we also grow varieties with broad leaves and curly leaves. Cultivation. - To prevent the plant from going to seed too quickly, it's a good idea to sow in the shade during the summer, so as to obtain a longer harvest. Cresson alénois can be useful for large-scale cultivation. In a short space of time, it produces seeds that can be sold commercially. In this circumstance, sowing is broadcast in April at a rate of 5 kilograms per hectare. For watercress to grow well, the soil must be fine, i.e. made uniform by harrowing and rolling. This crop requires no care until harvest time. This takes place in August and September. The watercress is mown, then left to dry in javelins. Finally, it is flailed and winnowed. The yield is four to five hundred francs per hectare. Crosnes see Épiaire. . ... .. 1 4 - SHALLOT Shallot, which Linnaeus named botanically Allium ascalonicum, based on Pliny's belief that the plant originated in Ascalon in Judea, is not considered a species by the most authoritative modern botanists. On the contrary, they tend (1) to regard it as a simple variety of the common onion. Indeed, while the characteristics derived from taste are different, all those derived from the vegetative organs and the flower are unmistakably similar. What's more, although the regions where it has been claimed to grow spontaneously have been explored, it has not been found in the wild. Finally, it very rarely produces seeds, which again indicates a kind of degeneration due to long cultivation and a profound change in its primitive state. The plant resembles the onion in its fistulous leaves and swollen, hollow stem; it differs in that its bulb branches early, forming a variable number of cloves that spread apart. - The bulbs are used as a condiment, either cooked or preserved in vinegar. (1) De Candolle, Orig, des plantes cultivées. Varieties. - There are two slightly different types, one the ordinary shallot (fig. 52), the other with more rounded, less branched bulbs, known as the Jersey shallot; plus a few local sub-varieties. Cultivation. - Shallots are grown in multiple stages, using bulbs that are planted in the same way as garlic. The soil must be deeply tilled. Avoid using freshly smoked soil, which could cause all or part of the plants to rot. Lines are drawn Om, 20 apart, along which the cloves are transplanted, keeping the same distance between plants. This planting is done in February and March, but for the Jersey Shallot it is preferable to do it in autumn, as this plant does not fear frosts. It takes early possession of the soil and provides bulbs which, reaching full maturity very early, keep much better than if planted in spring. Harvesting takes place when the leaves begin to turn yellow. Leaving bulbs too long in the ground can cause them to rot. This serious disadvantage, which frequently occurs in shallot plantations, can be remedied by removing any plants that seem to be affected by this rot. In Brittany, where this crop is grown on a large scale, the leaves are braided after they have dried, to form a sort of string of bulbs that young Bretons sell in the streets of Paris, along with garlic and bay leaves. The insects that attack shallots are the same as those that cause damage to leek and garlic crops. This newly-introduced vegetable is now widespread everywhere, and deserves to be. Rosary is native to Japan, where it has long been cultivated as a food plant. It is also used in China. It is a perennial plant with numerous underground, tuberous rhizomes formed by a succession of nodules resembling the swollen root collars of rosary oats. The simple or stalked stem, usually erect, bears opposite, rough, cordate-based leaves that are toothed and accuminate. The sessile flowers form false whorls or contracted cymes in the leaf axils. The flower, which is that of a labiate, bears a purplish corolla. Uses. - The swollen roots, no bigger than a finger and 5 to 6 centimeters long, are eaten cooked in water, then prepared in the same way as salsify, but with more finesse and a less firm consistency. They can also be made into pickles or used in vegetable salads. This new vegetable has been introduced and spread in France by the devoted care of a good man, Mr. Paillieux, who for many years has devoted his time to researching new vegetables, which he then spreads among the public. It is remarkable how quickly this vegetable spread, for it was only in 1882 that Mr. Paillieux received fresh rhizomes of the plant for the first time, enabling him to start cultivating it. No effort was spared to make it known, and today it is an almost popular vegetable. It would have been normal to give it the name Rosary, which is its real name. Instead, it was given the name Crosnes, the name of the village inhabited by Mr. Paillieux. Let's accept it as a tribute to the researcher's dedication. The following information is based on his observations, which we summarize below. Cultivation. - Epiaire grows in all types of soil, but compact clay soils make uprooting difficult if not impossible. It is therefore preferable to choose sandy or very loose soils. Plant in February or March in holes (mm 15 to Om, 20 deep) spaced Om, 40 apart in all directions, with three or four tubers per hole. The only cultivation care required is to keep the soil surface clean and loose by hoeing. Harvesting begins around December 1st in the Paris climate. Before this time, the tubers have not finished growing. As they don't start growing again until March, they can be left in the ground until then, and only pulled as and when they are needed for consumption, as frosts are not to be feared. Avoid leaving tubers exposed to the air for several days, as they will wilt and lose their value. Yields can be around 12,000 kilograms per hectare, but this is mainly a small-crop plant. One kilogram contains around 600 tubers. Its only enemy is the white grub. In cultivations with a large number of varieties, there are two types of Spinach, which some authors have claimed to be two species, based on the fact that one bears fruit with spines formed by the enlarged calyx, while the other has smooth fruit. This separation does not seem justified, and everything leads us to believe that round-fruited spinach is a product of cultivation (1) where, for a long time, only the spiny varieties were known. The cultivated species has not been found in a spontaneous state; however, following the indications given by ancient authors, there is every reason to believe that the species originated in Persia. Without making any distinction between the various cultivated types, they should be linked to the species designated by Linné as Spinacia oleracea. Spinach has long-stalked leaves with sagittate blades often over 2 decimeters long. The plant is grown as an annual or biennial. When Spinach flowers, it's easy to see that some plants have male flowers, while others have (1) De Candolle, Orig, des plantes cultivées. female ones. Spinach is therefore dioecious. The flowers, which are arranged in spikes of sessile cymes, are followed by the fruits (achenes), covered by the enlarged pieces of the calyx; these end, as we have said, in a point, in the varieties that are close to the type, while all those that are highly perfected by cultivation have smooth fruits. These seeds retain their germinative capacity for five years. Uses. - The cooked leaves of this widely used vegetable are eaten, with the undeniable advantage of providing green food even in the depths of winter. Varieties. - In addition to ordinary spinach, which is fairly close to the supposed primitive type of this plant, and whose cultivation is no longer practiced today, there are several varieties whose distinction is based on the size of the leaves, and the earliness or lateness of the plants of which they are composed. ANGLETERRE SPINACH. - This variety is widely grown by market gardeners, as it doesn't flower until very late in the spring. Its leaves are broad and erect. The seed is thorny. SPINACH SLOW TO BOLT. - Although it has a round seed, this variety is similar to the previous one in that it doesn't flower until very late in the spring. The ample leaves are sagittate, but blistered instead of noticeably smooth. HOLLAND SPINACH. - This is a good, cold-resistant variety, which makes it particularly sought-after for winter cultivation, as opposed to its predecessor, which is mainly reserved for spring. DYBONSRI. - Vegetable crop. 17 A fairly widespread sub-variety is the Spinach of Viroflay (fig. 53), whose leaves are very ample and provide an abundant harvest. Cultivation. - Spinach is grown at two times of the year, corresponding to two slightly different forms of production. On the one hand, there are autumn seedlings, which produce in autumn, winter and early spring; on the other hand, there are spring seedlings, which produce in spring and summer. Fig. 53 - Viroflay spinach. Autumn sowing begins on August 15th, and is repeated every fortnight until mid-October. The first sowings produce a first harvest towards the end of September. Those sown in September can be harvested during the winter; and finally, those sown in October do not produce until after the heavy rains. Spinach likes a fertile soil, which it is useful to fertilize especially, and which must be, above all, healthy and free from too much humidity during the winter, which would lead to rotting at the base and destruction of the seedling. The soil on which the seedlings are to be sown should be ploughed, then trodden and raked. Spinach is usually broadcast, spreading about 250 grams of seed per acre. The seed is then harrowed with a rake, after which a light layer of loam or straw is spread. Spinach emerges after about ten days, bearing two elongated cotyledonar leaves. For spinach sown in August, it's a good idea to harvest at the end of September or the beginning of October, otherwise the leaves will develop too much and risk spoiling in winter. Harvesting is done by cutting the leaves one by one with the fingernail; avoid harvesting by cutting the leaves with a knife, which would compromise subsequent harvests. This first harvest is used as an opportunity for thinning, if necessary, to leave an interval of at least Om, 10 to Om, 15 between plants. After this initial harvest, harvesting continues throughout the winter, until around May. In order to be able to harvest during very cold spells, it is advisable to place straw mats on top of the spinach beds, which are removed as soon as the frost has dropped to two or three degrees. These mats can be replaced by straw and long bedding. When May comes, spinach tends to come up, and a final harvest is made by cutting off the whole plant. To succeed this winter crop, which is by far the most advisable, spinach is sown in spring, from February to May. Spinach is sown either broadcast or in rows, but as it sets seed quickly at this time of year, it should be sown more tightly to obtain a higher yield, which is all the more justified as the plants only occupy the soil for a relatively short time. At this time of year, we sow at a rate of 400 grams per are, and most of the time only two harvests are made, sometimes even just one, when the plants tend to develop their stems and flower. It is essential to water this spring crop abundantly, if you want to obtain high quality products. Large-scale cultivation. - Spinach is grown in open fields in the suburbs of Paris, particularly around the towns of Versailles and Saint-Germain, exclusively in autumn. Spinach is broadcast in August, in the proportions we have indicated. Don't forget that this plant is greedy for fertilizer, and that it's useful to give the soil a fertilizer that can be buried by ploughing before sowing. One harrow stroke after sowing is enough to bury the seed. A similar crop yields three harvests: one in autumn, a second in December or January, and a third by cutting off the entire plant around April or May. The first and last harvests produce an abundant crop, with each cut yielding around 100 kilograms of leaves. For the winter harvest, the weight of the leaves is about half that. These leaves are sold in large quantities to commission agents, who then cook them and sell them in this state to fruit growers. The price of spinach leaves varies greatly according to the season. It is 15 to 20 francs for 100 kilograms of leaves in autumn, rising to 30 or even 40 francs in winter, before falling back to 10 francs in spring. This gives a total average price of 20 francs per 100 kilograms, and for the three harvests, a net product of 50 francs per acre. When cooked, Spinach diminishes significantly in weight, so that one kilogram of green leaves yields only 670 grams of cooked Spinach. The price of cooked spinach averages 40 centimes per kilogramme, which means that growers who are far from the centers of consumption would be well advised to cook and send them in this form. This would have the double advantage of reducing the volume and weight of shipments, while increasing their value. For the same quantity of sheets, T'are would obtain a sum of 66 francs, which would only be burdened by the low cost of baking. Seed carriers. - When it comes to harvesting seeds, spinach should be treated as a biennial plant, i.e. only those sown in August or September that have survived the winter should be harvested. Market gardeners harvest the leaves of the plants that will supply them with seed in the spring. It's best not to do this, but to leave the seed-bearing plants untouched, simply thinning them out and removing plants whose leaves don't correspond to the type you have in mind. Spinach flowers in June. As soon as flowering is over, we pull out all the male plants, which are no longer needed, and wait for the moment of maturity, which occurs at the end of July, to cut the seed-bearing plants. They are then threshed. The seeds are bagged and can be used for sowing for up to five years. The origins of broad bean cultivation (Vicia Faba, Linné) are lost in the mists of time, dating back to prehistoric times. The plant has never been found in a spontaneous state, and it is highly probable that it would have disappeared a long time ago due to the size of its seeds, which prevents any natural dissemination and makes it a target for animals of all kinds, if cultivation had not taken hold of it at a very early date and enabled it to reach us. The plant's vegetative organs are characterized by a robust stem with a few branches at the base. These stems are raised by four protruding angles, giving them a square appearance. The leaves are compound, pinnate and not odd. Papilionaceous flowers are white with a black spot in the center of the petals. They are borne in pauciflorous clusters in the leaf axils. The fruits are pods, sometimes erect, sometimes curving towards the ground. They contain a variable number of seeds, rarely more than eight. The seeds are large, flattened, kidney-shaped and have an easily detachable aril. They retain their germinative capacity for six years. Uses. - Broad beans are eaten as grains, either fresh or dried. The latter have the disadvantage of being covered with very thick husks that must be removed, as they cannot be eaten. Varieties. - Although it has been cultivated for a very long time, the broad bean has generally not varied much, and the number of different types of cultivation is relatively small. Here are two of the most commonly grown varieties. MARSH BEAN. - Plant about Om 80 high, pods in twos or threes, containing two to four very large seeds. WINDSOR BEAN. - Plant often taller than the previous one. Numerous pods, often solitary, containing one to three well-developed seeds. Grown in the Paris climate. - Fèves are hardy plants, but fear heavy frosts. In our climate, they are sown as soon as the temperature eases after the winter. Sowing takes place in February or March at the latest. They can be sown in any soil, but rich, moderately compact soils are best suited to broad beans. Seeds are planted in rows Om, 30 apart, spaced Om, 15 apart along the rows, and buried Om, 05 apart. To hasten plant development, it's a good idea to water when the weather turns dry. Fava beans are fast-growing, so they are fully developed by May. As soon as flowering begins, we pinch off the ends of the stems above about the tenth inflorescence. This has the dual effect of hastening the development of the preserved pods, and preventing the black aphid that attacks the herbaceous parts of the plant from wreaking havoc. Harvesting takes place either when the beans are two-thirds developed, or when dry. Cultivation in the Midi. - In the Midi region, seedlings should be sown in autumn, starting in September for the orange region and in October for the olive region. Sowing is carried out exactly as described above. These autumn sowings produce early-flowering Fava beans, whose pods can be harvested in March, April and May. Under these conditions, Fèves are capable of producing an advantageous product, as the pods sell in the spring for up to 30 francs per 100 kilogr. at the Paris halles. They belong to several botanical species, some indigenous, others, on the contrary, native to the temperate regions of South America. Sowing and selection on the one hand, and hybridization on the other, have produced a very considerable number of varieties and hybrids, which are widespread in gardens today. In practice, all these different types form two categories corresponding to different cultivation methods and requirements; on the one hand, they form the group of small-fruited strawberries or strawberries of the four satsons; on the other, large-fruited strawberries. All strawberry plants are perennials, their rhizomes producing two types of rameanx, some sterile and of indefinite elongation, bearing scale-like leaves from whose axils buds produce normal leaves, which are trifoliolate and stipular. These twigs root at the level of the buds they produce, and are known as runners or stolons (lig. 54). These rooted stolons can be used to propagate strawberry plants. The plant also produces other self-determining branches. The flowers are arranged in uniparous cymes, bearing a calicule, a calyx and a corolla, which is white and composed of five parts. After bearing numerous stamens, the flower's receptacle elongates into a kind of elevation, bearing an indefinite number of carpels that transform into small, indehiscent dried fruits (achenes). The edible part of the Strawberry is therefore not the fruit, as is often claimed, but the hypertrophied receptacle, whose tissue is gorged with adibles; it is nevertheless true that, in practice, U Fig. 54. - Stolon or strawberry runner. This is the part of the fruit that has retained its name, and we will refer to it as such. The fruit is surrounded by the calyx and calicule, which are persistent and form an induvie. Fruits vary infinitely in size, shape and color, but all contain sweet, mucilaginous substances mixed with essences that make them a pleasant-tasting food. The fact that they ripen in spring, when few other fruits are available, also contributes to their popularity. Finally, Strawberries have the advantage of being easy to force-feed. Uses. - Strawberries are eaten either raw or cooked. In the latter case, they are used to make highly prized jams and syrups. PETITES FRAISES. Small Strawberries seem to recognize a single botanical species as their ancestor: Linnaeus' Fragaria vesca, which grows wild in all the woods of the northern hemisphere. In practical terms, it differs 2 29 from all other strawberry plants in that both the type and the cultivated varieties are generally elongated, with white flesh and protruding seeds. All cultivated varieties have the advantage of sustained flowering throughout the fine season, when given the necessary care, which is why Fig. 55. -Fraisiers des quatre saisons (fig. 55). Varieties. - Varieties are generally less important than for large-fruited strawberries, for the reason that, as we shall see, the most common method of propagation is by sowing, and characteristics do not always reproduce with great fixity. However, there are certain types that we should aim for, because they correspond either to genuine qualities or to commercial requirements. At present, the most sought-after varieties are those whose fruits are bright red and whose elongated shape gives them the appearance of a small gherkin. IMPROVED DURU STRAWBERRY. - The fruit is long and bright red. This is one of the most widely grown varieties for the Paris market. It is very similar to an older variety with dark red fruit called Fratse Janus. STRAWBERRY WITHOUT NET. - This is an old variety whose cultivation has been rather neglected, as it does not produce sufficiently beautiful fruit. It has the particularity of not needing a net, which makes it ideal for edging vegetable gardens. Two different forms are grown, one with red fruit and the other with white. Sowing. - Sowing is a method of propagation that gives very good results, provided special care is taken and, above all, great care is taken in selecting the fruit to be sown. Four Seasons Strawberries are sown in March and April. They should be sown on beds with an average temperature of 15 to 18 degrees. The soil placed on the bed consists of a mixture of equal parts of potting soil and sandy soil or heather. It is placed in the trunk so that it comes to within 6 to 7 centimetres of the frame glass. After levelling the soil with a rake, it is lightly beaten with a planchette to make the surface absolutely even. The seeds are then scattered to form a tight seedbed, and covered with a thin layer of sandy soil. Water lightly with a fine-headed watering can, then replace the frame and cover with a mat until the seedling appears. Emergence takes place after about ten days, when the young plants appear with two very small cotyledonary leaves. From this point onwards, air should be supplied during the day, taking care to lift the frame on the side facing away from the wind to avoid drying out, and humidity maintained by frequent watering. In this way, you obtain healthy seedlings, and take advantage of a foggy day to remove the frames and leave them exposed to the direct action of the air. Seedlings can also be sown in the open air during May and June. In this case, it's best to choose a sunny location and keep the soil moist with constant watering. Seedlings sown in the open air are less attractive than those sown in beds or trays. As soon as the plants have four or five leaves, they can be transplanted. After watering the seedling, remove all the best seedlings, and after preparing the soil by ploughing and raking, draw lines Om, 15 apart, along which the strawberry plants will be transplanted. Two plants are often placed together, to produce larger clumps. When transplanting, which is done with a large planting tool, care must be taken not to bend the roots, but to press them in perpendicularly. Water immediately after transplanting, and repeat the watering frequently. If you want to obtain beautiful plants, it's a good idea to replant in August, which will multiply the plant's hair and make it more vigorous. Replanting is carried out using a trowel, removing the rootballs and keeping a distance of about Om.25 between the rows. If these plants produce either sterile or fruit-bearing shoots, they are removed and vigorous plants are obtained which can be used for planting. Another procedure consists, when the plants are strong enough to undergo the first transplanting, in planting them in rows Om, 50 apart, and covering the soil with a good layer of straw. Leave any nets that the plants are willing to produce. As soon as they are sufficiently rooted, they are removed and transplanted into beds in a nursery, to be used as seedlings the following year. This is the best method for obtaining strawberry plants that produce good quality fruit; however, it is the least followed, because of the time and labor required to do it properly. In either case, planting can be done early in the autumn, or in March. Strawberry plants planted in autumn will produce a full crop the following spring, and a smaller additional crop in autumn; they should be left to occupy the soil for three years, i.e. they should be uprooted when they have produced their third spring crop. On the other hand, Traisiers planted in spring will produce a full crop in autumn. They will remain in the ground for three years, which means that they will only be uprooted at the onset of winter in the third year of planting. This procedure will produce a steady crop, provided that new plantings are made every year at the times indicated. The soil chosen for planting should be fresh and substantial, if possible. Strawberry plants Fig. 56 - Basket used to pack small strawberries. also do well in sandy soil, provided they do not lack moisture, though this should not be too great. The plants are planted in four rows spaced Om, 35 apart, staggered Om, 45 apart. Once planted, the soil is covered with a layer of straw and watered. Frequent watering will be necessary throughout the fruiting period, and it will be useful to remove all netting as it occurs. Harvesting. - Harvesting begins around June 15th and continues until the end of September, provided that we take care to baste morning and evening. Production slows noticeably in July and early August, especially when watering is lacking. Harvesting takes place in the morning or evening; only the reddest strawberries are picked, and the stalks are removed by cutting them with a fingernail. The 4 Fig. 57. - Packing strawberries in Provence. Harvested strawberries are placed in pots or small baskets lined with vine leaves or strawberry plants. For sale, they are packed in lidded baskets (Fig. 56), containing one kilog. of fruit, as is done around Paris; these baskets are lined with a few leaves. In Provence, small stoneware pots (fig. 57) are used, in which the small strawberries are placed, then placed on top and held in place with a paper cone. DYBOWSKI. - Vegetable cultivation. 18 Harvesting the seed. - It's important to choose carefully the fruit that will provide the seed. Only well-colored fruit from fertile plants should be taken, from which all netting and poorly-formed fruit have been removed. Fruits from late August or early September are taken as seed, because they are the most ripe. When they are fully ripe and have taken on a beautiful vermilion-red color, we crush them in water, then pass the pulp through a fine cloth to separate the seed, which we dry in the shade and then bag. These seeds can only be used for two or three years, after they have lost their ability to germinate. LARGE-FRUITED STRAWBERRIES Most large-fruited strawberry plants are the result of hybridization between various botanical species. These include the Virginia strawberry (Fragarta rtrginiana, Ehrahrt), native to Canada, and the Chilean strawberry (Fragaria Chiloensis, Duchesne), which grows wild in southern Chile. To these should be added the Capron strawberry (Fragarta elattor, Ehrarht), of which only one or two varieties are grown, and these are not very widespread because of their distinctive, slightly musky taste. Varieties. - The number of varieties or hybrids cultivated today is extremely considerable, and many of these are of little value. The most widely cultivated varieties are STRAWBERRY MARGUERITE LEBRETON. - Robust and relatively fertile variety, with large, conical fruit, 3 Fig. 58. - Strawberry Marguerite Lebreton. Fig. 59. - Héricart de Thury strawberry. It is widely used in forced cultivation, to which it lends itself remarkably well because of its earliness (fig. 58). STRAWBERRY VICOMTESSE HÉRICART DE THURY. - Plant widely cultivated around Paris. Medium-sized, unevenly rounded fruit with juicy, fragrant flesh. An early variety suitable for forced cultivation (fig. 59). FRAISE Dr MORÈRE. - A vigorous variety with very large fruit and pink, sweet flesh; highly sought-after in the trade. Later than the two preceding varieties, it succeeds them in the order of maturity (fig. 60). JUCUNDA STRAWBERRY. - Late variety with large, dark-red fruit. Still a widely cultivated plant. Grown in the open air. - Seedlings do not faithfully reproduce the various large-fruited strawberry varieties. Fig. 60. - Strawberry Dr Morère. fruit, so this method of propagation is only used in the search for new varieties. When, on the other hand, the aim is to reproduce existing varieties, we use either nets or splinters that can be detached from the mother plants. If you want to propagate a variety of which you have only a limited number, you need to take special care of the plants that will provide the nets. Having obtained a few seedlings of the variety to be propagated during the summer, they are planted at a good exposure in the nursery, and when the cold comes, they are covered either with cloches or frames. Around March, the clodded plants are lifted and transplanted to a ploughed and smoked bed, spaced at Om, 40 apart in all directions. Mulch the soil, and if inflorescences appear, cut them out. It doesn't take long for the vines to produce numerous, vigorous threads, which are left to hang out on the ground. In July, we remove all the rooted nets, rid them of any yellow leaves they may bear, and plant them in a nursery at Om, 15 in each direction. Mulching and watering are necessary to obtain vigorous plants. Often, to obtain well-formed clumps, they are planted in- Fig. 61. - Strawberry Jucunda. seems to be two plants of equal strength; this procedure is always followed when a very large quantity of nets is available. If the aim is to propagate a common variety of which there are already many plants, there is no need to plant them in special beds beforehand; simply detach the most vigorous nets in the growing beds. In all cases, care must be taken to ensure that nursery plants do not produce new nets, which would be carefully removed if they did. Around mid-September, the strawberry plants should be planted. To do this, we need to prepare a plot of land that has not been used for strawberry planting for several years, as experience has shown that new plantings do not do well under these conditions. Strawberry rows should be spaced at Om, 35 apart, with plants spaced at Om, 50 to Om, 60 apart, depending on the vigor of the variety. Early-bearing varieties should be planted with a southern exposure, while late-bearing varieties should be planted with a northern exposure, so as to extend harvesting time as much as possible. Strawberries should be transplanted in rootballs and watered immediately after planting. The following spring, hoe the plants, taking care not to bury them, and cover the soil with mulch. Flowering takes place in May, and the fruits of the early varieties begin to ripen at the end of May. With the late varieties, harvesting lasts until July. Harvesting is carried out with the same equipment as for the Four Seasons Strawberry. According to M. Baltet, one hectare of strawberries in Brittany yields an average of 15,750 kilograms of fruit, at a price of O fr. 20 per kilogram, or 3,150 francs. Forced cultivation. - The most popular varieties for this type of cultivation are Marguerite Lebreton, Héricart de Thury and Dr. Morère; Fraisiers des quatre saisons are also used, but less frequently. Strawberry plants can be forced, either on the spot, or by transporting them on a bed; both methods give good results, but the second is the one most generally used. To do this, we use plants that we have nursed in July, and in September we put them in pots of Om, 16 to Om, 20 in diameter. In each of these pots, we place a clump made up, as we said, of two plants planted at the same time in the nursery. Potting should be done in pre-prepared soil. It should be made up of one-third free-range soil, or soil from lawns previously piled up and suitably rotted; to this should be added one-third potting soil which has not yet been used, and an equal proportion of sandy heather soil. After repotting, we bury the pots in the soil, water them and, when October comes, cover them with boxes and frames to which we give air until it freezes outside. At night, they are covered with straw mats. In January, or later if you like, build up a layer of new manure, half of which is mixed with annealed manure or leaves. Refill the layer with sandy soil or light potting compost, in which to bury the pots, at a rate of twenty-four per frame, as soon as the layer reaches a temperature of 12°. It's important not to overheat and not to exceed the temperature indicated above, so a thermometer should be placed in the bed. In February and March, when the strawberry plants are in full bloom, the temperature can be allowed to rise to around 16°. Water when the soil dries out a little, but avoid giving too much water, especially during flowering, as this could cause the flowers to rot or leak. Before flowering, the soil is covered with mulch to prevent the fruit from getting dirty; often, inflorescences are even supported with small wooden forks. It's very important in this crop not to set the temperature too high, and to reduce watering to what's strictly necessary to avoid excess humidity; with this dual aim in mind, air is given whenever the outside temperature permits. Harvesting usually begins after two and a half months of forcing. Harvesting can continue for around three weeks. Another procedure, still using the seedling prepared in the nursery, consists in planting in September in plots Imn, 30 wide, in which four rows of strawberry plants are placed at Om, 30 on the rows. A path of Om 50 is left between each bed. In October, the boxes and frames are placed, and when January comes, the paths are dug and stoves are set up to the height of the windows. The same care is taken with maintenance, and the harvest takes about two and a half months. Finally, we can simply cover strawberry beds, specially planted as we have just indicated, with boxes and frames, without establishing layers in the paths. This method produces fruit in great abundance from the beginning of May. As in the previous case, care must be taken to provide air in order to avoid too great a rise in temperature. With this cultivation method, yields are more or less equal to those obtained with open-ground cultivation. Animal and insect pests. - Strawberries are very fond of ferrets and rals. They often wreak considerable havoc in forced cultivation. Traps should be set for them. Slugs of all kinds frequently attack strawberries. The only way to destroy them is to place a layer of rancid butter on each slab. If you visit these boards early in the morning, you'll find the slugs attracted by the smell of butter, which are easy to destroy. The strawberry plant's most fearsome enemy is undoubtedly the larva of the chafer (Melalonta vulgaris) or white grub, which cuts all the roots, destroying the plant at fruiting time. The only way to destroy them is to pull up the strawberry plants as soon as you see them wilting, and look for the beetle larva, which is usually easy to find because of its size. Finally, the larvae of the Julius fragarium tipula attack the fruit, devouring its entire interior. There is no practical way to defend against the ravages of this insect. Taken as a whole, beans, grown all over the world, refer to several different botanical species. On the contrary, all the countless varieties grown in our climate originate from a single species, the common bean (Phaseolus vulgarts, Linnaeus). Beans are cultivated in our climate as annuals, but they can last longer if the temperature conditions are right. Its stems are long and voluble, and all varieties with this character are said to have oars, because of the need to provide them with supports; often its stems remain short and not voluble, which constitutes the so-called dwarf varieties. It seems that these two categories have existed for as long as beans have been cultivated; however, these characteristics are not always absolutely fixed, and it is not uncommon to see dwarf varieties producing here and there a few plants of beans with voluble stems. Beans have pinnate leaves, composed of three slightly cordiform, acuminate leaflets; the leaves are arranged in alternating order. The flowers, generally white, are arranged in single clusters, averaging three to ten flowers. They have a papilionaceous corolla with a spiral-shaped carina. The single-located ovary is followed by a fruit (pod), usually called a husk, which contains seeds of different shapes, colors and numbers, depending on the variety. Bean fruits have an endocarp which is sometimes hard and parchment-like; sometimes, on the contrary, this part of the fruit becomes fleshy. This makes up, on the one hand, Beans with parchment or for shelling, and on the other, Beans without parchment or mange-tout, so called because the whole pod is eaten. Bean seeds are either white or colored, and the husks that cover them are more or less thick, giving them very different organoleptic qualities. In all cases, these seeds are a first-rate foodstuff, as the seed coats contain a significant proportion of a nitrogenous substance, known as tegumine, associated with the starch. Numerous hypotheses have been put forward as to the origin of the bean, but nothing to date allows us to settle the question definitively, for the reason that nowhere has the plant been found in a spontaneous state. It is nevertheless true that the presence of its cultivation could not be authentically established, as having been made at a time prior to the discovery of America, that, in any case, from that time, this culture took a great extension, and that the varieties multiplied from that day; that finally, among the seeds found in Peruvian tombs, it was possible to link some of them to the Beans proper. All these clues together allow us to assume, if not establish definitively, that this plant originated in South America. - Beans are eaten as young pods, when they are known as green Hartcots. The mange-tout are used for the same purpose, with the advantage that they can still be used while the beans are still formed. The seeds are used either green or dry. Varieties. - There are innumerable varieties of bean; we will limit ourselves to indicating those most commonly used in both small and large-scale farming. But all these varieties should be separated into two groups, depending on whether they are dwarf or climbing, as they correspond to two different growing methods. Dwarf beans are most commonly grown in gardens, and are the only ones used for early production. They have the great advantage over those in the second category of being able to develop rapidly and not requiring stakes, which are often costly. I. - DWARF STRING BEANS. A. - Varieties with white seeds. HOLLAND FLAGEOLET BEAN. - Flageolets are the most widely known and esteemed of the shelling beans. The bean is small, depressed, and has a greenish tint which gives it a pleasant appearance and makes it sought after for consumption as a green or dry bean. FLAGEOLET BEAN WITH EMBOSSED LEAVES. - A small variety which, for this very reason, is much sought-after in forced cultivation. It is also sown in the open, where it produces abundant, early yields. It is characterized by its unevenly blistered leaves. It is grown for green consumption (fig. 62). Haricor rlageoler D'ÉTaMpEs. - Ample, abundant foliage; very early flowering, giving rise to Fig. 62 - Flageolet bean with embossed leaves. numerous pods. Like its predecessor, this variety is mainly grown for green consumption, either of the pods or the beans. Haricor FlageolEr CHEVRiER. - In recent years, a number of varieties have been sown whose beans remain almost green after drying. The Chevrier bean is one of the first varieties of this type. Apart from the advantage of coloring, this variety has the disadvantage of being delicate in many circumstances. The green color of the bean is partly due to the variety and partly to the fact that it is harvested before full maturity. B. - Varieties with colored beans. VAVIN CHOCOLATE BEAN. - Variety similar to Flageolets in shape and size of beans, Fig. 63. - Haricot de Bagnolet. but these are of a brown color which has earned them their name. It is especially used for the large-scale cultivation of early vegetables in southern France and Algeria. BELGIAN BLACK BEAN. - Small variety, well suited to forced cultivation. Green pods, sometimes variegated with purple, containing small, black seeds when ripe. Grown exclusively for green beans. HARICOT DE BAGNOLET. - This variety is larger than the previous one. The pod is straight and fruiting is abundant. The beans are purple, blackish. This is one of the most widely grown varieties around Paris for the production of green beans (fig. 63). 11. - DWARF BEANS WITHOUT PARCHMENT. HARICOT NOIR D'ALGER. - This variety, with its black beans, is widely cultivated, as its pods retain the property of being able to be eaten green for a long time. III. - STRING BEANS WITH PARCHMENT. A. - White-grain varieties. SOISSONS BEAN. - This is the most commonly used variety in this category. The voluble branches can grow to a height of around 2 meters; its flowering is prolonged and produces an abundant crop. The pods are long, curved and contain the largest seeds of the genus, highly sought-after for everyday consumption (fig. 64). B. - Varieties with colored beans. HARICOT ROUGE DE CHARTRES. - This bean belongs almost exclusively to large-scale cultivation; it is eaten only as beans. These are dark wine-red. It is a productive variety.
