Grown in the open air, in the Paris climate. - Beans thrive in loose, deeply tilled soil containing decomposed fertilizers. Sloping, south-facing soils are ideal for early sowing. The earliest you can start sowing is towards the end of April, if you don't want to use shelters, as beans are very sensitive to cold. You can bring them forward by about a fortnight, taking care to cover them every evening with straw mats laid on top of the bean beds. Sowing can continue until the end of June, if the beans are to be harvested as beans, and until the end of August if they are to be harvested green. Seedlings are sown either in bunches or in rows. The first of these two systems is used almost exclusively for dwarf varieties. In rows spaced Om, 40 to Om, 50 apart, pocks are opened at equal distances, either with a hoe or a spade, and five or six seeds are placed in them, spaced slightly apart, and covered with about Qu 05 of soil. In large-scale cultivation, we often sow in rays, on which the beans are spaced 09, 10 apart, but it is always preferable to sow in bunches - these sowings are generally done with a seed drill - this is how they are practiced around Paris, When we grow beans, it is necessary, whether we adopt rays or bunches, to leave a space between the rowsDYBONSKI. - Vegetable growing. 19 of about Om, 80. One and a half liters per are are sown in rays, and 2 liters in bunches. Beans germinate after ten or fifteen days. When they have emerged from the soil and are bearing their first leaves, the first hoeing is carried out to fill in the hollows left by sowing and to remove weeds. After hoeing, it's time to give the varieties that need it the support it requires. This can be done either by hoeing, or by cutting branches from the coppice. If beans are planted in bunches, place a single twig in the center of the clump. If the seedlings are planted in rays, the reams are inserted every two or three feet, taking care to incline them so that the ends of the reams of two neighboring rays meet at their apexes. This arrangement, by leaving the passage free every two rows, facilitates harvesting. After the reams have been laid, or in any case when the beans begin to show their first flowers, the ground is hoeed a second time, and the soil is raked over the bean stalks, making them slightly ridged. Harvesting begins around July for early beans eaten green, and in August for beans. Beans continue to produce until frost. Beans for green consumption should be harvested as soon as the pod has reached at most half of its full development. E4 EST Beans intended to provide dry grains should be harvested in fine weather, when the pods, having turned yellow, begin to dry out completely. Flageolet beans whose green color is to be preserved should be harvested before the pods have completely dried out. Once harvested, the beans are tied in bunches, left to dry out on the ground if the weather is fine, then taken into a shed or attic, where they are hung to dry out completely. Only when drying is complete can the seeds in the pods be extracted by flail threshing, but they can be kept fresher by extracting them from the pods only as and when needed. Bean yields vary greatly from year to year, and are generally higher the hotter and wetter the summer. In years of drought, however, yield is very low if Ton has not been able to water the crop. If the same beans are harvested green, then in fresh beans and finally dry, a maximum of 45 kilograms of green beans, 8 liters of fresh beans and 4 liters of dry beans can be obtained per acre. If harvested exclusively dry, they can yield over 20 liters per acre. Green beans can be preserved very easily, provided they are stored in stoneware jars, in which a bed of beans and a layer of gray salt are placed alternately. They should be washed with plenty of water before cooking. - Beans are grown in Algeria, Spain and, to a lesser extent, in the Mediterranean region, with a view to producing early products that are shipped to Paris and England. In recent years, this type of production has become so important that forced cultivation in the North of France has been greatly reduced. Mr. José Congiu provided us with the following information on the very important crops grown in the province of Malaga. They have the advantage of relating exactly to the procedures followed in Algeria. In the Malaga area alone, around 300 hectares of beans are grown annually, with the produce destined exclusively to supply the Paris markets during the winter. Bean growers bring in the seeds they need from Paris, usually the variety known as Vayin chocolate. Growers are well advised to bring their seeds from more northerly countries than their own, as experience has shown that this produces earlier yields than seeds harvested locally. For export crops, sowing takes place at two different times: in August on the one hand, and in December on the other. In both cases, seed is sown in bunches in well-prepared soil, with four or five seeds per bunch. The lines are drawn at Om, 45, and the clumps are spaced Om, 25 apart. This arrangement facilitates the hoeing essential to this crop. If the weather is dry, it is urgent to water, which is done by irrigating every four or five days. Ilaricots begin to produce about forty days after sowing, so that those sown in December produce from January onwards, and the harvest continues until April. Those sown in August produce their pods from October to December; this double sowing makes it easy to obtain a continuous product throughout the winter months. Yields. - Harvesting is entirely green, so we pick everything the plants produce. The yield varies from year to year, and also according to the land planted. It reaches its peak when the beans are sown in good exposure and frequently irrigated. Under these conditions, between 3,000 and 3,500 kilograms of green beans are produced per hectare. Sales prices are extremely variable, depending on when the crop is harvested: from December to February, beans sell for no less than 1.50 to 1.80 francs per kilogram. But this price falls rapidly, to O fr. 30 and even O fr. 20 per kilo in April and May, the prices obtained for sale on the spot. Forced cultivation. - Early bean production has greatly diminished since the produce is imported during the winter from southern regions. As a result, the cultivation of beans on beds, which used to be practiced by market gardeners, has now been completely abandoned by these growers. However, it is still a useful crop for vegetable gardens in rural areas, where communications with major centers are difficult. We cannot recommend this type of production from a commercial point of view. Beans are grown as early as possible, either with the help of heat produced by thermosiphons, or on layers. Only the second of these two methods needs to be considered here, as thermosiphon cultivation is beyond the scope of this book. Beans are sown on hot beds, starting in January, using early varieties of flageolet. The seeds are broadcast and covered with a small layer of potting soil. As soon as the plants have sprouted, which takes about three days, they are transplanted either to a nursery under a different frame, to be planted ten days later, or directly into the ground, which is a less efficient procedure, as the plants are less stocky. In all cases, the plants must be sunk right down to the cotyledons, and to do this, the layer is covered with about Om, 20 of potting soil. The plants are placed in three rows per frame, and transplanted, two by two, leaving a space of Om, 12 between each clump thus formed. Do not over-water, as this will rot the plants. Harvesting takes place two and a half months after sowing, and should be repeated every two or three days. To obtain a continuous yield, two or three seedlings are sown on a bed, and from April onwards, they are sown in the open ground covered with a frame. Finally, to achieve the same yield as in the open ground, you can sow in April under a frame and transplant at the beginning of May, provided you cover the plants overnight with straw mats. Harvesting seeds. - Beans destined for seed can simply be harvested from plants sown in beds, taking care not to harvest green. This procedure is sufficient for all common varieties, but for very advanced and early breeds, better results are obtained by harvesting the seeds only from plants that have been transplanted. Although theoretically beans retain their germinative capacity almost indefinitely, since seeds extracted from Tournefort's herbarium have germinated after more than eighty years, in practice preference should be given to seeds from the previous year, which germinate faster and give more robust plants than old seeds. This plant, of which many species and varieties are known today, is represented in our cultivation only by the Chinese yam (Dioscorea batatas, Decaisne), which was introduced to France in 1848 by M. de Montigny, French consul in Chang-Haï. Yam is a perennial plant with an underground rhizome. Its stems, which can reach 3 to 4 meters in length and are voluble, bear alternate leaves that frequently become opposed by training; these are sagittate, cordiform at the base and with pinnate-pedal venation; at their axils are born bulbils whose size varies from that of a pea to that of a hazelnut. The flowers are dioecious and arranged in variously composed clusters. The most interesting organ, the one for which the plant is cultivated, is that peculiar kind of fleshy rhizome, which in reality is no more than a disproportionately enlarged bud or bulblet. This is an annual organ; the previous year's rhizome is replaced the following year by a larger one. In its second year, it reaches a length of no less than Om, 60 to Om, 90. Its shape is very special: very small near the surface of the ground, it gradually increases in diameter, only to decrease again and end in a mossy point (fig. 65). At its widest, its diameter is often equal to Om, 06 or Om, 10. A gray envelope covered with small rootlets conceals a very white flesh which, when broken, exudes a slightly viscous substance. The rhizome of the yam is devoid of any special flavor, which is good for spreading its use, and is very rich in a starch vaguely reminiscent in shape of the potato, but with grains of a much more even size. Uses. - Rhizomes are eaten in the same way as potatoes, which they resemble; but their taste is much finer and lacks the unpleasant flavor found in many poor-quality potatoes. Cultivation. - Sowing is not used for multipli- Fig. 65. - Chinese yam. cation, as it would produce results too slowly. Moreover, yams do not ripen in our climate, and it is only in the Midi or in Algeria that we can hope to obtain fertile seeds. It would be in our interest to plant seedlings which, through intelligent selection, would perhaps lead to an RF type of yam whose rhizomes, being shorter and stubbier, would be easier to pull up. Were it not for the serious drawback of extracting yams from the soil, it is certain that the plant would long ago have taken its place in vegetable gardens and even in large-scale farming. There are various ways of propagating yams. The one that gives the quickest results is to use the upper, tapering part of the rhizomes removed for consumption, as well as the entire rhizome, when its length is only about Olil, 15. This method of propagation has only one drawback, which is the difficulty of obtaining a sufficient number of organs for planting each year. So, if we were to grow this plant on a large scale, we would have to resort to one of the following two methods. The first, and simplest, is to collect all the little bulblets that have developed in the leaf axils during the summer, in the autumn, when the half-dried plants have let them fall to the ground. These bulblets are stored over winter in a cellar, where they are stratified in sand. In March, they are pricked out at Om, 10 in each direction, in a bed in the vegetable garden, and in autumn, they form small rhizomes, Om, 15 in length, to be used for planting the following year. Another method is to take cuttings in May or June, and give them a length of Om, 10 or so. These cuttings are transplanted close together, under cloches, along a north-facing wall. When they have taken root, the cloches are removed. They are watered several times during the summer, and at the end of autumn as many small bulbils are produced as cuttings. Kept over winter, these bulblets can be used in spring to form plants exactly like those that have developed spontaneously in the axils of aerial leaves. Any soil is suitable for this crop, provided it is rich in fertilizer and sufficiently moist; in dry soils, harvesting is always poor. The soil is ploughed deeply, then levelled and the prepared seedlings, stored in the cellar, are transplanted using a planter sunk deep enough so that the rhizome ending at the top is Om 05 below ground level. A spacing of Om, 30 to Om, 40 is maintained in all directions between the plants. M. de Villepin, director of the Pilletière farm-school, who has been involved with yam since its introduction to France, cultivates it in a slightly different way, with the best results, it seems. Around February, he builds a bed covered with his frames, under which flower pots are arranged close together. In each of these pots, filled with potting soil, he plants either a fragment of a large rhizome or an aerial bulb. It doesn't take long for the yams to develop well. At the beginning of May, when frosts are no longer to be feared, he digs a deep hole in the soil intended for them. Then, from Om, 50 to Om, 50 in all directions, a hole is dug in the ground with a stake, which is driven in as far as the hole will allow. This hole is filled with potting soil, and one of the pots prepared under the frames is planted in it. As soon as the plant has risen to Om.40, it is given a stake against which it wraps, then irrigated during the summer and given one or two hoeings. Harvesting takes place in autumn, and M. de Villepin obtains 40,000 kilograms of yams per hectare using this method. This method has the advantage of yielding an abundant product, thanks to the use of beds in spring; it only has the disadvantage of requiring a lot of labor and raw material, consisting of potting soil and bedding manure. In ordinary cultivation, the crop is harvested either in autumn of the first year, when only rhizomes 0u30 to Om, 40 long are obtained, or only in the second year, so as to produce twice the size, and therefore twice the yield, without the need for additional expense. This biennial cultivation is very successful, as Yams have little fear of the cold and can withstand a frost of 15 degrees if a few leaves or large litter are thrown on the ground. However, the great drawback that makes the cultivation of this excellent plant so infrequent is the difficulty of uprooting it. The rhizomes sink vertically into the soil, and to extract them, it is necessary to open a gauge Om, 80 deep at one end of the cultivated field, and then gradually break up the soil in front of you with a hook, taking great care not to damage the extremely fragile yams. This method is costly, and has the added disadvantage of mixing in poor subsoil when the soil is not deep. A patient experimenter, Mr. Chapellier, has tried to breed a variety with shorter roots, but his results have not yet been completely successful. To prevent the roots from sinking, he advises planting them in pots, but the result is a twisted, poorly formed root. Yams uprooted in November and placed in cays keep very well until March or April. They are not attacked by any insect, nor are they known to suffer from any parasitic disease. .-. .. ".. HTAF.P. The very many varieties of cultivated lettuce found in vegetable gardens all seem to recognize as their origin the plant designated by Linnaeus as Lactuca scartola, found in a spontaneous state in almost all of the ancient world, and particularly throughout temperate Europe and northern Africa. The Greeks and Romans already cullivated it, but varieties were few and far between at the time. Today, the number has increased considerably. Lettuces are characterized by leaves that are more or less ample and elongated, depending on the variety; together, they form a large terminal bud, sometimes globular and pressed against the ground, which constitutes the lettuce proper, or head lettuce. At other times, the bud elongates into a rounded cylinder at the top, which characterizes the category of Roman lettuces. Lettuces are sometimes annuals, sometimes biennials; when the time comes to flower, a numerous-branched stem rises from the center of the leaves, ending in flower-head cymes. These bear only a small number of light yellow flowers, followed by flattened elliptical fruits (achenes), sometimes white, sometimes black, which are improperly called seeds; they retain their germinative powers for four to five years. APPLE LETTUCE Varieties. - These lettuces, all of which form more or less globular apples, have leaves of infinitely varying size, color and degree of division of the leaf blades. They constitute varieties whose hardiness and consequently cultivation requirements differ greatly. They are subdivided into spring, summer and winter lettuces, but this classification is by no means absolute, and almost all varieties can be moved from one category to another, provided they are cultivated appropriately. The most commonly used varieties are as follows: Spring varieties. These varieties have the characteristic of developing rapidly, making them particularly suitable for either forced cultivation or cultivation in the open ground, in a sheltered situation. Because of the short time they take to develop, they are unsuitable for summer cultivation, as they quickly flower under the influence of high heat. GOTTE LETTUCE WITH WHITE SEEDS. - Low-growth variety. Leaves are soft green, turning yellowish in parts exposed to direct sunlight. The plant is stocky, forming a small apple on the ground. Despite its small size, this variety is widely used, especially in forced cultivation, where it is particularly useful for its rapid development. It is hardy and, in a sheltered location, can withstand the cold of winter. GoTte A GRaINE NOIRE. - Differs from Y - 4 Fig. 66. - Black-seeded gotte lettuce. by the color of its seeds and its even greater earliness. It is widely used in market gardening, although its head never becomes hard (fig. 66). CREPE LETTUCE WITH BLACK SEEDS. - Light foliage, slightly more developed than in the preceding varieties; widely used for early vegetables. GEORGE LUEE. - This variety, which is still more or less confined to market gardens around Paris, is taking on a greater growth habit than all those mentioned above; despite this, it lends itself very well to forced second-season cultivation. It is the most suitable lettuce for the first spring planting. Summer and autumn varieties. All the varieties included in this second category are characterized by the fact that they flower less quickly than the preceding ones, and are therefore more resistant to the heat of the summer season. LAZY BROWN LETTUCE. - A vigorous plant with ample, dark-green foliage marked with reddish-brown, forming a hard head. Its name comes from the fact that it is slow to bolt; its seeds are black. PALATINE LETTUCE. - This variety, also known as L. rousse, forms a head with numerous leaves colored reddish-brown on the outside. Its seeds are black. These two varieties are the most widely grown around Paris, and are easy to sell at market stalls. LAITTE BATAVIA BLONDE. - Batavia lettuce forms a bulky, medium-hard head. Its leaves are embossed and toothed at the edges. The Batavia breed of lettuce has given rise to numerous variations, some of which are very similar to Romaine; they therefore represent a sort of transition between the two types, Lettuce and Romaine. Winter varieties. This group is made up of hardy plants that can easily overwinter in the open air in the Paris climate. The product they produce is of a less delicate quality than that produced by the two preceding categories, but their ease of cultivation, and the early spring produce they produce, make them much sought-after, particularly in rural potasers. PASSION LETTUCE. - This plant has dark green leaves with red spots. The head is medium-sized and rounded. The seed is white. All DYBOWSRI. - Vegetable cultivation. 20 varieties, this is certainly the hardiest. It is only suitable for winter cultivation (fig. 67.). LArue MoriNe. - Variety with weaker development than the preceding ones, bearing very ample green leaves. Hard, full apple. White seed. Uses. - Lettuces are all used in salads: they are all the more sought-after as their leaves are softer; for this reason, those supplied by forced cultivation are generally more highly esteemed than those grown in the open air. Fig. 67. - Passion lettuce. They are also eaten cooked and variously seasoned. Growing in the open air. - To be able to plant lettuces early in the spring, they should be sown in the autumn and overwintered under cover. Pancake, gottes and Georges lettuces, which are usually used in this way, should be sown in the second half of October. Sowing is done broadcast, on top of an old layer of potting soil; lightly baste, and emergence takes place after four to five days. As soon as the cotyledons are well developed and the first leaves begin to appear, it's time to transplant. This can be done under cloches or under a frame. In the former case, the soil is laid out in "ados", covered with a few centimetres of potting soil. Each bed receives three rows of cloches (fig. 68), under each of which 24 to 30 young lettuce plants are transplanted. When transplanting is to be done under a frame, the soil should be placed in the trunk so that it reaches approximately Om, 08 of the glass, and a distance of Om, 06 should be maintained between the plants. After transplanting, lightly baste the plants, then, when they have recovered, give them air until the day when the cold begins to set in, it becomes necessary not only to keep the cloches and frames closed, but even to surround them with litter or leaves and cover them with straw mats at night. Once the frosts have passed, air is gradually introduced to accustom the young plants to its action. Finally, in February, later or later depending on the severity of the year, we completely remove the shelters, leaving the young plant, which by then has three or four leaves, exposed to the air for a week or so, after which it can be definitively planted out in the open air. The first plantings are made in a well-sheltered hillside; then, from the first days of March, you can plant in a square. The soil should be well loosened and rich in potting soil. Transplanting is done in staggered rows Om, 20 or Om, 25 apart, depending on the variety. A few radish seeds are often sown before transplanting. A few waterings are useful; they are given in the morning so that the excess water has time to evaporate before the cold weather that is to be feared during the night sets in. The plant thus preserved under glass can be used for successive plantings until April. This method of cultivation produces lettuces that develop rapidly and give hard, well-shaped apples. To follow on from this first season, Gcorges lettuces are sown either in the open air or under cloches at the beginning of March. The resulting seedlings are planted directly in a full square. Finally, in March, we start sowing Palatine and Lazy Lettuces, which we renew every two or three weeks to ensure sustained production. The last seedlings are sown in July and August, when other lettuces take over from the lettuces. Throughout the summer months, lettuces are easy to grow: they are sown in good soil and watered frequently, then transplanted into ploughed, smoked beds. At this time of year, however, lettuce plants need to be watered frequently if they are to give good results. For this reason, it is useful to cover the soil with a mulch to retain water and prevent it from drying out too quickly. In market gardens, lettuces are watered abundantly every day. Some lettuces, as we have said, can withstand the cold of winter, such as the Passion variety. This variety should be sown in the second half of September, in the open ground, with enough light to prevent the plant from withering. As soon as the plant has four or five leaves, it is transplanted to a good exposure, leaving a distance of about Om, 40 between the plants. After transplanting, watering is carried out to help the plant take root. In normal winters, there's no need to protect the lettuce plant, which will get through the bad season without a hitch; but if the thermometer falls to more than 8 or 10 degrees below zero, and if the plant is not protected by snow, it's a good idea to cover it with a bit of litter, which can be removed as soon as the cold has passed. At the end of winter, lettuce develops rapidly and can be harvested towards the end of March or in April. Sometimes, young lettuces are delivered for consumption when they have five or six leaves, either by using the remains of unused plants for this purpose, or by sowing them specially for this particular purpose. In these conditions, we use early varieties whose seeds are scattered either singly in a bed specially set aside for this purpose, or between other vegetables such as cabbages, beans, etc. This process produces what is known as "cutting lettuce", because it is harvested by cutting above the root; no special variety is assigned to this crop, but all can be used, provided they are fast-growing. Forced cultivation. - Lettuces, and in particular all fast-growing varieties, do very well with forced cultivation. As a result, this method of production has been very popular for many years now. Paris market gardeners produce large quantities of lettuces throughout the winter, some of which are sold at market halls, and a large proportion of which are exported abroad, where they command premium prices at this time of year. The varieties most frequently used are Laitues gottes, crêpes and Georges, the latter being reserved for the last crops grown under chassis. Market gardeners in Paris build the first beds for their lettuces around the middle of October. These layers are made by mixing equal parts of dry manure, preserved in millstones and known as annealed manure, with fresh manure. These piles are given a height of about Qu 40 and covered with potting soil to a thickness of Qm. !5. When the layer is ready for use, seven rows of gotte lettuces are planted, with seven plants per row, making a total of forty-nine lettuces per frame. The plant used for this purpose was sown at the end of August or the beginning of September, then transplanted under cloche as soon as the first leaf appeared. The same plant can be used for subsequent crops. These lettuces are harvested at the beginning of December, when the central leaves have begun to form a small head. As soon as the lettuce has been delivered for consumption, the frames and boxes are removed, the layer of potting soil is removed, and the manure is reworked by adding about half the original quantity of new manure. Care must be taken in this operation to mix the new manure thoroughly with the old to allow the mass to heat up again. When the layer is ready for use, forty-nine plants of lettuce from the autumn sowing are planted in the same way as before. At the beginning of February, or by the middle of the month at the latest, the lettuces are harvested, and the soil in the frame becomes free again, so a third generation of lettuce is planted, without the need to reshuffle the bed this time. Lettuces are usually sold by the hundred. The packaging consists of large conical handles, which market gardeners use to transport most of their vegetables. Many early lettuces are shipped abroad, usually by commission agents who come to the growers' premises to buy the lettuces on the spot. Selling prices are extremely variable, depending on the season. During the winter, lettuces are sold for 10 to 12 francs per cent, but this price is halved in the spring. ROMAN LETTUCE Although some botanists have thought it useful to separate the Romaine variety from the Lactuca sativa variety, making it the Lactuca romana variety, we see no reason for this separation. In the latter, the head, instead of remaining short and often almost globular as in the Lettuces, elongates into a kind of cylinder of varying height; but this characteristic alone is insufficient to make the Romaine a separate species, especially as it is not, as we have said, absolutely fixed. Uses. - Like head lettuces, Romaines are used to make salads. They differ in that the leaves are firmer and crunchier. Varieties. - The Romaines that are widely grown are not very different in appearance; however, each variety corresponds to a distinct cultivation method, so it's worth mentioning them here. They are distinguished less by their shape than by the coloring of the leaves. ROMAINE VERTE MARAICHERE. - A variety with dark green leaves. Used especially for forced cultivation. It has produced a form used by market gardeners, known as Romaine plate, because during the first period of vegetation the leaves form a sort of flat cup, then gradually rise to form a very large head. ROMAINE BLONDE MARAICHÈRE. - Light green leaves. This variety is used for outdoor cultivation (fig. 69). ROMAINE ROUGE D'HIVER. - Dark red leaves. This variety is used for outdoor winter cultivation because of its resistance to cold. Open-air cultivation. - As with lettuces, Romaine must be sown in autumn towards the end of September or beginning of October, so that it can be planted early in the spring. As soon as the plant takes its first leaf, it is transplanted, preferably under cloches, as we have indicated for Lettuces. Green Romaine and sometimes blond Romaine are used for sowing. Whenever the weather permits, i.e. when it is not freezing, it is advisable to give the plants some air by sowing Fig. 69. - Romaine blonde maraîchère. vant les cloches sur des crémaillères, sinon le plantait étioler. In mild winters, despite all precautions, the plant may grow too vigorously. In such cases, it is necessary to delay the growth of the plant by uprooting it and replanting it in the same place; this replanting causes a salutary delay in vegetation. Frames are rarely used to protect Romaine plants over winter; the use of cloches is infinitely preferable. In February, Romaine plants sown in autumn can already be used for costiere planting. In March, they can be planted in the open air in a square. For these plantings, the soil should be prepared by ploughing and covered either with a layer of compost or decomposed mulch. Romaines are planted at Om, 35 in all directions. Red Romaines are planted in autumn, like those just mentioned; but as they are hardy and resist cold well, as long as it doesn't exceed 12 to 14 degrees, they are planted directly in autumn. It's a good idea to plant them not in a square, but in a sheltered hillside. As soon as the days become warm and sunny in March, it's a good idea to water the plants, but this should be done in the morning, so that the excess water has time to evaporate during the day, and any frosts that may still occur at this time of year are not to be feared. When the Romaine apple is well formed, it is tied with a strand of rye straw, soaked in water beforehand, and pieced to make it completely supple. This binding must be done in dry weather, as it has the effect of hastening and increasing the whitening of the leaves making up the apple. Romames sown in autumn can be harvested towards the end of April or in May. To succeed this first season, Romaine blonde seedlings should be sown at the beginning of March. It's a good idea to shelter the seedling with a frame, and even use a bed if you're in a hurry to harvest. As soon as the plant has acquired four or five leaves, it can be transplanted directly into a well-smoked, mulched square. Watering must be as frequent as it is copious, if you want to obtain well-developed Romaines that don't flower until they have formed their buds. Sowing can continue throughout the summer months, without the need for a bed or even a frame from April onwards; but Romaine crops grown during the summer months do not do very well, so Romaine is usually not sown until the end of May. Later crops will only succeed if they are watered copiously. Watering should only be done in the evening or morning, and never during the day, as this could cause the Romaine leaves to stain. Forced cultivation. - Romaines do well in forced cultivation, provided they are placed under a bell and not under a frame, as is the case for lettuces. As a result of this requirement, this early crop cannot be grown in the dead of winter, as cloches provide less protection against frost than frames. The seedling to be used for bedding is sown in the first days of October, under a bell or under a lightly shaded frame, if the weather is fine. A fortnight or so after sowing, the seedlings are transplanted under a bell as described above. The seedlings are then kept on the bedding until the time is right to plant them out on the bed. Layers for Romaine cultivation are built up from the end of December to the end of February; they are given a thickness of about Om, 45 for the first ones and Om, 35 for the last ones. Equal parts of annealed and new manure are used. The layer is topped up with about Om, 18 of potting soil, then bells are placed on top of the layer, staggered in three rows. On these layers we plant either a single Romaine plate, or a Romaine verte and three Laitues gottes; but for some years now this second arrangement has been abandoned, as experience has shown that these lettuces harm each other. When planting, take care to make a sort of hole in the soil with the planting tool, so as to form an opening beneath the Romaine plant. This procedure ensures that the roots are not burned by excessive heat. In addition, at the edge of each bell, we push in a little of the compost to form a small opening in the soil, allowing the air trapped under the bell to communicate with the outside atmosphere. These aeration conditions are essential to obtain fully developed lettuces. For Romaine grown on beds in February, we plant one plant under each bell and another between the bells, exposed to the open air. As soon as the Romaine planted under a bell has been harvested, it is replaced on the feet planted in the open air. This process can produce two or even three successive seasons of Romaine in a single layer. Romaines are sold in bunches of four. At the height of the season, they are sold in bundles of thirty-two. Romaines de primeur usually fetch 2 francs to 2 fr. 50 per four in February and early March. But this price drops rapidly, and in spring the thirty-two plants are sold for only 6 to 7 francs, sometimes even less. Growing for seed. - To obtain good lettuce or Romaine seed, it's best to use either plants sown in autumn and planted in spring, or those sown early on the bed. In all cases, when the Lettuce or Romaine plants have reached full head, choose those with the best apples; remove them in rootballs and replant them at Om, 50 in all directions. As soon as the flowering stem rises from the center of the leaves, it should be staked, and it is often useful to remove the leaves at the base, which could rot and destroy the whole stem. When these lettuces have flowered, the seeds are protected by placing a bell (fig. 70) at the top of the stile supporting the plant, to protect them from rain and from birds, which are fond of them. These seeds retain their germination capacity for four to five years. Diseases and pests. - Apart from slugs, which are very fond of young lettuce plants, these lettuces also have to contend with aphids, some of which (Aphis Sonchi) attack the roots, while others attack the inflorescences, causing great damage. The former are controlled by frequent watering, the latter by spraying with tobacco water... Fig. 70 - Lettuce plant in seed, sheltered by a bell. Lettuce also suffers from another plant pest, which in recent years has wreaked considerable havoc on lettuce crops. This parasite is known as the Lettuce whitefly (Peronospera gangliïformis). Mr. Max. Cornu (I), in a comprehensive study he made of this parasite, found that the only way to preserve oneself from this parasitic fungus was to carefully avoid the spread of its spores. To do this, firstly, all lettuces in which the disease manifests itself intensely should be dried out and then burned, and secondly, the same soil should not be used for growing lettuces for several years in succession, as the germs may remain in the soil and produce a blight on the lettuces which (1) M. Max. Cornu, Etude des Péronosporées (Mémoures de l'Acad. des sciences, 1882). more or less accentuated spots of disease. No treatment applied to the lettuces themselves would be successful, for the reason that the fungus grows inside the plant, and the parasite cannot be destroyed without killing the lettuce carrying it. The symptoms of this disease are white spots on the underside of the leaves. Affected plants develop poorly and, in all cases, all diseased parts end up rotting. These ravages are most noticeable when lettuces have to be packed for a few days, as is the case when they are shipped abroad. It is not uncommon for seemingly healthy lettuces to rot completely after two or three days' packing. Gardeners can't afford to take too much care to get rid of this pest. Lamb's lettuce (Valertanella olitoria, Linnaeus) is a biennial plant, meaning that when sown in autumn, it doesn't bear fruit until the following year. This plant, generally indicated as indigenous, seems to be widespread in France only in the subspontaneous state. It has escaped from cultivation and become naturalized in our fields, particularly in clay and clay-limestone soils. According to de Candolle (1), its true home is Sicily and Sardinia, where it is found in pastures. From there, it would have been imported into our crops. In any case, as the same author points out, its use seems to be absolutely modern, as there is no mention of it in cultivation works published in the seventeenth century. Lamb's lettuce has opposite, spatulate leaves. Pairs of leaves are close together on the stem, forming a more or less compact rosette on the ground, depending on the variety. In the spring of the second year, the stems lengthen and branch dichotomously to form inflo(1) Origins of cultivated plants. 4 , FE. tas *- resences in biparous cymes. The purplish, cmq-parted flowers give rise to fruits which, containing only one seed, do not open. It is these achenes that are commonly referred to as seeds; they are gray and small in volume, to the point that one gram contains around a thousand of them. They retain their ability to germinate for five years. Uses. - The whole plant is eaten as a salad. It is a very useful crop in the countryside, providing produce throughout the winter. Varieties. - Lamb's lettuce has formed a small number of varieties, of which one in particular is widely cultivated and deserves to be so: it is the one used by market gardeners. ROUND MOSHE. - The leaves of this variety are shorter than those of the type; the spatula shape is more accentuated. It is often referred to as M. double, which is due to the fact that the buds in the leaf axils all develop early, forming a rosette that becomes more and more branched, resulting in a fuller plant (fig. 71). This variety is the most productive, due to the volume it acquires, and should therefore be sown clear in the field. We have produced a few breeds with thick, blistered leaves, which have the advantage of wilting less easily and therefore lend themselves to long-distance transport. These qualities make them particularly suitable for market sales. Cultivation. - Lamb's lettuce is always sown directly on site. The soil in which this DYBONSKI. - Cultivation, 2nd ed. 21 is prepared by ploughing, then harrowed and suitably levelled with a rake. The first seedlings are sown around the middle of August. The seed is broadcast, avoiding sowing too tightly; the most suitable proportion is around 100 grams per are. The seed is buried with a light rake, and the soil is covered either with a highly decomposed mulch, or with compost. Fig. 71 - Round lamb's lettuce. If the weather is dry, germination should be hastened by a few not too violent basinings, to avoid ravining the soil and dragging the seed along, which would concentrate in places and give uneven emergence. Eight to ten days after sowing, Lamb's lettuce appears with two small, rounded, glaucous-green cotyledonary leaves. About two months after sowing, in October, the first Lamb's lettuces are harvested. Harvesting is done by cutting lettuce stalks flush with the ground with a knife, taking care to remove the stalks where the sowing is too tight, so as to thin it out. All Lamb's lettuce sown in August must be delivered for consumption before winter, which they would otherwise be unable to withstand. To succeed this first season of lamb's lettuce, we have taken care to sow other crops. These, begun as we have just said, around the middle of August, can be continued until around October, by renewing them several times during this period to obtain successive products. In a pinch, three sowings can be enough to provide for consumption throughout the entire Lamb's lettuce season. The first, sown in August, will produce in October; the second, sown in September, will produce throughout the winter; and the Lamb's lettuce whose seeds are left in the ground at the beginning of October can only be cut at the end of the winter and part of the spring. We must be very careful not to sow the lamb's lettuce seeds too close together, otherwise they will rot, and this rot will spread from one plant to the next, creating patches of lack in the square. For the same reason, seedlings must be kept free of weeds by weeding. Chickweed is particularly harmful, as it quickly invades the whole crop. Lamb's lettuce doesn't fear frost, so it can spend the winter unprotected. However, to be able to harvest it, even in snowy weather and heavy frosts, it is useful to cover the beds either with straw or litter, or, preferably, with straw mats supported by small stakes fitted with transversely placed wooden slats. The great advantage of using straw mats is that they can easily be removed and replaced when the weather turns bad again. The result is an abundance of lettuce throughout the winter, so it's a good idea to sow a lot of it to make sure you don't run out. The market gardeners of Paris sèment la Mâche très en grand dans leurs terres, car c'est un des rares légumes parmi ceux qu'ils cultivent, qui supporte les atteintes des gelées. Seeds. - To harvest the seed of this plant, seedlings sown in September are allowed to overwinter, taking care to remove any plants that are insufficiently doubled due to the weak development of the lateral buds into a rosette of leaves, as well as any whose leaves are too long and not very fleshy. Lamb's lettuce starts to flower in May. Once flowering is over, you need to keep an eye on when the fruit begins to ripen, as it falls off with the greatest of ease. When the plant starts to turn yellow, pull it up and lay it on a tarpaulin or canvas of some kind, so that the fruit can ripen and be easily removed by light beating. It's a good idea to label the bags with the date of harvest, as experience shows that while a two- or three-year-old seed will germinate in ten or fifteen days, a one-year-old seed will often take nearly a month to germinate. ... ..." ... ... . .. .. . . . .... . . MELON In gardens, Melons present themselves in such a multiplicity of forms that many botanists, on the basis of the fact that the plant had been found in the wild in various forms, felt authorized to classify all cultivated Melons into a number of different species. This question was taken up again in 1859 by M. Naudin, who after studying it experimentally and cultivating no less than a thousand Melons from all parts of the world where this crop is widespread, published a remarkable memoir (1) in which he links all cultivated Melons to Linné's Cucumis Afelo, whose innumerable forms should consequently only be considered as varieties, or races that can be perpetuated by sowing. The reason why melons, which grow wild in different parts of the world, have been made into several species is that this plant, which has the property of infinite variation, can take on very different forms. It is this very property, once well studied and understood by Mr. Naudin, that enabled him to link all melons to a single primitive type. (1) Ann. des se. nat. S. 4, vol. XI. All melons have this property of extreme variation, so much so that it is often very difficult to preserve pure varieties in cultivation. Soil, climate and cultivation methods are all causes whose influences are immediately felt not only in our cultivated melons, but even in those that seem to grow spontaneously. What's more, this plant hybridizes very easily, and it is rare for several varieties grown in close proximity to each other not to exert reciprocal influences due to pollen transport by insects. Melons have been found in a truly wild state in two distinct regions: in Africa, on the banks of the Niger, and in Asia, in English India. Melons are annual plants that can, in special circumstances, become perennial. Their long, sarmentose stems sometimes crawl along the ground, and sometimes climb up whatever supports are within reach; they hold themselves in this position by means of tendrils, which are stipules or the result of transformed axes. The leaves of Melons, arranged in alternating order, are webbed and covered with abundant hairs, as are the branches. The leaf blade is divided into five rounded lobes, more or less deeply incised depending on the variety. Melons are monoecious plants. Male flowers appear first, and are yellow with five divisions. Female flowers have an infertile ovary covered with long hairs when young. The fruit to which the female flowers give rise behaves very differently, depending on the variety under consideration, and also, for the same variety, on the conditions in which the plant is placed. In all cases, it's a voluminous berry containing a considerable number of seeds arranged in its early stages on three placentas, from which they detach when the fruit is ripe, and which are then found swimming in a kind of liquid thickened by the debris of the placental part, which has become deliquescent. As we have said, the general shape of the fruit varies greatly from one variety to another, as does the state of the surface. M. Naudin, taking these characteristics into account, has classified all melons into ten different categories. For those of us who are concerned here only with varieties of general cultivation, recognized by all as being the best, we will content ourselves with indicating two of these categories, which include all the melons usually grown in gardens. I. - CANTALOUPE MELONS. Varieties. - Cantaloupe melons produce fruit that is usually large in size. These fruits are marked by deep grooves which divide them on their surface into more or less pronounced segments, or ribs. The epicarp or rind of the fruit bears wart-like asperities, varying in number and size according to variety. The flesh is red or orange-red, with a pleasant, delicate fragrance. MELON NOIR DES CARMES. - A productive and remarkably early variety, particularly suited to early fruit production. The fruit has a diameter of about Om, 15 to Om, 18; it bears few warts, its flesh is dark red and of very good quality. MELON PRESCOTT A FOND BLANC. - Vigorous plant producing fruits from Om, 25 to Om, 30 in diameter. Prominent ribs covered with large warts (fig. 72). Flesh orange-red, sweet and very Fig. 72. - Prescott cantaloupe melon with white base. fine. Unquestionably one of the best melons, if not the best of all. It is suitable for market gardening, where it is commonly used. It has a sub-variety with smaller fruit, less prominent ribs and dark green mottling. This is the prescott petit hâtif melon, which is very well suited to early cultivation. There are a great many other sub-varieties of prescott melon, which need not be described because they are local. Since melons are essentially plants subject to variation, any gardener who cultivates them over a certain number of years can create a special variety for himself through selection, once he has recognized its real qualities. II. - EMBROIDERED MELONS. Varieties. - Embroidered melons differ from the previous varieties in that the ribs on the fruit Fig. 73. - Melon sucrin de Tours. are much less prominent. Their surface has no warts, but is covered with a network of sinuous, protruding lines that give the skin a mottled, often grayish appearance. The flesh, although not as thick overall, nevertheless provides a roughly equal quantity of edible material for the diet, because the bark is not very thick. The flesh is less orange-red than in cantaloupes; it is also often white or greenish. Although sweeter than melons in the first category, it lacks the finesse of cantaloupes. These melons are less prized than those described above. They are grown mainly in the south of France, where their hardiness makes them ideal for open-air production. MARKET MELON. - Medium-sized, yellowish-green fruit with shallow ribs. Musky flesh, quite pleasant to the taste, hardy variety. SUCRIN DE TOURS MELON. - Fruit with shallow ribs, covered with conspicuous embroidery. Fruit diameter usually around Om, 15. Firm red flesh of very good quality (fig. 73). CAVAILLON MELON. - Vigorous plant producing oblong fruit covered with sparse embroidery, particularly in the grooves of the ribs, which are not very pronounced. Very sweet, fragrant green flesh. This variety is especially suited to cultivation in the south of France and Algeria, as its fruit is rarely of good quality when summer heat is low. There are several different forms of this variety, some with green flesh, others with red flesh. All are suited to southern cultivation. Cultivation. - Melons are plants that only vegetate and bear fruit if they are kept at a constantly high temperature; the slightest chill is enough to damage the vegetative organs and compromise any fruiting. For these reasons, it is only in the climate of the South of France that these plants can be grown in the open air, and even then it is necessary to let the season of white frosts pass before entrusting them to the action of the open air. In the climate of Paris, cultivation in the open air is rarely practiced, as the yield is too random. We are obliged to compensate for the lack of atmospheric heat by supplying it artificially. At any time of year, this type of cultivation can only be carried out on beds, but these will vary greatly in their construction according to the time of year at which you wish to operate. Melons lend themselves very well to forced cultivation, so they can be grown very early in the season, provided you know how to vary the circumstances according to the needs of the moment. In all cases, melons thrive in rich soil, provided it is not too light. Soil alone is therefore unsuitable, and you'll get more vigorous plants and more beautiful fruit by mixing it in equal parts with good, free-flowing soil. Bedding culture. - Although, as we have said, provided the melons are given the warmth they need to thrive, they can be cultivated at almost any time of the year, in practice the first sowings on beds are only done in the second half of January. If you sow earlier, not only would you have to provide a lot of heat to combat the rigors of the outside air, but you'd also have to worry about insufficient light, which would be detrimental to the plant's development. In January, we build a layer to a height of Om, 60. The materials used for this construction consist of fresh horse manure mixed with about a third of annealed manure, i.e. preserved in millstones since the summer. When the layer has heated up and become uniform in temperature, the melon seeds are sown into the compost, which, as we have recommended, has been mixed with clean earth. These are either placed in troughs or pricked out one by one with a finger. It is advisable to sow seeds of very early ripening varieties at the same time as those of slightly later ripening varieties. For example, sow early prescott melons and white prescott at the same time. This will extend the harvesting season. As soon as the seed has been sown, cover the frame with thick straw mats to prevent heat loss. Five or six days later, the melons emerge from the soil, and the mats are removed during the day and replaced only at night. The young plant develops rapidly if the heat is around 25 degrees, and you can see its tigelle and the two cotyledons it carries, rapidly gaining strength. When the cotyledons are well-developed and the center

starts to emerge a young leaf, the time has come to transplant them. For this purpose, a new layer similar to the first is prepared. The seedlings are then transplanted either into the ground, at a distance of Om, 15 in all directions, or into Om, 10 diameter cups previously placed in the soil covering the layer. This second method is preferable, as it allows the young plants to be transported later without the slightest delay caused by transplanting. In all cases, the seedlings should be transplanted one by one, and pushed down to the cotyledons, so that adventitious roots can be formed over the entire buried portion. After transplanting, water lightly and close the trays, which can be left covered with their mats for the first day, to help the plants take root. After a few days, the young melon plants produce their first leaves. When there are three of them, it's time for the first pruning. This is done about 1 cm above the second leaf. This operation is called "ététage", and should be carried out with a sharp penknife to obtain a clean, easy-to-heal section, and as soon as possible, since Fig. 74 - Melon plant having undergone first pruning. the section of an already large branch would heal badly (fig. 74). As soon as a new bud begins to develop in the axil of each of the two retained leaves, it's time to proceed with pruning. All these preliminary operations take between three weeks and a month at the most. Sown in mid-January, it's not until mid-February that the melons can be set. Setting out. - To proceed with planting, we build a new layer in the conditions we have indicated above. If only a small crop is to be grown, for example ten to fifteen frames, it is essential to build large stoves around the trunks, measuring around Om, 50. When, on the other hand, as in the case of Paris market gardeners, the crop is grown over a very large area, these stoves become unnecessary, as in these conditions there is no heat loss to the sides, and only the frames at the edge of the bed need to be surrounded by stoves. In all cases, the paths between the boxes should be filled with manure up to the height of the frames. Inside the chests, soil is placed, which, as we have said, must be mixed with potting soil to a height of about Om.20, so that there is only Om.15 of this soil on the surface of the glazing. Once the layer has warmed up to a temperature of 25 to 30 degrees, the plants are planted at a rate of two feet per frame. Some gardeners plant three plants, but this has its disadvantages, especially when growing vigorous, fast-growing varieties. If two plants are planted, the melons are placed along a line that divides the bed into two equal parts. If, on the other hand, three plants are planted, two are placed along a line drawn towards the upper third of the frame, and one along a line drawn towards the lower third. 1 - 4 Plants that have been raised in pots are removed from their pots and planted out, sinking them down to the cotyledons. The soil should be covered with a light layer of mulch. The buds in the axils of the two retained leaves soon elongate, forming two branches, one pointing upwards and the other downwards on the frame. Each of these arms, when sufficiently elongated, is pruned above the third or, better still, the fifth leaf. The result of this pruning is a new generation of buds; all those located in the axils of the retained leaves will deyelope, which means that the branches of this third generation will number six or ten. These branches often bear both male and female flowers. It's a good idea to fertilize these flowers, because if the fruits knot, if they develop, we'll gain time, but often they abort, so we remove them and prune again with two leaves in order to obtain fourth-generation branches which, in turn, will give abundant fertile flowers. We know that insects visiting flowers carry pollen from male flowers to the organs of female flowers, unconsciously fertilizing them. When forced cultivation takes place in the cold season, it is rare that the plants can be given air and that these insects can play their useful role. Artificial fertilization is therefore necessary. Taking male flowers from which the corolla has been removed, the pollen is shaken into the female flower (which can be recognized by the swelling below the flower, which is the ovary that will become the young melon). To proceed more methodically, you can take the pollen with a brush and place it on the stigma of the female flower. Fruit selection. - As soon as the young fruits, known as "maille" after flowering, start to swell, it's time to choose which ones to keep and remove all the others. Gardeners who want to obtain the best possible results leave only one fruit per plant; often, however, and particularly when the plants are vigorous, it is more advantageous to leave two fruits. In all cases, all others are removed at the latest when they are the size of a hen's egg. They can be pickled in vinegar, making a pleasant condiment. Preserved fruit must be chosen with the greatest care. They should be well formed and not have an overdeveloped eye, i.e. the point of insertion of the flower, which would later give them a defective shape. Fruit-bearing shoots should be pruned to one leaf above the point of fruit insertion. Later on, it will be necessary to ensure that no new fruit is produced, which can be removed as soon as they appear. For this reason, you should frequently visit the melon frames and remove any new branches that may develop. Melons like frequent watering, but this should be avoided until the meshes have been tied, as this could cause all the flowers to run off. Once the fruit is well formed, DYBONSKI. - Culture, 2nd ed. 22 the whole plant should be bathed frequently, avoiding pouring too much water over the base of the plant, which could cause it to rot. The water used should be at a temperature of 12 to 15 degrees. An additional harvest can sometimes be obtained by preserving a new, ripe mesh when the first fruit is almost ripe. This produces what is known as a "regain", which is more often than not a fruit of inferior quality. If, instead of keeping just one fruit, you prefer to leave two, you'll need to select them from two branches far apart to ensure that they come to the right place. Harvesting. - It takes an average of three months of cultivation before the fruit can be harvested. This may come sooner or later, depending on the warmth of the soil and the state of the season. You can tell that a fruit is approaching maturity when its color becomes lighter, and small cracks appear near the insertion of the stalk. The time has come to cut the fruit, which is done by removing a fragment of the stem that produced it. Melons should never be cut until they are absolutely yellow in color and have a strong odor, as they would then be of poor quality. Ripening generally takes place thirty to forty days after the knot is tied. Second-season cultivation. - To ensure continuous production, new melon seedlings are sown in February. These seedlings can be renewed and continued at three-week intervals until mid-June. This crop is grown under the same conditions as those described above. Melons should be given the same general care and pruning, but it should be borne in mind that as the season progresses, the temperature becomes higher, and that consequently, to provide the plants with the same degree of warmth, it is no longer necessary to make such thick layers. In April and May, a trench is dug in the ground, Om 25 to Om 30 deep and 1 m wide. The soil is thrown back to the right and left, and the trench is filled with manure. The soil is then placed back on top of the layer, where boxes and frames are placed. Finally, in May, with a similar layout, you can place bells 1.20 m apart on the trench, under each of which you plant a melon plant. As soon as the pruned branches begin to grow too long to fit inside the bell, it is lifted onto three racks and left above the plant until summer. Cultivation care is the same, i.e. straw the soil and baste frequently after fruit formation. Pruning is always the same. Growing in the Midi. - In the south of France and in Algeria, melons are easy to grow if you want to obtain fruit in the normal season. Seedlings are sown on a bed in April and prepared by transplanting into pots. From mid-May onwards, the melons are planted in the open ground on I-meter-wide tees, in the middle of which manure pots are made every 1.5 meters, on which the melon vines are planted. It is advisable to follow the same pruning methods as those described above, but in most cases only prune twice, after which the plants are left to their own devices. Under the influence of high temperatures, the vigor of the plant is much greater than in our artificial cultivations, and it is possible to leave two or three fruits on each plant without damaging the quality of the product. When growing varieties with embroidered fruit, this number is often exceeded, but it must be remembered that the size of the fruit is always inversely proportional to the number left on each plant. Choosing the seed carrier. - For seed, we choose the best-formed melon, with thick, well-colored flesh and a delicate fragrance. But if all these characteristics are of value, there is another which is perhaps of even greater importance: that the melon from which you wish to obtain seed should come from a garden where only one variety is grown. Melons are highly capable of hybridizing with each other, so if you're not careful, you may harvest seeds of perfect quality, but the following year you'll end up with nothing but degenerate plants. The influence of hybridization is of no importance when it comes to harvesting the fruit, but it is crucial when it comes to obtaining good seeds capable of perpetuating the shape and quality of the fruit that produced them. These seeds retain their germination capacity for five to seven years. Animal and plant parasites. - Melons are frequently attacked by parasitic animals that wreak havoc. On the one hand, there's the mite (Acarus cueumeris), which in practice is given the name "gray" because of the color it turns the attacked organs. It's difficult to get rid of, but the disease is alleviated by frequent drenching of the underside of the leaves with a decoction of labac or a light emulsion of black sayon and petroleum. - The same treatment can be applied against aphids, which attack young melon shoots. This plant still suffers from other diseases, the causes of which are still poorly defined and for which no effective treatment is known. These include canker, which eats away at the branches and sometimes the fruit; nail (I), or tissue rot; and powdery mildew, due to the presence of a parasitic fungus which is not very dangerous and which can be partially destroyed by applications of sulfur flower.
