His tools - spades, rakes, hoes - must be of various sizes, all solid, well fitted and easy to handle, so that they can never fail him when needed. The best spade for market gardening is the Flemish spade (figure 1), with a blade that is longer than it is wide, as wide at the bottom as it is at the top, not too heavy, sharp and slightly curved lengthwise. This peach, used since time immemorial by gardeners in northern France, is beginning to be appreciated and adopted in all market gardens; there is no other like it. Iron tine forks, straight or curved, are used for loading and unloading manure, making beds, digging up rooted vegetables, and giving the soil rapid and highly effective surface cultivation, especially in times of prolonged drought. Hoes, of which the market gardener usually uses two models, provide very good service; they only have the disadvantage of being very tiring for the worker, who can only use them by bending over in an awkward position. The square-bladed hoe (figure 2) is the most widely used; the two-toothed flat or bident hoe (figure 3) is advantageous in slightly hard soils that are not totally free of couch grass or other weedy roots. The iron-toothed rake is the market gardener's harrow; he needs rakes of various sizes, some made of wood, with slightly curved cylindrical iron tines, others made entirely of iron, with long pointed tines, close together, to work on compact soils whose surface needs to be precisely loosened and pulverized. One of the most useful uses of the rake in market gardening is to cover broadcast seedlings, mixing the seeds exactly with the soil on the surface of the beds, which, like carrots and onions, need to be very lightly buried. The hoe or serfouette (figure 4), armed on one side with two sturdy tines and on the other with a sharp blade, is the most practical of all gardening tools for hoeing and weeding row crops; this is its special purpose; it is also used to mark out gullies and open holes or pits for certain seeds whose volume requires them to be buried fairly deeply. The watering can, which the market gardener uses so frequently that it never leaves his hands, so to speak, from spring to autumn, must be neither too small, which would unnecessarily multiply the number of trips from the beds to the basin, nor too large, which would make it too heavy to carry: a capacity of 10 to 12 liters is the most suitable. Almost everywhere in France, the cylindrical Belgian watering cans previously used only in the North, and the old Parisian watering cans with their very bulging bellies, have been abandoned. The flat-sided watering can (fiZgure 5), which can be carried without spreading the arms, has rightly been substituted for some twenty years. A small portable pump (figure 6), whose spout can be fitted with a watering can at will, is useful for watering the beds closest to the basin, saving time and effort: the use of this useful instrument saves part of the labor involved in transporting the water to the site to be watered. To understand the importance of this saving, you need to have seen Parisian market gardeners, during the heatwaves, running around with a watering can in each hand, constantly keeping cool, during the longest droughts, naturally scorching soils, where everything would perish, if you stopped watering them for a single moment. Habit alone can make these robust and courageous men endure such hard work; it's a great thing to spare them at least some of it, with the help of the portable pump. Gardening tools are not the most expensive part of the market gardener's equipment; he needs a more or less considerable number of chests covered with glass frames for the beds, which are, so to speak, the soul of his cultivation. He also needs a good assortment of glass cloches and straw mats, either to cover the cloches and frames as needed, or to create temporary shelters by means of stakes planted in a line, from east to west, from which straw mats are suspended to form espaliers facing due south. With all his equipment in working order, the market gardener can begin his operations. Gardening operations. For the market gardener, as for the farmer, the most important operation is ploughing. In the market garden, ploughing is carried out all year round, and at all times; the ordinary depth of this multiplied ploughing is never less than the length of a spade iron (30 to 35 centimetres), when this instrument is used. The worker begins by digging a pit, from which he transports the earth with a wheelbarrow to the ex1. tremity of the plank by which he is to finish his work. This pit is what gardeners call the "gauge"; it's said of a good ploughman: "He spades well; we'd bury him in his gauge. Other, shallower ploughing is done with the square hoe, the bident, or the iron-tined fork. When the soil, which has been well loosened by one or more previous ploughings, is only hardened at the surface by drought, it can be shaped very well with the fork, which produces large clods that are easy to break up and pulverize with the heavy, pointed-tine rake. In such circumstances, this method is as good as ploughing with a spade. If it is necessary to repeat ploughing for each crop in the market garden, it is no less necessary to repeat weeding as long as weeds invade, and hoeing as often as a crust forms on the surface of the cultivated soil. This crust often becomes very hard after only a few days of drought following a heavy rain that has beaten or, as gardeners say, leaded the surface of the soil. If it is not divided by hoeing, it squeezes the root collar of the plants, significantly retarding their growth. As already mentioned, watering is of vital importance in market gardening. Parisian market gardeners have the principle that if a vegetable garden is not watered thoroughly, it would be better if it were not watered at all: so they never say "water", but "wet" the soil, pouring in 10 to 12 litres of water per square metre in the form of rain, and repeating this irrigation three or four times a day. In the North, and in our neighboring departments along the Atlantic and English Channel coasts, the frequency of rainfall means that watering is not as frequent or as extensive; in the South, watering with a watering can would be unbearable: market gardens are watered in the same way as irrigated meadows, by means of gutters through which water is introduced to thoroughly soak the vegetable beds. But we insist that watering too little does more harm to the soil than leaving it dry. Indeed, a small quantity of water poured onto weathered soil evaporates, cooling the surface layer before the cultivated plants have had time to take advantage of it; it would have been better for them to abstain from watering. Vegetables. In order for the vegetable gardener to understand exactly the needs of each type of plant under his care, and the special cultivation they require, he must arrange them in a methodical order, based not on their botanical characteristics, but on the analogy of the useful products he wishes to obtain from them. Considered from this point of view, vegetable plants are presented in the following order, arranged in four natural divisions: 4th section. - Plants with edible seeds; - - - Plants with edible leaves and flowers; Plants with edible fruit; Root vegetables. These plants are subject to special cultivation requirements, which are not very different for those in the same section. FIRST SECTION, Edible seeded vegetables, This section includes all vegetables in the botanical sense of the term. The common feature of these plants is the shape of the pods or siliques which enclose their seeds, and which in botany are called vegetables; for this reason, they all belong to the Leguminosae family. The first section includes beans, peas, broad beans and lentils. Beans. Brought to Europe from the Indies at a time when no precise date can be assigned, the bean has produced a wide variety of species through cultivation: today there are no fewer than 300. All have retained the temperament of the primitive species; all perish as soon as the temperature drops to just half a degree below zero. The bean, of whatever variety, can therefore only be grown in the open air from the moment it stops freezing to the moment it does not yet freeze. As far as cultivation is concerned, beans fall into two distinct divisions: string beans and dwarf beans. Originally, all beans were rowed, i.e. their long, voluble stems needed support, and wrapped themselves around the stems of neighboring plants: hence the need to row them. Some varieties, by flowering early and abundantly at the bottom of the stems, have lost the ability to grow taller: they have become dwarf beans. Among string beans, the first rank belongs to the white Soissons bean, with very large strings; then come the saber bean, which owes its name to the particular shape of its long pods, and the princess bean, the best of the many varieties known as mange-tout, because when the bean has already reached its normal volume, the pods are still tender and very tasty. The first two beans are grown mainly for their dry beans; the third is eaten fresh. Gardeners who grow beans to sell their dry beans are wise to stick to white beans and exclude colored beans, which are particularly suitable for large-scale cultivation; dry white beans always sell better than colored beans. There's a reason for this, well known to buyers: when not all the beans from the annual harvest have been sold during the year, and the old are mixed with the new, the cooking of this vegetable is uneven and difficult. On the contrary, it's very obvious with white beans: those from the previous year have a yellowish tinge that makes them stand out from the new, glossy white beans; there's no mistaking it. This consumer preference for white beans as a dry vegetable should prompt the market gardener to refrain from growing others, when their produce is not to be sold fresh. Beans require light rather than strong soil, and fear both extremes of drought and humidity. In the Paris climate, beans are sown from May 10 to 15, which is the best time to harvest them when they are fully ripe. If you intend to harvest only green beans and beans for fresh shelling, sowing can be continued fortnightly until July. Beans are usually planted in clumps of five or seven, depending on the size of the plants. The soil, ploughed and smoked as for any other garden crop, is furrowed with shallow lines, drawn with the hoe along a chalk line, some along the length of the garden beds, others across; the points where these lines meet mark the place of the bean clumps. The distance is 50 centimetres for large pole beans, and only 40 centimetres for dwarf beans. Open a hole 5 to 6 centimetres deep with a hoe, and throw five or seven beans into each hole, taking care not to let them touch each other. If a good supply of sieved wood ash is available, it's a good idea to throw a handful over the beans before covering them with soil; no soil improver has a more direct effect than wood ash or even peat ash on bean vegetation. When the soil is neither too dry nor too wet, the reams can be planted at the same time as the seed is sown. In lowland areas often swept by strong winds, the stalks are inclined in two rows, one towards the other, and attached two by two 1 decimeter from the top, which gives them great strength. If the soil is too dry, the bean undergoes half-sprouting which, for lack of moisture, cannot be completed; it languishes and never produces vigorous plants; if it is too wet and the temperature is not mild enough, it rots and does not emerge. Bean emergence is often hampered by the crust that forms on the surface of the soil following heavy rainfall after sowing; this crust must be broken up without delay, using the teeth of a very small hoe, otherwise the beans will fail to emerge. The best dwarf beans for market gardening are the hâtif de Hollande and the flageolet de Paris. The former wins for earliness, the latter for fecundity. This latter arrangement is preferable in cool soils, wherever the climate is subject to frequent rainfall: in this case, air currents are established between the rows of beans, encouraging the rapid evaporation of superfluous moisture. In a dry climate, it's better to sow in clumps, as the clumps form a thick shade and retain the soil's freshness better. When the soil is very damp and the climate very wet, both of which are unfavorable conditions for growing beans, you can avoid burying the seedlings and only place them at suitable distances on well raked soil. The soil is then placed on top of the beans in the form of a small eminence, so that they grow much better than if they had been buried. In Belgium, a particular method is used for bean sowing, which can be followed with advantage in all our departments north of the Seine. The soil, suitably ploughed and smoked, is levelled with a rake; then holes or "poquets" are dug at the required distances, according to the type of bean to be sown, in which nothing is sown. A barrel on a wheelbarrow is brought along the path separating the vegetable garden beds, filled with liquid manure or manure juice, mixed with diluted human fertilizer, a mixture known to northern farmers as Flemish fertilizer. Half a liter of this fertilizer is poured into each hole, after which the holes are filled and the soil raked, as if the pots had not been dug. A fortnight later, in the place corresponding to this liquid fertilizer, the beans are placed on the ground without being buried, and a little earth is brought in on top in the form of a mound to cover them. Their roots, meeting in the ground the fertilizer given to them, take full advantage of it, and the beans grow with exceptional vigor. When the beans are well established, they are given a first hoeing, followed by a second a fortnight later; it doesn't take long for them to cover the whole ground, which prevents further weed development. To save time and obtain early green beans in the open air, we sow early dwarf beans on a warm bed, under a frame, which we transplant into the field as soon as the outside temperature allows, and which then receive the same cultivation care as those of the same species sown in the field. Green beans and runner beans should only be harvested with care, either to avoid uprooting the plants, or to avoid dropping the flowers, which adhere poorly to the stalk. String beans grown as a dry vegetable should be harvested three or four times, as part of the pods ripen; without this precaution, a large proportion of the first-ripe beans would spoil in the pods and be lost. Beans destined for sowing the following year are kept in the pods; they are shelled only when ready for sowing. Contrary to the rules that apply to other crops, beans can be sown several years in a row in the same place without any noticeable decrease in yield, either in quantity or quality, and without any appreciable loss of soil fertility. Peas. Peas, which like beans originate in Asia, are slightly less sensitive than beans to the effects of the cold; they can withstand (with the exception of chickpeas, an entirely southern variety) a slight frost of one or two degrees centigrade. Cultivation has given rise to many pea varieties, though fewer than those of the bean. Gardeners distinguish between two series of peas, those with oars and those without oars, or dwarf peas; the latter are particularly prized for their earliness. The best row peas for market gardening are Champigny, Marly, Clamart and Knight's wrinkled peas. None of these peas is very early; all prefer light, sandy soil, smoked the previous year for another crop, to very fertile, recently smoked soil; in these conditions, peas of all kinds grow too much stem and leaf, flower little and give almost no grain. The best dwarf peas are the Michaux de Hollande, the earliest of all, the Prince Albert pea, and the Queen of the Dwarfs English pea, whose stem does not rise more than 25 centimeters. All these peas are precocious and perfectly suited to market gardening, occupying little space and giving way very early to other crops. It's worth noting that it's not in the market gardener's interest to grow peas all the way to maturity, except for those he intends to use for the following year's seedlings. He only cultivates peas for the purpose of harvesting fresh shelled peas, known as green peas; dry peas, which are used in considerable quantities for maritime supplies, are produced not by market gardening, but by large-scale cultivation. Row peas are only sown in spring, around the first half of March. They are sown in rows or bunches, like beans; five or six peas are placed in each hole; clumps are spaced 25 centimetres apart in all directions. When sown in rows, they are spaced 30 or 40 centimetres apart, depending on the presumed development of the plants. A little sifted wood ash sprinkled over the peas at sowing time is just as useful for them as for beans. Eight to ten days after the peas have emerged, they are given a first hoeing, then a second ten or fifteen days later, and the reams are placed. When peas are grown on a large scale, the oars are a fairly expensive item. For medium-sized species, this expense can be avoided by the following procedure. Between each row of peas and at the same distance, sow a row of bog beans, which grow at the same time as the peas, and whose straight, firm stems serve to support the flexible pea stems. This method of cultivation applied to Knight's wrinkled peas and Marly peas, which require very large oars, would give only mediocre results; the stems of the peas, rising much higher than those of the broad beans, would lack support at the top, and would not be very productive. Champigny peas, on the other hand, and all medium-height varieties, produce about as much when supported by rows of broad beans as when they are rowed, because the height of their stems only slightly exceeds those of the broad beans. Rowless peas can be sown at two specific times, at the end of November and the beginning of February. November seedlings can only be sown at the foot of a wall in a south-facing position. In mild winters, the central stem of the pea freezes alone, while the root resists; it returns to vegetation very early, and produces lateral stems which flower and bear fruit very early; but if the winter is a little severe, everything freezes. The same is often true of peas of the same dwarf, early varieties, sown in the first days of February. If they don't have a hard frost later on, they flower and bear fruit at almost the same time as peas sown in November that have withstood the winter. If they freeze, we hasten to replace them with seedlings sown in the same place in the first fortnight of March. When early dwarf peas are in full flower, cut off the tops of the stems, whose flowers are for the most part sterile; this removal hastens grain formation in the pods at the bottom of the stems. No matter how it is cultivated, early dwarf peas are never very productive; but when they are successful, the green peas they produce very early are sold at advantageous prices, and the land, quickly cleared, can be used for another crop; this is almost the equivalent of a catch crop. The chickpea, completely different from all other peas, is dwarfed and not very productive, except in the most southerly of our départements; its stem and leaves resemble those of the lentil. Chickpeas are sown in spring, in the same conditions as early dwarf peas; they flower little and are never very heavy. Its grain is rarely intended for consumption as a fresh vegetable; it is harvested as a dry vegetable, consumed princĩpally as a puree, with a very pronounced flavor, pleasant only for those accustomed to it. Broad beans. The broad bean, native to Egypt, is sensitive to cold to about the same degree as the poïs; we have several varieties, some with high stems, others quite dwarfed. High-stemmed beans are rarely grown in market gardens; they are grown mainly in open fields for maritim supplies. In vegetable gardens, they are mainly grown in large garden varieties, such as the N iarais bean and the Windsor bean, an English variety whose beans remain green when fully ripe. Among the dwarf varieties, the Julienne bean, early and of very good quality, is the most suitable for market cultivation. Two beans are placed in each hole, spacing the clumps 30 centimetres apart, in rows spaced 50 centimetres apart for large varieties, and 40 centimetres apart for dwarf varieties. When the plar nts are about 1 decimeter high, they are carefully hoeled and lightly buttressed. Later, if they are overgrown with weeds, they are weeded once or twice: then, when they are in full bloom, all the flowering tops are removed, to encourage the formation of beans in the lower pods, which are the only fertile ones. To speed up the bean harvest, you can sow them in a nursery, either under a bell or in the open air, at the foot of a wall facing south, from the end of January onwards; they soon sprout and give quite delicate seedlings that would perish if they weren't sheltered under a blanket of long litter every time it froze; you uncover the beans when it stops freezing. After the end of the extreme cold, around February 15th, weather permitting, the beans are transplanted indoors, two by two, observing the same distances as for in-place sowing. This procedure saves eight to ten days on the natural vegetative growth of beans sown in the open. The bean's enemy is the black aphid, which invades almost instantly, sucking the stems and leaves and killing the plant. If you notice it in time, and the area infested with black aphids is not too large, you can stop their disastrous multiplication by sprinkling the beans with a strong infusion of smoking tobacco known as caporal. Boiling water is poured over the tobacco, at a rate of 60 grams of tobacco per 10 liters of water; the infusion is used to water the beans as soon as it has completely cooled. The market gardener does not let the beans ripen; they are harvested green and sold as a fresh vegetable. A curious experiment, which anyone can verify, consists in cutting the stems of early-growing broad beans at ground level as soon as the green pods have been harvested; the stump immediately sprouts new stems, which flower and bear fruit before the end of autumn. When the beans are about half the normal height for their species, Milan or Brussels sprouts are planted in the gaps between the rows, or carrots are sown; as soon as the bean crop is removed, the land is taken up by another crop, and no time is lost, without any reduction in the fresh bean product. Lentils. Lentils are rarely used in market gardening, because they are the least productive of the leguminous vegetable plants; they flower very little, and each of the pods that follow their flowers contains no more than two seeds. On the other hand, lentils, never eaten as a fresh vegetable, are the most nutritious of all pulses. The plant is native to Asia; Scripture attests that lentils have been cultivated for human consumption in Eastern countries since ancient times. Lentils are sown in the same way as bush beans, under the same soil and fertilizer conditions, and with the same spacing between clumps. The plant must be hoeed at least twice and carefully weeded; it is very sensitive to weeds. The cultivation of lentils is only mentioned here because of the excellence of their seeds; they are so unfruitful that their yield barely covers the cost of cultivation. Those that are commercially available are the product not of market gardening, but of field cultivation. Two distinct species of lentils are grown, the common lentil and the queen lentil; the grain of the latter is grayish-brown, smaller than that of the common species, which is the more widely cultivated of the two. PLANTS WITH EDIBLE LEAVES AND FLOWERS. This section includes a wide variety of vegetable plants belonging to botanical families far removed from one another. These plants occupy a very large place in the market garden and in the cuisine of all European peoples. The vegetable plants whose leaves are eaten are, firstly, cabbages, celery, cardoons, rhubarb, sorrel, spinach, tetragonia, asparagus and salads; and secondly, parsley, chervil, tarragon and civet. These last two plants are mainly grown as salad accessories. There are only two vegetable plants whose flowers are eaten, but their cultivation is one of the most important: cauliflower and artichoke. Cabbage. Cabbage, a member of the Cruciferae family, is one of the oldest cultivated vegetable plants. The health-giving properties of this plant, in addition to its edible qualities, had not escaped the notice of the ancients: history records that, during the four centuries when Rome dispensed with doctors, cabbage, in various forms, but above all as a herbal tea, was the only medicine against all illnesses. This harmless remedy had the merit of letting nature take its course, and of not preventing healing when the ailment was not fatal in itself. The main varieties of cabbage used in market gardening form several groups, including: 1° cabbages with round heads, smooth leaves and blistered leaves, the most esteemed of which are Alsatian white cabbage, sauerkraut cabbage or quintal cabbage; red cabbage, similar in all respects to the above, except for the color of its violet-red leaves; Milan or Savoy cabbage, also known as curly cabbage, with its many sub-varieties, and Brussels sprouts. 2nd group: cone-headed cabbages, the best of which are the cœur de bœuf or pain de sucre; the Y'ork cabbage, the most delicate of this series; the Pomeranian cenic cabbage, good and very voluminous. 3rd group: green cabbages, all of which have in common the characteristic of not peeling, of remaining constantly green, and of withstanding the cold without shelter in the open air. The best green cabbages are: green curly, variegated curly and tricolored curly. The cabbages in this group are the most restricted in use; they are grown only in market gardens in northern France, on the borders of Belgium, where they are widely cultivated and highly prized. All cabbages thrive in strong, fertile soils, with abundant manuring from horned cattle. The soil must be prepared by two deep ploughings; the lighter it is, the more manure needs to be ploughed into it for the cabbages to form large, tender apples. Cabbages, whatever their variety, cannot be sown in the field. The seedling is raised in a nursery and planted permanently when sufficiently developed. When the cabbage plant obtained from sowing has taken its first leaves, it is transplanted in rows, 8 or 10 centimetres apart in all directions. Here, it gains strength for twenty to twenty-five days, while awaiting final planting. It's always a good idea to plant only cabbage plants that are already strong; they always produce the best results. When the soil in the market garden is only mediocrely fertile, as is the case in recently created marshes, to obtain the most beautiful cabbages, you must water them once a week with a watering can without a sheaf, using liquid fertilizer. Cabbages are such a healthy and sought-after vegetable that the market gardener must ensure that markets are supplied with them at all times of the year. To this end, he sows cabbage seed in spring, in the first fortnight of March, which gives him good seedlings to plant in May; he thus obtains summer cabbages delivered for consumption in July and August. He sows a second time in April and May, to have seedlings to transplant in June, whose apples, formed in September, October and November, are kept for sale throughout the winter. A final sowing takes place from August 15th to September 15th, earlier or later, depending on the temperature; sowings are delayed when late summer droughts are prolonged. The seedlings from these sowings are transplanted into beds at the foot of a south-facing wall; if sheltered with straw mats or long litter, they overwinter well in the Paris climate, and can be planted very early in the spring. Conical-headed cabbages are the best for these late sowings; they form their heads the earliest the following spring. By adopting this method, the market gardener has cabbages to sell almost all year round. Brussels sprouts require special care. This cabbage, which belongs to the Savoy cabbage group, always ends up forming a small head at the top of its very tall stem, but it is not grown for this purpose. The armpits of its leaves give rise to very small, hard, tightly packed cabbages of excellent flavor, which have the property of withstanding the cold very well as long as it does not exceed 5 or 6 degrees, especially in a situation sheltered from the north winds. Brussels sprouts can therefore be harvested successively, and markets can be supplied with them for most of the winter. For this purpose, first sow in March to obtain seedlings for planting in May, and harvest small cabbages in September and October; sow a second time in May: the seedlings from these latter sowings give good seedlings for transplanting at the end of June. Brussels sprouts from the last planting are lifted into a clod at the start of winter and placed in a gauge at the foot of a wall facing south, where they can be kept until the end of winter. In this way, Brussels sprouts can be harvested in March and April, and sold with advantage at a time when there are hardly any other fresh vegetables to bring to market. Celery, a member of the Umbelliferae family, is nicknamed "the good herb" in the south of France, where it is found in abundance among the grasses of the damp meadows near the Mediterranean coast. Used as a seasoning, celery facilitates the digestion of a wide range of dishes; it particularly counteracts the cooling properties of certain salads with which it can be combined. Several species of celery are grown, the most prized of which are common, white, red, pink, curly and celeriac, a species entirely different from other cultivated celery. Celery is sown in a nursery, in the open air, in a bed with a southern exposure; the seedlings must be light, so that the plant has become robust by the time it is put in place towards the end of May. Celery is only really good and suitable for its intended use when it has been blanched by shrivelling. To this end, prepare the ground for transplanting as follows. After ploughing it thoroughly and smoking it extensively, we divide it into planks one meter wide, but without separating the planks by paths. From two to two planks, the earth is removed and an ados is formed, resulting in pits alternating with ados: the depth of the pits should be 35 to 40 centimetres. In each pit, four rows of celery are planted, in lines spaced 20 centimetres apart; the plants in the lines are 25 centimetres apart; they must be watered abundantly. As the celery grows in length, the leaves are tied together with rushes or rye straw, and a first ridging is made using some of the soil from the ados. The plant, which you must not tire of watering unless the weather is rainy, continues to elongate; you successively give it a second tie, a second ridging, and later a third, so that all the soil put in ados is used up. The ribs of the celery leaves become white and tender as they wither, while their warm, aromatic flavor softens and becomes more pleasant. At the onset of winter, celery plants are removed in clods, without untying them; their roots are planted in fresh sand, either in the cellar or in a damp-free place where frost cannot reach them; celery will keep there until spring. If you want to grow celery all year round, sow the seed in January and February, so as to have enough seedlings to plant as soon as the weather permits. Celery root, an excellent species widely cultivated by market gardeners in Belgium, Holland and parts of Germany, is little grown in France, because it is rarely used in French cuisine. The seed is sown either on a bed or in the open air, like that of common celery; it is planted in rows, 30 centimetres apart in all directions; it does not need to be ridged. 2. As celery root can only grow and produce good yields with watering, each bed is surrounded by a projecting edge, so that water from watering cannot run off into the paths separating the beds. The useful part of celery is not the root, but the root collar, which, in good, well-smoked soil, watered relentlessly, becomes very voluminous. Celery root from the latest plantings is kept in the cellar, like common celery: it can be delivered for consumption throughout the winter. Before starting to grow this type of celery, the market gardener must make sure that he will find a suitable placement for it; although it is an excellent vegetable, it is not suitable for all consumers. Cardoon. Cardoon, which might just as well be called thistle, since it is a true thistle like the artichoke, its close relative, is, like celeriac, a vegetable that the market gardener should cultivate only with reserve, and by consulting the state of the market. It's eaten all over France, especially in the big cities; but it's rarely eaten, and if too much is produced at once, it may be difficult to find a place for it. Several species of cardoon are grown, all native to southern Europe. The most esteemed are: cardon de Paris, the best of all, cardon d'Espagne, cardon plein and cardon de Tours. The latter, although as good as the others, is less cultivated, because its leaves are armed with prickles that are more or less troublesome for the gardener. n 1 Atiud mtâ-h miemad et Cardoon, a member of the Compositae family, sinks its roots deep into the soil. When the soil has been well ploughed and fertilized, lines are drawn lengthwise and widthwise, 80 centimetres apart in all directions. At the points where these lines intersect, pits 50 centimetres in diameter and 30 centimetres deep are dug and filled with half-decomposed manure; a layer of loam one decimetre thick is spread over the well-trampled manure. Sow three cardoon seeds in each hole, to obtain three plants, of which the two least vigorous will be removed later. Sowing in place in this way should only be done in April, when any return of late cold weather is no longer to be feared. These seedlings are transplanted from May 10 to 15, under the same conditions of fertilization and spacing as for sowing in situ. Cardoon seedlings need to be watered every day it doesn't rain; this seed only sprouts after thirty days. As the seedling develops quite slowly, you can make use of the intervals by growing radishes and chervil, or transplanting early lettuce seedlings. These can be harvested before the cardoons have taken over the whole field. The leaves, whose fleshy ribs are the only edible part of the plant, only reach their full length towards the end of September, when the seed has been sown. At this point, they need to be bleached. Once the leaves have been bundled together with three ties of rye straw, they are covered with a shirt of straw, the spikes of which must be in their natural position; the shirts are held together with three ties; the thicker they are, the more rapid and complete the leaf erosion. To keep the straw in place, the base of each tuft of cardoon is mounded so as to cover the bottom of each straw sleeve with earth, which keeps it in place even in strong winds. We don't blanch all the cardoons at once; once etiolated, they would soon rot; we only blanch the quantity that needs to be sent to market each week. Rhubarb. The petioles or tails of the leaves of various rhubarb varieties, and the jams made from these cooked leaves, sieved through an iron sieve and combined with sugar, have not yet taken on the same importance in French cuisine as they do in English. Near Paris, Tours, Montpellier and other towns inhabited for part of the year by numerous English families, it will be to his advantage to grow rhubarb in proportion to the presumed output; elsewhere, the product of this crop would not sell. Several varieties of rhubarb are grown, the most popular of which are the early Ayton, the wavy rhubarb, the Prince Albert and the currant rhubarb. Rhubarb, a member of the Polygonaceae family, multiplies by separating rooted offshoots. Nothing is hardier than this plant, which thrives in all soils and exposures; as the plant grows, it must be planted at a distance of one meter in all directions. As the leaf ribs or petioles lengthen, the base of the plant is milled to whiten them; the leaves are harvested for sale, leaving only those closest to the center, which grow and are picked in turn. When rhubarb is ready to flower, a bud forms in the center of the leaves, destined to become the plant's flowering stalk; it has been suggested that this central shoot should be processed like cauliflower. Although this vegetable has been highly praised under the name rhufleur, we are among those who regard it as mediocre, incapable of competing with choufleur. However, it is necessary to point out that the word rhubarb wrongly awakens in the mind of the French consumer the idea of a purgative and a medicinal flavor. This flavor, as well as the medicinal properties of rhubarb, reside exclusively in the root; the ribs of the leaves and the central bud are completely devoid of it and have, all prejudices aside, no taste whatsoever reminiscent of pharmacy. Sorrel. Sorrel, a type of the rumex genus, is one of the vegetable plants that French cuisine can least do without. Although it does not nourish in the true sense of the word, cooked and chopped sorrel seasons eggs, meat and fish, and helps to digest them; its pleasant acidity compensates for what it lacks in nutritional properties. Several varieties of sorrel are grown, the best of which are Belleville sorrel and the broad-leafed Dutch sorrel. For summer consumption, we also grow virgin sorrel, so named because it produces neither flowers nor seeds. Sorrel can be propagated either by sowing in place, in the borders around vegetable garden squares, or by dividing clumps in spring. Near large cities, market gardeners plant entire beds of sorrel, with clumps spaced 25 centimetres apart, so that they cover the whole ground. As the first frosts approach, a thick bed of straw or long litter is spread over these beds; under this shelter, winter does not interrupt the vegetation of the sorrel, whose underdeveloped leaves sell for a good price throughout the bad season. Every time the weather gets milder, the cover is moved, to be put back in place in case of frost; in this way, the market gardener has tender sorrel to take to market all year round. The more sun sorrel is exposed to, the more acidic it becomes; it is milder when grown in the shade, with a northern exposure. Sorrel requires no cultivation care other than removing the flower stalks as they form: this is not necessary when only virgin sorrel is grown. Although a plantation of sorrel can last almost indefinitely, the plant being perennial to the highest degree, it is a good idea to renew plantations every three years if you want to obtain a constant abundance of good leaves. Like sorrel, spinach is devoid of nutritive properties, and does not make up for this defect with a strong flavor. Nevertheless, it is widely consumed in France, and its cultivation is indispensable in the market garden. Spinach is especially advantageous because of the short time it takes to grow, which means it can be used to fill in a garden square left vacant by another crop when the bad season approaches. Spinach, a member of the Atripliaceae family, is dioecious and biennial; it bears male and female flowers on separate stems, and does not set seed until the second year. Spinach seed is broadcast, either in spring or late summer. The products of this 3 crop are not sufficiently valuable to allow it to be tended and fertilized on its own; spinach benefits from the remains of the fertilizer given to a previous crop. Several varieties of spinach are grown, the two best of which are the round-seeded Dutch spinach and the Esquernes spinach, both with broader leaves and better taste than the common species. Spinach of these two varieties should be thinned out when fully emerged, so that the clumps are about 20 to 25 centimetres apart. The first frosts that hit spinach give the leaves a faded appearance and a semi-transparency that could make them look lost; to restore their good appearance, dip them for a good quarter of an hour in very cold water; take them out to let them drain well and lay them on the ground on clean straw, in a frost-free place. As soon as it has dried out, the spinach returns to its original state, making it just as good for cooking as if it hadn't suffered from the cold. Every year, a portion of the previous year's spinach is set aside as seed. The male plants are pulled out after flowering; the seeds of the female plants are harvested as soon as they have reached maturity. Tetragonia. This New Zealand plant, introduced to Europe towards the end of the last century, is so similar in flavor to spinach that, when cooked with the same seasoning, it is impossible to distinguish one from the other. Tetragonia has the advantage over spinach of not going to seed during the heat of summer; as we know, when spinach does go to seed, its leaf product, the only edible part of the plant, becomes nil. Despite this property, tetragonia is rarely cultivated in vegetable gardens, because the gap it is intended to fill, as a replacement for spinach, occurs in a season when the market garden is over-supplied with vegetables of superior value, which make spinach and tetragonia scorned. This plant is grown from point to point like spinach: it just needs to be sown very lightly, as its creeping stems take up a lot of space. Asparagus. Asparagus is one of the most important crops to grow in a market garden; its products are always sought-after and sold at a good price; there is never enough in proportion to demand. Asparagus, a member of the Aspariginea family, has a particular vegetation characteristic that must be taken into account before starting to grow it. It requires a lot of manure, and only begins to repay the gardener's advances with its produce after four years. Land that has previously borne asparagus, which has died of old age, can no longer produce asparagus unless it has been given over to other crops for 10 to 12 years; otherwise, asparagus refuses to grow there. It is therefore important to make sure that the land on which you intend to establish an asparagus plantation has not borne asparagus for at least 10 years; without this information, asparagus cultivation, carried out in the most rational way, on land that is best suited to this plant, may fail completely. Asparagus cultivation is not like many other garden crops, possible only in the vicinity of cities, where thousands of horses, either luxury or draught, make large quantities of manure available for gardening. The old method of piling up masses of largely wasted manure under asparagus is now abandoned; asparagus cultivation can produce excellent produce by absor3 bing as much fertilizer as any other garden crop, but nothing more. There are two methods for creating a large asparagus plantation, both equally good in terms of the final result: sowing in place, or planting out. In-place sowing is more economical; it's the procedure generally followed in very large-scale cultivation. Here's how it works. The entire plot is divided into one-meter-wide beds, as for celery. From every other bed, 25 centimetres of soil is removed and transferred to the next bed, creating a series of pits alternating with ados. The bottom of the pits is broken up with a spade, and heavily manured with horse or cattle manure; cattle manure is the best. The soil, smoked and well levelled with a rake, is covered with a thin layer of only 5 to 6 centimetres of good loam from broken layers; the asparagus seed is sown in this loam, in three lines for each pit. The two lines adjacent to the edge of the pit should be 25 centimetres apart; the third line occupies the middle of each pit, at equal distance from the other two lines. The seeds are placed, two in each hole, 25 centimetres apart in the lines. When the seed emerges, the young asparagus, similar to a green thread, can barely be seen; weeding must wait until it is 5 to 6 centimetres high. Asparagus seedlings must be weeded by hand; this work can only be entrusted to attentive workers, otherwise part of the plant will be pulled up with the weeds. A second and, if necessary, third weeding is carried out to prevent the weed from smothering the asparagus plant. Ados are used to grow dwarf, early peas, York sprouts, dwarf beans, strawberries or other low-growing plants; the produce from these crops helps to wait for the asparagus crop. Every year, in November, the yellowed asparagus stalks are cut off at ground level, and a few centimetres of soil taken from the asparagus stalks is thrown back into the pits. In the spring of the second year, the asparagus beds are covered with half a layer of fertilizer, and weeded if necessary during the summer months; the same cultivation is continued in the following years; asparagus harvesting does not begin until the fourth year. From then on, well-established asparagus beds in good soil - light and sandy rather than clayey and compact - can remain productive for twelve to fifteen years without interruption. After five or six years, the asparagus plants have disappeared, and the beds are levelled: every year, 4 to 5 centimetres of soil are removed to replenish the asparagus beds. Soil is then taken from the place where the teenagers were, for annual replanting. When the asparagus plantation is exhausted, it forms its own ados separated by pits in which asparagus cultivation can be restarted, in new soil, with every chance of success. The soil of the asparagus farm, exhausted as far as as asparagus is concerned, is as fertile as its nature requires for all kinds of other vegetable crops. The second method differs from the first in only one respect: instead of sowing the asparagus seed in situ, we plant two-year-old asparagus claws raised in nurseries, which we place in the pits prepared as above, and at the distances indicated for sowing. Each asparagus claw consists of a bundle of elongated tubers called fingers, joined together on a central tray. When planting the claws, care should be taken not to spread their fingers too far apart, as they break easily, and to place them on a mound made of a handful of potting soil, so that there is no gap underneath, which could lead to mildew and delay their growth. In claw plantations, the first large asparagus should not be harvested until the third year, although by the second year there are some large enough for consumption. Asparagus plants harvested too early are ruined and have no future. The method of planting clumps of asparagus saves a year, but the high cost of clumps often makes this method inapplicable to very large-scale cultivation. Each year, the central plate from which the asparagus claw fingers extend rises and moves closer to the soil surface; it is this particular feature of asparagus vegetation that obliges the grower to replenish the asparagus beds with soil every year. If this depth is not taken into account when the asparagus is harvested, the tray can be attacked, killing a large number of claws just as their produce is about to reward the gardener for three or four years of careful cultivation. To cut the asparagus between two burrows, special knives are used, the use of which requires a certain degree of skill and experience. The work of harvesting asparagus should only be entrusted to a trained hand. A certain number of asparagus stalks laden with berries are left in the field a little longer than others, in order to let them ripen completely and harvest the seeds for sowing, either in the field or in a nursery. When the skin of these berries is wrinkled and the seeds inside are black, they should be picked. After letting them dry out completely in the shade, they are macerated in water for twelve hours. The pulp then separates from the seeds when the berries are rubbed between the fingers; the seeds, carefully washed and dried, are kept in a dry place until sowing time. Asparagus seeds are sown in nurseries in the second week of March, or a little later in late spring. The soil is prepared as for any other garden crop; the asparagus seed is sown clear, in rows spaced 25 centimetres apart; they should be covered with no more than a centimetre of finely pulverized soil; if it is buried too deeply, it will not sprout. When pulling out the young claws, either to sell them or to use them in plantations, the soil must be carefully lifted on both sides, so as not to break the fingers, which are excessively fragile at this age. Although asparagus has long been cultivated in Europe, it has not produced any distinct varieties. Common asparagus, Ghent asparagus and Ulm asparagus are considered sub-varieties, differing only in the volume of their stalks. If you sow the seeds of the very common wild asparagus along the Rhône valley, and on the banks of ravines throughout the south of France, and then cultivate the plant resulting from these sowings, under the ordinary conditions of good cultivation, you will obtain in three or four years asparagus that is very similar to the common species. Forced asparagus. When you have a large plantation of asparagus in full yield, you can force a part of it every year by the following procedure. At the start of winter, wooden boxes similar to those used for glazed frames for all forced cultivations are placed on the beds to be forced. Instead of glazed frames, as forced cultivation of asparagus requires no light, the chests can be lined with thin boards or frames covered with coarse canvas. The inside of the trunks is filled with good manure recently taken from the stable, in full fermentation without being too damp; the trunks are covered, and whenever it freezes a little severely, a thick blanket of long litter is thrown over them. Unless the cold is very intense and persistent, asparagus should start to grow after fifteen to twenty days. This is ensured by carefully disturbing the manure, and the asparagus is harvested as it grows, so that its top end takes on the violet hue it needs to sell well. We take advantage of the middle of the day, when the temperature is mildest, to momentarily uncover the forced asparagus beds; we cover them in the afternoon. If all the asparagus supplied by the beds subjected to this treatment is harvested, the claws are exhausted and the land must be given over to other crops. However, if the harvest is stopped in time, and each claw is left with a sufficient number of young shoots to repair its losses and regain its vigor, the forced beds can be planted again after a year's rest, during which they produce their usual quota of asparagus in spring, at the ordinary time of their natural vegetation. It goes without saying that in Paris and all major cities, asparagus forced in winter fetches very good prices. Not all the beds that need to be forced during a winter season are forced at the same time; in this way, it is possible to have very fine forced asparagus to bring to market, from mid-December until the time when the first asparagus can be harvested in the open air. Salads. Vegetables whose leaves are eaten raw, seasoned with salt, oil and vinegar, play an important role in market gardening, especially in France, where lettuce is widely consumed by all ranks of society. A military proverb says that when the drum beats to call the soldier to his main meal, his drumbeat means: soupe et salade, soupe et salade! The origin of the word salade is uncertain; the most likely opinion is that it derives from the name of a helmet of a particular shape, once worn by the soldiers of the famous Sah-el-Eddin, whom the Crusaders called Saladin. During the siege of Naples, the soldiers of Charles VIII's army, lacking salad bowls, put lettuces from the surrounding gardens into this type of helmet, which was then called salad. On their return to France, where they introduced the use of salad, they named the dish after the helmet in which they had begun to eat it. According to this interpretation, there is a fairly direct relationship between the name of Sultan Saladin and that of salad. Those who believe that this name derives from Italian, because in Italy lettuces have been grown and eaten from ancient times to the present day, seem to be mistaken; for Italians have always called lettuce insalata, a term that only remotely resembles the French word salade. In market gardens, lettuce and chicory are mainly grown as salads, with lamb's lettuce and raipons also being eaten. In the North, red cabbage is also eaten as a salad, sliced very thinly and sprinkled with melted butter and vinegar; but this salad is not very popular anywhere else, and even in the North, red cabbage is never grown specifically for salad. Lettuce is the salad par excellence. In many départements, when the word "salad" is uttered, it is lettuce alone that is meant. The innumerable varieties of lettuce produced by cultivation are naturally classified into two sections, that of round-headed lettuces, which are the lettuces proper, and that of elongated-headed lettuces, better known by their vulgar name of romaine. The first section is subdivided into several groups, according to the temperament of the sub-varieties, which makes them suitable for cultivation in different seasons. Round lettuce, like romaine, was not cultivated very long ago in France. Letters written by Rabelais to his patron Cardinal d'Estrées from Rome in 1527 show that he sent him the first lettuce seeds to be sown in France; lettuce cultivation did not become common in our kitchen gardens until the end of the same century. Round-headed lettuces are divided into three groups: spring lettuces, summer lettuces and winter lettuces. The best spring lettuces are: dauphine, cordon rouge and petite blonde. The best summer lettuces are blonde de Versailles, blonde laesseuse, belle et bonne, royale and Batavia cabbage lettuce. The latter, the largest and hardiest of them all, forms enormous apples; it is the one that is cultivated in large quantities to make it 3. consumed by the pores, whose fattening it promotes by inducing them to sleep. It is also from this lettuce that we extract, by chemical processes, the calming principle called Tridace, which produces some of the effects of opium, without having its dangerous properties. The best winter lettuces are crepe, gotte and passion lettuces. In the romaine section, the most esteemed are: verte hâtive, alphange, maraichère d'été and blonde de Brunoy. In addition to the above-mentioned lettuces and romaines, there are innumerable sub-varieties, recommended for various reasons, and more or less well suited to the soil and local climate of the cantons where they are grown. The cultivation of all round-headed lettuces is the same: the seed, sown on a bed in late winter, or later on a bed in the open air, produces a plant which is placed at varying distances according to the size of the species, from 25 centimetres for the smallest to 40 centimetres for the largest. When transplanting lettuces, great care must be taken not to crush the root collar, which has very little consistency. The soil is covered with a good mulch of long litter, to keep it cool. The success of this cultivation depends entirely on the possibility of watering the lettuces frequently and abundantly; as soon as they suffer from drought, they go to seed, even the lazy lettuce, which is the most difficult of all to set. Forced cultivation of winter lettuces is achieved by transplanting the young plant from the bed where the seeds were sown to another warm or simply cold bed, uncovered from its frame. The soil in the layer must be very close to the glass of the frame, so that there is as little air as possible between the lettuce and the inner surface of the glass panes: this is what market gardeners call growing lettuce "à l'étouffée". Crepe lettuce and gotte lettuce are not good salads when grown stewed; if you brought similar lettuces to the market in summer, they would not find buyers; but in winter, when there are no better ones available, they are always easily sold at a good price. Romaine is grown in the same way as round lettuce in the open air, except for one point. When it's windy, it naturally caps itself, as market gardeners say, i.e. its leaves fold over each other at the top. To ensure that the inner leaves become white and tender, the romaines should be tied with a straw or rush tie around the middle of their height. The need for watering is the same for romaine as for round lettuces; if romaine doesn't climb as easily when it lacks water, it becomes hard, and its leaves look much more like fodder than salad. Green romaine is fortified under a bell in spring as follows. The seed sown on a bed in January and February is transplanted under large melon cloches, on an uncovered cold bed set up at the foot of a wall facing south. On this layer lined with potting soil, the hords of the cloches are first marked, tracing circles close together. The romaine plant is transplanted into these circles with the same care as for the round lettuce plant. The bells are then placed back on the romaine plants, which, by this method of forced cultivation, never become very good or very large; they are nonetheless of very good quality, because all they meet on the markets to compete with them are the crepe lettuces and forced gottes, which are even inferior to them in quality. Chicory. Chicory, of whatever variety, is a salad that is always a little firm, and whose bitterness is not to everyone's taste; it is, moreover, very healthy, and possesses the valuable property of being easy to preserve for consumption throughout the winter. The main varieties used in market gardening are curly endive, the best of which are Italian, Meaux and Rouen; the latter is known as stag's horn because of the shape of its leaves. Another variety of whole-leaf chicory, widely used as a winter salad, is also grown under the names escarole, escarole and endive. It should be noted that while curly-leaf and whole-leaf chicories are mainly grown as salads, this is not their only use: they are also used cooked and chopped like sorrel or spinach, either on their own or as an accompaniment to other dishes, fatty or lean. Chicory cultivation is similar to that of the Romans. The seed, sown early on a bed or in a flowerbed at the foot of a south-facing wall, will not germinate if it is over-covered; it must be spread over the soil and a little potting soil sifted on top; for these first sowings, which can be done outdoors from the end of February, Italian chicory is the most successful. The seedling is planted out, watered and tied like romaine, so that the leaves in the center of the plant whiten as a result of shrivelling; if these leaves elongate sufficiently, they are joined together later by a second tie. Other curly-leaf varieties can be sown throughout the summer, until July. Care should be taken to bind these lettuces only when the weather is dry; if a prolonged drought makes it necessary to water them after they have been bound, only the watering can without its sheaf should be used, so that water can be poured at the foot of each leaf without wetting the head. Escarole, known as endive throughout northern France, is best sown in July and August than in any other season, its growth being rapid when sufficiently watered, and is successively tied in September and October; it turns white before the first frosts, and can be stored in a cellar or storeroom, protected from frost, as a winter supply; it is less afraid of the cold than of dampness. In the market gardens around Lille, escarole is whitened by a more expeditious process than binding: when the leaves spread out on the ground have reached their full length, the gardener joins them together at their tips, tilts them all to the same side, and with a spade throws enough earth over the tips to contain them: the heart of the escarole thus treated whitens in a short time, as if it had been bound. From the moment they have undergone this operation, they must not be watered again; this method only works in light, dry soil. In addition to the chicory varieties described above, wild chicory is also grown as a salad; but this is not a very profitable crop, and is grown more in the field than in the garden. The market gardener, however, sows wild chicory seed in the borders throughout the summer; as it emerges, the leaves, only a few centimetres long, are picked and sold to be eaten as salad; they are only edible during the first period of their vegetation; later, they can only be used as rabbit food. Wild chicory sown in the open field, in mediocre soil, at a rate of one kilogram of seed per are, is used to prepare a very healthy but somewhat tough salad in winter, using the following procedure. At the start of winter, chicory is carefully pulled up so as not to break the roots, which should be kept as whole as possible. The plants are peeled one by one; all the leaves are removed, except those of the central shoot. The chicory thus prepared is bound into bunches, with the collars of all the roots at the same level. These bunches are taken to a perfectly dark cellar, where they are buried, either upright or horizontally, in a layer of warm manure, or simply in moderately moist soil. The long, white, etiolated leaves soon develop, and are sold as talad under the vulgar name of Capuchin beard. Lamb's lettuce. Lamb's lettuce, also known by the vulgar names of dodder, wheat salad and hare's ear, is so common throughout the bad season in all winter cereal fields, that we could dispense with cultivating it in market gardens, where it never holds a very large place. If it's true that its name derives from the need to chew it for a long time in order to swallow it, we can see that it has always been considered a hédiocre salad. Lamb's lettuce can be sown in August and September, and even as late as October, when the good weather extends into the late season. The flatter and more fertile the soil in which it is sown, the less hard it is; frost softens it considerably; it is only when the lamb's lettuce has been subjected to a few days of severe frost that it produces a salad that is more or less edible: that's all we can reasonably ask of it. Rapunzel. Like lamb's lettuce, raiponce grows wild everywhere in France; its stems, laden with pretty blue bells, adorn the foot of hedges and the edges of woods throughout the summer. It is equal in all respects, except size, to the cultivated raiponce; the root, white and tender, has a nutty flavor; the leaves are as soft and less hard than those of lamb's lettuce. If you want to harvest wild raiponces at the most suitable stage of development, so that they can accompany lamb's lettuce or forced lettuce salads at the beginning of spring, you need to look for them in places where, the previous summer, you noticed flowering plants, whose seeds must have multiplied raiponces by natural sowing; the time for this search begins at the end of February and ends in the first week of April; wild raiponces lose their value as salads from the moment their flowering stems form. Riponce seed can be sown from spring to late summer; but the plant from spring sowing is prone to bolting in autumn; besides, raiponces from spring sowing are good to pick at a time when the best lettuces abound in the market garden. Sow in July, without burying the seed, which should only be placed on the surface of the soil, otherwise it won't germinate. The roots can already be harvested in part at the end of winter; as the plant is insensitive to cold, winter does it no harm; its young shoots, together with its roots, provide an excellent early spring salad. Parsley. Although parsley is only used as a seasoning, it is so widely used in French cuisine that its presence in the market garden at any time of year is considered indispensable. Only two varieties, common parsley and curly parsley, are generally grown. Unfortunately, the common parsley closely resembles the large and especially the small hemlock, and this resemblance has more than once given rise to deplorable accidents. The best way to avoid them is to grow only curly parsley, whose leaves bear no resemblance to either the common or common hemlock, and so cannot give rise to any fatal misunderstandings. Parsley seed is sown mainly in borders, from the first fine days of March. Patience is essential, as it takes 5 to 6 weeks to sprout. The plant flowers and goes to seed in its second year; but if you take care to prevent flowering by cutting the stems as they form, you can extend its life for three years. Near large cities, where parsley is in great demand in winter, a bed is sown with a southern exposure; as the first frosts approach, this bed is covered with straw or long litter, which is moved during the mildest hours of the day. With this care, parsley sown in the open air doesn't freeze, and winter doesn't completely interrupt the growth of its leaves. When sowing parsley in summer, with a view to harvesting the leaves in winter, it's a good idea to cover the seedlings with moss that is kept constantly moist. From the thirty-fifth day onwards, the seedlings are visited daily, in order to remove the moss and remove it completely as soon as the parsley has emerged from the ground. Chervil. Chervil is frequently used, mainly as a salad ingredient. Chervil is an annual plant, which goes to seed as soon as the first warm spells arrive. Consequently, seedlings should be sown in light, cool soil, with a northern or eastern exposure, every eight or ten days during the summer. Chervil seeds set after 5 to 6 days; the plant requires no cultivation care other than a few waterings in times of drought. Common chervil closely resembles little hemlock; it is only lighter green, and the divisions of its leaves are less acute; but these differences are easily overlooked, and many cases of poisoning are the result. They could be avoided by adopting exclusively curly chervil, a variety as easy to grow as the common species; but curly chervil's strong flavour displeases most consumers. The market gardener is therefore strongly advised to weed his chervil beds himself or have them weeded before his eyes, so that he does not have to reproach himself for having left a few stalks of small hemlock on the beds, and for having sold a deadly poison mixed with a supply of lettuce. Tarragon, a very aromatic plant, has a much more limited use than parsley and chervil; it is included in salad supplies, and is also used to flavor the vinegar in which pickles are to be preserved. The plant is not important enough to be cultivated other than as a border plant in the driest part of the kitchen garden, as it is very sensitive to excess humidity. In France's average climate, tarragon rarely flowers or ripens seed; it is propagated exclusively by dividing clumps. In order to always have young, tender tarragon shoots at hand, it's a good idea to cut the whole plant down to ground level from time to time; older stems become too aromatic, and are too hard to be used as salad greens. Civet. Civet, the smallest of the bulbous plants permitted in the market garden, has a scent reminiscent of garlic and onion, but to a less pronounced and still pleasant degree. It is planted as a border plant along squares, and is only ever used in very small quantities. When you don't have occasion to use it, you sometimes forget to cut it; then it flowers, and the clumps thin out; you must therefore be careful to cut civet very often, even when you don't need it. Tufts should be split every two years; it's one of the most pleasant of all salad supplies. Cauliflower. Cauliflower is the most widely tasted of the edible flowering vegetable plants, and although it contains little solid matter, it is an excellent food that is healthy, pleasant to the taste and easy to digest. Cultivation has produced several very good varieties, known expressively as tender, semi-hard and hard. Tender cauliflower is the earliest-growing; it has narrow leaves and forms only small apples; semi-hard cauliflower, a little slower to form than the preceding variety, is the most widely grown; its apples are medium-sized and of excellent quality. Hard cauliflower is the hardiest of all, i.e. the least sensitive to cold; it is suitable for very large-scale cultivation, because it requires little care once it is in place, and can be grown with little more ceremony than the large Alsatian white cabbage. Its shortcoming, which makes it excluded by many gardeners, is its slow growth, which means it takes up a lot of land, but it produces very large, white, firm apples of the highest quality. The sub-varieties are, among the tender varieties, petit Salomon, early, very white, but not very developed; among the semi-hard varieties, gros Salomon, with a very voluminous apple, and among the hard varieties, choufleur Lenormand, recently obtained from seed by the gardener who gave it its name. The latter, in good soil, can become enormous; it's the best of the late cabbages. To have early spring cauliflowers, sow the early cauliflower seed between the two Notre-Dame days, as the gardeners say, i.e. from August 15 to September 15, a little earlier or later, depending on the state of the weather. The plant, as soon as it has four leaves, is transplanted under a cold frame as the first white frosts approach, which it cannot withstand; it is given plenty of air as long as it does not freeze; it thus spends the winter, thanks to assiduous care aimed at preserving it from the cold, and preventing it from withering away for want of air and light. In February or March, as soon as the season permits, the cauliflower plant is placed in the open air. Not all of those planted first succeed; the latest returns from the late cold sweep away some of them; those that survive, albeit small in volume, always fetch a good price. Two precautions are necessary for the successful cultivation of early cauliflowers: 1° at the time of planting, as little time as possible should elapse between uprooting and planting; 2° after watering the cauliflowers for a few days to ensure their recovery, they should not be watered for a fortnight, even in the event of drought; observation has shown that this procedure hastens apple formation by eight to ten days. To obtain cauliflowers that can be harvested immediately after the first season, we sow semi-hard cauliflower seed on a bed and under a frame in February and March, not so much to prevent the plant from freezing, now that the severe cold has passed, as to accelerate its growth. Another layer is kept ready, on which the seedling is transplanted a fortnight after it has emerged; it is not put out in the open until the end of April or the first days of May, when the temperature has completely eased. These second-seeded cauliflowers bear their apples in June and July. In the first days of May, sow the seed of ordinary hard cauliflower or Lenormand cauliflower in the open air, in a well-smoked bed; the plant requires no care other than a few weedings; it can be planted without prior transplanting, and subsequently treated like white cabbage, except for a few waterings which it may need in the event of a long drought. Late cauliflower doesn't bear its apples until late autumn. They can be stored in the same way as cabbages, and sold with advantage throughout the bad season, when markets are absolutely short of other fresh vegetables. Artichoke. Artichoke cultivation in France has suffered serious setbacks in recent years, due to the inconstancy of the seasons. Nevertheless, it remains one of the most advantageous market garden crops, wherever it is well managed, and it can be so wherever this plant can be given water and manure at discretion. The artichoke is a thistle that grows wild in southern Spain; it has been cultivated in France to produce very good varieties, the most highly regarded of which are: 1° the artichoke from Laon, with very divergent pointed scales, which is rightly considered the best of all; 2° the large artichoke from Tours, with scales stuck together and notched at the top; 3° the small artichoke without hay, from southern France. The edible part of the artichoke consists of the common receptacle of flowers picked before they bloom. Artichokes are propagated either by sowing their seeds, or by separating the offshoots or eyelets that grow in large numbers around the old plants; the second method of propagation is the most commonly used; the seedling does not constantly reproduce the variety that provided the seed; part of this plant bears leaves armed with prickles; it turns into a thistle, as gardeners say. However, this method of propagating artichokes is often necessary when, as a result of an exceptionally harsh winter, all the seedlings from the eyelets have perished. In such cases, when the seedling is strong enough, it is sorted out and any plants that do not seem to be true to species are eliminated. The carnation plant is detached from the

It overwinters with a good covering of long litter, which is removed in mild weather and replaced in snowy or frosty conditions. In spring, the grommets, rooted or not, are placed 80 centimetres or 1 metre apart. Each eyelet is fitted with a heel, making it easy to take as a cutting if it had no roots formed when it was placed. Holes 50 centimetres in diameter and the same depth are opened for planting; the soil extracted from the holes is mixed with its volume of half-consumed manure; the artichokes are planted in this mixture; a small circular pit is created around each plant to retain water from watering. For eight to ten days, the artichokes must be watered generously every evening; they are then given over to the natural course of their vegetation; some of them produce heads during September; but the plantation is only fully productive in its second year, when it has not been destroyed by winter, which it does not always get through without accident. At the onset of winter, artichoke vines are firmly ridged; the eyelets needed to maintain the plantation are removed, and the heart of the plant is left uncovered. Dry leaves or long litter are placed between the artichokes. In the event of frost, the artichokes are covered in no time at all, and uncovered with the same ease whenever the weather permits. Despite this care, frost in winter and rot in spring often depopulate the plantation. Moreover, if the work of covering and uncovering artichokes is possible in a market garden of mediocre size, it becomes materially impossible in a plantation of several hectares. The gardeners who cultivate the marshes known as hortillons around Amiens (Somme), overcome this difficulty by treating artichoke cultivation in the same way as any other annual vegetable. The plant is raised, put in place, smoked and watered as described above, and not left to its own devices as soon as it has taken possession of the land, as is the usual method; it continues to be watered generously three times a day. Watered in this way, the artichokes grow rapidly, producing all their heads in August and September. When all the artichokes have been harvested, the eyelets are detached from the stumps and placed in gauges for the following year's planting, after which all the artichokes are pulled up and thrown into the manure, which naturally saves the market gardener the trouble of protecting them from the cold during the bad season. It's easy to see that this type of annual artichoke cultivation is only possible when you can water constantly, as the gardeners of Amiens do, whose marshes are cut by canals derived from the Somme. But in France, there is no shortage of land suitable for market gardening, crossed by watercourses or close to a river or pond. It is there and not elsewhere that the annual cultivation of artichokes could and should be carried out on a large scale, and if this were the case, this excellent vegetable, whose price so often puts it beyond the reach of a large number of consumers, could be produced cheaply and in abundance; for the alternations of dearth and profusion that are the consequence of the artichoke's present mode of cultivation would be replaced by a very regular production, always proportionate to consumer needs. Artichokes, treated in the usual way, last for three years; after this time, the plantation must be renewed. Every year, a certain number of the most beautiful plants with well-formed heads are set aside at the end of autumn; these plants are lifted into rootballs and planted in fresh sand, in a sound cellar or any other frost-free location; in this way, a few artichokes are available for sale in winter. HII SECTION. PLANTS WITH EDIBLE FRUIT. Vegetable plants with edible fruit, although not as important for food as the plants in the previous sections, are nevertheless of great value to the market gardener, as their produce is always sought-after and easy to sell at good prices on the markets of large towns. These plants, a source of fortune for those who know how to cultivate them well, are strawberries, tomatoes, melons, cucumbers, pumpkins and various species of edible squash. Strawberries. Few fruits are more widely tasted than the strawberry: so there isn't a garden, large or small, where the strawberry plant isn't cultivated. Artificial or accidental cross-breeding of cultivated strawberry plants has produced a profusion of varieties, classified in two distinct sections. The first includes remontant strawberry plants, native to Europe, which can flower and bear fruit several times in the course of the summer; the second includes all strawberry plants of American origin, which do not remont, and bear fruit only once a year: 1° the Montlhéry strawberry, with large, square-shaped, very smoky fruit; 2° the Alpes des quatre saisons strawberry, known as the strawberry of all months, the most frankly remontant and the most widely grown of all strawberry plants; 3° the Saint-Gilles strawberry, a variety not very different from the previous one; 4° the Gaillon strawberry bush. The section of non-remontant strawberries, on the other hand, is very rich in very large-fruited sub-varieties, all of which have the same drawback for the gardener: they occupy the land uselessly all year round, and only bear fruit for a few weeks during the summer. A volume could be filled with a descriptive catalog of the strawberry varieties in this section; sowings go on every year, giving rise to new varieties that surpass and displace the old ones; anyone who, in his sowings, obtains a strawberry of this section as frankly remontant as the Alpine strawberry, will have made his fortune. In general, all fruits of this section, which end in a point, are very pronouncedly acidic, even when perfectly ripe; those with a more or less rounded tip are rather too sweet than too acidic. The most popular species at present (1861) are Prince Imperial, Goliath, Princess Alice Maude, Deptford Seedlny, Prince Albert, Wilmott superbe, Liège and Chile strawberries.
