These last two strawberry plants are remarkable, one for its great earliness, the other for the extraordinary volume of its fruit; of all known strawberry plants, it produces the largest strawberries. Remontant strawberries. These are the favorite strawberry plants of the market gardener, who can, with careful watering, bring strawberries from remontant strawberry plants to market for five months, and who would only sell strawberries for five weeks if he stuck to growing strawberry plants that don't remontant. Soil suitable for strawberry cultivation must be fertile, rather light than clayey; it is prepared by two careful ploughings with a spade and abundant manuring. If the soil is infested with white grubs (cockchafer larvae), before planting strawberries, you can sow it with rapeseed, which is then ploughed in a few days before planting. The white grubs, brought into contact with the rotted rapeseed, die immediately. This procedure does not completely free strawberry plants from white grubs; some hanncton eggs remain in the ground, hatching later and giving rise to new legions of larvae; but rapeseed, buried green as plant fertilizer, always destroys some of them; moreover, it is very favorable to strawberry plant vegetation. Strawberries can be propagated either by sowing, or by using seedlings from nets or runners, or by dividing tufts of varieties that do not run. Seedlings are mainly used in the hope of obtaining new varieties. A few of the most beautiful strawberries of the species you wish to propagate by sowing are left to ripen completely, then dried out. The seed is then detached from the fruit and sown immediately, in a mixture of equal parts of potting soil and heather earth. The seedling, which is very small at first, is pricked out in the open air and planted in the ground; it flowers and bears its first fruit the following year. The first runners to form, when the strawberry plants start growing again in spring, are the ones that provide the best plant; they are pulled up a month before planting. Each plant is peeled separately, cleaned of superfluous leaves, and prepared to form young roots by cutting off those already present, half of which are removed lengthwise. The plant thus dressed, according to the accepted expression, is put in nursery, in very close rows, in a slightly shaded garden bed. The best time for this operation is August; if there are droughts, the young strawberry plant should be watered every day. During September and, if the weather is mild, into the first fortnight of October, the nursery stock is planted, and the soil is covered with an abundant mulch of long litter. This mulch keeps the soil cool, prevents watering from compacting the soil too tightly around the roots of the strawberry plants, inhibits weed growth and, during the strawberry season, prevents the fruit from becoming soiled by direct contact with the soil. Strawberries from a well-mulched strawberry field can be served for dessert without first being washed, thus retaining all their delicate taste and fragrance. Gardeners can choose between two varieties of strawberry plants that do not spin: the red-fruited Gaillon bush and the white-fruited Gaillon bush, both of which are similar to the four-season Alpine strawberry plants in terms of foliage, fruit shape and quality. These two strawberry plants, because of the absence of netting, are especially suited to being planted as borders around vegetable garden squares. Once the strawberry plant has taken possession of the land where it has been planted, further cultivation is limited to removing the netting and frequent watering during the hot summer months. Only a certain number of strawberry plants are allowed to produce nets, in proportion to the quantity of plants presumed to be needed. A good field of remontant strawberry plants lasts three years in good conditions; it should be removed and renewed in the fourth year, on another part of the garden. In recent years, Parisian horticulture has introduced the following procedure for growing repeat strawberries. In June, when the strawberries are fully ripe, we harvest the ripest strawberries possible from the four seasons, press them without crushing them, and leave them exposed to the sun for two hours. After this time, the seed detaches easily; it loses its germinative properties in a very short time, and must be sown immediately. For this purpose, prepare a garden bed covered with 5 to 6 cm of good crumbled potting soil; the strawberry seed is spread over the potting soil without being buried. The seedling is covered with broken branches, over which a light blanket of long straw is spread. The water, sifted through the straw and undergrowth, moistens the seedlings sufficiently, without compressing the potting soil; this is an essential condition for success. The seedling, uncovered as soon as it has sprouted, is transplanted in staggered rows, 30 cm apart in all directions, into good garden soil, smoked in the spring for another crop. It soon starts to grow, flower and produce runners in all directions. Flowers and runners are removed as they appear. Strawberry beds are given a good hoeing before winter, and a few centimetres of good potting soil are spread on top to prevent them from heaving. In spring, strawberry plants are mulched with long litter, and watered generously, taking care to remove any netting or runners. Strawberry plants treated in this way and watered generously, whether it rains or not (this point is very important), flower and bear fruit without interruption, from May to November. Re-sowable strawberry plants should only be required to produce for one year, and the seedlings should be renewed every year, if the plant is not to degenerate; in this way, the strawberry field is maintained at maximum production, and the best strawberries that can be obtained in the kitchen garden are harvested in abundance.  Non-remontant strawberry plants. Non-remontant strawberry plants do not occupy a large place in the market garden; their large-scale cultivation is more profitable in the open field, where they thrive without watering or delicate cultivation care, due to their great hardiness. The plant, prepared in the same way as for remontant strawberries, is placed 30 or 40 centimetres apart in all directions, depending on the presumed size of the clumps. Flowering and fruit ripening precede the period of extreme heat and drought, so that lack of watering does not harm strawberry production. Once this time has passed, the strawberry field is cleared of superfluous runners several times during the summer, requiring no further work. The strawberry crop is small in the first year, very bountiful in the second and third, and small in the fourth, after which the field must be renewed. The market gardener grows only a few of the most sought-after non-remontant strawberry species, not so much for the sale of the fruit as for the plant, which lovers of choice varieties will gladly pay a good price for. One piece of information that may be of value to gout sufferers is that they can be, if not radically cured, at least very sensibly relieved, by eating strawberries at discretion throughout the fine season, and by making use of strawberry jam during the part of the year when there are no fresh strawberries. Forced strawberry cultivation. Forced cultivation of both remontant and non-remontant strawberry plants means that strawberries can be harvested just about every day of the year. The proof is in the fact that at the English court, as at that of the King of the Belgians, a dish of strawberries must be served for dessert in every season. Open-air strawberry cultivation produces ripe strawberries from June to October, and strawberries can be harvested as early as the first days of May, without any care other than covering the strawberry beds with frames supported by trunks during the bad season, and planting stakes behind the trunks supporting suspended straw mats forming a temporary espalier. Under the protection of this espalier, the well-watered strawberry plants flower early, and the ripening of their strawberries is twenty to thirty days ahead of the usual ripening of the same fruit in the open air. The problem to be solved is to grow ripe strawberries by forced cultivation, from November to May. For this purpose, strawberry plants are potted early in March, and the flowering stems and runners are removed throughout the summer as they appear. In October, the potted strawberry plants are placed under frames whose trunks are surrounded by highly compressed fermenting manure. The heat produced by the manure inside the frames causes the strawberry plants to bloom, producing strawberries in November and December. These strawberries are never very abundant, nor are they of very good quality; for, if it is possible to preserve them from the cold, it is not possible to provide them with sunshine in foggy and cold rainy weather; but in the end, a few passable strawberries are harvested, and there are always wealthy amateurs willing to pay a decent price for them. If you're going to grow strawberries on a large scale, you'll need to stock up in March and April with remontant strawberry plants, potted and treated in summer as described above. These strawberry plants are successively introduced into the pineapple greenhouse, or into vine-forcing tarpaulins, where they flower and produce ripe strawberries from January to April. Around Paris, market gardeners who specialize in the forced cultivation of strawberry plants are beginning to use the boiling water heating system known as the thermosyphon. The thermosyphon pipes run underground through a series of boxes covered with glass frames, under which artificial heat, graduated at will, makes the potted strawberry plants blossom and bear fruit all winter long. They are usually kept at a temperature of 10 to 12 degrees until flowering, rising to 15 or 20 degrees when the fruit ripens. During the time that potted strawberry plants spend under heated frames or in the greenhouse, they should be watered three times a day with water brought up to the temperature of the interior of the greenhouse. If they were to be watered with cold water, their vegetation would stall, and the success of forced strawberry cultivation would be compromised. Tomatoes. In the south of France, tomatoes are grown in large quantities; they are eaten sliced and seasoned in oil, pan-fried, with lots of onions. In the rest of France, tomato cultivation is less widespread, because near the big cities, where tomato sales are assured, this branch of cultivation, proportionate to the ease of selling the produce, is as advantageous as any other. Only two varieties of tomato are grown in the market garden, one with red fruit, the other with yellow fruit, both of the same temperament and suitable for the same uses. The red variety deserves preference, as it is easier to place. No vegetable is more sensitive to cold than the tomato. The seed can only be sown in the open ground in the first half of May; seedlings sown at this time are planted in June; they begin to flower in July and bear ripe fruit in September. This is the simplest way to grow tomatoes in all departments south of the Seine valley. North of this valley, and even in the climate of Paris, it's best to sow tomato seeds on warm soil, in February and March. It is not necessary to set up special beds for tomato seed sowing; tomato seed sowing can be done around the edges of melon beds; the plant is removed and put in place before the time when its proximity could disturb the melons. To speed up the growth of tomato plants transplanted into the open air, they are given the protection of a temporary espalier of straw mats supported by stakes, under the shelter of which the tomatoes flower early and bear ripe fruit in July and August; Those tomatoes that appear first on the market are always better sold than the others. When the plants are well loaded with fruit that has reached almost its normal volume, but is still green, the ends of the stems are pinched off, which, left to their own devices, would continue to elongate and flower; but the late-forming tomatoes would not reach maturity before the first cold spells, so there is no reason to regret their removal, which causes the sap to flow back onto the tomatoes from the first flowers. These tomatoes gain in volume, quality and earliness by pruning the ends of the stems that bear them. If you stretch a piece of wire or simple string over the stakes to which the straw mats are attached, the fruit-laden tomato stems can be palmed on these supports, allowing them to benefit more fully from the warmth of the espalier. When the first white frost catches tomatoes with half-ripe fruit, the fruit should not be considered lost. By placing them on a shelf in a well-heated kitchen for a few days, they can be turned into color. These tomatoes are just as good for cooking as the others, although they don't look quite as good. Melon. Few fruits are more pleasant and fragrant than the melon; and although this fruit can give fever to those who eat it excessively, it has no harmful properties for those who use it in moderation; its refreshing properties are even useful for health during hot weather. Cultivation in Europe has produced a multitude of melon varieties, the most esteemed of which are the early but not very large Carmelite black melon, the small Prescott, the common cantaloupe and the Portuguese cantaloupe. In France, the cultivation of the brodé melon, once known as the melon maraîcher par excellence, has more or less been abandoned because of its obvious inferiority to the preceding varieties. The lines of the old poet Lamonnoye are well known: G Les amis de l'heure présente Sont d'un naturel de melon: G Il faut goûter plus de trente Avant que d'en trouver un bon. D These verses applied to embroidered melons; they no longer make sense since only the good varieties are cultivated; today, it's the bad melons that are rare, as they no longer dare show themselves alongside the good ones on the markets, where they would find no buyers. Only one variety of embroidered melon, the Honfleur melon, very large and elongated, is still grown in large quantities in part of the Seine-Inférieure region, for export to England, where it is highly prized. From the Loire Valley onwards, our southern départements have their own local varieties of melon, grown in the open air with no more care than common vegetables, and sold at very low prices; they are mostly edible, but mediocre. Among the best is the sucré vert d'Angers, which is very good, but so small that it cannot be grown in a market garden. The cultivation of melons is not, as has long been repeated, a learned and difficult task, in which only the most skilled 9 gardeners can hope to succeed; on the contrary, it is easy and a sure success for anyone who practises it methodically and without carelessness: this is the most important point. As sensitive to the slightest cold as the tomato itself, the melon can only be grown in the open air between the time when it no longer freezes and the time when it does not yet freeze. This method of cultivating melons is not used by market gardeners in the Paris climate, because it offers too few favorable chances. A melon seed sown around the 10th of May produces a plant that flowers late, and can only ripen fruit in September and October. If the late-season heat fails, which is not uncommon, it ripens only imperfectly. In any case, melons grown in the open air only reach the market in autumn, the time of year when they are least sought-after and least profitable to sell. For all these reasons, the market gardener always starts growing melons on a warm bed, and continues under cloche or chassis, with the dual aim of having perfectly ripe melons and bringing them to market at the time when they sell best. The first seedlings are sown in January, on a warm layer of leaves, horse manure and tannin; these substances must be used in equal parts, moderately moistened, exactly mixed and well trampled into the pit, surrounded by its frame and topped by its glass sash. Melon seeds are not sown until the heat of the bed, covered with a decimeter of potting soil, has dropped to 20 or 25 degrees. Seedlings are best sown in pots rather than in the potting soil; the reason for this lies in the temperament of the plant. The melon suffers very little from transplanting, even when it is done with the greatest possible care and precaution. If it is sown in a pot, when the roots have developed too much to find enough food in the pot soil, it can be removed and placed in the potting soil, without causing any disturbance to its roots, and without producing a halt in the progress of its vegetation. Melon seed is sown in pots filled with potting soil and buried in the bed, not all at once, but in January, February and March, so as to harvest a succession of ripe melons from the first half of June to August. The market gardener takes care to set up a number of layers similar to those for seedlings, in proportion to the number of melon plants he intends to grow, calculating on the basis of one square meter of layer surface for each melon plant. To raise the seedlings from the March sowing, he can also set up a few layers in the open air, at the foot of a wall facing south; the melons will ripen their fruit there before the end of August under glass cloches known as melon cloches; but cloche melons are never as good as frame melons. Once the melon seed has risen in the pots, a little air and as much light as possible are given, whenever the weather allows the frames to be uncovered and half-opened, to prevent the young plant from melting, i.e. from perishing by shrivelling, a kind of accident that frequently takes a part of it away through no fault of the gardener, when the rigors of the cold thwart his operations. Soon the melon plant has taken on four leaves, and it's time to pinch it. This is the beginning of melon pruning, a delicate operation whose principles must be understood if it is to be carried out with discernment. If the melon is allowed to follow its natural growth path, it will produce a single, very long, sparsely-branched stem, the ends of which alone will bear female flowers, called meshes by gardeners, and destined to become melons. The number of meshes will be very limited, and they will be born very far from the root collar of the plant. Experience shows that the closer a melon is born to the collar, the better it is; it also teaches that the most perfect in shape are always the best. What, then, is the purpose of melon pruning? Firstly, to force it to produce a large number of shoots, so as to have a good number of meshes to choose from, and to be able to reserve fruits of the most regular shape, according to their species; secondly, to obtain the meshes on short stems, so that the fruits are as close as possible to the plant's collar. Once this point has been clarified, melon pruning can be practised successfully by the first-comer. The first pinch gives rise to two shoots which, pinched in turn when they have four leaves, each give rise to two others. These, pinched later, bring to eight the number of stalks on which meshes soon appear. The young fruits are allowed to grow large enough to allow us to judge their future; we then choose, with full knowledge of the facts, the two most beautiful; all the others are removed along with the stems bearing them. The surface of the bed is then covered with fresh straw or long litter, to prepare a clean, suitable bed for the melons, which grow rapidly from this point onwards. While they are growing, they should be watered often, but not too much at a time. In terms of pruning and watering, bell-grown melons are treated in the same way as frame-grown melons. Cucumbers. G Cucumbers, which are widely used in English cuisine and in several parts of Germany, are much less common in French cuisine. In Paris, cucumbers, which are brought to the markets in fairly large quantities, are almost all bought by the kitchens of hotels where English and Germans stay. Cucumbers are as sensitive to cold as melons, and can only be sown outdoors from May 10 to 15. Cucumbers are planted in beds one meter 30 centimeters wide, separated by service paths. In the center of each bed, holes 30 centimeters in diameter and 30 centimeters deep are opened. These holes are placed in rows, 80 centimetres apart; they are filled with half-consumed manure, which is covered with a decimetre of soil mixed with good loam in equal parts. The cucumber seeds, two of which are sown in each hole, sprout after a few days. The plant is pinched a first time to make it branch out; the branches produced by the first pinch are pinched in their turn absolutely like those of melons grown in the open air; for the two plants have the same temperament, and their vegetation follows the same course. When the fruit is well formed, in numbers proportionate to the vigor of the plants, the stems above the fruit are removed, and as they form, the subsequent shoots, whose growth would be detrimental to the fruit's enlargement, are cut off. Cucumbers require continual watering throughout the growing season, and the larger and better the plants are watered, the bigger and better the fruit. The small-fruited cucumber, known as gherkin, is grown in exactly the same way. The fruit is picked as soon as it has reached the size of a little finger, and sold for pickling in vinegar, one of the most popular seasonings in French cuisine. The many varieties of cucumber grown by English, Dutch, Belgian and German gardeners are scarcely known in France; in our market gardens, only the early Dutch cucumber, the early white cucumber, the Bonneuil white cucumber and the green gherkin are generally grown; the latter is the most profitable of all cucumbers. All cucumbers can be grown on beds and subjected to the same pruning and cultivation methods as forced melons; but in France, even in the vicinity of large cities, forced cucumbers on beds can rarely fetch prices that cover cultivation costs. The market gardener must be guided in this respect by the general rule, which prescribes that he should produce only what he is assured in advance of being able to sell easily and at a profit. Pumpkin. In France, pumpkins are widely consumed. For a long time, only the large common pumpkin was grown, with its enormous volume, empty interior and consequent susceptibility to mildew. For some years now, the variety known as the Siam ball has been preferred, with its flattened shape, thick flesh and almost no hollow inside, as good quality as the common species and easier to store, and the green-skinned Hungarian pumpkin, whose shape and properties are more or less the same as those of the Siam ball. All pumpkin species are as sensitive to cold as melons and cucumbers; they can only be sown outdoors from May 10 to 15. For this purpose, holes one metre in diameter and 50 centimetres deep are opened, filled with good manure and covered with one decimetre of good soil mixed with loam. Each similar hole is planted with three pumpkin seeds, which soon sprout: as soon as the plant has sprouted its first leaves, it needs copious watering. The stems of pumpkins are not pruned; they grow long and creep along the ground, where they sink hooks that act as roots and contribute to the plant's nourishment. The male flowers appear first at the bottom of the stems, followed by the mesh or female flowers at the top. Pumpkins continue to be watered generously, as the fruit swells visibly; stems that continue to elongate are trimmed to two or three leaves above the fruit. Pumpkins harvested in autumn, before the frosts, keep very well in a dry place away from the cold. Giraumon or Turkish bonnet is also grown in the same way. Its fruit is not very large, but very sweet and has a very delicate flavor. The same method of cultivation is also used for various species of edible squash, the best of which is the marrow squash, with small but very nourishing fruit. Picked just before ripening, this squash's numerous fruits can be seasoned in all sorts of ways. This vegetable is widely used in England, but not in France. The market gardener should only cultivate squash other than pumpkins, which are always in demand, when he is certain that the produce will find buyers. G IVth SECTION. ROOT VEGETABLES. Root vegetables are an important part of the diet; the cultivation of many of these vegetables is of great importance to the market gardener, who must supply city markets with them at all seasons, and who can count on the products of this branch of his industry being placed on good terms; the ease with which root vegetables can be preserved makes their sale especially advantageous in winter, when fresh vegetables become scarce. Root vegetables used in market gardening are: 1° carrots, 2° turnips, 3° radishes, 4° parsnips, 5° salsify, 6° potatoes, 7° Jerusalem artichokes. Root crops used in market gardening include carrots, turnips, radishes, parsnips, salsify, potatoes and Jerusalem artichokes. Bulbous vegetables are also included in this section, although bulbs are not strictly speaking roots, but buds from which true roots grow. These plants, which are as widely used and as necessary as seasoning as the other vegetables, are: onions, leeks, spring onions, garlic and shallots. §6 - Carrot. I G The origin of the carrot is not in doubt; the irrefutably authentic experiments carried out by M. Vilmorin have proved that, subjected to the care of market gardening, the carrot, found everywhere in the wild in Europe, reproduces the cultivated carrot within two generations. G Among the varieties of carrot produced by cultivation, none of which constitutes a distinct species, botanically speaking, the most voluminous belong to field cultivation, and are grown only for cattle feed; these carrots do not belong to market gardening. The varieties permitted in the 5. market garden are: 1° the early short carrot, known as the Holland spinach; 2° the Meaux carrot, red and half-long; 3° the yellow Flanders carrot; 4° the yellow Achicourt carrot; the red Alteringham carrot. The last three are equally suitable for human and animal consumption. Any good garden soil, provided it is not too strong, is suitable for carrots; they should not be sown on fresh fermenting manure, as this type of manuring causes the carrot to branch out in the ground, which deprives it of all its market value. Sowing on land that has been fertilized for another crop the previous year is best. Although the practice of broadcasting carrot seed is more generally followed, it is better to sow the seed very lightly, in rows spaced 20 to 25 centimetres apart. This arrangement allows the young carrot plant to be hoeed two or three times, which is particularly conducive to rapid root formation. The plant should be thinned out as soon as the carrots are the size of a little finger: in this state, they are a healthy, highly sought-after vegetable; those that are to acquire their full volume remain spaced 8 or 10 centimetres apart in the rows. In the Paris climate, early carrots can be sown as early as the end of February, or in the first fortnight of March at the latest. Sowing can be repeated in July; provided the young plant is sufficiently watered, carrots have time to acquire the natural volume of their variety before the first cold spells, to which, moreover, they are not very sensitive; this is an advantageous way for the market gardener to use land on which he has harvested spring vegetables. During the first period of its growth, the carrot's main enemy is a spider-like insect, the theridion, which bites young plants at the root collar to suck out their sweet sap, and kills them. The most economical way to get rid of the spider mite is to sprinkle powdered soot on carrot beds infested with the spider mite, and water thoroughly immediately afterwards. You can also use a strong infusion of corporal tobacco, poured over the carrots in the form of rain, with a watering can with a sheaf pierced with very fine holes; this last method is the safest, but as it is also the most expensive, it is only used in very small-scale cultivation. Near large towns, it is highly advantageous to force early carrots onto warm layers, mounted successively in the manner indicated for melon layers (page 74). These layers should be filled to 35 to 40 centimetres with a mixture of good soil and loam in equal parts, into which the carrot seed is sown; otherwise, as the carrots lengthen, they will encounter the manure in the layer, and this alone will compromise the success of this crop. Carrot seed is sown on the bed from December to March, from month to month; the carrots are harvested successively when they are about half their size; they are much sought-after and a good loss until the time of year when the first peas and other fresh vegetables abound on the markets. Carrots grown on a bed under a frame are very prone to sunburn, especially in March: rolled mats should always be kept within reach of the frame, and thrown over the windows as soon as it gets a little hot in the middle of the day. Carrots forced onto a bed should only be watered very sparingly, and only when absolutely necessary; in most cases, evaporation of moisture from the manure through the bed is sufficient. Turnips. Turnips are more suited to large-scale cultivation than to market gardening; however, three types of turnip are sown in the market garden: the long white turnip from Clairefontaine, the yellow turnip from Freneuse, and the small Nankin turnip from Finland. The cultivation of all these varieties is the same: the seed can be broadcast in spring, or sown in July and August. The latter is the most common time of year. Turnips should be lighted early; if they are too close together, and get in each other's way, they won't form roots, and will grow too much foliage. Garden turnips should only be grown in light, sandy soils; in very fertile fat soils, suitable for all other vegetable crops, turnips grow entirely in leaves; they have difficulty forming roots, which have neither their normal volume, nor the recommendable properties of their variety. In any case, it is one of the least sought-after and least expensive vegetables, so it should be given very limited space in the market garden. Radishes. There's nothing simpler than growing radishes, of which there are three good varieties: pink, white and yellow. The pink variety is the most widely adopted; we've given up on the petite rave, whose two varieties, one pink, the other purple, were very popular in France half a century ago. Radish is sown in a bed in the open air from the first days of March to the end of June; sowing can be repeated in autumn; it takes no more than 20 to 25 days for the radish to take on its normal volume from the moment the seed has emerged. It is essential to interrupt radish cultivation during the hottest part of the summer; at this time of year, despite abundant watering, you would only obtain radishes that are split at the bottom, hollow inside, hard and barely edible. In winter, radishes sown on a bed at the same time as lettuce plants produce produce that is always easy to sell at this time of year. Radishes, whether grown on a bed or in the ground, require a lot of potting soil and a lot of water; the products of this crop are of little value, but there are none in the market garden that can be obtained with less trouble and expense and in a shorter time. In most of France, the use of this root is limited to enhancing the flavour of broth in the traditional pot-au-feu. Only in a few northern cantons is the parsnip grown on a large enough scale to be delivered to the kitchen as a fresh vegetable, when it has reached about a third of its normal volume. There are two species, one short-rooted, suitable for vegetable gardens with shallow soil, the other long-rooted, which thrives only in soil that can be penetrated to a great depth. Parsnip seed is rather difficult to sow, because of the membrane that surrounds it; the best way to sow this seed is to spread it very thinly in rows spaced 20 centimetres apart. Later, the seedling is thinned out at a very young age, so that it is spaced at 20 centimetres in all directions. To ensure even sowing, the seed is covered with crumbled earth, or better still, potting soil, without using a rake to bury it. The surplus from parsnip cultivation is the same as for carrots. Parsnips grown to be eaten at a third of their growth are called sugar carrots by gardeners in Northern and Walloon Belgium; steamed, this root is a hot dish, with a very pronounced flavor, difficult to accept by consumers who are not used to it. Parsnips are the hardiest of root vegetables, and are not damaged by the cold of our harshest winters. Seedlings can also be sown in the spring; the produce from autumn sowing is available early in the summer; those from spring sowing can only be harvested in the off-season; they are reserved for winter supply. For, although parsnip consumption is never very substantial, it is nevertheless one of the root vegetables that the market gardener must be able to supply to his customers in every season. Scorzonera. In French kitchens, the scorsonera has almost universally dethroned its rival and close relative, the salsify, which has the same flavour and eating properties. Salsify is hardly ever grown in market gardens any more; in fact, its cultivation is very similar to that of the scorsonera. Like parsnips, salsify is completely insensitive to the effects of cold; so, without compromising the success of this crop, salsify seed can be sown in September, in deep, light soil, smoked in the spring for another crop. In this case, the plant occupies the soil for the whole of the following year's fine season, and produces roots that can be harvested as it enters its second winter. You can then uproot part of it and store it in the cellar, so as not to run out during hard frosts, and leave the rest in the ground, as the most intense cold has no effect on these roots. When scorsonera seed is sown in spring, in March or April, the roots have not yet reached their normal volume by the time winter sets in, and need another year of cultivation before they can be pulled out. Scorzonera and salsify show a phenomenon in their vegetation that is not reproduced in the vegetation of any other vegetable. These plants, from seed sown in spring, flower and bear seed during the autumn of their first year; the stems are cut to harvest the seed; the plants grow back in spring, flower and bear seed a second time, and their roots, now as large and long as they can be, have lost none of their nutritional properties. Other root vegetables, such as carrots, parsnips and turnips, become woody and no longer edible as soon as they go to seed. Scorzonera seed should be sown very close together, either in spring or autumn, because it never lifts more than partially, as fertilization of the flowers is often incomplete. The seed is broadcast on the ground, divided into plots separated by paths, and covered with a little soil taken from the same paths. This is one of the vegetable seeds most eagerly eaten by wild birds; to prevent their depredations, it's a good idea to hang scarecrows made of feathers planted in a piece of cork over the boards sown with scorsonera seed. Once the plant is well established, it requires no more care than weeding and a little watering in the event of prolonged drought. Potatoes. The potato is only used for early market gardening, so only the earliest varieties are planted, such as marjolin, chaville, shaw, and the two Belgian varieties known as sept semaines and neuf semaines, because of their rapid vegetation. To make them even more precocious, before winter the tubers intended for planting are exposed to the action of air and light, in a well-ventilated and above all well-lit room; in a short time, if care is taken to turn them over often and to open the windows as long as it doesn't freeze, the potatoes turn green on all their surfaces, and lose their eating properties. But instead of exhausting themselves by producing long, etiolated shoots, like those kept in a dark cellar, green potatoes develop short, vigorous, well-colored eyes. In January, we arrange them close together in flat baskets, and occasionally light a little fire in the room, so that the potato sprouts develop quickly, along with their rudimentary roots. In February, either in the middle or at the end of the month, depending on the state of the weather, the potatoes are put in place in the usual way, taking every precaution not to break either the stems or the roots. The tubers are harvested in May and June, when they are about two-thirds full. This crop would be too unproductive on its own to take its place in the market garden, if it didn't fit perfectly into a system of other crops, by means of what market gardeners call counter-planting. As soon as the early potatoes have been ridged, a cabbage, cauliflower or celery plant is planted in the gaps between the rows, having been prepared in advance. When the cabbages, cauliflowers or celery are ready for market, the land is planted with spinach or escarole, plants for which there is still enough of the summer left, and which can be harvested before the first serious cold weather arrives. Without this possibility of counterplanting the land occupied by early potatoes, this plant would never feature in the market garden. Jerusalem artichoke. If there is a poorly exposed corner of the market garden where the soil can only be raised to the same level of fertility with difficulty as the rest of the plot, this is the place for Jerusalem artichokes. Because of the strength of their stems and the breadth of their foliage, Jerusalem artichokes, planted in thick, tight rows, are eminently suitable for use as windbreaks. Planted in mediocre soil, they separate completely from the soil and are usually planted at the same distance as potatoes. However, if you intend to form a curtain of Jerusalem artichokes that will act as a shelter against strong winds, plant them in two or three parallel rows, one decimetre apart in all directions. The largest tubers can be cut, taking the precaution, as with large potatoes, of cutting them in advance and leaving the cuttings to dry out in the open air for two or three days before planting. The Jerusalem artichoke, although native to South America, does not freeze in the ground, even during the harshest winters in the climate of central France; the tubers can be left in the ground after the stems have been cut off towards the end of autumn, and the Jerusalem artichokes can be harvested only in proportion to consumption needs, which avoids any embarrassment in preserving them. When Jerusalem artichokes have been planted in a corner of the market garden, either in rows or in beds, it is almost never necessary to renew the planting; the tuber fragments that remain in the ground, having escaped uprooting, are sufficient for reproduction, so that you will always find roughly the same quantity to harvest every year, where they have been planted once. Bulbous vegetables. - Onions. Among the bulbous plants permitted in the market garden, the onion ranks first. Consumption of this plant is considerable in France, either for cooking, or for the preparation of burnt onions, intended to give at the same time a good taste and a beautiful color to fatty broth. Three main varieties of onion are grown: yellow, white and violet; yellow is the most widely used. Onion seed is sown in spring, in March and April, without manure, but with a good covering of compost. An onion sown on recent manure would grow all leafy; it would turn with difficulty, split in two, and the bulb harvest would be almost nil. When the young plant is well established, weed it, then thin it out, so that each plant has enough space to acquire its normal volume. Parisian market gardeners follow an excellent method in this respect: they sow onion seed and leek seed in equal parts. After an initial weeding, they let the young onion and leek plants grow together, until the latter is strong enough to be transplanted. Pulling out the leek starts to release the young onions, which are left to grow for a further two or three weeks. The bulbs are now about the size of a thumb; if further thinning is necessary, some are removed and sold fresh in bunches to season peas. The remaining ones, spaced sufficiently far apart, grow rapidly. Bulb formation is encouraged by twisting the leaves without detaching them. Onions can be harvested as soon as the leaves begin to yellow and fade, a sure sign that the bulbs will no longer grow. Onions are usually sorted into three sizes, and stored in a dry, frost-free place, but cool rather than too hot. A temperature that is a little too high encourages the onion's natural tendency to vegetate in spring, making it unsuitable for use as a seasoning. In the vicinity of Paris and other large cities, many white onion seeds are sown under the conditions described above; these onions are harvested when they have reached about two-thirds of the volume of their species. Being more precocious than the others, the white onion easily reaches half-ripeness at the time when the supply of yellow onions from the previous harvest is exhausted, which ensures its sale at advantageous prices. A few years ago, Mr. Nouvellon's method for growing onions was highly recommended. It consists of sowing the onion seed very close together in autumn, in a bed lined with potting soil. Once the plant has emerged from the soil, it is left to suffer from drought; the leaves soon wither, and the onions, which are very well formed, are no bigger than peas. They are pulled up in this state and kept dry for the following year's planting. In spring, they are planted in rows, 6 or 8 centimetres apart in all directions. The advantages of this method are that it spares the seed and produces onions of roughly the same size, but it is too labor-intensive for large-scale cultivation at a time of year when the market gardener is overloaded with work. Nouvellon's onion-growing method is not widely used, but it is suitable for small-scale cultivation when a moderate quantity of very fine onions is desired, without mixing in small ones. Leek. Although less common than onions, leeks are indispensable, if only as an accompaniment to stews. Leek seed is sown in nurseries, either alone or, as mentioned above, mixed with onion seed. Two species are accepted for market gardening: the long common leek and the large short Rouen leek. The plant is placed in rows, 5 to 7 centimetres apart in all directions; recovery is assured, provided the plant has been well dressed, as the saying goes, i.e. provided the tops of the leaves and about half the length of the roots have been removed. You mustn't sow all the leek seed at once, so as to have a good plant to put in place twice, in May and June. Leeks transplanted early should be cut in late autumn and early winter; if kept later, they will not freeze, as the cold has no effect on this plant; but they will come up and form flower stalks very early in the spring, which deprives them of their nutritional properties. However, there is always a period in spring and early summer when leeks are in short supply on the market, because the previous year's leeks have all come up, and the new crop has not yet reached its normal size. This disadvantage can be partially overcome by sowing a small amount of leek seed at the beginning of September; these late sowings must be very light. The plant is weeded and thinned out when it is deemed too thick. It thus spends the winter without being transplanted, and never becomes very large; but in the spring of the following year, it does not come up until much later than the others, so that it supplies the market until those transplanted first in the spring are ready for sale. Ciboule. Less common than leeks, chives are nonetheless useful enough as a seasoning for a host of dishes to make their cultivation indispensable in the market garden. Chives are sown in March under the same conditions as leeks; the seedling is transplanted when it is the size of a feather pipe; it is planted in rows, at a distance of at least 15 cm in all directions, because each plant forms a thick clump, so that the whole plot is covered. Chives are only used fresh, like leeks; although they are closely related to onions, they cannot be harvested and dried as a winter supply. In July, a second seedling of chives is sown; the plant, with a light covering of dry leaves or long litter, overwinters well in the Paris climate; it is put into place very early in the spring; it produces good clumps for sale long before those from the spring seedlings. We also have a variety of perennial spring onion that can be planted as a border around vegetable garden squares; once in place, it requires no cultivation care other than splitting the clumps to deliver a portion for consumption when they become too thick. Garlic. Garlic can only be grown successfully in light, rich, dry soil; if the plant suffers from excess humidity, it rots on the spot. Although garlic can flower and ripen its seed in the climate of the departments south of the Loire, garlic seed is never sown; the plant is multiplied by its very numerous cloves, wrapped in a common menbrane or tunic, which must not be removed until it is time to use them, either for cooking or for planting. Garlic cloves planted in rows, 8 or 10 centimetres apart, either in beds or in borders, only need to be weeded a few times. When the leaves turn yellow, it's time to pull out the garlic; it should remain on the ground for a few days, exposed to the air and sun; then it should be tied in bundles and hung in a dry place. Garlic is grown on a large scale only in the market gardens of our southern départements, where garlic is used in all dishes; it is also processed on a fairly large scale in the canton of Roscoff (Finistère), which supplies Paris. Shallots. Shallots, of which there are two known varieties, large and small, are grown in the same way as garlic, and thrive in the same soil. Shallot seed is not sown; it multiplies exclusively by dividing its cloves. Shallots vegetate very quickly; planted in March, they can be harvested as early as the end of May and in the course of June. When planting, care must be taken not to bury the shallot pods too deeply, as at least half of them must remain above ground. Without this precaution, they will rot on the spot, even when the soil is dry and it doesn't rain more than usual. Shallots are the most aromatic of the bulbous vegetable plants used in French cuisine as a seasoning; a very small quantity of chopped shallot adds a very strong flavor to a host of dishes; it does not have the disadvantage of garlic, whose flavor is so persistent that anyone who has eaten a dish heavily seasoned with garlic is sure to experience the same sensation as if he or she had eaten garlic continuously for several days in a row. Shallots, provided they are grown in soil that is perfectly free of humidity, do very well in the Paris climate, and can even be successfully cultivated north of the Seine valley. - SECTION. CULTIVATION OF SEED-BEARING PLANTS. § 7 - Double scale. The success of all branches of market gardening, even when carried out with the utmost care, can be compromised when poor quality seeds are sown, and it is not always possible to obtain good quality seeds commercially. It is therefore of the utmost importance to know how to cultivate seed-bearing plants properly, and to harvest the seeds of all kinds of vegetable plants in the best possible conditions. The best method for this special type of cultivation is that practised from time immemorial by gardeners in the Nancy area (Meurthe), under the name of "double-scale": here's what it consists of: first, the most beautiful specimens of each type of plant are chosen and cultivated as best as possible, and the seed is harvested and carefully sorted. This seed, already very good in itself, is not sold; it is sown separately in the best soil, with the richest fertilizer, and only the seed from this second generation is sold. It is on this method, practised with rare intelligence, that the reputation of Nancy's gardeners rests for the production of vegetable seeds; they supply all our eastern departments. It would be difficult to do better, but it is possible to do just as well throughout France, using the same simple process, with certain results and easy execution. In the course of this treatise, we have taken care to note those plants which, in the practice of market gardening, are never multiplied by sowing their seeds, because we have enough other means of propagation for them. The following list includes vegetable plants that can only be propagated by sowing, and for which the market gardener must cultivate the seed-bearing plants himself, if he wants to be sure of harvesting the seed in the best conditions. Bean. Pea. Broad bean. Lentils. Cabbage and cauliflower. Celery. Cardoon. Spinach. Sorrel. Asparagus. Lettuce. Chicory. Artichoke. Strawberry. Melon. Cucumber. Pumpkin. Carrot. Turnip. Radish. Parsnip. Scorsonera. Onions. Leek. Beans. To keep the best types of bean clean and unaltered, you must first isolate those you are planting as seed-bearing plants, i.e. keep them away from other types of bean which flower at the same time, and which could give rise to accidental cross-breeding; it is through the effect of such cross-breeding that, when you are sure you have only sown dwarf white beans, you can harvest variegated ones of various colors, which climb up like Soissons beans. As the pods ripen, they are harvested to keep them whole; the beans should not be shelled until they are planted; the pods that ripen first are always those that provide the most perfect beans of each variety. This care is especially necessary to preserve the purity of early dwarf flageolet beans; their precocity, which is their main merit, can only be preserved when sowing beans from the flowers that bloom first, whose pods often ripen nearly a month before the others. We insist on this point, because it happens quite often that the inexperienced gardener is surprised by the degeneration of his early beans from the second generation; there is no degeneration in the true sense of the word; there is only an omission of the essential care we have just indicated. Peas. The precocity of peas, a quality no less valuable for this vegetable than for beans, can be preserved by taking the same precautions. It is safe to sow very early and very late peas side by side; as they do not flower at the same time, the latter cannot exert any untoward influence on the earliness of the former; it is only necessary to avoid sowing peas of unequal earliness side by side, which flower at the same time. Peas reserved as seed-bearing plants should be topped very early, and the pods of the first flowers harvested as they ripen; this is enough to keep each variety of pea pure, with all the qualities that make it so popular with consumers. Marsh beans and lentils, whose produce is to be reserved for the following year's sowing, should be managed in the same way as peas and beans. The seeds of all vegetable plants in the legume family can retain their germinative powers for several years, but better results are obtained by sowing only the products of the previous harvest, preserved in the pods until the time comes to sow them. D Cabbage and Cauliflower. It is especially with cabbage of all kinds, as well as with cauliflower and broccoli, that it is useful to apply the excellent double-scale method described above (page 98). To obtain good seed from all head cabbages, it is first necessary to separate the seed-bearing plants of each species, as they all flower at the same time in spring, making accidental cross-breeding between neighbors inevitable. At the start of winter, the apples of cabbages that have been carefully marked as the best of each variety are cut off. The 6. cores are left in the place where the plant was transplanted to form the apple. From the first fine days at the end of February, the horizontal cut of each core is split into four by two incisions a few centimetres deep, crossing each other at right angles. This operation has the effect of hastening the growth of young shoots, which each quarter of a core soon produces. If several shoots develop, leave one on each side, so that it can vegetate more vigorously. As soon as the top of each shoot begins to flower, it is pinched back 5 or 6 centimetres, to encourage the growth of flowering side shoots. These in turn are pinched back in the same way when they are well advanced in flowering. This leaves only a small number of siliques on each flowering stalk, filled with the most perfect seeds possible. Cabbages that don't head, such as green cabbages and Brussels sprouts, don't have to undergo quite the same process; the central stem is left to rise after all the sprays, each of which represents a small cabbage head, have been harvested. This stem, when it is ready to flower, is pinched off to a decimetre in length; if the side shoots seem too numerous, part of it is cut off and the others pinched off, always on the principle that the seeds of the side shoots of plants in the Cruciferae family are better than those of the central shoots, and that these seeds are all the better for the fewer siliques left on each branch of the seed-bearers. The same method applies to harvesting the seeds of different varieties of cauliflower. Instead of letting the flowers of the most defective apples, which cannot be sold, rise, as is the vicious custom of many gardeners, the most perfect heads should be reserved for seed-bearing purposes, and, as soon as they flower, they should be summered and treated in the same way as the seed-bearing heads of other cabbage species. These seeds retain their germinative properties for several years; it is the two-year-old seeds that produce the best-formed plants. Celery. 1 It is important to select the most vigorous plants of each celery variety as seedbeds, using the double-scaling method. If, in the usual way, less robust plants are allowed to grow and flower, most of the seed is not fertilized and does not set. Seedbeds planted in deep, rich soil with a southern exposure should be given plenty of water until after flowering. As soon as the seeds are ripe, the stems are cut, bound into bundles and hung in a moisture-free place. When you want to use them for sowing, don't detach them all indiscriminately; those at the outer edges of the umbels are the best fertilized, and almost all of them sprout, whereas those in the center of the umbels, being only imperfectly fertilized, are largely sterile and don't sprout. The same precaution applies to sorting the seeds of all vegetable plants in the Umbelliferes family. Cardoon plants intended for use as seed carriers are planted, smoked and watered in the same way as the others, but care is taken not to bind their leaves and cover them, as is done with those whose etiolated ribs are to be delivered for consumption. As soon as the blossoms are ready to wilt, wrap them in a piece of gauze or very light muslin. Without this precaution, wild birds, particularly goldfinches, which are very fond of cardoon seeds, would devour them without even allowing them to reach full maturity. Spinach. Spinach does not bear seed until its second year; the plant is dioecious, that is, it bears male and female flowers on separate plants; in spinach seedlings whose seed is to be harvested, all the male plants must be kept, even though they cannot bear seed; otherwise, as the female flowers are only imperfectly fertilized, seedlings made with their seeds will grow very unevenly.  Sorrel. One of sorrel's faults is its tendency to grow uninterruptedly throughout the summer, from spring to autumn, so that the gardener is constantly busy cutting back useless flower stalks, which regrow as they are cut; these stalks are picked a little before the seeds are fully ripe, and fall as soon as they are ripe; they are taken to a shed, where the seed finishes ripening; it can then be harvested without loss. Asparagus. To harvest good asparagus seed, stalks laden with ripe berries are left standing until they turn yellow; these berries are not harvested until November, after which the stalks that produced them are cut to ground level. The berries are left to dry on a shelf in a healthy, well-ventilated room. Once they are completely dry, they are soaked in water for twenty-four hours, allowing the softened pulp to detach easily. The seeds, which should be of a nice black color, are washed out and dried in the shade for use in the following year's seedlings. Lettuce. In most lettuce plantations, especially if the soil is naturally dry and not sufficiently watered, there are always too many lettuces rising instead of plucking. If you want the seed to be good, and to produce a plant that's ready to peel well, you mustn't harvest the seed from lettuces that have bolted before they've formed a head. A few of the most beautiful apples of each variety are left to rise and flower, so that the seed can be harvested. Feather scarecrows should be placed near these seedpods to keep out the goldfinches, which are very eager to eat them. Seedbeds of each variety should be planted far enough apart to avoid accidental cross-breeding. Chicory. The seeds of the different varieties of curly endive, escarole and chicory can only be harvested from two-year-old plants, because wild chicory, from which all these varieties originate, is a biennial plant. We choose the most beautiful plants for seedbeds, and avoid tying them to bleach them, as we do with those to be eaten in salads. These plants need to be covered with leaves or dry litter, to protect them from the effects of heavy frosts. As with grainy lettuces, varieties should be carefully isolated to prevent cross-breeding from causing them to degenerate. Artichoke. Artichoke plants used as seedbeds should each retain only the head at the end of the central stem; side shoots and their heads should be removed as they appear. As soon as the flowers begin to fade, wrap them up like cardoon flowers, to protect them from bird damage. Artichoke seedpods should be kept away from cardoon seedpods. Strawberry runners and rooted offshoots of non-spinning varieties are more than sufficient for the propagation of this plant. There would be no point in harvesting the seed if experience had not shown that seedlings are useful for periodically rejuvenating good varieties and preserving all their valuable properties. The best strawberries of each species are left to ripen as fully as possible, then exposed to the sun to dry out completely, allowing the seed to detach easily. They should be sown without delay, as they are one of the quickest to lose their germination capacity. Melon. It is never necessary to cultivate melons separately for use as seed-bearing plants, but it is important to harvest for sowing only the seeds of the most beautiful fruits of each species, taken from a melon plantation where only one variety is grown; this point is very important to avoid failure resulting from degeneration by crossing. Cucumbers. Cucumber and gherkin seeds are only perfectly ripe when the fruit containing them has rotted. A certain number of the finest fruits of each variety should therefore be left to rot on the vine, and the seed separated by washing when the pulp begins to decompose. It is dried in the shade and kept dry for next year's sowing. D Pumpkin. No vegetable plants are more easily altered by crossbreeding than those of the Cucurbitaceae family, pumpkins, gourds and squashes of all kinds. The seed should therefore only be harvested from fruit grown far from plants whose vicinity could have caused them to crossbreed and degenerate. Carrot. The collar of seed-bearing carrots should not be cut off in the same way as carrots stored in cellars or silos. Once the best carrots of each variety have been selected, any leaves other than those in the center are cut off at the start of winter; the carrots are then planted in gauges at the foot of a wall facing south. During frosts, they are covered with leaves or dry litter, and uncovered whenever temperatures permit. In spring, the carrots thus preserved are planted 40 or 50 centimetres apart in all directions, depending on the volume of each variety. When the seed is ripe, the seed-laden stems are cut, bound into bundles and hung in a dry place. At sowing time, carrot seeds are detached from the umbels with the same precautions indicated for sorting celery seeds: if they are detached indiscriminately, you run the risk of sowing seeds, a large proportion of which are not fertilized and do not germinate. D Turnips and radishes. G Seed-bearing turnips and radishes should be chosen from among the best conformed of each species; the seed is more perfect and gives clearer plants when care is taken to head the seed-bearing plants, like those of cabbages, at the beginning of flowering, and to leave only a moderate number of siliques on each seed-bearing plant. Parsnips. E Seed-bearing parsnips are grown in exactly the same way as carrots, and the seeds are removed from the umbels with the same precautions. Scorsonera. D D We have seen (page 87) that scorsonera and salsify flower and bear seed two years in a row, contrary to the way other potaterous plants vegetate, which die after ripening their seed; the seed of these two plants can only be harvested from second-year seed-bearing plants. When harvesting onions, the most beautiful and best-formed of each variety should be set aside as seed carriers. Early in the spring, they are planted in good soil that was smoked the previous year. When the flower stalks, which are hollow and flimsy, begin to elongate, they are tied to stakes to prevent the wind from breaking them before the seed has ripened. When the onion seed is ripe, it forms a spherical bunch at the top of the stems; these bunches are tied into bundles and hung in a dry place; the seed is not peeled until it is time to use it for sowing. D Leek. Leeks go to seed in the spring of their second year. A few of the most vigorous plants are left as seed-bearing stock; their hardy temperament allows them to overwinter in the open air, without any protection. Like onions, flower stalks need to be supported by stakes; the seeds are kept in their capsules; they are only peeled when they are sown. Easy to consult, abundant in indications of all kinds, but precise in form, concise without obscurity, this Dictionary gives, as one would in conversation, on the various specialties it deals with, an answer that is at once engraved in the memory by definition and analysis. In addition to history and geography, this volume contains numerous bíographic articles and a few archaeological and philological notions. In the historical section, we have focused, for both ancient and modern times, on the essential facts, those most commonly remembered by mankind, and which mark a memorable date in the lives of peoples. Everything to do with France, with its ancient judicial, political and administrative institutions, has been the subject of particular attention and a little more extensive development, and it can be said that the collection of the various articles concerning our glorious homeland forms a substantial summary of its annals. In the geography section, we have always indicated the political changes, the primitive races, the invasions and emigrations, the population figures, the principal dynasties, and the dates of their rise and fall, so that, in this part of the book, statistics and history always complement the geography proper. In the biographical section, we have endeavored to summarize, in a few precise words, the most salient features of the talent or destiny of famous people; and in the articles on sovereigns, the character of their reign and the influence they exerted on the society of their time: we have, moreover, only dealt with the dead, the living not yet belonging to history. Never, we can say without fear of being accused of exaggeration, have a greater number of facts, dates and indications of all kinds been brought together in the same number of pages; never has a book of the same kind presented such conditions of cheapness and typographical elegance. G-Executed along the same lines as the Dictionnaire usuel de géographie et d'histoire, we have endeavored in the new Dictionary to present only essential facts, precise notions, simple and clear definitions, and to summarize, in a word, in an elementary form, the most varied notions of science brought up to date with the most recent discoveries. This Dictionary embraces all the cosmological sciences properly speaking, i.e. those whose object is the study of the marvels of creation, of the various elements that constitute it, of the phenomena of which it is the scene, and of the beings that populate it. The framework to be followed was thus clearly defined: it was to include astronomy, cosmography, geology, meteorology, zoology, botany, physics and chemistry. - The visible miracle of the world is the subject of this book. It is not, therefore, aimed at professional scientists, or at any particular speciality; it is addressed to all those whose curiosity is aroused by the spectacle of creation, and who wish to know the most important scientific explanations of the phenomena of nature and life. The Dictionary is preceded by a remarkably precise and accurate Introduction. In it, the author takes a look at the history of the sciences; he establishes their divisions and classifications, and reviews them in the three great periods of antiquity, the Middle Ages and modern times.
